Recommendation Adopt risk-based gating: automated scanning and policy for everything, manual review only for sensitive changes (auth, crypto, data access, infra), with clear SLAs for reviewers. Reversibility Highly reversible; policy tiers can be tuned as data on escapes and delays accumulates. De-risk Define sensitive-change criteria SLA for security reviewers Track escaped defects and review latency Embed security champions Interview tip: Frame it as shared goals: safe and fast. Show data on where defects really come from.

questions.q: The business wants a feature with a hard marketing deadline that needs a risky data migration. How do you respond?
questions.text: Context A launch date is fixed externally. The data migration is complex and untested at production scale. Clarify first What is the true hard constraint: date, scope or both? Can the feature launch without the migration? What is the cost of failure vs delay? Trade-offs Do everything by the deadline: meets date but high risk of outage or data corruption Launch reduced scope without migration: lower risk, partial value Delay: safest, but marketing and credibility cost Fixed dates force scope or risk trade-offs. The senior move is exposing options with consequences, not quietly absorbing risk. Recommendation Propose a phased launch: ship the visible feature on the old data model behind a flag, run the migration separately with rehearsals and rollback, then switch when proven. Reversibility Phasing keeps the decision reversible: the flag and dual-read path allow rollback. De-risk Rehearse migration on production-size copy Dual write/read with verification Feature flag with kill switch Go/no-go checkpoint dates Interview tip: Offer two or three concrete options with costs and let the business choose, rather than just saying no.

questions.q: Developers want to adopt a new language for a service while operations wants to keep the stack small. How do you decide?
questions.text: Context A team proposes Rust or Go for a performance-sensitive component, in a Java-heavy organisation. Clarify first Is the performance need real and measured? Who will maintain and be on call? Hiring and tooling implications? Trade-offs Adopt new language: best fit for the problem, engineering satisfaction, but fragmented skills, tooling, security scanning, on-call Stay on standard stack: consistency, shared libraries and expertise, but possible performance or fit compromise Allow with criteria: bounded experiments with platform support Every new technology has an ongoing tax in hiring, tooling, libraries, security and incident response, which must be paid by someone. Recommendation Require a written justification with measured benefit, a named long-term owner, platform support plan, and limit to a bounded component; otherwise stay with the standard stack. Reversibility Reversible if the component is small and has clear interfaces; costly if the language spreads. De-risk Pilot with success criteria Ensure CI, scanning and observability support Cross-train on-call Review after 6-12 months Interview tip: Technology choices are team and operations commitments, not only technical ones.

questions.q: Two teams disagree on whether to share a common component or each keep their own copy. How do you decide?
questions.text: Context Teams A and B both need similar functionality. Sharing couples their roadmaps; duplicating risks drift. Clarify first How similar are the needs really? Who would own the shared component? How stable is the interface? Trade-offs Shared component: reuse, consistency, one place to fix bugs, but coupling, ownership burden, lowest-common-denominator design Duplicate: autonomy and speed, but divergence and repeated fixes Inner-source library with clear owner and versioning: shared with governance Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Share when the need is stable and truly common, with an owner who treats it like a product. Recommendation Wait until at least a third use case shows the stable core, then extract with a dedicated owner, versioning and a contribution process; until then tolerate duplication. Reversibility Extraction later is feasible; premature sharing is hard to undo once many teams depend on it. De-risk Clear owner and SLA Semantic versioning Contribution guide Deprecation path Interview tip: Rule of three: duplicate twice, abstract on the third.

questions.q: Finance asks you to reduce cloud spend, but engineers say any cut risks reliability. How do you find the right balance?
questions.text: Context Cloud costs have increased 40% year over year. Reliability targets have been met only narrowly. Clarify first Where is spend concentrated and what is waste vs necessary headroom? What are SLOs and current error budget? Which savings are low-risk? Trade-offs Aggressive cuts: big savings but reliability risk Targeted waste removal: moderate savings, low risk Architecture changes for efficiency: larger long-term gains but engineering investment Waste and necessary redundancy look similar on a bill, so data on utilisation and SLOs is needed to tell them apart. Recommendation Start with visibility and zero-risk waste, then use SLO and error budget data to guide rightsizing, and only then consider architectural changes and purchasing commitments. Reversibility Most rightsizing is reversible quickly; deleting data or removing redundancy is not. De-risk Tag and attribute spend Change gradually with monitoring Error budget as the guardrail Review with finance monthly Interview tip: Use error budget as the shared currency between cost and reliability discussions.

questions.q: How do you decide whether to offer a managed Kubernetes platform to product teams or let them use serverless and PaaS options?
questions.text: Context Teams want different runtimes. The platform team has limited capacity and wants to avoid supporting everything. Clarify first What workload types exist (web, batch, streaming, ML)? Team skills and operational maturity? Compliance and networking requirements? Trade-offs Kubernetes platform: flexible, portable, rich ecosystem, but complexity, cluster operations, skills required Serverless/PaaS: low ops, fast start, but constraints, cost at scale, limited control Offer both with paved roads: choice, but double support The platform's job is to reduce cognitive load. The fewest runtimes that cover real needs is usually best. Recommendation Offer a primary paved road covering most workloads, often managed Kubernetes behind a simple deployment abstraction or a PaaS, with a documented exception path for serverless where it fits. Reversibility Reasonably reversible if apps are containerised and 12-factor, which keeps portability. De-risk Standardise on containers Abstract deployment config Measure adoption and satisfaction Review exceptions annually Interview tip: Hide the infrastructure complexity behind a simple interface; teams care about shipping, not clusters.

questions.q: How do you handle multi-tenancy in a shared cluster: namespaces, virtual clusters or separate clusters?
questions.text: Context Many teams share infrastructure. A noisy neighbour and a security scare prompted a review. Clarify first Trust level between tenants? Compliance isolation needs? Cost vs isolation appetite? Trade-offs Namespaces with quotas, network policies and RBAC: cheap, efficient, but shared control plane and kernel Virtual clusters: stronger API isolation, moderate cost, extra layer Cluster per team or environment: strongest isolation, higher cost and operations overhead Isolation strength rises with cost. Match it to trust and compliance needs rather than defaulting to the extremes. Recommendation Use namespaces with strong guardrails for trusted internal teams, separate clusters for regulated or untrusted workloads and for production vs non-production, managed through automation. Reversibility Moving workloads between models is possible with GitOps but effortful. De-risk Policy as code for quotas and network rules Node pools per sensitivity Cluster provisioning automation Regular access reviews Interview tip: Namespaces are an organisational boundary, not a hard security boundary.

questions.q: How would you approach standardising observability across teams that use different tools?
questions.text: Context Teams use a mix of logging, metrics and tracing tools. Incident response is slow because data is scattered. Clarify first What do responders struggle to find? Existing contracts and costs? Are there regulatory data constraints? Trade-offs Mandate one vendor: consistency and correlation, lower total cost possible, but migration effort and lock-in Open standards (OpenTelemetry) with pluggable backends: portability, gradual migration, but integration work Leave to teams: autonomy, but fragmented incident response The value is correlation across signals and services. Standard instrumentation matters more than the backend brand. Recommendation Standardise instrumentation and conventions on OpenTelemetry, with common labels and trace context, and consolidate backends gradually based on cost and capability. Reversibility Instrumentation standard is reversible at the backend level; that is exactly its benefit. De-risk Naming and tagging conventions Collector layer to decouple Cost controls and sampling Migration plan with incentives Interview tip: Standardise the data and context propagation, then the tool. Backends can change; instrumentation is expensive to redo.

questions.q: How do you design the developer onboarding path so a new service can reach production in a day?
questions.text: Context Creating a new service takes weeks of tickets across teams. Leadership wants speed without losing control. Clarify first What are the slowest steps today? Which controls are mandatory? Who owns each step? Trade-offs Manual tickets: control but slow Template + automation (service catalogue/scaffolder): fast and consistent, but upfront investment Free-form: maximum speed, minimum consistency and security The goal is to bake controls into the template so the secure, observable, compliant path is also the fastest. Recommendation Build a scaffolding workflow that creates the repo, pipeline, infrastructure, monitoring, alerts, security scans and catalogue entry from a template, with approvals automated by policy. Reversibility Templates can evolve; services created from them can be updated through automated upgrades. De-risk Template versioning and update mechanism Policy checks instead of manual approvals Measure lead time to first deploy Keep an escape hatch for unusual needs Interview tip: Track time-to-first-production-deploy as the platform's headline metric.

questions.q: How do you decide when to deprecate an internal platform component and migrate users off it?
questions.text: Context An old internal deployment tool is costly to maintain. A replacement exists but 60 teams still use the old one. Clarify first Why migrate: cost, risk, capability gap? How hard is migration per team? What happens if you don't? Trade-offs Mandate and deadline: quick, but friction and disruption Incentives and migration help: smoother, but longer and costs platform time Run both indefinitely: no disruption but permanent double cost Every legacy component taxes the platform team. But migration costs fall on users, so the platform must make it easy and justify it. Recommendation Set a published sunset date, provide automated migration tooling and hands-on support, track progress per team, escalate blockers, and stop new onboarding to the old tool immediately. Reversibility Deprecation timelines can be adjusted before the cutoff; after shutdown, rollback is hard, so keep a short read-only period. De-risk Stop new adopters first Migration scripts and office hours Weekly progress dashboard Executive sponsor for stragglers Interview tip: Stop the bleeding first: no new users on the old system, then migrate the existing ones.

questions.q: How do you prioritise technical debt across many teams when everything seems important?
questions.text: Context Each team has a long list of debt. Leadership wants a coherent plan, not 30 separate wish lists. Clarify first Which debt causes incidents or slows delivery most? What does fixing it unlock? What is the cost of delay? Trade-offs Fix by developer annoyance: popular, but may miss the impactful items Fix by risk and impact: aligned to business, needs data Fixed percentage of capacity: predictable, but can be spent on low value Debt is only worth paying when interest is high: incidents, slowed delivery, security exposure or blocked strategy. Recommendation Score items by impact on reliability, delivery speed, security and strategic blockers against effort, fund the top items explicitly with a baseline capacity allowance, and review quarterly. Reversibility The prioritisation can be revisited every quarter; the key is keeping a visible, ranked list. De-risk Link debt items to incident and cycle-time data Make debt visible in planning Define done and measure improvement Avoid gold-plating Interview tip: Translate debt into business terms: incidents, lead time, risk. That is what wins budget.

questions.q: What is the strangler fig pattern and when would you use it to replace a legacy system?
questions.text: Context A critical legacy system must be replaced. A big-bang rewrite has failed before. Clarify first Can traffic be routed at an interface? What functionality is most valuable or painful? How are data and state shared? Trade-offs Strangler: incremental replacement behind a facade, continuous delivery of value, lower risk, but temporary complexity running both Big-bang rewrite: clean slate, but long time with no value and high cutover risk Leave as is: no risk now, but growing cost Incremental migration delivers value early and limits the blast radius of each step, while a rewrite hides risk until the end. Recommendation Place a routing facade in front, move one capability at a time to the new implementation, keep data in sync during the transition, and retire legacy pieces as traffic moves. Reversibility Each step is individually reversible by routing back to the legacy system. De-risk Choose a seam with clear boundary Data synchronisation strategy Parallel run and comparison Track decommissioning milestones Interview tip: Start with a slice that is valuable but small, to prove the approach and build confidence.

questions.q: How do you decide whether to upgrade a major dependency now or defer it?
questions.text: Context A framework has a new major version. The current version has support for another year but the gap grows. Clarify first Support timeline and security patch availability? Breaking changes and test coverage? Does the new version unlock needed features? Trade-offs Upgrade now: smaller gap, benefits earlier, but disruption and risk while other work waits Defer: focus on features, but larger, riskier jump later and growing incompatibilities Incremental upgrade path: spread work in small steps Upgrades get harder with time as intermediate versions are skipped, but doing them with no benefit competes with product work. Recommendation Plan the upgrade ahead of end of support using incremental steps, invest first in tests, and use automation to apply mechanical changes; do not defer until it becomes an emergency. Reversibility Upgrades are generally one-way, but can be staged and feature-flagged by service. De-risk Test coverage first Automated codemods Canary upgrade in a low-risk service Track end-of-support dates Interview tip: Upgrade debt compounds. The cheapest time is usually sooner than the end-of-support panic.

questions.q: How do you deal with undocumented tribal knowledge in a critical legacy system when key people might leave?
questions.text: Context Only two engineers understand a core billing system. Both are overloaded and one is considering leaving. Clarify first What would break if they left? Where is the knowledge gap largest? How much time can they spare? Trade-offs Heavy documentation project: durable, but slow and may become stale Pairing and rotation: spreads knowledge actively, but takes time from experts Add tests and observability: encode knowledge as executable behaviour Do nothing: risky Bus factor is a business risk. The best documentation is executable: tests, runbooks and automation, plus real practice. Recommendation Reduce the bus factor with deliberate pairing and rotation, record decisions and runbooks, capture behaviour in characterisation tests, and rehearse incident scenarios with the broader team. Reversibility All actions are additive and low-risk. De-risk Prioritise by criticality Time-box expert capacity explicitly Run a game day on the system Record architecture decision records Interview tip: Documentation alone does not transfer skill. Make others do the work with the experts present.

questions.q: A team wants to introduce a big refactoring of core domain code before adding a new feature. How do you decide?
questions.text: Context The new feature touches messy code. Engineers say refactoring first will make it cleaner but delay delivery by weeks. Clarify first How tangled is the code and what's the risk of changing it? Is there test coverage? Will other features hit the same area soon? Trade-offs Refactor first: cleaner foundation, but delays feature and risks scope creep Feature first with workaround: faster, but more debt in a hot area Refactor as you go (preparatory refactoring): small steps tied to the feature Refactoring pays when the area is a hotspot of future change. Unbounded refactoring is a classic way to lose months. Recommendation Do just enough preparatory refactoring to make the feature easy, backed by tests, time-boxed and in small reviewable commits, and schedule larger clean-ups separately only if future work justifies them. Reversibility Small refactors are reversible; large ones need a flag or branch-by-abstraction. De-risk Characterisation tests first Time-box and checkpoint Separate refactor commits from behaviour change Re-assess after the feature Interview tip: Make the change easy, then make the easy change. Keep the first step small.

questions.q: How do you evaluate adopting a service mesh, eBPF-based networking or other infrastructure bets that promise large benefits?
questions.text: Context Vendors and conference talks push new networking tech. Your team is tempted by promised gains. Clarify first What concrete problem do we have today? What is the maturity and community of the tech? What do we lose if we wait? Trade-offs Adopt early: potential advantage, but immature, churn and risk Wait for maturity: safer, but possibly slower to capture benefit Pilot narrowly: learn at small cost New infrastructure is a long-term operational commitment. A real problem and a bounded pilot beat enthusiasm. Recommendation Tie any bet to a measurable problem, run a time-boxed pilot on non-critical workloads with success and exit criteria, and decide with data on operations cost, not demos. Reversibility Pilots are cheap to reverse, but wide adoption becomes sticky. De-risk Written success and exit criteria Pilot on low-risk workload Operational readiness review Budget the learning curve Interview tip: The question is not 'is it good?' but 'do we have the problem it solves, and can we run it?'

questions.q: How do you decide whether to migrate from on-premises to cloud, or the reverse, for a large estate?
questions.text: Context Costs, agility and risk arguments exist in both directions. Leadership wants a data-driven decision. Clarify first What are the drivers: agility, cost, capacity, compliance? Workload profile: steady vs spiky? Skills and contracts in place? Trade-offs Cloud: elasticity, managed services, speed, global reach, but variable cost, skills, potential lock-in On-prem: predictable cost for steady loads, control, but capital outlay, slower provisioning Hybrid: place by workload, but integration complexity Neither is universally cheaper. Steady heavy workloads can favour owned hardware, spiky and innovative workloads favour cloud. Recommendation Decide per workload with TCO modelling including people, migration and egress, migrate in waves starting with low-risk candidates, and keep the option to repatriate by avoiding unnecessary proprietary dependencies for steady-state workloads. Reversibility Neither direction is cheap to reverse at scale, so phase it and measure. De-risk Workload-by-workload TCO model Pilot wave with measured results Skills development plan Exit strategy and data egress costs Interview tip: Model total cost including people and migration. Sticker price comparisons mislead in both directions.

questions.q: How do you decide when to rewrite a product in a new architecture versus evolving the existing one?
questions.text: Context The current system is slow to change. The team proposes a ground-up rewrite on a modern stack with a 12-month timeline. Clarify first What exactly is blocking change: code, architecture, process, people? Can the old system keep running and evolving during the rewrite? What is the business case for 12 months of no new value? Trade-offs Rewrite: clean design, modern tooling, but long delivery, feature freeze pressure, second-system risk, losing hidden behaviour Evolve incrementally: continuous value and lower risk, but constrained by legacy and requires discipline Hybrid: strangler migration of the worst parts Rewrites often underestimate the hidden business logic embedded in old code and run long. The reasons for slowness may survive the rewrite. Recommendation Diagnose root causes first; prefer incremental modernisation using the strangler approach, and approve a rewrite only for components with clear boundaries, strong justification and a measured plan. Reversibility A rewrite is hard to reverse once the old system is neglected, so keep the old running with value delivery. De-risk Inventory hidden behaviour via tests Milestones delivering production value Parallel run Stop-loss decision points Interview tip: Ask what problem the rewrite solves that incremental change cannot. If the answer is vague, don't.

questions.q: How do you assess the build-versus-partner decision when entering a new market or capability with regulatory complexity?
questions.text: Context The company wants to offer payments or lending. Regulation, licences and integrations are heavy. Clarify first Is the capability core to the strategy? Regulatory burden and liability? Time to market and margin impact? Trade-offs Build in-house: control and margin, but licences, compliance, long time Partner/BaaS: speed and shared compliance, but margin share, dependency, less control Acquire: instant capability but integration and cost Regulation makes entry costly and slow. Partnering lets you test the market while deciding if building is worth the investment. Recommendation Start with a partner to validate demand and learn, design integration behind your own abstraction, and revisit building when volume and strategic importance justify the compliance investment. Reversibility Partnering is more reversible if contracts allow data portability and you hold the customer relationship. De-risk Contractual SLAs and exit terms Own the customer data and experience Compliance oversight of the partner Defined trigger for insourcing Interview tip: Define a trigger metric for when it becomes worth insourcing, so the decision is revisited deliberately.

questions.q: How do you scale an engineering organisation's architecture decision-making without a central architecture board becoming a bottleneck?
questions.text: Context As the company grows to 15 teams, big decisions queue behind one architect group and teams bypass it. Clarify first Which decisions truly need cross-team alignment? What's the current decision latency? Do teams trust the guidance? Trade-offs Central board approves everything: consistency, but slow and disconnected No governance: speed and autonomy, but fragmentation and duplicated effort Lightweight: ADRs, guilds, advice process, decision tiers: balance, but needs culture Most decisions are reversible and local. Only a few are one-way doors needing broad input. Recommendation Adopt the advice process with architecture decision records, classify decisions as reversible vs one-way, require broad consultation only for one-way or cross-cutting ones, and publish principles and paved roads. Reversibility The governance model can evolve; the important thing is measuring decision latency and outcomes. De-risk Clear decision classification ADR repository searchable Time-boxed consultation Architecture guild for shared learning Interview tip: Distinguish one-way doors from two-way doors. Move fast on the latter.

questions.q: How do you avoid the 'shared services team' becoming a dependency bottleneck as teams multiply?
questions.text: Context A shared database team, a shared QA team and a shared release team all have long queues. Clarify first Where are the longest queues? What expertise is truly scarce? Can work be self-served? Trade-offs Central shared teams: efficiency and expertise concentration, but queues and handoffs Embed capability into product teams: fast, but duplicated skills Platform/enablement model: shared tools and coaching so teams self-serve Handoffs and queues dominate lead time at scale. Expertise should spread through tooling, standards and coaching, not by routing every task through a team. Recommendation Convert shared service teams into enabling or platform teams that provide self-service tooling, guardrails and consultation, and embed specialists temporarily where needed. Reversibility Reorganisation is reversible but disruptive; move gradually by capability. De-risk Measure queue time and lead time Self-service before reorganisation Coaching and documentation Clear interaction modes between teams Interview tip: Look at flow: a team that everyone must wait for is a design flaw in the organisation, not a people problem.

questions.q: How do you manage the architecture when you acquire a company with a different stack?
questions.text: Context An acquired company has a working product on different cloud, language and auth systems. Leadership wants synergy. Clarify first What is the integration goal: shared customers, cost, unified product? How healthy is the acquired tech? Retention of key engineers? Trade-offs Full consolidation: long-term efficiency, but heavy cost and risk to the acquired product Keep separate: low disruption, but duplicated cost and inconsistent experience Selective integration at seams: identity, billing, data, with gradual convergence Forced rewrites often destroy the value you bought. Integrate where the customer or cost benefit is clear. Recommendation Integrate at the customer-facing seams first (SSO, billing, data sharing) via APIs, keep the acquired stack running, then converge infrastructure opportunistically where economics are clear. Reversibility Selective integration is reversible; full migration is not. De-risk Retain key engineers Security assessment early Integration roadmap with measurable benefits Avoid forcing rewrite for its own sake Interview tip: Let business outcomes, not technical neatness, set the integration order.

questions.q: What architectural practices keep a system evolvable as the team grows from 10 to 100 engineers?
questions.text: Context Growth is straining the codebase: merge conflicts, slow builds, unclear ownership, fragile deployments. Clarify first Where does coordination hurt most? Is ownership clear per component? What is the release frequency and failure rate? Trade-offs Strong module boundaries and ownership: scalable, but needs investment Everything shared: fast early, painful later Service-oriented split: independent flow, but operational overhead Conway's law: the architecture follows the organisation. Aligning boundaries to teams reduces coordination cost. Recommendation Establish clear domain boundaries aligned to teams, enforce them with tooling, invest in CI speed and automated testing, make ownership explicit in a catalogue, and adopt progressive delivery to keep releases safe. Reversibility Practices are incremental and reversible; boundaries evolve with domain understanding. De-risk Ownership catalogue Architectural fitness functions in CI Build and test speed budget Contract tests between domains Interview tip: Use automated architecture tests to stop boundaries decaying quietly.

questions.q: How would you reduce the blast radius and coordination cost of a large shared database schema used by many teams?
questions.text: Context One database schema is modified by dozens of teams; migrations cause conflicts and outages. Clarify first Which tables are shared and who owns them? How frequently do schemas change? Can ownership be split by domain? Trade-offs Keep shared schema with strict process: low initial change, but slow, risky Split into per-domain databases/schemas with APIs: autonomy, but data migration and joins lost Introduce read models/data products: decoupled reads, extra pipelines A shared schema is a shared mutable state across teams. The cost grows quadratically with the number of writers. Recommendation Assign clear table ownership, forbid cross-domain writes, expose data via APIs or published read models, and migrate gradually, starting with the most contentious tables. Reversibility Incremental and reversible per table with dual-read periods. De-risk Ownership map Expand-contract migrations Access controls enforcing ownership Dual-read validation during moves Interview tip: Start by enforcing who may write to each table. Ownership comes before any physical split.

questions.q: Your largest enterprise customer demands data residency in their own country, but you have only one region today. How do you respond architecturally?
questions.text: Context A large contract depends on in-country data storage within six months. Clarify first Which data must stay in-country: all or specific categories? Can processing happen elsewhere if data is not stored? How many customers will follow with similar demands? Trade-offs New regional stack for that country: full compliance, but cost, operations and duplication Region-aware data layer with partitioned tenant data: scalable for future, but design effort Cloud provider sovereign options: faster, but constraints One-off regions are expensive, so the design should anticipate more residency requirements while meeting this one first. Recommendation Introduce tenant-to-region placement in the data layer and a regional deployment of the necessary stack, using the new customer as the first tenant; automate provisioning so further regions are repeatable. Reversibility Costly to unwind but additive; placing tenants by region is a long-term capability. De-risk Identify all data flows including logs and backups Control-plane vs data-plane split Compliance review Automate region provisioning Interview tip: Think about backups, logs, analytics and support tooling too. Residency leaks often happen there.

questions.q: A vendor offers a heavily discounted three-year contract with deep integration. How do you evaluate the commitment?
questions.text: Context Procurement likes the 40% discount. Engineering worries about lock-in and the vendor's roadmap. Clarify first How critical is the product and how replaceable? Vendor's financial health and roadmap? What exit and portability terms are possible? Trade-offs Sign 3 years: savings, price certainty, but lock-in and stranded cost if needs change 1 year or monthly: flexibility, but higher price Sign with exit clauses and data portability: balanced but negotiation effort A discount is only valuable if you will actually use the product for the term and could leave if it fails you. Recommendation Negotiate shorter or ramped commitment, SLA credits, termination rights for chronic failure, data export guarantees, and limit deep integration behind an abstraction. Reversibility Contracts are hard to unwind; technical coupling is the larger lock-in, so manage it. De-risk Abstraction layer Exit plan and data export test Vendor viability check Usage forecast with margin Interview tip: Technical lock-in costs more than contractual lock-in. Check both.

questions.q: A security vulnerability requires an urgent change in a legacy module nobody understands. How do you make the change safely?
questions.text: Context A critical CVE affects a library used in an old module with no tests and no owner. Clarify first How exploitable and exposed is it? Can you mitigate without changing code? Who has any knowledge of the module? Trade-offs Quick patch and deploy: fast, but risk of regressions Compensating control first (WAF, config, network): buys time, imperfect Full understanding and refactor first: safest long-term, too slow for the threat The urgency demands layered response: reduce exposure immediately, then patch with a safety net. Recommendation Apply a compensating control now, write characterisation tests around the module's entry points, apply the minimal library upgrade or patch, deploy gradually with monitoring and rollback, then plan longer-term cleanup. Reversibility Canary and rollback make the change reversible. De-risk Characterisation tests Canary deploy Monitoring on error rate Assign an owner afterwards Interview tip: Reduce exposure first, then change code with a safety net. Never skip the follow-up ownership step.

questions.q: A fast-growing startup's monolith is hitting database limits. The CTO asks whether to shard, move to microservices or buy time. What do you advise?
questions.text: Context Primary database is at 80% CPU at peak, growth is 15% month over month, the team is 25 engineers. Clarify first What queries and tables dominate load? Read vs write ratio? How soon will the limit be hit? Trade-offs Optimise and scale up: quick, cheap, buys months, but ceiling Read replicas, caching, offload analytics: moderate effort, big relief for read-heavy loads Shard or split services: long-term scale, high complexity and risk Most early scaling problems are solved by query tuning, indexing, caching and replicas long before sharding is needed. Recommendation Buy time with profiling, indexes, caching, replicas and a bigger instance, while designing a data partitioning strategy for the tenant or domain boundary so sharding is ready if growth continues. Reversibility The first steps are reversible; sharding is a major commitment, so delay until data justifies it. De-risk Capacity forecast with trigger points Load testing Clear tenant/shard key design Avoid premature microservices Interview tip: Ask what the top five queries are. Often 80% of the load is a handful of fixable queries.

questions.q: How do you decide whether an internal tool should be open-sourced or kept private?
questions.text: Context A team built a useful internal tool and wants to publish it. Legal and security have concerns. Clarify first What is the actual problem and its cost? What are the constraints on time, skills and budget? What would make us reverse this? Trade-offs Option A: faster to start, but carries long-term cost Option B: more upfront effort, but sustainable Option C: a hybrid that limits risk The right choice depends on reversibility, cost of being wrong and the skills the team has today. Recommendation Open-source only if it is non-differentiating, free of secrets and internal assumptions, has a committed maintainer and a clear support policy; otherwise keep it internal. Reversibility Prefer the option that can be undone cheaply and revisit with data after a short trial. De-risk Run a time-boxed pilot Define success and exit criteria Record the decision in an ADR Interview tip: State the decision, the reasons and the conditions under which you would change it.

questions.q: How do you decide whether to adopt a new programming platform such as WebAssembly or a new runtime for a major system?
questions.text: Context Engineers are excited about a new runtime promising large performance and portability gains. Clarify first What is the actual problem and its cost? What are the constraints on time, skills and budget? What would make us reverse this? Trade-offs Option A: faster to start, but carries long-term cost Option B: more upfront effort, but sustainable Option C: a hybrid that limits risk The right choice depends on reversibility, cost of being wrong and the skills the team has today. Recommendation Run a bounded pilot against a measured problem, keep the integration behind a stable interface, and adopt widely only if the operational and hiring costs are acceptable. Reversibility Prefer the option that can be undone cheaply and revisit with data after a short trial. De-risk Run a time-boxed pilot Define success and exit criteria Record the decision in an ADR Interview tip: State the decision, the reasons and the conditions under which you would change it.

questions.q: What is the IAM model in AWS — how do principals, policies, and roles work?
questions.text: Principal types: IAM User, IAM Role, AWS Service, Federated identity Policy types: Identity-based, Resource-based, SCP (org-level), Permission boundary # Create role for EC2 to access S3: aws iam create-role --role-name ec2-s3-role --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name ec2-s3-role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess # Assume role for cross-account access: aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/CrossAccountRole --role-session-name session1 Least privilege principle: grant only the permissions needed for the task. IAM Roles are preferred over IAM Users for services — roles use temporary credentials via STS. SCPs (Service Control Policies) set maximum permissions for an entire AWS Organization account — they override IAM policies. Permission boundaries limit the maximum permissions an IAM entity can have, even if their policies allow more. IAM Access Analyzer: Automatically identifies resource policies granting external access. Run regularly to find unintended public S3 buckets, overly permissive role trust policies, and cross-account access. Essential for security posture management.

questions.q: What is AWS STS and how does it work — how do you implement cross-account access?
questions.text: # Cross-account role assumption: aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT-B:role/DeployRole --role-session-name deploy # Returns temporary credentials (expire in 1-12 hours): export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=... # Trust policy on target account role: {"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT-A:role/CIRole"}, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"} # OIDC federation for GitHub Actions: aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com STS issues temporary credentials for role assumption. Cross-account pattern: Account A has a role, Account B has a role with trust policy allowing Account A to assume it. Account A's CI pipeline assumes Account B's DeployRole to deploy resources there. No long-lived credentials needed. OIDC federation for GitHub Actions: GitHub OIDC token exchanges for AWS credentials — no IAM User access keys in CI.

questions.q: What is a VPC — how do you design a production-grade VPC architecture?
questions.text: aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 # 3-tier subnet layout per AZ: Public subnets: 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.1.0/24 — ALB, NAT Gateway Private subnets: 10.0.10.0/24, 10.0.11.0/24 — App servers, EKS nodes DB subnets: 10.0.20.0/24, 10.0.21.0/24 — RDS, ElastiCache # NAT Gateway (private subnet internet outbound): aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id public-subnet-id --allocation-id eip-id # VPC Flow Logs for security audit: aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-ids vpc-id --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs 3-tier VPC: public subnets for load balancers and NAT Gateways, private subnets for application workloads, isolated subnets for databases. Resources in private subnets cannot be reached from the internet but can reach out via NAT Gateway. Security Groups act as stateful firewalls per resource. NACLs act as stateless firewalls per subnet. Always deploy across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

questions.q: What is the difference between Security Groups and NACLs?
questions.text: # Security Group (stateful - per instance/ENI): aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-xxx --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0 aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-xxx # NACL (stateless - per subnet): aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-xxx --rule-number 100 --protocol tcp --port-range From=443,To=443 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow # NACL needs explicit DENY for outbound 443 response too (stateless) Security Groups: stateful (return traffic automatically allowed), attached to instances/ENIs, allow-only rules (no explicit deny). NACLs: stateless (must explicitly allow return traffic), subnet-level, allow and deny rules, numbered rules evaluated in order. Use Security Groups for most cases (simpler). Use NACLs as an additional layer for subnet-level blocking (block specific CIDR ranges, add defence-in-depth).

questions.q: What is EC2 — how do you choose the right instance type and purchase model?
questions.text: # Instance families: t4g/t3 — burstable general purpose (dev/test) m7i/m6i — balanced compute/memory (web servers) c7i/c6i — compute optimised (CPU-intensive workloads) r7i/r6i — memory optimised (databases, caches) p4/p3 — GPU instances (ML training) # Purchase models: On-Demand: pay per hour, no commitment, full price Reserved: 1-3 year commitment, up to 72% discount Savings Plans: flexible commitment ($/hour), up to 66% discount Spot: spare capacity, up to 90% discount, can be interrupted Right-size first, then optimise purchase model. Graviton (arm64) instances (t4g, m7g, c7g) offer 20-40% better price/performance for most workloads. Spot instances are ideal for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, and stateless auto-scaled workloads. Use Compute Savings Plans for baseline capacity (predictable load), Spot for peak/burst. AWS Cost Explorer Recommendations identifies right-sizing opportunities automatically.

questions.q: What is EKS — how does it differ from self-managed Kubernetes?
questions.text: eksctl create cluster --name prod --region us-east-1 --nodes 3 --node-type m6i.large aws eks update-kubeconfig --region us-east-1 --name prod # EKS managed node groups: eksctl create nodegroup --cluster prod --name workers --node-type m6i.large --nodes-min 2 --nodes-max 10 # Fargate profile (serverless pods): eksctl create fargateprofile --cluster prod --name fp-default --namespace default aws eks update-cluster-version --name prod --kubernetes-version 1.30 EKS: AWS manages the control plane (etcd, API server, scheduler) — you manage the data plane (nodes). Managed node groups handle node provisioning, AMI updates, and draining during upgrades. Fargate removes node management entirely — AWS runs each pod on isolated compute. Key EKS add-ons: aws-load-balancer-controller (ALB integration), EBS CSI driver, EFS CSI driver, VPC CNI. EKS Anywhere extends EKS to on-prem. Cluster upgrades: update control plane first, then node groups.

questions.q: What is the AWS Load Balancer Controller — how do you expose Kubernetes services on EKS?
questions.text: # Install ALB controller: helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system \ --set clusterName=prod --set serviceAccountName=aws-load-balancer-controller # Ingress with ALB: annotations: kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:xxx:certificate/xxx # NLB for TCP/UDP: service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "external" ALB controller provisions AWS ALBs/NLBs from Ingress and Service resources. target-type: ip routes directly to pod IPs (bypasses NodePort, more efficient). Use NLB for TCP/UDP or when you need static IPs. ALB supports path-based and host-based routing, HTTPS termination with ACM certificates, WAF integration, and authentication via Cognito/OIDC. One ALB per Ingress by default — use IngressGroup annotation to share an ALB across multiple Ingress resources (reduces cost).

questions.q: What are the storage options in AWS — EBS, EFS, S3 — when do you use each?
questions.text: EBS: block storage, single AZ, attached to one instance, high IOPS gp3: general purpose SSD, 3000 IOPS baseline, up to 16000 IOPS io2 Block Express: high performance DB (up to 256,000 IOPS) EFS: NFS shared filesystem, multi-AZ, auto-scales, multiple instances Use for: shared config, user uploads accessible from many pods S3: object storage, unlimited scale, 11 nines durability Use for: backups, static assets, data lake, ML training data aws s3 cp largefile.tar.gz s3://mybucket/ --storage-class INTELLIGENT_TIERING EBS: databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB) — single-instance block storage with consistent low latency. EFS: shared storage for multiple EC2 instances or Kubernetes pods (ReadWriteMany PVC via EFS CSI driver). S3: everything else at scale — virtually unlimited, 99.999999999% durability, versioning, lifecycle policies, event notifications. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage patterns — significant cost savings for data with unpredictable access.

questions.q: What is RDS — how do you set up a production-grade PostgreSQL on AWS?
questions.text: aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier mydb \ --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \ --engine postgres --engine-version 16 \ --master-username admin --manage-master-user-password \ --vpc-security-group-ids sg-xxx --db-subnet-group mysubnetgroup \ --multi-az --storage-encrypted --allocated-storage 100 # Read replica: aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica --source-db-instance-identifier mydb --db-instance-identifier mydb-read # RDS Proxy (connection pooling): aws rds create-db-proxy --db-proxy-name myproxy --engine-family POSTGRESQL Production RDS: Multi-AZ (synchronous replication to standby, auto-failover in 60-120 seconds), encryption at rest and in transit, Private subnet only (no public access), automated backups (7-35 day retention), Performance Insights enabled. RDS Proxy: connection pooling reduces connection overhead for Lambda or Fargate workloads. --manage-master-user-password stores credentials in Secrets Manager automatically — no password in IaC code.

questions.q: What is CloudWatch — how do you use it for production monitoring?
questions.text: # Custom metric: aws cloudwatch put-metric-data --namespace MyApp --metric-name ErrorCount --value 5 --unit Count # Alarm: aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name HighErrorRate \ --metric-name ErrorCount --namespace MyApp \ --statistic Sum --period 60 --threshold 10 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \ --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:alerts # Container Insights (EKS/ECS metrics): aws eks update-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name amazon-cloudwatch-observability # Log Insights query: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like "ERROR" | stats count(*) by bin(5m) CloudWatch covers metrics (custom + AWS service metrics), logs (CloudWatch Logs), alarms (SNS/PagerDuty integration), dashboards, and Logs Insights (query language for structured logs). Container Insights adds K8s-aware metrics (per pod, per namespace) to EKS. For complex observability: Managed Prometheus + Grafana is more powerful than CloudWatch dashboards, but CloudWatch is zero-setup for AWS services.

questions.q: How do you set up AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing?
questions.text: # Python instrumentation: from aws_xray_sdk.core import xray_recorder, patch_all patch_all() # auto-patches boto3, requests, mysql, etc. xray_recorder.configure(service="payments-service") # EKS: X-Ray daemon as DaemonSet: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws-samples/amazon-cloudwatch-container-insights/latest/k8s-deployment-manifest-templates/deployment-mode/daemonset/container-insights-monitoring/x-ray/xray-k8s-daemonset.yaml # OR: use OpenTelemetry → AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://aws-otel-collector:4317 X-Ray traces requests across Lambda, EC2, ECS, EKS, and API Gateway automatically with minimal SDK integration. Use AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) for standards-based tracing that works with both X-Ray and other backends — avoids vendor lock-in. X-Ray Service Map visualises service dependencies and latency between them automatically.

questions.q: How do you reduce AWS costs — what are the key levers?
questions.text: # Right-sizing (biggest lever): aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations --region us-east-1 # Commit-based discounts: Savings Plans: 1-3 year commitment, up to 66% off On-Demand Reserved Instances: 1-3 year, up to 72% off (less flexible) # Spot for non-critical workloads: EKS Karpenter: automatically uses Spot instances for node groups # S3 cost optimisation: aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --lifecycle-rules file://lifecycle.json S3 Intelligent-Tiering for unpredictable access patterns # Monitor spend: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2024-01-01,End=2024-01-31 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics AmortizedCost Cost optimisation hierarchy: (1) Eliminate waste (unused resources, over-provisioned instances), (2) Right-size (match instance type to actual utilisation), (3) Purchase model (Savings Plans for predictable baseline, Spot for burst), (4) Architecture (Fargate vs EC2, Lambda for variable workloads). AWS Compute Optimizer analyses usage and recommends right-sized instances. Budget alerts prevent surprise bills.

questions.q: How does AWS CodePipeline work — how does it compare to GitHub Actions?
questions.text: # CodePipeline stages: Source (CodeCommit/GitHub) → Build (CodeBuild) → Test (CodeBuild) → Deploy (CodeDeploy/ECS/EKS) # CodeBuild buildspec.yaml: phases: build: commands: - docker build -t $IMAGE_URI . - docker push $IMAGE_URI post_build: commands: - kubectl apply -f k8s/ --record # CodeDeploy for blue/green ECS: aws deploy create-deployment --application-name myapp --deployment-group-name prod CodePipeline is fully managed, integrates natively with AWS services, and keeps everything within your AWS account (no external secrets). CodeBuild runs build jobs in ephemeral containers. GitHub Actions is more flexible, has a larger action marketplace, and is preferred when the team already uses GitHub. For AWS-native shops: CodePipeline + CodeBuild + CodeDeploy is a coherent zero-ops CI/CD stack. For multi-cloud or GitHub-centric teams: GitHub Actions + AWS OIDC federation is simpler.

questions.q: What is Karpenter — how does it improve EKS auto-scaling?
questions.text: helm install karpenter oci://public.ecr.aws/karpenter/karpenter --version v0.33 -n karpenter # NodePool defines what nodes Karpenter can provision: spec: template: spec: requirements: - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type values: [spot, on-demand] - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type values: [m6i.large, m6i.xlarge, m5.large, m5.xlarge] nodeClassRef: name: default Karpenter replaces the Cluster Autoscaler with a more intelligent approach: it provisions nodes specifically shaped for pending pods (right instance type, right size) rather than scaling predefined node groups. Results: faster scaling (seconds vs minutes), better bin-packing (higher utilisation), automatic Spot diversification (uses many instance types to reduce interruption risk), and consolidation (replaces multiple underutilised nodes with one larger node). Reduces both cost and scaling latency significantly.

questions.q: What is AWS PrivateLink — when do you use it vs VPC peering vs Transit Gateway?
questions.text: VPC Peering: direct 1:1 VPC connection (non-transitive) PrivateLink: expose a service privately (NLB endpoint service) Transit Gateway: hub-and-spoke router for many VPCs VPN/Direct Connect: on-premises to AWS # PrivateLink endpoint: aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-xxx --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 --vpc-endpoint-type Interface # Transit Gateway (connects 3+ VPCs): aws ec2 create-transit-gateway aws ec2 attach-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxx --vpc-id vpc-xxx VPC Peering: simple 1:1 direct connection, non-transitive (A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C). PrivateLink: expose a service (NLB) to other VPCs privately — no full VPC peering, no CIDR overlap issues. Use for: SaaS services, internal platform services consumed across many VPCs. Transit Gateway: hub-and-spoke for 10+ VPCs — one attachment per VPC, full mesh routing. Preferred for large-scale multi-VPC architectures. Direct Connect: dedicated physical connection to AWS data centre for consistent low-latency or compliance requirements.

questions.q: An EC2 instance has high CPU but your application is not doing extra work — how do you investigate?
questions.text: ssh ec2-user@instance-ip top -bn1 | head -20 # overall CPU, top processes ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10 # top CPU-consuming processes mpstat -P ALL 1 5 # per-CPU utilisation sar -u 1 10 # system activity over time iostat -x 1 5 # CPU wait time (iowait) # Check for steal time (hypervisor contention): top → %st (steal) — if high: instance is CPU-constrained by hypervisor # Check CloudWatch metrics: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 Common causes: noisy neighbour (high steal time on shared hardware → move to dedicated instance or Nitro-based type), runaway process (find with ps aux), kernel processes (kworker, ksoftirqd — check dmesg for errors), memory pressure causing swap usage (check free -h), and for t2/t3: CPU credit exhaustion (check CPUCreditBalance CloudWatch metric — unlimited mode prevents throttling).

questions.q: How does Route 53 work — what routing policies do you use for production?
questions.text: aws route53 list-hosted-zones aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch file://record.json # Routing policies: Simple: single resource, no health checks Failover: primary + secondary, health-check-based failover Weighted: split traffic by weight (canary: 90%/10%) Latency: route to lowest-latency region Geolocation: route by user location (GDPR compliance, content localisation) Multivalue: return multiple IPs (basic load distribution) # Health check: aws route53 create-health-check --caller-reference $(date +%s) --health-check-config Type=HTTPS,FullyQualifiedDomainName=api.example.com,Port=443,ResourcePath=/health Failover routing + health checks = DNS-based disaster recovery. Weighted routing enables DNS-level canary deployments (10% to new region). Latency routing reduces global P99 latency significantly. Always attach health checks to production DNS records — Route 53 stops routing to unhealthy endpoints automatically. Route 53 Resolver enables DNS resolution between VPCs and on-premises networks.

questions.q: What is AWS Organizations and SCPs — how do you use them for multi-account governance?
questions.text: # SCP that prevents disabling CloudTrail: {"Effect":"Deny","Action":["cloudtrail:StopLogging","cloudtrail:DeleteTrail"],"Resource":"*"} # SCP that restricts to approved regions: {"Effect":"Deny","Action":"*","Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:RequestedRegion":["us-east-1","eu-west-1"]}}} # Check effective permissions (SCP + IAM): aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/MyRole --action-names s3:DeleteBucket Multi-account AWS: separate accounts for dev/staging/production, sandbox, security, logging. SCPs define the maximum permissions ceiling for an entire account — even the root user cannot exceed them. Common SCPs: prevent disabling security services (CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub), restrict to approved regions, prevent creating IAM users with console access, require MFA for sensitive actions. AWS Control Tower automates account vending and baseline security controls for new accounts.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot connectivity issues between AWS services?
questions.text: # Test connectivity from EC2/EKS pod: curl -v https://rds-endpoint:5432 # does TCP connect? nmap -p 5432 rds-endpoint # port scan traceroute rds-endpoint # path to host # VPC Flow Logs: check for REJECT aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /vpc-flowlogs --filter-pattern "REJECT" # Security Group: check inbound rules on RDS SG aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-rds-xxx # Route table: does private subnet route to target? aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-xxx # Reachability Analyzer: aws ec2 start-network-insights-analysis --network-insights-path-id path-xxx Systematic connectivity debugging: (1) Security Group inbound rules on the destination, (2) NACL rules on source and destination subnets, (3) Route table has a route to the destination, (4) VPC Flow Logs show REJECT if any, (5) EC2 Reachability Analyzer gives a visual path analysis with exact blocking point. Most connectivity issues are Security Group misconfiguration — check both source SG (outbound) and destination SG (inbound).

questions.q: How does S3 work — what are the key features for production use?
questions.text: aws s3 mb s3://mybucket --region us-east-1 # Versioning: aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket mybucket --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled # Block public access (essential): aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket mybucket --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true # Lifecycle rule (transition to Glacier after 90 days): aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket mybucket --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json # Pre-signed URL (temporary access): aws s3 presign s3://mybucket/file.txt --expires-in 3600 S3 production checklist: versioning enabled (recover deleted/overwritten objects), Block Public Access enabled (prevent accidental public buckets), bucket policies over ACLs, encryption at rest (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), access logging, and lifecycle policies to manage cost. Pre-signed URLs grant time-limited access to private objects without making them public — use for user file downloads. S3 Object Lock enables WORM (Write Once Read Many) for compliance data that must not be modified or deleted.

questions.q: What is AWS Fargate — when do you use EKS on Fargate vs EC2 node groups?
questions.text: # EKS Fargate profile: eksctl create fargateprofile --cluster prod --name fp-app \ --namespace production --labels app=myapp # Pod spec: no node selector needed — profile matches namespace/label # Each pod gets its own micro-VM (gVisor isolation) # No DaemonSets on Fargate (no node to run on) # EC2 node groups — use when you need: DaemonSets, privileged containers, GPU instances, custom AMIs Fargate: no node management, per-pod billing, stronger isolation (each pod in its own micro-VM), scales to zero. EC2: more control, cheaper at scale, required for DaemonSets/GPU/privileged containers. Hybrid: use Fargate for variable/bursty workloads (auto-scales without node management), EC2 for steady baseline (Savings Plan pricing). Fargate does not support node-level metrics (no Node Exporter) — use Container Insights for pod-level metrics instead.

questions.q: What is CloudTrail — how do you use it for compliance and audit?
questions.text: aws cloudtrail create-trail --name prod-trail --s3-bucket-name my-audit-bucket --is-multi-region-trail aws cloudtrail start-logging --name prod-trail # Query CloudTrail with Athena: SELECT eventname, useridentity.arn, sourceipaddress, eventtime FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = "DeleteBucket" AND eventtime > "2024-01-01" # Real-time: CloudWatch Events rule on CloudTrail aws events put-rule --event-pattern file://console-login-event.json CloudTrail logs every AWS API call — who did what, when, and from where. Enable in all regions (--is-multi-region-trail) and log to an S3 bucket with versioning and MFA delete protection. Enable CloudTrail Insights to detect unusual API activity (burst of DescribeInstances calls might indicate reconnaissance). Atop CloudTrail, AWS Config continuously records resource configuration and detects drift. GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs for threat detection.

questions.q: What is ElastiCache — Redis vs Memcached — how do you use it with EKS?
questions.text: aws elasticache create-replication-group --replication-group-id myredis \ --replication-group-description "prod redis" \ --engine redis --cache-node-type cache.r6g.large \ --num-cache-clusters 2 --multi-az-enabled # Access from EKS (in same VPC, private subnet): redis-cli -h myredis.abc.cache.amazonaws.com -p 6379 # Redis connection in Python: r = redis.Redis(host=os.environ["REDIS_HOST"], port=6379, ssl=True) Redis vs Memcached: Redis supports persistence, replication, data structures (sorted sets, streams), pub/sub, Lua scripting — use for session store, leaderboards, queues, rate limiting. Memcached: pure in-memory, simpler, multi-threaded — use when you need only simple key-value caching and maximum throughput. For production: ElastiCache Redis with Multi-AZ (automatic failover), encryption in transit (TLS), encryption at rest, and AUTH token. Access from EKS only via private subnet — never expose cache publicly.

questions.q: An EKS pod cannot reach an external API — how do you debug it?
questions.text: # Step 1: can the pod resolve DNS? kubectl exec mypod -- nslookup api.external.com # Step 2: can the pod reach the IP? kubectl exec mypod -- curl -v https://api.external.com --max-time 5 # Step 3: Check Security Group on the node aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-node-xxx # allow 443 outbound? # Step 4: Does NAT Gateway exist for the private subnet? aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-node # Step 5: VPC Flow Logs REJECT on the node IP # Step 6: If using VPC CNI, check pod IP in Security Group rules EKS pod connectivity path: pod → node Security Group → route table → NAT Gateway (if private subnet) → internet. VPC CNI assigns pod IPs from the VPC CIDR — Security Group rules must allow from pod IPs, not just node IPs (use Security Groups for Pods feature for pod-level SG enforcement). Common fix: NAT Gateway not in the route table for the node subnet, or Security Group blocking outbound 443.

questions.q: What is AWS Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store — when do you use each?
questions.text: # Secrets Manager: full lifecycle management aws secretsmanager create-secret --name prod/db/password --secret-string "mysecretpassword" aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db/password # Automatic rotation (Lambda function): aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/db/password --rotation-lambda-arn arn:xxx # Parameter Store: config + secrets (cheaper) aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/db/password --value "mysecret" --type SecureString aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/db/password --with-decryption Secrets Manager: auto-rotation (natively integrates with RDS, Redshift, ElastiCache), cross-account access, versioning, cost $0.40/secret/month. Parameter Store: free tier (Standard), cheaper at scale, does not support auto-rotation. Use Secrets Manager for credentials requiring rotation (database passwords, API keys). Use Parameter Store for configuration values and non-sensitive parameters. External Secrets Operator syncs both into Kubernetes Secrets automatically — no application code changes needed.

questions.q: What is AWS Cost Explorer and how do you use it to identify waste?
questions.text: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2024-01-01,End=2024-01-31 \ --granularity MONTHLY --metrics AmortizedCost \ --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE # Rightsizing recommendations: aws ce get-rightsizing-recommendation --service AmazonEC2 # Reserved Instance coverage report: aws ce get-reservation-coverage --time-period Start=2024-01-01,End=2024-01-31 # Savings Plan recommendations: aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP Cost Explorer workflow: identify top 5 services by spend (usually EC2, EKS, RDS, data transfer, S3), drill into each by region and resource type. Rightsizing recommendations identify over-provisioned EC2/RDS instances. Reservation coverage shows what % of On-Demand is covered by commitments — under 60% coverage means overspending. Tag all resources with environment, team, and project to enable per-team cost allocation. Use AWS Budgets to alert when spend exceeds threshold.

questions.q: What is AWS WAF — how do you configure it for EKS/ALB?
questions.text: # Create WAF Web ACL: aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name prod-waf --scope REGIONAL \ --default-action Allow={} --rules file://waf-rules.json # Attach to ALB: aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn WAF_ARN --resource-arn ALB_ARN # Key managed rule groups: AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet — OWASP Top 10 (SQLi, XSS) AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList — block known bad IPs AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet — log4j, Spring4shell # Rate limiting rule: {"Type":"RATE_BASED","Limit":2000,"AggregateKeyType":"IP"} AWS WAF protects ALBs, API Gateway, and CloudFront from common web attacks. Start with AWS Managed Rule Groups (no custom rules needed) — they cover OWASP Top 10 automatically. Rate limiting prevents DDoS and credential stuffing. WAF logs to S3/CloudWatch for security analysis. Shield Advanced (paid) adds DDoS protection, 24/7 AWS DDoS Response Team access, and attack cost protection. For EKS + ALB: attach WAF to the ALB ARN provisioned by the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

questions.q: How do you diagnose high latency in an AWS-hosted application?
questions.text: # Step 1: Which component is slow? (ALB access logs) aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name alb-access-logs --filter-pattern "[request_processing_time > 1]" # Step 2: Is it the application or the database? aws xray get-service-graph --start-time $(date -d "1 hour ago" +%s) --end-time $(date +%s) # Step 3: RDS Performance Insights aws pi get-resource-metrics --service-type RDS --identifier db-xxx --metric-queries file://queries.json # Step 4: EKS: check CPU throttling container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total rate # Step 5: Data transfer between AZs? (cross-AZ latency adds 1-3ms) Latency diagnosis layers: (1) DNS resolution time (Route 53 latency dashboard), (2) TLS handshake time (ALB target response time), (3) Application processing time (X-Ray trace waterfall), (4) Database query time (RDS Performance Insights, slow query log), (5) Resource constraints (CPU throttling on pods, RDS CPU/IOPS limits). Cross-AZ data transfer adds latency AND cost — colocate application pods and RDS read replicas in the same AZ when possible.

questions.q: How do you manage EKS cluster upgrades safely?
questions.text: # Check current version: aws eks describe-cluster --name prod --query cluster.version # Upgrade control plane first: aws eks update-cluster-version --name prod --kubernetes-version 1.30 aws eks wait cluster-active --name prod # Upgrade add-ons: aws eks update-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name kube-proxy --addon-version v1.30.0-eksbuild.1 aws eks update-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name vpc-cni aws eks update-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name coredns # Upgrade node groups: aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name prod --nodegroup-name workers EKS upgrade sequence: always control plane first, then add-ons, then node groups. One minor version at a time (1.28 → 1.29, not 1.28 → 1.30). Test on non-production cluster first. Check deprecated API versions in workloads before upgrading (kubectl convert + pluto for deprecated API detection). EKS supports two minor versions behind current — upgrade before support ends to maintain managed node group patching. Use managed node groups for node upgrades — they drain nodes automatically.

questions.q: Walk through a production incident where an EKS service is returning 503s.
questions.text: # Step 1: Check ALB target health: aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn tg-xxx # targets healthy? # Step 2: Check pods: kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=myapp # are pods Running? kubectl describe pod myapp-xxx -n prod # events show issues # Step 3: Check endpoints: kubectl get endpoints myapp -n prod # any IPs registered? # Step 4: Check logs: kubectl logs -l app=myapp -n prod --tail=50 | grep -i error # Step 5: Check HPA: kubectl get hpa -n prod # is max replicas reached? # Step 6: Check node capacity: kubectl get nodes # all Ready? kubectl top nodes # CPU/memory pressure? 503 from ALB means no healthy targets. Systematic checks: (1) ALB target group health — are pod IPs registered? (2) Pod status — any CrashLoopBackOff or Pending? (3) Kubernetes Endpoints — are pod IPs listed? (4) Readiness probe — is it passing? (5) Service selector — does it match pod labels? (6) Node capacity — are pods pending due to insufficient node resources? The most common cause: readiness probe failure (the pod starts but fails health check, so ALB never routes to it).

questions.q: What is the IAM policy evaluation logic — how are Allow, Deny, and boundaries resolved?
questions.text: # Evaluation order (simplified): 1. Explicit DENY anywhere -> DENY (always wins) 2. SCP (Organizations) -> must ALLOW or implicit deny 3. Resource-based policy / Identity policy -> needs an ALLOW 4. Permission boundary -> caps the max; must also allow 5. Session policy (assume-role) -> further caps # No explicit allow anywhere = implicit DENY The golden rule: an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow. A request is permitted only if every applicable layer allows it AND nothing denies it. SCPs and permission boundaries do not grant access — they set the maximum; you still need an identity/resource policy that allows the action. This is why a user can have AdministratorAccess yet be blocked by an SCP or boundary. Debugging access-denied: Use the IAM Policy Simulator and CloudTrail to see which policy denied a call. Decode the encoded authorization message with aws sts decode-authorization-message . The usual culprit is an SCP or permission boundary the user forgot about — not the identity policy.

questions.q: How do you securely give applications on EC2/EKS access to AWS without static keys?
questions.text: # EC2: instance profile (role) -> auto-rotated temp creds via IMDS: aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name app-profile # ALWAYS enforce IMDSv2 (token-required) to block SSRF credential theft: aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-xxx --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1 # EKS: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) via OIDC: eksctl create iamserviceaccount --cluster prod --name s3-reader --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess --approve # Or EKS Pod Identity (newer, simpler than IRSA): aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name prod --namespace app --service-account s3-reader --role-arn arn:... Never bake long-lived access keys into apps or images. On EC2 use an instance profile; on EKS use IRSA or Pod Identity so each pod gets a scoped role with temporary, auto-rotated STS credentials. For CI use OIDC federation (GitHub Actions, GitLab) instead of stored keys. IMDSv2 is critical: IMDSv1 let an SSRF bug fetch instance credentials with a single GET. IMDSv2 requires a session token (PUT then GET) and a hop limit of 1, which stops most SSRF-to-credential-theft attacks. Enforce it org-wide.

questions.q: What is AWS KMS — how do envelope encryption and key policies work?
questions.text: # Create a customer-managed key (CMK): aws kms create-key --description "app data key" # Envelope encryption: generate a data key, KMS returns plaintext + encrypted: aws kms generate-data-key --key-id alias/app --key-spec AES_256 # Encrypt locally with the plaintext data key, store the ENCRYPTED data key. # To decrypt: send encrypted data key back to KMS -> get plaintext key back. # Enable automatic annual rotation: aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id key-id Envelope encryption: KMS encrypts a small data key, not your large data. You encrypt the bulk data locally with the data key (fast, no size limit), then store the KMS-encrypted data key alongside it. KMS never sees your data. Access is controlled by the key policy (on the key itself) combined with IAM — both must allow. Grants give temporary, scoped key access. Key policy vs IAM: Unlike most services, a KMS key has its own resource policy that is authoritative — if the key policy does not allow the principal (directly or by delegating to IAM), no IAM policy can grant access. Locking yourself out of a key is a classic mistake; always keep the account root or an admin role in the key policy.

questions.q: How do you manage secrets in AWS? Compare Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store.
questions.text: # Secrets Manager: built-in rotation, JSON secrets, cross-region replication: aws secretsmanager create-secret --name prod/db --secret-string \'{"user":"app","pass":"..."}\' aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db # Rotation with a Lambda (e.g. RDS): aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/db --rotation-lambda-arn arn:... # SSM Parameter Store (cheaper, SecureString via KMS): aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/api-key --value "..." --type SecureString aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/api-key --with-decryption Secrets Manager: automatic rotation (native RDS/Redshift/DocumentDB integration), fine-grained resource policies, cross-region replication — but costs per secret + per API call. SSM Parameter Store: free standard tier, SecureString encrypted with KMS, hierarchical paths, great for config + simple secrets — but no built-in rotation. Use Parameter Store for config and low-churn secrets; Secrets Manager when you need automatic rotation or replication. Decision rule: Need rotation or cross-region secret replication -> Secrets Manager. Just need encrypted config/values cheaply -> Parameter Store SecureString. Both integrate with EKS via the Secrets Store CSI driver so pods mount secrets without app code changes.

questions.q: What are SCPs and how do you use AWS Organizations for multi-account governance?
questions.text: # Org structure: OUs (Organizational Units) group accounts by purpose: Root -> Security OU, Prod OU, Dev OU, Sandbox OU # SCP example: deny leaving the org + restrict regions: {"Effect":"Deny","Action":"*","Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:RequestedRegion":["us-east-1","eu-west-1"]}}} aws organizations attach-policy --policy-id p-xxx --target-id ou-xxx # Deny disabling CloudTrail / GuardDuty (guardrails): "Action":["cloudtrail:StopLogging","guardduty:DeleteDetector"], "Effect":"Deny" Multi-account is the AWS best practice for isolation: separate accounts per environment/team limit blast radius and simplify billing. SCPs are preventive guardrails applied to OUs/accounts — they set the maximum permissions even the account admin/root cannot exceed. Common SCPs: restrict regions, prevent disabling security services, block root usage, deny leaving the org. AWS Control Tower automates landing-zone setup with these guardrails. SCPs do not grant: they only filter. They also do not apply to the management (payer) account. Test SCPs carefully — an overly broad Deny can lock out an entire OU. Use Control Tower / well-architected landing zones rather than hand-rolling.

questions.q: How do you detect and respond to security threats in AWS? (GuardDuty, Security Hub, CloudTrail)
questions.text: # CloudTrail: record of every API call (the audit log — enable org-wide): aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail --s3-bucket-name audit-bucket --is-organization-trail # GuardDuty: ML threat detection (crypto-mining, creds exfil, recon): aws guardduty create-detector --enable # Security Hub: aggregates findings + CIS/AWS best-practice checks: aws securityhub enable-security-hub --enable-default-standards # Auto-respond with EventBridge -> Lambda (e.g. isolate instance): aws events put-rule --event-pattern \'{"source":["aws.guardduty"]}\' Layered detection: CloudTrail is the foundational audit trail (who did what, when). GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs with ML to flag threats (compromised credentials, crypto-mining, unusual API calls). Security Hub centralizes findings across accounts and runs compliance standards (CIS, PCI). Wire GuardDuty findings to EventBridge for automated response — quarantine an instance, revoke sessions, or alert. Incident response in AWS: On a compromised credential alert, immediately revoke the session (attach a Deny-all policy / disable the key), snapshot for forensics, and rotate. CloudTrail tells you the blast radius (what the credential touched). Detective helps visualize the attack path.

questions.q: What is the difference between identity-based, resource-based, and ABAC policies?
questions.text: # Identity-based: attached to a user/group/role (what THEY can do): {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*"} # Resource-based: attached to the RESOURCE (who can access IT) - has Principal: {"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::222:root"},"Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"..."} # ABAC: allow based on matching TAGS instead of listing every resource: "Condition":{"StringEquals":{"aws:ResourceTag/team":"${aws:PrincipalTag/team}"}} Identity-based policies attach to principals and grant them actions. Resource-based policies attach to resources (S3 buckets, SQS, Lambda, KMS) and include a Principal — they enable cross-account access without role assumption. ABAC (attribute-based access control) grants access by comparing tags on the principal and resource, so one policy scales to many resources/teams without editing it as you add resources. ABAC at scale: Tag resources and principals with team / project , then write a single policy that allows access only when the tags match. New projects need no policy changes — just consistent tagging. This is the modern approach for large multi-team orgs versus exploding lists of resource ARNs.

questions.q: How do you enforce encryption and prevent public exposure of S3 data org-wide?
questions.text: # Account-level Block Public Access (the master switch): aws s3control put-public-access-block --account-id 123 --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true # Default encryption (SSE-KMS) on a bucket: aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket b --server-side-encryption-configuration \'{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"aws:kms"}}]}\' # Bucket policy: deny any unencrypted PUT or non-TLS access: {"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:PutObject","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"aws:kms"}}} {"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:*","Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:SecureTransport":"false"}}} Defense in depth for S3: enable account-level Block Public Access (overrides any bucket-level mistake), set default encryption, and add bucket policies that deny unencrypted uploads and non-TLS requests. Enforce org-wide with an SCP requiring Block Public Access and via IAM Access Analyzer to flag any bucket exposed externally. The classic breach: a public S3 bucket leaking data.
