Account-level Block Public Access is the single most important control — it stops a misconfigured bucket policy or ACL from ever making data public, regardless of what someone sets later. Combine with Access Analyzer alerts.

questions.q: How does AWS WAF and Shield protect applications? When do you use each?
questions.text: # WAF web ACL on ALB / CloudFront / API Gateway: aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name app-acl --scope REGIONAL --default-action Allow={} # Managed rule groups (OWASP top 10, bad inputs, bot control): AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet, AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet, AWSManagedRulesBotControl # Rate-based rule (block IPs over N req / 5 min): {"RateBasedStatement":{"Limit":2000,"AggregateKeyType":"IP"}} # Shield Advanced (DDoS) + cost protection: aws shield subscribe-to-proactive-engagement WAF is a Layer 7 firewall: it inspects HTTP requests and blocks SQLi, XSS, bad bots, and abusive IPs via managed and custom rules, including rate limiting. Shield Standard (free, automatic) protects against common L3/L4 DDoS. Shield Advanced adds enhanced L3-L7 DDoS protection, 24/7 DDoS response team, and cost protection against scaling-driven bills during an attack. Place WAF on CloudFront for global edge filtering. Layering: CloudFront (edge) + WAF (L7 rules, rate limiting) + Shield (DDoS) + Security Groups (L3/4) gives defense in depth. For L7 floods, WAF rate-based rules and Bot Control are the right tool; for volumetric L3/4 attacks, Shield. Put the WAF as close to the edge (CloudFront) as possible to drop bad traffic early.

questions.q: A developer accidentally committed AWS access keys to a public GitHub repo. What do you do?
questions.text: # 1. IMMEDIATELY deactivate/delete the key (do not wait): aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id AKIA... --status Inactive --user-name dev aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id AKIA... --user-name dev # 2. Scope the blast radius via CloudTrail: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIA... # 3. Check for attacker persistence (new users/keys/roles, EC2 instances): aws iam list-users; aws ec2 describe-instances --query "Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId" Act in order: (1) revoke the credential first — minutes matter, attackers scrape public repos within seconds; (2) investigate what the key did via CloudTrail (it logs every API call by that key); (3) hunt for persistence the attacker may have created (new IAM users/keys, unexpected instances often spun up for crypto-mining, modified trust policies); (4) rotate anything the key could have read; (5) remediate the root cause. Prevent recurrence: Stop using long-lived keys — move to IAM roles, IRSA, and OIDC for CI. Add secret scanning (git-secrets, gitleaks, GitHub push protection) to block commits. AWS also auto-detects exposed keys and applies a quarantine policy, but never rely on that — assume compromise and respond fully.

questions.q: How do Auto Scaling Groups work? Explain scaling policies, health checks, and lifecycle hooks.
questions.text: # ASG with a launch template, spread across AZs: aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=web-lt --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 3 --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-a,subnet-b,subnet-c" # Target tracking (keep avg CPU at 50%): aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling --target-tracking-configuration \'{"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},"TargetValue":50}\' # Use ELB health checks (not just EC2): aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 120 ASGs maintain desired capacity, replace unhealthy instances, and scale on policies. Target tracking (keep a metric at a target) is the simplest and preferred over step scaling for most cases. Set health-check-type to ELB so instances failing the load balancer health check (not just crashed) get replaced. Lifecycle hooks pause launch/terminate so you can run setup or drain connections before an instance is added/removed. Production tips: Spread across 3 AZs for resilience; use a warm-up/grace period so new instances are not killed before the app starts; combine On-Demand + Spot via mixed instances policy for cost; and use instance refresh for rolling AMI updates without downtime.

questions.q: What is AWS Lambda — explain cold starts, concurrency, and when serverless fits.
questions.text: # Concurrency controls: aws lambda put-function-concurrency --function-name api --reserved-concurrent-executions 100 # Provisioned concurrency to eliminate cold starts on hot paths: aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name api --qualifier prod --provisioned-concurrent-executions 20 # Tune memory (also scales CPU) for price/performance: aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name api --memory-size 1024 --timeout 30 Lambda runs code without managing servers, scaling automatically per request and billing per ms. A cold start is the latency when a new execution environment spins up (init + your init code); it hits the first request and during scale-out. Mitigate with provisioned concurrency on latency-sensitive paths, smaller packages, and lightweight runtimes. Account concurrency is shared — use reserved concurrency to protect critical functions and cap others. When NOT to use Lambda: long-running jobs (15-min cap), very high steady throughput (can be costlier than containers), workloads needing persistent connections, or heavy/low-latency cold-start-sensitive paths without provisioned concurrency. Watch out for downstream limits — a Lambda scaling to thousands of concurrent executions can overwhelm an RDS connection pool (use RDS Proxy). Memory = CPU: Lambda CPU scales with memory, so raising memory can make a function finish faster AND cheaper. Use AWS Lambda Power Tuning to find the sweet spot.

questions.q: Compare ECS, EKS, and Fargate. How do you choose a container platform on AWS?
questions.text: # ECS on Fargate (no nodes to manage): aws ecs create-service --cluster prod --service-name api --task-definition api:3 --desired-count 3 --launch-type FARGATE # ECS on EC2 (you manage the instances, cheaper at scale): aws ecs create-cluster --cluster-name prod # + EC2 capacity provider # EKS = managed Kubernetes (portable, ecosystem): eksctl create cluster --name prod --fargate ECS is AWS-native, simpler, tightly integrated, no Kubernetes knowledge needed — great when you are all-in on AWS and want low operational overhead. EKS is managed Kubernetes — choose it for portability, the CNCF ecosystem (Helm, operators, service mesh), or existing K8s skills/workloads. Fargate is a launch type (works with both ECS and EKS): serverless containers, no node management, you pay per task vCPU/memory. Decision guide: Want simplest + AWS-only -> ECS. Need Kubernetes portability/ecosystem or multi-cloud -> EKS. Do not want to manage nodes/patching -> Fargate (with either). Steady high scale where node bin-packing saves money -> EC2 launch type. Many teams run EKS + Fargate for spiky/isolated workloads and managed node groups for the rest.

questions.q: How do you build immutable, hardened machine images and keep an AMI pipeline current?
questions.text: # EC2 Image Builder pipeline (build + test + distribute AMIs): aws imagebuilder create-image-pipeline --name golden --image-recipe-arn arn:... --infrastructure-configuration-arn arn:... # Or Packer to bake an AMI from a base + provisioning: packer build app.pkr.hcl # installs deps, agents, hardening, app # Reference the AMI by SSM parameter (auto-updates launch templates): aws ssm get-parameter --name /golden/ami/latest --query Parameter.Value Immutable infrastructure: bake a versioned golden AMI with the OS hardened (CIS benchmark), patches, agents (CloudWatch, SSM, security), and the app, then deploy by replacing instances — never patch in place. EC2 Image Builder or Packer automate the bake; Image Builder can run on a schedule to pull the latest patched base, run tests, and distribute across regions/accounts. Keeping current: Schedule the pipeline to rebuild from the newest patched base AMI, store the resulting AMI ID in an SSM parameter, and have launch templates reference that parameter so an instance refresh rolls out the new image. This gives a repeatable, auditable patch cadence without snowflake servers.

questions.q: How do Spot Instances work and how do you run production workloads on them safely?
questions.text: # Mixed instances policy: baseline On-Demand + Spot for the rest: aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --mixed-instances-policy \'{"InstancesDistribution":{"OnDemandBaseCapacity":2,"OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity":20,"SpotAllocationStrategy":"price-capacity-optimized"},"LaunchTemplate":{"Overrides":[{"InstanceType":"m6i.large"},{"InstanceType":"m5.large"},{"InstanceType":"m5a.large"}]}}\' # Handle the 2-minute interruption notice (IMDS or EventBridge): curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/instance-action Spot uses spare EC2 capacity at up to ~90% off but can be reclaimed with a 2-minute warning. Run them safely by: diversifying across many instance types and AZs (price-capacity-optimized strategy reduces interruptions), keeping workloads stateless/fault-tolerant, and handling the interruption notice to drain gracefully. Ideal for CI runners, batch, big-data, and stateless web tiers behind an ASG. Do not run on Spot: stateful singletons, databases, or anything that cannot tolerate sudden termination. For EKS, use the AWS Node Termination Handler (or Karpenter, which natively handles Spot interruptions and consolidation) to cordon and drain nodes on the 2-minute notice.

questions.q: What is Karpenter and how does it improve EKS node autoscaling vs Cluster Autoscaler?
questions.text: # Karpenter provisioner/NodePool: pick instances just-in-time by pod needs: apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1 kind: NodePool requirements: [karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category In [c,m,r], karpenter.sh/capacity-type In [spot,on-demand]] disruption: consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized # Karpenter watches unschedulable pods and launches the cheapest fitting node. Cluster Autoscaler scales fixed node groups (one instance type each) by adjusting ASG desired count — slower and coarse. Karpenter watches pending pods and provisions right-sized nodes directly from EC2 in seconds, choosing instance type, size, and Spot/On-Demand to fit the actual pod requirements. It also consolidates — repacking pods and terminating underutilized nodes to cut cost. Why it wins: faster scale-up (no pre-defined node groups), better bin-packing and cost via diverse instance selection + Spot, and automatic consolidation. The trade-off is more dynamic node churn, so set Pod Disruption Budgets and use do-not-disrupt annotations for sensitive workloads. Karpenter is now the recommended autoscaler for most EKS clusters.

questions.q: How do you design a highly available, multi-AZ architecture for a stateless web app?
questions.text: # ALB across 3 AZs -> ASG instances in private subnets in each AZ: Route 53 -> CloudFront -> ALB (3 AZs) -> ASG (min spread per AZ) -> RDS Multi-AZ # Health checks at every layer: aws elbv2 modify-target-group --target-group-arn tg --health-check-path /healthz # Stateless: session/state in ElastiCache or DynamoDB, not on the instance HA pattern: front with Route 53 + CloudFront, an ALB spanning at least 3 AZs, instances in an ASG spread across those AZs (so losing one AZ keeps you serving), and a Multi-AZ data tier (RDS Multi-AZ / DynamoDB). Keep the app tier stateless — store session and shared state in ElastiCache or DynamoDB so any instance can serve any request and instances are freely replaceable. Surviving an AZ failure: design so the remaining AZs have enough headroom to absorb the load (do not run at 100% across 3 AZs, or losing one overloads the other two). Health checks at each layer + ASG self-healing + Multi-AZ data give automatic recovery. This is the canonical AWS Well-Architected reliability design.

questions.q: What deployment strategies does AWS support (blue/green, canary, rolling) and how?
questions.text: # CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS / Lambda / EC2: aws deploy create-deployment --deployment-group-name bg --deployment-config-name CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes # Lambda weighted alias (canary 10% -> 100%): aws lambda update-alias --function-name api --name prod --function-version 5 --routing-config AdditionalVersionWeights={"4"=0.9} # ALB weighted target groups for traffic shifting: aws elbv2 modify-listener --default-actions ...ForwardConfig with weights Rolling: replace instances/tasks in batches (built into ASG/ECS) — simple, no extra cost, but mixed versions briefly run together. Blue/green: stand up a full new (green) environment, shift traffic, keep blue for instant rollback — zero-downtime and safe, at the cost of double resources during cutover. Canary: shift a small % of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then ramp — catches issues with minimal blast radius. Choosing: Use canary (CodeDeploy/Lambda weighted aliases) for risky changes where you want metric-gated rollout and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms. Use blue/green when you need instant rollback and can afford duplicate capacity. Rolling is fine for low-risk, backward-compatible changes. Always pair with health checks and automatic rollback alarms.

questions.q: How does EC2 instance metadata (IMDS) work and why is IMDSv2 a security requirement?
questions.text: # IMDSv1 (insecure): a single GET returns role credentials: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/role-name # IMDSv2: must first PUT to get a session token, then use it: TOKEN=$(curl -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300") curl -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ # Enforce v2 + hop limit 1 (blocks containers/SSRF reaching IMDS): aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-xxx --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1 IMDS exposes instance data and, crucially, the IAM role\'s temporary credentials at 169.254.169.254. IMDSv1\'s simple GET means any SSRF vulnerability (tricking the app into making a request to that URL) can exfiltrate role credentials. IMDSv2 requires a PUT-issued, short-lived session token and a low hop limit, which defeats most SSRF and prevents containers from casually reaching the host\'s credentials. This was the Capital One breach vector: an SSRF flaw fetched IMDSv1 credentials and accessed S3. Enforce IMDSv2 ( http-tokens required ) and a hop limit of 1 across the fleet via SCP/launch templates. It is one of the highest-impact, lowest-effort hardening steps in AWS.

questions.q: How do you patch and manage a fleet of EC2 instances at scale with Systems Manager?
questions.text: # SSM needs the agent + an instance role (no SSH/keys required): aws ssm describe-instance-information # which instances are managed # Patch Manager: baseline + maintenance window: aws ssm create-patch-baseline --name prod-baseline --approval-rules ... aws ssm create-association --name AWS-RunPatchBaseline --schedule-expression "cron(0 3 ? * SUN *)" # Run a command across the fleet (no SSH): aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript --targets Key=tag:env,Values=prod --parameters commands="yum update -y" # Session Manager: shell access without open SSH ports: aws ssm start-session --target i-xxx Systems Manager manages fleets without SSH: Patch Manager applies patch baselines on maintenance windows, Run Command executes scripts across tagged instances, State Manager enforces desired config, and Session Manager gives audited shell access through IAM (no bastion, no open port 22, full logging to CloudWatch/S3). Inventory and Compliance report what is installed and which instances are out of patch compliance. Why SSM over SSH: no inbound ports, no key management, every action is IAM-controlled and logged in CloudTrail/Session logs. Combine with immutable AMIs for the base and SSM for emergency fixes/compliance. Tag-based targeting lets you patch \'env=prod\' fleet-wide on a schedule with automatic rollback reporting.

questions.q: How do you connect VPCs and on-prem networks? Compare peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, Direct Connect.
questions.text: # VPC Peering (1:1, non-transitive): aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-a --peer-vpc-id vpc-b # Transit Gateway (hub-and-spoke, transitive, scales to hundreds of VPCs): aws ec2 create-transit-gateway; aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-id tgw --vpc-id vpc-a # Site-to-Site VPN (encrypted over internet): aws ec2 create-vpn-connection --type ipsec.1 --customer-gateway-id cgw --transit-gateway-id tgw # Direct Connect = dedicated private fiber (consistent low latency) VPC Peering is simple and cheap but non-transitive (A-B and B-C does not give A-C) and becomes a mesh nightmare beyond a few VPCs. Transit Gateway is a central hub that connects many VPCs and on-prem transitively — the standard for multi-VPC/multi-account at scale. Site-to-Site VPN gives encrypted connectivity over the internet (quick, variable latency). Direct Connect provides a dedicated physical link for consistent low latency and high throughput. Choosing: 2-3 VPCs -> peering. Many VPCs/accounts -> Transit Gateway. On-prem with cost sensitivity / quick setup -> VPN; on-prem needing predictable performance/bandwidth -> Direct Connect (often with a VPN backup for resilience). PrivateLink is the right answer when you only need to expose a single service, not whole-network routing.

questions.q: What is AWS PrivateLink and how does it differ from VPC peering and NAT?
questions.text: # Interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) to an AWS service or partner service: aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.secretsmanager --subnet-ids subnet-a --security-group-ids sg-x # Gateway endpoint (S3/DynamoDB only, free, route-table based): aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 --route-table-ids rtb-x # Expose YOUR service to other VPCs via an endpoint service (NLB-backed): aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint-service-configuration --network-load-balancer-arns arn:... PrivateLink exposes a specific service (an AWS service, or your own NLB-fronted service) as a private endpoint inside your VPC — traffic never traverses the internet, and there is no network-level route between the two VPCs (unlike peering, which joins whole address spaces). It avoids NAT Gateway data-processing costs for AWS API calls and prevents CIDR-overlap problems since only the one service is reachable. Endpoints save money + secure traffic: Use Gateway endpoints (free) for S3/DynamoDB, Interface endpoints for other AWS APIs so private subnets reach AWS services without a NAT Gateway. Use a PrivateLink endpoint service to offer your SaaS to customers privately. The key contrast: peering = whole-VPC routing; PrivateLink = one-service exposure, no overlap concerns.

questions.q: How does Route 53 work? Explain routing policies and health-check based failover.
questions.text: # Routing policies: Simple — one record, no logic Weighted — split traffic by % (canary, A/B, gradual migration) Latency — route to the lowest-latency region for the user Geolocation/Geoproximity — route by user location Failover — primary/secondary with health checks Multivalue — return multiple healthy IPs (simple client-side LB) # Health check driving failover: aws route53 create-health-check --health-check-config Type=HTTPS,ResourcePath=/healthz,FullyQualifiedDomainName=api.example.com Route 53 is DNS plus traffic management. Weighted records enable canary releases and blue/green at the DNS layer. Latency-based routing sends users to the nearest/fastest region. Failover routing pairs a primary and secondary with health checks so DNS stops returning the unhealthy endpoint. Alias records point to AWS resources (ALB, CloudFront, S3) for free and can sit at the zone apex (where CNAMEs cannot). Multi-region active-passive: Failover routing + health checks gives automatic regional failover; combine with latency routing for active-active. Remember DNS failover is bounded by TTL and client caching, so it is minutes-scale — pair with in-region (ALB/ASG) health for fast local recovery. Use ALIAS (not CNAME) at the apex for ALB/CloudFront.

questions.q: What is CloudFront and how do you use it for performance and security?
questions.text: # Distribution with an S3/ALB origin + OAC (no public bucket): aws cloudfront create-distribution --origin-domain-name bucket.s3.amazonaws.com # Cache behaviors by path (static long-cache, /api no-cache): /static/* -> cache 1y; /api/* -> forward to ALB, cache disabled # Invalidate after a deploy: aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123 --paths "/*" # Edge logic with CloudFront Functions / Lambda@Edge (auth, redirects, headers) CloudFront is a global CDN: it caches content at edge locations near users (lower latency, less origin load) and terminates TLS at the edge. Use Origin Access Control so the S3 origin is private and only CloudFront can read it. Per-path cache behaviors let you cache static assets aggressively while bypassing cache for dynamic APIs. It is also the best place to attach WAF and Shield for edge security and to add headers/redirects/auth via CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge. Performance + security combo: CloudFront (edge cache + TLS) + WAF (L7 rules) + Shield (DDoS) + OAC (private origin) is the standard edge stack. Set proper Cache-Control headers and use versioned asset filenames so you rarely need invalidations (which cost money and take time).

questions.q: Compare ALB, NLB, and Gateway Load Balancer. When do you use each?
questions.text: # ALB (L7 - HTTP/HTTPS, host/path routing, WebSockets, gRPC): aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --type application --subnets subnet-a subnet-b # NLB (L4 - TCP/UDP, ultra-low latency, static IP, millions of req): aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --type network --subnets subnet-a subnet-b # GWLB (insert appliances - firewalls/IDS - transparently): aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --type gateway ALB operates at Layer 7: routes by host/path/header, supports HTTPS termination, WebSockets, gRPC, redirects, and integrates with WAF and Cognito auth — the default for HTTP apps and Kubernetes Ingress. NLB operates at Layer 4: extreme performance/low latency, handles TCP/UDP, preserves source IP, provides static/Elastic IPs, and is used for non-HTTP protocols or when you need a fixed IP. Gateway Load Balancer transparently inserts third-party network appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS) into the traffic path. Quick rule: HTTP(S) with routing/auth/WAF -> ALB. Non-HTTP, need static IP, or millions of connections at lowest latency -> NLB. Need to run inline security appliances -> GWLB. For EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions ALBs for Ingress and NLBs for L4 Services.

questions.q: A NAT Gateway is generating huge data-processing costs. How do you diagnose and reduce it?
questions.text: # Find what is going through NAT with VPC Flow Logs: aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type Subnet --resource-ids subnet-priv --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs # Query: top talkers / destinations through the NAT ENI # Replace AWS API traffic with VPC endpoints (no NAT charges): aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --service-name ...s3 --route-table-ids rtb # S3/DynamoDB FREE aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --service-name ...ecr.dkr # ECR, etc. NAT Gateways charge both hourly and per-GB processed, so high egress from private subnets gets expensive. Diagnose with VPC Flow Logs to find the top destinations. The biggest win is usually adding VPC endpoints: S3/DynamoDB via free Gateway endpoints, and ECR/Secrets Manager/etc. via Interface endpoints, so that traffic to AWS services bypasses the NAT entirely. Common hidden cost: pulling container images from ECR or writing to S3 through the NAT Gateway. Gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB are free and eliminate that data-processing charge immediately. Also check cross-AZ NAT (place a NAT per AZ to avoid cross-AZ data charges) and chatty third-party calls that could be cached or batched.

questions.q: How do you debug why an EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot reach the internet?
questions.text: # Walk the path methodically: 1. Route table: does the private subnet have 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-gateway-id? aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-priv 2. NAT Gateway: is it in a PUBLIC subnet with an IGW route + an EIP? 3. Security Group: outbound allowed? (default allows all egress) 4. NACL: stateless - allow outbound AND inbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535)? 5. DNS: enableDnsSupport/enableDnsHostnames on the VPC? Systematic checklist: the private subnet route table must send 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway; the NAT Gateway itself must live in a public subnet that routes to the Internet Gateway and has an Elastic IP; the Security Group must allow the outbound traffic; and because NACLs are stateless, the outbound NACL must allow the request and the inbound NACL must allow the ephemeral return ports. Finally, confirm VPC DNS settings if name resolution fails. Most common cause: the NAT Gateway placed in a private subnet by mistake (it must be in a public subnet with an IGW route), or a missing 0.0.0.0/0 route in the private route table. The stateless-NACL ephemeral-port trap is the second most common — Security Groups handle return traffic automatically, NACLs do not.

questions.q: How do you design VPC CIDR and IP addressing to avoid running out of IPs or conflicts?
questions.text: # Plan non-overlapping CIDRs (critical for peering/TGW/VPN): Prod VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 Dev VPC: 10.1.0.0/16 On-prem: 10.100.0.0/16 # Reserve space; subnets sized for growth (each AZ gets a /20, etc.) # EKS eats IPs fast (VPC CNI assigns a VPC IP per pod): # mitigate with prefix delegation or a secondary CIDR for pods: aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block --vpc-id vpc-x --cidr-block 100.64.0.0/16 Choose non-overlapping RFC1918 ranges across all VPCs and on-prem up front — overlaps make peering, Transit Gateway, and VPN routing impossible to fix later without re-IP. Size subnets for growth (AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet). EKS with the VPC CNI assigns a real VPC IP to every pod, so clusters exhaust subnets quickly; use prefix delegation, larger subnets, or a secondary (e.g. 100.64.0.0/16 CGNAT) CIDR dedicated to pods. EKS IP exhaustion is a frequent production problem: pods Pending with \'insufficient IP addresses\'. Fixes: enable VPC CNI prefix delegation (assigns /28 blocks, far more pods per node), add a secondary CIDR for pod subnets, or use custom networking. Use IPAM (AWS VPC IP Address Manager) to plan and track allocation org-wide.

questions.q: What are VPC Flow Logs and how do you use them for security and troubleshooting?
questions.text: # Enable on a VPC/subnet/ENI, to CloudWatch or S3: aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-ids vpc-x --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type s3 --log-destination arn:aws:s3:::flowlogs # Fields include srcaddr, dstaddr, srcport, dstport, action (ACCEPT/REJECT), bytes # Analyze at scale with Athena over the S3 logs: SELECT srcaddr, dstaddr, sum(bytes) FROM flowlogs WHERE action=\'REJECT\' GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic (not payloads): source/dest IP and port, protocol, bytes, and whether the Security Group/NACL ACCEPTed or REJECTed it. Use them to troubleshoot connectivity (REJECT entries show what a firewall blocked), find top talkers driving NAT/data costs, detect exfiltration or port scans, and feed GuardDuty. Query large volumes cheaply with Athena over S3. Troubleshooting trick: when a connection mysteriously fails, Flow Logs tell you whether packets even arrived and whether a SG/NACL rejected them — instantly separating \'firewall blocked it\' from \'it never got there\' from \'app problem\'. For security, alerting on unexpected REJECT/ACCEPT patterns and large outbound transfers catches scans and data exfiltration.

questions.q: How do you architect a multi-region application on AWS? What are the hard parts?
questions.text: # Global routing: Route 53 latency/failover or Global Accelerator (anycast): aws globalaccelerator create-accelerator --name app # 2 static anycast IPs, fast failover # Data replication is the hard part: DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-region active-active) Aurora Global Database (1 primary write region, fast read replicas + failover) S3 Cross-Region Replication; ECR cross-region replication for images Compute is the easy part — replicate stacks per region behind Route 53 (latency or failover routing) or Global Accelerator for anycast IPs and sub-minute failover. The hard part is data : you must choose between active-active (DynamoDB Global Tables — handles multi-region writes with last-writer-wins) and active-passive (Aurora Global Database — single write region, fast cross-region replicas and promotion). You also must handle replication lag, conflict resolution, and consistency. Be honest about why: multi-region adds large cost and complexity; most needs are met by multi-AZ. Justify it by RTO/RPO (true regional DR or active-active latency). Decide write topology first (active-active vs active-passive), since that dictates the database choice and the whole architecture. Replication lag and split-brain are the recurring pain points interviewers probe.

questions.q: Explain S3 storage classes and lifecycle policies. How do you optimize storage cost?
questions.text: # Classes by access pattern: Standard — frequent access Intelligent-Tiering — auto-moves objects between tiers (unknown/changing access) Standard-IA / One Zone-IA — infrequent access, lower storage cost + retrieval fee Glacier Instant / Flexible / Deep Archive — archival, cheapest, retrieval latency # Lifecycle rule: transition + expire: aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket b --lifecycle-configuration \'{"Rules":[{"Status":"Enabled","Transitions":[{"Days":30,"StorageClass":"STANDARD_IA"},{"Days":90,"StorageClass":"GLACIER"}],"Expiration":{"Days":365}}]}\' Match class to access pattern: Standard for hot data, Standard-IA for infrequent, Glacier tiers for archives, and Intelligent-Tiering when access is unpredictable (it auto-tiers with no retrieval fees on the frequent/infrequent tiers). Lifecycle policies automate transitions to cheaper classes over time and expire old data. Also expire incomplete multipart uploads and old versions, which silently accumulate cost. Cost wins: Intelligent-Tiering is the safe default for unknown patterns (no retrieval fees, small monitoring charge). Use S3 Storage Lens to find buckets to optimize. Watch for the IA minimum object size/duration charges (small short-lived objects can cost more in IA than Standard). Always add a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads.

questions.q: Compare EBS, EFS, and S3. When do you use each, and which EBS volume types?
questions.text: # EBS = block storage, single-AZ, attaches to one EC2 (mostly): gp3 — general SSD (baseline 3000 IOPS, tune IOPS/throughput independently) io2 Block Express — high IOPS/durability (databases) st1/sc1 — throughput HDD / cold HDD (big sequential, logs, cheap) # EFS = managed NFS, multi-AZ, many instances share it: aws efs create-file-system --performance-mode generalPurpose --throughput-mode elastic # S3 = object storage over HTTP, infinite scale EBS is a network block device for a single instance (like a virtual disk) — use for boot volumes and databases; gp3 is the modern default (cheaper than gp2, decoupled IOPS/throughput), io2 Block Express for high-performance databases. EFS is managed NFS that many instances across AZs can mount simultaneously — use for shared filesystems and lift-and-shift apps needing POSIX. S3 is object storage accessed via API — use for backups, media, data lakes, and static assets. Quick rule: one instance, low-latency block + filesystem -> EBS (gp3 default, io2 for DBs). Shared across many instances/AZs -> EFS. Web-scale, durable, accessed by URL/API -> S3. Migrate gp2 to gp3 for an easy ~20% cost cut. Use EBS snapshots (incremental) for backups and DLM to automate them.

questions.q: How do S3 consistency, versioning, and Object Lock work? How do you protect against deletion?
questions.text: # Versioning (keeps every version; deletes add a delete marker): aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket b --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled # MFA Delete (require MFA to permanently delete versions): aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket b --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled --mfa "serial code" # Object Lock (WORM - compliance, immutable for a retention period): aws s3api put-object-retention --bucket b --key k --retention Mode=COMPLIANCE,RetainUntilDate=2027-01-01 S3 now provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations. Versioning keeps every version of an object so overwrites and deletes are recoverable (a delete just adds a delete marker). Object Lock enforces WORM (write-once-read-many): in Governance mode privileged users can override, in Compliance mode no one (not even root) can delete until the retention expires — the strongest defense against ransomware and malicious deletion. Ransomware/insider defense: versioning + MFA Delete + Object Lock (Compliance) makes backups immutable so an attacker with credentials still cannot erase them. Pair with Cross-Region Replication to a separate account for an air-gapped copy. This is the S3 equivalent of the 3-2-1-1-0 immutable-backup rule.

questions.q: How do you back up and recover AWS resources? Explain snapshots, AWS Backup, and DR strategies.
questions.text: # EBS snapshots are incremental; automate with Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup: aws backup create-backup-plan --backup-plan \'{"BackupPlanName":"daily","Rules":[{"RuleName":"daily","TargetBackupVaultName":"vault","ScheduleExpression":"cron(0 5 * * ? *)","Lifecycle":{"DeleteAfterDays":35}}]}\' # Cross-region/cross-account copy for DR + ransomware isolation: aws backup ... CopyActions to a vault in another region/account (locked vault) AWS Backup centralizes backups across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, and more with policy-based plans, retention, and cross-region/cross-account copies. EBS snapshots are incremental (only changed blocks) and stored in S3. For DR, pick a strategy by RTO/RTO: Backup & Restore (cheapest, hours), Pilot Light (core running, scale up on failover), Warm Standby (scaled-down full stack), or Multi-Site Active-Active (lowest RTO, highest cost). Test restores + isolate copies: an untested backup is not a backup — run restore drills and measure actual RTO. Copy backups to a separate region and a separate account with a locked Backup Vault (Vault Lock = WORM) so a compromised production account cannot delete your DR copies. Choose the DR tier by business RTO/RPO, not by default.

questions.q: How do you achieve high performance with S3 (throughput, large objects, many requests)?
questions.text: # Multipart upload for large objects (parallel parts, resumable): aws s3 cp big.bin s3://b/ --expected-size 5368709120 # CLI auto-multiparts # S3 scales to 3,500 PUT and 5,500 GET per second PER PREFIX -> spread keys # S3 Transfer Acceleration (upload via CloudFront edge): aws s3api put-bucket-accelerate-configuration --bucket b --accelerate-configuration Status=Enabled # Byte-range GETs to parallelize large downloads S3 scales horizontally per key prefix (3,500 writes / 5,500 reads per second each), so high-throughput workloads should distribute object keys across many prefixes rather than a sequential hot prefix. Use multipart upload for large objects (parallelism + resume on failure) and byte-range fetches to parallelize downloads. Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge for far-flung clients. For analytics, columnar formats + S3 Select / Athena reduce data scanned. Prefix design matters: the old advice to randomize key prefixes is less critical now (S3 auto-partitions), but a single sequential hot prefix can still bottleneck — spread high-rate keys. For data lakes, partition by query dimensions (date/region) and use Parquet so engines scan less. CRT-based clients/awscli get much higher throughput.

questions.q: What is S3 event-driven processing and how do you build it reliably?
questions.text: # S3 event notification -> SQS / SNS / Lambda / EventBridge: aws s3api put-bucket-notification-configuration --bucket b --notification-configuration \'{"QueueConfigurations":[{"QueueArn":"arn:...sqs","Events":["s3:ObjectCreated:*"]}]}\' # Prefer SQS (or EventBridge) in front of Lambda for buffering + retries + DLQ: S3 -> SQS -> Lambda (batch) , with a Dead Letter Queue for failures S3 can emit events on object create/delete to SQS, SNS, Lambda, or EventBridge — the basis of serverless pipelines (image processing, ingestion, ETL triggers). For reliability, put SQS or EventBridge between S3 and the consumer: it buffers spikes, enables batching and retries, and provides a dead-letter queue for poison messages, instead of invoking Lambda directly where bursts can throttle and failures vanish. Reliability patterns: use SQS for decoupling + DLQ; make consumers idempotent (events can be delivered more than once); for ordering or fan-out, use SNS-to-SQS or EventBridge. EventBridge adds rich filtering and many targets. Always have a DLQ and alarming on it so failed objects are not silently dropped.

questions.q: How do you securely share data across AWS accounts (S3, KMS, cross-account access)?
questions.text: # Bucket policy granting another account (resource-based): {"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT-B:root"},"Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::b/*"} # If SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must ALSO allow Account B: aws kms put-key-policy ... # grant kms:Decrypt to ACCOUNT-B principal # Modern: enforce bucket-owner ownership so cross-account writes are owned by you: aws s3api put-bucket-ownership-controls --bucket b --ownership-controls Rules=[{ObjectOwnership=BucketOwnerEnforced}] Cross-account S3 sharing needs both a resource-based bucket policy allowing the other account/role and, if the data is SSE-KMS encrypted, a KMS key policy that also grants that principal kms:Decrypt — forgetting the KMS half is the most common failure. Use BucketOwnerEnforced ownership so objects written by another account are owned by the bucket owner (ACLs are disabled). For richer governance, use AWS RAM or Lake Formation. The classic cross-account gotcha: the bucket policy allows access but downloads fail with AccessDenied because the KMS key policy was not updated. Both the bucket policy AND the KMS key policy must permit the external principal. Also prefer assuming a role over root-account principals, and scope to specific prefixes.

questions.q: What is a data lake on AWS and how do the core services fit together?
questions.text: # S3 = storage layer (raw / cleaned / curated zones): s3://lake/raw/ s3://lake/processed/ s3://lake/curated/ # Glue = catalog + ETL (crawlers infer schema into the Data Catalog): aws glue start-crawler --name lake-crawler # Athena = serverless SQL over S3; Lake Formation = governance/permissions: SELECT * FROM curated.orders WHERE dt=\'2026-06-01\' -- pay per TB scanned An AWS data lake centers on S3 as cheap, durable storage organized into zones (raw, processed, curated). AWS Glue provides the Data Catalog (a metastore of table schemas) and serverless ETL; crawlers infer schemas. Athena runs serverless SQL directly over S3 (priced per data scanned), and Lake Formation centralizes fine-grained permissions. Use columnar Parquet + partitioning to cut cost and speed queries; Redshift Spectrum or EMR handle heavier analytics. Cost + performance: Athena bills per TB scanned, so store data as partitioned Parquet/ORC and only scan needed partitions/columns — this can cut query cost by 10-100x versus raw JSON/CSV. Lake Formation gives table/column/row-level access control across the lake, which raw IAM cannot easily express.

questions.q: An application reports 'AccessDenied' reading from an encrypted S3 bucket. How do you debug?
questions.text: # Check each layer that can deny: 1. Identity policy: does the role allow s3:GetObject on this bucket/prefix? 2. Bucket policy: any explicit Deny? Does it require a VPC endpoint / TLS / KMS? 3. KMS key policy: does the role have kms:Decrypt on the bucket key? aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket b ; aws kms get-key-policy --key-id k --policy-name default 4. Block Public Access / SCP / VPC endpoint policy restricting access? aws cloudtrail lookup-events ... # find the exact denying call + decode message S3 AccessDenied is a layered problem: the identity policy, the bucket policy (which may add explicit Denies for non-TLS, wrong KMS key, or non-endpoint access), the KMS key policy (for SSE-KMS data you need kms:Decrypt), and any SCP or VPC endpoint policy can each block. Work top-down, and use CloudTrail plus aws sts decode-authorization-message to see precisely which policy denied the request. For encrypted buckets, suspect KMS first: the object is readable per S3 policy but the role lacks kms:Decrypt on the key, so the download fails. An explicit Deny in the bucket policy (e.g. requiring SecureTransport or a specific endpoint) is the second usual cause. Remember: any explicit Deny anywhere overrides all Allows.

questions.q: How do you choose between RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, and ElastiCache?
questions.text: RDS — managed relational (MySQL/Postgres/etc.), Multi-AZ, read replicas Aurora — AWS cloud-native relational, 5x MySQL throughput, storage auto-grows DynamoDB — serverless key-value/document, single-digit-ms at any scale ElastiCache — in-memory (Redis/Memcached), caching + sessions + leaderboards Pick by data model and scale needs. RDS for standard relational workloads where you want a managed engine. Aurora when you want relational + higher performance, faster failover, and storage that scales automatically (and Serverless v2 for variable load). DynamoDB for massive scale, predictable low latency, and serverless ops with a key-value/document access pattern designed around your queries. ElastiCache to offload reads, store sessions, and accelerate hot data in front of a database. Access pattern drives the choice: known relational queries + joins -> RDS/Aurora. Hyper-scale with well-defined key-based access -> DynamoDB (model the table from the access patterns, not normalized like SQL). Reduce DB load / sub-ms reads -> ElastiCache in front. A common production stack is Aurora + ElastiCache + DynamoDB for different workloads.

questions.q: How does Aurora differ from standard RDS architecturally? Explain the storage layer and failover.
questions.text: # Aurora cluster: writer + up to 15 readers share ONE distributed storage volume: aws rds create-db-cluster --engine aurora-postgresql --db-cluster-identifier prod aws rds create-db-instance --db-cluster-identifier prod --db-instance-class db.r6g.large --engine aurora-postgresql # writer # Add readers (also failover targets): aws rds create-db-instance --db-cluster-identifier prod ... # reader # Cluster endpoint = writer; reader endpoint load-balances reads Standard RDS replicates by streaming to separate full copies (Multi-AZ standby, async read replicas). Aurora decouples compute from storage: a shared, distributed, auto-healing storage volume replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs, with up to 15 reader instances reading the same storage. Failover just promotes a reader (no data copy needed) so it is typically under 30 seconds, and storage grows automatically up to 128TB. Why it matters: Aurora gives faster failover (promote a reader, not rebuild), cheaper read scaling (readers share storage, no replication overhead), and continuous backup to S3. Use the reader endpoint for read scaling, the cluster endpoint for writes. Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine-grained increments for spiky workloads. Global Database extends it across regions.

questions.q: How do you scale a relational database on AWS? (read replicas, connection pooling, partitioning)
questions.text: # Read replicas to offload reads: aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica --db-instance-identifier replica1 --source-db-instance-identifier prod # RDS Proxy to pool connections (critical for Lambda/serverless): aws rds create-db-proxy --db-proxy-name prod-proxy --engine-family POSTGRESQL --auth ... --role-arn ... # Vertical scale (bigger instance) is the simplest first step Scale reads with read replicas (route SELECTs to the reader endpoint), but writes still go to one primary — so the write path scales vertically (bigger instance) until you must shard/partition the data. Connection management is a frequent bottleneck: each connection costs memory, and serverless/many-instance apps exhaust the DB. RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections, smooths failovers, and is essential when Lambda fan-out would otherwise open thousands of connections. Connection exhaustion is the classic serverless-meets-RDS failure: Lambda scales to thousands of concurrent executions, each opening a DB connection, and the database runs out. RDS Proxy fixes this by multiplexing. Caching (ElastiCache) and read replicas relieve read pressure; eventually, sharding or moving hot tables to DynamoDB addresses write scaling.

questions.q: How do you model data in DynamoDB? Explain partition keys, GSIs, and single-table design.
questions.text: # Partition key (PK) + optional sort key (SK) define the primary key: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name app --attribute-definitions AttributeName=PK,AttributeType=S AttributeName=SK,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=PK,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=SK,KeyType=RANGE --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST # Query a partition + sort range (efficient): aws dynamodb query --key-condition-expression "PK = :u AND begins_with(SK, :p)" # GSI for an alternate access pattern (different PK/SK) DynamoDB performance depends on key design. The partition key determines data distribution — choose a high-cardinality key to spread load and avoid hot partitions. The sort key enables range queries within a partition. Global Secondary Indexes provide additional access patterns with different keys. Single-table design stores multiple entity types in one table (using composite PK/SK like USER#123 / ORDER#456) so related items are co-located and retrievable in one query. Model from access patterns, not entities: unlike SQL, you design DynamoDB around the exact queries the app makes (no ad-hoc joins). List every access pattern first, then design PK/SK and GSIs to satisfy them. Avoid Scans (full table reads). Hot partitions and unbounded item collections are the main pitfalls; use write sharding for very hot keys.

questions.q: How do you handle DynamoDB capacity, throttling, and cost? (on-demand vs provisioned)
questions.text: # On-demand: pay per request, instant scaling, no capacity planning: --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST # Provisioned + auto scaling: cheaper for steady predictable load: aws dynamodb update-table --table app --billing-mode PROVISIONED --provisioned-throughput ReadCapacityUnits=100,WriteCapacityUnits=50 aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target ... # auto-scale RCU/WCU # DAX for microsecond cached reads: aws dax create-cluster --cluster-name app-dax --node-type dax.r5.large On-demand mode auto-scales per request with no planning — ideal for spiky or unknown traffic and new apps, but pricier per request at steady high volume. Provisioned mode with auto scaling is cheaper for predictable load. Throttling occurs when you exceed capacity or hit a hot partition; the SDK retries with backoff, but persistent throttling means under-provisioning or poor key distribution. DAX provides a microsecond in-memory cache for read-heavy workloads. Avoid throttling + control cost: distribute keys to prevent hot partitions, use on-demand for spiky/unpredictable and provisioned+autoscaling for steady baseline. Watch ThrottledRequests and ConsumedCapacity in CloudWatch. Use DAX for hot reads, TTL to auto-expire old items (free deletes), and reserved capacity for committed savings.

questions.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime database migration or major version upgrade on RDS/Aurora?
questions.text: # DMS for migration with ongoing replication (CDC) until cutover: aws dms create-replication-task --migration-type full-load-and-cdc --source-endpoint-arn ... --target-endpoint-arn ... # Blue/green deployment for RDS/Aurora upgrades (managed, with sync): aws rds create-blue-green-deployment --source arn:...:cluster:prod --target-engine-version 15.4 # Switch over when ready (fast, with safeguards): aws rds switchover-blue-green-deployment --blue-green-deployment-identifier bgd-xxx For engine/version upgrades, RDS/Aurora Blue/Green Deployments create a synchronized green copy at the new version, keep it replicating from blue, let you test it, then switch over in about a minute with safeguards (and blue retained for rollback). For cross-engine or cross-platform migrations, AWS DMS does a full load plus change-data-capture so the source stays live until you cut over, minimizing downtime. Minimize risk: Blue/Green for in-place version upgrades (test the green, fast reversible switchover). DMS + Schema Conversion Tool for heterogeneous migrations (e.g. Oracle -> Aurora PostgreSQL) with CDC so the app keeps writing to the source until cutover. Always rehearse the cutover, keep rollback ready, and validate data parity before switching.

questions.q: How do you secure a database on AWS? (network isolation, encryption, IAM auth, rotation)
questions.text: # Put DB in private/isolated subnets, no public access: aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --no-publicly-accessible # SG: allow only the app tier SG on the DB port: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id db-sg --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group app-sg # Encryption at rest (KMS) + in transit (TLS); IAM database auth: aws rds create-db-instance ... --storage-encrypted --kms-key-id k --enable-iam-database-authentication Layer the controls: place the database in private/isolated subnets with no public accessibility, and restrict the Security Group to allow only the application tier\'s Security Group on the DB port (not CIDR ranges). Enable encryption at rest with KMS and enforce TLS in transit. Use IAM database authentication (token-based, no static DB passwords) or Secrets Manager with automatic rotation for credentials. Best practices stack: private subnets + SG-referencing-SG (not 0.0.0.0/0) + KMS encryption + TLS enforced + IAM auth or Secrets Manager rotation + audit logging (e.g. pgAudit, enhanced monitoring) shipped to CloudWatch. Never make a production DB publicly accessible. Use RDS Proxy to also centralize Secrets-Manager-backed credentials.

questions.q: What is ElastiCache used for, and how do you design caching to avoid stampedes and staleness?
questions.text: # Redis cluster (replication + Multi-AZ failover): aws elasticache create-replication-group --replication-group-id app --engine redis --num-node-groups 3 --replicas-per-node-group 2 --automatic-failover-enabled --multi-az-enabled # Patterns: cache-aside (lazy), write-through, TTL on every key # Prevent stampede: add jitter to TTLs, use a lock/single-flight on miss ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey or Memcached) accelerates reads, stores sessions, rate-limit counters, leaderboards, and pub/sub. The common pattern is cache-aside: read from cache, on miss read the DB and populate the cache with a TTL. Guard against a cache stampede (many concurrent misses hammering the DB when a hot key expires) by adding random jitter to TTLs and using a lock or single-flight so only one request rebuilds the value. Manage staleness with appropriate TTLs or explicit invalidation on write. Production caching concerns: stampede/thundering-herd on expiry (jittered TTL + single-flight), staleness (TTL vs write-through vs invalidation trade-off), and what happens if the cache is down (the DB must absorb the load — size for it or use a circuit breaker). Use Redis cluster mode + Multi-AZ for HA, and never store the only copy of data in a cache.

questions.q: How do you monitor and tune RDS/Aurora performance? (Performance Insights, slow queries)
questions.text: # Enable Performance Insights (top SQL, wait events, load): aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --enable-performance-insights # Enhanced Monitoring (OS-level metrics) + CloudWatch: aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --monitoring-interval 60 --monitoring-role-arn arn:... # Slow query log to CloudWatch Logs: aws rds modify-db-instance --cloudwatch-logs-export-configuration EnableLogTypes=postgresql Performance Insights is the primary tool: it visualizes database load by wait event and shows the top SQL statements driving load, so you can see whether you are CPU-bound, I/O-bound, lock-bound, or waiting on a specific query. Enhanced Monitoring adds OS-level metrics (process list, memory, I/O). Export slow query logs to CloudWatch, and watch key CloudWatch metrics: CPU, FreeableMemory, Read/WriteLatency, DiskQueueDepth, and DatabaseConnections. Tuning workflow: use Performance Insights to find the top wait + top SQL, then fix at the source — add an index, rewrite the query, add a read replica or cache for read-heavy load, or scale up if genuinely resource-bound. High connections + low throughput suggests connection pooling (RDS Proxy). Lock waits point to long transactions. Always tie a CloudWatch alarm to replica lag and connection count.

questions.q: How do you achieve database high availability and disaster recovery on AWS?
questions.text: # Multi-AZ (synchronous standby, automatic failover - HA within a region): aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --multi-az # Cross-region read replica / Aurora Global Database (DR across regions): aws rds create-db-cluster --global-cluster-identifier global --source-region us-east-1 ... # Automated + manual snapshots, cross-region snapshot copy Distinguish HA from DR. HA within a region: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover (no data loss, ~60s); Aurora replicates storage across 3 AZs and promotes a reader on failure. DR across regions: cross-region read replicas or Aurora Global Database (sub-second replication, fast regional promotion) protect against a regional outage. Automated backups + cross-region snapshot copies provide point-in-time recovery. Match the mechanism to RTO/RPO: Multi-AZ for in-region HA (automatic, near-zero RPO). For regional DR, Aurora Global Database gives the lowest RTO/RPO (typically <1s lag, <1min promotion); cross-region replicas/snapshots are cheaper with higher RTO. Test failover and document the promotion runbook — automatic in-AZ, often manual cross-region.

questions.q: How does CloudWatch work? Explain metrics, alarms, dashboards, and custom metrics.
questions.text: # Alarm on a metric (e.g. high CPU) -> SNS / Auto Scaling action: aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name high-cpu --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --statistic Average --period 300 --threshold 80 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --evaluation-periods 2 --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:... # Publish a custom (business) metric: aws cloudwatch put-metric-data --namespace MyApp --metric-name OrdersPlaced --value 1 --unit Count # Composite alarm to reduce noise (alarm only if A AND B) CloudWatch collects metrics (AWS service metrics free; custom metrics you publish), evaluates alarms against thresholds over evaluation periods, and triggers actions (SNS notification, Auto Scaling, EC2 recovery). Dashboards visualize them. Custom metrics let you alarm on business/app signals (orders/sec, queue depth). Composite alarms combine conditions to cut noise, and anomaly-detection alarms learn normal bands instead of fixed thresholds. Good alerting: alert on symptoms users feel (latency, error rate, saturation) not every low-level metric; use evaluation periods and M-of-N to avoid flapping; composite alarms to reduce noise; and anomaly detection for metrics without an obvious fixed threshold. Tie alarms to runbooks. Embedded Metric Format lets you emit metrics from logs cheaply.

questions.q: How do you implement centralized logging on AWS for EC2, containers, and Lambda?
questions.text: # CloudWatch Logs is the hub; agents/drivers ship logs: EC2: CloudWatch agent -> log groups EKS: Fluent Bit DaemonSet -> CloudWatch Logs / OpenSearch Lambda: automatic -> /aws/lambda/fn log group # Query across logs with Logs Insights: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() by bin(5m) # Metric filter -> turn a log pattern into a metric + alarm Centralize on CloudWatch Logs (or stream to OpenSearch for full-text search/Kibana, or S3 for cheap retention + Athena). On EC2 use the CloudWatch agent; on EKS run Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet to ship container logs; Lambda logs automatically. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights for ad-hoc queries, metric filters to convert log patterns (e.g. count of ERROR) into alarmable metrics, and subscription filters to stream logs to other systems in real time. Make logs useful + affordable: emit structured JSON logs (queryable fields), set retention per log group (logs default to never-expire and quietly cost money), and archive to S3 for long-term/compliance with lifecycle to Glacier. Use metric filters to alert on log-derived signals, and correlate logs with traces via a request/trace ID.

questions.q: What is distributed tracing on AWS (X-Ray / OpenTelemetry) and why does it matter?
questions.text: # Instrument with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) or X-Ray SDK: # Each request gets a trace ID propagated across services -> a service map: API GW -> Lambda -> DynamoDB / RDS, with timing on each hop # Enable X-Ray on Lambda: aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name api --tracing-config Mode=Active Distributed tracing follows a single request as it traverses multiple services, attaching a trace ID and recording timing at each hop. X-Ray (and the vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry via ADOT) builds a service map and breaks down latency per segment, so in a microservices/serverless system you can see exactly which downstream call is slow or failing — something logs and per-service metrics alone cannot show. Why it matters: in distributed systems, \'the API is slow\' is useless without knowing which of ten services caused it. Tracing localizes the slow/failing hop, reveals fan-out and N+1 calls, and ties together logs/metrics by trace ID (the three pillars of observability). Prefer OpenTelemetry (ADOT) for portability across vendors. Sample to control cost while keeping error/slow traces.

questions.q: How do you define and monitor SLOs, SLIs, and error budgets on AWS?
questions.text: # SLI: a measured signal (e.g. % of requests < 300ms AND 2xx/3xx) # SLO: the target (e.g. 99.9% over 30 days). Error budget = 0.1% = ~43m/month # Compute from ALB/CloudWatch metrics or Application Signals: good = sum(2xx+3xx under latency); total = sum(all); availability = good/total # CloudWatch Application Signals can track SLOs natively now SLIs are the measured indicators users care about (availability, latency, error rate); an SLO is the target for an SLI over a window (e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed under 300ms over 30 days); the error budget is the allowed failure (100% minus the SLO). On AWS, derive SLIs from ALB/CloudWatch metrics or X-Ray, alert on budget burn rate (fast burn = page now, slow burn = ticket), and use the budget to balance reliability work against feature velocity. Alert on burn rate, not raw thresholds: multi-window burn-rate alerts (e.g. 2% of budget in 1h) catch real user impact while ignoring harmless blips, reducing pager fatigue. The error budget creates a shared, objective rule: if the budget is spent, prioritize reliability over features. CloudWatch Application Signals can now track service SLOs directly.

questions.q: How do you monitor and observe an EKS cluster end to end?
questions.text: # Managed Prometheus + Grafana, or Container Insights: aws amp create-workspace --alias prod # Amazon Managed Prometheus # Container Insights (CloudWatch) for cluster/pod metrics + logs: aws eks ... + CloudWatch agent / ADOT collector as a DaemonSet # Key signals: node CPU/mem, pod restarts, pending pods, HPA, control-plane logs aws eks update-cluster-config --name prod --logging \'{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator"],"enabled":true}]}\' Cover all layers: control plane (enable EKS control-plane logging — api/audit/authenticator to CloudWatch), nodes (CPU/memory/disk, NotReady), and workloads (pod restarts/CrashLoopBackOff, pending pods, HPA behavior, container CPU/memory vs limits). Use Amazon Managed Prometheus + Managed Grafana (or CloudWatch Container Insights) for metrics, Fluent Bit for logs, and ADOT/X-Ray for traces. kube-state-metrics and node-exporter feed the standard dashboards/alerts. EKS-specific alerts that matter: pods Pending (out of IPs or node capacity), CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled containers (limits too low), nodes NotReady, HPA at max replicas, and PersistentVolume issues. Enable audit logging for security/forensics. Container Insights gives a fast managed start; Managed Prometheus/Grafana gives the full Kubernetes-native experience.

questions.q: What is EventBridge and how do you use it for event-driven architecture and automation?
questions.text: # Rule matching AWS or custom events -> targets (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions...): aws events put-rule --name ec2-stop --event-pattern \'{"source":["aws.ec2"],"detail-type":["EC2 Instance State-change Notification"],"detail":{"state":["stopped"]}}\' aws events put-targets --rule ec2-stop --targets Id=1,Arn=arn:aws:lambda:... # Scheduler for cron-like jobs; custom event bus for app events EventBridge is a serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, SaaS partners, and your own apps to targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, etc.) based on content-filtering rules. It powers two big patterns: operational automation (react to AWS events — auto-remediate, tag, notify) and application event-driven architecture (decouple microservices via a custom event bus). EventBridge Scheduler replaces cron for scheduled invocations with retries and dead-letter support. EventBridge vs SNS/SQS: use EventBridge when you need rich content-based routing, many AWS/SaaS sources, schema registry, and fan-out to many target types; SNS for simple pub/sub fan-out; SQS for buffered point-to-point work queues. Add a DLQ to rules so unmatched/failed deliveries are not lost, and use the schema registry to keep producers/consumers in sync.

questions.q: How do you do automated remediation and self-healing on AWS?
questions.text: # EC2 auto-recovery alarm (recover impaired instance): aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name recover --metric-name StatusCheckFailed_System --namespace AWS/EC2 --alarm-actions arn:aws:automate:us-east-1:ec2:recover ... # GuardDuty finding -> EventBridge -> Lambda/SSM Automation (isolate, snapshot): aws ssm start-automation-execution --document-name AWS-StopEC2Instance ... # Config rule + auto-remediation (e.g. re-enable encryption / fix SG): aws configservice put-remediation-configurations ... Self-healing combines detection with automated action. Built-in: ASG replaces unhealthy instances, EC2 alarm-based auto-recovery, ECS/EKS restart failed tasks/pods. Event-driven: GuardDuty/Config/CloudWatch -> EventBridge -> Lambda or SSM Automation documents to remediate (isolate a compromised instance, revert an open Security Group, re-enable encryption, restart a service). AWS Config rules can auto-remediate drift from desired state. Guardrails for automation: make remediations idempotent and safe, log every action (CloudTrail/SSM), and add a human-approval step for destructive actions. Common wins: auto-close public Security Groups, auto-tag untagged resources, auto-recover impaired instances, and quarantine GuardDuty-flagged instances. Start with notify-only, then promote trusted remediations to automatic.

questions.q: How do you debug a latency spike in a production AWS application?
questions.text: # 1. Confirm + localize with the service map (X-Ray/traces): which segment got slow? API GW? a downstream service? the DB? # 2. ALB/Target metrics: TargetResponseTime, 5xx, RejectedConnectionCount # 3. Resource saturation: CPU, memory, DB connections, queue depth # 4. DB: Performance Insights top SQL + waits; replica lag # 5. Correlate with recent deploys/config changes/traffic Work outside-in. Confirm user impact (ALB TargetResponseTime/p99, error rate), then use traces to localize which hop slowed down — front end, a specific microservice, or the database. Check saturation on that component (CPU, memory, connection pool, queue depth, Lambda concurrency/throttles). For DB-driven spikes, Performance Insights shows the top SQL and wait events. Always ask \'what changed?\' — most spikes follow a deploy, config change, or traffic surge. Common AWS latency causes: a slow/locking DB query or replica lag, connection-pool exhaustion (add RDS Proxy), Lambda cold starts or concurrency throttling, an undersized/over-scaled tier, a NAT or DNS bottleneck, or a downstream third-party call. Tracing + Performance Insights together usually pinpoint it fast. Mitigate first (scale out, roll back), then root-cause.

questions.q: How do you set up effective alerting that avoids both missed incidents and pager fatigue?
questions.text: # Alert on symptoms (SLO/golden signals), route by severity: Page: user-facing SLO burn (high error rate, latency breach) Ticket: slow-burn budget, capacity trending, non-urgent # Reduce noise: composite alarms, anomaly detection, M-of-N evaluation aws cloudwatch put-composite-alarm --alarm-rule "ALARM(errors) AND ALARM(latency)" # SNS -> on-call tool (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with escalation Effective alerting pages humans only for things that need immediate action and affect users. Alert on symptoms (the four golden signals / SLO burn rate), not every underlying metric. Tier by severity: page for fast SLO burn, ticket for slow burn or capacity warnings, dashboard for the rest. Cut noise with composite alarms (require multiple conditions), anomaly detection, and M-of-N evaluation periods to avoid flapping. Every page should map to a runbook. The balance: too-sensitive alerts cause pager fatigue (people ignore real ones); too-loose miss incidents. Use multi-window burn-rate alerts so you page on genuine user impact and ticket on slow degradation. Continuously prune alerts that never lead to action, and review every page in retro: was it actionable? If not, fix or delete it.

questions.q: How does ECS networking work? Explain awsvpc mode, task vs service, and ECS vs EKS trade-offs.
questions.text: # awsvpc mode — each task gets its own ENI + private IP + security group: "networkMode": "awsvpc" # task-level isolation, SGs per task (recommended) # bridge/host modes = older, share the host network (port conflicts) # Task definition (the blueprint) vs Service (keeps N tasks running): aws ecs register-task-definition --cli-input-json file://task.json aws ecs create-service --cluster prod --task-definition app:3 \\ --desired-count 4 --load-balancers targetGroupArn=tg-arn,containerName=app,containerPort=8080 A task definition is the immutable blueprint (image, CPU/memory, env, IAM task role); a task is a running instance of it; a service maintains a desired count, registers with a load balancer, and replaces failed tasks. In awsvpc mode each task gets its own ENI, private IP, and security group — first-class VPC networking and per-task SG isolation (the recommended mode, required on Fargate). ECS vs EKS : ECS is AWS-native, simpler, no control-plane to learn, deeply integrated; EKS gives portable Kubernetes and its ecosystem at the cost of operational complexity. Interview tip: Distinguish the three nouns clearly (task def = blueprint, task = running copy, service = desired-count manager + LB). Recommend awsvpc mode for per-task SGs and clean IP-per-task (and note it consumes ENIs, which has density limits). On ECS vs EKS, the mature take: ECS if you\'re all-in on AWS and want simplicity; EKS if you need Kubernetes portability/ecosystem/skills. Mention the IAM task role (per-

questions.q: How do you autoscale on EKS? Compare Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter, and HPA/KEDA.
questions.text: # HPA — scale PODS on metrics: kubectl autoscale deployment api --cpu-percent=60 --min=3 --max=20 # Cluster Autoscaler — scale NODES via ASGs (node-group bound): # adds nodes when pods are Pending; tied to predefined node groups # Karpenter — provisions right-sized nodes directly, fast, no node groups: kubectl apply -f nodepool.yaml # picks instance types/Spot to fit pending pods # KEDA — event-driven pod scaling (SQS depth, Kafka lag, scale-to-zero): kubectl apply -f scaledobject.yaml Two dimensions: scale pods and scale nodes . HPA scales pod replicas on CPU/memory/custom metrics; KEDA extends that to event sources (queue depth, Kafka lag) and enables scale-to-zero. For nodes, Cluster Autoscaler adds/removes nodes within predefined ASG node groups when pods can\'t schedule. Karpenter is the modern replacement: it provisions right-sized nodes directly from the EC2 fleet (choosing instance types and Spot) to exactly fit pending pods, scales faster, and consolidates underutilized nodes — better bin-packing and cost. Interview tip: Separate pod scaling (HPA/KEDA) from node scaling (Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter) — interviewers test whether you conflate them. The current best-practice pairing is HPA/KEDA + Karpenter : Karpenter\'s just-in-time right-sized provisioning and consolidation beat Cluster Autoscaler\'s fixed node groups on speed and cost. KEDA\'s scale-to-zero and queue-based scaling is the answer for spiky event workloads.

questions.q: How do you secure containers on AWS? Cover image scanning, task roles, and runtime security.
questions.text: # Scan images in ECR (on push) — block deploys on criticals: aws ecr put-image-scanning-configuration --repository-name app --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true aws ecr start-image-scan --repository-name app --image-id imageTag=v1 # enhanced = Inspector # Least-privilege per pod/task (not the node): eksctl create iamserviceaccount ... # IRSA / EKS Pod Identity # Pod hardening: non-root, read-only rootfs, drop caps, seccomp: securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } } Defense in depth across the lifecycle: scan images in ECR (scan-on-push, or Inspector enhanced scanning) and fail builds on critical CVEs; use minimal/distroless base images. Give each pod/task its own IAM role (IRSA/Pod Identity, ECS task role) so a compromised container has minimal blast radius — never the node role. Harden the runtime: non-root user, read-only root filesystem, drop all Linux capabilities, NoNewPrivileges , seccomp/AppArmor profiles. Enforce policy with admission controllers (OPA/Kyverno) and detect at runtime with GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring or Falco. Restrict node IMDS (hop-limit) so pods can\'t steal node creds. Interview tip: Hit the lifecycle: build (scan + distroless), deploy (admission policy, per-pod IAM, hardened securityContext), runtime (GuardDuty EKS/Falco). The two highest-value AWS-specific points: per-pod IAM (IRSA/Pod Identity, not the node role) to contain blast radius, an

questions.q: How does ECR work, and what's a good image strategy (tagging, lifecycle, multi-arch)?
questions.text: # Auth + push: aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com # Immutable tags so a tag can never be overwritten (supply-chain safety): aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --repository-name app --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE # Lifecycle policy to expire old/untagged images (cost + clutter): aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name app --lifecycle-policy-text file://lifecycle.json # Multi-arch (amd64 + arm64/Graviton) with buildx: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t REPO:v1 --push . ECR is the managed private registry, IAM-controlled and KMS-encrypted, with scan-on-push and cross-region/cross-account replication. A solid strategy: immutable tags (a deployed tag can never change underneath you — pin to the digest for true reproducibility), tag with the git SHA (not just latest ), lifecycle policies to expire untagged/old images so storage and risk don\'t pile up, and multi-arch manifests so the same tag runs on x86 and Graviton (arm64) for cost/perf. Replicate to other regions for DR and pull-latency. Interview tip: The standout practices: immutable tags + deploy by digest (kills the \'latest moved under me\' and tag-overwrite supply-chain risks), git-SHA tags for traceability, and lifecycle policies to control cost/clutter. Multi-arch images for Graviton savings is a current cost-optimization signal. Mention scan-on-push and cross-region replication for DR. Avoid latest in production deploy

questions.q: What is a service mesh on EKS (App Mesh / Istio), and when is it worth the complexity?
questions.text: # A mesh adds a sidecar proxy (Envoy) per pod to handle service-to-service traffic: - mTLS between services (encryption + identity) without app changes - traffic shaping: canary/weighted routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking - observability: per-call metrics/traces at the proxy # Lighter alternatives before a full mesh: - VPC Lattice (AWS-native service-to-service connectivity/auth) - Cilium/eBPF for mTLS + network policy without sidecars A service mesh injects a sidecar proxy alongside each pod and moves cross-service concerns out of application code: mTLS (mutual auth + encryption), fine-grained traffic management (weighted/canary routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection), and uniform observability (golden-signal metrics and traces per hop). It\'s worth it when you have many services, need zero-trust mTLS everywhere, or want advanced rollout/resilience controls centrally. It\'s not worth it for a handful of services — the operational complexity, latency, and resource overhead of sidecars outweigh the benefit. Interview tip: Show judgment, not enthusiasm: a mesh\'s value (mTLS, canary routing, retries/circuit-breaking, per-hop telemetry) scales with the number of services, but sidecars add latency, memory, and a steep operational learning curve. For small fleets, native retries + ALB + IAM/TLS suffice. Mention sidecar-less options (Cilium eBPF, Ambient mesh, AWS VPC Lattice) as the modern trend reducing that overhead. \'Don\'t add a mesh for 5 ser

questions.q: How do you handle persistent storage and stateful workloads in containers on AWS?
questions.text: # EBS CSI — block storage, single-AZ, ReadWriteOnce (one node): storageClassName: ebs-sc # great for databases needing low-latency block I/O # EFS CSI — shared NFS, multi-AZ, ReadWriteMany (many pods): storageClassName: efs-sc # shared files across pods/AZs (slower than EBS) # StatefulSet gives stable identity + per-pod PVC: kubectl apply -f statefulset.yaml # stable network id + own volume per replica Containers are ephemeral, so persistent state lives on volumes via CSI drivers. EBS CSI attaches block volumes (ReadWriteOnce, AZ-bound, low latency) — ideal for databases, but a pod with an EBS volume is pinned to that volume\'s AZ. EFS CSI provides shared NFS (ReadWriteMany, multi-AZ) for content many pods read/write, at higher latency. Use StatefulSets for stable pod identity and per-replica PVCs. The pragmatic AWS answer, though, is often to not self-host state in the cluster: use managed RDS/DynamoDB/ElastiCache/S3 and keep the cluster stateless — far less operational risk than running databases on Kubernetes. Interview tip: Map access modes to drivers: EBS = RWO/single-AZ/fast (databases, pinned to an AZ — a scheduling gotcha), EFS = RWX/multi-AZ/shared (slower). StatefulSets for stable identity + PVC-per-pod. The senior judgment call interviewers want: prefer managed data services (RDS/DynamoDB/S3) over stateful workloads in-cluster — keep Kubernetes stateless when you can; reach for in-cluster state only when there\'s a real reason.

questions.q: How do you do zero-downtime deployments and safe rollbacks for containers on AWS?
questions.text: # Kubernetes rolling update with surge/unavailable controls + probes: strategy: { rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 } } readinessProbe: ... # don\'t send traffic until the pod is actually ready kubectl rollout status deploy/api; kubectl rollout undo deploy/api # instant rollback # ECS rolling or blue/green via CodeDeploy: deploymentConfiguration: { minimumHealthyPercent: 100, maximumPercent: 200 } # CodeDeploy canary shifts 10% then the rest, auto-rollback on alarms Zero-downtime relies on health-gated gradual replacement. In Kubernetes, a rolling update with maxUnavailable:0 + readiness probes ensures new pods receive traffic only when ready and old pods drain (preStop + terminationGracePeriodSeconds ). For richer safety, blue/green (deploy a parallel version, switch the service/target group, roll back by switching back) or canary (shift a small % first, watch metrics, then proceed). ECS does the same via rolling config or CodeDeploy blue/green with canary traffic shifting and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms. Interview tip: The mechanics that matter: readiness probes (gate traffic), maxUnavailable:0 /surge (always enough healthy capacity), and graceful shutdown (preStop + grace period to drain in-flight requests). Then escalate to canary/blue-green with automatic rollback on alarms — the senior point is that rollback should be automatic and metric-driven, not a human noticing. ECS+CodeDeploy and Argo Rollouts/Flagger are good names to drop.

questions.q: An EKS pod is stuck in Pending / CrashLoopBackOff / ImagePullBackOff. How do you debug each?
questions.text: kubectl describe pod # Events at the bottom are the #1 clue # Pending -> no node fits: resources, taints, AZ/volume affinity, no capacity kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp; kubectl top nodes # CrashLoopBackOff -> container starts then exits; read its logs: kubectl logs --previous # logs from the crashed instance # ImagePullBackOff -> registry/auth/tag issue: # wrong tag, ECR perms on the node/pod role, or cross-account/region pull Always start with kubectl describe pod — the Events list usually names the cause. Pending = scheduler can\'t place it: insufficient CPU/memory (check requests vs kubectl top nodes ), taints without tolerations, node selectors/affinity, or an EBS volume pinning the pod to an AZ with no capacity (then Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter should add a node — if not, check IAM/limits). CrashLoopBackOff = the container keeps exiting: read logs --previous , check the command/args, missing config/secrets, failing liveness probe, or OOMKilled (check limits in describe ). ImagePullBackOff = can\'t pull the image: wrong tag/digest, ECR permissions on the node/pod IAM role, or wrong region/account. Interview tip: Give a crisp per-state playbook anchored on describe pod Events.
