Map causes: Pending=scheduling (resources/taints/affinity/AZ-volume/capacity), CrashLoop=app exit (logs --previous, config/secrets, OOMKilled, bad probe), ImagePull=registry/auth/tag. The AWS-specific gotchas that score: ECR pull permissions via the pod/node IAM role, and EBS volumes p

questions.q: Explain the AWS cost levers: Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances vs Spot, and how to choose.
questions.text: On-Demand -> no commitment, full price (baseline / unpredictable) Reserved Inst -> 1-3yr commit to a specific family/region, up to ~72% off Savings Plans -> 1-3yr commit to a $/hr spend, more flexible: Compute SP -> any region/family/Lambda/Fargate (most flexible, ~66%) EC2 SP -> locked to a family in a region (bigger discount) Spot -> spare capacity, up to ~90% off, interruptible Match commitment to predictability. Cover your steady baseline with Savings Plans (Compute SP is the modern default — applies across EC2 families/regions, Fargate, and Lambda, so you don\'t over-commit to one shape) or RIs where you want the deepest discount on a fixed family. Run fault-tolerant/burst capacity on Spot (up to 90% off, handle interruptions). Leave truly unpredictable or short-lived workloads on On-Demand . The strategy: right-size first, then layer commitments on the stable floor and Spot on the variable top. Interview tip: The framework is baseline vs burst: Savings Plans/RIs on the predictable floor, Spot on the elastic peak, On-Demand for the unpredictable middle. Recommend Compute Savings Plans over standard RIs for flexibility (covers Fargate/Lambda, no family lock-in) unless a deep family-specific RI fits. Critical caveat: right-size before committing — a 3-year RI on an oversized instance locks in waste. Mention coverage/utilization reports to avoid under/over-committing.

questions.q: How do you find and eliminate wasted AWS spend? Walk through a cost-optimization audit.
questions.text: # Cost Explorer: group by service/tag, find the top movers + anomalies: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --granularity MONTHLY --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE ... # Compute Optimizer: right-sizing recommendations from real utilization: aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations # Common waste to hunt: - idle/oversized EC2 + RDS; unattached EBS volumes + old snapshots - unassociated Elastic IPs; idle NAT Gateways; orphaned load balancers - S3 with no lifecycle policy; over-provisioned gp2; dev running 24/7 A systematic audit: (1) Visibility — Cost Explorer grouped by service and by tag to see where money goes and catch anomalies; enforce cost-allocation tags. (2) Right-size — Compute Optimizer/Cost Explorer recommendations to shrink over-provisioned EC2/RDS/EBS based on actual utilization. (3) Eliminate waste — delete unattached EBS, old snapshots, idle NAT Gateways/EIPs/LBs, and add S3 lifecycle rules to tier/expire data. (4) Schedule — stop non-prod outside business hours. (5) Commit — Savings Plans on the right-sized baseline + Spot for burst. (6) Architect — Graviton, serverless for spiky loads, reduce cross-AZ/NAT data transfer. Interview tip: Show an ordered method: visibility (tagging + Cost Explorer) -> right-size (Compute Optimizer) -> kill waste (unattached EBS, idle NAT/EIP/LB, snapshots, no-lifecycle S3) -> schedule non-prod -> commit (SP/Spot) -> architect (Graviton, serverless, cut data-transfer). The order matters — right-size before committing. Namin

questions.q: Why is data transfer so expensive on AWS, and how do you minimize it?
questions.text: # The expensive flows (often surprising on the bill): Internet egress -> data OUT to internet is charged (in is free) Cross-AZ -> traffic between AZs charged BOTH directions ($0.01/GB each way) NAT Gateway -> per-GB data processing on TOP of egress Cross-Region -> most expensive inter-region # Cheaper paths: - VPC Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB = FREE (avoid NAT + egress) - CloudFront for internet egress (cheaper + cached); keep traffic same-AZ Data transfer is metered along many edges and adds up silently. Internet egress is charged per GB (ingress is free). Cross-AZ traffic is charged in both directions — chatty multi-AZ services (or a load balancer routing across AZs to backends) can rack up real cost. NAT Gateway charges a per-GB processing fee on top of egress, so routing S3/package traffic through NAT is doubly wasteful. To minimize: use VPC Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB (free, bypasses NAT and egress), Interface Endpoints/PrivateLink to keep traffic private, CloudFront for cheaper cached internet egress, keep chatty traffic within an AZ, and compress/batch. Interview tip: The points that reveal real bill experience: cross-AZ is charged both ways (chatty cross-AZ chatter + the NAT data-processing fee are top hidden costs), and S3/DynamoDB Gateway Endpoints are free and remove both NAT processing and egress for that traffic — a frequent quick win. CloudFront for egress, AZ-affinity for chatty services, and PrivateLink to avoid NAT round-trips round it out. \'Ingre

questions.q: How do you optimize S3 storage costs? Explain storage classes, lifecycle, and Intelligent-Tiering.
questions.text: # Storage classes by access pattern: Standard -> frequent access Standard-IA / One Zone-IA -> infrequent (lower storage, retrieval fee) Glacier Instant / Flexible / Deep Archive -> archive (cheapest, slower retrieval) Intelligent-Tiering -> auto-moves objects between tiers by access (no retrieval fees) # Lifecycle policy: transition + expire automatically: aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket b --lifecycle-configuration file://lc.json Match the storage class to the access pattern: Standard for hot data, Standard-IA for infrequent (cheaper storage, per-GB retrieval fee), Glacier tiers for archives (cheapest, retrieval latency from instant to hours), One Zone-IA for reproducible data you can afford to lose with an AZ. Lifecycle policies automate transitions (e.g. logs: Standard -> IA at 30d -> Glacier at 90d -> expire at 365d) and clean up incomplete multipart uploads and old versions. When access patterns are unpredictable , Intelligent-Tiering auto-moves objects between frequent/infrequent/archive tiers with no retrieval fees (small monitoring charge) — set-and-forget. Interview tip: Lead with \'class to access pattern + lifecycle to automate\'. The most-tested judgment: use Intelligent-Tiering when access is unpredictable (it avoids the IA/Glacier retrieval-fee surprise by moving data automatically), and use explicit lifecycle transitions when you know the pattern (logs aging out). Don\'t forget cleanup rules (incomplete multipart uploads, old noncurrent ver

questions.q: What is FinOps, and how do you build cost accountability across engineering teams?
questions.text: # Foundation: consistent cost-allocation tags (enforced, not optional): tags: { team: payments, env: prod, service: checkout, cost-center: 4021 } # Enforce tags at creation with SCP / Config / tag policies: aws organizations create-policy --type TAG_POLICY ... # Show teams their spend + alert on anomalies: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --group-by Type=TAG,Key=team ... # per-team chargeback aws ce create-anomaly-monitor ... # automatic spend-spike detection aws budgets create-budget ... # per-team budgets + alerts FinOps is the practice of bringing financial accountability to cloud spend — making engineering, finance, and product share ownership of cost as a first-class metric. The mechanics: enforce cost-allocation tags (team/service/env/cost-center) so spend can be attributed; use multi-account structure so accounts map to teams/environments; give each team visibility into their own cost (dashboards, showback/chargeback); set budgets and anomaly alerts ; and bake cost into engineering decisions (architecture reviews, CI cost estimates with Infracost). The cultural shift — engineers see and own their bill — drives more savings than any single tool. Interview tip: Frame FinOps as culture + accountability, not just \'turn on Cost Explorer\'. The enablers: enforced tagging (via tag policies/SCP/Config — un-enforced tags are useless), per-team showback/chargeback so cost is visible to the people who create it, budgets + anomaly detection, and account-per-team isolation. questions.q: How do you reduce RDS and database costs without hurting performance?
questions.text: # Right-size from real metrics (CPU, connections, IOPS, memory): aws compute-optimizer get-rds-database-recommendations # Commit to baseline with Reserved Instances (DBs are steady -> good RI fit): aws rds purchase-reserved-db-instances-offering --reserved-db-instances-offering-id ... # Offload reads to replicas (smaller primary); cache hot reads: # ElastiCache in front of RDS; Aurora Serverless v2 for variable load # gp3 storage instead of provisioned IOPS where possible; stop non-prod DBs Databases are usually steady-state, so they\'re strong Reserved Instance candidates once right-sized. Reduce the instance you need by right-sizing from real utilization (Compute Optimizer), offloading reads to read replicas and a cache (ElastiCache) so the primary can be smaller, and choosing gp3 storage instead of pricey provisioned IOPS unless you genuinely need it. For variable/intermittent load, Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity to demand (and scales non-prod down). Stop or downsize non-prod databases off-hours, tier old data to cheaper storage or archive, and watch backup/snapshot and cross-AZ replication costs. Interview tip: The ordered play: right-size (real metrics) -> reduce load (replicas + cache so the primary shrinks) -> commit (RIs on the steady baseline) -> storage (gp3 vs provisioned IOPS) -> non-prod scheduling/serverless. The insight that impresses: a cache/read-replica lets you run a smaller primary, compounding savings, and Aurora Serverless v2 fits spiky/dev workloa

questions.q: How do Graviton (arm64) and serverless change the cost equation? When do they pay off?
questions.text: # Graviton: ~20-40% better price/performance, broadly supported: instance types: t4g, m7g, c7g, r7g; RDS/ElastiCache/Lambda all support arm64 # Build multi-arch so the same image runs on x86 and arm64: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t REPO:v1 . # Serverless: pay-per-use beats always-on for spiky/low-duty workloads: # Lambda/Fargate: no idle cost; but steady high load -> reserved EC2 cheaper Graviton (AWS arm64 CPUs) typically delivers 20-40% better price/performance for general workloads (web servers, microservices, caches, many databases) and is supported across EC2, Lambda, Fargate, RDS, and ElastiCache — often a near-free win once you build multi-arch images and validate your dependencies on arm64. Serverless (Lambda/Fargate) eliminates idle cost: it\'s cheapest for spiky, event-driven, or low-duty-cycle workloads where you\'d otherwise pay for idle servers. But for steady, high-utilization workloads, a committed/reserved EC2 or container fleet is cheaper than per-invocation pricing — run the breakeven math. Interview tip: Two distinct levers. Graviton is the low-risk, high-ROI move (build multi-arch, test arm64 compatibility, switch — 20-40% off across many services). Serverless is workload-shape-dependent: a win for spiky/intermittent (no idle pay), a loss for steady high throughput (do the cost-per-hour breakeven vs reserved compute). The mature answer rejects \'serverless is always cheaper\' and frames both as utilization-driven decision

questions.q: How do you forecast spend, set budgets, and catch cost anomalies before they blow up?
questions.text: # Budgets with threshold alerts (and optional actions): aws budgets create-budget --budget file://budget.json # alert at 80%/100%/forecasted # Cost Anomaly Detection — ML baseline, alerts on unusual spikes: aws ce create-anomaly-monitor --anomaly-monitor file://monitor.json aws ce create-anomaly-subscription ... # email/SNS when anomalies exceed $threshold # Forecast from trend: aws ce get-cost-forecast --metric UNBLENDED_COST --granularity MONTHLY --time-period ... Proactive cost control combines forecasting, guardrails, and detection. AWS Budgets set spend (or usage/RI-coverage) thresholds per account/team/tag with alerts at actual and forecasted percentages — and can trigger actions (e.g. apply a restrictive policy). Cost Anomaly Detection builds an ML baseline of normal spend per service/account and alerts on unusual spikes (a misconfigured job, a leaked key spinning up instances, a runaway data-transfer) before the monthly bill reveals it. Cost forecasts project the trend so you see overruns coming. Combine with per-team budgets and tag-based attribution so alerts reach the team that owns the spend. Interview tip: The key distinction: Budgets = threshold guardrails you define (including forecasted-to-exceed alerts and budget actions), Anomaly Detection = ML catching the unexpected (a spike you didn\'t set a threshold for — like a compromised key launching crypto-mining or a runaway pipeline). Routing alerts to the owning team via tags closes the loop. \'Catch it in days,

questions.q: Explain the AWS native CI/CD stack (CodePipeline, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy). When use it vs GitHub Actions?
questions.text: # CodePipeline orchestrates stages; CodeBuild builds; CodeDeploy deploys: Source (CodeCommit/GitHub) -> Build (CodeBuild) -> Test -> Deploy (CodeDeploy/ECS/CFN) # CodeBuild spec: buildspec.yml: phases: { build: { commands: [ "docker build -t $REPO:$TAG ." ] } } # CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS with automatic rollback on alarm: appspec: { Resources: [...], Hooks: { BeforeAllowTraffic: lambda-validate } } The native stack: CodePipeline orchestrates the stages, CodeBuild runs builds/tests in managed containers (buildspec.yml), and CodeDeploy handles deployment strategies (in-place, blue/green, canary) with hooks and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms. It\'s fully IAM-integrated, runs inside your account/VPC, and needs no third-party credentials. GitHub Actions (or GitLab CI) is often preferred for developer experience, marketplace ecosystem, and keeping CI next to the code — authenticating to AWS via OIDC (no stored keys). Many teams use Actions for build/test and CodeDeploy for the AWS-side deployment, or go fully GitHub-native. Interview tip: Know what each piece does and give a balanced \'when\': native stack shines for tight IAM/VPC integration, compliance (everything in-account), and AWS-managed deploys (CodeDeploy blue/green + alarm rollback); GitHub Actions wins on DX, ecosystem, and being where the code lives (use OIDC to auth, no static keys). The pragmatic answer is often hybrid. Mentioning CodeDeploy\'s automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms shows deployment-safe

questions.q: What is Infrastructure as Code on AWS? Compare CloudFormation, CDK, and Terraform.
questions.text: # CloudFormation — AWS-native declarative YAML/JSON, managed state (stacks): aws cloudformation deploy --template-file tpl.yaml --stack-name prod --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM # CDK — write infra in TypeScript/Python; synthesizes to CloudFormation: cdk deploy # real programming language, loops/abstractions, AWS-native state # Terraform — multi-cloud HCL, external state, huge provider ecosystem: terraform plan; terraform apply # state in S3 + DynamoDB lock CloudFormation is AWS-native declarative IaC with state managed by AWS (stacks, change sets, drift detection, automatic rollback) — no state file to babysit, but AWS-only and verbose. CDK lets you author in a real language (TypeScript/Python) with loops and reusable constructs, then synthesizes to CloudFormation — great developer ergonomics, still AWS-native state. Terraform uses HCL, manages its own state (typically S3 + DynamoDB lock), and supports many providers — the choice for multi-cloud or when you want one tool across AWS/GCP/Azure/SaaS. All enable versioned, reviewable, repeatable infra. Interview tip: Decide by ecosystem + state model: AWS-only and want managed state/no state file -> CloudFormation (or CDK for nicer authoring); multi-cloud or richest provider ecosystem and comfortable owning remote state -> Terraform. The key technical contrast is state : CFN manages it for you; Terraform makes you manage it (S3 backend + DynamoDB locking — and protect/encrypt it). CDK = imperative authoring, declarative CFN undern

questions.q: How do you manage Terraform state safely for a team (remote state, locking, drift)?
questions.text: # Remote backend: S3 for state + DynamoDB for locking (prevents concurrent apply): terraform { backend "s3" { bucket="tf-state" key="prod/terraform.tfstate" region="us-east-1" dynamodb_table="tf-locks" encrypt=true } } # Detect drift (real infra vs state): terraform plan -detailed-exitcode # exit 2 = drift detected # Isolate blast radius: separate state per environment/component (workspaces or dirs) Team-safe Terraform centers on the state file . Store it remotely (S3, encrypted, versioned) so everyone shares one source of truth, and use a lock (DynamoDB table) so two applies can\'t run simultaneously and corrupt state. Separate state per environment and per component (small blast radius — a network change can\'t accidentally affect the database stack), via directories or workspaces. Run plan in CI on PRs for review and apply only after merge (gated, with OIDC auth). Detect drift with scheduled plan -detailed-exitcode and never edit resources in the console (it desyncs state). Interview tip: The non-negotiables: remote encrypted/versioned state (S3) + locking (DynamoDB) — explain why locking matters (concurrent applies corrupt state). Then blast-radius isolation (state per env/component), PR-gated plan/apply in CI with OIDC, and drift detection. The cardinal rule to state out loud: no manual console changes — they cause drift and the next apply may revert or conflict. Mention terraform import for adopting existing resources and protecting state secrets.

questions.q: What is GitOps, and how do you implement it on EKS with ArgoCD or Flux?
questions.text: # Git is the single source of truth; a controller reconciles cluster -> Git: # ArgoCD watches a repo and syncs manifests into the cluster: argocd app create api --repo https://git/infra --path k8s/prod \\ --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc --sync-policy automated --self-heal # Deploy = merge a PR that changes the image tag; ArgoCD applies it. # Drift: if someone kubectl-edits live, self-heal reverts to Git. GitOps makes Git the single source of truth for cluster state: you describe the desired state declaratively in a repo, and an in-cluster controller ( ArgoCD or Flux ) continuously reconciles the live cluster to match Git. Deployments become Git operations (merge a PR bumping an image tag), giving you review, audit, and one-command rollback ( git revert ). The controller pulls from Git (no CI system needs cluster credentials), and self-heal reverts any manual kubectl drift back to the declared state. It separates CI (build/test/push image, update manifest) from CD (the controller syncs). Interview tip: The defining ideas: Git as source of truth + continuous reconciliation + pull-based (cluster pulls from Git, so no external CI holds kube creds — a security win over push pipelines). Benefits: auditable history, easy rollback (revert the commit), and automatic drift correction (self-heal). Clarify the CI/CD split: CI builds and updates the manifest/tag in Git; the GitOps controller (Argo/Flux) does the actual deploy. Mention app-of-apps and progressive delivery (Arg

questions.q: How do you build a secure software supply chain (signing, SBOM, scanning) in a pipeline?
questions.text: # Scan dependencies + image in CI; fail on criticals: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH $REPO:$TAG # Generate an SBOM (software bill of materials): syft $REPO:$TAG -o spdx-json > sbom.json # Sign the image (keyless) so deploys can verify provenance: cosign sign $REPO@$DIGEST; cosign verify $REPO@$DIGEST # Admission control: only run signed images from trusted registries A secure supply chain protects everything from source to running container. In the pipeline: scan dependencies and the built image (Trivy/Grype, ECR scanning, Inspector) and fail on critical CVEs; generate an SBOM (Syft) so you know exactly what shipped and can answer \'are we affected by CVE-X?\' instantly. Sign images (cosign/Sigstore) and verify signatures at deploy time with an admission controller (Kyverno/OPA) so only signed, provenance-verified images from trusted registries run. Pin dependencies and base-image digests, use OIDC (no static CI keys), and aim toward SLSA provenance attestations for build integrity. Interview tip: Cover the stages: scan (deps + image, gate on severity), SBOM (Syft — the \'what\'s in it\' artifact that makes the next CVE a 5-minute query), sign + verify (cosign + admission control so unsigned/untrusted images can\'t deploy), and provenance (SLSA attestations). Tie it to real incidents (Log4Shell, SolarWinds, xz) to show why it matters. The standout point is verifying signatures at admission, not just signing — signing without enforcement is theater.

questions.q: How do you implement progressive delivery (canary, feature flags, automated rollback)?
questions.text: # Canary: shift a small % of traffic, watch metrics, then proceed or abort: # Argo Rollouts / Flagger automate the analysis + rollback: steps: [ {setWeight: 10}, {pause: {duration: 5m}}, {analysis: success-rate}, {setWeight: 50} ] # Analysis queries Prometheus/CloudWatch; auto-rollback if error rate/latency breach: metric: error-rate # Feature flags decouple deploy from release (LaunchDarkly / AppConfig): aws appconfig start-deployment ... # flip features without redeploying Progressive delivery reduces deployment risk by rolling out gradually and automating the safety checks. A canary shifts a small traffic slice to the new version, runs automated analysis against real metrics (error rate, latency, saturation from Prometheus/CloudWatch), and only proceeds if healthy — otherwise it auto-rolls-back . Tools like Argo Rollouts and Flagger orchestrate this on Kubernetes. Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, AWS AppConfig) decouple deploy from release : ship code dark, then enable it for a cohort/percentage at runtime (and kill-switch it instantly) without a redeploy. Interview tip: The core insight: rollback should be automatic and metric-driven , not a human paging at 3am — canary + automated analysis (Argo Rollouts/Flagger querying SLO metrics) gives that. The second is decoupling deploy from release via feature flags (ship dark, enable progressively, instant kill-switch), which also enables A/B tests and limits blast radius. Define the metrics that gate promotion (error rate, p99 late

questions.q: How do you design pipelines for multiple environments and safe production promotion?
questions.text: # Promote the SAME artifact through environments (build once): build -> push image (immutable digest) -> deploy dev -> test -> staging -> prod # Config differs per env, NOT the artifact (12-factor): # env-specific values via Parameter Store / Secrets Manager / Helm values # Prod gated by approval + checks: CodePipeline manual approval action / GitHub environment protection rules The cardinal rule: build once, promote the same immutable artifact (by digest) through dev -> staging -> prod — never rebuild per environment (that defeats the purpose of testing). Environment differences live in configuration (Parameter Store/Secrets Manager, Helm values), not in the artifact, following 12-factor. Each environment mirrors prod as closely as practical. Production promotion is gated : required passing tests/scans, manual approval (CodePipeline approval action / GitHub environment protection), and ideally automated canary analysis. Account-per-environment isolates blast radius, with the pipeline assuming a cross-account deploy role via OIDC/STS. Interview tip: The principle interviewers want stated explicitly: build once, promote the same artifact — rebuilding for prod means you tested something different. Config (not code) varies by env. Then production guardrails: gated approvals, required checks, canary, and account-per-env isolation with cross-account assume-role (OIDC, no static keys). Mention staging parity with prod and that secrets/config come from Parameter Store/Secrets Manage

questions.q: A deployment succeeded but the app is broken in production. How do you respond and prevent recurrence?
questions.text: # 1. Roll back FIRST (restore service), diagnose after: kubectl rollout undo deploy/api # or shift traffic to blue / revert the GitOps commit # 2. Confirm recovery via the same metrics that detected the break: # error rate, p99 latency, saturation back to baseline? # 3. Diagnose on the failed version (logs, traces, config diff, what changed): kubectl logs ...; compare config/env between good and bad releases Treat it as an incident: mitigate before root-causing . Roll back immediately to the last known-good version (Kubernetes rollout undo , blue/green traffic switch back, or git revert in GitOps) — restoring service beats finding the cause in the moment. Verify recovery with the metrics that flagged the issue. Then diagnose the failed release: logs/traces, the config/env diff between good and bad, the migration or dependency that changed. Prevent recurrence : the deploy \'succeeded\' but broke prod means your health checks were too shallow — add real readiness/health validation, smoke tests post-deploy, canary with metric-based auto-rollback, and a blameless postmortem producing the specific guardrail (test/alarm/check) that would have caught it. Interview tip: Lead with roll back first, diagnose second (mitigate over investigate). The deeper insight interviewers reward: a \'successful\' deploy that broke prod is a validation gap — your pipeline checked \'pods started\' not \'app works.\' Fix it with deeper health checks, post-deploy smoke tests, and canary + automated metri

questions.q: Users report intermittent 5xx errors from an app behind an ALB. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: # Distinguish WHO is erroring — ALB vs target — via ALB metrics + logs: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count -> the ALB itself (no healthy targets, timeouts) HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count -> the app returned 5xx # Enable + query ALB access logs (per-request detail): # fields: elb_status_code, target_status_code, target_processing_time, target:port # Check target health + the usual intermittent causes: aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn tg-arn First localize the 5xx: ALB CloudWatch metrics separate ELB 5xx (the load balancer — e.g. 502 from a target connection reset, 503 no healthy targets, 504 target timeout) from Target 5xx (the app actually returned an error). Enable ALB access logs and inspect elb_status_code vs target_status_code and target_processing_time per request. For intermittent errors, suspect: some targets failing health checks (flapping in/out), idle-timeout mismatches (app keep-alive shorter than ALB\'s 60s -> 502s), connection/thread pool exhaustion under load, a slow dependency causing 504s, or one bad instance in the pool. Correlate error timestamps with target health, deploys, and traffic spikes. Interview tip: The first move that signals competence: split ELB 5xx vs Target 5xx (CloudWatch + access logs) — they point at completely different layers. Know the ALB code meanings: 502 = bad/reset target connection (classic keep-alive/idle-timeout mismatch — set the app\'s keep-alive higher than the ALB), 503 = no healthy targets, 504 = target too slow. \'Intermit

questions.q: An EC2 instance can't reach the internet (or a service can't be reached). How do you debug connectivity?
questions.text: # Walk the VPC path systematically: 1. Security Group -> allows the traffic (outbound + the inbound on target)? 2. NACL -> subnet allows BOTH directions (stateless, ephemeral ports)? 3. Route table -> 0.0.0.0/0 -> IGW (public) or NAT (private)? right target? 4. Public IP / NAT -> public subnet needs a public IP; private needs NAT GW # Confirm with VPC Reachability Analyzer + Flow Logs: aws ec2 create-network-insights-path ...; aws ec2 start-network-insights-analysis ... Walk the VPC layers in order. Security Group (stateful, per-ENI) — does it allow the traffic? NACL (stateless, per-subnet) — does it allow both directions, including the ephemeral return ports (the classic stateless trap)? Route table — is there a default route to an Internet Gateway (public subnet) or NAT Gateway (private subnet)? Does the instance have a public IP (public path) or is NAT correctly placed (private path)? Then DNS (can it resolve?) and the target\'s own SG. VPC Reachability Analyzer tests the path declaratively and tells you exactly which hop blocks it; VPC Flow Logs show ACCEPT/REJECT per flow to confirm where packets die. Interview tip: Recite the ordered VPC checklist: SG -> NACL (both directions + ephemeral ports!) -> route table (IGW vs NAT) -> public IP/NAT placement -> DNS -> target SG. The two highest-yield gotchas: the stateless NACL ephemeral-return-port trap, and a private subnet missing a NAT route (or NAT in the wrong subnet). Naming Reachability Analyzer (pinpoints the blocking h

questions.q: RDS is slow or hitting high CPU/connections. How do you diagnose and stabilize it?
questions.text: # Performance Insights: find the top SQL + wait events (the fastest path): # shows DB load by waits (CPU, IO, lock) and the worst queries # Enhanced Monitoring + CloudWatch: CPU, FreeableMemory, Read/WriteIOPS, connections: DatabaseConnections near max_connections -> connection exhaustion # Inspect slow queries + plans: EXPLAIN ANALYZE the-query; # missing index? full scan? bad plan? # Stabilize: add read replica, RDS Proxy (pool conns), scale, add index Use Performance Insights first — it visualizes DB load by wait event and surfaces the top SQL, immediately telling you whether you\'re CPU-bound, I/O-bound, or lock-bound and which queries are responsible. Pair with CloudWatch/Enhanced Monitoring (CPU, freeable memory, IOPS/burst-credit exhaustion, DatabaseConnections vs max_connections ). Common causes: a missing index causing full scans (confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE ), connection exhaustion (too many short-lived connections from many app instances/Lambdas), a runaway query, or undersized storage IOPS. Stabilize by killing the offending query, adding the index, offloading reads to a read replica , pooling connections with RDS Proxy (especially for Lambda), and scaling the instance/storage. Interview tip: Go to Performance Insights first (top SQL + wait-event breakdown is the fastest root-cause). Then the AWS-specific stabilizers that impress: RDS Proxy for connection-pool exhaustion (the canonical Lambda-hammering-RDS fix), read replicas to offload reads, and watching for st

questions.q: How do you debug latency in a distributed AWS application using X-Ray and CloudWatch?
questions.text: # X-Ray distributed tracing: see the full request path + per-segment time: # service map shows which hop (ALB -> service -> DynamoDB -> downstream) is slow # instrument with the X-Ray SDK / ADOT (OpenTelemetry) -> traces to X-Ray # CloudWatch: correlate with metrics + use ServiceLens to unify traces/metrics/logs: # p50/p99 latency per service, then drill into the slow trace # CloudWatch Logs Insights to query structured logs by request id: fields @timestamp, duration | filter requestId="abc" | sort duration desc In distributed systems, aggregate latency hides where the time goes — use distributed tracing . X-Ray (or OpenTelemetry via ADOT) stitches a request across services into one trace with per-segment timing and a service map , so you can see which hop (the database call, a downstream API, a cold-started Lambda) owns the latency. Correlate with CloudWatch percentile metrics (watch p99 , not averages — averages hide tail latency) and ServiceLens to jump from a latency spike to the offending traces and logs. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query structured logs by request/trace ID for the full story of a slow request. Interview tip: The core principle: distributed latency needs tracing , not just metrics — X-Ray/OTel localizes the slow hop via the service map and per-segment timing. The metric-literacy point that lands: look at p99/p99.9 , not averages (tail latency is what users feel and averages mask). Tie it together with ServiceLens (traces+metrics+logs) and structured

questions.q: Your monthly AWS bill spiked unexpectedly. How do you find the cause fast?
questions.text: # Cost Explorer: group by SERVICE, then by USAGE_TYPE + REGION to isolate: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --granularity DAILY \\ --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE # Find WHEN it started (daily granularity) and WHICH account/tag (group by tag): # Check Cost Anomaly Detection findings for the flagged root cause # Common spikes: data transfer, NAT, forgotten big instances, runaway Lambda/logs, leaked credentials launching instances (check CloudTrail + GuardDuty) Move from coarse to fine in Cost Explorer : group by service to find which service jumped, switch to daily granularity to pin when it started, then group by usage type , region , and tag/account to isolate the exact driver. Check Cost Anomaly Detection — it often already identifies the root cause. Frequent culprits: a surge in data transfer (cross-AZ/egress) or NAT Gateway processing, a forgotten large/GPU instance or oversized RDS, runaway Lambda invocations or CloudWatch Logs ingestion, an un-lifecycled S3 bucket, or — critically — leaked credentials spinning up instances for crypto-mining (correlate with CloudTrail RunInstances and GuardDuty findings). Interview tip: Show the drill-down method: service -> daily (when) -> usage type/region/tag (what + who). Lean on Cost Anomaly Detection for an instant lead. The two answers that stand out: the sneaky-but-common drivers (data transfer/NAT, logs ingestion, forgotten instances) and treating a sudden compute spike as a possible security inciden

questions.q: An AWS service is returning throttling/RateExceeded errors. How do you handle and prevent it?
questions.text: # Symptoms: ThrottlingException, RateExceeded, ProvisionedThroughputExceeded, 429/503 # Handle: retry with EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF + JITTER (SDKs do this by default): retry: base * 2^attempt + random_jitter # never tight-loop retries (makes it worse) # DynamoDB: switch to on-demand or raise provisioned capacity / fix hot partition: # Lambda: raise reserved concurrency or the account concurrency limit # API-level: request a service quota increase (Service Quotas console) Throttling means you exceeded a rate limit — either an API request quota or a resource throughput limit . Handle it gracefully with exponential backoff + jitter (the AWS SDKs do this automatically — don\'t tight-loop retries, which amplify the problem and can cause retry storms). Then address the root cause by service: DynamoDB — switch to on-demand capacity, raise provisioned RCU/WCU, or fix a hot partition (poor partition-key design concentrating load); Lambda — reserved/account concurrency limits; Kinesis — shard count; general APIs — request a Service Quotas increase. Smooth bursty producers with a queue (SQS) so you process at a sustainable rate, and cache to cut call volume. Interview tip: First answer is always exponential backoff with jitter (and that SDKs do it — naive fixed retries cause retry storms). Then root-cause by service: the standout is DynamoDB hot partitions (bad partition key -> one partition throttles while capacity looks fine overall) and the on-demand-vs-provisioned trade-off. Mention buff

questions.q: How do you investigate a security incident in AWS (compromised credentials or instance)?
questions.text: # 1. Detect/scope via the audit trail: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=Username,AttributeValue=the-key # GuardDuty findings often flag it first (unusual API calls, crypto-mining, recon) # 2. Contain — revoke the credential / isolate the instance: aws iam delete-access-key / update-access-key --status Inactive # kill the key # attach a deny-all SG, isolate the instance (don\'t terminate -> preserve evidence) # 3. Eradicate + recover: rotate ALL secrets, rebuild from clean AMI/IaC Run the IR loop with AWS tooling. Detect/scope : GuardDuty usually surfaces it (anomalous API calls, mining, credential use from a new geo); CloudTrail is the authoritative audit log to trace exactly what the compromised principal did and when. Contain without destroying evidence: disable/delete the exposed access keys or detach the role policy, and for a compromised instance attach an isolation security group (deny all) and snapshot it for forensics — don\'t terminate (you\'d lose volatile evidence). Eradicate/recover : rotate all potentially exposed secrets, revoke active STS sessions, rebuild the instance from a known-good AMI/IaC (don\'t \'clean\' it), and remove any persistence the attacker added (new IAM users/keys, backdoor roles). Then close the entry vector (the leaked key, the SSRF, the public bucket) and post-mortem. Interview tip: Map the IR phases to AWS services: GuardDuty (detect) + CloudTrail (scope — what did they do) -> contain (disable keys, isolate ins

questions.q: How do you build effective observability on AWS (metrics, logs, traces, alarms, SLOs)?
questions.text: # Three pillars, unified: Metrics -> CloudWatch (+ custom/EMF), Container Insights, Prometheus/AMP Logs -> CloudWatch Logs + Logs Insights (structured JSON), centralized Traces -> X-Ray / ADOT (OpenTelemetry) -> ServiceLens ties all three # Alarm on SYMPTOMS (SLOs), not just causes; use composite alarms to cut noise: aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --metric-name p99Latency ... # alert on user-facing pain Good observability combines the three pillars and ties them together. Metrics (CloudWatch, EMF for custom, Container Insights for EKS/ECS, or Prometheus/AMP) for the numbers; structured logs (JSON to CloudWatch Logs, queried with Logs Insights, centralized across accounts) for detail; traces (X-Ray or OpenTelemetry via ADOT) for request flow — unified in ServiceLens so you pivot from a metric spike to the traces and logs behind it. Alert on symptoms/SLOs (user-facing: error rate, p99 latency, availability — the golden signals) rather than every cause, use composite alarms to reduce noise, and define SLOs/error budgets so alerting and release decisions are driven by user impact, not vanity metrics. Propagate a trace/correlation ID through everything. Interview tip: Name the three pillars and how to unify them (ServiceLens / OpenTelemetry-ADOT), then the maturity points: alert on symptoms (SLOs/golden signals), not causes — page on user-facing pain (p99 latency, error rate), not CPU at 80%; use composite alarms to fight alert fatigue; and define SLOs + error budgets to make ale

questions.q: What are IAM permissions boundaries, and how are they different from SCPs and session policies?
questions.text: A permissions boundary is a managed policy that sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can ever have. Effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary. SCPs do the same at account level and session policies at session level. aws iam put-role-permissions-boundary --role-name dev-role --permissions-boundary arn:aws:iam::123456789012:policy/DevBoundary aws iam get-role --role-name dev-role --query 'Role.PermissionsBoundary' Interview tip: The classic use is delegated administration: let teams create roles, but only roles that carry the boundary.

questions.q: Why use IAM Identity Center (SSO) instead of IAM users for people, and how do permission sets work?
questions.text: Identity Center gives people short-lived credentials via your identity provider, one login across accounts, and central assignment. A permission set is a template that is turned into an IAM role in each assigned account. aws configure sso aws sso login --profile prod-admin aws sts get-caller-identity --profile prod-admin Interview tip: Say that long-lived IAM user access keys for humans are the first thing a security review flags.

questions.q: How do you use IAM Access Analyzer to reach least privilege?
questions.text: Access Analyzer finds resources shared outside your zone of trust, flags unused access and permissions, and can generate a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity. Policy validation catches errors before deploy. aws accessanalyzer list-findings --analyzer-arn <arn> --filter '{"status":{"eq":["ACTIVE"]}}' aws accessanalyzer start-policy-generation --policy-generation-details principalArn=<role-arn> aws accessanalyzer validate-policy --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY --policy-document file://p.json Interview tip: Start broad in dev, then tighten using generated policies from real usage, rather than guessing in advance.

questions.q: Gateway versus interface VPC endpoints: what is the difference and when do you use each?
questions.text: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, are free, and work through route table entries. Interface endpoints use PrivateLink, create ENIs with private IPs in your subnets, cost per hour and per GB, and support many services. aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-1 --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 --route-table-ids rtb-1 aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.ecr.api --subnet-ids subnet-1 --security-group-ids sg-1 Interview tip: Adding an S3 gateway endpoint is the quickest cut to NAT Gateway data charges.

questions.q: Site-to-Site VPN versus Direct Connect: how do you choose and design for resilience?
questions.text: VPN is quick to set up, encrypted over the internet, and limited to about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel with variable latency. Direct Connect is a private dedicated link with consistent latency and higher bandwidth, but takes weeks and is not encrypted by default. aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections --query 'VpnConnections[].VgwTelemetry' aws directconnect describe-virtual-interfaces Interview tip: The usual answer: Direct Connect as primary, VPN as backup, and MACsec or VPN over Direct Connect if encryption is required.

questions.q: How does Route 53 Resolver work for hybrid DNS between AWS and on-premises?
questions.text: The VPC resolver at the base of the VPC CIDR plus 2 answers queries. Inbound endpoints let on-prem DNS query AWS private zones. Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send chosen domains to on-prem DNS servers. aws route53resolver create-resolver-endpoint --direction INBOUND --security-group-ids sg-1 --ip-addresses SubnetId=subnet-1 SubnetId=subnet-2 aws route53resolver create-resolver-rule --rule-type FORWARD --domain-name corp.example.com --target-ips Ip=10.1.0.2 Interview tip: Put at least two IPs in different zones on each endpoint and share forwarding rules through AWS RAM.

questions.q: What are EC2 placement groups, and when would you use cluster, spread or partition?
questions.text: Cluster packs instances close together in one zone for low latency and high throughput. Spread puts each instance on distinct hardware, up to 7 per zone. Partition groups instances into racks that do not share hardware, for large distributed systems. aws ec2 create-placement-group --group-name hpc --strategy cluster aws ec2 run-instances --placement GroupName=hpc --instance-type c6in.32xlarge --count 4 --image-id <ami> Interview tip: Cluster groups can fail with insufficient capacity, so launch all instances at once and use a single instance type.

questions.q: When does Lambda cost more than containers, and how do you decide between them?
questions.text: Lambda charges per request and per GB-second, so it is cheap for spiky or idle workloads and expensive for steady high-volume traffic. Containers on Fargate or EC2 are cheaper at constant utilisation, but you manage scaling and idle capacity. aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name api --query '[MemorySize,Timeout]' aws compute-optimizer get-lambda-function-recommendations Interview tip: Do a break-even calculation with real request rate, duration and memory rather than choosing by fashion.

questions.q: How do Auto Scaling warm pools and instance refresh help with deployments and scale-out speed?
questions.text: A warm pool keeps pre-initialised stopped or running instances ready, so scale-out skips long boot and bootstrap time. Instance refresh replaces instances in an ASG gradually when the launch template or AMI changes, with a minimum healthy percentage. aws autoscaling put-warm-pool --auto-scaling-group-name web --pool-state Stopped --min-size 2 aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name web --preferences '{"MinHealthyPercentage":90,"InstanceWarmup":120}' Interview tip: Use lifecycle hooks so warm instances finish their setup before they enter service.

questions.q: Managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Fargate and Karpenter on EKS: how do you choose?
questions.text: Managed node groups automate provisioning and rolling updates of EC2 workers. Self-managed gives full control over the AMI and bootstrap. Fargate runs each pod in its own microVM with no nodes to manage. Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes on demand. aws eks create-nodegroup --cluster-name prod --nodegroup-name ng-1 --subnets subnet-1 subnet-2 --node-role <arn> aws eks describe-nodegroup --cluster-name prod --nodegroup-name ng-1 --query 'nodegroup.updateConfig' Interview tip: A common production answer is managed node groups or Karpenter for general workloads, plus Fargate for small isolated jobs.

questions.q: EKS Pod Identity versus IRSA: how do they give pods AWS permissions, and which is better?
questions.text: IRSA uses the cluster's OIDC provider and a service account annotation, with a trust policy per cluster. EKS Pod Identity uses an agent and an association between a service account and a role, with one reusable trust policy and no OIDC setup per cluster. aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name prod --namespace app --service-account web --role-arn <arn> kubectl annotate sa web eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=<arn> # IRSA Interview tip: Mention that both avoid node-wide instance profile permissions, which every pod on the node would share.

questions.q: How do ECS task definitions, services and task roles fit together, and what is the difference between the execution role and the task role?
questions.text: A task definition describes containers, CPU, memory and roles. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running behind a load balancer. The execution role lets ECS pull images and write logs; the task role is what your application code uses to call AWS APIs. aws ecs register-task-definition --cli-input-json file://td.json aws ecs update-service --cluster prod --service web --task-definition web:42 --force-new-deployment aws ecs describe-services --cluster prod --services web --query 'services[0].events[:5]' Interview tip: Mixing the two roles up is the most common ECS permissions bug in interviews and in production.

questions.q: Compare EBS gp3, io2 and st1 volumes, and explain how snapshots work.
questions.text: gp3 is general-purpose SSD with baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s that you can raise independently. io2 provides provisioned, high-durability IOPS for databases. st1 is throughput-optimised HDD for large sequential workloads. Snapshots are incremental and stored in S3. aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-1 --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 --throughput 250 aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-1 --description nightly aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-1 Interview tip: Moving gp2 to gp3 online is a free cost and performance win, which interviewers like to hear.

questions.q: What are S3 presigned URLs, and how do you use them securely for uploads and downloads?
questions.text: A presigned URL embeds temporary credentials and a signature so a client can GET or PUT one object without AWS credentials. It inherits the permissions of whoever signed it and expires after the time you set. aws s3 presign s3://bucket/report.pdf --expires-in 300 python -c "import boto3; print(boto3.client('s3').generate_presigned_url('put_object', Params={'Bucket':'b','Key':'k'}, ExpiresIn=300))" Interview tip: Keep expiry short, pin the key and content type, and remember the URL is a bearer token: anyone who has it can use it.

questions.q: EFS performance and throughput modes: how do you pick and avoid surprises?
questions.text: EFS is elastic NFS storage. Throughput modes are Elastic, Provisioned and Bursting; performance mode is General Purpose for almost all workloads. Metadata-heavy small-file patterns and cross-AZ mounts are the usual sources of slowness. aws efs describe-file-systems --query 'FileSystems[].[FileSystemId,ThroughputMode,PerformanceMode]' aws efs update-file-system --file-system-id fs-1 --throughput-mode elastic mount -t efs -o tls,iam fs-1:/ /mnt/efs Interview tip: Mount using the mount target in the same availability zone as the client to avoid cross-AZ latency and charges.

questions.q: RDS Multi-AZ versus read replicas: what does each give you, and do they replace each other?
questions.text: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby for high availability and automatic failover, and you cannot read from the classic standby. Read replicas use asynchronous replication to scale reads and can be cross-region. They solve different problems. aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --multi-az --apply-immediately aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica --db-instance-identifier prod-ro1 --source-db-instance-identifier prod aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --force-failover Interview tip: Add that replica lag means reads can be stale, so read-your-own-writes paths must use the primary.

questions.q: How do DynamoDB Streams and TTL work, and what are they used for?
questions.text: Streams capture an ordered 24-hour log of item changes, which Lambda or Kinesis consumers can process. TTL deletes expired items for free in the background, within a day or two of expiry, and the deletions also appear in the stream. aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name sessions --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt aws dynamodb update-table --table-name orders --stream-specification StreamEnabled=true,StreamViewType=NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES Interview tip: TTL is not exact: expired items can stay readable, so filter on the timestamp in queries.

questions.q: What does RDS Proxy do, and when is it worth using?
questions.text: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, reduces failover time by holding connections, and can use IAM auth with Secrets Manager credentials. It is most useful with Lambda or apps that open many short connections. aws rds create-db-proxy --db-proxy-name app-proxy --engine-family POSTGRESQL --auth AuthScheme=SECRETS,SecretArn=<arn> --role-arn <arn> --vpc-subnet-ids subnet-1 subnet-2 aws rds describe-db-proxy-targets --db-proxy-name app-proxy Interview tip: Watch for session pinning, because pinned connections cannot be shared and reduce the benefit.

questions.q: How do you use CloudWatch Logs Insights to investigate an incident quickly?
questions.text: Logs Insights runs a purpose-built query language over log groups. You filter, parse fields, aggregate and chart. Structured JSON logs make fields queryable immediately, so you can find error spikes, top offenders and slow requests in seconds. fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() by bin(5m) filter status >= 500 | stats count() as c by path | sort c desc | limit 10 fields @timestamp, duration | stats pct(duration, 99) by bin(1m) Interview tip: Query cost is per GB scanned, so narrow the time range and log groups first.

questions.q: What does CloudWatch Container Insights give you for ECS and EKS, and what are its limits?
questions.text: Container Insights collects cluster, node, pod and task level CPU, memory, network and storage metrics and performance logs, with prebuilt dashboards. It is easy to enable but can be expensive at scale and is less flexible than Prometheus. aws eks create-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name amazon-cloudwatch-observability aws ecs update-cluster-settings --cluster prod --settings name=containerInsights,value=enhanced Interview tip: Point out the cost lever: metrics and logs are charged per metric and per GB, so review which are enabled.

questions.q: What are CloudWatch composite alarms and anomaly detection, and how do they cut alert noise?
questions.text: A composite alarm combines other alarms with AND, OR and NOT rules so you page only when several symptoms agree. Anomaly detection learns the normal band for a metric, accounting for time-of-day patterns, and alarms outside that band. aws cloudwatch put-composite-alarm --alarm-name checkout-down --alarm-rule "ALARM(high-5xx) AND ALARM(low-orders)" aws cloudwatch put-anomaly-detector --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name RequestCount --stat Sum Interview tip: Alert on user-facing symptoms and use the cause alarms as suppressed inputs or dashboards.

questions.q: Compute Savings Plans versus EC2 Instance Savings Plans versus Reserved Instances: how do you choose and avoid over-commitment?
questions.text: Compute Savings Plans commit to a dollar-per-hour spend and apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda in any region and family. EC2 Instance plans give a deeper discount for one family in one region. Reserved Instances are tied to specific instance attributes. aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP --term-in-years ONE_YEAR --payment-option NO_UPFRONT --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS aws ce get-savings-plans-coverage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 Interview tip: Commit to your stable baseline, around 60 to 70 percent, never to peak usage.

questions.q: How do you use Compute Optimizer and rightsizing recommendations without hurting performance?
questions.text: Compute Optimizer analyses CloudWatch utilisation, usually 14 days, and recommends smaller or different instance types, EBS volumes, Lambda memory and ECS on Fargate sizes. Validate against peak, memory metrics and business cycles before acting. aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations --query 'instanceRecommendations[].[instanceArn,finding,recommendationOptions[0].instanceType]' aws compute-optimizer put-recommendation-preferences --resource-type Ec2Instance --enhanced-infrastructure-metrics Active Interview tip: Memory is not collected by default, so install the CloudWatch agent or the recommendation misses the key signal.

questions.q: How do you design a tagging strategy that really supports cost allocation?
questions.text: Define a small mandatory set such as owner, team, environment, cost-center and application. Activate them as cost allocation tags, enforce with tag policies, SCPs and IaC checks, and handle untaggable spend with account structure and shared-cost rules. aws organizations create-policy --type TAG_POLICY --name std-tags --content file://tags.json aws ce list-cost-allocation-tags --status Inactive aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=team --query 'ResourceTagMappingList[].ResourceARN' Interview tip: Tags only apply from activation onward, so activate early. Tag policies check values but do not stop untagged resources by themselves.

questions.q: How do you let GitHub Actions or another CI system deploy to AWS without static access keys?
questions.text: Use OpenID Connect federation. Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for the CI issuer, then a role whose trust policy allows web identity from that provider with conditions on repository and branch. The job exchanges its token for temporary credentials. aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity --role-arn <arn> --role-session-name ci --web-identity-token $TOKEN Interview tip: Always constrain the sub claim to a specific repo and branch or environment. A trust policy that accepts any repository is a real vulnerability.

questions.q: How do ECS blue/green deployments with CodeDeploy work?
questions.text: CodeDeploy launches a new task set behind a second target group, shifts the ALB listener traffic all at once, linearly or as a canary, runs lifecycle hook tests, and can roll back automatically on alarms. The old task set is kept briefly for fast rollback. aws deploy create-deployment --application-name web --deployment-group-name prod --revision file://appspec.json aws deploy get-deployment --deployment-id d-ABC123 --query 'deploymentInfo.status' Interview tip: Use a test listener port and a BeforeAllowTraffic hook to smoke test before real users see the new version.

questions.q: A Lambda function in a VPC times out when calling RDS or an external API. How do you debug it?
questions.text: Check the function's subnets, security groups and routes. Reaching RDS needs a security group rule from the function to the database port. Reaching the internet needs a NAT Gateway, since Lambda in a VPC has no public IP. Also check the timeout and connection reuse. aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name f --query 'VpcConfig' aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-1 aws logs tail /aws/lambda/f --follow Interview tip: Timeouts, rather than refusals, usually mean a dropped packet: missing route, security group or NACL.

questions.q: An ALB target group shows targets as unhealthy. How do you find out why?
questions.text: Read the health check reason code, then verify the path, port and success codes match what the app serves, the security group allows the ALB to reach the target, the app is listening, and timeouts and thresholds are realistic. aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn> aws elbv2 describe-target-groups --target-group-arns <arn> --query 'TargetGroups[0].[HealthCheckPath,HealthCheckPort,Matcher]' curl -v http://<target-ip>:8080/health Interview tip: The reason field, such as Target.Timeout or Target.ResponseCodeMismatch, tells you which layer to look at.

questions.q: New EKS worker nodes launch but never join the cluster. What do you check?
questions.text: Verify the node IAM role is mapped through an access entry or aws-auth, the bootstrap script and cluster name are correct, the node can reach the API endpoint and required AWS endpoints, security groups allow control plane traffic, and the CNI and kubelet start. aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name prod kubectl get cm aws-auth -n kube-system -o yaml sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50 aws ec2 get-console-output --instance-id i-1 Interview tip: Check the console output or system log first. Bootstrap errors usually appear there in plain text.

questions.q: A pod using IRSA gets 'WebIdentityErr' or AccessDenied from STS. What is wrong?
questions.text:
Check that the service account annotation and the pod's token projection exist, the OIDC provider is registered in IAM, and the role trust policy's sub and aud conditions exactly match the namespace and service account name. kubectl get pod

-o yaml | grep -E 'AWS_ROLE_ARN|AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE' aws iam get-role --role-name app --query 'Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument' aws eks describe-cluster --name prod --query 'cluster.identity.oidc.issuer' Interview tip: The pod must be restarted after annotating the service account, because the token is injected at pod creation.

questions.q: An EC2 instance fails a system or instance status check. What do you do?
questions.text: System check failure points to AWS hardware or host, so stop and start the instance to move it to new hardware. Instance check failure points to the OS: boot problems, full disk, kernel panic, or bad network config. Use console output and screenshot, or attach the volume to a rescue instance. aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids i-1 aws ec2 get-console-output --instance-id i-1 --latest aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-1 && aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-1 Interview tip: Remember reboot keeps the host, but stop then start usually migrates the instance. Instance store data is lost on stop.

questions.q: A VPC peering connection is active but instances cannot reach each other. What do you check?
questions.text: Both VPCs need route table entries pointing the other CIDR to the peering connection, security groups and NACLs must allow the traffic, CIDRs must not overlap, and peering is not transitive. DNS resolution across peering must be enabled if you use private names. aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --query 'VpcPeeringConnections[].[VpcPeeringConnectionId,Status.Code]' aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=route.vpc-peering-connection-id,Values=pcx-1 aws ec2 modify-vpc-peering-connection-options --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-1 --requester-peering-connection-options AllowDnsResolutionFromRemoteVpc=true Interview tip: Reachability Analyzer shows exactly which hop blocks the path.

questions.q: Private hosted zone names resolve in one VPC but not another. How do you fix it?
questions.text: A private hosted zone only answers queries from VPCs associated with it. Associate the other VPC, which for cross-account VPCs needs an authorization and association call, and make sure enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames are on. aws route53 list-hosted-zones-by-vpc --vpc-id vpc-2 --vpc-region eu-west-1 aws route53 associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone --hosted-zone-id Z123 --vpc VPCRegion=eu-west-1,VPCId=vpc-2 aws ec2 describe-vpc-attribute --vpc-id vpc-2 --attribute enableDnsSupport Interview tip: For cross-account, first run create-vpc-association-authorization in the zone's account, then associate from the VPC's account.

questions.q: A CloudFormation stack is stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. How do you recover?
questions.text: Find the resource that failed to roll back in the stack events, fix the cause such as a manually changed or deleted resource, then use ContinueUpdateRollback, optionally skipping the stuck resources. Afterwards, address drift and retry the update. aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name app --query 'StackEvents[?contains(ResourceStatus, `FAILED`)].[LogicalResourceId,ResourceStatusReason]' aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name app --resources-to-skip MyBucket aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name app Interview tip: Skipping a resource leaves it out of sync, so you must reconcile it manually afterwards.

questions.q: An ECS deployment keeps failing and rolling back because new tasks fail health checks. How do you get to the cause?
questions.text: Look at the service events and stopped task reasons, then the container logs and exit code. Common causes are a wrong container port or health check path, missing secrets or environment, a slow startup that needs a grace period, and insufficient memory. aws ecs describe-services --cluster prod --services web --query 'services[0].events[:10]' aws ecs describe-tasks --cluster prod --tasks <arn> --query 'tasks[0].[stoppedReason,containers[0].exitCode]' aws logs tail /ecs/web --since 15m Interview tip: Set healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds for slow-starting apps so the load balancer does not kill them during startup.

questions.q: The root EBS volume is almost full on a production instance. How do you expand it without downtime?
questions.text: Modify the volume size online, then grow the partition and filesystem inside the OS, with growpart and resize2fs or xfs_growfs. You can modify once every six hours per volume. Take a snapshot first, and find what filled the disk. aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-1 --size 200 lsblk; sudo growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1 sudo xfs_growfs -d / # or: sudo resize2fs /dev/nvme0n1p1 du -xh / --max-depth=2 | sort -h | tail Interview tip: Check inodes with df -i as well. A disk can be full of tiny files while showing free space.

questions.q: Important objects were deleted from an S3 bucket. How do you recover them, and how do you prevent a repeat?
questions.text: If versioning was on, the delete only added a delete marker, so remove the marker or copy the earlier version back. Without versioning, check replication targets, backups, or AWS Backup. Prevent with versioning, MFA delete, Object Lock and restrictive policies. aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket b --prefix path/ aws s3api delete-object --bucket b --key path/file --version-id <delete-marker-id> aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket b --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled Interview tip: Deleting a specific version is permanent, so only users who truly need it should have s3:DeleteObjectVersion.

questions.q: After an RDS Multi-AZ failover, the application kept failing for several minutes. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.text: The endpoint DNS changes to the new primary, but apps cache DNS or hold dead connections. Use short DNS TTL honoured by the runtime, connection validation and retry with backoff, pool limits, and RDS Proxy to shield clients. aws rds describe-events --source-identifier prod --source-type db-instance --duration 120 dig +short prod.abc.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod --force-failover Interview tip: Test failover on purpose in staging. It is the only way to know your connection handling works.

questions.q: A DynamoDB table is throttling even though consumed capacity is below the provisioned limit. What is happening?
questions.text: A hot partition. Traffic concentrated on a few partition keys exceeds the per-partition limits, about 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads per second. Fix the key design with higher-cardinality keys, write sharding, caching, or on-demand mode, and check for hot GSIs. aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/DynamoDB --metric-name WriteThrottleEvents --dimensions Name=TableName,Value=orders --start-time 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z --period 300 --statistics Sum aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name orders Interview tip: Contributor Insights shows the most accessed partition keys directly, so enable it during diagnosis.

questions.q: Aurora read replicas show growing replica lag. How do you diagnose it?
questions.text: Aurora replicas share storage, so lag is normally milliseconds. Growing lag usually means heavy write volume, long-running queries on the replica blocking replay, an undersized replica, or a large transaction. Check AuroraReplicaLag, CPU, and Performance Insights. aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name AuroraReplicaLag --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=prod-ro1 --start-time 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-21T06:00:00Z --period 60 --statistics Maximum SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS dur, query FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY dur DESC LIMIT 5; Interview tip: In Aurora, a replica that is smaller than the writer can struggle to apply changes during heavy write bursts.

questions.q: The CloudWatch bill is suddenly very high. Where do you look and how do you cut it?
questions.text: Break the CloudWatch charges down by usage type. Log ingestion and storage, custom metrics with high-cardinality dimensions, detailed monitoring, vended logs such as VPC Flow Logs, and API polling are the usual drivers. aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-21 --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"SERVICE","Values":["AmazonCloudWatch"]}}' --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE aws logs describe-log-groups --query 'sort_by(logGroups,&storedBytes)[-10:].[logGroupName,storedBytes,retentionInDays]' Interview tip: Setting a retention period on every log group is the cheapest quick win, because the default is to keep logs forever.

questions.q: Savings Plan coverage dropped after migrating workloads to Fargate and Graviton. What happened and what do you do?
questions.text: Instance-specific commitments, like EC2 Instance Savings Plans or RIs, do not cover Fargate, and changing architecture can leave commitments unused while new usage is billed on-demand. Review coverage and utilisation, and prefer Compute Savings Plans. aws ce get-savings-plans-utilization --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-21 aws ce get-savings-plans-coverage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-21 --granularity MONTHLY Interview tip: Plan commitments around the target architecture, and keep some baseline uncommitted while migrations are in flight.

questions.q: Lambda throttling in one function is starving other functions in the account. How do you contain it?
questions.text: All functions in a region share the account concurrency limit. Set reserved concurrency on important functions to guarantee capacity and on noisy ones to cap them, add queues to smooth bursts, request a quota increase, and alarm on throttles. aws lambda put-function-concurrency --function-name checkout --reserved-concurrent-executions 200 aws lambda get-account-settings --query 'AccountLimit.[ConcurrentExecutions,UnreservedConcurrentExecutions]' aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/Lambda --metric-name Throttles --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=ingest --start-time 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-21T06:00:00Z --period 60 --statistics Sum Interview tip: Reserved concurrency is both a guarantee and a hard cap for that function, so size it carefully.

questions.q: Instances in an Auto Scaling group keep terminating and relaunching in a loop. How do you stop it and find the cause?
questions.text: Usually the health check fails right after launch, from slow bootstrap, a wrong health check path, or an ELB check starting before the app is up. Look at scaling activity history, set a health check grace period, and test the launch template in isolation. aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name web --max-items 10 aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web --health-check-grace-period 600 aws autoscaling suspend-processes --auto-scaling-group-name web --scaling-processes Terminate Interview tip: Suspending the Terminate process lets you keep one failing instance alive to inspect, but resume it afterwards.

questions.q: ECS tasks fail with CannotPullContainerError. How do you diagnose it?
questions.text: The task cannot fetch its image. Check the image name and tag, the execution role's ECR permissions, network path to ECR and S3 (NAT or endpoints) for private subnets, registry rate limits, and available disk or image size. aws ecs describe-tasks --cluster prod --tasks <arn> --query 'tasks[0].stoppedReason' aws ecr describe-images --repository-name web --image-ids imageTag=v42 aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <acct>.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com Interview tip: Private Fargate tasks need ecr.api, ecr.dkr and the S3 gateway endpoint, or a NAT Gateway.

questions.q: An EKS control plane upgrade is blocked or add-ons break afterwards. How do you plan to avoid that?
questions.text: Check upgrade insights for deprecated APIs, confirm add-on and node versions are compatible, upgrade one minor version at a time, upgrade add-ons and managed node groups after the control plane, and use PodDisruptionBudgets that allow drains. aws eks list-insights --cluster-name prod --filter category=UPGRADE_READINESS aws eks describe-addon-versions --kubernetes-version 1.33 --addon-name vpc-cni aws eks update-cluster-version --name prod --kubernetes-version 1.33 Interview tip: A PDB with maxUnavailable zero and a single replica makes node drains hang forever, so audit PDBs before the upgrade.

questions.q: A CloudWatch alarm sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA and never fires during a real outage. What is wrong?
questions.text: The alarm is not receiving data points, or the missing-data treatment hides the problem. A crashed service emits no metrics, so default behaviour stays in insufficient data. Set treat missing data to breaching, or alarm on a heartbeat or the absence of metrics. aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names api-5xx --query 'MetricAlarms[0].[StateValue,TreatMissingData,Period,EvaluationPeriods]' aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name api-heartbeat --metric-name RequestCount --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 5 --threshold 1 --comparison-operator LessThanThreshold --treat-missing-data breaching Interview tip: Alerting on error counts alone fails when the service is completely down, so also alarm on lack of traffic.

questions.q: A Lambda or ECS service runs but no logs appear in CloudWatch. What do you check?
questions.text: Check the role has logs:CreateLogStream and PutLogEvents, the log group exists or can be created, the task definition log driver and options are right, network access to the logs endpoint exists from private subnets, and the app actually writes to stdout. aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/f aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition web --query 'taskDefinition.containerDefinitions[0].logConfiguration' aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role-arn> --action-names logs:PutLogEvents Interview tip: For ECS, the execution role does log delivery, not the task role.

questions.q: Assuming a role across accounts fails with 'not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRole'. How do you fix it?
questions.text: Cross-account access needs two sides: the caller's identity policy allows sts:AssumeRole on the target role, and the target role's trust policy names the caller's account or principal. Check conditions such as ExternalId, MFA, and SCPs. aws iam get-role --role-name Deploy --query 'Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument' aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/Deploy --role-session-name test aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <caller-arn> --action-names sts:AssumeRole --resource-arns <role-arn> Interview tip: If the trust policy names an account root, the caller still needs its own explicit allow. Both sides must agree.

questions.q: A dead-letter queue is filling up with messages. How do you investigate and drain it safely?
questions.text: Inspect messages and attributes to find why processing failed: poison payloads, bugs, downstream outages, or visibility timeout too short. Fix the cause, then redrive messages back to the source queue, and alarm on queue depth and age. aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url <dlq> --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible aws sqs receive-message --queue-url <dlq> --max-number-of-messages 5 --attribute-names All --message-attribute-names All aws sqs start-message-move-task --source-arn <dlq-arn> --destination-arn <source-queue-arn> Interview tip: Only redrive after the bug is fixed, or the messages will just return to the DLQ and burn retries.

questions.q: What is Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) — how does RBAC work in Azure?
questions.text: # Assign a role to a user/SP on a resource group: az role assignment create --assignee user@company.com \ --role "Contributor" --scope /subscriptions/SUB/resourceGroups/prod-rg # List role assignments: az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/SUB --output table # Create custom role: az role definition create --role-definition file://custom-role.json # Workload Identity for AKS pods (no secrets): az aks update --resource-group rg --name aks --enable-workload-identity --enable-oidc-issuer Azure RBAC: 4 fundamental roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator) plus 100+ built-in roles. Scope hierarchy: Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource. Assign at the highest appropriate scope — a Contributor on a Resource Group can manage everything in it. Service Principals (app identities) and Managed Identities replace username/password for service authentication. Workload Identity: AKS pod federated with Entra ID service principal — no credential files, auto-rotating tokens.

questions.q: What is a Managed Identity in Azure — how does it differ from a Service Principal?
questions.text: # System-assigned Managed Identity (tied to resource lifecycle): az vm identity assign --resource-group rg --name myvm # auto-enabled for VM # User-assigned Managed Identity (reusable across resources): az identity create --resource-group rg --name myapp-identity az vm identity assign --resource-group rg --name myvm --identities myapp-identity # Grant identity access to Key Vault: az keyvault set-policy --name myvault --object-id <identity-object-id> \ --secret-permissions get list # In application code: no credentials needed credential = DefaultAzureCredential() # uses Managed Identity when on Azure Managed Identity: Azure manages the credential lifecycle — no secrets to rotate, no credential leaks. System-assigned: created with the resource, deleted when the resource is deleted, 1:1 relationship. User-assigned: independent lifecycle, can be assigned to multiple resources — use when multiple services share the same identity. Service Principal with certificate/secret: use when Managed Identity is not available (cross-tenant, CI/CD outside Azure). For AKS: Workload Identity is the Kubernetes-aware equivalent.

questions.q: What is a Virtual Network (VNet) — how do you design one for production AKS?
questions.text: az network vnet create --resource-group rg --name prod-vnet --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/8 # Subnets: az network vnet subnet create --vnet-name prod-vnet --name aks-nodes --address-prefixes 10.240.0.0/16 az network vnet subnet create --vnet-name prod-vnet --name aks-pods --address-prefixes 10.241.0.0/16 az network vnet subnet create --vnet-name prod-vnet --name ingress --address-prefixes 10.242.0.0/24 az network vnet subnet create --vnet-name prod-vnet --name db-subnet --address-prefixes 10.243.0.0/24 # NSG on subnet: az network nsg create --resource-group rg --name aks-nsg az network vnet subnet update --vnet-name prod-vnet --name aks-nodes --network-security-group aks-nsg AKS uses Azure CNI (recommended for production): each pod gets a real VNet IP, enabling native VNet routing, NSG-level pod traffic control, and direct pod-to-service communication. Plan address space carefully: AKS clusters can have many pod IPs (N nodes × max_pods_per_node). Use Azure CNI Overlay or Cilium for larger clusters where IP exhaustion is a concern. Private AKS: API server on private IP, accessible only from VNet or peered networks.

questions.q: What is AKS — what does Azure manage vs what you manage?
questions.text: az aks create --resource-group rg --name prod-aks \ --node-count 3 --node-vm-size Standard_D4s_v5 \ --enable-managed-identity --network-plugin azure \ --enable-workload-identity --enable-oidc-issuer \ --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 3 --max-count 10 az aks get-credentials --resource-group rg --name prod-aks # Upgrade cluster: az aks upgrade --resource-group rg --name prod-aks --kubernetes-version 1.30 Azure manages: control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler), node OS security patches (auto-upgrade options), control plane SLA (99.95% with AZs). You manage: node pools, workloads, networking within VNet, RBAC for Kubernetes objects. Key AKS add-ons: Azure Monitor (Container Insights), Azure Key Vault CSI driver (mount secrets as volumes), Azure Policy for Kubernetes (OPA Gatekeeper policies), NGINX/AGIC ingress. Upgrade: control plane first, then node pools (az aks nodepool upgrade).

questions.q: What is the Application Gateway Ingress Controller (AGIC) — how does it work?
