questions.text: az network application-gateway create --resource-group rg --name appgw \ --sku Standard_v2 --capacity 2 --vnet-name prod-vnet --subnet ingress az aks enable-addons --resource-group rg --name prod-aks \ --addons ingress-appgw --appgw-id /subscriptions/.../applicationGateways/appgw # Ingress resource uses AGIC annotations: kubernetes.io/ingress.class: azure/application-gateway appgw.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true" AGIC provisions Azure Application Gateway rules from Kubernetes Ingress resources. Application Gateway is an L7 load balancer with WAF, SSL termination, URL routing, and session affinity. AGIC watches Ingress resources and translates them to App Gateway routing rules automatically. Alternative: NGINX ingress controller (simpler, more portable, no Azure dependency). Use AGIC when you need WAF integration, autoscaling (App Gateway v2 scales pods automatically), or Azure-native PaaS integration.

questions.q: What are the storage options in Azure — Blob, Disk, Files, NetApp?
questions.text: Azure Blob: object storage (S3 equivalent), hot/cool/archive tiers Azure Disk: block storage, attached to single VM (EBS equivalent) Premium SSD (P10-P80), Ultra Disk (sub-ms latency) Azure Files: SMB/NFS shared filesystem (EFS equivalent) Azure NetApp: enterprise NFS for latency-sensitive workloads # AKS persistent volume: kubectl get storageclass # managed-premium, azurefile-csi, etc. kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml # request a managed disk or Azure Files share # AKS CSI drivers handle provisioning and attachment AKS storage: managed-premium StorageClass provisions Azure Premium SSD disks (ReadWriteOnce). azurefile-csi provisions Azure Files shares (ReadWriteMany — shared across pods). For databases: Premium SSD or Ultra Disk. For shared config or user uploads: Azure Files. For backup/archives: Blob with lifecycle management. Azure NetApp Files: high-performance NFS for SAP, Oracle, or latency-sensitive Linux workloads — expensive but very fast.

questions.q: What is Azure SQL Managed Instance — how does it differ from Azure SQL Database?
questions.text: # Azure SQL Database (PaaS, serverless option): az sql db create --resource-group rg --server myserver --name mydb --service-objective S3 # Azure SQL Managed Instance (full SQL Server engine in VNet): az sql mi create --resource-group rg --name mymi --subnet /subscriptions/.../subnets/mi-subnet \ --admin-user sqladmin --admin-password <password> # Connection string: mymi.public.abc123.database.windows.net,3342 # or private endpoint Azure SQL Database: fully managed PaaS, serverless option (scales compute to zero when idle), geo-redundancy. Best for: new applications, microservices, variable load. Azure SQL Managed Instance: 99% SQL Server compatibility, runs in your VNet, supports SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries, CLR, linked servers. Best for: lift-and-shift of on-prem SQL Server workloads. PostgreSQL Flexible Server: fully managed PostgreSQL in your VNet, high availability with zone-redundant standby, read replicas.

questions.q: What is Azure Monitor — how do you use it with AKS?
questions.text: # Enable Container Insights on AKS: az aks enable-addons --addons monitoring --name prod-aks --resource-group rg \ --workspace-resource-id /subscriptions/.../workspaces/myworkspace # KQL query in Log Analytics: KubeEvents | where Reason == "OOMKilling" | project TimeGenerated, Name, Message ContainerLog | where LogEntry contains "ERROR" | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated,5m), ContainerName # Metric alert: az monitor metrics alert create --name cpu-high --resource $AKS_ID \ --condition "avg Percentage CPU > 80" --action $ACTION_GROUP_ID Azure Monitor: metrics (platform + custom), logs (Log Analytics workspace), alerts (metric and log-based), dashboards, Application Insights (APM for application code). Container Insights adds AKS-aware views: node/pod CPU/memory, controller health, container logs. KQL (Kusto Query Language) is the query language for Log Analytics — powerful for aggregation, joining tables, and time-series analysis. For Prometheus-compatible metrics: Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus + Azure Managed Grafana (zero-ops equivalent of kube-prometheus-stack).

questions.q: What is Azure Managed Prometheus and Managed Grafana — how do you set them up?
questions.text: # Enable Managed Prometheus on AKS: az aks update --resource-group rg --name prod-aks \ --enable-azure-monitor-metrics \ --azure-monitor-workspace-resource-id /subscriptions/.../accounts/mypromws # Create Managed Grafana: az grafana create --name mygrafana --resource-group rg # Link Prometheus workspace to Grafana: az grafana data-source create --name mygrafana --definition file://prometheus-datasource.json # Same Prometheus PromQL, same Grafana dashboards, zero infra to manage Azure Managed Prometheus: Prometheus-compatible (same SDKs, ServiceMonitors, PromQL, recording rules) but fully managed — no StatefulSets, no storage management. Stores data in Azure Monitor Workspace. Azure Managed Grafana: managed Grafana service, auto-connected to Azure data sources (Azure Monitor, Managed Prometheus, Log Analytics). For AKS teams, this is the zero-ops path to full observability — equivalent to GCP Managed Prometheus on the Azure side.

questions.q: How does Azure DevOps work — Pipelines, Repos, Artifacts?
questions.text: # azure-pipelines.yml: trigger: [main] pool: {vmImage: ubuntu-latest} stages: - stage: Build jobs: - job: BuildTest steps: - task: Docker@2 inputs: {command: buildAndPush, containerRegistry: my-acr} - stage: Deploy environment: production # requires approval jobs: - deployment: DeployAKS strategy: runOnce: deploy: steps: - task: KubernetesManifest@1 Azure DevOps is a complete platform: Repos (Git hosting), Pipelines (CI/CD), Boards (Agile), Artifacts (package registry), Test Plans. Pipelines: multi-stage YAML, environment gates (manual approval), service connections (to Azure subscriptions, Docker registries, Kubernetes clusters). Azure Container Registry (ACR) is the native image registry — use Managed Identity for AKS to pull from ACR without credentials. GitHub Actions + OIDC federation is increasingly preferred over Azure DevOps Pipelines for teams on GitHub.

questions.q: How do you deploy to AKS from a CI/CD pipeline securely?
questions.text: # GitHub Actions: OIDC federation (no credentials) - uses: azure/login@v2 with: client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }} tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }} subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }} - uses: azure/aks-set-context@v3 with: {resource-group: rg, cluster-name: prod-aks} - run: kubectl apply -f k8s/ # Or: update Helm values / Kustomize manifests in GitOps repo # ArgoCD or Flux watches the manifests repo and syncs to AKS OIDC federation: configure a Federated Identity Credential on an Entra ID app/managed identity, mapping it to the GitHub Actions OIDC token. No client secret needed — GitHub OIDC token exchanges for a short-lived Azure access token. The service principal needs AKS Cluster User role + deployment permissions in Kubernetes RBAC. For GitOps: the pipeline pushes to the manifests repo, ArgoCD/Flux handles the actual kubectl apply — this keeps deployment credentials out of CI entirely.

questions.q: What is Azure Private Endpoint — how does it differ from Service Endpoint?
questions.text: # Private Endpoint (private IP in your VNet for PaaS service): az network private-endpoint create --resource-group rg --name mydb-pe \ --vnet-name prod-vnet --subnet db-subnet \ --private-connection-resource-id /subscriptions/.../servers/mydb \ --group-id sqlServer --connection-name mydb-conn # DNS: mydb.database.windows.net resolves to 10.x.x.x (private IP) az network private-dns zone create --resource-group rg --name privatelink.database.windows.net # Service Endpoint (extend VNet identity to public endpoint): az network vnet subnet update --vnet-name prod-vnet --name db-subnet --service-endpoints Microsoft.Sql Private Endpoint: PaaS service (SQL, Storage, Key Vault) gets a private IP in your VNet — traffic never leaves Azure backbone network, service can disable public access. Full network isolation. Service Endpoint: optimises routing from subnet to Azure backbone but the service still has a public IP — less secure than Private Endpoint. Use Private Endpoints for production databases and storage. Private DNS zones are required to resolve PaaS service hostnames to private IPs.

questions.q: What is Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets — how does it work with AKS node pools?
questions.text: # AKS node pool = VMSS under the hood az aks nodepool add --resource-group rg --cluster-name prod-aks \ --name gpunodes --node-vm-size Standard_NC6s_v3 --node-count 1 \ --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 0 --max-count 5 # Manual scale: az aks nodepool scale --resource-group rg --cluster-name prod-aks --name workers --node-count 5 # Node pool upgrade: az aks nodepool upgrade --resource-group rg --cluster-name prod-aks --name workers --kubernetes-version 1.30 AKS node pools are backed by VMSS — the Cluster Autoscaler scales VMSS instances based on pending pod requirements. Multiple node pools: system pool (system-critical pods — use at least Standard_D2s_v3), user pools (workload pods), specialised pools (GPU, spot). Spot node pools: 60-90% cost savings, can be evicted with 30 seconds notice — use for batch jobs or fault-tolerant workloads with toleration. Node auto-provisioning (KEDA-based) is the Azure equivalent of Karpenter for dynamic node type selection.

questions.q: What is Azure Functions and when do you use it vs containers on AKS?
questions.text: az functionapp create --resource-group rg --name myfunc \ --storage-account mystorage --consumption-plan-location eastus \ --runtime python --runtime-version 3.11 --functions-version 4 # Deploy function: func azure functionapp publish myfunc # Trigger types: HTTP, Timer, Service Bus, Event Hub, Blob, Cosmos DB # KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) on AKS: helm install keda kedacore/keda -n keda # Scale to zero based on queue depth, no Functions needed Azure Functions: serverless, scales to zero, pay-per-execution, up to 10-minute timeout (Premium plan: unlimited). Best for: event-driven processing, short-lived tasks, variable/unpredictable traffic. AKS: persistent workloads, long-running processes, stateful services. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) brings Functions-like scale-to-zero to AKS — scale pods based on queue depth, event hub lag, or custom metrics. For platform teams: KEDA on AKS is often preferred over Functions for standardisation (same K8s tooling everywhere).

questions.q: How does Azure Key Vault integrate with AKS — what are the patterns?
questions.text: # Key Vault CSI Driver (mount secrets as volumes): az aks enable-addons --addons azure-keyvault-secrets-provider --name prod-aks --resource-group rg # SecretProviderClass: spec: provider: azure parameters: vaultName: myvault objects: | array: - objectName: db-password objectType: secret # Pod mounts /mnt/secrets-store/db-password as a file # External Secrets Operator (sync to K8s Secrets): kubectl get externalsecret db-credentials # syncs Key Vault → K8s Secret Two patterns: CSI Driver mounts secrets as files/env vars directly from Key Vault (no K8s Secret created). External Secrets Operator syncs Key Vault secrets into native K8s Secrets (applications read normal K8s Secrets — no Key Vault SDK needed). CSI Driver is more secure (secret never stored in etcd). ESO is more compatible (works with any application that reads K8s Secrets). Both use Workload Identity — no credentials in pod specs.

questions.q: What is Azure DDoS Protection — how does it work with Application Gateway?
questions.text: # Enable DDoS Network Protection on VNet: az network ddos-protection create --resource-group rg --name myplan az network vnet update --resource-group rg --name prod-vnet --ddos-protection-plan myplan # App Gateway WAF policy: az network application-gateway waf-policy create --resource-group rg --name mywaf az network application-gateway waf-policy managed-rules rule-set add \ --policy-name mywaf --type OWASP --version 3.2 az network application-gateway update --name appgw --waf-policy mywaf DDoS Network Protection: volumetric and protocol attacks mitigated automatically at the Azure network edge — L3/L4 DDoS. WAF on Application Gateway: L7 attacks (SQLi, XSS, command injection) — OWASP 3.2 managed rules + custom rules. Together they cover all DDoS layers. For AKS exposed via Application Gateway: App Gateway WAF protects against web attacks, DDoS Protection handles volumetric attacks. Azure DDoS Response Team available 24/7 with Standard plan for attack assistance.

questions.q: How do you debug a CrashLoopBackOff pod on AKS?
questions.text: kubectl get pods -n prod kubectl describe pod myapp-xxx -n prod # check Events section kubectl logs myapp-xxx -n prod --previous # logs from crashed container kubectl logs myapp-xxx -n prod -c initcontainer # init container logs # Check resource limits: kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A10 Allocated # Check events for OOMKill: kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep -i oom # Exec into a working pod for comparison: kubectl run debug --image=myapp:v1 --rm -it -- /bin/sh CrashLoopBackOff: container starts, crashes, Kubernetes restarts it, exponential backoff kicks in. Common causes: application error on startup (missing env var, failed DB connection), OOMKill (memory limit too low), liveness probe failing and killing a healthy container, init container failing (dependency not ready), and permission errors (file not readable, port binding failure). Always check --previous logs first — current container may have no logs if it crashes immediately.

questions.q: How do you optimise AKS costs on Azure?
questions.text: # Spot node pools for non-critical workloads: az aks nodepool add --name spot --spot-max-price -1 --priority Spot --eviction-policy Delete # Right-size nodes with Azure Advisor: az advisor recommendation list --category Cost --output table # Stop/start AKS cluster (dev/test): az aks stop --resource-group rg --name dev-aks # pause billing on nodes az aks start --resource-group rg --name dev-aks # Azure Reservations (1-3 year VM commitment): # 40-72% savings on VM compute vs PAYG # Microsoft Azure Hybrid Benefit (if you have Windows Server licences) AKS cost levers: Spot node pools for batch/fault-tolerant workloads (60-80% savings), right-sizing via Azure Advisor and Container Insights metrics, stopping dev/test clusters outside business hours, Azure Reserved VM Instances for predictable baseline (1-3 year commitment), and cluster consolidation (fewer larger clusters vs many small ones). Container Insights + Azure Cost Management tags enable per-namespace, per-team cost allocation for chargeback.

questions.q: How do you configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaling on AKS?
questions.text: kubectl autoscale deployment myapp --cpu-percent=70 --min=3 --max=20 # Custom metric HPA (KEDA): apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1 kind: ScaledObject spec: scaleTargetRef: {name: myapp} minReplicaCount: 0 maxReplicaCount: 50 triggers: - type: azure-servicebus metadata: queueName: orders queueLength: "10" # scale when queue depth exceeds 10 messages/replica HPA v2: scale on CPU, memory, custom metrics (Prometheus), or external metrics (Azure Service Bus queue depth). KEDA extends HPA to scale on any event source (Service Bus, Event Hub, Storage Queue, HTTP traffic, Cron schedule). Scale-to-zero with KEDA: pods go to 0 when queue is empty, scale up when messages arrive — impossible with native HPA. Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes to accommodate scaled-up pods. The full stack: KEDA scales pods → Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes.

questions.q: An AKS pod is running but the Service is not routing traffic to it — how do you debug?
questions.text: # Step 1: Check pod is actually Ready kubectl get pods -l app=myapp -o wide # STATUS and READY columns # Step 2: Check Service selector matches pod labels kubectl describe service myapp # Selector vs pod labels # Step 3: Check Endpoints kubectl get endpoints myapp # should list pod IPs # Step 4: Check readiness probe kubectl describe pod myapp-xxx | grep -A5 Readiness # Step 5: Test directly to pod IP kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl http://10.240.0.5:8080/health # Step 6: NSG blocking pod subnet traffic? az network nsg rule list --resource-group MC_rg_prod-aks_eastus --nsg-name aks-nsg Most common causes: readiness probe failing (pod Running but not Ready, so Endpoints are empty), Service selector does not match pod labels (typo in label name/value), pod listening on wrong port (containerPort != service targetPort), and on AKS with Azure CNI: NSG rule blocking traffic between subnets. If Endpoints is empty, check selector. If Endpoints has IPs but traffic fails, check the port and readiness probe.

questions.q: What is Azure Cosmos DB — when do you use it?
questions.text: az cosmosdb create --resource-group rg --name mycosmosdb \ --default-consistency-level Session --locations regionName=eastus az cosmosdb sql database create --account-name mycosmosdb --name mydb az cosmosdb sql container create --account-name mycosmosdb --database-name mydb \ --name mycontainer --partition-key-path /userId --throughput 400 Cosmos DB: globally distributed NoSQL database with multi-model API (SQL/Core, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). Turnkey global distribution — replicate to any Azure region with one click. Five consistency levels (Strong to Eventual). 99.999% availability SLA with multi-region writes. Use for: globally distributed apps where latency matters, high-throughput workloads that need horizontal scale, flexible schema documents. Partition key choice is critical — poor partitioning causes hot partitions and throttling. Use Autoscale throughput to avoid over-provisioning.

questions.q: What is Azure Front Door — how does it differ from Application Gateway?
questions.text: az afd profile create --resource-group rg --profile-name myfd --sku Premium_AzureFrontDoor az afd endpoint create --resource-group rg --profile-name myfd --endpoint-name api az afd origin-group create --resource-group rg --profile-name myfd --origin-group-name backends az afd origin create --origin-group-name backends --host-name app1.eastus.cloudapp.azure.com --origin-host-header app1.eastus.cloudapp.azure.com Application Gateway: regional (single Azure region), L7 load balancer, WAF, best for intra-region traffic. Azure Front Door: global CDN and L7 load balancer, routes to the nearest healthy backend across regions, edge PoPs in 100+ locations worldwide. Use Front Door for: global user base (reduces latency by routing to nearest region), global failover (health-check-based routing away from unhealthy regions), DDoS + WAF at the edge, and SSL offload at the CDN edge. The combination: Front Door (global) → App Gateway (regional WAF) → AKS is a common enterprise pattern.

questions.q: How do you use Azure Monitor alerts and action groups for incident response?
questions.text: # Action Group (where to send alerts): az monitor action-group create --resource-group rg --name ops-team \ --action email ops ops-team@company.com \ --action webhook pagerduty https://events.pagerduty.com/integration/xxx/enqueue # Metric alert: az monitor metrics alert create --name pod-oom --resource $AKS_ID \ --condition "count kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason where reason includes OOMKilled > 0" \ --action /subscriptions/.../actionGroups/ops-team # Log alert (KQL): az monitor scheduled-query create --resource-group rg --name high-errors \ --condition-query "ContainerLog | where LogEntry contains "ERROR" | summarize count() > 10" Action Groups define who gets notified and how (email, SMS, webhook, PagerDuty, Logic App, Azure Function). Reuse action groups across multiple alerts — update once, changes everywhere. Metric alerts fire within 1-5 minutes. Log alerts (KQL) fire within 5-15 minutes. Smart Groups automatically cluster related alerts to reduce noise. Alert processing rules can suppress alerts during maintenance windows without disabling them.

questions.q: AKS nodes are NotReady — how do you diagnose and recover?
questions.text: kubectl get nodes # which nodes are NotReady? kubectl describe node mynode | tail -30 # Events section kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=mynode # pods on the node # SSH to node (via AKS debug pod): kubectl debug node/mynode -it --image=mcr.microsoft.com/cbl-mariner/busybox:2.0 chroot /host journalctl -u kubelet --since "10 minutes ago" | tail -50 systemctl status kubelet # Check node resource pressure: kubectl describe node mynode | grep -A10 Conditions Common causes: kubelet crash (check journalctl -u kubelet), disk pressure (check ephemeral storage, /var/log, container image cache), memory pressure (OOMKiller killed kubelet), network plugin failure (Azure CNI misconfiguration), or node unresponsive (Azure VM health issue). For persistent node failures: cordon, drain, and delete the node — the VMSS will provision a replacement automatically. AKS Node Auto-Repair detects and replaces unhealthy nodes automatically in managed node pools.

questions.q: What is Azure Policy — how do you enforce governance on AKS workloads?
questions.text: # Assign built-in policy to subscription: az policy assignment create --name require-pod-limits \ --policy "/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyDefinitions/e345eecc-fa47-480f-9e88-67dcc122b164" \ --scope /subscriptions/SUB \ --params "{"allowedContainerImagesRegex":{"value":"myregistry.azurecr.io/.*"}}" # Enable Azure Policy add-on for AKS (OPA Gatekeeper): az aks enable-addons --addons azure-policy --name prod-aks --resource-group rg kubectl get constrainttemplate # Gatekeeper constraint templates kubectl get k8srequiredlabels # custom constraints Azure Policy for Kubernetes: uses OPA Gatekeeper under the hood to enforce policies at pod admission time. Built-in policies: require resource limits, require readiness/liveness probes, restrict privileged containers, require specific labels, allow only images from approved registries. Policy effects: Audit (log violations), Deny (block non-compliant deployments). Policies can be assigned at Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group scope — inherit hierarchically. Essential for SOC2, CIS Benchmark, and internal governance requirements.

questions.q: What is Azure Spot VMs — how do you use them with AKS safely?
questions.text: # Create spot node pool: az aks nodepool add --resource-group rg --cluster-name prod-aks \ --name spot --priority Spot --eviction-policy Delete \ --spot-max-price -1 --node-vm-size Standard_D4s_v5 # Toleration for spot nodes: tolerations: - key: "kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority" operator: "Equal" value: "spot" effect: "NoSchedule" # Use node affinity to target spot nodes explicitly Spot VMs: 60-80% cheaper, can be evicted with 30 seconds notice when Azure needs capacity. Design workloads for eviction: use Pod Disruption Budgets to ensure minimum replicas survive eviction, use spot for stateless horizontal workloads (batch processing, CI runners, ML training). Never run stateful services on spot without replication. Use multiple VM sizes in the spot pool to increase capacity availability. SPOT_INSTANCE_TERMINATION_NOTICE environment variable (via metadata service) gives 30 seconds warning — use a SIGTERM handler to checkpoint state.

questions.q: What is Azure Service Mesh (Istio add-on) — when do you enable it on AKS?
questions.text: # Enable Istio service mesh on AKS: az aks mesh enable --resource-group rg --name prod-aks az aks mesh enable-ingress-gateway --resource-group rg --name prod-aks --ingress-gateway-type external # Enable sidecar injection for namespace: kubectl label namespace production istio.io/rev=asm-1-18 # Traffic management: kubectl apply -f virtual-service.yaml # canary: 90/10 traffic split kubectl apply -f destination-rule.yaml # circuit breaker, mTLS Service mesh adds: mTLS between services (zero-trust networking), traffic management (canary, circuit breaker, retries), and L7 observability (per-service golden signals, distributed traces). AKS Istio add-on: managed Istio (Azure updates the control plane). When to enable: you need mTLS for compliance, advanced traffic management (canary without redeployment), or need L7 metrics between services without code instrumentation. Cost: every pod gets a sidecar proxy — 15-20% overhead in CPU/memory. Not worth it for small clusters or simple architectures.

questions.q: How does Azure Backup work — how do you protect AKS data?
questions.text: # Azure Backup for AKS (preview/GA depending on region): az dataprotection backup-vault create --resource-group rg --vault-name myvault --storage-settings type=LocallyRedundant az dataprotection backup-policy create --resource-group rg --vault-name myvault --policy file://aks-policy.json # Velero (open-source, multi-cloud alternative): velero install --provider azure --plugins velero/velero-plugin-for-microsoft-azure:v1.8 \ --bucket velero-backups --secret-file ./credentials-velero velero backup create prod-backup --include-namespaces production velero restore create --from-backup prod-backup AKS data protection: Azure Backup for AKS (persistent volume snapshots + Kubernetes resource backup), Velero (open-source, backs up K8s resources and PVs to Azure Blob). Backup strategy: take daily snapshots of PVs, backup Kubernetes manifests (or rely on GitOps — manifests are already in Git), test restore quarterly. For stateful workloads: the database backup policy (RTO/RPO) usually determines the backup frequency more than the Kubernetes backup policy.

questions.q: How do you investigate high memory usage in an AKS cluster?
questions.text: # Node-level memory: kubectl top nodes # memory usage % kubectl describe node mynode | grep -A10 Allocated # memory requests vs capacity # Pod-level memory: kubectl top pods -n prod --sort-by=memory # top memory consumers kubectl describe pod myapp-xxx | grep -A5 Limits # configured limits # OOMKill events: kubectl get events -n prod | grep OOMKill # Container Insights KQL: KubePodInventory | join KubeNodeInventory on Computer | where OomKilled == true # Node memory saturation (leaves no room for burst): container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.9 Memory investigation path: identify top memory-consuming pods (kubectl top pods), compare actual usage against memory limits (if close to limit, OOMKill risk), check if any pods were recently OOMKilled (kubectl get events), and verify memory requests are accurate (over-requested memory causes node waste, under-requested causes OOMKill). Increase memory limits for legitimate high-memory workloads. For memory leaks: take heap dumps, analyse with application-specific profiling tools. Node memory pressure (allocatable - requests) must remain positive or new pods cannot schedule.

questions.q: Walk through diagnosing a production AKS performance issue reported by users.
questions.text: Principal-level systematic diagnosis — cover the full investigation flow. Step 1: Quantify — error rate, P99 latency, affected users (Azure Monitor) Step 2: Golden signals — which signal is anomalous? (Grafana or Insights) Step 3: Recent changes — kubectl rollout history, recent CI/CD deployments Step 4: Pod health — kubectl get pods -n prod (any Pending/CrashLoop?) Step 5: Node health — kubectl get nodes (all Ready?) Step 6: CPU throttling — container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total Step 7: Database — RDS/Cosmos DB slow query logs, connection pool exhaustion Step 8: Downstream — is a dependency (external API, cache) slow? Step 9: Network — NSG blocking? Private Endpoint DNS resolution? Step 10: Rollback if recent change — restore known-good state first The most common production AKS performance issues: CPU throttling (invisible, silent), memory pressure causing pod eviction, HPA not scaling fast enough (scale-up latency), Cluster Autoscaler slow to provision nodes, database connection pool exhaustion, and cross-AZ data transfer causing latency. Rollback first if there was a recent deployment — restore the known-good state, then diagnose at leisure without user impact.

questions.q: How do you design hub-and-spoke network topology in Azure for multiple workloads?
questions.text: # Hub VNet (shared services: firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute, DNS): az network vnet create -g net-rg -n hub-vnet --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16 # Spoke VNets (per workload/environment): az network vnet create -g app-rg -n spoke-prod --address-prefix 10.1.0.0/16 # Peer spoke to hub (and hub to spoke): az network vnet peering create -g app-rg --vnet-name spoke-prod -n to-hub \\ --remote-vnet hub-vnet --allow-vnet-access --allow-forwarded-traffic # Route spoke egress through hub firewall via UDR: az network route-table route create -g net-rg --route-table-name spoke-rt \\ -n default --address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 --next-hop-type VirtualAppliance \\ --next-hop-ip-address 10.0.1.4 # Azure Firewall private IP Hub-and-spoke centralises shared services (Azure Firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute gateways, DNS) in a hub VNet, with workloads isolated in spoke VNets peered to it. Spokes do not peer to each other (transitive peering is not automatic) — inter-spoke traffic routes through the hub firewall via User-Defined Routes, giving a central inspection and policy point. This is the standard enterprise topology: it isolates blast radius per spoke, centralises egress control and logging, and scales by adding spokes. Interview tip: the key facts are that VNet peering is non-transitive (spokes need the hub to talk, forced via UDR to the firewall) and that the hub centralises egress/inspection. Mentioning Azure Virtual WAN as the managed evolution of hub-and-spoke shows current knowledge.

questions.q: What is Azure Firewall vs NSG vs Application Gateway WAF — when do you use each?
questions.text: NSG: L3/L4 stateful allow/deny on subnet/NIC (free, basic) Azure Firewall: L3-L7 managed firewall, FQDN filtering, threat intel, central egress App Gateway WAF: L7 web protection (OWASP), SQLi/XSS, for HTTP(S) apps # NSG rule: az network nsg rule create -g rg --nsg-name aks-nsg -n allow-https \\ --priority 100 --destination-port-ranges 443 --access Allow --protocol Tcp # Azure Firewall app rule (FQDN egress): az network firewall application-rule create -g rg -f myfw --collection-name egress \\ -n allow-mcr --protocols Https=443 --target-fqdns mcr.microsoft.com --action Allow These operate at different layers and are complementary, not alternatives. NSGs are free, basic L3/L4 stateful filters attached to subnets/NICs — your first line for segment-to-segment rules. Azure Firewall is a managed, scalable L3–L7 firewall with FQDN filtering, threat intelligence, and centralised egress control (placed in the hub). Application Gateway WAF protects HTTP(S) apps from L7 attacks (OWASP rules: SQLi, XSS). A typical stack: NSGs for micro-segmentation, Azure Firewall for centralised egress in the hub, WAF for inbound web traffic. Interview tip: frame them by layer and purpose — NSG (cheap L4 segmentation), Azure Firewall (managed L7 egress/inspection, FQDN rules), WAF (inbound web-app protection). Knowing they layer together (defence in depth) rather than compete is the senior framing.

questions.q: How does DNS resolution work for Private Endpoints, and what breaks if it is misconfigured?
questions.text: # Private Endpoint gives the PaaS service a private IP in your subnet. # A Private DNS Zone maps the service FQDN to that private IP: az network private-dns zone create -g rg -n privatelink.database.windows.net az network private-dns link vnet create -g rg -z privatelink.database.windows.net \\ -n vnet-link --virtual-network prod-vnet --registration-enabled false # Verify resolution from inside the VNet: nslookup mydb.database.windows.net # MUST return 10.x.x.x (private), not public IP A Private Endpoint creates a private IP for a PaaS service, but clients still connect using the public FQDN (e.g. mydb.database.windows.net ). The magic is a Private DNS Zone (e.g. privatelink.database.windows.net ) linked to your VNet: it overrides resolution so the FQDN returns the private IP instead of the public one. If the zone is missing or not linked to the VNet, the FQDN resolves to the public IP — and if the service has public access disabled, the connection fails entirely. Interview tip: the classic failure is "Private Endpoint created, but the app still cannot connect" — almost always missing/unlinked Private DNS Zone, so the FQDN resolves public while public access is off. Always verify with nslookup from inside the VNet returning a private IP. This is one of the most common real-world Azure networking incidents.

questions.q: What is the difference between Azure Load Balancer, Application Gateway, and Front Door?
questions.text: Azure Load Balancer: L4 (TCP/UDP), regional, ultra-low latency, no app awareness Application Gateway: L7 (HTTP/S), regional, WAF, URL routing, SSL termination Front Door: L7, GLOBAL, CDN + edge WAF, multi-region routing/failover # Common enterprise chain: # Front Door (global edge) -> App Gateway (regional WAF) -> AKS internal LB -> pods They differ by OSI layer and scope. Load Balancer is L4 (TCP/UDP), regional, extremely fast, with no HTTP awareness — use for non-HTTP or raw performance. Application Gateway is L7, regional, with WAF, path/host routing, and SSL termination — use for HTTP apps needing web features in one region. Front Door is L7 but global : a CDN with edge PoPs that routes users to the nearest healthy region, with edge WAF and global failover — use for a worldwide user base or multi-region HA. They compose: Front Door for global routing/failover into per-region App Gateways. Interview tip: the discriminators are layer (L4 vs L7) and scope (regional vs global). "Global users / multi-region failover" → Front Door; "regional web app with WAF" → App Gateway; "raw TCP/low latency" → Load Balancer. Naming the Front Door → App Gateway → AKS chain shows real architecture experience.

questions.q: How do you connect on-premises networks to Azure — VPN Gateway vs ExpressRoute?
questions.text: # Site-to-Site VPN (over public internet, IPsec): az network vnet-gateway create -g rg -n vpn-gw --vnet hub-vnet \\ --gateway-type Vpn --vpn-type RouteBased --sku VpnGw2 # ExpressRoute (private dedicated circuit via a provider): az network express-route create -g rg -n er-circuit \\ --bandwidth 1000 --provider Equinix --peering-location "Silicon Valley" --sku-tier Standard VPN Gateway connects on-prem to Azure over the public internet via encrypted IPsec tunnels — quick to set up, lower cost, but subject to internet variability and lower throughput. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit through a connectivity provider that bypasses the public internet entirely — consistent low latency, high bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps), and an SLA. Use VPN for dev/test, smaller workloads, or as a backup path; use ExpressRoute for production, latency-sensitive, high-throughput, or compliance-driven connectivity. A common HA design uses ExpressRoute primary with VPN as failover. Interview tip: the trade-off is internet-based (VPN: cheap, fast to deploy, variable) vs private circuit (ExpressRoute: consistent, high-bandwidth, SLA, more cost/lead-time). Mentioning ExpressRoute-primary + VPN-failover as a resilient hybrid pattern is a strong senior detail.

questions.q: What are Azure Management Groups and how do you structure subscriptions at enterprise scale?
questions.text: # Management Group hierarchy (governance applied top-down): az account management-group create --name Corp --display-name Corporate az account management-group create --name Prod --parent Corp az account management-group create --name NonProd --parent Corp # Move a subscription under a management group: az account management-group subscription add --name Prod --subscription SUB_ID # Policies/RBAC assigned at MG level inherit to all child subscriptions Management Groups sit above subscriptions, forming a hierarchy (Tenant Root → Management Groups → Subscriptions → Resource Groups) where Azure Policy and RBAC assignments inherit downward. The enterprise pattern (Cloud Adoption Framework "landing zones") groups subscriptions by purpose — e.g. separate Platform, Prod, and NonProd management groups — so governance (allowed regions, required tags, security baselines) is defined once at the group level and automatically applies to every subscription beneath it. Subscriptions become units of isolation, billing, and scale limits. Interview tip: the key insight is inheritance — assign policy/RBAC at the management-group level so it cascades, rather than per-subscription. Referencing the Azure landing-zone / Cloud Adoption Framework structure (platform vs workload subscriptions under management groups) signals enterprise governance maturity.

questions.q: What is Conditional Access in Entra ID and how does it strengthen security?
questions.text: # Conditional Access policy intent (configured in Entra ID): # IF user accesses [Azure Management] # AND sign-in risk is medium/high OR location is outside corp network # THEN require MFA AND a compliant/managed device # ELSE block # Common controls: require MFA, require compliant device, block legacy auth, # restrict by location/IP, require approved client app Conditional Access is Entra ID’s policy engine that evaluates signals at sign-in — user/group, application, device state, location, and real-time risk — and enforces controls like requiring MFA, demanding a compliant managed device, or blocking access. Instead of "always require MFA," it applies controls contextually: low-risk sign-in from a managed device on the corporate network passes seamlessly, while a risky sign-in from an unknown location is challenged or blocked. Blocking legacy authentication protocols (which bypass MFA) is one of the highest-impact policies. Interview tip: frame it as risk-based, context-aware access — the foundation of Zero Trust on Azure. The single most impactful policy to mention is blocking legacy auth , since it closes the gap attackers use to bypass MFA. Pairing Conditional Access with Identity Protection (risk signals) is the complete answer.

questions.q: How do Azure RBAC and Kubernetes RBAC interact on AKS?
questions.text: # Two RBAC layers on AKS: # 1. Azure RBAC: who can manage the CLUSTER resource (az aks ...) az role assignment create --assignee user@co.com \\ --role "Azure Kubernetes Service Cluster User Role" --scope $AKS_ID # 2. Kubernetes RBAC: what you can do INSIDE the cluster (kubectl) # Option A: AKS-managed Entra integration maps Entra groups -> K8s RBAC az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --enable-azure-rbac # use Azure RBAC for K8s authz too # Then assign K8s-scoped Azure roles: az role assignment create --assignee $GROUP_ID \\ --role "Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader" --scope $AKS_ID/namespaces/prod AKS has two distinct authorization layers. Azure RBAC controls operations on the cluster resource (creating/scaling the cluster, getting credentials). Kubernetes RBAC controls actions inside the cluster (which pods/secrets a user can read). With Entra integration, users authenticate via Entra ID and their group membership maps to Kubernetes Roles/RoleBindings. Enabling "Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization" lets you manage even in-cluster permissions through Azure role assignments scoped to namespaces — unifying both layers under Entra/Azure RBAC. Interview tip: the crisp distinction is "Azure RBAC = permission to manage the cluster object; Kubernetes RBAC = permission to act on objects within the cluster." Note that getting a kubeconfig (Cluster User role) does not grant in-cluster permissions — K8s RBAC still gates that. Mapping Entra groups to namespaces is the production patte

questions.q: What is Privileged Identity Management (PIM) and why use just-in-time access?
questions.text: # PIM makes privileged roles ELIGIBLE rather than permanently ACTIVE: # - user is 'eligible' for Owner/Contributor, not standing-assigned # - to use it: activate the role (time-boxed, e.g. 4 hours) # - activation can require: MFA, justification, approval, ticket number # Eligible assignment via Graph/PIM (conceptual): # role: Contributor scope: prod-sub type: Eligible maxDuration: PT4H PIM implements just-in-time, time-bound privileged access. Instead of users holding standing admin rights (a constant attack surface), they are made eligible for a role and must activate it on demand — with optional MFA, business justification, approval workflow, and an automatic expiry. This shrinks the window during which privileged credentials are exploitable, creates an audit trail of every elevation, and enforces least privilege over time. It is central to limiting the blast radius of a compromised admin account. Interview tip: the security principle is "no standing privilege." PIM converts permanent admin into time-boxed, justified, approved, audited elevation. Mentioning that activation can require approval + MFA + a ticket, and that everything is logged, demonstrates you understand privileged-access security, not just RBAC basics.

questions.q: How do you architect a private (API-server-isolated) AKS cluster and still allow CI/CD access?
questions.text: # Private cluster: API server gets a private IP, no public endpoint az aks create -g rg -n prod-aks --enable-private-cluster \\ --private-dns-zone system --enable-managed-identity # CI/CD reaches the private API server via one of: # - self-hosted runners inside the VNet (or a peered VNet) # - 'az aks command invoke' (runs kubectl in an AKS-managed pod, no network line-of-sight) az aks command invoke -g rg -n prod-aks --command "kubectl get pods -n prod" # - private endpoint + private DNS for the API server FQDN A private AKS cluster places the Kubernetes API server on a private IP with no public endpoint, so management traffic never traverses the internet. The challenge is that CI/CD and operators now lack a direct line of sight to the API server. Solutions: run self-hosted CI runners inside the VNet (or a peered/hub VNet), use az aks command invoke (which executes your kubectl/helm inside an AKS-managed pod that already has cluster access, requiring no network path), or wire up a Private Endpoint with Private DNS for the API server FQDN so VPN/ExpressRoute-connected clients resolve it privately. Interview tip: private cluster = no public API endpoint, which forces a decision about how pipelines reach it. The elegant, low-infrastructure answer is az aks command invoke (no VNet line-of-sight needed); the scalable answer is in-VNet self-hosted runners. Knowing the Private DNS requirement for the API FQDN rounds it out.

questions.q: How do you secure secrets end-to-end on Azure: Key Vault, rotation, and access?
questions.text: az keyvault create -g rg -n myvault --enable-rbac-authorization true # RBAC (preferred over access policies): az role assignment create --assignee $MI_OBJECT_ID \\ --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope $VAULT_ID # Store + rotate: az keyvault secret set --vault-name myvault -n db-password --value <v> # Auto-rotation policy / event-grid trigger to rotate and update consumers # Consume from AKS via CSI driver or Workload Identity (no creds in pod) End-to-end secret security on Azure: store secrets/keys/certs in Key Vault with RBAC authorization (granular, auditable — preferred over legacy access policies), grant access to Managed Identities / Workload Identity rather than shared credentials, enable soft-delete and purge protection so secrets cannot be permanently lost or maliciously deleted, and automate rotation (Key Vault rotation policies or Event Grid-triggered functions that rotate the credential and update dependents). Pods consume secrets via the CSI driver or ESO with no credentials embedded. All access is logged for audit. Interview tip: hit the full lifecycle — storage (Key Vault, RBAC, purge protection), access (Managed Identity, no shared secrets), rotation (automated, not manual), and consumption (CSI/Workload Identity, nothing in pod specs). Calling out RBAC authorization over access policies, and soft-delete/purge protection, shows current best practice.

questions.q: What causes SNAT port exhaustion on AKS and how do you fix it?
questions.text: # Symptom: outbound connections intermittently fail/timeout under load # Diagnose via Azure Monitor / LB metrics: SNAT port utilization, failed connections # Fixes: # 1. Increase allocated outbound SNAT ports (Standard LB outbound rule): az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --load-balancer-outbound-ports 2048 # 2. Add more outbound public IPs (more SNAT ports total): az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --load-balancer-managed-outbound-ip-count 4 # 3. Use a NAT Gateway for the node subnet (far larger SNAT scale): az network nat gateway create -g rg -n aks-nat --public-ip-addresses natip Azure performs SNAT (source NAT) for pod egress through the cluster’s load balancer, and each public IP provides a limited pool of SNAT ports. Workloads making many concurrent outbound connections (chatty microservices, lots of external API calls) can exhaust the port pool, causing intermittent connection failures and timeouts that are hard to diagnose. Fixes: allocate more SNAT ports per node, add more outbound public IPs (each adds ports), or — the most scalable — attach a NAT Gateway to the node subnet, which provides vastly more SNAT ports and better handles bursty egress. Interview tip: SNAT exhaustion is a classic, hard-to-spot AKS production issue — intermittent outbound failures under load with healthy pods. The senior answer names the symptom, points to LB SNAT metrics, and recommends NAT Gateway as the durable fix (plus connection reuse/pooling in the app to reduce port churn).

questions.q: How do you implement Workload Identity on AKS and why is it better than pod-managed identity?
questions.text: # 1. Enable OIDC issuer + workload identity on the cluster: az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity # 2. Create a managed identity and federate it to a K8s service account: az identity create -g rg -n app-mi az identity federated-credential create -g rg -n app-fc --identity-name app-mi \\ --issuer $(az aks show -g rg -n prod-aks --query oidcIssuerProfile.issuerUrl -o tsv) \\ --subject system:serviceaccount:prod:app-sa # 3. Annotate the K8s service account; pod uses it, gets tokens automatically Workload Identity federates a Kubernetes service account with an Entra ID managed identity via the cluster’s OIDC issuer. Pods using that service account receive short-lived, automatically-rotated Entra tokens to access Azure resources (Key Vault, Storage, SQL) — with no secrets stored anywhere. It replaces the deprecated pod-managed identity (aad-pod-identity) , which relied on a node-level component intercepting metadata requests and had scaling, latency, and security drawbacks. Workload Identity is the current standard: cleaner (native OIDC federation), more secure (no intercepting daemon), and scalable. Interview tip: say explicitly that Workload Identity replaces the deprecated aad-pod-identity, and explain the mechanism: OIDC federation maps a K8s service account to an Entra identity, pods get auto-rotating tokens, zero stored credentials. This is the most current AKS identity answer and a strong signal you track the platform’s evolution.

questions.q: Explain Azure CNI vs kubenet vs CNI Overlay for AKS networking.
questions.text: Azure CNI (standard): every pod gets a real VNet IP (fast, NSG-controllable, IP-hungry) kubenet: pods get internal IPs, UDR-routed (IP-efficient, more limits) [legacy] Azure CNI Overlay: pods on an overlay network, nodes use VNet IPs (scales huge, IP-efficient) # Overlay (recommended for large clusters): az aks create -g rg -n prod-aks --network-plugin azure --network-plugin-mode overlay \\ --pod-cidr 10.244.0.0/16 The choice trades VNet integration against IP consumption. Azure CNI (standard) gives every pod a routable VNet IP — best network performance and NSG-level pod control, but consumes VNet address space fast (nodes × max-pods), risking IP exhaustion. kubenet conserves IPs (pods get internal addresses, UDR-routed) but is legacy with feature limits. Azure CNI Overlay is the modern recommendation for large clusters: pods run on a separate overlay CIDR while nodes use VNet IPs — giving near-CNI performance with massive scale and minimal VNet IP usage. Cilium-powered CNI adds eBPF dataplane and network policy. Interview tip: the deciding factor is IP address planning at scale. "Large cluster, limited VNet IP space" → Azure CNI Overlay (or Cilium). "Need every pod directly addressable in the VNet" → standard Azure CNI. Calling kubenet legacy and recommending Overlay/Cilium for new large clusters reflects current AKS guidance.

questions.q: How do you set up cross-tenant or B2B access securely in Entra ID?
questions.text: # Invite an external (guest) user via B2B collaboration: az ad user invite --invited-user-email partner@vendor.com \\ --invite-redirect-url https://portal.azure.com # Cross-tenant access settings control what guests can do: # - inbound: which external tenants/users may be invited # - outbound: which external resources your users may access # - trust MFA/device claims from the home tenant (avoid double-MFA) # Entitlement management: access packages with approval + expiry for guests Entra B2B collaboration invites external users as guest identities in your tenant; they authenticate with their home-tenant credentials but are governed by your policies. Cross-tenant access settings let you control inbound/outbound collaboration per partner tenant and optionally trust the partner’s MFA/device claims (avoiding double prompts). For governance at scale, Entitlement Management bundles resources into access packages with approval workflows and automatic expiry/recertification, so guest access does not linger. Conditional Access still applies to guests, so you can require MFA and restrict what external identities reach. Interview tip: the secure pattern is B2B guests (not shared accounts) + cross-tenant access settings (scoped trust, optional MFA pass-through) + Entitlement Management (time-bound, approved, recertified access) + Conditional Access on guests. Emphasising expiry/recertification shows you think about guest-access sprawl, a real governance risk.

questions.q: How do you design egress control and force-tunneling for AKS in a regulated environment?
questions.text: # Route all node/pod egress through Azure Firewall in the hub: az network route-table route create -g rg --route-table-name aks-rt \\ -n to-fw --address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 --next-hop-type VirtualAppliance \\ --next-hop-ip-address 10.0.1.4 # Associate UDR to the node subnet; set AKS outbound type: az aks create -g rg -n prod-aks --outbound-type userDefinedRouting ... # Allow required AKS egress FQDNs on the firewall (mcr.microsoft.com, etc.) In regulated environments, you must control and inspect all outbound traffic. Set the AKS outbound type to userDefinedRouting and use a User-Defined Route to force 0.0.0.0/0 egress through Azure Firewall in the hub, where you allow only required destinations (by FQDN/tag) and log everything. AKS itself needs specific egress FQDNs (the Microsoft Container Registry, AKS API, Ubuntu/security repos, etc.), so the firewall ruleset must permit those or the cluster breaks. This gives a single, auditable egress chokepoint that satisfies compliance requirements for traffic inspection and data-exfiltration prevention. Interview tip: the mechanism is outboundType=userDefinedRouting + UDR → Azure Firewall + an allow-list of required AKS FQDNs. The gotcha to mention: lock down egress and remember AKS has mandatory egress endpoints — over-tight rules silently break image pulls and node bootstrap. Centralised, logged egress is the compliance story.

questions.q: What is Defender for Cloud and how does it improve AKS/Azure security posture?
questions.text: # Enable Defender plans (CSPM + workload protection): az security pricing create -n Containers --tier Standard az security pricing create -n VirtualMachines --tier Standard # Defender for Containers provides: # - image vulnerability scanning (in ACR + at runtime) # - K8s runtime threat detection (suspicious exec, crypto-mining) # - secure-score recommendations + regulatory compliance dashboards Microsoft Defender for Cloud combines posture management (CSPM) with workload protection (CWPP). For posture, it continuously assesses configuration against best practice and regulatory standards (CIS, PCI, SOC2), producing a Secure Score and prioritized remediation. Defender for Containers adds AKS-specific protection: scanning images in ACR and at runtime for vulnerabilities, detecting runtime threats (suspicious kubectl exec , crypto-mining, privilege escalation), and surfacing Kubernetes misconfigurations. It turns security from periodic audits into continuous monitoring with actionable, ranked recommendations. Interview tip: split it into posture (CSPM: Secure Score, compliance dashboards, config recommendations) and protection (CWPP: image scanning, runtime threat detection). For AKS specifically, name Defender for Containers’ image scanning + runtime detection. Tying it to compliance frameworks (CIS/PCI/SOC2) connects security to audit requirements interviewers care about.

questions.q: How do you achieve multi-region active-active networking on Azure?
questions.text: # Global L7 entry with health-based routing + failover: az afd profile create -g rg --profile-name global-fd --sku Premium_AzureFrontDoor # Origins in each region (regional App Gateway / AKS LB), health-probed # Data tier: geo-distributed (Cosmos DB multi-region writes) or paired-region replication # Per-region VNets (no overlapping CIDRs) for future peering/global VNet peering # DNS: Front Door for HTTP; Traffic Manager for non-HTTP/DNS-level failover Active-active multi-region means each region runs a full stack serving live traffic, with global routing distributing users and failing over automatically. Azure Front Door (or Traffic Manager for non-HTTP) provides the global entry point, health-probing each region and routing to the nearest healthy one. Each region has its own VNet (non-overlapping CIDRs so they can be peered) and regional ingress (App Gateway/AKS). The hard part is data : use a globally-distributed store (Cosmos DB with multi-region writes) or carefully designed cross-region replication, accepting the consistency trade-offs that active-active writes imply. Interview tip: separate the easy part (stateless compute replicated per region behind Front Door) from the hard part (multi-region data consistency). Mention Front Door for global HTTP routing/failover, non-overlapping VNet CIDRs, and that the real design challenge is the data tier (Cosmos multi-region writes vs replication latency/consistency). That framing reads as principal-level.

questions.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime AKS cluster upgrade in production?
questions.text: # 1. Upgrade the control plane first: az aks upgrade -g rg -n prod-aks --control-plane-only --kubernetes-version 1.30 # 2. Upgrade node pools with surge (extra nodes added before draining old): az aks nodepool update -g rg --cluster-name prod-aks -n workers \\ --max-surge 33% # 33% extra capacity during rollout az aks nodepool upgrade -g rg --cluster-name prod-aks -n workers --kubernetes-version 1.30 # Ensure PodDisruptionBudgets protect minimum replicas during node drains AKS upgrades the control plane and node pools separately. Upgrade the control plane first (it stays available with AZ-backed SLA), then roll node pools. Node-pool upgrade cordons and drains each node, rescheduling pods elsewhere — so zero downtime depends on two things: max-surge (adds extra nodes before draining, avoiding capacity dips) and PodDisruptionBudgets (guarantee a minimum number of replicas stay running during evictions). Without PDBs, a drain can take all replicas of a service down at once; without surge, you lose capacity mid-rollout. Interview tip: the two pillars of zero-downtime upgrades are max-surge (capacity during the rollout) and PDBs (availability during drains), plus readiness probes so traffic only hits ready pods. Mention upgrading control plane before nodes, and validating in a non-prod cluster first. Blue/green node pools are the advanced option for risk-averse upgrades.

questions.q: How do you implement a canary or blue-green deployment on AKS?
questions.text: # Blue-green: two deployments, switch Service selector kubectl apply -f green-deploy.yaml # new version alongside blue kubectl patch service myapp -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}' # cutover # Canary with Istio (AKS mesh add-on) weighted routing: # VirtualService: 90% -> v1 subset, 10% -> v2 subset, shift gradually # Progressive delivery (automated): Argo Rollouts / Flagger # analyze golden-signal metrics, auto-promote or auto-rollback Blue-green runs two full versions; you flip the Service selector (or ingress) from blue to green for an instant cutover, with instant rollback by flipping back — simple, but doubles resources momentarily and shifts 100% at once. Canary shifts a small traffic percentage to the new version (10% → 50% → 100%), limiting blast radius and letting you observe before full rollout — best done with a mesh (Istio) or ingress weighting. Progressive delivery tools (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) automate canary analysis: they watch error rate/latency and auto-promote on success or auto-rollback on regression. Interview tip: blue-green = instant switch + easy rollback but all-or-nothing; canary = gradual, metric-observed, smaller blast radius. The senior addition is automated progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts/Flagger) that gates promotion on golden-signal metrics and rolls back automatically — turning safe deploys into the default rather than a manual ritual.

questions.q: What are resource requests and limits, and how do they affect scheduling and QoS on AKS?
questions.text: resources: requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi} # used for SCHEDULING + guarantee limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi} # hard cap (CPU throttled, memory OOMKilled) # QoS classes derived from requests/limits: # Guaranteed: requests == limits (highest priority, last evicted) # Burstable: requests < limits # BestEffort: none set (first evicted under pressure) Requests are what the scheduler reserves — a pod is placed only where its requested CPU/memory fits, and requests act as the guaranteed floor. Limits are the hard ceiling: exceeding the CPU limit causes throttling (silent slowdowns), exceeding the memory limit causes OOMKill . The relationship sets the pod’s QoS class : Guaranteed (requests=limits) pods are evicted last; Burstable next; BestEffort (nothing set) first. Accurate requests are critical: too high wastes node capacity (nothing else schedules), too low risks OOMKill and noisy-neighbour contention. Interview tip: nail the effects — requests drive scheduling + QoS + eviction order; CPU limit → throttling, memory limit → OOMKill. The common production mistake is mis-set requests (over-request wastes money, under-request causes evictions/OOM). Mentioning that CPU throttling is silent (no events, just latency) is a strong real-world detail.

questions.q: How do you choose between AKS, Azure Container Apps, and Azure Container Instances?
questions.text: ACI: single containers, fast start, per-second billing, no orchestration Container Apps: serverless containers on managed K8s+KEDA+Dapr, scale-to-zero AKS: full Kubernetes, maximum control + ecosystem, you run the platform # ACI as AKS virtual-node burst target (Virtual Kubelet): az aks enable-addons --addons virtual-node -g rg -n prod-aks --subnet-name aci-subnet It is a control-vs-simplicity spectrum. ACI runs individual containers with no orchestration — great for short tasks, burst, or CI jobs (per-second billing, fast start), and can back AKS virtual nodes for burst capacity. Container Apps is serverless containers on a managed Kubernetes+KEDA+Dapr foundation: scale-to-zero, built-in ingress, revisions/canary, microservices features — without operating a cluster. AKS gives full Kubernetes: maximum control, the entire ecosystem (operators, CRDs, mesh), and the responsibility of running the platform. Choose by how much Kubernetes control you actually need. Interview tip: "do you need to run Kubernetes or just run containers ?" ACI for one-off/burst, Container Apps for serverless microservices without cluster ops, AKS when you need full K8s control/ecosystem. For a platform team standardising on K8s tooling, AKS; for product teams wanting velocity without platform overhead, Container Apps. That decision framing is what they want.

questions.q: How does the AKS Cluster Autoscaler work and how do you tune it?
questions.text: az aks nodepool update -g rg --cluster-name prod-aks -n workers \\ --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 3 --max-count 20 # Tunable behaviour (autoscaler profile): az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --cluster-autoscaler-profile \\ scale-down-delay-after-add=10m scale-down-unneeded-time=10m \\ scale-down-utilization-threshold=0.5 The Cluster Autoscaler watches for pods that cannot be scheduled due to insufficient resources and adds nodes (scaling the underlying VMSS) up to max-count ; it removes nodes that stay underutilized long enough, down to min-count . It scales on pending pods (unschedulable due to requests), not on raw utilization — which is why accurate pod requests are essential. Tuning levers control scale-down aggressiveness: how long to wait after adding a node, how long a node must be unneeded, and the utilization threshold below which a node is a removal candidate. Interview tip: the crucial insight is that it scales on unschedulable pods driven by resource requests , not actual usage — so wrong requests break autoscaling. Pair it mentally with HPA/KEDA (scale pods) → Cluster Autoscaler (scale nodes). Mention scale-down tuning and that node provisioning has latency (minutes), which is why surge/headroom matters for spiky load.

questions.q: What is the difference between availability sets, availability zones, and region pairs?
questions.text: Availability Set: spreads VMs across fault/update domains WITHIN a datacenter Availability Zones: physically separate datacenters within a region (AZ1/AZ2/AZ3) Region Pairs: two regions paired for geo-redundancy + sequential updates # AKS across zones: az aks create -g rg -n prod-aks --zones 1 2 3 --node-count 3 These are increasing levels of fault isolation. Availability Sets spread VMs across fault and update domains within a single datacenter — protecting against rack/hardware and maintenance failures, but not a datacenter outage. Availability Zones are physically separate datacenters within a region (independent power/cooling/network) — protecting against a whole-datacenter failure; spreading AKS nodes across zones survives a zone outage. Region Pairs are two regions linked for geo-redundancy, with platform updates rolled sequentially (never both at once) and prioritized recovery — protecting against a regional disaster. Interview tip: map each to the failure it survives — Availability Set (rack/host within a DC), Availability Zone (whole datacenter within a region), Region Pair (entire region). For production AKS, spread node pools across zones ; for DR, replicate to the paired region . Knowing AZs are physically distinct DCs (not just logical) is the differentiator.

questions.q: How do you secure the software supply chain for AKS container images?
questions.text: # Scan images in ACR (Defender) + in CI before push: az acr task create -n scan --registry myacr --cmd "trivy image \$IMG" ... # Sign images (Notation / cosign) and store signatures in ACR: notation sign myacr.azurecr.io/app:v1 # Enforce: only signed images from approved registries (Azure Policy / ratify + Gatekeeper): kubectl get constrainttemplate # e.g. allow only myacr.azurecr.io/*, signed Supply-chain security for AKS spans build, registry, and admission. Scan images for vulnerabilities in CI and continuously in ACR (Defender for Containers). Sign images (Notation/cosign) so their provenance can be verified, storing signatures alongside the image in ACR. Enforce at the cluster with Azure Policy / Ratify + Gatekeeper: admit only images from approved registries that are signed and pass vulnerability gates, blocking anything else. Pull from ACR using Workload Identity (no registry credentials in pods). This closes the gap between "image built" and "image running." Interview tip: structure it as scan → sign → enforce-at-admission, plus credential-less ACR pulls via managed identity. Naming Ratify/Gatekeeper (or Azure Policy) to block unsigned/unapproved images at admission is the detail that shows you can make the policy preventive, not advisory — the same SLSA-style thinking interviewers probe for.

questions.q: How do you design for graceful shutdown and pod termination on AKS?
questions.text: # Pod termination sequence: # 1. Pod marked Terminating; removed from Service Endpoints # 2. preStop hook runs (e.g. sleep to drain in-flight) # 3. SIGTERM sent to container; app should finish in-flight, stop accepting new # 4. After terminationGracePeriodSeconds, SIGKILL lifecycle: {preStop: {exec: {command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"]}}} terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 When a pod is terminated (scale-down, rollout, node drain), Kubernetes removes it from Service Endpoints and sends SIGTERM , then SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds . For zero dropped requests, the app must catch SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections, and finish in-flight work. A common race: endpoint removal and SIGTERM are near-simultaneous, but load balancers/kube-proxy take a moment to stop routing — so a short preStop sleep (or app-level drain) avoids sending traffic to a pod that already began shutting down. Set the grace period longer than the worst-case request duration. Interview tip: the sequence (Endpoint removal → preStop → SIGTERM → grace → SIGKILL) plus the classic race (LB still routing briefly after termination starts) is the answer. The fix — a preStop drain delay and a SIGTERM handler — demonstrates you have debugged real "occasional 502s during deploy" issues, which is exactly the production signal.

questions.q: What are taints, tolerations, node selectors, and affinity — and when do you use each?
questions.text: # Taint a node pool so only tolerating pods land there (e.g. GPU/spot): az aks nodepool add ... --node-taints sku=gpu:NoSchedule tolerations: [{key: sku, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule}] # nodeSelector / nodeAffinity to ATTRACT pods to nodes: nodeSelector: {agentpool: gpunodes} # podAntiAffinity to spread replicas across nodes/zones (HA): # topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone Taints repel pods from a node pool unless they carry a matching toleration — used to reserve special pools (GPU, spot, system) for the right workloads. Node selectors / node affinity attract pods to nodes with certain labels (e.g. schedule onto the GPU pool). The two work together: taint the GPU pool so general pods stay off it, and use affinity/selector so GPU pods target it. Pod anti-affinity spreads replicas across nodes/zones for HA (so one node/zone failure does not take all replicas), while pod affinity co-locates related pods. Topology spread constraints are the modern way to balance across zones. Interview tip: the mental model is "taints repel, affinity/selectors attract." Reserve specialized pools with taint+toleration and target them with affinity. For HA, use pod anti-affinity / topology spread across zones so replicas survive a zone loss. Giving the GPU/spot pool example and the zone-spread example shows practical scheduling experience.

questions.q: How do you right-size AKS node pools and pods to balance cost and reliability?
questions.text: # Observe actual usage to set requests (Container Insights / Prometheus): kubectl top pods --all-namespaces --sort-by=memory # VPA in recommendation mode suggests requests/limits: kubectl get vpa myapp -o yaml # target recommendations # Match node VM size to pod shape (avoid stranded capacity): # many small pods -> general-purpose; memory-heavy -> E-series; CPU-heavy -> F-series Right-sizing has two layers. At the pod level, set requests from observed usage (Container Insights/Prometheus, or VPA in recommendation mode): over-requesting strands node capacity (you pay for unused reservation and block scheduling), under-requesting causes OOMKills and contention. At the node level, pick VM sizes that match the workload shape so requested resources pack efficiently — mismatched node sizes leave "stranded" CPU or memory that nothing can use. Combine with Cluster Autoscaler bounds, spot pools for tolerant workloads, and bin-packing awareness to minimize idle capacity while keeping enough headroom for bursts and node failures. Interview tip: tie cost to correctness — accurate requests are the lever for both reliability (no OOM/contention) and cost (no stranded capacity). Mention VPA recommendations to set requests from real data, matching node SKU to pod shape to avoid stranded resources, and keeping failure/burst headroom. This connects FinOps to reliability, a strong platform-engineering angle.

questions.q: How do liveness, readiness, and startup probes differ, and what happens when they are misconfigured?
questions.text: livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}, periodSeconds: 10} readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8080}, periodSeconds: 5} startupProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5} # liveness fail -> container RESTARTED # readiness fail -> pod removed from Service Endpoints (no traffic), NOT restarted # startup running -> liveness/readiness suppressed until startup passes Liveness answers "is this container healthy?" — failure causes a restart . Readiness answers "can it serve traffic now?" — failure removes the pod from Service Endpoints (no traffic) but does not restart it. Startup protects slow-starting apps: while it runs, liveness/readiness are suppressed, so a slow boot is not mistaken for a crash. Misconfiguration is a top production cause of outages: a too-aggressive liveness probe restarts healthy-but-busy pods (CrashLoop under load); a liveness probe that should be readiness restarts pods that are merely warming up; missing readiness sends traffic to not-yet-ready pods (errors during rollout). Interview tip: "liveness restarts, readiness gates traffic, startup buys boot time." The classic bug to cite: using liveness where readiness was needed, so heavy load makes the probe fail and Kubernetes restarts perfectly healthy pods — a self-inflicted CrashLoop. Recommending startup probes for slow apps and conservative liveness thresholds shows hard-won experience.

questions.q: How do you run stateful workloads (databases) on AKS, and when should you not?
questions.text: # StatefulSet + persistent volumes for stable identity/storage: # - volumeClaimTemplates -> per-pod PVC (managed-premium / Ultra disk) # - stable network IDs (pod-0, pod-1) for clustering # Operators manage complex stateful systems (e.g. Postgres, Kafka operators) # BUT: managed PaaS is usually better: # Azure SQL / PostgreSQL Flexible Server / Cosmos DB -> Azure handles HA, backup, patching Kubernetes can run stateful workloads via StatefulSets (stable pod identity, ordered rollout, per-pod persistent volumes) and operators that automate clustering, failover, and backups. But for most databases, managed PaaS (Azure SQL, PostgreSQL Flexible Server, Cosmos DB) is the better choice: Azure handles HA, patching, backups, and point-in-time restore, removing enormous operational burden and risk. Run databases on AKS only when you have a strong reason — a mature operator, specific version/extension needs, cost at scale, or portability requirements — and the team to operate them. Otherwise, keep stateful data in managed services and AKS for stateless compute. Interview tip: the senior answer is "you can with StatefulSets + operators, but usually shouldn’t — use managed PaaS." Articulate the trade-off: operators give control/portability but you own HA/backup/patching; PaaS offloads all of that. Knowing when not to put a DB on Kubernetes is a stronger signal than knowing how to.

questions.q: What is KEDA and how does it enable event-driven and scale-to-zero workloads on AKS?
questions.text: az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --enable-keda apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1 kind: ScaledObject spec: scaleTargetRef: {name: worker} minReplicaCount: 0 # scale to ZERO when idle maxReplicaCount: 100 triggers: - type: azure-servicebus metadata: {queueName: jobs, messageCount: "5"} KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) extends the HPA to scale workloads on event sources — Service Bus/Storage Queue depth, Event Hub lag, Kafka, Prometheus metrics, cron schedules, HTTP traffic, and dozens more — rather than just CPU/memory. Critically, it supports scale-to-zero : when there are no events (empty queue), pods drop to zero, and the first event scales them back up. This brings serverless economics (pay only when working) to standard Kubernetes workloads, letting platform teams standardise on AKS tooling instead of splitting between Functions and K8s. It is the managed Azure equivalent of running KEDA yourself. Interview tip: KEDA = "HPA, but on any event source, with scale-to-zero." The scale-to-zero capability (impossible with native HPA) is the headline. Frame it as the reason a platform team can keep event-driven and batch workloads on AKS rather than Azure Functions — one toolchain, same observability, same RBAC — which is the standardisation argument interviewers like.

questions.q: How do you handle GPU workloads (ML/AI) on AKS efficiently?
questions.text: # GPU node pool, scale-to-zero when idle, tainted for GPU pods only: az aks nodepool add -g rg --cluster-name prod-aks -n gpu \\ --node-vm-size Standard_NC6s_v3 --node-taints nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule \\ --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 0 --max-count 8 # NVIDIA device plugin exposes GPUs; pod requests them: resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}} # Consider spot GPU pools + checkpointing for training jobs GPU efficiency on AKS centres on not paying for idle accelerators. Put GPUs in a dedicated node pool that is tainted (so only GPU workloads land there) and autoscales from zero — nodes spin up when GPU jobs queue and back down to zero when idle, since GPU VMs are very expensive. The NVIDIA device plugin advertises GPUs so pods request them via nvidia.com/gpu limits. For training, use spot GPU pools with checkpointing (huge savings, tolerate eviction) and consider GPU sharing/MIG for inference to pack multiple workloads onto one GPU. Interview tip: the cost lever is scale-to-zero on a tainted GPU pool (idle GPUs are the budget killer), plus spot + checkpointing for training and MIG/time-slicing for inference packing. Mentioning the NVIDIA device plugin and taints (keep non-GPU pods off pricey nodes) shows you have actually run GPU workloads, not just read about them.

questions.q: How do you implement network policies to restrict pod-to-pod traffic on AKS?
questions.text: # Enable a network policy engine at cluster creation (Azure NPM or Cilium): az aks create -g rg -n prod-aks --network-plugin azure --network-policy cilium # Default-deny ingress in a namespace, then allow specific flows: kind: NetworkPolicy spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}} policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: frontend}}}] ports: [{port: 8080}] By default all pods can talk to all pods. Network Policies implement micro-segmentation — but only if the cluster runs a policy engine (Azure NPM or, increasingly, Cilium /eBPF), chosen at cluster creation. The strong pattern is default-deny per namespace, then explicit allow rules for legitimate flows (e.g. frontend→api on port 8080), so a compromised pod cannot freely move laterally. This is zero-trust networking inside the cluster, complementing NSGs (which operate at subnet level, not pod level). Cilium adds richer L7-aware policy and better performance. Interview tip: two key facts — (1) network policy requires a policy engine enabled at cluster creation (you cannot add it trivially later), and (2) the secure design is default-deny + explicit allows for lateral-movement containment. Recommending Cilium (eBPF, L7-aware) for new clusters reflects current AKS direction and signals depth beyond basic NetworkPolicy YAML.

questions.q: What is Bicep and how does it compare to ARM templates and Terraform on Azure?
questions.text: // main.bicep — concise, typed DSL transpiled to ARM JSON resource aks 'Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters@2024-02-01' = { name: 'prod-aks' location: location properties: { dnsPrefix: 'prod' agentPoolProfiles: [...] } } az deployment group create -g rg --template-file main.bicep ARM templates are Azure’s native JSON IaC — powerful but verbose and hard to read. Bicep is a concise, typed DSL that transpiles to ARM JSON: same engine and full day-one resource coverage, far better authoring (modules, type safety, simpler syntax), and no state file (Azure Resource Manager is the source of truth). Terraform is multi-cloud, has a rich provider ecosystem and explicit state management, and is preferred when you span clouds or want a single IaC tool everywhere. Rule of thumb: Bicep for Azure-only shops wanting native tooling and instant new-feature support; Terraform for multi-cloud or existing-Terraform organisations. Interview tip: Bicep = "ARM made usable," Azure-native, stateless (ARM is the truth), day-one resource support; Terraform = multi-cloud, stateful, broad ecosystem. The decision driver is "Azure-only vs multi-cloud" and existing tooling/skills. Noting Bicep’s immediate support for new Azure features (vs Terraform provider lag) and its lack of a state file to manage is the nuanced comparison.

questions.q: How do you debug intermittent image pull failures (ImagePullBackOff) on AKS?
questions.text: kubectl describe pod myapp-xxx | grep -A10 Events # exact pull error # Common causes & checks: # - auth: AKS identity lacks AcrPull on the registry az aks check-acr -g rg -n prod-aks --acr myacr.azurecr.io # - wrong tag/digest or image deleted from ACR # - registry throttling / rate limits (Docker Hub anonymous pulls) # - private registry not reachable (Private Endpoint / firewall egress) # - node disk pressure evicting image cache ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet cannot pull the image; kubectl describe pod Events shows the precise reason. Common causes: authorization (the AKS managed identity lacks the AcrPull role — verify with az aks check-acr ), a wrong/missing tag or digest , registry throttling (notably anonymous Docker Hub rate limits — mirror to ACR), the private registry being unreachable (missing Private Endpoint/DNS or egress firewall rule blocking it), or node disk pressure evicting the image cache. Intermittent (not constant) failures point toward throttling, transient network/egress issues, or a flaky registry rather than a static misconfiguration. Interview tip: lead with "read the describe Events for the exact error," then enumerate auth (AcrPull / az aks check-acr ), tag/digest, rate-limiting (Docker Hub → mirror to ACR), private-registry reachability, and disk pressure. The intermittent qualifier specifically implicates throttling or transient egress — calling that out shows diagnostic precision.
