questions.q: How do you plan and execute a migration of VMs/workloads from on-prem to Azure?
questions.text: # Assess: discover + dependency-map + right-size (Azure Migrate) # Azure Migrate appliance inventories on-prem, suggests target SKUs + cost # Choose a strategy per workload (the 5/6 R's): # Rehost (lift-shift VMs) | Replatform (e.g. -> AKS/PaaS) | Refactor # Repurchase (SaaS) | Retire | Retain # Migrate: Azure Migrate replication -> test failover -> cutover A disciplined migration runs Assess → Plan → Migrate → Optimize. Assess with Azure Migrate: discover servers, map dependencies (so you do not break inter-app communication), and right-size target SKUs with cost estimates. Plan a strategy per workload using the "R’s": Rehost (lift-and-shift VMs — fastest), Replatform (move to PaaS/AKS for managed benefits), Refactor (re-architect cloud-native), Repurchase (SaaS), Retire , Retain . Migrate via replication, then test failover in Azure before the real cutover to minimize downtime. Optimize afterward for cost and reliability. Group workloads into waves by dependency so related systems move together. Interview tip: structure the answer as Assess (Azure Migrate: discovery, dependency mapping, right-sizing) → strategy per workload (the R’s) → wave-based migration with test failover before cutover → post-migration optimization. Emphasising dependency mapping and migration waves (move interdependent apps together) is what separates a real migration plan from "just move the VMs."

questions.q: Pods are stuck in Pending on AKS. Walk through the diagnosis.
questions.text: kubectl describe pod myapp-xxx | grep -A15 Events # scheduler's reason is here # Common reasons & checks: # - Insufficient cpu/memory: no node fits the requests kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Allocated # - No node matches nodeSelector/affinity/taints # - PVC unbound (storage class / disk quota) kubectl get pvc # - Cluster Autoscaler at max-count or failing to add nodes kubectl -n kube-system logs -l app=cluster-autoscaler | tail A Pending pod means the scheduler cannot place it — and kubectl describe pod Events states exactly why. The usual causes: insufficient resources (no node satisfies the pod’s CPU/memory requests — and the Cluster Autoscaler is at max-count or cannot add nodes), scheduling constraints (nodeSelector/affinity/taints with no matching node), or an unbound PVC (storage class issue, disk quota, or zone mismatch between pod and volume). Follow the Events message to the specific cause rather than guessing. Interview tip: always "read the scheduler’s reason in describe Events first." Then map: insufficient resources → requests vs node capacity + autoscaler state; unschedulable due to affinity/taints → node labels/taints; volume not bound → PVC/storage class/zone. Mentioning the autoscaler-at-max and PVC-zone-affinity cases shows real AKS troubleshooting depth.

questions.q: Users report intermittent 502/504 errors from an AKS app behind Application Gateway. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: # Layered check: client -> Front Door/AppGW -> ingress -> Service -> pod # 1. App Gateway backend health: az network application-gateway show-backend-health -g rg -n appgw # 2. Endpoints populated + pods Ready: kubectl get endpoints myapp ; kubectl get pods -l app=myapp # 3. Probe mismatch (AppGW health probe path/port vs app) # 4. Pod restarts / OOM during traffic: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep -i -E 'oom|killed|restart' # 5. Timeouts: AppGW request-timeout < app response time 502/504s behind App Gateway point to the gateway being unable to get a healthy response from the backend. Work the path top-down: check App Gateway backend health (unhealthy backends → probe misconfiguration: wrong path/port/host, or app health endpoint failing), confirm Kubernetes Endpoints are populated and pods are Ready (empty Endpoints = readiness failing = 502s), look for pod restarts/OOM coinciding with errors (capacity issue under load), and check timeouts (504 when the app’s response time exceeds App Gateway’s request-timeout). "Intermittent" usually means capacity/scaling lag or a subset of unhealthy pods, not a total misconfiguration. Interview tip: demonstrate layered diagnosis (AppGW health → Endpoints/readiness → pod restarts/OOM → timeouts) rather than jumping to one cause. 502 = backend unreachable/unhealthy (often readiness/probe), 504 = backend too slow (timeout). Tying "intermittent" to scaling lag or a few bad pods, and checking AppGW backend health first, is th

questions.q: What are the golden signals and how do you implement them for an AKS service?
questions.text: # Four golden signals (per service): # Latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket) # Traffic: sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) # Errors: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / total # Saturation: container CPU throttling, memory working set vs limit # Managed Prometheus scrapes; Managed Grafana dashboards; alert on SLO burn The four golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — are the minimal set that characterise a service’s health. On AKS, instrument the app to expose Prometheus metrics (request duration histograms, request counts by status), scrape them with Azure Managed Prometheus , and visualise/alert via Managed Grafana . Latency uses high percentiles (P99, not average — averages hide tail pain); errors as a ratio of failed to total requests; saturation from CPU throttling and memory-vs-limit. Alert on SLO burn rate (you are consuming the error budget too fast) rather than raw thresholds, to reduce noise and catch real degradation. Interview tip: name all four signals and how each is measured (P99 latency, request rate, 5xx ratio, throttling/memory-pressure for saturation). The senior addition is alerting on SLO burn rate not static thresholds — it ties monitoring to user-facing reliability and cuts alert fatigue. Mentioning Managed Prometheus + Managed Grafana keeps it Azure-specific.

questions.q: An AKS deployment rollout is stuck (not progressing). How do you investigate and recover?
questions.text: kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod # shows it's stuck kubectl get pods -l app=myapp # new ReplicaSet pods state? kubectl describe deployment myapp | grep -A5 Conditions # ProgressDeadlineExceeded? kubectl describe pod <new-pod> # why new pods won't go Ready # Recover: kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp # roll back to last good ReplicaSet kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp A stuck rollout means the new ReplicaSet’s pods are not becoming Ready, so the Deployment will not progress (and after progressDeadlineSeconds reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded ). Investigate the new pods: are they Pending (scheduling/resources), CrashLoopBackOff (app failing on the new version), or not passing readiness (bad config, failing dependency)? kubectl describe on the deployment (Conditions) and the new pods pinpoints it. The rolling-update strategy intentionally protects you — it will not tear down old healthy pods until new ones are Ready — so the old version keeps serving. Recover quickly with kubectl rollout undo to the previous ReplicaSet, then debug the new version offline. Interview tip: the reassuring fact to state: a rolling update will not kill the old version until new pods are Ready, so a stuck rollout usually is not an outage — buy time with rollout undo , then diagnose. Identifying the new-pod failure mode (Pending vs CrashLoop vs readiness) and knowing maxUnavailable / maxSurge govern the rollout shows command of deployments.

questions.q: How do you write effective KQL queries in Log Analytics for AKS incident investigation?
questions.text: // Error spike by container over time: ContainerLogV2 | where LogMessage has 'ERROR' | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), ContainerName | render timechart // OOMKilled pods: KubePodInventory | where ContainerStatusReason == 'OOMKilled' | project TimeGenerated, Namespace, Name, Node=Computer // Correlate node + pod: KubeNodeInventory | join kind=inner KubePodInventory on Computer KQL (Kusto Query Language) is the query engine for Log Analytics. Effective incident KQL follows a pattern: filter early (time range + where on the relevant table/field), summarize with bin() for time-bucketed aggregation, render as a timechart to spot the onset, and join tables (e.g. KubePodInventory with KubeNodeInventory ) to correlate pod issues with node conditions. Key AKS tables: ContainerLogV2 (app logs), KubePodInventory / KubeNodeInventory (object state), KubeEvents (cluster events). Use has / contains for log text and summarize ... by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) to see when an issue began. Interview tip: the method matters more than memorising tables — filter→summarize-by-bin→render to find onset, then join to correlate (pod↔node). Naming the AKS tables ( ContainerLogV2 , KubePodInventory , KubeEvents ) and the OOMKilled query shows you have actually investigated AKS incidents in Log Analytics, not just read docs.

questions.q: A node has disk pressure and is evicting pods. How do you diagnose and resolve it?
questions.text: kubectl describe node mynode | grep -A5 Conditions # DiskPressure=True kubectl get events | grep -i evict # Inspect node disk (via debug pod): kubectl debug node/mynode -it --image=mcr.microsoft.com/cbl-mariner/busybox:2.0 chroot /host; df -h; du -sh /var/lib/containerd/* /var/log/* # Common culprits: image cache bloat, runaway container logs, ephemeral PV growth # kubelet GC settings: imageGCHighThresholdPercent, evictionHard nodefs DiskPressure on a node triggers kubelet eviction of pods to reclaim space, causing disruption. Diagnose by confirming the condition ( describe node → Conditions) and inspecting what filled the disk via a debug pod: usually image cache bloat ( /var/lib/containerd ), runaway container logs (apps logging excessively, no rotation), or ephemeral storage growth (emptyDir/temp files). Resolve immediately by reclaiming space (kubelet image GC, log rotation), and durably by setting log limits, sizing node OS/ephemeral disks adequately, capping ephemeral-storage requests/limits, and tuning kubelet GC thresholds. Excessive app logging is a frequent root cause. Interview tip: name the eviction mechanism (DiskPressure → kubelet evicts), then the top culprits: image cache, container logs without rotation, ephemeral storage. Durable fixes (log rotation/limits, ephemeral-storage limits, bigger/managed OS disk, kubelet GC tuning) beyond the immediate cleanup show you fix root cause, not just symptoms.

questions.q: How do you set up SLOs, error budgets, and burn-rate alerting on Azure?
questions.text: # Define SLI (e.g. availability = good requests / total) and SLO (99.9% / 30d) # Error budget = 1 - SLO = 0.1% of requests may fail over the window # Burn-rate alert (Managed Prometheus): fast burn = page, slow burn = ticket // fast burn (2% of budget in 1h): (1 - (sum(rate(good[5m]))/sum(rate(total[5m])))) > 14.4 * (1-0.999) # Track budget consumption on a Managed Grafana SLO dashboard An SLO is a target on a service-level indicator (e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days). The error budget is the allowable failure (0.1% here) — a concrete budget you can "spend." Burn-rate alerting fires based on how fast you are consuming that budget: a fast burn (e.g. 2% of the monthly budget in an hour) pages immediately, while a slow burn raises a low-urgency ticket. Implement SLIs as Prometheus queries, compute burn rate, and alert via Managed Prometheus rules, visualising budget consumption in Managed Grafana. This replaces noisy static thresholds with alerts tied directly to user-facing reliability. Interview tip: define the chain SLI → SLO → error budget → burn-rate alert, and contrast multi-window burn rates (fast burn pages, slow burn tickets) with naive static thresholds. The point interviewers want: alert on budget burn , not raw CPU/error spikes — it aligns paging with actual user impact and the error-budget policy governs release decisions.

questions.q: Cross-region or cross-AZ latency is degrading an AKS app. How do you investigate?
questions.text: # Is traffic crossing zones/regions unnecessarily? # - pods + their DB/cache in the SAME zone? (topology-aware routing) kubectl get pods -o wide # node -> zone mapping # Enable topology-aware hints so Services prefer same-zone endpoints: # service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto # Check DB/cache region vs cluster region; Private Endpoint in correct region # Measure: distributed traces (App Insights) to find the slow hop Latency from topology usually means traffic is crossing zone or region boundaries it should not. Investigate where each hop lives: are pods and their database/cache in the same zone/region , or is the app in one region calling a data store in another? Use topology-aware routing (topology-aware hints) so Kubernetes Services prefer same-zone endpoints, reducing cross-AZ hops (which also cuts cross-AZ data-transfer cost). Verify PaaS dependencies (SQL, Cosmos, cache) are in the cluster’s region with correctly-placed Private Endpoints. Distributed tracing (Application Insights) pinpoints exactly which hop is slow rather than guessing. Interview tip: two angles — (1) is traffic needlessly crossing AZ/region (fix with topology-aware routing / co-locating data), and (2) measure the actual slow hop with distributed tracing rather than assuming. Noting that cross-AZ traffic costs money and latency, and that topology-aware hints keep traffic same-zone, connects performance to cost — a platform-level insight.

questions.q: How do you implement distributed tracing for microservices on AKS?
questions.text: # Instrument with OpenTelemetry (vendor-neutral), export to App Insights: # OTEL SDK in app -> OTEL Collector (DaemonSet) -> Azure Monitor/App Insights # Propagate trace context (W3C traceparent) across service calls # Application Insights distributed trace view: end-to-end span waterfall # Correlate traces with logs (trace_id) and metrics for full context Distributed tracing follows a single request across service boundaries, revealing where latency and errors actually occur in a microservice call chain. The modern approach uses OpenTelemetry (vendor-neutral instrumentation) in each service, propagating W3C trace context ( traceparent header) so spans link into one trace, exported via an OTel Collector to Application Insights / Azure Monitor. The App Insights trace view shows the end-to-end span waterfall — making it obvious that, say, a 2s request spent 1.8s in a downstream database call. Correlating trace_id across traces, logs, and metrics gives full-context debugging. Interview tip: emphasise OpenTelemetry (avoid vendor lock-in) + W3C context propagation + export to App Insights, and the payoff: you find the slow hop in a microservice chain instead of guessing per-service. Mentioning trace↔log↔metric correlation via trace_id (the "three pillars of observability" tied together) is the senior framing.

questions.q: A Managed Identity / Workload Identity token is failing in a pod. How do you debug auth failures?
questions.text: # Symptom: app gets 401/403 calling Key Vault/Storage/SQL kubectl describe sa app-sa -n prod # has azure.workload.identity/client-id annotation? kubectl describe pod | grep -i 'azure.workload.identity/use' # label present? # Federated credential subject must match exactly: # system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa-name> az identity federated-credential list -g rg --identity-name app-mi # Target RBAC: does the identity have the role on the resource? az role assignment list --assignee <client-id> --scope <resource-id> Workload Identity auth failures (401/403 from Key Vault/Storage/SQL) usually trace to one of three mismatches. (1) Service account wiring : the K8s service account must have the azure.workload.identity/client-id annotation and the pod must use that SA with the azure.workload.identity/use label. (2) Federated credential subject mismatch : the federated credential’s subject must exactly equal system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name> — a namespace or name typo breaks token exchange. (3) Missing target RBAC : the managed identity authenticated fine but lacks the role (e.g. Key Vault Secrets User) on the specific resource. Check each in order. Interview tip: structure it as authentication vs authorization. Auth (getting a token): SA annotation + pod label + exact federated-credential subject ( system:serviceaccount:ns:sa ). Authorization (using it): the identity needs the right Azure role on the target resource. The most common silent bug is the federated subject typo — call

questions.q: How do you reduce alert fatigue and design an effective on-call alerting strategy on Azure?
questions.text: # Principles: # - alert on SYMPTOMS (user-facing SLO burn), not every cause # - every page must be ACTIONABLE and URGENT; else ticket/dashboard # - group related alerts (Azure Monitor Smart Groups) # - suppress during maintenance (alert processing rules) # - severity tiers -> action groups (P1 page, P3 email) Alert fatigue comes from too many non-actionable, cause-based alerts. The fixes: alert on symptoms (user-facing SLO burn) rather than every internal cause, so one page corresponds to real impact instead of dozens of correlated cause-alerts; make every page actionable and urgent — if it is not, downgrade it to a ticket or dashboard; group related alerts (Azure Monitor Smart Groups cluster correlated alerts into one); suppress during known maintenance (alert processing rules) without disabling; and use severity tiers routed to different action groups (P1 pages PagerDuty, P3 emails). The test for any alert: "does a human need to do something now?" Interview tip: the core principle is "page on symptoms (SLO burn), not causes," and "every page must be actionable+urgent." Add tactical Azure mechanisms (Smart Groups for de-duplication, alert processing rules for maintenance suppression, severity→action-group routing). Framing on-call health as a designed system, with the "actionable now?" test, is exactly the SRE maturity interviewers probe.

questions.q: An Azure SQL / database-backed AKS app is hitting connection pool exhaustion. How do you fix it?
questions.text: # Symptom: 'timeout acquiring connection' / max pool size reached under load # Check: pods x replicas x per-pod pool size vs DB max connections # e.g. 20 pods x 100 pool = 2000 > Azure SQL connection limit # Fixes: # - right-size per-pod pool; ensure connections are RETURNED (no leaks) # - add a proxy/pooler (PgBouncer for PostgreSQL) to multiplex # - scale DB tier or use read replicas for read-heavy load Connection pool exhaustion appears as "timeout acquiring connection" or max-pool-reached errors under load. The arithmetic is the key insight: total connections = replicas × per-pod pool size, which can blow past the database’s connection ceiling as pods scale out (20 pods × 100-connection pools = 2000 connections — far above many tiers). Causes are over-sized per-pod pools, connection leaks (connections borrowed but never returned), or simply more replicas than the DB can serve. Fixes: right-size the per-pod pool relative to replica count, fix leaks (always release connections), introduce a connection pooler/proxy (e.g. PgBouncer for PostgreSQL) to multiplex many app connections onto few DB connections, and scale the DB tier or add read replicas for read-heavy load. Interview tip: lead with the math — replicas × pool-size vs DB max connections — because that scaling interaction is what surprises teams when pods autoscale. Then: right-size pools, fix leaks, add a pooler (PgBouncer) to multiplex, scale tier/read-replicas. The pooler-to-multiplex answer is the one that signals

questions.q: How do you monitor and control Azure costs in real time (FinOps on AKS)?
questions.text: # Cost visibility: # - Azure Cost Management: budgets, alerts, anomaly detection # - tags (team/env/cost-center) for showback/chargeback # - OpenCost / Kubecost on AKS for per-namespace/pod cost allocation az consumption budget create --budget-name prod --amount 50000 --time-grain Monthly # Controls: spot pools, autoscaler bounds, reservations/savings plans, rightsizing FinOps on Azure combines visibility, allocation, and control. Visibility : Azure Cost Management for budgets, cost alerts, and anomaly detection; consistent tagging (team/env/cost-center) so spend maps to owners. For AKS specifically, shared cluster cost is opaque — tools like OpenCost/Kubecost allocate cost per namespace/pod/team, enabling showback/chargeback. Control : spot node pools for tolerant workloads, Cluster Autoscaler bounds and rightsized requests (the biggest waste source), and Reservations/Savings Plans for predictable baseline (40–72% off). The cycle is inform → allocate → optimize, made continuous with budgets and anomaly alerts. Interview tip: structure as visibility (Cost Management + tagging + Kubecost/OpenCost for per-namespace AKS allocation) → control (spot, rightsizing, reservations/savings plans). The AKS-specific insight is that a shared cluster hides per-team cost until you add allocation tooling. Tying rightsized requests to both cost and reliability, and naming reservations vs savings plans, reads as platform/FinOps maturity.

questions.q: DNS resolution is failing intermittently inside AKS pods. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: # Test from a pod: kubectl run dnsutils --rm -it --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.3 \\ -- nslookup kubernetes.default # Check CoreDNS health + load: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns | tail # Common causes: CoreDNS under-provisioned, ndots:5 search-domain amplification, # conntrack table full, upstream (Azure DNS / private zone) issues Intermittent in-pod DNS failures are a classic AKS pain point. Diagnose by testing resolution from a debug pod and checking CoreDNS health/logs in kube-system . Common causes: CoreDNS under-provisioned for query volume (add replicas / enable autoscaling, or use NodeLocal DNSCache to offload), the ndots:5 default causing search-domain amplification (each external lookup tries several suffixes first — fix with fully-qualified names or tuned dnsConfig ), conntrack table exhaustion on busy nodes dropping UDP DNS packets, or upstream issues resolving Private DNS Zones. Intermittency usually points to load/capacity (CoreDNS or conntrack) rather than a static misconfig. Interview tip: the AKS-savvy answer names CoreDNS capacity (scale it / NodeLocal DNSCache), the ndots:5 search-domain amplification (use FQDNs to cut lookups), and conntrack exhaustion dropping UDP under load. Recommending NodeLocal DNSCache as the durable fix for intermittent DNS at scale is a strong, specific signal.

questions.q: How do you centralize logs across multiple AKS clusters and subscriptions?
questions.text: # Container Insights -> Log Analytics workspace(s) # - one central workspace, or per-team workspaces + cross-workspace KQL: union workspace('ws-a').ContainerLogV2, workspace('ws-b').ContainerLogV2 # Governance via Azure Policy: enforce Container Insights on all AKS # Retention/cost: tiered (interactive vs archive), table-level retention # Diagnostic settings route platform logs/metrics to the workspace too Centralised logging across clusters/subscriptions uses Log Analytics workspaces fed by Container Insights and resource diagnostic settings . Two patterns: a single central workspace (simplest querying, but governance/cost concentration) or per-team/per-environment workspaces with cross-workspace KQL ( union workspace(...) across two workspaces) for global queries while preserving access boundaries. Enforce coverage with Azure Policy (require Container Insights on every AKS so no cluster is unmonitored), and manage cost/retention with tiered storage (interactive vs cheap archive) and table-level retention. Diagnostic settings also route platform (control-plane) logs and metrics into the same workspace for correlation. Interview tip: address the central-vs-federated workspace trade-off (single = easy queries; per-team + cross-workspace KQL = access isolation), enforcement via Azure Policy (no unmonitored clusters), and cost control via tiered retention. Mentioning cross-workspace union queries and policy-enforced coverage shows you think about observability at fleet scale, no

questions.q: A scheduled job / CronJob on AKS is not running or is overlapping. How do you debug?
questions.text: kubectl get cronjob -n prod # LAST SCHEDULE, SUSPEND status kubectl get jobs -n prod # did Jobs get created? kubectl describe cronjob mycron -n prod # events: missed schedules? # Key fields: # concurrencyPolicy: Forbid|Allow|Replace # overlap behaviour # startingDeadlineSeconds # missed-schedule tolerance # successfulJobsHistoryLimit / failedJobsHistoryLimit CronJob issues fall into "not running" and "overlapping." For not running : check the CronJob is not Suspend=true , that its schedule (cron syntax, and the cluster’s timezone assumptions) is correct, and the events for "missed schedule" — if the controller was down or busy past startingDeadlineSeconds , a run is skipped. For overlapping : the concurrencyPolicy governs behaviour — Allow (default) lets runs overlap (problematic for non-idempotent jobs), Forbid skips a new run if the previous is still going, Replace kills the old and starts fresh. Also check whether created Jobs themselves fail (image/permission/resource issues) versus the schedule never firing. Interview tip: split the problem (not-firing vs overlapping) and map to fields: Suspend/schedule/startingDeadlineSeconds for missed runs; concurrencyPolicy (Forbid/Replace) for overlap of long or non-idempotent jobs. Distinguishing "schedule never created a Job" from "Job created but failed" is the diagnostic precision interviewers look for.

questions.q: How would you build a production-grade observability stack for AKS from scratch?
questions.text: # Metrics: Azure Managed Prometheus (scrape) + Managed Grafana (dashboards) # Logs: Container Insights -> Log Analytics (KQL), tiered retention # Traces: OpenTelemetry -> Application Insights (distributed tracing) # Alerting: SLO burn-rate rules -> action groups (PagerDuty/email by severity) # Correlate: trace_id across metrics/logs/traces; golden-signal dashboards A complete stack covers the three pillars plus alerting and correlation. Metrics : Azure Managed Prometheus scrapes app and infra metrics (golden signals), visualised in Managed Grafana — zero-ops, PromQL-compatible. Logs : Container Insights ships to Log Analytics for KQL investigation, with tiered retention for cost. Traces : OpenTelemetry instrumentation exporting to Application Insights for end-to-end request tracing. Alerting : SLO burn-rate rules routed by severity to action groups (page vs ticket). The glue is correlation — shared trace_id linking a metric anomaly to the relevant logs and the exact slow trace — plus standardised golden-signal dashboards per service so any on-call engineer can navigate any service the same way. Interview tip: present it as three pillars (metrics/logs/traces) + alerting + correlation, naming the managed Azure components (Managed Prometheus, Managed Grafana, Log Analytics, App Insights, OTel). The senior differentiators: alert on SLO burn (not thresholds), correlate via trace_id, and standardise golden-signal dashboards so the stack is usable under pressure — designing for the

questions.q: How do you conduct a blameless post-incident review after an AKS production outage?
questions.text: # Structure: # 1. Timeline: detection -> diagnosis -> mitigation -> resolution (with timestamps) # 2. Impact: users affected, duration, SLO/error-budget burn # 3. Root cause(s): the 'why' chain, not a person # 4. What went well / what was hard (detection gaps, tooling gaps) # 5. Action items: owned, dated, tracked to completion A blameless post-incident review focuses on systems and conditions , not individual fault — because punishing people hides information, while psychological safety surfaces the real contributing factors. Build a precise timeline (detection → diagnosis → mitigation → resolution with timestamps), quantify impact (affected users, duration, error-budget burn), and trace root cause(s) as a chain of "why" (often multiple latent factors aligning, not a single cause). Capture what helped and what slowed response (detection gaps, missing runbooks, confusing dashboards), and turn findings into owned, dated action items tracked to completion. The output is organisational learning and concrete prevention, not blame. Interview tip: emphasise blameless (systems not people — because blame suppresses the truth you need), a factual timeline, impact quantified against the error budget, multi-factor root cause (not "human error"), and trackable action items with owners. Mentioning that the error-budget burn from the incident informs release-pace decisions ties the postmortem into the broader SRE practice.

questions.q: How do you design high availability and disaster recovery for Azure SQL Database?
questions.text: # In-region HA is built in (zone-redundant for Premium/Business Critical): az sql db update -g rg -s srv -n mydb --zone-redundant true # Cross-region DR options: # - Active geo-replication: readable secondaries in other regions # - Auto-failover groups: automatic failover + stable connection endpoint az sql failover-group create -g rg -s primarysrv -n fg \\ --partner-server secondarysrv --add-db mydb --failover-policy Automatic Azure SQL provides layered resilience. In-region HA is automatic; higher tiers (Premium/Business Critical) add zone redundancy , surviving a datacenter (zone) failure transparently. For regional DR , active geo-replication creates readable secondary replicas in other regions (also useful for offloading reads), while auto-failover groups add automatic regional failover plus a stable listener endpoint — so the app connects to the failover-group name and Azure redirects to whichever region is primary, requiring no connection-string change on failover. Choose RPO/RTO targets, then match the tier and replication accordingly, and rehearse failover. Interview tip: layer the answer — built-in HA → zone redundancy (DC failure) → geo-replication / auto-failover groups (region failure). The detail that lands: auto-failover groups give a stable endpoint so the app needs no change on failover, and you should define RPO/RTO and actually test failover. Tying tier choice to RPO/RTO shows you design DR to requirements, not by default.

questions.q: How do you perform a zero/low-downtime schema migration for a database backing an AKS app?
questions.text: # Expand/contract (parallel change) across multiple deploys: # 1. EXPAND: add new column/table (nullable/default) — backward compatible # 2. deploy app that writes BOTH old+new, reads old (or new) # 3. BACKFILL existing rows in batches # 4. switch app to read/write new only # 5. CONTRACT: drop old column — only after no code uses it Low-downtime schema changes use the expand/contract (parallel change) pattern, never a breaking change in one step. Expand : add the new structure backward-compatibly (nullable column, new table) so old code still works. Deploy code that writes to both old and new shapes. Backfill existing data in batches (avoiding long locks). Switch the app to use the new shape. Finally contract : remove the old structure — only once no running version references it. Each step is independently deployable and rollbackable, which is exactly what keeps a rolling AKS deploy (old and new pods coexisting) from breaking against the schema. Interview tip: the key is decoupling schema changes from code changes across multiple deploys so old and new app versions both work during a rolling update. The trap to name: dropping a column in the same release that stops using it breaks rollback (old pods expect the column). Mentioning batched backfills to avoid lock contention shows production DB experience.

questions.q: When do you choose Cosmos DB vs Azure SQL vs PostgreSQL Flexible Server?
questions.text: Cosmos DB: global distribution, NoSQL, horizontal scale, tunable consistency Azure SQL: relational, strong consistency, T-SQL, transactions, PaaS PostgreSQL Flex: open-source relational, extensions, in-VNet, cost-effective # Decision drivers: data model, consistency, scale shape, global reach, portability Match the store to the workload. Cosmos DB : globally distributed, horizontally scalable NoSQL with tunable consistency and single-digit-ms latency worldwide — for global apps, high write throughput, flexible schemas, where partitioning is designed well. Azure SQL : managed relational with strong consistency, rich T-SQL, and transactions — for relational workloads needing ACID and complex queries, especially Microsoft-stack apps. PostgreSQL Flexible Server : managed open-source Postgres with extensions (PostGIS, etc.), VNet integration, and cost efficiency — for relational workloads valuing portability/open-source and no cloud lock-in. The drivers are data model (relational vs document), consistency needs, scale shape (vertical vs global horizontal), and portability. Interview tip: decide by data model + consistency + scale + portability, not popularity. "Global, high-throughput, flexible schema, partition-able" → Cosmos; "relational/ACID, Microsoft stack" → Azure SQL; "open-source relational, portable, cost-sensitive" → PostgreSQL Flexible Server. Flagging that Cosmos’s partition-key design makes or breaks it is the senior caveat.

questions.q: How do you secure Azure Storage accounts for production?
questions.text: # Disable public access; require private connectivity: az storage account update -g rg -n acct --public-network-access Disabled az network private-endpoint create ... --group-id blob # private endpoint + DNS # Enforce: HTTPS only, min TLS 1.2, no shared-key (use Entra/RBAC): az storage account update -g rg -n acct --https-only true --min-tls-version TLS1_2 \\ --allow-shared-key-access false # Access via Entra RBAC (Managed Identity) + SAS with short expiry where needed Production storage hardening: disable public network access and reach the account via a Private Endpoint (with Private DNS) so traffic stays on the Azure backbone; enforce HTTPS and TLS 1.2+ ; and disable shared-key access in favour of Entra ID RBAC with Managed Identities — eliminating long-lived account keys that leak and never rotate. Where temporary delegated access is needed (e.g. uploads), use short-expiry, narrowly-scoped SAS tokens (ideally user-delegation SAS tied to Entra). Enable soft-delete/versioning for recovery and immutability/legal-hold where compliance requires. Encryption at rest is on by default (optionally with customer-managed keys). Interview tip: the high-impact moves are disabling public access (→ Private Endpoint) and disabling shared-key access (→ Entra RBAC/Managed Identity), because account keys are the classic leak. Add TLS enforcement, short-lived user-delegation SAS, and soft-delete/versioning. Leading with "kill the account keys, use identity" signals modern Azure security think

questions.q: How do Azure Storage redundancy options (LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS) differ and how do you choose?
questions.text: LRS: 3 copies in ONE datacenter (cheapest; DC failure = data loss) ZRS: 3 copies across availability ZONES in a region (survives a DC/zone loss) GRS: LRS + async copy to PAIRED REGION (regional DR; secondary not readable) GZRS: ZRS + async copy to paired region (zone + region resilience) RA-GRS / RA-GZRS: adds READ access to the secondary region Redundancy tiers trade durability/availability against cost. LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter — cheapest, but a datacenter loss loses data. ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in the region — survives a zone/datacenter failure. GRS adds asynchronous replication to the paired region for regional disaster recovery (secondary is not readable unless you fail over). GZRS combines zone redundancy with cross-region replication — the most resilient. The RA- variants make the secondary region readable, useful for read scale or regional read-availability. Choose by required resilience: ZRS for in-region HA, G(Z)RS for regional DR, RA- when you need read access to the secondary. Interview tip: map each to the failure it survives — LRS (none beyond disk), ZRS (zone/DC), GRS (region, no read), GZRS (zone+region), RA-* (adds secondary read). For production data you typically want at least ZRS (in-region resilience) and G(Z)RS for DR. Noting that GRS secondary is not readable until failover (unless RA-) is the detail people miss.

questions.q: How do Azure Reservations, Savings Plans, and Spot pricing differ, and when do you use each?
questions.text: Reservations: 1/3-yr commit to SPECIFIC VM size/region -> up to ~72% off baseline Savings Plans: 1/3-yr commit to hourly COMPUTE SPEND (flexible across SKUs/regions) Spot: spare capacity, ~60-90% off, evictable with short notice PAYG: on-demand, full price, no commitment These are the core cost levers. Reservations commit to a specific VM family/region for 1–3 years — deepest discount (up to ~72%) but least flexible (locked to that SKU/region). Savings Plans commit to an hourly compute spend rather than a specific SKU — slightly less discount but flexible across instance sizes and regions, ideal when your baseline is steady but the exact VM mix shifts. Spot uses spare capacity at 60–90% off but can be evicted on short notice — for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads (batch, CI, ML training). The strategy: cover predictable baseline with reservations/savings plans, run tolerant/bursty workloads on spot, and leave only true variability on pay-as-you-go. Interview tip: the decision frame is commitment vs flexibility vs interruptibility. Reservations (max discount, rigid SKU) for stable known shapes; Savings Plans (flexible spend commit) for steady-but-shifting compute; Spot for interruptible workloads. The portfolio answer — reservations/savings for baseline + spot for tolerant + PAYG for spikes — is what a FinOps-aware platform engineer says.

questions.q: How do you handle read scaling and caching for a database-backed service on Azure?
questions.text: # Read replicas (offload reads): # Azure SQL: active geo-replication / named replicas (readable secondaries) # PostgreSQL Flexible Server: read replicas # Cache hot data (Azure Cache for Redis): az redis create -g rg -n mycache --sku Premium --vm-size P1 # Patterns: cache-aside, write-through; set TTLs; guard against stampede Scale reads in two complementary ways. Read replicas offload read traffic from the primary: Azure SQL named replicas / geo-replication and PostgreSQL Flexible Server read replicas let read-heavy workloads (reporting, dashboards) hit secondaries while the primary handles writes — mind the small replication lag (eventual consistency on replicas). Caching with Azure Cache for Redis serves hot data from memory, dramatically cutting database load and latency. Common patterns: cache-aside (app checks cache, falls back to DB, populates cache) and write-through; always set sensible TTLs and protect against cache stampedes (e.g. request coalescing, jittered expiry) so a cold cache does not hammer the DB. Interview tip: two levers — read replicas (offload reads, accept replication lag / eventual consistency on the replica) and Redis caching (cache-aside pattern, TTLs, stampede protection). Naming the replication-lag trade-off and cache-stampede mitigation shows you have run these at scale, not just enabled them.

questions.q: How do you implement lifecycle management and tiering for cost-efficient blob storage?
questions.text: # Tiers: Hot (frequent), Cool (30+ days), Cold (90+), Archive (rare, hours to rehydrate) # Lifecycle policy moves/expires blobs automatically by age: # if baseBlob > 30 days -> tierToCool # if baseBlob > 90 days -> tierToArchive # if baseBlob > 365 days -> delete az storage account management-policy create --account-name acct --policy @policy.json Blob storage has access tiers priced for different access patterns: Hot (frequent access, higher storage cost, lower access cost), Cool and Cold (infrequent, lower storage cost, higher access/retrieval cost, minimum retention periods), and Archive (rarely accessed, cheapest storage, but data must be rehydrated over hours before reading). Lifecycle management policies automate this: rules move blobs to cooler tiers as they age and delete them past a retention threshold — e.g. logs go Hot → Cool at 30 days → Archive at 90 → deleted at a year. This matches storage cost to actual access patterns automatically, a major lever for data-heavy workloads. Interview tip: describe tiers by access pattern + the trade-off (cooler = cheaper storage but pricier/slower retrieval, Archive needs rehydration), then automate with lifecycle policies (age-based tier transitions + expiry). The Archive rehydration latency (hours) is the gotcha to mention — it disqualifies Archive for anything needing quick reads.

questions.q: How do you back up and restore data, and test DR, for production databases on Azure?
questions.text: # Azure SQL: automated backups + Point-In-Time Restore (PITR) within retention az sql db restore -g rg -s srv -n mydb --dest-name mydb-restored --time "2026-06-01T10:00:00Z" # Long-term retention (LTR) for compliance (weekly/monthly/yearly) # Cosmos DB: continuous backup + PITR; PostgreSQL: automated backups + PITR # DR test: restore to a copy, validate, document RTO/RPO actually achieved Managed Azure databases provide automated backups with point-in-time restore (PITR) within a configurable retention window — you can restore to any moment (e.g. just before a bad deploy or accidental delete). For compliance, long-term retention keeps weekly/monthly/yearly backups for years. Cosmos DB and PostgreSQL Flexible Server offer equivalent continuous-backup/PITR. The crucial discipline is testing restores : regularly restore to a copy, validate the data, and measure the actual RTO/RPO achieved against your targets — an untested backup is not a backup. Document the runbook so recovery under pressure is repeatable. Interview tip: automated backups + PITR + LTR is the baseline; the senior point is "test the restore and measure real RTO/RPO" — untested backups fail when you need them. Mention restoring to a copy (never over the prod DB) for validation, and tying retention/LTR to compliance requirements. The "untested backup isn’t a backup" line resonates.

questions.q: A team’s Azure bill spiked unexpectedly. Walk through investigating and controlling it.
questions.text: # 1. Cost Management: cost analysis grouped by service / resource group / tag # -> what jumped, when, and which resource/team owns it # 2. Cost anomaly alerts should have flagged it; check the spike onset # 3. Common causes: untagged orphans, over-provisioned SKUs, egress/data transfer, # forgotten dev resources, log ingestion blowout, autoscale runaway # 4. Controls: budgets+alerts, policy to require tags, rightsizing, reservations Investigate top-down in Azure Cost Management : open cost analysis and group by service, resource group, and tag to find what jumped, when , and who owns it . Correlate the onset with deployments or config changes. Common culprits: over-provisioned or accidentally-large SKUs, orphaned/untagged resources nobody owns, data egress / cross-region transfer , forgotten dev/test resources left running, log ingestion blowout (a chatty app flooding Log Analytics), or runaway autoscaling. Then control it: set budgets with alerts and anomaly detection so the next spike is caught early, enforce required tags via Azure Policy for accountability, rightsize, and apply reservations/savings plans to the stable baseline. Interview tip: method first — Cost Management grouped by service/RG/tag to localise the spike, then map to common causes (orphans, oversized SKUs, egress, log ingestion, autoscale). The preventive close (budgets + anomaly alerts + policy-enforced tagging for ownership) shows you turn a fire-drill into a standing control. Mentioning log-ingestion bl

questions.q: How do persistent volumes work on AKS, and how do you handle volume issues across zones?
questions.text: # CSI drivers provision PVs: Azure Disk (RWO) vs Azure Files (RWX) kubectl get storageclass # managed-csi (disk), azurefile-csi (files) # Azure Disk is ZONE-PINNED: a pod using it must schedule in the disk's zone # -> use zone-redundant storage class or topology-aware volume binding # volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer (bind disk in the pod's zone) AKS provisions persistent volumes through CSI drivers : Azure Disk (block, ReadWriteOnce — one pod) for databases/stateful pods, and Azure Files (SMB/NFS, ReadWriteMany — shared across pods) for shared content. The key cross-zone gotcha: a standard Azure Disk is pinned to a single zone , so a pod mounting it can only schedule in that zone — if that zone is unavailable or the scheduler wants another zone, the pod gets stuck Pending. Fixes: use WaitForFirstConsumer volume binding (provision the disk in the zone where the pod actually lands) and/or zone-redundant storage classes, and for cross-zone shared access prefer Azure Files (RWX). For HA databases, replicate at the data layer rather than relying on a single zonal disk. Interview tip: distinguish Azure Disk (RWO, zone-pinned ) from Azure Files (RWX, shareable), then nail the classic failure: a pod stuck Pending because its zonal disk’s zone does not match an available node. The fix — WaitForFirstConsumer binding and zone-aware/ zone-redundant storage — is the AKS-specific detail that shows real stateful-workload experience.

questions.q: How do you choose a Cosmos DB partition key and avoid hot partitions?
questions.text: # Good partition key: HIGH cardinality + EVEN access distribution # - good: /userId, /tenantId (if balanced), /deviceId # - bad: /status (few values), /date (today gets all writes = hot) # Symptoms of a bad key: 429 throttling on some partitions, uneven RU usage # Composite/synthetic keys to spread load when natural key is skewed Cosmos DB partitions data by the partition key , and each logical partition has a throughput (RU) and storage ceiling. A good key has high cardinality (many distinct values) and even access distribution so reads/writes spread across partitions — /userId or /tenantId (if balanced) work well. A poor key concentrates load: low-cardinality values ( /status ) or time-based keys ( /date , where today’s partition takes all writes) create hot partitions that throttle (HTTP 429) while others sit idle. When the natural key is skewed, use a synthetic/composite key (e.g. combine tenant + a hash suffix) to spread load. Partition key is effectively immutable, so getting it right up front is critical. Interview tip: the rule is high cardinality + even distribution; the anti-patterns are low-cardinality and time-based keys (today = hot partition). Symptoms: per-partition 429 throttling with uneven RU consumption. Mentioning synthetic/composite keys for skewed data and that the partition key is essentially immutable (design it correctly the first time) is the depth interviewers want.

questions.q: How do you allocate and chargeback shared AKS cluster costs to teams?
questions.text: # Shared cluster cost is opaque without allocation tooling: # - OpenCost / Kubecost: per-namespace/pod/label cost (compute + storage + network) # - map namespaces/labels -> teams; report showback or chargeback # Azure side: resource tags + Cost Management for non-K8s resources # Governance: require team/cost-center labels via Gatekeeper/Azure Policy A shared AKS cluster bills as a few VMs, hiding which team consumes what. Cost-allocation tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) attributes the node cost down to namespaces, workloads, and labels by measuring each pod’s resource requests/usage — producing per-team cost for compute, storage, and (with config) network. Map namespaces or team labels to owning teams, then publish either showback (visibility to drive behaviour) or chargeback (actual cross-charging). Enforce the required team/cost-center labels at admission (Gatekeeper/Azure Policy) so untagged workloads cannot escape allocation. Pair with Azure tags + Cost Management for the non-Kubernetes resources (databases, storage, networking). Interview tip: the core insight is that Kubernetes hides per-team cost until you add allocation (Kubecost/OpenCost mapping namespaces/labels → teams). Distinguish showback (visibility) from chargeback (cross-charging), and stress enforcing cost labels at admission so allocation is complete. This is a concrete FinOps-on-Kubernetes answer that platform interviewers value.

questions.q: How do you handle data residency, encryption, and compliance for Azure data services?
questions.text: # Residency: pin resources to compliant regions; Azure Policy 'allowed locations' # Encryption at rest: on by default; customer-managed keys (CMK) in Key Vault for control # Encryption in transit: enforce TLS 1.2+; private endpoints to avoid public paths # Compliance: Defender for Cloud regulatory dashboards (PCI/HIPAA/ISO/SOC2) Compliance for data services spans residency, encryption, and evidence. Data residency : keep data in approved regions — enforce with an Azure Policy "allowed locations" so no resource is created outside compliant geographies. Encryption at rest is on by default with Microsoft-managed keys; for regulatory control over the key lifecycle, use customer-managed keys (CMK) stored in Key Vault (you can rotate/revoke, controlling access to your own data). Encryption in transit : enforce TLS 1.2+ and use Private Endpoints so data never traverses public networks. For evidence , Defender for Cloud’s regulatory compliance dashboards continuously assess your estate against PCI/HIPAA/ISO/SOC2 and produce audit-ready reports. Interview tip: cover residency (policy-enforced allowed regions), encryption at rest (default + CMK when you must control keys), in transit (TLS + private endpoints), and continuous compliance evidence (Defender regulatory dashboards). The CMK point — customer-managed keys give you rotation/revocation control over your data’s encryption — is the nuance that signals real compliance work.

questions.q: How do you handle database connection management and resilience from AKS pods?
questions.text: # Use Managed Identity / Workload Identity (no DB passwords in pods) # Connection pooling: size pool to (replicas x pool) < DB max connections # Resilience: retry with exponential backoff + jitter on transient errors # Handle failover: reconnect logic; for Azure SQL use failover-group listener # PgBouncer sidecar/Deployment to multiplex for PostgreSQL at scale Robust DB access from AKS combines security, efficiency, and resilience. Auth : use Workload/Managed Identity so pods get tokens instead of storing DB passwords. Pooling : size connection pools with the replicas-×-pool-size-vs-DB-limit math in mind, and at scale front PostgreSQL with PgBouncer to multiplex. Resilience : implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient faults (Azure SQL throttling, brief failovers), and reconnection logic that handles failover — for Azure SQL, connect to the failover-group listener so the app does not need a new connection string when the primary moves regions. Validate connections on borrow and set sensible timeouts so a stuck DB does not cascade into pod-wide hangs. Interview tip: hit auth (Workload Identity, no stored passwords), pooling (the replicas×pool math + PgBouncer), and resilience (retry w/ backoff+jitter, failover-group listener for transparent reconnection). Mentioning connection validation and timeouts to prevent a slow DB from hanging all pods shows you have debugged cascading failures, not just happy-path connectivity.

questions.q: What is the FinOps operating model and how would you roll it out for an Azure platform?
questions.text: # FinOps phases (continuous loop): Inform -> Optimize -> Operate # Inform: tagging, cost allocation (Cost Mgmt + Kubecost), showback dashboards # Optimize: rightsizing, spot, reservations/savings plans, kill orphans # Operate: budgets+anomaly alerts, policy guardrails, regular cost reviews # Make engineers cost-aware: surface cost in PRs (Infracost), per-team dashboards FinOps is a cultural+operational practice giving engineering accountability for cloud cost, run as a continuous loop: Inform (visibility — consistent tagging, cost allocation via Cost Management and Kubecost for shared clusters, per-team showback dashboards), Optimize (rightsizing from real usage, spot for tolerant workloads, reservations/savings plans for baseline, eliminating orphaned resources), and Operate (budgets and anomaly alerts, policy guardrails like required tags and allowed SKUs, regular cross-functional cost reviews). Rollout: start by making cost visible and attributable (you cannot optimize what you cannot see), then drive optimization with engineers — surface cost in PRs (Infracost) and give teams dashboards so cost becomes a design input, not an afterthought. Interview tip: name the Inform→Optimize→Operate loop and stress that visibility/attribution comes first (tagging + allocation), because optimization without ownership stalls. The platform-engineering angle: embed cost into the developer workflow (Infracost in PRs, per-team dashboards, policy guardrails) so engineers self-serve cost-aware

questions.q: How do you migrate a database to Azure with minimal downtime?
questions.text: # Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) — online (minimal-downtime) mode: # 1. initial full load of source -> target # 2. continuous replication of ongoing changes (CDC) to keep target current # 3. validate target; brief cutover window when lag ~0 # 4. repoint app connection string -> target; decommission source Minimal-downtime database migration uses online migration (continuous replication) rather than a big-bang export/import. Azure Database Migration Service in online mode does an initial full load, then continuously replicates ongoing changes (change data capture) so the target stays in near-sync with the live source. You validate the target while the source still serves traffic, then take a brief cutover when replication lag approaches zero — stop writes momentarily, let the last changes drain, repoint the application connection string to the target, and decommission the source. Downtime shrinks to the seconds/minutes of cutover rather than the hours a full dump/restore would take. Plan rollback (keep the source intact until validated) and test the cutover beforehand. Interview tip: contrast online (DMS continuous replication → tiny cutover) with offline (dump/restore → long downtime). The minimal-downtime pattern is full-load + CDC + cutover-at-low-lag + connection repoint. Emphasising validation before cutover and keeping the source as rollback until verified shows you treat a migration as a reversible, tested operation.

questions.q: How do you architect for data durability and recovery across an Azure platform?
questions.text: # Layered durability: # - storage redundancy (ZRS/GZRS) for infra-level resilience # - DB automated backups + PITR + long-term retention # - app-data backups (Velero/Azure Backup for AKS PVs) # - immutable/soft-delete to defend against accidental + malicious deletion # - tested restores + documented RTO/RPO per data class Durable-by-design means layering protections and matching them to data criticality. Infrastructure : choose storage redundancy (ZRS for zone resilience, GZRS for region) appropriate to the data. Databases : automated backups with PITR plus long-term retention for compliance. Application/cluster data : back up AKS persistent volumes and Kubernetes state (Velero/Azure Backup), or rely on GitOps for manifests. Defence in depth against deletion : soft-delete, versioning, and immutability/legal-hold so neither accidents nor ransomware can permanently destroy data. Critically, define RTO/RPO per data class and test restores regularly — the architecture is only as good as the last successful recovery drill. Document runbooks so recovery is repeatable under pressure. Interview tip: present durability as layers (storage redundancy → DB backups/PITR → app/PV backups → immutability/soft-delete) tied to per-data-class RTO/RPO, with tested restores as the non-negotiable. Calling out immutability/soft-delete as ransomware/accident defence, and "tested restore or it doesn’t count," is the principal-level framing that goes beyond "we have backups."

questions.q: How do you set up GitHub Actions to deploy to AKS using OIDC (no stored secrets)?
questions.text: # 1. Create an Entra ID app + federated credential mapped to the GitHub repo: az ad app create --display-name github-deployer az ad app federated-credential create --id <APP_ID> --parameters '{ "name":"gh-main","issuer":"https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com", "subject":"repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main","audiences":["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]}' # 2. Grant the SP AKS + RBAC permissions (least privilege) az role assignment create --assignee <APP_ID> --role 'Azure Kubernetes Service Cluster User Role' --scope <AKS_ID> # 3. Workflow uses azure/login with id-token: write permission permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read } OIDC federation removes long-lived client secrets entirely: the GitHub Actions job presents a signed OIDC token, Azure verifies it against the federated credential (matched on issuer + subject = repo/branch), and issues a short-lived access token. The subject claim scopes which repo/branch/environment can assume the identity. The workflow needs id-token: write permission to request the OIDC token. No secret ever lives in GitHub.

questions.q: How do you implement progressive delivery (canary / blue-green) on AKS?
questions.text: # Argo Rollouts (canary with automated analysis): kubectl argo rollouts get rollout myapp --watch # Rollout spec: steps with traffic weights + analysis gates strategy: canary: steps: - setWeight: 10 - pause: {duration: 5m} # bake time - analysis: {templates: [{templateName: success-rate}]} # auto-abort on regression - setWeight: 50 - pause: {duration: 5m} # Flagger is the alternative (works with Istio/AGIC/NGINX + Prometheus metrics) Progressive delivery shifts traffic to the new version gradually while watching metrics, auto-rolling-back on regression. Argo Rollouts and Flagger are the two main tools on AKS: they integrate with a traffic provider (Istio add-on, AGIC, or NGINX) to split traffic and with Managed Prometheus to evaluate success-rate/latency. Blue-green keeps two full environments and flips traffic at once (instant rollback, double the resources); canary ramps gradually (smaller blast radius, slower). The key safety feature is the automated analysis gate that aborts the rollout if golden signals degrade.

questions.q: How do you manage Helm releases safely in a production AKS pipeline?
questions.text: helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart \\ --namespace prod --create-namespace \\ --values values-prod.yaml \\ --atomic --timeout 5m \\ --set image.tag=$GIT_SHA helm history myapp -n prod # see revision history helm rollback myapp 3 -n prod # roll back to a known-good revision helm diff upgrade myapp ./chart # (helm-diff plugin) preview changes --atomic is the production-critical flag: if the upgrade fails or times out, Helm automatically rolls back to the previous revision, so you never end up in a half-applied state. Pin the image tag to the immutable Git SHA (not latest ) for traceability and reproducible rollbacks. helm diff (plugin) previews exactly what will change before applying — the Helm equivalent of a Terraform plan. helm history + helm rollback give you fast, revision-based recovery.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to handle environment-specific config across dev/staging/prod on AKS?
questions.text: # Kustomize overlays (base + per-env patches): base/ # common manifests overlays/dev/ # kustomization.yaml patches base overlays/staging/ overlays/prod/ kubectl apply -k overlays/prod # Helm: one chart, per-env values files: helm upgrade --install app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml # Secrets per env: Key Vault (separate vault or scoped secrets) + CSI/ESO Two dominant patterns: Kustomize overlays (a shared base plus per-environment patches — no templating, declarative) and Helm values files (one chart, one values file per environment). Both keep a single source of truth for the common shape and isolate only what differs (replica counts, resource sizes, hostnames, feature flags). Environment-specific secrets come from separate Key Vaults (or scoped secrets) via the CSI driver or External Secrets Operator — never baked into the manifests. With GitOps, each environment maps to a path/branch the controller syncs.

questions.q: How do you secure the supply chain for container images deployed to AKS?
questions.text: # 1. Build + push to ACR; scan on push: az acr task create --name scan --image myapp:{{.Run.ID}} --context <git> --file Dockerfile # Microsoft Defender for Containers scans ACR images for CVEs # 2. Sign images (Notation / cosign): notation sign myregistry.azurecr.io/myapp@sha256:... # 3. Enforce signature + no-CVE at admission (Azure Policy / Ratify + Gatekeeper): kubectl get constrainttemplate # verify-image-signature constraint # 4. Only allow images from your ACR (Azure Policy: allowed registries) Defense in depth across the image lifecycle: scan images for vulnerabilities on push (Microsoft Defender for Containers / Trivy in CI), sign them (Notation or cosign) to prove provenance, and enforce at admission that only signed images from your trusted ACR with no critical CVEs can run — via Azure Policy for AKS (Gatekeeper) plus Ratify for signature verification. Pin by digest ( @sha256: ) not mutable tags. This closes the gap between "built securely" and "what actually runs in the cluster."

questions.q: How do you roll back a bad deployment on AKS quickly?
questions.text: # Native Kubernetes Deployment rollback: kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp -n prod kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp -n prod # to previous revision kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp -n prod --to-revision=5 # to a specific one kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod # watch it complete # Helm: helm rollback myapp <rev> -n prod # GitOps: git revert the manifest commit → Argo/Flux auto-syncs back The fastest mechanism depends on how you deploy. Plain Deployments keep a revision history, so kubectl rollout undo reverts to the prior ReplicaSet near-instantly. Helm uses helm rollback to a known-good revision. With GitOps , you git revert the offending manifest commit and the controller reconciles the cluster back — keeping the rollback auditable in Git. Always confirm with rollout status . The principle echoes Terraform: rollback is roll-forward to a previous known-good desired state.

questions.q: How do you manage database schema migrations safely during AKS deployments?
questions.text: # Run migrations as a separate, gated step — not in app startup: kubectl create job --from=cronjob/migrate migrate-$GIT_SHA -n prod # or an initContainer / Helm pre-upgrade hook: annotations: { "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade, "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5" } # Expand/contract pattern across deploys: # 1) add column (backward compatible) 2) deploy code using it # 3) backfill 4) later: drop old column Treat migrations as a distinct, gated pipeline step (a Job or Helm pre-upgrade hook), not something the app runs on startup — so a rolling deploy does not race multiple replicas trying to migrate. Use the expand/contract pattern so old and new app versions both work against the schema during the rollout: add the new structure first, deploy code, backfill, and only later remove the old — each as a separate, independently-rollbackable change. This is what makes zero-downtime deploys and safe rollbacks possible with a stateful database.

questions.q: How do you design Entra ID / RBAC for least privilege across many teams and subscriptions?
questions.text: # Management Group hierarchy mirrors org; policy + RBAC inherit down: Root MG → Platform MG / BU MGs → subscriptions (prod/nonprod) → RGs # Assign roles to Entra GROUPS, never individual users: az role assignment create --assignee-object-id <GROUP_ID> --assignee-principal-type Group \\ --role 'Contributor' --scope <RG_ID> # PIM for just-in-time elevation of privileged roles: # eligible (not active) assignments; activate with approval + time limit Structure subscriptions under a Management Group hierarchy that mirrors the org, so RBAC and Azure Policy inherit downward consistently. Assign roles to Entra ID groups (driven by your IdP/HR system), never to individuals — so joining/leaving a team automatically grants/revokes access everywhere. Default people to least privilege (Reader), grant Contributor narrowly at the right scope, and use Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for just-in-time, time-bound, approval-gated elevation of high-risk roles (Owner, User Access Administrator) instead of standing admin. Manage these assignments as code (Terraform/Bicep) for auditability.

questions.q: A pod on AKS needs to access Azure SQL without storing credentials. How do you set it up?
questions.text: # 1. Enable Workload Identity on the cluster (OIDC issuer + addon): az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity # 2. Create a user-assigned managed identity + federated credential to the K8s SA: az identity create -g rg -n app-mi az identity federated-credential create --identity-name app-mi -g rg \\ --issuer <OIDC_ISSUER_URL> --subject system:serviceaccount:prod:app-sa # 3. Grant the MI access to SQL (Entra-auth), annotate the ServiceAccount: # serviceAccount annotation: azure.workload.identity/client-id: <MI_CLIENT_ID> # 4. App uses DefaultAzureCredential → token → SQL (no password) Workload Identity federates a Kubernetes ServiceAccount with an Entra ID managed identity via OIDC. The pod’s projected SA token is exchanged for an Entra token, which authenticates to Azure SQL using Entra authentication — no connection-string password anywhere. Setup: enable the OIDC issuer + workload-identity add-on, create a managed identity with a federated credential whose subject is the SA, grant that identity SQL access, and annotate the SA with the identity’s client-id. In code, DefaultAzureCredential() transparently picks up the workload identity. This is the modern, secret-less replacement for the deprecated pod-managed-identity (aad-pod-identity).

questions.q: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud and how does it fit an AKS security posture?
questions.text: # Enable Defender plans: az security pricing create --name Containers --tier Standard az security pricing create --name KeyVaults --tier Standard # Defender for Containers provides: # - image vulnerability scanning (ACR + running images) # - runtime threat detection (suspicious exec, crypto-mining, etc.) # - K8s hardening recommendations (CIS benchmark) # Secure Score tracks posture; export findings to SIEM (Sentinel) Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the CNAPP/CSPM layer: it continuously assesses your security posture against benchmarks (CIS, regulatory), surfaces misconfigurations with a Secure Score , and — with Defender for Containers — scans images for CVEs, detects runtime threats (anomalous process execution, crypto-mining, reverse shells in pods), and recommends AKS hardening. Findings flow into Microsoft Sentinel (SIEM) for correlation and response. It complements (does not replace) admission-time controls like Azure Policy/Gatekeeper: Defender detects and recommends, Policy prevents.

questions.q: How do you implement per-team / per-namespace cost allocation (showback) on AKS?
questions.text: # 1. Tag resources for cost attribution (team, env, cost-center): az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --tags team=payments env=prod costcenter=cc-123 # 2. AKS Cost Analysis add-on (OpenCost-based) for namespace-level breakdown: az aks update -g rg -n prod-aks --enable-cost-analysis # 3. Azure Cost Management: group by tag, set budgets + alerts: az consumption budget create --budget-name payments-monthly --amount 5000 ... # 4. OpenCost / Kubecost for in-cluster pod-level cost Cluster costs are shared, so allocation needs a breakdown inside the cluster plus tagging outside . The AKS Cost Analysis add-on (built on OpenCost) attributes node cost to namespaces/workloads by their resource requests, giving per-team showback. Combine with consistent resource tags (team/env/cost-center) so Azure Cost Management can group spend, and set per-team budgets with alerts . For finer pod-level granularity and chargeback, OpenCost/Kubecost map CPU/memory/storage/network to teams. The platform move: make this self-service so teams see their own spend and own optimizing it.

questions.q: AKS spend spiked unexpectedly this month. How do you investigate and bring it down?
questions.text: # 1. Where did it grow? Cost Management cost analysis, group by service/resource: az consumption usage list --start-date 2026-05-01 --end-date 2026-05-31 -o table # 2. Common culprits: # - Cluster Autoscaler scaled out (a workload over-requesting CPU/mem) # - egress / cross-AZ / cross-region data transfer # - orphaned managed disks / public IPs / load balancers from deleted workloads # - logging volume into Log Analytics (ingestion is billed by GB) # 3. Right-size requests, add Spot pools, set Log Analytics daily cap Start in Azure Cost Management to find what grew (group by service and resource). Frequent AKS cost spikes come from: the Cluster Autoscaler adding nodes because a workload over-requests resources (fix the requests), a surge in data transfer (egress, cross-AZ chatter), orphaned resources left by deleted workloads (unattached disks, idle public IPs/load balancers), and Log Analytics ingestion (logs are billed per GB — a chatty app or debug logging can dominate the bill). Remediate with right-sizing, Spot node pools for tolerant workloads, a Log Analytics daily cap, and a sweep for orphaned resources. Then add a budget alert so the next spike is caught early.

questions.q: How do you decide between Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, and Spot for AKS compute?
questions.text: # Reserved VM Instances: 1 or 3 year, specific VM family/region, up to ~72% off # Azure Savings Plans: 1 or 3 year hourly $ commitment, flexible across VM types/regions # Spot: up to ~90% off, evictable with 30s notice, no SLA # Typical mix for an AKS estate: # baseline system + steady workloads → Reserved / Savings Plan # bursty / batch / fault-tolerant → Spot node pools # unpredictable spikes → on-demand Match the commitment to the workload’s predictability. Reserved Instances give the deepest discount but lock you to a VM family/region — best for a stable, known baseline. Savings Plans trade a little discount for flexibility (an hourly $ commitment that applies across VM types/regions) — better when your instance mix evolves. Spot is cheapest but evictable — only for fault-tolerant, stateless, or batch workloads with PodDisruptionBudgets. The mature AKS pattern blends all three: cover the steady baseline with a Savings Plan/Reservations, run tolerant workloads on Spot pools, and leave a thin on-demand layer for unpredictable bursts.

questions.q: How do you define and track SLOs for a service running on AKS?
questions.text: # Pick SLIs from golden signals (availability, latency): # Availability SLI (PromQL): good requests / total requests sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) # Latency SLI: fraction of requests under threshold histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) # SLO: 99.9% availability over 28d → error budget = 0.1% # Alert on BURN RATE, not raw threshold (multiwindow: fast + slow burn) Define SLIs (measurable signals like success ratio and latency-under-threshold) from Managed Prometheus, set an SLO target (e.g. 99.9% over 28 days), and derive the error budget (the allowed unreliability). The key practice is alerting on burn rate — how fast you are consuming the error budget — using multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts (a fast-burn alert pages immediately on a severe spike; a slow-burn alert warns on gradual erosion). This pages on user-impacting problems while suppressing noise, and the error budget becomes the objective input to the velocity-vs-reliability decision (freeze risky changes when the budget is spent).

questions.q: How do you implement distributed tracing for microservices on AKS?
questions.text: # Instrument with OpenTelemetry (vendor-neutral SDK + auto-instrumentation): # app emits spans → OTel Collector (DaemonSet/Deployment) → backend # Backends: Application Insights, or Managed Grafana + Tempo/Jaeger # Service mesh (Istio add-on) can emit spans without code changes, # but app must propagate trace context headers (traceparent / b3) # Correlate traces ↔ logs ↔ metrics via trace_id OpenTelemetry is the standard: instrument services with the OTel SDK (or auto-instrumentation), emit spans to an OTel Collector running in-cluster, and export to a backend — Azure Application Insights (native APM) or Grafana Tempo/Jaeger. The critical detail is context propagation : each service must forward the trace headers ( traceparent ) so spans stitch into one end-to-end trace; even an Istio sidecar emitting spans relies on the app passing the headers through. The big win is correlating traces with logs and metrics by trace_id , so you can jump from a latency spike to the exact slow span across services.

questions.q: Intermittent 5xx errors appear only under load on AKS. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: # 1. Confirm pattern: do 5xx correlate with traffic/HPA scaling events? kubectl get hpa -n prod -w # is it scaling fast enough? # 2. CPU throttling (silent killer under load): rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m]) > 0 # 3. Connection / pool exhaustion to DB or upstream: # DB max_connections hit; app connection pool too small # 4. Readiness flapping under load → pods pulled from Endpoints kubectl get events -n prod | grep -i unhealthy # 5. Node-level: conntrack table full, SNAT port exhaustion (egress) Load-only 5xx point to a resource that saturates under pressure. Work the likely causes: CPU throttling (CFS limits choke the app silently — check throttled-seconds; often the fix is higher/removed CPU limits), HPA scaling too slowly (requests pile up before new pods arrive — tune target + scale-up behavior, or pre-scale), connection-pool / DB max-connections exhaustion , readiness probes flapping under load (pods get yanked from Endpoints, concentrating load on the rest), and at node level SNAT/conntrack exhaustion for high outbound connection counts. Correlate the 5xx timeline with scaling events and golden signals to localize which one it is, then load-test the fix.

questions.q: An AKS cluster upgrade is stuck or failing. How do you handle it?
questions.text: az aks show -g rg -n prod-aks --query provisioningState # Failed / Upgrading? kubectl get nodes # mixed versions? a node stuck draining? kubectl describe node <stuck> # cordoned, pods not evicting? # common blocker: a PodDisruptionBudget that can't be satisfied blocks drain kubectl get pdb -A # retry the upgrade (idempotent), or upgrade control plane and node pools separately: az aks upgrade -g rg -n prod-aks --control-plane-only az aks nodepool upgrade -g rg --cluster-name prod-aks -n workers --kubernetes-version 1.30 AKS upgrades go control-plane-first, then node pools, draining nodes one at a time. The most common stall is a node that cannot drain because a PodDisruptionBudget can never be satisfied (e.g. minAvailable equals replica count), or a pod with no controller / long terminationGracePeriod. Diagnose with provisioningState , node versions, and PDBs. Fixes: relax the blocking PDB, ensure replicas can tolerate one-node disruption, then retry (the operation is idempotent). Upgrading the control plane and node pools separately (and one pool at a time) isolates failures and limits blast radius. Always upgrade non-prod first and stay within the supported version skew.

questions.q: Capstone: design the production readiness checklist for a new service going live on AKS.
questions.text: Reliability: liveness+readiness+startup probes; resource requests/limits; PDB; multi-AZ; HPA Rollout: immutable image by digest; canary/blue-green; --atomic Helm; tested rollback Security: Workload Identity (no secrets); Key Vault CSI; signed images; NetworkPolicy; non-root Networking: Private Endpoints for data; NSGs; ingress + TLS; WAF if internet-facing Observability: golden-signal dashboards; SLOs + burn-rate alerts; structured logs; tracing Data: backups + tested restore; expand/contract migrations; connection-pool sizing Cost: right-sized requests; Spot where tolerant; tags for showback; budget alert Ops: runbook; on-call + escalation; capacity/load test; chaos/failure drill A production-readiness review is the staff-level synthesis of everything: reliability (correct probes, requests/limits, PodDisruptionBudgets, multi-AZ spread, autoscaling), safe rollout (immutable digests, progressive delivery, atomic deploys, a tested rollback), security (secret-less Workload Identity, Key Vault integration, signed images enforced at admission, NetworkPolicies, non-root containers), networking (Private Endpoints for data, ingress TLS, WAF when exposed), observability (golden-signal dashboards, SLOs with burn-rate alerts, logs, tracing), data (backups with tested restores, expand/contract migrations), cost (right-sizing, Spot, tagging, budgets), and operational readiness (runbook, on-call, load and failure testing). The signal interviewers want: you treat "going live" as a deliberat

questions.q: What is the difference between Azure RBAC roles and Microsoft Entra roles, and where does each apply?
questions.text: Azure RBAC controls access to Azure resources (subscriptions, resource groups, VMs, storage) using role assignments at a scope. Entra roles control the identity directory itself: users, groups, apps, Conditional Access. They are separate systems with separate assignment points. az role assignment create --assignee <id> --role 'Contributor' --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/app-rg az role assignment list --assignee <id> --all -o table az rest --method get --url https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/directoryRoles Interview tip: Mention the elevate-access toggle for Global Administrators, which is the bridge between the two worlds, and that it should be rare and audited.

questions.q: System-assigned versus user-assigned managed identities: when do you use each?
questions.text: A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and deleted with it. A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to many resources and survives their deletion. Both give tokens without secrets. az identity create -g app-rg -n web-uami az vm identity assign -g app-rg -n vm1 --identities web-uami az role assignment create --assignee-object-id <principalId> --role 'Storage Blob Data Reader' --scope <storage-id> Interview tip: User-assigned identities let you pre-create role assignments before the resource exists, which avoids deployment ordering problems.

questions.q: Explain Azure Policy effects such as Audit, Deny, Modify and DeployIfNotExists, and how you roll out a new policy safely.
questions.text: Audit flags non-compliance only. Deny blocks the request. Modify adds or changes properties like tags. DeployIfNotExists deploys a related resource, such as diagnostic settings, when missing.
