Worked example: (illustrative) " S: A major customer faced intermittent data export failures across three teams. T: I volunteered as the owner. A: I gathered evidence, coordinated the teams, gave the customer regular updates and verified the fix with them. R: Resolved in a week; the customer sent a thank-you."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you made a long-term investment that paid off later.
questions.text: STAR cues: S — the situation and the cost of the investment. T — your decision to invest. A — how you justified and executed it. R — the later payoff. What to demonstrate: Long-term thinking and persuasion. Show: You explained the future benefit and measured the return. Trap: Claiming credit for luck. Worked example: (illustrative) " S: I pushed for infrastructure as code before it was urgent. T: I believed it would pay back in reliability and speed. A: I proposed a gradual migration, started with new services, and wrote modules and guides. R: A year later we rebuilt an environment in an hour after a failure."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you mentored someone who later outgrew your guidance.
questions.text: STAR cues: S — the mentee and their goals. T — your role as mentor. A — how you supported and adapted. R — their growth and your learning. What to demonstrate: Generosity and growth mindset. Show: You helped them find their own path and celebrated their success. Trap: Taking credit or holding them back. Worked example: (illustrative) " S: A junior engineer wanted to become a strong systems engineer. T: I mentored them for a year. A: I set goals together, gave stretch tasks, reviewed work, and connected them to specialists as they advanced. R: They became the team's go-to for a subsystem and later taught me."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to correct a mistake in front of others.
questions.text: STAR cues: S — the mistake and the audience. T — your decision to speak up. A — how you corrected it and framed it. R — reaction and learning. What to demonstrate: Integrity and composure. Show: You corrected promptly and plainly, without excuses. Trap: Hiding it or over-dramatising. Worked example: (illustrative) " S: I presented an incorrect capacity number to leadership. T: I noticed the error afterwards. A: I emailed a correction the same day, explained the cause and the revised conclusion. R: Leaders appreciated the transparency and the decision was unaffected."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you used the error budget or SLOs to guide a prioritisation decision.
questions.text: STAR cues: S — the feature pressure and the reliability data. T — your responsibility for reliability. A — how you used SLO data to inform the decision. R — outcome. What to demonstrate: Data-informed trade-offs between reliability and features. Show: You presented budget data and proposed a clear action. Trap: Using SLOs as a weapon. Worked example: (illustrative) " S: The error budget for the quarter was nearly exhausted with a feature launch planned. T: I advised on whether to proceed. A: I showed the budget burn, recommended a staged rollout behind a flag and a pause on risky changes. R: The launch went well with no further budget loss."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you led a post-incident cleanup that took months and kept it on track.
questions.text: STAR cues: S — the incident and the list of follow-ups. T — you owned the closure. A — tracking, prioritising, reporting. R — completion and benefits. What to demonstrate: Follow-through and visibility. Show: You broke work into milestones and reported progress regularly. Trap: Letting actions fade. Worked example: (illustrative) " S: A major outage produced twenty follow-up actions. T: I was assigned to drive them to completion. A: I prioritised by risk reduction, assigned owners, held a biweekly review and reported to leadership. R: All critical actions closed within a quarter and a repeat outage did not occur."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you learned from a near miss that never became an incident.
questions.text: STAR cues: S — the near miss and how you noticed it. T — your decision to investigate. A — analysis and actions taken. R — improvement. What to demonstrate: Learning from weak signals. Show: You treated it as a learning opportunity and fixed the systemic cause. Trap: Ignoring it because nothing broke. Worked example: (illustrative) " S: A deployment almost wiped a production config due to a wrong environment variable. T: I caught it in review minutes before. A: I wrote a short near-miss review, added environment validation and a confirmation guard. R: The guard blocked a similar mistake months later."

questions.q: What is CI/CD — difference between continuous integration, delivery, and deployment?
questions.text: CI: merge + build + test on every commit (catch integration bugs early) CD (Delivery): artifact is always releasable; deploy is a manual trigger CD (Deployment): every passing commit auto-deploys to production CI catches bugs when they are cheap to fix. Continuous Delivery ensures the pipeline always produces a deployable artifact. Continuous Deployment removes all manual gates. Most teams use CI + Delivery with a manual production gate as the sweet spot. DORA metrics: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, MTTR. Elite teams deploy multiple times/day with under 1 hour lead time. Your CI/CD design directly determines these numbers.

questions.q: What is an immutable artifact — why do you never rebuild for production?
questions.text: docker build -t myapp:${GITHUB_SHA} . # tag = git commit SHA docker push registry/myapp:${GITHUB_SHA} # Same image promoted through all stages: registry/myapp:abc1234 → staging → production (never rebuilt) docker tag registry/myapp:$SHA registry/myapp:v1.2.3 # tag on release Build once, deploy everywhere. Never rebuild for production — different environment, compiler version, or timestamp can produce a different binary. The image that passed staging tests is exactly the binary deployed to production. Use Git SHA as the image tag for traceability: any deployed image maps directly to its source commit.

questions.q: How do you structure secrets in CI/CD pipelines — what are the best practices?
questions.text: # GitHub Actions: repository secrets (encrypted) env: {API_KEY: "${{ secrets.API_KEY }}"} # GCP Workload Identity Federation (no keys at all): - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2 with: workload_identity_provider: projects/123/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/pool/providers/github service_account: deploy@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com Hierarchy: hardcoded (never) → env var in CI settings (basic) → secrets manager (good) → Workload Identity/OIDC (best — no static credentials). Workload Identity Federation: GitHub OIDC token exchanges for a short-lived GCP access token. No service account key files anywhere. This is the production standard for GitHub Actions + GCP pipelines.

questions.q: How does GitHub Actions work — workflows, jobs, and steps?
questions.text: on: push: {branches: [main]} pull_request: {branches: [main]} push: {tags: ["v*.*.*"]} jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: make test deploy: needs: test environment: production # requires manual approval Workflows trigger on events. Jobs run in parallel by default — use needs: for ordering. environments add manual approval gates and environment-specific secrets. Matrix builds run the same job across multiple configs (Node 18/20/22) simultaneously. Actions are reusable steps (uses:).

questions.q: How do you implement a full GitHub Actions pipeline for a containerised app?
questions.text: jobs: ci: # runs on every PR steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: make lint test - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master # CVE scan deploy-staging: # runs on merge to main needs: ci if: github.ref == "refs/heads/main" steps: - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2 # Workload Identity - run: docker push && update GitOps manifests repo deploy-production: # runs on semver tag if: startsWith(github.ref, "refs/tags/v") environment: production # manual approval gate PR → CI (lint, test, build, scan) — no deploy. Merge to main → staging deploy automatically. Tag push (v1.2.3) → production with manual approval. Build the image once in the CI job, reference the same digest in deploy jobs. Environment protection rules block production until a required reviewer approves.

questions.q: How do you use dependency caching and matrix builds to speed up pipelines?
questions.text: strategy: matrix: node: [18, 20, 22] fail-fast: false # Dependency caching: - uses: actions/cache@v4 with: path: ~/.npm key: npm-${{ hashFiles("**/package-lock.json") }} restore-keys: npm- # Docker layer caching: - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: cache-from: type=gha cache-to: type=gha,mode=max Matrix builds run N jobs simultaneously — test 3 Node versions in the same CI time as one. Cache key = hash of lock files — invalidated only when dependencies change. Docker layer cache reuses unchanged layers. These two optimisations alone typically reduce pipeline time by 70-80% for Node.js or Python projects.

questions.q: How does Google Cloud Build work — how do you write a cloudbuild.yaml?
questions.text: steps: - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker args: [build, -t, IMAGE:$SHORT_SHA, .] - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker args: [push, IMAGE:$SHORT_SHA] - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/gke-deploy args: [run, --filename=k8s/, --cluster=prod, --location=us-central1] options: {machineType: E2_HIGHCPU_8, logging: CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY} Steps run sequentially (use waitFor for parallel). Built-in substitutions: $PROJECT_ID, $SHORT_SHA (7-char commit SHA), $BRANCH_NAME, $TAG_NAME. Triggers connect to GitHub repos on push, PR, or tag. The Cloud Build service account needs IAM permissions for every GCP resource it accesses (Artifact Registry, GKE, Secret Manager).

questions.q: How do you integrate Cloud Build with Artifact Registry and Binary Authorization?
questions.text: # Build and push to Artifact Registry: - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker args: [push, us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/repo/app:$SHORT_SHA] # Container Analysis scans automatically on push # Attest after scan passes: - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/gcloud args: [container, binauthz, attestations, sign-and-create, --artifact-url, DIGEST, --attestor, vuln-scan-passed, --keyversion, KMS_KEY] # Binary Authorization on GKE rejects unattested images Supply chain: Cloud Build → push to Artifact Registry → Container Analysis auto-scans → if no critical CVEs, sign image digest with KMS key → attestation created → GKE admission controller verifies attestation before running pod. Unsigned images are rejected at the cluster level. This is SLSA Level 3 for GCP-native pipelines.

questions.q: How does ArgoCD implement GitOps — what is the sync loop?
questions.text: argocd app create myapp --repo https://github.com/org/manifests \ --path apps/myapp/overlays/prod \ --sync-policy automated --self-heal --prune argocd app sync myapp # manual sync argocd app diff myapp # what would change argocd app rollback myapp 3 # rollback to revision 3 ArgoCD continuously reconciles cluster state with the Git manifests repo. Every 3 minutes (or on webhook) it compares desired state (Git) with actual state (cluster). auto-sync=true → applies changes automatically. self-heal=true → reverses manual kubectl changes. prune=true → deletes resources removed from Git. Result: Git is the only way to change cluster state. Rollback = git revert in the manifests repo.

questions.q: What is the App-of-Apps pattern — how do you bootstrap a cluster with ArgoCD?
questions.text: # Root app manages child Application CRDs: argocd app create root-app --repo https://github.com/org/manifests --path cluster/apps cluster/apps/ monitoring.yaml # Application → monitoring stack ingress.yaml # Application → ingress-nginx myapp.yaml # Application → myapp manifests # Apply root-app once → ArgoCD manages everything else # ApplicationSet for multi-cluster/environment generation Bootstrap a new cluster: apply the root app, ArgoCD installs everything else. Entire cluster config is in Git — any new cluster is bootstrapped identically. ApplicationSet generates Applications dynamically from templates (one template for all environments, or all clusters in a fleet). This is how platform teams manage dozens of clusters with a single GitOps repo.

questions.q: How do you handle secrets in GitOps — what integrates with ArgoCD?
questions.text: # External Secrets Operator (recommended for GCP): kubectl get externalsecret db-password # syncs Secret Manager → K8s Secret # Sealed Secrets (encrypt in Git): kubeseal --fetch-cert --controller-name sealed-secrets kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=pass=mysecret \ --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubeseal -o yaml > sealed-secret.yaml git add sealed-secret.yaml # safe to commit encrypted # Vault Agent Injector: vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true" # injects secret as pod file Never commit plain Kubernetes Secrets (base64 is not encryption). External Secrets Operator: secrets in GCP Secret Manager, ESO syncs into K8s Secrets — never in Git. Sealed Secrets: encrypted in Git, cluster-specific key, simpler ops. Vault: most powerful, most complex, handles dynamic credentials. For GCP + GitOps: ESO + Secret Manager is the production standard.

questions.q: What types of tests belong in CI — how do you keep pipelines under 10 minutes?
questions.text: Unit tests: < 2 min — every commit (fast, isolated) Integration tests: 5-10 min — against real dependencies (DB, cache) Contract tests: < 5 min — API contracts between services E2E / smoke: 10-20 min — post-deploy on staging (not blocking PR) # Speed techniques: pytest -x -q -n auto # parallel, fail-fast jest --findRelatedTests # only tests for changed files docker compose up -d db redis # real deps for integration Keep PR pipeline under 10 minutes — developers abandon longer pipelines. Parallelize tests (pytest-xdist, jest --maxWorkers). Fail fast (-x). Split slow E2E into a post-merge pipeline. The test pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, minimal E2E.

questions.q: How do you implement shift-left security in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.text: # Pre-commit: detect-secrets, lint, basic SAST # CI pipeline: trivy image myapp:$SHA --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL # container CVE scan npm audit --audit-level=high # dependency audit checkov -d terraform/ # IaC misconfiguration tflint --recursive # Terraform lint # GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS): - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3 # SAST Shift-left: find security issues earlier when cheaper to fix. Pre-commit (seconds), CI (minutes), staging (hours), production (expensive). Failing CI on CRITICAL CVEs prevents known vulnerabilities from reaching production. IaC scanning catches misconfigured infrastructure before it is deployed. Cost of a security fix grows 10x at each stage.

questions.q: How do you design a multi-environment pipeline with promotion gates?
questions.text: PR open → CI (lint, test, scan) — no deployment Merge main → auto-deploy dev → smoke tests Tag v* → auto-deploy staging → integration tests → manual gate Approve → deploy production → smoke → monitor 30min # GitHub Actions environment protection: environment: production protection_rules: required_reviewers: [tech-lead, sre-team] Build once, promote the same image through environments. Each gate validates the artifact is safe for the next stage. Dev: fast feedback. Staging: full integration + performance baseline. Production: manual approval + automated canary. If staging tests fail, the artifact does not proceed. The promotion decision is based on data (test results, metrics), not opinion.

questions.q: How do you handle database migrations in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.text: # Init container (migration before new pods start): initContainers: - name: migrate image: myapp:$VERSION command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"] # Pre-deploy Kubernetes Job: kubectl apply -f migration-job.yaml kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/db-migration --timeout=5m kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml # only after migration succeeds # Expand-contract for zero-downtime migrations: 1. Add nullable column 2. Deploy (writes both) 3. Backfill 4. Deploy (reads new) 5. Drop old column Never run migrations in app startup — multiple replicas race. Init containers or pre-deploy Jobs run once, sequentially. Expand-contract ensures both old and new app versions work with the same schema simultaneously — required for rolling deployments. Always test migration on a production data snapshot in staging first.

questions.q: How do you implement rollback in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.text: # Fast: kubectl rollout undo (seconds) kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp --to-revision=3 # Safe: GitOps revert (auditable, goes through pipeline) git revert HEAD --no-edit && git push origin main # ArgoCD auto-syncs # Automated: Argo Rollouts analysis template kubectl argo rollouts abort myapp # manual abort # Redeploy previous tag: kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=registry/myapp:v1.2.2 GitOps revert is the production standard — creates audit trail, goes through the normal pipeline, tests run, visible to the team. Automated rollback (Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate): if error rate crosses threshold within 5 minutes of deploy, rollback automatically with no human required. This is the highest-maturity deployment safety mechanism.

questions.q: How do you monitor ArgoCD and alert on sync failures?
questions.text: # Key Prometheus alerts: argocd_app_health_status{health_status="Degraded"} > 0 argocd_app_sync_status{sync_status="OutOfSync"} > 0 argocd_app_sync_total{phase="Failed"} # rate increasing # Check app status: argocd app list argocd app get myapp kubectl get applications -n argocd -o wide Alert on Degraded health (app not running), OutOfSync for more than 30 minutes (sync may have failed silently), and increasing sync failure rate. ArgoCD exposes a Prometheus metrics endpoint. Integrate ArgoCD notifications to Slack for deployment success/failure messages in the team channel — this replaces manual deploy status checking.

questions.q: CI passes but deployments fail in production — how do you debug the gap?
questions.text: # Verify correct image is deployed: kubectl get deployment myapp -o jsonpath=".spec.template.spec.containers[0].image" # Check env vars in production: kubectl exec myapp-pod -- env | sort # Check rollout events: kubectl describe deployment myapp | grep -A10 Conditions kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n production | tail -20 # Pod logs after deploy: kubectl logs -l app=myapp --since=10m | grep -i error Common gaps: secrets present in CI but missing in production (not created as K8s Secrets), resource limits too low (CI runs without limits), network policies blocking production connections, readiness probe timeout too short (production dependencies are slower than CI). Check each systematically rather than guessing.

questions.q: A CI pipeline takes 45 minutes — how do you find and fix the bottleneck?
questions.text: # Check step timing in GitHub Actions workflow run UI # Most common bottlenecks: 1. No caching: npm install / pip install every run (5-15 min) 2. Docker build without layer cache (10-20 min) 3. Sequential jobs that could be parallel 4. Full test suite when only affected tests needed 5. Shallow clone not used (full git history download) # Fixes: actions/cache@v4 for dependencies cache-from: type=gha for Docker layers fetch-depth: 1 for shallow clone Profile before optimising — look at GitHub Actions step timings. Usually one step accounts for 80% of the time. Dependency caching alone often reduces pipeline from 20 minutes to 3 minutes. Parallelise independent jobs (lint + test + security scan run simultaneously). The 10-minute target for PR pipelines is achievable for most services with proper caching.

questions.q: How do you use reusable workflows and composite actions for pipeline standardisation?
questions.text: # Reusable workflow (.github/workflows/deploy.yaml): on: workflow_call: inputs: environment: {type: string, required: true} secrets: GCP_WIF_PROVIDER: {required: true} # Caller: jobs: deploy: uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yaml with: {environment: production} secrets: inherit Reusable workflows: define deploy-to-gke once, call it from 10 service repos. Composite actions: bundle multiple steps (setup-gcp, setup-docker) into one action. For a platform team managing many service repos, reusable workflows enforce pipeline standards without managing each repo individually. Teams get consistent CI/CD by convention.

questions.q: What is a feature flag — how does it decouple deployment from release?
questions.text: # Simple env var flag: if os.getenv("ENABLE_NEW_PAYMENT_FLOW") == "true": return new_payment_flow(request) return legacy_payment_flow(request) # Managed (LaunchDarkly / GrowthBook / Flagsmith): if ld_client.variation("new-payment-flow", user, False): return new_payment_flow(request) # Gradual rollout: 1% users → 10% → 50% → 100% # Instant rollback: flip flag off — no deployment needed Feature flags decouple deployment (code in production) from release (users see it). Merge incomplete features behind a flag — enables trunk-based development without long-lived branches. Gradual rollout to 1%, monitor metrics, increase. Instant rollback: disable the flag in seconds, no deployment required. Also enables A/B testing and canary releases without Kubernetes traffic splitting complexity.

questions.q: How do you implement contract testing between microservices?
questions.text: # Pact: consumer-driven contract testing # Consumer defines expected interactions: pact.given("user exists").upon_receiving("GET /users/123") .will_respond_with(200, body={"id":123, "name":"Alice"}) # Provider verifies it satisfies all consumer contracts: pact verify --provider=payments-api --pact-url=pact-broker/contracts.json Contract tests catch API breaking changes before deployment without needing both services running. Much faster than E2E tests. The consumer defines what it expects, the provider verifies it can satisfy those expectations. Essential in microservice architectures where teams develop services independently. Catches "provider broke consumer without knowing" — the most common integration failure mode.

questions.q: How do you prevent secrets from leaking in CI/CD pipeline output?
questions.text: # Mask secrets immediately in GitHub Actions: echo "::add-mask::$SECRET" # masks in all subsequent output # Never echo secrets: echo $SECRET # BAD — visible in logs # Docker build: use --secret (not build args): docker build --secret id=token,env=GITHUB_TOKEN . # not in image history # Scan logs for accidental exposure: gitleaks detect --source . --verbose Common leak vectors: echo in debug scripts, error messages printing full environment, curl with Authorization headers in verbose mode, Docker build args (visible in image history). Use --secret flag for sensitive values in Docker builds — they do not persist in image layers. Use Workload Identity Federation to eliminate static credential files entirely — nothing to leak.

questions.q: How do you measure CI/CD pipeline performance — what are the key metrics?
questions.text: # DORA metrics: Deployment frequency: how often do you deploy to production? Lead time for changes: commit to production time (hours vs days) Change failure rate: % of deploys causing an incident MTTR: how fast do you recover from failure? # Pipeline-specific metrics: PR cycle time PR open → merge CI pass rate % of pipeline runs that succeed Pipeline P95 duration 95th percentile build time Cache hit rate % of builds using cached deps Elite teams: deploy multiple times/day, <1 hour lead time, <5% change failure rate, <1 hour MTTR. If lead time is days, the bottleneck is usually manual approval gates, slow test suites, or large PRs. Track these in a dashboard and treat pipeline improvements as engineering work, not housekeeping.

questions.q: How do you debug a flaky CI test — passes locally, fails intermittently in CI?
questions.text: # Common causes: 1. Timing (sleep() instead of wait_until()) 2. Port conflicts in parallel test runs 3. Shared mutable state between tests (test pollution) 4. External service dependencies (network timeouts) 5. Resource contention on CI runner (CPU throttling) # Debug: run the test 10 times in isolation pytest tests/test_payment.py -v --count=10 # Replace sleep with polling: wait_until(lambda: service.ready(), timeout=30) @pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=3) # short-term quarantine Flaky tests erode trust in CI — engineers start ignoring failures. Track flakiness rate per test (failures/runs), prioritise high-flakiness tests. Short-term: retry logic. Long-term: fix root cause. Never leave a flaky test untracked — it will eventually mask a real failure at the worst possible time.

questions.q: How do you optimise Cloud Build for speed and cost?
questions.text: # Faster machine type: options: {machineType: E2_HIGHCPU_8} # 8 vCPU, 4x cost but 6-8x faster # Docker layer caching via Artifact Registry: - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker args: [build, --cache-from, IMAGE:latest, -t, IMAGE:$SHORT_SHA, .] # Parallel steps: - id: test waitFor: [build] - id: scan waitFor: [build] # runs in parallel with test Cloud Build billing: per build-minute x machine type. E2_HIGHCPU_8 is typically net-cheaper for CPU-bound builds (6-8x faster, only 4x more expensive). Parallelise steps with waitFor. Docker layer caching from Artifact Registry significantly reduces build time. Private worker pools let builds access VPC resources (Cloud SQL, private GKE) without public exposure.

questions.q: How do you use ApplicationSets for multi-cluster deployments?
questions.text: apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: ApplicationSet spec: generators: - clusters: {} # all registered clusters template: spec: source: path: apps/myapp/overlays/{{name}} destination: server: {{server}} ApplicationSet generates N ArgoCD Applications from one template — one per cluster, environment, or Git branch. Cluster generator deploys to every registered cluster automatically. Git generator creates an app per subdirectory. Matrix generator combines both. This scales GitOps to 100+ clusters with a single template definition. New cluster registration → automatic app deployment → zero manual configuration.

questions.q: What is pipeline as code — how do you version and test it?
questions.text: # Pipeline config lives in the application repo: .github/workflows/ci.yaml # GitHub Actions cloudbuild.yaml # Cloud Build # Test locally: act -j test # run GitHub Actions locally (act tool) cloud-build-local --dryrun cloudbuild.yaml # Lint pipeline files: actionlint .github/workflows/*.yaml # Pipeline changes go through PR review like code Pipeline as code: CI/CD config in the same repo as the application. Changes go through PR review. Prevents pipeline drift across teams. Enables rollback (git revert the pipeline change). Provides audit trail. Test on a feature branch before merging — open a test PR, verify the pipeline behaves as expected. Changes to the pipeline are as significant as changes to the application code.

questions.q: How do you implement canary deployments in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.text: # Argo Rollouts canary strategy: spec: strategy: canary: steps: - setWeight: 10 # 10% traffic to new version - pause: {duration: 5m} - analysis: # check error rate templates: [{templateName: error-rate}] - setWeight: 50 - pause: {duration: 10m} - setWeight: 100 kubectl argo rollouts get rollout myapp --watch Canary: route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, measure golden signals, progressively increase if healthy, automatically rollback if metrics degrade. Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate queries Prometheus: if error rate exceeds threshold during the canary phase, rollback automatically. This limits blast radius — a bad deploy affects only 10% of users before automatic rollback. The metrics-driven promotion is the key advantage over simple rolling updates.

questions.q: Design a complete CI/CD platform for 20 engineers across 10 microservices on GCP.
questions.text: Principal-level platform design question — architecture, developer experience, and governance. Source: GitHub + branch protection + CODEOWNERS + signed commits CI: GitHub Actions reusable workflows (canonical pipeline per language) Registry: GCP Artifact Registry + Container Analysis auto-scan CD: ArgoCD + two-repo GitOps (app repo / manifests repo) Secrets: External Secrets Operator + GCP Secret Manager Security: Binary Authorization + Workload Identity Preview: Ephemeral environments per PR (short-lived GKE namespace) Metrics: DORA dashboard (deploy freq, lead time, CFR, MTTR) Platform team owns: reusable workflow templates, manifests repo structure, ArgoCD ApplicationSet config, DORA metrics dashboard. Service teams only write application code — CI/CD is inherited by using the platform Dockerfile conventions and reusable workflows. Goal: a new service is production-deployable within 1 day of creation, using the same pipeline as all other services. Platform SLO: commit to production in under 30 minutes including manual approval. Developer experience first: A fast, reliable pipeline is the platform team's product. Track pipeline P95 duration and treat improvements as feature work.

questions.q: What is trunk-based development and why does it suit CI/CD?
questions.text: Developers merge small changes to one main branch at least daily, using short-lived branches and feature flags. It keeps integration continuous and avoids long-lived branch merge pain. git switch -c fix/login-timeout git pull --rebase origin main git push origin fix/login-timeout Interview tip: Say that flags, not branches, hide unfinished work.

questions.q: What are the DORA metrics and how do they relate to CI/CD?
questions.text: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Together they measure delivery speed and stability. git log --merges --since=30.days --oneline | wc -l kubectl rollout history deploy/app Interview tip: Emphasise that speed and stability are measured together.

questions.q: What is the difference between a build artifact and a deployment manifest, and why version both?
questions.text: The artifact is the built binary or image; the manifest says how and where to run it. Versioning both gives reproducible, auditable releases. docker build -t app:1.4.2 . helm template app ./chart --set image.tag=1.4.2 Interview tip: Mention that rollbacks need both to be recoverable.

questions.q: What is a monorepo versus polyrepo pipeline strategy, and how does CI handle each?
questions.text: A monorepo holds many services; CI must detect which changed. Polyrepo has one pipeline per repo but harder cross-repo changes. git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD | cut -d/ -f1 | sort -u Interview tip: Talk about path filters and build caching.

questions.q: What are the stages of a typical modern CI pipeline in order, and why that order?
questions.text: Lint and unit tests first, then build, scan, integration tests, publish artifact. Cheap fast checks come first to fail early. make lint test docker build -t app:$SHA . trivy image app:$SHA Interview tip: Explain fail-fast and cost ordering.

questions.q: What is a build agent or runner, and how do you choose between hosted and self-hosted?
questions.text: A runner executes pipeline jobs. Hosted is simple and clean; self-hosted gives control, private network access and cost savings at scale. docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash Interview tip: Cover isolation, ephemeral runners and secrets.

questions.q: What is semantic versioning and how do you automate releases from commits?
questions.text: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH conveys compatibility. Conventional commit messages let tools calculate the next version and changelog automatically. git commit -m 'feat: add retry to client' npx semantic-release --dry-run Interview tip: Mention breaking change markers.

questions.q: How do you restrict permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN in a workflow?
questions.text: Set permissions at the workflow or job level to the minimum scopes and default to read-only. permissions: contents: read id-token: write Interview tip: Least privilege per job.

questions.q: How do you authenticate a workflow to AWS, Azure or GCP without long-lived secrets?
questions.text: Use OpenID Connect federation: the workflow gets a short-lived token the cloud trusts based on repository, branch and environment claims. permissions: id-token: write contents: read Interview tip: Scope the trust policy to branch or environment.

questions.q: Why pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, and how do you keep them updated?
questions.text: Tags can be moved; a SHA is immutable. Use an update bot to propose reviewed bumps. uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha> # v4.1.1 Interview tip: Supply chain risk.

questions.q: How do you design environment protection and approvals for production deployments?
questions.text: Use environments with required reviewers, wait timers, branch restrictions and environment-scoped secrets. environment: production needs: [build, test] Interview tip: Gate on environment, not on person.

questions.q: How do concurrency groups prevent overlapping deployments?
questions.text: A concurrency key cancels or queues runs sharing the same group so two deploys do not race. concurrency: group: deploy-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: false Interview tip: Cancel for CI, queue for deploy.

questions.q: How do you build and publish a container image securely with provenance in a workflow?
questions.text: Build with a pinned builder, sign the image, generate an SBOM and attach provenance attestations. docker buildx build --provenance=true --sbom=true -t reg/app:$SHA --push . cosign sign reg/app@sha256:... Interview tip: Sign the digest, not the tag.

questions.q: How do you reduce cost and time of workflows that run on every pull request?
questions.text: Use path filters, caching, concurrency cancel, smaller matrices and skip drafts. on: pull_request: paths: ['src/**','package.json'] Interview tip: Measure before optimising.

questions.q: What is the danger of pull_request_target and how do you handle workflows for forks?
questions.text: It runs with secrets in the base repository context; checking out untrusted fork code there can leak secrets. on: pull_request # avoid checkout of PR head under pull_request_target Interview tip: Never run untrusted code with secrets.

questions.q: How do you use substitutions and variables in Cloud Build safely?
questions.text: Built-in substitutions like $SHORT_SHA and user-defined ones starting with an underscore let one config serve many environments. gcloud builds submit --substitutions=_ENV=staging,_REGION=us-central1 # cloudbuild.yaml: ${_ENV} Interview tip: User substitutions must start with underscore.

questions.q: How do you run Cloud Build in a private pool and why?
questions.text: Private pools run builds in a VPC-connected, customer-owned environment, allowing access to private resources and custom machine sizes. gcloud builds worker-pools create ci-pool --region=us-central1 --peered-network=projects/p/global/networks/n Interview tip: Use for private repos and databases.

questions.q: How do you speed up Docker builds in Cloud Build using caching?
questions.text: Use Kaniko or BuildKit cache, pull the previous image as cache-from, and order Dockerfile layers by change frequency. docker build --cache-from $IMAGE:latest -t $IMAGE:$SHORT_SHA . Interview tip: Cache is lost between ephemeral workers.

questions.q: How do you deploy to Cloud Run from Cloud Build with a gradual rollout?
questions.text: Deploy a new revision with no traffic, test it using a tag URL, then shift traffic in stages and roll back by re-pointing traffic. gcloud run deploy app --image $IMG --no-traffic --tag canary gcloud run services update-traffic app --to-tags canary=10 Interview tip: Revisions are immutable.

questions.q: How do you control who can trigger builds and what the build can access in Cloud Build?
questions.text: Use a dedicated user-managed service account with least privilege per trigger, and restrict trigger configuration with IAM. gcloud builds triggers create github --service-account=projects/p/serviceAccounts/ci@p.iam.gserviceaccount.com Interview tip: Avoid the default broad build account.

questions.q: How do you implement build provenance and attestations on Google Cloud?
questions.text: Cloud Build generates SLSA provenance; Binary Authorization verifies attestations before deployment. gcloud artifacts docker images describe $IMG --show-provenance Interview tip: Verify at admission, not just generate.

questions.q: How do you handle drift and self-healing in ArgoCD?
questions.text: Automated sync with selfHeal reverts manual cluster changes to match Git; prune removes resources deleted from Git. syncPolicy: automated: prune: true selfHeal: true Interview tip: Self-heal can fight emergency changes.

questions.q: What are sync waves and hooks in ArgoCD and when do you use them?
questions.text: Waves order resource creation within a sync; hooks run jobs at phases like PreSync and PostSync. argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1" argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync Interview tip: Use for migrations and CRD ordering.

questions.q: How do you structure repositories and environments for ArgoCD: Kustomize overlays or Helm values?
questions.text: A base plus per-environment overlays or values files; promote by changing the image tag or revision per environment. kustomize build overlays/prod helm template app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml Interview tip: Directory per environment beats branch per environment.

questions.q: How do you secure ArgoCD itself: RBAC, projects and SSO?
questions.text: Use AppProjects to restrict repos, clusters and namespaces; SSO with group-based RBAC; disable the default admin. argocd proj create team-a --src 'https://git.example/team-a/*' --dest 'https://kubernetes.default.svc,team-a-*' Interview tip: Projects are the multi-tenant boundary.

questions.q: How does Argo Rollouts enable canary and blue-green deployments?
questions.text: A Rollout resource replaces Deployment, shifting traffic by steps and analysing metrics to promote or abort automatically. kubectl argo rollouts get rollout app --watch kubectl argo rollouts promote app Interview tip: Analysis makes it automatic.

questions.q: How do you manage multi-cluster deployments and cluster registration in ArgoCD?
questions.text: Register clusters as secrets, use ApplicationSets with cluster generators, and keep a hub-and-spoke or per-cluster instance model. argocd cluster add prod-east --name prod-east kubectl get secret -n argocd -l argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type=cluster Interview tip: Hub-and-spoke vs per-cluster instance.

questions.q: How do you roll back with ArgoCD and why is git revert preferred?
questions.text: Revert the commit in Git so history and cluster agree; UI rollback is temporary when auto-sync is on. git revert <sha> && git push argocd app history app argocd app rollback app <id> Interview tip: Git is the source of truth.

questions.q: What is the test pyramid and how does it shape pipeline design?
questions.text: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests; the pipeline runs cheap tests first. pytest -m unit -q pytest -m integration Interview tip: Inverted pyramids make slow, flaky pipelines.

questions.q: How do you test infrastructure as code in a pipeline?
questions.text: Validate syntax, lint, policy-check the plan, and run integration tests in a temporary environment. terraform fmt -check && terraform validate tflint terraform plan -out tfplan && conftest test tfplan.json Interview tip: Plan is the unit test of IaC.

questions.q: How do you handle test data and ephemeral environments for integration tests?
questions.text: Use containers or per-PR namespaces with seeded, disposable data and automatic teardown. docker compose up -d db kubectl create ns pr-123 && helm install app ./chart -n pr-123 Interview tip: Never use shared mutable test databases.

questions.q: How do you quarantine and manage flaky tests without hiding real failures?
questions.text: Detect by rerun statistics, move to a quarantine suite with an owner and deadline, and track the flake rate. pytest --reruns 0 -p no:randomly pytest --count=50 tests/test_x.py Interview tip: Retries hide, quarantine tracks.

questions.q: What is mutation testing or coverage gating, and are coverage thresholds useful?
questions.text: Coverage shows what code ran, not whether tests assert behaviour. Mutation testing checks whether tests catch injected bugs. pytest --cov=app --cov-fail-under=80 mutmut run Interview tip: Use coverage as a floor, not a goal.

questions.q: How do you scan for secrets in repositories and block them in CI?
questions.text: Use pre-commit and CI secret scanners, block on detection, rotate any leaked secret and scan history. gitleaks detect --source . --redact gitleaks protect --staged Interview tip: A leaked secret must be rotated, not just deleted.

questions.q: What is an SBOM and how do you generate and use it in a pipeline?
questions.text: A software bill of materials lists components and versions in an artifact, enabling vulnerability lookup and licence checks. syft packages app:1.4.2 -o spdx-json > sbom.json grype sbom:sbom.json Interview tip: Store it with the artifact.

questions.q: How do you apply SAST, DAST and dependency scanning without drowning developers in noise?
questions.text: Tune rules, fail only on high severity new findings, show results in pull requests and track exceptions with expiry. semgrep --config auto --error --severity ERROR trivy fs --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 . Interview tip: Fail on new, not old.

questions.q: How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline itself against supply chain attacks?
questions.text: Pin dependencies and actions, least-privilege tokens, isolated ephemeral runners, signed artifacts and protected branches. npm ci --ignore-scripts pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt Interview tip: Treat the pipeline as production.

questions.q: How do you enforce policy as code for Kubernetes manifests in the pipeline?
questions.text: Validate manifests with OPA/Conftest or Kyverno CLI in CI and enforce the same rules at admission in the cluster. conftest test deploy/*.yaml kyverno apply policies/ --resource deploy/ Interview tip: Shift left, enforce at the gate.

questions.q: How do you manage the approvals and separation of duties required by compliance in CI/CD?
questions.text: Automate evidence, require peer review and protected branches, and separate who writes from who approves production. # branch protection: require 1 approval, status checks, linear history Interview tip: Pipelines can generate audit evidence.

questions.q: How do you implement blue-green deployment in a pipeline and what are the risks?
questions.text: Deploy to the idle environment, test, switch traffic, keep the old one for rollback; database compatibility is the main risk. kubectl apply -f green.yaml kubectl patch svc app -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}' Interview tip: Schema changes must be backwards compatible.

questions.q: How do you handle configuration and secrets differences across environments without rebuilding?
questions.text: Build once, inject environment configuration at deploy time from config maps, parameter stores and secret managers. helm upgrade app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml kubectl create secret generic app --from-literal=... Interview tip: Same artifact, different config.

questions.q: How do you design pipelines for a microservice that depends on shared libraries?
questions.text: Version and publish libraries, use dependency updates automatically, and run compatibility or contract tests downstream. npm publish --provenance renovate # opens bump PRs Interview tip: Avoid lockstep releases.

questions.q: How do you implement automated rollback based on metrics after a deployment?
questions.text: Define SLO-based health checks, observe a bake period, and automatically revert if error rate or latency breach thresholds. kubectl rollout status deploy/app --timeout=300s kubectl rollout undo deploy/app Interview tip: Choose a few strong signals.

questions.q: What is a deployment freeze or change window, and how do you handle it in modern CI/CD?
questions.text: A period when production changes are restricted. Automate enforcement and keep an emergency path. # pipeline rule: block prod deploys if calendar freeze=true unless label=hotfix Interview tip: Frequent small releases reduce the need for freezes.

questions.q: How do you build a pipeline for database schema changes with zero downtime?
questions.text: Use versioned migrations with expand and contract, run them as a controlled step, and keep changes backwards compatible. flyway migrate alembic upgrade head Interview tip: Never couple a destructive change to the app release.

questions.q: How do you promote releases across environments using the same artifact and gates?
questions.text: Build once, deploy the same digest to dev, staging and production with automated tests and approvals between stages. crane copy reg/app@sha256:... reg/prod/app@sha256:... argocd app set app --helm-set image.digest=sha256:... Interview tip: Promotion changes pointers, not binaries.

questions.q: A pipeline works on one runner but fails on another. How do you investigate?
questions.text: Compare tool versions, environment variables, OS, permissions, network and caches; make the environment reproducible. env | sort docker run --rm -it $BUILD_IMAGE bash Interview tip: Reproduce in the same image.

questions.q: A deployment is stuck in progress and pods never become ready. What do you check?
questions.text: Describe the pods, check events, probes, image pulls, resource requests and config or secret mounts. kubectl rollout status deploy/app kubectl describe pod -l app=app kubectl logs deploy/app --previous Interview tip: Events first.

questions.q: Builds suddenly became slow after a dependency update. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: Compare timing per step, check cache hits, dependency resolution and network, and bisect the change. time npm ci docker build --progress=plain . Interview tip: Timing data per step first.

questions.q: A rollback did not fix the problem. What could explain that?
questions.text: State outside the code changed: database migrations, configuration, feature flags, caches, dependencies or data. kubectl rollout history deploy/app git diff v1.4.1 v1.4.2 -- config/ Interview tip: Rollback only reverts code.

questions.q: Terraform apply in the pipeline failed halfway. How do you recover safely?
questions.text: Do not rerun blindly: check state and lock, review what was created, then re-plan and apply the remainder. terraform state list terraform plan terraform force-unlock <id> Interview tip: State is the source of truth, so protect it.

questions.q: Docker builds work locally but fail in CI with permission or network errors. What do you check?
questions.text: Check runner user and permissions, registry credentials, proxy and DNS, build context size and rate limits. docker info docker login reg.example.com docker build --no-cache --progress=plain . Interview tip: Look at auth and rate limits first.

questions.q: ArgoCD shows an application as OutOfSync forever even after syncing. What is happening?
questions.text: Usually a controller or webhook mutates fields, or defaults differ from the manifest. Configure ignore differences or fix the manifest. argocd app diff app argocd app get app --show-operation Interview tip: Read the diff.

questions.q: Intermittent pipeline failures show 'connection reset' or timeouts when downloading dependencies. What do you do?
questions.text: Add a caching proxy or mirror, retries with backoff, pin versions and check runner network egress. npm config set fetch-retries 5 pip install --retries 5 -r requirements.txt Interview tip: Reduce dependence on the public internet.

questions.q: A secret rotation broke deployments across many pipelines. How do you prevent a repeat?
questions.text: Centralise secrets in a manager, reference them by name, rotate with overlap, and test rotation in staging. aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id ci/registry Interview tip: Dual validity during rotation.

questions.q: Design the approach to deploy 50 microservices with consistent pipelines but team autonomy.
questions.text: Provide a golden-path template with reusable pipeline components, let teams extend it, and enforce guardrails centrally. uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/build-deploy.yml@v3 Interview tip: Paved road, not forced road.

guides.title: Coding & Scripting for SRE / Platform — InterviewHub

questions.q: Write a Bash script that exits on any error, unset variable, or failed pipe. Why does each flag matter?
questions.text: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -Eeuo pipefail IFS=$'\n\t' This is the standard "strict mode" preamble for any production Bash script. -e exits on the first command that returns non-zero, -u treats unset variables as an error (catches typos in var names), and -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last. -E ensures an ERR trap is inherited by functions/subshells. Without pipefail, cmd_that_fails | grep x returns grep’s exit code and silently masks the real failure. Gotcha: set -e does NOT trigger inside if conditions or commands joined by && / || . Code like grep x file in an if won’t abort the script even with -e.

questions.q: How do you safely handle filenames with spaces or newlines in a Bash loop?
questions.text: # BAD: breaks on spaces/newlines/globs for f in $(ls); do rm "$f"; done # GOOD: null-delimited, handles every filename find . -type f -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do printf '%s\n' "$f" done Never parse ls and never leave variables unquoted in word-splitting contexts. The robust pattern is find -print0 piped to read -d '' , which separates entries by NUL bytes — the only character that can’t appear in a filename. IFS= prevents trimming, -r stops backslash mangling. Always quote: "$f" , not $f . Unquoted expansion re-splits on IFS and expands globs — the cause of countless "rm deleted the wrong thing" incidents.

questions.q: Write a function with a trap that cleans up a temp directory even if the script is interrupted.
questions.text: tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmpdir"; } trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM # ... work in "$tmpdir" ... A trap ... EXIT runs the cleanup on normal exit, errors (with -e), and signals — so the temp dir never leaks. Adding INT/TERM makes Ctrl-C and kill clean up too. Use mktemp -d rather than a hard-coded path: it creates a unique directory with safe permissions and avoids races/symlink attacks in /tmp . Why SREs care: Scripts that leak temp files or half-written state on interruption are a classic source of "disk full" pages and corrupted runs. Idempotent cleanup is table stakes.

questions.q: How do you parse command-line flags in a Bash script (e.g. -e env -v)?
questions.text: verbose=0; env="" while getopts ":e:v" opt; do case "$opt" in e) env="$OPTARG" ;; v) verbose=1 ;; \?) echo "bad flag: -$OPTARG" > exit 2 ;; :) echo "-$OPTARG needs an arg" > exit 2 ;; esac done; shift $((OPTIND-1)) getopts is the built-in for short flags. A colon after a letter ( e: ) means it takes an argument exposed as $OPTARG ; a leading colon enables silent error handling so you can print your own messages. After the loop, shift $((OPTIND-1)) drops the parsed flags so $@ holds the remaining positional args. For long flags ( --env ), getopts won’t help — use a manual while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; case "$1" in --env) ... ;; esac; shift loop, or switch to Python for anything complex.

questions.q: Write a one-liner to find the top 5 IPs by request count in an Nginx access log.
questions.text: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5 # with %: awk '{c[$1]++} END{for(i in c) print c[i],i}' access.log | sort -rn | head -5 The classic pipeline: awk extracts the first field (client IP), sort | uniq -c counts duplicates (uniq needs sorted input), and sort -rn | head ranks descending. The pure-awk version uses an associative array to count in a single pass — faster on large logs because it avoids the first sort. Interview favorite: Knowing uniq -c requires pre-sorted input, and that an awk hash map does it in one pass, signals real command-line fluency.

questions.q: How do you check if a remote TCP port is open without nc/telnet installed?
questions.text: # Bash built-in /dev/tcp pseudo-device if timeout 3 bash -c 'echo > /dev/tcp/db.internal/5432' 2>/dev/null; then echo "port open" else echo "port closed/unreachable" fi Bash has a built-in /dev/tcp/HOST/PORT pseudo-device — opening it attempts a TCP connection, so you can health-check ports on minimal containers that lack nc , telnet , or curl . Wrapping it in timeout prevents hanging on a filtered/dropped port. Container-friendly: Distroless and Alpine images often strip networking tools. /dev/tcp needs nothing but bash, making it ideal for readiness probes and debug.

questions.q: Write a retry-with-backoff wrapper in Bash for a flaky command.
questions.text: retry() { local max=$1; shift; local n=1 delay=1 until "$@"; do (( n++ > max )) && { echo "failed after $max" > return 1; } echo "attempt $n in ${delay}s..." >&2 sleep "$delay"; delay=$(( delay * 2 )) done } # usage: retry 5 curl -fsS https://api.internal/health This runs "$@" (the command + args) until it succeeds or hits the max attempts, doubling the delay each time (exponential backoff). "$@" preserves argument boundaries. For production you’d add jitter ( delay + RANDOM%delay ) so many clients don’t retry in lockstep and create a thundering herd. Cap the retries: Unbounded retries against a down dependency turn a blip into a self-sustaining overload. Always bound attempts and total time.

questions.q: What is the difference between $@ and $* and "$@" and "$*"?
questions.text: $* → all args as ONE word, split on IFS $@ → all args, split on IFS (usually same as above) "$*" → ONE string: "arg1 arg2 arg3" (joined by first IFS char) "$@" → EACH arg preserved as a separate quoted word ← almost always what you want The only one that correctly preserves arguments containing spaces is "$@" — it expands to each argument individually quoted. Use it whenever you forward args to another command. "$*" is occasionally useful when you genuinely want one joined string (e.g. building a log message). Rule of thumb: If you’re passing arguments through, it’s "$@" every time. Getting this wrong silently corrupts paths with spaces.

questions.q: How do you redirect stdout and stderr, and what does 2>&1 actually do?
questions.text: cmd > out.log 2> err.log # separate files cmd > all.log 2>&1 # both to one file (order matters!) cmd &> all.log # bash shorthand for the above cmd 2>&1 | tee log # both into a pipe 2>&1 means "make file descriptor 2 (stderr) point to wherever fd 1 (stdout) currently points." Order is critical: > file 2>&1 works, but 2>&1 > file sends stderr to the old stdout (the terminal) because the redirect of stdout happens after stderr was already duplicated. Common need: To pipe stderr through a filter, you must 2>&1 first — pipes only carry stdout by default.

questions.q: Write a script that processes a CSV and sums a numeric column with awk.
questions.text: # sum column 3 of a comma-separated file, skipping header awk -F',' 'NR>1 { sum += $3 } END { printf "%.2f\n", sum }' data.csv # group-by: sum col3 per category in col1 awk -F',' 'NR>1 { s[$1]+=$3 } END { for (k in s) print k, s[k] }' data.csv -F',' sets the field separator, NR>1 skips the header row, and $3 is the third column. awk auto-initializes numeric vars to 0, so sum += $3 just works. The group-by version uses an associative array keyed by the category column — awk’s killer feature for ad-hoc log/CSV analysis. Real CSVs are messy: Quoted fields containing commas break naive -F',' . For those, use a real parser (Python’s csv module) rather than awk.

questions.q: How do you write an idempotent script that creates a config only if it doesn't exist?
questions.text: config=/etc/app/config.yml if [[ ! -f "$config" ]]; then install -D -m 0640 -o app -g app /dev/stdin "$config" key: value EOF echo "created $config" else echo "$config exists, skipping" fi Idempotency means running the script repeatedly yields the same end state without side effects. Guard creation with [[ ! -f ]] , and use install to atomically create the file with the right mode and ownership in one step (it also creates parent dirs with -D ). A heredoc supplies the content. Why it matters: Config-management and bootstrap scripts run over and over (cron, cloud-init, CI). Non-idempotent scripts duplicate entries, reset permissions, or clobber edits.

questions.q: What’s the difference between [ ], [[ ]], and (( )) in Bash?
questions.text: [ "$a" = "$b" ] # POSIX test, needs quoting, string = [[ $a == "$b" ]] # bash test: safer, supports == pattern, && || [[ $s =~ ^v[0-9]+$ ]] # regex match (( x > 5 && y [ ] is the old POSIX test command — portable but fragile (word-splitting, needs careful quoting). [[ ]] is the bash keyword: no word-splitting inside, supports == globbing, =~ regex, and && / || . (( )) is arithmetic evaluation with C-like operators and no $ needed on variables. Default to [[ ]] for tests and (( )) for numbers in bash scripts. Reserve [ ] for strict POSIX sh compatibility.

questions.q: How do you tail logs from multiple files and act on a matching pattern in real time?
questions.text: tail -F /var/log/app/*.log | while read -r line; do if [[ "$line" == *"FATAL"* ]]; then echo "$line" | mail -s "FATAL on $(hostname)" oncall@co.com fi done tail -F (capital F) follows files by name and survives log rotation (reopens when the file is recreated), unlike -f which follows the inode and goes silent after rotation. Piping into a while read loop lets you pattern-match each line and trigger an action — a poor-man’s alerting hook. Don’t build real monitoring this way: It’s fine for quick debugging, but for production use a log shipper (Promtail/Fluent Bit) + alerting. A shell loop has no buffering, dedup, or backpressure handling.

questions.q: Write a script to check disk usage and alert if any mount exceeds 85%.
questions.text: threshold=85 df -P | awk -v t="$threshold" 'NR>1 { gsub(/%/,"",$5) if ($5+0 >= t) printf "WARN %s at %s%%\n", $6, $5 }' df -P forces POSIX output (one line per filesystem, stable columns). awk strips the % from the use-percent column with gsub , coerces it to a number ( $5+0 ), and prints the mount point ( $6 ) if over threshold. Passing the threshold via -v keeps it parameterized. Inode exhaustion is a sneaky cousin: a disk can be 30% full but out of inodes (many tiny files). Check df -iP too — a frequent cause of "no space left" with free space showing.

questions.q: How do you run commands in parallel in Bash and wait for all to finish?
questions.text: # background jobs + wait for host in web1 web2 web3; do ssh "$host" 'systemctl restart app' & done wait # block until all background jobs complete # bounded parallelism with xargs printf '%s\n' web{1..9} | xargs -P4 -I{} ssh {} uptime Appending & backgrounds each job; wait with no args blocks until they all finish. For controlled concurrency, xargs -P4 runs at most 4 at once — important so you don’t fork 500 SSH sessions and exhaust resources. GNU parallel is the richer tool if available. Capture failures: Plain wait doesn’t tell you which job failed. Collect PIDs and wait $pid individually, or write per-host exit codes to files, if you need to know what broke.

questions.q: What does 'local' do in a Bash function and why does it matter?
questions.text: counter=0 bump() { local counter=99; echo "inside: $counter"; } bump # inside: 99 echo "$counter" # 0 (global untouched) By default all Bash variables are global — assigning inside a function mutates the caller’s scope, a notorious source of action-at-a-distance bugs. local scopes a variable to the function and its callees. Always declare function-internal variables local to avoid clobbering globals or other functions’ state. Subtle trap: local var=$(cmd) masks cmd ’s exit code (local always returns 0). Split into local var; var=$(cmd) || return 1 if you need to check it.

questions.q: How do you safely use variables in a command that might be empty or undefined?
questions.text: ${VAR:-default} # use default if VAR unset OR empty ${VAR:=default} # assign default to VAR if unset/empty ${VAR:?must be set} # exit with error message if unset/empty ${VAR:+value} # use 'value' only if VAR IS set These parameter-expansion forms handle missing config cleanly. :- supplies a fallback, := sets it, :? fails fast with a message (great for required env vars), and :+ conditionally adds something only when set (e.g. appending a flag). Combined with set -u , :? gives you self-documenting required-variable checks. Pattern: : "${DATABASE_URL:?DATABASE_URL is required}" at the top of a script makes missing config fail immediately with a clear message instead of mysteriously later.

questions.q: Write a healthcheck script that returns proper exit codes for a load balancer.
questions.text: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail if curl -fsS --max-time 2 http://localhost:8080/healthz >/dev/null; then exit 0 # healthy else exit 1 # unhealthy → LB removes from rotation fi Health checks communicate via exit codes: 0 = healthy, non-zero = unhealthy. curl -f makes HTTP ≥400 return non-zero, -sS stays quiet but still shows real errors, and --max-time bounds the check so a hung backend doesn’t hang the probe. The LB or orchestrator interprets the exit code to route traffic. Check the right thing: A good health endpoint verifies the app can do real work (DB reachable, deps OK) — but keep liveness cheap and local so a downstream blip doesn’t cause mass restarts.

questions.q: How do you debug a Bash script that’s behaving unexpectedly?
questions.text: bash -x script.sh # trace every expanded command set -x ... set +x # trace just a section PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-}: ' # richer trace bash -n script.sh # syntax check without running shellcheck script.sh # static analysis — catches most bugs set -x prints each command after expansion so you see exactly what ran with what values — the single most useful Bash debugging tool. Customizing PS4 adds file/line/function context. bash -n checks syntax without executing. And shellcheck is essential: it statically flags quoting bugs, unset vars, and footguns before they bite. Run shellcheck in CI: Treat its warnings as errors. It catches the vast majority of the quoting and subtlety bugs that make Bash scripts fragile.

questions.q: When should you STOP using Bash and switch to Python/Go?
questions.text: Stay in Bash: glue, pipelines, <100 lines, calling other CLIs Switch when: real data structures, JSON/HTTP parsing, error handling, arithmetic/floats, testing, or it exceeds ~100–200 lines Bash excels at orchestrating other programs and text pipelines. But once you need structured data (parsing JSON, nested maps), robust error handling, floating-point math, unit tests, or the script grows past a couple hundred lines, Bash becomes a liability — fragile quoting, no real types, painful debugging. That’s the signal to move to Python (or Go for a distributed binary). Rule of thumb: "If I’m reaching for jq three times and an array of structs, this should be Python." Knowing when to switch is itself a senior signal.

questions.q: What’s the difference between a list, tuple, set, and dict — and when do you use each?
questions.text: list [..] ordered, mutable, dupes ok → sequences tuple (..) ordered, immutable, hashable → fixed records, dict keys set {..} unordered, unique, O(1) membership → dedup, fast "in" dict {k:v} key→value, O(1) lookup, ordered(3.7+) → mappings Choose by access pattern. Need ordered mutable data → list. Need an immutable, hashable group (or a dict key) → tuple. Need uniqueness or fast membership tests → set (checking x in big_set is O(1) vs O(n) for a list). Need key-based lookup → dict. Picking the wrong one turns O(1) operations into O(n) and is a top cause of "why is my script slow on big input." SRE example: Diffing two large lists of hostnames? Convert to sets — set_a - set_b is near-instant; nested list loops are O(n²).

questions.q: Explain list comprehensions and when they’re better (or worse) than a loop.
questions.text: squares = [x*x for x in nums if x > 0] by_host = {h: ping(h) for h in hosts} # dict comp uniq = {line.strip() for line in f} # set comp # generator (lazy, memory-friendly): total = sum(x*x for x in nums) Comprehensions are concise and fast for building a collection by transforming/filtering an iterable. Prefer them for simple map/filter logic. Use a generator expression (parentheses) when you only iterate once or the data is large — it’s lazy and avoids building the whole list in memory. Drop back to a plain loop when there’s side effects, multiple statements, or the logic hurts readability. Don’t over-nest: A triple-nested comprehension with two conditions is write-only code. If you can’t read it aloud, use a loop.

questions.q: How do you read a large file line-by-line without loading it all into memory?
questions.text: # GOOD: iterates lazily, constant memory with open("huge.log") as f: for line in f: process(line) # BAD: loads entire file into RAM lines = open("huge.log").read().splitlines() A file object is itself a lazy iterator — for line in f reads one line at a time with buffering, so memory stays flat regardless of file size. Using .read() or .readlines() pulls the whole file into RAM and will OOM on multi-GB logs. The with block guarantees the file handle closes even on exception. For huge files, combine with a generator pipeline: a function that yield s parsed records keeps the whole flow streaming and composable.

questions.q: Write a function that parses a log line into a structured dict. Handle malformed lines.
questions.text: import re PATTERN = re.compile( r'(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<ts>[^\]]+)\] ' r'"(?P<method>\S+) (?P<path>\S+)[^"]*" (?P<status>\d+)') def parse(line): m = PATTERN.match(line) if not m: return None # caller skips/counts bad lines d = m.groupdict() d["status"] = int(d["status"]) return d Use a compiled regex with named groups for readable, fast parsing (compile once at module level, not per call). Return None (or raise a custom exception) on non-matching lines so the caller decides how to handle bad input — real logs always contain garbage lines, partial writes, and format drift. Convert types (status → int) at the boundary. Robustness: Count and log the malformed-line rate. A sudden spike in unparseable lines is itself a signal (deploy changed the log format, or something is corrupting output).

questions.q: Explain *args and **kwargs with a practical example.
questions.text: def run(cmd, *args, timeout=30, **opts): full = [cmd, *args] print(full, timeout, opts) run("kubectl", "get", "pods", timeout=10, namespace="prod") # ['kubectl','get','pods'] 10 {'namespace':'prod'} *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. They let you write flexible wrappers (decorators, CLI runners, retry helpers) that forward arbitrary arguments to an inner function via inner(*args, **kwargs) . The same * / ** also unpack a list/dict back into a call. Forwarding pattern: A retry/timing decorator typically signs as def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return fn(*args, **kwargs) so it works for any wrapped function.

questions.q: What is a context manager and how do you write one with contextlib?
questions.text: from contextlib import contextmanager import time @contextmanager def timed(label): start = time.monotonic() try: yield finally: print(f"{label}: {time.monotonic()-start:.3f}s") with timed("query"): run_query() A context manager guarantees setup/teardown around a block via with — the canonical use is releasing resources (files, locks, connections) even on exception. The @contextmanager decorator turns a generator into one: code before yield is setup, code in finally after yield always runs as teardown. Use time.monotonic() for durations (it never goes backward, unlike wall-clock). Why finally matters: Putting teardown in finally ensures cleanup runs even if the wrapped block raises — the whole point over manual setup/teardown.

questions.q: How do you handle exceptions properly — and what are the anti-patterns?
questions.text: # GOOD: specific, logged, re-raised or handled try: resp = client.get(url, timeout=5) except requests.Timeout: log.warning("timeout on %s", url); raise except requests.HTTPError as e: log.error("http %s", e.response.status_code); raise # BAD: try: ... except: pass # swallows everything, incl KeyboardInterrupt Catch the most specific exceptions you can handle, do something meaningful (log with context, retry, clean up), and re-raise if you can’t actually recover. The cardinal sins: bare except: (catches SystemExit / KeyboardInterrupt too), except Exception: pass (silently hides bugs), and catching broadly just to log-and-continue. Silent failures are how data corruption and "why didn’t the alert fire" incidents happen. Never swallow silently: except: pass is the most dangerous two lines in production Python — it converts crashes into invisible wrong behavior.

questions.q: What’s the difference between is and == ? Show a gotcha.
questions.text: a == b # value equality (calls __eq__) a is b # identity: same object in memory x = [1,2]; y = [1,2] x == y # True (same contents) x is y # False (different objects) if val is None: ... # correct None check == compares values; is compares object identity. Use is only for singletons — None , True , False ( if x is None ). Using is for value comparison appears to work for small ints and short strings due to interning, then breaks unpredictably for larger values. That intermittent breakage is the classic gotcha. Always if x is None , never if x == None — and never is for numbers/strings you actually want to compare by value.

questions.q: Explain mutable default arguments — the classic Python footgun.
questions.text: # BUG: default list is created ONCE, shared across calls def add(item, bucket=[]): bucket.append(item); return bucket add(1) # [1] add(2) # [1, 2] ← surprise! same list # FIX: def add(item, bucket=None): bucket = [] if bucket is None else bucket bucket.append(item); return bucket Default argument values are evaluated once at function-definition time, not per call. A mutable default (list, dict, set) is therefore shared across every call that doesn’t override it, accumulating state — a subtle, data-dependent bug. The fix is the None sentinel pattern: default to None and create a fresh object inside the function. Interview staple: This is asked constantly because it trips up even experienced devs and silently corrupts state in long-running services.

questions.q: How do you make an HTTP request with retries and timeouts using requests?
questions.text: import requests from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter, Retry s = requests.Session() retries = Retry(total=4, backoff_factor=0.5, status_forcelist=[429,500,502,503,504], allowed_methods=["GET","PUT","DELETE"]) s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries)) r = s.get(url, timeout=(3, 10)) # (connect, read) r.raise_for_status() Always set an explicit timeout — without it, requests can hang forever and freeze your service. The Retry adapter gives automatic exponential backoff ( backoff_factor ) only on retryable statuses, and only on idempotent methods by default (don’t blindly retry POSTs). raise_for_status() turns 4xx/5xx into exceptions so failures aren’t silently ignored. The #1 production bug: Forgetting timeout= . A single hung upstream call with no timeout cascades into your service’s thread pool and takes you down.

questions.q: What’s the difference between deepcopy and a shallow copy?
questions.text: import copy a = {"tags": ["x"]} b = a.copy() # shallow: new dict, SAME inner list b["tags"].append("y") a["tags"] # ['x','y'] ← mutated! c = copy.deepcopy(a) # fully independent nested copy A shallow copy duplicates the top-level container but the nested objects are shared references — mutating a nested list/dict shows up in both copies. copy.deepcopy recursively copies everything, giving full independence (at higher cost). This bites when you copy config dicts or default templates and then mutate them per-iteration. Cheaper alternative: If your data is simple/serializable, prefer immutable structures or rebuild rather than deepcopy in hot paths — deepcopy is slow on large nested objects.

questions.q: How do you parse and emit JSON safely, including from a subprocess?
questions.text: import json, subprocess out = subprocess.run(["kubectl","get","pods","-o","json"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout data = json.loads(out) names = [p["metadata"]["name"] for p in data["items"]] print(json.dumps({"pods": names}, indent=2)) Get machine-readable output ( -o json ) and parse with json.loads rather than scraping text. subprocess.run(..., check=True) raises if the command fails (don’t ignore exit codes), text=True decodes bytes to str, and capture_output grabs stdout. Emit with json.dumps for structured output other tools can consume. Never subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) with interpolated user input — that’s shell injection. Pass a list of args (no shell) so arguments can’t be reinterpreted.

questions.q: What are generators and why are they useful for SRE data processing?
questions.text: def read_errors(path): with open(path) as f: for line in f: if "ERROR" in line: yield line.rstrip() # pipeline stays lazy end-to-end: errs = read_errors("app.log") first_ten = list(itertools.islice(errs, 10)) A generator produces values lazily with yield , computing each only when requested. This keeps memory flat over huge or infinite streams and lets you build composable pipelines (filter → map → take) that never materialize the full dataset. Perfect for log processing, paginated API consumption, and streaming transforms where the data won’t fit in RAM. Composability: Chain generators — each stage pulls one item at a time — so a multi-GB log flows through filtering and parsing using constant memory.

questions.q: How do you use argparse to build a proper CLI tool?
questions.text: import argparse p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="deploy tool") p.add_argument("service") p.add_argument("-e","--env", required=True, choices=["dev","prod"]) p.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true") p.add_argument("-n","--replicas", type=int, default=3) args = p.parse_args() if args.dry_run: print("would deploy", args.service) argparse gives you typed args, required flags, choices validation, defaults, and auto-generated --help and error messages for free. Use type=int for conversion, action="store_true" for booleans, and choices to constrain values (catching typos like --env prdo at parse time). A --dry-run flag is essential for any tool that mutates infrastructure. For larger CLIs with subcommands, argparse subparsers or libraries like click / typer scale better and reduce boilerplate.

questions.q: Explain decorators with a retry decorator example.
questions.text: import functools, time def retry(times=3, delay=1): def deco(fn): @functools.wraps(fn) def wrap(*a, **kw): for i in range(times): try: return fn(*a, **kw) except Exception: if i == times-1: raise time.sleep(delay * 2**i) return wrap return deco @retry(times=5) def fetch(): ... A decorator wraps a function to add behavior (retries, timing, auth, caching) without touching its body. This three-layer form takes arguments: outer retry captures config, deco receives the function, wrap runs the logic and forwards *a, **kw . @functools.wraps preserves the original name/docstring — omit it and tracebacks/introspection break. Always use @functools.wraps on the inner wrapper, or your decorated functions all report as wrap in logs and stack traces.

questions.q: What is the difference between threading, multiprocessing, and asyncio? When use each?
questions.text: threading → I/O-bound, shared memory, limited by the GIL for CPU multiprocessing→ CPU-bound, true parallelism, separate memory asyncio → high-concurrency I/O (1000s of connections), single thread Python’s GIL means threads don’t run CPU-bound Python code in parallel — so use threads for I/O-bound work (waiting on network/disk) where the GIL is released during the wait. Use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work to get real parallelism across cores. Use asyncio when you have huge numbers of concurrent I/O operations and want efficient single-threaded cooperative concurrency without thread overhead. SRE lens: A script that fans out to 500 hosts is I/O-bound → threads or asyncio. A script crunching numbers over a big dataset is CPU-bound → multiprocessing.

questions.q: How do you run shell commands from Python the right way?
questions.text: import subprocess # preferred: list args, no shell, check errors r = subprocess.run(["df","-h","/"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=10) print(r.stdout) # streaming for long-running: with subprocess.Popen(["tail","-f","log"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True) as p: for line in p.stdout: handle(line) Use subprocess.run with a list of arguments and shell=False (the default) to avoid shell-injection. check=True raises on non-zero exit, timeout= prevents hangs, and text=True gives str instead of bytes. For long-running or streaming commands use Popen and iterate stdout line by line. Avoid os.system and shell=True with any interpolated input — both are injection-prone and hard to error-check. The list form is safer and clearer.

questions.q: How do you structure logging in a Python service (not print)?
questions.text: import logging, sys logging.basicConfig( level=logging.INFO, stream=sys.stdout, format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s') log = logging.getLogger(__name__) log.info("starting", extra={"svc": "api"}) log.error("failed: %s", err) # lazy %-format, not f-string Use the logging module, not print — it gives levels, timestamps, module names, and configurable handlers/formatters. Log to stdout in containers (let the platform collect it; don’t manage files). Get a logger per module with getLogger(__name__) . Pass args lazily ( log.info("x %s", val) ) so formatting is skipped when the level is disabled. Structured logging: In production, emit JSON logs (via python-json-logger or structlog) so fields are queryable in Loki/Elasticsearch — far more useful than free-text lines.

questions.q: What are type hints and how do they help in platform code?
questions.text: from typing import Optional def scale(svc: str, replicas: int, ns: str = "default") -> Optional[dict]: ... # check statically, no runtime cost: $ mypy deploy.py Type hints annotate expected types; they’re not enforced at runtime but enable static checkers ( mypy , pyright ) to catch type bugs before deploy, and they dramatically improve editor autocomplete and readability. In platform/tooling code consumed by other engineers, hints act as machine-checked documentation of your function contracts. Adopt gradually: Add hints to public function signatures first and run mypy in CI. Even partial typing catches a surprising number of "passed the wrong thing" bugs.
