questions.q: How do you write a unit test with pytest, including a fixture and a mock?
questions.text: import pytest from unittest.mock import patch @pytest.fixture def sample(): return {"cpu": 95, "host": "web1"} def test_alerts_on_high_cpu(sample): assert should_alert(sample) is True @patch("mymod.requests.get") def test_fetch(mock_get): mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {"ok": True} assert fetch_status() == {"ok": True} pytest uses plain assert and gives rich failure output. A @pytest.fixture provides reusable test data/setup injected by parameter name. @patch replaces external dependencies (HTTP, subprocess, cloud SDKs) with mocks so tests are fast, deterministic, and don’t hit real systems. Test behavior at the boundaries: high-CPU → alert, API failure → handled. Mock the edges, not your logic: Patch network/cloud calls so tests are hermetic, but exercise your real decision logic — that’s where the bugs are.

questions.q: Explain Big-O. Why does an SRE/platform engineer care about it?
questions.text: O(1) constant — dict/set lookup O(log n) logarithmic — binary search, balanced tree O(n) linear — single loop / scan O(n log n) — good sorts O(n²) quadratic — nested loop over same data ← danger at scale Big-O describes how runtime/memory grows with input size, ignoring constants. It matters because tooling that’s fine on 100 items can melt on 1,000,000 — the classic SRE incident is a script that worked in staging and timed out on prod-scale data. Recognizing an accidental O(n²) (a list in check inside a loop) and fixing it to O(n) with a set is everyday platform work. Real example: "Find duplicates" with nested loops is O(n²); with a set it’s O(n). On a million-row log that’s the difference between seconds and hours.

questions.q: Find the duplicate hostnames across two large lists efficiently.
questions.text: # O(n) with sets a = set(list_a) b = set(list_b) common = a & b # in both only_a = a - b # in a, not b missing = b - a # in b, not a Convert both to sets and use set algebra: intersection ( & ), difference ( - ), symmetric difference ( ^ ). Each set build is O(n) and lookups are O(1), so the whole diff is O(n) — versus the naive nested-loop approach at O(n²). This is the bread-and-butter pattern for reconciling inventories (DNS vs cloud, desired vs actual state). Drift detection: "What’s in Terraform state but not in the cloud?" is exactly state - actual — a one-line set difference.

questions.q: Count the frequency of each status code in a log — in one pass.
questions.text: from collections import Counter counts = Counter(parse(l)["status"] for l in open("a.log")) print(counts.most_common(5)) # manual equivalent with defaultdict: from collections import defaultdict c = defaultdict(int) for l in open("a.log"): c[parse(l)["status"]] += 1 collections.Counter is the idiomatic O(n) frequency counter — feed it any iterable and it tallies, with .most_common(k) giving the top-k for free. defaultdict(int) is the manual version (auto-initializes missing keys to 0, avoiding KeyError ). Both do it in a single streaming pass with constant extra logic. Counter does math too: You can add/subtract Counters to combine tallies from multiple files — handy for aggregating per-shard stats.

questions.q: Explain binary search and a real platform use case.
questions.text: import bisect # find first log index at/after a target timestamp i = bisect.bisect_left(timestamps, target_ts) # classic implementation: lo, hi = 0, len(arr) while lo < hi: mid = (lo+hi)//2 if arr[mid] < x: lo = mid+1 else: hi = mid Binary search finds an element (or insertion point) in a sorted array in O(log n) by halving the search range each step. Python’s bisect module gives this for free. SRE use: jumping to a timestamp in a sorted log/time-series, or "git bisect" style — finding the first bad commit/deploy among many in log(n) steps instead of checking each. git bisect is literally binary search over your commit history to find which change introduced a regression — the same O(log n) idea applied to debugging.

questions.q: How would you implement a simple rate limiter (token bucket)?
questions.text: import time class TokenBucket: def __init__(self, rate, cap): self.rate=rate; self.cap=cap self.tokens=cap; self.ts=time.monotonic() def allow(self, n=1): now=time.monotonic() self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.ts)*self.rate) self.ts=now if self.tokens>=n: self.tokens-=n; return True return False A token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a cap ; each request consumes tokens, and is allowed only if enough are available. It permits short bursts (up to capacity) while bounding the long-run average rate — the standard algorithm behind API rate limiting and client-side throttling. Using monotonic() avoids clock-adjustment bugs. Why token bucket: Unlike a fixed window, it smooths bursts and has no boundary spikes; it’s what most API gateways and SDKs use under the hood.

questions.q: What’s a hash map collision and why does dict performance matter?
questions.text: avg case: O(1) insert / lookup / delete collisions resolved by probing/chaining worst case: O(n) if many keys collide (rare, adversarial) A dict/hash map stores keys by hashing them to buckets; a collision is two keys hashing to the same bucket, resolved by open addressing or chaining. Average operations are O(1), which is why dicts/sets are the go-to for fast lookup. Worst case degrades to O(n) under pathological/adversarial keys, but for normal SRE data this effectively never happens — the practical takeaway is "lookups are cheap, use them." Keys must be hashable: Only immutable types (str, int, tuple) can be dict keys — that’s why you can’t key by a list, and why tuples exist as frozen records.

questions.q: How do you find the top-K items from a massive stream without sorting everything?
questions.text: import heapq # top 10 slowest requests by latency, streaming top = heapq.nlargest(10, stream, key=lambda r: r["ms"]) # or maintain a fixed min-heap of size K: h=[] for r in stream: heapq.heappush(h, (r["ms"], r)) if len(h)>K: heapq.heappop(h) # drop smallest Sorting the whole stream is O(n log n) and needs all data in memory. A min-heap of size K keeps only the current top-K: push each item, and when the heap exceeds K, pop the smallest. That’s O(n log K) time and O(K) memory — ideal for "top 10 slowest endpoints" over a huge log you can’t fully load. heapq.nlargest/nsmallest does exactly this internally — reach for it before writing a manual heap.

questions.q: Explain the sliding window technique with an SRE example.
questions.text: # max requests in any 60s window from sorted timestamps from collections import deque win=deque(); best=0 for t in timestamps: # sorted win.append(t) while win[0] <= t-60: win.popleft() best=max(best, len(win)) A sliding window maintains a moving range over a sequence, adding new elements and evicting ones that fall out of range — turning many O(n²) "check every subarray" problems into O(n). A deque gives O(1) appends and pops from both ends. SRE use: computing peak request rate over a rolling time window, or a moving average of latency. Rolling metrics: Burn-rate alerting and "requests in the last N seconds" are sliding-window computations — the same pattern you’d code by hand.

questions.q: How do you safely chunk a huge list to process in batches (e.g. API bulk calls)?
questions.text: def chunks(seq, size): for i in range(0, len(seq), size): yield seq[i:i+size] for batch in chunks(host_ids, 100): api.bulk_update(batch) # 100 at a time # lazy version for iterators (3.12+): itertools.batched from itertools import batched Batching avoids hitting API payload limits, request-size caps, or memory blowups when operating on huge collections. The generator yields successive slices of size ; for arbitrary iterators (not just lists), itertools.batched (3.12+) or an islice loop works without slicing. Combine with rate limiting and retries for robust bulk operations. Tune the batch size: Too small = many round-trips (slow); too large = timeouts/memory. Pick based on the API’s documented limits, not a guess.

questions.q: What’s the difference between O(n) memory and O(1) memory, and why prefer streaming?
questions.text: # O(n) memory — whole file in RAM data = open("huge.log").readlines() errors = [l for l in data if "ERR" in l] # O(1) memory — stream, count only n = sum(1 for l in open("huge.log") if "ERR" in l) O(n) memory grows with input size; O(1) (constant) memory does not. Streaming processes one record at a time and keeps only a small running state (a count, a sum, a fixed-size heap), so it handles arbitrarily large inputs that would never fit in RAM. For SRE log/metric processing, always ask "do I need all the data at once, or can I stream?" — usually streaming wins. OOM-killer territory: Loading a 50GB log with .readlines() on a 4GB box gets your process killed. Stream it.

questions.q: How would you deduplicate log lines while preserving order?
questions.text: seen = set(); out = [] for line in stream: if line not in seen: seen.add(line); out.append(line) # 3.7+ shortcut (insertion-ordered dict): deduped = list(dict.fromkeys(stream)) A plain set(stream) dedups but loses order. To keep first-seen order, track a seen set for O(1) membership and append only new items — O(n) time. The slick one-liner dict.fromkeys exploits dict’s guaranteed insertion order (3.7+) to dedup-and-preserve in one expression. Memory note: Dedup needs O(unique) memory to remember what was seen. For truly massive cardinality, a probabilistic structure (Bloom filter) trades a tiny false-positive rate for huge memory savings.

questions.q: Explain recursion vs iteration — and the risk of recursion in Python.
questions.text: # recursive dir walk — risks RecursionError on deep trees def walk(path): for e in os.scandir(path): if e.is_dir(): yield from walk(e.path) else: yield e.path # Python default recursion limit ≈ 1000 Recursion expresses tree/nested problems naturally; iteration uses an explicit loop/stack. Python has no tail-call optimization and a default recursion limit (~1000 frames), so deep recursion raises RecursionError and each frame costs memory. For deep or unbounded structures (huge directory trees, large graphs), convert to an iterative approach with an explicit stack/queue. Practical rule: Recursion is fine for shallow, bounded depth (parsing, small trees). For anything that could be thousands deep, iterate with a stack.

questions.q: How do you merge K sorted streams (e.g. logs from many servers) by timestamp?
questions.text: import heapq # each src is an iterator of (timestamp, line), already sorted merged = heapq.merge(*sources, key=lambda x: x[0]) for ts, line in merged: print(ts, line) heapq.merge lazily merges multiple already-sorted iterables into one sorted stream using a heap, in O(total log K) time and O(K) memory — it never loads all logs at once. This is exactly how you’d interleave per-server log files into a single chronological view for incident analysis without sorting the combined multi-GB dataset. Precondition: Each input must already be sorted by the merge key (per-server logs usually are by time). heapq.merge only does the K-way interleave, not a full sort.

questions.q: What is an LRU cache and how do you add one in Python?
questions.text: from functools import lru_cache @lru_cache(maxsize=1024) def resolve(hostname): # expensive DNS / API lookup return slow_lookup(hostname) # inspect / clear: resolve.cache_info() resolve.cache_clear() An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache stores recent results and evicts the least-recently-used entry when full, giving O(1) get/put. @functools.lru_cache memoizes a function’s return value keyed by its arguments — perfect for expensive, repeatable lookups (DNS, config fetches, API calls with stable answers). Bound maxsize so the cache can’t grow unbounded. Cache invalidation: lru_cache never expires entries on its own — only on eviction. For data that changes, you need TTL logic (use cachetools.TTLCache ) or you’ll serve stale results.

questions.q: How do you detect anomalies in a metric series with simple statistics?
questions.text: import statistics as st mean = st.mean(window); sd = st.pstdev(window) # flag points more than 3 standard deviations out for x in series: if sd and abs(x-mean) > 3*sd: flag(x) A simple, explainable anomaly check is the z-score: flag points more than ~3 standard deviations from the rolling mean. It’s cheap and good for roughly-normal metrics (latency, request rate). For real systems prefer a rolling/EWMA baseline so it adapts, and be aware it assumes normality — spiky or seasonal metrics need percentile-based or seasonal methods instead. Know the limits: z-score breaks on skewed or seasonal data (daily traffic cycles). Mention MAD (median absolute deviation) or percentile thresholds as more robust alternatives.

questions.q: Reverse-engineer: a script is slow. How do you profile and find the bottleneck?
questions.text: python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py # function-level timing # line-level: pip install line_profiler; @profile + kernprof import timeit; timeit.timeit(stmt, number=1000) # micro-bench # memory: pip install memory_profiler Measure before optimizing — intuition about hot spots is usually wrong. cProfile shows where cumulative time goes by function; line_profiler drills to specific lines; timeit micro-benchmarks small snippets; memory_profiler finds memory hogs. Find the actual bottleneck, fix that one thing, then re-measure. Amdahl’s law: Optimizing code that’s 2% of runtime is wasted effort. Profile, attack the biggest slice (often an accidental O(n²) or repeated I/O), re-profile.

questions.q: How do you implement exponential backoff with jitter correctly?
questions.text: import random def backoff(attempt, base=0.5, cap=30): # full jitter: random between 0 and the capped exp delay exp = min(cap, base * (2 ** attempt)) return random.uniform(0, exp) Exponential backoff doubles the wait per attempt ( base * 2**n ) up to a cap, so retries don’t hammer a struggling service. Jitter randomizes the delay so many clients don’t retry in lockstep — without it, every client that failed at the same instant retries simultaneously, creating a synchronized thundering herd. "Full jitter" (random between 0 and the delay) is the AWS-recommended variant. Jitter is not optional: Backoff without jitter still produces correlated retry spikes after an outage. The randomization is what actually spreads the load.

questions.q: What data structure powers a Bloom filter and when would an SRE use one?
questions.text: bit array + k hash functions add(x): set bits hash1(x)..hashk(x) maybe(x): all those bits set? → "possibly present" guarantee: no false negatives; small false-positive rate A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic set: it tells you an element is definitely not present or possibly present, using a bit array and several hash functions — a fraction of the memory of a real set. SRE uses: "have I already alerted on this fingerprint?", dedup at massive scale, or a cheap pre-check before an expensive lookup (skip the DB hit if the Bloom filter says "definitely not there"). Trade-off: You accept a tunable false-positive rate in exchange for huge memory savings. Never use it where a false "yes" is unacceptable without a confirming check.

questions.q: Write a Python script to page through a paginated REST API and collect all results.
questions.text: def fetch_all(url, session): items=[] while url: r=session.get(url, timeout=10); r.raise_for_status() body=r.json() items.extend(body["items"]) url=body.get("next") # None when no more pages return items Most APIs cap results per page and return a cursor/next-link. Loop until there’s no next page, accumulating items. Reuse a Session (connection pooling + shared retry/auth), always set a timeout, and check status. For very large result sets, yield each page instead of building one giant list, to stay memory-friendly. Respect rate limits: Honor Retry-After / X-RateLimit-Remaining headers and back off — hammering a paginated API across thousands of pages will get you throttled or banned.

questions.q: How do you authenticate to a cloud API and avoid hardcoding credentials?
questions.text: # NEVER hardcode keys. Prefer, in order: 1. Workload identity / IRSA / instance metadata (no static keys) 2. Secrets manager (Vault, AWS SM, GCP Secret Manager) 3. Env vars injected at runtime import boto3 # auto-uses role/metadata creds s3 = boto3.client("s3") # no keys in code The credential hierarchy: best is keyless — workload identity (GKE), IRSA (EKS), or instance metadata, where the cloud injects short-lived rotated credentials your SDK picks up automatically. Next best is a secrets manager fetched at runtime. Env vars are acceptable when injected by the platform. Never commit keys to code or Git — it’s the most common cause of cloud breaches. Static long-lived keys are the enemy: They leak via Git history, logs, and screenshots. Use short-lived, automatically-rotated identity wherever possible.

questions.q: Write an idempotent script to ensure a resource exists (create-or-update pattern).
questions.text: def ensure_bucket(client, name): existing = {b["Name"] for b in client.list_buckets()["Buckets"]} if name in existing: log.info("bucket %s exists", name); return False client.create_bucket(Bucket=name) log.info("created %s", name); return True Idempotent automation checks current state and only acts if needed, so re-running causes no errors or duplicates — essential because automation reruns on retries, cron, and CI. The "ensure" pattern: read desired vs actual, converge the difference. Return whether a change was made so callers can report drift. This is the philosophy behind Terraform/Ansible — declare the end state, not the steps. Reconcile, don’t imperatively create: "Make it so X exists" is safe to run repeatedly; "create X" fails the second time. Always write the former.

questions.q: How do you parse YAML safely in Python (e.g. a Kubernetes manifest)?
questions.text: import yaml with open("deploy.yaml") as f: doc = yaml.safe_load(f) # NOT yaml.load replicas = doc["spec"]["replicas"] # multi-document files (--- separated): for d in yaml.safe_load_all(open("all.yaml")): print(d["kind"]) Always use yaml.safe_load , never yaml.load without a safe loader — the unsafe loader can instantiate arbitrary Python objects and execute code from a malicious YAML file (a real RCE vector). For K8s manifests with multiple documents separated by --- , use safe_load_all which yields each document. Security: yaml.load(untrusted) is a known remote-code-execution risk. safe_load only builds plain dicts/lists — use it for anything you didn’t write yourself.

questions.q: Write a script that sends a Slack/webhook alert with structured payload.
questions.text: import requests, os def notify(text, level="warning"): hook = os.environ["SLACK_WEBHOOK"] # from secret, not code payload = {"attachments":[{ "color": {"warning":"#daa","error":"#f00"}.get(level,"#ccc"), "text": text}]} r = requests.post(hook, json=payload, timeout=5) r.raise_for_status() POST a JSON payload to the incoming-webhook URL (kept in an env var/secret, never in code). Set a short timeout so a slow Slack doesn’t block your script, and check the response. Structure the message (color by severity, fields) so on-call can triage at a glance. This is the building block for custom alerting hooks from scripts and cron jobs. Don’t spam: Add dedup/throttling so a flapping condition doesn’t fire 500 Slack messages — that’s how alert fatigue starts.

questions.q: How do you write a script that’s safe to run from cron (locking, logging, exit codes)?
questions.text: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -Eeuo pipefail exec 9>/var/lock/myjob.lock flock -n 9 || { echo "already running"; exit 0; } exec >>/var/log/myjob.log 2>&1 # all output to log echo "$(date -Is) start" # ... work ... Cron jobs need three things: a lock so overlapping runs don’t collide ( flock -n exits if another instance holds it), explicit logging (cron’s environment is minimal and output otherwise vanishes or emails root), and correct exit codes. Also set full paths and required env vars — cron runs with a bare PATH and no profile, a classic "works in my shell, fails in cron" trap. The cron environment is not your shell: No aliases, minimal PATH, different locale. Always use absolute paths and source needed env explicitly.

questions.q: How do you template config files in Python (e.g. generate per-environment configs)?
questions.text: from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("templates"), undefined=__import__("jinja2").StrictUndefined) tmpl = env.get_template("app.conf.j2") out = tmpl.render(env="prod", replicas=5, region="us-east1") open("app.conf","w").write(out) Jinja2 templating generates config from a template plus variables — the engine behind Ansible and Helm-style rendering. Use StrictUndefined so a missing variable raises an error instead of silently rendering blank (which causes broken configs that fail mysteriously at runtime). Keep templates in version control and render per-environment. Fail loud on missing vars: StrictUndefined turns "forgot to set region" into an immediate template error, not a config with an empty region that breaks in prod.

questions.q: Write a script to back up a directory and rotate old backups.
questions.text: ts=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S) tar czf "/backups/data-$ts.tgz" -C /var/lib/app data # keep only the 7 most recent ls -1t /backups/data-*.tgz | tail -n +8 | xargs -r rm -f Timestamp each backup for ordering and traceability. The rotation pipeline lists backups newest-first ( ls -1t ), skips the 7 most recent ( tail -n +8 ), and removes the rest — xargs -r avoids running rm with no args. This bounds disk usage so backups don’t silently fill the volume (a frequent self-inflicted outage). Untested backups aren’t backups: Add a periodic restore test. Plenty of teams discover their backups were corrupt or empty only during a real incident.

questions.q: How do you handle secrets in a script without leaking them in logs or process list?
questions.text: # BAD: visible in ps/history curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ... # token in ps args? no—env is ok mysql -u root -p"$PASS" # ← password visible in ps! # GOOD: read from file / stdin / env mysql --defaults-extra-file=/run/secrets/my.cnf read -rs TOKEN < /run/secrets/token Secrets passed as command-line arguments appear in ps , shell history, and process listings — any user on the box can read them. Pass secrets via environment variables, files with restricted permissions ( 0600 ), or stdin instead. Also avoid set -x while handling secrets (it echoes them to logs), and scrub secrets from error output. Two leak vectors people forget: command-line args (visible in ps ) and set -x trace output. Both expose secrets to anyone with shell/log access.

questions.q: Write a Python health-aggregator that checks N endpoints concurrently.
questions.text: from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed def check(url): try: return url, requests.get(url, timeout=3).status_code except Exception as e: return url, f"ERR {e}" with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20) as ex: futs=[ex.submit(check,u) for u in urls] for f in as_completed(futs): print(*f.result()) Health checks are I/O-bound (waiting on the network), so threads give real speedup despite the GIL. ThreadPoolExecutor bounds concurrency (don’t open 5000 sockets at once), submit schedules work, and as_completed yields results as they finish. Each check catches its own exceptions so one bad endpoint doesn’t crash the whole sweep. Bound the pool: max_workers caps concurrent connections so you don’t exhaust file descriptors or overwhelm the targets you’re checking.

questions.q: How do you make a long-running script gracefully handle SIGTERM (e.g. in a container)?
questions.text: import signal, sys stop=False def handle(sig, frame): global stop; stop=True signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handle) signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, handle) while not stop: do_work_chunk() cleanup(); sys.exit(0) Kubernetes sends SIGTERM before SIGKILL during pod shutdown. A graceful handler sets a flag, finishes the current unit of work, flushes/commits, and exits cleanly within the termination grace period — avoiding corrupted state, lost messages, or half-done writes. Don’t do heavy work inside the handler; just signal the main loop to wind down. Respect the grace period: If cleanup takes longer than terminationGracePeriodSeconds , K8s SIGKILLs you. Keep shutdown fast or checkpoint progress.

questions.q: How do you diff desired vs actual state and only apply changes?
questions.text: desired = load_desired() # {name: spec} actual = fetch_actual() to_create = desired.keys() - actual.keys() to_delete = actual.keys() - desired.keys() to_update = {k for k in desired&actual.keys() if desired[k] != actual[k]} for k in to_create: create(k, desired[k]) # etc. This reconciliation loop is the core of declarative automation (Terraform, K8s controllers): compute the set difference between desired and actual state, then create/update/delete only what differs. Using sets makes the diff O(n) and the intent explicit. Always support a --dry-run that prints the plan without applying — so humans can review before infrastructure changes. Plan then apply: Show the diff first (like terraform plan ). Surprising deletes are how reconciliation scripts cause outages.

questions.q: Write a script to roll-restart pods/services one at a time, verifying health between each.
questions.text: for pod in $(kubectl get pods -l app=api -o name); do kubectl delete "$pod" kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=120s || exit 1 sleep 5 # let it settle before the next done A safe rolling restart takes down one instance at a time and waits for the replacement to become healthy before proceeding — preserving capacity and catching a bad rollout early (the || exit 1 stops the loop if health never recovers). This "verify between steps" pattern prevents the disaster of restarting everything at once and discovering too late that the new version is broken. One at a time + health gate: Restarting all replicas simultaneously turns a bad deploy into a full outage. The gate between steps is what makes it safe.

questions.q: How do you safely do find-and-replace across many config files?
questions.text: # preview first — NO in-place edit yet grep -rl 'old.host.com' /etc/app/ # then edit, with a backup suffix grep -rl 'old.host.com' /etc/app/ \ | xargs sed -i.bak 's/old\.host\.com/new.host.com/g' Always preview the affected files ( grep -rl ) before mutating anything. Then sed -i.bak edits in place but keeps a .bak backup so you can revert. Escape regex metacharacters (the dots in a hostname) to avoid matching unintended text. For anything important, do it in version control so the diff is reviewable and revertible. Unescaped dots bite: s/old.host.com/.../ matches oldXhostYcom too. Escape literal dots ( \. ) or you’ll corrupt unexpected lines.

questions.q: How do you build a small CLI that wraps kubectl/cloud commands for your team?
questions.text: import subprocess, click @click.group() def cli(): pass @cli.command() @click.argument("svc") @click.option("--ns", default="default") def logs(svc, ns): subprocess.run(["kubectl","logs","-l",f"app={svc}","-n",ns]) if __name__=="__main__": cli() An internal CLI encodes team conventions and guardrails over raw commands — standard namespaces, label selectors, safety checks — so engineers don’t memorize long invocations or make dangerous mistakes. click (or typer ) gives subcommands, options, and help with minimal boilerplate. This is platform engineering in miniature: paving a golden path as a tool. Guardrails in the wrapper: e.g. refuse to run destructive commands against prod without a confirmation flag — the CLI becomes where you enforce safety.

questions.q: How do you read configuration from multiple sources with precedence (flags > env > file > default)?
questions.text: def get(key, cli_val=None): if cli_val is not None: return cli_val # 1 flags if key.upper() in os.environ: # 2 env return os.environ[key.upper()] if key in file_cfg: return file_cfg[key] # 3 file return DEFAULTS[key] # 4 default The 12-factor precedence chain: explicit CLI flags override environment variables, which override a config file, which overrides built-in defaults. This gives operators flexibility (override one value at runtime without editing files) while keeping sane defaults. Resolve each setting through the same ordered lookup so behavior is predictable and documented. Make precedence visible: A --show-config that prints the effective values and where each came from saves hours of "why is it using that value?" debugging.

questions.q: Write a script to wait for a condition (e.g. service ready) with timeout.
questions.text: deadline=$(( $(date +%s) + 120 )) # 2-min timeout until curl -fsS localhost:8080/ready >/dev/null 2> do (( $(date +%s) > deadline )) && { echo "timed out"; exit 1; } echo "waiting..."; sleep 3 done echo "ready" Polling-with-timeout is everywhere in deploy automation: wait for a service to pass readiness, a DB migration to finish, a resource to provision. Always bound the wait with a deadline so a stuck dependency fails the pipeline instead of hanging forever. Use a fixed poll interval (or backoff) and emit progress so logs show it’s alive, not frozen. Bounded waits only: An unbounded "wait until ready" in CI will hang a build agent indefinitely when something’s actually broken. The timeout converts a hang into a clear failure.

questions.q: How do you make automation observable — metrics/logs from your scripts?
questions.text: # emit a Prometheus-style metric to the pushgateway cat <<EOF | curl --data-binary @- \ http://pushgw:9091/metrics/job/backup backup_success{host="$(hostname)"} 1 backup_duration_seconds $SECONDS EOF Cron jobs and automation fail silently unless you instrument them. Emit a success/failure metric and duration to a Pushgateway (for short-lived jobs) or write structured logs your shipper collects — then alert on "backup_success == 0" or "job hasn’t reported in 25h". This turns invisible batch failures into actionable alerts instead of discovering a week-old broken backup during an incident. Alert on absence: The most valuable batch-job alert is "this job didn’t run/report when expected" — a job that silently stops running emits no failure at all.

questions.q: How do you extract specific fields from kubectl output for scripting?
questions.text: # jsonpath — built into kubectl kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' # custom columns kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName # or pipe JSON to jq kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '.items[].metadata.name' For reliable scripting, get structured output ( -o json / -o jsonpath ) and parse it — never grep/awk the human-readable table, whose columns and spacing change between versions. jsonpath and custom-columns are built in; jq is more powerful for filtering and transforming. This is the difference between automation that survives a kubectl upgrade and automation that silently breaks. Never parse the default table: Column order, widths, and added columns vary by version and flags. Structured output is the contract; the table is not.

questions.q: Write a jq filter to list pods not in Running state.
questions.text: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ' .items[] | select(.status.phase != "Running") | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) \(.status.phase)"' jq is the standard tool for slicing JSON on the command line. .items[] iterates the list, select(...) filters, and "\(.field)" string-interpolates for clean output. -r emits raw strings (no quotes). This one-liner finds problem pods across all namespaces — a common triage starting point during an incident. Phase isn’t the whole story: A pod can be Running but not Ready (failing readiness). For real health, also check .status.conditions[] where type=="Ready" .

questions.q: How do you script against the Kubernetes API directly in Python?
questions.text: from kubernetes import client, config config.load_incluster_config() # or load_kube_config() locally v1 = client.CoreV1Api() for p in v1.list_pod_for_all_namespaces().items: if p.status.phase != "Running": print(p.metadata.namespace, p.metadata.name, p.status.phase) The official Python client talks to the API server directly — better than shelling out to kubectl for anything non-trivial (typed objects, watch streams, error handling). load_incluster_config() uses the pod’s service-account token when running inside the cluster; load_kube_config() uses your local kubeconfig. This is how you build controllers, operators, and custom automation. RBAC scope it: Give the service account only the verbs/resources it needs (least privilege). A script that only reads pods shouldn’t have delete on secrets.

questions.q: How do you safely run a command across many EC2 instances / VMs?
questions.text: # Prefer agent-based (SSM) over raw SSH at scale aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \ --targets Key=tag:env,Values=prod \ --parameters 'commands=["systemctl restart app"]' # raw SSH fan-out (small scale), bounded parallelism: printf '%s\n' "${hosts[@]}" | xargs -P5 -I{} ssh {} 'uptime' At scale, prefer a managed mechanism (AWS SSM, Ansible, Salt) over hand-rolled SSH loops — they handle auth, auditing, bounded concurrency, and partial failures. If you do fan out over SSH, bound parallelism ( xargs -P ), set ConnectTimeout , and capture per-host results so you know exactly which hosts failed rather than a vague aggregate error. Blast radius: A "restart everything" fan-out with no canary or batching can take down a whole fleet at once. Batch it, verify health between batches.

questions.q: Write a script to clean up untagged/old cloud resources (cost hygiene).
questions.text: import boto3, datetime as dt ec2 = boto3.client("ec2") cutoff = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc) - dt.timedelta(days=30) for v in ec2.describe_volumes( Filters=[{"Name":"status","Values":["available"]}])["Volumes"]: if v["CreateTime"] < cutoff: print("would delete", v["VolumeId"]) # dry-run first! Orphaned resources (unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers) quietly burn money. A cleanup script finds resources matching "wasteful" criteria (unattached + older than N days) and removes them. Always dry-run first — print what would be deleted, have a human review, and ideally require an explicit tag or grace period before any destructive action. Destructive automation needs guardrails: dry-run by default, an allow/deny tag (e.g. keep=true ), and a confirmation flag. Auto-deleting cloud resources has ended careers.

questions.q: How do you stream and follow logs from multiple pods in a script?
questions.text: # all pods of a deployment, prefixed, following kubectl logs -f -l app=api --all-containers --prefix --tail=50 # or use stern for multi-pod tailing stern api --since 10m Modern kubectl logs can follow ( -f ) a label selector across pods with --prefix to show which pod each line came from. For richer multi-pod tailing across deployments, stern is the de-facto tool (color-coded by pod, regex filtering). During an incident, aggregated live logs across replicas are essential to spot which instance is misbehaving. Bound it: --tail and --since prevent pulling gigabytes of history. For real analysis, query your log backend (Loki) rather than streaming from the cluster.

questions.q: How do you compute resource usage / find the noisy-neighbor pod by script?
questions.text: # top pods by CPU across the cluster (needs metrics-server) kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu | head # memory: kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head # script: flag pods near their limits via /metrics or PromQL kubectl top (backed by metrics-server) gives live CPU/memory per pod; sorting surfaces the heaviest consumers — the first step in finding a noisy neighbor or a leaking pod. For real analysis, query Prometheus: compare usage against requests/limits to find pods being throttled (CPU) or at OOM risk (memory near limit). Scripted, this feeds rightsizing and capacity work. Usage vs limits: High CPU isn’t bad if under limit; the signal is sustained throttling or memory creeping toward the limit (OOMKill incoming).

questions.q: Write a kubectl wait / rollout verification snippet for a deploy script.
questions.text: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml if ! kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=180s; then echo "rollout failed — rolling back" >&2 kubectl rollout undo deploy/api exit 1 fi kubectl rollout status blocks until the new ReplicaSet is fully available or the timeout hits, returning non-zero on failure — so your deploy script can detect a bad rollout and automatically rollout undo to the previous revision. This automated rollback-on-failure is what makes scripted deploys safe: a broken image self-heals instead of sitting half-deployed. Mitigate before diagnose: Auto-rollback restores service first; you investigate the bad build afterward. That’s the SRE deploy reflex encoded in a script.

questions.q: How do you generate Kubernetes manifests programmatically and validate them?
questions.text: # render then validate before applying python gen_manifests.py > out.yaml kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f out.yaml # API-side validation kubeconform -strict out.yaml # schema validation # in Python, build dicts and yaml.safe_dump them Generate manifests as Python dicts and yaml.safe_dump them, or template with Jinja/Helm. Critically, validate before applying: --dry-run=server runs real API admission (catches policy/webhook rejections), and kubeconform / kubeval checks schema offline in CI. Catching a malformed manifest in CI beats discovering it when the apply half-succeeds in prod. Two validation layers: offline schema check (fast, in CI) plus server dry-run (catches admission webhooks/policies the schema can’t). Use both.

questions.q: How do you handle pagination and throttling when listing many cloud resources?
questions.text: import boto3 ec2 = boto3.client("ec2") # paginators handle NextToken + retries automatically for page in ec2.get_paginator("describe_instances").paginate(): for r in page["Reservations"]: for i in r["Instances"]: handle(i) Cloud list APIs paginate and throttle. SDK paginators handle the NextToken loop for you and integrate with the SDK’s built-in exponential-backoff retry on throttling errors — far more robust than a hand-rolled loop. For very large accounts, process each page as it arrives (don’t accumulate everything) and respect rate limits to avoid RequestLimitExceeded . Don’t reinvent retries: The SDK already does exponential backoff on throttling. Hand-rolled list loops usually forget this and fail on large accounts.

questions.q: Write a script that snapshots then validates a database backup.
questions.text: set -Eeuo pipefail snap="bk-$(date +%F-%H%M)" pg_dump -Fc "$DATABASE_URL" -f "/backups/$snap.dump" # validate: restore to a throwaway DB and run a sanity query createdb verify_$snap pg_restore -d verify_$snap "/backups/$snap.dump" psql -d verify_$snap -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM users' | grep -q '[1-9]' dropdb verify_$snap A backup you haven’t restored is a hope, not a backup. This script dumps, then actually restores into a throwaway database and runs a sanity query to confirm the data is present and the dump isn’t corrupt — then cleans up. Automating restore-verification is what separates teams that recover in an incident from teams that discover their backups were empty. Test restores on a schedule: Corruption, partial dumps, and permission changes silently break backups. Only a real restore proves they work.

questions.q: How do you write a script that’s portable across Linux distros / shells?
questions.text: #!/bin/sh # POSIX sh, not bash, for max portability # avoid bashisms: [[ ]], arrays, ${x^^}, <<< command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "need jq" > exit 1; } # detect package manager: if command -v apt-get; then PM="apt-get"; elif command -v dnf; then PM="dnf"; fi For scripts that must run anywhere (containers, Alpine, BSD, minimal images), target POSIX sh and avoid bash-only features. Check for required tools with command -v and fail clearly if missing. Detect distro differences (package manager, paths) rather than assuming. Alpine uses busybox with leaner utilities, so flags you rely on in GNU coreutils may not exist. Test on the real target: A script that works on your Ubuntu laptop may break in an Alpine container (busybox sed / grep differ). Run it where it’ll actually run.

questions.q: Why is Go popular for platform/SRE tooling over Python?
questions.text: + single static binary — no runtime/deps to ship + fast, compiled, low memory + first-class concurrency (goroutines, channels) + the ecosystem language: K8s, Terraform, Prometheus, Docker − more verbose, slower to prototype than Python Go compiles to a single static binary you can drop on any host or into a scratch container — no interpreter, no dependency hell. It’s fast and memory-light, has built-in concurrency, and is the language the entire cloud-native stack is written in (Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus, etcd, Docker). For distributed tools and anything you ship as a binary, Go wins; for quick scripts and glue, Python is faster to write. Rule of thumb: Quick automation/glue → Python/Bash. A daemon, controller, or CLI you distribute as a binary → Go.

questions.q: Explain goroutines and channels with a worker-pool example.
questions.text: jobs := make(chan string, 100) results := make(chan int, 100) for w := 0; w < 5; w++ { // 5 workers go func() { for j := range jobs { results <- process(j) } }() } for _, j := range tasks { jobs <- j } close(jobs) A goroutine is a lightweight thread (thousands are cheap); go func(){} launches one. Channels pass data between them safely without locks. The worker-pool pattern bounds concurrency: a fixed set of goroutines pulls jobs off a channel, so you process work in parallel without spawning unbounded goroutines. This is the idiomatic way to fan out network/IO work in Go tooling. "Share memory by communicating": Channels let goroutines coordinate without manual mutexes — fewer race conditions than thread+lock models.

questions.q: How does Go error handling work and why no exceptions?
questions.text: f, err := os.Open(path) if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("opening %s: %w", path, err) // wrap } defer f.Close() Go returns errors as explicit values instead of throwing exceptions, forcing you to handle (or deliberately ignore) each one at the call site — verbose, but it makes failure paths visible and hard to silently skip. Wrapping with %w preserves the error chain for errors.Is / errors.As inspection. panic exists but is reserved for truly unrecoverable programmer errors, not normal failures. Add context when wrapping: fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err) builds a breadcrumb trail so the final error tells you the whole failure path, not just the leaf cause.

questions.q: What is defer and how do SREs use it for cleanup?
questions.text: resp, err := http.Get(url) if err != nil { return err } defer resp.Body.Close() // runs when function returns mu.Lock(); defer mu.Unlock() defer schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, regardless of how it returns (normal or error). It keeps cleanup right next to acquisition — open then defer Close() , lock then defer Unlock() — so you never forget to release resources. Deferred calls run in LIFO order. It’s Go’s equivalent of a context manager / finally . Defer in loops: defer fires at function return, not loop-iteration end — deferring inside a long loop leaks resources until the function exits. Close explicitly per-iteration or wrap the body in a function.

questions.q: How do you build and ship a Go tool as a minimal container?
questions.text: # build a static binary CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o app ./cmd/app # multi-stage Dockerfile → tiny image FROM golang:1.22 AS build ... go build ... FROM gcr.io/distroless/static # or scratch COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] Go’s static binaries enable tiny, secure images. Build with CGO_ENABLED=0 for a fully static binary, then use a multi-stage Dockerfile: a fat builder stage compiles, and the final stage is distroless/static or scratch with just the binary — a few MB, minimal attack surface, no shell or package manager for attackers to abuse. Distroless > Alpine for Go: Since the binary is static, you don’t need a libc or shell at all. Smaller image, far fewer CVEs to patch.

questions.q: What’s the Go concurrency gotcha with loop variables and goroutines?
questions.text: // pre-1.22 BUG: all goroutines saw the final i for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { go func() { fmt.Println(i) }() // often prints 3,3,3 } // fix (pre-1.22): capture per iteration for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { i := i; go func(){ fmt.Println(i) }() } Before Go 1.22, loop variables were shared across iterations, so goroutines closing over i all read its final value — a notorious concurrency bug. The fix was shadowing ( i := i ) or passing as an argument. Go 1.22 changed loop semantics so each iteration gets its own variable, fixing it by default — but you’ll still see the old pattern in existing code and older interview questions. Know your version: On Go <1.22 this bites; on ≥1.22 it’s fixed. Mention both — it shows you track language evolution.

questions.q: What makes a script production-grade vs a throwaway one-liner?
questions.text: ✓ strict mode / error handling, non-zero exit on failure ✓ idempotent + dry-run for anything destructive ✓ logging, observability, clear messages ✓ input validation + required-config checks ✓ timeouts, retries, graceful shutdown ✓ tests + shellcheck/lint in CI; documented usage A throwaway script just needs to work once on known input. Production-grade means it survives bad input, partial failures, reruns, and interruption — with error handling, idempotency, dry-run, logging, timeouts, and tests. The mindset shift: assume everything can fail and the script will run unattended at 3am. That’s what separates tooling other people can trust from a personal hack. The 3am test: "Would I trust this to run unattended in prod and fail safely?" If not, it needs error handling, idempotency, and observability first.

questions.q: How do you make any mutating script safe with a dry-run mode?
questions.text: DRY_RUN=${DRY_RUN:-1} # default to SAFE run() { if [[ "$DRY_RUN" == 1 ]]; then echo "DRY: $*"; else "$@"; fi } run rm -rf "$old_dir" run kubectl delete pod "$p" Route every destructive action through a run wrapper that either prints (dry-run) or executes. Default to dry-run so the safe behavior is the accidental one — a human must consciously pass DRY_RUN=0 to actually mutate. This lets operators preview exactly what a script will do before committing, turning "oops it deleted prod" into "the plan looked wrong, I stopped." Default to safe: If dry-run is opt-in, someone will run the destructive path by accident. Make execution the explicit, deliberate choice.

questions.q: A script worked in staging but fails in prod. How do you debug systematically?
questions.text: 1. Read the actual error + exit code (don’t guess) 2. Diff the environments: versions, env vars, perms, data scale, network 3. Reproduce minimally; add set -x / verbose logging 4. Check scale: O(n²) or memory fine on 100 rows, dies on 10M 5. Check perms/secrets/network policy differences "Works here, fails there" almost always comes down to an environment difference: tool versions, missing env vars, tighter permissions/RBAC, network policy, locale, or — very commonly — data scale (prod has 1000x the rows and exposes an O(n²) or memory bug). Debug methodically: capture the real error, diff the two environments systematically, reproduce small, then turn on tracing. Resist guessing. Scale is the usual culprit: Code that’s instant on staging’s tiny dataset can time out or OOM on prod volume. Test with prod-like data sizes.

questions.q: How do you prevent and detect common shell-injection / command-injection bugs?
questions.text: # VULNERABLE: user input in a shell string os.system(f"ping {user_host}") # user_host="x; rm -rf /" # SAFE: arg list, no shell subprocess.run(["ping","-c","1", user_host]) # Bash: quote everything, validate input [[ "$host" =~ ^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+$ ]] || exit 1 Command injection happens when untrusted input is interpolated into a shell string — the attacker smuggles in ; , && , or backticks to run their own commands. The fix is to never build shell strings from input: pass arguments as a list with shell=False , so the OS treats them as literal arguments. In Bash, quote all expansions and validate input against a strict allowlist pattern. The root cause is string-building: Any time user/external data becomes part of a command string , you have a potential injection. Pass args as a list, not a string.

questions.q: How do you structure a larger automation codebase so a team can maintain it?
questions.text: cli/ entrypoints (argparse/click) lib/ reusable modules (clients, parsing, config) tests/ pytest unit + integration pyproject.toml pinned deps, lint/format config README + --help + type hints + CI (lint+test) Past a few scripts, treat automation like real software: separate thin CLI entrypoints from reusable library logic, write tests, pin dependencies, and enforce lint/format/type-check in CI. Add type hints and a README so the next engineer (or you in six months) can understand and safely change it. The goal is that anyone on the team can fix a bug without fear — not a pile of one-off scripts only the author understands. Bus-factor: Tested, documented, linted automation survives the author leaving. A folder of clever undocumented scripts is technical debt waiting to break.

questions.q: Live coding: parse a log, compute error rate per endpoint, alert if any exceeds 5%. Walk through it.
questions.text: from collections import defaultdict total=defaultdict(int); errors=defaultdict(int) for line in open("access.log"): rec=parse(line) # {path,status}; skip None if not rec: continue total[rec["path"]]+=1 if rec["status"]>=500: errors[rec["path"]]+=1 for path,n in total.items(): rate=errors[path]/n if rate>0.05 and n>=100: # ignore low-traffic noise alert(f"{path}: {rate:.1%} errors ({errors[path]}/{n})") The structure interviewers want: stream the file (constant memory), parse defensively (skip malformed lines), tally totals and errors per endpoint with defaultdict in one pass (O(n)), then compute the rate and alert. The crucial nuance is the minimum-volume guard ( n>=100 ): a path with 2 requests and 1 error is 50% but statistically meaningless — alerting on it creates noise. Mention edge cases out loud: empty file, all-bad lines, division by zero. What earns the offer: Streaming not loading, defensive parsing, one-pass O(n) counting, and especially the low-traffic guard — it shows you think about alert quality, not just code that "works."

questions.q: How do you use dataclasses, and when are they better than a plain dict or NamedTuple?
questions.text: from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) class Host: name: str cpu: int = 0 tags: list = field(default_factory=list) # never a mutable default! h = Host('web1', cpu=4) A @dataclass auto-generates __init__ , __repr__ , and __eq__ from typed fields — far more readable and self-documenting than a bare dict, with attribute access and type hints. frozen=True makes instances immutable and hashable (usable as dict keys/set members); slots=True cuts memory and speeds attribute access. Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults to avoid the shared-default footgun. Over dict: typed fields catch typos ( h.cpuu is an AttributeError, d['cpuu'] a silent KeyError later), and the class documents the shape. Over NamedTuple: dataclasses support defaults, mutation, and inheritance more cleanly.

questions.q: Explain the GIL precisely — what it does and does not prevent.
questions.text: # GIL = Global Interpreter Lock: one thread runs Python bytecode at a time CPU-bound threads -> NO speedup (serialized by GIL) I/O-bound threads -> YES speedup (GIL released during I/O waits) multiprocessing -> true parallelism (separate interpreters, no shared GIL) # Python 3.13+: experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) can disable it The GIL is a mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so pure-Python CPU work does not parallelize across threads. It does not block I/O concurrency: the GIL is released during blocking syscalls (network, disk), so threads overlap I/O effectively. C extensions (numpy) can also release it during heavy compute. For CPU parallelism use multiprocessing (or 3.13's experimental free-threaded build). Why it exists: it simplifies CPython's memory management (reference counting) and C-extension safety. The free-threaded work (PEP 703) is the long-term path to removing it without breaking the ecosystem.

questions.q: How do you profile memory and find a leak in a long-running Python service?
questions.text: import tracemalloc tracemalloc.start() snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot() # ... run workload ... snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot() for stat in snap2.compare_to(snap1, 'lineno')[:10]: print(stat) # top growth by source line # also: tracemalloc, objgraph, or memory_profiler / py-spy for live procs tracemalloc (stdlib) snapshots allocations by source line; diffing two snapshots taken over time pinpoints what keeps growing — the signature of a leak. In Python, 'leaks' are usually unbounded growth: an ever-growing cache/list, lingering references in a module-level dict, or a closure capturing large objects. py-spy can profile a running process without restarting it, which is invaluable in prod. Common culprit: an unbounded @lru_cache (no maxsize), a module-level list that's appended forever, or registering callbacks/observers without ever deregistering them. Bound your caches and audit module-level mutable state.

questions.q: What is the difference between __str__ and __repr__, and why do both matter?
questions.text: class Job: def __init__(self, id): self.id = id def __repr__(self): return f'Job(id={self.id!r})' # unambiguous, dev-facing def __str__(self): return f'job {self.id}' # readable, user-facing j = Job('x'); print(j) # uses __str__ -> 'job x' j # uses __repr__ -> Job(id='x') [j] # containers use __repr__ __repr__ is the unambiguous developer representation (ideally something you could paste back to recreate the object); it's what you see in the REPL, in tracebacks, and inside containers. __str__ is the human-readable form used by print() and str() . If you define only one, define __repr__ — Python falls back to it for str() , and good reprs make debugging logs and stack traces vastly more useful. SRE relevance: a meaningful __repr__ turns a useless <Job object at 0x7f...> in your error logs into Job(id='abc') — the difference between a fast diagnosis and a guessing game.

questions.q: How do you write async code with asyncio to fan out 1000 HTTP requests efficiently?
questions.text: import asyncio, aiohttp async def fetch(session, url): async with session.get(url, timeout=aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=5)) as r: return url, r.status async def main(urls): sem = asyncio.Semaphore(50) # bound concurrency async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s: async def bound(u): async with sem: return await fetch(s, u) return await asyncio.gather(*(bound(u) for u in urls)) asyncio runs thousands of concurrent I/O operations on a single thread via an event loop — ideal for high-fan-out network work without the overhead of thousands of threads. asyncio.gather runs coroutines concurrently and collects results; a Semaphore bounds how many run at once so you don't open 1000 sockets and exhaust file descriptors or hammer the target. Always set per-request timeouts. Don't block the loop: a single synchronous/CPU-bound call inside a coroutine freezes the entire event loop and stalls every other task. Keep async code non-blocking; offload CPU work to an executor.

questions.q: Explain the difference between == on floats and why it bites in production.
questions.text: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 # False! -> 0.30000000000000004 import math math.isclose(0.1+0.2, 0.3) # True (relative tolerance) math.isclose(a, b, abs_tol=1e-9) # for values near zero # money: use Decimal, never float from decimal import Decimal; Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') # exact 0.3 Floats are binary IEEE-754 and cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 . Never compare floats with == ; use math.isclose with appropriate tolerances. For money or anything requiring exact decimal arithmetic, use Decimal — float rounding errors in billing or financial calculations are real incidents. The classic bug: summing many floats accumulates error, and == threshold checks flake intermittently. For currency, Decimal (or integer cents) is mandatory, not optional.

questions.q: How does Python's import system work, and what causes circular import errors?
questions.text: # circular: a.py imports b, b.py imports a -> ImportError / partial module # fixes: import b # import the MODULE, use b.func() lazily def handler(): from b import thing # deferred import inside the function # or: extract the shared piece into a third module both import Importing runs the module top-to-bottom once, caching it in sys.modules . A circular import fails when module A (mid-execution) imports B, which imports A again — but A isn't finished, so the name B wants isn't defined yet. Fixes: import the module rather than names from it (resolve attributes lazily at call time), defer the import inside a function, or refactor the shared dependency into a third module. Circular imports usually signal a layering problem. Design signal: a circular import often means two modules are too entangled. The cleanest fix is extracting the shared abstraction, not just deferring the import.

questions.q: How do you safely handle and clean up resources when multiple can fail (ExitStack)?
questions.text: from contextlib import ExitStack with ExitStack() as stack: files = [stack.enter_context(open(p)) for p in paths] conn = stack.enter_context(db.connect()) # all of files + conn are cleaned up in reverse order on exit, # even if one of them (or the body) raises ExitStack manages a dynamic number of context managers — you don't know how many files/connections until runtime. Each enter_context registers cleanup; when the with block exits (normally or via exception), everything is closed in reverse (LIFO) order. This avoids deeply nested with statements and guarantees partial setup is fully unwound if a later resource fails to open. Why it matters: opening N resources where resource K fails would leak the first K-1 without ExitStack. It makes 'open many, clean up all, even on partial failure' correct and readable.

questions.q: What are Python's f-string pitfalls and the right way to log structured data?
questions.text: # BAD: f-string formats EVEN when the log level is disabled (wasted work) log.debug(f'processing {expensive()}') # GOOD: lazy %-args, formatted only if DEBUG is enabled log.debug('processing %s', expensive_repr) # structured: log.info('request done', extra={'path': path, 'ms': dur, 'status': code}) f-strings are great for general formatting but wrong for logging: the string is built eagerly even when that log level is suppressed, wasting CPU on hot paths. Use the logger's lazy %s arguments so formatting only happens if the message is actually emitted. For machine-queryable logs, attach fields via extra= (or use structlog) so you can filter by path / status in Loki/Elasticsearch instead of regexing free text. Subtle perf bug: log.debug(f'...') in a tight loop computes the string a million times even in production where DEBUG is off. The %s form skips it.

questions.q: How do you pin dependencies and build reproducible Python environments?
questions.text: # modern: pyproject.toml + a lockfile uv pip compile pyproject.toml -o requirements.txt # fully pinned + hashes uv pip sync requirements.txt # exact, reproducible install # or pip-tools: pip-compile / pip-sync pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt # verify integrity Reproducibility means every install resolves to the identical versions. Declare loose constraints in pyproject.toml , then compile a fully-pinned lockfile (with hashes) committed to the repo, and install from that in CI/prod. Hashes ( --require-hashes ) verify supply-chain integrity. Tools like uv or pip-tools separate 'what I want' (pyproject) from 'exactly what's installed' (lockfile) — the same pattern as package-lock.json or Cargo.lock. Unpinned = irreproducible: pip install requests with no lock gives different versions on different days, causing 'works on my machine' and surprise breakages when a transitive dep ships a bad release.

questions.q: Explain __enter__/__exit__ — write a class-based context manager for a lock with timeout.
questions.text: import time class FileLock: def __init__(self, path, timeout=10): self.path, self.timeout = path, timeout def __enter__(self): deadline = time.monotonic() + self.timeout while not self._try_acquire(): if time.monotonic() > deadline: raise TimeoutError(self.path) time.sleep(0.1) return self def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb): self._release() # runs even if the with-body raised return False # don't suppress exceptions A class context manager implements __enter__ (setup, returns the resource) and __exit__ (teardown, always runs). __exit__ receives any exception info; returning False lets the exception propagate (returning True would swallow it — rarely what you want). This pattern guarantees the lock is released even if the protected block raises, and the timeout prevents waiting forever on a stuck lock. Always release in __exit__: putting release there (not after the with-body) is what makes it exception-safe. Return False so you don't accidentally hide errors that occurred inside the block.

questions.q: How do you validate and parse external input robustly (e.g. with pydantic)?
questions.text: from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator class Config(BaseModel): replicas: int env: str @field_validator('replicas') @classmethod def positive(cls, v): if v < 1: raise ValueError('replicas must be >= 1') return v cfg = Config(**yaml.safe_load(open('c.yaml'))) # raises on bad input Parsing untrusted/external data (config files, API payloads, env) is where bugs and security issues enter. pydantic validates types and constraints at the boundary and produces typed objects, so the rest of your code works with guaranteed-valid data. It fails fast with clear messages on bad input instead of letting a malformed value cause a confusing error deep in the call stack. This is the 'parse, don't validate' discipline. Validate at the edge: convert raw dicts to validated models the moment data enters your program. Downstream code then trusts the types, and errors point at the actual source (the bad input), not a distant symptom.

questions.q: What is the walrus operator and a genuinely useful SRE use case?
questions.text: # assign-and-test in one expression (3.8+) while (chunk := f.read(8192)): process(chunk) # avoid calling expensive thing twice: if (m := PATTERN.search(line)) is not None: handle(m.group('ip')) # filter + reuse in a comprehension: results = [y for x in data if (y := transform(x)) is not None] The walrus := assigns within an expression. Its best uses: reading in chunks until empty (assign and test the read in the loop condition), capturing a regex match once and reusing it, and computing a value in a comprehension's filter to reuse in the output without calling the function twice. Used sparingly it removes duplicate calls and tightens loops; overused it hurts readability. Use it for: 'compute once, test, then reuse' patterns — especially regex matches and chunked reads. Don't sprinkle it everywhere; clarity beats cleverness.

questions.q: How do you handle timezones correctly in Python (a frequent production bug)?
questions.text: from datetime import datetime, timezone from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo # stdlib 3.9+ now = datetime.now(timezone.utc) # ALWAYS aware, in UTC # convert for display only: now.astimezone(ZoneInfo('Asia/Kolkata')) # parse ISO with offset: datetime.fromisoformat('2026-01-15T10:00:00+05:30') # AVOID: datetime.now() -> naive, ambiguous, bug magnet Store and compute in UTC with timezone-aware datetimes; convert to local time only for display. Naive datetimes (no tzinfo) are ambiguous and the source of countless bugs — comparing naive and aware raises, and datetime.now() silently uses local time. Use datetime.now(timezone.utc) and zoneinfo for conversions. For durations use time.monotonic() , which is immune to clock changes and DST. The DST/log-correlation trap: mixing naive local timestamps across servers in different zones makes log correlation impossible and breaks scheduling around DST transitions. UTC everywhere internally is the only safe rule.

questions.q: What's the difference between shallow iteration and copying when mutating during a loop?
questions.text: # BUG: modifying a list while iterating it skips elements / errors for x in items: if bad(x): items.remove(x) # WRONG # FIX: iterate a copy, or build a new list for x in items[:]: # iterate a shallow copy if bad(x): items.remove(x) items = [x for x in items if not bad(x)] # cleaner: rebuild # dict: for k in list(d): if ...: del d[k] Mutating a collection while iterating it corrupts the iteration — lists skip elements (indices shift), and dicts/sets raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration . The fixes: iterate over a copy ( items[:] or list(d) ) so the original can be mutated safely, or — usually cleaner — build a new filtered collection with a comprehension instead of removing in place. Prefer rebuilding: items = [x for x in items if keep(x)] is clearer and bug-free versus in-place removal. Reach for it before copy-and-mutate.

questions.q: How do you make a CPU-bound task use all cores with multiprocessing safely?
questions.text: from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor def crunch(chunk): return heavy_compute(chunk) if __name__ == '__main__': # REQUIRED on spawn platforms with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex: results = list(ex.map(crunch, chunks)) For CPU-bound work, ProcessPoolExecutor runs tasks in separate processes (each with its own GIL), achieving true multicore parallelism. The if __name__ == '__main__' guard is mandatory on spawn-based platforms (Windows/macOS default) — without it, child processes re-import and re-run your module, causing infinite process spawning. Arguments and return values must be picklable, since they're serialized between processes. Two real gotchas: (1) the __main__ guard, or you fork-bomb yourself; (2) IPC overhead — passing big objects between processes can cost more than the parallelism saves. Chunk work coarsely to amortize the serialization cost.

questions.q: How do you write a generator-based streaming pipeline for ETL on huge data?
questions.text: def read(path): with open(path) as f: yield from f def parse(lines): for line in lines: if (r := try_parse(line)): yield r def enrich(records): for r in records: yield {**r, 'host': lookup(r['ip'])} # compose — stays lazy, constant memory end to end: for out in enrich(parse(read('huge.log'))): sink(out) Chaining generators builds a pull-based pipeline where each stage processes one item at a time and passes it on — no stage ever materializes the full dataset, so memory stays flat regardless of input size. Each function does one transform (read → parse → enrich), making the pipeline composable and testable in isolation. This is the idiomatic Python pattern for ETL over multi-GB logs or unbounded streams. Why streaming wins: the whole flow uses constant memory and starts producing output immediately (no waiting to load everything). Each stage is independently unit-testable with a small fake iterable.

questions.q: How do you debug a hung Python process in production without restarting it?
questions.text: py-spy dump --pid 12345 # instant stack trace of every thread, no restart py-spy top --pid 12345 # live flame-graph-style view # built-in: send SIGQUIT for a faulthandler traceback (if enabled) python -X faulthandler app.py # then faulthandler dumps on fatal signals # or attach: import pdb; or signal a thread to print stacks py-spy is the SRE's best friend: it samples a running Python process from outside (no code changes, no restart, negligible overhead) and dumps every thread's stack — instantly showing where a hang is stuck (a blocking call with no timeout, a deadlock, an infinite loop). Restarting a hung prod process destroys the evidence; py-spy lets you diagnose the live state first. faulthandler is the stdlib fallback for crash tracebacks. The #1 finding: a hung process is usually blocked on a network call with no timeout. py-spy dump points straight at the offending stack frame, turning a mystery hang into a one-line fix.

questions.q: How do you write an ERR trap that prints the failing command and line number?
questions.text: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -Eeuo pipefail trap 'echo "ERROR line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (exit $?)" >&2' ERR # now any failing command reports exactly where and what failed some_command_that_might_fail An ERR trap fires whenever a command exits non-zero (with set -e ). Printing $LINENO and $BASH_COMMAND tells you exactly which line and command failed — turning a silent abort into an actionable error. The -E flag is what makes the ERR trap propagate into functions and subshells; without it, failures inside functions won't trigger the trap. Production pattern: combine strict mode + an ERR trap that logs line/command, so a 200-line deploy script that dies tells you precisely where instead of just exiting with a bare code.

questions.q: What is the difference between a subshell and a command group, and when does it matter?
questions.text: ( cd /tmp; do_stuff ) # SUBSHELL: cd is local, doesn't affect caller { cmd1; cmd2; } # GROUP: same shell, cd/vars persist x=1; ( x=2 ); echo $x # 1 (subshell change is lost) x=1; { x=2; }; echo $x # 2 (group mutates current shell) result=$(cmd) # command substitution also runs in a subshell ( ) runs commands in a subshell — a child process with its own copy of variables and working directory, so changes (cd, variable assignments) don't leak back. { } is a command group running in the current shell, so its side effects persist. This matters constantly: a cd inside $(...) or a pipe stage won't affect your script, and variables set inside a piped while loop vanish because the pipe spawns a subshell. The classic gotcha: cmd | while read x; do count=$((count+1)); done — count is 0 afterward because the loop ran in a subshell. Use process substitution while ...; done < <(cmd) to keep the loop in the current shell.

questions.q: How do you use process substitution and why is it better than temp files?
questions.text: # compare output of two commands without temp files diff <(kubectl get pods -o name) <(cat expected.txt) # feed a command's output where a FILE is expected while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < <(generate) # tee to multiple processors generate | tee >(gzip > out.gz) >(wc -l > count.txt) > /dev/null Process substitution <(cmd) presents a command's output as a filename (a /dev/fd pipe), so tools that expect file arguments ( diff , comm ) can consume command output directly — no temp files to create, secure, and clean up. >(cmd) works the other direction for output. Crucially, while read < <(cmd) keeps the loop in the current shell (unlike cmd | while ), so variables set inside persist. Two wins: no temp-file race conditions or leaks, and it sidesteps the subshell-variable-loss problem of pipes. diff <(a) <(b) is the canonical example.

questions.q: How do you parse long options (--env=prod) robustly in a Bash script?
questions.text: while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do case "$1" in --env=*) env="${1#*=}"; shift ;; # --env=prod --env) env="$2"; shift 2 ;; # --env prod --dry-run) dry=1; shift ;; --) shift; break ;; # end of options -*) echo "unknown: $1" > exit 2 ;; *) args+=("$1"); shift ;; # positional esac done getopts only handles short flags, so for long options you write a manual while/case loop. Handle both --env=prod (split on = with ${1#*=} ) and --env prod (consume $2 , shift 2 ) forms, collect positionals into an array, and reject unknown flags. The -- sentinel signals end-of-options so remaining args starting with - are treated as positional. When the flag logic gets complex, that's the signal to switch to Python's argparse — robust long-option parsing in Bash is verbose and easy to get subtly wrong.

questions.q: Explain mapfile/readarray and why it's better than a for-loop over command output.
questions.text: # read all lines into an array safely (handles spaces, no word-split) mapfile -t pods < <(kubectl get pods -o name) echo "got ${#pods[@]} pods" for p in "${pods[@]}"; do echo "$p"; done # vs the fragile classic: for p in $(kubectl ...) -> splits on whitespace mapfile -t (aka readarray ) reads lines into an array, one element per line, with -t stripping the trailing newline. It correctly handles entries with spaces and avoids the word-splitting and glob-expansion bugs of for x in $(cmd) . You then iterate with "${arr[@]}" (quoted) to preserve each element. It's the safe, modern way to capture command output line-by-line into a list. Why it's safer: for f in $(ls) breaks on any filename with a space and expands globs; mapfile -t arr < <(find ...) with quoted expansion handles every case correctly.

questions.q: How do you safely create and use temporary files/dirs (avoiding /tmp races)?
questions.text: tmp=$(mktemp) # unique file, mode 600, in $TMPDIR tmpd=$(mktemp -d) # unique directory trap 'rm -rf "$tmp" "$tmpd"' EXIT INT TERM # NEVER: tmpfile=/tmp/myapp.$$ (predictable name = symlink-attack risk) mktemp atomically creates a uniquely-named temp file/dir with safe permissions (0600/0700), defeating the predictable-name race where an attacker pre-creates or symlinks /tmp/myapp.PID to hijack or read your data. Pair it with a trap ... EXIT cleanup so temp files never leak on exit, error, or interrupt. Hard-coded /tmp paths are both a security hole and a source of collisions between concurrent runs. Predictable temp names are a CVE class: /tmp/foo.$$ is guessable; an attacker can symlink it to a sensitive file before you write. Always mktemp .

questions.q: What does 'set -o pipefail' fix, and what's the remaining gotcha with pipelines?
questions.text: set -o pipefail cmd_that_fails | grep x # now returns failure, not grep's success # inspect each stage's exit code: false | true | false echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}" # 1 0 1 -> per-stage exit codes By default a pipeline's exit status is only the last command's, so failing_cmd | grep x reports success if grep succeeds — silently masking the real failure. set -o pipefail makes the pipeline fail if any stage fails. The remaining nuance: to know which stage failed, inspect the PIPESTATUS array, which holds each command's individual exit code. Debugging tip: ${PIPESTATUS[@]} right after a pipeline tells you exactly which stage broke — invaluable when a multi-stage pipe fails and pipefail only tells you 'something did.'

questions.q: How do you write a portable script that detects and adapts to GNU vs BSD tools?
questions.text: # sed -i differs: GNU 'sed -i' vs BSD 'sed -i ""' if sed --version >/dev/null 2> then SED_INPLACE=(sed -i) # GNU else SED_INPLACE=(sed -i '') # BSD/macOS fi "${SED_INPLACE[@]}" 's/a/b/' file # also: date, stat, readlink, grep -P differ across GNU/BSD/busybox GNU coreutils (Linux), BSD utils (macOS), and busybox (Alpine) have subtly different flags — sed -i , date formatting, stat , readlink -f , and grep -P are common divergences. Detect the variant (e.g. sed --version succeeds only on GNU) and branch, storing the command in an array. For maximum portability, stick to POSIX-specified flags, or require GNU coreutils explicitly and check for them up front. The frequent offender: sed -i needs an empty backup arg on BSD/macOS but not GNU. A script that works on your Mac silently corrupts files in an Alpine container, or vice versa.

questions.q: How do you implement a mutex/lock so only one instance of a script runs at a time?
questions.text: exec 9>/var/lock/myjob.lock # open fd 9 on a lock file if ! flock -n 9; then # non-blocking: fail if held echo 'another instance is running' > exit 0 fi # fd 9 (and thus the lock) is auto-released when the script exits # blocking variant with timeout: flock -w 30 9 || exit 1 flock on a dedicated lock file gives a robust mutex. Opening the file on a file descriptor and locking it means the lock is automatically released when the process exits (even on crash) — no stale lock files to clean up, unlike a manual [ -f lockfile ] check which leaks on kill. -n fails immediately if another instance holds it; -w N waits up to N seconds. Essential for cron jobs that must not overlap. Don't roll your own with a flag file: if [ -f lock ]; then exit; fi; touch lock has a race (two instances pass the check) and leaks the file on crash. flock is atomic and self-cleaning.

questions.q: How do you safely handle 'rm -rf' with variables to avoid catastrophic deletion?
questions.text: # DANGER: if $dir is empty/unset -> rm -rf / (with set -u it errors first) rm -rf "$dir"/ # SAFE patterns: : "${dir:?dir must be set}" # fail loud if empty/unset [[ -n "$dir" && "$dir" != "/" ]] || exit 1 rm -rf -- "${dir:?}" # :? guards empty; -- ends options The infamous rm -rf "$dir"/ deletes everything if $dir is empty (becomes rm -rf / ). Defenses: set -u to error on unset vars, the ${dir:?msg} expansion to fail loudly when empty, an explicit non-empty/non-root check, and -- to stop a path starting with - being read as a flag. For destructive operations, validate the target rigorously and prefer a dry-run that prints what would be deleted. Real outages have happened from an unset variable in rm -rf "$VAR/" . Always guard with ${VAR:?} and a non-root check before any recursive delete.

questions.q: How do you read a config/env file into a script without 'source'-ing untrusted code?
questions.text: # UNSAFE: source runs ARBITRARY code in the file source config.env # a line like rm -rf / would execute # SAFER: parse KEY=VALUE lines explicitly while IFS='=' read -r key val; do [[ $key =~ ^[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*$ ]] || continue # validate key declare "$key=$val" done < config.env source file executes the file as shell code — if the file is attacker-controlled or has a typo with a command, it runs. For a simple KEY=VALUE config, parse it explicitly: split on = , validate the key matches an identifier pattern, and assign with declare . This treats the file as data, not code, eliminating the command-execution risk. Sourcing config is a code-execution vector: any command in the file runs with your script's privileges. Only source files you fully control; parse anything external.

questions.q: What's the difference between 'exec', backgrounding, and 'nohup' for process control?
