questions.text: exec myprog # REPLACE the shell with myprog (no new process) myprog & # run in background, dies if shell/terminal closes nohup myprog & # background, survives terminal hangup (SIGHUP) setsid myprog # fully detach into a new session (daemon-like) exec 2>/var/log/x # exec with redirects: redirect script's own fds exec cmd replaces the current shell process with cmd — useful as the last line of a wrapper (no extra shell lingering), and for redirecting the script's own file descriptors ( exec >log 2>&1 ). & backgrounds a job but it receives SIGHUP when the terminal closes. nohup ignores SIGHUP so the job survives logout. setsid fully detaches into its own session. Knowing these is key for launching long-running processes correctly. Container entrypoints use exec: exec myapp as the final line makes your app PID 1, so it receives signals (SIGTERM) directly for graceful shutdown — wrapping it in a shell that doesn't exec swallows those signals.

questions.q: How do you measure and improve the performance of a slow shell script?
questions.text: time ./script.sh # wall/user/sys time overview PS4='+ $(date +%s.%N) ${LINENO}: '; set -x # timestamped trace # common fix: avoid spawning a process per line # SLOW: while read l; do echo "$l" | grep x; done (fork per line) # FAST: do it in ONE awk/grep pass over the whole file awk '/x/{...}' file Shell scripts are usually slow because they fork a new process per iteration (calling grep / sed / cut inside a loop over thousands of lines). time gives the overview; a timestamped PS4 trace shows where time goes. The big win is almost always replacing per-line external commands with a single pass through awk (or moving to Python) — turning thousands of fork+exec calls into one. The rule: if you're calling an external command inside a loop body, you can usually replace the whole loop with one awk invocation that's 100x faster. Process spawning is the hidden cost.

questions.q: How do you handle signals and ensure children are cleaned up (no orphans)?
questions.text: child_pids=() cleanup() { kill "${child_pids[@]}" 2>/dev/null; wait; } trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM long_task & child_pids+=($!) # record each child PID another_task & child_pids+=($!) wait When a script spawns background children and is then killed, the children can be orphaned and keep running. Track each child's PID ( $! after & ), and in a trap on EXIT/INT/TERM, kill them and wait for cleanup. This guarantees that interrupting the parent tears down the whole process tree — important for scripts that launch workers, port-forwards, or tunnels you don't want leaking. Orphaned port-forwards/tunnels are a classic leak: a script that backgrounds kubectl port-forward and exits without killing it leaves a dangling process holding the port. Trap + tracked PIDs fix it.

questions.q: How do you correctly quote a variable used inside a command run over SSH?
questions.text: # The remote shell re-parses the command -> double quoting needed host=server1; path='/var/log/my app' # BAD: remote splits on the space in the path ssh "$host" "ls $path" # GOOD: let printf %q produce a remote-safe quoted string ssh "$host" "ls $(printf '%q' "$path")" SSH concatenates its arguments and runs them through the remote shell, which re-parses and re-splits the string — so local quoting alone isn't enough; the value must survive a second round of shell parsing. printf '%q' produces a string safely re-quoted for shell input, so a path with spaces or special characters is interpreted literally on the remote side. This double-quoting subtlety is a frequent source of remote-command bugs. Remember the two shells: your local shell parses once, the remote shell parses again. printf %q (or here-doc with quoted delimiter) is how you make values survive the second parse intact.

questions.q: How do you build a robust deploy/rollback shell function with state verification?
questions.text: deploy() { local prev; prev=$(current_version) || return 1 if ! apply_new_version; then echo 'apply failed' > return 1 fi if ! verify_healthy; then echo 'health check failed, rolling back' >&2 rollback_to "$prev"; return 1 fi echo "deployed, previous was $prev" } A safe deploy function captures the current state before changing anything (so rollback has a target), applies the change, then verifies health — and automatically rolls back to the captured previous version if verification fails. This 'capture → apply → verify → auto-rollback' structure encodes the SRE deploy reflex: never leave the system in a broken half-deployed state, and restore service first, investigate later. Capture-before-change is the key: recording prev up front is what makes rollback possible. A deploy that mutates first and figures out rollback later has no safe state to return to.

questions.q: When and how should you use 'trap DEBUG' or 'set -T' for advanced debugging?
questions.text: # print every command with its line number before it runs trap 'echo "[L$LINENO] $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' DEBUG # time each command (rough): trap 'echo "$(date +%s.%N) $BASH_COMMAND"' DEBUG set -T # make DEBUG/RETURN traps inherit into functions A DEBUG trap runs before every command, giving finer-grained tracing than set -x — you can log line numbers, time individual commands, or inspect state at each step. set -T makes the DEBUG and RETURN traps propagate into functions (analogous to how -E propagates ERR). This is a heavier debugging tool for when set -x and shellcheck haven't found a subtle ordering or state bug. Use sparingly: DEBUG traps fire constantly and slow execution, so reserve them for isolating a tricky bug — then remove. For everyday debugging, set -x + shellcheck cover most cases.

questions.q: How does context.Context work, and why is it essential in Go services?
questions.text: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second) defer cancel() // always cancel to free resources req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, 'GET', url, nil) resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req) // aborts if ctx times out // propagate ctx down the call chain so cancellation flows everywhere func work(ctx context.Context) error { select { case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err(); ... } } context.Context carries deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values across API boundaries and goroutines. It's how you implement timeouts and propagate cancellation: when a request is cancelled or times out, every downstream call watching the context ( ctx.Done() ) stops, freeing goroutines and connections. Passing ctx as the first parameter through your call chain is idiomatic Go and the foundation of well-behaved services. Why SREs care: without context propagation, a cancelled client request leaves backend goroutines and DB queries running — leaking resources under load. Context is how cancellation flows end-to-end so work stops when the caller gives up.

questions.q: Explain Go's race detector and how you find concurrency bugs.
questions.text: go test -race ./... // run tests with the race detector go run -race main.go // or run the program with it // it instruments memory access and reports data races at runtime: // WARNING: DATA RACE // Read at 0x... by goroutine 7 / Write at 0x... by goroutine 8 A data race is two goroutines accessing the same memory concurrently with at least one write and no synchronization — undefined behavior that manifests as intermittent corruption. Go's built-in race detector ( -race ) instruments memory accesses and reports the exact conflicting reads/writes with stack traces when they occur. Run your tests and integration suites with -race in CI; it catches bugs that are nearly impossible to find by inspection. It only finds races that actually execute: the detector is dynamic, so you need test coverage that exercises the concurrent paths. A race in an untested code path won't be caught — run race-enabled tests with realistic concurrency.

questions.q: How do you synchronize goroutines correctly — channels vs sync.Mutex vs sync.WaitGroup?
questions.text: var mu sync.Mutex; mu.Lock(); shared++; mu.Unlock() // protect shared state var wg sync.WaitGroup for _, j := range jobs { wg.Add(1); go func(j Job){ defer wg.Done(); do(j) }(j) } wg.Wait() // wait for all to finish ch := make(chan int); go func(){ ch <- compute() }(); v := <-ch // pass data Pick the tool by intent. Channels pass data/ownership between goroutines ('share by communicating') — best for pipelines and handing off results. sync.Mutex protects shared mutable state accessed by multiple goroutines (a counter, a map). sync.WaitGroup waits for a set of goroutines to complete. Use a mutex when goroutines genuinely share memory; use channels when you can pass ownership instead — fewer locks means fewer deadlocks. Idiom: 'Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.' Prefer channels for coordination, reserve mutexes for genuinely shared state like a concurrent counter or cache.

questions.q: What are Go interfaces, and how do they enable testable, decoupled code?
questions.text: type Store interface { // small interface = the dependency Get(ctx context.Context, k string) ([]byte, error) } func Handler(s Store) { ... } // depends on the interface, not a concrete type // real: type RedisStore struct{}; func (r RedisStore) Get(...){...} // test: type fakeStore struct{}; func (f fakeStore) Get(...){ return ..., nil } Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly — any type with the right methods implements them, no implements keyword. Depending on a small interface (rather than a concrete type) decouples your code from implementations: production code injects the real one, tests inject a fake/mock. Idiomatic Go favors small interfaces (often one method) defined where they're used , not where the implementation lives — 'accept interfaces, return structs.' Accept interfaces, return structs: functions take narrow interfaces (so callers can substitute fakes in tests), but return concrete types (so callers get full functionality). This is the core of testable Go design.

questions.q: How do you avoid goroutine leaks, and how do you detect them?
questions.text: // LEAK: goroutine blocks forever on a channel no one reads/closes go func(){ ch <- result }() // if nothing ever receives, it leaks // FIX: use context cancellation or a buffered/closed channel go func(){ select { case ch <- result: case <-ctx.Done(): } }() // detect: runtime.NumGoroutine(), or goleak in tests defer goleak.VerifyNone(t) // uber-go/goleak fails test on leaks A goroutine leaks when it blocks forever — typically waiting to send/receive on a channel that's never read/closed, or looping without a cancellation path. Leaked goroutines accumulate, consuming memory and eventually degrading the service. Prevent it by giving every goroutine a way out: a select with ctx.Done() , a closed channel, or a buffered channel. Detect leaks with runtime.NumGoroutine() monitoring or uber-go/goleak in tests. The silent killer under load: a handler that spawns a goroutine per request which can block forever will slowly exhaust memory. Every goroutine needs a guaranteed termination path — usually via context.

questions.q: What is the difference between value and pointer receivers, and when does it matter?
questions.text: type Counter struct{ n int } func (c Counter) Get() int { return c.n } // value: gets a COPY func (c *Counter) Inc() { c.n++ } // pointer: mutates original // value receiver on a big struct copies it every call (cost) // pointer receiver needed to MUTATE, and for sync.Mutex fields (don't copy a lock!) A value receiver operates on a copy, so it can't mutate the original and copies the whole struct each call. A pointer receiver shares the original, enabling mutation and avoiding copies of large structs. Rules of thumb: use pointer receivers if the method mutates, if the struct is large, or if it contains a sync.Mutex (copying a locked mutex is a bug). Keep receiver types consistent across a type's methods. Copying a mutex is a real bug: a value receiver on a struct containing a sync.Mutex copies the lock, so the copy guards nothing. go vet flags this. Use pointer receivers for any struct holding a lock.

questions.q: How do you write table-driven tests in Go (the idiomatic pattern)?
questions.text: func TestParse(t *testing.T) { tests := []struct{ name, in string; want int; wantErr bool }{ {'valid', '200', 200, false}, {'bad', 'xx', 0, true}, } for _, tt := range tests { t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) { got, err := Parse(tt.in) if (err != nil) != tt.wantErr { t.Fatalf('err = %v', err) } if got != tt.want { t.Errorf('got %d want %d', got, tt.want) } }) } } Table-driven tests define a slice of test cases (input + expected output) and loop over them, running each as a subtest with t.Run . This is the idiomatic Go testing style: adding a case is one line, each subtest reports independently (and can run in parallel), and the structure forces you to enumerate edge cases explicitly. It scales far better than copy-pasted test functions. Why it's standard: subtests give per-case names in output, failures pinpoint the exact case, and the table makes the set of behaviors you're verifying visible at a glance. It's how the Go standard library tests itself.

questions.q: How do you handle JSON marshaling/unmarshaling robustly in Go?
questions.text: type Pod struct { Name string `json:'name'` Status string `json:'status,omitempty'` // omit if empty Labels map[string]string `json:'labels,omitempty'` } var p Pod if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &p); err != nil { return err } // always check! out, _ := json.Marshal(p) // unknown/dynamic shape: json.RawMessage or map[string]any Struct tags ( json:'name' ) map Go fields to JSON keys; omitempty drops zero-valued fields from output. Always check the Unmarshal error — malformed JSON is common with external data. For unknown or dynamic structures, unmarshal into map[string]any or defer parsing with json.RawMessage . Be aware that absent fields become Go zero values, so you sometimes need a pointer ( *int ) to distinguish 'absent' from 'zero'. Zero vs absent: a missing JSON number unmarshals to 0 , indistinguishable from an explicit 0 . Use a pointer field ( *int ) when you must tell 'not provided' from 'provided as zero' — a frequent config-parsing subtlety.

questions.q: What does 'go vet' and static analysis catch, and how do you wire up linting?
questions.text: go vet ./... // built-in: suspicious constructs golangci-lint run // aggregates many linters (staticcheck, etc.) // catches: printf format mismatches, copied mutexes, unreachable code, // shadowed err, unchecked errors, nil-map writes, ... gofmt -l . / goimports // formatting + import hygiene go vet catches correctness issues the compiler allows but are almost always bugs: Printf format/argument mismatches, copied locks, unreachable code, struct-tag typos. golangci-lint bundles many linters (staticcheck, errcheck, ineffassign) into one fast pass. Run both in CI alongside gofmt / goimports for consistent formatting. This catches a class of bugs before code review and keeps a codebase uniform across a team. CI gate: go vet + golangci-lint + gofmt -l (fail if anything's unformatted) as required checks keeps Go code correct and consistent — the equivalent of shellcheck for Bash or mypy for Python.

questions.q: How do you implement graceful shutdown of a Go HTTP server?
questions.text: srv := &http.Server{Addr: ':8080', Handler: mux} go func(){ srv.ListenAndServe() }() stop := make(chan os.Signal, 1) signal.Notify(stop, syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM) <-stop // wait for signal ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second) defer cancel() srv.Shutdown(ctx) // stop accepting, drain in-flight Graceful shutdown stops accepting new connections while letting in-flight requests finish within a deadline — critical in Kubernetes, which sends SIGTERM before SIGKILL. You catch the signal, then call srv.Shutdown(ctx) , which closes listeners and waits for active handlers to complete (up to the context timeout) before returning. Without this, a rolling deploy drops in-flight requests, causing user-visible errors during every deploy. Match the grace period: the shutdown timeout should fit within Kubernetes' terminationGracePeriodSeconds , or the pod gets SIGKILLed mid-drain. Combine with a readiness probe flipping to not-ready so traffic stops arriving first.

questions.q: What are common Go memory/performance pitfalls SREs should know?
questions.text: // 1. slice holding a huge backing array alive: small := big[:10] // still references big's full array -> copy if needed // 2. appending in a loop without pre-allocating: s := make([]T, 0, n) // pre-size to avoid repeated reallocations // 3. string concatenation in a loop -> use strings.Builder // 4. defer in a hot loop -> accumulates until function returns Key Go performance traps: a small slice of a large array keeps the whole backing array in memory (copy the sub-slice to release it); growing a slice without pre-allocating capacity causes repeated reallocations and copies; concatenating strings with + in a loop is O(n²) (use strings.Builder ); and defer inside a tight loop accumulates deferred calls until the function returns (leaking resources). Profile with pprof to find the real hot spots. pprof is built in: import _ 'net/http/pprof' exposes CPU/heap/goroutine profiles over HTTP — the standard way to find allocation hot spots and goroutine leaks in a running Go service.

questions.q: How do you structure a Go project and manage dependencies with modules?
questions.text: go mod init github.com/org/tool // creates go.mod go get github.com/x/y@v1.2.3 // add a pinned dependency go mod tidy // prune unused, add missing // layout: // cmd/tool/main.go entrypoint(s) // internal/... private packages (un-importable externally) // pkg/... public reusable packages Go modules ( go.mod / go.sum ) pin dependencies with versions and checksums for reproducible, verifiable builds — commit both files. go mod tidy keeps them accurate. The conventional layout puts entrypoints under cmd/ , private packages under internal/ (the compiler forbids external imports of internal ), and shared libraries under pkg/ . go.sum hashes give supply-chain integrity — a tampered dependency fails verification. internal/ is enforced: packages under internal/ can only be imported by code in the same module subtree — a compiler-enforced boundary for keeping implementation details private, unlike Python's convention-only underscore prefix.

questions.q: How do you wrap and inspect errors with errors.Is / errors.As / %w?
questions.text: var ErrNotFound = errors.New('not found') func get(k string) error { return fmt.Errorf('get %s: %w', k, ErrNotFound) } // inspect the chain: if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) { /* handle 404 */ } var perr *os.PathError if errors.As(err, &perr) { log.Print(perr.Path) } // extract a typed error Wrapping with %w in fmt.Errorf preserves the underlying error in a chain while adding context. errors.Is checks whether any error in the chain matches a sentinel (like ErrNotFound ) — robust to wrapping, unlike == . errors.As extracts a specific error type from the chain so you can read its fields. This lets you add context at each layer yet still make decisions on the root cause at the top. Wrap with context, match on cause: each layer adds fmt.Errorf('doing X: %w', err) so the final message is a breadcrumb trail, while errors.Is/As at the top still classifies the original failure correctly.

questions.q: How do you build a small concurrent CLI that respects timeouts and cancellation?
questions.text: ctx, cancel := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt) defer cancel() // Ctrl-C cancels the context g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx) // golang.org/x/sync/errgroup for _, u := range urls { u := u g.Go(func() error { return check(ctx, u) }) // bounded fan-out } if err := g.Wait(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } // first error cancels rest signal.NotifyContext ties Ctrl-C/SIGTERM to context cancellation, so an interrupt cleanly stops all work. errgroup runs a group of goroutines, propagates the first error, and cancels the shared context so siblings stop early — exactly what you want for fan-out tasks (health checks, parallel fetches). Each goroutine watches ctx for cancellation. This is the idiomatic pattern for a robust concurrent CLI tool. errgroup is the go-to: it combines WaitGroup semantics with error propagation and context cancellation — the clean way to fan out work where any failure should abort the rest, common in SRE tooling.

questions.q: Live coding: write a Go function to find the top-K slowest requests from a stream. Walk through it.
questions.text: import 'container/heap' // maintain a MIN-heap of size K; the root is the smallest of the top-K type Req struct{ Path string; MS int } // heap holds the K largest seen so far func topK(reqs []Req, k int) []Req { h := &minHeap{}; heap.Init(h) for _, r := range reqs { if h.Len() < k { heap.Push(h, r) } else if r.MS > (*h)[0].MS { heap.Pop(h); heap.Push(h, r) // evict smallest, add bigger } } return *h } The interview-grade structure: maintain a min-heap of size K. Push until it holds K items; thereafter, if a new request is slower than the heap's smallest (the root), evict the root and push the new one. This keeps only the top-K in O(n log K) time and O(K) memory — never sorting or holding the whole stream, so it scales to an unbounded log. Walk through edge cases aloud: k larger than the input, ties, empty stream. What earns the offer: choosing a size-K min-heap over sorting everything (O(n log K) vs O(n log n), O(K) vs O(n) memory), explaining why the min-heap root is the eviction candidate, and naming the streaming/constant-memory property — that's the SRE-grade answer.

questions.q: How do you use here-documents and here-strings, and when are they better than echo?
questions.text: A here-doc feeds multi-line text to a command's stdin; a here-string feeds one string. They avoid quoting and escaping problems with echo. cat <<'EOF' > app.conf port=8080 EOF grep -c error <<< "$LOG" Interview tip: Quote the delimiter to stop expansion.

questions.q: How do you use arrays and associative arrays in Bash safely?
questions.text: Indexed arrays hold lists; associative arrays (declare -A) map keys to values. Always expand with quotes: "${arr[@]}". files=(a.txt 'b c.txt') for f in "${files[@]}"; do echo "$f"; done declare -A port=([web]=80 [db]=5432) echo "${port[db]}" Interview tip: Quote "${arr[@]}" to preserve elements with spaces.

questions.q: How does parameter expansion help with defaults, trimming and substitutions?
questions.text: ${var:-default}, ${var#prefix}, ${var%suffix} and ${var//a/b} do common string work without external tools. echo "${ENV:-dev}" f=report.tar.gz; echo "${f%.tar.gz}" echo "${path//\//_}" Interview tip: Prefer built-in expansion over spawning sed.

questions.q: How do you read a file line by line in Bash without breaking on spaces or backslashes?
questions.text: Use while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done while IFS= read -r line; do printf '%s\n' "$line"; done < hosts.txt while IFS=, read -r name ip; do echo "$name $ip"; done < list.csv Interview tip: Redirect the file in, do not pipe, to keep variables.

questions.q: How do you implement structured logging and log levels in a Bash script?
questions.text: Write a small log function with levels and timestamps, send logs to stderr, and keep stdout for data. log(){ printf '%s %s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$1" "${*:2}" > } log INFO 'starting backup' Interview tip: stderr for logs, stdout for results.

questions.q: What are the common Bash pitfalls with set -e, and when does it not stop the script?
questions.text: set -e is ignored in conditions, after && or ||, in command substitutions inside assignments with local, and in pipelines without pipefail. set -Eeuo pipefail local out; out=$(cmd) # separate declaration from assignment Interview tip: Treat set -e as a safety net, not a design.

questions.q: How do you write a Bash function that returns data and status correctly?
questions.text: Return status with return, data by printing to stdout and capturing with $(...), or via a nameref for multiple values. get_ip(){ hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'; } ip=$(get_ip) fill(){ local -n out=$1; out=(a b c); } Interview tip: Return codes are 0-255 only.

questions.q: How do you use xargs and find together safely and efficiently?
questions.text: Use find -print0 with xargs -0 for safe filenames, and -P for parallelism, or use find -exec ... +. find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -print0 | xargs -0 -r rm -f find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 -P4 -n50 gzip Interview tip: -print0 and -0 always go together.

questions.q: How do you write a Bash script that reads from stdin or a file argument like standard Unix tools?
questions.text: Default to stdin when no file is given, using "${1:--}" and cat or redirect, and detect a terminal with test -t. input="${1:--}" cat -- "$input" | wc -l [ -t 0 ] && echo 'reading from terminal' Interview tip: A dash means stdin by convention.

questions.q: How do you measure elapsed time and add a timeout to a command in Bash?
questions.text: Use SECONDS or date +%s for timing, and the timeout command to kill long-running processes. start=$SECONDS; run_job; echo "took $((SECONDS-start))s" timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10 60 ./long.sh Interview tip: Use kill-after to escalate.

questions.q: How do you use pathlib instead of os.path, and what are the benefits?
questions.text: Path objects model filesystem paths with operators and methods, making code more readable and portable. from pathlib import Path p = Path('/var/log') / 'app' / 'x.log' print(p.suffix, p.exists()) [f for f in Path('.').rglob('*.yaml')] Interview tip: Use / to join paths.

questions.q: How do you use the subprocess module to capture output, enforce timeouts and avoid shell injection?
questions.text: Pass a list of arguments, avoid shell=True, set timeout and check=True, and capture text output. r = subprocess.run(['kubectl','get','pods','-o','json'], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30, check=True) json.loads(r.stdout) Interview tip: A list of args avoids the shell.

questions.q: How do you handle configuration with environment variables and validate it at startup?
questions.text: Read env vars into a typed settings object, apply defaults, and fail fast with clear errors when required values are missing. import os PORT = int(os.environ.get('PORT','8080')) DB = os.environ['DB_URL'] from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings Interview tip: Fail at startup, not at 3 a.m.

questions.q: How do you write robust retry logic with the tenacity library or a custom decorator?
questions.text: Retry only on transient errors, with exponential backoff and jitter, a stop condition, and logging of attempts. from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_random_exponential, retry_if_exception_type @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5), wait=wait_random_exponential(max=30), retry=retry_if_exception_type(ConnectionError)) Interview tip: Never retry non-idempotent calls blindly.

questions.q: What is the difference between a list comprehension, a generator expression and map/filter?
questions.text: A list comprehension builds a list now; a generator expression yields lazily; map and filter are lazy iterators but less readable. squares = [x*x for x in range(10)] total = sum(x*x for x in range(10**7)) Interview tip: Use generators for large pipelines.

questions.q: How do you use collections like Counter, defaultdict and deque for operational scripts?
questions.text: Counter tallies, defaultdict removes key checks, deque gives fast appends and pops at both ends and bounded windows. from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque Counter(codes).most_common(5) last = deque(maxlen=100) Interview tip: deque(maxlen) is a free sliding window.

questions.q: How do you work with dates and durations, such as computing time since last deploy?
questions.text: Use timezone-aware datetime in UTC, timedelta for durations, and ISO 8601 for parsing and output. from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta now = datetime.now(timezone.utc) age = now - datetime.fromisoformat('2026-10-01T10:00:00+00:00') age > timedelta(hours=6) Interview tip: Store UTC, convert for display.

questions.q: How do you write and organise Python modules and packages for a team's internal tooling?
questions.text: Use a src layout, pyproject.toml, clear module boundaries, entry points, tests and a linter and formatter. pyproject.toml src/mytool/__init__.py src/mytool/cli.py tests/test_cli.py pip install -e . Interview tip: Make it installable, not a pile of scripts.

questions.q: How do you handle large CSV or JSON files efficiently in Python?
questions.text: Stream with csv.reader or json lines, process in chunks, and use pandas chunking or DuckDB for heavy analytics. import csv with open('big.csv', newline='') as f: for row in csv.DictReader(f): ... pd.read_csv('big.csv', chunksize=100000) Interview tip: Avoid json.load on multi-GB files.

questions.q: How do you use virtual environments and tools like pip-tools, Poetry or uv for reproducible installs?
questions.text: Isolate per project with venv, lock exact versions with hashes, and install from the lock file in CI and production. python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate pip-compile --generate-hashes requirements.in pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt Interview tip: Separate abstract and locked requirements.

questions.q: What are Python's common performance pitfalls in scripts, and how do you fix them?
questions.text: String concatenation in loops, repeated list membership tests, unnecessary I/O, and global lookups; use join, sets, batching and profiling. items = set(big_list) if x in items: ... ''.join(parts) Interview tip: Profile first.

questions.q: How do you test code that calls external APIs or the cloud SDK without real calls?
questions.text: Mock the client boundary with unittest.mock or a stubber, use recorded responses, and keep a few real integration tests separate. from unittest.mock import patch @patch('mytool.client.get_instances', return_value=[]) moto # mock AWS services Interview tip: Mock at your own boundary, not deep internals.

questions.q: How do you build a simple REST API client class with sessions, auth, timeouts and pagination?
questions.text: Wrap requests.Session, set default headers and timeouts, retry adapters, and expose an iterator for pages. s = requests.Session() s.headers['Authorization'] = f'Bearer {token}' s.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=Retry(total=3, backoff_factor=0.5, status_forcelist=[429,500,502,503]))) Interview tip: requests has no default timeout.

questions.q: How do you find the two sum pair or detect duplicates using a hash set?
questions.text: Store seen values in a hash set or map and check complements in one pass for O(n) time. seen = {} for i, x in enumerate(nums): if target - x in seen: return seen[target - x], i seen[x] = i Interview tip: Trade memory for time.

questions.q: Explain the two-pointer technique with a practical example.
questions.text: Two indexes move through a sorted or linear structure to solve in O(n) what would take O(n²), such as pair sums or merging. l, r = 0, len(a)-1 while l < r: s = a[l]+a[r] if s == t: break l, r = (l+1, r) if s < t else (l, r-1) Interview tip: Needs sorted data or a monotonic property.

questions.q: How do you detect a cycle or compute dependency order, such as for a deploy plan?
questions.text: Model dependencies as a directed graph, run a topological sort, and a failure to order all nodes means a cycle. from graphlib import TopologicalSorter list(TopologicalSorter({'app':{'db','cache'},'db':set()}).static_order()) Interview tip: graphlib is in the standard library.

questions.q: How do you implement a simple circuit breaker or a sliding-window rate counter?
questions.text: Track recent failures or timestamps in a bounded structure and open the circuit when a threshold is exceeded, then probe after a cooldown. from collections import deque window = deque() while window and window[0] < now-60: window.popleft() window.append(now) Interview tip: States: closed, open, half-open.

questions.q: How do you find the most recent N events or compute a moving average efficiently?
questions.text: Use a deque with maxlen, maintaining a running sum so each update is O(1). from collections import deque w = deque(maxlen=5); total = 0 for x in stream: if len(w)==w.maxlen: total -= w[0] w.append(x); total += x; avg = total/len(w) Interview tip: Update incrementally, do not recompute.

questions.q: Explain heaps and priority queues and give an operations use case.
questions.text: A heap gives O(log n) insert and extract-min; use it for top-K, scheduling and merging sorted streams. import heapq heapq.heappush(h, (priority, item)) heapq.heappop(h) heapq.nlargest(5, data, key=...) Interview tip: Python heapq is a min-heap.

questions.q: How do you compute percentiles like p95 and p99 from large latency data, and what are the pitfalls?
questions.text: Sort or use selection for exact values; use histograms or t-digest for streaming; never average percentiles. import statistics statistics.quantiles(lat, n=100)[94] import numpy as np np.percentile(lat, [95,99]) Interview tip: You cannot average p99s across hosts.

questions.q: What is the difference between BFS and DFS, and where do they appear in infrastructure scripts?
questions.text: BFS explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS goes deep first and suits traversal, cycle detection and tree walks. from collections import deque q = deque([start]); seen = {start} while q: n = q.popleft() for m in graph[n]: if m not in seen: seen.add(m); q.append(m) Interview tip: Always track visited nodes.

questions.q: How do you build a script that safely rotates credentials or API keys with zero downtime?
questions.text: Create the new credential, update consumers, verify, then revoke the old one; support overlap and have a rollback. aws iam create-access-key --user-name ci aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id OLD --status Inactive aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id OLD Interview tip: Deactivate before delete.

questions.q: How do you write a script that audits cloud resources and produces a report?
questions.text: List resources across accounts with pagination, normalise to a common structure, apply rules, and output CSV or JSON. aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name,Tags]' --output json paginator = client.get_paginator('describe_volumes') Interview tip: Use paginators and read-only roles.

questions.q: How do you build a ChatOps or webhook-driven automation safely?
questions.text: Authenticate and verify requests, authorise by user and action, make actions idempotent and audited, and require confirmation for risky ones. hmac.compare_digest(sig, expected) # verify signing secret and timestamp Interview tip: Verify signatures and limit blast radius.

questions.q: How do you automate certificate expiry checks and renewal alerts?
questions.text: Scan endpoints and stores for not-after dates, alert at multiple thresholds, and automate renewal where possible. echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate openssl x509 -checkend 1209600 -noout -in cert.pem Interview tip: Alert at 30, 14 and 7 days.

questions.q: How do you automate environment cleanup, like removing old preview environments?
questions.text: Tag with owner and expiry, list by tag, delete in dependency order, and run on a schedule with dry-run and notifications. kubectl get ns -l preview=true -o json | jq -r '.items[]|select(.metadata.creationTimestamp < "2026-10-01")|.metadata.name' Interview tip: Label everything with ttl and owner.

questions.q: How do you write a drift-detection script for configuration or infrastructure?
questions.text: Compare desired state from code with actual state from APIs, report differences, and optionally remediate with approval. terraform plan -detailed-exitcode kubectl diff -f manifests/ Interview tip: Exit code 2 means changes.

questions.q: How do you implement a safe bulk operation, such as updating tags on thousands of resources?
questions.text: Plan first, batch, throttle, make it idempotent and resumable, log each change, and start with a small canary subset. for chunk in chunks(resources, 20): apply(chunk); time.sleep(1) Interview tip: Dry-run, canary, then scale.

questions.q: How do you use the official Kubernetes Python client to list and patch resources safely?
questions.text: Load kubeconfig or in-cluster config, use typed API clients, handle pagination and ApiException, and patch with strategic merge. from kubernetes import client, config config.load_kube_config() v1 = client.CoreV1Api() v1.list_namespaced_pod('default', limit=100) apps.patch_namespaced_deployment(name, ns, {'spec':{'replicas':3}}) Interview tip: Use in-cluster config inside pods.

questions.q: How do you write a script that drains and upgrades nodes one at a time safely?
questions.text: Cordon, drain respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, upgrade, uncordon, and verify health before the next node. kubectl cordon node1 kubectl drain node1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=300s kubectl uncordon node1 Interview tip: PDBs may block drains, which is intentional.

questions.q: How do you query cloud resources with the CLI and JMESPath or jq for scripting?
questions.text: Use --query with JMESPath for server-side filtering and --output json piped into jq for further shaping. aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:env,Values=prod --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text gcloud compute instances list --format='value(name,zone)' Interview tip: Filter at the API where possible.

questions.q: How do you write a custom Kubernetes operator or controller loop conceptually, and when is it worth it?
questions.text: A controller watches objects, compares desired and actual state, and reconciles idempotently; use one for domain logic that needs continuous convergence. kubebuilder init --domain example.com # reconcile(): get object, diff state, create/update, update status Interview tip: Reconcile must be idempotent and level-triggered.

questions.q: How do you read and write files and handle errors idiomatically in Go?
questions.text: Use os and bufio, check every error, defer Close, and wrap errors with context. f, err := os.Open(path) if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("open %s: %w", path, err) } defer f.Close() sc := bufio.NewScanner(f) Interview tip: Check the error from Close on writes.

questions.q: How do you make HTTP requests in Go with timeouts, and why is the default client risky?
questions.text: The default client has no timeout. Create an http.Client with Timeout, use context per request, and close the response body. c := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second} req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil) resp, err := c.Do(req) defer resp.Body.Close() Interview tip: Always close and drain the body.

questions.q: How do you use select with channels for timeouts and multiple events in Go?
questions.text: select waits on several channel operations; combine with time.After or ctx.Done for timeouts and cancellation. select { case r := <-results: use(r) case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err() case <-time.After(5*time.Second): return errTimeout } Interview tip: Prefer ctx.Done over time.After in loops.

questions.q: How do you use sync.WaitGroup and errgroup to run concurrent tasks and collect errors?
questions.text: WaitGroup waits for goroutines; errgroup also propagates the first error and cancels siblings with a context. g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx) g.SetLimit(8) for _, u := range urls { u := u; g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, u) }) } err := g.Wait() Interview tip: Limit concurrency with SetLimit.

questions.q: How do you build a CLI in Go with flags or Cobra and good exit codes?
questions.text: Use the flag package for simple tools or Cobra for subcommands, return errors from run functions, and exit non-zero in main only. func main(){ if err := run(os.Args[1:]); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) } } Interview tip: Keep os.Exit in main so defers run.

questions.q: How do you write benchmarks and use pprof in Go to find performance problems?
questions.text: Write BenchmarkXxx functions with b.N, run go test -bench, and use CPU and heap profiles via pprof to find hotspots. go test -bench=. -benchmem go test -cpuprofile cpu.out -bench . go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.out Interview tip: Measure allocations too.

questions.q: How do you review someone else's automation script before it runs in production?
questions.text: Check safety first: scope, idempotency, dry-run, error handling, secrets, blast radius, logging and rollback; then readability and tests. shellcheck script.sh git diff main -- scripts/ Interview tip: Ask what happens if it runs twice, or half-fails.

questions.q: When do you choose a script versus a proper service or tool, and how do you decide?
questions.text: Scripts suit short, low-risk, single-owner tasks; move to a tool or service when it needs reliability, shared use, state, concurrency or auditing. # signals: >200 lines, multiple users, runs unattended, needs retries/state Interview tip: Promote code deliberately before it becomes critical.

guides.title: Container Lifecycle Management & Deployments Interview Guide

questions.q: What is a container — how does it differ from a virtual machine?
questions.text: A container is a lightweight, isolated process that shares the host OS kernel but has its own filesystem, network stack, and process namespace. A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS kernel. Key differences VM: Hypervisor → Guest OS kernel → Application (heavy, slow boot) Container: Host kernel → Namespaces + cgroups → Application (lightweight, fast) VM size: GBs (full OS). Container size: MBs (app + deps only) VM boot: 30-60 seconds. Container start: milliseconds Isolation: VM = hardware-level. Container = kernel-level (namespaces) Containers use Linux namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) for isolation and cgroups for resource limits. The shared kernel means containers are less isolated than VMs — a kernel exploit can potentially escape a container. VMs provide stronger isolation but at the cost of resource overhead. In practice: run containers on VMs in cloud environments — you get both the performance of containers and the isolation of VMs. Interview tip: Mention that containers are not magic — they are simply Linux processes with namespace and cgroup constraints applied. docker run is ultimately a fork() + clone() with specific flags. This depth shows you understand the kernel primitives underneath.

questions.q: Explain the Docker architecture — daemon, client, registry, and image layers.
questions.text: Components Docker CLI (client) → sends API requests over Unix socket or TCP dockerd (daemon) → manages images, containers, networks, volumes containerd → container runtime (manages container lifecycle) runc → OCI runtime (actually creates the container) Registry → stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, GCR, ECR) docker info # daemon configuration docker system df # disk usage by images, containers, volumes docker system prune -a # remove all unused resources Docker is a layered architecture. The CLI sends requests to dockerd via REST API. dockerd delegates to containerd for container lifecycle. containerd uses runc (or another OCI runtime) to actually create the container. Image layers are content-addressed (SHA256 digest) and shared across containers using copy-on-write. This layering means two containers based on the same ubuntu image share those base layers in storage. Kubernetes context: Kubernetes deprecated dockershim in 1.24 — it now uses containerd or CRI-O directly via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). Docker images still work because they follow the OCI image spec. The change only affects the runtime, not images or Dockerfiles.

questions.q: What is the difference between docker run, docker start, and docker exec?
questions.text: docker run nginx:latest # create NEW container from image + start it docker start <container-id> # start an EXISTING stopped container docker exec -it <id> /bin/sh # run command in RUNNING container docker attach <id> # attach to PID 1 stdin/stdout of running container docker run -d --name web nginx # detached (background) with name docker run --rm nginx ls / # run + auto-remove on exit docker run -it ubuntu bash # interactive + TTY (for debugging) docker run = docker create + docker start. It pulls the image if not cached, creates a new container layer, and starts the process. docker exec enters a running container by joining its namespaces — it does not start a new container. docker attach connects your terminal to PID 1 — sending Ctrl+C will stop the container. Use exec for debugging, not attach, to avoid accidentally stopping production containers. docker attach danger: Attaching to a production container and pressing Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to PID 1, which may stop the container. Always use docker exec -it for interactive debugging of running containers.

questions.q: What do docker ps, docker inspect, and docker stats reveal — when do you use each?
questions.text: docker ps # running containers: ID, image, status, ports docker ps -a # all containers including stopped docker ps --format "table {{.Names}} {{.Status}} {{.Ports}}" docker inspect <container> # full JSON config: mounts, env, network, PID docker inspect -f "{{.State.Pid}}" <container> # extract specific field docker inspect -f "{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}" <container> docker stats # live CPU, memory, net I/O, block I/O per container docker stats --no-stream # snapshot (not live) docker top <container> # processes inside container (from host perspective) docker inspect is the most powerful diagnostic tool — it shows the full container configuration as JSON: environment variables, mounted volumes, network settings, restart policy, health check config, and the container PID on the host. Use -f with Go template syntax to extract specific fields in scripts. docker stats shows real-time resource consumption — critical for detecting containers approaching their limits before an OOM kill. Production use: docker inspect -f "{{.State.Pid}}" lets you get the container PID to enter its namespaces with nsenter, run strace, or examine /proc — invaluable when a container lacks debugging tools (distroless images).

questions.q: How does docker networking work — what are the default network drivers?
questions.text: docker network ls # list networks docker network inspect bridge # inspect default bridge network docker network create mynet # create user-defined bridge docker run --network mynet nginx # attach container to network docker run --network host nginx # share host network namespace docker run --network none nginx # no network (fully isolated) Network drivers: bridge (default — virtual switch, NAT for external access, containers communicate by IP), host (container shares host network namespace — best performance, no port mapping needed, no isolation), overlay (multi-host networking for Docker Swarm), macvlan (assign MAC address directly, appears as physical device), none (no networking). User-defined bridge networks enable DNS resolution by container name — the default bridge network does not support this. User-defined bridge vs default: Always create user-defined bridge networks. They provide automatic DNS resolution (containers reach each other by name), better network isolation, and dynamic connect/disconnect. The default bridge network requires --link (deprecated) for DNS and is considered legacy.

questions.q: Container exits immediately after docker run — how do you debug it?
questions.text: docker run myimage # exits immediately docker ps -a # show stopped container docker logs <container-id> # see output/errors before exit docker inspect <id> --format "{{.State.ExitCode}}" # exit code docker inspect <id> --format "{{.State.Error}}" # error message # Debug: override entrypoint to get a shell docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh myimage # Or run with sh -c to see what CMD does: docker run -it myimage sh -c "echo starting; exec myapp; echo done" A container exits when PID 1 exits. If your ENTRYPOINT or CMD exits immediately (wrong command, missing binary, startup error), the container stops. Common causes: wrong CMD (typo in binary name — container gets exec error), application crashes on startup (missing env var, DB not reachable), foreground process not running (supervisord/init not used for multi-process), or script runs and exits cleanly. Check docker logs first, then override the entrypoint to drop to a shell for interactive investigation. Shell vs exec form: CMD ["app"] (exec form) runs app as PID 1. CMD "app" (shell form) runs /bin/sh -c "app" as PID 1, and app is a child — it won't receive SIGTERM. Always use exec form in Dockerfiles for production containers so your app handles signals correctly.

questions.q: What are Docker image layers — how does the copy-on-write filesystem work?
questions.text: docker image history myimage # show all layers and sizes docker image inspect myimage # full image metadata including layers docker diff <container> # changes made in container layer vs image dive myimage # interactive layer explorer (third-party tool) Docker images are built as a stack of read-only layers. Each Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new layer. Layers are content-addressed by SHA256 and shared across images — if 10 images use the same ubuntu:22.04 base, that layer is stored once. When a container starts, a thin read-write layer is added on top. Copy-on-write: when a container modifies a file from a lower layer, that file is copied to the writable layer first — the original layer is unchanged. This means reading unmodified files from lower layers is fast; modifying large files adds I/O overhead. Layer caching in CI: Docker build cache reuses layers if the instruction and all previous layers haven't changed. Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing: base image → system deps → app deps (package.json/requirements.txt) → app code. This maximizes cache hits and speeds up builds significantly.

questions.q: How do you write an optimized production Dockerfile — what are the best practices?
questions.text: Best practices # 1. Use specific base image tags (not :latest) FROM node:20.11-alpine3.19 # pinned version + minimal base # 2. Multi-stage build (separate build from runtime) FROM node:20-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ # copy deps manifest first (cache layer) RUN npm ci --only=production COPY . . RUN npm run build FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime # fresh minimal runtime stage RUN adduser -D -u 1001 appuser # non-root user WORKDIR /app COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules USER appuser # drop privileges EXPOSE 3000 ENTRYPOINT ["node", "dist/server.js"] # exec form (not shell form) Key practices: pin base image versions (avoid supply chain surprises), use Alpine or distroless for minimal attack surface and image size, multi-stage builds to exclude build tools from production image, copy dependency manifests before source code to maximize layer cache, run as non-root user, use exec form ENTRYPOINT, add .dockerignore to exclude .git, node_modules, test files. Distroless images: Google's distroless images (gcr.io/distroless/nodejs) contain only the runtime and your app — no shell, no package manager, no utilities. Attack surface is minimal. Downside: no shell for debugging. Use a debug variant (distroless:debug) that includes busybox for troubleshooting.

questions.q: What is a multi-stage build — what problems does it solve?
questions.text: # Without multi-stage: production image includes compiler, build tools, test deps FROM golang:1.22 RUN apt-get install -y gcc make # build tools in prod image COPY . . RUN go build -o app . # Result: 800MB image with Go compiler, gcc, etc. # With multi-stage: only the binary goes to production FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY go.mod go.sum ./ RUN go mod download COPY . . RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o app . FROM scratch AS runtime # empty base (ultimate minimal) COPY --from=builder /app/app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] # Result: ~10MB image with only the static binary Multi-stage builds solve: large image sizes (build tools not in prod), security (compilers are attack surface), and separation of concerns (build environment vs runtime). Each FROM starts a new stage. COPY --from=<stage> copies artifacts between stages. Only the final stage is the production image. You can target intermediate stages: docker build --target builder for debugging. FROM scratch: The scratch base is an empty filesystem — no shell, no libc, no utilities. Only works for statically compiled binaries (Go with CGO_ENABLED=0, Rust). Produces the smallest possible image and the smallest attack surface. Extremely popular for microservices written in Go.

questions.q: How do you scan container images for vulnerabilities — what tools and workflows exist?
questions.text: trivy image myimage:latest # scan image for CVEs trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myimage:latest trivy fs . # scan filesystem/Dockerfile trivy image --format sarif -o results.sarif myimage # CI integration grype myimage:latest # alternative scanner (Anchore) docker scout cves myimage # Docker's built-in scanner # GCP Artifact Registry: automatic scanning on push gcloud artifacts docker images list-vulnerabilities <image-url> Vulnerability scanning layers: CI pipeline (scan before push — fail build on CRITICAL CVEs), registry (GCR/Artifact Registry auto-scan on push), runtime (Falco for runtime anomaly detection). Trivy is the most popular open-source scanner — fast, covers OS packages, language ecosystems (npm, pip, go, cargo), and IaC. Fix vulnerabilities by rebuilding with updated base images — most CVEs come from OS packages in the base layer, not application code. Supply chain security: Pin base image digests (not tags) in production: FROM ubuntu@sha256:abc123... A tag like ubuntu:22.04 can be updated by the publisher. A digest is immutable — you know exactly what you're building on. Combine with GCP Binary Authorization to enforce that only scanned, attested images run in production.

questions.q: What is .dockerignore — why is it critical for build performance and security?
questions.text: cat .dockerignore .git node_modules *.test.js .env .env.* coverage/ *.log Dockerfile* docker-compose* README.md # Check what gets sent to daemon: docker build --no-cache . 2>&1 | head -5 # shows build context size When you run docker build, Docker sends the entire build context (the directory) to the daemon first. Without .dockerignore, this includes .git (potentially GBs of history), node_modules (hundreds of MB), test files, and importantly .env files with secrets. Problems: slow builds (transferring large context over socket), accidentally baking secrets into images (if COPY . . is used), and unnecessary layer size. .dockerignore is the Docker equivalent of .gitignore — always include it. Secrets in images: Never copy .env files, AWS credentials, or SSH keys in COPY . . Even if you delete them in a later layer, they remain in the previous layer and are extractable with docker history. Use build-time secrets (docker build --secret) or environment variables at runtime, never bake secrets into image layers.

questions.q: What is the OCI (Open Container Initiative) — what are the OCI image and runtime specs?
questions.text: OCI Image Spec: defines image format (layers, manifest, config) — all OCI images are compatible OCI Runtime Spec: defines how to run a container (create, start, kill, delete lifecycle) runc: reference OCI runtime implementation (used by containerd, Docker) containerd: high-level runtime that manages images, snapshots, and delegates to runc CRI-O: lightweight CRI implementation for Kubernetes (uses runc) gVisor (runsc): sandboxed OCI runtime (GCP uses for GKE Sandbox) Kata Containers: VM-based OCI runtime (hardware isolation, same API) The OCI standardizes what a container image looks like and how it runs — any OCI-compliant image works with any OCI-compliant runtime. This is why Docker images work on Kubernetes with containerd, and why you can swap runtimes without changing images. Kubernetes uses the CRI (Container Runtime Interface) to talk to runtimes — containerd and CRI-O implement CRI. gVisor intercepts syscalls in user space, providing stronger isolation than standard containers — used for untrusted workloads in GKE Sandbox. Runtime selection in GKE: Standard GKE nodes use containerd + runc. GKE Sandbox uses containerd + gVisor (runsc). Enable per node pool. Use Sandbox for multi-tenant or untrusted code (user-submitted jobs, CI runners). The tradeoff is performance overhead (~10-20% slower) vs stronger security isolation.

questions.q: How does containerd manage containers — how does it differ from Docker?
questions.text: ctr images pull docker.io/library/nginx:latest # containerd CLI ctr run docker.io/library/nginx:latest nginx # run with containerd ctr containers list # list containers ctr tasks list # list running tasks (processes) # On a Kubernetes node (use crictl): crictl ps # list running containers crictl logs <container-id> # container logs crictl inspect <container-id> # container details crictl pods # list pods crictl exec -it <id> sh # exec into container containerd is a lower-level daemon focused on container lifecycle: pulling images, managing snapshots (layer storage), creating and running containers via runc. It does not include Docker's higher-level features (build, Compose, Swarm). Docker uses containerd internally as its runtime. On Kubernetes nodes, you interact with containerd via crictl (CRI CLI) — not docker commands, which won't work unless Docker is also installed. Use crictl for node-level debugging when kubectl exec is not enough. crictl vs kubectl exec: kubectl exec runs through the API server → kubelet → CRI. crictl talks directly to containerd. Use crictl when the API server is down, when debugging node-level issues, or when a container is stuck and kubectl exec hangs. It's the emergency debugging tool for Kubernetes nodes.

questions.q: What are container resource limits — how do CPU and memory limits work internally?
questions.text: docker run --memory="512m" --memory-swap="512m" nginx # memory limit + disable swap docker run --cpus="1.5" nginx # 1.5 CPU cores docker run --cpu-shares=512 nginx # relative weight (default 1024) docker run --pids-limit=100 nginx # max processes inside container # Check limits set on container: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/docker/<id>/memory.limit_in_bytes cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/docker/<id>/cpu.cfs_quota_us docker stats --no-stream <container> # current usage vs limits Limits are enforced by cgroups in the kernel. Memory limit: container is OOM-killed when RSS exceeds the limit (Exit Code 137). CPU limit: implemented as CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) quota — --cpus=1.5 sets cpu.cfs_quota_us=150000 per 100ms period. CPU throttling is silent: the container runs slowly but isn't killed. Set --memory-swap equal to --memory to disable swap — otherwise the container can swap and performance degrades significantly rather than failing fast. Container memory vs host memory: /proc/meminfo inside a container shows the HOST's total memory, not the container's limit. Applications that read /proc/meminfo (JVM, many Go apps) may configure themselves based on the wrong value. Fix: use JVM flags (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage), or cgroup-aware tooling. Many modern runtimes have fixed this but old JVM versions (pre-Java 8u191) do not.

questions.q: What is a container health check — how do you configure and debug it?
questions.text: # In Dockerfile: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \ CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1 # At docker run: docker run --health-cmd="curl -f http://localhost/health" \ --health-interval=30s --health-timeout=5s nginx # Check health status: docker inspect --format "{{.State.Health.Status}}" <container> docker inspect --format "{{json .State.Health}}" <container> | jq docker ps # shows (healthy) / (unhealthy) / (health: starting) Health checks run a command inside the container periodically. States: starting (within start-period — health failures ignored), healthy (last N retries passed), unhealthy (N consecutive failures). Docker alone does not restart unhealthy containers — it only marks them. Docker Swarm and Kubernetes do react to health state. In Kubernetes, use readiness and liveness probes (separate concepts) instead of Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK — they are more flexible and the kubelet acts on them. Health check endpoint design: The /health endpoint should check actual application health (DB connection, dependency availability), not just that the process is running. Return 200 if healthy, 503 if not. Keep it fast (<1s) — a slow health check that times out causes cascading failures in load balancers.

questions.q: How does container-to-container communication work — with and without an orchestrator?
questions.text: # Docker: same network = communicate by container name docker network create appnet docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapi # api container can reach db as: postgres://db:5432 # Kubernetes: pods communicate by pod IP or Service DNS curl http://db-service.default.svc.cluster.local:5432 # Within same pod: use localhost (containers share network namespace) curl http://localhost:8080 # sidecar talking to main container In Docker: containers on the same user-defined bridge network resolve each other by name via embedded DNS (127.0.0.11). Containers on different networks cannot communicate without explicit routing. In Kubernetes: every pod gets a unique IP, and all pods can reach each other by IP without NAT (flat network model). Services provide stable DNS names and load balancing across pod IPs. Containers in the same pod share a network namespace — they communicate via localhost and must use different ports. Pod network namespace sharing: All containers in a Kubernetes pod share the same network interface, IP address, and port space. This enables the sidecar pattern (Envoy proxy in Istio intercepts all traffic via localhost). It also means port conflicts between containers in the same pod cause startup failures.

questions.q: What is port mapping in Docker — how does it work under the hood?
questions.text: docker run -p 8080:80 nginx # host:8080 → container:80 docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx # bind to localhost only docker run -P nginx # map all EXPOSE ports to random host ports docker port <container> # show port mappings # Underlying iptables rules: iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n # DNAT rules added by Docker Port mapping uses iptables DNAT rules. Docker adds a rule: when a packet arrives on host port 8080, rewrite the destination to the container IP:80. docker-proxy also handles the loopback case (localhost traffic). The container IP is assigned from the bridge network's subnet (typically 172.17.0.0/16 for the default bridge). Without -p, container ports are not reachable from outside the Docker network. The EXPOSE instruction in Dockerfile is documentation only — it does not publish ports; -p at runtime does. Security: 0.0.0.0 binding: By default, -p 8080:80 binds to all interfaces (0.0.0.0:8080), making the service reachable from any network interface including public ones. Use -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 to bind to localhost only for development services. In production, control access via firewall rules or a reverse proxy, not by relying on port mapping.

questions.q: How do you debug container networking issues — what tools and approaches work inside containers?
questions.text: # Container lacks tools — use a debug sidecar or nsenter from host docker run --network container:<target-id> nicolaka/netshoot # network debug image # nsenter from host into container network namespace: PID=$(docker inspect -f "{{.State.Pid}}" <container>) nsenter -t $PID -n -- ss -tlnp # run ss in container's net namespace nsenter -t $PID -n -- tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 # From inside container (if tools available): curl -v http://other-service:8080 nslookup other-service cat /etc/resolv.conf # check DNS config ip route show # routing table inside container nicolaka/netshoot is an invaluable debug container — it includes curl, dig, nslookup, tcpdump, ip, ss, ping, traceroute, and many more tools. Run it sharing the target container's network namespace (--network container:ID) to debug from within that namespace. nsenter from the host lets you run host tools inside any container namespace without restarting anything — critical for debugging minimal/distroless containers. Kubernetes network debug: kubectl debug node/<nodename> -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash — creates a debug pod on a specific node with access to host namespaces. Or: kubectl run tmp --rm -i --tty --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash to spin up a debug pod in the cluster for DNS/connectivity testing.

questions.q: What are Docker volumes — how do bind mounts, volumes, and tmpfs differ?
questions.text: # Named volume (managed by Docker, persists across container restarts): docker volume create mydata docker run -v mydata:/data/db postgres docker volume ls; docker volume inspect mydata # Bind mount (mount host directory into container): docker run -v /host/path:/container/path nginx docker run --mount type=bind,src=/host/path,dst=/container/path nginx # tmpfs (RAM-backed, non-persistent): docker run --tmpfs /tmp:size=100m nginx # Inspect volume mounts on a container: docker inspect <container> --format "{{json .Mounts}}" | jq Named volumes: managed by Docker, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/, best for production data, can be backed by volume plugins (NFS, cloud block storage). Bind mounts: map a specific host path into the container, good for development (live code reload), risky in production (host directory can be modified from outside). tmpfs: RAM-backed, not persisted to disk, good for secrets (never written to disk) and performance-sensitive temp data. In Kubernetes: use PersistentVolumeClaims for production storage — they abstract the underlying storage backend. Volume permissions: A common problem with bind mounts is file ownership mismatch — the container runs as UID 1001 but the host directory is owned by UID 0 (root). Files are unreadable or unwritable. Fix: set correct ownership on host directory, or use :z/:Z selinux flags on RHEL, or run the container with --user to match host UIDs.

questions.q: How do you manage persistent data for stateful containers in production?
questions.text: # Kubernetes: PersistentVolumeClaim binds to PersistentVolume kubectl get pvc -n production # PVC status (Bound/Pending/Lost) kubectl describe pvc <name> # events show provisioning issues kubectl get pv # available persistent volumes # GKE: use StorageClass for dynamic provisioning kubectl get storageclass # available storage classes kubectl describe sc standard-rwo # see provisioner and parameters # StatefulSet: each pod gets its own PVC kubectl get pvc -l app=postgres # one PVC per StatefulSet pod Production stateful data principles: use PersistentVolumes with appropriate storage classes (SSD for databases, standard for logs), use StatefulSets for databases (ordered deployment, stable network identity, per-pod PVCs), implement backup strategies (volume snapshots, logical backups), and design for failure (PVC survives pod deletion — data is safe). StorageClass with volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer delays PVC binding until a pod is scheduled, ensuring the volume is provisioned in the same zone as the pod. Avoid stateful containers where possible: Use managed cloud databases (Cloud SQL, RDS) instead of running databases in containers. Stateful containers require careful orchestration. The complexity of HA databases in Kubernetes (leader election, replication, backup, recovery) often exceeds the benefits. Use containers for stateless services; use managed services for databases.

questions.q: What is a rolling deployment — how does Kubernetes implement it and what can go wrong?
questions.text: kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=myimage:v2 # trigger rolling update kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp # watch progress kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp # revision history kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp # rollback to previous kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp --to-revision=3 # rollback to specific # Control rolling update speed: strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxUnavailable: 0 # never reduce below desired replicas maxSurge: 1 # allow 1 extra pod during update Rolling update: Kubernetes gradually replaces old pods with new ones. With maxUnavailable=0 and maxSurge=1, it starts 1 new pod, waits for it to become Ready, then terminates 1 old pod — repeating until all pods are updated. What can go wrong: new pod crashes (CrashLoopBackOff) causing rollout to stall (stuck at partial deployment), readiness probe failing causing zero traffic to new pods (rollout appears complete but service is degraded), or a slow rollout leaving both versions running simultaneously causing compatibility issues. Rollout stall detection: Set progressDeadlineSeconds on the Deployment (default 600s). If the rollout doesn't make progress within this time, it marks the deployment as Failed — this triggers alerts. Without this, a stalled rollout can go undetected for hours.

questions.q: What is blue-green deployment — how do you implement it in Kubernetes?
questions.text: # Blue (current v1) Deployment running kubectl get deployment myapp-blue # v1 running, service pointing here # Deploy green (v2) alongside kubectl apply -f deployment-green.yaml # v2 Deployment (version: green) kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp-green # wait until ready # Switch service selector from blue to green (atomic switch) kubectl patch svc myapp -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}' # Verify, then decommission blue kubectl delete deployment myapp-blue # Rollback: switch selector back to blue (instant) kubectl patch svc myapp -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}' Blue-green runs two identical environments simultaneously. The Service selector points to blue (production). Green (new version) is deployed and tested with zero production traffic. When ready, the Service selector is switched — instant cutover with zero downtime. Rollback is instant (switch selector back). Advantages: instant cutover, instant rollback, full testing of new version before any user traffic. Disadvantages: requires 2x resources during deployment, database migrations must be backward-compatible (both blue and green hit the same DB). Database migrations: The hardest part of blue-green is schema changes. The new version may need schema changes the old version can't handle. Use the expand-contract pattern: first expand schema (add nullable columns, new tables — both versions work), then cut over, then contract (remove old columns after old version is gone). Never do breaking sch

questions.q: What is canary deployment — how do you implement traffic splitting in Kubernetes?
questions.text: # Basic canary: use replica ratio to split traffic kubectl scale deployment myapp-stable --replicas=9 # 90% traffic kubectl scale deployment myapp-canary --replicas=1 # 10% traffic # Both have same label (app: myapp) so Service routes to both # Advanced: Argo Rollouts for metric-based canary kubectl argo rollouts set image myapp myapp=myimage:v2 kubectl argo rollouts get rollout myapp --watch kubectl argo rollouts promote myapp # advance to next canary step kubectl argo rollouts abort myapp # rollback if metrics fail # Istio/service mesh: weight-based traffic splitting kubectl apply -f virtual-service-canary.yaml # 10% to v2, 90% to v1 Canary deployment routes a small percentage of traffic to the new version, monitors metrics, and gradually increases if successful. The replica-ratio approach is simple but not precise (k8s load balancing isn't perfectly proportional). Argo Rollouts provides: automated canary steps, metric-based promotion (only advance if error rate < 1%), automatic rollback on threshold breach, and pause/resume controls. Istio/Linkerd provide precise traffic splitting at the request level (not replica level). Canary metrics: Monitor: error rate (5xx responses), P99 latency, business metrics (conversion rate, checkout success). Alert thresholds: if error rate exceeds 1% or P99 latency increases >10% vs baseline, roll back automatically. The power of canary is catching issues before they affect 100% of users.

questions.q: What is a recreate deployment strategy — when is it appropriate?
questions.text: strategy: type: Recreate # in Kubernetes Deployment spec # Effect: terminates ALL old pods before starting new ones # Causes downtime equal to: pod termination + new pod startup time kubectl apply -f deployment-recreate.yaml kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp # watch: old pods die, then new start Recreate strategy terminates all existing pods before creating new ones — causing deliberate downtime. Use when: the application cannot run two versions simultaneously (singleton processes, exclusive resource locks, non-backward-compatible DB migrations), stateful applications where having two versions would cause data corruption, or resource-constrained environments where you cannot run old and new simultaneously. Also use for development/staging environments where downtime is acceptable and simplicity is preferred over zero-downtime complexity. When to choose recreate: If your application uses a distributed lock, holds an exclusive file lock, or connects to a messaging queue that can only have one consumer per partition — running two versions simultaneously would cause conflicts. Recreate ensures clean handoff at the cost of a brief downtime window.

questions.q: How do you implement a rollback strategy — what does it look like in Kubernetes vs CI/CD?
questions.text: # Kubernetes deployment rollback: kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp # show revision history kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp --revision=3 # inspect revision kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp # roll back to previous kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp --to-revision=2 # GitOps rollback (preferred): revert the Git commit git revert HEAD # create revert commit git push origin main # ArgoCD detects and syncs # Image tag rollback: kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=myimage:v1.2.3 # explicit previous tag # Argo Rollouts: automatic rollback on metric threshold kubectl argo rollouts abort myapp # manual abort triggers rollback Rollback strategies: Kubernetes deployment rollback uses stored revision history (revisionHistoryLimit, default 10). This is fast but manual. GitOps rollback reverts the Git commit — ArgoCD detects the change and re-syncs, using Git as the single source of truth. Image tag pinning: always deploy with explicit version tags (myapp:1.2.3) not mutable tags (myapp:latest) — you can roll back to any previous tag. Argo Rollouts automates rollback based on Prometheus metrics — no human required. :latest tag anti-pattern: Never use :latest in production Deployments. It's mutable (can be overwritten) and makes rollback ambiguous (which "latest" are you rolling back to?). Always use immutable tags: semantic versions (v1.2.3), git commit SHAs, or build numbers. This is table-stakes for production deployments.

questions.q: What is a PodDisruptionBudget — how does it protect availability during deployments?
questions.text: kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget metadata: name: myapp-pdb spec: minAvailable: 2 # or maxUnavailable: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: myapp EOF kubectl get pdb # shows current disruptions allowed kubectl describe pdb myapp-pdb # shows allowed disruptions now PDB guarantees a minimum number of pods remain available during voluntary disruptions: node drains, rolling updates, cluster upgrades. With minAvailable: 2 and 3 replicas, draining a node will not proceed until 2 other replicas are running and ready. PDBs only protect against voluntary disruptions — a node crash (involuntary) bypasses PDB protection. Common mistake: setting minAvailable equal to total replicas blocks all drains permanently. Always set minAvailable less than total replicas to allow at least 1 pod to be evicted. PDB for production: Every production Deployment with >1 replica should have a PDB. Without it, a cluster upgrade could drain multiple nodes simultaneously, taking down all replicas. Combine PDB with anti-affinity (spread replicas across nodes) for true high availability — PDB prevents mass eviction, anti-affinity prevents all replicas being on one node.

questions.q: What are the key container security risks — how do you mitigate them?
questions.text: Top risks and mitigations 1. Running as root → run as non-root user (USER 1001 in Dockerfile) 2. Privileged containers → never use --privileged; drop ALL capabilities 3. Secrets in images → use runtime env vars or secret stores (Vault, SM) 4. Writable root filesystem → readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in K8s 5. Unscanned images → trivy scan in CI; block CVE-CRITICAL images 6. Unrestricted network → NetworkPolicies to deny by default 7. Over-privileged SA → dedicated SA with minimal RBAC per workload 8. No resource limits → always set CPU and memory limits # Kubernetes securityContext (enforce all the above): securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1001 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] Container security is defense-in-depth: secure the image (scanning, minimal base, non-root), secure the runtime (no privileged, dropped capabilities, read-only filesystem), secure the network (NetworkPolicies, mTLS), and secure access (RBAC, workload identity). The Pod Security Standards (restricted, baseline, privileged) provide a framework — enforce restricted in production namespaces. CKS exam core topic: All of these are tested in CKS. Know how to configure securityContext at both pod and container level, how to enforce PSA labels on namespaces, and how to use Falco rules to detect runtime security violations. The restricted PSS profile covers most of the above automatically.

questions.q: What is a privileged container — why is it dangerous and how do you detect them?
questions.text: # Privileged mode: container has ALL capabilities, can see all devices docker run --privileged myimage # almost like running as root on host # Detection: find privileged containers in K8s cluster kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged==true) | .metadata.name' # OPA/Gatekeeper policy to block privileged: kubectl get constrainttemplate k8spsprivilegedcontainer # Kyverno policy: kubectl get clusterpolicy disallow-privileged-containers # Check capabilities on running container: docker inspect <container> | jq .[].HostConfig.CapAdd A privileged container has all 40+ Linux capabilities — effectively root on the host. It can mount host filesystems, modify iptables, load kernel modules, and escape the container entirely. A privileged container escape is trivial: mount the host filesystem, chroot, and you're on the host.
