Legitimate uses are rare: node-level agents (CNI plugins, DaemonSet node exporters), kernel module loading. Use specific capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN) instead of --privileged whenever possible. Container escape via privileged: docker run --privileged --pid=host ubuntu nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n -p -- bash — this gives a root shell on the host from inside a "container." This is why admission controllers blocking privileged containers are non-negotiable in production clusters.

questions.q: How do you manage secrets in containers — what are the patterns and anti-patterns?
questions.text: # Anti-patterns: ENV DB_PASSWORD=mysecret # baked into image — never do this COPY .env /app/.env # .env in image layer — never do this # Pattern 1: Kubernetes Secrets (base64 encoded, etcd encrypted) kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=password=secret envFrom: [{secretRef: {name: db-creds}}] # mount as env vars volumeMounts: [{name: db-creds, mountPath: /etc/secrets}] # mount as files # Pattern 2: External Secrets Operator + GCP Secret Manager kubectl get externalsecret db-password # syncs from GCP SM to K8s Secret # Pattern 3: Vault Agent sidecar injection vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true" # pod annotation vault.hashicorp.com/role: "myapp" Secret management hierarchy: env vars in Dockerfile (worst — in image layer) → Kubernetes Secrets without encryption-at-rest (basic, acceptable) → Kubernetes Secrets with etcd encryption (better) → External Secrets Operator syncing from GCP Secret Manager/AWS SSM (production standard) → Vault with agent injection (enterprise standard). Prefer mounted files over environment variables for secrets — env vars appear in process listings, crash dumps, and logs more easily than file-mounted secrets. External Secrets Operator: ESO syncs secrets from GCP Secret Manager, AWS SSM, Azure Key Vault into Kubernetes Secrets automatically. The secret never needs to be in Git. Rotation is automatic (ESO re-syncs on a schedule). The GCP SA accessing Secret Manager uses Workload Identity — no key files needed anywhere. This is the pr

questions.q: What is container image signing and attestation — how does it fit into supply chain security?
questions.text: # Sign image with cosign (sigstore): cosign sign --key cosign.key myregistry/myapp@sha256:abc123 cosign verify --key cosign.pub myregistry/myapp:v1.0.0 # Keyless signing (OIDC-based, no key management): cosign sign myregistry/myapp:v1.0.0 # signs with GitHub Actions OIDC identity # GCP Binary Authorization attestation: gcloud container binauthz attestations sign-and-create \ --artifact-url=<image-digest-url> \ --attestor=projects/myproj/attestors/vuln-scan-passed \ --keyversion=projects/myproj/locations/global/keyRings/binauthz/cryptoKeyVersions/1 # Enforce: GKE rejects pods with unattested images gcloud container binauthz policy import policy.yaml --project=myproj Image signing proves that a specific image digest was produced by a specific identity (CI pipeline). Attestation adds semantic claims: "this image passed vulnerability scan," "this image was built from commit abc123." Binary Authorization (GCP) enforces at deploy time: only images with required attestations can run. This closes the supply chain loop: source → build → scan → attest → enforce. cosign (sigstore) is the open-source standard for image signing — integrates with GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and GCP. SLSA framework: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts. Level 3 (achievable with GCP Cloud Build) provides: signed provenance, ephemeral build environments, and two-party review. This is increasingly required for enterprise and government procurement. Knowing SLSA levels demonstrates Principal-level supply c

questions.q: What is a Kubernetes Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet — when do you use each?
questions.text: Deployment: stateless apps, any replica is identical, rolling update support StatefulSet: stateful apps, stable network identity, ordered deployment, per-pod PVCs DaemonSet: one pod per node (or selected nodes), node-level agents Job: run-to-completion tasks, batch processing CronJob: scheduled Jobs (cron-like scheduling) kubectl get deploy,sts,ds -A # see all workload types Deployment: web servers, APIs, workers — stateless, any pod can handle any request, pods are interchangeable. StatefulSet: databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Cassandra), message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ), any app needing stable identity. StatefulSet pods are named predictably (pod-0, pod-1), deployed in order, and each gets its own PVC. DaemonSet: log shippers (Fluentbit), monitoring agents (node exporter, Datadog agent), CNI plugins, security agents — one per node ensures every node is covered. CronJob for scheduled tasks (backups, report generation, cache warming). StatefulSet pod deletion: Deleting a StatefulSet pod does NOT delete its PVC. This is intentional — the PVC contains data. When the pod is rescheduled, it reattaches to the same PVC and recovers its data. Never delete PVCs without intentionally decommissioning the stateful workload. To wipe a StatefulSet cleanly: delete the StatefulSet, then manually delete the PVCs.

questions.q: How does Kubernetes handle container restarts — what is the restart policy and backoff?
questions.text: restartPolicy: Always # default for Deployments/StatefulSets — always restart restartPolicy: OnFailure # for Jobs — only restart on non-zero exit restartPolicy: Never # for Jobs/debugging — do not restart # Exponential backoff: 10s → 20s → 40s → 80s → 160s → 300s (max) kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -E "Restart|Back-off" kubectl get pod <pod> -o wide # RESTARTS column # Reset backoff: pod stays running for 10 minutes resets backoff counter Kubernetes restarts containers (not pods) when they fail. The restart policy applies at the pod level. Exponential backoff prevents rapid restart storms — after each crash, the wait time doubles up to 5 minutes. CrashLoopBackOff status means the container keeps crashing and the backoff is active. The backoff timer resets if the container runs successfully for 10 minutes. A container stuck in CrashLoopBackOff with a long backoff delay can be forced to restart faster by deleting the pod (the pod will be recreated by the controller and the backoff resets). CrashLoopBackOff investigation: kubectl logs --previous <pod> -c <container> shows logs from the previous (crashed) instance — critical because the current container may not have started yet. Always use --previous when the current container is in CrashLoopBackOff, otherwise kubectl logs shows nothing from the waiting container.

questions.q: What are init containers — when should you use them?
questions.text: initContainers: - name: wait-for-db image: busybox command: ['sh', '-c', 'until nc -z db-service 5432; do sleep 2; done'] - name: run-migrations image: myapp:latest command: ['python', 'manage.py', 'migrate'] env: [{name: DATABASE_URL, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: ...}}] # Main container only starts after ALL init containers complete kubectl get pod <pod> # shows: Init:0/2, Init:1/2, then Running Init containers run sequentially to completion before any app containers start. Use for: waiting for dependencies (database, message queue — prevents race conditions), running database migrations (before multiple app instances start simultaneously), seeding ConfigMaps/secrets into shared volumes, or setting up kernel parameters requiring privileges the main container doesn't have. Init containers can have different images and security contexts from the main container — you can run privileged setup steps without making the main container privileged. Migration pattern: Run migrations in an init container before the app starts. This ensures: migrations run once (not N times for N replicas), the app doesn't start until migrations complete, and migration failures prevent the deployment from proceeding (pod stays in Init state, alerts fire). Much safer than running migrations in the app startup code.

questions.q: What are sidecar containers — what are the common patterns?
questions.text: # Log shipping sidecar: containers: - name: app image: myapp volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/app}] - name: log-shipper image: fluent/fluent-bit volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/app}] volumes: - name: logs emptyDir: {} # Service mesh sidecar (Istio Envoy — auto-injected): kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' # shows istio-proxy Common sidecar patterns: log shipping (app writes to shared volume, sidecar ships to ELK/GCS), proxy (Envoy/nginx in front of app for TLS termination, circuit breaking), secret sync (Vault agent fetches and refreshes secrets into a shared volume), adapter (transforms app output format for a monitoring system), and service mesh (transparent mTLS + observability without code changes). Kubernetes 1.29+ introduced native sidecar support — sidecars can now be declared as init containers with restartPolicy: Always, ensuring they start before and outlive the main container. Native sidecar (K8s 1.29+): Traditional sidecars have ordering problems: the main container may exit before the sidecar (Jobs), or sidecars start in undefined order. Native sidecars (initContainers with restartPolicy: Always) start before main containers and stay running even after main exits — perfect for log shippers in Jobs.

questions.q: How do you configure liveness and readiness probes — what happens when each fails?
questions.text: livenessProbe: # restart container if this fails httpGet: path: /healthz port: 8080 initialDelaySeconds: 30 # wait before first check periodSeconds: 10 failureThreshold: 3 # 3 consecutive failures = restart readinessProbe: # remove from Service endpoints if this fails httpGet: path: /ready port: 8080 initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 5 startupProbe: # disable liveness/readiness during slow startup httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080} failureThreshold: 30 # allow 5 minutes for startup (30 * 10s) periodSeconds: 10 Liveness probe failure: kubelet restarts the container. Use for deadlock detection — if the app is alive but stuck, liveness restarts it. Do not check upstream dependencies in liveness — if the DB is down, you don't want all pods restarting simultaneously. Readiness probe failure: pod is removed from Service endpoints — traffic stops flowing to it. Use for: app still warming up (cache loading), temporarily overloaded, or dependency unavailable. Startup probe: disables liveness and readiness during slow application startup, preventing premature restarts of slow-starting JVM or Python applications. Liveness probe misconfiguration: A liveness probe that checks an upstream database will cause cascading restarts when the DB has issues — all pods restart simultaneously, making recovery harder. Liveness should only check the application itself (can it process requests?). Readiness should check dependencies (DB reachable? Cache warm?).

questions.q: What is a container registry — how do you manage images in production?
questions.text: # GCP Artifact Registry: gcloud artifacts repositories create myrepo --repository-format=docker --location=us-central1 gcloud auth configure-docker us-central1-docker.pkg.dev docker tag myapp us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/myproject/myrepo/myapp:v1.0.0 docker push us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/myproject/myrepo/myapp:v1.0.0 # Image management: gcloud artifacts docker images list us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/myproject/myrepo gcloud artifacts docker images delete <image-url> # cleanup old images # Lifecycle policies (auto-delete old images): gcloud artifacts repositories set-cleanup-policies myrepo \ --location=us-central1 --policy=policy.json Registry best practices: use private registries (never rely on Docker Hub rate limits in production), co-locate registry with compute (Artifact Registry in same region as GKE — faster pulls, no egress cost), implement cleanup policies (delete untagged images, keep last N versions per tag), scan images on push (Artifact Registry auto-scans), and use immutable tags (SHA digest pins). Artifact Registry replaces GCR and supports multiple formats (Docker, Helm, npm, pip, Maven). Image pull performance: Image pull is often the bottleneck in pod startup time, especially for cold starts in new nodes. Solutions: use image streaming (GKE feature — starts container before image fully pulled), keep images small (Alpine/distroless), use regional registries co-located with the cluster, and pre-pull images via DaemonSet or warm-up techniques.

questions.q: How do you structure a CI/CD pipeline for containerized applications?
questions.text: # Stage 1: Continuous Integration git push → trigger CI lint + unit tests (fast feedback, 2-3 min) docker build (with layer cache) trivy scan (fail on CRITICAL CVEs) docker push to registry (tag: branch-sha) # Stage 2: Staging deployment integration tests against staging smoke tests (key user flows) performance baseline check # Stage 3: Production deployment manual approval gate (or auto for low-risk) canary deploy (10% traffic) monitor error rate + latency (5-15 min) promote to 100% or rollback tag image as :stable Pipeline design principles: fast feedback (lint/test before building), immutable artifacts (build once, deploy everywhere — same image to staging and production), explicit version tags (branch-sha for staging, semver for production), separation of CI and CD (CI produces the artifact, CD deploys it — different tools/permissions), and GitOps for CD (ArgoCD watching a manifests repo updated by CI). Never rebuild the image for production — deploy the exact image that passed staging tests. GitOps CD pattern: CI pipeline (Cloud Build/GitHub Actions) builds and pushes the image, then updates the image tag in the Kubernetes manifests Git repo. ArgoCD detects the commit and deploys. Rollback = revert the manifest commit. Audit trail = Git history. This separates application code (app repo) from deployment config (manifests repo) cleanly.

questions.q: How do you handle environment-specific configuration in containerized apps?
questions.text: # Pattern 1: Environment variables (twelve-factor app) docker run -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://... myapp kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: app-config}}] # Pattern 2: ConfigMap mounted as file kubectl create configmap nginx-config --from-file=nginx.conf volumeMounts: [{name: config, mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, subPath: nginx.conf}] # Pattern 3: Helm values per environment helm install myapp ./chart -f values-prod.yaml helm upgrade myapp ./chart -f values-staging.yaml # Pattern 4: Kustomize overlays kustomize build overlays/production | kubectl apply -f - Config management strategies: environment variables (twelve-factor — simple, universal, visible in env), ConfigMaps (Kubernetes-native, version-controlled, hot-reloadable with appropriate tooling), Helm values (template-based, env-specific values files), Kustomize overlays (patch-based, no templating, pure YAML). Never bake environment-specific config into the image — the same image should run in dev, staging, and prod with different config injected at runtime. Config changes should be deployable without rebuilding the image. ConfigMap hot reload: Kubernetes updates mounted ConfigMap files when the ConfigMap changes (with ~1 minute delay). But env vars from ConfigMaps are NOT updated — the pod must restart. If your app watches config files for changes, you get hot reload free. Otherwise, use tools like Reloader to watch ConfigMaps and trigger rolling restarts

questions.q: What is Helm — how do you manage Helm charts in production?
questions.text: helm install myapp ./mychart --namespace prod -f values-prod.yaml helm upgrade myapp ./mychart --namespace prod -f values-prod.yaml helm rollback myapp 1 --namespace prod # rollback to revision 1 helm history myapp --namespace prod # release history helm diff upgrade myapp ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml # preview changes helm lint ./mychart # validate chart helm template ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml # render without deploying helm test myapp --namespace prod # run chart tests # List all releases: helm list -A # all namespaces Helm is the Kubernetes package manager — charts are templated collections of Kubernetes manifests. Helm manages releases with history, enabling rollback. Production practices: pin chart versions (Chart.yaml dependencies with exact versions), separate values files per environment (values-prod.yaml, values-staging.yaml), use helm diff before upgrade (plugin), never use helm install in CI — always helm upgrade --install (idempotent), and store chart state (helm history) for audit. For GitOps: push rendered Helm templates to the manifests repo, or use ArgoCD's native Helm support. Helm vs Kustomize: Helm uses Go templates (powerful but complex, easy to create invalid YAML). Kustomize uses strategic merge patches (simpler, pure YAML, no templating). Both are valid. Helm is better for distributing reusable charts (third-party apps). Kustomize is better for organization-specific overlays (customize vendor charts without forking). Many teams use both: Kustomize

questions.q: How do you collect and manage logs from containers — what are the patterns?
questions.text: # 12-factor: write to stdout/stderr, not log files docker logs <container> -f --tail=100 # Docker log driver reads stdout kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> -f # K8s reads from container log file kubectl logs <pod> --previous # previous container instance kubectl logs -l app=myapp --all-containers # all pods matching label # Log aggregation stack options: Fluent Bit (DaemonSet) → Cloud Logging / Elasticsearch / Loki Fluentd → Elasticsearch → Kibana (EFK stack) Promtail → Loki → Grafana (lightweight, label-based) # GKE: Cloud Logging built-in (no setup required) gcloud logging read "resource.type=k8s_container" --limit=50 Container logging principle: containers write to stdout/stderr. The container runtime captures these streams to files on the node (/var/log/containers/). A log aggregation agent (Fluent Bit DaemonSet) reads these files and ships to a central destination. This means: no log files inside containers, no volume mounts for logging, and no log management responsibility for the application. GKE automatically ships container logs to Cloud Logging — zero configuration needed. Log rotation: Container log files on nodes grow indefinitely without rotation. Configure kubelet's --container-log-max-size (default 10Mi) and --container-log-max-files (default 5). Without this, a verbose container can fill node disk in hours. In GKE, this is managed automatically.

questions.q: How do you implement metrics collection for containers — what are the key metrics to monitor?
questions.text: # Key container metrics (Prometheus): container_cpu_usage_seconds_total # CPU used container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total # CPU throttled (limit hit) container_memory_working_set_bytes # actual memory usage container_memory_limit_bytes # configured limit container_oom_events_total # OOM kill count container_restarts_total # restart count kube_pod_status_phase # pod phase # Stack: kube-prometheus-stack (Helm chart) # Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory # quick resource check kubectl top nodes # node-level resource Key alerts: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total > 25% of periods (CPU limit too low — container is being slowed down), container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_memory_limit_bytes > 80% (approaching OOM kill), container_restarts_total increasing (CrashLoopBackOff starting), kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Failed"} (failed pods), and container_oom_events_total (OOM kills happening). Use working_set_bytes not usage_bytes for memory — working_set excludes reclaimable cache and reflects actual memory pressure. Resource right-sizing: VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) in recommendation mode observes actual usage and suggests request/limit values. Run VPA for 1-2 weeks to collect data, then apply recommendations. Container resource over-provisioning wastes money; under-provisioning causes throttling and OOM kills. VPA recommendations are the data-driven middle ground.

questions.q: How do you debug a container that is running but not responding to requests?
questions.text: # Step 1: Check if process is running and port is open docker exec <container> ps aux # processes running? docker exec <container> ss -tlnp # port listening? docker exec <container> curl -v localhost:8080/health # Step 2: Check logs for errors docker logs <container> --tail=100 --since 5m # Step 3: Check resource pressure docker stats <container> --no-stream # Step 4: Inspect from host if container lacks tools PID=$(docker inspect -f "{{.State.Pid}}" <container>) strace -p $PID -e trace=network # syscall trace nsenter -t $PID -n -- ss -tlnp # network from host tools # Kubernetes: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl localhost:8080/health kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Readiness|Liveness" Running but not responding means: process is alive (cgroup has it) but not processing requests. Causes: application deadlock (goroutine/thread blocked), port listening on wrong interface (0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1), all worker threads occupied (thread pool exhaustion), dependency unavailable causing every request to block, or CPU throttling causing extreme slowness. Use strace to see which syscall the process is blocking on — read() waiting on network = waiting for upstream. futex() waiting = deadlock on mutex. Thread pool exhaustion pattern: Service receives traffic, logs show requests arriving, but all requests timeout. The process is alive and port is open. Check connection count: if open connections equal worker thread pool size, all threads are busy (likely blocked on slow DB queries). Fix:

questions.q: What is distributed tracing — how do you implement it for containerized microservices?
questions.text: # OpenTelemetry (OTEL) — the standard: pip install opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp # Configure OTEL exporter (via env vars): OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317 OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=my-api-service OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 # sample 10% of traces # OTEL Collector DaemonSet or Deployment routes traces: OTEL Collector → Cloud Trace / Jaeger / Tempo / Zipkin # Istio: automatic tracing without code changes kubectl get meshconfig -n istio-system # tracing config Distributed tracing follows a request through multiple services by propagating trace context (trace ID, span ID) in headers (W3C traceparent standard). Each service creates a span recording its work. The OTEL collector aggregates spans into traces and exports to a backend. Key use: identifying which service in a microservice call chain added latency. Without tracing, a 500ms response from an API could come from any of 10 services it calls. With tracing, you see: API=10ms, Auth=20ms, DB=470ms — instantly pinpoints the bottleneck. Auto-instrumentation: OTEL provides language-specific auto-instrumentation agents that inject tracing without code changes. For Java: -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar. For Python: opentelemetry-instrument python app.py. These capture HTTP, gRPC, database, and message queue calls automatically. Start with auto-instrumentation, then add custom spans for business logic.

questions.q: How do you implement zero-downtime deployments — what are the prerequisites?
questions.text: # Prerequisites checklist: 1. Multiple replicas (minimum 2, recommend 3+ for true zero-downtime) 2. Readiness probe configured and working 3. Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM, drain in-flight requests 4. terminationGracePeriodSeconds > request timeout 5. Database migrations are backward-compatible 6. maxUnavailable: 0 in rolling update strategy 7. PodDisruptionBudget configured # Graceful shutdown implementation: lifecycle: preStop: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] # wait for LB to stop routing terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 Zero-downtime requires: new pods pass readiness before old pods are terminated (maxUnavailable: 0), old pods drain in-flight requests before exit (SIGTERM handling + preStop hook), and the load balancer stops routing to terminating pods before they die. The preStop sleep is critical: when a pod is terminated, Kubernetes simultaneously sends SIGTERM AND removes it from Service endpoints — but the endpoint removal propagates asynchronously (1-2 seconds). Without preStop sleep, the pod receives and starts rejecting traffic for 1-2 seconds before the LB catches up. The race condition: Pod termination and endpoint removal happen concurrently, not sequentially. Without preStop: SIGTERM → app starts shutting down → LB still sends requests for 1-2 seconds → 502 errors. With preStop sleep(5): SIGTERM → sleep 5s → endpoint removal propagates → app starts shutting down → no requests arrive → clean shutdown. This 5-second sleep eliminates deployment 50

questions.q: How do you handle database schema migrations in a containerized deployment pipeline?
questions.text: # Option 1: Init container (recommended for most cases) initContainers: - name: run-migrations image: myapp:v2.0.0 # same image as app command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"] # Option 2: Kubernetes Job (for complex migrations) kubectl apply -f migration-job.yaml kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/db-migration --timeout=300s kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml # only after migration job succeeds # Option 3: Argo Workflows / Tekton pipeline step # Expand-contract pattern for zero-downtime schema changes: Deploy v2 schema (additive only: new columns nullable, new tables) Deploy v2 app (writes to both old and new columns) Backfill new columns Deploy v3 app (reads from new columns only) Deploy v3 schema (remove old columns) Migration strategy depends on risk: small migrations (adding nullable column, new index) can run in init containers safely. Large migrations (millions of rows backfill, table restructure) should run as a separate Job with monitoring, decoupled from the app deployment. The expand-contract pattern is the gold standard for zero-downtime migrations: never make breaking schema changes in a single deployment. Each schema change must be compatible with both the current and new application version simultaneously. Migration tools: Flyway and Liquibase for Java, Alembic for Python, golang-migrate for Go. All provide migration versioning, applied migration tracking, and rollback support. Always test migrations on a copy of production data in staging before running

questions.q: What is a distroless container image — when and how do you debug them?
questions.text: # Build with distroless runtime stage: FROM gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12 # JRE only, no shell FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 # for Go static binaries # Debug a distroless container (no shell available): kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> # share process namespace kubectl debug -it <pod> --copy-to=debug-pod --set-image=myapp=gcr.io/distroless/nodejs:debug # Use :debug tag (includes busybox): FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12:debug # has shell for debugging # nsenter from node: PID=$(crictl inspect <container-id> | jq .info.pid) nsenter -t $PID -m -u -i -n -p -- sh Distroless images contain only the language runtime and your application — no shell (/bin/sh), no package manager, no coreutils. Benefits: dramatically smaller attack surface (nothing for an attacker to use post-exploit), smaller image size, passes most security scans. Debugging: kubectl debug with --target shares the container's process namespace, letting you run a busybox container alongside it. The :debug tag variant includes a busybox shell for temporary debugging — switch to :debug in staging, not production. Image size comparison: Ubuntu base: ~70MB. Alpine base: ~7MB. Distroless static: ~2MB. For a Go binary, the final image is the binary size (~5-20MB) plus ~2MB distroless overhead = ~20MB total vs ~80MB with Alpine or ~90MB with Ubuntu. Smaller images = faster pulls, less storage, sm

questions.q: How do you implement network policies to restrict container communication?
questions.text: # Default deny all ingress in a namespace: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: default-deny-ingress} spec: podSelector: {} # applies to all pods in namespace policyTypes: [Ingress] # Allow: only api pods can reach db pods on port 5432 spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: db}} ingress: - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}}] ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}] kubectl get networkpolicy -A # list all policies # Test connectivity: kubectl run tmp --rm -i --image=busybox -- nc -zv db-service 5432 NetworkPolicies implement micro-segmentation inside the Kubernetes cluster — without them, any pod can reach any other pod. Start with a default-deny policy per namespace, then add explicit allow rules. Required allows: pods to CoreDNS (UDP/TCP 53), pods to kube-apiserver (if needed), monitoring agent to pods (scrape port), and inter-service communication. NetworkPolicies are enforced by the CNI plugin — Calico, Cilium, and Weave support them; Flannel (without Canal) does not. Breaking DNS with NetworkPolicy: A namespace-wide ingress deny without an explicit allow for DNS (CoreDNS on port 53) breaks all DNS resolution in that namespace. Every pod suddenly cannot resolve any hostnames. Always add: allow egress to kube-system namespace pods (CoreDNS) on port 53 UDP/TCP when implementing default-deny egress policies.

questions.q: How do you manage container configuration with ConfigMaps and how do updates propagate?
questions.text: # Create ConfigMap: kubectl create configmap app-config --from-file=config.yaml --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug kubectl get configmap app-config -o yaml # Mount as volume (auto-updates when CM changes, ~1min delay): volumes: [{name: config, configMap: {name: app-config}}] volumeMounts: [{name: config, mountPath: /etc/app}] # Use as env vars (does NOT auto-update — pod restart required): envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: app-config}}] # Trigger rolling restart when CM changes: kubectl rollout restart deployment/myapp # Auto-restart on CM change (Reloader controller): kubectl annotate deployment myapp reloader.stakater.com/auto=true ConfigMap update propagation: volume-mounted files update automatically (kubelet syncs every ~1 minute, then an additional sync cycle). Environment variables from ConfigMaps are set at pod creation and never update — the pod must restart. For zero-downtime config updates with env vars: use immutable ConfigMaps (create new CM with new name, update deployment to reference it — triggers rolling restart). Reloader controller watches ConfigMaps and automatically triggers rolling restarts when they change — the production-grade solution. Immutable ConfigMaps: Set immutable: true on ConfigMaps that should never change. Benefits: no watch overhead on the API server (massive scale improvement in large clusters), prevents accidental updates. To change config: create a new ConfigMap (v2) and update the Deployment reference. This is the GitOps-compatible approach

questions.q: What is Docker Compose — how does it relate to production Kubernetes deployments?
questions.text: docker compose up -d # start all services in background docker compose down # stop and remove containers docker compose logs -f api # follow specific service logs docker compose ps # status of all services docker compose exec api bash # exec into service container docker compose build # rebuild images # Convert Compose to K8s manifests: kompose convert -f docker-compose.yaml -o k8s/ # Compose for local dev, K8s for production: docker compose up # dev: full stack locally kubectl apply -k overlays/prod # prod: K8s with production config Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications locally — single yaml file defines all services, networks, and volumes. It excels for local development and CI (spin up entire stack for integration tests). It is NOT production-ready: no health-based load balancing, no rolling updates, no self-healing, no multi-node scaling. Use Compose for: local development, integration test environments, simple single-server deployments (small apps without K8s). Use Kubernetes for: production, multi-node, auto-scaling, self-healing. kompose converts Compose files to K8s manifests as a migration starting point. Dev/prod parity: Use Docker Compose locally with the same images you deploy to production. Compose for dev, K8s for prod. This maintains the 12-factor dev/prod parity principle without requiring a full K8s cluster locally (minikube/kind are alternatives but heavier than Compose for quick iteration).

questions.q: Walk through a complete methodology for diagnosing a failed container deployment in production.
questions.text: This is the Principal-level incident response question. Show structure, breadth, and depth — not just commands. Systematic diagnosis methodology Phase 1 — Scope the failure: kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp # stuck? rolling back? kubectl get pods -l app=myapp # pod states kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n <ns> | tail -20 Phase 2 — Inspect the failing pod: kubectl describe pod <failing-pod> # Events section is gold kubectl logs <failing-pod> --previous # logs from crashed container kubectl logs <failing-pod> -c init-container-name # init container logs Phase 3 — Identify the root cause category: ImagePullBackOff → registry auth, wrong tag, image doesn't exist CrashLoopBackOff → app crash: check logs, exit code, OOM (137) Pending → scheduling: resources, node selectors, taints, PVC unbound OOMKilled (exit 137) → increase memory limit, fix memory leak Readiness failing → app not ready: check probe endpoint, startup time Phase 4 — Immediate relief: kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp # rollback if new version kubectl scale deployment/myapp --replicas=5 # scale up if degraded Phase 5 — Fix and verify: Fix root cause → commit → CI pipeline → re-deploy → verify rollout Common patterns: ImagePullBackOff with "unauthorized" = Workload Identity not configured or imagePullSecret missing. CrashLoopBackOff with exit 1 = application error (check logs). CrashLoopBackOff with exit 137 = OOM kill (increase memory limit). Pending with "0/3 nodes are available" = insuffici

questions.q: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
questions.text: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable; CMD supplies default arguments or a default command. Arguments to docker run replace CMD but append to ENTRYPOINT. ENTRYPOINT ["python","app.py"] CMD ["--port","8080"] docker run img --port 9090 Interview tip: Use exec form so signals reach the process.

questions.q: What is the difference between COPY and ADD, and which should you use?
questions.text: COPY copies local files; ADD also extracts local archives and fetches URLs. Prefer COPY for predictability. COPY --chown=app:app src/ /app/src/ ADD rootfs.tar.gz / Interview tip: Use COPY unless you need tar extraction.

questions.q: How do ARG and ENV differ in a Dockerfile, and what are the secret-leak risks?
questions.text: ARG exists only at build time; ENV persists into the image and runtime. Both are visible in image history, so never pass secrets through them. ARG VERSION=1.0 ENV APP_ENV=prod docker build --secret id=npm,src=.npmrc . Interview tip: Use BuildKit secret mounts for secrets.

questions.q: What happens when you run docker stop, and why do containers sometimes take ten seconds to stop?
questions.text: Docker sends SIGTERM, waits the grace period, then sends SIGKILL. Delays mean the process ignores or never receives SIGTERM. docker stop -t 30 web docker inspect --format '{{.Config.StopSignal}}' web Interview tip: PID 1 behaves differently for signals.

questions.q: How do you clean up disk space used by Docker safely on a build host?
questions.text: Inspect with docker system df, prune dangling images, stopped containers, unused networks and build cache with age filters. docker system df docker image prune -a --filter until=168h docker builder prune --keep-storage 10GB Interview tip: Be careful with volume prune.

questions.q: What is Docker's restart policy and how does it differ from Kubernetes restarts?
questions.text: Policies like no, on-failure, always and unless-stopped control daemon-level restarts; Kubernetes uses pod restartPolicy and controllers. docker run --restart unless-stopped nginx docker update --restart on-failure:5 web Interview tip: Use on-failure with a cap for crash loops.

questions.q: How do you copy files in and out of containers and when is it appropriate?
questions.text: docker cp works for debugging; production data should use volumes or object storage, not manual copies. docker cp web:/var/log/app.log ./app.log kubectl cp ns/pod:/tmp/dump ./dump Interview tip: Treat container filesystems as disposable.

questions.q: How do you choose a base image: Alpine, Debian slim, distroless or scratch?
questions.text: Balance size, compatibility, debuggability and attack surface. Alpine uses musl, distroless has no shell, scratch is empty for static binaries. FROM gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot FROM python:3.12-slim Interview tip: Smaller is not always better if it breaks libc compatibility.

questions.q: How do you make image builds reproducible?
questions.text: Pin base images by digest, pin package versions, use lock files, avoid latest and timestamps, and build in a controlled environment. FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest> pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.lock Interview tip: latest is not a version.

questions.q: How do you reduce image size without breaking the application?
questions.text: Multi-stage builds, slim bases, combined RUN steps with cleanup, dockerignore, and removing build tools and caches. RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* docker history --no-trunc img Interview tip: Cleanup must be in the same layer.

questions.q: What is an image digest versus a tag, and why does it matter for deployments?
questions.text: A tag is a movable label; a digest is the immutable content hash. Deploy by digest for exact, verifiable artifacts. docker pull nginx@sha256:... docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' app:1.4 Interview tip: Tags can be overwritten.

questions.q: How do you run containers as non-root and why does it matter?
questions.text: Create a user in the image, set USER, drop capabilities and, in Kubernetes, set runAsNonRoot and a read-only root filesystem. RUN adduser --system --uid 10001 app USER 10001 securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true readOnlyRootFilesystem: true Interview tip: Use a numeric UID.

questions.q: What are Linux namespaces and cgroups, and how do containers use them?
questions.text: Namespaces isolate what a process sees; cgroups limit what it can use. A container is a process with both applied. lsns cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash Interview tip: No hypervisor is involved.

questions.q: What is the difference between runc, containerd, CRI-O and Docker?
questions.text: runc is the low-level OCI runtime; containerd and CRI-O are higher-level runtimes managing images and lifecycle; Docker adds a developer-friendly engine on top. crictl ps ctr -n k8s.io containers list Interview tip: Kubernetes talks CRI, not Docker.

questions.q: How do you investigate a container killed by OOM, and how do you set memory limits properly?
questions.text: Check exit code 137 and OOMKilled in status, review memory metrics, then size requests and limits from observed usage with headroom. kubectl describe pod p | grep -A5 'Last State' dmesg | grep -i 'killed process' Interview tip: Heap limits must sit below container limits.

questions.q: How does CPU limiting work in containers and why can it cause latency?
questions.text: CPU limits use CFS quota per period; hitting the quota throttles the process even when the node has idle CPU. cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]) Interview tip: Throttling hurts tail latency.

questions.q: What is the container lifecycle from image pull to termination in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Schedule, pull image, create sandbox and network, run init containers, start containers with probes, serve traffic, then preStop and SIGTERM on termination. kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp kubectl describe pod p Interview tip: Events narrate each phase.

questions.q: How does Docker's default bridge network provide NAT and DNS, and how do user-defined bridges differ?
questions.text: The default bridge uses iptables NAT and no name resolution between containers; user-defined bridges add automatic DNS and better isolation. docker network create app-net docker run --network app-net --name db postgres iptables -t nat -L -n Interview tip: Use user-defined networks.

questions.q: How do you debug DNS problems inside a container or pod?
questions.text: Check resolv.conf, test lookups with nslookup or dig, review CoreDNS logs and ndots behaviour, and test search domains. cat /etc/resolv.conf nslookup kubernetes.default kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Interview tip: ndots:5 multiplies queries.

questions.q: What is the difference between ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and Ingress?
questions.text: ClusterIP is internal; NodePort exposes on each node; LoadBalancer provisions a cloud LB; Ingress routes HTTP by host and path through a controller. kubectl expose deploy web --port 80 --type ClusterIP kubectl get ingress Interview tip: One Ingress can front many services.

questions.q: How does kube-proxy implement Services, and what are iptables versus IPVS modes?
questions.text: kube-proxy programs node rules that translate service virtual IPs to pod endpoints; iptables mode is rule-chain based, IPVS uses kernel load balancing with better scale. iptables-save | grep KUBE-SVC ipvsadm -Ln Interview tip: Services have no process listening on the VIP.

questions.q: How does service discovery work in Docker Compose and Kubernetes, and what are the pitfalls of caching DNS?
questions.text: Both give services DNS names; clients that cache resolved IPs forever can miss changes after pods are replaced. curl http://db:5432 curl http://orders.shop.svc.cluster.local Interview tip: Honour DNS TTL in your client.

questions.q: What is the difference between PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass?
questions.text: A PV is storage; a PVC is a request for it; a StorageClass defines how to dynamically provision PVs. kubectl get pv,pvc,sc kubectl describe pvc data-0 Interview tip: Reclaim policy decides what happens on delete.

questions.q: What are the access modes ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany and ReadWriteOncePod?
questions.text: They define how many nodes or pods can mount a volume and with what permission; block disks are usually RWO, shared file systems support RWX. accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] kubectl get pvc -o wide Interview tip: RWO limits to one node, not one pod.

questions.q: How do you handle a full volume on a running stateful workload?
questions.text: Identify what consumes space, free it safely or expand the PVC online if the class allows, and add alerts and retention. kubectl exec pod -- df -h kubectl patch pvc data-0 -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"200Gi"}}}}' Interview tip: Check allowVolumeExpansion first.

questions.q: How do volume snapshots and backups work for containerised stateful workloads?
questions.text: CSI snapshots capture a point-in-time copy of a volume; application-consistent backups also need quiescing or native tools. kubectl get volumesnapshot velero backup create daily --include-namespaces prod Interview tip: Test restores regularly.

questions.q: What are emptyDir and ephemeral volumes, and when should containers use them?
questions.text: emptyDir is scratch space tied to the pod lifetime, optionally memory-backed; use it for caches and temporary files, not persistent data. volumes: - name: tmp emptyDir: medium: Memory sizeLimit: 256Mi Interview tip: Set sizeLimit to avoid node pressure.

questions.q: How do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control a rolling update?
questions.text: maxSurge sets how many extra pods can be created above desired; maxUnavailable sets how many may be unavailable; together they set rollout speed and capacity. strategy: rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 25% maxUnavailable: 0 Interview tip: maxUnavailable 0 keeps full capacity.

questions.q: How do you achieve graceful shutdown so rolling updates drop no requests?
questions.text: Handle SIGTERM, fail readiness first, delay with preStop to allow endpoint propagation, then drain connections within the grace period. lifecycle: preStop: exec: command: ["sleep","10"] terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 Interview tip: Endpoint removal is asynchronous.

questions.q: What are Kubernetes Jobs and CronJobs, and what are their failure modes?
questions.text: Jobs run to completion with retries; CronJobs create Jobs on a schedule. Watch concurrency policy, backoff limit, deadlines and missed schedules. kubectl create job --from=cronjob/backup manual-1 concurrencyPolicy: Forbid backoffLimit: 3 Interview tip: Make job work idempotent.

questions.q: How do you use resource requests, limits and QoS classes to protect critical pods?
questions.text: Requests drive scheduling; limits cap usage. QoS class Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort decides eviction order under node pressure. kubectl get pod p -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}' kubectl top pods Interview tip: Equal requests and limits give Guaranteed.

questions.q: What is the horizontal pod autoscaler and what can make it behave badly?
questions.text: HPA adjusts replicas based on metrics like CPU or custom metrics; problems include missing requests, slow metrics, flapping and dependency limits. kubectl autoscale deploy web --cpu-percent=60 --min=3 --max=20 kubectl describe hpa web Interview tip: CPU percent is relative to requests.

questions.q: How do you deploy a stateful database in containers, and when should you not?
questions.text: Use StatefulSets with persistent volumes, anti-affinity, backups and an operator, but consider managed services for critical data. kubectl get sts,pvc topologySpreadConstraints: - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone Interview tip: Operators encode operational knowledge.

questions.q: What are Linux capabilities and seccomp, and how do you harden a container with them?
questions.text: Capabilities split root privileges into units; seccomp filters system calls. Drop all capabilities, add back only what is needed, and use the runtime default seccomp profile. securityContext: capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault capsh --print Interview tip: Drop ALL, then add.

questions.q: What are Pod Security Standards and admission controls, and how do you roll them out?
questions.text: Privileged, baseline and restricted profiles enforced per namespace via labels; roll out in audit and warn modes before enforce. kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted Interview tip: Audit first, then enforce.

questions.q: How do you detect and respond to a compromised container in a cluster?
questions.text: Use runtime detection, audit logs and network telemetry; isolate the pod, preserve evidence, rotate credentials and rebuild from a clean image. kubectl label pod p quarantine=true --overwrite kubectl get events -A | grep -i exec Interview tip: Isolate, then investigate.

questions.q: How do Kubernetes RBAC and service accounts apply to workloads, and what are common mistakes?
questions.text: Roles grant verbs on resources; bindings attach them to users or service accounts. Avoid cluster-admin, wildcard rules and default service account tokens. kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:app:web automountServiceAccountToken: false Interview tip: Test permissions with can-i.

questions.q: How do you scan and control third-party container images in an organisation?
questions.text: Use an approved internal registry, mirror and scan upstream images, enforce signatures and allowlists at admission, and rebuild regularly. trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed app:1.4 cosign verify --key cosign.pub reg/app@sha256:... Interview tip: Approve sources, not just images.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Deployment, ReplicaSet and Pod, and how does a rollout use them?
questions.text: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage Pods; each rollout creates a new ReplicaSet and scales old ones down. kubectl get rs -l app=web kubectl rollout history deploy/web Interview tip: Never edit ReplicaSets directly.

questions.q: How does the scheduler decide where to place a pod, and how do affinity, taints and tolerations influence it?
questions.text: It filters nodes by constraints then scores the rest; node affinity attracts, taints repel, anti-affinity and spread constraints distribute replicas. kubectl describe pod p | grep -A10 Events tolerations: - key: dedicated operator: Equal value: gpu effect: NoSchedule Interview tip: FailedScheduling events state the reason.

questions.q: What are ConfigMaps and Secrets, and what are the security limits of Kubernetes Secrets?
questions.text: Both inject configuration; Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted by default, so enable encryption at rest, restrict RBAC and prefer external secret managers. kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=... kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d Interview tip: Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

questions.q: How do namespaces, ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges support multi-tenancy?
questions.text: Namespaces separate teams; quotas cap aggregate resources; limit ranges set defaults and bounds per container. kubectl create quota team-a --hard=cpu=20,memory=64Gi,pods=100 -n team-a kubectl describe limitrange -n team-a Interview tip: Namespaces are not a security boundary alone.

questions.q: What is a Kubernetes operator or CRD and how is it different from a Helm chart?
questions.text: A CRD adds a new resource type; an operator is a controller that manages it continuously. Helm templates and installs manifests but does not run ongoing logic. kubectl get crd helm template web ./chart | kubectl diff -f - Interview tip: Helm installs; operators operate.

questions.q: How do you scan, sign and promote container images in a pipeline?
questions.text: Build once, scan, sign the digest, push to a registry, and promote the same digest across environments, verifying at admission. trivy image app@sha256:... cosign sign app@sha256:... crane copy dev/app@sha256:... prod/app@sha256:... Interview tip: Promote by digest.

questions.q: How do you run integration tests with containers in CI using Testcontainers or Compose?
questions.text: Start real dependencies in disposable containers, wait for readiness, run tests, and tear down. docker compose up -d --wait docker compose down -v Interview tip: Wait for health, not just start.

questions.q: How do you do multi-architecture image builds (amd64 and arm64)?
questions.text: Use buildx with QEMU emulation or native builders to produce a manifest list so each platform pulls the right image. docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t reg/app:1.4 --push . docker buildx imagetools inspect reg/app:1.4 Interview tip: Native builders beat emulation for speed.

questions.q: How do you manage image tagging and retention policies in a registry?
questions.text: Tag immutably with commit SHA and semantic versions, protect release tags, and expire old untagged or unused images. gcloud artifacts repositories set-cleanup-policies repo --policy=policy.json aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name app --lifecycle-policy-text file://policy.json Interview tip: Enable tag immutability.

questions.q: How do you deploy the same image to multiple environments with different configuration using Helm or Kustomize?
questions.text: Keep the chart or base generic and supply per-environment values or overlays; promote only the image reference and config changes via Git. helm upgrade --install web ./chart -f values/prod.yaml --set image.digest=sha256:... kubectl apply -k overlays/prod Interview tip: Config differences should be small and visible.

questions.q: How do you design container logging so logs survive pod restarts and remain searchable?
questions.text: Write to stdout and stderr in structured form; a node agent ships them to a central store with metadata, retention and rotation. kubectl logs pod --previous docker run --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 img Interview tip: Do not write log files inside containers.

questions.q: Which container and Kubernetes metrics should you alert on, and which only on dashboards?
questions.text: Alert on symptoms such as errors, latency and saturation risks; keep resource detail like per-container CPU on dashboards. kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total container_memory_working_set_bytes / kube_pod_container_resource_limits Interview tip: Page on user impact.

questions.q: How do you use kubectl debug and ephemeral containers to troubleshoot a running pod?
questions.text: Attach a temporary container with debugging tools to an existing pod's namespaces, without restarting or changing the image. kubectl debug -it pod/web --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app kubectl debug node/n1 -it --image=busybox Interview tip: Works for distroless images.

questions.q: How do you set up readiness, liveness and startup probes correctly to avoid restart storms?
questions.text: Startup probe protects slow starts, readiness controls traffic, liveness restarts only deadlocked processes; do not check dependencies in liveness. startupProbe: httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080} failureThreshold: 30 periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: httpGet: {path: /live, port: 8080} Interview tip: Liveness should be cheap and local.

questions.q: How do you trace a request across containers and correlate traces with logs and metrics?
questions.text: Propagate trace context headers, instrument with OpenTelemetry, put trace IDs in logs, and use exemplars to link metrics to traces. traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-01 OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://collector:4317 Interview tip: Trace ID in every log line.

guides.title: Database Performance Interview Guide (97 Q&A) — InterviewHub

questions.q: What is a database index and how does a B-tree index work internally?
questions.text: An index is a separate data structure that allows the database engine to find rows without scanning every row in the table. Without an index, every query does a full sequential scan — O(n). With a B-tree index, lookups are O(log n). B-tree mechanics B-tree: balanced tree where each node holds sorted keys + pointers to children Leaf nodes: hold actual index entries → pointers to heap (table) rows Height: typically 3-4 levels for millions of rows (log base 100 of 10M ≈ 3.5) -- PostgreSQL: inspect index usage SELECT schemaname, tablename, indexname, idx_scan, idx_tup_read FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan; B-tree supports: equality (=), range (<, >, BETWEEN), ORDER BY, IS NULL. It does NOT efficiently support: leading wildcard LIKE ('%foo'), full-text search, geometric queries, or array containment. For those, use specialized index types: GIN (full-text, arrays), GiST (geometric, range types), BRIN (large sequential tables like timestamps), Hash (equality-only, tiny). Interview tip: Always explain the trade-off — indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update all indexes on that table). Every additional index has a write-amplification cost. In write-heavy tables, too many indexes hurt overall throughput.

questions.q: When does a query NOT use an index even though one exists — what are the common pitfalls?
questions.text: -- Function wrapping prevents index use: WHERE UPPER(email) = 'FOO@BAR.COM' -- scans table (function on column) WHERE email = UPPER('foo@bar.com') -- uses index (function on literal) -- Type mismatch: WHERE user_id = '123' -- user_id is INT, implicit cast kills index -- Leading wildcard: WHERE name LIKE '%smith' -- full scan (no prefix to match in B-tree) WHERE name LIKE 'smith%' -- uses index (prefix match) -- Low cardinality: planner may prefer seq scan if index selectivity is poor WHERE status = 'active' -- if 90% of rows are 'active', seq scan wins The planner may also skip an index if: the table is small (sequential scan is faster for tiny tables), statistics are stale (ANALYZE hasn't run), or the cost estimate is wrong (adjust random_page_cost for SSD). Force index use for debugging with SET enable_seqscan = off (PostgreSQL) or FORCE INDEX (MySQL) — but never use these in production as permanent fixes. Implicit casts: Passing a string where an integer is expected causes a cast on every row — the index is useless. Always match parameter type to column type. In ORMs, inspect the generated SQL to catch type mismatches.

questions.q: What is a composite index — how does column order affect its usefulness?
questions.text: CREATE INDEX idx_user_status ON orders (user_id, status, created_at); -- This index supports these queries efficiently: WHERE user_id = 5 -- uses index (leftmost prefix) WHERE user_id = 5 AND status = 'shipped' -- uses index WHERE user_id = 5 AND status = 'shipped' AND created_at > '2024-01-01' -- full use -- These are NOT efficiently supported: WHERE status = 'shipped' -- skips leftmost column, full scan WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' -- skips two leftmost columns The leftmost prefix rule: a composite index on (A, B, C) can be used for queries filtering on A, A+B, or A+B+C — but not B alone or C alone. Column order rule: put equality columns first, then range columns last (range condition stops further index use for subsequent columns). Put the most selective column first within the equality group to minimize the rows scanned. Design heuristic: For a query WHERE user_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at , the ideal index is (user_id, status, created_at) — the ORDER BY is satisfied by the index, eliminating a sort step. This pattern (equality + range/sort) is one of the most common index optimization patterns.

questions.q: What is an index covering query — what is a covering index?
questions.text: -- Without covering index: index lookup → heap fetch for each row SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com'; -- index on email, heap fetch for name -- With covering index: no heap fetch needed CREATE INDEX idx_email_name ON users (email) INCLUDE (name); -- PostgreSQL 11+ CREATE INDEX idx_email_name ON users (email, name); -- MySQL covering index -- EXPLAIN shows "Index Only Scan" in PostgreSQL if covered EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com'; A covering index contains all columns needed by the query — the database never needs to go back to the heap (table) for additional data. This eliminates random I/O for heap fetches, which is often the most expensive part of an index lookup. In PostgreSQL, use INCLUDE to add non-key columns to the index without affecting sort order. In MySQL, all columns in the SELECT and WHERE must be in the index for an Index Only Scan (key-only lookup). When to use: Covering indexes are most valuable for high-frequency, read-heavy queries on large tables. The trade-off is larger index size and slower writes. Profile first — don't preemptively add INCLUDE columns to every index.

questions.q: What is index bloat — how do you detect and fix it?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: check index bloat SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'i' ORDER BY pg_relation_size(oid) DESC LIMIT 20; -- Extension for detailed bloat estimate: SELECT * FROM pgstattuple('idx_name'); -- requires pgstattuple extension -- Fix: rebuild the index (non-blocking in PG 12+) REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_name; -- MySQL: check index fragmentation SELECT TABLE_NAME, DATA_FREE FROM information_schema.TABLES WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'mydb'; OPTIMIZE TABLE tablename; -- rebuilds and defragments (locks table in older MySQL) Index bloat occurs when deleted/updated rows leave dead entries in the index. B-tree pages become sparse — more disk reads per lookup, more cache pressure. In PostgreSQL, VACUUM reclaims heap space but index bloat accumulates over time and requires REINDEX. Triggers for rebuilding: index is significantly larger than it should be, slow queries despite the index being used, or after bulk deletes/updates of a large fraction of the table. REINDEX vs REINDEX CONCURRENTLY: Plain REINDEX locks the table — do not use in production. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL 12+) builds a new index alongside the old one and swaps atomically. Takes 2x space temporarily but causes zero downtime.

questions.q: How do you read and interpret a query execution plan (EXPLAIN ANALYZE)?
questions.text: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT) SELECT ...; -- PostgreSQL full analysis EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON SELECT ...; -- MySQL (8.0+) -- Key nodes to understand (PostgreSQL): Seq Scan -- full table scan (look for large row_count × cost) Index Scan -- uses index, then fetches heap rows Index Only Scan -- covers query without heap fetch (best case) Bitmap Heap Scan -- combines multiple indexes, batches heap fetches Hash Join -- builds hash table on smaller relation (good for large joins) Nested Loop -- for each outer row, probe inner (good when inner is small/indexed) Merge Join -- both sides sorted, merge in order (good for large sorted relations) Key metrics: actual rows vs estimated rows (big discrepancy = stale statistics → run ANALYZE), actual time per node (find the expensive node), Buffers hit vs read (cache hit rate — more hits = better), and loops × time (nested loop with many loops can be very expensive). The plan reads bottom-up — the innermost node executes first. Rows estimate vs actual: If estimated rows = 1 but actual rows = 100,000, the planner underestimated selectivity and may have chosen a bad join order or wrong index. Fix: ANALYZE tablename to refresh statistics, or increase default_statistics_target for skewed columns.

questions.q: What is the N+1 query problem — how do you detect and fix it?
questions.text: -- N+1 pattern: 1 query to get list + N queries to get related data SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 100; -- 1 query SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1; -- query per order (N=100) SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 2; -- ... repeated 100 times -- Fix: JOIN or IN clause SELECT o.*, u.name FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id LIMIT 100; -- Or: batch load with IN SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (1,2,3,...,100); -- 1 query for all users -- Detection in PostgreSQL: log slow queries SET log_min_duration_statement = 10; -- log queries taking > 10ms N+1 queries are invisible in development (small datasets) but catastrophic in production (thousands of records). An ORM loading relationships lazily is the primary cause. Detection: pg_stat_statements (shows query frequency — same query called 10,000 times/minute), slow query log, or APM tools showing many identical fast queries. Fix at the ORM level: eager loading (Hibernate's JOIN FETCH, Rails' includes, Sequelize's include). DataLoader pattern: For GraphQL APIs, use DataLoader to batch and deduplicate queries within a single request — collects all IDs needed, fires one IN query. This solves N+1 at the API layer without changing the data model.

questions.q: A query was fast last week and is now slow — what do you investigate?
questions.text: -- Step 1: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare to expected plan EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...; -- Step 2: Check if statistics are stale SELECT last_analyze, last_autoanalyze, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'tablename'; ANALYZE tablename; -- refresh statistics manually -- Step 3: Check data growth SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('tablename')); SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tablename; -- has table grown 10x? -- Step 4: Check if index is being used (or was dropped) SELECT * FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'tablename'; Common causes: table grew past the threshold where the planner switches from index scan to seq scan (statistics are stale, planner doesn't know it grew), an index was accidentally dropped during a migration, autovacuum is behind and dead tuple bloat is skewing statistics, data distribution changed (a value that was rare is now 50% of rows — index no longer selective), or a schema migration changed a column type breaking index compatibility. Plan regression after deploy: A schema migration (adding a column, changing a type, adding a constraint) triggers a statistics reset. The planner may choose a different plan for a few minutes until autovacuum/autoanalyze catches up. This causes a classic "deploy → slow queries → recovers on its own in 5 minutes" pattern.

questions.q: What are window functions and when do they outperform subqueries or self-joins?
questions.text: -- Rank users by order count per region — window function SELECT user_id, region, order_count, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY order_count DESC) AS rank FROM user_stats; -- Running total SELECT date, revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative FROM daily_revenue; -- Lag/Lead: compare to previous row SELECT date, revenue, LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS prev_day_revenue FROM daily_revenue; Window functions operate over a "window" of rows related to the current row without collapsing them (unlike GROUP BY). They are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING but before ORDER BY and LIMIT. Performance advantage: the database scans the result set once and computes the window in-memory — a self-join or correlated subquery to achieve the same result would require multiple scans. Common functions: RANK, DENSE_RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTILE, SUM/AVG/COUNT with OVER. Frame specification matters: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (running total) vs ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (7-day rolling average). Getting the frame wrong produces silently incorrect results — always verify with sample data.

questions.q: How do you optimize a slow JOIN query — what strategies do you apply?
questions.text: -- Ensure join columns are indexed on both sides: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id); -- foreign key columns often missing indexes -- Filter early — push WHERE conditions to reduce join input size: -- Bad: join everything then filter SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE o.status = 'active'; -- Better (if planner doesn't auto-push): use subquery to pre-filter SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'active') o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id; -- Check join order: smaller result set as outer loop in nested loop join SET join_collapse_limit = 1; -- disable PostgreSQL join reorder (for testing only) Join optimization checklist: index join columns (especially FK columns — databases don't auto-create FK indexes), ensure statistics are fresh (planner needs accurate row counts for join order), avoid functions on join columns, avoid SELECT * (retrieve only needed columns to reduce data movement), and consider materialized CTEs for complex multi-step transformations (reused intermediate results). For very complex multi-table joins, break into steps using temp tables or CTEs with MATERIALIZED hint. Join algorithm choice: Hash Join is best for large unsorted datasets. Nested Loop is best when the inner table is small or well-indexed. Merge Join requires both sides sorted. If the planner picks the wrong algorithm, stale statistics are usually the cause.

questions.q: What is VACUUM in PostgreSQL — why is it critical for performance?
questions.text: -- Check autovacuum status per table: SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 20; -- Manual vacuum (non-blocking): VACUUM tablename; -- Full vacuum (rewrites, reclaims disk — locks table): VACUUM FULL tablename; -- never in production without planning -- Check transaction ID wraparound risk: SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY age DESC; PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) — UPDATE and DELETE create new row versions, leaving old "dead tuples" in place. VACUUM reclaims this space for reuse. Without regular vacuuming: table bloat (dead tuples waste disk and slow sequential scans), statistics become inaccurate (planner makes bad decisions), and transaction ID wraparound risk grows (a PostgreSQL-specific catastrophic failure that forces the DB into read-only mode to prevent data corruption). Transaction ID wraparound: PostgreSQL uses 32-bit transaction IDs. When age approaches 2 billion, PostgreSQL forces a VACUUM FREEZE. If you ignore autovacuum and this limit is exceeded, the DB shuts down in read-only mode. Monitor age(datfrozenxid) and alert above 1.5 billion. This has caused real production outages.

questions.q: How do you identify and kill long-running queries in PostgreSQL?
questions.text: -- Find long-running queries: SELECT pid, now() - pg_stat_activity.query_start AS duration, query, state FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state != 'idle' AND query_start -- Find blocking locks: SELECT blocked.pid, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, blocked.query AS blocked_query, blocking.query AS blocking_query FROM pg_stat_activity blocked JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) > 0; -- Cancel query (graceful): SELECT pg_cancel_backend(pid); -- Kill connection (immediate): SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid); Long-running queries hold locks that block other queries. An idle transaction (BEGIN without COMMIT/ROLLBACK) is especially dangerous — it holds locks indefinitely even though the query is done. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min' to auto-terminate idle-in-transaction sessions. Set statement_timeout per role to prevent runaway queries. Always investigate before terminating — a long-running VACUUM ANALYZE is legitimate. Lock hierarchy: ALTER TABLE takes an AccessExclusiveLock — it blocks all reads and writes. Plan schema migrations carefully: use tools like pg_repack or pgroll for zero-downtime migrations that avoid heavy locking. Never run ALTER TABLE in production during peak hours.

questions.q: What is pg_stat_statements — how do you use it to find the worst queries?
questions.text: -- Enable (requires postgresql.conf restart): shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements' CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements; -- Top 10 queries by total time: SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time/1000 AS total_sec, mean_exec_time AS avg_ms, rows FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10; -- Top 10 by average latency (worst per-call performance): SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time AS avg_ms FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE calls > 100 ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10; -- Reset stats: SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset(); pg_stat_statements normalizes queries (replaces literals with $1, $2 placeholders) and tracks total execution time, call count, rows, shared blocks hit/read, and I/O timing. Use it to find: the query with highest total time (highest impact to optimize), queries called millions of times with even small latency (N+1 detection), and queries with low cache hit rate (high blks_read vs blks_hit — missing from shared_buffers). This is the first tool to reach for during a performance investigation. Production standard: Always have pg_stat_statements enabled. The overhead is minimal (<5% CPU) and the visibility is invaluable. Cloud SQL, RDS, and Cloud Spanner all have equivalent query insights dashboards built on the same principle.

questions.q: How do you tune PostgreSQL memory settings — what are the key parameters?
questions.text: shared_buffers = 25% of RAM # PostgreSQL's own page cache effective_cache_size = 75% of RAM # hints to planner about OS cache work_mem = 4MB–256MB # per-sort / per-hash operation maintenance_work_mem = 256MB–2GB # for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE wal_buffers = 64MB # WAL write buffer (auto-tuned in PG 12+) -- Check buffer hit rate (should be > 99%): SELECT sum(blks_hit)*100.0 / (sum(blks_hit)+sum(blks_read)) AS cache_hit_rate FROM pg_stat_database; work_mem is the most commonly misunderstood parameter. It's allocated per sort/hash operation per query — a complex query with multiple sort nodes and 100 parallel connections can use work_mem × nodes × connections of RAM simultaneously. Setting it too high causes OOM; too low causes disk sorts (look for "Disk: true" in EXPLAIN output). Set a low default and use SET work_mem = '256MB' per session for analytics queries. shared_buffers should be 25% of RAM for dedicated PostgreSQL hosts. work_mem × connections math: 100 connections × 10 sort nodes × 256MB work_mem = 256GB potential peak RAM. Always calculate the worst-case memory footprint before setting work_mem globally high.

questions.q: How does the InnoDB buffer pool work — how do you tune it?
questions.text: -- Check buffer pool hit rate (should be > 99%): SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_buffer_pool_%'; -- Calculate hit rate: SELECT (1 - (Innodb_buffer_pool_reads / Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests)) * 100 AS hit_rate; -- Set buffer pool size (my.cnf): innodb_buffer_pool_size = 70-80% of RAM # for dedicated MySQL server innodb_buffer_pool_instances = 8 # reduce mutex contention (1 per GB) -- Warm up buffer pool after restart: innodb_buffer_pool_dump_at_shutdown = ON innodb_buffer_pool_load_at_startup = ON InnoDB buffer pool is MySQL's combined page cache and index cache — it's the most impactful single parameter for MySQL performance. It caches both data pages and index pages. A warm buffer pool serves reads from memory; a cold pool (after restart) has high I/O until pages are loaded. Enable dump/load to persist the "hot set" across restarts, dramatically reducing the post-restart performance dip. Multiple instances: With a large buffer pool (> 8GB), split into 8 instances ( innodb_buffer_pool_instances=8 ). Each instance has its own mutex, reducing lock contention for concurrent access. Without this, a single mutex on a 64GB buffer pool becomes a bottleneck.

questions.q: What is the MySQL slow query log — how do you use it and what do you look for?
questions.text: -- Enable slow query log: slow_query_log = ON slow_query_log_file = /var/log/mysql/slow.log long_query_time = 1 # log queries > 1 second log_queries_not_using_indexes = ON # catch full scans regardless of time -- Analyze with mysqldumpslow: mysqldumpslow -s t -t 10 /var/log/mysql/slow.log # top 10 by total time mysqldumpslow -s c -t 10 /var/log/mysql/slow.log # top 10 by count -- Or with pt-query-digest (more detailed): pt-query-digest /var/log/mysql/slow.log | head -100 The slow query log captures queries exceeding long_query_time . Enable log_queries_not_using_indexes to catch full scans even on fast small tables — they will degrade as data grows. Use pt-query-digest from Percona Toolkit for structured analysis: fingerprinted query patterns, sorted by total execution time, with response time distribution. This is the equivalent of PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements but file-based. Performance Schema: MySQL 5.6+ has Performance Schema — enables events_statements_summary_by_digest for real-time query analytics without a log file. Use this in production for live query profiling without the disk I/O overhead of the slow log.

questions.q: What is MySQL replication lag — how do you detect and reduce it?
questions.text: -- Check replication lag on replica: SHOW SLAVE STATUSG -- "Seconds_Behind_Master" field SHOW REPLICA STATUSG -- MySQL 8.0+ syntax -- Enable parallel replication (MySQL 5.7+): replica_parallel_workers = 8 # number of parallel apply threads replica_parallel_type = LOGICAL_CLOCK # dependency-based parallelism -- Reduce binlog event size: binlog_row_image = MINIMAL # only log changed columns, not full row Replication lag sources: single-threaded replica applying multi-threaded primary writes (solve with parallel replication), long-running transactions on primary blocking replica, large bulk operations, or network latency between primary and replica. Monitor Seconds_Behind_Master but also compare GTID positions for more accurate lag measurement. In cloud: Cloud SQL and RDS replicas have built-in parallel apply. Reading stale data: If your application reads from a replica, it may read data that hasn't been replicated yet. Implement read-your-writes consistency by routing writes AND the subsequent reads for the same user session to the primary (or wait for replica to catch up using WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET).

questions.q: What is connection pooling — why is it essential for database performance?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: each connection is a forked process (~5-10MB RAM each) -- 1000 direct connections = 5-10GB RAM overhead on the DB server -- PgBouncer config (pgbouncer.ini): pool_mode = transaction # most efficient — connection returned after each transaction max_client_conn = 10000 # clients can connect to PgBouncer default_pool_size = 25 # actual connections to PostgreSQL -- Check PgBouncer stats: psql -p 6432 pgbouncer -c "SHOW POOLS;" psql -p 6432 pgbouncer -c "SHOW STATS;" PostgreSQL opens a new OS process per connection — expensive at scale. A 500-connection PostgreSQL instance with 8 cores is wasting 492 connections waiting (CPU can only run 8 at once). PgBouncer multiplexes thousands of application connections onto a small pool of actual DB connections. Pool modes: session (connection held for full session), transaction (returned after each transaction — most efficient), statement (returned after each statement — incompatible with multi-statement transactions). Cloud SQL / RDS: Cloud SQL has built-in connection pooling via the Auth Proxy. For high-concurrency apps, still use PgBouncer in front — Cloud SQL's max_connections is often the bottleneck, not the Auth Proxy. Run PgBouncer as a sidecar in Kubernetes or as a dedicated service.

questions.q: Database is running out of connections — how do you diagnose and fix the connection exhaustion?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: check current connections SELECT count(*), state, wait_event_type, wait_event FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state, wait_event_type, wait_event ORDER BY count DESC; SELECT setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'max_connections'; -- Find connections by application: SELECT application_name, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY application_name ORDER BY count DESC; -- MySQL: SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected'; SHOW PROCESSLIST; -- active queries + sleeping connections Root causes: application not returning connections to pool (connection leak — missing finally/close() blocks), pool size set too large (each app instance claims N connections, N × pods exceeds max_connections), connection pool not configured (every request opens a new connection), or idle connections not timed out (sleeping connections accumulating). Fix immediately: restart the leaking service, reduce pool size, or increase max_connections temporarily. Fix permanently: add connection pooling layer (PgBouncer), fix the connection leak in code, set idle connection timeouts.
