Kubernetes scale-out: When HPA scales from 5 to 50 pods, a pool of 20 connections per pod = 1000 connections to PostgreSQL. Plan for max_pod_replicas × pool_size when sizing PostgreSQL max_connections. PgBouncer decouples this — all 50 pods connect to PgBouncer's 1000-connection capacity, which maps to 25 real DB connections.

questions.q: What is a database deadlock — how do you detect, prevent, and recover from it?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL deadlock detection (automatic, logged): tail -f /var/log/postgresql/postgresql.log | grep deadlock -- Or check pg_locks for current lock waits: SELECT l.pid, l.locktype, l.relation::regclass, l.mode, l.granted FROM pg_locks l WHERE NOT l.granted; -- MySQL: show last deadlock SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUSG -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section -- Prevention: always acquire locks in the same order -- Transaction 1: lock table A, then table B -- Transaction 2: lock table A, then table B (not B then A) A deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs — they wait forever. PostgreSQL detects deadlocks automatically and kills one transaction (the victim) with an error. MySQL InnoDB does the same. Both log the deadlock details. Prevention: acquire locks in a consistent global order across all transactions, keep transactions short (reduce lock hold time), and use SELECT FOR UPDATE to explicitly lock rows in the order you'll update them. Application handling: Deadlock victims receive an error (error code 40P01 in PostgreSQL). Application code MUST handle this with retry logic — deadlocks are normal under high concurrency. A deadlock-prone query that isn't retried will surface as a user-visible error under load.

questions.q: What is WAL in PostgreSQL — how does WAL enable replication and point-in-time recovery?
questions.text: -- WAL (Write-Ahead Log): all changes written to WAL before modifying data pages -- Check WAL directory size: SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) FROM pg_ls_waldir(); -- WAL archiving (for PITR): archive_mode = on archive_command = 'gsutil cp %p gs://my-wal-archive/%f' # copy WAL to GCS -- Streaming replication settings: wal_level = replica # minimum for replication max_wal_senders = 10 # max replica connections wal_keep_size = 1GB # keep WAL on primary for slow replicas WAL ensures durability (data is never lost if fsync is on) and enables both streaming replication (replica receives WAL stream continuously) and PITR (replay archived WAL segments to any point in time). Replicas in streaming replication continuously apply WAL — they are always slightly behind the primary (replication lag). If a replica falls too far behind and the primary discards WAL it hasn't received, the replica must be rebuilt from a base backup. PITR for Cloud SQL: Cloud SQL automatically archives WAL to GCS. Enable PITR in Cloud SQL config — it retains 7 days of WAL by default. For compliance workloads, this is your RTO/RPO safety net: restore to any second within the retention window.

questions.q: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication — when do you choose each?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: configure synchronous replication synchronous_standby_names = 'replica1' # in postgresql.conf -- Per transaction override: SET synchronous_commit = local; # don't wait for replica (lower durability) SET synchronous_commit = remote_write; # wait until replica has WAL in OS buffer SET synchronous_commit = on; # wait until replica has WAL fsynced (full sync) -- Check replication lag in bytes: SELECT client_addr, state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn, (sent_lsn - replay_lsn) AS lag_bytes FROM pg_stat_replication; Async replication: primary commits as soon as WAL is locally fsynced. Replica applies WAL asynchronously. Pros: zero write latency overhead. Cons: data loss risk on primary failure (replica may be seconds behind). Sync replication: primary waits for replica to acknowledge WAL before returning to client. Pros: zero data loss (RPO=0). Cons: every write waits for a network round-trip to the replica — adds latency. Use sync for financial transactions and compliance workloads; async for high-throughput workloads that can tolerate seconds of potential data loss. Quorum commit: PostgreSQL supports ANY 1 (replica1, replica2) — commit acknowledged when any 1 of 2 replicas confirm. This combines sync durability with high availability — if one replica goes down, the other still satisfies the quorum.

questions.q: A read replica is significantly lagging — what are the causes and how do you fix it?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: check replication lag SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replication_lag; -- Check if replica is in recovery: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(); -- Check for replication slot bloat (replica not consuming WAL): SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS lag FROM pg_replication_slots; -- MySQL: check replica threads SHOW REPLICA STATUSG -- check SQL_Delay, Seconds_Behind_Source Lag causes: single-threaded WAL apply unable to keep up with parallel primary writes (enable parallel apply), long-running transactions on replica blocking WAL application, heavy read queries on the replica consuming I/O needed for WAL apply (dedicated replica for analytics vs serving reads), or replication slot not being consumed (slot accumulates WAL — can fill disk on primary). A replication slot with a lagging consumer is a disk bomb — always set max_slot_wal_keep_size as a safety limit. Replication slot danger: An inactive replication slot causes the primary to retain ALL WAL since the slot's last confirmed LSN. If a logical replication consumer (like Debezium CDC) goes down for hours, the primary's /pg_wal directory can fill the disk, causing a primary outage. Monitor slot lag closely.

questions.q: How does schema design impact database performance — what are the key design decisions?
questions.text: -- Choose appropriate data types (smaller = faster): INT (4 bytes) vs BIGINT (8 bytes) — use INT until you need > 2 billion rows VARCHAR(255) vs TEXT — TEXT is fine in PostgreSQL (same storage), avoid in MySQL for indexing TIMESTAMPTZ vs TIMESTAMP — always TIMESTAMPTZ in PostgreSQL (stores in UTC) UUID vs BIGINT — UUID as PK causes index fragmentation (random inserts); use BIGSERIAL or ULIDs -- Normalization vs denormalization trade-off: 3NF: minimize redundancy, maximize consistency (OLTP workloads) Denormalized: pre-compute joins for read performance (OLAP / reporting) Key decisions: primary key type (UUID v4 causes B-tree fragmentation on insert-heavy tables — use sequential UUIDs/ULIDs/BIGSERIAL), column ordering (PostgreSQL aligns types — grouping 8-byte columns together reduces padding/wasted space), NOT NULL constraints (NULLable columns require extra storage bits and complicate query logic), and partitioning (range/list/hash partitioning for large tables improves query performance and maintenance operations like archival). ULID over UUID: ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) is time-ordered and random-suffix — it's globally unique like UUID but sequential like BIGSERIAL. New inserts always go to the rightmost B-tree leaf page instead of randomly scattered across the tree. Dramatically less index fragmentation and better cache locality for recent-data queries.

questions.q: What is table partitioning — when should you use it and what are the pitfalls?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL declarative partitioning: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, data JSONB) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at); CREATE TABLE events_2024_q1 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-04-01'); CREATE TABLE events_2024_q2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-04-01') TO ('2024-07-01'); -- Partition pruning: check if query prunes partitions EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at > '2024-06-01'; -- should show only q2+ -- MySQL: check partition info SELECT PARTITION_NAME, TABLE_ROWS FROM information_schema.PARTITIONS WHERE TABLE_NAME = 'events'; Partitioning benefits: partition pruning (query only scans relevant partitions), faster archival (DROP old partition instead of DELETE millions of rows — near-instant), parallel query across partitions, and index sizes per partition stay manageable. Use for: time-series data (partition by month/quarter), multi-tenant data (partition by tenant_id), or any table growing beyond 50-100M rows. Pitfall: queries without a partition key in WHERE clause scan ALL partitions — worse than an unpartitioned table if the key is missing. Partition key in every query: A partitioned table is only beneficial if your hot queries filter on the partition key. If your most common query does WHERE user_id = ? but the table is partitioned by created_at , you get no pruning — and the overhead of partition routing adds cost. Partition key must match your query patterns.

questions.q: What is database normalization vs denormalization — how do you decide in practice?
questions.text: -- Normalized (3NF): separate tables, joins at query time users(id, name, email) + orders(id, user_id, total) → JOIN on user_id -- Denormalized: store user_name in orders to avoid join orders(id, user_id, user_name, total) → no join needed -- Hybrid: JSONB column for flexible attributes without schema changes ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN attributes JSONB; CREATE INDEX idx_attributes_gin ON products USING GIN (attributes); -- queryable Normalized (3NF): eliminates data redundancy, simplifies writes (update one place), enforces consistency. Good for OLTP where writes are frequent. Denormalized: precomputes data, eliminates join overhead, simplifies read queries. Good for read-heavy analytics and reporting. In practice: start normalized, denormalize only where profiling shows join cost is a bottleneck. Materialized views are a middle ground — normalized source, precomputed denormalized view refreshed on schedule. JSONB for flexible attributes: Store semi-structured or highly variable data in PostgreSQL JSONB columns with GIN indexes. You get schema flexibility without an EAV (Entity-Attribute-Value) anti-pattern, and JSONB is fully queryable with operators like @> (containment) and ->> (field extraction).

questions.q: When do you choose a NoSQL database over a relational database?
questions.text: Use cases for NoSQL: Document (MongoDB, Firestore): variable schema, nested objects, rapid iteration Key-Value (Redis, Memorystore): caching, sessions, counters, pub/sub Wide-Column (Bigtable, Cassandra): time-series, IoT, 100M+ rows, write-heavy Graph (Neo4j, Neptune): relationship traversal, social networks, fraud detection Search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch): full-text search, log analytics, faceted search Choose NoSQL when: data doesn't fit a relational model (variable schema, deeply nested), write throughput exceeds what a single PostgreSQL instance can handle horizontally (Cassandra/Bigtable scale horizontally), or you need a specific access pattern that relational databases serve poorly (graph traversal, full-text search). Don't choose NoSQL to avoid learning SQL or as a premature optimization — most apps scale to tens of millions of rows fine on PostgreSQL with proper indexing. Multi-document transactions: Most NoSQL databases have weak or no cross-document transactions. If your data model requires atomic updates across multiple "records" (like transferring money between accounts), a relational database with ACID transactions is the correct choice. NoSQL consistency models (eventual, causal) require careful application-level handling.

questions.q: How do you optimize Redis for production — what are the key performance and reliability concerns?
questions.text: -- Check memory usage and eviction policy: redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory|mem_fragmentation" redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy # eviction when memory full -- Set for cache workloads: CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru # evict least recently used -- Find memory hogs: redis-cli --bigkeys # scan for large keys redis-cli MEMORY USAGE key_name # bytes for specific key -- Check slow log: redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10 # last 10 slow commands redis-cli CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 10000 # log commands > 10ms Redis is single-threaded for command processing — one slow command (KEYS *, LRANGE with huge list, SORT without index) blocks all other clients. Never run KEYS * in production — use SCAN with COUNT for iteration. Large values (>1MB per key) slow serialization and network transfer. Pipeline multiple commands to reduce round-trips. Use Redis Cluster for horizontal scaling or Sentinel for HA without sharding. For GCP: Cloud Memorystore (managed Redis) handles replication and failover automatically. KEYS * in production: KEYS * is O(n) and blocks the entire Redis instance while it scans. On an instance with 10 million keys, it can block for seconds. Use SCAN 0 COUNT 100 for iterating keys — it returns a cursor and is non-blocking.

questions.q: What is Bigtable/HBase — when is wide-column the right choice and how do you model data for it?
questions.text: -- Bigtable row key design (all access is by row key prefix scan): -- Bad: monotonic timestamp as row key → hot spot on latest tablet row_key = "2024-01-15T10:30:00#user123" -- all writes go to same server -- Good: salted / reversed timestamp row_key = "user123#~2024-01-15T10:30:00" -- spread across tablets -- Or: hash prefix for write distribution row_key = "hash(user_id)[0:4]#user123#timestamp" gcloud bigtable instances list cbt read <table> prefix="user123" count=10 Bigtable is designed for: massive scale (petabytes), high write throughput (millions of writes/second), and time-series or event data. Data model: one big sorted table — all queries are row key lookups or prefix scans. No secondary indexes, no joins, no SQL. Row key design IS your data model — you must design rows to support your access patterns. Hot spots (all writes going to one tablet) are the #1 performance problem — salt or hash the row key to distribute writes. When NOT to use Bigtable: If your queries need secondary indexes, ad-hoc filters, or SQL-like flexibility, use Cloud Spanner or PostgreSQL. Bigtable's power comes from its access pattern constraints — brute-forcing relational patterns onto it produces worse results than just using a relational DB.

questions.q: How do you tune Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) for production on GCP?
questions.text: -- Key Cloud SQL flags to configure: max_connections = 200 # size based on pool config, not raw app connections shared_buffers = 25% of RAM # Cloud SQL sets this automatically based on tier work_mem = 16MB # adjust for analytics queries pg_stat_statements.track = all # enable query insights log_min_duration_statement = 1000 # log queries > 1s -- Check Cloud SQL metrics in Cloud Monitoring: cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/cpu/utilization cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/memory/utilization cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/disk/read_ops_count cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/postgresql/num_backends Cloud SQL-specific: use SSD storage for production (HDD is 3x cheaper but 10x slower IOPS). Enable automatic storage increase to avoid disk-full outages. Use private IP (no public IP) and connect via Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. Enable Query Insights (built-in pg_stat_statements visualization). Choose the right machine tier — CPU is usually not the bottleneck; RAM (for shared_buffers + OS cache) and IOPS matter most. For read scaling, add read replicas in the same region as the consumers. Read replica for analytics: Route OLAP/reporting queries to a read replica to protect the primary from analytical workload interference. Use a larger replica tier if needed — you can size primary and replicas independently in Cloud SQL.

questions.q: What is Cloud Spanner — when should you choose it over Cloud SQL?
questions.text: -- Spanner: globally distributed, horizontally scalable, ACID relational DB -- When to choose Spanner: ✓ Need > 30,000 QPS on a single table (beyond single Cloud SQL node) ✓ Multi-region writes with external consistency (banking, booking systems) ✓ Zero-downtime horizontal scaling without sharding logic in app ✓ 99.999% SLA requirement -- When NOT to choose Spanner: ✗ Small to medium workloads (< $500/month budget) ✗ Complex analytical queries (use BigQuery instead) ✗ Requires stored procedures or PL/pgSQL (use Cloud SQL) Spanner uses TrueTime (GPS + atomic clock synchronization) to achieve external consistency across regions — a property no other globally distributed database provides. Primary key design is critical (avoid monotonic keys — causes hot splits). Interleaved tables (Spanner's parent-child relationship) co-locate related rows on the same Spanner node, eliminating cross-node joins for the most common access pattern. Cost: ~$0.90/node-hour for a single processing unit — significantly more than Cloud SQL. Justify with the SLA and scale requirements. Cloud SQL → Spanner migration trigger: When you start sharding Cloud SQL manually (splitting users across multiple DB instances by ID range), that's the signal you should have moved to Spanner. Spanner eliminates application-level sharding entirely.

questions.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime schema migration on a large table in production?
questions.text: -- Problem: ALTER TABLE on a 500M row table takes hours and locks the table -- Solution: online schema change tools -- PostgreSQL: pg_repack or pgroll pg_repack --table tablename --jobs 4 dbname # online table repack -- MySQL: pt-online-schema-change (Percona) or gh-ost (GitHub) pt-online-schema-change --alter "ADD COLUMN flag TINYINT DEFAULT 0" D=mydb,t=mytable --execute gh-ost --alter "ADD COLUMN flag TINYINT DEFAULT 0" --database mydb --table mytable --execute -- Manual expand-contract pattern: Step 1: Add new nullable column (fast, no data rewrite) Step 2: Deploy code to write to both old and new column Step 3: Backfill new column in batches (UPDATE WHERE id BETWEEN x AND y) Step 4: Deploy code to read from new column Step 5: Drop old column The expand-contract (blue-green schema) pattern is the safest for zero-downtime migrations. Never add NOT NULL columns without defaults in a single step — it locks the table for the full rewrite. Add as nullable first, backfill, then add the constraint. Use batched backfills with rate limiting to avoid overwhelming the database during migration. Adding NOT NULL without default: ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR NOT NULL on a 100M row table rewrites every row immediately under an exclusive lock. Always add nullable first, backfill, then add NOT NULL constraint. PostgreSQL 11+ allows NOT NULL with a constant default without rewrite — but complex defaults still rewrite.

questions.q: How do you take and restore a database backup safely — what are RTO and RPO?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: logical backup (portable, slow for large DBs) pg_dump -Fc -j 4 dbname > backup.dump # parallel custom format pg_restore -Fc -j 4 -d targetdb backup.dump -- Physical backup (faster, same PG version required) pg_basebackup -D /backup/base -Ft -z -P # full base backup -- PITR: restore base backup + replay WAL to target time recovery_target_time = '2024-01-15 14:30:00' # in recovery.conf / postgresql.conf -- Test your restore regularly: pg_restore ... && psql -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM critical_table;" # verify RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long can the system be down? Drives backup restore speed requirements. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data loss is acceptable? Drives backup frequency and replication lag tolerance. A daily backup gives RPO of 24 hours (you lose up to a day of data). WAL archiving gives RPO of minutes (replay WAL up to the last archived segment). Streaming replication with sync commit gives RPO of zero. Test restores monthly — an untested backup is an untested failure. Cloud SQL PITR: Enable in Cloud SQL with one flag. GCP retains base backups + WAL for up to 7 days. Restore to any second within that window. This makes Cloud SQL's RTO/RPO significantly better than self-managed PostgreSQL with manual WAL archiving.

questions.q: Database disk is filling up — how do you diagnose and resolve it without downtime?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL: find largest objects SELECT schemaname, tablename, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(schemaname||'.'||tablename)) AS size FROM information_schema.tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(schemaname||'.'||tablename) DESC LIMIT 20; -- Check for WAL accumulation: SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) FROM pg_ls_waldir(); -- Check for bloated tables vs actual live data: SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10; -- Run VACUUM to reclaim dead tuple space: VACUUM VERBOSE ANALYZE tablename; -- Emergency: drop old partitions, truncate log tables DROP TABLE events_2022_q1; -- instant, no VACUUM needed Disk space culprits: table bloat from dead tuples (VACUUM to reclaim), WAL accumulation from inactive replication slots or archive failure, index bloat, and log data growth. Immediate actions: run VACUUM on bloated tables, drop old partitions (instant disk recovery), check and fix WAL archiving, drop unused indexes. Long-term: implement automated archival/deletion of old data, monitor disk usage with alerts at 70% and 85% full. Replication slot disk bomb: An inactive replication slot silently accumulates WAL — primary cannot remove WAL that the slot hasn't consumed. This is the most common cause of unexpected disk exhaustion in production PostgreSQL. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size = 10GB in postgresql.conf as a safety cap.

questions.q: How do you handle database connection pool exhaustion in a Kubernetes environment?
questions.text: -- Architecture: pods → PgBouncer → PostgreSQL -- PgBouncer as a Kubernetes Deployment: kubectl get pods -l app=pgbouncer -n db kubectl exec -it pgbouncer-pod -- psql -p 6432 pgbouncer -c "SHOW POOLS;" -- Key metrics to watch: cl_waiting: clients waiting for a connection (> 0 = pool exhausted) sv_active: active server connections sv_idle: idle server connections available -- Scale response: increase pool_size in PgBouncer config -- Or: scale PgBouncer horizontally (multiple replicas with shared backend) In Kubernetes, connection exhaustion is amplified by HPA scaling — 50 pods × 20 pool connections = 1000 connections. Architecture: each app pod connects to PgBouncer (ClusterIP Service), PgBouncer maintains a small pool of actual PostgreSQL connections. PgBouncer itself can be scaled horizontally — multiple PgBouncer replicas share the backend PostgreSQL connection budget. Use transaction-mode pooling for highest efficiency. Monitor cl_waiting in PgBouncer — any clients waiting means the pool is undersized. Pgpool vs PgBouncer: PgBouncer is lightweight and fast — best for connection pooling only. Pgpool-II adds load balancing, query caching, and connection pooling but is heavier. For most Kubernetes deployments, PgBouncer is the right choice. Pgpool only if you need its additional features.

questions.q: What is a partial index — when does it dramatically outperform a full index?
questions.text: -- Full index on status column: indexes ALL rows including completed orders CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status); -- Partial index: only indexes rows where status = 'pending' CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders (user_id, created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; -- This query uses the partial index efficiently: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND user_id = 123 ORDER BY created_at; -- Check index size comparison: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx_orders_pending')); Partial indexes index only a subset of rows that match a WHERE condition. If your table has 100M orders but only 10,000 are 'pending' (the rows you query 99% of the time), a partial index on pending orders is 10,000x smaller, fits in cache, and is dramatically faster than a full index. Classic use cases: active/inactive flags (index only active), soft deletes (index only non-deleted), unprocessed queue items (index only unprocessed status). Real-world impact: A table with 500M rows where 0.01% are "active" — a full index is 500M entries; a partial index on active rows is 50K entries. The partial index fits entirely in shared_buffers; the full index is a cold disk read. This single change can reduce query time from seconds to microseconds.

questions.q: What are CTEs (WITH clauses) — when do they help vs hurt performance?
questions.text: -- PostgreSQL 12+: CTEs are NOT optimization fences by default WITH active_users AS ( SELECT id FROM users WHERE status = 'active' ) SELECT o.* FROM orders o JOIN active_users u ON o.user_id = u.id; -- Force materialization (pre-12 behavior, optimization fence): WITH active_users AS MATERIALIZED ( SELECT id FROM users WHERE status = 'active' ) -- Prevent materialization (inline the CTE): WITH active_users AS NOT MATERIALIZED ( SELECT id FROM users WHERE status = 'active' ) -- Recursive CTE: tree traversal WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS ( SELECT id, name, parent_id FROM employees WHERE parent_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, e.parent_id FROM employees e JOIN org_tree o ON e.parent_id = o.id ) SELECT * FROM org_tree; In PostgreSQL before version 12, CTEs were optimization fences — the planner couldn't push filters through them, and they were always materialized (computed once, stored in memory). In PG 12+, simple CTEs are inlined by default. When to use MATERIALIZED: when the CTE is referenced multiple times and computing it once saves repeated scans. When to avoid: CTE on a large table with a filter that could be pushed to an index — use a subquery instead so the planner can optimize. Recursive CTEs: Recursive CTEs are the correct tool for hierarchical data (org charts, category trees, graph traversal). They outperform application-level recursion by orders of magnitude. Learn the pattern — it comes up in any job involving hierarchical data.

questions.q: What is logical replication in PostgreSQL — how does it differ from physical replication?
questions.text: -- Physical replication: streams WAL byte-for-byte (same PG version required) -- Logical replication: streams row-level changes (flexible — cross-version, cross-DB) -- Set up logical replication: wal_level = logical # in postgresql.conf (requires restart) -- On publisher: CREATE PUBLICATION my_pub FOR TABLE users, orders; -- On subscriber: CREATE SUBSCRIPTION my_sub CONNECTION 'host=primary ...' PUBLICATION my_pub; -- Check replication status: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_subscription; Logical replication use cases: zero-downtime major version upgrades (logical rep from old to new version), selective table replication (replicate only specific tables to analytics DB), cross-database aggregation, and CDC (Change Data Capture) with tools like Debezium. Physical replication is better for HA replicas (faster, lower overhead, full DB copy). Logical replication allows schema differences between publisher and subscriber — the subscriber can have additional indexes, different column ordering, or even a different DB system (via Debezium → Kafka). Replication slot management: Logical replication uses replication slots. A slot for a Debezium consumer that goes offline for 24 hours will accumulate 24 hours of WAL on the primary. Always monitor slot lag and set max_slot_wal_keep_size to prevent disk exhaustion.

questions.q: How do you efficiently store and query time-series data in a relational database?
questions.text: -- Partition by time range (monthly or quarterly): CREATE TABLE metrics (ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, host TEXT, value FLOAT) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts); CREATE TABLE metrics_2024_01 PARTITION OF metrics FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01'); -- Composite index: (host, ts) for common access pattern CREATE INDEX ON metrics_2024_01 (host, ts DESC); -- BRIN index: very cheap for sequential time data CREATE INDEX ON metrics_2024_01 USING BRIN (ts); -- tiny index, good for seq scans -- Or: TimescaleDB extension for automated time-series management SELECT create_hypertable('metrics', 'ts', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '1 week'); Time-series patterns: always include timestamp in indexes as the trailing sort column (most queries are "latest N for entity X"), use DESC sort on timestamp index to serve "latest" queries from the leftmost pages, partition by time for fast archival (drop old partitions instead of DELETE), and use BRIN indexes for append-only time-ordered data (BRIN is 1000x smaller than B-tree for sequential data). For high-cardinality metrics (Prometheus-style), use TimescaleDB or a purpose-built TSDB (Victoria Metrics, InfluxDB). TimescaleDB: TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension that adds automatic time-based partitioning (hypertables), continuous aggregates, and data retention policies. It's fully compatible with standard PostgreSQL — same SQL, same tools, same connection pooling. For serious time-series workloads on PostgreSQL, it's the right tool.

questions.q: How do you implement database observability — what metrics, logs, and alerts matter most?
questions.text: -- Critical PostgreSQL metrics to monitor: SELECT sum(blks_hit)*100.0/(sum(blks_hit)+sum(blks_read)) FROM pg_stat_database; -- cache hit rate > 99% SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; -- active connections SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock'; -- lock waits SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() FROM pg_stat_replication; -- replica lag SELECT age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 1; -- XID age -- Export to Prometheus: postgres_exporter --web.listen-address=:9187 --config.file=config.yml Alert thresholds: cache hit rate <99% (increase shared_buffers or add RAM), connection count >80% of max_connections (add PgBouncer or scale), replication lag >30s (investigate replica), transaction ID age >1.5B (urgent VACUUM needed), disk >80% full (archival or resize), lock wait time >5s (investigate blocking query). Use postgres_exporter with Prometheus + Grafana for the full metrics pipeline, or Cloud SQL's built-in Query Insights for managed deployments. Principal-level practice: Build SLO-based DB alerting — not just "query_time > 1s" but "99th percentile query latency error budget burn rate". This separates platform observability maturity from ad-hoc monitoring. Treat the database as a service with its own SLO, not just infrastructure to watch.

questions.q: What is a materialized view — how do you use it for performance and when does it go stale?
questions.text: -- Create a materialized view (stores results on disk): CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; WITH DATA; -- Refresh (blocks reads in PostgreSQL by default): REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue; -- Non-blocking refresh (PostgreSQL 9.4+, requires unique index on matview): CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON monthly_revenue (month); REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue; -- Query the matview like a regular table: SELECT * FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month >= '2024-01-01'; Materialized views precompute expensive aggregations and store the result. Great for: dashboards and reporting queries that aggregate millions of rows (run once, query many times), denormalizing normalized data for read performance, and caching the result of complex multi-table joins. Stale data: the matview reflects the data at the last REFRESH time — it does not auto-update. Schedule REFRESH CONCURRENTLY via pg_cron or external scheduler. For near-real-time data, TimescaleDB Continuous Aggregates incrementally update materialized views as new data arrives. pg_cron for scheduled refresh: SELECT cron.schedule('refresh-revenue', '0 * * * *', 'REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue'); — refreshes hourly with no application code change needed. pg_cron runs inside PostgreSQL, survives container restarts, and has no external dependency.

questions.q: What is EXPLAIN in MySQL — how do you interpret the output to find performance problems?
questions.text: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123 AND status = 'pending'; EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON SELECT ...; -- detailed JSON output (MySQL 8+) EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...; -- actually executes + shows real times (MySQL 8.0.18+) -- Key columns in EXPLAIN output: type: ALL=full scan(bad), index=index scan, range=range scan, ref=non-unique index, eq_ref=unique, const=best key: which index was chosen (NULL = no index used) rows: estimated rows examined (multiply across joins for total cost) Extra: "Using filesort"=expensive sort, "Using temporary"=temp table, "Using index"=covering index(good) type column priority (best to worst): system > const > eq_ref > ref > range > index > ALL. Seeing type=ALL on a large table is a red flag — add an index. "Using filesort" means MySQL cannot satisfy ORDER BY with an index — add the sort column to the index. "Using temporary" means a temp table was created for GROUP BY or ORDER BY — restructure the query or add a covering index. rows × loops (for nested queries) gives the total row examination cost. Index hints: If MySQL picks the wrong index, use FORCE INDEX (idx_name) temporarily to confirm it's an optimizer issue, then fix by updating statistics ( ANALYZE TABLE ) rather than permanently forcing an index. Forced indexes break silently when the data distribution changes.

questions.q: What is optimistic vs pessimistic locking — when do you choose each?
questions.text: -- Pessimistic locking: lock the row before reading (prevent concurrent updates) BEGIN; SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 1 FOR UPDATE; -- row is now locked UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = 1; COMMIT; -- Optimistic locking: no lock, use version column to detect conflict SELECT id, quantity, version FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 1; -- In application: compute new_quantity = quantity - 1 UPDATE inventory SET quantity = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE product_id = 1 AND version = ?; -- if 0 rows updated: conflict, retry Pessimistic locking: acquire a lock before reading. Safe but reduces concurrency — all readers of the same row must queue. Use when: conflict probability is high (hot inventory items, bank account balances), the operation must not fail (you can't retry). Optimistic locking: no locks, detect conflicts at write time using a version counter. Use when: conflict probability is low (most reads are followed by a write that doesn't conflict), read-heavy workloads (no lock contention). ORM frameworks (Hibernate, ActiveRecord) support optimistic locking natively via a version column. SELECT FOR UPDATE scope: A lock acquired with SELECT FOR UPDATE is released only at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A slow application-level operation between the lock acquisition and the commit holds the lock for that entire duration — blocking all other writers. Keep critical section (SELECT FOR UPDATE → UPDATE → COMMIT) as short as possible.

questions.q: How do you handle database migrations safely in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.text: -- Tools: Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic (Python), golang-migrate, sqitch -- Flyway example migration versioning: V1__Create_users_table.sql V2__Add_email_index.sql V3__Add_status_column.sql -- Run in CI/CD: flyway migrate -url=jdbc:postgresql://... -user=app -password=... -locations=filesystem:./migrations -- Safe migration checklist: ✓ Add columns as nullable (no NOT NULL without default) ✓ Add indexes CONCURRENTLY (non-blocking) ✓ Never rename columns (use add + backfill + drop) ✓ Never change column types directly (add new column, migrate data) ✓ Use expand-contract for breaking schema changes Schema migrations in CI/CD: migrations run automatically on deploy, schema and code changes must be backward-compatible for the duration of a rolling deployment (both old and new code run simultaneously against the new schema). Add columns before deploying code that uses them; drop columns only after all code references to them are removed. Use migration tools that track applied versions and are idempotent. Separate DDL migrations (fast, schema only) from data migrations (slow, batched) to avoid long deployment windows. GitOps for migrations: Commit migration files to Git alongside application code. The deployment pipeline applies pending migrations before starting the new app version. Migration history is version-controlled and auditable. Failed migrations should be caught in staging — never let an untested migration near production schema.

questions.q: Walk through your methodology for diagnosing a production database performance incident.
questions.text: This is the Principal-level systems thinking question. The interviewer wants structure, prioritization, and depth — not a random list of commands. Incident triage methodology Phase 1 — Quantify: what's actually slow? Which query/table/operation? Since when? Phase 2 — Immediate relief: kill blocking queries, kill long-running idle transactions Phase 3 — Identify hottest queries: pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC Phase 4 — Explain the worst query: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) — look for seq scans, bad estimates Phase 5 — Check system resources: CPU, I/O wait, memory pressure, connection count Phase 6 — Check for lock contention: pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock' Phase 7 — Check for bloat: n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum — is VACUUM behind? Phase 8 — Implement fix: index, query rewrite, or VACUUM Phase 9 — Verify and document: before/after metrics, root cause, prevention Common root causes by symptom: sudden slowdown with high I/O wait → autovacuum running or index bloat. Sudden slowdown after deploy → plan regression (stale stats after schema change, run ANALYZE). Gradual slowdown over weeks → data growth past index threshold, table bloat. Spike-and-recover pattern → lock contention from long transactions. Steady increase in query time → N+1 queries introduced in new code or missing index on growing table. Principal-level deliverable: After any performance incident, write a postmortem with: the query/queries involved, the root cause (index missing, stats

questions.q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
questions.text: A clustered index defines the physical row order (the table is the index); non-clustered indexes are separate structures pointing back to rows. CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX ix ON orders(id); -- SQL Server CLUSTER orders USING orders_pkey; -- PostgreSQL one-time Interview tip: InnoDB primary key is the clustered index.

questions.q: What is index selectivity and cardinality, and why do they matter?
questions.text: Selectivity is the fraction of rows a value matches; high-cardinality columns make better index candidates because they narrow results. SELECT count(DISTINCT status)::float/count(*) FROM orders; SELECT n_distinct FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename='orders'; Interview tip: Low-selectivity indexes are often ignored.

questions.q: How do you find unused and duplicate indexes and safely remove them?
questions.text: Check index usage statistics over a full business cycle, find overlapping definitions, then drop in a controlled change with a rollback plan. SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan; DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_old; Interview tip: Reset windows can hide seasonal use.

questions.q: What are the different index types in PostgreSQL: B-tree, hash, GIN, GiST and BRIN?
questions.text: B-tree is the default for equality and ranges; GIN suits arrays, JSONB and full text; GiST handles geometric and nearest-neighbour; BRIN is tiny for naturally ordered huge tables; hash is equality only. CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops); CREATE INDEX ON events USING brin (created_at); Interview tip: BRIN needs physical correlation.

questions.q: What is an index-only scan and what prevents it in PostgreSQL?
questions.text: The query is answered from the index alone without visiting the table, but only if the visibility map shows pages as all-visible. CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total); EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT total FROM orders WHERE customer_id=7; Interview tip: VACUUM keeps the visibility map fresh.

questions.q: How do you use pagination efficiently: OFFSET versus keyset pagination?
questions.text: OFFSET scans and discards rows so deep pages get slower; keyset (seek) pagination uses an indexed last-seen value and stays fast. SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100000; SELECT * FROM items WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 50; Interview tip: Order by a unique indexed key.

questions.q: How do you speed up COUNT(*) on large tables?
questions.text: Use estimates from statistics, maintain counters, count with index-only scans, or cache; exact counts require scanning visible rows. SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname='orders'; SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '1 day'; Interview tip: Ask whether exactness is really needed.

questions.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and IN versus EXISTS?
questions.text: UNION removes duplicates by sorting or hashing; UNION ALL just appends. EXISTS can stop at the first match and is often better than IN for correlated checks. SELECT id FROM a UNION ALL SELECT id FROM b; SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM items i WHERE i.order_id=o.id); Interview tip: Default to UNION ALL if duplicates are impossible.

questions.q: How do you optimise queries that use LIKE with wildcards or full-text search?
questions.text: Leading wildcards cannot use B-tree indexes; use trigram indexes, full-text search indexes or a search engine. CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm; CREATE INDEX ON users USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops); SELECT * FROM docs WHERE tsv @@ to_tsquery('english','deploy & rollback'); Interview tip: Prefix patterns can use B-tree with the right operator class.

questions.q: How do you handle bulk inserts and updates efficiently?
questions.text: Batch rows, use COPY or multi-row inserts, disable unnecessary indexes temporarily, commit in chunks and avoid per-row round trips. COPY orders FROM '/data/orders.csv' CSV; INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,'a'),(2,'b'),(3,'c'); Interview tip: Round trips dominate small inserts.

questions.q: How do prepared statements and the plan cache affect performance and security?
questions.text: Prepared statements parse once and bind parameters, saving planning time and preventing SQL injection; generic plans can misestimate skewed data. PREPARE q(int) AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=$1; EXECUTE q(42); SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan; Interview tip: Always parameterise, never concatenate.

questions.q: What is MVCC in PostgreSQL and how does it cause bloat?
questions.text: Each update creates a new row version; old versions remain until vacuum removes them, so heavy updates need vacuum capacity. SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='orders'; SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM orders LIMIT 1; Interview tip: Long transactions block cleanup.

questions.q: What is transaction ID wraparound and how do you prevent it?
questions.text: Transaction IDs are 32-bit and wrap; vacuum freezes old rows to avoid data becoming invisible, and failing to vacuum can force the database into read-only shutdown. SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC; VACUUM (FREEZE, VERBOSE) big_table; Interview tip: Alert well before 1.5 billion.

questions.q: How do you tune autovacuum for a hot table?
questions.text: Lower scale factors per table, raise cost limit or workers, and monitor dead tuples and vacuum duration. ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000); SELECT * FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum; Interview tip: Defaults suit small tables, not huge ones.

questions.q: What is table and index bloat repair with pg_repack, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and VACUUM FULL?
questions.text: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table with an exclusive lock; pg_repack and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuild online with minimal locking. REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_orders_created; pg_repack -d appdb -t orders Interview tip: Avoid VACUUM FULL on live systems.

questions.q: How do you use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to find I/O problems?
questions.text: Buffers show shared hits versus reads; many reads mean cache misses and disk I/O. Compare estimated and actual rows to spot bad statistics. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE) SELECT ...; SET track_io_timing = on; Interview tip: Actual versus estimated rows is the first check.

questions.q: How does InnoDB use the redo log, undo log and doublewrite buffer?
questions.text: Redo ensures durability, undo supports rollback and MVCC, and doublewrite protects against torn pages. SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit'; Interview tip: Flush setting trades durability for speed.

questions.q: How do gap locks and next-key locks cause deadlocks in InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ?
questions.text: Range scans lock gaps between index records to prevent phantoms; concurrent inserts into the same gap can deadlock. SELECT * FROM t WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE; SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK Interview tip: READ COMMITTED reduces gap locking.

questions.q: How do you choose between MySQL replication formats and what is GTID replication?
questions.text: Row-based replication is the safest; GTIDs give each transaction a global ID, making failover and replica repointing much simpler. SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_format'; CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1; Interview tip: Use ROW format and GTIDs.

questions.q: How do you perform online schema changes in MySQL with gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change?
questions.text: These tools create a shadow table, copy data in chunks while capturing changes, and swap tables atomically with minimal blocking. gh-ost --alter='ADD COLUMN notes TEXT' --database=app --table=orders --execute pt-online-schema-change --alter 'ADD INDEX ix(c)' D=app,t=orders --execute Interview tip: Always test with dry-run first.

questions.q: What are common causes of MySQL replication lag and how do you reduce them?
questions.text: Single-threaded apply, large transactions, heavy replica reads, I/O limits and missing indexes on replicas; use parallel replication and smaller transactions. SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G SET GLOBAL replica_parallel_workers=8; Interview tip: Large transactions serialise apply.

questions.q: How do you size a database connection pool correctly?
questions.text: Pool size should match what the database can run concurrently, often cores times two plus disks, not the number of clients; more connections increase contention. SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state; pool_size = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count) Interview tip: Smaller pools are often faster.

questions.q: What are the PgBouncer pooling modes and their trade-offs?
questions.text: Session mode holds a server connection per client; transaction mode releases after each transaction (best multiplexing, restricts session features); statement mode is rarely used. pool_mode = transaction default_pool_size = 20 max_client_conn = 2000 SHOW POOLS; Interview tip: Transaction mode breaks session state.

questions.q: How do you find and handle idle-in-transaction sessions?
questions.text: They hold locks and block vacuum; find them in pg_stat_activity and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='idle in transaction' ORDER BY age DESC; ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout='60s'; Interview tip: A forgotten BEGIN can bloat the whole database.

questions.q: How do you handle connection storms after a database restart or failover?
questions.text: Use jittered retries, connection limits, pooler queues and gradual ramp-up so clients do not overwhelm the recovering database. max_connections = 500 retry delay = base * 2^n + random(0, base) Interview tip: Thundering herd needs jitter.

questions.q: What is max_connections and what are the memory implications of raising it?
questions.text: Each connection uses memory for backend state and work_mem per operation; raising limits without pooling risks out-of-memory and slowdowns. SHOW max_connections; SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_backend_memory_contexts_total) -- per-backend memory Interview tip: Pool instead of raising the limit.

questions.q: What is a replication slot in PostgreSQL and what risks does it carry?
questions.text: A slot makes the primary retain WAL until the consumer confirms it; an inactive slot makes WAL pile up and can fill the disk. SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS lag FROM pg_replication_slots; SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('old_slot'); Interview tip: Alert on retained WAL size.

questions.q: How do you do a zero-downtime failover with a replicated database and what can go wrong?
questions.text: Detect failure reliably, fence the old primary, promote the most caught-up replica, redirect traffic and rebuild; risks are split brain and data loss with async replication. pg_ctl promote -D /var/lib/postgresql/data patronictl failover cluster Interview tip: Fence the old primary.

questions.q: How do you route reads to replicas safely given replication lag?
questions.text: Send only lag-tolerant reads to replicas, use read-your-writes strategies for recent writers, and monitor lag with fallbacks to the primary. SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS lag; SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) FROM pg_stat_replication; Interview tip: Not all reads are equal.

questions.q: What is the difference between logical and physical backups and when would you use each?
questions.text: Physical backups copy data files and WAL for fast full restore and PITR; logical backups dump SQL or rows, which are portable but slower. pg_basebackup -D /backup -X stream -P pg_dump -Fc appdb > appdb.dump Interview tip: Test the restore, not just the backup.

questions.q: What is change data capture and how do logical decoding or binlog readers support it?
questions.text: CDC streams row-level changes from the database log to downstream systems with low overhead, avoiding polling and dual writes. CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE orders; debezium connector reading WAL via a replication slot Interview tip: Handle schema changes and slot lag.

questions.q: How do you choose data types that affect performance and storage?
questions.text: Use the smallest suitable types, avoid text for numbers, use timestamps with time zone appropriately and consistent types for join keys. ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint; CREATE TABLE t (id bigint, created_at timestamptz, amount numeric(12,2)); Interview tip: Mismatched types prevent index use.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs of UUIDs versus auto-increment integers as primary keys?
questions.text: Integers are compact and ordered; UUIDs are globally unique and safe to generate anywhere but larger and random unless time-ordered. id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY id uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() Interview tip: Consider UUIDv7 or ULID for ordering.

questions.q: How do you design indexes and tables for multi-tenant applications?
questions.text: Include tenant_id in keys and indexes, choose shared schema, schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant by isolation needs, and guard against noisy neighbours. CREATE INDEX ON orders (tenant_id, created_at); ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; Interview tip: Lead with tenant_id in composite indexes.

questions.q: When should you use JSONB columns versus relational columns?
questions.text: Use JSONB for sparse, evolving or document-like attributes; use relational columns for core, frequently filtered fields needing constraints and joins. CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload); SELECT payload->>'plan' FROM accounts WHERE payload @> '{"active": true}'; Interview tip: Promote hot JSON fields to columns.

questions.q: How do foreign keys affect performance and should you always use them?
questions.text: They guarantee integrity but add checks on writes and need indexes on the referencing column; use them by default and remove only with a clear reason. CREATE INDEX ON order_items (order_id); ALTER TABLE order_items ADD CONSTRAINT fk FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE; Interview tip: Index the child column.

questions.q: How does DynamoDB partitioning work and how do you avoid hot partitions?
questions.text: Items are spread by partition key hash; uneven access concentrates load on one partition. Use high-cardinality keys, write sharding and adaptive capacity. pk = f"{user_id}#{random.randint(0,9)}" aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name events Interview tip: Design keys from access patterns first.

questions.q: What are the eviction policies in Redis and how do you choose one?
questions.text: When memory is full Redis evicts by policy such as allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl or noeviction; choose by whether the data is a cache or a store. CONFIG SET maxmemory 2gb CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru Interview tip: Never use noeviction for a pure cache.

questions.q: How do you prevent cache stampedes and keep a cache consistent with the database?
questions.text: Use request coalescing, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate and explicit invalidation on writes; accept eventual consistency where possible. SET lock:key 1 NX EX 10 TTL = base + random(0, 60) Interview tip: Two hard problems: invalidation and naming.

questions.q: How does MongoDB indexing and the aggregation pipeline affect performance?
questions.text: Compound indexes follow the equality-sort-range rule; the pipeline should filter and project early so stages can use indexes. db.orders.createIndex({customerId:1, createdAt:-1}) db.orders.find({customerId:7}).explain('executionStats') Interview tip: Equality, sort, range.

questions.q: What consistency models exist in distributed NoSQL stores and how do you tune them?
questions.text: Eventual, read-your-writes, strong and tunable quorum consistency; choose per operation based on correctness needs and latency. CONSISTENCY QUORUM; -- Cassandra cqlsh aws dynamodb get-item --consistent-read Interview tip: R + W > N gives strong reads in quorum systems.

questions.q: How do you use RDS or Cloud SQL read replicas, Multi-AZ and high availability correctly?
questions.text: HA standby is for failover durability, not read scaling; read replicas scale reads asynchronously; know the failover time and test it. aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,MultiAZ]' aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier db --force-failover Interview tip: Standbys do not serve reads in classic Multi-AZ.

questions.q: How do you tune IOPS and storage on cloud managed databases?
questions.text: Match provisioned or burst IOPS and throughput to the workload; watch queue depth, burst balance and storage autoscaling limits. aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --metric-name DiskQueueDepth ... gcloud sql instances patch db --storage-auto-increase Interview tip: Burst credits run out.

questions.q: What is Amazon Aurora and how does its architecture differ from standard PostgreSQL or MySQL?
questions.text: Aurora separates compute from a shared, distributed storage layer replicated six ways across three zones; replicas read the same storage, giving fast failover and low replica lag. aws rds describe-db-clusters aws rds failover-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier prod Interview tip: Storage is shared, not copied per replica.

questions.q: How do you monitor a managed database effectively with cloud-native tools?
questions.text: Combine instance metrics, enhanced monitoring, performance insights and logs; alert on saturation and replication, not just CPU. aws pi get-resource-metrics ... gcloud sql operations list --instance db Interview tip: Use Performance Insights for top SQL.

questions.q: How do you plan a major version upgrade of a production database with minimal downtime?
questions.text: Test on a clone, check extension and application compatibility, use logical replication or blue-green deployments for near-zero downtime, and keep a rollback path. pg_upgrade --check aws rds create-blue-green-deployment ... Interview tip: Rehearse with production-like data.

questions.q: How do you investigate sudden latency spikes on a database that otherwise looks healthy?
questions.text: Correlate with locks, checkpoints, autovacuum, cache misses, plan changes, noisy neighbours and I/O limits using wait events and time-series. SELECT wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC; SELECT * FROM pg_stat_bgwriter; Interview tip: Wait events show where time goes.

questions.q: How do you set up and use slow query logging and query analysis tools?
questions.text: Log queries over a threshold, aggregate with tools like pg_stat_statements, pgBadger or pt-query-digest, and fix the top offenders by total time. ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = '500ms'; pt-query-digest slow.log | head -50 Interview tip: Rank by total time, not single slowest.

questions.q: How do you capacity-plan a database: CPU, memory, storage and growth?
questions.text: Track trends in data size, working set, QPS and latency, project growth, and size for peak plus headroom with a plan for scaling up or out. SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(current_database())); SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_catalog.pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 10; Interview tip: The working set should fit in memory.

questions.q: How do you archive or purge old data from huge tables without hurting production?
questions.text: Partition by time and drop partitions, or delete in small batches with indexes, throttling and monitoring; archive first to cheaper storage. ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2024_01; DELETE FROM logs WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM logs WHERE created_at < now()-interval '1 year' LIMIT 5000); Interview tip: Dropping a partition is instant; deleting is not.

questions.q: How do you handle a runaway query or lock pile-up in production?
questions.text: Identify the blocker with the lock graph, assess impact, cancel or terminate it, and then fix the root cause with timeouts and query changes. SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid))>0; SELECT pg_cancel_backend(pid); Interview tip: Cancel before terminate.

questions.q: How do you run safe load tests against a database before a launch?
questions.text: Use production-like data volume and distribution, replay realistic workloads, ramp gradually, measure percentiles and resources, and isolate from production. pgbench -c 50 -j 4 -T 300 -f workload.sql appdb sysbench oltp_read_write --threads=64 run Interview tip: Test with realistic data skew.

questions.q: What’s wrong with storing secrets in environment variables, and what are the alternatives?
questions.text: # env vars leak via: /proc/<pid>/environ ← readable by same-uid processes docker inspect, crash dumps, child processes (inherited) CI logs that echo the environment Env vars are better than hardcoding but still leak: they’re inherited by every child process, visible in /proc/<pid>/environ , captured in crash dumps and docker inspect , and often accidentally printed in CI logs. They’re acceptable for low-sensitivity config but weak for high-value secrets. Better: mount secrets as files from a secrets manager (tmpfs, mode 0400), or fetch them at runtime via a sidecar/agent so they never persist. Pragmatic stance: Env vars injected by the platform from a secrets manager (not committed anywhere) are fine for most apps. Reserve file-mount/dynamic secrets for the crown jewels.

questions.q: How does HashiCorp Vault’s dynamic secrets model improve on static credentials?
questions.text: # app requests a short-lived DB credential on demand vault read database/creds/readonly # → username/password valid for e.g. 1h, auto-revoked after Static credentials live forever, get shared, leak, and are painful to rotate. Vault’s dynamic secrets are generated on demand, scoped to a single consumer, and have a short TTL — Vault creates a unique DB user per request and automatically revokes it when the lease expires. This shrinks the blast radius (a leaked credential is useless in an hour), gives per-app attribution, and makes rotation automatic rather than a manual fire drill. Why SREs love it: "Rotate all DB passwords" becomes a non-event — credentials are ephemeral by design, so there’s nothing long-lived to rotate.

questions.q: Explain the difference between encryption at rest and envelope encryption with a KMS.
questions.text: data → encrypted with a DEK (data encryption key) DEK → encrypted with a KEK (key encryption key) held in KMS store: ciphertext + wrapped DEK; KEK never leaves the KMS/HSM Envelope encryption uses two layers: a local data key (DEK) encrypts the actual data, and a master key (KEK) in the KMS encrypts the DEK. You store the ciphertext alongside the wrapped DEK; to decrypt, you ask the KMS to unwrap the DEK. The KEK never leaves the KMS/HSM, so compromising your storage doesn’t expose the master key, and you can rotate the KEK without re-encrypting all data — just re-wrap the DEKs. Why two keys: Encrypting gigabytes directly with a KMS call is slow and rate-limited. The DEK does bulk crypto locally; the KMS only handles the tiny DEK.

questions.q: How do you manage secrets in Kubernetes — and why are native Secrets not enough?
questions.text: # native Secrets are only base64 — NOT encrypted echo "cGFzc3dvcmQ=" | base64 -d → password # harden: EncryptionConfiguration (etcd at-rest) + RBAC + ESO Kubernetes Secrets are merely base64-encoded, stored in etcd, and readable by anyone with get access in the namespace — not real encryption. Hardening: enable EncryptionConfiguration so etcd encrypts secrets at rest (ideally KMS-backed), lock down RBAC so few principals can read them, and prefer the External Secrets Operator or Secrets Store CSI driver to sync from Vault/cloud secrets managers rather than committing Secret manifests. Never commit Secret YAML to Git — base64 is encoding, not encryption. Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or an external store so Git never holds plaintext-equivalent secrets.

questions.q: What is the External Secrets Operator and how does it work?
questions.text: apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1 kind: ExternalSecret spec: secretStoreRef: {name: vault-backend, kind: SecretStore} target: {name: db-creds} data: [{secretKey: password, remoteRef: {key: prod/db, property: pw}}] The External Secrets Operator (ESO) syncs secrets from an external source of truth (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) into native Kubernetes Secrets. You declare an ExternalSecret CR pointing at a backend; ESO fetches the value and materializes a K8s Secret, refreshing it on a schedule. This keeps the authoritative secret outside the cluster and out of Git, while apps still consume a normal Secret — no app changes needed. GitOps-friendly: You commit the ExternalSecret reference (no sensitive data) to Git; the actual value lives in Vault. Best of both worlds.

questions.q: How do you detect secrets that have already been committed to a Git repo?
questions.text: gitleaks detect --source . --redact # scan working tree + history trufflehog git file://. --only-verified # verifies live creds # pre-commit hook to PREVENT new ones: gitleaks protect --staged Tools like gitleaks and trufflehog scan the entire Git history (not just the current tree) for high-entropy strings and known credential patterns; trufflehog can even verify whether a found key is still live. Run them in CI to block PRs and as a pre-commit hook to stop secrets before they’re ever committed. Scanning history matters because a secret deleted in a later commit still lives in the Git objects forever. Detection isn’t remediation: A committed secret must be rotated , not just deleted. Removing it from history (BFG/filter-repo) doesn’t help if someone already cloned the repo — assume it’s compromised.

questions.q: Explain secret rotation — what makes it hard and how do you automate it?
questions.text: # the dual-credential pattern for zero-downtime rotation: 1. create new credential (v2) alongside old (v1) 2. roll apps to v2; verify all healthy 3. revoke v1 only after confirming nothing uses it Rotation is hard because of the cutover window: revoke too early and live apps break; too late and a leaked credential stays valid. The safe approach is overlapping credentials — issue the new one, migrate consumers, verify, then revoke the old. Automate with Vault dynamic secrets (rotation is implicit via short TTLs) or cloud-managed rotation (AWS Secrets Manager rotation Lambdas). Track which services use which credential so you know when it’s safe to revoke. Best rotation is no rotation: Short-lived dynamic credentials make rotation continuous and automatic, eliminating the risky manual cutover entirely.

questions.q: What is SOPS and when would you use it over a secrets manager?
questions.text: # encrypt only the values, keep keys readable, commit to Git sops --encrypt --kms arn:aws:kms:... secrets.yaml > secrets.enc.yaml sops --decrypt secrets.enc.yaml # decrypts on demand SOPS (Secrets OPerationS) encrypts the values in a YAML/JSON/env file while leaving keys in plaintext, so the file stays diff-friendly and commitable to Git. It encrypts with a KMS/age/PGP key, so only authorized principals can decrypt. Use it for GitOps secret-in-repo workflows where you want secrets versioned alongside config and don’t want to run a full Vault — common in smaller teams or for bootstrapping config. SOPS vs Vault: SOPS = encrypted files in Git, simple, static. Vault = central service, dynamic secrets, audit, leasing. SOPS for config-as-code; Vault for scale and dynamic needs.

questions.q: How do you prevent secrets from leaking into logs and observability tooling?
questions.text: # scrub at multiple layers: app: redact known fields before logging (password, token, authz) pipeline: log-shipper regex filters (Fluent Bit/Logstash) code review + linters that flag logging of secret vars Secrets leak into logs via stack traces, request/response dumps, and debug logging of config objects. Defend in depth: redact sensitive fields in the app before they’re logged (allowlist what you log, not denylist), add scrubbing filters in the log pipeline as a backstop, mask values in error reporters (Sentry), and never log full request headers (Authorization). Treat logs as a potential exfiltration channel — anyone with log access effectively has those secrets. Debug logging is the usual culprit: "log the whole config to debug startup" dumps every secret. Redact at the source; a downstream filter is only a safety net.

questions.q: What is workload identity (IRSA / GKE Workload Identity) and why is it better than keys?
questions.text: # pod assumes a cloud IAM role via its K8s service account # EKS (IRSA): SA annotated with an IAM role ARN # GKE: SA bound to a GCP service account # → SDK gets short-lived, auto-rotated creds. No stored keys. Workload identity lets a pod’s Kubernetes service account map to a cloud IAM identity, so the SDK receives short-lived, automatically-rotated credentials from the metadata/token service — there are no static access keys to store, leak, or rotate. It’s the keyless ideal: credentials are ephemeral, scoped per-workload (least privilege), and tied to the pod’s identity, giving clean audit trails. This eliminates the #1 cloud breach vector: long-lived keys in code/config. The endgame: No long-lived cloud keys anywhere in your cluster. Every workload gets just-in-time, just-enough, auto-expiring credentials.

questions.q: How do you handle secret sprawl across many services and environments?
questions.text: central source of truth (Vault / cloud SM) + naming convention: <env>/<team>/<service>/<secret> e.g. prod/payments/api/db-pw + per-path access policies + audit + automated inventory Secret sprawl — the same credential copied into a dozen places — makes rotation impossible and breaches inevitable. Fix it with a single authoritative store, a consistent hierarchical naming scheme so access policies map cleanly to teams/envs, least-privilege path policies, and audit logging of every read. Periodically inventory which workloads read which secrets so you can answer "what’s affected if this leaks?" instantly. One source of truth: The moment a secret exists in two places, rotation breaks. Reference the central store everywhere; never copy values around.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege applied to secret access?
questions.text: # scope each policy tightly: path "prod/payments/*" { capabilities = ["read"] } # not "*" # + deny by default, time-bound tokens, per-service identity Least privilege means each identity can read only the specific secrets it needs, nothing more — the payments service can read prod/payments/* , not all of prod/* . Combine path-scoped read-only policies, deny-by-default, per-service identities (not shared accounts), and short-lived tokens. This bounds the blast radius: a compromised service exposes only its own secrets, and audit logs cleanly attribute every access to one identity. Blast-radius thinking: Design so that "service X is compromised" leaks the minimum. Broad wildcard policies turn one breach into total compromise.

questions.q: How do you securely pass secrets into a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.text: # use the platform’s secret store + OIDC, not plaintext vars # GitHub Actions → OIDC federation to cloud (no stored keys): permissions: {id-token: write} - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: {role-to-assume: arn:..., aws-region: us-east-1} The modern approach is OIDC federation: the CI runner presents a signed identity token to the cloud, which exchanges it for short-lived credentials — no long-lived keys stored in the CI system at all. For other secrets, use the platform’s encrypted secret store (masked in logs), scope them to specific environments/branches, and require approvals for production. Never put secrets in plaintext workflow files or unmasked variables. CI is a prime target: It has access to everything it deploys. Static cloud keys in CI are a top breach vector — OIDC eliminates them.

questions.q: What goes in a secret-leak incident response runbook?
questions.text: 1. REVOKE/rotate the credential immediately (assume compromised) 2. scope: where used? audit logs for anomalous use? 3. contain: disable affected identity, check for lateral movement 4. remediate: remove from history, fix the leak source 5. postmortem: how did it leak, how to prevent When a secret leaks, treat it as compromised regardless of exposure duration. Rotate/revoke first — speed matters more than investigation. Then scope the damage (audit logs for the credential’s usage), contain (disable the identity, look for lateral movement and new IAM users/keys an attacker may have created), remediate the leak source, and run a blameless postmortem. Removing the secret from Git history is necessary but never sufficient — rotation is what actually closes the exposure. Rotate before you investigate: Every minute a leaked key stays valid is risk. Kill it first, analyze second.

questions.q: What is a software supply-chain attack? Give real examples.
questions.text: SolarWinds (2020) — build system compromised, signed malware shipped Codecov (2021) — CI script altered, exfiltrated env secrets xz/liblzma (2024)— malicious maintainer backdoored a core library npm/PyPI typosquats — malicious lookalike packages A supply-chain attack compromises software before it reaches you — via a dependency, build system, or distribution channel — so you ship the attacker’s code while trusting your own pipeline. Because the malicious code arrives through a trusted path (a signed update, a popular library), traditional perimeter defenses miss it. The xz backdoor showed even a single trusted maintainer can poison a library used by millions; SolarWinds showed build-system compromise scales to thousands of victims. Why it’s the hot topic: Your code is increasingly other people’s code — hundreds of transitive dependencies. The attack surface is everything you didn’t write.

questions.q: What is an SBOM and why does it matter?
questions.text: # generate a Software Bill of Materials syft packages dir:. -o spdx-json > sbom.json trivy image --format cyclonedx myapp:1.2 > sbom.cdx.json An SBOM is a complete, machine-readable inventory of every component and dependency (and version) in your software — like an ingredients label. It matters because when a new CVE drops (Log4Shell), the first question is "are we affected, and where?" Without an SBOM that takes days of manual hunting; with one it’s a query. Standard formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, generated by tools like syft or trivy . Regulators and customers increasingly require them. Log4Shell lesson: Teams with SBOMs answered "are we vulnerable?" in minutes. Teams without spent a frantic week grepping build manifests across hundreds of services.

questions.q: Explain artifact signing with Sigstore/cosign and how verification works.
questions.text: cosign sign myregistry/app@sha256:abc... # keyless, OIDC identity cosign verify --certificate-identity ci@org.com \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions... app@sha256:abc Signing proves an artifact came from a trusted builder and wasn’t tampered with. Sigstore/cosign enables keyless signing: the signer authenticates via OIDC (e.g. the CI’s identity), gets a short-lived certificate, signs, and the signature + certificate are logged in a public transparency log (Rekor). Verification checks the signature, that the signer identity matches your expected builder, and that it’s in the transparency log — no long-lived signing keys to manage or leak. Keyless is the breakthrough: Traditional signing fails because the signing key leaks. Sigstore ties signatures to ephemeral OIDC identities + a public audit log instead.

questions.q: What is SLSA and what do its levels mean?
questions.text: SLSA = Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts L1: provenance exists (how it was built) L2: signed provenance, hosted build service L3: hardened, non-falsifiable provenance, isolated builds SLSA is a framework of incremental maturity levels for build integrity. The core idea is provenance — verifiable metadata about how, where, and from what sources an artifact was built. Higher levels demand stronger guarantees: signed provenance, builds on a trusted hosted service, isolated/ephemeral build environments that can’t be tampered with, and provenance an attacker can’t forge. It gives you a roadmap to answer "can I trust that this binary was built from the source I think it was?" Provenance is the heart: SLSA is about being able to trace an artifact back to its exact source and build process, with cryptographic proof that the chain wasn’t altered.

questions.q: How do you scan container images for vulnerabilities and what are the gotchas?
questions.text: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:1.2 grype myapp:1.2 --fail-on high # scan at build (CI) AND continuously (registry/runtime) Scanners (Trivy, Grype, Clair) compare the packages in an image against CVE databases. Scan in CI to block vulnerable builds and continuously re-scan images already in your registry — new CVEs are discovered daily for images that haven’t changed. Gotchas: scanners produce false positives (a CVE in a package you don’t actually invoke) and false negatives (vendored deps, language libs they miss), and CVSS severity ≠ your real risk. Use VEX statements to suppress non-exploitable findings rather than ignoring scans. Scan continuously, not just at build: An image built clean today can be "critical" tomorrow when a new CVE lands. A one-time CI scan gives false comfort.

questions.q: What is dependency confusion and how do you defend against it?
questions.text: # attacker publishes a PUBLIC package matching your INTERNAL name # at a higher version → resolver pulls the malicious public one # defend: scoped names, explicit registry, namespace reservation Dependency confusion exploits package managers that check public registries alongside private ones: an attacker publishes a malicious public package with the same name as your internal package but a higher version, and the resolver fetches theirs. Defenses: use scoped/namespaced names tied to your org, configure the package manager to pull internal packages only from your private registry (no public fallback for those names), reserve your namespaces on public registries, and pin/verify with lockfiles and checksums. Higher version wins: Many resolvers pick the highest available version across all configured registries. Scoping and registry pinning break that attack path.

questions.q: Why are lockfiles and pinned dependencies a security control, not just reproducibility?
questions.text: # pin to exact versions + integrity hashes package-lock.json / poetry.lock / go.sum ← hash-verified # unpinned: "requests>=2.0" → silently pulls a poisoned 2.99 Lockfiles record exact versions and cryptographic hashes of every dependency, so a build always pulls the precise, verified bytes you tested. Without pinning, a range like >=2.0 means a compromised maintainer can publish a malicious patch release that silently enters your build. The integrity hashes also detect registry tampering — if the downloaded package doesn’t match the recorded hash, the build fails. So lockfiles are both reproducibility and a tamper-detection control. Hashes catch swaps: Even if an attacker replaces a package in the registry, the lockfile’s hash mismatch stops the build cold.

questions.q: What is provenance/attestation and how does it differ from an SBOM?
questions.text: SBOM → WHAT is in the artifact (the ingredients) Provenance → HOW/WHERE it was built (the recipe + kitchen) # in-toto attestation: signed statement about the build An SBOM describes what components an artifact contains; provenance (attestation) describes how it was produced — which source commit, which builder, what steps, signed so it can’t be forged. They’re complementary: the SBOM lets you answer "am I affected by CVE-X?", provenance lets you answer "was this really built from our trusted pipeline?" The in-toto framework standardizes signed attestations linking source → build → artifact. Together they close the loop: SBOM (contents) + provenance (origin) + signature (integrity) = you can trust both what’s inside and where it came from.

questions.q: How do you secure your CI/CD pipeline against being the attack vector?
questions.text: ✓ ephemeral, isolated build runners (no shared state) ✓ pin action/orb versions by SHA, not floating tags ✓ least-privilege tokens, OIDC not static keys ✓ no secrets to PRs from forks; require review for workflow changes CI is high-value: it can read your secrets and push to production. Harden it by running builds in ephemeral isolated environments (a poisoned build can’t persist), pinning third-party actions/plugins to immutable SHAs (a floating tag can be repointed to malicious code), using short-lived OIDC credentials instead of stored keys, scoping tokens to least privilege, and never exposing secrets to pull requests from forks.
