questions.q: What are reproducible builds and why do they matter for supply-chain security?
questions.text: A reproducible build yields bit-for-bit identical output from the same source, so independent parties can verify that a binary matches its claimed source and detect tampering in the build environment. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$(git log -1 --format=%ct) make build sha256sum dist/app-linux-amd64 diffoscope build-a/app build-b/app docker buildx build --provenance=true --sbom=true . Interview tip: Common blockers are timestamps, file ordering, embedded paths and non-pinned dependencies.

questions.q: How do you secure a private package registry and prevent typosquatting and malicious packages?
questions.text: Proxy public registries through an internal repository manager, allowlist packages, scope private namespaces, add cooldown periods and malware scanning, require lockfiles and integrity hashes, and block install scripts where possible. npm config set ignore-scripts true pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt npm audit signatures npm config set @acme:registry https://registry.internal/ Interview tip: Install scripts execute with developer or CI privileges at install time, so treat new packages like running unknown code.

questions.q: How do you assess and respond to a compromised maintainer or malicious release of a dependency you use?
questions.text: Identify exposure through SBOMs and lockfiles, pin or roll back to a known good version, rotate any secrets exposed to affected builds, check for indicators of compromise, and block the version at the registry proxy. npm ls malicious-pkg --all grep -R 'malicious-pkg' */package-lock.json git log --all -S'malicious-pkg@1.2.4' --oneline npm view malicious-pkg time --json Interview tip: If the bad version ran in CI, assume that job's secrets were exposed and rotate them.

questions.q: What is in-toto and how does it add verifiable steps to a software supply chain?
questions.text: in-toto defines a layout of required steps and who may perform them, and each step emits signed link metadata. A verifier checks that every step happened, by the right party, with matching materials and products. in-toto-run --step-name build --key builder.key --materials src/ --products dist/ -- make in-toto-verify --layout root.layout --layout-keys owner.pub cosign attest --type slsaprovenance --predicate prov.json $IMAGE Interview tip: Think of it as a signed checklist across the pipeline, so a skipped scan or an unauthorised build step is detectable.

questions.q: How do you vet container base images and maintain an internal golden image pipeline?
questions.text: Choose minimal, maintained bases, build golden images centrally with patching, scanning and signing, publish by digest, and rebuild on a schedule and on CVE triggers. Teams must use the approved images. docker buildx imagetools inspect registry/golden/python:3.12 trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry/golden/python:3.12 cosign sign registry/golden/python@sha256:abc crane digest registry/golden/python:3.12 Interview tip: Distroless or minimal images shrink the attack surface and the noise from scanners.

questions.q: How do you verify provenance of third-party binaries and tools downloaded in pipelines?
questions.text: Pin versions, verify checksums and signatures from a trusted source, prefer package managers with verification, mirror approved tools internally, and avoid piping curl to bash. curl -fsSLO https://host/tool_1.2.3_linux_amd64.tar.gz && sha256sum -c tool.sha256 cosign verify-blob --certificate-identity=release@org --certificate-oidc-issuer=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com --signature tool.sig tool.tar.gz gpg --verify tool.tar.gz.asc tool.tar.gz Interview tip: A checksum fetched from the same place as the binary only proves integrity in transit, not authenticity. Verify a signature.

questions.q: How do you use Pod Security Standards with namespace labels and exemptions in practice?
questions.text: Label namespaces with enforce, audit and warn levels (privileged, baseline, restricted). Start with warn and audit to find violations, fix workloads, then enforce. Exempt only specific system namespaces or users. kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted kubectl label --dry-run=server --overwrite ns --all pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline kubectl get ns --show-labels Interview tip: The server-side dry-run label shows which existing pods would violate a level before you enforce it.

questions.q: What is a securityContext and which settings give the best hardening for a typical application pod?
questions.text: runAsNonRoot, a numeric UID, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, drop ALL capabilities, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault, and no hostPath or host namespaces. Mount writable emptyDirs only where needed. securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:app kubectl exec pod -- id Interview tip: Test with the restricted Pod Security level. If your manifest passes it, you have the main hardening in place.

questions.q: How do you audit and reduce excessive Kubernetes RBAC permissions?
questions.text: Review bindings with tools such as kubectl-who-can, rbac-tool and audit logs, remove cluster-admin and wildcard grants, prefer namespaced Roles, avoid access to secrets and exec, and generate least-privilege roles from observed usage. kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .subjects' kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:app -n prod kubectl who-can get secrets -n prod rbac-tool lookup -e '.*admin.*' Interview tip: Access to create pods, read secrets, or exec into pods is effectively privilege escalation, so treat those verbs as sensitive.

questions.q: How do you secure the container runtime with gVisor, Kata Containers or user namespaces for untrusted workloads?
questions.text: Sandboxed runtimes add a boundary between workload and host kernel: gVisor intercepts syscalls in user space, Kata runs pods in lightweight VMs, user namespaces map root in the container to an unprivileged host user. Use via RuntimeClass. kubectl get runtimeclass spec: runtimeClassName: gvisor spec: hostUsers: false kubectl run test --image=alpine --overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"kata"}}' -- sleep 3600 Interview tip: Sandboxing trades some performance and compatibility for a stronger isolation boundary. Apply it where tenants are untrusted.

questions.q: How do you protect Kubernetes nodes with hardened OS images, minimal access and kubelet settings?
questions.text: Use minimal immutable node OS images, disable SSH, restrict kubelet anonymous access and read-only port, enable authorization webhook mode, apply patches by replacing nodes, and monitor with runtime tools. kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/NODE/proxy/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.authentication' kube-bench run --targets node curl -k https://NODE:10250/pods kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets Interview tip: Test that the kubelet port rejects unauthenticated requests. An open kubelet API means remote command execution on pods.

questions.q: How do you secure etcd, including encryption at rest, access control and backups?
questions.text: Restrict etcd to the API server with mTLS, isolate network access, enable encryption of Secrets at rest using a KMS provider, encrypt and access-control backups, and monitor access. Managed control planes handle much of this. ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --cacert ca.crt --cert client.crt --key client.key endpoint health kubectl get secret db -o yaml apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: EncryptionConfiguration resources: - resources: [secrets] providers: [kms: {name: kms, endpoint: unix:///kms.sock}] etcdctl snapshot save backup.db Interview tip: Base64 in a Secret is not encryption. Without encryption at rest, anyone with etcd or backup access reads every secret.

questions.q: What is Kubernetes audit logging, and how do you design an audit policy that is useful without being overwhelming?
questions.text: Audit logs record API requests by who, what and when. A policy sets levels (None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse) by resource. Log secrets at Metadata only, log writes in detail, drop noisy reads, and ship logs to a SIEM. --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml --audit-log-path=/var/log/audit.log - level: Metadata resources: [{group: "", resources: ["secrets","configmaps"]}] - level: RequestResponse verbs: ["create","patch","delete"] resources: [{group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}] jq 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.resource=="pods/exec")' audit.log Interview tip: Never log request bodies for secrets, or the audit log itself becomes a store of secrets.

questions.q: How do you secure ingress and API gateways, including TLS, WAF integration and rate limiting?
questions.text: Terminate TLS with modern settings and managed certificates, enforce HTTPS and HSTS, add a WAF, rate-limit and authenticate at the edge, restrict admin paths, and keep ingress controllers patched and isolated. nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true" nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "20" kubectl get ingress -A -o wide testssl.sh https://api.example.com Interview tip: The ingress controller is internet-facing and highly privileged, so treat it as critical, patch quickly, and limit its RBAC.

questions.q: How do you handle image pull secrets and registry authentication securely in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Use workload or node identity for cloud registries to avoid static pull secrets, scope credentials read-only per registry, rotate them, and attach pull secrets to service accounts rather than each pod. kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=registry --docker-username=u --docker-password=p kubectl patch sa default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}' aws ecr get-login-password | head -c 10 Interview tip: With cloud registries, node or workload IAM roles remove the need to store pull credentials in the cluster at all.

questions.q: How do you write and test Rego policies with conftest and OPA unit tests?
questions.text: Write policies as deny rules over structured input, test them with opa test using fixtures for allowed and denied cases, and run conftest in CI against manifests or Terraform plan JSON. Include messages that explain the fix. conftest test deployment.yaml -p policy/ opa test policy/ -v opa eval -i input.json -d policy/ 'data.main.deny' deny[msg] { input.kind == "Deployment"; not input.spec.template.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot; msg := "pods must run as non-root" } Interview tip: Test both the denied and allowed paths, and include edge cases like missing fields, because Rego treats undefined as false.

questions.q: What is Kyverno's verifyImages and how does it enforce signed images?
questions.text: verifyImages is a Kyverno rule type that checks image signatures or attestations at admission, using cosign keys or keyless identities, and can mutate tags to digests. Unverified images are rejected. kubectl get clusterpolicy verifyImages: - imageReferences: ["registry.example.com/*"] attestors: - entries: - keyless: { issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com", subject: "https://github.com/acme/*" } cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/acme/.*' registry.example.com/app@sha256:abc Interview tip: Verify against an identity (who built it), not just that some signature exists. Any attacker can sign with their own key.

questions.q: How do you use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and CEL as a native alternative to webhook-based policy engines?
questions.text: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy lets the API server evaluate CEL expressions in-process, so no external webhook is needed. It is fast, reliable and simple for common checks, with bindings selecting where to apply. kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy,validatingadmissionpolicybinding validations: - expression: "object.spec.replicas <= 10" message: "replicas must be 10 or fewer" kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deployment.yaml Interview tip: No webhook means no availability dependency and no extra latency, but CEL has less power than Rego for complex logic.

questions.q: How do you build a policy exception process that is auditable and time-bound?
questions.text: Exceptions are requested as code, linked to a ticket and owner, approved by security, scoped narrowly, and given an expiry. Dashboards track active exceptions, and automation removes or flags expired ones. kubectl get policyexception -A apiVersion: kyverno.io/v2 kind: PolicyException metadata: { name: legacy-root, annotations: { expires: "2026-12-31", ticket: "SEC-1042" } } kubectl get policyexception -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations.expires < "2026-10-21")' Interview tip: An exception without an expiry becomes permanent policy. Make the default end date short.

questions.q: How do you scan Helm charts and Kubernetes manifests in CI with kube-linter, kubesec, Trivy and Checkov?
questions.text: Render charts to manifests, then run linters and scanners for misconfigurations such as privileged pods, missing limits and latest tags. Fail on high severity, report the rest, and keep rules consistent with admission policy. helm template release ./chart -f values-prod.yaml > rendered.yaml kube-linter lint rendered.yaml trivy config rendered.yaml --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 checkov -f rendered.yaml --framework kubernetes Interview tip: Scan the rendered output with production values, since misconfigurations often come from values files, not the chart defaults.

questions.q: What is the difference between preventive, detective and corrective controls in policy as code?
questions.text: Preventive controls block bad changes (admission, CI gates, SCPs), detective controls find issues after the fact (CSPM, audits, drift detection), corrective controls fix automatically or via remediation workflow. Mature programs layer all three. aws organizations list-policies --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY kubectl get constraints aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule kubectl get clusterpolicy -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.validationFailureAction}' Interview tip: Preventive controls are cheapest per incident, but detective ones are needed for what you could not or did not prevent.

questions.q: How do you enforce tagging, ownership and cost-allocation standards through policy?
questions.text: Define required tags, enforce on creation via IaC policy checks and cloud tag policies or SCPs, detect gaps with scanning, and tie tags to ownership for alerts and cost reports. Inherit tags automatically where possible. aws organizations create-policy --type TAG_POLICY --name required-tags --content file://tags.json az policy assignment create --name require-owner --policy 'Require a tag on resources' conftest test plan.json -p policy/tags.rego gcloud asset search-all-resources --query='-labels:owner' Interview tip: Tags let a security finding find its owner. An unowned resource is an unfixed finding.

questions.q: How do you use AWS Organizations SCPs, Azure Policy and GCP organisation policies as preventive guardrails?
questions.text: They set boundaries above individual accounts or projects: deny dangerous actions, restrict regions and services, require encryption. They limit what even admins can do inside, and complement IAM rather than replace it. aws organizations list-policies --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY az policy assignment list --scope /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/prod gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --organization=ORG_ID {"Effect":"Deny","Action":"*","Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:RequestedRegion":["eu-west-1"]}}} Interview tip: Guardrails set the maximum permissions, they don't grant any. Test them in a sandbox OU first because a bad deny can break pipelines.

questions.q: How do you secure serverless and managed container platforms (Lambda, Cloud Run, Fargate) differently from VMs?
questions.text: The provider secures the host, so focus shifts to code, dependencies, per-function IAM roles, secrets handling, event input validation, network egress controls and logging. Use least privilege per function and short timeouts. aws lambda get-function --function-name fn --query 'Configuration.Role' aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $ROLE --action-names s3:DeleteBucket gcloud run services describe svc --format='value(spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName)' Interview tip: One shared over-privileged role for all functions is the classic serverless mistake. Give each function its own scoped role.

questions.q: How do you use IAM Access Analyzer, Policy Sentinel-style tools or CIEM to find unused and external access?
questions.text: Analyzers find resources shared outside the account or organisation and permissions unused over a period, and generate least-privilege policies from CloudTrail activity. Run continuously and route findings to owners. aws accessanalyzer list-findings --analyzer-arn $ARN --filter '{"status":{"eq":["ACTIVE"]}}' aws accessanalyzer start-policy-generation --policy-generation-details principalArn=$ROLE aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn $ROLE gcloud recommender recommendations list --recommender=google.iam.policy.Recommender Interview tip: Unused permissions and unused roles are free attack surface. Remove them on a schedule.

questions.q: How do you design and secure cross-account access in AWS using roles and external IDs?
questions.text: Use IAM roles assumed via sts:AssumeRole, with trust policies naming exact principals, conditions such as MFA or source organisation, and external IDs for third parties to prevent confused deputy attacks. Avoid long-lived user keys. aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::222233334444:role/audit --role-session-name me {"Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"sts:ExternalId":"abc123"}}} aws iam get-role --role-name audit --query Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument Interview tip: The external ID stops a third party from being tricked into using their access to your account on someone else's behalf.

questions.q: How do you secure DNS and prevent subdomain takeover?
questions.text: Inventory DNS records, remove dangling CNAMEs pointing to deprovisioned cloud resources, monitor for them continuously, use DNSSEC and registrar locks, and tie DNS changes to resource lifecycle in IaC. dig +short CNAME old.example.com curl -sI https://old.example.com | head -3 subjack -w subdomains.txt -t 50 -ssl aws route53 list-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --query "ResourceRecordSets[?Type=='CNAME']" Interview tip: Delete the DNS record in the same change that deletes the cloud resource it points to.

questions.q: How do you build a cloud incident response capability with forensic snapshots, isolation and log preservation?
questions.text: Prepare in advance: centralised immutable logs, a dedicated forensics account, runbooks, and automation to isolate (quarantine security group, disable keys), snapshot disks and memory, and preserve evidence with chain of custody. aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-0abc --groups sg-quarantine aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0abc --description 'IR case 1042' aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id AKIA... --status Inactive --user-name suspect aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket ir-evidence Interview tip: Isolate, don't terminate. Terminating a compromised instance destroys memory and volatile evidence.

questions.q: How do you handle authentication and session security with OAuth2, OIDC and JWT correctly?
questions.text: Use authorization code flow with PKCE, validate issuer, audience, signature and expiry, keep tokens short-lived with refresh rotation, store them safely, and never put sensitive data in unencrypted JWTs. curl -s https://issuer/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .jwks_uri jwt decode $TOKEN code_challenge=$(echo -n $VERIFIER | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=') Interview tip: Reject tokens with alg none and pin accepted algorithms. Never trust the header to choose verification behaviour.

questions.q: How do you secure file uploads and prevent SSRF, path traversal and deserialization vulnerabilities?
questions.text: For uploads: validate type by content, limit size, rename files, store outside the web root with no execute permission. For SSRF: allowlist destinations and block internal ranges. Avoid unsafe deserialization and canonicalise paths. file --mime-type upload.bin realpath --relative-base=/srv/uploads "$path" curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ # must be blocked from app pods grep -R 'pickle.loads\|ObjectInputStream' src/ Interview tip: Never trust the filename or Content-Type header from a client. Both are attacker-controlled.

questions.q: What is software composition analysis and how do you prioritise findings beyond CVSS scores?
questions.text: SCA finds known vulnerabilities in dependencies. Prioritise by reachability, exploit availability (EPSS, KEV), exposure of the service, data sensitivity and fix availability, not CVSS alone. trivy fs --scanners vuln . osv-scanner -r . grype dir:. --only-fixed curl -s https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve=CVE-2021-44228 Interview tip: CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities list is a strong signal that a CVE is being used in attacks right now.

questions.q: How do you perform threat modeling with STRIDE on a new feature, and make it lightweight for agile teams?
questions.text: Draw a data flow diagram, mark trust boundaries, apply STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) to each element, record mitigations and track them as tickets. Keep sessions short and recurring. pytm --dfd threat_model.py | dot -Tpng -o dfd.png threatdragon # open model file gh issue create --title 'Mitigate: JWT replay on /refresh' --label threat-model Interview tip: Focus on trust boundaries. The interesting threats are where data crosses from one trust level to another.

questions.q: How do you secure GraphQL and gRPC APIs differently from REST?
questions.text: GraphQL needs query depth and complexity limits, introspection control, per-field authorisation and batching limits. gRPC needs mTLS, per-method authz, message size limits and reflection control. Both still need validation and rate limiting. query { a { b { c { d } } } } # depth attack graphql-armor --max-depth 7 --max-cost 1000 grpcurl -plaintext host:50051 list grpcurl -cacert ca.pem host:443 describe svc.Service Interview tip: GraphQL's single endpoint hides authorisation gaps. Check permissions per field and per object, not per URL.

questions.q: What are secure coding guardrails for AI-assisted or third-party generated code in the pipeline?
questions.text: Treat generated or copied code as untrusted: run the same SAST, SCA, secret scanning and review as human code, require tests, restrict secrets exposure to tools, and check licences and provenance. semgrep --config auto --error src/ gitleaks protect --staged trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,license . git log --format='%an %s' --since=1.week | grep -i 'generated' Interview tip: The review burden shifts to verifying behaviour. Require tests and a human who understands the change before merge.

questions.q: How do you implement rate limiting, bot protection and abuse prevention for public endpoints?
questions.text: Apply layered limits at the edge and the application per IP, per user and per token, with token bucket algorithms, progressive challenges, anomaly detection, and returning 429 with Retry-After. Protect sensitive flows such as login and signup more tightly. limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login:10m rate=5r/m; curl -i https://api.example.com/login # expect 429 + Retry-After aws wafv2 list-rule-groups --scope REGIONAL kubectl get envoyfilter -A Interview tip: Limit by identity (account, API key) as well as IP, since attackers rotate IPs and many legitimate users share one.

questions.q: How do you map security controls to compliance frameworks like SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS without duplicating effort?
questions.text: Build one control library, map each control to multiple framework requirements, automate evidence collection from systems, and run continuous control monitoring. Audit once, satisfy many. aws configservice get-compliance-summary-by-config-rule inspec exec cis-baseline -t aws:// steampipe query "select * from aws_s3_bucket where not versioning_enabled" git log --since=90.days --format='%h %an %s' -- policy/ Interview tip: Evidence from Git history, tickets and system configuration is stronger and cheaper than screenshots collected before the audit.

questions.q: How do you run effective access reviews and manage the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle?
questions.text: Automate provisioning from the HR system, use role-based groups, review privileged access frequently and general access periodically, remove access on moves and exits immediately, and keep evidence of reviewers' decisions. aws iam generate-credential-report && aws iam get-credential-report aws iam list-users --query 'Users[?PasswordLastUsed<`2026-07-01`].UserName' gh api orgs/acme/members --paginate -q '.[].login' gcloud asset search-iam-policies --scope=organizations/ID --query='policy:user:*' Interview tip: Access that nobody reviews tends to grow forever. Make inactive access expire by default.

questions.q: How do you design a vulnerability management SLA policy and handle exceptions?
questions.text: Set remediation deadlines by severity and exposure (for example critical internet-facing in days, low in quarter), measure compliance, require risk-accepted exceptions with owner, compensating controls and expiry, and escalate breaches. trivy image --severity CRITICAL --format json app:1.4 | jq '.Results[].Vulnerabilities | length' gh api repos/org/repo/dependabot/alerts -q '.[] | select(.state=="open") | .security_advisory.severity' | sort | uniq -c jq '.[] | select(.due < now)' findings.json Interview tip: Track mean time to remediate and the percentage within SLA per team. Trends show whether the program is working.

questions.q: How do you run a security champions program and embed security into engineering teams at scale?
questions.text: Recruit volunteer engineers per team, give them training, tooling and a direct line to security, align incentives, share metrics, and make secure paths the easy default through paved roads and templates. gh repo create org/secure-service-template --template gh api orgs/acme/teams/security-champions/members -q '.[].login' semgrep ci --config p/owasp-top-ten Interview tip: Champions amplify the security team, but only if they get time allocated and recognition for the role.

questions.q: What is a security posture dashboard and which metrics should it show to executives and engineers?
questions.text: Executives need risk trend, time to remediate critical issues, coverage, incident metrics and compliance status. Engineers need actionable per-service findings, SLA status and ownership. Avoid vanity counts. jq '[.findings[]|select(.severity=="CRITICAL")]|length' findings.json promql: sum by (team) (vuln_open{severity="critical"}) promql: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(vuln_remediation_seconds_bucket[30d])) by (le)) Interview tip: A single big number such as total vulnerabilities rewards the wrong behaviour. Show risk-weighted and trend-based metrics.

questions.q: A developer pastes a production database password into a public GitHub issue. What do you do in the first hour?
questions.text: Rotate the credential immediately, remove or redact the content (knowing it is already scraped), check database logs for use since exposure, invalidate sessions, and then fix the process with scanning and training. aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/db psql -c "select usename, client_addr, backend_start from pg_stat_activity" gh api -X DELETE repos/org/repo/issues/comments/123 aws cloudtrail lookup-events --start-time 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z Interview tip: Redaction does not help. Public content is scraped within minutes, so rotation is the only real remediation.

questions.q: A scanner flags a critical CVE in a base image used by 80 services. How do you drive remediation at scale?
questions.text: Confirm exploitability and exposure, rebuild the golden image with the patch, let a bot open PRs across services, prioritise internet-facing ones, track progress on a dashboard, and use admission policy to block old digests after the deadline. syft registry/golden/python:3.12 -o json | jq '.artifacts[]|select(.name=="libfoo")' grype registry/golden/python:3.12 --only-fixed gh search prs --owner acme 'bump base image' --state open kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | grep old-digest Interview tip: Central base image plus automated update PRs turns an 80-repo problem into one patch and one rollout.

questions.q: Falco alerts that a shell was spawned in a production pod and an outbound connection to an unknown IP was made. Walk through your response.
questions.text: Treat it as likely compromise. Preserve evidence, isolate the pod with network policy rather than deleting, capture logs and filesystem, identify the entry point, check lateral movement and credentials, then rebuild and rotate. kubectl label pod web-7d9 quarantine=true --overwrite kubectl apply -f networkpolicy-quarantine.yaml kubectl logs web-7d9 --previous > pod.log kubectl debug web-7d9 -it --image=busybox --target=app Interview tip: Cordon the node and snapshot before deleting anything, so forensics remain possible.

questions.q: GuardDuty or a similar service reports crypto-mining on an EC2 instance. What is your process?
questions.text: Verify the finding, isolate the instance, preserve snapshots, identify how it got in (exposed service, leaked key, vulnerable app), revoke credentials, hunt for other affected resources and persistence, then rebuild. aws guardduty get-findings --detector-id $D --finding-ids $F aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-0abc --groups sg-quarantine aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=i-0abc aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=iam-instance-profile.arn,Values=*role* Interview tip: Check for new IAM users, access keys, and additional instances in other regions. Attackers often persist and scale out.

questions.q: You enforce a new admission policy and it blocks a critical production deployment during an incident. What do you do?
questions.text: Restore service first using a documented, audited bypass or exception, then fix the root cause. Afterwards review why audit mode did not catch it and improve rollout, communication and escape hatches. kubectl annotate ns prod policies.kyverno.io/exclude=true --overwrite kubectl get clusterpolicy -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,ACTION:.spec.validationFailureAction kubectl patch clusterpolicy require-nonroot --type merge -p '{"spec":{"validationFailureAction":"Audit"}}' Interview tip: Pre-agree the emergency path. During an incident, nobody should be inventing how to switch a policy to audit mode.

questions.q: An auditor asks for evidence that all production changes were reviewed and approved in the last quarter. How do you produce it?
questions.text: Query Git and the deployment system: list production deploys, map each to a merged PR with approvals and passing checks, flag exceptions such as emergency changes with retroactive review, and provide the protection settings as evidence. gh pr list --state merged --base main --search 'merged:2026-07-01..2026-09-30' --json number,reviews,mergedBy --limit 500 gh api repos/org/repo/branches/main/protection git log --first-parent --merges main --since=2026-07-01 --until=2026-09-30 --format='%h %s' jq '[.[]|select(.reviews|length==0)]' prs.json Interview tip: Automate the query so evidence takes minutes, and treat unreviewed changes as findings to explain, not hide.

questions.q: What is the GCP IAM model — how do principals, roles, and policies work together?
questions.text: GCP IAM controls who (principal) can do what (role) on which resource (policy binding). A policy is a collection of role bindings attached to a resource. Core concepts gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project> # view project-level policy gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <project> --member="user:x@y.com" --role="roles/viewer" gcloud iam roles describe roles/container.admin # inspect permissions in a role Principals: Google accounts, service accounts, groups, domains, allUsers/allAuthenticatedUsers. Roles: Basic (Owner/Editor/Viewer — avoid in prod), Predefined (fine-grained per service), Custom (least privilege). IAM policies are additive — no explicit deny. Resource hierarchy: Org → Folder → Project → Resource. Policies inherited downward. Interview tip: Mention that IAM conditions allow attribute-based access control (restrict by time, IP, resource tag). This is the Principal-level nuance interviewers listen for.

questions.q: A service account has too many permissions — how do you audit and enforce least privilege?
questions.text: gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project> --format=json | jq '.bindings[] | select(.members[] | contains("serviceAccount:"))' gcloud policy-intelligence query-activity --project=<project> # what permissions were actually used gcloud iam service-accounts list --project=<project> Use Policy Analyzer and IAM Recommender — GCP automatically suggests permission reductions based on 90-day usage history. Recommender shows which permissions are granted but never used. Create custom roles with only the permissions actually needed. Audit with Cloud Asset Inventory for org-wide SA permission scan. Automated enforcement: Enable IAM Recommender via Security Command Center and set up alerts for high-risk recommendations. This is how platform teams scale least-privilege across hundreds of SAs without manual audits.

questions.q: What is Workload Identity Federation — how does it replace service account keys?
questions.text: Workload Identity Federation lets external workloads (GitHub Actions, AWS, Azure, on-prem) authenticate to GCP using their native identity — no service account key files needed. gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create <pool> --location=global gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc <provider> --workload-identity-pool=<pool> --issuer-uri=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding <sa> --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member="principalSet://..." Flow: external system gets OIDC token → exchanges with GCP STS → gets short-lived access token → calls GCP APIs. No keys to rotate, no keys to leak. For GKE specifically, Workload Identity maps a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a GCP ServiceAccount — pods call GCP APIs without key files. Never use SA key files in production. They don't expire by default, are hard to rotate, and are the #1 source of GCP credential leaks. Workload Identity is the production standard for every external integration.

questions.q: IAM policy change accidentally removed access — how do you recover?
questions.text: gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project> --format=json > backup.json # always backup first gcloud projects set-iam-policy <project> backup.json # restore from backup gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.methodName="SetIamPolicy"' --limit=5 --format=json # audit who changed what If you locked yourself out of a project: use a break-glass account (org-level admin) to restore access. Check Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity) for the exact SetIamPolicy call — it records the before/after policy diff. For org-level lockout, contact GCP Support with proof of ownership. Prevention: Use Terraform for IAM management — all changes go through PR review and state diff. Never make manual IAM changes in production. Store IAM policy backups in GCS with versioning.

questions.q: How does GCP Service Account impersonation work and when should you use it?
questions.text: gcloud --impersonate-service-account=<sa>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com compute instances list gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding <target-sa> --member="serviceAccount:<caller-sa>" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator" Impersonation lets one SA act as another SA — short-lived credentials, full audit trail, no key exchange. Use it for: pipeline SA impersonating deployment SA (privilege separation), breaking glass scenarios, testing SA permissions without a key. Requires roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on the target SA. Security pattern: Human users never get SA keys — they impersonate SAs via their own identity. The audit log shows both the human and the SA identity, giving full traceability. This is the recommended model for developer access to production resources.

questions.q: GKE cluster upgrade is failing — how do you troubleshoot and manage it safely?
questions.text: gcloud container clusters describe <cluster> --zone=<zone> | grep -A5 currentMaster gcloud container operations list --filter="status=RUNNING" # any pending operations gcloud container clusters upgrade <cluster> --master # upgrade control plane first GKE upgrades: control plane first (automatic with release channels), then node pools. Enable surge upgrade on node pools: adds extra nodes during upgrade so pods are never disrupted. Set --max-surge=1 --max-unavailable=0 for zero-downtime node upgrades. Use release channels (Rapid/Regular/Stable) instead of manual version pinning — GKE manages the upgrade cadence for you. Production pattern: Use Regular channel for production. Rapid for dev/staging to catch issues early. Stable only if you have compliance requirements for specific versions.

questions.q: GKE nodes are experiencing high memory pressure — how do you diagnose and fix?
questions.text: kubectl top nodes # current usage kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A10 "Allocated resources" kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> # pods on node Distinguish between: requested memory (scheduling pressure), used memory (actual pressure), and allocatable memory (total minus OS and kubelet reservation). GKE reserves memory for OS and system daemons — subtract this from VM memory. Fix: scale node pool, enable cluster autoscaler, set accurate memory requests, or move memory-heavy workloads to dedicated node pools. GKE Autopilot advantage: No node management — GCP provisions and manages nodes automatically based on pod requests. Memory pressure becomes a pod scheduling concern, not a node ops concern. Recommend Autopilot for new clusters unless you need node-level customization.

questions.q: How do you configure GKE Workload Identity for a pod to access GCP services?
questions.text: gcloud container clusters update <cluster> --workload-pool=<project>.svc.id.goog gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding <gcp-sa>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member="serviceAccount:<project>.svc.id.goog[<namespace>/<ksa>]" kubectl annotate serviceaccount <ksa> -n <ns> iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=<gcp-sa>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com Workload Identity is the recommended way for GKE pods to call GCP APIs. The pod's Kubernetes SA is bound to a GCP SA — the metadata server on the node exchanges the KSA token for a GCP access token transparently. No key files, automatic rotation, full audit trail per pod. Common mistake: Forgetting to annotate the Kubernetes ServiceAccount OR forgetting the IAM binding on the GCP SA. Both are required. Test with kubectl exec -- gcloud auth list from the pod.

questions.q: GKE cluster autoscaler is not scaling up — how do you debug?
questions.text: kubectl describe configmap cluster-autoscaler-status -n kube-system # autoscaler decisions kubectl get events -n <ns> | grep -i "FailedScheduling|ScaleUp" gcloud container clusters describe <cluster> | grep -A5 autoscaling Autoscaler won't scale if: node pool is at max size (increase maxNodeCount), pods have PodAntiAffinity preventing placement on a new node, node selector/taint rules prevent the pod from running on any new node type, or the pending pod requests are larger than the node pool's instance type. Check the cluster-autoscaler-status ConfigMap — it explains why scale-up was skipped. Scale-down issue: Autoscaler won't remove a node if any pod has a local PVC (emptyDir with data), PodDisruptionBudget blocks eviction, or pod has cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false" annotation.

questions.q: How do you set up a private GKE cluster and what are the connectivity implications?
questions.text: gcloud container clusters create <name> --enable-private-nodes --master-ipv4-cidr=172.16.0.0/28 --enable-ip-alias gcloud container clusters update <name> --enable-master-authorized-networks --master-authorized-networks=<cidr> Private clusters: nodes have no public IPs — only RFC1918 addresses. Control plane is in a GCP-managed VPC peered to your VPC. Implications: nodes need Cloud NAT for outbound internet (image pulls, external APIs), kubectl access requires authorized networks or VPN/bastion, and inter-node traffic stays on Google's network. Use Master Authorized Networks to restrict control plane API access to specific CIDRs. Image pull: Private nodes cannot reach Docker Hub directly. Either mirror images to Artifact Registry, configure Cloud NAT, or use GKE's image streaming feature. This catches teams off-guard the first time.

questions.q: VPC network is misconfigured — traffic between VMs is not working. How do you debug?
questions.text: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="network=<vpc>" # all firewall rules gcloud compute networks subnets describe <subnet> --region=<region> gcloud compute connectivity-tests create test1 --source-instance=<vm1> --destination-instance=<vm2> --protocol=TCP --destination-port=80 Debug layers: (1) Firewall rules — default VPC allows internal traffic, custom VPCs do not. (2) Routes — is there a route to the destination subnet? (3) VM network tags — firewall rules target tags, not IPs. (4) Shared VPC — is the subnet in the correct host project? Use Connectivity Tests (Network Intelligence Center) to trace packet path and identify exactly where traffic is dropped. Network Intelligence Center: Far faster than manual firewall rule analysis. It simulates the packet path and shows the exact firewall rule accepting or blocking traffic. Always use this before manually scanning rule lists.

questions.q: How does Cloud Load Balancing work in GCP — what type do you choose for which scenario?
questions.text: # External HTTP(S) LB: global, anycast IP, URL-based routing, Cloud CDN integration # Internal HTTP(S) LB: regional, private IP, for internal microservices # TCP/UDP Network LB: regional, preserves client IP, for non-HTTP protocols gcloud compute backend-services describe <name> --global # inspect LB backend config External HTTPS LB is GKE Ingress default — uses Google's global anycast network, enabling traffic to enter from the nearest PoP worldwide. Backend health is checked via GCP health checks. Premium Tier networking routes traffic on Google's backbone; Standard Tier uses public internet. GKE Ingress note: Backend pods must pass GCP health checks or they're marked unhealthy in the LB backend. Check pod readiness AND GCP health check path/port alignment. A common source of 502 errors after deployment.

questions.q: Cloud NAT is not working — VMs cannot reach the internet. How do you debug?
questions.text: gcloud compute routers describe <router> --region=<region> # NAT router config gcloud compute routers get-nat-mapping-info <router> --region=<region> # active NAT mappings gcloud logging read 'resource.type="nat_gateway"' --limit=20 # NAT logs Check: Cloud Router exists in the correct region, NAT config covers the correct subnet (AUTO or manual subnet selection), VM has no public IP (NAT only applies to VMs without external IPs), and NAT IP allocation is not exhausted. Enable Cloud NAT logging for dropped connection visibility. Port exhaustion: Each NAT IP supports ~64K ports. High-connection workloads (like GKE pods doing many outbound calls) can exhaust NAT ports. Allocate additional NAT IPs or increase min-ports-per-VM in the NAT config.

questions.q: How does VPC peering vs Shared VPC vs VPN differ — when do you use each?
questions.text: # VPC Peering: direct connectivity, no transitive routing, both projects manage own firewall # Shared VPC: central host project owns subnets, service projects use them # Cloud VPN / Interconnect: connect to on-premises or other clouds gcloud compute networks peerings list # view existing peerings VPC Peering: peer-to-peer, low latency, no transitive routing (A-B and B-C peering doesn't give A-C connectivity). Shared VPC: org-recommended for multi-project architectures — network team owns subnets, app teams deploy into them. VPN: encrypted tunnel over internet. Dedicated/Partner Interconnect: high-bandwidth on-prem connectivity (99.99% SLA for dedicated). Enterprise pattern: Shared VPC with a hub-and-spoke topology. Central connectivity project (VPN/Interconnect) peered to the Shared VPC host. App projects are service projects. Network security team controls firewall rules centrally.

questions.q: DNS resolution is failing for a GCP resource — how do you troubleshoot Cloud DNS?
questions.text: gcloud dns managed-zones list # list DNS zones gcloud dns record-sets list --zone=<zone> # inspect records gcloud compute instances ssh <vm> -- "dig +short <hostname> @169.254.169.254" gcloud dns policies list # DNS policies on VPC Check: DNS zone is attached to the correct VPC network (private zones must be authorized for the network), record TTL (stale cache), DNS policy enabling/blocking forwarding, and VPC DNS settings. For GKE, CoreDNS queries go to the metadata server (169.254.169.254) which proxies to Cloud DNS. Hybrid DNS: For on-prem DNS resolution from GCP, use Cloud DNS inbound forwarding (creates forwarding IP in subnet) and configure on-prem DNS to forward GCP domain queries to it.

questions.q: GCS bucket is returning 403 errors — how do you debug access issues?
questions.text: gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy gs://<bucket> # bucket-level IAM gsutil acl get gs://<bucket>/<object> # object-level ACL gcloud logging read 'resource.type="gcs_bucket" protoPayload.status.code=403' --limit=10 gcloud auth application-default print-access-token # verify caller identity 403 causes: caller SA lacks roles/storage.objectViewer or storage.objectAdmin, bucket has uniform bucket-level access disabled with conflicting ACLs, VPC Service Controls perimeter blocking access, or bucket CORS config rejecting the origin. Check if Uniform Bucket-Level Access is enabled — it disables ACLs and uses IAM only. VPC Service Controls: If the bucket is inside a service perimeter, only requests from within the perimeter are allowed. A SA outside the perimeter gets 403 even with correct IAM. Check SC perimeter config first when IAM looks correct.

questions.q: BigQuery query costs are unexpectedly high — how do you investigate and control costs?
questions.text: SELECT * FROM region-us.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS_BY_PROJECT WHERE total_bytes_billed > 1000000000 ORDER BY creation_time DESC LIMIT 20; bq query --dry_run 'SELECT ...' # estimate cost before running Cost controls: partition tables by date and require partition filter (rejects full scans), cluster tables on common filter columns, use column selection (avoid SELECT *), set project-level custom quotas (max bytes per day/user), use flat-rate slots for predictable cost vs on-demand pricing. Audit with INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS to find expensive queries and their authors. Partitioned tables + partition filter: Setting require_partition_filter = true forces all queries to include a WHERE clause on the partition column. This single change can reduce BigQuery costs by 90% for time-series data.

questions.q: Cloud Spanner is showing high latency — how do you diagnose performance issues?
questions.text: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql <db> --instance=<inst> --sql='SELECT * FROM SPANNER_SYS.QUERY_STATS_TOP_HOUR ORDER BY avg_latency_seconds DESC LIMIT 10' gcloud spanner instances describe <inst> # node count Spanner latency causes: hot spots from monotonically increasing keys (use UUID or bit-reversed sequences as primary keys), insufficient nodes (scale up processing units), large read/write transactions, missing secondary indexes causing full scans, or high-priority CPU above 65%. Use Query Execution Plans to identify slow operations. Hot spot pattern: Using timestamps or auto-increment IDs as Spanner primary keys creates hot spots on the last split. Always use UUID v4 or hash-prefixed keys. This is the most common Spanner performance mistake.

questions.q: Cloud SQL instance is not accepting connections — how do you debug?
questions.text: gcloud sql instances describe <instance> | grep -E "state|ipAddresses" gcloud sql connect <instance> --user=root # direct test ./cloud_sql_proxy -instances=<project>:<region>:<instance>=tcp:5432 Connection issues: Cloud SQL Auth Proxy not running (recommended connection method — handles IAM auth and TLS), authorized networks not including the client IP (for public IP instances), SA missing roles/cloudsql.client, instance is stopped or in maintenance, max connections reached. Use PgBouncer or Cloud SQL's built-in connection pooling for high-concurrency apps. GKE pattern: Run Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar container in each pod, or as a Deployment with a ClusterIP Service. The sidecar pattern is simpler; the shared proxy pattern reduces total connections to Cloud SQL.

questions.q: Compute Engine VM is unreachable via SSH — how do you recover access?
questions.text: gcloud compute instances describe <vm> --zone=<zone> | grep -E "status|networkInterfaces" gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output <vm> --zone=<zone> # boot/OS logs gcloud compute ssh <vm> --zone=<zone> --tunnel-through-iap # SSH via IAP (no public IP needed) Recovery options: IAP TCP tunneling bypasses firewall rules and public IP requirement — just needs roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor. For SSH key issues: use OS Login (recommended) which ties SSH access to GCP IAM identity. Serial console output shows OS-level boot errors. For disk issues, detach disk, attach to recovery VM, repair, reattach. OS Login vs metadata SSH keys: OS Login is the recommended approach — maps Linux user accounts to Google identities, respects IAM, audit logs every login. Metadata SSH keys are unmanaged and hard to audit at scale.

questions.q: Cloud Run service is returning 500 errors — how do you debug?
questions.text: gcloud run services describe <service> --region=<region> # configuration gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" severity=ERROR' --limit=20 gcloud run services update-traffic <service> --to-revisions=LATEST=0,<prev-rev>=100 --region=<region> # rollback traffic Cloud Run 500 causes: application panic/crash (check container logs), container fails to start within 4 minutes (startup probe/timeout), container port mismatch (must listen on $PORT env var), exceeded concurrency limit causing queue buildup, cold start timeout, or dependency unavailable. Roll back traffic to previous revision while debugging. PORT env var: Cloud Run injects the $PORT environment variable. Your container must listen on this port — hardcoding port 8080 works only if you explicitly set it. Many teams hardcode the port and then are confused when the service returns 502.

questions.q: VM instance group is not autoscaling as expected — how do you debug MIG autoscaling?
questions.text: gcloud compute instance-groups managed describe <mig> --zone=<zone> # autoscaler config gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances <mig> --zone=<zone> gcloud compute instance-groups managed describe-autoscaler <mig> --zone=<zone> # scaling decisions Autoscaler decisions are based on: CPU utilization, HTTP LB serving capacity, Cloud Monitoring metrics, or schedule. Debug: check autoscaler status (ACTIVE/ERROR), verify metric is being emitted, check min/max instance bounds, and confirm instance template is valid. Cooldown period (default 60s) prevents rapid scale oscillation. Predictive autoscaling: GCP MIG autoscaler supports predictive mode — it learns traffic patterns and scales proactively before load spikes. Enable with --autoscaling-mode=ONLY_SCALE_OUT initially to avoid unexpected scale-in.

questions.q: How do you set up comprehensive observability in GCP — metrics, logs, and traces?
questions.text: gcloud monitoring alerting-policies list # existing alerts gcloud logging sinks list # log routing destinations gcloud trace list --project=<project> # recent traces Key setup: install Ops Agent on VMs for system metrics and logs, configure log-based metrics for business events, create alerting policies on SLO burn rates (not just thresholds), export logs to BigQuery for long-term analysis, and use Cloud Trace with OpenTelemetry SDK for distributed tracing. Create Uptime Checks for external endpoint monitoring. SLO-based alerting: Alert on error budget burn rate, not raw error rate. GCP Cloud Monitoring supports SLO burn rate alerting natively — use it over simple threshold alerts.

questions.q: Cloud Logging is missing expected logs — how do you investigate log routing issues?
questions.text: gcloud logging sinks list --project=<project> # log sinks and filters gcloud logging read 'resource.type="gce_instance"' --limit=5 # test query gcloud logging write test-log "test message" --severity=INFO # inject test log Missing logs causes: log exclusion filter on the default sink dropping logs before they reach Log Bucket, application writing to stdout but log agent not configured, resource not exporting logs to Cloud Logging, log retention period expired (default 30 days), or log sink misconfigured. Check the _Default sink's exclusion filters first. Cost vs retention: Logs are expensive at scale. Use log exclusions to drop high-volume low-value logs. Route important logs to BigQuery for long-term analysis. Set log-based alerts for critical errors instead of keeping all logs hot.

questions.q: How do you create custom dashboards and alerting policies in Cloud Monitoring?
questions.text: gcloud monitoring dashboards create --config-from-file=dashboard.json gcloud monitoring alerting-policies create --policy-from-file=alert.yaml kubernetes.io/container/cpu/request_utilization # pod CPU vs request loadbalancing.googleapis.com/https/backend_latencies # LB latency Build dashboards around golden signals: latency (p50/p99), traffic (RPS), errors (5xx rate), saturation (CPU/memory). Use Monitoring Query Language (MQL) for complex aggregations. Set up notification channels (PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Slack) before creating alerts. Dashboard as code: Export dashboard JSON, store in Git, deploy via Terraform google_monitoring_dashboard resource. All observability config should be IaC — dashboards deleted in UI get recreated automatically.

questions.q: How does VPC Service Controls work — when and how do you configure it?
questions.text: gcloud access-context-manager perimeters list --policy=<policy> gcloud access-context-manager perimeters create <name> --policy=<policy> --resources=projects/<num> --restricted-services=storage.googleapis.com VPC Service Controls creates a security perimeter around GCP services — requests from outside the perimeter are denied even with valid IAM credentials. Use for: data exfiltration prevention, compliance (HIPAA, PCI-DSS), restricting BigQuery/GCS to internal access only. Configure access levels for exceptions. Dry-run mode logs violations without enforcing — use this first to identify legitimate traffic to allowlist. Breakage risk: VPC-SC can break service integrations. Always run in dry-run mode for 2+ weeks before enforcing. Audit the violation logs thoroughly. A wrong VPC-SC config can cause widespread service outages.

questions.q: Security Command Center is showing high-severity findings — how do you triage and remediate?
questions.text: gcloud scc findings list --organization=<org> --filter="severity=HIGH AND state=ACTIVE" --format=json gcloud scc findings update <finding> --organization=<org> --state=INACTIVE # mark resolved SCC finding categories: vulnerabilities (CVEs in container images), misconfigurations (public GCS buckets, open firewall rules, SA key age), threats (anomalous API calls, cryptomining, data exfiltration), and compliance violations. Prioritize: CRITICAL > HIGH, then by asset criticality. Integrate SCC with SIEM for SOC workflows. Quick wins: SCC often flags public GCS buckets, overly permissive firewall rules (allow all ingress), and stale SA keys (>90 days). Fix these first — they're high impact, low effort. Set up SCC notifications to PagerDuty for CRITICAL findings.

questions.q: How do you implement Binary Authorization for GKE — ensuring only verified images run in production?
questions.text: gcloud container binauthz policy export > policy.yaml # export current policy gcloud container binauthz attestations sign-and-create --artifact-url=<digest-url> --attestor=<attestor> --keyversion=<kms-key> gcloud container clusters update <cluster> --binauthz-evaluation-mode=PROJECT_SINGLETON_POLICY_ENFORCE Binary Authorization enforces that only cryptographically attested images run on GKE. CI pipeline: build image → scan with Trivy/Container Analysis → if no critical CVEs, sign the image digest with KMS → attestation stored. GKE admission controller verifies attestation before allowing pod creation. Unsigned images are rejected. For Interview context: Binary Authorization is the gold standard for supply chain security in GKE. Being able to describe this end-to-end at a Principal level demonstrates mature GCP security thinking.

questions.q: A GCP service account key was accidentally committed to GitHub — what do you do?
questions.text: gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable <key-id> --iam-account=<sa> # disable immediately gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete <key-id> --iam-account=<sa> # then delete gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.authenticationInfo.serviceAccountKeyName="<key-id>"' --limit=50 # audit usage Incident response: (1) Disable the key immediately. (2) Audit Cloud Audit Logs for any usage of the compromised key. (3) Delete the key. (4) Rotate all secrets that the SA had access to. (5) Remove from Git history and force-push. (6) Enable Secret Scanning in GitHub. (7) Migrate to Workload Identity to eliminate keys entirely. Never rely on Git history deletion alone. Assume the key was already scraped by automated bots. The key is compromised — disable it first, investigate second.

questions.q: How do you implement a production-grade CI/CD pipeline on GCP using Cloud Build?
questions.text: steps: - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker args: [build, -t, IMAGE, .] - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/gke-deploy args: [run, --filename=k8s/, --cluster=<c>, --location=<z>] gcloud builds triggers create github --repo-name=<repo> --branch-pattern=main --build-config=cloudbuild.yaml Production pipeline: PR trigger → lint + test → build image → push to Artifact Registry → scan with Container Analysis → run integration tests in staging → deploy to staging → gate on test results → deploy to production. Use Cloud Build substitution variables for environment-specific config. Separate SA per environment with minimal permissions. GitOps alternative: Use Cloud Build to update the image tag in a GitOps repo → ArgoCD picks up the change and syncs to GKE. This separates CI (Cloud Build) from CD (ArgoCD) cleanly — the recommended pattern for production GKE deployments.

questions.q: Terraform is being used to manage GCP infrastructure — what GCP-specific best practices apply?
questions.text: terraform { backend "gcs" { bucket = "tf-state-<project>" prefix = "prod" } } gcloud iam roles create terraform_deployer --project=<project> --permissions=compute.instances.create,... GCP-specific Terraform best practices: store state in GCS with object versioning. Use Workload Identity for CI/CD — no SA key files. Enable GCS state locking (native, no DynamoDB equivalent needed). Organize by resource hierarchy: one root module per project/environment. Use google_project_service to manage API enablement. API enablement: Add google_project_service resources for every API your Terraform uses, with disable_on_destroy = false to avoid breaking dependent resources during teardown.

questions.q: How do you manage GCP project structure and resource hierarchy at an enterprise scale?
questions.text: gcloud resource-manager folders list --organization=<org-id> gcloud organizations get-iam-policy <org-id> # org-wide policies gcloud org-policies set-policy --organization=<org-id> constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention.yaml Recommended structure: Org → [Bootstrap, Common, Environments] folders → [network, security, prod, staging, dev] projects. One project per environment per application (project as blast radius boundary). Shared VPC host project for networking. Use Organization Policies (constraints) for guardrails: disable SA key creation, enforce resource location, require OS Login. Landing Zone pattern: Use Google's Cloud Foundation Toolkit (Terraform modules) for bootstrapping the org hierarchy. Don't design from scratch — the CFT encodes GCP best practices accumulated from thousands of enterprise deployments.

questions.q: GCP bill is unexpectedly high — how do you investigate and optimize costs?
questions.text: gcloud billing budgets list --billing-account=<account> # existing budget alerts SELECT service.description, SUM(cost) as total FROM `billing_dataset.gcp_billing_export` WHERE DATE(usage_start_time) = CURRENT_DATE()-1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC Investigation: export billing data to BigQuery (enable billing export first), query by service/project/label/SKU. Common culprits: undeleted persistent disks after VM deletion, unused static IPs, GKE nodes with low utilization, inter-region egress traffic, BigQuery on-demand scan costs. Use committed use discounts (CUDs) — 1-year CUD saves ~37%, 3-year ~55%. Label-based cost attribution: Tag all resources with team, env, application labels. Filter billing export by label to charge back costs to teams. Without labels, cost attribution becomes a guessing game at scale.

questions.q: GKE cluster costs are too high — what optimization strategies do you apply?
questions.text: kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory # find over-provisioned pods gcloud container node-pools create spot-pool --cluster=<cluster> --spot --machine-type=e2-standard-4 GKE cost optimization: (1) Spot/Preemptible VMs for batch/stateless workloads (60-90% cheaper), (2) Right-size node pools using VPA recommendations, (3) Enable cluster autoscaler to scale down idle nodes, (4) Use E2 machine family (cost-optimized), (5) Schedule dev/staging clusters to scale to zero overnight, (6) Enable GKE usage metering to attribute costs per namespace/team. Autopilot cost model: GKE Autopilot charges per pod CPU/memory request — no idle node cost. For variable workloads with low off-peak usage, Autopilot is often significantly cheaper than Standard mode clusters with persistent node pools.

questions.q: How do you implement cost governance and FinOps practices on GCP?
questions.text: gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=<account> --display-name="Prod Budget" --budget-amount=5000USD --threshold-rule=percent=0.5 --threshold-rule=percent=0.9 gcloud recommender recommendations list --project=<project> --recommender=google.compute.instance.MachineTypeRecommender --location=<region> FinOps on GCP: (1) Budget alerts per project/team, (2) Billing export to BigQuery + Looker Studio dashboards for real-time spend visibility, (3) Enforce resource labels via Organization Policy, (4) Use GCP Recommender API for automatic right-sizing suggestions, (5) Committed Use Discounts for baseline compute, (6) Monthly cost review with team leads. Principal-level ownership: A Platform Engineer builds the cost visibility tooling and governance framework. Attribute costs to teams, surface anomalies automatically, make the data self-serve. The goal is teams making cost-aware decisions independently.

questions.q: How do you manage Organization Policies to enforce guardrails across all GCP projects?
questions.text: gcloud org-policies list --organization=<org-id> # all active policies gcloud org-policies describe constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation --organization=<org-id> gcloud org-policies set-policy policy.yaml --organization=<org-id> Key Organization Policies for security: iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation (enforce Workload Identity), storage.publicAccessPrevention (no public GCS buckets), compute.requireOsLogin, compute.restrictCloudSQLInstances (private-only), gcp.resourceLocations (restrict to specific regions). Policies inherit downward and can be overridden at lower levels unless enforced. Policy inheritance override: Use inheritFromParent: false with an empty allow list to enforce a deny-all at org level that cannot be overridden by child resources.

questions.q: Cloud Interconnect is experiencing packet loss — how do you diagnose hybrid connectivity issues?
questions.text: gcloud compute interconnects describe <interconnect> # operational state gcloud compute interconnects attachments describe <attachment> --region=<region> gcloud compute routers get-status <router> --region=<region> # BGP session status Interconnect issues: BGP session down (check advertised routes and ASN config), VLAN attachment misconfiguration, physical layer issues (contact GCP Support), or route advertisement missing. For Partner Interconnect, the ISP manages the physical layer — open ticket with both GCP Support and the ISP simultaneously. Redundancy: Always provision 2 VLAN attachments in different metropolitan areas for Dedicated Interconnect (99.99% SLA requires this). A single attachment gives only 99.9% SLA.

questions.q: How do you implement multi-cluster GKE architecture for high availability?
questions.text: gcloud container fleet memberships list # GKE Fleet registered clusters gcloud container fleet ingress enable --config-membership=<cluster> # Multi-cluster Ingress gcloud container fleet multi-cluster-services enable Multi-cluster patterns: Multi-cluster Ingress with a Global Load Balancer routes traffic to the nearest healthy cluster (active-active), GKE Fleet for unified management and policy enforcement across clusters, Config Sync (ACM) for GitOps-driven config consistency. Deploy stateless workloads active-active across regions; stateful workloads with primary-replica across zones within a region. GKE Fleet: Registers clusters under a common management plane. Enables Fleet-wide policy enforcement, Config Sync across all clusters, unified observability, and multi-cluster service mesh (Anthos Service Mesh). This is the production pattern for 5+ cluster environments.

questions.q: How do you implement a secure software supply chain on GCP?
questions.text: gcloud artifacts repositories create <repo> --repository-format=docker --location=<region> gcloud artifacts docker images list <region>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo> --show-occurrences gcloud builds submit --config=cloudbuild-sign.yaml # build, scan, attest in pipeline Supply chain security layers: (1) Source — branch protection, code review, secret scanning. (2) Build — Cloud Build with hermetic builds, provenance attestation (SLSA). (3) Artifact — Artifact Registry with Container Analysis, vulnerability policy gates. (4) Deploy — Binary Authorization enforces only attested images. (5) Runtime — Falco/GKE security posture for anomaly detection. SLSA framework: GCP Cloud Build supports SLSA Level 3 provenance — cryptographic proof that a specific source commit produced a specific image via a specific build process. This is the industry direction for supply chain security and a strong Principal-level talking point.

questions.q: How would you design a complete GCP Platform Engineering architecture for a growing product company?
questions.text: This is the end-to-end system design question. A Principal Platform Engineer owns this entire picture. # Foundation: Org hierarchy via Cloud Foundation Toolkit (Terraform) # Identity: Workload Identity everywhere, OS Login for VMs, no SA keys # Networking: Shared VPC + Cloud NAT + Private GKE + Cloud Interconnect # Compute: GKE Autopilot for apps, Cloud Run for stateless APIs, Cloud SQL + Spanner for data # CI/CD: Cloud Build + Artifact Registry + ArgoCD + Binary Authorization # Observability: Cloud Monitoring + Cloud Logging + Cloud Trace + SLO alerting # Security: VPC-SC + SCC + Org Policies + KMS + Secret Manager # Cost: Billing export → BigQuery → Looker dashboards + team labels + CUDs The Platform team's output is a paved road: developers deploy applications without knowing GCP internals. Golden paths (IaC modules, CI/CD templates, observability standards) make the right thing the easy thing. Platform team measures success by developer deployment frequency and MTTR — not by individual infrastructure components. Interview framing: A Principal Platform Engineer at a security-focused company also owns the security posture of the platform itself. Tie every architectural decision back to: least privilege, auditability, data protection, and supply chain integrity. That combination — platform reliability + security-first thinking — is exactly what the role requires.

questions.q: Basic, predefined and custom roles in GCP IAM: which should you use and why avoid basic roles?
questions.text: Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) are very broad and span almost every service. Predefined roles are curated per service and job. Custom roles let you pick exact permissions but need maintenance. Prefer predefined, and custom only when none fit. gcloud iam roles describe roles/storage.objectViewer gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-proj --member=group:sre@corp.com --role=roles/logging.viewer gcloud iam roles create deployer --project=my-proj --file=role.yaml Interview tip: Say Editor can modify almost everything, including creating service accounts, so it is a privilege escalation path.

questions.q: What are IAM Conditions and IAM deny policies, and how do they differ from allow policies?
questions.text: Allow policies grant access. IAM Conditions add attributes such as time, resource name or tag to a binding. Deny policies explicitly block permissions for principals, evaluated before allow, and apply at the organization, folder or project level. gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-proj --member=user:a@corp.com --role=roles/compute.admin --condition='expression=request.time < timestamp("2026-12-31T00:00:00Z"),title=temp' gcloud iam policies create no-key-creation --attachment-point=cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/organizations/123 --kind=denypolicies --policy-file=deny.json Interview tip: Deny always wins over allow, so deny policies are a strong guardrail against mistakes in lower-level grants.

questions.q: What are the risks of the default service accounts in GCP, and how do you remove them from your design?
questions.text: The Compute Engine default service account is created with the Editor role in older projects and is attached to VMs by default. Any process on the VM inherits it. Use dedicated, least-privilege service accounts per workload and enforce with org policy. gcloud iam service-accounts list --project my-proj gcloud compute instances create vm1 --service-account=app-sa@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform gcloud resource-manager org-policies enable-enforce iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts --project my-proj Interview tip: Name the org policy iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts, which stops new projects from granting Editor to default accounts.

questions.q: How do you use IAM Recommender and Policy Intelligence to reach least privilege?
questions.text: IAM Recommender analyses 90 days of permission usage and suggests removing or replacing roles. Policy Troubleshooter explains why access was granted or denied. Policy Analyzer shows who can access what. Together they support audits and cleanup. gcloud recommender recommendations list --project=my-proj --location=global --recommender=google.iam.policy.Recommender --format=json gcloud policy-troubleshoot iam //storage.googleapis.com/projects/_/buckets/b --principal-email=a@corp.com --permission=storage.objects.get Interview tip: Apply recommendations through code review, and test in a lower environment, because rarely used permissions such as disaster recovery may not appear in the usage window.

questions.q: GKE Autopilot versus Standard: how do you choose?
questions.text:
Autopilot manages nodes, scaling and hardening, and bills per pod resource request. Standard gives control over node pools, machine types, DaemonSets and kernel settings, and bills per node. Choose Autopilot unless you need that control. gcloud container clusters create-auto prod --region europe-west1 gcloud container clusters create std --region europe-west1 --num-nodes 1 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 1 --max-nodes 5 kubectl describe pod

| grep -i 'autopilot\|cpu\|memory' Interview tip: In Autopilot, requests are what you pay for, so accurate sizing directly cuts the bill.

questions.q: What are GKE release channels and maintenance windows, and how do they keep clusters current safely?
questions.text: Rapid, Regular and Stable channels deliver Kubernetes versions at different cadences with different soak time. Cluster and node auto-upgrade follow the channel. Maintenance windows and exclusions control when upgrades happen. gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --release-channel regular gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --maintenance-window-start 2026-10-25T02:00:00Z --maintenance-window-end 2026-10-25T06:00:00Z --maintenance-window-recurrence 'FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SU' gcloud container get-server-config --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(channels)' Interview tip: Run dev on Rapid or Regular and production on Stable, so a version has been tested before it reaches production.

questions.q: How does the GKE Gateway API work compared with classic Ingress?
questions.text: Gateway API separates roles: platform teams define a Gateway tied to a load balancer, app teams attach HTTPRoutes. It supports header routing, traffic splitting, multi-cluster gateways and policies, with Google Cloud load balancers behind it. kubectl get gatewayclass kubectl apply -f gateway.yaml # gatewayClassName: gke-l7-global-external-managed kubectl describe httproute web-route Interview tip: Mention backend policies for health checks, timeouts and Cloud Armor attached through GCPBackendPolicy.

questions.q: What are GKE node pools, node auto-provisioning and compute classes, and when do you use each?
questions.text: Node pools are groups of identical nodes you define. Node auto-provisioning creates new pools automatically to fit pending pods within limits. Custom compute classes let workloads request ordered preferences, such as Spot first then on-demand, or specific machine families. gcloud container node-pools create highmem --cluster prod --region europe-west1 --machine-type n2-highmem-8 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 10 gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --enable-autoprovisioning --max-cpu 500 --max-memory 2000 Interview tip: Always set resource limits for autoprovisioning so a bad deployment cannot create unlimited nodes.

questions.q: What do Config Sync and Config Connector do in a GitOps setup on GKE?
questions.text: Config Sync continuously applies Kubernetes manifests from a Git repo to clusters and reverts drift. Config Connector exposes Google Cloud resources, such as buckets and Pub/Sub topics, as Kubernetes custom resources so they can be managed the same way. gcloud beta container fleet config-management apply --membership=prod --config=apm.yaml kubectl get storagebucket,pubsubtopic -n infra nomos status Interview tip: Alternatives to mention: Argo CD or Flux for sync, and Terraform for cloud resources. The principle is Git as the source of truth.

questions.q: How would you design a Shared VPC for a multi-team organisation on GCP?
questions.text: A host project owns the VPC and subnets, and service projects attach to it. Network admins control the network while project teams use subnets via the compute.networkUser role. This centralises firewalling and IP planning while keeping project-level billing and IAM. gcloud compute shared-vpc enable host-proj gcloud compute shared-vpc associated-projects add svc-proj --host-project host-proj gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding host-proj --member=group:team-a@corp.com --role=roles/compute.networkUser Interview tip: Grant networkUser at the subnet level, not the whole host project, so teams can only use their own subnets.

questions.q: What are Private Google Access and Private Service Connect, and how do they keep traffic off the internet?
questions.text: Private Google Access lets VMs with only internal IPs reach Google APIs. Private Service Connect creates a private endpoint with an internal IP in your VPC for Google APIs, or for services published by others, with no peering or shared address space. gcloud compute networks subnets update app-subnet --region europe-west1 --enable-private-ip-google-access gcloud compute addresses create psc-apis --global --purpose=PRIVATE_SERVICE_CONNECT --addresses=10.10.0.5 --network=prod gcloud compute forwarding-rules create pscapis --global --network=prod --address=psc-apis --target-google-apis-bundle=all-apis Interview tip: PSC is the answer when someone asks for private access to a SaaS or a producer's service across organisations without overlapping IP problems.

questions.q: How do hierarchical firewall policies and VPC firewall rules work together?
questions.text: Firewall policies can be attached to the organization, folders or networks and are evaluated top-down before VPC rules. Rules can allow, deny or delegate to the next level with goto_next. Use tags or service accounts to target workloads. gcloud compute network-firewall-policies create corp-baseline --global gcloud compute network-firewall-policies rules create 100 --firewall-policy corp-baseline --global-firewall-policy --action deny --direction INGRESS --src-ip-ranges 0.0.0.0/0 --layer4-configs tcp:22,tcp:3389 gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter='network:prod' --sort-by=priority Interview tip: Prefer secure tags or service account targets over network tags, since network tags can be set by anyone with VM edit rights.

questions.q: How do Cloud DNS private zones, forwarding and peering work for hybrid name resolution?
questions.text: Private zones answer names only for attached VPCs. Forwarding zones send queries for a domain to on-premises DNS. Inbound server policies let on-premises resolvers query Cloud DNS.
