DNS peering shares zones between VPCs without full network peering. gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-private --dns-name=corp.internal. --visibility=private --networks=prod --description=internal gcloud dns managed-zones create onprem-fwd --dns-name=onprem.example.com. --visibility=private --networks=prod --forwarding-targets=10.200.0.2 gcloud dns policies create inbound --networks=prod --enable-inbound-forwarding Interview tip: Hub-and-spoke DNS: host private zones in a central project and use DNS peering from spokes.

questions.q: GCS storage classes, Autoclass and lifecycle rules: how do you optimise storage cost?
questions.text: Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive trade lower storage price for higher retrieval cost and minimum storage duration, all with the same millisecond access. Lifecycle rules transition or delete by age. Autoclass moves objects automatically based on access. gsutil lifecycle set lifecycle.json gs://my-bucket gcloud storage buckets update gs://my-bucket --enable-autoclass gcloud storage objects update gs://my-bucket/old.log --storage-class=COLDLINE Interview tip: Remember early deletion fees: Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90, Archive 365.

questions.q: Signed URLs and signed policy documents in Cloud Storage: how do you give temporary access safely?
questions.text: A signed URL grants time-limited access to one object using the signer's credentials. Prefer V4 signing with a service account that has minimal access, via impersonation instead of key files. Policy documents control browser uploads. gcloud storage sign-url gs://bucket/report.pdf --duration=10m --impersonate-service-account=signer@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding signer@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com --member=user:a@corp.com --role=roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator Interview tip: Avoid downloading service account keys just to sign. IAM Credentials signBlob works with impersonation.

questions.q: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk and Filestore: how do you choose block and file storage on GCP?
questions.text: Persistent Disk (balanced, SSD, standard) is the default block storage. Hyperdisk lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently for demanding databases. Filestore provides managed NFS for shared access, including by GKE pods. gcloud compute disks create data1 --size=500GB --type=pd-balanced --zone=europe-west1-b gcloud compute disks create fast1 --size=1TB --type=hyperdisk-balanced --provisioned-iops=20000 --provisioned-throughput=800 --zone=europe-west1-b gcloud filestore instances create shared --zone=europe-west1-b --tier=ENTERPRISE --file-share=name=vol1,capacity=1TB --network=name=prod Interview tip: Regional persistent disks replicate synchronously across two zones, which helps stateful workloads fail over without data loss.

questions.q: How do managed instance group rolling updates, autohealing and health checks work together?
questions.text: A MIG replaces instances gradually to a new template using maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Autohealing recreates VMs that fail an application-level health check after an initial delay. Load balancer health checks are separate and only control traffic. gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig --version=template=web-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0 --region=europe-west1 gcloud compute instance-groups managed update web-mig --health-check=app-hc --initial-delay=300 --region=europe-west1 gcloud compute instance-groups managed describe web-mig --region=europe-west1 Interview tip: Set the autohealing initial delay longer than your slowest boot, or healthy-but-booting VMs will be killed in a loop.

questions.q: Spot VMs on GCP: how do they work and how do you use them safely?
questions.text: Spot VMs are heavily discounted instances that Google can stop at any time with a 30-second notice and have no maximum runtime. Use them for stateless, batch or fault-tolerant work with checkpointing, and mix with on-demand capacity for baseline. gcloud compute instances create worker1 --provisioning-model=SPOT --instance-termination-action=STOP --machine-type=e2-standard-4 curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/preempted gcloud container node-pools create spot-pool --cluster prod --spot --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 20 Interview tip: Poll the preempted metadata flag or handle the ACPI shutdown signal so work can checkpoint within the 30 seconds.

questions.q: What are OS Login and IAP TCP forwarding, and why use them instead of SSH keys and public IPs?
questions.text: OS Login ties SSH access to IAM identities, so access and sudo are granted by roles and logged, with no key distribution. IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH or RDP through Google's identity-aware proxy to VMs that have no external IP. gcloud compute project-info add-metadata --metadata enable-oslogin=TRUE gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-proj --member=group:ops@corp.com --role=roles/compute.osAdminLogin gcloud compute ssh vm1 --tunnel-through-iap --zone=europe-west1-b Interview tip: IAP needs a firewall rule allowing 35.235.240.0/20 on port 22, a detail interviewers like to hear.

questions.q: How do you define SLIs and SLOs in Cloud Monitoring and alert on error budget burn?
questions.text: Create a service, define a request-based or window-based SLI from a metric such as load balancer request count and latency, set an SLO target over a rolling or calendar window, and add burn-rate alerting policies on the error budget. gcloud monitoring slos create --service=checkout --display-name='99.9% availability' --goal=0.999 --rolling-period=28d --request-based-sli=... gcloud alpha monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=burn-rate.yaml Interview tip: Use two burn-rate windows, fast and slow, to catch sudden outages and slow leaks without constant noise.

questions.q: How do Cloud Logging sinks, log-based metrics and exclusion filters work together?
questions.text: Sinks route matching logs to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or another bucket. Log-based metrics turn log patterns into metrics for dashboards and alerts. Exclusion filters drop logs before storage to cut cost. The _Required bucket cannot be disabled. gcloud logging sinks create audit-to-bq bigquery.googleapis.com/projects/sec-proj/datasets/audit --log-filter='logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com"' --include-children --organization=123 gcloud logging metrics create http_5xx --log-filter='resource.type="k8s_container" AND jsonPayload.status>=500' gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-days=30 Interview tip: Remember to grant the sink's writer identity access on the destination, a step people often forget.

questions.q: What is Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, and when is it better than self-hosting Prometheus?
questions.text: It is a managed, Prometheus-compatible backend (Monarch) that stores metrics globally, queried with PromQL. You keep exporters and PodMonitoring resources, but avoid running storage, sharding and retention yourself. Charges are per sample ingested. kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/prometheus-engine/main/examples/pod-monitoring.yaml kubectl get podmonitoring -A gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --enable-managed-prometheus Interview tip: Cost is driven by sample count, so control cardinality and scrape interval.

questions.q: How do you use Secret Manager safely from applications on GCP, and handle rotation?
questions.text: Store secrets in Secret Manager with versions and IAM at the secret level. Applications use their workload identity to access the latest or a pinned version. Rotation publishes Pub/Sub notifications that trigger a function to create a new version. gcloud secrets create db-password --replication-policy=automatic printf 's3cr3t' | gcloud secrets versions add db-password --data-file=- gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password --member=serviceAccount:app@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor Interview tip: Pin to a version number in production and move it deliberately, rather than reading latest, to avoid surprise breakage during rotation.

questions.q: What are customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS, and when are they worth the overhead?
questions.text: By default Google encrypts data with Google-managed keys. CMEK lets you control a Cloud KMS key used to encrypt supported services, giving you rotation control, the ability to disable or destroy the key to cut access, and separate duties. It adds operational responsibility. gcloud kms keyrings create prod --location=europe-west1 gcloud kms keys create bucket-key --keyring=prod --location=europe-west1 --purpose=encryption --rotation-period=90d --next-rotation-time=2026-12-01T00:00:00Z gcloud storage buckets update gs://secure-bucket --default-encryption-key=projects/p/locations/europe-west1/keyRings/prod/cryptoKeys/bucket-key Interview tip: If the key is disabled or destroyed, the data becomes unreadable. Protect key admin access and enable key destruction scheduling delays.

questions.q: Which Cloud Audit Logs types exist, and which must you enable explicitly?
questions.text: Admin Activity logs are always on and free. System Event logs are always on. Data Access logs record reads and data writes but are off by default for most services (except BigQuery) and must be enabled. Policy Denied logs record security policy denials. gcloud projects get-iam-policy my-proj --format='yaml(auditConfigs)' gcloud logging read 'logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity" AND protoPayload.methodName="SetIamPolicy"' --limit 10 gcloud projects set-iam-policy my-proj policy-with-auditconfigs.yaml Interview tip: Data Access logs can be voluminous and costly, so enable them for sensitive services and exempt noisy service accounts.

questions.q: What does Cloud Deploy add on top of Cloud Build for delivery to GKE and Cloud Run?
questions.text: Cloud Build builds and tests artifacts. Cloud Deploy manages delivery pipelines across targets with promotion, approvals, canary and blue-green strategies through Skaffold, rollback, and a release audit trail. gcloud deploy apply --file=clouddeploy.yaml --region=europe-west1 gcloud deploy releases create rel-042 --delivery-pipeline=web --region=europe-west1 --images=web=europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/proj/repo/web:42 gcloud deploy rollouts promote rel-042 --delivery-pipeline=web --region=europe-west1 Interview tip: The key sentence: Build creates the artifact once, Deploy promotes the same artifact through environments.

questions.q: How do Cloud Build private pools and triggers work, and why use them for builds that touch private resources?
questions.text: Default workers run in a Google-managed network with no access to your VPC. Private pools run in a peered network, giving builds access to private registries, databases or GKE control planes, with custom machine sizes and VPC Service Controls support. gcloud builds worker-pools create private-pool --region=europe-west1 --peered-network=projects/host/global/networks/prod --worker-machine-type=e2-standard-4 gcloud builds triggers create github --name=main-build --repo-name=app --repo-owner=corp --branch-pattern='^main$' --build-config=cloudbuild.yaml --service-account=projects/p/serviceAccounts/builder@p.iam.gserviceaccount.com Interview tip: Use a dedicated user-specified service account per trigger instead of the legacy default Cloud Build account.

questions.q: How do committed use discounts work on GCP, and how do they differ from sustained use discounts?
questions.text: Committed use discounts trade a one or three year commitment for a lower price, either resource-based (vCPU, memory) or spend-based (flexible). Sustained use discounts are automatic for some machine types and run-time, and are limited to older series. Combine with Spot for variable work. gcloud compute commitments create web-cud --region=europe-west1 --plan=12-month --resources=vcpu=64,memory=256GB gcloud billing accounts list bq query 'SELECT service.description, SUM(cost) FROM `billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXX` GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC' Interview tip: Buy commitments for the steady baseline only, and review utilisation of the commitment monthly.

questions.q: How do you set up billing export to BigQuery and labels to attribute GCP costs to teams?
questions.text: Enable standard and detailed usage cost export to a BigQuery dataset, standardise resource labels such as team and env enforced by policy, use folders and projects as the main boundary, and build dashboards with Looker Studio on the export data. bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT labels.value AS team, SUM(cost) FROM `billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_X`, UNNEST(labels) AS labels WHERE labels.key="team" GROUP BY 1' gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=ABC --display-name=team-a --budget-amount=5000USD --threshold-rule=percent=0.8 Interview tip: Labels apply only from when they are set. They are not retroactive, so enforce them at resource creation.

questions.q: BigQuery on-demand versus capacity (slot) pricing: how do you choose and control query cost?
questions.text: On-demand charges per TB scanned and shares a pool of slots. Capacity pricing buys dedicated slots with editions and autoscaling, giving predictable cost for heavy workloads. Control cost with partitioning, clustering, selecting only needed columns, and quotas. bq query --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT * FROM `proj.ds.events` WHERE dt = "2026-10-20"' bq query --maximum_bytes_billed=10000000000 --use_legacy_sql=false '...' bq mk --reservation --location=EU --edition=ENTERPRISE --slot_capacity=100 prod-res Interview tip: Always partition large tables on a date column and require a partition filter to prevent accidental full scans.

questions.q: GKE pods are Pending with 'Insufficient' errors or IP allocation failures. How do you diagnose it?
questions.text:
Distinguish resource shortage from IP exhaustion. Check pod events, node allocatable versus requests, autoscaler status, and the pod secondary range utilisation. VPC-native clusters allocate a /24 slice of the pod range per node, which can run out. kubectl describe pod

| tail -15 kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODCIDR:.spec.podCIDR gcloud container clusters describe prod --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(ipAllocationPolicy,defaultMaxPodsConstraint)' Interview tip: Lower max pods per node or add a discontiguous pod range to extend a cluster that ran out of pod IPs.

questions.q: A GKE Ingress or Gateway returns 502 errors and the backend shows as unhealthy. What do you check?
questions.text: The Google load balancer health check must succeed against the pod. Check that firewall rules allow Google health check ranges, the readiness probe and health check path match, container-native NEGs are in use, and the app listens on the target port. kubectl describe ingress web gcloud compute backend-services get-health k8s1-abc-web-80 --global gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter='sourceRanges:(130.211.0.0/22 35.191.0.0/16)' Interview tip: The load balancer health check is derived from the readiness probe by default, but only if the path and port are compatible.

questions.q: A GKE node auto-upgrade broke workloads. How do you reduce the blast radius next time?
questions.text: Identify what changed: a Kubernetes version removing an API or changing behaviour, node image changes, or workloads that cannot tolerate disruption. Use release channels with soak, maintenance windows and exclusions, surge settings, PDBs, and test in staging. gcloud container operations list --filter='operationType:UPGRADE_NODES' --limit 5 kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30 gcloud container node-pools update pool1 --cluster prod --region europe-west1 --max-surge-upgrade 2 --max-unavailable-upgrade 0 Interview tip: For a risky window, use a maintenance exclusion, and for a rollback create a new pool on the old version if the old minor is still supported.

questions.q: A pod using Workload Identity cannot access Google APIs and gets 403 or metadata server errors. How do you fix it?
questions.text:
Check that Workload Identity is enabled on the cluster and node pool, the Kubernetes service account is annotated with the Google service account, the IAM binding grants roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser to the right namespace and name, and the GSA has the needed permissions. kubectl get sa app -n prod -o yaml | grep iam.gke.io gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy app-gsa@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com kubectl exec

-- curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/email Interview tip: The member format is serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA]. A typo there is the most common cause.

questions.q: The GKE cluster autoscaler is not adding nodes though pods are Pending. What are the usual causes on GCP?
questions.text: Quota limits (CPUs, IPs, disks), max node count reached, no node pool that fits the pod's requests, selectors or zone constraints, a PVC bound to a zone with no capacity, or stockouts of a machine type in a zone. kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=NotTriggerScaleUp gcloud container clusters describe prod --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(autoscaling,nodePools[].autoscaling)' gcloud compute regions describe europe-west1 --format='yaml(quotas)' | grep -B1 -A1 'CPUS\|IN_USE_ADDRESSES' Interview tip: Use multiple zones and machine types, or node auto-provisioning, to reduce zonal stockout failures.

questions.q: Cloud Run cannot connect to Cloud SQL or a private service in your VPC. How do you set up connectivity?
questions.text: Cloud Run is serverless and outside your VPC by default. Use the Cloud SQL connection (unix socket via the Auth proxy built-in) for Cloud SQL, and Direct VPC egress or a Serverless VPC Access connector for private IPs, with correct firewall rules and egress setting. gcloud run deploy api --image=... --add-cloudsql-instances=proj:europe-west1:db gcloud run deploy api --image=... --network=prod --subnet=run-subnet --vpc-egress=private-ranges-only gcloud run services describe api --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(spec.template.metadata.annotations)' Interview tip: The Cloud Run service account needs the Cloud SQL Client role, a frequent missing piece.

questions.q: A Pub/Sub subscription backlog keeps growing. How do you investigate and fix it?
questions.text: Compare publish rate to ack rate, check oldest unacked message age, subscriber errors and ack deadline expirations, then scale subscribers, tune flow control, fix poison messages with dead-letter topics, and look at downstream dependencies. gcloud monitoring time-series list --filter='metric.type="pubsub.googleapis.com/subscription/num_undelivered_messages"' gcloud pubsub subscriptions describe orders-sub --format='yaml(ackDeadlineSeconds,deadLetterPolicy,retryPolicy)' gcloud pubsub subscriptions update orders-sub --dead-letter-topic=orders-dlq --max-delivery-attempts=5 Interview tip: Alert on oldest_unacked_message_age, not just message count, since age directly maps to user-visible delay.

questions.q: Cloud NAT drops connections with 'OUT_OF_RESOURCES' or allocation failures under load. What is the cause and fix?
questions.text: Each NAT IP provides about 64,512 ports, divided among VMs. When a VM exhausts its allocated ports to the same destination, new connections fail. Raise minimum ports per VM, add NAT IPs, enable dynamic port allocation, and reuse connections. gcloud compute routers nats describe nat1 --router=rtr1 --region=europe-west1 gcloud compute routers nats update nat1 --router=rtr1 --region=europe-west1 --enable-dynamic-port-allocation --min-ports-per-vm=128 --max-ports-per-vm=4096 gcloud logging read 'resource.type="nat_gateway" AND jsonPayload.allocation_status="DROPPED"' --limit 10 Interview tip: Connection pooling and keep-alive in the application is the cheapest fix, since it removes the need for so many ports.

questions.q: A request is denied by VPC Service Controls and the team cannot reach a service from their CI system. How do you investigate and fix it safely?
questions.text: Look up the violation in audit logs (Policy Denied) for the unique ID, which shows the source identity, network, service and which rule it breached. Fix with an ingress or egress rule scoped to the specific identity, project and method, or an access level, rather than loosening the perimeter. gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.metadata.violationReason="RESOURCES_NOT_IN_SAME_SERVICE_PERIMETER"' --limit 5 --format=json gcloud access-context-manager perimeters describe prod-perimeter --policy=POLICY_ID gcloud access-context-manager perimeters dry-run update prod-perimeter --policy=POLICY_ID --add-ingress-policies=ingress.yaml Interview tip: Test changes in dry-run mode first, which logs would-be violations without enforcing.

questions.q: A deployment fails with 'Permission denied' even though the engineer has Owner. Which other layers could be blocking it?
questions.text: Owner can still be blocked by organisation policies, IAM deny policies, VPC Service Controls, missing API enablement, billing issues, or quotas. Use Policy Troubleshooter and the error's details to find which layer denied the call. gcloud policy-troubleshoot iam //cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/projects/my-proj --principal-email=a@corp.com --permission=compute.instances.create gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --project=my-proj gcloud services list --enabled --project=my-proj | grep compute Interview tip: Read the full error. Organisation policy errors name the constraint, like constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess.

questions.q: Terraform on GCP fails with 'API has not been used in project' or 'service account does not have permission'. How do you make it reliable?
questions.text: Enable required APIs explicitly with google_project_service, wait for propagation using dependencies, grant the Terraform service account the needed roles, and check the right quota project and impersonation settings. Split bootstrap from application stacks. gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com container.googleapis.com --project my-proj terraform apply -var=impersonate_sa=tf-deployer@admin-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project my-proj Interview tip: Use depends_on or the service resource output as a dependency so resources do not race the API enablement.

questions.q: GKE cannot pull images from Artifact Registry and shows 403 or ImagePullBackOff. What do you check?
questions.text:
The node service account needs Artifact Registry Reader on the repository, the repository must be in a reachable location, private clusters need Private Google Access, and image paths must be exact. Check cross-project permissions and VPC Service Controls. kubectl describe pod

| grep -A5 Events gcloud artifacts repositories get-iam-policy repo --location=europe-west1 gcloud artifacts docker images list europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/proj/repo Interview tip: With custom node service accounts, remember to grant them the Reader role. Only the default account may have had it implicitly.

questions.q: A large GCP network egress charge appeared. How do you find the traffic and reduce it?
questions.text: Use billing export by SKU to see whether it is internet egress, inter-region, inter-zone or CDN. Then VPC Flow Logs and Network Intelligence to find sources and destinations. Reduce with Cloud CDN, regional co-location, compression, caching, and private paths. bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT sku.description, SUM(cost) c FROM `billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_X` WHERE service.description="Compute Engine" AND sku.description LIKE "%Egress%" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY c DESC' gcloud compute networks subnets update app --region=europe-west1 --enable-flow-logs --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-5-min gcloud compute backend-services update web --enable-cdn --global Interview tip: Cross-zone and cross-region traffic inside the same app is a quiet cost, so check topology before blaming the internet.

questions.q: Cloud Logging costs have exploded. How do you identify the source and reduce them without losing important logs?
questions.text: Use Logs Explorer and the log volume metrics to see bytes ingested by resource and log name. Typical culprits are debug logging, load balancer or VPC flow logs, and chatty GKE containers. Add exclusion filters, sampling, routing to cheaper storage, and retention changes. gcloud logging metrics list gcloud logging sinks update _Default --add-exclusion=name=drop-health,filter='httpRequest.requestUrl=~"/healthz"' gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-days=14 Interview tip: The logging/billing/bytes_ingested metric by resource_type quickly shows who generates the volume.

questions.q: A log sink to BigQuery is not receiving data. What do you check?
questions.text: Verify the sink's filter matches entries, the sink's writer identity has BigQuery Data Editor on the dataset, the destination dataset exists in an allowed location, the sink is not disabled or excluded upstream, and check for sink errors in the logs. gcloud logging sinks describe audit-to-bq bq show --format=prettyjson proj:audit | grep -i location gcloud logging read 'logName:"logging.googleapis.com%2Fsink_error"' --limit 5 Interview tip: The writer identity is created per sink. Copy it from the describe output and grant it on the destination, every time.

questions.q: A managed instance group keeps recreating instances in an autohealing loop. How do you stop it and find the cause?
questions.text: Instances are failing the autohealing health check, often because the initial delay is too short, the check path or port is wrong, a firewall blocks health check ranges, or the app crashes under load. Disable autohealing temporarily, inspect an instance, then fix. gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-errors web-mig --region=europe-west1 gcloud compute instance-groups managed update web-mig --clear-autohealing --region=europe-west1 gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output <vm> --zone=europe-west1-b | tail -50 Interview tip: The serial port output shows startup script failures, which are a frequent root cause for new instances never becoming healthy.

questions.q: A Cloud VPN tunnel is established but BGP is down or routes are missing on-premises. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: Check tunnel status and IKE logs, then BGP peer settings: ASNs, link-local IPs, MD5 if used, and Cloud Router advertised routes. Verify firewalls on both sides and that overlapping ranges are not present. Use route and learned-route views. gcloud compute vpn-tunnels describe tun1 --region=europe-west1 --format='yaml(status,detailedStatus)' gcloud compute routers get-status rtr1 --region=europe-west1 gcloud compute routers update-bgp-peer rtr1 --peer-name=peer1 --region=europe-west1 --advertisement-mode=CUSTOM --set-advertisement-ranges=10.10.0.0/16 Interview tip: Tunnel up and BGP down usually points to an ASN or link-local address mismatch, or a firewall dropping TCP 179.

questions.q: A Compute Engine persistent disk is almost full. How do you grow it online and avoid a repeat?
questions.text: Resize the disk with gcloud, which works while attached, then grow the partition and filesystem in the guest. Take a snapshot first. Find the cause of growth and add monitoring with the Ops Agent for disk usage alerts. gcloud compute disks snapshot data1 --zone=europe-west1-b --snapshot-names=pre-resize gcloud compute disks resize data1 --size=600GB --zone=europe-west1-b sudo growpart /dev/sdb 1 && sudo resize2fs /dev/sdb1 Interview tip: Disks can only grow, never shrink, so go up in measured steps.

questions.q: A Security Command Center finding reports a publicly accessible Cloud Storage bucket. How do you respond?
questions.text: Confirm whether the exposure is intended, then remove public access, enable public access prevention and uniform bucket-level access, check access logs for what was read, and fix the pipeline or policy that allowed it. Use org policy to stop recurrence. gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy gs://my-bucket --format=json | grep -E 'allUsers|allAuthenticatedUsers' gcloud storage buckets update gs://my-bucket --public-access-prevention --uniform-bucket-level-access gcloud resource-manager org-policies enable-enforce storage.publicAccessPrevention --organization=123 Interview tip: Check Data Access audit logs, if enabled, to see whether anyone actually read objects while it was public.

questions.q: Spot VM or Spot GKE node preemptions are causing batch jobs to fail. How do you make them resilient?
questions.text: Make work restartable: checkpoint progress, make tasks idempotent, use a queue so unfinished tasks return, handle the shutdown signal to save state, diversify zones and machine types, and keep a small on-demand pool to guarantee completion. gcloud compute instances describe worker1 --zone=europe-west1-b --format='value(scheduling.provisioningModel)' kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector status.phase=Failed gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.methodName="compute.instances.preempted"' --limit 10 Interview tip: Measure preemption frequency. If a job is shorter than the typical time between preemptions, retries are cheap.

guides.title: Git in Production Environments — Interview Guide

questions.q: How does Git store data internally — what is the object model?
questions.text: Git is a content-addressable filesystem. Every piece of data is stored as an object identified by its SHA-1 (now SHA-256 in new repos) hash of its content. There are four object types. Object types blob — stores file content (not filename, not path) tree — stores directory listing: blob/tree references + names + permissions commit — stores tree pointer + parent commit(s) + author + message tag — annotated tag: pointer to commit + tagger + message git cat-file -t <sha> # show object type git cat-file -p <sha> # print object content git cat-file -p HEAD # inspect current commit git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree} # inspect current tree find .git/objects -type f # see all stored objects A commit is a snapshot, not a diff. It stores a pointer to the full tree at that moment. The efficiency comes from sharing: if 99% of files are unchanged, those blobs are reused. Git computes diffs on the fly when you run git diff — it is not stored. This immutable, content-addressed model is what makes branching and merging cheap, and what makes rewriting history (rebase, amend) create new objects rather than modifying existing ones. Interview depth: Understanding that a branch is just a file in .git/refs/heads/ containing a SHA, and HEAD is just a file containing either a branch name or a SHA (detached HEAD), reveals you understand Git at the plumbing level — not just the porcelain commands.

questions.q: What is the difference between git fetch, git pull, and git pull --rebase?
questions.text: git fetch origin # download remote changes, do NOT modify working tree git fetch origin main # fetch specific branch only git pull # fetch + merge (creates merge commit if diverged) git pull --rebase # fetch + rebase local commits on top of remote git pull --rebase=interactive # fetch + interactive rebase (squash/reorder) # Set rebase as default pull strategy: git config --global pull.rebase true # See divergence before pulling: git fetch origin && git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main git fetch is always safe — it updates remote-tracking branches (origin/main) but never touches your working directory or local branches. git pull = fetch + merge: if your local branch has diverged, it creates a merge commit, producing an ugly history. git pull --rebase replays your local commits on top of the fetched remote, keeping history linear. For feature branch development, --rebase is almost always preferred. Set pull.rebase=true globally to make this the default and avoid accidental merge commits. Never rebase shared branches: git pull --rebase on a branch others are working on rewrites commit SHAs. Anyone else who has pulled that branch now has diverged history. Only rebase local commits that have not been pushed, or use rebase on your private feature branch before merging to main.

questions.q: Explain HEAD, staging area, and working tree — what are the three trees of Git?
questions.text: Working Tree — files on disk as you see them in your editor Index (Stage) — snapshot prepared for next commit (.git/index) HEAD — pointer to last commit on current branch git status # compares all three trees git diff # working tree vs index (unstaged changes) git diff --staged # index vs HEAD (staged, what will be committed) git diff HEAD # working tree vs HEAD (all uncommitted changes) cat .git/HEAD # see what HEAD points to git ls-files --stage # show index contents The three-tree model explains every Git operation: git add moves changes from working tree to index. git commit creates a new commit from the index and advances HEAD. git checkout branch moves HEAD to the branch and updates both index and working tree to match that commit. git reset --soft HEAD~1 moves HEAD back but leaves index and working tree untouched. git reset --hard HEAD~1 moves HEAD back AND resets index AND working tree — destructive. Understanding which trees each command touches is the key to avoiding data loss. The mental model: Every Git command moves data between these three trees. Before running any destructive operation, ask: which of the three trees does this affect? git reset --hard affects all three (dangerous). git reset --soft affects only HEAD (safe). This framework prevents most common Git mistakes.

questions.q: What is a detached HEAD state — how do you get into it and how do you get out?
questions.text: git checkout v1.2.3 # checking out a tag → detached HEAD git checkout abc1234 # checking out a commit SHA → detached HEAD cat .git/HEAD # shows SHA instead of ref: refs/heads/branch git status # "HEAD detached at abc1234" # Recover: create a branch to save your work git checkout -b my-experiment # create branch at current detached HEAD git switch -c my-experiment # modern syntax # Or discard: go back to a branch git checkout main # HEAD re-attaches to main branch git switch main # modern syntax Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit SHA instead of a branch name. You can make commits in this state, but they are not on any branch — when you switch away, they become unreachable and will eventually be garbage collected (git gc). Any work done in detached HEAD state must be saved to a branch before switching away. Detached HEAD is not an error — it is intentional when inspecting historical commits, checking out tags for a build, or doing temporary experiments. Recovering lost commits: If you made commits in detached HEAD and switched away, use git reflog to find the SHA of your last commit in that state, then git checkout -b rescue <sha> to create a branch at that point. git reflog keeps all recent HEADs for 30-90 days.

questions.q: What is git stash — how do you use it effectively in a team environment?
questions.text: git stash # stash tracked changes (index + working tree) git stash push -u # include untracked files git stash push -m "WIP: auth refactor" # named stash git stash list # show all stashes git stash show -p stash@{0} # show diff of top stash git stash pop # apply top stash + remove from stash list git stash apply stash@{2} # apply specific stash (keep in list) git stash drop stash@{0} # remove specific stash git stash branch feature/new stash@{0} # create branch from stash git stash clear # drop ALL stashes (destructive) Stash is a stack of partial work saves. Use it when you need to switch context quickly without committing incomplete work. In team environments, stash is local — stashes are not pushed to remote and are not visible to teammates. Stash pop can conflict if the stashed changes conflict with the current state of the branch — treat it like any other merge conflict. For longer-term WIP storage, create a WIP commit (git commit -m "WIP: [description]") and push it to a remote branch — this backs up work and is visible to the team. Stash is not a backup: Stashes are stored in .git/refs/stash and are lost if you delete the repo or if something corrupts .git. For work you care about, commit to a branch and push. Never rely on stash as long-term storage for important work.

questions.q: What is a Git branch internally — how do branches and tags differ?
questions.text: cat .git/refs/heads/main # branch file: just a 40-char SHA cat .git/refs/tags/v1.0.0 # lightweight tag: same as branch git cat-file -p v1.0.0 # annotated tag: separate tag object git branch # list local branches git branch -vv # show tracking info + last commit git branch -a # local + remote-tracking branches git branch --merged main # branches merged into main (safe to delete) git branch --no-merged main # branches NOT yet merged (caution deleting) git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0" # annotated tag (recommended) git tag v1.2.0 # lightweight tag (just a pointer) A branch is simply a file containing a 40-character commit SHA. When you commit, Git updates that file to point to the new commit. Creating a branch costs almost nothing — one file write. Tags also point to commits, but annotated tags are tag objects (with tagger identity, date, message) pointing to the commit. The key difference: branches move automatically with new commits; tags are permanently fixed to a specific commit. Use annotated tags for releases (they have metadata), lightweight tags for private/temporary markers. Branch naming conventions: Consistent naming enables automation. Common patterns: feature/TICKET-123-description, fix/TICKET-456-bug-name, chore/update-dependencies, release/v1.2.0, hotfix/critical-payment-bug. CI/CD pipelines can use these patterns: deploy to staging on feature/*, deploy to production on release/*, auto-create GitHub releases on tags matching v*.*.*.

questions.q: What branching strategies exist — GitFlow vs trunk-based development vs GitHub Flow?
questions.text: Strategy comparison GitFlow: main + develop + feature/* + release/* + hotfix/* GitHub Flow: main + feature/* (PR → merge → deploy) Trunk-Based: main only + short-lived feature branches (merge daily) Release Flow: main + release/vX.Y branches for production fixes GitFlow: well-defined for teams releasing versioned software (mobile apps, desktop software). Drawback: complex, long-lived branches cause integration pain, release branches create merge debt. GitHub Flow: simple two-tier model ideal for continuous deployment teams — branch off main, PR, merge, deploy. Every merge to main triggers a deployment. Trunk-Based Development: developers commit directly to main (or merge short-lived branches within 1-2 days). Requires feature flags to hide incomplete work. Enables true continuous integration — the most advanced practice used by Google, Facebook, Microsoft. Platform Engineer recommendation: For a Platform Engineering team deploying infrastructure and tooling, trunk-based development or GitHub Flow is usually best — they enable fast iteration and simple CI/CD pipelines. GitFlow is overkill unless you have strict versioned releases or multiple concurrent release streams (like firmware or on-prem product versions). Match the strategy to release cadence: continuous delivery = trunk-based, versioned releases = GitFlow.

questions.q: How do you protect the main branch in production — what branch protection rules matter?
questions.text: # GitHub Branch Protection Rules (Settings → Branches → Add rule): Require pull request before merging Require approvals: minimum 1 (production: 2) Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed Require review from Code Owners (CODEOWNERS file) Require status checks to pass before merging: - CI tests (unit, integration) - Security scan (Trivy, Snyk) - Lint / code quality Require branches to be up to date before merging Require signed commits Do not allow bypassing the above settings (even admins) Restrict who can push to matching branches Branch protection rules enforce your deployment gates at the VCS level — they cannot be bypassed by individuals (when "do not allow bypassing" is checked). CODEOWNERS file maps paths to required reviewers: infrastructure changes require the platform team, security-sensitive files require the security team. "Dismiss stale approvals" prevents the attack where code is approved, then bad commits are added after approval. Require status checks ensures no merge without passing CI — this is the first line of defense against broken deployments. Admin bypass: Repository admins can bypass branch protection by default. Enable "Do not allow bypassing the above settings" to protect even from admin push. For compliance (SOC2, PCI-DSS), this setting is required — auditors look for it specifically. Create a separate break-glass procedure for genuine emergencies that is logged and reviewed.

questions.q: How do you handle long-running feature branches — what problems do they create?
questions.text: # Long-lived branch problems: git log --oneline main..feature/big-refactor | wc -l # 200 commits behind main git diff main...feature/big-refactor --stat # massive diff # Keep feature branch updated: git fetch origin git rebase origin/main # replay feature commits on latest main # Or merge main into feature (creates merge commits but is safer): git merge origin/main # merge latest main into feature # Feature flags to ship incomplete code: if feature_enabled("new-payment-flow", user_id): return new_payment_flow() return legacy_payment_flow() Long-lived feature branches accumulate merge debt — the longer a branch lives, the more diverged it becomes from main, and the harder the eventual merge. Problems: large conflict resolution effort, integration surprises (your feature works alone but not with other merged features), delayed feedback (bugs discovered late). Solutions: sync the feature branch with main daily (rebase or merge), break large features into smaller mergeable increments, and use feature flags to merge incomplete code to main safely while hiding it from users. Feature flags decouple deployment from feature release — the ultimate solution to long-lived branches. Branch age SLO: Set a team agreement: no feature branch lives longer than 2-3 days without being merged or rebased onto main. A branch older than 1 week is a smell — the feature should be broken down smaller or feature-flagged. Enforcing this SLO prevents the "big bang" merge nightmare.

questions.q: What are Git worktrees — how do they help when working on multiple branches simultaneously?
questions.text: git worktree add ../hotfix-123 hotfix/payment-crash # checkout branch in new dir git worktree add -b feature/new-api ../new-api origin/main # new branch + dir git worktree list # show all worktrees git worktree remove ../hotfix-123 # remove worktree git worktree prune # clean up stale worktree metadata Worktrees let you check out multiple branches simultaneously in different directories, all sharing the same .git repository (no duplicate .git overhead). Use cases: context switching between a feature branch and an urgent hotfix without stashing, comparing two branches side by side, running tests on two branches concurrently. Without worktrees, you would need to stash, switch, work, switch back, unstash — error-prone and slow. With worktrees, each branch is a separate directory you can switch between instantly. Practical pattern: Keep your main working directory on the main branch (for reference). Create worktrees for each active feature. Your editor can open multiple directories. When you finish a worktree, run git worktree remove to clean up. This workflow eliminates stash entirely for multi-branch work.

questions.q: What is the difference between merge and rebase — which do you use when?
questions.text: # Merge: preserves history, creates merge commit git checkout main git merge feature/login # creates merge commit (two parents) # Rebase: rewrites history, linear result git checkout feature/login git rebase main # replay feature commits on top of main git checkout main git merge feature/login # now fast-forward only (no merge commit) # Fast-forward merge (when no divergence): git merge --ff-only feature # fail if not fast-forwardable # No-ff merge (always create merge commit): git merge --no-ff feature # preserves feature branch boundary Merge preserves the true history — you can see when branches diverged and merged. Merge commits are noise in a linear history but accurately represent what happened. Rebase rewrites history to be linear — all commits appear as if they were made sequentially on main. Rebase produces cleaner git log output but obscures the true timeline. Rule of thumb: rebase your private feature branch before merging to main (clean history), never rebase commits already pushed to shared branches (rewrites history others depend on). Many teams use squash-and-merge for PRs (one clean commit per feature) as a middle ground. The golden rule of rebase: Never rebase commits that exist outside your local repository. If others have based work on those commits, rebasing creates parallel histories with the same changes under different SHAs — the definition of a nightmare merge situation.

questions.q: How do you resolve merge conflicts — what is your systematic approach?
questions.text: git merge feature/payments # triggers conflict git status # see conflicting files (both modified) git diff # show conflict markers in files # Conflict markers in file: <<<<<<< HEAD (current branch) current branch version ======= incoming branch version >>>>>>> feature/payments # Use a merge tool: git mergetool # opens configured diff tool (vimdiff, VS Code, etc.) git config merge.tool vscode # Accept one side entirely: git checkout --ours file.txt # keep current branch version git checkout --theirs file.txt # keep incoming branch version git add file.txt git merge --continue # Abort and start over: git merge --abort Systematic conflict resolution: (1) understand what each side is trying to do (read the commits, not just the diff), (2) decide on the correct semantics (not just text), (3) resolve with proper understanding of both changes, (4) run tests after resolution. Mechanical resolution (accept all ours/theirs) is dangerous — the result may compile but be logically wrong. Configure a visual merge tool (VS Code, IntelliJ, vimdiff) — three-way diff showing base/ours/theirs makes resolution faster and safer. rerere (Reuse Recorded Resolution): git config --global rerere.enabled true — Git records how you resolved conflicts and automatically reapplies the same resolution if the same conflict occurs again (common during long rebases). Essential for large rebases with recurring conflict patterns.

questions.q: What is a squash merge — when is it appropriate vs a regular merge?
questions.text: git merge --squash feature/login # stage all feature changes as one commit git commit -m "feat: add login with OAuth2 (#PR-456)" # GitHub/GitLab: Squash and Merge button in PR UI # Check if PR was squashed: git log --oneline main | head -5 # clean single commits per feature # Squash local commits before pushing: git rebase -i HEAD~5 # interactive rebase last 5 commits # then change pick to squash/s for commits to collapse Squash merge collapses all commits from a feature branch into a single commit on main. Advantages: clean linear history on main (one meaningful commit per feature), individual commits on feature branches can be messy WIP commits without polluting main. Disadvantages: you lose the detailed commit history of the feature (all those "fix typo" and "WIP" commits are gone), making blame/bisect less granular. Use squash-and-merge for: small features where the PR is the unit of change, teams with messy commit discipline. Use regular merge with --no-ff for: large features where individual commits provide meaningful history, or when you want to preserve detailed blame information. Team consistency: Pick one merge strategy and enforce it. If you use squash-and-merge, every PR becomes one commit — consistent and clean. If you use regular merge, require conventional commits (feat:, fix:, chore:) so the history is meaningful. Mixing strategies makes the history confusing.

questions.q: How does git cherry-pick work — what are its risks in production?
questions.text: git cherry-pick abc1234 # apply single commit to current branch git cherry-pick abc1234..def5678 # apply range of commits git cherry-pick -x abc1234 # add "(cherry picked from commit abc)" to message git cherry-pick --no-commit abc1234 # stage changes without committing git cherry-pick --abort # abort if conflicts # Common use: backport a fix to a release branch git checkout release/v1.2 git cherry-pick <fix-commit-sha> git push origin release/v1.2 Cherry-pick copies a commit to another branch, creating a new commit with the same changes but a different SHA. Production use cases: backporting a security fix to multiple release branches, hotfixing production without pulling in other in-progress changes, picking a fix from a feature branch before the full feature is ready. Risks: cherry-picked commits create duplicate history — the same logical change exists as two different SHAs in two branches, causing confusion in git log and git blame. If the cherry-picked commit depends on other commits for context, applying it in isolation can cause subtle bugs. Cherry-pick debt: Heavy cherry-pick usage across multiple release branches creates significant merge debt. Backports must be carefully tracked — use the -x flag to leave a trail in the commit message. Some teams use a bot (like GitHub's backport action) to automate cherry-picks to release branches when a fix is merged to main.

questions.q: How do you perform an interactive rebase — what operations does it support?
questions.text: git rebase -i HEAD~5 # interactive rebase last 5 commits git rebase -i origin/main # rebase commits not yet on main # Interactive rebase operations: pick — use commit as-is reword — use commit, edit message only edit — pause to amend commit (add/remove files) squash — meld into previous commit (keep both messages) fixup — meld into previous commit (discard this message) drop — remove this commit entirely exec — run shell command after this commit (for testing) break — pause here (for manual inspection) # Reorder commits by reordering lines in the editor # After editing: git rebase --continue or git rebase --abort Interactive rebase lets you rewrite the last N commits before pushing. Use it to: squash WIP/fixup commits before a PR, reorder commits for logical clarity, edit commit messages to follow conventions, remove a commit that was accidentally included, or split a large commit into smaller ones (edit, then unstage and recommit in parts). Run it only on commits that haven't been pushed to shared branches. Many developers run git rebase -i origin/main before every PR to clean up their commit history. exec for safety: Add exec make test between commits during a rebase to verify tests pass at each step. If a test fails mid-rebase, Git pauses and lets you fix it before continuing. This is invaluable when rebasing complex branches where order matters.

questions.q: How do you write good commit messages — what conventions matter in production?
questions.text: # Conventional Commits format: type(scope): short description (50 chars max) Longer body explaining WHAT and WHY (not HOW), 72 chars per line. HOW is in the code. WHY is in the commit message. Closes #123 # Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, ci, perf # Examples: feat(auth): add OAuth2 login with Google provider fix(payments): prevent double-charge on network timeout chore(deps): upgrade axios from 0.27 to 1.6.0 ci(github-actions): add matrix build for node 18 and 20 # Breaking change: feat!: remove deprecated v1 API endpoints BREAKING CHANGE: /api/v1 endpoints removed, use /api/v2 Good commit messages are engineering documentation. The subject line answers "what does this commit do?" — use imperative mood ("add feature" not "added feature"). The body answers "why was this change made?" — context that cannot be inferred from the code. Conventional Commits enables automation: semantic-release auto-generates changelogs and version bumps based on commit type (feat → minor bump, fix → patch, BREAKING CHANGE → major). CI/CD pipelines can enforce message format with commitlint. The "why" is priceless: "Fix off-by-one error in loop" describes what. "Fix off-by-one error in loop causing silent data loss when processing batches at partition boundaries (found via Datadog alert at 2024-01-15 02:30 UTC)" tells you why anyone should care. Three months later, that context is gold for whoever bisects a regression to this commit.

questions.q: How do you use git log effectively to navigate project history?
questions.text: git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate # visual branch graph git log --since="2 weeks ago" --author="Eknatha" git log --grep="payment" --oneline # search commit messages git log -S "function processPayment" # search for code added/removed (pickaxe) git log -G "processPayment" # search using regex (pickaxe) git log --follow -p -- src/auth.ts # history of a specific file (follows renames) git log main..feature/login # commits on feature not yet on main git log feature/login..main # commits on main not yet on feature git log --merges --oneline # only merge commits git shortlog -sn # contributor commit count summary git log --format="%H %ai %ae %s" --since="1 month ago" > audit.log git log -S (the "pickaxe") is one of the most powerful debugging tools — it finds every commit that added or removed a specific string, even across renames and moves. Use it to answer "when did this function first appear?" or "which commit deleted this configuration key?". git log --follow tracks a file through renames. Two-dot notation (A..B) shows commits reachable from B but not A — what's unique to one branch relative to another. Three-dot (A...B) shows commits reachable from either but not both — symmetric difference. git log aliases: Add to ~/.gitconfig: alias.lg = log --oneline --graph --all --decorate. Then git lg gives a beautiful branch graph. Share aliases across the team via a dotfiles repo to standardize the Git experience.

questions.q: What is git blame — how do you use it productively for incident investigation?
questions.text: git blame src/payments/processor.go # annotate each line with last commit git blame -L 45,60 src/payments/processor.go # specific line range git blame -w src/payments/processor.go # ignore whitespace changes git blame -M src/payments/processor.go # detect moved lines within file git blame -C src/payments/processor.go # detect lines copied from other files # If blame shows a refactor commit (not the original change): git log -p <refactor-commit> -- src/payments/processor.go # Then blame at the parent of that commit: git blame <refactor-commit>^ -- src/payments/processor.go # GitHub: "View blame" then "View as of this commit" to walk back through history git blame is most useful for incident investigation: "which commit introduced this behavior?" and "who can explain this code?". The -w flag prevents refactoring commits (whitespace/formatting changes) from obscuring the actual logic author. -M and -C detect when code was moved or copied, attributing to the original author rather than whoever moved it. When blame shows a trivial commit (formatting, rename), use git log on that commit to trace back to the original change. Blame culture: git blame is a code archaeology tool, not a blame assignment tool. Use it to understand context and find the person who can explain the code — not to assign fault. "Who wrote this?" should lead to "let me ask them about the context" not "I found who broke it."

questions.q: What is git bisect — how do you use it to find which commit introduced a bug?
questions.text: git bisect start git bisect bad # current commit has the bug git bisect good v1.2.0 # last known good version # Git checks out the middle commit — test it: make test # does the bug exist? git bisect good # no bug here git bisect bad # bug present # Repeat until Git identifies the first bad commit git bisect reset # return to original HEAD when done # Automated bisect with a test script: git bisect start HEAD v1.2.0 git bisect run ./test-for-bug.sh # 0=good, non-zero=bad git bisect uses binary search through commit history to find the first bad commit. With 1000 commits between good and bad, it takes only ~10 steps (log2(1000)). The automated form (git bisect run) is the most powerful: provide a script that returns 0 if the bug is absent, non-zero if present, and Git binary-searches automatically. This reduces what would be hours of manual investigation to minutes. Essential for production incident root cause analysis when you know the bug was introduced between two versions. Production use: When a Kubernetes cluster upgrade introduces a regression, or a dependency update breaks behavior, git bisect against a tag range (git bisect start HEAD v1.8.0) with an automated test script finds the exact commit. Even complex bugs become tractable — the exponential reduction in search space is transformative.

questions.q: How do you amend commits — what is the difference between amend, fixup, and reset?
questions.text: # Amend last commit (message or content): git add forgotten-file.txt git commit --amend # opens editor for message change git commit --amend --no-edit # keep message, just add staged changes # Fixup commit (for interactive rebase cleanup): git commit --fixup abc1234 # create "fixup! <original message>" commit git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main # auto-squashes fixups into targets # Reset to unstage or undo commits: git reset HEAD~1 # undo last commit, keep changes staged (--mixed) git reset --soft HEAD~1 # undo last commit, keep changes staged git reset --hard HEAD~1 # undo last commit, DISCARD changes (destructive) git reset HEAD file.txt # unstage a specific file Amend rewrites the last commit — creates a new SHA. Use it before pushing; after pushing requires force-push. Fixup commits are WIP commits meant to be squashed into a specific earlier commit — they follow a naming convention ("fixup! original commit message") that --autosquash understands. Reset --soft is the safest reset: undoes the commit but keeps all changes staged for recommitting. Reset --mixed (default) unstages changes but keeps them in working tree. Reset --hard destroys changes — use with extreme care and verify with git diff HEAD first. After pushing: git commit --amend followed by git push rewrites published history. Force-push is required. On shared branches this is catastrophic — anyone who has pulled the original commit now has a diverged history. Only amend commits that exist only in your local

questions.q: How does the pull request / merge request workflow work in practice — what makes a good PR?
questions.text: # PR workflow steps: 1. Create feature branch from main 2. Make focused commits (one logical change per commit) 3. Push branch, open PR with descriptive title and body 4. CI runs automatically (tests, lint, security scan) 5. Reviewers approve (check required status checks pass) 6. Author addresses feedback with new commits or rebases 7. Squash or merge to main 8. CD pipeline deploys automatically # Keep PRs small: Ideal PR: under 400 lines changed, single concern, reviewable in 20 min Large PR: split into a stacked PR series or use feature flags A good PR has: a clear title (conventional commit format), a description explaining what changed and why (not how), screenshots/recordings for UI changes, a link to the ticket/issue, and a testing notes section. Small PRs get reviewed faster, merged sooner, and have fewer conflicts. Studies show review quality degrades sharply above 400 lines of diff. Large PRs often signal either a feature that wasn't broken down small enough, or a refactoring that should be done incrementally. Review latency (time from PR opened to first review) is a key developer experience metric. PR description template: Create a .github/pull_request_template.md with sections for: What does this PR do, Why is it needed, How to test, Screenshots (if applicable), Related issues. A template nudges contributors toward completeness without requiring it.

questions.q: What are Git hooks — how do you use them in a team environment?
questions.text: # Client-side hooks (run locally): .git/hooks/pre-commit # run before committing (lint, test) .git/hooks/commit-msg # validate commit message format .git/hooks/pre-push # run before pushing (integration tests) .git/hooks/post-checkout # run after checkout (install deps?) # Server-side hooks (run on remote): pre-receive # validate pushes before accepting post-receive # trigger deployments after push update # per-branch validation # Share hooks with the team using husky (Node.js): npx husky init echo "npx lint-staged" > .husky/pre-commit echo "npx commitlint --edit" > .husky/commit-msg # Or pre-commit (Python, language-agnostic): pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install Client-side hooks are not pushed to remote (they live in .git/hooks which is not tracked). Use husky or pre-commit framework to share hooks via package.json or .pre-commit-config.yaml. Pre-commit hooks: run linters (fast, targeted — only on changed files using lint-staged), validate commit message format with commitlint (enforces conventional commits). Pre-push hooks: run tests (heavier, only on push). Server-side hooks on GitHub/GitLab: use branch protection required status checks instead — they cannot be bypassed by clients. Slow hooks hurt DX: A pre-commit hook that runs the full test suite makes every commit painful. Run only fast checks in pre-commit (lint, format, type-check — under 30 seconds). Run tests in pre-push or CI. Developers will git commit --no-verify to bypass slow hooks, defeating their pu

questions.q: What is a monorepo — what are the Git-specific challenges and how do you address them?
questions.text: # Monorepo: all services/packages in one repository repo/ services/api/ services/worker/ libraries/shared/ infrastructure/terraform/ # Sparse checkout (only clone what you need): git clone --no-checkout --filter=blob:none <url> git sparse-checkout set services/api libraries/shared # Git LFS for large files: git lfs track "*.pkl" "*.bin" "infrastructure/certificates/*.pem" git lfs ls-files # Shallow clone for CI (faster, less history): git clone --depth=1 <url> # CODEOWNERS for monorepo path-based ownership: services/api/ @api-team infrastructure/ @platform-team libraries/shared/ @core-team Monorepo challenges: large repository size (slow clones, deep history), cross-service CI (every commit triggers every service's tests), and ownership conflicts (who approves changes to shared libraries?). Solutions: sparse checkout (only materialize needed paths), Git LFS for binary files, shallow clones in CI (--depth=1 is sufficient for most CI tasks), path-based CODEOWNERS for automated review assignment, and affected-service detection (only run tests for services with changed files). Tools like Nx, Turborepo, and Bazel provide monorepo-aware build and test systems. Affected-change detection: git diff --name-only origin/main HEAD | xargs -I{} dirname {} | sort -u gives changed directories. A CI pipeline can use this to only test and deploy the services whose code actually changed — reducing CI time from 30 minutes to 3 minutes on a monorepo with 20 services.

questions.q: How do you manage Git submodules in production — what are the pitfalls?
questions.text: git submodule add <url> vendor/lib # add submodule git submodule update --init --recursive # initialize after clone git clone --recurse-submodules <url> # clone with all submodules git submodule update --remote # update to latest remote git submodule foreach git pull origin main # update all submodules cat .gitmodules # submodule config git submodule status # show SHA each submodule is at # Check for uncommitted submodule changes: git submodule foreach git status Submodules pin a specific commit of another repository inside your repo. Use cases: vendoring third-party code at a known version, sharing infrastructure modules between repos. Pitfalls: forgetting --recurse-submodules on clone (submodule directories are empty), updating the submodule SHA without pushing the change (others get empty directories), detached HEAD confusion (submodules always check out a specific commit, not a branch), and two-step push requirement (push submodule changes before pushing parent). Most teams prefer Git subtree or package management (npm, pip, go modules) over submodules for dependency management. Submodule footgun: After git submodule update --remote, you must commit the updated SHA in the parent repo. If you forget, everyone else who pulls your commit gets the old submodule version. The submodule SHA embedded in the parent is what controls which version everyone gets — not the remote submodule's default branch.

questions.q: What is git reflog — how does it save you from disasters?
questions.text: git reflog # every HEAD movement in last 90 days git reflog show main # reflog for specific branch git reflog --date=iso # with timestamps # Recover from accidental reset --hard: git reflog # find the SHA before the reset git reset --hard HEAD@{3} # go back to that point # Recover accidentally deleted branch: git reflog # find last commit SHA on the branch git checkout -b recovered-branch abc1234 # recreate branch at that SHA # Recover dropped stash: git fsck --lost-found # find dangling commits (stash objects) git show dangling-sha # inspect the recovered stash content git reflog is the ultimate safety net — it records every position HEAD has been, including commits on deleted branches, before resets, before rebases. The reflog is local only (not pushed to remote) and expires after 90 days (configurable). Before running any destructive operation (reset --hard, rebase, branch deletion), note the current SHA — you can always return to it via reflog. "I accidentally reset --hard and lost my work" is recoverable within 90 days. "I force-pushed and others have no local copy" is trickier but often still recoverable via their reflogs. Before any dangerous operation: Run git log --oneline -5 and note the current SHA. Then run the operation. If something goes wrong, git reset --hard <noted-sha> is your escape hatch. This 5-second habit has saved countless hours of lost work.

questions.q: How do you undo a bad commit that has already been pushed to main?
questions.text: # Option 1: git revert (SAFE — adds new commit undoing changes) git revert abc1234 # create new commit that reverses abc1234 git revert HEAD~3..HEAD # revert last 3 commits git revert --no-commit abc1234 # stage the revert without committing git push origin main # normal push (no force needed) # Option 2: git reset + force push (DANGEROUS on shared branches) git reset --hard HEAD~1 # undo last commit locally git push --force-with-lease origin main # force push (safer than --force) # --force-with-lease: fails if remote has commits you haven't fetched # Option 3: revert a merge commit git revert -m 1 <merge-commit-sha> # -m 1 = keep the mainline parent Revert is the only safe option for shared branches — it adds a new commit that inverts the bad commit, preserving history. Reset + force-push rewrites history: anyone who has pulled the bad commit now has a diverged history and will need to reset or rebase. Use force-push only on private branches you own entirely. --force-with-lease is safer than --force: it refuses to push if someone else has pushed since your last fetch, preventing you from overwriting their work. For a bad merge commit, revert -m 1 specifies which parent (mainline = first parent) to keep. Force-push on main: Even with --force-with-lease, force-pushing to main in a team causes pain for everyone. If you must force-push main: (1) communicate to the team, (2) have everyone run git fetch origin && git reset --hard origin/main afterward. Better: prevent it with bran

questions.q: How do you recover a deleted branch that was not merged?
questions.text: # Step 1: find the last commit SHA on the deleted branch git reflog | grep "branch-name" # if you remember the branch name git reflog | head -30 # scan recent HEADs git fsck --lost-found # find unreferenced commits (dangling) # Step 2: recreate the branch git checkout -b recovered-branch <sha> git switch -c recovered-branch <sha> # If branch was remote-only and locally pulled: git checkout -b recovered origin/deleted-branch # if remote still has it # If deleted from GitHub PR: # GitHub keeps deleted PR branches — Restore Branch button in PR # Or: GitHub API: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/refs A "deleted" branch just removes the pointer file — the commits are still in the object database until garbage collected. As long as git gc has not run and the commits are in the reflog (within 90 days), recovery is straightforward. GitHub retains deleted branch commits for the lifetime of the repository and provides a "Restore branch" button on closed PRs — use this for recently deleted remote branches. The nuclear recovery option is git fsck --lost-found which writes all unreferenced objects to .git/lost-found/ — parse through the dangling commits to find your branch tip. Prevention: Configure GitHub to never auto-delete branches after merge (uncheck "Automatically delete head branches" in repo settings). Instead, delete branches manually after confirming the merge is stable in production. This gives a window to restore if the deployment reveals a problem.

questions.q: How do you handle a corrupted Git repository — what are recovery steps?
questions.text: git fsck --full # check object database integrity git fsck --lost-found # find dangling objects # Common corruption: corrupted pack file cd .git/objects/pack ls -la # find .pack and .idx files git verify-pack -v pack-*.idx # verify pack integrity # Rebuild pack from loose objects: git gc --aggressive # repack all objects # If pack is corrupt: remove and re-fetch from remote rm .git/objects/pack/pack-*.pack .git/objects/pack/pack-*.idx git fetch --all # re-download all objects from remote # Nuclear option: fresh clone git clone <remote-url> repo-recovered # Copy uncommitted work from corrupted repo: rsync -av --exclude=".git" corrupted-repo/ repo-recovered/ Repository corruption is rare in normal operation but can happen due to hardware failure, full disk during a write, or process kill during git gc. git fsck --full validates every object in the database. For pack corruption (most common): delete the corrupt pack files and re-fetch from remote. For missing objects: git fetch restores anything that exists on the remote. The nuclear option (fresh clone + copy working tree) recovers most situations. Prevention: never let the disk fill up during git operations, avoid killing git gc mid-run. CI/CD prevention: Configure CI runners to use --depth=1 shallow clones — this uses a single pack file with no history. If it corrupts, rm -rf and clone again. Never reuse CI workspaces between jobs without git clean -fdx — stale objects from previous runs can cause mysterious errors.

questions.q: How does Git handle large binary files — what is Git LFS and when do you need it?
questions.text: git lfs install # initialize LFS in repo git lfs track "*.psd" "*.zip" "*.bin" # track patterns in LFS git lfs track "models/*.pkl" cat .gitattributes # LFS tracking rules git add .gitattributes large-file.psd git lfs ls-files # list LFS-tracked files git lfs status # LFS file status git lfs fetch --all # fetch all LFS objects # Check LFS usage: git lfs env # LFS configuration git lfs migrate info # analyze what should be in LFS git lfs migrate import --include="*.bin" # retroactively move to LFS Git stores every version of every file — committing a 100MB binary file 100 times uses 10GB of repository storage. Git LFS replaces large files with text pointers in the repository and stores the actual content on a separate server. Without LFS: slow clones (everyone downloads all versions of binaries), repository size bloat, GitHub's 100MB file size limit blocks pushes. With LFS: the repository stays small (pointers are tiny), large files are fetched on demand. Use LFS for: ML model files, compiled binaries, design assets, test fixtures with large data files. LFS in CI: CI runners must have Git LFS installed and configured. A checkout without LFS support leaves pointer files instead of actual content — builds fail with missing files. Add GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1 to CI environments that don't need LFS files to speed up checkouts, and explicitly fetch only needed LFS files.

questions.q: What is a CODEOWNERS file — how does it scale code review in large teams?
questions.text: cat .github/CODEOWNERS # Global owners (review everything): * @core-team # Path-specific owners: infrastructure/ @platform-team security/ @security-team services/payments/ @payments-team @security-team *.Dockerfile @platform-team **/terraform/** @platform-team # Individual file owners: .github/workflows/ @devops-team package.json @frontend-lead CODEOWNERS automatically assigns reviewers based on which files changed in a PR. Combined with branch protection "Require review from Code Owners," changes to critical paths cannot merge without approval from the responsible team. Last matching pattern wins in CODEOWNERS. This scales code review: the security team is automatically notified of changes to payment processing; the platform team reviews all Dockerfiles and Terraform changes; no manual tagging of reviewers needed. Reduces both review latency and the risk of changes slipping through without appropriate domain review. Ownership granularity: Start with coarse ownership (teams own directories) and refine as pain points emerge. Over-granular CODEOWNERS (every file has an owner) creates review bottlenecks — every PR needs 10 different approvals. The goal is ensuring the right people see relevant changes, not creating approval bureaucracy.

questions.q: How do you handle secrets accidentally committed to a Git repository?
questions.text: # IMMEDIATE: revoke/rotate the exposed secret first (before anything else) # Step 1: Remove from history using git-filter-repo (modern tool): pip install git-filter-repo git filter-repo --path secrets.env --invert-paths # remove file from history git filter-repo --replace-text patterns.txt # replace secret values # patterns.txt: LITERAL:actual-secret==>REDACTED # Step 2: Force-push all branches and tags: git push origin --force --all git push origin --force --tags # Step 3: Notify all contributors to re-clone (their local copies have the secret) # Step 4: Contact GitHub Support to purge caches # Prevention: pre-commit secrets detection pip install detect-secrets && detect-secrets scan > .secrets.baseline pip install git-secrets && git secrets --install Assume the secret is compromised the moment it is pushed — GitHub notifications, webhooks, and CI systems may have already processed it. Rotation/revocation is the only true fix; history rewriting is secondary cleanup. git filter-repo is the modern replacement for the deprecated BFG Repo Cleaner and git filter-branch. After rewriting, force-push, and have every contributor re-clone — their local copies still contain the secret in reflog/pack files. GitHub can purge cached views of the old content but the exposed window may have been enough for automated scanners. GitHub automatically scans for secrets: GitHub Secret Scanning detects common secret patterns (AWS keys, GCP service account keys, GitHub tokens) and notifies the prov

questions.q: What is git rebase --onto — how do you use it to transplant a branch?
questions.text: # Situation: feature-b was branched off feature-a, but feature-a is delayed # You want to move feature-b commits directly onto main git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b # Syntax: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch> # Moves commits on feature-b that are NOT on feature-a onto main # Another use: remove a range of commits from a branch git rebase --onto HEAD~5 HEAD~2 # remove commits 3-5 (keep 1-2 and 6+) # Preview what will be rebased: git log --oneline feature-a..feature-b # commits that will move --onto is the Swiss Army knife of rebasing — it lets you specify exactly what commits to move and where to put them. The three-argument form: newbase (where to put them), upstream (defines what commits to move — everything NOT on upstream), branch (the branch to rebase). Use cases: extracting part of a branch into its own PR, moving a branch stacked on another branch to base it directly on main, and surgically removing a range of commits from the middle of a branch history. Stacked PRs pattern: Teams using stacked PRs (each feature branch built on top of another) use --onto frequently. When the bottom PR merges, use git rebase --onto main old-base next-branch to rebase the dependent branch onto the updated main. Tools like Graphite and ghstack automate this workflow.

questions.q: How does Git integrate with CI/CD — what triggers what in a typical pipeline?
questions.text: # GitHub Actions trigger patterns: on: push: branches: [main, release/**] # any push to main or release branches pull_request: branches: [main] # any PR targeting main push: tags: [v*.*.*] # semantic version tags workflow_dispatch: {} # manual trigger schedule: - cron: "0 2 * * *" # nightly at 2am UTC # Path filtering (only run when relevant files change): push: paths: - "services/api/**" - "!**.md" # exclude markdown changes CI/CD pipelines are triggered by Git events — push, pull_request, tag creation, and schedule. Path filters prevent unnecessary pipeline runs: a docs commit should not redeploy the API. Tag-based triggers enable release workflows: creating a semver tag triggers a production deployment pipeline. The canonical pattern: feature branch push → PR CI (test, scan), main branch push → staging deployment, tag push → production deployment. Separate jobs per service in a monorepo with path filters keep CI fast and cheap. GitOps pattern: In a GitOps model, the pipeline does not deploy directly. Instead, it updates the image tag in a separate manifests repository. ArgoCD detects the manifest change and deploys. The deployment history is the Git history of the manifests repo. Rollback = git revert in the manifests repo. This separation of application code (app repo) and deployment config (manifests repo) is the production standard for Kubernetes deployments.

questions.q: What is semantic versioning and how do you automate releases with Git tags?
