questions.text: # SemVer: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.4.1) MAJOR: breaking change (incompatible API change) MINOR: new feature (backward-compatible) PATCH: bug fix (backward-compatible) # Manual tagging: git tag -a v2.4.1 -m "Release v2.4.1: fix payment timeout" git push origin v2.4.1 # Automated: semantic-release (reads conventional commits): npx semantic-release # determines version bump from commits # feat: → minor bump (1.2.0 → 1.3.0) # fix: → patch bump (1.2.0 → 1.2.1) # BREAKING CHANGE → major bump (1.2.0 → 2.0.0) # Get latest tag: git describe --tags --abbrev=0 git describe --tags # v2.4.1-3-gabc1234 (tag + commits since + sha) Semantic versioning communicates the impact of a release. semantic-release automates the entire release process: reads conventional commits since last release, determines version bump, creates Git tag, generates CHANGELOG.md, publishes to npm/PyPI/etc., and creates a GitHub Release — all from a single CI step. git describe generates version strings for non-release builds: v2.4.1-3-gabc1234 means "3 commits after v2.4.1, current SHA is abc1234" — perfect for Docker image tags in feature branch builds. Docker image tagging strategy: Production: v2.4.1 (exact semver tag). Staging: main-abc1234 (branch-sha). Feature: feature-login-def5678. Never use :latest in production. Use git describe --tags for builds that need a version string but aren't on a tag yet. This makes every deployed image traceable to an exact Git commit.

questions.q: How do you use Git in a GitOps workflow — what does the repository structure look like?
questions.text: # Two-repo GitOps pattern: app-repo/ # application source code src/ Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yaml # builds image, updates manifests repo manifests-repo/ # deployment config (ArgoCD watches this) apps/ myapp/ base/kustomization.yaml overlays/ staging/kustomization.yaml # image: myapp:main-abc1234 production/kustomization.yaml # image: myapp:v2.4.1 # CI pipeline update step: cd manifests-repo kustomize edit set image myapp=myregistry/myapp:main-${GITHUB_SHA::8} git commit -m "ci: deploy myapp main-${GITHUB_SHA::8} to staging" git push origin main # ArgoCD detects the push and syncs the cluster GitOps treats the Git repository as the single source of truth for cluster state. Benefits: every deployment is a Git commit (full audit trail), rollback is git revert, drift detection (ArgoCD alerts when cluster state diverges from manifests), and no direct kubectl access needed for deployments. The manifests repo should have the same branch protections as the app repo — a push to the manifests repo triggers a production deployment. PR-based changes to manifests provide review gates for infrastructure changes. Manifests repo access control: The CI pipeline service account has push access to the manifests repo only for the staging overlay path. Production overlay changes require a human PR. This enforces a promotion gate: staging deploys automatically, production requires intentional human action. This is the security model for GitOps in regulated environments.

questions.q: How do you handle Git in CI/CD runners — what configuration matters for performance and security?
questions.text: # Shallow clone for CI (most CI only needs current code, not full history): git clone --depth=1 --single-branch --branch main <url> # Or in GitHub Actions: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: fetch-depth: 1 # shallow (default) fetch-depth: 0 # full history (for git describe, semantic-release) # Credential management for CI: git config credential.helper store # use credential store git config url."https://token@github.com/".insteadOf "https://github.com/" # Avoid git gc in CI (slow, not needed per-run): git config gc.auto 0 # Cache the repo between runs: - uses: actions/cache@v4 with: path: .git key: git-cache-${{ github.sha }} CI performance: shallow clones (--depth=1) reduce checkout time from minutes to seconds for large repos with deep history. Full history (fetch-depth: 0) is needed for semantic-release (reads all commits), git describe (walks tags), and coverage reports that diff against base. Disable gc.auto in CI — automatic garbage collection wastes runner time. Cache the .git directory between runs to avoid re-downloading the full pack each time. CI credentials: use short-lived tokens (GITHUB_TOKEN in GitHub Actions, Workload Identity in GCP) rather than long-lived PATs or SSH keys. git clean in CI: Always run git clean -fdx before building in a reused workspace — leftover artifacts from previous builds cause non-deterministic failures. Better: use ephemeral runners (each job gets a fresh container) to eliminate workspace state entirely. GitHub Actions hosted runners a

questions.q: What is GPG commit signing — how and why do you enable it?
questions.text: gpg --full-generate-key # generate GPG key pair gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long git config --global user.signingkey <KEY-ID> git config --global commit.gpgsign true # sign all commits git config --global tag.gpgsign true # sign all tags git commit -S -m "feat: add OAuth2" # sign a single commit git log --show-signature # verify signatures in log git verify-commit <sha> # verify specific commit signature # GitHub: upload public key at Settings → SSH and GPG keys # GitHub shows "Verified" badge on signed commits # Modern alternative: SSH commit signing (simpler, same key as auth): git config --global gpg.format ssh git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub GPG/SSH signing cryptographically proves that commits were made by the holder of a private key — not just by anyone with the email address set in git config. Without signing, anyone can make commits attributed to your email by running git config user.email "you@company.com". Signed commits provide non-repudiation: you cannot deny making a commit that is signed with your key. Required for compliance in high-security environments (FedRAMP, some PCI-DSS scopes). GitHub's "Require signed commits" branch protection setting enforces this at the repository level. SSH vs GPG: SSH signing (Git 2.34+) uses the same key you use to authenticate to GitHub — simpler key management, no GPG daemon needed. For most teams, SSH signing is sufficient and easier to set up. GPG provides a stronger trust model (Web of Tru

questions.q: How do you audit Git repository access and detect suspicious activity?
questions.text: # GitHub audit log (organization level): gh api /orgs/{org}/audit-log?phrase=action:git.push --paginate # Key events to monitor: git.push # who pushed where, when protected_branch.policy_override # branch protection bypassed member.added # new member with write access repository.create/delete # repo creation or deletion oauth_application.token_revoked # credential revocation event # GitHub Advanced Security: secret scanning + code scanning alerts gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/secret-scanning/alerts # Local: recent pushes and clones git log --all --format="%H %ai %ae %s" # full commit audit trail # Detect force-push on main: # GitHub webhook on push event: compare forced=true attribute Git audit trails answer: who pushed what, when, and from where. GitHub organization audit logs export to SIEM (Splunk, Chronicle) for centralized security monitoring. Key anomaly signals: force-push to main (should never happen if protected), new admin added outside normal IAM process, push outside business hours from unknown IP, secret scanning alert for a new commit, large binary files pushed (possible data exfiltration). For regulated environments, enable GitHub's audit log streaming to GCS or S3 for immutable long-term retention. SOC2 requirement: Demonstrating access control and auditability for the code repository is a core SOC2 CC6.1 and CC6.2 control. The evidence: branch protection rules preventing direct push, required PR reviews, signed commits, and exported audit logs showing all acce

questions.q: How do you prevent sensitive data from entering a Git repository — what tools exist?
questions.text: # Pre-commit hooks for local detection: pip install detect-secrets detect-secrets scan > .secrets.baseline # create baseline detect-secrets audit .secrets.baseline # review findings # Add to .pre-commit-config.yaml: repos: - repo: https://github.com/Yelp/detect-secrets hooks: [{id: detect-secrets}] # git-secrets (AWS Labs): git secrets --install git secrets --register-aws # add AWS pattern detection git secrets --add "PRIVATE KEY" # GitHub Secret Scanning (server-side, automatic): gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/secret-scanning/alerts # CI scan: truffleHog git <repo-url> --only-verified # scan history for secrets gitleaks detect --source . --verbose Defense in depth for secret prevention: (1) developer workstation pre-commit hooks (detect-secrets, gitleaks) — fast feedback before commit, (2) CI pipeline scan on every PR (truffleHog, gitleaks) — catches anything that bypassed hooks, (3) GitHub Advanced Security server-side scanning — automatic, no configuration needed, alerts provider directly, (4) periodic full history scans — finds secrets in old commits. .gitignore for .env files and cloud credential files. Developer training: secrets in environment variables or secret managers, never in files committed to Git. .gitignore is not security: .gitignore prevents accidental addition of files but can be bypassed with git add -f. A misplaced git add . in the wrong directory commits everything. Pre-commit secret scanning provides a safety net even when .gitignore fails. Neither is a r

questions.q: What is git gc — how does garbage collection work and when does it matter?
questions.text: git gc # manual garbage collection git gc --aggressive # more thorough repacking (slow) git gc --prune=now # immediately prune unreachable objects git count-objects -v # show loose object count and size git cat-file --batch-check --batch-all-objects | wc -l # total object count # Pack files vs loose objects: ls -lh .git/objects/pack/ # pack files (compressed collections) find .git/objects -type f | grep -v pack | wc -l # loose object count # Auto-gc threshold: git config gc.auto # default 6700 loose objects triggers auto-gc git config gc.autoPackLimit # default 50 pack files triggers repacking Git gc packs loose objects into pack files, prunes unreachable objects, and compresses pack files. Loose objects are created by every git add, commit, and object operation. Git auto-runs gc when loose objects exceed gc.auto (default 6700). Pack files store delta-compressed objects — a pack of 1000 commits might be smaller than the 1000 loose objects because similar objects (consecutive commits on similar trees) compress together well. git gc --aggressive runs more expensive delta compression, useful for repositories with degraded performance from frequent rebases or large binary file history. Performance tuning: On a server-side bare repository receiving many pushes, auto-gc can trigger mid-push and cause timeouts for users. Set gc.auto=0 and schedule gc in a cron job during off-peak hours. Server-side git gc also releases space from large files removed via git filter-repo — the actual

questions.q: What is git shallow clone — when and how do you use it safely?
questions.text: git clone --depth=1 <url> # only last commit (fastest) git clone --depth=50 <url> # last 50 commits git clone --shallow-since="1 month ago" <url> git fetch --depth=1 # deepen or re-shallow an existing clone git fetch --unshallow # convert shallow back to full clone git log --oneline | wc -l # count available commits in shallow clone # Check if repo is shallow: cat .git/shallow # exists if shallow clone # CI: fetch just enough for comparison: git fetch --depth=2 origin main # enough for git diff HEAD~1 Shallow clones download only the last N commits, dramatically reducing clone time for repositories with deep history. Use in CI/CD (--depth=1 is sufficient for most builds), local exploration of large repos, or when disk space is limited. Limitations: git log history is truncated, git blame may not show original author, git describe may not find tags, and git bisect cannot traverse beyond the shallow boundary. For operations that need full history: git fetch --unshallow before running semantic-release, git describe, or full git bisect. The grafts mechanism in .git/shallow tells Git where history is artificially truncated. CI checkout strategy: Use fetch-depth: 1 for build jobs (fastest). Use fetch-depth: 0 for semantic-release, changelog generation, and coverage diff jobs (needs full history). Separate these into different jobs rather than always fetching full history for every CI run. This optimization alone can reduce CI checkout time by 80% on repos with years of history.

questions.q: What is git sparse-checkout — how do you use it for monorepos?
questions.text: git clone --no-checkout --filter=blob:none <url> myrepo cd myrepo git sparse-checkout init --cone # enable cone mode (recommended) git sparse-checkout set services/api libraries/shared # only these paths git checkout main # now materializes only specified paths git sparse-checkout add services/worker # add another path git sparse-checkout list # show configured paths git sparse-checkout disable # back to full checkout # Check what files are materialized: git ls-files | head -20 Sparse-checkout downloads all objects but only materializes (writes to disk) the files in specified paths. Combined with --filter=blob:none (partial clone), even the object database is lazily populated — Git fetches blob content only when needed. This enables working with monorepos containing hundreds of services without checking out the full tree. A monorepo with 10GB of files across 50 services can be worked with as if it were a small single-service repo — only your service's files are on disk. CI runners for specific services use sparse-checkout to only test the changed service. --filter=blob:none: The partial clone filter tells Git not to download file content (blobs) until they are needed. The repository structure (commits, trees) is downloaded, but file content is lazy-fetched. Combine with sparse-checkout for maximum efficiency in large monorepos: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout. This is how engineers at Google and Meta work with their multi-GB monorepos locally.

questions.q: How does Git handle line endings across operating systems — what is core.autocrlf?
questions.text: # Settings: git config core.autocrlf true # Windows: CRLF in working tree, LF in repo git config core.autocrlf input # macOS/Linux: LF everywhere, convert CRLF on add git config core.autocrlf false # no conversion (if you manage via .gitattributes) # Recommended: use .gitattributes to be explicit (not per-dev settings): cat .gitattributes * text=auto eol=lf # auto-detect text files, normalize to LF *.sh text eol=lf # shell scripts must be LF (breaks on CRLF) *.bat text eol=crlf # batch files must be CRLF *.png binary # binary files: no conversion # Fix existing CRLF in repo: git add --renormalize . # re-apply .gitattributes to all files .gitattributes is the right solution — it defines line ending behavior at the repository level, independent of developer OS settings. autocrlf relies on each developer having the right setting, which breaks in mixed teams. text=auto eol=lf normalizes all text files to LF in the repository and on checkout — the modern standard for cross-platform projects. Shell scripts with CRLF line endings will fail on Linux ("command not found" errors from the invisible character). Binary files must be marked as such to prevent corruption from line ending conversion. CI failures from line endings: A common source of mysterious CI failures: script works on Windows developer machine, fails on Linux CI runner with "/bin/bash: bad interpreter: No such file or directory" because the shebang line has appended. Enforce *.sh text eol=lf in .gitattributes to prevent

questions.q: What is git bundle — how do you use it for air-gapped environments?
questions.text: # Create a bundle of the full repository: git bundle create repo.bundle --all # everything: all branches, tags git bundle create incremental.bundle HEAD ^origin/main # only new commits git bundle create release.bundle v1.2.0 v1.3.0 # between two tags # Verify a bundle: git bundle verify repo.bundle # Clone from a bundle: git clone repo.bundle myrepo # Fetch from a bundle into existing repo: git fetch repo.bundle main:refs/remotes/origin/main # List what a bundle contains: git bundle list-heads repo.bundle git bundle creates a single file that contains a complete Git repository or a subset of it — it can be transferred via USB drive, email, or any file transfer mechanism. Use cases: transferring code to air-gapped networks (common in defense, government, financial), offline backup of a repository, sharing a specific range of commits without granting repository access. The bundle is treated like a remote: you can clone from it, fetch from it, and push to it. It is a complete git transport over a file rather than a network. Infrastructure use case: Terraform modules or Ansible roles for air-gapped environments. CI/CD in a locked-down network: the pipeline bundle is created on an internet-connected machine, transferred physically, and applied on an isolated server. This pattern is common in regulated industries (finance, government, utilities) where production networks have no internet access.

questions.q: How do you set up and use Git aliases for productivity — what are the most useful ones?
questions.text: git config --global alias.st "status -sb" git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all --decorate" git config --global alias.last "log -1 HEAD --stat" git config --global alias.unstage "reset HEAD --" git config --global alias.undo "reset --soft HEAD~1" git config --global alias.wip "commit -am WIP" git config --global alias.unwip "reset HEAD~1" git config --global alias.aliases "config --get-regexp alias" git config --global alias.whoami "config user.email" # Shell command aliases (prefix with !): git config --global alias.recent "for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate refs/heads/ --format="%(refname:short) %(committerdate:relative)"" git config --global alias.contributors "shortlog --summary --numbered --no-merges" git config --global alias.nuke "!git reset --hard && git clean -fdx" Aliases reduce cognitive overhead for frequently used command sequences. Store aliases in ~/.gitconfig and share them via a dotfiles repository so the team has a consistent Git experience. The wip/unwip pattern is a fast way to save and restore work-in-progress: git wip saves everything in a single commit, git unwip restores it. The nuke alias resets to a known clean state — useful in CI cleanup or development experiments. Aliases that start with ! execute as shell commands, enabling multi-step sequences. Dotfiles repo: Keep ~/.gitconfig, ~/.zshrc, and other config files in a dotfiles repository. New developers clone it and run an install script to get the full team configuration. This

questions.q: How do you manage hotfixes in production — what is the workflow when main has moved ahead?
questions.text: # Situation: production is running v2.3.0, main is at v2.5.0-dev # Critical bug found in production that needs immediate fix # Step 1: Create hotfix branch from the production tag git checkout v2.3.0 git checkout -b hotfix/payment-crash-v2.3.1 # Step 2: Fix the bug, commit git commit -m "fix(payments): prevent crash on null currency code" # Step 3: Create release tag git tag -a v2.3.1 -m "Hotfix release v2.3.1" git push origin hotfix/payment-crash-v2.3.1 v2.3.1 # Step 4: Cherry-pick or merge the fix back to main git checkout main git cherry-pick <fix-commit-sha> # port fix to main git push origin main # Step 5: Deploy v2.3.1 tag to production via CI/CD Hotfix workflow: branch from the production tag (not main, which may have incompatible changes), apply the minimal fix, tag the hotfix release, push the tag (which triggers the CI/CD production deployment pipeline), and then cherry-pick the fix back to main so it is not lost. The critical mistake is forgetting step 4 — the hotfix gets deployed to production but the fix is never ported back to the development branch, re-introducing the bug in the next release. Set a team process: every hotfix must have a tracking ticket requiring a cherry-pick confirmation before the ticket is closed. Test the hotfix: The temptation to skip testing under production pressure is real. At minimum: run the specific test case that exercises the bug, and deploy to staging first even if it takes 10 minutes. A bad hotfix deployed under pressure that cau

questions.q: How do you use git format-patch and git am for email-based workflows?
questions.text: git format-patch origin/main # create .patch files for new commits git format-patch -1 HEAD # patch for just last commit git format-patch HEAD~3..HEAD # last 3 commits as patches git format-patch --stdout > changes.patch # single file # Apply patches: git am 0001-feat-add-payment-logging.patch git am *.patch # apply all patches in order git am --3way *.patch # use 3-way merge for conflicts git am --abort # if it goes wrong # Review a patch before applying: git apply --check 0001-*.patch # dry run (no changes) git apply --stat 0001-*.patch # show what would change format-patch creates patches in the mbox email format — the original Linux kernel contribution workflow. Each patch is a self-contained commit with author, date, message, and diff. git am applies patches as commits, preserving authorship. Still used in: Linux kernel development, projects that accept contributions via email list, transferring commits between repositories without shared remote access, and distributing fixes to customers who cannot access your source repository. In air-gapped deployments, patches transfer specific code changes between environments where direct git push is not possible. Modern equivalent: For most teams, PRs replaced the format-patch workflow. But knowing format-patch is valuable for: contributing to open-source projects that use mailing lists (Linux kernel, Git itself, many BSD projects), generating change documentation for security-sensitive deployments where reviewers need a portable

questions.q: What is git bisect run — how do you automate regression hunting in CI?
questions.text: # Automated bisect with a test script: cat test-regression.sh #!/bin/bash make build 2>/dev/null || exit 125 # exit 125 = skip this commit ./run-specific-test.sh payment-flow # 0 = good, non-zero = bad git bisect start HEAD v1.8.0 # bad=HEAD, good=v1.8.0 git bisect run ./test-regression.sh # automated binary search git bisect reset # clean up when done # Exit codes for bisect run: 0 — commit is good (no regression) 1-127 (not 125) — commit is bad (has regression) 125 — skip this commit (cannot test, e.g., build fails) # CI integration: run bisect as part of incident response git bisect start --first-parent HEAD <last-known-good-tag> exit 125 (special to bisect) skips commits where the test cannot run — build failures, missing dependencies, or intermediate states that are untestable. --first-parent on a merge-heavy repo restricts bisect to the mainline, ignoring merge commits where the regression was introduced via a side branch. For CI incident response, a fully automated bisect script can run overnight and identify the exact regression commit in a repository with 500 commits since the last known good release — all without human intervention. Production incident automation: Integrate bisect into your incident runbook: when a regression is detected (monitoring alert), the on-call automation kicks off a git bisect run job in CI targeting the deployment range. By the time a human looks at the incident, the root commit is already identified. This is the highest-leverage use of gi

questions.q: How do you deal with a merge gone wrong after pushing — the "undo a published merge" scenario?
questions.text: # Scenario: merged feature to main, pushed, but it broke production # Option 1: git revert the merge commit (SAFE, preferred) git log --merges --oneline -5 # find the merge commit SHA git revert -m 1 <merge-commit-sha> # -m 1 = mainline parent git push origin main # This undoes all changes from the merge as a new commit # When the fix is ready, re-merge the feature branch: git revert <revert-of-merge-sha> # revert the revert (re-enables the feature) git merge feature/broken-feature # merge with actual fixes # Option 2: Reset + force-push (DANGEROUS, coordinate with team) git reset --hard <sha-before-merge> git push --force-with-lease origin main Reverting a merge commit requires -m to specify which parent to keep (mainline = 1). The result is a new commit that undoes all changes introduced by the merge. Critical follow-up: when you fix the feature branch and want to re-merge, you MUST first revert the revert. If you simply merge the feature branch again, Git sees that all those commits were already "merged" (the revert is a descendant) and only applies the new fix commits — the original feature code stays missing. This is the most common mistake in the "revert a bad merge" pattern. Revert the revert: After reverting a merge, if you just merge the branch again later, Git thinks the original commits are already merged (by the revert) and skips them. You must: git revert <revert-commit> (revert the revert) to re-enable the original changes, THEN apply your fix. Forgetting this s

questions.q: Walk through your methodology for onboarding a new repository to production Git standards.
questions.text: This is the Principal-level systems thinking question — designing the Git governance model, not just using commands. Production Git standards checklist Phase 1 — Repository setup: Branch protection on main: require PR, 1+ approvers, status checks, signed commits CODEOWNERS file: map directories to owning teams .gitignore: comprehensive (OS files, IDE files, build artifacts, .env) .gitattributes: line endings, binary files, LFS configuration README.md: setup instructions, branching model, PR process Phase 2 — Developer tooling: .pre-commit-config.yaml: secrets detection, lint, format, commit-msg PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md: standard PR description format Conventional commits enforced via commitlint Phase 3 — CI/CD integration: Required status checks: tests, security scan, lint Semantic versioning: semantic-release or manual tag policy Branch → environment mapping: feature/* → preview, main → staging, tag → prod Phase 4 — Security: GitHub Advanced Security: secret scanning + code scanning enabled Audit log streaming to SIEM or GCS Deploy keys or Workload Identity (no PATs with long expiry) Signed commits required (SSH or GPG) Phase 5 — Documentation: Git workflow documented in team wiki (branching model, release process, hotfix process) Runbook: what to do if X (force push needed, secret exposed, branch deleted) A well-governed Git repository is invisible to developers — the guardrails prevent mistakes without getting in the way. The goal: any engineer can contribute safely withou

questions.q: A force-push overwrote a colleague’s commits on a shared branch. How do you recover them?
questions.text: Force-push does not delete the old commits immediately — they become unreferenced but stay in the object database until garbage collection. Recovery is almost always possible if you act before gc runs. Recover the lost commits git reflog show origin/feature # if you have a local tracking ref # On the machine that had the old commits, the reflog is the goldmine: git reflog # find the SHA before the force-push git log -g --oneline <branch> # reflog as log # Restore the branch to the pre-force-push SHA: git branch recovered-feature <good-sha> git push origin recovered-feature # If no local copy exists, ask the colleague — their reflog has it: git fsck --lost-found # find dangling commits server-side or local The reflog is per-clone and local — it is not pushed. So the colleague whose work was overwritten almost certainly still has the commits in their own reflog or local branch. The fastest fix is usually to have them re-push, or to cherry-pick their dangling commits back on. Prevention beats recovery: enable branch protection with "Require force pushes to be done via the API" disabled, or block force-push entirely on shared branches. Use git push --force-with-lease instead of --force — it refuses to overwrite if the remote moved since your last fetch, which would have prevented this incident.

questions.q: You committed a secret (API key) and pushed it. What is the correct remediation?
questions.text: Order matters: rotate first, scrub second. The moment a secret hits a remote, assume it is compromised — scrubbing history does not un-leak it. Step 1 — rotate immediately # Revoke/rotate the leaked credential at the provider. This is non-negotiable # and comes BEFORE any git surgery. The key is already public. Step 2 — purge from history # git-filter-repo is the modern, recommended tool (filter-branch is deprecated): git filter-repo --path config/secrets.yml --invert-paths # remove a file git filter-repo --replace-text expressions.txt # redact a string # expressions.txt: AKIA1234567890==>REDACTED # Then force-push the rewritten history: git push origin --force --all git push origin --force --tags Everyone with a clone must re-clone or hard-reset, because their history still contains the secret. Open PRs based on old history must be recreated. Coordinate this — a half-purged history where some forks still carry the secret is the common failure. The secret may already be cached: GitHub keeps unreferenced commits accessible via their SHA for a window, and forks/caches/CI logs may retain it. Rotation is the only reliable mitigation. Add secret scanning (gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning) and a pre-commit hook so it never happens again.

questions.q: How do you recover a deleted branch when you do not remember its last commit SHA?
questions.text: A branch is just a ref — a pointer to a commit. Deleting it removes the pointer, not the commits. The reflog records every position HEAD and branches have held. git reflog # scan for the last commit on the deleted branch git reflog --date=iso # add timestamps to locate it # Once you find the SHA (e.g. the 'checkout: moving from feature-x' entry): git branch feature-x <sha> # recreate the branch at that commit # If reflog was pruned, search dangling commits: git fsck --no-reflogs --lost-found git fsck --unreachable | grep commit The reflog entry you want usually reads like checkout: moving from feature-x to main — the SHA on that line is the tip of the branch right before you left it. git fsck --lost-found is the fallback when the reflog itself has been pruned (default expiry is 90 days for reachable, 30 for unreachable). Interview signal: knowing that "delete" in Git almost never means "gone" — and that the reflog + fsck + the 90/30-day gc grace windows are your safety net — shows you understand Git is append-only at the object level.

questions.q: A bad commit is buried 20 commits back on main and is already deployed. How do you undo it safely?
questions.text: On a shared, deployed branch you must not rewrite history — use git revert, which creates a new commit that inverses the bad one. Reset/rebase would force-push and break everyone. git revert <bad-sha> # creates an inverse commit, safe on shared branches git revert <sha1> <sha2> <sha3> # revert several, newest-first ordering matters git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> # revert a merge commit, -m picks the mainline parent git revert --no-commit <sha> # stage the inverse without committing (batch) git revert is the production-safe undo: it moves forward, never rewrites, so it is reproducible across every clone and deploy. For a merge commit you must specify the parent to keep with -m 1 (usually mainline). Reverting a merge has a subtle gotcha: re-merging that branch later will skip the reverted changes — you typically revert-the-revert or rebase to bring them back. reset vs revert: git reset --hard rewrites history and is only safe on private, unpushed branches. On main/shared branches always revert . Confusing the two is how teams lose work.

questions.q: Walk me through git bisect to find which commit introduced a regression.
questions.text: git bisect does a binary search across history to find the first bad commit — O(log n) instead of checking each commit. With 1000 commits, that is ~10 tests instead of 1000. git bisect start git bisect bad # current commit is broken git bisect good v2.3.0 # this older tag/commit was fine # Git checks out a midpoint; you test, then mark: git bisect good # or git bisect bad # repeat until Git prints 'X is the first bad commit' git bisect reset # return to original HEAD Automate it git bisect run ./test.sh # script: exit 0 = good, non-zero = bad, 125 = skip git bisect run pytest tests/test_regression.py The killer feature is git bisect run with a test script — Git drives the entire search automatically, marking each midpoint by the script’s exit code. A script returning 125 tells Git to skip an untestable commit (e.g. one that does not build). Production use: bisect plus a reliable reproduction script turns "somewhere in the last release something broke" into a precise commit + author + diff in minutes. Mention pairing it with a minimal repro test — that is what makes it fast and trustworthy.

questions.q: What does git rebase --onto do, and when would you use it in production?
questions.text: git rebase --onto transplants a range of commits onto a new base — it answers "move these specific commits somewhere else," which plain rebase cannot express cleanly. git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch> # Example: you branched feature off the wrong base (dev), want it on main: git rebase --onto main dev feature # Drop a range of commits: replay commits AFTER <bad> onto <bad>'s parent: git rebase --onto <bad>~1 <bad> feature # Move a sub-branch off a feature that itself got rebased: git rebase --onto main old-feature-tip sub-feature Read it as: take the commits in (upstream, branch] and replay them starting from newbase . The classic production use is fixing a branch that was cut from the wrong parent, or surgically removing a middle commit by replaying everything after it onto its parent. Only on private branches. Like all rebase, this rewrites commit SHAs. Never rebase commits others have already pulled — coordinate or use a fresh branch.

questions.q: How do you split one large commit into several smaller logical commits?
questions.text: Use interactive rebase to mark the commit for editing, reset it to unstage its changes, then re-commit in logical chunks. git rebase -i <commit>~1 # opens the todo list # change 'pick' to 'edit' (or 'e') for the target commit, save # Git stops at that commit. Undo it but keep the changes staged-then-unstaged: git reset HEAD~ # commit's changes now in working tree, unstaged # Now stage and commit in pieces: git add -p file1.py # interactively stage hunks git commit -m 'refactor: extract validation helper' git add file2.py && git commit -m 'feat: add retry logic' git rebase --continue # finish the rebase git add -p (patch mode) is the key tool — it lets you stage individual hunks within a file, so one messy commit becomes several clean, reviewable ones. This is how you turn "WIP: everything" into a tidy, bisectable history before opening a PR. Why it matters: small, single-purpose commits make code review faster, bisect precise, and reverts surgical. Interviewers ask this to see if you treat history as a communication tool, not just a save button.

questions.q: Explain git cherry-pick and a real scenario where it is the right tool.
questions.text: cherry-pick applies the diff introduced by a specific commit onto your current branch, creating a new commit with a new SHA. It copies a change without merging the whole branch. git cherry-pick <sha> # apply one commit here git cherry-pick <sha1>..<sha2> # a range (exclusive of sha1) git cherry-pick -x <sha> # record 'cherry picked from commit ...' in message git cherry-pick -n <sha> # apply without committing (stage only) git cherry-pick --abort # bail out on conflict Real scenario — hotfix to multiple release branches # A security fix lands on main. You must also ship it on release/2.3 and release/2.4: git checkout release/2.3 && git cherry-pick -x <fix-sha> git checkout release/2.4 && git cherry-pick -x <fix-sha> The canonical production use is back-porting a hotfix from main to one or more maintenance release branches. -x records the original SHA in the message, giving an audit trail of where the change came from — valuable when the same fix exists in several branches. Cherry-pick duplicates commits (new SHA), which can cause confusing "already applied" conflicts when those branches later merge. Prefer merging where possible; cherry-pick when you need only one change, not the whole branch.

questions.q: You ran git reset --hard and lost uncommitted work. Is anything recoverable?
questions.text: Committed work is recoverable via reflog. Truly uncommitted, never-staged changes are usually gone — but staged changes may survive in dangling blobs. # If the work was ever committed (even via a WIP commit): git reflog && git reset --hard <sha> # If it was staged (git add) but not committed, the blobs may be dangling: git fsck --lost-found ls .git/lost-found/other/ # recovered blob contents land here git cat-file -p <blob-sha> # inspect a recovered blob The honest answer: reset --hard on changes that were only in the working tree (never git add ed, never committed) destroys them — Git never had a copy. If you had staged them, git fsck --lost-found can surface the blobs because add writes objects to the database. This is the strongest argument for committing early and often, even as throwaway WIP. Habit that saves you: commit WIP frequently (you can always squash later), and consider git stash before destructive operations — stashes are recoverable via reflog too.

questions.q: What is the difference between git reset --soft, --mixed, and --hard?
questions.text: All three move the branch pointer (HEAD) to a target commit; they differ in what they do to the staging area (index) and the working tree. git reset --soft <sha> # move HEAD only; index + working tree untouched git reset --mixed <sha> # move HEAD + reset index; working tree untouched (DEFAULT) git reset --hard <sha> # move HEAD + reset index + reset working tree (DESTRUCTIVE) Mental model --soft : changes from undone commits become STAGED (ready to recommit) --mixed : changes become UNSTAGED but kept in files --hard : changes are DISCARDED entirely Common uses: --soft HEAD~1 to undo the last commit but keep everything staged (to recommit with a better message or combine). --mixed (default) to unstage everything while keeping edits. --hard only when you genuinely want the working tree to match the target commit and accept losing local changes. --hard is the dangerous one and the only one that touches your working files. Always check git status first and consider git stash as a reversible alternative.

questions.q: How do you abort or recover from a merge or rebase that went wrong mid-operation?
questions.text: Git keeps a record of where you started before the operation. Both merge and rebase have explicit abort commands, and ORIG_HEAD / reflog are the fallback. # Mid-merge with conflicts you want to bail on: git merge --abort # restores pre-merge state # Mid-rebase gone wrong: git rebase --abort # restores pre-rebase state # Already finished a bad rebase/merge and want the old tip back: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD # ORIG_HEAD = where you were before git reflog && git reset --hard <pre-op-sha> # if ORIG_HEAD was overwritten --abort is the clean in-progress escape hatch. If the operation already completed and you only realize afterward it was wrong, ORIG_HEAD points at the commit you were on before the last merge/rebase/reset — a one-command rescue. The reflog is the universal backstop. Interview depth: mentioning ORIG_HEAD (auto-set by merge, rebase, reset, pull) distinguishes you — most people only know --abort and panic once the operation has finished.

questions.q: When would you use git revert vs git reset for undoing changes, in a team context?
questions.text: The deciding question: has the commit been shared (pushed to a branch others use)? Shared → revert. Private/unpushed → reset is fine. git revert <sha> # NEW inverse commit, history preserved, SHAs stable — SHARED branches git reset <sha> # MOVES branch pointer, rewrites history — PRIVATE branches only On main or any branch teammates have pulled, reset rewrites history and forces everyone to recover their clones — it breaks the team. revert moves forward by adding an inverse commit, so it is reproducible everywhere and leaves an auditable trail of "we undid this, here is why." On your own un-pushed feature branch, reset is the cleaner choice because nobody else depends on those SHAs yet. Rule of thumb: "reset rewrites the past, revert writes a new future." If anyone else might have the commits, never rewrite — revert.

questions.q: A teammate’s rebase created duplicate commits after a merge. How do you diagnose and clean it up?
questions.text: Duplicate commits (same change, different SHAs) appear when a branch is rebased after some of its commits already reached the target via merge or cherry-pick. Git sees them as distinct objects. git log --oneline --graph main feature # visualize the divergence git cherry -v main feature # shows commits in feature not in main (- = already there) git range-diff main...old-feature main...feature # compare two versions of a branch Clean up # Interactive rebase to drop the duplicated commits: git rebase -i main # delete the 'pick' lines for commits already present upstream # Or, if main already has everything, just fast-forward and abandon the dupes: git checkout feature && git reset --hard main # if feature should equal main git cherry and the newer git range-diff are the diagnostic tools — they tell you which commits are genuinely new versus already-applied-with-a-different-SHA. Once identified, an interactive rebase drops the duplicates. Root cause: this usually means the team mixes merge and rebase on the same branch without a clear policy. Pick one integration strategy per branch and document it to prevent recurrence.

questions.q: Explain the reflog: what it records, where it lives, and its expiry behavior.
questions.text: The reflog is a local, per-clone log of every position your refs (HEAD and branches) have pointed to. It is your time machine and the foundation of nearly all Git recovery. git reflog # HEAD reflog (default) git reflog show main # a specific branch's reflog git reflog --date=iso # with timestamps git log -g # reflog formatted as full log cat .git/logs/HEAD # the raw reflog file It records resets, checkouts, commits, merges, rebases, pulls — every ref movement, with the before/after SHA and a reason. Crucially it is local and never pushed , so it survives operations that rewrite shared history, and each developer has their own. Expiry defaults: reachable entries are pruned after 90 days ( gc.reflogExpire ), unreachable after 30 ( gc.reflogExpireUnreachable ). Why interviewers love it: "How would you recover X?" almost always has the same root answer — the reflog. Understanding it is local, append-only, and time-bounded shows you know why Git rarely loses committed work.

questions.q: Compare trunk-based development with GitFlow. When would you choose each in production?
questions.text: They optimize for different release cadences. Trunk-based suits continuous deployment; GitFlow suits versioned, scheduled releases. Trunk-based development main is always releasable; short-lived branches (hours/days) merge fast Feature flags hide incomplete work instead of long-lived branches Pairs with CI/CD: every merge can deploy; small batches, low merge pain GitFlow Long-lived develop + main; feature/* release/* hotfix/* branches Explicit release branches for stabilization before a versioned ship Heavier process; more merge overhead; suits desktop/mobile/firmware releases For a SaaS shipping many times a day, trunk-based wins — long-lived branches cause painful merges and hide integration risk, while feature flags decouple deploy from release. GitFlow earns its complexity when you ship discrete versions on a schedule (mobile app store releases, on-prem software) and need a dedicated stabilization window. Staff-level nuance: the question behind the question is "do you understand that branching strategy follows deployment model, not fashion?" Trunk-based without CI maturity and feature flags is dangerous; GitFlow on a high-velocity SaaS is needless friction.

questions.q: How would you structure Git for a monorepo with 200 engineers? What breaks at scale?
questions.text: At scale, vanilla Git struggles with repo size, checkout time, and CI fan-out. The strategy is partial adoption of scaling tooling plus ownership boundaries. Scaling techniques git clone --filter=blob:none <url> # partial clone: fetch blobs on demand git sparse-checkout set path/to/team # check out only your subtree git maintenance start # background gc, commit-graph, prefetch # Commit-graph + multi-pack-index speed up log/blame on huge histories Ownership & CI CODEOWNERS # auto-assign reviewers per path Affected-only CI: build/test only what changed (Bazel, Nx, Turborepo) Merge queue to serialize merges and avoid semantic conflicts at HEAD What breaks first: clone/checkout time (fix with partial clone + sparse-checkout), CI cost from running everything on every change (fix with affected-target detection via Bazel/Nx), and merge races (fix with a merge queue). CODEOWNERS enforces review boundaries so 200 engineers do not all review everything. Real-world: Google, Meta, and Microsoft run massive monorepos but on custom VFS layers (VFS for Git, EdenFS). For most orgs, partial clone + sparse-checkout + a build system with affected-target detection + a merge queue is the pragmatic stack before you need custom infrastructure.

questions.q: What is a merge queue (merge train) and what problem does it solve?
questions.text: A merge queue serializes merges into a protected branch, testing each PR against the actual post-merge state rather than its stale base. It eliminates "green PR breaks main" caused by semantic conflicts. The problem it solves PR-A and PR-B both pass CI against main independently Both merge — but combined they break main (semantic conflict, no textual conflict) Example: A renames a function, B adds a new caller of the old name How the queue works Queue builds a speculative branch: main + A + B in order CI runs against that combined state; only then are merges finalized If the combined build fails, the offending PR is ejected, not merged Without a queue, each PR is tested in isolation against a base that may be stale by merge time. The queue tests the real integrated result, so main stays green even at high merge volume. GitHub, GitLab, and tools like Mergify/Bors provide this. Speculative/parallel execution keeps throughput high by optimistically testing several queue positions at once. When to introduce it: when merge volume is high enough that "passed CI but broke main" happens regularly. It is a hallmark of a mature platform org and a strong thing to mention for a Platform/SRE role.

questions.q: How do you handle a long-running feature branch that has drifted far from main?
questions.text: Drift causes painful "big bang" merges and integration risk. The fix is to integrate continuously and, ideally, avoid long-lived branches altogether. Keep it current git fetch origin git rebase origin/main # replay your work on latest main (private branch) # or merge main in regularly if the branch is shared: git merge origin/main git rerere # reuse recorded conflict resolutions across rebases Better: avoid the situation Break the feature into small, independently-mergeable PRs behind a flag Merge incomplete-but-safe slices to main continuously (feature-flagged off) Tactically, rebase or merge main into the branch frequently (daily) so conflicts stay small, and enable git rerere so you do not re-resolve the same conflicts on each rebase. Strategically, the real answer is to stop creating long-lived branches: decompose the work into small PRs that land behind a feature flag, integrating continuously. The deeper signal: a branch that drifted "far from main" is usually a process smell. Interviewers want to hear you address the root cause (batch size) not just the symptom (the painful merge).

questions.q: Describe a safe hotfix workflow for a critical production bug.
questions.text: A hotfix must ship fast without bypassing safety, and must not be lost from mainline. The pattern: branch from the production tag, fix, deploy, then back-merge. git checkout -b hotfix/CVE-fix v2.3.1 # branch from the EXACT deployed tag, not main # make the minimal fix, commit git tag v2.3.2 && git push origin v2.3.2 # tag the patched release # deploy v2.3.2 to production # Back-merge so main/develop also gets the fix: git checkout main && git merge hotfix/CVE-fix git push origin main Branching from the deployed tag (not from current main) is the critical detail — main may contain unreleased changes you do not want in an emergency hotfix. After shipping, you must back-merge into main/develop or the fix silently disappears in the next release (a classic "we fixed it twice" bug). Keep safety on: even under pressure, the hotfix should go through CI, a fast review, and ideally a canary. Speed comes from a small diff and a pre-agreed expedited process — not from skipping checks.

questions.q: What goes in a good PR, and how do you keep reviews fast and effective at scale?
questions.text: PR throughput is a platform concern: slow reviews are often a team’s biggest hidden bottleneck. The levers are PR size, context, and tooling. Anatomy of a reviewable PR Small: <400 lines changed where possible (review quality drops sharply after) Single purpose: one logical change, not five unrelated fixes Clear description: what, why, how to test; link the issue Self-reviewed: author leaves inline notes on non-obvious choices Platform levers CODEOWNERS for auto-routing to the right reviewers Required checks (tests, lint, security) green before human review Draft PRs for early feedback; merge queue for serialized integration Track PR cycle time (open→merge) and review latency as team health metrics The single highest-leverage factor is small PRs — review quality and speed both collapse on large diffs. Automate everything a machine can check (format, lint, tests, coverage, security) so humans review design and correctness, not style. Measure cycle time so review friction is visible and improvable. Platform framing: treat "PR cycle time" as a DORA-adjacent metric you own and optimize. That reframes code review from a chore into a system you engineer — exactly the staff/platform perspective.

questions.q: How do you manage release versioning and tagging in an automated pipeline?
questions.text: Automated versioning removes human error and ties versions to commit semantics. The dominant pattern is Semantic Versioning driven by Conventional Commits. git tag -a v2.4.0 -m 'release: ...' # annotated tags carry metadata; use for releases git push origin v2.4.0 git describe --tags # human-readable version from nearest tag # semantic-release / release-please derive the version automatically: feat: ... → minor bump fix: ... → patch bump feat!: / BREAKING CHANGE: → major bump Conventional Commits let tooling (semantic-release, release-please, changesets) compute the next version, generate a changelog, create the tag, and publish — all from commit messages. Always use annotated tags for releases (they store author/date/message and are objects), not lightweight tags. git describe gives a deterministic version string for builds. Why this matters for platform: deterministic, automated versioning is a prerequisite for reliable rollbacks and provenance. The version on a running pod should map unambiguously to a tag and a commit SHA.

questions.q: Explain Git submodules vs subtrees vs a package manager for sharing code.
questions.text: All three share code across repos but differ in coupling, history, and operational pain. The right choice depends on how tightly versioned and how often updated the shared code is. Submodules git submodule add <url> libs/shared # Parent repo pins an exact SHA of the child; explicit, but easy to forget to update git submodule update --init --recursive # required after clone (common footgun) Subtrees git subtree add --prefix=libs/shared <url> main --squash # Child code is merged INTO parent history; no special clone steps, but bigger repo Submodules keep repos separate and pin exact versions, but add clone/checkout friction and a steep learning curve (detached HEADs, forgotten updates). Subtrees vendor the code into the parent so clones "just work," at the cost of a larger repo and awkward upstream contribution. For most teams, neither beats a real package manager (npm, PyPI, Go modules, an internal registry) with semantic versioning — it gives clean version constraints, caching, and dependency resolution. Default recommendation: reach for a package manager + internal artifact registry first. Use submodules only when you genuinely need source-level coupling (e.g. vendoring a fork you patch). Subtrees are niche.

questions.q: How do you enforce commit message conventions and pre-commit quality gates across a team?
questions.text: Consistency comes from automation, not documentation. Local hooks give fast feedback; server-side checks are the real enforcement. Local (fast feedback) # .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework): - lint, format (ruff/black/prettier), trailing-whitespace - detect-secrets / gitleaks - commitlint via commit-msg hook (enforce Conventional Commits) pre-commit install # wires up the git hooks locally Server-side (real enforcement) Branch protection: required status checks must pass to merge CI re-runs lint/format/tests/secret-scan (local hooks can be bypassed) Required signed commits; required linear history if desired Local hooks (via the pre-commit framework) catch issues before they leave the laptop and keep feedback fast. But local hooks can be skipped ( --no-verify ), so the authoritative gate is server-side : branch protection with required CI checks that re-run the same validations. Belt and suspenders — local for speed, server for guarantee. Platform mindset: ship the hook config in-repo so it is versioned and consistent, and make CI the source of truth. Never rely on humans remembering to run checks.

questions.q: A repo is too big and slow to clone/work with. What are your options?
questions.text: Diagnose whether the problem is history size, working-tree size, or large binaries — each has a different fix. Reduce what you fetch git clone --depth 1 <url> # shallow clone: only latest commit (CI use) git clone --filter=blob:none <url> # partial clone: history without blobs git sparse-checkout set <paths> # check out only part of the tree Fix large binaries git lfs track '*.psd' # Git LFS: store big files outside main history git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M # purge huge blobs from history If clone is slow because of deep history , use shallow ( --depth ) or partial ( --filter=blob:none ) clones. If the working tree is huge, sparse-checkout limits it. If the cause is large binaries bloating history , that is the real disease: migrate them to Git LFS and purge the originals with filter-repo, then everyone re-clones. Background git maintenance keeps things fast over time. Prevention: binaries in Git history are permanent dead weight — every clone pays for them forever. Add a pre-commit size check and an LFS policy so large files never enter normal history.

questions.q: How would you design a branching and deploy mapping for multiple environments (dev/staging/prod)?
questions.text: Map Git refs to environments deterministically so every deploy is traceable to a commit. The cleanest model pairs trunk-based development with promotion by tag/SHA, not by long-lived environment branches. Recommended: promote artifacts, not branches main merge → build immutable artifact, deploy to staging automatically git tag v2.4.0 → promote the SAME artifact to production rollback → redeploy previous tag's artifact (no rebuild) Anti-pattern to avoid Long-lived dev/staging/prod branches that drift and require cherry-picks Rebuilding per environment (the prod artifact differs from what you tested) The key principle: build the artifact once and promote that exact artifact through environments — staging tests the literal bytes that will run in prod. Tying promotion to tags/SHAs gives precise traceability and trivial rollback (redeploy the prior tag). Long-lived environment branches are an anti-pattern: they drift, demand error-prone cherry-picks, and let staging diverge from prod. GitOps angle: with Argo CD/Flux, a separate config repo holds the desired state per environment, and promotion is a commit that bumps the image tag. Git becomes the audit log of every environment change — strong for a platform role.

questions.q: What is git worktree and how does it help in production/dev workflows?
questions.text: git worktree lets one repository have multiple working directories checked out simultaneously, sharing a single object store — no second clone needed. git worktree add ../hotfix main # new working dir on main, alongside your feature work git worktree add ../review pr-123 # check out a PR to review without stashing git worktree list # see all worktrees git worktree remove ../hotfix # clean up when done The classic use: you are deep in a feature branch when a P1 hotfix lands. Instead of stashing, switching, fixing, switching back, and unstashing, you spin up a worktree on a separate directory, fix there, and your feature work stays untouched. Because worktrees share the object database, they are far cheaper than a second clone (no re-fetch, shared history). Other uses: running a long build on one branch while coding on another, reviewing a PR without disrupting your context, or building two versions side by side. A clean, underused feature worth mentioning.

questions.q: How do you implement and enforce a code review / approval policy with branch protection?
questions.text: Branch protection turns review policy into an enforced gate rather than a convention. Configure it on the default and release branches. Typical protection rules Require N approving reviews before merge (often 1–2) Require review from CODEOWNERS for touched paths Dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed Require status checks (tests, lint, security) to pass Require branches up to date / require linear history Require signed commits; restrict who can push; block force-push & deletion CODEOWNERS plus "require review from code owners" routes each change to the people who actually own that code. "Dismiss stale approvals" prevents the trick of getting approved, then pushing different code. Requiring up-to-date branches (or a merge queue) prevents semantic conflicts. For regulated environments, require signed commits and restrict who can administer the rules. Watch the admin bypass: decide deliberately whether admins can bypass protection. For high-compliance repos, "include administrators" should be on — otherwise the controls are theater. Audit who has the power to change the rules.

questions.q: Explain GPG/SSH commit signing: why, how, and how to enforce it.
questions.text: Signing cryptographically proves who authored a commit, defeating identity spoofing (anyone can set user.email to yours). It is increasingly required for supply-chain security. git config user.signingkey <key-id> git config commit.gpgsign true # sign all commits automatically git commit -S -m 'msg' # sign a single commit explicitly git tag -s v2.4.0 # sign a tag # SSH signing (simpler than GPG, since Git 2.34): git config gpg.format ssh git config user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub git log --show-signature # verify signatures Without signing, commit author fields are pure metadata — trivially forged. Signing binds commits to a verified key. Enforcement happens server-side: GitHub/GitLab can require signed commits via branch protection and show a "Verified" badge. SSH signing (Git 2.34+) is now the easy path — reuse your existing SSH key, no GPG keyring management. Supply-chain context: signed commits + signed tags + provenance (SLSA) are how you prove what shipped came from who you think. For a platform/security-adjacent role, framing signing as part of supply-chain integrity (not just "nice to have") lands well.

questions.q: What is GitOps and how does Git become the source of truth for infrastructure?
questions.text: GitOps declares desired system state in Git; an automated controller continuously reconciles the live environment to match. Git becomes the single source of truth and the audit log for infrastructure. Core loop Desired state (manifests/Helm/Kustomize) committed to a config repo Controller (Argo CD / Flux) watches the repo Controller diffs desired vs live cluster state and reconciles automatically Drift (manual kubectl change) is detected and reverted to match Git Why it is powerful Every change is a reviewed, signed, auditable commit (who/what/when/why) Rollback = git revert + auto-reconcile (no imperative kubectl needed) No human has prod credentials; the controller pulls and applies The shift is from push (CI runs kubectl/terraform against prod) to pull (an in-cluster controller pulls the declared state and applies it). Benefits: a complete audit trail in Git, trivial rollback via revert, automatic drift correction, and no CI system holding prod credentials. The config repo is typically separate from app code so deploys are decoupled from builds. Platform relevance: GitOps is core to modern platform engineering. Mentioning the push→pull inversion, drift detection, and "rollback is just git revert" demonstrates current, production-grade knowledge.

questions.q: Why should CI not use a long-lived Personal Access Token, and what replaces it?
questions.text: Long-lived PATs are static, broad, and rarely rotated — a single leak (in logs, env dumps, a compromised runner) is a durable breach. The modern replacement is short-lived, identity-based credentials. Better options OIDC federation: CI exchanges a signed identity token for short-lived cloud creds (GitHub Actions ↔ AWS/GCP/Azure Workload Identity — no stored secrets) GitHub App installation tokens: scoped, auto-expiring (~1h), per-repo Deploy keys: single-repo, read-only by default, instead of account-wide PATs Fine-grained PATs with explicit repo + permission scope and short expiry (last resort) OIDC federation is the gold standard: the CI job presents a cryptographically signed identity token, the cloud provider verifies it against a trust policy and issues credentials valid for minutes — nothing long-lived is ever stored. For Git operations, GitHub App tokens or deploy keys replace account-wide PATs with scoped, expiring access. Leak blast radius: a leaked 1-hour OIDC credential expires before most attackers can use it; a leaked PAT with no expiry is exploitable indefinitely. Always prefer ephemeral, scoped identity over static secrets.

questions.q: How do you prevent secrets from ever entering Git history?
questions.text: Defense in depth: stop secrets at the developer’s machine, catch them in CI, and scan continuously — because a single push to a remote is effectively permanent exposure. Layers Pre-commit: gitleaks / detect-secrets hook blocks the commit locally Server-side: push protection (GitHub) rejects pushes containing secret patterns CI: re-scan (local hooks can be bypassed with --no-verify) Continuous: scheduled secret scanning across all repos + alerting .gitignore for known secret files (.env, *.pem, credentials.json) And do not store secrets in Git at all Use a secrets manager: Vault, AWS/GCP Secrets Manager, sealed-secrets for k8s Inject at runtime via env/volume, never commit plaintext config The most reliable prevention is architectural: secrets should live in a secrets manager and be injected at runtime, so there is nothing to leak into Git in the first place. Layer on pre-commit scanning (fast, local), server-side push protection (cannot be bypassed), and CI re-scanning (catches --no-verify ). Treat any committed-and-pushed secret as compromised — rotate it. Interview framing: lead with "the best fix is not to put secrets in Git at all," then layer scanning as defense in depth. That ordering shows you address root cause before symptom.

questions.q: Explain how you would build a deployment pipeline triggered by Git events.
questions.text: Map Git events to pipeline stages so the workflow is automatic and traceable. The trigger model defines the deploy semantics. Event → action mapping PR opened/updated → build + test + security scan + deploy ephemeral preview env Merge to main → build immutable artifact + deploy to staging Tag vX.Y.Z → promote the SAME artifact to production (canary → full) Manual approval → gate between staging and prod for high-risk changes Key properties Build once, promote the same artifact (don't rebuild per environment) Every artifact tagged with its commit SHA for traceability Automated rollback: redeploy previous tag on health-check failure Webhooks (or the CI provider’s native triggers) fire on push/PR/tag events. The disciplined design builds the artifact once on merge and promotes that exact artifact — PR previews validate features in isolation, staging tests the literal prod bytes, and a tag promotes to prod with a canary. Tagging artifacts by SHA makes "what is running in prod?" answerable and rollback deterministic. Safety in the pipeline: required green checks before merge, ephemeral preview environments per PR, canary/progressive delivery to prod, and automated rollback on SLO breach. Git events drive it; observability gates it.

questions.q: What is a signed/verified release and how does it fit into supply-chain security (SLSA)?
questions.text: A verified release proves provenance: that an artifact was built from specific source by a specific trusted process, unmodified. It closes the gap where attackers tamper between source and deploy. The chain of trust Signed commits → prove who authored the source Signed tags → prove which exact source is the release Signed artifacts → cosign sign <image> (Sigstore) Provenance attestation → SLSA: who built it, from what source, with what builder Verify at deploy → cosign verify; admission controller blocks unsigned images SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) formalizes this into levels: at higher levels the build runs on a hardened, isolated builder that emits signed provenance linking the artifact back to the exact source commit. Sigstore/cosign make signing keyless (tied to OIDC identity). At deploy, an admission controller (e.g. Kyverno, Connaisseur) refuses to run images lacking a valid signature and provenance. Why it matters: attacks like SolarWinds and the xz backdoor exploited the gap between trusted source and shipped artifact. Signing the whole chain — commit → tag → artifact → provenance, verified at admission — is how you defend it. Strong material for a platform/security role.

questions.q: How do Git hooks work, and where do server-side vs client-side hooks fit?
questions.text: Hooks are scripts Git runs at lifecycle events. Client-side hooks live in each clone (advisory); server-side hooks run on the remote (enforcing). Client-side (local, bypassable) pre-commit # lint/format/secret-scan before a commit is created commit-msg # validate message format (Conventional Commits) pre-push # run quick tests before pushing # Bypassable with --no-verify — fast feedback, not enforcement Server-side (authoritative) pre-receive # reject a push that violates policy (protected paths, signed commits) update # per-branch ref checks post-receive # trigger CI/CD, notifications after accepted push Client hooks give fast feedback but cannot be trusted as gates — developers can skip them. Real enforcement is server-side: pre-receive can reject pushes that break policy. On hosted platforms (GitHub/GitLab) you usually do not write raw server hooks; you use branch protection and required CI checks, which serve the same enforcement role. Distribute client hooks via the pre-commit framework so they are versioned and consistent. Common mistake: relying on client-side hooks for security/compliance. They are convenience, not control. Anything that must be guaranteed belongs in server-side enforcement or CI.

questions.q: A dependency was compromised via a malicious commit. How do you investigate using Git?
questions.text: Git forensics: use history, blame, and signatures to establish what changed, when, by whom, and whether it was authentic. git log --all --source --oneline -- <suspect-file> # full history of the file git log -p -- <file> # see every diff to the file over time git blame -w -C <file> # who last touched each line (ignore whitespace/moves) git log --show-signature # which commits are cryptographically verified git log --since='2 weeks ago' --author='...' # scope by time/author git diff <last-good-tag> HEAD -- <path> # what changed since known-good Start from the last known-good tag and diff forward to isolate the introduced change. git blame -C attributes lines (the -C detects moved/copied code, defeating obfuscation by relocation). --show-signature reveals whether the malicious commit was signed by a trusted key or spoofed — unsigned or unexpected-author commits in a signed repo are red flags. The reflog on build machines can reveal what was actually checked out and built. Lesson from xz: the attack used a trusted maintainer identity over time, so signature checks alone were insufficient — provenance and behavioral review matter too. Mention that detection combines Git forensics with build provenance and anomaly detection, not history inspection alone.

questions.q: How do you handle database migrations safely in a Git-driven deploy?
questions.text: Migrations are the riskiest part of a deploy because they are stateful and often irreversible. The pattern is versioned, ordered, expand/contract migrations decoupled from code deploys. Principles Versioned migration files in Git, applied in order (Flyway/Liquibase/Alembic) Expand/contract: add column → deploy code using it → backfill → drop old (separate deploys) Backward-compatible: new code must work with old schema and vice versa during rollout Migrations run as a distinct, gated pipeline step — not silently in app startup The core technique is expand/contract (parallel change): never make a breaking schema change in one step. Add the new structure (expand), ship code that writes to both/reads new, backfill data, then later remove the old (contract) — each as a separate, independently-rollbackable deploy. This keeps old and new app versions both functional during a rolling deploy, which is what makes zero-downtime and rollback possible. The trap: a migration that drops a column in the same deploy that stops using it means you cannot roll back the code without a forward fix — the old code expects the column that is now gone. Decouple schema changes from code changes across multiple deploys.

questions.q: What does git fsck check, and how is it used for integrity verification?
questions.text: git fsck (file system check) verifies the integrity and connectivity of the object database — confirming objects are not corrupt and references resolve. git fsck # verify object integrity + connectivity git fsck --full # check all objects including packed git fsck --unreachable # list objects not reachable from any ref git fsck --lost-found # write dangling commits/blobs for recovery git fsck --connectivity-only # faster: skip content hash verification It validates that each object’s content still matches its SHA (detecting bit-rot or tampering, since the hash is the address) and that the commit/tree/blob graph is fully connected. Two main uses: integrity — detect repository corruption, e.g. after a disk issue; and recovery — --lost-found surfaces dangling objects (orphaned commits from a bad reset, deleted branches) so you can rescue lost work. Security angle: because Git is content-addressed, fsck detecting a hash mismatch means an object was altered — a tamper signal. SHA-1 collision concerns drove the move toward SHA-256 repos; mentioning that shows depth.

questions.q: How would you implement automatic rollback tied to Git in a deploy system?
questions.text: Rollback should be a fast, deterministic Git/artifact operation triggered by health signals — not a manual scramble. The design depends on building immutable, versioned artifacts. GitOps-style rollback git revert <deploy-commit> # revert the config commit that bumped the image # controller (Argo/Flux) auto-reconciles cluster back to previous state argocd app rollback <app> <revision> # explicit rollback to a prior synced revision Pipeline-driven rollback Health check / SLO breach after deploy → redeploy previous tag's artifact Progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts/Flagger): auto-abort canary on metric regression Keep last-known-good tag/SHA recorded for instant redeploy Because you build the artifact once and tag it by SHA, rollback is simply "redeploy the previous tag" — no rebuild, fully deterministic. In GitOps, rollback is git revert of the config change, and the controller reconciles automatically, preserving the audit trail. Progressive delivery tools watch metrics during a canary and auto-abort/rollback on regression before full traffic shifts. Make rollback boring: the best rollback is automatic and metric-driven (canary abort) so a human never has to decide under pressure. Pair Git-based rollback with health gates and you get safe deploys by default.

questions.q: Explain ephemeral preview environments per pull request and how Git drives them.
questions.text: A preview environment is a temporary, fully-functional deployment spun up automatically for each PR, letting reviewers and stakeholders test the change in isolation before merge. Lifecycle driven by Git events PR opened → CI builds the branch + deploys a namespaced env (pr-123.preview.app) PR updated → redeploy the env with the new commit PR merged/closed → tear down the env (free resources) Implementation Kubernetes namespace per PR, or vcluster, or platform (Vercel/Netlify) preview Seeded/ephemeral data; isolated dependencies; unique URL posted back to the PR Git events are the triggers: opening a PR creates the env, pushing updates it, closing it tears it down. The value is testing the actual running change — not just reading a diff — with a shareable URL for designers, PMs, and QA. The hard parts are data isolation (each env needs realistic but safe data) and cost control (auto-teardown is essential). Platform value: preview environments dramatically improve review quality and shift testing left. Building this as a self-service capability is a strong platform-engineering deliverable to cite.

questions.q: How do you audit who changed what in a repository for compliance?
questions.text: Git itself records authorship and content; the hosting platform adds the access and administrative audit layer. Compliance needs both. From Git git log --all --pretty=fuller # author AND committer + timestamps git log --show-signature # verified identity (not just claimed) git blame -w <file> # line-level attribution git log --follow -- <file> # history across renames From the platform (the real audit trail) Audit log: who merged, who changed branch protection, who added access Stream audit events to SIEM / immutable storage (tamper-evident) Required signed commits so 'author' is verified, not spoofable Git’s author field is self-reported and forgeable, so for compliance you require signed commits (verified identity) and rely on the platform’s audit log for who-merged-what, who-changed-settings, and access grants. Streaming those audit events to a SIEM or immutable store gives a tamper-evident record. git log --pretty=fuller distinguishes author (wrote it) from committer (applied it) — relevant after rebases/cherry-picks. Key insight for auditors: unsigned commit metadata is not evidence — it can be forged. Verified signatures + platform audit logs are the defensible record. State this explicitly; it shows you understand the trust model.

questions.q: What is the difference between merge, squash-merge, and rebase-merge for integrating PRs?
questions.text: Three ways a PR lands on main, each shaping history differently. The choice is a team policy trade-off between traceability and tidiness. The three strategies Merge commit : preserves all PR commits + a merge commit; full history, busier graph Squash-merge : collapses the PR into ONE commit on main; clean linear history Rebase-merge : replays PR commits onto main individually; linear, no merge commit Squash-merge is the most common default: main gets one tidy, revertible commit per PR, and messy WIP commits vanish — great for clean history and easy reverts, at the cost of losing intra-PR granularity (bisect lands on big commits). Merge commits preserve everything and clearly delineate PR boundaries, but clutter the graph. Rebase-merge keeps individual commits in a linear history but rewrites their SHAs and can be confusing if PR commits were not curated. Recommendation to state: squash-merge for most product teams (clean, revertible, one-commit-per-feature), reserving merge commits for cases where preserving individual commits matters (e.g. a curated series). Consistency per repo matters more than the specific choice — and enforce it in branch settings.

questions.q: How do you handle access control and least privilege across many repositories?
questions.text: Scale access control through groups, roles, and automation — never per-user, per-repo grants, which drift into over-permissioning. Principles & mechanisms Teams/groups map to roles; assign repos to teams, users to teams (not repos directly) Least privilege: read by default, write/maintain/admin only where needed CODEOWNERS for review authority ≠ write access (separate concerns) Time-bound / just-in-time elevation for admin actions Automate via IaC: Terraform GitHub provider manages teams + repo access in Git Periodic access reviews; remove dormant access; SSO + SCIM deprovisioning The scalable model is role/group-based: define teams that map to responsibilities, grant repos to teams, and add people to teams — so offboarding (remove from group / SCIM deprovision) instantly revokes everywhere. Manage all of it as code (Terraform GitHub provider) so access itself is reviewed via PR and audited in Git. Default to read; grant write/admin narrowly; review periodically to catch privilege creep. Managing access as code is the platform-engineering move: access changes become reviewable, auditable commits, and there is no manual console drift. Pair with SSO/SCIM so identity lifecycle drives access automatically.

questions.q: Explain the three-way merge algorithm Git uses.
questions.text: Git merges using three inputs: the two branch tips and their common ancestor (merge base). The ancestor is what lets Git tell "added" from "deleted" and minimize false conflicts.
