The three points git merge-base main feature # find the common ancestor commit # Git compares: BASE ↔ OURS and BASE ↔ THEIRS # For each hunk: if only one side changed it vs base → take that side # if both sides changed the same region → CONFLICT A two-way diff (just comparing the two tips) cannot tell whether a line was added on one side or deleted on the other. The merge base resolves this: changes present on one side but not the base are applied cleanly; only regions changed on both sides relative to the base become conflicts. This is why Git auto-merges most concurrent edits to different parts of a file. Recursive/ort strategy: when branches have multiple merge bases (criss-cross merges), Git’s default ort strategy merges the bases themselves first to synthesize a virtual ancestor. Mentioning ort (which replaced recursive as default) signals current knowledge.

questions.q: How do you resolve a complex merge conflict methodically?
questions.text: Conflicts are resolved by understanding intent on both sides, not by blindly picking ours/theirs. Tooling and discipline keep it safe. git status # list conflicted files git diff # see conflict markers in context git checkout --conflict=diff3 <file> # show BASE too, not just ours/theirs git mergetool # launch a visual 3-way merge tool git add <file> # mark resolved git merge --continue # or commit git checkout --ours <file> # take our version wholesale (use deliberately) git checkout --theirs <file> # take their version wholesale Enable diff3 conflict style so you see the common base alongside both sides — understanding what each side changed from is essential to merging intent rather than guessing. Resolve, then re-run the tests before continuing; a syntactically-resolved conflict can still be semantically wrong. For repetitive conflicts across rebases, enable git rerere to record and replay resolutions. Do not blindly --theirs/--ours a whole file to make conflicts disappear — that silently drops the other side’s changes. The most dangerous conflict resolution is one that compiles but loses someone’s work.

questions.q: What is git rerere and when does it pay off?
questions.text: rerere = "reuse recorded resolution." Git remembers how you resolved a specific conflict and auto-applies the same resolution if that exact conflict recurs. git config rerere.enabled true # Resolve a conflict once; Git records the before/after # Next time the identical conflict appears (e.g. on re-rebase), Git auto-resolves it git rerere status # show what rerere is tracking git rerere diff # show recorded resolutions It pays off in two situations: rebasing a long-lived branch repeatedly onto a moving main (you would otherwise re-resolve the same conflicts each time), and maintaining a long-running merge between two diverging branches. Without rerere, every rebase re-presents conflicts you already solved; with it, the resolution is replayed automatically. Subtle but loved: few engineers know rerere. Citing it for "I keep re-resolving the same conflict on each rebase" shows you have done real long-branch maintenance and know the ergonomic fixes.

questions.q: Explain packfiles, loose objects, and what git gc does.
questions.text: Git stores objects two ways: loose (one file per object, fast to write) and packed (many objects delta-compressed into a packfile, efficient to store/transfer). gc converts and optimizes. ls .git/objects/ # loose objects in 2-char-prefixed dirs ls .git/objects/pack/ # packfiles (.pack) + indexes (.idx) git gc # pack loose objects, prune, build commit-graph git gc --aggressive # recompute deltas more thoroughly (slow) git count-objects -vH # see loose vs packed sizes git repack -ad # repack everything into one pack New objects start loose (cheap to create). Over time git gc (run automatically) packs them into packfiles using delta compression — storing similar objects as deltas against each other, which dramatically shrinks repo size and speeds up clones/fetches (the network transfers packs). gc also prunes unreachable objects past the grace window and builds the commit-graph for fast history traversal. Operational note: git maintenance start schedules background gc, prefetch, and commit-graph updates — the modern, incremental replacement for periodic gc --aggressive , keeping large repos fast without disruptive full repacks.

questions.q: How does Git handle large binary files, and what is Git LFS doing under the hood?
questions.text: Git is built for text: it stores full snapshots and delta-compresses similar objects. Binaries do not delta well, so each version bloats history permanently. Git LFS solves this with pointers. The problem Every version of a 50MB binary is stored in full in history — forever Clones must download all historical versions; repo balloons How LFS works git lfs track '*.psd' # writes patterns to .gitattributes # On commit, the file is replaced in Git by a small text POINTER: # version, oid (sha256), size # The real bytes go to a separate LFS store; fetched on checkout on demand git lfs ls-files # list LFS-tracked files LFS replaces the binary in Git history with a tiny pointer file (an OID + size); the actual content lives in a separate LFS server and is downloaded only for the versions you check out. So history stays small and clones are fast, because you do not drag every historical revision of every asset. .gitattributes records which patterns are LFS-managed. Caveat: LFS needs server support and adds operational complexity (storage quotas, a separate store, migration of existing history with git lfs migrate ). For truly large or non-versioned assets, an object store (S3/GCS) referenced by URL is sometimes the better answer than putting them in Git at all.

questions.q: What is the commit-graph file and how does it speed up Git operations?
questions.text: The commit-graph is an auxiliary file caching commit metadata and a precomputed reachability structure, so Git avoids walking and parsing commit objects one by one. git commit-graph write --reachable # build it git config core.commitGraph true # enable usage (default in modern Git) git config fetch.writeCommitGraph true # generation numbers enable fast 'is A an ancestor of B?' answers Operations like git log --graph , git merge-base , git tag --contains , and ahead/behind counts require traversing and parsing many commit objects. The commit-graph stores parents, commit dates, and generation numbers in a single memory-mappable file, turning expensive walks into fast lookups. On large repos this is the difference between sub-second and multi-second history queries. Where it shows up: it is part of the modern large-repo toolkit alongside partial clone, sparse-checkout, and git maintenance . Mentioning generation numbers (fast ancestry tests) demonstrates real internals knowledge.

questions.q: When and why would you use git merge --no-ff vs a fast-forward merge?
questions.text: A fast-forward merge just moves the branch pointer forward when there is no divergence — leaving no record that a branch existed. --no-ff forces a merge commit to preserve that boundary. git merge feature # fast-forwards if main hasn't diverged (no merge commit) git merge --no-ff feature # always create a merge commit, recording the branch git merge --ff-only feature # refuse to merge unless it can fast-forward --no-ff preserves feature-branch boundaries in history — you can see "these commits were one PR" and revert the whole feature with a single revert -m 1 of the merge commit. Useful for traceability and easy feature-level rollback. Fast-forward (or squash) keeps history linear and uncluttered. --ff-only is a safety setting (often on git pull ) that refuses to silently create merge commits, forcing you to rebase intentionally. Policy angle: --no-ff + meaningful merge commits gives feature-level grouping and one-shot reverts; squash gives the cleanest linear log. State the trade-off (traceability vs tidiness) and that consistency per repo matters.

questions.q: Explain how git stash works internally and its common pitfalls.
questions.text: A stash is not magic storage — it is real commits. Git creates commit objects capturing your work and parks them on a special ref, leaving your working tree clean. git stash # stash tracked changes git stash -u # include untracked files git stash push -m 'wip: parser' # named stash git stash list # refs/stash + reflog of stashes git stash show -p stash@{0} # view a stash's diff git stash pop # apply + drop git stash apply # apply, keep in list cat .git/refs/stash # the stash ref (a commit) Internally a stash builds (at least) two commits — one for the index, one for the working tree — with your current commit as parent, stored under refs/stash as a stack (reflog). Because they are real commits, a dropped or popped stash is recoverable via the reflog / fsck even though it is off the stash list. Pitfalls: (1) git stash ignores untracked files unless you add -u — people lose new files this way. (2) pop can conflict and then NOT drop the stash, causing confusion. (3) stashes are easy to forget — prefer short-lived WIP commits or worktrees for anything beyond a quick context switch.

questions.q: What are Git refspecs and how do they control fetch/push behavior?
questions.text: A refspec maps refs between a remote and your local repo — <src>:<dst> with an optional leading + for force. It is the rule behind every fetch and push. # Default fetch refspec for 'origin': +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/* # all remote branches → origin/* (force-update) git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main git push origin local-branch:remote-branch # push local to a differently-named remote ref git push origin :stale-branch # empty src = DELETE the remote branch git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main # Gerrit-style review push The + prefix allows non-fast-forward (force) updates — which is why your local origin/* tracking refs always update even after upstream rebases, while your own branches do not. Custom refspecs let you fetch/push to differently-named refs, fetch only specific branches, or delete remote branches (empty source). Understanding refspecs explains seemingly-magic behaviors like "why does fetch update origin/main but not my main?" Configured in .git/config under each remote’s fetch = line. Editing it (e.g. to fetch only one branch) is a real technique for limiting traffic on huge repos.

questions.q: How do you keep a fork in sync with upstream, and integrate upstream changes cleanly?
questions.text: A fork needs both the upstream and your origin as remotes; you sync by fetching upstream and rebasing or merging your changes on top. git remote add upstream <original-repo-url> git remote -v # origin (your fork) + upstream git fetch upstream git checkout main git rebase upstream/main # replay your changes on latest upstream (clean) # or: git merge upstream/main # if you prefer merge commits / shared branch git push origin main # update your fork # For a feature branch you're contributing back: git rebase upstream/main feature && git push --force-with-lease origin feature Add the original as upstream , fetch it, and integrate. For a personal fork you control, rebasing onto upstream/main keeps your contribution a clean series on top of current upstream — exactly what maintainers want to review. Use --force-with-lease when re-pushing a rebased feature branch on your fork (safe force). Keep your fork’s main a clean mirror of upstream and do work on feature branches. Open-source etiquette: rebase your PR branch onto current upstream before review so it applies cleanly, and keep the commit series tidy. This is the workflow interviewers expect from anyone who contributes to OSS.

questions.q: What is git replace / git notes, and a scenario where each is useful?
questions.text: Both attach or substitute information without rewriting the original immutable history — useful when you must annotate or virtually edit history you cannot change. git notes — attach metadata to commits git notes add -m 'reviewed-by: ...' <sha> git log --show-notes # Use: CI results, review metadata, ticket links, attached to commits after the fact git replace — virtual object substitution git replace <old-sha> <new-sha> # transparently swap one object for another # Use: graft histories, fix a broken object, or stitch a shallow/old history on git notes attaches mutable annotations (review info, CI status, references) to immutable commits without changing their SHAs — handy for adding context after the fact. git replace creates a transparent substitution so tools see a different object in place of another, without rewriting history — classically used to graft a truncated/imported history onto an older archive, or to test a fix for a corrupt object. Niche but telling: these are advanced plumbing. Knowing they let you annotate or virtually-edit history non-destructively (vs filter-repo which rewrites SHAs) signals deep familiarity.

questions.q: Explain octopus merges and when (or whether) to use them.
questions.text: An octopus merge combines more than two branches in a single merge commit (3+ parents). Git can do it, but only for conflict-free integrations. git merge branch-a branch-b branch-c # one merge commit with multiple parents git log --graph # shows the multi-parent merge Octopus merges are restricted to cases where the branches do not conflict — the default octopus strategy bails out if conflict resolution is needed, because resolving an N-way conflict is impractical. The legitimate use is integrating many independent, non-overlapping topic branches at once (historically used in some integration workflows). In practice they are rare and usually a smell. Mostly avoid: octopus merges make history hard to read and bisect, and signal that you are batching integrations in a way that hides risk. Modern teams prefer merging PRs individually (often through a merge queue), which keeps each integration testable and revertible. Know it exists; rarely reach for it.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large legacy repository to a cleaner structure or remove bloat?
questions.text: Rewriting large repos is done with git-filter-repo (filter-branch is deprecated and slow). The work is high-impact but disruptive, so plan the coordination. pip install git-filter-repo git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M # purge huge files from all history git filter-repo --path keep/this/ --path also/this/ # keep only certain paths (extract a subdir) git filter-repo --path-rename old/:new/ # restructure paths across history git filter-repo --invert-paths --path secrets/ # remove a path entirely # Then everyone re-clones; force-push the rewritten history filter-repo can purge oversized blobs, extract a subdirectory into its own repo (preserving that path’s history), rename/restructure paths across all of history, or remove sensitive files. Because it rewrites every commit SHA, the rollout is the hard part: communicate a freeze, do the rewrite, force-push, and have everyone re-clone (old clones and open PRs are invalidated). Plan the cutover like a deploy: announce a window, freeze merges, rewrite, verify with git fsck and a diff of tip trees, force-push, then unfreeze. Half-migrated states (some forks on old history) are the failure mode — coordinate explicitly.

questions.q: What causes "merge conflict" vs "semantic conflict," and how do you defend against each?
questions.text: A textual merge conflict is when both sides edit the same lines — Git detects it. A semantic conflict is when both sides merge cleanly but the combined code is broken — Git cannot see it. Textual conflict Both branches change the same region → Git inserts conflict markers Defense: small PRs, frequent integration, clear ownership of files Semantic conflict (the dangerous one) Branch A renames a function; Branch B adds a new call to the OLD name Both merge cleanly (different lines) — but main no longer compiles/works Defense: merge queue (test the COMBINED state), strong test suite, CI on main Textual conflicts are visible and Git forces you to resolve them. Semantic conflicts are insidious precisely because each PR is green in isolation and they merge without markers — the breakage only appears in the integrated result. The structural defense is a merge queue that builds and tests the actual post-merge state, plus a comprehensive test suite that catches the integration failure. Staff-level point: "passed CI but broke main" is almost always a semantic conflict. Naming the merge queue as the systemic fix (rather than "be more careful") shows you solve it at the platform level.

questions.q: What exactly is HEAD, and what is a detached HEAD state?
questions.text: HEAD is a reference to "where you are now" — normally a pointer to a branch name, which in turn points to a commit. Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly at a commit, not at a branch. cat .git/HEAD # normally: ref: refs/heads/main git checkout <sha> # detaches HEAD onto a specific commit git checkout v2.3.0 # checking out a tag also detaches # In detached state, new commits belong to NO branch: git switch -c rescue # create a branch to keep detached-state commits git switch - # return to previous branch Normally HEAD → branch → commit, so committing advances the branch. In detached HEAD , HEAD → commit directly: you can look around and even commit, but those commits are not on any branch and become unreachable (garbage-collectable) once you leave — unless you create a branch to anchor them. It happens when you check out a SHA, tag, or remote-tracking ref directly. The classic data-loss trap: making commits in detached HEAD, then switching away — the commits look gone. They are in the reflog for the grace period, so git reflog + git branch rescue <sha> recovers them. Always create a branch before committing in detached state.

questions.q: What is the difference between git switch/restore and git checkout?
questions.text: git checkout was historically overloaded — it switched branches AND restored files, causing confusion and accidents. Git 2.23 split it into two focused commands. # Switching branches: git switch main # switch to an existing branch (clear intent) git switch -c feature # create + switch git switch - # toggle to previous branch # Restoring files: git restore file.py # discard working-tree changes to a file git restore --staged file.py # unstage (keep working-tree changes) git restore --source=HEAD~2 file.py # restore file from an older commit switch handles branch operations; restore handles file content operations. The old git checkout file.py silently discarded your changes with no undo — a notorious footgun — because the same verb also meant "switch branch." The split makes intent explicit and reduces accidental data loss. checkout still works for backward compatibility. Why it matters: recommending switch / restore shows you keep current and care about reducing destructive ambiguity — a small but real signal of modern Git fluency.

questions.q: Explain the staging area (index) and why it exists.
questions.text: The index (staging area) is an intermediate layer between your working tree and the repository — it holds the proposed contents of the next commit, letting you compose commits deliberately. git add file.py # stage whole file git add -p # stage selected hunks interactively git status # staged vs unstaged vs untracked git diff # working tree vs index (unstaged changes) git diff --staged # index vs HEAD (what will be committed) git restore --staged file.py # unstage cat .git/index # binary index file (not human-readable) The index lets you craft a commit that is a subset of your working changes — you can have edits in ten files but stage only the three that form one logical change, using git add -p to even select specific hunks. This is what enables clean, single-purpose commits. The two-stage model (working tree → index → commit) is core to Git and surprises newcomers from systems that commit the whole working state. Interview depth: explaining git diff (tree vs index) vs git diff --staged (index vs HEAD) shows you truly understand the three states. The index is also why reset --soft/--mixed/--hard behave differently.

questions.q: How do remote-tracking branches work, and what is the relationship to local branches?
questions.text: Remote-tracking branches (e.g. origin/main ) are local, read-only bookmarks of where a remote branch was at your last fetch. They are not the remote, and not editable directly. git branch -vv # show local branches + their upstream + ahead/behind git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main git fetch # updates origin/* tracking refs (not your branches) git status # 'ahead 2, behind 1' compares to tracking branch git push -u origin feature # set upstream while first pushing origin/main is a cache: git fetch updates it to the remote’s latest, but your local main moves only when you merge/rebase or pull. The "ahead/behind" in git status compares your branch to its upstream tracking branch. This separation is deliberate — fetch is safe (only updates tracking refs), while integrating remote work into your branch is a separate, explicit step you control. Mental model: three layers — the remote (server), origin/* (your last-known snapshot of it), and your local branches (your work). fetch syncs the middle layer; merge/rebase/pull bridges middle to local. This explains why fetch never surprises you with changed files.

questions.q: What is the difference between .gitignore, .git/info/exclude, and assume-unchanged?
questions.text: Three mechanisms to not track files, differing in scope and intent: shared, local-only, and "ignore changes to a tracked file." .gitignore # committed, shared with the team (project-wide) .git/info/exclude # local-only ignores, NOT committed (personal) ~/.config/git/ignore # global ignores for all your repos # For ALREADY-tracked files (.gitignore won't ignore those): git rm --cached file # stop tracking, keep on disk git update-index --skip-worktree config.local # ignore local changes to a tracked file git update-index --assume-unchanged big.bin # perf hint: assume file unchanged .gitignore is committed and shared — for build artifacts, deps, OS files everyone should ignore. .git/info/exclude is your private, uncommitted ignore list. Critically, .gitignore only affects untracked files — to stop tracking something already committed you must git rm --cached it. --skip-worktree is the right tool for "keep this tracked file but ignore my local edits" (e.g. a config template you tweak locally); --assume-unchanged is only a performance hint, not a reliable ignore. Common confusion: adding a file to .gitignore after it is already tracked does nothing — Git keeps tracking it. You must untrack with git rm --cached first. And do not use --assume-unchanged to hide local config edits; it is unreliable — use --skip-worktree .

questions.q: How would you design a branch naming and lifecycle convention for a large team?
questions.text: Conventions reduce cognitive load and enable automation. Encode type, scope, and traceability in the name, and define a clear lifecycle. Naming pattern feature/JIRA-123-short-description fix/JIRA-456-null-pointer hotfix/CVE-2025-xxxx release/2.4.0 # type/ticket-slug — parseable by automation, traceable to a ticket Lifecycle Short-lived: branch → PR → review → merge → auto-delete on merge Auto-delete merged branches; flag/clean stale branches (>30 days) periodically Branch → environment mapping handled by tags/artifacts, not long-lived branches A type/ticket-slug convention makes branches self-documenting and machine-parseable (CI can route by type, link to tickets, derive changelogs). The lifecycle should favor short-lived branches with auto-deletion on merge, and a periodic sweep of stale branches — a repo with hundreds of dead branches is a navigation and tooling burden. Tie versioning to tags, not to permanent environment branches. Platform framing: branch hygiene (auto-delete, stale cleanup, parseable names) is a small thing that compounds at scale. Owning it as policy + automation is the platform-engineering instinct interviewers look for.

questions.q: Explain the difference between author and committer on a commit.
questions.text: Git records two identities per commit: the author (who wrote the change) and the committer (who created this commit object). They are usually the same but diverge after history rewriting. git log --pretty=fuller # shows both Author/AuthorDate and Commit/CommitDate git show --format=fuller <sha> # When they differ: # rebase — committer becomes the rebaser, author stays original # cherry-pick — same: author preserved, committer is you # applying a patch / PR on someone's behalf When you rebase, cherry-pick, amend, or apply someone else’s patch, Git preserves the original author (and author date) but sets the committer to you with a new commit date. This is why a rebased branch shows old author dates but new commit dates. It matters for attribution (the author gets credit) and for audit (the committer shows who actually rewrote/applied it). Audit relevance: git log --pretty=fuller distinguishing the two is useful in forensics — e.g. spotting that a commit was authored long ago but committed (rebased/applied) recently by someone else. Both fields are self-reported, hence the need for signing.

questions.q: What is a tracking branch vs an upstream branch, and how do you set them?
questions.text: An upstream (tracking) relationship links a local branch to a remote-tracking branch so Git knows what to compare against and where to push/pull by default. git push -u origin feature # push AND set origin/feature as upstream git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main git branch -vv # see each local branch's upstream + ahead/behind git status # uses upstream to report ahead/behind # Without upstream set, bare 'git push'/'git pull' may error or need full args Setting an upstream lets you run bare git push / git pull (Git knows the target), and powers the "ahead 3, behind 1" status. -u on first push is the common way to establish it. git branch -vv shows the full picture: local branch, its upstream, and divergence. Without an upstream, Git relies on push.default config and may require explicit origin branch arguments. Config to know: push.default = simple (the modern default) pushes the current branch to its upstream of the same name — safe behavior. Understanding upstreams explains a lot of "why did push go there / why this ahead-behind" confusion.

questions.q: How does git diff work, and what are the most useful diff options in practice?
questions.text: Git computes diffs on demand (it stores snapshots, not diffs) by comparing trees. The comparison endpoints depend on the flags. git diff # working tree vs index (unstaged) git diff --staged # index vs HEAD (what's about to commit) git diff HEAD # working tree vs last commit (all changes) git diff main..feature # tip-to-tip difference git diff main...feature # changes on feature SINCE it diverged (merge-base) git diff -w # ignore whitespace git diff --stat # summary: files + insertions/deletions git diff --color-moved # distinguish moved code from added/deleted The endpoints matter: no args = unstaged, --staged = staged, HEAD = everything since last commit. The two-dot vs three-dot distinction is a frequent interview point: main..feature is a raw tip comparison, while main...feature shows what feature added since branching off the merge base — usually what you want for "what does this PR change." --color-moved and -w make reviews of refactors far clearer. Underused gem: git diff --color-moved highlights relocated code differently from genuine changes — invaluable when reviewing a refactor that moved blocks around. Mentioning two-dot vs three-dot semantics signals real fluency.

questions.q: How do you clean up local and remote branches safely at scale?
questions.text: Stale branches accumulate and clutter tooling. Clean them with awareness of what is merged and what is gone from the remote. git fetch --prune # remove local origin/* refs for deleted remote branches git branch --merged main # local branches already merged into main (safe to delete) git branch -d feature # delete merged branch (refuses if unmerged) git branch -D feature # force-delete (use with care) git branch --no-merged main # branches NOT yet merged (review before deleting) # Find stale branches by last-commit date: git for-each-ref --sort=committerdate refs/heads/ --format='%(committerdate:short) %(refname:short)' git push origin --delete old-branch # delete a remote branch git fetch --prune clears local tracking refs for branches deleted on the remote (otherwise origin/* accumulates ghosts). --merged / --no-merged separate safe deletions from ones needing review. The lowercase -d is safe (refuses unmerged branches); -D forces and can lose work. git for-each-ref sorted by date finds the truly stale ones programmatically. Automate it: enable "auto-delete head branches on merge" in the platform, run a periodic job listing branches older than N days with no open PR, and prune tracking refs on fetch. Branch hygiene as automation, not manual chores.

questions.q: What happens, object by object, when you make a commit?
questions.text: A commit triggers a cascade of object creation in the content-addressed store. Understanding it demystifies why commits are snapshots and why SHAs change on rewrite. The sequence 1. git add → blob objects written for changed file contents (hashed by content) 2. git commit → tree objects built from the index (directory → blob/tree mapping) 3. a commit object is written: points to the root tree + parent commit(s) + author/msg 4. the current branch ref is updated to point at the new commit SHA 5. HEAD (via the branch) now resolves to the new commit Each step produces immutable, SHA-addressed objects: blobs (file contents), trees (directory snapshots referencing blobs/subtrees), and a commit (root tree + parents + metadata). The commit is a full snapshot (via the tree), not a diff. Only the branch ref — a tiny file in .git/refs/heads/ — is mutated to point at the new commit. This is why amending or rebasing creates entirely new objects with new SHAs: you cannot edit an immutable object, only create a replacement and move the ref. The payoff insight: "a branch is just a movable pointer; commits are immutable snapshots." Explaining the blob→tree→commit→ref chain is the single clearest demonstration that you understand Git’s data model rather than just its commands.

questions.q: Explain the tradeoffs of rebasing vs merging for keeping a feature branch current.
questions.text: Both bring main’s latest into your feature branch; they differ in resulting history and safety. The right choice depends on whether the branch is shared. Rebase onto main git rebase main # replay your commits on top of latest main + Linear, clean history; no merge-bubble clutter + Your changes read as if written against current main - Rewrites SHAs — unsafe if others share the branch - Must resolve conflicts per-commit; force-push needed after Merge main in git merge main # bring main into feature via a merge commit + Non-destructive; safe on shared branches; resolve conflicts once - Adds merge commits; busier, non-linear history Rebase gives a clean, linear history and is ideal for a private feature branch you will open as a PR — reviewers see a tidy series against current main. Merge is non-destructive and the safe choice when others share the branch, at the cost of merge bubbles. The cardinal rule: never rebase commits that others have already pulled (the "golden rule of rebasing") — it rewrites shared history and forces everyone to recover. Golden rule of rebasing: only rebase commits that exist solely in your local/private branch. Once pushed and pulled by others, integrate with merge instead. Violating this is the most common cause of team-wide Git chaos.

questions.q: How do tags differ from branches, and lightweight vs annotated tags?
questions.text: Both are refs pointing at commits, but a branch moves as you commit while a tag is a fixed marker. Tags come in two flavors with different metadata and trust properties. git tag v2.4.0 # LIGHTWEIGHT: just a name → commit pointer git tag -a v2.4.0 -m 'Release 2.4.0' # ANNOTATED: a real tag OBJECT (tagger, date, msg) git tag -s v2.4.0 # signed annotated tag (GPG/SSH) git push origin v2.4.0 # tags are NOT pushed by default git push origin --tags # push all tags git describe --tags # nearest tag + distance (version strings) A branch ref advances with each commit; a tag ref stays put — it marks a specific point (a release). Lightweight tags are just a name pointing at a commit (like a branch that never moves). Annotated tags are full objects storing the tagger, date, message, and an optional signature — and they are what you should use for releases, because they carry provenance and can be verified. Remember tags are not pushed automatically. Always annotate releases: annotated (ideally signed) tags give you an auditable, verifiable release marker; lightweight tags are fine for private/local bookmarks. git describe turning tags into deterministic version strings is the basis of many CI versioning schemes.

questions.q: Capstone: design a complete Git strategy for a 50-engineer SaaS deploying many times a day.
questions.text: Tie together branching model, integration, deploy mapping, safety, and governance into one coherent system suited to high-velocity SaaS. Branching & integration Trunk-based: short-lived branches off main, merged within a day Feature flags decouple deploy from release (ship dark, enable gradually) Squash-merge to main: one clean, revertible commit per PR Merge queue: serialize merges, test the combined state, keep main always green Deploy & rollback Build artifact ONCE on merge; promote same artifact: staging → (tag) → prod canary GitOps (Argo/Flux) with a config repo as source of truth; rollback = git revert Progressive delivery with auto-abort on SLO/metric regression Safety & governance Branch protection: required green checks, CODEOWNERS review, no force-push to main Signed commits; secret scanning + push protection; pre-commit hooks shipped in-repo OIDC (no long-lived PATs) for CI → cloud; access managed as code (Terraform) Auto-delete merged branches; track PR cycle time as a health metric The through-line: optimize for small batches integrated continuously and shipped safely . Trunk-based + feature flags + a merge queue keeps main releasable at high volume. Build-once/promote with GitOps gives traceable deploys and one-command (revert) rollback. Branch protection, signed commits, secret scanning, and OIDC enforce safety without slowing people down. Every guardrail is automated so contributing is easy and mistakes are caught by tooling, not heroics. What ties it together

questions.q: What is the difference between git restore, git reset and git checkout -- file for discarding changes?
questions.text: restore is the modern, single-purpose command for files; reset moves branch pointers and optionally the index; checkout -- file is the older overloaded form of restore. Know which tree each one touches. git restore file.txt git restore --staged file.txt git restore --source=HEAD~2 file.txt git reset HEAD file.txt Interview tip: restore without flags only touches the working tree. Add --staged to touch the index.

questions.q: What is the difference between git config at system, global and local levels, and how do includeIf rules help?
questions.text: Config is layered: system, global (user), local (repo), plus worktree. Later levels override earlier ones. includeIf loads different identity or settings depending on the repo path. git config --list --show-origin git config --global user.email me@example.com git config --local core.hooksPath .githooks [includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"] path = ~/.gitconfig-work Interview tip: Use show-origin to debug where a surprising setting comes from.

questions.q: What does git status show beyond changed files, and how do you read ahead/behind information?
questions.text: Status shows the branch, its upstream, ahead/behind counts, staged and unstaged changes, untracked files and in-progress operations like a rebase or merge. Short and branch flags make it scriptable. git status -sb git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD git status --porcelain=v2 --branch git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short) %(upstream:track)' refs/heads Interview tip: Porcelain output is stable across versions, so scripts should use it instead of parsing the human format.

questions.q: How do you use git add -p to craft clean commits from messy working changes?
questions.text: Patch mode stages individual hunks, letting you split unrelated edits into separate logical commits. Use s to split hunks and e to edit them manually. git add -p git add -p src/api.py git diff --staged git restore -p file.txt Interview tip: Review with git diff --staged before committing, so you know exactly what is in the commit.

questions.q: What are Git's merge-base and how do triple-dot and double-dot ranges differ?
questions.text: merge-base is the best common ancestor of two commits. A..B means commits reachable from B but not A; A...B in log means those in either but not both; in diff, A...B compares B to the merge-base. git merge-base main feature git log main..feature --oneline git log main...feature --left-right --oneline git diff main...feature Interview tip: For reviewing a PR, diff with triple dots shows only the branch's own changes, ignoring main's newer commits.

questions.q: How does git switch -c and git branch --set-upstream-to differ from push -u when creating feature branches?
questions.text: switch -c creates and checks out a local branch. Upstream tracking links it to a remote branch so status, pull and push know the counterpart. push -u does the push and sets tracking in one step. git switch -c feature/login git push -u origin feature/login git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/feature/login git config push.autoSetupRemote true Interview tip: push.autoSetupRemote removes the need for -u on the first push.

questions.q: What is a release branch strategy and how do you backport a fix to several maintained versions?
questions.text: Maintain release/x.y branches for supported versions. Fix on main first, then cherry-pick with -x to each supported release branch, test, and tag patch releases. Automation labels PRs for backports. git switch release/2.4 git cherry-pick -x abc1234 git tag -a v2.4.3 -m 'Patch release' git branch --contains abc1234 -r Interview tip: Always fix forward on main first so the bug cannot reappear in the next release.

questions.q: How do feature flags reduce the need for long-lived branches?
questions.text: Flags let incomplete work merge to main behind a switch, decoupling deploy from release. Branches stay short, integration is continuous, and rollout can be gradual and instantly reversible. if (flags.isEnabled('new-checkout', user)) { newFlow() } else { oldFlow() } git log --since=2.weeks --merges --oneline | wc -l git branch --sort=committerdate --format='%(committerdate:short) %(refname:short)' Interview tip: Flags are debt. Track and delete them after rollout, or the codebase fills with dead paths.

questions.q: How do you rename the default branch from master to main without breaking clones and CI?
questions.text: Rename on the host, which can set redirects; update local clones with branch -m and upstream changes; fix CI triggers, protection rules, deploy configs, docs and webhooks; communicate with a short checklist. git branch -m master main git fetch origin git branch -u origin/main main git remote set-head origin -a Interview tip: Search the whole organisation for hard-coded master references in pipelines, badges and scripts before cutting over.

questions.q: What is stacked branching (stacked PRs) and when is it worth the complexity?
questions.text: Stacked branches build each change on top of the previous one so large work is reviewed as small dependent pull requests. Tools automate rebasing the stack when a lower branch changes. git switch -c part1 && git switch -c part2 git rebase --onto part1 old-part1 part2 git rebase --update-refs main git push --force-with-lease origin part1 part2 Interview tip: The update-refs flag moves all intermediate branch pointers during a rebase, which makes stacks far easier to maintain.

questions.q: What merge strategies and options does Git offer (ort, recursive, ours, theirs, subtree), and when do they matter?
questions.text: The default ort strategy handles most merges. -X ours/theirs resolve conflicting hunks automatically in favour of one side; -s ours discards the other branch's changes entirely. Choose carefully because both can hide mistakes. git merge -s ort -X patience feature git merge -X theirs feature git merge -s ours obsolete-branch git merge -s subtree vendor/lib Interview tip: -X ours only affects conflicting hunks. -s ours keeps your tree and records the merge, ignoring all of theirs.

questions.q: How do you configure and use a mergetool and diff3/zdiff3 conflict style to make resolution easier?
questions.text: The diff3 and zdiff3 styles include the common ancestor in conflict markers, so you can see what each side changed. A three-way mergetool shows base, local and remote side by side. git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 git mergetool git checkout --ours file && git checkout --theirs file git diff --base file Interview tip: Seeing the base version often makes the right resolution obvious, instead of guessing between two competing blocks.

questions.q: How do you merge a branch that has already been squash-merged elsewhere without getting duplicate conflicts?
questions.text: After a squash merge, the original commits are not ancestors of main, so Git sees them as unmerged. Rebase the child branch with --onto to drop the already-squashed commits, or delete and recreate from main. git rebase --onto main old-feature child-feature git log main..child-feature --oneline git cherry -v main child-feature Interview tip: git cherry marks commits already applied upstream with a minus, which helps identify what is truly new.

questions.q: What is git merge --abort versus git reset --merge, and how do you safely back out of a merge in progress?
questions.text: merge --abort restores the pre-merge state when no uncommitted changes would be lost. reset --merge is the lower-level equivalent. If the merge was already committed locally, use reset to ORIG_HEAD or revert if it was pushed. git merge --abort git reset --merge git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> Interview tip: Commit or stash your local edits before merging so an abort can cleanly restore the starting point.

questions.q: How does git rebase --autosquash with fixup commits streamline addressing review feedback?
questions.text: Create fixup! commits targeting earlier commits with git commit --fixup, then run an interactive rebase with --autosquash to reorder and squash them automatically into their targets. git commit --fixup=abc1234 git rebase -i --autosquash main git config --global rebase.autoSquash true git push --force-with-lease Interview tip: Reviewers can see the incremental fixup commits during review, and you squash them away just before merge.

questions.q: How do you use git log -S and -G (pickaxe) to find when a piece of code was added or removed?
questions.text: -S finds commits where the number of occurrences of a string changed; -G finds commits whose diff matches a regex. Combine with -p and --follow to trace code through history. git log -S'MAX_RETRIES' --oneline git log -G'timeout\s*=\s*\d+' -p -- src/ git log -L :parseConfig:src/config.py git log --follow -p -- path/to/file Interview tip: -L traces the history of a function or line range, which often beats blame for understanding how code evolved.

questions.q: How do you rewrite history across an entire repository using git filter-repo, and what are the consequences?
questions.text: filter-repo is the supported replacement for filter-branch. It rewrites every commit to drop paths, replace text or change authors. All hashes change, so everyone must reclone and open PRs break. git filter-repo --path secrets.env --invert-paths git filter-repo --replace-text expressions.txt git filter-repo --mailmap mailmap.txt git clone --mirror repo.git && cd repo.git Interview tip: Always work on a fresh mirror clone and keep a backup, because the operation is destructive and rewrites everything.

questions.q: What is a good strategy for using git blame effectively, including ignoring formatting-only commits?
questions.text: Use blame with -w, -M and -C to ignore whitespace and detect moved code, and configure blame.ignoreRevsFile so bulk reformatting commits don't hide the real author and reason. git blame -w -M -C file.py git blame -L 40,60 file.py echo <format-commit-sha> >> .git-blame-ignore-revs git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs Interview tip: Blame tells you who last touched a line, not who wrote the logic. Follow the commit message and PR for the why.

questions.q: How do you generate a changelog and release notes from Git history reliably?
questions.text: Use conventional commit messages or PR labels, then generate notes from the range between tags with git log or tooling. Consistency in commit format is what makes automation trustworthy. git log v1.4.0..v1.5.0 --pretty='- %s (%h)' --no-merges git describe --tags --abbrev=0 git log --grep='^feat' v1.4.0..HEAD --oneline git shortlog -sn v1.4.0..HEAD Interview tip: Generated notes are only as good as the commit messages, so enforce a convention with a commit-msg hook or CI check.

questions.q: How can you find which commits touched a file but are not in a release, using git cherry, branch --contains and tag --contains?
questions.text: Use contains queries to see which branches or tags include a commit, and git log with ranges to list what is on main but not yet in a release tag. git tag --contains abc1234 git branch -r --contains abc1234 git log v2.3.0..origin/main --oneline -- path/ git cherry -v release/2.3 main Interview tip: This answers the common production question: is my fix in the build that is deployed?

questions.q: How do you design a code review workflow using draft pull requests, required checks and CODEOWNERS?
questions.text: Draft PRs signal work in progress, required status checks prevent merging broken code, CODEOWNERS routes review to the right people, and branch protection enforces it all. Keep PRs small to keep review fast. gh pr create --draft --fill gh pr checks --watch gh pr ready gh pr merge --squash --auto Interview tip: Measure time-to-first-review and PR size. Long reviews usually mean oversized changes, not slow reviewers.

questions.q: What is the forking workflow and when is it used instead of shared-repo branches?
questions.text: Contributors fork the upstream repo, push to their fork, and open PRs back. It suits open source and cross-organisation work where contributors lack write access, with upstream as a read-only remote. git remote add upstream https://host/org/repo.git git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main git push origin feature git remote -v Interview tip: Keep the fork's main in sync with upstream, and always branch from the updated main, not from your fork's stale copy.

questions.q: How would you set up Git workflows for a team using conventional commits, semantic-release and protected tags?
questions.text: Enforce commit format in PRs, let a release job read commits since the last tag to compute the next semver, create the tag and changelog, and protect tags so only the release job can create them. git commit -m 'feat(api): add pagination' git commit -m 'fix!: change error format' -m 'BREAKING CHANGE: ...' npx semantic-release --dry-run git tag -l 'v*' --sort=-v:refname | head Interview tip: Dry runs in pull requests show the version bump a change would cause before it merges.

questions.q: How do you handle a merge freeze or release train in a busy monorepo?
questions.text: Use a merge queue or protected release branch, cut the release at a known commit, allow only approved fixes after the cut, and communicate freeze windows clearly with automation enforcing them. git switch -c release/2026-10 <cut-sha> git cherry-pick -x <approved-fix> gh api repos/org/repo/rulesets git log release/2026-10..main --oneline | wc -l Interview tip: Prefer cutting a release branch over freezing main, so everyone else can keep merging.

questions.q: What Git practices help with working across time zones and asynchronous teams?
questions.text: Small PRs with clear descriptions, branch naming and ownership conventions, automated checks to give instant feedback, rebasing discipline, and written decision records so work does not block on someone being online. git log --since='yesterday' --format='%an %s' --no-merges gh pr list --search 'review:required' git config --global pull.rebase true git config --global fetch.prune true Interview tip: The goal is that a reviewer in another time zone can approve without a call, from the description and CI results alone.

questions.q: How do you recover lost commits that are no longer reachable from any branch, such as after a reset or a dropped stash?
questions.text: Use reflog for recent HEAD positions, git fsck --lost-found for dangling commits, and unreachable stash commits via fsck. Create a branch at the recovered SHA before gc prunes it. git reflog git fsck --lost-found --no-reflogs git branch rescue <sha> git stash apply <dropped-stash-sha> Interview tip: Unreachable objects survive until gc prunes them, typically after at least two weeks, so act promptly.

questions.q: You pushed to the wrong branch (for example main) by mistake. What do you do?
questions.text: Act quickly: tell the team, check whether CI or deploys have picked it up, then revert on the shared branch (or force-reset only if policy allows and nobody has pulled), and move the commits to the right branch. git revert <sha> git branch correct-branch <sha> git push --force-with-lease origin <good-sha>:main git log origin/main --oneline -5 Interview tip: Reverting is the safe default on shared branches. Force-resetting main is a last resort and needs agreement.

questions.q: How do you fix a repository where git pull says 'refusing to merge unrelated histories'?
questions.text: The two histories share no common ancestor, for example after reinitialising or a history rewrite. Decide whether to reclone, rebase onto the new history, or deliberately merge with --allow-unrelated-histories. git merge-base HEAD origin/main git log --oneline --graph --all | head git pull --allow-unrelated-histories git rebase --onto origin/main <old-base> mybranch Interview tip: Usually this signals a rewritten or recreated remote, so understand why before forcing a merge.

questions.q: How do you undo a git rebase that you already finished, using ORIG_HEAD and the reflog?
questions.text: After a completed rebase, ORIG_HEAD or the reflog entry before the rebase points at the old tip. Reset the branch to it to restore the pre-rebase history, if you have not pushed or are willing to force-push. git reflog git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD git reset --hard 'HEAD@{5}' git rebase --abort Interview tip: ORIG_HEAD is overwritten by later risky commands, so the reflog is the more reliable record.

questions.q: What is git fsck, git prune and git gc --prune, and what should you never run during an incident?
questions.text: fsck verifies and lists problems or dangling objects, prune deletes unreachable objects, and gc packs and optionally prunes. During recovery, avoid gc/prune or clearing reflog until you've saved what you need. git fsck --full git count-objects -vH git gc --prune=never git reflog expire --expire=never --all Interview tip: Before recovery, copy the whole .git directory. Then experiment on the copy.

questions.q: How do you review a pull request effectively, and what do you look for?
questions.text: Start with intent and design, then correctness, tests, security, performance and operability, and finally style. Check the diff in context, run it if risky, and give specific, kind, actionable comments. gh pr checkout 482 gh pr diff 482 git diff main...HEAD --stat gh pr review 482 --comment -b 'Question about error handling' Interview tip: Approve with confidence or ask for changes with reasons. Vague approvals and nitpick floods both waste time.

questions.q: How do you use git range-diff to review a force-pushed update to a pull request?
questions.text: range-diff compares two versions of a patch series commit by commit, so reviewers see what changed between the old and new push rather than rereading everything. git range-diff main old-feature new-feature git range-diff main...old-tip main...new-tip git fetch origin pull/482/head:pr-new git log --oneline main..pr-new Interview tip: Save the old tip before the author force-pushes (via reflog or remote-tracking history) to be able to compare.

questions.q: What is the difference between --force and --force-with-lease, and how do you protect shared branches?
questions.text: --force overwrites the remote ref unconditionally. --force-with-lease refuses if the remote moved since you last fetched, protecting others' work. Combine with branch protection that blocks force pushes on shared branches. git push --force-with-lease git push --force-with-lease=feature:abc1234 git push --force-if-includes git config --global alias.pf 'push --force-with-lease' Interview tip: Background fetches can silently update your lease reference. Use force-if-includes for extra safety.

questions.q: How do you work with Git across multiple remotes, such as mirrors and a vendor repo?
questions.text: Add named remotes, fetch each separately, push to specific ones, and configure pushurl for mirroring. Track which remote is origin and keep upstream read-only to avoid confusion. git remote add vendor https://vendor/repo.git git remote set-url --add --push origin git@mirror:org/repo.git git fetch --all --prune git push mirror --mirror Interview tip: A mirror push overwrites everything on the destination, so use it only for dedicated read-only mirrors.

questions.q: How do you handle line-ending and whitespace issues across a mixed Windows, Mac and Linux team using .gitattributes?
questions.text: Commit a .gitattributes with text=auto and explicit eol rules for scripts, so normalisation is repo-wide and independent of each developer's autocrlf setting. Renormalise once when introducing it. * text=auto *.sh text eol=lf *.bat text eol=crlf git add --renormalize . Interview tip: Shell scripts with CRLF endings fail on Linux with a confusing 'bad interpreter' error, so pin them to LF.

questions.q: How do you speed up CI checkouts for large repositories using partial clone, shallow fetch and caching?
questions.text: Use fetch-depth limits, blobless or treeless partial clones, sparse checkout and runner-local reference caches. Fetch full history only for jobs that truly need it, like version computation. git clone --filter=blob:none --depth=1 URL git sparse-checkout set services/api git fetch --unshallow git clone --reference /cache/repo.git URL Interview tip: Release jobs that compute versions from tags need full history, so give them a separate checkout configuration.

questions.q: How do you build a pipeline that tests only what changed in a monorepo?
questions.text: Compute the changed paths between the PR and its merge base, map them to affected projects via a dependency graph, and run only those jobs, while always running full tests on main or on shared-config changes. git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD git diff --name-only $(git merge-base origin/main HEAD) HEAD -- services/api/ paths: ['services/api/**'] nx affected --target=test --base=origin/main Interview tip: Path filters alone miss dependency changes. A change to a shared library must trigger every consumer.

questions.q: How do you securely trigger deployments from Git tags or merges, and prevent unauthorised releases?
questions.text: Protect release branches and tags, require approvals through environment rules, use OIDC short-lived credentials in the deploy job, and restrict who can create tags. Deploy from immutable artifacts built once. git tag -a v1.8.0 -m 'Release 1.8.0' && git push origin v1.8.0 on: push: tags: ['v*.*.*'] environment: production # requires reviewers git verify-tag v1.8.0 Interview tip: Build once and promote the same artifact through environments instead of rebuilding per stage.

questions.q: How do you handle flaky tests and failed CI blocking merges without weakening the quality gate?
questions.text: Detect and quarantine flaky tests with tracking, retry sparingly with visibility, fix root causes with owners and SLAs, and keep required checks reliable. Never normalise re-running until green. pytest --lf --maxfail=1 pytest -p no:randomly --count=20 tests/test_payment.py::test_retry gh run rerun --failed git log --since=30.days --format='%h' -- tests/ | wc -l Interview tip: Track flake rate per test. A quarantine list without owners and deadlines becomes a graveyard.

questions.q: How do you configure and enforce SSH commit signing and verify signatures in CI?
questions.text: Set gpg.format ssh and user.signingkey, enable commit.gpgsign, and register the public key as a signing key on the host. Verify with an allowed signers file in CI and enforce through branch rules. git config --global gpg.format ssh git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub git config --global commit.gpgsign true git verify-commit HEAD Interview tip: SSH signing is simpler than GPG for most teams because developers already manage SSH keys.

questions.q: How do you scan Git history for secrets and set up preventive controls like pre-commit hooks and push protection?
questions.text: Run scanners such as gitleaks or trufflehog over full history, add pre-commit and CI scans, and enable server-side push protection. Treat any found secret as compromised and rotate it. gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts='--all' trufflehog git file://. --only-verified pre-commit run gitleaks --all-files git log --all -S'AKIA' --oneline Interview tip: Defence in depth: local hook for speed, CI scan as a safety net, and server push protection that cannot be bypassed.

questions.q: How do you secure a Git hosting platform's access using SSO, SSH certificates, deploy keys and least-privilege tokens?
questions.text: Enforce SSO and MFA, use SSH certificates or short-lived tokens instead of static keys, give CI read-only deploy keys or app tokens scoped to a repo, and review access regularly. ssh-keygen -s ca_key -I alice -n git -V +12h alice.pub git config --get-regexp '^url\..*insteadof' gh api orgs/acme/members --paginate -q '.[].login' gh auth status Interview tip: Prefer GitHub App or OIDC-issued tokens, which expire quickly and can be limited to specific repos and permissions.

questions.q: What risks do Git hooks, .gitattributes filters and submodule URLs pose when cloning untrusted repositories?
questions.text: Client hooks are not cloned, but malicious configs, filters, submodule URLs and aliases can execute code if you run commands in a hostile repo. Inspect first, disable risky features and keep Git patched. git clone --no-checkout URL && cat .gitmodules git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null status git config --global protocol.ext.allow never git config --global protocol.file.allow user Interview tip: Treat cloning and then building untrusted code the same as running untrusted code. Use a sandbox.

questions.q: How do you meet audit and compliance requirements for Git, such as separation of duties and immutable history?
questions.text: Enforce protected branches, required reviews by someone other than the author, signed commits, audit log export, retention, and tagged releases linking commit to ticket and approval. Ensure admins cannot bypass without trace. gh api repos/org/repo/branches/main/protection git log --format='%H %an %GS %G?' origin/main | head git log --merges --first-parent main --format='%h %s' gh api orgs/acme/audit-log --paginate Interview tip: Auditors want evidence: who approved, what checks passed, when it deployed. Make that traceable from a single commit.

questions.q: What are partial clones and promisor remotes, and how do they differ from shallow clones?
questions.text: Shallow clones truncate history by depth. Partial clones keep full history but defer downloading objects (blobs or trees) until needed, using a promisor remote. Partial keeps log and blame working. git clone --filter=blob:none URL git clone --filter=tree:0 URL git clone --depth=1 URL git config remote.origin.promisor Interview tip: Blobless clones suit developers who need history. Shallow clones suit throwaway CI builds.

questions.q: What are Git maintenance and scheduled background tasks, and how do they keep large repositories fast?
questions.text: git maintenance runs prefetch, commit-graph updates, incremental repack and loose-object cleanup on a schedule, keeping operations fast without blocking developers. Register repos with maintenance start. git maintenance start git maintenance run --task=incremental-repack git config maintenance.strategy incremental git count-objects -vH Interview tip: Prefetch keeps remote-tracking refs fresh in the background, so fetch and pull feel instant.

questions.q: How does Git's fsmonitor and untracked cache speed up git status in huge working trees?
questions.text: fsmonitor uses OS file-change notifications to avoid scanning the whole tree, and the untracked cache remembers directory states. Together they make status near-instant on large repositories. git config core.fsmonitor true git config core.untrackedCache true git update-index --untracked-cache GIT_TRACE_PERFORMANCE=1 git status Interview tip: Measure with trace performance before and after. Gains are largest on big trees with few changes.

questions.q: What is git notes and how can it attach metadata such as build or review info to commits without changing their hashes?
questions.text: Notes store extra text in a separate ref linked to a commit, leaving the commit and its hash untouched. They suit post-hoc metadata like CI results, but must be pushed and fetched explicitly. git notes add -m 'Deployed to prod 2026-10-12' <sha> git log --show-notes git push origin refs/notes/* git fetch origin refs/notes/*:refs/notes/* Interview tip: Notes are not pushed or fetched by default, which is why teams often forget them. Configure refspecs.

questions.q: What is git sparse-index and how do cone-mode sparse checkouts reduce index size?
questions.text: Cone-mode sparse checkout restricts the working tree to chosen directories efficiently. The sparse index additionally collapses excluded directories into single entries, shrinking the index and speeding commands. git sparse-checkout init --cone git sparse-checkout set services/api libs/common git sparse-checkout list git sparse-checkout reapply Interview tip: Cone mode uses directory patterns, which are much faster than arbitrary gitignore-style patterns.

questions.q: How would you design a repository migration from SVN or Perforce to Git, preserving history and minimising disruption?
questions.text: Plan scope and history depth, map authors, convert with git svn or a migration tool, split or trim large files, validate against the source, run both systems briefly, then cut over with training and updated CI. git svn clone --stdlayout --authors-file=authors.txt URL repo git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M git lfs migrate import --include='*.psd' git count-objects -vH Interview tip: Often the right choice is migrating recent history only, keeping the old system read-only as an archive.

questions.q: Your CI pipeline reports that main is broken after a merge that passed on the PR branch. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.text: Two PRs each passed alone but conflict semantically on main. Revert or fix forward quickly, find the culprit with the merge history or bisect, and prevent recurrence with a merge queue or up-to-date branch requirement. git log --first-parent main --oneline -10 git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> git bisect start HEAD <last-green> git bisect run ./ci/test.sh Interview tip: Restore green first (revert), investigate second. A broken main blocks everyone.

questions.q: A developer's laptop was lost with unpushed work and the repo contains secrets in config. What do you do?
questions.text: Treat credentials as compromised: revoke tokens and SSH keys, rotate secrets, review audit logs for use. Assess which work was lost, and put in place habits like pushing WIP branches and using disk encryption. gh api user/keys gh auth token --revoke gh api orgs/acme/audit-log -f phrase='actor:alice' git push origin HEAD:wip/alice-$(date +%F) Interview tip: Full-disk encryption makes a lost device an inconvenience rather than a breach, so verify it is mandatory.

questions.q: Two teams keep overwriting each other's changes in a shared config file. How do you fix the workflow, not just the conflicts?
questions.text: Find why they edit the same file: split it into per-team files, add CODEOWNERS, generate it from sources, or move to an API or schema. Short-lived branches and a merge queue reduce collisions. git log --format='%an' -- config/app.yaml | sort | uniq -c git log --since=1.month --oneline -- config/app.yaml | wc -l git blame -w config/app.yaml | head -30 Interview tip: Frequent conflicts in one file are a design smell: the file has too many reasons to change.

questions.q: A release tag was pushed to the wrong commit and the artifact was already published. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Do not silently move the tag. Publish a corrected new version, deprecate or yank the bad one, document, and protect tags from moves. Moving a published tag breaks reproducibility and caches. git tag -v v1.8.0 git rev-parse v1.8.0^{commit} git tag -a v1.8.1 <correct-sha> -m 'Fix wrong release commit' git push origin v1.8.1 Interview tip: Treat published versions as immutable. Fix by releasing forward, not by rewriting tags.

questions.q: A contributor's pull request contains an obfuscated change in a build script. How do you review it and protect CI?
questions.text: Do not run it with secrets. Review the diff carefully, decode the obfuscation in a sandbox, ask the author for justification, run CI without secrets for forks, and require maintainer approval for workflows. gh pr diff 731 | less git diff main...pr-731 -- scripts/ .github/ echo 'ZWNobyBoaQ==' | base64 -d gh pr checkout 731 --detach Interview tip: Workflow files and build scripts are the highest-risk parts of a PR, since they execute with CI privileges.

questions.q: You accidentally committed to the wrong branch locally. How do you move the commit to the correct branch cleanly?
questions.text: Create or switch to the right branch, cherry-pick the commit there, then reset the wrong branch back to its previous commit. If unpushed, this is entirely local and safe. git switch correct-branch git cherry-pick <sha> git switch wrong-branch && git reset --hard HEAD~1 git branch new-branch && git reset --hard origin/main Interview tip: Creating a new branch at the current commit first is the simplest way to keep the work safe before resetting.

questions.q: A new engineer asks why their git pull created a messy merge commit every time. How do you explain and fix their setup?
questions.text: Pulling merges by default, creating a merge commit when branches diverged. Set pull.rebase or pull.ff only, fetch and inspect first, and explain when each is appropriate. git config --global pull.rebase true git config --global pull.ff only git fetch && git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline git config --global rebase.autoStash true Interview tip: Fetch first, look, then decide. Pull hides that decision inside a single command.

questions.q: What is Helm and what problems does it solve in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned charts with templates and values, renders them per environment and manages install, upgrade and rollback as releases. Helm 3 is client-only and stores release state as namespace secrets. helm install myapp ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml helm list -A Interview tip: Say chart plus values equals release.

questions.q: Explain the core Helm concepts: chart, release, repository and values.
questions.text: A chart is the package, a release is an installed instance with numbered revisions, a repository publishes charts through HTTP index or OCI, and values are configuration merged over chart defaults at render time. helm history myapp helm get values myapp Interview tip: Say one chart, many releases, each upgrade a revision.

questions.q: What are the essential Helm commands you use daily?
questions.text: Daily commands are search, show, template, lint, install, upgrade --install, list, status, get, history, rollback, uninstall, plus create, package and dependency update for authoring. Use the diff plugin and atomic and wait flags for safer upgrades. helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart -n prod --create-namespace --atomic --wait helm template myapp ./chart -f values.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f - Interview tip: Say lint, template, diff, then upgrade --install --atomic.

questions.q: How does helm install work internally, from command to running resources?
questions.text: Helm loads the chart, merges values, renders Go templates to manifests, validates them, orders resources by kind, stores the release record as a namespace secret, applies resources through the Kubernetes API with hooks, optionally waits for readiness and prints notes. kubectl get secrets -n prod -l owner=helm helm install myapp ./chart --debug --dry-run Interview tip: Say render client-side, store release as a secret, apply via API.

questions.q: What is the difference between helm install, helm upgrade and helm upgrade --install?
questions.text: Install creates a release and fails if it exists; upgrade changes an existing release and creates a revision; upgrade --install does either, so it is idempotent for pipelines. Supply complete values each time and use atomic and wait. helm upgrade --install myapp oci://registry/charts/myapp --version 1.4.2 -f prod.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m Interview tip: Say upgrade --install with full values each run.

questions.q: How does Helm store release state, and what happened to Tiller?
questions.text: Helm 2 used a privileged in-cluster Tiller; Helm 3 removed it, acts with the caller's RBAC, and stores each revision as a secret named sh.helm.release.v1 in the release namespace. Restrict access to those secrets since they contain values. kubectl get secret sh.helm.release.v1.myapp.v3 -n prod helm upgrade myapp ./chart --history-max 10 Interview tip: Say no Tiller, state in namespace secrets.

questions.q: When would you use Helm compared with Kustomize or plain manifests?
questions.text: Plain manifests suit small static setups, Kustomize gives patch-based overlays without templating, and Helm adds packaging, versioning, dependencies, hooks and release management. Use Helm for third-party or configurable apps, Kustomize for simple variants, or combine them. helm template myapp ./chart | kubectl kustomize kubectl apply -k overlays/prod Interview tip: Say Helm packages and versions; Kustomize patches.

questions.q: How do you install and configure Helm, and manage Kubernetes context and namespaces?
questions.text: Install a pinned Helm binary, verify kubeconfig context and namespace before acting, pass kube-context and namespace explicitly in automation, use create-namespace carefully, configure repositories or OCI logins and give CI least-privilege access. helm version kubectl config current-context helm list -n prod --kube-context prod-eu Interview tip: Say always pass context and namespace in pipelines.

questions.q: What does helm uninstall remove, and what can be left behind?
questions.text: Uninstall removes manifest resources and runs delete hooks, optionally keeping history. PVCs from stateful sets, CRDs, resources with the keep policy, namespaces and runtime-created objects can remain, so review and clean them explicitly. helm uninstall myapp -n prod --keep-history kubectl get pvc,crd -n prod Interview tip: Say PVCs and CRDs survive uninstall by design.

questions.q: What are Helm plugins and which ones are useful?
questions.text: Plugins add Helm subcommands; install from trusted sources and pin versions. Useful ones are helm-diff for previewing upgrades, helm-secrets with SOPS, helm-unittest for template tests, helm-docs for documentation and mapkubeapis for removed APIs. helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff --version 3.9.0 helm diff upgrade myapp ./chart -f prod.yaml Interview tip: Say helm diff before every production upgrade.

questions.q: How does Helm templating work, and what are the built-in objects?
questions.text: Helm renders Go templates with Sprig functions, exposing Values, Release, Chart, Files, Capabilities and Template objects. Use whitespace control for valid YAML, underscore files for helpers and template with debug to inspect output. metadata: name: {{ .Release.Name }}-web namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }} helm template myapp ./chart --debug Interview tip: Say the dot is context; Values, Release and Chart are its parts.

questions.q: How do you use conditionals and loops in Helm templates?
questions.text: Use if/else for optional blocks, noting empty values are false; range for lists and maps, where dot is rebound so use $ for the root; with for optional nested values; and nindent and whitespace trimming to keep YAML valid. {{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }} {{- range .Values.ingress.hosts }} - host: {{ . | quote }} {{- end }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say $ is the root inside range and with.

questions.q: What are named templates and _helpers.tpl, and how do include and template differ?
questions.text: Define reusable fragments with define in _helpers.tpl and call them with include, which returns a string that can be piped to indent or nindent; template cannot be piped. Pass context explicitly and prefix names with the chart name since they are global. {{- define "mychart.labels" -}} app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }} {{- end }} labels: {{- include "mychart.labels" . | nindent 4 }} Interview tip: Say include plus nindent, never template for helpers.

questions.q: Which Sprig and Helm template functions do you use most, such as default, required, quote, toYaml and tpl?
questions.text: Common functions are default for fallbacks, required for mandatory values, quote for safe strings, toYaml with nindent for pass-through blocks, tpl for templated values, trunc for name limits, sha256sum for checksums and lookup for cluster reads. image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }} apiUrl: {{ required "apiUrl is required" .Values.apiUrl | quote }} resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 2 }} Interview tip: Say required for mandatory values, toYaml for blocks.

questions.q: How do you trigger a rolling restart of pods when a ConfigMap or Secret changes?
questions.text: Add a pod template annotation with the sha256sum of the rendered ConfigMap or Secret so changes alter the pod template and trigger a rolling update. Alternatives are Reloader-style controllers or apps that reload files themselves. spec: template: metadata: annotations: checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} Interview tip: Say checksum annotation to force a rolling update.

questions.q: How do you debug a Helm template that renders the wrong output or fails?
questions.text: Use helm lint, then helm template with --debug and --show-only to inspect output, dry-run for server-side validation, and print values with toYaml to check. Common causes are indentation, rebound dot, missing quotes, nil nested keys and whitespace trimming. helm template myapp ./chart --debug --show-only templates/deployment.yaml helm template myapp ./chart | kubeconform -strict -summary Interview tip: Say template --debug, then kubeconform.

questions.q: How do you handle optional blocks and nested values safely to avoid nil pointer errors?
questions.text: Define defaults for every parent map in values.yaml, guard nested access with if, with or hasKey, use dig for safe traversal with a default, control features with enabled flags and fail early with required or a values schema. {{ dig "service" "annotations" "team" "unknown" .Values }} {{- if and .Values.ingress .Values.ingress.enabled }} Interview tip: Say defaults for parents, dig for safe reads.

questions.q: How do you write a chart that supports multiple Kubernetes API versions?
questions.text: Use Capabilities.APIVersions.Has and KubeVersion in helpers to pick apiVersion and fields, pass kube-version and api-versions flags when templating offline, declare kubeVersion in Chart.yaml, drop old versions on a schedule and use mapkubeapis for existing releases. {{- if .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "networking.k8s.io/v1/Ingress" }} apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 {{- end }} helm template x ./chart --kube-version 1.29.0 --api-versions networking.k8s.io/v1/Ingress Interview tip: Say Capabilities, plus CI across several versions.

questions.q: Why are Kubernetes resource names limited to 63 characters in charts, and how do you build safe names?
questions.text: DNS label rules cap many names at 63 characters, so use the fullname helper that combines release and chart names, truncates and trims hyphens, account for suffixes, provide name overrides and keep selectors stable since they are immutable. {{- define "mychart.fullname" -}} {{- printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name .Chart.Name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" -}} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say fullname helper, truncate to 63, keep selectors stable.

questions.q: How do you manage whitespace and indentation problems in Helm templates?
questions.text: Use dashes in braces to trim whitespace, nindent or indent to place multi-line output at the correct depth, check rendered output with helm template and a YAML linter and move complex logic into helpers. {{- with .Values.nodeSelector }} nodeSelector: {{- toYaml . | nindent 2 }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say dash trims, nindent places.

questions.q: How are Helm values merged, and what is the order of precedence?
questions.text: Order is chart values.yaml, parent overrides for subcharts, values files in sequence, then set flags. Maps merge recursively but lists are replaced; null deletes a default. Prefer complete values files in Git over reuse-values. helm upgrade --install app ./chart -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.4.2 helm get values app --all Interview tip: Say maps merge, lists replace.

questions.q: How do you organise values files for multiple environments?
questions.text: Use a shared base values file plus small per-environment, region or cluster overlays applied in order, keep them in Git with the chart version pinned separately, store secrets elsewhere and validate all layers with a schema and rendered diffs in CI. helm upgrade --install app ./chart -f values/base.yaml -f values/prod.yaml -f values/prod-eu.yaml diff <(helm template app ./chart -f values/base.yaml -f values/stg.yaml) <(helm template app ./chart -f values/base.yaml -f values/prod.yaml) Interview tip: Say base plus thin overlays, secrets elsewhere.

questions.q: What is values.schema.json and why should every chart have one?
