questions.text: A values.schema.json defines types, enums, required fields and patterns; Helm validates merged values on install, upgrade, lint and template, catching typos and bad input early and documenting options. Keep it in sync with values.yaml. { "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#", "type": "object", "required": ["image"], "properties": {"replicaCount": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1}} } Interview tip: Say schema fails fast with a clear message.

questions.q: What are the differences between --set, --set-string, --set-file and --set-json?
questions.text: Set infers types; set-string forces strings for tag-like values; set-file loads file content; set-json passes structured JSON. Prefer values files for reviewability and reserve set for a few dynamic values like image tags, and never for secrets. helm upgrade app ./chart --set-string image.tag=1.20 --set-file tls.crt=./tls.crt --set-json 'tolerations=[{"key":"gpu","operator":"Exists"}]' Interview tip: Say set-string stops 1.20 becoming 1.2.

questions.q: How do you design a good values.yaml for a chart others will consume?
questions.text: Group values logically with consistent names, safe defaults, documented comments and helm-docs, enabled flags for optional parts, standard extension points like annotations and tolerations, secret references, stable names across versions and a schema. image: repository: nginx tag: "" resources: {} autoscaling: enabled: false helm-docs --chart-search-root . Interview tip: Say values are the chart's API; version them like one.

questions.q: How do global values work, and how do values flow to subcharts?
questions.text: Parents override subchart values under the subchart's name or alias; subcharts cannot read parent values except those under the global key, shared with all. Use import-values for the reverse, conditions and tags to toggle subcharts, and keep global small. postgresql: auth: database: app global: imageRegistry: registry.example.com Interview tip: Say down by name, shared by global.

questions.q: How do you handle sensitive values in Helm without committing them in plain text?
questions.text: Prefer referencing secrets created by External Secrets, CSI drivers or Sealed Secrets; otherwise encrypt values with SOPS and helm-secrets. Remember release records contain values, so restrict access, enable encryption at rest, rotate and scan for leaks. sops --encrypt --age $AGE_PUB values-secret.yaml > values-secret.enc.yaml helm secrets upgrade --install app ./chart -f values-secret.enc.yaml Interview tip: Say reference secrets, don't embed them.

questions.q: What are the problems with --reuse-values and how do you avoid configuration drift?
questions.text: Reuse-values keeps old computed values so new chart defaults are ignored and the release drifts from Git. Pass full values files every time, treat Git as truth, audit with get values and use GitOps reconciliation. helm get values app --all -o yaml > live.yaml helm upgrade app ./chart -f values/base.yaml -f values/prod.yaml Interview tip: Say Git is the truth; avoid reuse-values.

questions.q: How do you pass complex structures such as lists of maps, multiline strings and typed numbers through values?
questions.text: Use values files with native YAML and block scalars, render with toYaml and quote, use set-json or set-string on the command line, watch float and boolean coercion, and embed files with the Files object or set-file. config: | log_level: info retries: 3 data: app.conf: |- {{- .Values.config | nindent 4 }} {{- (.Files.Glob "files/*").AsConfig | nindent 2 }} Interview tip: Say quote versions; large ints go wrong.

questions.q: How would you validate and test values and rendered output before deploying?
questions.text: Layer schema validation, helm lint --strict, rendering to kubeconform and policy checks with conftest or Kyverno, server-side dry-run and helm diff, helm-unittest assertions, and chart-testing installs in kind, all in CI. helm lint ./chart --strict -f values/prod.yaml helm template app ./chart -f values/prod.yaml | kubeconform -strict -kubernetes-version 1.29.0 helm unittest ./chart Interview tip: Say lint, schema, policy, dry-run, diff, install test.

questions.q: How do you provide sensible defaults for resources, replicas and autoscaling in a reusable chart?
questions.text: Ship safe modest defaults or documented empty blocks, render resources with toYaml, omit replicas when HPA is enabled to avoid upgrade resets, expose PDB, spread and probes, offer size presets and give measured production examples. {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }} replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say omit replicas when the HPA owns scaling.

questions.q: What is the structure of a Helm chart and what does each part do?
questions.text: Chart.yaml has metadata and dependencies, values.yaml and optional schema hold configuration, templates contains manifests, helpers, notes and tests, charts holds subcharts, crds holds CRDs, Chart.lock pins dependencies and .helmignore excludes files. helm create mychart && tree mychart Interview tip: Say Chart.yaml, values, templates, charts, crds.

questions.q: What is the difference between chart version and appVersion, and how should you version charts?
questions.text: Chart version is semver for the package and is used by Helm for resolution and upgrades; appVersion is informational, often the default image tag. Bump the chart version with every change, major for breaking changes, and never overwrite a published version. apiVersion: v2 name: myapp version: 2.3.0 appVersion: "1.18.4" helm package ./myapp --version 2.3.1 --app-version 1.18.5 Interview tip: Say chart version is the package; appVersion is the app.

questions.q: How do chart dependencies and subcharts work?
questions.text: Declare dependencies in Chart.yaml with versions, aliases, conditions and tags; dependency update resolves and writes Chart.lock, dependency build restores it for reproducible CI. Subcharts share the release but are isolated by values, and stateful ones are often better as separate releases. dependencies: - name: postgresql version: 15.x.x repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts condition: postgresql.enabled helm dependency build ./chart Interview tip: Say lock file plus dependency build for reproducibility.

questions.q: What are library charts and when are they useful?
questions.text: A library chart of type library contains only named templates and is consumed as a dependency via include, centralising labels, deployments and policies for many services. Benefits are consistency and less boilerplate; risks are indirection and wide blast radius, so version and test it carefully. type: library {{ include "common.deployment" (dict "root" . "name" "web") }} Interview tip: Say library charts share templates, not manifests.

questions.q: How do Helm hooks work and what are typical uses?
questions.text: Hooks are annotated jobs or pods that run at lifecycle points such as pre-upgrade or post-install, ordered by weight and cleaned by delete policy. Use for migrations, backups and tests, but make them idempotent, set timeouts and remember rollbacks do not undo them. metadata: annotations: "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0" "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded Interview tip: Say hooks run jobs at lifecycle points; clean them up.

questions.q: How do you manage Custom Resource Definitions with Helm?
questions.text: Files in crds install first without templating and are never upgraded or deleted by Helm. Manage updates with a separate CRD chart, a kubectl or GitOps step, or templated CRDs with a keep policy, and test upgrades because removal destroys custom resources. kubectl apply --server-side -f https://example.com/crds-v2.yaml helm upgrade --install app ./chart --skip-crds Interview tip: Say Helm installs CRDs once and never touches them again.

questions.q: How do you write and run Helm tests?
questions.text: Test manifests in templates/tests carry the helm.sh/hook: test annotation and run only on helm test, passing on exit code zero. Use them as smoke checks in pipelines with cleanup policies, alongside unit tests and chart-testing in kind. metadata: annotations: "helm.sh/hook": test spec: containers: - name: probe image: curlimages/curl command: ["curl", "-fsS", "http://{{ include \"mychart.fullname\" . }}:80/healthz"] helm test app --logs Interview tip: Say helm test is a post-deploy smoke test.

questions.q: How do you package and structure charts for many microservices: one chart per service, umbrella charts or a shared generic chart?
questions.text: One chart per service gives independence, umbrella charts couple services into one release, and a shared generic chart centralises practice. Often a library chart plus thin per-service charts, or generic chart with per-service values, balances consistency and autonomy. helm upgrade --install orders oci://registry/charts/generic-app --version 3.2.0 -f services/orders/values.yaml Interview tip: Say balance autonomy against consistency.

questions.q: How do you create a chart from scratch with helm create and turn the scaffold into something production-ready?
questions.text: Start from helm create, trim unused files, fix names and labels, add PDB, spread, security context, resources and probes, document values with helm-docs and a schema, add checksums, unit and smoke tests, CI lint and publish with proper versions. helm create webapp helm lint webapp --strict && helm-docs Interview tip: Say scaffold, harden, document, test, publish.

questions.q: How do Helm rollbacks work, and what are their limits?
questions.text: Rollback applies a previous revision's manifest as a new revision, running rollback hooks. It does not revert data, migrations, CRDs or manual changes cleanly, depends on retained history, and in GitOps should be done by reverting Git. helm history app -n prod helm rollback app 7 -n prod --wait --timeout 5m Interview tip: Say rollback reverts manifests, not data.

questions.q: What do --atomic, --wait, --timeout and --cleanup-on-fail do in an upgrade?
questions.text: Wait polls until resources are ready within the timeout, atomic implies wait and rolls back on failure or removes a failed install, and cleanup-on-fail deletes new resources from a failed upgrade. Set realistic timeouts and capture events before rollback. helm upgrade --install app ./chart --atomic --timeout 10m --cleanup-on-fail Interview tip: Say atomic makes failed deploys revert themselves.

questions.q: What does a Helm release in a failed or pending state mean, and how do you recover from pending-upgrade or failed states?
questions.text: Pending states mean an operation was interrupted; check history and processes, then helm rollback to the last good revision or, as last resort, fix or delete the stuck revision secret. Prevent with atomic, timeouts and serialised pipelines. helm history app -n prod helm rollback app 12 -n prod kubectl get secret -n prod -l owner=helm,name=app,status=pending-upgrade Interview tip: Say rollback first; edit secrets last.

questions.q: How does Helm compute upgrades with the three-way strategic merge, and what happens to manual changes made with kubectl?
questions.text: Helm patches using old manifest, live state and new manifest, so manual changes to fields the chart does not set persist while chart-set fields are overwritten and removed fields deleted. Avoid manual edits, use helm diff and GitOps, and consider server-side apply. helm diff upgrade app ./chart -f values.yaml --three-way-merge kubectl get deploy app -o yaml | diff - rendered.yaml Interview tip: Say compare old, live and new.

questions.q: How do you adopt existing Kubernetes resources into a Helm release, or move a release between namespaces?
questions.text: To adopt resources add the managed-by Helm label and the release-name and release-namespace annotations; to move a release, install a new one in the target namespace, migrate data and traffic, then remove the old. Releases are namespaced so direct moves are unsupported. kubectl label deploy app app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm kubectl annotate deploy app meta.helm.sh/release-name=app meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=prod Interview tip: Say label and annotate to adopt.

questions.q: What deployment strategies can you implement with Helm, such as blue-green and canary?
questions.text: Helm does rolling updates via deployment strategy; blue-green uses two releases and switches service or ingress, canary uses a small second release or weighted ingress, mesh, Argo Rollouts or Flagger for metric-driven promotion. Use backward-compatible migrations. helm upgrade --install app-green ./chart --set color=green kubectl patch svc app -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"color":"green"}}}' Interview tip: Say Helm ships; a rollout controller shifts traffic.

questions.q: How do you manage Helm release history and cleanup, and what is --history-max?
questions.text: Each revision is a secret, so cap them with --history-max (default 10) to protect etcd and listing speed, balancing rollback depth. Use Git and logs for audit, clean kept history and avoid large embedded files that hit secret size limits. helm upgrade --install app ./chart --history-max 5 kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm --no-headers | wc -l Interview tip: Say cap revisions; Git is the audit trail.

questions.q: How do you handle database migrations alongside Helm upgrades safely?
questions.text: Use expand-and-contract migrations so old and new versions coexist, run them once as a pre-upgrade hook job or a dedicated pipeline step with locks, timeouts and idempotency, back up beforehand and never ship destructive changes together with the code that stops using the data. metadata: annotations: "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation spec: backoffLimit: 0 Interview tip: Say schema changes must be backward compatible.

questions.q: How do you use helm diff and a dry-run to review a change before production?
questions.text: helm diff upgrade compares the rendered new manifests with live state, including three-way drift, and is run in pull requests with read-only credentials; dry-run adds server-side validation. Suppress secret values and review image, selector and removed resources. helm diff upgrade app ./chart -f values/prod.yaml -n prod --suppress-secrets --context 3 helm upgrade app ./chart --dry-run --debug Interview tip: Say review the rendered diff, not just the values.

questions.q: How do you roll back safely when only part of a multi-release application is broken?
questions.text: Identify the culprit release, roll back only that release with helm rollback, respect compatibility order between dependent services, use feature flags, check data migrations and in GitOps revert the commit. Separate releases make partial rollback possible. helm rollback payments 14 -n prod --wait helm history payments -n prod --max 5 Interview tip: Say separate releases allow surgical rollbacks.

questions.q: How do Helm chart repositories work, and how do they differ from OCI registries?
questions.text: HTTP repositories serve an index.yaml plus chart archives; OCI registries store charts as artifacts, pushed and pulled by reference with no index and reuse existing registry auth, replication and scanning. Pin by version or digest. helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update helm push mychart-1.2.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts Interview tip: Say OCI reuses the registry you already run.

questions.q: How do you publish a chart to an OCI registry and consume it securely?
questions.text: Package, log in with a token or CI identity, helm push to an oci URL, and consume by pinned version or digest. Use immutable tags, push permissions, scanning, signing and verification, with pull credentials in GitOps tools. helm package ./chart && helm push chart-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/org/charts helm install app oci://ghcr.io/org/charts/chart --version 1.4.0 Interview tip: Say immutable, pinned, signed.

questions.q: How do you sign and verify Helm charts, and what is provenance?
questions.text: Helm provenance signs the packaged chart with PGP into a .prov file and verifies on install; OCI charts are often signed with cosign. Protect keys, publish public keys and enforce verification in GitOps tools or admission policy with pinned digests. helm package --sign --key 'ci' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg ./chart helm install app ./chart-1.4.0.tgz --verify --keyring pub.gpg cosign sign ghcr.io/org/charts/chart:1.4.0 Interview tip: Say sign in CI, verify at deploy.

questions.q: How would you set up an internal chart repository with ChartMuseum, Harbor or cloud registries?
questions.text: Prefer an existing OCI-capable registry such as Harbor, ECR, ACR, GAR or GHCR; use ChartMuseum when HTTP repository semantics are needed. Plan auth, TLS, retention, backups and mirroring of third-party charts, with publishing only from tested main-branch pipelines. helm registry login harbor.example.com --username robot$ci helm push chart-1.0.0.tgz oci://harbor.example.com/platform Interview tip: Say reuse the registry you already have.

questions.q: How do you safely consume third-party charts such as Bitnami, ingress-nginx or Prometheus stacks?
questions.text: Vet third-party charts by reading rendered output, pin versions, review diffs between versions, mirror or vendor them, override images to approved internal digests, customise via values or post-renderers, scan and test in staging and assign an owner for regular upgrades. helm template ingress ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx --version 4.11.3 -f values.yaml > rendered.yaml helm upgrade --install ingress ./ingress-nginx-4.11.3.tgz --post-renderer ./kustomize-post.sh Interview tip: Say pin, mirror, read the render, own the upgrade.

questions.q: What is the helm pull, helm show and helm search workflow for evaluating a chart?
questions.text: Search for the chart, helm show chart, readme, values and crds to read defaults, helm pull --untar to inspect templates, compare versions by diffing extracted directories, then helm template with intended values and a dry-run before installing. helm search repo nginx --versions | head helm show values bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.0 > defaults.yaml helm pull bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.0 --untar Interview tip: Say read before you install.

questions.q: How do you automate chart releases with chart-releaser or a CI pipeline?
questions.text: On merge to main: lint, unit tests, version-bump check, package, publish with chart-releaser or helm push, sign and tag. Use ct list-changed, protected branches and short-lived credentials, never overwrite versions and let Renovate propose consumer bumps. ct lint --target-branch main cr package charts/app && cr upload -o org -r charts && cr index -o org -r charts --push Interview tip: Say version bump enforced, publish only from main.

questions.q: How do you search for and evaluate charts on Artifact Hub, and what signals indicate a trustworthy chart?
questions.text: Artifact Hub helps discovery; judge charts by verified publisher, signing, recent maintenance, documentation, schema, safe defaults, image scan results and licence, then read the rendered output and scan it. Popularity is not proof of safety. helm search hub prometheus --max-col-width 80 helm show chart prometheus-community/prometheus Interview tip: Say discovery is not endorsement.

questions.q: How do you work with private repositories and authentication in Helm, including in CI?
questions.text: Add repositories with masked secrets at run time, log in to OCI with short-lived workload-identity tokens, keep pull-only credentials for deploys and push rights for the release job, isolate Helm config per job, rotate tokens and keep TLS verification enabled. aws ecr get-login-password | helm registry login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com helm repo add internal https://charts.example.com --username $U --password $P Interview tip: Say short-lived tokens, least privilege.

questions.q: How do you keep a chart repository healthy: versioning rules, retention, deprecation and breaking changes?
questions.text: Enforce immutable semver versions, document breaking changes with majors, changelogs and upgrade guides, deprecate via Chart.yaml and notes, retain versions in use, automate tests and scans, define supported Kubernetes ranges and assign owners. deprecated: true kubeVersion: ">=1.27.0-0" ct lint --check-version-increment Interview tip: Say treat the repo like a product with consumers.

questions.q: How do you integrate Helm into a CI/CD pipeline, from lint to production deployment?
questions.text: PRs run lint, schema, render, kubeconform, policy, unit tests, scans, kind install tests and a diff; merges publish chart and image; deploys use upgrade --install with atomic and wait, smoke tests, approvals and metric checks, promoting identical artefacts with environment values. helm lint chart --strict && helm unittest chart helm upgrade --install app oci://reg/charts/app --version $V -f env/$ENV.yaml -n $NS --atomic --wait --timeout 10m Interview tip: Say same artefact, different values.

questions.q: What is GitOps with Helm, and how do Argo CD and Flux deploy Helm charts?
questions.text: GitOps controllers reconcile Helm charts from Git or registries: Argo CD renders with helm template and applies manifests without Helm release records, while Flux's HelmRelease runs real Helm actions with retries, remediation and drift detection. Changes flow through pull requests. apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2 kind: HelmRelease spec: interval: 10m chart: spec: chart: app version: 1.4.x sourceRef: {kind: HelmRepository, name: internal} argocd app diff app-prod Interview tip: Say Argo renders and applies; Flux runs Helm.

questions.q: How do you promote a release across dev, staging and production using Helm?
questions.text: Publish chart and image once, keep per-environment values in Git, promote by reviewed commits or automation through dev, staging and production with test, soak and approval gates, check parity with rendered diffs and roll back by reverting. diff <(helm template a ./chart -f env/stg.yaml) <(helm template a ./chart -f env/prod.yaml) yq -i '.image.tag = "1.4.2"' env/stg.yaml Interview tip: Say build once, promote by config commits.

questions.q: How do you test Helm charts automatically in CI with chart-testing, kind and unit tests?
questions.text: Use ct for change detection, lint and install tests in kind with several ci values files, helm-unittest for fast rendering assertions, kubeconform and policy checks across Kubernetes versions, and upgrade tests from the previous chart version in a CI matrix. ct lint-and-install --target-branch main --charts charts/app helm unittest charts/app Interview tip: Say render tests, install tests, then upgrade tests.

questions.q: How do you manage Helm deployments securely from CI, including credentials and least privilege?
questions.text: Use OIDC workload identity for short-lived cluster tokens, namespace-scoped RBAC per environment, protected production approvals, masked secrets from a vault, ephemeral runners, pinned actions and plugins, admission policies and signature verification. kubectl create rolebinding ci-deploy --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=ci:deployer -n app-prod helm upgrade --install app ./chart -n app-prod --kube-as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer Interview tip: Say short-lived identity, narrow RBAC.

questions.q: How would you handle a failed Helm deployment in a pipeline, including diagnostics and notifications?
questions.text: Use wait and timeouts, then on failure capture status, events, pod logs and describe output with secrets redacted, roll back and verify health, fail the job, record the deployment as failed and notify with links. Retry only transient errors and turn recurring causes into checks. kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30 kubectl logs -n prod -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=app --tail=100 --all-containers Interview tip: Say capture evidence first, then recover.

questions.q: What are Helm post-renderers and how can Kustomize be combined with Helm in a pipeline?
questions.text: A post-renderer is an executable that receives rendered YAML on stdin and returns modified YAML, often via kustomize, letting you patch upstream charts without forking. Include it in tests and diffs, and beware of hidden transformations and breakage on upstream renames. helm upgrade --install app ./chart --post-renderer ./post-render.sh #!/bin/sh cat > all.yaml && kustomize build . Interview tip: Say patch the render, don't fork the chart.

questions.q: How do you handle multi-cluster and multi-region Helm deployments?
questions.text: Layer values per environment, region and cluster from an inventory, roll out in waves with health gates, and use GitOps fleet tooling such as Argo CD ApplicationSets or Flux to generate per-cluster apps. Monitor drift, test version matrices and limit blast radius. generators: - clusters: selector: matchLabels: {env: prod} helm upgrade --install app ./chart -f values/base.yaml -f values/region/eu-west-1.yaml --kube-context eu-west-1 Interview tip: Say fleet generators and wave rollouts.

questions.q: How do you automate chart and image version updates with Renovate or Dependabot in a Helm and GitOps workflow?
questions.text: Renovate opens pull requests for chart and image version bumps in Chart.yaml, values, Flux and Argo manifests; configure grouping, schedules and auto-merge for safe patches, require review for majors and critical components, and rely on CI rendered diffs to catch breaking changes. { "extends": ["config:recommended"], "packageRules": [{"matchUpdateTypes": ["patch"], "automerge": true}] } Interview tip: Say small frequent bumps beat big risky ones.

questions.q: How do you prevent two pipelines from deploying the same Helm release at the same time?
questions.text: Use per-environment concurrency groups or locks that queue deployments without cancelling a running upgrade, deploy production only from protected branches, rely on GitOps single-controller reconciliation, use atomic and timeouts and alert on stuck pending releases. concurrency: group: deploy-prod-${{ inputs.release }} cancel-in-progress: false Interview tip: Say queue deploys; never kill one midway.

questions.q: What are the main security risks of Helm charts and how do you reduce them?
questions.text: Charts can create privileged pods, broad RBAC, mutable images and plaintext secrets. Reduce risk with trusted pinned and signed sources, rendered-manifest scanning, admission policy, least-privilege installers, secret references, network policies and protected release secrets. helm template app ./chart | kubescape scan - helm template app ./chart | trivy config - Interview tip: Say scan the render; enforce policy at admission.

questions.q: How do you apply Pod Security Standards and secure defaults inside a chart?
questions.text: Default to non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, read-only root filesystem, seccomp runtime default, no host access, resource limits and minimal RBAC with token automount off; test against restricted namespaces and assert defaults with unit tests. securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]} seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} kubectl label ns app pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted Interview tip: Say the chart's defaults should pass restricted.

questions.q: How is RBAC used by Helm itself, and what permissions does a deployer need?
questions.text: Helm uses the caller's RBAC: namespaced deployers need create, update and delete on the chart's kinds plus release secrets, while cluster-scoped resources need elevated rights. Give app pipelines namespace roles, separate platform pipelines for CRDs and operators, avoid cluster-admin and limit RBAC-creating rights. kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n app-prod --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer Interview tip: Say Helm has no powers of its own; RBAC rules.

questions.q: How do you scan Helm charts and rendered manifests for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations?
questions.text: Render charts per environment and run Checkov, Kubescape, Trivy or kube-linter plus conftest or Kyverno policies, extract and scan images and generate SBOMs, fail PRs on severity thresholds with expiring exceptions, and re-scan registries and enforce at admission. helm template app ./chart -f values/prod.yaml > out.yaml && checkov -f out.yaml grep -E 'image:' out.yaml | awk '{print $2}' | sort -u | xargs -n1 trivy image Interview tip: Say scan the render with real values.

questions.q: How do you secure the Helm release secrets and the data they contain?
questions.text: Release secrets hold values and manifests in base64, not encryption, so restrict RBAC, enable etcd encryption at rest, keep real secret values out of Helm by referencing external secrets, cap history, audit access and rotate anything exposed. kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n app-prod --as=dev-user helm get values app -n prod Interview tip: Say anyone who reads release secrets reads your values.

questions.q: How do you use SOPS, helm-secrets and External Secrets together with Helm?
questions.text: SOPS encrypts values files for Git and helm-secrets decrypts at deploy time, but decrypted values still land in release records. External Secrets or CSI drivers sync secrets from a vault so charts reference only names; prefer them for runtime credentials. apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1 kind: ExternalSecret spec: secretStoreRef: {name: vault, kind: ClusterSecretStore} target: {name: db-credentials} dataFrom: - extract: {key: prod/db} Interview tip: Say SOPS for Git, External Secrets for runtime.

questions.q: How do you enforce policy on Helm deployments with Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper or admission webhooks?
questions.text: Kyverno or Gatekeeper admission policies enforce registries, no latest tags, non-root, limits, labels and signatures on whatever Helm applies. Roll out audit then enforce with expiring exceptions, and run the same policies in CI on rendered manifests. kyverno apply policies/ --resource rendered.yaml kubectl get policyreport -A Interview tip: Say audit first, enforce next, test in CI.

questions.q: How do you secure the supply chain for Helm charts and the images they deploy?
questions.text: Build in protected pipelines, publish immutable signed charts and images with SBOMs and attestations, pin by digest, mirror upstream content, verify signatures at deployment and admission with fail-closed policy, and keep provenance for incident response. cosign sign --yes registry/app@sha256:abc123 cosign verify registry/app@sha256:abc123 --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/org/.*' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Interview tip: Say sign, attest, pin by digest, verify at admission.

questions.q: What should you check before installing a chart that creates ClusterRoles, webhooks or CRDs?
questions.text: Review ClusterRoles for wildcards, secrets and escalate or bind rights; webhooks for failurePolicy, selectors, timeouts and backend availability; CRDs for conflicts, versions and upgrade ownership. Render and diff, test in a non-production cluster and prepare emergency removal steps. helm template x ./chart | yq 'select(.kind=="ClusterRole" or .kind=="ValidatingWebhookConfiguration")' kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations Interview tip: Say cluster-scoped means cluster-wide blast radius.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot a Helm install or upgrade that fails with 'cannot re-use a name that is still in use' or 'resource already exists'?
questions.text: Name in use means a release record exists, so check helm list --all, then upgrade --install, uninstall or rename. Resource already exists means an unowned or other-release object, so inspect its Helm labels and annotations, adopt it, delete it safely or fix naming, especially for cluster-scoped objects. helm list -A --all | grep app kubectl get clusterrole app -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}' Interview tip: Say find the owner before deleting anything.

questions.q: Helm upgrade fails with 'another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress'. What do you do?
questions.text: A stuck pending revision blocks new operations. Confirm nothing is running, view history, then helm rollback to the last good revision; for first installs uninstall and retry; as last resort back up and delete the stuck revision secret. Prevent with atomic, timeouts and non-cancelling pipelines. helm history app -n prod helm rollback app <last-deployed> -n prod kubectl get secret -n prod -l name=app,status=pending-upgrade -o name Interview tip: Say rollback to clear the pending state.

questions.q: A Helm upgrade fails with 'UPGRADE FAILED: ... field is immutable'. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Immutable field errors come from changing selectors, volume claim templates, job specs or service IPs. Delete and recreate the object, orphan-delete stateful sets to keep pods and data, migrate PVCs, and prevent recurrence by keeping selectors stable and testing upgrades from the previous chart version. kubectl delete statefulset db -n prod --cascade=orphan helm upgrade db ./chart -n prod Interview tip: Say selectors are forever; treat changing them as breaking.

questions.q: Helm reports 'Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: timed out waiting for the condition'. How do you find the real cause?
questions.text: Timeout means readiness never arrived. Inspect pods, describe and events for scheduling, PVC, image pull, probe and crash issues, read current and previous logs, check hooks and quotas, increase the timeout only for slow healthy starts, then retry with atomic. kubectl get pods,pvc,events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp kubectl describe pod -n prod -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=app kubectl logs -n prod <pod> --previous Interview tip: Say Helm only reports; pods and events explain.

questions.q: How do you diagnose 'YAML parse error', 'nil pointer evaluating interface' and 'error converting YAML to JSON' during rendering?
questions.text: Render with helm template --debug and --show-only. YAML errors usually mean bad indentation, missing nindent, unquoted special strings or tabs; nil pointers come from missing parent maps or rebound dot. Add defaults, guards, dig, $ for root, a schema and unit tests. helm template app ./chart --debug --show-only templates/deployment.yaml 2>&1 | head -60 helm lint ./chart --strict Interview tip: Say read the rendered output around the reported line.

questions.q: How do you handle Helm errors caused by removed or deprecated Kubernetes APIs, such as 'no matches for kind ... in version'?
questions.text: Scan with pluto, kubent or kubeconform before upgrading clusters, update chart apiVersions and fields with Capabilities checks if needed, use mapkubeapis to fix stored release metadata, ensure CRDs exist first and verify releases with dry-run upgrades afterwards. pluto detect-helm -o wide helm mapkubeapis app -n prod --dry-run Interview tip: Say scan for deprecated APIs before cluster upgrades.

questions.q: A release shows 'deployed' but the application is not working. How do you investigate?
questions.text: Deployed does not mean working. Check pods, events and logs, compare helm get values and manifest with intent, verify config, secrets, permissions, service endpoints and selectors, ingress and network policies, diff against a healthy environment or previous revision and roll back to confirm. helm get values app -n prod --all && helm get manifest app -n prod | less kubectl get endpoints app -n prod helm diff revision app 11 12 -n prod Interview tip: Say verify the render, then the wiring.

questions.q: How do you debug Helm hooks that hang, fail or leave resources behind?
questions.text: Watch hook jobs and pods during the operation, read logs and events, check ordering and dependencies since pre-hooks run before release resources exist, tune weights, delete policies, backoff limit and deadlines, inspect with helm get hooks and clean leftovers manually. helm get hooks app -n prod kubectl get jobs,pods -n prod -w kubectl logs job/app-migrate -n prod Interview tip: Say pre-hooks run before your resources exist.

questions.q: How do you restrict which charts, registries and namespaces teams can deploy to in a shared cluster?
questions.text: Use namespace-scoped RBAC, quotas, network policies and Pod Security labels, admission policy limiting registries and requiring signatures, GitOps tenant constraints like AppProjects or Flux impersonation, internal chart mirrors and audited exceptions. apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: AppProject spec: sourceRepos: ["https://git.example.com/team-a/*"] destinations: [{namespace: team-a-*, server: "*"}] clusterResourceWhitelist: [] Interview tip: Say tenants get namespaces, not cluster scope.

questions.q: A Helm upgrade changed or deleted resources unexpectedly. How do you find out why and prevent it?
questions.text: Diff revisions with helm diff revision or helm get manifest to see rendering changes, then trace causes like changed defaults, missing values files, reuse-values, renamed keys or resource renames. Prevent with pre-upgrade diffs, full values in Git, pinned versions and the keep resource policy. helm diff revision app 11 12 -n prod metadata: annotations: "helm.sh/resource-policy": keep Interview tip: Say always diff before prod and protect stateful resources.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot Helm dependency errors, such as 'found in Chart.yaml, but missing in charts/ directory' or lock file mismatches?
questions.text: Missing or mismatched dependencies need helm dependency build to restore the locked set or dependency update to re-resolve and rewrite Chart.lock. Check repositories, auth and constraints, commit the lock, and run dependency build before lint, package and template in CI. helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update helm dependency build ./chart Interview tip: Say commit the lock; build in CI.

questions.q: How do you use the lookup function, and what are its limitations?
questions.text: Lookup reads live cluster objects during rendering, for example to keep an existing secret. It returns empty offline, so helm template, diff and Argo CD render differently; it needs read RBAC and makes output nondeterministic. Always handle empty results and use it sparingly. {{- $s := lookup "v1" "Secret" .Release.Namespace "db-pass" }} {{- if $s }} password: {{ index $s.data "password" }} {{- else }} password: {{ randAlphaNum 24 | b64enc }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say lookup is empty offline; handle both cases.

questions.q: How do you generate stable random values, such as passwords, in Helm without changing them on every upgrade?
questions.text: Random functions regenerate on every render. Keep secrets stable by reusing existing objects with lookup, requiring supplied values, creating them with a one-time hook, or generating them outside Helm with External Secrets or operators. Deterministic hashes are stable but only as strong as their seed. helm upgrade --install db ./chart --set auth.existingSecret=db-credentials Interview tip: Say never leave randAlphaNum in an upgradeable secret.

questions.q: What are the Helm SDK and Helm in Go or Python automation, and when would you use them instead of the CLI?
questions.text: The Helm SDK is a Go library exposing install, upgrade, rollback and template actions, used by controllers like Flux. For scripts the CLI with JSON output and exit codes is simpler; from Python call it with argument lists and timeouts. Use the SDK for long-running platform services. helm list -A -o json | jq '.[] | {name, namespace, status, chart}' subprocess.run(['helm','upgrade','--install',rel,chart,'-n',ns,'--atomic'], check=True, timeout=900) Interview tip: Say CLI for pipelines, SDK for controllers.

questions.q: How would you write unit tests for chart templates with helm-unittest?
questions.text: helm-unittest suites in the tests directory set values and assert on rendered documents with equal, contains, isKind, hasDocuments, failedTemplate and snapshots. They run fast without a cluster; cover defaults, toggles, security settings and required-value errors, and complement install tests. suite: deployment templates: [deployment.yaml] tests: - it: omits replicas when autoscaling set: {autoscaling.enabled: true} asserts: - notExists: {path: spec.replicas} helm unittest ./chart Interview tip: Say test toggles and failure cases, not only defaults.

questions.q: How do you manage Helm releases with Helmfile or similar tools for many releases and environments?
questions.text: Helmfile declares repositories, releases, versions and per-environment values in one file, applies only changed releases with diffs and dependency ordering via needs. It suits bootstrapping and push pipelines; GitOps controllers add continuous reconciliation and are preferred for production. releases: - name: ingress namespace: ingress chart: ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx version: 4.11.3 values: [values/ingress.yaml] helmfile -e prod diff && helmfile -e prod apply Interview tip: Say Helmfile is declarative push; GitOps is declarative pull.

questions.q: How do you design charts for stateful applications such as databases, and what are the pitfalls?
questions.text: Use StatefulSets with headless services, volume claim templates, PDBs, spread and meaningful readiness, but expect immutable template fields, persistent PVCs, credential stability and upgrade compatibility issues. Prefer operators for production databases, back up before upgrades and test restores. volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: {name: data} spec: accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] resources: {requests: {storage: {{ .Values.persistence.size }}}} kubectl get pvc -n prod Interview tip: Say data outlives the release; plan for it.

questions.q: How would you migrate from raw manifests or Kustomize to Helm, or from Helm to GitOps-native tooling, with minimal risk?
questions.text: Convert one app at a time, render and diff until output matches live objects, preserve selectors, adopt resources via Helm labels and annotations or run in parallel then cut over. For GitOps, point controllers at the same chart and values, check hooks and lookups, rehearse in staging with backups. helm template app ./chart -f values.yaml | kubectl diff -f - kubectl annotate deploy app meta.helm.sh/release-name=app meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=prod --overwrite Interview tip: Say diff until it's boring, then adopt.

questions.q: What are common Helm anti-patterns and best practices you would enforce in code review?
questions.text: Avoid hard-coded values, complex templates, forks, floating versions, secrets in values, reuse-values, unstable selectors, missing limits and probes, hooks for heavy work and untested charts. Enforce schema, tests, diffs, pinned versions and digests, atomic deploys and GitOps, with a review checklist. helm lint . --strict && helm unittest . && helm template . | kubeconform -strict helm upgrade --install app . --atomic --wait --timeout 10m Interview tip: Say simple templates, pinned versions, tested upgrades.

questions.q: How do you handle breaking changes when upgrading a major chart version, for example a third-party chart that renamed values?
questions.text: Read upgrade notes, diff default values and templates between versions, rehearse in staging with backups and helm diff, update renamed values, apply CRD steps manually, consider intermediate versions or blue-green for risky changes, verify with tests and promote with a rollback plan. helm pull repo/chart --version 14.0.0 --untar --untardir new && helm pull repo/chart --version 13.5.2 --untar --untardir old && diff -ru old new | less helm diff upgrade app repo/chart --version 14.0.0 -f values.yaml Interview tip: Say rehearse in staging with diff and backups.

questions.q: How do you build and use Helm OCI dependencies and chart caching in air-gapped or restricted environments?
questions.text: Mirror reviewed charts and images into an internal OCI registry, point dependencies and image values at it, keep Chart.lock and vendored archives for offline builds, transfer signed bundles for fully disconnected networks, verify digests and signatures and refresh on a regular approved cadence. helm pull oci://public.example/charts/app --version 1.4.0 && helm push app-1.4.0.tgz oci://registry.internal/charts skopeo copy docker://public/app:1.4.0 docker://registry.internal/app:1.4.0 Interview tip: Say mirror, pin, verify, rewrite image registries.

questions.q: How do you ship NetworkPolicies with a chart so workloads are isolated by default?
questions.text: Render NetworkPolicies that select the chart's pods, deny by default and allow declared ingress and egress including DNS, database and monitoring paths, expose sources and destinations as values, note that the CNI must enforce policies and test allowed and denied paths. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy spec: podSelector: matchLabels: {{- include "app.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }} policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] ingress: - from: - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: ingress-nginx}} ports: [{port: 8080}] Interview tip: Say default deny, then declare what is allowed.

questions.q: How do charts handle service accounts and cloud identities such as IRSA or Workload Identity?
questions.text: Create a dedicated service account with user-supplied annotations for IRSA, Workload Identity or Azure workload identity, allow existing accounts, disable token automount unless needed, grant minimal namespaced Roles, and manage the cloud-side roles separately. serviceAccount: create: true automount: false annotations: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/app-prod Interview tip: Say identity per workload, permissions least.

questions.q: How do you manage image pull secrets and private registries in charts?
questions.text: Expose imagePullSecrets as names of externally managed secrets, prefer cloud identity or node-level credentials, avoid creating registry secrets from plain values, use global settings for subcharts and use read-only, rotated tokens. Debug by checking namespace, server name and service account references. imagePullSecrets: - name: regcred kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password="$TOKEN" -n app Interview tip: Say reference pull secrets; don't template passwords.

questions.q: How do you integrate cert-manager and TLS into a chart and handle mutual TLS between services?
questions.text: Use cert-manager annotations for ingress and Certificate resources for in-cluster TLS with issuer, DNS names and renewal settings, mount the secret and reload on renewal; for mTLS add client usage, trust bundles and verification, or let a service mesh handle it. Alert on expiry. apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1 kind: Certificate spec: secretName: {{ include "app.fullname" . }}-tls issuerRef: {name: {{ .Values.tls.issuer }}, kind: ClusterIssuer} dnsNames: - {{ include "app.fullname" . }}.{{ .Release.Namespace }}.svc Interview tip: Say the chart requests certs; cert-manager issues and renews.

questions.q: How do you handle vulnerability management for the images and dependencies a chart deploys over time?
questions.text: Scan images at build and on a schedule, keep SBOMs to query affected deployments, rebuild minimal bases regularly, track chart and image updates with bots, scan running clusters, triage by reachability with deadlines and expiring exceptions, and gate with admission policy. trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed registry/app:1.4.2 syft registry/app:1.4.2 -o spdx-json > sbom.json Interview tip: Say vulnerabilities arrive after release; keep scanning.

questions.q: Pods crash or are OOMKilled right after a Helm upgrade. How do you find what changed?
questions.text: Diff the failing and good revisions for image, env, config, resources, probes and security context, then describe pods for last state and exit codes and read previous logs. OOM suggests limits or leaks; start-up crashes suggest config or permissions. Roll back to restore service, then reproduce in staging. helm diff revision app 11 12 -n prod kubectl describe pod -n prod <pod> | sed -n '/Last State/,/Ready/p' kubectl logs -n prod <pod> --previous Interview tip: Say diff the revisions, then read the previous container's logs.

questions.q: Helm fails with 'Kubernetes cluster unreachable', 'Unauthorized' or 'forbidden'. How do you troubleshoot connection and permission errors?
questions.text: Check context and kubeconfig, then API reachability, VPN, firewalls and expired certs for unreachable; refresh tokens or exec plugins for Unauthorized; and use kubectl auth can-i plus the error's user, verb and resource to grant narrow RBAC for forbidden. Print identity safely in CI. kubectl config current-context && kubectl cluster-info kubectl auth can-i create secrets -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer helm list -n prod --debug Interview tip: Say reachability, then authn, then authz.

questions.q: You changed values but the deployed behaviour did not change. What are the possible causes?
questions.text: Verify that the right files and order were used, key names and nesting match the template, subchart values sit under the subchart name, reuse-values is not retaining old settings, and that pods restarted. Compare helm get values --all, get manifest and the live object, and check image pull policy and GitOps sync. helm get values app -n prod --all | grep -i replica helm get manifest app -n prod | grep -n 'replicas' kubectl exec -n prod deploy/app -- env | grep APP_ Interview tip: Say trace the value from file to manifest to pod.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot chart download and repository errors such as 404, x509, 401 or 'failed to fetch'?
questions.text: 404 means wrong name, version or stale index; 401/403 means credentials or redirect issues; x509 means an untrusted CA, expired cert or intercepting proxy, fixed with a CA file, never skipping verification. Check DNS and proxies for timeouts and clear caches. helm repo update && helm search repo app --versions | head curl -fsSI https://charts.example.com/index.yaml helm pull app/chart --ca-file internal-ca.pem --version 1.4.0 Interview tip: Say fix trust, don't disable verification.

questions.q: How do you investigate an Ingress or Service that stopped working after a Helm upgrade?
questions.text: Diff service and ingress between revisions, check Service endpoints for selector or readiness mismatches, verify port names and numbers, inspect the ingress class, host, path, TLS and controller logs, test from inside the cluster to isolate layers, then check DNS and load balancer health. kubectl get endpoints app -n prod kubectl describe ingress app -n prod kubectl run t --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sv http://app.prod.svc:80/healthz Interview tip: Say follow the path: DNS, LB, ingress, service, pod.

questions.q: How do you write a Helm plugin, and when is it worthwhile?
questions.text: A plugin is a directory with plugin.yaml and a script or binary, receiving Helm environment variables and optional install hooks; Go gives portable binaries. Use plugins for repeated Helm-specific operations, pin and review them, and prefer a plain script when that is enough. name: "myplugin" version: "0.1.0" usage: "check chart standards" command: "$HELM_PLUGIN_DIR/bin/myplugin" helm plugin install https://git.example.com/platform/helm-myplugin --version 0.1.0 Interview tip: Say plugins run with your permissions; vet them.

questions.q: What are the limits on release size, and how do you deal with very large charts or manifests?
questions.text: Each revision is a secret limited to roughly one megabyte, so large embedded files, many CRDs or huge manifests can break installs. Use helmignore, move assets and CRDs out, split umbrella charts into several releases, cap history and monitor etcd. helm get manifest app -n prod | wc -c kubectl get secret sh.helm.release.v1.app.v5 -n prod -o json | wc -c Interview tip: Say a release record must fit in one Kubernetes object.

questions.q: How do alias, import-values and condition on dependencies work together in advanced chart composition?
questions.text: Alias includes the same chart several times with separate values, condition and tags toggle dependencies by values, and import-values pulls subchart values up for the parent's templates. Powerful but complex, so document values and use sparingly. dependencies: - name: redis alias: cache version: 19.x.x repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts condition: cache.enabled - name: redis alias: queue version: 19.x.x repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts condition: queue.enabled Interview tip: Say alias for multiples, condition for optionals.

questions.q: How do you verify and enforce provenance of OCI charts with Flux or Argo CD at deploy time?
questions.text: Flux can verify cosign signatures on OCI chart sources with expected identity and issuer and refuses to reconcile on failure; with Argo CD, enforce through admission policy and pipeline checks. Reference by digest, scope the signing identity to the release workflow, test with unsigned charts and alert on failures. apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta2 kind: OCIRepository spec: url: oci://ghcr.io/org/charts/app verify: provider: cosign matchOIDCIdentity: - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com subject: ^https://github.com/org/charts/.* Interview tip: Say verification must block deployment, not just warn.

questions.q: How do you design a Helm-based platform for many teams, with golden-path charts, guardrails and self-service?
questions.text: Publish a few library-based golden-path charts with secure defaults, let teams supply short values, enforce guardrails in CI and admission, scaffold services for self-service, provide extension points and approved exceptions, bump consumers by automated pull requests and track adoption. helm upgrade --install orders oci://registry.example.com/platform/web-service --version 3.4.0 -f services/orders/values.yaml -n orders Interview tip: Say a paved road with guardrails and escape hatches.

questions.q: What is the version skew policy between Helm and Kubernetes, and why does it matter?
questions.text: Each Helm minor supports a range of Kubernetes versions, so pin Helm in CI, upgrade it with clusters, set kubeVersion in charts and check releases for removed APIs before upgrading the control plane. helm version --short kubectl version kubeVersion: ">=1.27.0-0 <1.32.0-0" Interview tip: Say pin the client; check removed APIs before cluster upgrades.

questions.q: How do you inspect an installed release with helm status, get, history and show?
questions.text: Use helm list, status, get values/manifest/hooks/notes and history to inspect a release, and show to inspect a chart. Compare revisions with the diff plugin and check effective values against Git. helm get values app -n prod --all helm get manifest app -n prod --revision 7 > r7.yaml helm history app -n prod Interview tip: Say get is for releases; show is for charts.

questions.q: How do namespaces work with Helm releases, and what does --create-namespace do?
questions.text: Releases and their records live in a namespace; use the release namespace value in templates, prefer platform-created namespaces with quotas and policies over --create-namespace in production, and name cluster-scoped resources with the release to avoid clashes. helm install app ./chart -n team-a --create-namespace metadata: namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }} Interview tip: Say namespaces are governed by platform, not by helm flags.

questions.q: What is the difference between helm lint, helm template and helm install --dry-run?
questions.text: Lint checks chart structure and templates offline, template renders manifests locally for validation, and dry-run adds server-side checks through the API without creating anything. Use all three plus diff in a pipeline. helm lint ./chart --strict -f values/prod.yaml helm template app ./chart -f values/prod.yaml | kubeconform -strict helm upgrade --install app ./chart --dry-run=server Interview tip: Say lint the chart, template the output, dry-run the cluster.

questions.q: When would you choose a Kubernetes operator instead of a Helm chart to manage an application?
questions.text: Charts apply manifests and stop; operators continuously reconcile and encode operational logic such as backups and failover. Use charts for stateless and simple apps, operators for complex stateful systems, and often a chart to install the operator. helm install cnpg cnpg/cloudnative-pg -n cnpg-system --create-namespace kubectl apply -f cluster.yaml Interview tip: Say charts install; operators operate.

questions.q: How do you generate several resources from a list in values, for example multiple CronJobs or Ingress hosts?
questions.text: Define a list or map in values and range over it in one template, emitting a document separator and a resource per item, using $ for root context, combined names, defaults and required fields. Use schema validation and keep loops readable. {{- range $name, $job := .Values.cronjobs }} --- apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: {{ include "app.fullname" $ }}-{{ $name }} spec: schedule: {{ $job.schedule | quote }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say one template, many resources, via range.

questions.q: How do you load and use files inside a chart with .Files, Files.Glob, AsConfig and AsSecrets?
questions.text: Files.Get reads one packaged file, Files.Glob selects many and AsConfig or AsSecrets turn them into ConfigMap or Secret data; run through tpl if they contain expressions. Avoid large or sensitive files because the chart is stored in the release record. data: {{- (.Files.Glob "files/*.conf").AsConfig | nindent 2 }} data: init.sh: |- {{- .Files.Get "files/init.sh" | nindent 4 }} Interview tip: Say real files beat giant YAML strings.

questions.q: How do you use semverCompare, fail and NOTES.txt to make a chart helpful and safe?
questions.text: Use semverCompare for version-aware templates, fail with clear messages for invalid combinations a schema cannot express, required for mandatory values, and NOTES.txt to show access instructions, secrets retrieval and warnings after install. {{- if and .Values.autoscaling.enabled .Values.replicaCount }} {{- fail "set either autoscaling.enabled or replicaCount, not both" }} {{- end }} {{- if semverCompare ">=1.25-0" .Capabilities.KubeVersion.Version }} Interview tip: Say fail early with a message that explains the fix.

questions.q: Which string, list and dictionary functions from Sprig do you use for safe name and label handling?
questions.text: Use trunc and trimSuffix for 63-character limits, replace for illegal characters, printf and join for building strings, dict to pass multiple arguments to includes, merge and hasKey for maps, and sha256sum or b64enc for checksums and secrets. Wrap common logic in helpers. {{ printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name .Chart.Name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }} {{ .Chart.Version | replace "+" "_" | trunc 63 | quote }} {{ include "app.container" (dict "root" . "name" "web") }} Interview tip: Say wrap fiddly logic in one helper.

questions.q: How do you write a template that merges user-supplied annotations, labels or env vars with chart defaults without duplicates?
questions.text: Use merge or mergeOverwrite in a helper to combine standard labels, global values and user extras, render with toYaml, keep selector labels immutable, convert env maps to sorted lists or append extra lists, and test that defaults survive and overrides apply. {{- define "app.labels" -}} {{- $base := dict "app.kubernetes.io/name" .Chart.Name "app.kubernetes.io/instance" .Release.Name -}} {{- merge $base (.Values.extraLabels | default dict) | toYaml -}} {{- end }} {{- range $k, $v := .Values.env }} - name: {{ $k }} value: {{ $v | quote }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say merge into one map; never touch selectors.

questions.q: How do you document chart values so users know what each option does?
questions.text: Comment each key in values.yaml in a parseable format, generate the readme table with helm-docs in pre-commit or CI, add a values schema, document upgrades and examples, keep a changelog of renamed or removed values and test that examples render. # -- Number of replicas # @default -- 1 replicaCount: 1 helm-docs --chart-search-root charts Interview tip: Say generate the table; don't hand-write it.

questions.q: How should image tags and digests be handled in chart values?
questions.text: Expose repository, tag, digest and pullPolicy; default the tag to appVersion, avoid mutable tags, prefer digests, build image strings in a shared helper with an optional global registry prefix for mirrors, and enforce with admission policy. {{- define "app.image" -}} {{- $r := printf "%s%s" (default "" .Values.global.imageRegistry) .Values.image.repository -}} {{- if .Values.image.digest }}{{ $r }}@{{ .Values.image.digest }}{{ else }}{{ $r }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}{{ end -}} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say immutable tags or digests, one helper.

questions.q: How do you size resources and autoscaling per environment using values without duplicating whole files?
questions.text: Keep a modest base values file and override only scale settings per environment, optionally with size presets, omit replicas when autoscaling is on, base requests on measured usage and VPA advice, scale PDBs and spread constraints, and diff rendered environments. # values/prod.yaml resources: requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi} autoscaling: enabled: true minReplicas: 4 maxReplicas: 20 targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 65 Interview tip: Say thin overrides: only scale differs.

questions.q: How do you deploy the same chart for many tenants or customers safely using values?
questions.text: Create a release and namespace per tenant with small tenant values over shared defaults, generate them with ApplicationSets, Flux or Helmfile, isolate with quotas, network policies and per-tenant secrets, upgrade in waves, label observability by tenant and validate files with a schema. generators: - git: repoURL: https://git.example.com/platform/tenants files: - path: "tenants/*.yaml" Interview tip: Say generate tenants; don't copy them.

questions.q: How do you use JSON Schema conditionals and references in values.schema.json for stronger validation?
questions.text: Use if/then/else to require fields when features are enabled, oneOf for exclusive alternatives, $ref definitions for reuse, patterns and enums for formats, and additionalProperties false to catch typos where appropriate. Test valid and invalid values against the schema. { "if": {"properties": {"ingress": {"properties": {"enabled": {"const": true}}}}}, "then": {"properties": {"ingress": {"required": ["host"]}}} } Interview tip: Say schemas can express dependencies, not just types.

questions.q: How do you add init containers, sidecars and extra volumes to a chart in a flexible way?
questions.text: Expose initContainers, extraContainers, extraVolumes and extraVolumeMounts as values rendered with toYaml and tpl, apply security defaults and resource requests to extras, document the format and use native sidecars for better ordering on recent Kubernetes. {{- with .Values.extraContainers }} {{- tpl (toYaml .) $ | nindent 8 }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say expose extension points instead of forcing forks.

questions.q: How do you template Ingress and Gateway API resources in a chart across different controllers?
questions.text: Expose enabled, class, annotations, hosts, paths and TLS for Ingress, pass controller annotations through, support cert-manager, optionally render Gateway API HTTPRoute referencing a platform Gateway, default to no public exposure and test combinations. {{- if .Values.httpRoute.enabled }} apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute spec: parentRefs: {{- toYaml .Values.httpRoute.parentRefs | nindent 4 }} hostnames: {{- toYaml .Values.httpRoute.hostnames | nindent 4 }} {{- end }} Interview tip: Say pass controller specifics through; default to private.

questions.q: How do you template PodDisruptionBudgets, HorizontalPodAutoscalers and topology spread correctly in a chart?
questions.text: Expose minAvailable or maxUnavailable (not both) for PDBs and avoid budgets that block drains with a single replica; omit replicas when the HPA is enabled; provide soft topology spread defaults using selector labels; require resource requests and test combinations. apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget spec: maxUnavailable: {{ .Values.pdb.maxUnavailable }} selector: matchLabels: {{- include "app.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }} Interview tip: Say availability objects must match selectors and replicas.

questions.q: How do you handle Jobs and CronJobs in a chart, including migrations, ttl and history settings?
questions.text: Jobs are immutable, so recreate them with hooks and delete policies, unique names or ttlSecondsAfterFinished. Give migrations backoff and deadlines; for CronJobs expose schedule, time zone, concurrencyPolicy Forbid by default, history limits and suspend, and make work idempotent. spec: schedule: {{ .Values.cron.schedule | quote }} concurrencyPolicy: Forbid successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3 jobTemplate: spec: ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 backoffLimit: 2 Interview tip: Say jobs are immutable; recreate them deliberately.

questions.q: How do you support configuration of the application's own config file in a chart, and avoid breaking changes?
questions.text: Choose structured values rendered by template, a free-form block mounted as-is, or a hybrid with an extraConfig merge; store in a ConfigMap or Secret, add a checksum annotation, document migrations between formats and validate with the application's config test. data: app.yaml: |- {{- toYaml .Values.config | nindent 4 }} annotations: checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} Interview tip: Say structure what you must, pass through the rest.

questions.q: How do you achieve zero-downtime upgrades with a Helm-deployed application?
questions.text: Expose rolling update settings with maxUnavailable zero, accurate readiness and startup probes, preStop delay and sufficient grace period with SIGTERM handling, PDBs, multiple spread replicas, backward-compatible migrations, and use --atomic --wait. Test under load. strategy: rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0} lifecycle: preStop: exec: {command: ["sleep", "10"]} terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 Interview tip: Say Helm applies; Kubernetes settings deliver zero downtime.

questions.q: What do --force, --recreate-pods and --reset-then-reuse-values do on upgrade, and when are they appropriate?
questions.text: Force deletes and recreates resources when patching fails, risking downtime and data loss. Recreate-pods is gone in favour of checksums. Reuse-values keeps old values and ignores new defaults, reset-values drops them, and reset-then-reuse reapplies prior overrides on new defaults. Prefer full values files. helm upgrade app ./chart --reset-then-reuse-values helm upgrade app ./chart -f values/base.yaml -f values/prod.yaml Interview tip: Say reproducible upgrades come from complete values files.

questions.q: What naming and structure conventions do you use for release names, namespaces and labels across a platform?
questions.text: Use short stable release names, a documented namespace scheme, the recommended app.kubernetes.io labels through a shared helper, required organisational labels for team, owner and cost, and CI or admission checks to enforce them. labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }} app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }} app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }} team: {{ .Values.team }} Interview tip: Say conventions let tooling group things reliably.

questions.q: How do you recover when a namespace or release is stuck in Terminating or deletion hangs after helm uninstall?
questions.text: Check the namespace conditions and list all remaining resources to find finalizers waiting on missing controllers, volumes or cloud load balancers. Fix the cause first; as a last resort patch the finalizer away and clean up orphaned external resources. Uninstall operators after their custom resources. kubectl get ns stuck -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get -n stuck --ignore-not-found kubectl patch foo/bar -n stuck -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}' --type=merge Interview tip: Say find the blocker; remove finalizers only as a last resort.

questions.q: How do you plan and execute a Helm release freeze, hotfix or emergency rollback process?
questions.text: Define freezes with enforced exceptions, a hotfix path that keeps tests, diffs, atomic deploys and metric checks, and a rehearsed rollback using helm rollback or Git revert while pausing GitOps syncs. Communicate, record versions, plan for data changes and review afterwards. helm history app -n prod --max 5 helm rollback app 41 -n prod --wait argocd app set app --sync-policy none Interview tip: Say rehearse rollback before you need it.

questions.q: What are the benefits and pitfalls of pinning chart dependencies and application images by digest?
questions.text: Digests pin exact content, guard against tag overwrite and compromise and make rollbacks exact, but they are opaque and need automation to update, careful mirroring and scheduled rebuilds for security patches. Combine with signature verification and admission policy. image: registry.example.com/app@sha256:3f1a... crane digest registry.example.com/app:1.4.2 Interview tip: Say pin by digest, automate the updates.

questions.q: How do you mirror public charts and images into a private registry, using skopeo, crane or oras?
questions.text: Copy OCI charts with oras or crane and images with skopeo or crane, preserving digests; derive the image list from rendered manifests, scan and sign, override registry values, drive it from an approved list and schedule it with retention and alerts. crane copy ghcr.io/org/charts/app:1.4.0 registry.internal/charts/app:1.4.0 skopeo copy --all docker://nginx:1.27 docker://registry.internal/mirror/nginx:1.27 helm template app ./chart | grep 'image:' | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '"' | sort -u Interview tip: Say mirror what the chart actually references.

questions.q: How do you publish chart metadata for Artifact Hub, including annotations, icons and verified publisher status?
questions.text: Fill Chart.yaml metadata, add artifacthub.io annotations such as changes, images and licence, publish artifacthub-repo.yml to prove ownership for the verified badge, sign charts, keep a good readme and automate metadata in the release pipeline. annotations: artifacthub.io/changes: | - kind: added description: HTTPRoute support artifacthub.io/license: Apache-2.0 Interview tip: Say metadata is part of the release.

questions.q: How do you migrate an organisation from an HTTP chart repository to OCI without breaking consumers?
questions.text: Create the OCI registry, republish all existing versions with verified digests, dual-publish during transition, update dependencies, GitOps sources and docs, provide discovery through Artifact Hub or a catalogue, watch old-repo access logs, announce deprecation and then make it read-only. for f in archive/*.tgz; do helm push $f oci://registry.example.com/charts; done helm dependency update ./chart Interview tip: Say dual-publish, move consumers, then retire.

questions.q: How do you handle development and pre-release chart versions with semantic versioning?
questions.text: Use semver pre-release identifiers for PR and release-candidate builds, publish them to a short-retention dev area, rely on Helm excluding them from normal ranges unless --devel, avoid plus-sign metadata for OCI tags, keep versions immutable and clean up old ones. helm package ./chart --version 1.5.0-rc.1 helm install app oci://registry/charts/app --version 1.5.0-rc.1 helm search repo app --devel --versions Interview tip: Say pre-release versions never leak into stable ranges.

questions.q: What does a GitHub Actions workflow for building, testing and publishing a Helm chart look like?
questions.text: PR jobs run chart-testing lint and install in kind, unit tests, kubeconform and policy checks and a diff; release jobs authenticate with OIDC, check the version bump, push the OCI chart, sign with cosign and attach an SBOM. Use minimal token permissions and pinned actions. permissions: contents: read packages: write id-token: write steps: - uses: helm/chart-testing-action@v2 - run: ct lint-and-install --target-branch main - run: helm push chart-*.tgz oci://ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/charts Interview tip: Say OIDC, minimal permissions, pinned actions.

questions.q: Should you deploy with the Terraform helm_release resource or the Helm CLI, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.text: helm_release gives one workflow with dependency ordering and drift detection, but plans hide the rendered manifest diff, state may hold secrets and failures can desync state. Use it for rarely changed platform add-ons and GitOps or the CLI for frequently deployed applications. resource "helm_release" "ingress" { name = "ingress-nginx" repository = "https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx" chart = "ingress-nginx" version = "4.11.3" namespace = "ingress" atomic = true } Interview tip: Say Terraform for add-ons, GitOps for apps.

questions.q: How do Argo CD sync waves and hooks relate to Helm hooks and weights?
questions.text: Argo CD renders with helm template and maps Helm hooks to PreSync and PostSync hooks, while its own sync-wave annotations order resources by wave with health gates. Behaviour differs from the CLI, such as install versus upgrade hooks, so test charts under the real tool. metadata: annotations: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1" argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync Interview tip: Say Argo applies manifests; it doesn't run Helm lifecycle.

questions.q: How do you create preview environments per pull request with Helm?
questions.text: On each PR, build the image, install a release in a per-PR namespace with a unique hostname and small resources, post the URL, enforce quotas and TTL cleanup, use seeded test data and no production secrets, uninstall on close, and use ApplicationSet PR generators with approval for forks. helm upgrade --install pr-123 ./chart -n preview-pr-123 --create-namespace --set image.tag=$SHA --set ingress.host=pr-123.preview.example.com --atomic helm uninstall pr-123 -n preview-pr-123 && kubectl delete ns preview-pr-123 Interview tip: Say every preview has an owner and an expiry.

questions.q: How do you combine Helm with progressive delivery tools such as Argo Rollouts or Flagger?
questions.text: The chart renders a Rollout for Argo Rollouts, or a Canary resource for Flagger, exposing strategy, weights, analysis and metrics as values. Helm only starts the change; the pipeline must wait for rollout status, and failed analysis aborts automatically while Git should be reconciled to the reverted version. strategy: canary: steps: - setWeight: 10 - pause: {duration: 5m} - setWeight: 50 - pause: {duration: 10m} kubectl argo rollouts status app -n prod --timeout 30m Interview tip: Say Helm ships the version; the controller shifts the traffic.

guides.title: Kubernetes Production Interview Guide (170 Q&A) — InterviewHub

questions.q: What happens when a pod is stuck in Pending state — how do you debug it?
questions.text: Pending means the scheduler cannot place the pod on any node. The root cause is almost always resource constraints, node selectors, taints, or missing PVCs. Debug commands kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> # check Events section — scheduler message is here kubectl get nodes -o wide # confirm nodes are Ready kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources" # check capacity kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' -n <ns> Common causes: insufficient CPU/memory on all nodes (scale node pool or reduce requests), node selector / affinity rules not matching any node, taint with no matching toleration, PVC stuck in Pending (storage class issue), or image pull waiting on volume mount. Interview tip: Mention the scheduler's filter + score pipeline — Pending means the filter phase eliminated all nodes. The Events section tells you which predicate failed.

questions.q: Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff — how do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.text: CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts, crashes, Kubernetes restarts it, and it crashes again — with exponential backoff delay (10s → 20s → 40s → max 5min). kubectl logs <pod> --previous # logs from the crashed container kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> -f # follow live logs kubectl describe pod <pod> # check Exit Code and Last State Exit code meanings: 0 = success (CMD exited cleanly — check your ENTRYPOINT), 1 = app error, 137 = OOMKilled (increase memory limit), 139 = segfault, 143 = SIGTERM (graceful shutdown issue). Fix the application error, check liveness probe config, verify env vars and secrets are mounted correctly. OOMKilled pattern: If Exit Code is 137 consistently, increase resources.limits.memory or find the memory leak. Kubernetes never lies about OOM.

questions.q: Pod is in ImagePullBackOff — how do you resolve it?
questions.text:
kubectl describe pod # check Events for exact pull error kubectl get secret -o jsonpath='{.data..dockerconfigjson}' | base64 -d kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server= --docker-username= --docker-password=

Causes: image tag does not exist, wrong registry URL, missing or expired imagePullSecret , registry authentication failure, or network policy blocking egress to the registry. Verify the image exists with docker pull from the node. Check the service account has the pull secret attached. GKE/GCP context: For GCR/Artifact Registry, use Workload Identity — no secrets needed. The node SA must have roles/artifactregistry.reader .

questions.q: A Deployment is not rolling out — pods are stuck in old version. How do you debug?
questions.text: kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> # check rollout progress kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> # list revisions kubectl describe deployment <name> # check conditions kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> # rollback to previous kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=2 # rollback to specific Common blockers: new pods are CrashLoopBackOff so the rolling update stalls (maxUnavailable / maxSurge config), readiness probe failing so new pods never become Ready, resource quota exceeded so new pods can't schedule, or PodDisruptionBudget blocking old pod termination. Principal-level answer: Explain the maxUnavailable and maxSurge parameters and how they control rollout speed vs availability tradeoff. A stuck rollout with maxUnavailable: 0 means the new pod must become Ready before the old one is removed.

questions.q: A StatefulSet pod is not coming up — how do you troubleshoot?
