questions.text: kubectl describe pod <sts-pod-0> # StatefulSet pods start sequentially kubectl get pvc -n <ns> # check PVC binding status kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> # storage provisioner events StatefulSets have ordered, sequential pod creation — pod-1 won't start until pod-0 is Running and Ready. PVC binding failure is the most common blocker. Check: storage class exists and has a provisioner, the provisioner pod itself is running, correct access modes (ReadWriteOnce vs ReadWriteMany), and sufficient storage quota. Critical difference from Deployments: Deleting a StatefulSet pod does NOT delete its PVC. If you need to wipe data, delete the PVC explicitly. This is intentional — protect stateful data.

questions.q: How do you handle a pod that is consuming too much CPU or memory in production?
questions.text: kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> # current resource usage kubectl top pod --sort-by=memory # find top consumers kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A4 Limits # check current limits Immediate: if OOMKilling, increase memory limit with kubectl set resources deployment . Long term: add Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in recommendation mode to get right-sized request/limit suggestions. Set resource requests accurately — they affect scheduling; limits affect throttling/OOM. CPU vs memory: CPU throttling is silent — the pod runs slowly. Memory OOM kills the container. Both cause degraded performance. Use Prometheus metrics ( container_cpu_throttled_seconds_total ) to detect CPU throttling in production.

questions.q: A Service is not routing traffic to pods — how do you debug?
questions.text: kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> # if empty — label selector mismatch kubectl describe svc <svc> # check selector labels kubectl get pods --show-labels -n <ns> # verify pod labels match selector kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl <svc>:<port> # test from inside cluster The most common cause is empty Endpoints — the service selector doesn't match any pod labels. Also check: targetPort matches the container port (not the service port), pods are in Ready state (only Ready pods get endpoints), and kube-proxy / CNI is functioning on the node. Quick test: kubectl run tmp --image=curlimages/curl -it --rm -- curl http://<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local to test DNS resolution and connectivity in one command.

questions.q: DNS resolution is failing inside the cluster — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes.default # basic DNS check kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns # CoreDNS health kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50 kubectl describe cm coredns -n kube-system # check Corefile config Check CoreDNS pods are Running. Check ConfigMap for Corefile syntax errors. Verify the pod's /etc/resolv.conf points to the cluster DNS IP (usually 10.96.0.10). Network policies can block DNS (UDP 53) from pods to CoreDNS — always allow this in custom NetworkPolicies. Common trap: A NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} (deny all) will break DNS unless you explicitly allow egress to CoreDNS on port 53 UDP/TCP.

questions.q: Ingress is not routing traffic — how do you debug Ingress issues?
questions.text: kubectl describe ingress <name> -n <ns> # check rules and backend kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx # controller running? kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx <controller-pod> -f # access + error logs kubectl get events -n <ns> | grep ingress Troubleshooting layers: (1) Is the Ingress controller running and has an external IP? (2) Does the IngressClass match the controller? (3) Is the backend Service and port correct? (4) Does the host header in the request match the Ingress rule? (5) Is TLS cert valid for the hostname? Check controller logs — nginx/envoy logs show exactly which requests arrive and why they fail. GKE context: GKE Ingress uses a GCP HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Provisioning takes 5–10 minutes. Check GCP Console → Load Balancers for backend health status — unhealthy backends mean readiness probe failures.

questions.q: Network Policy is blocking traffic unexpectedly — how do you debug?
questions.text: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns> -o yaml # review all policies in namespace kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> # ingress/egress rules # Test connectivity: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nc -zv <target-ip> <port> NetworkPolicies are additive for allow rules but the default (if any policy selects a pod) is deny-all for unmatched traffic. Debug by temporarily removing NetworkPolicies to confirm they are the cause, then add back one by one. Check both ingress rules on the destination pod AND egress rules on the source pod. Important: NetworkPolicies are enforced by the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, etc.). If your CNI doesn't support them (like Flannel without addons), policies are silently ignored. Verify CNI support first.

questions.q: PersistentVolumeClaim is stuck in Pending — how do you fix it?
questions.text: kubectl describe pvc <name> -n <ns> # provisioner events are here kubectl get sc # list storage classes kubectl describe sc <name> # check provisioner and parameters kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep provisioner Causes: no default StorageClass defined, StorageClass provisioner pod is not running, access mode mismatch (requesting ReadWriteMany on a block storage that only supports ReadWriteOnce), storage quota exceeded, or the volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer means PVC binds only when a pod using it is scheduled. WaitForFirstConsumer: With this binding mode, the PVC stays Pending until a pod claims it. This is correct behavior for topology-aware provisioning (e.g., AWS EBS in a specific AZ).

questions.q: A pod lost its persistent data after restart — how do you investigate?
questions.text: kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 Volumes # check volume mounts kubectl get pvc -n <ns> # PVC still bound? kubectl describe pv <pv-name> # reclaim policy Root causes: pod was using emptyDir instead of a PVC (emptyDir is ephemeral — wiped on pod restart), PVC had reclaimPolicy: Delete and the pod/PVC was deleted, or the volume was mounted at wrong path. Always use PVCs with reclaimPolicy: Retain for production stateful data. Confirm the data directory in the container matches the mountPath in the pod spec. Never use emptyDir for production data. It survives container restarts within the same pod but is destroyed when the pod is evicted or deleted.

questions.q: How do you secure secrets in Kubernetes — what are the risks of using Kubernetes Secrets natively?
questions.text: Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded (not encrypted) by default. Anyone with RBAC access to get secrets can read them. They are stored in etcd — if etcd is compromised without encryption-at-rest, all secrets are exposed. Production hardening # Enable etcd encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration) # Use external secret stores: External Secrets Operator + AWS SSM/GCP Secret Manager # Use Vault Agent Injector for sidecar-based secret injection kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A | grep secrets # audit RBAC Best practice: Never store secrets in Git (even encrypted tfvars). Use External Secrets Operator to sync from GCP Secret Manager — secrets live in GCP, K8s Secret is auto-synced and rotated. This is the production standard.

questions.q: A pod is running as root — how do you harden the pod security posture?
questions.text: # In pod spec: securityContext runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1000 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } Use Pod Security Admission (PSA) with enforce: restricted label on namespaces in production. Audit existing pods with kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext' . For CKS exam: know the difference between privileged, baseline, and restricted PSA profiles. CKS relevance: This is a core CKS domain. Know how to audit with kube-bench , configure PSA, and use Falco for runtime security detection.

questions.q: RBAC is misconfigured — a service account has too much access. How do you audit and fix?
questions.text: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -A5 <sa-name> kubectl describe clusterrolebinding <name> Follow least-privilege principle: avoid ClusterRoleBindings when a RoleBinding scoped to a namespace suffices. Avoid binding to default service accounts. Audit with tools like rbac-tool or kubectl-who-can . Never use cluster-admin for application service accounts. Common mistake: Helm deployments often create ClusterRoleBindings for convenience. Audit every Helm chart's RBAC manifests before applying to production.

questions.q: How do you detect and prevent privilege escalation in a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.text: # Runtime detection: Falco with default ruleset falco -r /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml # detects privileged container exec, etc. # Admission control: OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies kubectl get constrainttemplate # OPA Gatekeeper policies Prevention layers: PSA restricted profile blocks privileged containers at admission, NetworkPolicies limit lateral movement, Falco detects anomalous runtime behavior (unexpected exec, file writes in /etc), and audit logging captures API server activity. For CKS: know how to write Falco rules and Kyverno ClusterPolicies. Audit logging: Enable API server audit policy. Without it, you cannot do forensics after a breach. This is often missed in self-managed clusters.

questions.q: Pods are not being scheduled on specific nodes — how do you control pod placement?
questions.text: kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd # add node label kubectl taint node <node> key=value:NoSchedule # add taint Placement mechanisms (in order of preference for production use): (1) nodeSelector — simple label match, (2) Node Affinity — richer rules with preferred vs required, (3) Pod Affinity/AntiAffinity — place pods relative to other pods, (4) Taints + Tolerations — node-side repulsion with pod-side override. For high availability: use topologySpreadConstraints to spread pods across zones evenly. Production pattern: Use AntiAffinity with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname to ensure Deployment replicas land on different nodes. Use zone-level spread for HA across AZs.

questions.q: Nodes are under resource pressure — how do you handle node eviction and resource management?
questions.text: kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A10 Conditions # MemoryPressure, DiskPressure kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -A # recently evicted pods kubectl top nodes # resource utilization Kubelet evicts pods under memory or disk pressure using QoS classes: BestEffort (no requests/limits) evicted first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed (requests = limits). Set accurate resource requests to avoid BestEffort classification for production pods. Use PodDisruptionBudgets to limit voluntary evictions during node drain/maintenance. Best practice: Set requests = limits for memory on critical pods (Guaranteed QoS). Never leave requests unset in production — the scheduler and eviction manager both rely on them.

questions.q: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) is not scaling — how do you debug?
questions.text: kubectl describe hpa <name> -n <ns> # check current metrics and conditions kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io # metrics-server available? kubectl top pods -n <ns> # verify metrics are flowing HPA requires metrics-server to be running. Common failures: metrics-server not installed, pod resource requests not set (HPA computes utilization % of requests — without requests it cannot calculate), scale-down cooldown period active (default 5min), or minReplicas == maxReplicas. For custom metrics HPA, verify Prometheus Adapter is running and the metric is registered as an APIService. Production tip: Always set both CPU and memory HPA targets. CPU alone misses memory-bound workloads. For GKE, use custom metrics from Cloud Monitoring for queue-depth-based scaling.

questions.q: Node is NotReady — how do you diagnose and recover?
questions.text: kubectl describe node <node> # check Conditions and Events kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> # pods on the node # SSH to node: systemctl status kubelet # kubelet running? journalctl -u kubelet -n 100 # kubelet logs systemctl status containerd # container runtime NotReady causes: kubelet stopped/crashed, container runtime (containerd/docker) failed, network plugin (CNI) crashed, node OOM at OS level, disk full, or certificate expired. Fix: restart kubelet and containerd. For a fully unrecoverable node, drain it ( kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data ) and replace it. Node drain before delete: Always drain before deleting/replacing a node to gracefully evict pods and respect PodDisruptionBudgets.

questions.q: How do you debug a pod that is Running but application is not responding?
questions.text: kubectl logs <pod> -f --tail=100 # live application logs kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh # exec into container kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl localhost:<port>/health kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 Readiness # readiness probe status Running state only means the container process is alive — the application inside may be deadlocked, misconfigured, or healthy-checked incorrectly. Check: readiness probe endpoint is responding (if not, pod is excluded from Service endpoints), application logs for panics/errors, env vars/configmaps mounted correctly, and network connectivity to dependencies (DB, cache). Readiness vs Liveness: Readiness probe failure removes pod from Service endpoints (traffic stops). Liveness probe failure restarts the container. Use both strategically — don't make liveness probe too aggressive or you'll cause unnecessary restarts under load.

questions.q: How do you set up effective observability for a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.text: Production observability has three pillars: metrics, logs, and traces. # Metrics: Prometheus + Grafana (kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart) # Logs: Fluent Bit (DaemonSet) → Elasticsearch/Loki → Grafana/Kibana # Traces: OpenTelemetry Collector → Jaeger/Tempo # Alerting: Prometheus AlertManager with PagerDuty/OpsGenie Key metrics to alert on: pod restart rate, HPA at max replicas, PVC usage %, node CPU/memory %, etcd latency, API server request latency, and coredns error rate. Set up dashboards for: cluster overview, namespace resource usage, and per-deployment golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation). GKE context: GKE Autopilot includes managed Prometheus. For a GCP-focused role, Google Cloud Monitoring + Cloud Logging reduces operational overhead significantly vs self-managed Prometheus stack.

questions.q: Kubernetes API server is slow or unresponsive — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_request_duration kubectl get --raw /healthz # API server health # Check etcd: etcdctl endpoint health kubectl top nodes # control plane node pressure Causes: etcd performance degradation (high disk latency — use SSDs for etcd), too many LIST operations (watch storms from controllers), control plane node under memory/CPU pressure, too many objects in etcd (clean up unused resources), or webhook latency (admission webhooks adding round-trip time to every API call). Webhook timeout: Misconfigured admission webhooks with long timeouts can make every API call slow. Set failurePolicy: Ignore and short timeouts for non-critical webhooks. Check webhook latency with apiserver_admission_webhook_admission_duration_seconds .

questions.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime Kubernetes cluster upgrade?
questions.text: # 1. Upgrade control plane first (one minor version at a time) kubectl drain <control-plane-node> --ignore-daemonsets # 2. Upgrade kubelet and kubectl on control plane node # 3. Upgrade worker nodes one by one: kubectl drain <worker-node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data kubectl uncordon <worker-node> # after upgrade Rules: upgrade only one minor version at a time (1.28 → 1.29, not 1.28 → 1.30). Control plane must be upgraded before workers. Ensure PodDisruptionBudgets are set so draining doesn't violate availability. Test in staging first. For GKE: use GKE's managed upgrade with surge upgrade enabled (adds extra nodes during upgrade). GKE shortcut: Enable auto-upgrade with maintenance windows and surge upgrade. GKE handles the upgrade orchestration — you define the maintenance policy and it does the rest safely.

questions.q: etcd is unhealthy — how do you recover a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.text: etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=<ip>:2379 etcdctl member list # check cluster membership # Restore from snapshot: etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore etcd is the source of truth for the entire cluster. If the majority of etcd members are down, the cluster is read-only (no writes). Recovery steps: restore from a snapshot backup, reconfigure the etcd data directory, restart the etcd service, then restart kube-apiserver. Always take regular etcd snapshots in production (automated, stored in durable object storage). etcd quorum: A 3-node etcd cluster tolerates 1 failure. A 5-node cluster tolerates 2. Never run single-node etcd in production. For GKE and managed services, etcd is managed for you — this question is more relevant for self-managed clusters (CKA/CKS exam domain).

questions.q: How do you drain a node safely without causing downtime?
questions.text: kubectl cordon <node> # prevent new pods from scheduling kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60 kubectl uncordon <node> # re-enable scheduling after maintenance Before draining: verify PodDisruptionBudgets allow eviction (if PDB has minAvailable: 100% and only 1 replica, drain will hang). Ensure other nodes have capacity to absorb the evicted pods. DaemonSet pods are ignored by default ( --ignore-daemonsets ). Pods using emptyDir require --delete-emptydir-data flag to proceed. Production checklist: Check HPA max replicas, PDB definitions, and node capacity before draining. Schedule drains during low-traffic windows for safety.

questions.q: Certificate expired in the cluster — how do you renew Kubernetes certificates?
questions.text: kubeadm certs check-expiration # list all cert expiry dates kubeadm certs renew all # renew all control plane certs systemctl restart kubelet # restart to pick up new certs openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates kubeadm-managed clusters: certs expire after 1 year by default. Rotate before expiry using kubeadm certs renew . After renewal, restart all control plane components. Set up a monitoring alert for cert expiry (Prometheus x509_cert_expiry metric). For managed clusters (GKE/EKS), certificate rotation is handled automatically. Expired cert symptoms: kubectl commands fail with TLS errors, pods can't pull images, webhooks fail. This is a full cluster outage scenario — certificate monitoring is non-negotiable.

questions.q: How do you implement GitOps for Kubernetes using ArgoCD?
questions.text: GitOps principle: Git is the single source of truth for cluster state. ArgoCD continuously reconciles cluster state with the Git repository. argocd app create myapp --repo <git-url> --path k8s/ --dest-server <cluster> argocd app sync myapp # manual sync argocd app get myapp # health and sync status argocd app diff myapp # what would change on sync ArgoCD polls the repo (default 3min) or uses Git webhooks for instant sync. Set sync policy to automated with prune: true and selfHeal: true for fully automated GitOps. Use ApplicationSets for multi-cluster or multi-environment deployments from a single template. Interview differentiator: Mention the App-of-Apps pattern for bootstrapping cluster infrastructure. ArgoCD manages ArgoCD itself — the entire cluster config is in Git.

questions.q: How do you implement a blue-green or canary deployment in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Blue-green: two full deployments (blue=current, green=new). Switch traffic at the Service level. Canary: route a percentage of traffic to new version. # Blue-green: patch service selector to switch kubectl patch svc myapp -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}' # Canary with Argo Rollouts: kubectl argo rollouts get rollout myapp --watch kubectl argo rollouts promote myapp # advance canary steps Native Kubernetes: use multiple Deployments with weighted Services or Ingress traffic splitting. Production-grade: use Argo Rollouts or Flagger with analysis templates — they automate canary promotion/rollback based on Prometheus metrics (error rate, latency). This is far more sophisticated than manual Deployment switching. Principal-level answer: Describe analysis-driven progressive delivery — canary receives 10% traffic, if P99 latency stays under threshold for 10min, promote to 25%, then 50%, then 100%. Argo Rollouts automates this entire workflow.

questions.q: CI/CD pipeline is failing to deploy to Kubernetes — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: # Check: kubectl is configured with correct kubeconfig kubectl config current-context # verify target cluster kubectl auth can-i create deployment --as=system:serviceaccount:cicd:deployer # Check: image was pushed to registry before apply kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> --timeout=120s Common pipeline failures: kubeconfig not configured or expired token, CI service account lacks RBAC permissions (create/update deployments, secrets), image not yet pushed when apply runs (race condition), wrong namespace or context, or Helm values file referencing wrong environment. Always check kubectl auth can-i with the pipeline's service account identity. GKE pipeline pattern: Use Workload Identity Federation to authenticate GitHub Actions to GCP — no service account key files needed. OIDC token exchange is the production standard.

questions.q: How do you handle pod disruption during node maintenance to maintain availability?
questions.text: # Create PodDisruptionBudget kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget metadata: { name: myapp-pdb } spec: minAvailable: 2 selector: { matchLabels: { app: myapp } } EOF kubectl get pdb -n <ns> # check current disruptions allowed PDBs guarantee that at least N pods (or at most X% are unavailable) during voluntary disruptions (drain, eviction). Set minAvailable: "50%" or maxUnavailable: 1 . PDBs only apply to voluntary disruptions — a node crash is involuntary and PDBs don't protect against it. Combine PDBs with proper replica counts and anti-affinity for full HA. PDB trap: A PDB with minAvailable equal to current replicas will block all drains. Always set minAvailable to less than total replicas.

questions.q: How do you manage multi-tenancy in a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.text: Multi-tenancy means multiple teams/applications share a cluster safely with isolation and fair resource usage. # Namespace per team/environment with ResourceQuota: kubectl create quota team-quota --hard=cpu=10,memory=20Gi,pods=50 -n team-a # LimitRange for default resource requests: kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml -n team-a Isolation layers: Namespaces (logical), ResourceQuota (resource limits per namespace), LimitRange (per-pod defaults and limits), NetworkPolicies (network isolation), RBAC (API access isolation), PSA (security posture enforcement per namespace). For stronger isolation between untrusted tenants, use separate node pools with taints/tolerations per tenant, or separate clusters. Principal recommendation: Soft multi-tenancy (namespace isolation) for trusted teams. Hard multi-tenancy (separate clusters or node pools) for compliance-sensitive or untrusted workloads.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot high latency in a microservices application running on Kubernetes?
questions.text: kubectl top pods -n <ns> --sort-by=cpu # CPU-saturated pods # Check Prometheus golden signals per service: # http_request_duration_seconds (latency), http_requests_total (traffic), error rate kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl -s /metrics | grep duration Systematic approach: (1) Identify which service in the call chain is slow using distributed traces (Jaeger/Tempo), (2) Check if the slow pod is CPU-throttled (increase limits or HPA), (3) Check DNS resolution latency (ndots:5 config causes multiple DNS lookups), (4) Check network policy overhead, (5) Check external dependency (DB, cache) latency. Use service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) for automatic tracing and traffic metrics. DNS latency fix: Set dnsConfig.options: [{name: ndots, value: "1"}] to reduce spurious DNS lookups. This alone can reduce P99 latency by hundreds of milliseconds in chatty microservices.

questions.q: How do you implement image security scanning in a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.text: # CI: trivy image <image>:<tag> # scan before push # Admission: OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno to block unscanned images # Runtime: Falco to detect anomalous container behavior # Registry: GCR/Artifact Registry with Container Analysis API Defense in layers: (1) Scan in CI pipeline — block PRs with critical CVEs, (2) Admission webhook — only allow images from approved registries with scan results, (3) Use digest pinning ( image: repo/app@sha256:abc... ) not mutable tags in production, (4) Enable runtime scanning with Falco, (5) Regularly re-scan deployed images for newly discovered CVEs. GCP Artifact Registry: Enables automatic vulnerability scanning with Container Analysis. Combine with Binary Authorization to enforce only attested images run in production — a cryptographic proof of scan completion.

questions.q: How do you design a production-grade Kubernetes platform for multiple teams — what does a Principal Platform Engineer own here?
questions.text: This is the Principal-level systems design question. The answer spans infrastructure, developer experience, and organizational patterns. # Infrastructure: IaC (Terraform) for cluster provisioning, GitOps (ArgoCD) for config # Developer experience: internal developer platform, self-service namespace creation # Reliability: multi-region clusters, cross-cluster traffic routing # Governance: OPA/Kyverno policies, admission webhooks, cost attribution A Principal Platform Engineer owns: cluster lifecycle (provisioning, upgrades, capacity planning), golden paths (opinionated templates teams use to deploy safely), reliability SLOs for the platform itself, security posture enforcement, observability standards, and developer productivity metrics. The platform should make the right thing the easy thing — teams deploy to production without thinking about Kubernetes internals. Interview context: Frame your answer around mentoring — a Principal defines the standards other engineers follow. Show you think in terms of platforms and APIs, not just individual cluster operations. That's what separates a Staff/Principal from a Senior engineer.

questions.q: Explain init containers vs sidecar containers. When do you use each in production?
questions.text: Both add containers to a pod beyond the main app, but they differ in lifecycle. Init containers run to completion before app containers start, sequentially; sidecars run alongside the main container for its whole life. Init container — runs once, before app initContainers: - name: wait-for-db image: busybox command: ['sh','-c','until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done'] Use init containers for: waiting on a dependency, running DB migrations, fetching config/secrets, setting kernel params, cloning a git repo into a shared volume. Sidecar — runs for the pod's lifetime Use sidecars for: log shippers, service-mesh proxies (Envoy), metrics exporters, config reloaders. Since K8s 1.28+ native sidecars are initContainers with restartPolicy: Always — they start before the app and shut down after it, fixing the old job-sidecar termination problem. Interview tip: The native sidecar (1.29 GA) solved two long-standing pain points: sidecars now start before the main container (so the proxy is ready first) and don't block Job completion. Mention this — it shows you track recent K8s.

questions.q: What is the difference between resources.requests and resources.limits? What happens at each boundary?
questions.text: Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are the hard ceiling the runtime enforces. They drive scheduling, QoS class, and eviction order. resources: requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" } # scheduler reserves this limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" } # hard cap What happens at the boundary CPU is compressible: exceeding the CPU limit throttles the container (CFS quota), it is not killed. Memory is incompressible: exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOMKilled (exit 137). Requests affect which node it lands on and the QoS class. QoS classes (eviction priority) Guaranteed : requests == limits for all resources (evicted last) Burstable : requests < limits (evicted middle) BestEffort : no requests/limits set (evicted first) Production gotcha: Setting a CPU limit can cause latency spikes from CFS throttling even when the node has spare CPU. Many teams set CPU requests but omit CPU limits for latency-sensitive workloads, while always setting memory limits to prevent node OOM.

questions.q: Walk through the full pod lifecycle and termination sequence. Why do graceful shutdowns fail?
questions.text: Understanding termination is key to zero-downtime deploys. The sequence is not just "send SIGTERM." Termination sequence 1. Pod marked Terminating; removed from Endpoints (stops getting new traffic) 2. preStop hook runs (if defined) 3. SIGTERM sent to PID 1 in each container 4. Wait up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s) 5. SIGKILL if still running Why graceful shutdown fails The endpoint removal (step 1) and SIGTERM (step 3) happen in parallel , not in order — kube-proxy/ingress may still route traffic for a moment after SIGTERM. The app can get requests after it started shutting down. lifecycle: preStop: exec: { command: ["sh","-c","sleep 5"] } # let endpoint removal propagate terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 Interview tip: The classic fix is a preStop sleep of a few seconds so load balancers de-register the pod before SIGTERM, plus an app that handles SIGTERM by draining in-flight requests. Also ensure PID 1 actually receives SIGTERM (use an init like tini if your entrypoint is a shell that swallows signals).

questions.q: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet vs Job/CronJob — when do you choose each?
questions.text: Picking the right workload controller is a common design question. The four Deployment : stateless, interchangeable replicas; rolling updates StatefulSet : stable identity + ordered start/stop + per-pod storage DaemonSet : one pod per node (agents) Job/CronJob : run-to-completion / scheduled batch StatefulSet guarantees Stable network ID ( pod-0 , pod-1 ...), stable storage (PVC per pod via volumeClaimTemplates ), ordered rollout and scale-down (reverse order). Use for databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper, anything needing identity or per-replica disks. DaemonSet examples Log collectors (Fluent Bit), node monitoring (node-exporter), CNI agents, storage daemons, security agents — anything that must run on every node. Interview tip: A frequent trap: "can I run a database as a Deployment?" Technically yes with a single replica, but you lose stable identity and ordered operations. For HA stateful systems use a StatefulSet (or better, an operator like CloudNativePG / Strimzi that manages the StatefulSet plus failover logic).

questions.q: How do liveness, readiness, and startup probes differ? What's the danger of a bad liveness probe?
questions.text: The three probe types serve different purposes and conflating them causes outages. livenessProbe : is it alive? FAIL -> restart the container readinessProbe : ready for traffic? FAIL -> remove from Service endpoints startupProbe : has it finished booting? gates the other two for slow starters The danger of a bad liveness probe If a liveness probe is too aggressive (short timeout, low threshold) or depends on a downstream service, a transient blip restarts healthy containers. Under load this creates a restart storm — the very thing you didn't want. Liveness should check only "is this process wedged," never "is my database up." readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 3 livenessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 8080 } initialDelaySeconds: 15 failureThreshold: 3 Rule: Readiness can depend on dependencies (so you stop serving when DB is down); liveness must NOT — it should only detect a deadlocked process. A liveness probe that pings the DB will restart-loop your whole fleet during a DB incident.

questions.q: Explain HPA, VPA, and how they conflict. How does HPA actually compute replica count?
questions.text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales replica count; Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts requests/limits. They fight if both target CPU/memory. HPA formula desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas * (currentMetric / targetMetric) ) # e.g. 4 pods at 80% CPU, target 50%: # ceil(4 * 80/50) = ceil(6.4) = 7 replicas HPA reads metrics from metrics-server (resource metrics) or custom/external metrics adapters (Prometheus Adapter, KEDA). It has a stabilization window to avoid flapping and won't scale on missing metrics. The HPA/VPA conflict Both reacting to CPU/memory will oscillate. Safe combos: HPA on CPU + VPA on memory in recommendation -only mode, or HPA on custom metrics (RPS, queue depth) + VPA on resources. Never both on the same signal in Auto mode. Interview tip: For event-driven scaling (queue length, Kafka lag, scale-to-zero), name KEDA — it extends HPA with external scalers. For node-level scaling mention Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter. Showing the formula and the HPA/VPA conflict is what separates a real answer.

questions.q: Explain taints, tolerations, node affinity, and pod affinity/anti-affinity with a real use case.
questions.text: These control where pods land. Taints repel; affinities attract; anti-affinity spreads. Taints + tolerations (node repels unless pod tolerates) kubectl taint nodes gpu-node-1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule # pod must tolerate to land there: tolerations: - { key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule } Effects: NoSchedule (don't place), PreferNoSchedule (soft), NoExecute (evict existing pods too). Node affinity (pod selects nodes) + pod anti-affinity (spread) affinity: podAntiAffinity: # spread replicas across nodes requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: - labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } } topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname Real use case GPU nodes tainted so only ML workloads (with tolerations + node affinity for gpu=true ) land there. Web tier uses pod anti-affinity across topology.kubernetes.io/zone so a zone failure never takes all replicas. Interview tip: For simple even spreading prefer topologySpreadConstraints over anti-affinity — it scales better and supports maxSkew . Anti-affinity (especially required ) can leave pods Pending if there aren't enough distinct nodes.

questions.q: What are topologySpreadConstraints and why are they preferred over pod anti-affinity?
questions.text: Topology spread constraints distribute pods evenly across failure domains (zones, nodes) with a tunable skew, scaling far better than anti-affinity. topologySpreadConstraints: - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule # or ScheduleAnyway (soft) labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } } Why preferred over anti-affinity Pod anti-affinity is O(N^2) to evaluate (every pod checked against every other) and is binary — a pod either can or can't co-locate. Spread constraints are evaluated more efficiently and let you say "keep zones within 1 pod of each other" with maxSkew , giving even distribution instead of just "not together." whenUnsatisfiable DoNotSchedule = hard (pod stays Pending if it would violate skew); ScheduleAnyway = best-effort. Combine zone-level and node-level constraints for resilient placement. Gotcha: With DoNotSchedule and a cluster that lacks enough zones/nodes, pods go Pending. Use ScheduleAnyway for soft spreading, or ensure your node pools actually span the topology keys you reference.

questions.q: How does the kube-scheduler decide where to place a pod? Explain the filter and score phases.
questions.text: The scheduler runs a two-phase pipeline per pending pod: filter (which nodes can run it) then score (which is best ). Filter (predicates) — eliminate infeasible nodes - NodeResourcesFit : enough allocatable CPU/mem for requests? - NodeAffinity : node selector / affinity match? - TaintToleration : tolerates the node's taints? - NodeUnschedulable : node cordoned? - VolumeBinding : can required PVCs bind here? Score (priorities) — rank feasible nodes - NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation : even CPU/mem usage - ImageLocality : node already has the image - InterPodAffinity / TopologySpread - LeastAllocated vs MostAllocated : spread vs bin-pack Highest-scoring node wins; the pod is bound (a write to the API setting nodeName ), then kubelet on that node starts it. Interview tip: Pending almost always means the filter phase rejected every node — kubectl describe pod Events shows which predicate failed (insufficient cpu, untolerated taint, no matching affinity, unbound PVC). You can customize scoring via the scheduler framework or run multiple scheduler profiles.

questions.q: Explain PodDisruptionBudgets. How do they interact with node drains and upgrades?
questions.text: A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many pods of an app can be voluntarily disrupted at once, protecting availability during drains, upgrades, and autoscaling. apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget spec: minAvailable: 2 # or maxUnavailable: 1 selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } } Voluntary vs involuntary PDBs only govern voluntary disruptions: kubectl drain , cluster autoscaler scale-down, node pool upgrades. They do not protect against involuntary events (node crash, OOM, kernel panic). Interaction with drains kubectl drain uses the Eviction API, which respects PDBs. If evicting a pod would violate minAvailable , the eviction is blocked and the drain waits. A misconfigured PDB (e.g. minAvailable equal to replica count) makes drains hang forever. Production gotcha: minAvailable: 100% or a PDB on a single-replica Deployment deadlocks node maintenance — the node can never be safely drained. Always leave headroom (e.g. maxUnavailable: 1 ) and run >=2 replicas for anything with a PDB.

questions.q: What is a ConfigMap vs Secret, and how do you safely roll config changes without downtime?
questions.text: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive config; Secrets hold sensitive data (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default). Both can be mounted as volumes or injected as env vars. Env var vs volume mount — a key difference Env vars are read once at container start — changing the ConfigMap does NOT update them; you must restart the pod. Volume-mounted ConfigMaps/Secrets are updated in place (eventually, via kubelet sync) but the app must re-read the file. Rolling config safely # Trigger a rollout when config changes: hash the config into an annotation kubectl rollout restart deployment/web # simplest manual trigger # or use a checksum annotation in the pod template so the hash change rolls pods Security note: Secrets are only base64-encoded in etcd by default. Enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider) and restrict RBAC on secrets. Better: pull from an external store (Vault, cloud Secret Manager) via CSI Secrets Store or External Secrets Operator so secrets never live in etcd/git. Interview tip: Mention the immutable: true field on ConfigMaps/Secrets — it improves performance (kubelet stops watching) and prevents accidental edits; you roll a new named object instead.

questions.q: How do you debug a pod that's running but the application inside is misbehaving (no shell in image)?
questions.text: Distroless/scratch images have no shell, so kubectl exec fails. Use ephemeral debug containers. kubectl debug — ephemeral container kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> -- sh # shares the target container's process namespace — see its PIDs, /proc, network Debug a node kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=ubuntu # host PID/net/IPC, /host mount Copy a pod with a shell for deeper work kubectl debug <pod> -it --copy-to=debug-pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot --share-processes Other tools: kubectl logs --previous for crashed instances, kubectl cp to pull files, kubectl port-forward to hit the app locally, and nsenter / crictl on the node for runtime-level inspection. Interview tip: kubectl debug with --target and process-namespace sharing is the modern answer for distroless images. netshoot is the go-to debug image (dig, curl, tcpdump, ss). This shows you operate hardened, shell-less production images.

questions.q: Explain rolling update strategy parameters (maxSurge, maxUnavailable) and how to do a safe canary.
questions.text: Deployment rollout speed and safety are governed by two knobs. strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 25% # extra pods above desired during rollout maxUnavailable: 0 # never drop below desired (safest) maxUnavailable: 0 + maxSurge: 1 gives zero-downtime: a new pod must be Ready before an old one is removed. Larger surge = faster but more resource use. Canary without extra tooling # Run a small second Deployment with the new image + same Service selector # 1 canary pod alongside 9 stable -> ~10% traffic, watch metrics, then promote Canary with tooling Argo Rollouts or Flagger give progressive delivery: automated step weights (10%->50%->100%), metric analysis, and auto-rollback on SLO breach — far safer than manual. Interview tip: Tie in the earlier termination point — zero-downtime needs maxUnavailable: 0 AND readiness probes AND preStop drain. All three together. Mention DB migrations must be backward-compatible (expand/contract) since old and new pods run simultaneously mid-rollout.

questions.q: What is pod priority and preemption? How can it cause cascading evictions?
questions.text: PriorityClasses let higher-priority pods preempt (evict) lower-priority ones when the cluster is full. apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1 kind: PriorityClass metadata: { name: high-priority } value: 1000000 globalDefault: false When a high-priority pod can't schedule, the scheduler finds the lowest-priority pods whose removal would make room and evicts them (respecting PDBs where possible). Cascading eviction risk If many high-priority pods arrive, they can evict a wave of low-priority pods, which then re-queue and may themselves trigger node scale-up or further churn. Misused priorities (everything "high") defeat the purpose and cause thrash. Gotcha: System-critical components use reserved classes system-cluster-critical / system-node-critical . Don't assign these to app workloads. Preemption can disrupt lower-priority pods even when they have PDBs if no other placement exists. Keep a sane priority hierarchy and use it sparingly. Interview tip: Good real use: give batch/CI jobs low priority so they yield to production traffic during spikes, and use Cluster Autoscaler with priority expander so preemption is a bridge until new nodes come online.

questions.q: A pod was OOMKilled but the app's heap looks fine. What else could consume the memory limit?
questions.text: The cgroup memory limit counts everything in the container, not just your app's heap. OOMKills with a "healthy" heap usually come from overlooked memory users. Hidden memory consumers - Page cache from heavy file I/O (counts toward cgroup memory) - Off-heap / native allocations (JNI, mmap, direct ByteBuffers in JVM) - tmpfs / emptyDir{medium: Memory} volumes count against the limit - Thread stacks (many threads x stack size) - The JVM/runtime itself not being container-aware (old runtimes) Diagnosis kubectl describe pod <pod> # Last State: OOMKilled, exit 137 kubectl top pod <pod> --containers # live usage # on node: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max and memory.current JVM gotcha: Pre-Java 10 JVMs ignored cgroup limits and sized the heap from host RAM -> instant OOM. Use a container-aware JVM and -XX:MaxRAMPercentage . For Node.js, set --max-old-space-size below the limit. Interview tip: Mention that emptyDir with medium: Memory and writable page cache both count against the limit — a surprising number of OOMKills are tmpfs or log files, not the heap.

questions.q: How does the Cluster Autoscaler work, and how is Karpenter different?
questions.text: Cluster Autoscaler (CA) adds/removes nodes when pods can't schedule or nodes are underused. Karpenter is a newer, more flexible alternative. Cluster Autoscaler Watches for Pending pods that fail only due to insufficient resources -> scales up a node group (ASG/MIG). Scales down nodes that are underutilized and whose pods can move elsewhere (respecting PDBs, local storage, etc.). Works on fixed, pre-defined node groups. Karpenter — group-less, just-in-time - No node groups: picks instance types per pending pods' actual needs - Faster: provisions nodes in seconds, bin-packs across instance types - Consolidation: actively repacks workloads onto fewer/cheaper nodes - Native spot handling and instance diversification Scale-down blockers: CA won't remove a node running a pod without a controller, a pod with local storage, a pod that can't be moved due to PDB, or kube-system pods lacking a PDB. A single such pod can pin an expensive node up indefinitely. Interview tip: Karpenter's consolidation + per-pod instance selection usually cuts cost vs CA's fixed groups. Mention the scale-down blockers — they're the #1 reason "autoscaling isn't saving money."

questions.q: Explain how a Service selects pods and what happens when none are Ready. How do headless Services differ?
questions.text: A Service is a stable virtual IP that load-balances to a dynamic set of pod IPs chosen by a label selector. The glue is the Endpoints/EndpointSlice object. Selector -> EndpointSlice kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> # only READY pods appear here; not-ready pods are excluded from routing If no pods are Ready, the EndpointSlice is empty and connections fail (connection refused / timeout). This is why readiness probes matter — a failing readiness check pulls the pod from the endpoints, not the Service. Headless Service (clusterIP: None) spec: clusterIP: None # no virtual IP / no proxying selector: { app: db } DNS returns the individual pod IPs (A records) instead of one VIP. Used with StatefulSets so clients can address specific pods ( db-0.db.ns.svc ) — essential for databases and peer discovery. Interview tip: Distinguish the Service types: ClusterIP (internal VIP), NodePort (port on every node), LoadBalancer (cloud LB), ExternalName (CNAME), and Headless (no VIP, direct pod DNS). Headless + StatefulSet is the standard pattern for stateful peer-aware systems.

questions.q: Walk through exactly how a packet travels from one pod to another pod on a different node.
questions.text: This is the canonical CNI question. The path crosses veth pairs, the node's network namespace, and an overlay or routed fabric. The path (pod A on node1 -> pod B on node2) 1. Pod A sends to Pod B's IP; leaves via eth0 (one end of a veth pair) 2. Other veth end is in node1's root netns, attached to a bridge / CNI datapath 3. Routing: node knows Pod B's IP belongs to node2's pod CIDR 4. Encapsulation (overlay: VXLAN/Geneve) OR direct routing (no overlay) 5. Across the node network to node2 6. Decapsulate -> node2 routes to Pod B's veth -> Pod B eth0 Overlay vs routed Overlay (Flannel VXLAN, Calico IP-in-IP): pod traffic is encapsulated; works anywhere but adds overhead. Routed/native (Calico BGP, GKE/EKS VPC-native): pod IPs are real routable addresses in the VPC; lower overhead, integrates with cloud routing. Interview tip: The K8s networking model requires: every pod gets its own IP, pods communicate without NAT, and nodes can reach all pods. CNI plugins implement this. Mention eBPF-based Cilium replacing kube-proxy/iptables for performance, and that the veth pair + per-node pod CIDR is the core mechanism. Knowing overlay-vs-routed trade-offs signals depth.

questions.q: How does kube-proxy implement Services? Compare iptables vs IPVS vs eBPF modes.
questions.text: kube-proxy programs the node's datapath so a Service's virtual IP load-balances to backend pods. The mode determines how. iptables mode (default historically) Installs iptables rules: Service VIP DNAT'd to a random backend pod IP. Simple and robust, but rule evaluation is O(N) — thousands of Services create huge rule chains and slow updates. IPVS mode Uses the kernel's IPVS (hash tables) for O(1) lookup and real LB algorithms (round-robin, least-conn, etc.). Scales to thousands of Services far better than iptables. eBPF (Cilium, kube-proxy replacement) # Cilium can REPLACE kube-proxy entirely: # Service load-balancing done in eBPF at the socket/XDP layer # - no iptables rule explosion, lower latency, better observability Interview tip: The progression iptables -> IPVS -> eBPF is about scaling Service count and cutting latency. In large clusters, iptables rule churn becomes a real bottleneck (slow Service updates, CPU on rule eval). eBPF/Cilium is the modern direction — name it and explain why (no linear rule chains).

questions.q: Explain Kubernetes DNS. How is a Service name resolved and what are common DNS failure modes?
questions.text: CoreDNS resolves Service and pod names cluster-wide. Understanding the resolution path and its pitfalls is key to debugging "intermittent" failures. Resolution svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local # fully qualified Service name # A pod's /etc/resolv.conf: search ns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local nameserver 10.96.0.10 # the CoreDNS Service ClusterIP options ndots:5 The ndots:5 performance trap ndots:5 means any name with fewer than 5 dots is first tried against every search-domain suffix. api.example.com (2 dots) becomes 4+ failed lookups before the real one. High-QPS apps generate massive DNS load and latency from this. Common failure modes - CoreDNS pods under-resourced / not enough replicas (use autoscaler) - ndots:5 amplifying lookups (use FQDN with trailing dot, or NodeLocal DNSCache) - conntrack race on UDP (old kernels) -> intermittent 5s timeouts - NetworkPolicy accidentally blocking egress to CoreDNS Interview tip: Name NodeLocal DNSCache as the standard fix — a per-node DNS cache that cuts CoreDNS load and avoids the UDP conntrack 5s-timeout bug. The ndots:5 trap and using fully-qualified names (trailing dot) for external hosts is a classic senior optimization.

questions.q: What is an Ingress vs a Service of type LoadBalancer vs the Gateway API? When use each?
questions.text: These expose workloads externally at different layers and maturity levels. Service type LoadBalancer L4 (TCP/UDP). Provisions one cloud load balancer per Service — simple but one LB (and cost) per Service, no HTTP routing. Ingress L7 HTTP(S) routing through a shared ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, cloud LB). Host/path-based routing, TLS termination, one LB for many Services. The long-standing standard, but the spec is limited and vendors bolt on features via annotations. Gateway API — the successor # Role-oriented: GatewayClass (infra) / Gateway (cluster-op) / HTTPRoute (app dev) # Expressive routing (header/method/weight), protocol-aware, portable across vendors # Replaces annotation-soup of Ingress; supports traffic splitting natively Interview tip: Use LoadBalancer for raw TCP/non-HTTP; Ingress for HTTP routing today; and know the Gateway API is the future (GA, role separation, native traffic splitting and multi-protocol). Mentioning Gateway API and why it exists — to fix Ingress's expressiveness and annotation portability problems — signals current knowledge.

questions.q: Explain NetworkPolicies. Why is a pod 'open' by default and how do you implement zero-trust?
questions.text: By default, all pods can talk to all pods — the cluster is flat and open. NetworkPolicies add firewall rules, but only if the CNI enforces them. Default-open, then default-deny # Start zero-trust: deny all ingress in a namespace apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: default-deny-ingress } spec: podSelector: {} # all pods in namespace policyTypes: [Ingress] # no ingress rules = deny all ingress Then add explicit allow rules per app. The moment a pod is selected by any policy, it switches from allow-all to allow-only-what's-listed. Allow specific traffic ingress: - from: - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: frontend } } ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }] Critical: NetworkPolicies are enforced by the CNI — Flannel (basic) ignores them; Calico/Cilium enforce them. A policy with no enforcing CNI is a silent no-op. Also remember to allow egress to CoreDNS (port 53) in default-deny-egress namespaces, or DNS breaks. Interview tip: Zero-trust = default-deny + explicit allows per flow. Cilium adds L7-aware policies (allow only GET /api ) and identity-based rules via eBPF, going beyond the L3/L4 stock NetworkPolicy.

questions.q: You have intermittent 5-second latency on some pod-to-service calls. What's the likely cause?
questions.text: Intermittent ~5s delays on DNS or new connections are a fingerprint of the classic conntrack/DNS race on UDP. The root cause On older kernels, parallel DNS lookups (A and AAAA sent simultaneously over UDP) hit a race in the kernel conntrack DNAT insertion; one packet is dropped, and the client waits for the 5s DNS retransmit timeout . The ndots:5 setting multiplies lookups, increasing the chance. Fixes - NodeLocal DNSCache (queries go to a local cache over TCP-ish path; avoids the race) - single-request-reopen / use-vc in resolv.conf options - reduce ndots / use FQDN for external names - upgrade kernel (the conntrack race is fixed in newer kernels) How to confirm kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c 'time nslookup my-svc' # ~5s = the tell # tcpdump on the node for DNS retransmits; check CoreDNS latency metrics Interview tip: The 5-second-exactly pattern is the giveaway — it maps to the DNS UDP retransmit timer. NodeLocal DNSCache is the canonical fix and a great thing to name. This question tests whether you've actually operated clusters, not just read docs.

questions.q: Explain the PV / PVC / StorageClass model and dynamic provisioning end to end.
questions.text: Kubernetes decouples storage requests (PVC) from storage implementation (PV) via StorageClass-driven dynamic provisioning. The objects StorageClass : the "type" of storage + provisioner (e.g. gp3, ssd) PVC : a pod's REQUEST for storage (size, access mode, class) PV : the actual provisioned volume (bound 1:1 to a PVC) Dynamic provisioning flow 1. Pod references a PVC 2. PVC names a StorageClass 3. The CSI provisioner for that class creates a real disk (EBS/PD/etc.) 4. A PV is created and BOUND to the PVC 5. The volume is attached + mounted into the pod Access modes & binding ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany , ReadWriteMany (needs NFS/EFS-style backend), ReadWriteOncePod (single pod). volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until a pod is scheduled, so the disk lands in the right zone. Interview tip: The WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode is a key production detail — without it, a disk can be created in zone-a while the pod schedules to zone-b and can never mount it. Always use it for zonal block storage.

questions.q: What is the CSI architecture? Walk through what happens when a volume is attached to a pod.
questions.text: The Container Storage Interface standardizes how K8s talks to storage backends via out-of-tree drivers. It has a controller plane and a node plane. Components CSI Controller (Deployment): Provision/Delete + Attach/Detach (talks to cloud API) CSI Node (DaemonSet) : Stage + Publish (mounts on the actual node) Sidecars: external-provisioner, external-attacher, node-driver-registrar Attach -> mount sequence 1. ControllerPublishVolume : attach disk to the node (cloud API call) 2. NodeStageVolume : format + mount to a global staging path on node 3. NodePublishVolume : bind-mount staging path into the pod's mount namespace Detach reverses it on pod deletion. The split (stage once per node, publish per pod) lets multiple pods share a staged volume where allowed. Interview tip: CSI also enables snapshots, volume expansion, and cloning as standardized features. A common failure: a volume stuck attaching because the previous node didn't cleanly detach (force-detach / VolumeAttachment cleanup needed). Knowing the controller-vs-node split explains why some failures are cloud-side (attach) vs node-side (mount).

questions.q: A StatefulSet pod is stuck and its PVC won't move to a new node. Why, and how do you resolve it?
questions.text: StatefulSet pods bind to specific PVCs and (for block storage) specific zones — that stickiness is by design but causes stuck-pod scenarios. Why it's stuck - ReadWriteOnce block volume can attach to only ONE node at a time - If the old node died uncleanly, the volume is still "attached" to it - The pod can't start on a new node until the volume detaches - Zonal disk (EBS/PD) can only mount in its own zone -> pod pinned to that zone Resolution kubectl get volumeattachment # find the stale attachment kubectl get pods -o wide # confirm pod can't bind # If node is truly gone: delete the Node object so the attach-detach # controller force-detaches; then the pod can reschedule + mount. kubectl delete node <dead-node> Danger: Never force-detach a volume that might still be written to by a live node — RWO exists to prevent two writers corrupting data. Only force-detach when you're certain the old node is dead. This is why split-brain protection matters for stateful workloads. Interview tip: Mention that the cloud's node-not-ready timeout (often ~6 min) gates automatic force-detach, which is why a failed-node stateful pod takes minutes to recover. For faster failover, operators (e.g. CloudNativePG) handle promotion at the app layer rather than relying on volume reattach.

questions.q: How do you expand a PVC, take snapshots, and back up stateful data in Kubernetes?
questions.text: CSI standardizes volume expansion, snapshots, and (via tools) backup of stateful workloads. Online volume expansion # StorageClass must have allowVolumeExpansion: true kubectl patch pvc <pvc> -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}' # CSI grows the disk; filesystem resize often happens online (no pod restart on modern CSI) Volume snapshots apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: VolumeSnapshot spec: volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-snapclass source: { persistentVolumeClaimName: data-db-0 } # restore by creating a PVC with dataSource pointing at the snapshot Application-consistent backups Snapshots are crash-consistent, not app-consistent — quiesce the DB (or use its native backup) for consistency. Velero backs up cluster objects + PV snapshots together and restores to another cluster (DR). Gotcha: You can only grow a PVC, never shrink it. And a snapshot of a running database without flushing/locking may be unrestorable — pair CSI snapshots with the DB's own consistent-backup hooks. Interview tip: Name Velero for cluster-level backup/DR and stress crash-consistent vs application-consistent — the distinction interviewers look for in anyone who's restored real stateful data.

questions.q: How does service mesh mTLS work in Kubernetes, and what's the cost of running a mesh?
questions.text: A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) injects a sidecar proxy per pod that transparently encrypts and authenticates service-to-service traffic with mutual TLS. How mTLS works - Control plane issues short-lived per-workload certs (SPIFFE identity) - Sidecar proxies intercept all pod traffic (via iptables/eBPF redirect) - Proxy A presents its cert, proxy B verifies + presents its own -> mutual auth - Traffic encrypted in transit; app code unchanged What the mesh adds beyond mTLS Uniform retries/timeouts/circuit-breaking, traffic splitting (canary), L7 observability (golden signals for every call), and authorization policies — all without app changes. The cost - Per-pod sidecar: extra CPU/memory + ~1 hop of latency per call - A control plane to operate and upgrade - Debugging complexity (traffic goes through proxies) - Overkill for a handful of services Interview tip: Be balanced: mesh gives free mTLS + observability + traffic control, but the sidecar tax (resources, latency, ops) is real. Mention Linkerd (lighter) vs Istio (feature-rich) and the move to sidecar-less / ambient / eBPF (Cilium) meshes to cut the per-pod overhead.

questions.q: Explain dual-stack, IP exhaustion, and pod CIDR sizing problems at scale.
questions.text: At scale, pod/Service IP ranges become a hard constraint that must be planned up front — you can't easily resize them later. The exhaustion problem - Each node gets a slice of the pod CIDR (e.g. /24 = 254 pods/node) - Cluster pod CIDR (e.g. /16) caps total nodes x pods-per-node - VPC-native clusters consume REAL VPC IPs for pods -> can exhaust the VPC - Resizing the cluster CIDR usually means rebuilding the cluster Mitigations - Size the pod CIDR generously at creation (plan for peak nodes x density) - Reduce per-node max pods if IPs are tight - Use non-VPC-routable pod ranges / IP masquerade where appropriate - Secondary ranges / custom CNI IPAM to extend address space Dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack assigns both families to pods/Services, easing IPv4 exhaustion. Requires CNI + cloud support and careful Service ipFamilyPolicy config. Interview tip: The headline is "CIDR sizing is a day-0 decision you can rarely undo." On EKS, the classic fix for VPC IP exhaustion is prefix delegation or custom networking; on GKE, planning the secondary ranges. Showing you'd capacity-plan IPs before cluster creation signals real scale experience.

questions.q: When would you use emptyDir, hostPath, local PV, and network storage? Trade-offs of each?
questions.text: Different volume types suit different needs — ephemeral scratch vs node-local performance vs durable network storage. The options emptyDir : ephemeral, lives with the pod; gone on pod delete (scratch, cache) hostPath : mounts a node directory; tied to that node; risky (security, portability) local PV : node-local disk as a PV; high perf, but pod pinned to that node network PV : EBS/PD/NFS/Ceph; durable, survives node loss, portable across nodes Trade-offs emptyDir is fast and simple but non-durable (and medium: Memory counts against the mem limit). hostPath breaks scheduling portability and is a security risk (don't use in multi-tenant). local PV gives NVMe-class performance for databases but loses HA — node dies, data is stranded; rely on app-level replication. Network PV is durable and reschedulable but slower and zone-bound. Interview tip: Local PV is the right call for performance-critical stateful systems that handle their own replication (Cassandra, Kafka) — you trade K8s-level durability for speed and let the app replicate. Network PV is the default for everything that needs the volume to follow the pod. Flag hostPath as a smell outside of node-agent DaemonSets.

questions.q: How do you expose a gRPC or long-lived connection service correctly behind a Kubernetes LB?
questions.text: L4 load balancers and HTTP/2 (gRPC) interact badly with the default Service round-robin, causing uneven load. The problem gRPC multiplexes many requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection. A connection-level (L4) LB pins that connection to one backend pod, so all requests from a client hit one pod — load is uneven, and new pods get no traffic until clients reconnect. Fixes - Use an L7 proxy that load-balances per-REQUEST (Envoy/Ingress with HTTP/2, or a service mesh) instead of per-connection - Client-side load balancing: headless Service -> client sees all pod IPs, balances requests itself (gRPC name resolver + round_robin policy) - Periodic connection recycling (MAX_CONNECTION_AGE) to redistribute Gotcha: Scaling up a gRPC service often doesn't relieve load because existing connections never move. You must force rebalancing (request-level LB, headless+client LB, or connection max-age) — adding replicas alone does nothing. Interview tip: This is a favorite "have you actually run gRPC on K8s" question. The crisp answer: per-connection L4 balancing breaks HTTP/2 multiplexing; solve with request-level L7 balancing, client-side LB via headless Service, or connection age limits.

questions.q: What is the Operator pattern and how does it manage stateful applications via CRDs?
questions.text: An Operator encodes human operational knowledge (deploy, backup, failover, upgrade) into a controller that reconciles a Custom Resource toward desired state. The mechanism CRD: defines a new type, e.g. kind: PostgresCluster CR : an instance: "I want a 3-node Postgres, v16, with backups" Operator (controller): watches CRs -> reconciles reality to match (creates StatefulSet, Services, secrets, runs failover, schedules backups) Why for stateful apps StatefulSets give identity + storage but not application logic. An Operator adds the domain smarts: primary election, automated failover, point-in-time restore, version upgrades with data migration, scaling with rebalancing. Examples CloudNativePG / Zalando (Postgres), Strimzi (Kafka), Elastic Operator, Prometheus Operator. The reconcile loop (observe -> diff -> act) is the same control-loop pattern as built-in controllers. Interview tip: Frame Operators as "automating the on-call runbook." The CRD extends the K8s API; the controller is just another reconcile loop. For production databases on K8s, an Operator is strongly preferred over a hand-rolled StatefulSet because it handles the hard parts — failover and backups — that raw StatefulSets don't.

questions.q: How does external traffic reach a pod end-to-end (cloud LB to container)? What is externalTrafficPolicy?
questions.text: External ingress traverses a cloud LB, a node port, kube-proxy, and finally the pod. externalTrafficPolicy changes the hop behavior and source-IP visibility. The path Internet -> Cloud LB -> NodePort on a node -> kube-proxy -> pod # With type=LoadBalancer, the cloud LB targets node ports across the fleet externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster vs Local Cluster (default): LB hits any node; kube-proxy may forward to a pod on ANOTHER node -> extra hop, SNAT hides the real client source IP, even load Local: only nodes that HAVE a backend pod accept traffic; no second hop, PRESERVES client source IP, but load can be uneven (depends on pod placement) Implications Local preserves client IP (needed for allowlists, geo, logging) and avoids a hop, but requires the LB health check to only target nodes with pods, and pod distribution affects balance. Interview tip: The source-IP question is the heart of it: default Cluster policy SNATs and loses the client IP; switch to Local to preserve it (or use proxy protocol / X-Forwarded-For at L7). Knowing the extra-hop and load-balance trade-off of Local shows real network operations experience.

questions.q: How do you run a database on Kubernetes safely? What are the real risks and mitigations?
questions.text: Running stateful databases on K8s is viable but demands care — the risks are around data safety during node/volume failures. The real risks - Volume reattach delay on node failure (minutes) -> downtime - RWO split-brain if force-detach is misused -> data corruption - Naive rescheduling moving a pod away from its zonal disk - An aggressive liveness probe restarting a healthy-but-slow DB - etcd/control-plane issues cascading to data-plane churn Mitigations - Use an Operator (CloudNativePG, Strimzi) for failover + backups, not raw StatefulSet - App-level replication (>=3 replicas) so a lost node/volume isn't data loss - StatefulSet + headless Service + per-pod PVC + anti-affinity across zones - Conservative probes; PDBs; tested restore (Velero / native backups) - Local NVMe PV + app replication for performance-critical stores Honest take: For mission-critical OLTP, many teams still use managed DBs (Cloud SQL, RDS) and keep K8s for stateless tiers. Running DBs on K8s is best when an Operator handles failover/backup and the DB replicates at the application layer. Interview tip: The mature answer weighs build-vs-buy: K8s-hosted DB (control, portability, cost) vs managed DB (operational safety). If on K8s, an Operator + app-level replication + tested backups are non-negotiable.

questions.q: Explain Kubernetes RBAC. How do Roles, ClusterRoles, and bindings actually combine?
questions.text: RBAC governs who can do what on which resources. Four objects compose: Role/ClusterRole (permissions) and RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding (who gets them). The four objects Role : permissions WITHIN a namespace ClusterRole : cluster-wide permissions (or reusable across namespaces) RoleBinding : grant a Role (or ClusterRole) to subjects in a namespace ClusterRoleBinding : grant a ClusterRole cluster-wide A subtle combination A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole — this grants that ClusterRole's permissions but scoped to the binding's namespace. This is how you define a permission set once (ClusterRole) and apply it per-namespace. rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods","pods/log"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"] RBAC is additive only — there are no deny rules. Permissions accumulate from all bindings a subject has. You restrict by granting less, never by denying. Audit with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<user> . Interview tip: Least privilege: prefer namespaced Roles over ClusterRoles, bind to specific ServiceAccounts not default , and avoid wildcards ( verbs: ["*"] ). Mention kubectl auth can-i for verification — it shows you actually audit RBAC.

questions.q: What replaced PodSecurityPolicy? Explain Pod Security Admission and its three levels.
questions.text: PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) was removed in 1.25. Pod Security Admission (PSA) is the built-in replacement — a namespace-label-driven admission controller enforcing the Pod Security Standards. Three standards privileged : unrestricted (no constraints) baseline : prevents known privilege escalations (no hostNetwork, no privileged) restricted : hardened best-practice (non-root, drop ALL caps, seccomp, RO rootfs) Three modes, set via namespace labels kubectl label ns prod \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted # enforce = block; warn = allow but warn; audit = log to audit only You can enforce baseline while warning on restricted, easing migration. Limitation: PSA is namespace-level and coarse (3 fixed profiles). For fine-grained or custom policy (registry allowlists, required labels, specific seccomp profiles), use a policy engine — OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno — alongside or instead of PSA. Interview tip: Know the timeline (PSP deprecated 1.21, removed 1.25 -> PSA). The restricted profile maps to the hardening you'd describe anyway: runAsNonRoot, drop all capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no privilege escalation, read-only root FS.

questions.q: How do you harden a pod's securityContext for a CKS-level restricted workload?
questions.text: A hardened securityContext minimizes the blast radius if a container is compromised. This is core CKS material. The hardened spec securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1000 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault What each does runAsNonRoot : refuse to run as UID 0 allowPrivilegeEscalation: block setuid/gaining more privs than parent readOnlyRootFilesystem : container can't write its own FS (use emptyDir for tmp) drop ALL capabilities : remove all Linux caps, add back only what's needed seccompProfile : restrict syscalls to the runtime default allowlist Never: privileged: true (full host access), mounting the Docker socket, hostPID/hostNetwork/hostIPC unless an agent truly needs it, or running as root. Each is a container-escape vector. Interview tip: If the app needs to bind a low port, add NET_BIND_SERVICE back rather than running as root. Mention AppArmor/SELinux profiles and a read-only rootfs + writable emptyDir for /tmp as the standard pattern. This is exactly what the PSA restricted profile enforces.

questions.q: Explain how a container escape could happen and the layered defenses against it.
questions.text: A container is a process with namespaces + cgroups, not a VM. Escapes exploit misconfigurations or kernel bugs to reach the host. Common escape vectors - privileged: true -> near-full host access - Mounting the host Docker/containerd socket -> control the runtime - hostPath mount of / or /var -> read/write host files - CAP_SYS_ADMIN and friends -> many escape primitives - Kernel exploit (shared kernel) -> break out via a vuln - Writable /proc or host PID ns -> tamper with host processes Layered defenses (defense in depth) 1. Don't grant privilege: drop caps, no privileged, no host mounts/namespaces 2. seccomp + AppArmor/SELinux: restrict syscalls and file access 3. Run as non-root + read-only rootfs 4. Stronger isolation: gVisor (userspace kernel) or Kata (microVM) per pod 5. Runtime detection: Falco/Tetragon alert on suspicious syscalls 6. Patch nodes (kernel) promptly Interview tip: The headline: containers share the host kernel, so isolation is only as strong as the kernel + your constraints. For hostile multi-tenant workloads, name gVisor or Kata Containers (VM-level isolation) as the answer when namespaces aren't enough, and Falco for runtime threat detection.

questions.q: How does Workload Identity (GKE) / IRSA (EKS) work and why is it better than node service accounts?
questions.text: Workload Identity binds a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a cloud IAM identity so pods get short-lived, scoped cloud credentials without static keys. The mechanism # K8s SA -> annotated to map to a cloud IAM role/SA # Pod requests a projected SA token (OIDC) -> exchanged for cloud creds # Creds are short-lived, auto-rotated, scoped to that workload's IAM role Why better than node SA / static keys Node SA : EVERY pod on the node inherits the node's cloud permissions (over-broad; a compromised pod gets node-level cloud access) Static keys : long-lived secrets in env/Secret -> leak risk, manual rotation Workload Id : per-pod least-privilege, no stored secret, auto-rotated Anti-pattern: Giving the node's service account broad cloud IAM and relying on it for pod access — any pod (and any attacker who lands in one) gets those permissions. Disable legacy metadata access and use Workload Identity / IRSA so each workload gets only its own role. Interview tip: This maps directly to your earlier secrets point — Workload Identity solves the bootstrapping problem (how a pod proves who it is) without a stored secret. On EKS it's IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) via OIDC; on GKE it's Workload Identity. Per-pod least privilege is the win.

questions.q: What is admission control? Compare validating/mutating webhooks, OPA Gatekeeper, and Kyverno.
questions.text: Admission controllers intercept API requests after authn/authz but before persistence, to validate or mutate objects — the enforcement point for policy. Two webhook types Mutating webhook : can MODIFY the object (inject sidecar, add labels, set defaults) Validating webhook : can ACCEPT or REJECT (enforce policy), runs after mutating Policy engines OPA Gatekeeper : policies in Rego (powerful, steeper learning curve) ConstraintTemplates + Constraints; great for complex logic Kyverno : policies as YAML/Kubernetes-native (easier to read/write) validate, mutate, generate, and verifyImages in one tool Typical policies Require resource limits, block :latest tags, enforce allowed registries, require labels/probes, disallow privileged, verify image signatures (cosign). Gotcha: A failing/slow validating webhook with failurePolicy: Fail can block ALL API writes (including system controllers) — a self-inflicted outage. Scope webhooks narrowly (namespaceSelector, objectSelector) and consider failurePolicy: Ignore for non-critical policies. Interview tip: Kyverno (YAML-native, simpler) vs Gatekeeper/OPA (Rego, more powerful) is the comparison to make. Both replace the removed PSP for custom policy and integrate supply-chain checks (image signature verification).

questions.q: Explain supply-chain security for containers: image scanning, signing, SBOM, and admission.
questions.text: Supply-chain security ensures only trusted, verified images run. The pillars are scanning, SBOM, signing, and admission enforcement. The pipeline 1. SCAN : Trivy/Grype scan image for CVEs in build CI (fail on criticals) 2. SBOM : generate a Software Bill of Materials (Syft) -> know what's inside 3. SIGN : cosign signs the image + attestations (provenance, SLSA) 4. ADMIT : cluster admission verifies signature before allowing the image to run Admission-time verification # Kyverno / Gatekeeper / sigstore policy-controller: # reject any image that is unsigned or not from an allowed registry, # and verify the cosign signature + SLSA provenance attestation Hardening the image itself Minimal/distroless base, non-root user, pinned digests (not tags), multi-stage builds to drop build tooling, no secrets baked in. Interview tip: Name the concrete tools: Trivy/Grype (scan), Syft (SBOM), cosign/sigstore (sign + verify), SLSA (provenance framework), and admission verification via Kyverno/policy-controller. Pinning by digest and verifying signatures at admission closes the "someone pushed a malicious :latest" gap.

questions.q: How do you manage secrets securely in Kubernetes beyond the built-in Secret object?
questions.text: Native Secrets are only base64-encoded in etcd and easily over-exposed. Production setups keep secrets out of etcd/git and inject them just-in-time. Layered improvements 1. Encryption at rest: EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider (so etcd holds ciphertext, not base64) 2. Tight RBAC on the secrets resource + audit access 3. External Secrets Operator: sync from Vault/cloud Secret Manager into K8s Secrets 4. CSI Secrets Store: mount secrets directly from Vault/cloud at pod runtime (nothing persisted in etcd) 5. Vault dynamic secrets: short-lived, per-request DB creds that auto-expire GitOps + secrets Never commit plaintext secrets. Use Sealed Secrets (encrypted, safe in git, decrypted in-cluster) or reference an external store via External Secrets Operator so git holds only a pointer. Anti-pattern: Plaintext secrets in a Git repo, in container env baked into the image, or shared across all namespaces. Any of these turns one leak into total compromise. Interview tip: The strongest answer mirrors your secrets-management design point: prefer dynamic, short-lived secrets (Vault) and runtime injection (CSI Secrets Store) so credentials never sit in etcd or git, and solve identity via Workload Identity rather than a stored token.

questions.q: Walk through securing the Kubernetes API server and control plane (CKS perspective).
questions.text: The API server is the front door to the cluster; hardening it and the control plane is foundational CKS content.
