API server hardening - Strong authn (OIDC / cloud IAM), no anonymous auth - Least-privilege RBAC; no wildcard cluster-admin handouts - Enable audit logging (who did what, when) - Restrict network exposure: private control plane / authorized networks - Disable insecure port; TLS everywhere; rotate certs etcd — the crown jewels - Encrypt etcd at rest (KMS); etcd holds ALL cluster data + secrets - mTLS between API server and etcd; restrict etcd network access - Regular encrypted etcd backups (and test restore) Node + kubelet Kubelet authn/authz on (no anonymous), rotate kubelet certs, restrict kubelet API, run CIS Benchmark checks ( kube-bench ), keep nodes patched. Interview tip: Name kube-bench (CIS Benchmark) and audit logging explicitly. Stress that etcd is the highest-value target — its compromise = all secrets — so encryption at rest + mTLS + restricted access + tested backups are non-negotiable. On managed clusters (GKE/EKS) the provider handles much of this; know what's yours vs theirs.

questions.q: What runtime security threats exist after a pod is running, and how do Falco/Tetragon help?
questions.text: Build-time scanning misses runtime threats — a compromised running container behaving maliciously. Runtime security detects and responds to that. Runtime threats - Reverse shell spawned in a container - Unexpected process execution (crypto miner, recon tools) - Sensitive file reads (/etc/shadow), writes to system dirs - Unexpected outbound network connections (C2, exfiltration) - Privilege escalation attempts, container escape behavior Falco / Tetragon Falco : rules over syscalls (kernel module/eBPF) -> alert on suspicious behavior e.g. "shell spawned in a container", "write below /etc" Tetragon : eBPF-based observability + ENFORCEMENT (can kill offending processes) These complement, not replace, prevention: even a hardened container can be exploited via an app vuln, and runtime detection catches the post-exploitation behavior. Interview tip: Frame the layers: prevent (scan, sign, harden) + detect/respond (Falco/Tetragon at runtime). eBPF is the modern data source — low overhead, kernel-level visibility. Tetragon's ability to enforce (kill the process) not just alert is a notable distinction to mention.

questions.q: How do you implement multi-tenancy securely in a shared cluster? What are the isolation boundaries?
questions.text: Multi-tenancy on one cluster trades cost-efficiency for weaker isolation than separate clusters. You stack namespace-level controls to approximate isolation. Isolation layers per tenant Namespace : the basic boundary (one+ per tenant) RBAC : tenant SAs scoped to their namespaces only ResourceQuota : cap CPU/mem/object counts per namespace (noisy-neighbor) LimitRange : default + max requests/limits per pod NetworkPolicy : default-deny cross-namespace traffic PSA / policy : enforce restricted pod security per namespace Node isolation : taints + RuntimeClass (gVisor/Kata) for hostile tenants The hard truth about the boundary Namespaces are NOT a hard security boundary — they share the same kernel, control plane, and (by default) nodes. A kernel exploit or control-plane bug crosses namespaces. When soft multi-tenancy isn't enough: For untrusted/hostile tenants, use separate clusters, dedicated node pools per tenant (taints + node affinity), and sandboxed runtimes (gVisor/Kata). "Hard" multi-tenancy of untrusted code on shared nodes is genuinely difficult. Interview tip: Distinguish soft multi-tenancy (trusted internal teams — namespace + quota + RBAC + NetworkPolicy suffices) from hard multi-tenancy (untrusted — separate clusters or VM-isolated runtimes). Stating that a namespace is not a security boundary is the senior insight.

questions.q: Explain ServiceAccount tokens, token projection, and why auto-mounting can be a risk.
questions.text: Every pod gets a ServiceAccount; its token authenticates to the API server. Mismanaged, it's an easy lateral-movement path. The risk of auto-mount # By default the SA token is mounted into every pod at: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token # If the pod doesn't need the API, that's an unnecessary credential an # attacker can steal to talk to the API server with the SA's RBAC. Mitigations automountServiceAccountToken: false # on the SA or the pod, if API access unneeded # Use bound, projected tokens (default in 1.22+): short-lived, audience-scoped, # auto-rotated -- vs the old never-expiring Secret-based tokens. Bound service account tokens Modern tokens are time-bound, audience-bound, and tied to the pod's lifetime (projected volume), so a leaked token expires and can't be replayed elsewhere — unlike legacy long-lived Secret tokens. Interview tip: Two crisp points: (1) disable token auto-mount for pods that don't call the API (least privilege), and (2) bound/projected tokens (1.22+) replaced the old non-expiring Secret tokens, shrinking the blast radius of a leak. Pair with tight RBAC on the SA so even a stolen token does little.

questions.q: A CVE drops for your base image fleet-wide. Walk through your response process.
questions.text: This tests incident process for supply-chain/runtime vulnerabilities — triage, assess, remediate, verify. 1. Triage / assess exposure - Is it exploitable in our context? (network-reachable? privileged? present in the path?) - Inventory affected images via SBOMs / registry scan (Trivy across all images) - Severity + exploit availability -> prioritize 2. Contain (if actively exploited) - NetworkPolicy to limit blast radius, or scale down exposed services - Runtime detection (Falco) for exploitation signs - Admission rule to block the vulnerable image from new scheduling 3. Remediate + roll out - Patch base image, rebuild, rescan to confirm fixed - Roll out via normal CD (canary -> fleet), backward-compatible - For urgent: prioritized rollout of the most-exposed services first 4. Verify + prevent recurrence Re-scan the fleet to confirm zero affected images remain; add/enforce the CVE gate in CI; consider digest pinning and signed images. Interview tip: Lead with exposure assessment — not every critical CVE is reachable in your setup, and triage prevents a needless fire drill. SBOMs make "which images are affected" answerable in minutes instead of days; mention them as the reason you can respond fast.

questions.q: What's the difference between authentication, authorization, and admission in the API request flow?
questions.text: Every API request passes through three sequential gates. Knowing the order clarifies where a given control lives. The request pipeline Request -> [1 AuthN] -> [2 AuthZ] -> [3 Admission] -> persisted to etcd 1. Authentication : WHO are you? (certs, OIDC tokens, SA tokens, cloud IAM) 2. Authorization : are you ALLOWED? (RBAC / ABAC / Webhook / Node authorizer) 3. Admission : SHOULD this specific object be allowed/mutated? (mutating webhooks, then validating webhooks/PSA/policy) Where controls live "User X can't authenticate" -> AuthN (bad/expired cert or token) "User X forbidden to list pods" -> AuthZ (RBAC missing the verb) "Pod rejected: must run non-root" -> Admission (PSA/policy engine) "Sidecar auto-injected" -> Admission (mutating webhook) Interview tip: The crisp framing: authN = identity, authZ = permission, admission = policy on the object itself. Mutating admission runs before validating admission. This mental model lets you instantly place where any security control or failure belongs — a clean way to structure a security answer.

questions.q: How do you scan and harden a cluster against the CIS Benchmark? What does kube-bench check?
questions.text: The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is the standard hardening checklist; kube-bench automates checking a cluster against it. What kube-bench checks - Control plane component flags (api-server, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd) - File permissions/ownership of config files and certs - kubelet configuration (anonymous auth off, authz mode, cert rotation) - etcd encryption + TLS settings - Logging/auditing enabled Running it kube-bench run --targets master,node,etcd,policies # outputs PASS/FAIL/WARN per CIS control with remediation steps Managed vs self-managed On GKE/EKS/AKS the provider hardens the control plane (you can't set those flags), so node/policy checks are your responsibility. On self-managed (kubeadm), you own all of it. Interview tip: Pair kube-bench (CIS config hardening) with kube-hunter (active pen-test of the cluster) and Trivy (workload/image scanning) for a full posture check. Knowing that managed clusters shift control-plane checks to the provider — and what remains yours (nodes, RBAC, policies, workloads) — shows real operational understanding.

questions.q: Explain seccomp, AppArmor, and SELinux in the context of containers. When use each?
questions.text: These are Linux kernel security modules that constrain what a container can do — defense in depth below the K8s layer. The three seccomp : filters which SYSCALLS a process may make (allowlist/denylist) AppArmor : path-based MAC -> restrict file access, capabilities, network per profile SELinux : label-based MAC -> enforce policy via security labels on processes/files In Kubernetes securityContext: seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } # blocks ~dangerous syscalls # AppArmor via annotation/profile; SELinux via seLinuxOptions RuntimeDefault seccomp blocks dozens of rarely-needed, dangerous syscalls with near-zero effort — the easiest high-value hardening. Custom profiles tighten further but need testing (a missing syscall crashes the app). When each seccomp: always enable RuntimeDefault as a baseline. AppArmor: Debian/Ubuntu nodes, path-based file/cap restriction. SELinux: RHEL/CoreOS nodes, label-based enforcement (default on OpenShift). Interview tip: The pragmatic answer: turn on seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault everywhere (huge win, trivial cost), then layer AppArmor or SELinux depending on your node OS. These operate at the kernel boundary, complementing RBAC/NetworkPolicy which operate at the K8s API/network layers.

questions.q: How would you detect and respond to a compromised pod that's mining crypto or beaconing out?
questions.text: This blends runtime detection, network controls, and incident response — a realistic security scenario. Detection signals - CPU pegged at 100% with no legitimate workload change (mining) - Unexpected outbound connections to unknown IPs/pools (beaconing/C2) - Falco alerts: unexpected process spawn, shell in container, outbound to mining pool - New processes not in the image; writes to unexpected paths Response 1. Isolate: apply a deny-all NetworkPolicy to the pod (cut C2/exfil) 2. Preserve: snapshot for forensics BEFORE killing (capture evidence) 3. Cordon the node if escape suspected; check for lateral movement 4. Terminate the pod; rotate any credentials it could access (SA token, secrets) 5. Root cause: which CVE / misconfig / leaked cred let them in? 6. Remediate the entry vector; redeploy clean; verify Prevention going forward Egress NetworkPolicies (default-deny egress stops beaconing), runtime detection (Falco/Tetragon), least-privilege SA + tight RBAC so a compromised pod can't pivot, hardened securityContext to limit escape. Interview tip: Order matters: isolate (network) and preserve evidence before you kill the pod — terminating first destroys forensics and the attacker may have persistence elsewhere. Then rotate credentials the pod could reach and hunt for lateral movement. Egress controls are the prevention headline: default-deny egress would have blocked the beaconing outright.

questions.q: How do you monitor a Kubernetes cluster? What are the layers and the key metrics at each?
questions.text: Cluster monitoring spans several layers; each has signals you must watch. Prometheus + Grafana is the de-facto stack. The layers Cluster/control plane : apiserver latency, etcd health, scheduler/controller queues Nodes : CPU/mem/disk/network, node conditions, kubelet health Workloads : pod restarts, OOMKills, readiness, HPA behavior Application : RED (rate, errors, duration) / golden signals Kubernetes objects : kube-state-metrics (deployment replicas, PVC status...) Where metrics come from node-exporter : node-level OS metrics kube-state-metrics : object state (desired vs ready replicas, pod phase) cAdvisor (in kubelet): per-container resource usage metrics-server : live CPU/mem for HPA + kubectl top app /metrics : your service's RED metrics (instrumented) Key alerts Pods crash-looping, nodes NotReady, PVCs near full, HPA at max replicas, apiserver/etcd latency high, certificate expiry, persistent OOMKills. Interview tip: Structure the answer by layer and cite the exporters by name (node-exporter, kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor) — that specificity shows hands-on monitoring experience. Tie app monitoring to RED/golden signals and mention kube-prometheus-stack as the batteries-included Helm chart.

questions.q: Explain how Prometheus discovers and scrapes targets in Kubernetes. What is ServiceMonitor?
questions.text: Prometheus uses Kubernetes service discovery to find scrape targets dynamically as pods come and go. Service discovery + scraping # Prometheus watches the K8s API for pods/services/endpoints # kubernetes_sd_configs roles: pod, service, endpoints, node, ingress # Relabeling picks which targets to scrape and rewrites labels # Then it pulls /metrics from each target on an interval Prometheus Operator: ServiceMonitor / PodMonitor apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1 kind: ServiceMonitor spec: selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } } endpoints: - { port: metrics, interval: 30s, path: /metrics } The Operator turns ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor CRDs into Prometheus scrape config automatically — you declare "scrape services with this label" instead of editing prometheus.yml. Scale gotcha: Pull model + high-cardinality labels (per-pod, per-request-id) explode memory and TSDB size. Keep label cardinality bounded. For huge fleets use sharding/federation or a remote-write backend (Thanos, Mimir, Cortex) for long-term storage and global query. Interview tip: Explain relabeling as the filter mechanism, ServiceMonitor as the declarative Operator-native way to register scrape targets, and cardinality as the #1 thing that kills Prometheus — mirroring the TSDB cardinality point from system design.

questions.q: What are the three pillars of observability and how do you implement them in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Metrics, logs, and traces together let you understand and debug a distributed system. Each answers a different question. The three pillars Metrics : what & how much (aggregates, alerting) -> Prometheus Logs : what happened (discrete events, detail) -> Loki / ELK / Cloud Logging Traces : where & why slow (request path) -> Jaeger / Tempo / OTel Implementation in K8s Metrics : Prometheus scrapes /metrics; Grafana dashboards; Alertmanager Logs : DaemonSet collector (Fluent Bit/Promtail) tails container stdout -> ships to Loki/Elasticsearch (don't write logs to pod disk) Traces : OpenTelemetry SDK/collector; propagate trace context across services The glue: correlation Propagate a trace/correlation ID through all services and include it in logs + spans, so you can pivot metric alert -> trace (which hop) -> logs (root cause). Interview tip: Stress the workflow: a metric alert tells you something's wrong, a trace localizes the slow service, logs give the why — and correlation IDs tie them together. Name OpenTelemetry as the vendor-neutral instrumentation standard and that container logs should go to stdout for a DaemonSet collector, never to files on the pod.

questions.q: How do you do centralized logging in Kubernetes? Why not write logs to files in the pod?
questions.text: Containers are ephemeral, so logs must leave the pod immediately. The standard pattern is stdout -> node collector -> central store. The pattern App -> stdout/stderr -> container runtime writes to /var/log/containers/*.log on the node -> DaemonSet collector (Fluent Bit / Fluentd / Promtail) tails those -> ships to Loki / Elasticsearch / Cloud Logging -> Grafana / Kibana to query Why NOT log to a file in the pod - Pod deleted -> logs gone (ephemeral filesystem) - Files count against the container's storage/memory (emptyDir) - No central search; can't correlate across pods - Log rotation inside the container is fragile Enrichment The collector adds K8s metadata (namespace, pod, labels, node) so you can filter logs by workload. Use structured (JSON) logs for queryability. Interview tip: "Log to stdout, let a DaemonSet ship it" is the canonical answer. Mention Loki (label-indexed, cheaper, pairs with Grafana) vs the EFK/ELK stack (full-text, heavier). The key principle: treat logs as a stream that leaves the pod instantly, never as files on ephemeral storage.

questions.q: How do you define SLOs and alert on them for a Kubernetes service? Explain burn-rate alerting.
questions.text: SLOs turn reliability into a measurable target; burn-rate alerting fires on the rate of error-budget consumption, not raw thresholds. SLI / SLO / error budget SLI : the measured signal (e.g. % of requests < 300ms and 2xx/3xx) SLO : the target (e.g. 99.9% success over 30 days) Error budget : 100% - SLO = 0.1% of requests may fail in the window Why burn-rate beats static thresholds Alerting "error rate > 1%" is noisy (fires on harmless blips) or slow. Burn-rate measures how fast you're spending the error budget: a fast burn (budget gone in hours) pages immediately; a slow burn (budget gone in days) is a ticket. # Multi-window, multi-burn-rate (Google SRE): # fast: 14.4x burn over 1h -> page (budget exhausts in ~2 days at this rate) # slow: 3x burn over 6h -> ticket # Requires BOTH a short and long window to fire (avoids flapping) Interview tip: Burn-rate, multi-window alerting (from the Google SRE book) is the senior answer — it ties alert urgency to budget impact, cutting noise while catching real fast-burn incidents quickly. Implement SLIs as Prometheus recording rules and alerts in Alertmanager.

questions.q: Walk through what happens when a node goes NotReady. What's the timeline to pod rescheduling?
questions.text: Node failure recovery has a deliberately conservative timeline to avoid flapping — knowing it explains why recovery "takes minutes." The timeline 1. kubelet stops posting heartbeats (node lease) 2. After ~40s (node-monitor-grace-period) node -> NotReady 3. Node controller waits ~5min (pod eviction timeout) before evicting 4. Pods marked for deletion; controllers (Deployment/RS) create replacements elsewhere 5. For StatefulSet + RWO volume: must detach from dead node first (more delay) Why so slow on purpose Aggressive eviction on a brief network blip would cause needless churn and double-scheduling. The grace periods trade recovery speed for stability. Speeding it up where needed - Tune node-monitor / eviction timeouts (carefully) - Run enough replicas across nodes/zones so one node loss = no outage - For stateful: app-level replication/failover beats waiting for volume reattach Interview tip: The honest takeaway: K8s self-heals node failure in minutes , not seconds, because of intentional grace periods — so availability comes from running redundant replicas across failure domains, not from fast rescheduling. Stateful workloads are slower still due to volume detach; that's why operators handle failover at the app layer.

questions.q: How do you upgrade a Kubernetes cluster safely with zero downtime? Control plane and nodes.
questions.text: Cluster upgrades follow version-skew rules and a control-plane-first, then-nodes order, draining nodes gracefully. Order + skew rules 1. Upgrade control plane first (api-server, then controller-manager/scheduler) 2. Then nodes (kubelet) -- kubelet may be up to 3 minor versions behind apiserver 3. One minor version at a time (no skipping, e.g. 1.28 -> 1.29 -> 1.30) 4. Upgrade addons/CRDs as required by the new version Node upgrade (rolling, drained) kubectl cordon <node> # stop new pods kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data # evict (respects PDBs) # upgrade kubelet / replace node, then: kubectl uncordon <node> Managed clusters (GKE/EKS) automate this with surge upgrades — spin up new-version nodes, drain old ones, respecting PDBs. Pre-flight: Check deprecated/removed APIs in the target version (e.g. kubectl deprecations / pluto) — a removed API version breaks manifests/controllers. Verify PDBs allow draining (no single-replica deadlocks). Back up etcd first. Interview tip: The headline rules: control plane before nodes, one minor at a time, PDBs make drains safe, and check for removed APIs before upgrading. Zero downtime depends on the same trio as deploys — multiple replicas, readiness probes, PDBs.

questions.q: What is etcd's role, and how do you back up and restore it? What happens if etcd is unhealthy?
questions.text: etcd is the cluster's single source of truth — every object's desired state. Its health gates the entire control plane. Role A distributed key-value store (Raft consensus) holding all API objects, secrets, and config. The API server is essentially a typed front-end over etcd. Backup ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save snapshot.db \ --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert=... --cert=... --key=... # store the snapshot encrypted, off-cluster; schedule regularly Restore etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore # point etcd at the restored data dir, restart control plane If etcd is unhealthy Lose quorum (need majority of an odd-numbered cluster, e.g. 2 of 3) and the API becomes read-only or unavailable — no scheduling, no changes. Running pods keep running (kubelet is autonomous) but nothing can change. Disk-full or high latency on etcd degrades the whole control plane. Interview tip: Key facts: odd-sized etcd (3 or 5) for quorum, regular tested snapshot restores, and that a healthy data plane survives a brief control-plane/etcd outage (existing pods run) but no changes are possible. On managed clusters the provider runs etcd; on self-managed it's your most critical backup.

questions.q: How do you do capacity planning and bin-packing for a cluster? How do requests drive cost?
questions.text: Cluster cost is driven by node count, which is driven by pod requests (not actual usage) and how well pods bin-pack onto nodes. Requests drive scheduling and cost # The scheduler reserves based on REQUESTS, not real usage. # Over-requesting -> nodes "full" of reservations while actually idle -> wasted $$ # Under-requesting -> overcommit -> contention, OOMKills, noisy neighbors Right-sizing - Measure actual usage (Prometheus / VPA recommendations) -> set requests to ~p90+headroom - Bin-pack: fewer, fuller nodes (MostAllocated scoring / Karpenter consolidation) - Separate node pools by workload shape (CPU-heavy vs mem-heavy vs GPU) - Use Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter to match node count to demand The trade-off Tight bin-packing cuts cost but raises blast radius (more pods per node) and reduces burst headroom. Spreading improves resilience but costs more. Balance per workload criticality. Interview tip: The crisp insight interviewers want: requests, not usage, determine cost — the most common waste is over-provisioned requests reserving capacity that sits idle. VPA in recommendation mode + dashboards of request-vs-usage is how you find it. Karpenter's consolidation actively bin-packs to cut node count.

questions.q: Explain GitOps with Argo CD or Flux. How does it differ from push-based CI/CD for clusters?
questions.text: GitOps makes Git the single source of truth for cluster state; an in-cluster agent continuously reconciles the live cluster toward the repo. Pull-based reconciliation Git repo (desired manifests) vs push-based CI/CD Push (traditional): CI has cluster credentials, runs `kubectl apply` from outside - external system holds prod creds (bigger attack surface) - no continuous drift detection; manual changes go unnoticed Pull (GitOps): cluster agent pulls; no external creds; drift auto-corrected Benefits Git is the audit log + rollback (revert a commit), drift detection/self-heal, no cluster creds in CI, declarative and reviewable. Argo CD has a rich UI + sync waves; Flux is lightweight and CRD-driven. Interview tip: The security angle is the strongest differentiator: pull-based GitOps means CI never holds cluster credentials and the agent continuously corrects drift. Mention app-of-apps (Argo) for managing many apps, sync waves for ordering, and that Git revert = instant rollback. This ties to your CI/CD and platform work.

questions.q: How do you manage configuration across many environments? Helm vs Kustomize vs both.
questions.text: Multi-environment config (dev/stage/prod) needs templating or overlays. The two dominant tools take different approaches. Helm — templating + packaging - Charts: templated YAML + values.yaml per environment - Package manager: versioning, dependencies, releases, rollback - Good for: distributing apps, complex parameterization - Downside: Go templating in YAML can get gnarly Kustomize — overlays, no templating - base/ + overlays/{dev,prod}: patch the base declaratively - No templating language: pure YAML merge/patch (kubectl -k built in) - Good for: env-specific tweaks to the same base manifests Both together (common) Helm to package/version the app + Kustomize to apply env-specific patches on the rendered output. Argo CD and Flux support both natively. Interview tip: The trade-off: Helm is powerful (packaging, dependencies, releases) but templating-heavy; Kustomize is simpler and template-free but lacks packaging/versioning. Many teams use Helm for third-party charts + Kustomize for their own overlays. Mention that secrets still need separate handling (External Secrets/Sealed Secrets) regardless of which you pick.

questions.q: A service's p99 latency spiked but p50 is fine. How do you investigate in Kubernetes?
questions.text: A p99-only spike means a subset of requests are slow — tail latency. The investigation walks the layers from app to infra. Likely causes (tail latency) - CPU throttling: CFS limits throttling some pods (check container_cpu_cfs_throttled) - One slow/unhealthy pod behind the Service (uneven load) - GC pauses, cold caches, lock contention on some requests - Noisy neighbor on a node; or a node with degraded disk/network - Downstream dependency tail (DB slow queries) on some calls - DNS 5s timeouts on a fraction of lookups Investigation path 1. Traces: find the slow requests, see WHICH hop adds latency (Jaeger/Tempo) 2. Per-pod metrics: is one replica slow? (uneven -> bad pod / placement) 3. CFS throttling metric: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total 4. Node-level: is one node degraded? kubectl top nodes, node metrics 5. Check GC/lock/app metrics; DB slow-query log for downstream Interview tip: The tell is p50-fine/p99-bad = tail, so look for what affects some requests: CPU throttling (very common — a CPU limit throttling bursty pods), one bad replica, or a downstream tail. Distributed tracing is the fastest way to localize the slow hop. Mentioning cfs_throttled shows you've debugged this for real.

questions.q: How do you implement multi-cluster Kubernetes? When do you need it and what are the patterns?
questions.text: Multi-cluster runs workloads across several clusters for HA, geo-distribution, isolation, or scale beyond a single cluster's limits. Why multi-cluster - Region/DR: survive a region or cluster failure - Geo: serve users from the nearest cluster (latency) - Isolation: hard tenant/blast-radius separation (prod vs nonprod, per-team) - Scale: beyond a single cluster's node/object limits - Compliance/data residency Patterns + tooling GitOps fleet : Argo CD / Flux manage many clusters from one repo (app-of-apps) Multi-cluster services : route/failover across clusters (mesh: Istio multi-cluster) Global LB / GeoDNS : direct users to the right cluster Fleet management : Rancher, Anthos, Cluster API for provisioning at scale The cost Operational complexity multiplies: config consistency, cross-cluster networking/identity, observability aggregation, and data replication across clusters. Don't over-reach: A single well-run regional cluster with multi-zone node pools already survives zone failures. Reach for multi-cluster only when you need cross-region DR, hard isolation, or scale a single cluster can't meet — the complexity is real. Interview tip: Lead with "why" — most HA needs are met by one multi-zone cluster; multi-cluster is for region-level DR, hard isolation, or scale limits. Then name GitOps (Argo/Flux) for fleet config and Cluster API/Rancher/fleet tools for provisioning. Be honest about the complexity tax.

questions.q: How do you debug high control-plane (API server) latency or throttling in a large cluster?
questions.text: At scale the API server and etcd become bottlenecks. Symptoms: slow kubectl, controller lag, scheduling delays, client throttling (429s). Common causes - Too many/large objects (huge Secrets/ConfigMaps, thousands of CRs) - Expensive LIST calls without pagination (list all pods cluster-wide) hammering etcd - A hot controller / operator with a tight reconcile loop - etcd slow (disk latency) -> everything slows - High watch churn; large events volume Investigation - apiserver_request_duration_seconds (latency by verb/resource) - apiserver_flowcontrol_* (APF / Priority and Fairness throttling) - etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration (etcd disk health) - audit log: who's making expensive LISTs? rate-limit/fix that client Mitigations API Priority and Fairness (APF) to isolate misbehaving clients, paginated/field-selector LISTs, fix chatty controllers, fast etcd disks, prune large objects/events, scale control plane (or rely on managed autoscaling). Interview tip: Name API Priority and Fairness (APF) — it prevents one client's flood from starving the control plane and is where you see throttling. The classic culprit is an operator or script doing unpaginated full LISTs against etcd. etcd disk latency underlies many control-plane slowdowns. This is a strong large-cluster operations signal.

questions.q: What are finalizers and why does a namespace or resource get stuck Terminating?
questions.text: Finalizers are pre-deletion hooks: a resource with finalizers won't be removed until each finalizer is cleared, letting controllers do cleanup first. How they work # metadata.finalizers: [ "example.com/cleanup" ] # Delete sets deletionTimestamp but the object STAYS until the controller # finishes cleanup and removes its finalizer -> then it's actually deleted. Why stuck Terminating - The controller responsible for the finalizer is gone/broken -> never clears it - A namespace stuck Terminating: a resource in it has a finalizer that can't complete (common with broken CRDs / orphaned custom resources / failed APIService) - Dependent resources can't be cleaned up (external system unreachable) Resolution (carefully) kubectl get ns <ns> -o json | jq '.spec.finalizers=[]' \ | kubectl replace --raw /api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/finalize -f - # Force-removing a finalizer SKIPS the cleanup it guarded -> may orphan resources Caution: Force-clearing finalizers can leak external resources (cloud LBs, disks) the controller would have cleaned up. Fix the broken controller/CRD first if possible; force-clear only as last resort. Interview tip: Explain that Terminating-but-stuck almost always = an uncleared finalizer waiting on a dead/broken controller. A frequent real case is a leftover APIService/CRD whose controller is gone, blocking namespace deletion. Knowing the finalize subresource trick (and its risk) shows real cleanup experience.

questions.q: How do you handle node maintenance, draining, and surge upgrades without impacting workloads?
questions.text: Safe node maintenance hinges on cordon + drain respecting PDBs, plus enough redundancy that losing a node is invisible. The drain workflow kubectl cordon <node> # mark unschedulable (no new pods) kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets \ --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=... # evict via Eviction API (honors PDBs) # ... do maintenance / replace node ... kubectl uncordon <node> # back into rotation What makes it non-disruptive - PDBs ensure minAvailable replicas stay up during eviction - maxUnavailable:0 + readiness ensures replacements are Ready before old ones leave - Topology spread / anti-affinity so replicas weren't all on this node - DaemonSets stay (--ignore-daemonsets); emptyDir data is acknowledged lost Surge upgrades (managed) GKE/EKS surge upgrades create extra new-version nodes first, then cordon+drain old ones, keeping capacity constant — tune surge/unavailable to balance speed vs cost. Interview tip: The drain honoring PDBs is the safety mechanism — but a bad PDB (single replica, minAvailable=replicas) makes drain hang forever. So the real prerequisites are: >=2 replicas, sane PDBs, topology spread, and readiness probes. Surge upgrades keep capacity flat during the roll.

questions.q: How do you instrument and trace a request across multiple microservices on Kubernetes?
questions.text: Distributed tracing follows a single request across service hops by propagating a trace context, revealing where latency and errors occur. How tracing works # Entry point creates a trace_id + root span # Each service: create a child span, propagate context via headers # (W3C traceparent header) to the next service # Spans shipped to a collector -> assembled into one trace (waterfall view) Implementation with OpenTelemetry - Instrument apps with OTel SDK (auto-instrumentation for many languages) - OTel Collector (DaemonSet/Deployment) receives + exports spans - Backend: Jaeger / Tempo / cloud trace - Service mesh can add spans for service-to-service hops automatically Sampling 100% tracing is expensive at scale. Head sampling (decide upfront) is cheap but may miss rare errors; tail sampling (decide after seeing the trace) keeps slow/error traces — better signal, more infra. Interview tip: The crux is context propagation — the W3C traceparent header carried hop to hop is what stitches spans into one trace. Name OpenTelemetry as the standard, mention a service mesh can auto-instrument the network hops, and discuss tail vs head sampling (tail keeps the interesting traces). Correlating trace IDs into logs closes the loop with the three pillars.

questions.q: Design a CI/CD pipeline that builds and deploys to Kubernetes. What are the stages?
questions.text: A production K8s pipeline separates CI (build/test/scan/push) from CD (deploy/verify), ideally with GitOps for the deploy half. CI stages 1. Lint + unit test 2. Build image (reproducible, pinned base) -> tag with git SHA (not :latest) 3. Scan: Trivy/Grype for CVEs (fail on criticals) 4. SBOM (Syft) + sign image (cosign) 5. Push to registry by digest 6. Update the deployment manifest / Helm values with the new digest (commit to GitOps repo) CD stages (GitOps) 7. Argo CD / Flux detects the repo change -> syncs to cluster 8. Progressive rollout (canary / blue-green via Argo Rollouts) 9. Automated verification: smoke tests + SLO/metric checks 10. Auto-promote or auto-rollback on failure Anti-patterns: deploying :latest (non-reproducible, can't roll back to a known image), giving CI direct cluster-admin creds (use GitOps pull instead), and skipping the scan/sign gate. Interview tip: The senior structure is CI pushes an artifact + opens a commit to a config repo; CD is a pull-based GitOps agent. Tag by immutable git SHA/digest so every deploy is reproducible and rollback is just pointing at the prior digest. Mentions of scan/sign/SBOM gates show supply-chain awareness.

questions.q: How do you build container images inside a Kubernetes cluster without the Docker daemon?
questions.text: Mounting the Docker socket into a CI pod is a major security risk (root on the node). Daemonless builders solve this. Why not docker-in-docker / docker.sock # Mounting /var/run/docker.sock = container can control the host daemon # -> effectively root on the node (container escape). Avoid in CI. # DinD (privileged) is also insecure + slow. Daemonless builders Kaniko : builds from a Dockerfile in an unprivileged container, pushes to registry Buildah : daemonless OCI builds (rootless capable) BuildKit : can run rootless; advanced caching, used by `docker buildx` Cloud Native Buildpacks : no Dockerfile -> auto-detect + build (pack / kpack) Caching for speed Layer caching (Kaniko cache, BuildKit registry cache) is essential or builds are slow. kpack/Buildpacks rebase only changed layers. Interview tip: The headline: never mount the Docker socket in CI — use Kaniko or BuildKit rootless to build unprivileged inside the cluster. Buildpacks (kpack) remove the Dockerfile entirely and standardize images. This is a security + supply-chain answer as much as a build one.

questions.q: Explain progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts. How do canary and blue-green differ?
questions.text: Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment controller with one that supports canary and blue-green strategies plus automated analysis. Canary — gradual shift strategy: canary: steps: - setWeight: 10 - pause: { duration: 5m } - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: success-rate }] } - setWeight: 50 - pause: {} - setWeight: 100 Shifts a small % of traffic to the new version, runs metric analysis, and auto-rolls-back if SLOs degrade — then ramps up. Blue-green — instant switch - Stand up the full new version (green) alongside old (blue) - Test green via a preview Service - Flip the Service selector blue -> green instantly (and back to roll back) Trade-offs Canary: gradual risk exposure, less spare capacity, slower; great with metric analysis. Blue-green: instant cutover + instant rollback, but needs 2x capacity and exposes all users at once at the flip. Interview tip: Tie the choice to risk + cost: canary for gradual, metric-gated rollout (best default); blue-green for fast cutover/rollback when you can afford double capacity and want an instant switch. The killer feature is automated analysis -> auto-rollback on SLO breach, removing humans from the rollback decision.

questions.q: How do you secure a CI/CD pipeline that deploys to Kubernetes end to end?
questions.text: Pipeline security spans source, build, artifact, and deploy — each a potential supply-chain entry point. Layered controls Source : protected branches, signed commits, required reviews, no secrets in git Build : ephemeral runners, no docker.sock, pinned base images, scan (Trivy) Artifact: SBOM (Syft), sign (cosign), push by digest, immutable tags Deploy : GitOps pull (CI holds no cluster creds), admission verifies signatures Runtime: least-privilege SA, NetworkPolicy, runtime detection (Falco) Credentials - OIDC federation from CI -> cloud (no long-lived keys stored in CI) - Short-lived, scoped tokens; rotate; never echo secrets in logs - Pull-based GitOps so prod cluster creds never live in the CI system Admission enforcement Cluster rejects unsigned images / disallowed registries (Kyverno/sigstore policy-controller), closing the loop so even a compromised CI can't deploy an unverified image. Interview tip: Frame it as SLSA-style supply-chain integrity: every step adds provenance, and admission verification at the cluster is the final gate. The two biggest wins: OIDC (no static cloud keys in CI) and pull-based GitOps (no cluster creds in CI) — both remove the most-stolen credentials from the pipeline.

questions.q: How do you manage Helm releases in CI/CD, and how do rollbacks work?
questions.text: Helm packages and versions releases; in CI/CD you template values per environment and rely on release history for rollback. Release flow helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart \ -f values-prod.yaml \ --set image.tag=$GIT_SHA \ --atomic --timeout 5m # --atomic: auto-rollback if the upgrade fails/times out Rollback helm history myapp # list revisions helm rollback myapp 4 # revert to revision 4 # Each upgrade stores a revision (in a Secret) -> rollback is reverting to it Helm in GitOps With Argo CD/Flux you usually don't run helm upgrade directly — the agent renders the chart and applies it; rollback = git revert of the values/chart version. This keeps git as the source of truth and audit log. Gotcha: --atomic + --timeout are important — without them a partially-applied failed upgrade leaves the release in a broken state. Also CRDs are not upgraded by Helm by default (Helm only installs CRDs on first install) — manage CRD upgrades explicitly. Interview tip: Mention --atomic (auto-rollback on failure) as the safety flag, that Helm stores revision history for rollback, and that in GitOps the rollback is a git revert rather than a helm rollback . The CRD-upgrade caveat is a real-world gotcha that signals experience.

questions.q: How do you run CI jobs themselves on Kubernetes (e.g. ephemeral runners)? Trade-offs?
questions.text: Running CI on K8s gives elastic, isolated, ephemeral build capacity — each job in a fresh pod — instead of static always-on runners. The pattern - GitHub Actions runner controller / GitLab K8s executor / Tekton / Argo Workflows - Each pipeline job -> a fresh pod (clean env, no state bleed between builds) - Scale to zero when idle; burst to many pods under load (HPA/KEDA on queue depth) Trade-offs / challenges + Elastic + cost-efficient (scale to zero), isolated, reproducible + Reuse cluster autoscaling + spot nodes for cheap build capacity - Build caching is harder (ephemeral pods lose local cache) -> use registry/remote cache - Image builds need daemonless (Kaniko/BuildKit) since no docker.sock - Cold-start latency for new pods/nodes; secrets must be injected securely Scaling on demand KEDA scales runner pods on queue depth (pending jobs), and Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter add nodes — often on spot instances for cheap, interruptible build capacity. Interview tip: The wins are isolation + scale-to-zero economics; the catches are caching (use remote/registry cache) and daemonless image builds. Name KEDA for queue-based runner autoscaling and spot nodes for cost — a nice tie-in to FinOps and autoscaling topics.

questions.q: How do you handle database schema migrations safely during a Kubernetes rolling deploy?
questions.text: During a rolling update, old and new app versions run simultaneously against one database — so migrations must be backward-compatible. This is the expand/contract pattern. The problem A rolling deploy means for a window both v1 and v2 pods are live. A destructive migration (drop/rename a column) breaks whichever version doesn't expect it. You cannot atomically swap schema + all pods. Expand / contract (parallel change) 1. EXPAND : add new column/table (additive, both versions still work) 2. MIGRATE: deploy code that writes BOTH old+new, reads new (backfill data) 3. CONTRACT: after all pods are v2 and data migrated, drop the old column # each step is backward-compatible with the version before it Where to run migrations - Init container or a Job (gated before rollout), NOT in every pod's startup race - Ensure idempotency + locking so concurrent pods don't double-run Never do a destructive, non-backward-compatible migration in the same deploy as the code that needs it — mid-rollout the old pods will error. Split across releases (expand now, contract later). Interview tip: Expand/contract (a.k.a. parallel change) is the expected answer. Stress that rolling deploys force backward-compatible schemas because two versions share the DB, and run migrations as a gated Job, not racing in pod startup. This connects to the zero-downtime rollout point from the pods section.

questions.q: What's the difference between a Deployment rollback and a GitOps rollback? Which is safer?
questions.text: Both revert to a prior state, but one is imperative and ephemeral, the other declarative and auditable. kubectl rollout undo kubectl rollout undo deployment/web # revert to previous ReplicaSet kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=3 # Fast, but: it diverges from git -> the live state no longer matches the repo GitOps rollback git revert <bad-commit> && git push # repo is source of truth # Argo/Flux syncs the cluster back -> live state matches git again Why GitOps is safer With GitOps, an imperative rollout undo creates drift — the agent will detect the live state differs from git and may re-sync forward to the "bad" version, undoing your manual rollback. The correct rollback is reverting the commit so git and cluster agree. Gotcha: Doing kubectl rollout undo on a GitOps-managed app is a trap — Argo CD sees drift and re-applies the repo (the broken version) unless auto-sync is paused. Always roll back in git for GitOps-managed workloads. Interview tip: The insight: in a GitOps world, the cluster is not the source of truth — git is. Manual rollout undo fights the reconciler. Safer rollback = git revert, which preserves auditability and keeps the reconcile loop consistent. Showing you understand drift vs source-of-truth is a strong platform signal.

questions.q: How do you schedule GPU or other specialized hardware workloads? What's the device plugin model?
questions.text: GPUs and other devices aren't native K8s resources — the device plugin framework advertises them as schedulable resources on nodes. Device plugin model # A DaemonSet (e.g. NVIDIA device plugin) runs on GPU nodes: # - discovers GPUs, registers them with kubelet as nvidia.com/gpu # - pods request them like any resource: resources: limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 } Placement - Taint GPU nodes (nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) so only GPU pods land there - GPU pods add a matching toleration + node affinity for the GPU node label - Node labels often auto-applied by NVIDIA GPU Operator / node feature discovery Sharing + efficiency GPUs are expensive and not natively shareable; options include time-slicing, MIG (multi-instance GPU partitioning), and MPS to pack multiple workloads per GPU. The NVIDIA GPU Operator manages drivers, plugin, and monitoring. Interview tip: The device plugin framework (DaemonSet advertising vendor.com/resource to kubelet) is the general mechanism — works for GPUs, FPGAs, NICs. Pair with taints (keep non-GPU pods off pricey nodes) + affinity. Mention MIG/time-slicing for GPU cost efficiency — a nice FinOps tie-in given how expensive GPU nodes are.

questions.q: How do you alert effectively without alert fatigue? What makes a good vs bad Kubernetes alert?
questions.text: Good alerting pages humans only for actionable, user-impacting problems. Most cluster noise should be dashboards or tickets, not pages. Bad alerts (cause fatigue) - Cause-based on transient states: "pod restarted once", "CPU > 80% for 1 min" - Non-actionable: nothing for the on-call to do - Per-pod noise in a fleet that self-heals - Static thresholds that flap Good alerts (symptom + actionable) - Symptom-based: user-facing SLO breach (error rate / latency burn-rate) - "Deployment has 0 available replicas for 5m" (real outage) - "PVC > 90% and filling" (will fail soon, actionable) - Has a runbook link + clear owner Principles Alert on symptoms (is the user affected?) not causes; use burn-rate/multi-window to cut flapping; route non-urgent signals to tickets/dashboards; every page must be actionable with a runbook. Interview tip: The Google SRE principle — alert on symptoms, not causes — is the headline. A single node at 80% CPU isn't a page; users seeing errors is. Burn-rate alerting (from the SLO question) reduces noise. Demonstrating you'd ruthlessly cut non-actionable alerts shows on-call maturity.

questions.q: How does Cilium / eBPF change Kubernetes networking, and why are teams adopting it?
questions.text: Cilium uses eBPF to run networking, security, and load-balancing logic in the kernel datapath, replacing iptables-based kube-proxy and unlocking richer features. What eBPF replaces - kube-proxy iptables/IPVS -> eBPF Service load-balancing (no rule explosion) - L3/L4 NetworkPolicy -> eBPF enforcement + identity-based (not IP-based) policy - Adds L7-aware policy (allow only GET /api), DNS-aware policy - Hubble: deep network observability (flow visibility) from eBPF Why teams adopt it - Performance at scale: no linear iptables chains; lower latency - Identity-based security: policy follows workload identity, not ephemeral pod IPs - Observability: Hubble shows every flow without sidecars - kube-proxy replacement + sidecar-less service mesh (ambient/eBPF mesh) The shift eBPF lets you run programmable logic in the kernel safely, so networking/security/observability move from userspace proxies and iptables into the datapath — faster and more flexible. Interview tip: Connect to earlier points: iptables kube-proxy doesn't scale (linear rule eval), and IP-based NetworkPolicy is brittle as pods churn. Cilium's eBPF gives O(1) LB, identity-based policy, L7 awareness, and Hubble observability — and is moving toward sidecar-less service mesh. Naming Hubble and identity-based policy signals current knowledge.

questions.q: How do you handle stateful workload disaster recovery across regions in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Stateful DR needs both the data (replicated/backed up off-region) and the ability to reconstitute the workload in another region/cluster. Data layer - App-level replication across regions (DB native: Postgres streaming/logical, Kafka MirrorMaker) -> warm standby, low RPO - Volume snapshots replicated cross-region (object storage) -> higher RPO - Velero: backs up K8s objects + PV snapshots, restore to another cluster RTO / RPO drive the design RPO (data loss tolerance): continuous replication = near-zero; snapshots = minutes/hrs RTO (downtime tolerance): warm standby = minutes; backup-restore = hours # Tighter RPO/RTO = more cost (active-active / continuous replication) Failover orchestration Promote the standby (operator or runbook), repoint DNS/global LB to the DR region, and reconcile the workloads there (GitOps applies the same manifests to the DR cluster). Untested DR is no DR: regularly run restore drills (Velero restore, standby promotion) and measure actual RTO/RPO — backups that have never been restored routinely fail when you need them. Interview tip: Lead with RPO/RTO defining the architecture and cost, then map: continuous app-level replication (low RPO/RTO, costly) vs Velero snapshot/restore (cheaper, higher RPO/RTO). Stress tested restore drills and that GitOps makes re-deploying the workload to the DR cluster trivial — data is the hard part, not manifests.

questions.q: How do you debug 'my cluster is slow' when you don't know the layer? Give a systematic approach.
questions.text: "Cluster is slow" is ambiguous — a systematic top-down sweep localizes it to control plane, node, network, or app. Narrow the scope first - Slow kubectl/deploys? -> control plane (apiserver/etcd) - Slow app responses? -> app, network, or node resource - Specific service or whole cluster? one node or all? - When did it start? correlate with a deploy / scale event / upgrade Layer-by-layer checks Control plane: apiserver_request_duration, APF throttling, etcd fsync latency Nodes: kubectl top nodes; disk/network saturation; node conditions Workloads: kubectl top pods; CFS throttling; OOMKills; restart counts Network: DNS latency (the 5s tell), NetworkPolicy drops, conntrack table full App/deps: traces for slow hop; downstream DB latency Common culprits etcd on slow disk, CPU CFS throttling, DNS (ndots/5s timeouts), conntrack table exhaustion on busy nodes, a chatty controller hammering the API, a noisy neighbor. Interview tip: Show method, not guessing: scope it (control plane vs data plane vs network), correlate with a change, then drill the suspect layer with specific metrics. Naming the usual suspects — etcd disk latency, CFS throttling, DNS 5s timeouts, conntrack exhaustion, APF throttling — proves you've actually chased these down.

questions.q: What is a Job and CronJob, and how do you make batch workloads reliable on Kubernetes?
questions.text: Jobs run pods to completion; CronJobs schedule Jobs. Reliability comes from tuning retries, parallelism, deadlines, and concurrency. Job knobs spec: completions: 5 # run to 5 successful pods parallelism: 2 # 2 at a time backoffLimit: 4 # retries before marking failed activeDeadlineSeconds: 600 # hard time cap ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 # auto-clean finished jobs CronJob concurrency concurrencyPolicy: Forbid # don't start a new run if the last is still going # (Allow / Forbid / Replace) startingDeadlineSeconds: 100 # skip missed runs older than this successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3 Reliability concerns Make jobs idempotent (they can re-run on retry/restart), set deadlines so a hung job doesn't run forever, use ttlSecondsAfterFinished to avoid pile-up, and handle the at-least-once nature (a job pod can run more than once). Gotcha: Default concurrencyPolicy: Allow can overlap runs if a job runs longer than its schedule interval — pile-ups and double-processing. Use Forbid or Replace for non-idempotent work, and design jobs to be idempotent regardless. Interview tip: Emphasize idempotency (Kubernetes gives at-least-once, a pod may re-run), concurrencyPolicy to prevent overlap, and activeDeadlineSeconds / ttlSecondsAfterFinished for hygiene. For complex DAGs of jobs, mention Argo Workflows. These details separate "I wrote a CronJob" from "I run reliable batch."

questions.q: How do descheduler and rebalancing work? Why doesn't Kubernetes rebalance pods on its own?
questions.text: The scheduler places pods once and never moves them — so over time the cluster drifts out of balance. The Descheduler evicts pods so they get rescheduled better. Why K8s doesn't rebalance # Scheduling is a one-time decision at pod creation. # After that, nodes get added/drained, pods come/go, requests change -> # the original placement becomes suboptimal, but nothing moves pods automatically. The Descheduler # Runs as a Job/CronJob; evicts pods matching strategies, e.g.: - RemoveDuplicates : spread replicas off the same node - LowNodeUtilization : drain under-used nodes' candidates to rebalance - RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpread / InterPodAntiAffinity (rule drift) - RemovePodsViolatingNodeTaints Evicted pods are recreated by their controllers and rescheduled per current state. It respects PDBs and won't evict un-replicated pods. Caution: The descheduler causes churn (evictions = brief disruption). Tune it and rely on PDBs so it doesn't disrupt availability. Karpenter's consolidation does similar rebalancing for cost by repacking nodes. Interview tip: The key concept: scheduling is one-shot, so the cluster needs an external rebalancer (Descheduler, or Karpenter consolidation) to correct drift after nodes/pods change. Mentioning that eviction churn must be bounded by PDBs shows you'd deploy it safely, not blindly.

questions.q: How do you manage CRDs and operators at scale? What are the upgrade and versioning pitfalls?
questions.text: CRDs extend the API; operators act on them. At scale, CRD versioning and operator upgrades become a real source of outages if mishandled. CRD versioning - CRDs support multiple versions (v1alpha1, v1beta1, v1) with a conversion webhook - Stored version + served versions; migrating stored objects needs care - Schema validation (OpenAPI) gates what users can submit Upgrade pitfalls - Helm does NOT upgrade CRDs by default (only installs on first install) -> CRD changes get silently skipped; operator expects new schema -> breaks - A breaking CRD schema change can invalidate existing CRs - Conversion webhook down -> CRs unreadable -> operator + deletes stuck (finalizers!) - Operator RBAC drift after upgrade Safe practice Version CRDs additively, test conversion webhooks, manage CRD upgrades explicitly (not via Helm's skip), and stage operator upgrades in nonprod. Watch for the finalizer-stuck-Terminating failure mode when a conversion webhook or operator is unhealthy. Interview tip: The two pitfalls interviewers love: (1) Helm skips CRD upgrades, so schema changes get missed, and (2) a down conversion webhook makes CRs unreadable and blocks deletion (ties back to finalizers/stuck-Terminating). Treating CRDs as a versioned API with backward-compatible evolution is the senior framing.

questions.q: You inherit an undocumented production cluster. How do you assess its health, risk, and cost?
questions.text: A structured audit across reliability, security, and cost gives you a prioritized risk picture fast — a realistic senior/staff scenario. 1. Inventory + reliability - Versions: kubelet/control-plane version, is it EOL? upcoming forced upgrade? - Workloads without requests/limits, PDBs, multiple replicas, anti-affinity - Single points of failure: single-replica critical services, one-zone deploys - Backups: is etcd backed up? are stateful PVs backed up? ever restored? 2. Security posture - kube-bench (CIS), kube-hunter; Trivy scan running images - RBAC sprawl: who has cluster-admin? kubectl auth can-i audits - privileged pods, hostPath/hostNetwork, no NetworkPolicies, secrets in env/git - Pod Security Admission enforced? image signing/registry allowlist? 3. Cost - Request-vs-usage gap (over-provisioned requests = wasted nodes) - Idle/under-utilized nodes; oversized node pools; no autoscaling - Orphaned PVs/LBs; right-sizing via VPA recommendations / Kubecost Then prioritize Rank by risk x effort: backups + EOL version + cluster-admin sprawl are usually top. Document findings, quick wins first, build a remediation roadmap. Interview tip: Structure beats trivia here — assess across reliability, security, cost, then prioritize by risk. Name concrete tools (kube-bench, Trivy, Kubecost, VPA) and the highest-impact gaps (no backups, EOL version, over-broad RBAC, no NetworkPolicies, request bloat). This is exactly the platform-ownership framing senior interviews probe for.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Pod, a ReplicaSet and a Deployment, and why do you almost never create bare Pods?
questions.text: A Pod is the smallest runnable unit, a ReplicaSet keeps N identical Pods alive, and a Deployment manages ReplicaSets so you get rolling updates and rollbacks. A bare Pod is not rescheduled if its node dies. kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=web kubectl rollout history deploy/web kubectl describe rs <name> | grep -i 'controlled by' Interview tip: Say the ownership chain out loud: Deployment owns ReplicaSet owns Pod. It shows you understand where rollouts really happen.

questions.q: What are the Kubernetes QoS classes and how do they decide who gets evicted first?
questions.text:
Guaranteed means every container has requests equal to limits for CPU and memory. Burstable means at least one request or limit is set. BestEffort means none are set. Under node pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable pods exceeding requests, and Guaranteed last. kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}' kubectl describe node | grep -A8 'Allocated resources' Interview tip: Mention that QoS is derived, not configured, and that the OOM killer also uses it through oom_score_adj.

questions.q: How do Namespaces, ResourceQuota and LimitRange work together to share a cluster fairly?
questions.text: A Namespace is the scope. ResourceQuota caps the total a namespace can consume or create, and LimitRange sets per-pod or per-container defaults and bounds, so a pod without requests still gets sensible ones. kubectl describe quota -n team-a kubectl describe limitrange -n team-a kubectl create quota q --hard=cpu=20,memory=64Gi,pods=100 -n team-a Interview tip: A quota on CPU or memory forces every pod to declare them, so pair it with a LimitRange default or deployments will be rejected.

questions.q: Compare ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName Services. When do you pick each?
questions.text: ClusterIP is internal only. NodePort opens a port on every node. LoadBalancer asks the cloud for an external load balancer in front of a NodePort. ExternalName is only a DNS CNAME to something outside the cluster. kubectl get svc -o wide kubectl expose deploy web --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=ClusterIP Interview tip: Add that most production traffic enters through one Ingress or Gateway rather than one cloud load balancer per Service, because of cost.

questions.q: Name the control plane components and describe what each one does.
questions.text: kube-apiserver is the only front door and talks to etcd. etcd stores state. kube-scheduler assigns pods to nodes. kube-controller-manager runs reconciliation loops. cloud-controller-manager talks to the cloud API. On nodes, kubelet and kube-proxy do the work. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' Interview tip: Stress that every component talks only to the API server, never to each other directly. That one fact explains most debugging paths.

questions.q: ConfigMap as environment variables versus as a mounted volume: which one updates live, and what are the consequences?
questions.text: Environment variables are read at container start and never change. Mounted ConfigMap files are refreshed by the kubelet within a minute or so, except when mounted with subPath, which never updates. kubectl set env deploy/web --from=configmap/app-config kubectl rollout restart deploy/web kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/config/app.yaml Interview tip: Mention a checksum annotation on the pod template, a common Helm trick, to force a rollout when the config changes.

questions.q: What are the postStart and preStop lifecycle hooks, and how do they interact with graceful shutdown?
questions.text:
postStart runs right after the container is created, without any ordering guarantee against the entrypoint. preStop runs before SIGTERM is sent and is used to drain connections. Both count toward terminationGracePeriodSeconds. kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.lifecycle kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}' Interview tip: A short sleep in preStop is a common fix for 502s during rollouts, because endpoint removal and SIGTERM race each other.

questions.q: How does kubectl rollout undo work, and where are revisions stored?
questions.text: Each pod-template change creates a new ReplicaSet, and the Deployment keeps old ones up to revisionHistoryLimit. Undo scales an old ReplicaSet back up and the current one down. Scaling or changing replicas alone does not create a revision. kubectl rollout history deploy/web kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=3 kubectl annotate deploy/web kubernetes.io/change-cause='bump to 1.4.2' Interview tip: In a GitOps setup, prefer reverting the commit. A manual undo will be overwritten at the next sync.

questions.q: Explain how a Helm chart is structured and what helm template, helm upgrade --install and helm diff are for.
questions.text: A chart has Chart.yaml, values.yaml and a templates folder. helm template renders manifests locally with no cluster. helm upgrade --install is idempotent deploy. helm diff, a plugin, shows what would change before you apply. helm template web ./chart -f values-prod.yaml helm upgrade --install web ./chart -n prod --atomic --timeout 5m helm diff upgrade web ./chart -n prod Interview tip: Use --atomic or --wait in CI so a failed release rolls itself back instead of leaving a half-deployed state.

questions.q: What is an EndpointSlice, and why did it replace the Endpoints object?
questions.text: Endpoints stored every pod IP of a Service in one object, so a change to one pod rewrote and resent the whole thing to every node. EndpointSlices shard that into small chunks, default 100 endpoints each, which scales far better. kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web kubectl get endpoints web -o yaml Interview tip: Mention that kube-proxy and the ingress controllers now watch EndpointSlices, so large Services update much faster.

questions.q: How do you manage access to multiple clusters with kubeconfig contexts without making mistakes?
questions.text: A kubeconfig holds clusters, users and contexts. A context binds one cluster, one user and a default namespace. Switch with kubectl config use-context, or better, use the KUBECONFIG variable per shell and a prompt that shows the context. kubectl config get-contexts kubectl config use-context prod-eu -n payments kubectl --context=staging get pods kubectl auth whoami Interview tip: Name a real habit: a coloured prompt for prod, and short-lived credentials from SSO or an exec plugin rather than static tokens.

questions.q: When do you use kubectl debug node, and how is it different from SSH to the node?
questions.text: kubectl debug node/ starts a privileged pod on that node with the host filesystem mounted at /host. It gives you host-level access without opening SSH, and the access is audited through the API server. kubectl debug node/ip-10-0-1-5 -it --image=busybox chroot /host journalctl -u kubelet --since '10 min ago' Interview tip: Delete the debug pod afterwards, and mention that on managed or immutable OS nodes this is often the only way in.

questions.q: What are static pods, and which cluster components commonly run as static pods?
questions.text: Static pods are defined as manifest files in a directory on a node, and the kubelet runs them directly with no API server involved. A mirror pod is created in the API so you can see them. kubeadm control plane components use this. ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests grep staticPodPath /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'apiserver|etcd' Interview tip: This is why you edit a file on the control plane node, not use kubectl edit, to change the API server flags in a kubeadm cluster.

questions.q: What do the kubelet and the container runtime each do, and what is CRI?
questions.text: The kubelet is the node agent that makes pods match the spec. It talks to a container runtime such as containerd or CRI-O through the Container Runtime Interface, a gRPC API. Docker Engine support through dockershim was removed in 1.24. crictl ps crictl pods systemctl status kubelet containerd journalctl -u kubelet -f Interview tip: If asked about dockershim, say images built with Docker still run fine, because they are OCI images.

questions.q: What does volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer solve, and why does it matter on multi-zone clusters?
questions.text: With Immediate binding, a zonal disk is created before the pod is scheduled, possibly in a zone where the pod cannot run. WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until the pod is scheduled, so the disk is created in the same zone as the node. kubectl get sc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,MODE:.volumeBindingMode kubectl describe pvc data-0 | grep -i 'waiting for first consumer' Interview tip: A PVC showing Pending with this mode is normal until a pod uses it. Do not misread it as a failure.

questions.q: Explain the PersistentVolume access modes: ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany and ReadWriteOncePod.
questions.text: RWO allows one node to mount read-write, not one pod. ROX allows many nodes read-only. RWX allows many nodes read-write and needs a shared filesystem such as NFS or EFS. RWOP restricts the volume to a single pod. kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,MODES:.spec.accessModes kubectl explain pvc.spec.accessModes Interview tip: Point out the RWO trap: several pods on the same node can still share an RWO volume.

questions.q: What is the PersistentVolume reclaim policy, and when would you choose Retain over Delete?
questions.text: Delete removes the underlying disk when the PVC is deleted, which is the default for dynamic provisioning. Retain keeps the disk and the PV in Released state, so data survives and an admin can recover it. kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,POLICY:.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy kubectl patch pv <pv> -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}' Interview tip: Say that Retain is not a backup. It only prevents accidental deletion, so you still need snapshots.

questions.q: What is the difference between an Ingress resource and an Ingress controller, and how do you terminate TLS?
questions.text: An Ingress resource is only routing rules in the API. An Ingress controller, such as NGINX, Traefik or a cloud ALB controller, watches those rules and configures a real proxy. TLS is terminated at the controller using a certificate stored in a Secret. kubectl get ingressclass kubectl describe ingress web kubectl get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}' Interview tip: Mention that without an installed controller an Ingress object does nothing, which is a common first-day surprise.

questions.q: How does cert-manager issue and renew certificates inside a cluster?
questions.text: You define an Issuer or ClusterIssuer, such as Let's Encrypt or Vault. A Certificate resource, or an annotated Ingress, requests a cert. cert-manager completes the ACME challenge, stores the result in a Secret, and renews it before expiry. kubectl get clusterissuer,certificate -A kubectl describe certificate web-tls cmctl status certificate web-tls Interview tip: Name the usual failure: the HTTP-01 challenge is blocked by a redirect or a firewall. DNS-01 avoids it and supports wildcards.

questions.q: What are good practices for Kubernetes labels, selectors and annotations?
questions.text:
Labels identify and select; annotations hold non-identifying metadata. Use the recommended app.kubernetes.io set, keep selectors stable because Deployment selectors are immutable, and never put secrets or large data in either. kubectl get pods -l 'app.kubernetes.io/name=web,tier in (frontend,api)' kubectl label pod

debug=true --overwrite kubectl get pods --show-labels Interview tip: A well-known trap: if a Service selector matches pods from two Deployments, traffic is split between them.

questions.q: What are native sidecar containers, and how do they differ from the old sidecar pattern?
questions.text:
Native sidecars are init containers with restartPolicy Always. They start before the app, keep running alongside it, are restarted independently, and are stopped after the app ends. This fixes ordering and Job completion problems of regular sidecars. kubectl explain pod.spec.initContainers.restartPolicy kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.status.initContainerStatuses[*].name}' Interview tip: The headline benefit is that a Job with a log or proxy sidecar can now actually complete.

questions.q: Why do many teams remove CPU limits, and what does CFS throttling have to do with it?
questions.text: CPU limits are enforced by the CFS quota in 100 ms periods. A multi-threaded app can use its whole quota in a few milliseconds and then be paused for the rest of the period, which hurts tail latency even when the node is idle. rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]) kubectl top pod --containers Interview tip: Keep CPU requests accurate, since requests drive scheduling and fair sharing. Memory limits you should keep.

questions.q: How do you write a default-deny NetworkPolicy that still lets pods resolve DNS?
questions.text: Create an empty podSelector policy with both Ingress and Egress types, then add an egress allow to the kube-dns pods on UDP and TCP 53 in the kube-system namespace. Without that rule, all name lookups break. kubectl apply -f default-deny.yaml kubectl exec test -- nslookup kubernetes.default kubectl describe netpol -n prod Interview tip: Always confirm your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy. Some, like plain Flannel, silently ignore it.

questions.q: What is Kubernetes audit logging, and how would you use it to investigate an incident?
questions.text: The API server can record every request according to an audit policy, with levels None, Metadata, Request and RequestResponse. Logs go to a file or webhook, and you query who did what, to which resource, when, and from where. kube-apiserver --audit-policy-file=... --audit-log-path=... jq 'select(.verb=="delete" and .objectRef.resource=="secrets")' audit.log Interview tip: On managed clusters, enable the provider's control plane logs, because audit is often off by default.

questions.q: What is the difference between metrics-server and Prometheus, and where does kubectl top get its data?
questions.text: metrics-server keeps only current CPU and memory in memory for kubectl top and the HPA. It stores no history. Prometheus scrapes many metrics and stores time series for dashboards, alerting and analysis. kubectl top nodes kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics Interview tip: If kubectl top fails, check the metrics-server pod and the v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io APIService first.

questions.q: What is KEDA, and when would you use it instead of the standard HPA?
questions.text: KEDA scales workloads on event sources such as queue length, Kafka lag or cron schedules, and can scale to zero. It feeds the HPA with external metrics. The plain HPA mostly scales on CPU and memory and cannot go to zero. kubectl get scaledobject -A kubectl describe scaledobject worker kubectl get hpa Interview tip: Scale-to-zero suits workers, not user-facing APIs, because of cold start latency.

questions.q: Pods are being evicted because of DiskPressure on a node. How do you investigate and prevent a repeat?
questions.text: The kubelet evicts pods when nodefs or imagefs falls under its threshold, and also garbage-collects images. Find what is filling the disk: container logs, images, emptyDir, or writable layers. kubectl describe node <n> | grep -A5 Conditions kubectl debug node/<n> -it --image=busybox -- du -xh /host/var/lib --max-depth=2 | sort -h | tail crictl images; crictl rmi --prune Interview tip: Name three preventers: log rotation limits, ephemeral-storage requests and limits, and image garbage collection thresholds.

questions.q: A Deployment rollout finished but some old pods are stuck in Terminating forever. What is going on?
questions.text:
A pod stays Terminating when a finalizer blocks it, the node is unreachable so the kubelet cannot confirm deletion, the process ignores SIGTERM and the grace period is very long, or a volume cannot be unmounted. kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers} {.metadata.deletionTimestamp}' kubectl describe pod

| tail -20 kubectl delete pod

--force --grace-period=0 Interview tip: Force delete is a last resort. For StatefulSets it can allow two pods with the same identity, which risks data corruption.

questions.q: ImagePullBackOff happens only on some nodes, not all. How do you find the cause?
questions.text:
If the same image works on some nodes, the problem is node-specific: registry rate limits per IP, missing credentials or a node role without ECR access, DNS or proxy issues on that node, or a full disk. kubectl get pod

-o wide kubectl describe pod

| grep -A10 Events crictl pull # run on the failing node kubectl debug node/ -it --image=busybox Interview tip: Docker Hub anonymous pull limits are a classic. Use authenticated pulls or a pull-through cache.

questions.q: A Service works from inside the cluster but is unreachable from outside through its NodePort. How do you debug?
questions.text: Check the layers in order: pod readiness and endpoints, kube-proxy rules on the node, cloud security groups or firewall for the port range 30000-32767, externalTrafficPolicy, and whether the node you hit has a local pod. kubectl get svc web -o wide; kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web curl -v http://<nodeIP>:<nodePort> sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-NODEPORTS | grep <port> Interview tip: With externalTrafficPolicy Local, nodes without a local pod drop the traffic. This is by design and preserves the source IP.

questions.q: Every pod creation suddenly fails with a webhook timeout or certificate error. What happened and how do you recover?
questions.text: A validating or mutating admission webhook is unreachable or its serving certificate expired, and its failurePolicy is Fail, so the API server rejects all matching requests. Disable or fix the webhook configuration to unblock. kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> kubectl logs -n gatekeeper-system deploy/gatekeeper-controller-manager Interview tip: Exempt kube-system and the webhook's own namespace, and set a timeout. The webhook that guards pods must not depend on pods it blocks.

questions.q: etcd reports 'mvcc: database space exceeded' and the cluster turns read-only. How do you recover?
questions.text: etcd hits its quota, default 2 GB, raises a NOSPACE alarm and only accepts reads and deletes. Compact the history, defragment, then disarm the alarm. Find out what grew: usually events or a controller writing too much. ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status -w table rev=$(etcdctl endpoint status -w json | jq '.[0].Status.header.revision'); etcdctl compact $rev etcdctl defrag; etcdctl alarm disarm Interview tip: Take a snapshot before you touch anything, and defrag one member at a time because it blocks that member.

questions.q: A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating. What are the likely causes and how do you narrow them down?
questions.text:
The pod is scheduled but the kubelet cannot finish setup. Typical causes are a failing volume mount or attach, a missing ConfigMap or Secret, CNI problems assigning an IP, or the runtime failing to pull or create the sandbox. kubectl describe pod

| sed -n '/Events/,$p' kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=

journalctl -u kubelet | grep Interview tip: Events usually name the culprit in one line, such as FailedMount, FailedCreatePodSandBox or FailedAttachVolume.

questions.q: External lookups from pods are slow and some calls take about five seconds. How do ndots and CoreDNS play a role?
questions.text:
The default ndots:5 makes the resolver try several search-domain suffixes before the real name, multiplying queries. Combined with the UDP conntrack race, timeouts of 5 seconds appear. Use fully qualified names, tune ndots, and add NodeLocal DNSCache. kubectl exec

-- cat /etc/resolv.conf kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50 kubectl top pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Interview tip: A trailing dot on external hostnames, api.example.com., skips the search path entirely.

questions.q: Pods cannot get IP addresses because the node ran out of IPs. How does that happen on EKS and what are the options?
questions.text: With the AWS VPC CNI, each pod uses a real VPC IP drawn from the ENIs attached to the node, so the instance type's ENI and IP limits cap pods per node and small subnets run dry. Use prefix delegation, custom networking or larger subnets. kubectl describe node <n> | grep -i 'pods:' kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=aws-node --tail=30 aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[].[SubnetId,AvailableIpAddressCount]' Interview tip: Say the formula: max pods = ENIs x (IPs per ENI - 1) + 2. It shows you know why small instances fit few pods.

questions.q: A pod fails with 'Multi-Attach error for volume' after a node failure. Why, and how do you resolve it safely?
questions.text:
A ReadWriteOnce block volume is still attached to the failed node, so the CSI attacher will not attach it elsewhere until the old attachment is released. Wait for the force-detach timeout, or confirm the node is truly down and remove the VolumeAttachment. kubectl get volumeattachment | grep kubectl describe pod

| grep -i multi-attach kubectl delete volumeattachment # only after node is confirmed gone Interview tip: Never force the detach while the old node might still be writing. That can corrupt the filesystem.
