questions.q: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler keeps flapping between scale up and scale down. How do you stabilise it?
questions.text: Flapping comes from noisy metrics, short windows, a target near the natural load level, or slow pod startup. Use stabilizationWindowSeconds, scaling policies, a better metric, and readiness so new pods are counted correctly. kubectl describe hpa web kubectl get hpa web -w kubectl get hpa web -o yaml | grep -A12 behavior Interview tip: Scale up fast, scale down slowly is the usual rule. The behavior field lets you set each direction separately.

questions.q: Users see 502 errors for a few seconds on every deployment. How do you make rollouts truly zero-downtime?
questions.text:
Traffic is still sent to terminating pods, or new pods receive traffic before they are ready. Add accurate readiness probes, a preStop sleep, SIGTERM handling, enough grace period, a PodDisruptionBudget and sensible maxUnavailable. kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy}' kubectl describe pod

| grep -A6 -E 'Readiness|Liveness' kubectl rollout status deploy/web Interview tip: Also check keep-alive and idle timeouts on the load balancer, because they can differ from the app's.

questions.q: The Cluster Autoscaler is not adding nodes even though pods are Pending. How do you investigate?
questions.text:
Check why the pods are Pending and whether a new node would help. Common reasons: node group at max size, pod requests larger than any node type, taints or affinity no node group satisfies, quotas, or the autoscaler not discovering the group. kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler | grep -i -E 'scale-up|no.*node group' kubectl get cm cluster-autoscaler-status -n kube-system -o yaml kubectl describe pod

| grep -A5 Events Interview tip: The status ConfigMap and the pod's TriggeredScaleUp or NotTriggerScaleUp event usually spell out the reason.

questions.q: A secret was committed to a Git repository and used in a Kubernetes manifest. What is your response?
questions.text: Treat it as compromised: rotate the credential first, then remove it from the cluster and history, check audit logs and cloud logs for use, and put a control in place such as secret scanning and an external secret manager. git log -S'AKIA' --all --oneline kubectl get secret app-creds -o yaml | grep -c data trufflehog git file://. --only-verified Interview tip: Rewriting Git history is not enough. Anyone who cloned already has it, so rotation is the only real fix.

questions.q: A developer gets 'forbidden' from kubectl exec. How do you find the missing RBAC permission quickly?
questions.text: Read the error, which names the user, verb, resource and namespace. Use kubectl auth can-i with impersonation, check bindings that reference the user or groups, and remember exec needs create on pods/exec, not just get on pods. kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n prod --as dev@corp.com kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o wide | grep dev@corp.com kubectl auth can-i --list -n prod --as dev@corp.com Interview tip: For group-based access from OIDC, verify the group claim actually reaches the API server, since bindings to a group do nothing otherwise.

questions.q: Packets are intermittently dropped and dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full'. What do you do?
questions.text: The node's connection tracking table is exhausted, usually by many short connections, high-traffic DNS over UDP, or leaked entries. Raise nf_conntrack_max and hashsize, reduce connection churn, and consider eBPF datapaths that avoid conntrack. sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max conntrack -S sudo sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288 Interview tip: Track the count over max ratio as a node metric and alert on it before drops start.

questions.q: You suspect a memory leak in a service. How do you confirm it from Kubernetes and Prometheus data?
questions.text:
Look for a sawtooth that never returns to baseline in container working set memory, restarts with OOMKilled, and a steady upward trend across days. Then use a profiler or heap dump in a staging copy to find the cause. container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~"web-.*"} kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}' deriv(container_memory_working_set_bytes[1h]) > 0 Interview tip: Use working set, not RSS or usage, since the working set is what the OOM killer compares to the limit.

questions.q: Prometheus keeps running out of memory. How do you find the high-cardinality metrics and fix them?
questions.text: Memory scales with active time series. Find the biggest metrics and labels, drop or relabel unbounded labels like user ID or full URL, reduce scrape targets, and shard or move long-term storage to Thanos, Mimir or similar. topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"})) curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/status/tsdb | jq '.data.seriesCountByMetricName[:10]' promtool tsdb analyze /prometheus Interview tip: The TSDB status page and promtool analyze show the worst offenders in seconds.

questions.q: An Argo CD application is stuck OutOfSync or Progressing. How do you diagnose it?
questions.text: OutOfSync means live state differs from Git: check the diff, defaulted fields, and controllers mutating resources. Progressing means health checks have not passed: pods not ready, a hook stuck, or a CRD with no health definition. argocd app diff web argocd app get web --show-operation kubectl describe application web -n argocd argocd app sync web --dry-run Interview tip: Use ignoreDifferences for fields that other controllers legitimately change, such as replicas managed by the HPA.

questions.q: helm upgrade failed and the release is stuck in 'pending-upgrade'. How do you recover?
questions.text: A previous Helm operation was interrupted, leaving a lock-like release status. Check history, roll back to the last deployed revision, or if no rollback is possible remove the stuck release Secret, then fix the chart and upgrade again with --atomic. helm history web -n prod helm rollback web 7 -n prod kubectl get secret -n prod -l owner=helm,name=web,status=pending-upgrade helm upgrade --install web ./chart -n prod --atomic Interview tip: Cancelling CI in the middle of a Helm run is the usual cause. Make pipeline jobs non-cancellable during deploy.

questions.q: After a node scale-down or zone issue, pods are packed unevenly and one zone holds most replicas. How do you fix and prevent it?
questions.text: The scheduler only places pods at creation time and does not rebalance. Use topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew, whenUnsatisfiable settings, PodDisruptionBudgets, and optionally the descheduler to rebalance existing pods. kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide --sort-by=.spec.nodeName kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone kubectl rollout restart deploy/web Interview tip: Add minDomains or use nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy in newer versions to make spread behave predictably with autoscaling.

questions.q: Users get 504 Gateway Timeout or 413 errors through the Ingress for certain requests. Where do you look?
questions.text: 504 means the proxy gave up waiting for the backend, so check upstream timeouts and slow pods. 413 means the request body exceeds the proxy limit. Tune per-Ingress annotations, but first find out why the backend is slow. kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller | grep -E ' 504 | 413 ' kubectl annotate ingress web nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout='120' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size='50m' --overwrite Interview tip: Raising the timeout hides a slow backend. Check the application latency first and the load balancer idle timeout in front too.

questions.q: A cluster upgrade is planned and some manifests use deprecated APIs. How do you avoid breaking workloads?
questions.text: Find the deprecated and removed API versions in use, in live objects and in Git or Helm charts, convert them before upgrading, and upgrade one minor version at a time, with add-ons checked for compatibility. kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis pluto detect-files -d ./manifests kubent kubectl convert -f old.yaml --output-version networking.k8s.io/v1 Interview tip: Check the Kubernetes deprecation guide for each target version. Removals such as PodSecurityPolicy or old Ingress versions have broken real clusters.

questions.q: A Kubernetes Job never finishes, and a CronJob has missed several schedules. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: A Job hangs if pods keep failing under backoffLimit, a sidecar keeps running, or the container never exits. A CronJob misses runs because of concurrencyPolicy, startingDeadlineSeconds, suspended state, or too many missed starts. kubectl describe job nightly-report kubectl get cronjob nightly -o yaml | grep -E 'suspend|concurrencyPolicy|startingDeadline' kubectl logs job/nightly-report Interview tip: Set activeDeadlineSeconds and ttlSecondsAfterFinished so stuck Jobs terminate and finished ones are cleaned up.

questions.q: How do you find and kill a process consuming excessive CPU or memory?
questions.text: Identify top -o %CPU # sort by CPU (press M to sort by memory) htop # interactive, easier to read ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -15 # snapshot sorted by CPU ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -15 # snapshot sorted by memory pidof nginx # find PID by name pgrep -fl java # find PIDs matching pattern + show cmdline Kill kill -15 <pid> # SIGTERM — graceful shutdown (try this first) kill -9 <pid> # SIGKILL — force kill (use when -15 fails) killall nginx # kill all processes named nginx pkill -f "java.*myapp" # kill by regex matching full command line Always try SIGTERM (15) first — it allows the process to clean up (flush buffers, close connections, remove temp files). SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored — the kernel terminates the process immediately with no cleanup. Use SIGKILL only when SIGTERM fails or the process is unkillable. Interview tip: Explain the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL. A process ignoring SIGTERM is either buggy or intentionally handling it (e.g., daemontools keeping a service alive). SIGKILL always works except for zombie processes — which cannot be killed at all (must reap the parent).

questions.q: What is a zombie process — why does it appear and how do you deal with it?
questions.text: A zombie process has finished executing but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not yet read its exit status via wait(). It holds no resources — just a PID slot. ps aux | grep 'Z' # Z state = zombie ps -el | grep defunct # another way to list zombies cat /proc/<zombie-pid>/status | grep PPid # find parent PID kill -SIGCHLD <parent-pid> # signal parent to reap children You cannot kill a zombie with kill -9 — it has no running code. The fix is to signal or restart the parent process so it calls wait() to reap the zombie. If the parent is buggy and never reaps children, the parent itself must be killed — init (PID 1) will then adopt and reap the orphaned zombie. A few zombies are harmless; hundreds indicate a parent process leak. PID table exhaustion: Each zombie holds one PID. Linux has a PID limit (default 32768, check /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max). Thousands of zombies can exhaust PIDs, preventing any new process from starting — a full system outage. Monitor zombie count in production.

questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread — how does Linux manage them?
questions.text: In Linux, threads and processes are both represented as "tasks" and created with clone(). The difference is what they share. ps -eLf | grep <pid> # show all threads of a process (LWP = Light Weight Process) cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep Threads # thread count for a process ls /proc/<pid>/task/ # each subdirectory = one thread pstree -p <pid> # show process tree with PIDs Process: separate address space, file descriptors, signal handlers. Thread: shares address space, heap, file descriptors with siblings — has its own stack and registers. fork() creates a new process (copy-on-write). clone() with CLONE_VM|CLONE_FILES creates a thread. In Linux, the scheduler sees threads and processes equally — both are schedulable tasks. This matters when diagnosing CPU usage: a Java app with 200 threads can show 200 entries in /proc/<pid>/task. Practical use: When a Java or Go application is using unexpected CPU, use top -H -p <pid> to see per-thread CPU usage. This pinpoints which specific thread (and thus which goroutine or Java thread) is spinning.

questions.q: How does process scheduling work in Linux — what is load average and when is it a problem?
questions.text: uptime # load average: 1min 5min 15min cat /proc/loadavg # same, plus running/total tasks and last PID nproc # number of CPU cores sar -u 1 5 # CPU utilization over 5 samples vmstat 1 5 # r column = runnable processes (key metric) Load average = average number of tasks in runnable OR uninterruptible sleep (D state, waiting for I/O) state. It is NOT CPU percentage. A load of 1.0 on a 4-core system means 25% utilization — fine. A load of 8.0 on a 4-core system means the queue is 2× overloaded. Rule of thumb: load / nproc > 1.0 for sustained periods = investigate. High load with low CPU% = I/O bound (disk or network). High load with high CPU% = CPU bound. Check vmstat's 'r' (runnable) and 'b' (blocked on I/O) columns to distinguish. D-state processes: Processes in D (uninterruptible sleep) are waiting for I/O and cannot be killed. They inflate load average significantly. ps aux | awk '$8=="D"' lists D-state processes. High D-state count with high load and low CPU = storage I/O bottleneck.

questions.q: What are Linux signals — which ones matter most for DevOps/Platform engineers?
questions.text: kill -l # list all signals SIGHUP (1) — reload config (nginx, sshd respond to this) SIGINT (2) — Ctrl+C (interrupt from terminal) SIGTERM (15) — graceful shutdown request (catchable) SIGKILL (9) — force kill (cannot be caught or ignored) SIGSTOP (19) — pause process (cannot be caught, Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP) SIGCHLD (17) — child process changed state (parent notified) SIGUSR1/2 — user-defined (apps use for log rotation, graceful reload) SIGHUP is commonly used to reload configuration without restart — nginx, sshd, and many daemons reload their config on SIGHUP. SIGUSR1 is used by nginx for log rotation (reopens log files after they've been moved). In containers: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM when terminating a pod, then SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Make sure your application handles SIGTERM to drain connections gracefully — otherwise you get 502 errors during deployments. Kubernetes graceful shutdown: When a pod is deleted, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to PID 1 inside the container. If your app is not PID 1 (it's a child of a shell script), it may never receive SIGTERM. Use exec form in Dockerfile (ENTRYPOINT ["app"]) not shell form (ENTRYPOINT app) so your app is PID 1.

questions.q: What is /proc filesystem — what useful information can you extract from it?
questions.text: cat /proc/cpuinfo # CPU model, cores, flags cat /proc/meminfo # memory breakdown: MemTotal, MemFree, Cached, Buffers cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline # full command line of a process (null-separated) cat /proc/<pid>/environ # environment variables of a running process cat /proc/<pid>/fd/ | ls -la # open file descriptors cat /proc/<pid>/net/tcp # TCP connections for a process's namespace cat /proc/<pid>/limits # ulimits for the process cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness # kernel tunable cat /proc/net/dev # network interface statistics /proc is a virtual filesystem exposing kernel data structures as files. Everything is readable as text. Key use cases: inspect a running process's open files and connections without any external tool, read kernel tunables (all /proc/sys/ entries are tunable via sysctl), and debug networking issues per-namespace. In containers, /proc/1/environ reveals environment variables of PID 1 — useful for debugging misconfigured containers. Security note: /proc/<pid>/environ may expose secrets passed as env vars to processes. Ensure container runtimes and OS permissions restrict cross-process /proc access. This is why Kubernetes recommends using mounted Secrets files instead of env vars for sensitive values.

questions.q: Filesystem is full but du shows available space — how do you find and recover the space?
questions.text: This classic problem occurs when a file is deleted but a process still has it open — the inode is not freed until the file handle is closed. df -h # shows filesystem usage (may show 100% full) du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20 # find largest directories du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head -10 # common culprit # Find deleted-but-open files (holding space): lsof +L1 # list files with link count 0 (deleted but open) lsof | grep deleted # same, different filter # Recover without restart: truncate the file via its fd: truncate -s 0 /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd-number> The truncate trick is invaluable in production — it empties the file in-place without closing it, immediately freeing disk space without restarting the process holding it open. Common culprits: log files being written to after logrotate moved them, application keeping a large temp file open, or a core dump file being written by a crashing process. Inode exhaustion: df -h shows space available but writes fail with "No space left on device". Check inodes: df -i . Inode exhaustion happens when millions of tiny files are created (email queues, session files, package manager caches). Fix: delete many small files or reformat with larger inode ratio.

questions.q: What are hard links vs soft links — when does the distinction matter?
questions.text: ln /etc/hosts /tmp/hosts_hard # hard link (same inode) ln -s /etc/hosts /tmp/hosts_soft # soft link (symlink, new inode) ls -li /etc/hosts /tmp/hosts_hard # same inode number = hard link ls -la /tmp/hosts_soft # shows -> /etc/hosts stat /etc/hosts # see link count (nlink) Hard link: another directory entry pointing to the same inode. The file is not deleted until ALL hard links are removed AND no process has it open. Hard links cannot span filesystems. Soft link: a special file containing a path to the target. If the target is deleted, the symlink dangles. Symlinks can span filesystems and can point to directories. Practical distinction: logrotate uses hard links when rotating logs to ensure no log entries are lost. Container image layers use hard links to share files between layers without duplication. Finding dangling symlinks: find /etc -type l ! -exec test -e {} ; -print — finds symlinks whose targets don't exist. Dangling symlinks from removed packages are common and harmless but can confuse diagnostics.

questions.q: How do Linux file permissions work — explain chmod, chown, SUID, SGID, and sticky bit?
questions.text: ls -la /etc/passwd # -rw-r--r-- root root chmod 755 script.sh # rwxr-xr-x (octal) chmod u+x,g-w,o-rwx file # symbolic notation chown user:group file # change owner and group chmod u+s /usr/bin/sudo # set SUID bit (runs as file owner) chmod g+s /shared/dir # set SGID on dir (new files inherit group) chmod +t /tmp # sticky bit (only owner can delete their files) find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null # find all SUID files Permission bits: 3 sets of rwx for owner/group/other. Octal: 4=read, 2=write, 1=execute. SUID on executables: runs with file owner's privileges (passwd, sudo use this). SGID on directories: new files inherit the directory's group — used for shared project directories. Sticky bit on directories: users can only delete their own files (used on /tmp to prevent users deleting each other's temp files). SUID security risk: SUID binaries run with elevated privileges — a vulnerability in a SUID binary is a privilege escalation vector. Audit with find / -perm /4000 and investigate unexpected SUID files. This is a standard security hardening step and CKS exam topic.

questions.q: What is the Linux Virtual Filesystem (VFS) — why does everything in Linux appear as a file?
questions.text: ls /proc # process info as files ls /sys/class/net # network interfaces as files ls /dev # hardware devices as files cat /dev/urandom | head -c 10 | od -An -tu1 # read from random device echo "data" > /dev/tcp/example.com/80 # write to network socket as file (bash) mount | head -10 # see all mounted filesystems including virtual ones The VFS (Virtual File System) is an abstraction layer in the kernel that provides a uniform interface (open, read, write, close) for all I/O — whether talking to disk, a device, a network socket, or kernel data structures. "Everything is a file" means you can use standard Unix tools on all of these. tmpfs is a RAM-backed filesystem (used by /run, /tmp). cgroups and namespaces are exposed via /sys/fs/cgroup and /proc/<pid>/ns — this is how container runtimes manage container isolation. Container relevance: Kubernetes uses /proc and /sys to inspect container processes. The kubelet reads cgroup memory limits from /sys/fs/cgroup. Understanding VFS helps debug "why does my container think it has 128GB RAM" (it's reading from /proc/meminfo which shows host memory, not container limits).

questions.q: How do you find large files, find files modified recently, and find files by type across a filesystem?
questions.text: # Large files: find / -type f -size +100M 2>/dev/null | sort -k5 -rn find /var -type f -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} ; # Recently modified (last 60 minutes): find /etc -type f -mmin -60 2>/dev/null find / -newer /tmp/reference_file 2>/dev/null # modified after reference file # By type: find / -type f -name "*.log" -mtime +30 -delete # delete logs older than 30 days find /proc -type l -name "exe" -exec ls -la {} ; 2>/dev/null # running binaries # By permission: find /etc -perm /o+w 2>/dev/null # world-writable files (security audit) find is the Swiss Army knife of filesystem queries. Key options: -type (f=file, d=dir, l=symlink), -size (+/-N[ckMG]), -mtime/-mmin (modified N days/minutes ago), -perm, -user, -group. Combine with -exec to act on results. Use 2>/dev/null to suppress permission errors. For disk cleanup automation, combine find with -delete or pipe to xargs rm. locate vs find: locate filename searches a pre-built database (fast but stale). find walks the filesystem in real time (slower but current). Use locate for quick lookups, find for scripts and when recency matters. Update locate db with updatedb .

questions.q: What is LVM (Logical Volume Manager) — how do you extend a filesystem online?
questions.text: pvdisplay # physical volumes vgdisplay # volume groups lvdisplay # logical volumes # Extend an LV and resize filesystem online: lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/lv_data # extend LV by 10GB resize2fs /dev/vg0/lv_data # resize ext4 filesystem (online) xfs_growfs /mount/point # resize XFS (must use mount point) # Add a new disk to an existing VG: pvcreate /dev/sdb # initialize new disk as PV vgextend vg0 /dev/sdb # add PV to VG lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/vg0/lv_data # use all new free space LVM adds a virtualization layer between physical disks and filesystems: Physical Volumes (disks) → Volume Groups (pools) → Logical Volumes (virtual disks). Benefits: online resize, snapshots (for consistent backups), striping across disks. Ext4 supports online grow (resize2fs on mounted filesystem). XFS supports online grow but NOT shrink. Neither supports online shrink — unmount first. Cloud disk resize workflow: In GCP/AWS, resize the persistent disk in the console/CLI → resize the partition (if needed, using growpart or parted) → resize the LV (if LVM) → resize the filesystem. All steps can be done on a running system for ext4 and XFS.

questions.q: How do you diagnose network connectivity issues on Linux — what is your systematic approach?
questions.text: # Layer by layer approach: ip link show # L2: interfaces up? carrier detected? ip addr show # L3: IP addresses assigned? ip route show # L3: default route exists? ping -c 4 8.8.8.8 # L3: can reach internet? ping -c 4 <gateway-ip> # L3: can reach gateway? traceroute -T -p 443 <host> # L3: where does routing break? nc -zv <host> <port> # L4: is the port open? curl -v https://<host> # L7: does the app respond? ss -tlnp # what is listening on which port? iptables -L -n -v # any firewall rules blocking? Work bottom-up: physical link → IP config → routing → port reachability → application. Each layer narrows the problem. If ping works but nc fails: the network path is fine but the service isn't listening or is firewalled. If ping fails but the gateway pings: routing issue. If the gateway doesn't ping: either IP misconfigured or L2/L1 issue. ss vs netstat: ss is the modern replacement for netstat — faster (reads from kernel directly), more features. Learn ss: ss -tlnp (TCP listen), ss -tnp state established (active connections), ss -s (summary stats).

questions.q: How do iptables work — how do you debug and write firewall rules?
questions.text: iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers # list all rules with packet counts iptables -t nat -L -n -v # NAT table rules (DNAT, SNAT) iptables -t mangle -L -n # mangle table (QoS, TTL) # Allow incoming SSH: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT # Block specific IP: iptables -I INPUT 1 -s 1.2.3.4 -j DROP # Log dropped packets (for debugging): iptables -A INPUT -j LOG --log-prefix "DROPPED: " --log-level 4 iptables -A INPUT -j DROP # Save rules (Debian/Ubuntu): iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4 iptables processes packets through chains (INPUT, OUTPUT, FORWARD) in tables (filter, nat, mangle). Rules are processed in order — first match wins. Default chains have a policy (ACCEPT or DROP). Kubernetes uses iptables extensively: kube-proxy writes DNAT rules for every Service (ClusterIP → pod IPs), and NetworkPolicies generate iptables rules per pod. Understanding iptables is essential for debugging why a Kubernetes service isn't reachable. iptables vs nftables: Modern Linux (RHEL 8+, Debian 11+) uses nftables as the backend. iptables commands still work via iptables-nft compatibility layer. Kubernetes is migrating kube-proxy to nftables mode. Know both exist; iptables syntax still dominates CKA/CKS exams.

questions.q: How do you capture and analyze network traffic on Linux?
questions.text: tcpdump -i eth0 -n port 80 # capture HTTP on eth0 tcpdump -i any host 10.0.0.5 # all traffic to/from IP tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/cap.pcap # write to file for Wireshark tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' # capture RST packets tcpdump -i any port 53 -n # DNS queries # tshark (Wireshark CLI): tshark -i eth0 -f "port 443" -T fields -e http.request.uri # extract URIs # ss with detailed TCP info: ss -tin dst 10.0.0.5 # TCP internals: rtt, cwnd, retransmits tcpdump is the primary packet capture tool. Filters use Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax: host, port, proto, src/dst, and/or/not. Key patterns: capture DNS (port 53) to debug resolver issues, capture RST packets to find rejected connections, capture SYN packets to see connection attempts. Always write to file (-w) for complex analysis in Wireshark. In Kubernetes, use kubectl-sniff or a debug container in the pod's network namespace to capture from a running pod. Bandwidth measurement: iperf3 -s on server, iperf3 -c <server> on client. Use nload or iftop for real-time bandwidth monitoring per interface. nethogs shows bandwidth per process — invaluable for finding which process is saturating the network.

questions.q: How do you configure static IP, routes, and DNS on a Linux server?
questions.text: # Modern (systemd-networkd / netplan on Ubuntu 18+): cat /etc/netplan/01-netcfg.yaml netplan apply # apply config changes # Legacy (ifcfg files on RHEL/CentOS): cat /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0 # Runtime changes (not persistent): ip addr add 10.0.0.100/24 dev eth0 ip route add default via 10.0.0.1 ip route add 192.168.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.254 # DNS: cat /etc/resolv.conf # current nameservers resolvectl status # systemd-resolved status resolvectl dns eth0 8.8.8.8 # set DNS for interface Network configuration has fragmented across tools: legacy ifupdown (/etc/network/interfaces), RHEL's NetworkManager (/etc/sysconfig), and modern systemd-networkd with Netplan (Ubuntu). Cloud instances typically use DHCP with cloud-init setting initial config. Changes to /etc/resolv.conf may be overwritten by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager — edit the source config, not resolv.conf directly. Cloud metadata routes: Cloud VMs have a link-local route to 169.254.169.254 (metadata server). Never remove this route — it's used by the guest agent, credential fetching, and Workload Identity. Check with ip route show | grep 169.254 .

questions.q: What is /etc/hosts and /etc/nsswitch.conf — how does DNS resolution order work?
questions.text: cat /etc/nsswitch.conf | grep hosts # resolution order # Typical: hosts: files dns (check /etc/hosts first, then DNS) cat /etc/hosts # static hostname → IP mappings getent hosts example.com # test resolution using NSS (respects nsswitch) strace -e trace=network getent hosts example.com # trace exactly what happens # Override DNS for testing (add to /etc/hosts): echo "1.2.3.4 staging.example.com" >> /etc/hosts nsswitch.conf controls resolution order for hosts, users, groups, and more. "files dns" means: check /etc/hosts first, then query nameservers in /etc/resolv.conf. "dns files" reverses this. In containers: /etc/hosts is writable by the container runtime (Kubernetes adds pod IPs to /etc/hosts). The ndots option in /etc/resolv.conf controls how many dots a hostname needs before it's treated as fully qualified — critical for Kubernetes DNS performance. getent vs nslookup: nslookup and dig bypass nsswitch and query DNS directly. getent hosts uses the full NSS stack including /etc/hosts. Use getent when you want to test exactly what the application sees. Use dig when you want to test DNS specifically.

questions.q: How do you diagnose high CPU usage on a Linux server?
questions.text: top # real-time CPU per process top -1 # show per-CPU breakdown (press 1 in top) mpstat -P ALL 1 5 # per-CPU utilization: usr, sys, iowait, si (softirq) sar -u 1 5 # CPU utilization history ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%cpu,%mem --sort=-%cpu | head -15 # Find which CPU is hot (for IRQ affinity issues): cat /proc/interrupts | sort -k2 -rn | head -10 # Profile what the CPU is actually doing: perf top # live kernel/userspace profiling (needs perf pkg) perf record -g -p <pid> sleep 10 && perf report # flame graph data CPU breakdown: us (user), sy (system/kernel), ni (niced), id (idle), wa (I/O wait), hi (hardware IRQ), si (software IRQ), st (stolen by hypervisor). High sy = kernel-intensive work (syscall-heavy, iptables rules, context switching). High si = network interrupt processing (high-traffic network interface). High wa = I/O bound. High us = application CPU. Use perf for deep profiling — it shows exactly which function the CPU spends time in. Stolen CPU (st): In VMs, high %st means the hypervisor is not scheduling your VM's vCPUs promptly — the physical host is overcommitted. No application-level fix; escalate to the cloud provider or move to a dedicated host. On GCP/AWS, st > 5% consistently signals a noisy-neighbor problem.

questions.q: How do you diagnose memory issues — OOM killer, swap usage, and memory leaks?
questions.text: free -h # overview: total, used, free, buff/cache, available cat /proc/meminfo # detailed breakdown vmstat -s # memory stats summary # OOM killer events: dmesg | grep -i "oom|killed process|out of memory" journalctl -k | grep -i oom # systemd journal kernel messages # Per-process memory: cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep -E "VmRSS|VmSwap|VmPeak" smem -r -k | head -15 # accurate memory accounting per process # Swap: swapon --show # swap devices and usage cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness # 60=default, 1=avoid swap, 100=aggressive swap Available memory (not Free) is what matters — Linux uses RAM for cache aggressively. Available = free + reclaimable cache. A system with 500MB free but 20GB available is healthy. OOM killer: when available memory is exhausted, the kernel scores processes by OOM score (larger RSS and lower priority = higher score) and kills the highest scorer. Check dmesg for "Killed process" to identify OOM victims. Kubernetes OOM: A container that hits its memory limit gets OOM-killed (Exit Code 137). The kernel's OOM killer operates inside the container's cgroup. Set memory limits accurately — too low causes constant OOMKills, too high allows memory leaks to grow unchecked. Always set both requests and limits for memory in production pods.

questions.q: How do you diagnose I/O performance issues — high disk latency or throughput problems?
questions.text: iostat -xz 1 5 # per-disk: r/w IOPS, throughput, await, util% iotop -o # per-process I/O (like top but for disk) iotop -bod 1 # batch mode for logging pidstat -d 1 5 # per-process disk I/O stats # Key iostat columns: await = average I/O wait time (ms). > 20ms SSD / > 100ms HDD = problem util% = disk utilization. > 80% = saturated r_await = read latency, w_await = write latency # Check for I/O scheduler: cat /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler # current I/O scheduler # Benchmark disk: fio --name=randread --rw=randread --bs=4k --size=1G --runtime=30 --iodepth=32 iostat await is the most important metric — it measures how long I/O requests wait in the device queue plus actual I/O time. High await with low util% = high queue depth or device latency. High util% = device saturated. Use iotop to identify which process is causing I/O. For cloud VMs: disk IOPS and throughput are limited by the disk type and VM type — check GCP/AWS console for throttling metrics. Page cache tuning: Linux caches disk reads/writes in RAM. vm.dirty_ratio (default 20%) = max RAM used for dirty (unwritten) pages before sync. High dirty_ratio delays writes but improves throughput. Lower it for databases that need durable writes. vm.dirty_background_ratio = when background writeback starts.

questions.q: What are the key sysctl parameters every Platform Engineer should know?
questions.text: sysctl -a | grep <param> # view current value sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 # set temporarily echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" >> /etc/sysctl.conf # persist sysctl -p # reload /etc/sysctl.conf # Networking: net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 # enable IP routing (required for K8s) net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1 # iptables sees bridged traffic (K8s CNI) net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 # reuse TIME_WAIT sockets net.core.somaxconn = 65535 # max listen backlog (for high-conn services) net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 65535 # SYN queue size net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 1024 65535 # ephemeral port range # Memory: vm.swappiness = 1 # minimize swap (for DB servers) vm.overcommit_memory = 1 # allow overcommit (Redis requirement) vm.max_map_count = 262144 # max mmap regions (Elasticsearch) # File descriptors: fs.file-max = 2097152 # system-wide fd limit fs.inotify.max_user_watches = 524288 # for IDE/file watchers (K8s needs this) These parameters are the standard tuning set for production Kubernetes nodes. net.ipv4.ip_forward and bridge-nf-call-iptables are required for pod networking. inotify limits are hit by development tools and Kubernetes controllers watching many files. Redis requires vm.overcommit_memory=1 to avoid background save failures. Elasticsearch requires vm.max_map_count=262144 for memory-mapped index files. Kubernetes node requirements: kubeadm preflight checks validate several of these sysctl values. Failing preflight on a new node is almost always a missing sysctl setting. Kee

questions.q: How do you use strace and lsof to debug a misbehaving application?
questions.text: # strace: trace system calls made by a process strace -p <pid> # attach to running process strace -p <pid> -e trace=network # only network syscalls strace -p <pid> -e trace=file # only file syscalls strace -c -p <pid> sleep 10 # count syscalls over 10s (summary) strace -T -p <pid> 2>&1 | grep -v "0.0000" # show slow syscalls only # lsof: list open files and connections lsof -p <pid> # all open files for process lsof -i :8080 # what process is using port 8080 lsof -u www-data # all files opened by user lsof -i TCP -s TCP:ESTABLISHED # all established TCP connections lsof +D /var/log # all processes with files open in /var/log strace reveals exactly what a process is doing at the kernel level — which files it's opening, which sockets it's connecting to, what errors it's getting. Use -T to show time spent per syscall (find slow operations). Use -e trace=network to focus on network activity. lsof answers "what has this port/file/directory open?" — essential for finding port conflicts and leaked file descriptors. strace overhead: strace adds significant overhead (2-10x slowdown) — it intercepts every syscall. Use it for debugging, not production monitoring. For production-safe tracing, use bpftrace or perf with eBPF probes.

questions.q: How do you audit and harden SSH configuration on a Linux server?
questions.text: cat /etc/ssh/sshd_config # current config # Key hardening settings: PermitRootLogin no # never allow direct root SSH PasswordAuthentication no # keys only (no password brute force) PubkeyAuthentication yes AllowUsers deployer admin # whitelist specific users Port 22 # consider non-standard port (obscurity only) MaxAuthTries 3 ClientAliveInterval 300 # disconnect idle sessions after 5 min X11Forwarding no UseDNS no # skip DNS lookup (faster login) systemctl reload sshd # apply config changes # Audit login attempts: journalctl -u sshd | grep "Failed|Accepted" | tail -20 lastb | head -20 # failed login attempts last | head -20 # successful logins Disable password authentication immediately on any internet-facing server — this eliminates 99% of brute-force attacks. Use key-based authentication exclusively. AllowUsers creates an explicit whitelist — accounts not listed cannot SSH even with valid keys. Consider fail2ban for automatic IP banning after repeated failures. For cloud environments, prefer IAP (Identity-Aware Proxy) or Systems Manager Session Manager over direct SSH — no need to expose port 22 at all. GCP OS Login: OS Login ties SSH access to GCP IAM identity — add roles/compute.osLogin to a user's IAM policy instead of managing authorized_keys files. Login events appear in Cloud Audit Logs. No SSH key management required. Enable org-wide with Organization Policy.

questions.q: What are Linux capabilities — how do they reduce attack surface compared to running as root?
questions.text: capsh --print # current process capabilities cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep Cap # hex-encoded capability sets capsh --decode=0000000000003000 # decode capability hex getcap /usr/bin/ping # view capabilities on a binary setcap cap_net_bind_service+ep /usr/bin/node # bind ports <1024 without root # In containers (K8s securityContext): securityContext: capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] Linux capabilities split root privileges into ~40 distinct units. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE: bind ports below 1024. CAP_SYS_PTRACE: trace/debug processes. CAP_NET_ADMIN: configure network interfaces, iptables. CAP_SYS_ADMIN: almost everything (avoid). Running as root grants all capabilities. Running as non-root with specific capabilities is far safer — compromise of the process gives only those specific privileges. In Kubernetes, drop ALL capabilities and add back only what's needed — this is the "restricted" Pod Security Standard requirement. Interview depth: Explaining capabilities vs root shows security maturity. A common follow-up is "how does a container escape work?" — many escapes rely on containers having CAP_SYS_ADMIN or running as root with --privileged. Dropping capabilities and running as non-root eliminates most container escape vectors.

questions.q: How do you use auditd to track file access and command execution on a Linux system?
questions.text: systemctl status auditd # auditd running? # Add audit rules: auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes # watch file for writes/attribs auditctl -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers_changes auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k command_exec # log all commands auditctl -l # list current rules # Query audit log: ausearch -k passwd_changes # search by key ausearch -ua 1000 # all events for UID 1000 aureport --summary # summary report aureport -x --summary # executable summary cat /var/log/audit/audit.log | grep execve # raw log auditd provides kernel-level audit logging — it captures syscall events with full context (who, what, when, from which process). Rules watch files (-w) or syscalls (-a). The -k flag tags rules with a searchable key. Use for compliance requirements (PCI-DSS, CIS benchmarks), incident forensics, and detecting privilege escalation attempts. Export logs to SIEM (Splunk, Chronicle) for long-term retention and alerting. Performance impact: Auditing every execve syscall generates enormous log volume on busy servers. Be selective: watch sensitive files (/etc/passwd, /etc/sudoers, /etc/ssh/) and specific directories rather than logging every command system-wide. Use rate limiting with -F to reduce noise.

questions.q: What is SELinux / AppArmor — how do mandatory access controls work?
questions.text: # SELinux (RHEL/CentOS): getenforce # Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled sestatus # detailed SELinux status setenforce 0 # set Permissive (for testing, NOT production) ausearch -m avc -ts recent # SELinux denial messages sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log # human-readable denial explanations restorecon -Rv /var/www/html # fix file context after copy # AppArmor (Ubuntu/Debian): aa-status # profile status aa-complain /usr/sbin/nginx # put nginx profile in complain mode aa-enforce /usr/sbin/nginx # enforce nginx profile journalctl | grep apparmor # AppArmor denials DAC (Discretionary Access Control) = traditional Unix permissions — file owner controls access. MAC (Mandatory Access Control) = kernel enforces policies that override file permissions. SELinux labels every file, process, and port with a security context — access is only allowed when the policy explicitly permits it. A web server process confined by SELinux cannot read /etc/shadow even if the file permissions allow it. In containers: seccomp and AppArmor profiles restrict syscalls and filesystem access — GKE's default runtime/default seccomp profile blocks ~100 risky syscalls. Never permanently disable SELinux. "setenforce 0" is a debug step, not a fix. If SELinux is blocking a legitimate operation, generate the correct policy addition with audit2allow. Disabling SELinux on a RHEL production server is a security failure and a compliance violation.

questions.q: How do you manage disks and partitions on Linux — MBR vs GPT?
questions.text: lsblk # block devices tree view fdisk -l # list all disks and partitions blkid # show UUID and filesystem type per partition # Create partition (GPT, modern): gdisk /dev/sdb # GPT partition tool parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 0% 100% # Format: mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1 # create ext4 filesystem mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1 # create XFS filesystem # Mount persistently: echo "UUID=xxxx /data ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2" >> /etc/fstab mount -a # test fstab without reboot MBR (Master Boot Record): max 4 primary partitions, max 2TB disk. GPT (GUID Partition Table): 128 partitions, up to 9.4 ZB. Use GPT for all new disks. Always use UUID in /etc/fstab instead of device names (/dev/sdb) — device names can change on reboot, UUIDs are stable. The nofail mount option prevents boot failure if the disk is missing (important for data disks that may not always be attached). Cloud disk attach workflow: Attach disk in GCP/AWS console → lsblk to see new device → mkfs if new disk → blkid to get UUID → add to /etc/fstab with nofail → mount -a to verify. This is a daily operation for platform engineers managing data volumes.

questions.q: What is RAID — what levels matter and when do you use software RAID in production?
questions.text: # Software RAID with mdadm: mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sdb /dev/sdc # RAID 1 cat /proc/mdstat # RAID status mdadm --detail /dev/md0 # detailed array status mdadm --manage /dev/md0 --add /dev/sdd # add spare/replace failed disk # Common RAID levels: RAID 0: striping — max performance/capacity, zero redundancy (any disk failure = data loss) RAID 1: mirroring — 2 disks, full redundancy, 50% capacity RAID 5: striping + parity — 3+ disks, 1 disk fault tolerance, (n-1) capacity RAID 6: striping + 2 parity — 2 disk fault tolerance RAID 10: RAID 1+0 — mirrored stripes, best performance + redundancy, 50% capacity In cloud environments, RAID is largely replaced by cloud storage redundancy (GCP Persistent Disks, AWS EBS have built-in replication). Use software RAID on bare metal or when you need: local NVMe RAID 0 for extreme IOPS (databases, scratch storage), or RAID 10 for bare-metal database servers. RAID is not a backup — it protects against disk failure, not data corruption or accidental deletion. RAID 5 rebuild risk: During rebuild after a disk failure, the remaining disks are under stress. A second failure during rebuild (common for old drives from the same batch) causes total data loss. RAID 6 or RAID 10 is safer for production. Many DBAs prefer RAID 10 over RAID 5 for write-heavy databases.

questions.q: How do you diagnose and fix filesystem corruption on Linux?
questions.text: dmesg | grep -i "error|corrupt|EXT4-fs|XFS" # kernel filesystem errors journalctl -k | grep -i "filesystem|ext4|xfs" # journal filesystem messages # Check and repair ext4 (must be unmounted): umount /dev/sdb1 # unmount first fsck -y /dev/sdb1 # check and auto-fix ext4 e2fsck -f -y /dev/sdb1 # more thorough ext4 check # XFS repair (must be unmounted): xfs_check /dev/sdb1 # check (read-only) xfs_repair /dev/sdb1 # repair XFS # Remount read-only if filesystem errors detected: mount -o remount,ro /data # prevent further corruption Filesystem corruption causes: improper shutdown (power loss during writes), hardware failure (failing disk, bad RAM causing bit flips), kernel bugs, or full filesystem (writes failing partially). When the kernel detects errors, it remounts the filesystem read-only to prevent further damage. Fix: fsck/xfs_repair on unmounted filesystem. For production systems: always have journaling enabled (ext4 journal, XFS journal) to minimize corruption on unclean shutdown. Root filesystem fsck: You can't unmount the root filesystem while the system is running. Boot into rescue/single-user mode, or use a live CD, to run fsck on the root partition. Modern Linux runs fsck automatically on boot if the filesystem was not cleanly unmounted.

questions.q: Explain the Linux boot process — from power-on to login prompt.
questions.text: 1. BIOS/UEFI — hardware init, finds bootable disk 2. Bootloader (GRUB2) — loads kernel + initramfs from /boot 3. Kernel init — decompresses, initializes hardware, mounts initramfs 4. initramfs — temporary root FS with drivers to mount real root FS 5. Kernel mounts real root filesystem (from /etc/fstab or kernel cmdline) 6. systemd (PID 1) starts — reads /etc/systemd/system/default.target 7. systemd activates services in dependency order 8. getty (login prompt) or display manager starts # Debug boot: journalctl -b # all logs from current boot journalctl -b -1 # logs from previous boot (useful after crash) systemd-analyze # total boot time systemd-analyze blame # time per service (find slow boot services) systemd-analyze critical-chain # critical path of boot GRUB2 is the bootloader on most modern Linux. It reads /boot/grub/grub.cfg, loads the kernel image and initrd. The kernel cmdline (visible in /proc/cmdline) can pass parameters: root= (root device), quiet (suppress messages), ro (mount root read-only initially). systemd replaces sysvinit — it parallelizes service startup and tracks dependencies. Containers skip all of this — the kernel is provided by the host, the container runtime starts PID 1 directly. Rescue mode: If systemd fails to start (corrupted unit file, bad fstab), boot with systemd.unit=rescue.target on the kernel cmdline in GRUB. Or append init=/bin/bash for a root shell before systemd starts. These rescue techniques are tested in CKA.

questions.q: How do you manage services with systemd — what are the key commands and unit file structure?
questions.text: systemctl status nginx # service status + recent logs systemctl start/stop/restart nginx systemctl enable nginx # start on boot (creates symlink in wants/) systemctl disable nginx # remove from boot systemctl daemon-reload # reload unit files after editing systemctl list-units --type=service --state=failed journalctl -u nginx -f # follow nginx service logs journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" # Create a custom service unit: cat /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service [Unit] Description=My Application After=network.target [Service] Type=simple User=myapp ExecStart=/usr/bin/myapp --config /etc/myapp/config.yaml Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Unit files define services, timers, sockets, and mounts. The [Service] section key settings: Type (simple, forking, notify, oneshot), ExecStart/ExecStop/ExecReload, Restart (always/on-failure/on-abnormal), User/Group for privilege dropping, Environment/EnvironmentFile for config. After=network.target ensures networking is up before the service starts. systemd replaces both /etc/init.d scripts and cron (use .timer units instead of cron for systemd-managed services). Restart policies: Restart=on-failure restarts only on non-zero exit code. Restart=always restarts even on clean exit (good for long-running services). RestartSec=5 adds a delay to prevent rapid restart loops from hammering the system. Combine with StartLimitIntervalSec and StartLimitBurst to limit restart frequency.

questions.q: A server is not booting — how do you diagnose and recover from boot failures?
questions.text: # From GRUB: edit kernel cmdline (press 'e' on GRUB entry) Append: systemd.unit=rescue.target # boot to rescue shell Append: init=/bin/bash # bypass systemd entirely Remove: quiet splash # see all boot messages # In rescue shell: mount -o remount,rw / # remount root read-write journalctl -b -p err # errors from this boot systemctl list-units --failed # which units failed fsck /dev/sda1 # check root filesystem cat /etc/fstab # check for bad entries # For cloud VMs — rescue disk approach: # Snapshot the boot disk → detach → attach to rescue VM → mount → fix → reattach Common boot failures: bad /etc/fstab entry (missing nofail on non-critical disk causes boot hang), corrupted filesystem (fsck needed), failed systemd service in required boot chain (disable or fix the unit), kernel panic (bad kernel module — boot old kernel from GRUB), or full root filesystem (can't write to disk). For cloud VMs: use serial console access (GCP Serial Console, AWS EC2 Serial Console) to see boot messages without needing SSH. fstab mistakes: A typo in /etc/fstab is one of the most common ways to break a server. Always test with mount -a before rebooting. Use nofail for non-root filesystems so a missing disk doesn't halt boot. Never reboot after editing fstab without testing.

questions.q: How do you manage users, groups, and sudo on a Linux system?
questions.text: useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G sudo deployer # create user with home dir and sudo usermod -aG docker,sudo existing_user # add to groups (-a = append) passwd deployer # set password userdel -r olduser # delete user + home dir id username # show UID, GID, groups groups username # list groups cat /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1 # list all users # sudo configuration: visudo # edit /etc/sudoers safely deployer ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl # passwordless specific command %ops ALL=(ALL) ALL # all users in ops group get full sudo cat /etc/sudoers.d/deployer # per-user sudo config in drop-in dir Always use visudo to edit sudoers — it validates syntax before saving, preventing lockout from a syntax error. Use /etc/sudoers.d/ for per-user/group configs instead of editing the main sudoers file. NOPASSWD should be limited to specific commands, never ALL, to minimize risk. For cloud environments: prefer IAM-based access (OS Login for GCP) over managing local users — it scales and audits better. Group membership: Users must log out and back in after group changes for new groups to take effect (the login shell reads group membership at session start). Or use newgrp docker to start a new shell with the updated group without logging out.

questions.q: What is PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) — how does it control login?
questions.text: cat /etc/pam.d/sshd # PAM config for SSH login cat /etc/pam.d/sudo # PAM config for sudo cat /etc/pam.d/common-auth # included by most PAM configs # PAM module types: auth — verify identity (password, LDAP, 2FA, SSH key) account — check account restrictions (expiry, time of day, lockout) session — setup/teardown session (mount home, set env, log) password — manage password changes # Control flags: required — must pass, failure continues chain (reveals all errors at end) requisite — must pass, failure stops chain immediately sufficient — if passes, stop chain (success without later checks) optional — result ignored PAM is the Linux authentication framework — it makes authentication pluggable without recompiling applications. SSH, sudo, login, su all use PAM. Common modules: pam_unix (local passwords), pam_ldap (LDAP auth), pam_google_authenticator (TOTP 2FA), pam_limits (enforce ulimits on login), pam_faillock (account lockout after failed attempts). When an SSH login is slow, PAM modules (especially LDAP or DNS lookups) are often the cause. PAM misconfiguration: A syntax error or wrong module path in a PAM config file can make it impossible to log in via that method. Always test on a second open session before closing the current one. pam_tally2/pam_faillock can lock out all users including root — know how to unlock: faillock --user root --reset .

questions.q: How do you implement and audit access controls using ACLs (Access Control Lists)?
questions.text: getfacl /shared/project # view current ACLs setfacl -m u:alice:rwx /shared/project # give alice rwx setfacl -m g:devteam:rx /shared/project # give devteam r-x setfacl -m d:g:devteam:rx /shared/project # default ACL for new files setfacl -x u:alice /shared/project # remove alice's ACL setfacl -b /shared/project # remove all ACLs # Find files with ACLs: find / -acl 2>/dev/null # files with extended ACLs ls -la /shared/project # + sign after permissions = has ACL POSIX ACLs extend standard rwx permissions — you can grant specific users or groups access to files without changing the owning user/group or using SUID/SGID. Default ACLs on directories propagate to newly created files inside — critical for shared project directories where you want consistent permissions on all files. The + in ls -la output indicates ACLs are present. Filesystem must be mounted with acl option (ext4/XFS support ACLs natively, enabled by default in modern Linux). Practical use case: A shared /data/project directory owned by root:engineering. Engineers need write access, CI service account needs read-only. Without ACLs: you need complex group arrangements. With ACLs: setfacl -m u:ci-user:rx and u:alice:rwx solves it cleanly without touching group membership.

questions.q: What are essential bash scripting practices for production automation scripts?
questions.text: #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail # exit on error, undefined var, pipe failure set -x # trace (print each command before execution) # Trap for cleanup on exit: trap 'cleanup; echo "Script failed on line $LINENO"' ERR trap cleanup EXIT # Safe variable use: var="${1:-default_value}" # parameter with default [ -z "${VAR:-}" ] && echo "VAR is empty" # Avoid word splitting with quotes: file="my file.txt"; rm "$file" # quotes prevent word splitting # Lockfile to prevent concurrent runs: LOCKFILE=/tmp/myscript.lock exec 200>"$LOCKFILE"; flock -n 200 || { echo "Already running"; exit 1; } # Logging: log() { echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] $*" | tee -a /var/log/myscript.log; } set -euo pipefail is the most important line in any production bash script. -e: exit on command failure. -u: treat unset variables as errors (catches typos). -o pipefail: a pipe fails if any command in it fails (without this, false | echo "ok" succeeds). trap ERR catches failures and cleans up temp files, releases locks. Never write production scripts without these — a missing set -e means errors are silently ignored and the script continues in a broken state. set -e caveats: set -e has surprising behavior: it doesn't trigger inside if conditions ( if grep foo file; then ), function calls assigned to variables, or expressions after || and &&. Test scripts thoroughly and consider using explicit error checking for critical commands: cmd || { echo "cmd failed"; exit 1; } .

questions.q: How do you write efficient text processing pipelines with grep, awk, sed, and sort?
questions.text: # grep — search and filter: grep -r "ERROR" /var/log/ --include="*.log" -l # recursive, filenames only grep -E "ERROR|WARN" app.log | grep -v "expected" # exclude pattern grep -c "404" access.log # count matches grep -A3 -B1 "Exception" app.log # context lines # awk — columnar processing: awk '{print $1, $NF}' access.log # first and last field awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd # users with UID >= 1000 awk '{sum+=$NF} END {print "Total:", sum}' file # sum last column awk '/START/,/END/' logfile # print between patterns # sed — stream editing: sed -i 's/old_value/new_value/g' config.yaml # in-place replacement sed -n '10,20p' largefile # print lines 10-20 sed '/^#/d; /^$/d' config.yaml # remove comments + blank lines # sort + uniq — aggregation: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10 # top IPs The Unix pipeline philosophy: each tool does one thing, compose them. grep filters lines, awk processes columns, sed transforms text, sort orders, uniq counts. Mastering these four tools means you can process any log file, config file, or data stream without writing a Python script. The top-IPs pipeline is a classic — learn it and adapt it for any log analysis task. Performance tip: For large files, grep is faster than awk for pure pattern matching. Place the most selective filter first in a pipeline — filter early to reduce data flowing to later stages. For very large log files (>10GB), consider ripgrep (rg) which is significantly faster than GNU gre

questions.q: How do you schedule tasks with cron and systemd timers — what are the differences?
questions.text: # cron: crontab -e # edit current user's crontab crontab -l # list current user's crontab cat /etc/crontab # system crontab ls /etc/cron.d/ /etc/cron.daily/ # drop-in cron directories # Format: min hour dom month dow command */5 * * * * /usr/bin/check_disk.sh # every 5 minutes 0 2 * * 0 /usr/bin/weekly_backup.sh # Sunday at 2am @reboot /usr/bin/startup.sh # on reboot # systemd timer: cat /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer [Timer] OnCalendar=Sun *-*-* 02:00:00 Persistent=true # run if missed while system was off systemctl enable --now backup.timer systemctl list-timers --all # list all timers and next run time cron advantages: simple, universal, familiar. Disadvantages: no dependency management, no logging (output goes to email or /dev/null), no retry on failure, skips if system was off. systemd timer advantages: full journal logging, dependencies (OnActiveSec, After=network.target), Persistent=true to catch missed runs, easy to disable/enable without crontab editing, integrated with systemctl status. For new automation on systemd systems, prefer timers. Keep cron for simple one-liners and scripts deployed to mixed environments. Cron PATH: cron runs with a minimal environment — PATH is typically just /usr/bin:/bin. Scripts that work interactively fail in cron because commands aren't found. Always use absolute paths in cron scripts or set PATH explicitly at the top of the script.

questions.q: Server is responding slowly — walk through your systematic diagnosis approach.
questions.text: # Step 1: System-wide snapshot (60 seconds of data) uptime # load average trend vmstat 1 10 # CPU, memory, swap, I/O, processes iostat -xz 1 5 # disk I/O breakdown free -h # memory: available is the key metric ss -s # socket summary (connection counts) # Step 2: Find the bottleneck top -b -n 1 -o %CPU # CPU hogs top -b -n 1 -o %MEM # memory hogs iotop -b -n 1 -o # I/O hogs iftop # network bandwidth hogs # Step 3: Check for specific conditions dmesg | tail -20 # kernel errors (OOM, disk errors, etc.) journalctl -p err -n 50 # systemd error messages ps aux | awk '$8=="D"' | wc -l # D-state process count The USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) is the framework: for each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check utilization (how busy is it?), saturation (is there a queue?), and errors. A slow server is always one of these. vmstat's columns tell the story: r (runnable queue), b (blocked), wa (I/O wait), si/so (swap in/out). Swapping to disk is catastrophic for performance — si/so > 0 means memory is exhausted. USE method in 60 seconds: This is the Brendan Gregg "60-second Linux performance analysis" checklist. In an interview, recite this flow — uptime → dmesg → vmstat → mpstat → pidstat → iostat → free → sar → top. It demonstrates structured thinking, not random command firing.

questions.q: How do you investigate a server that was compromised — what do you look for?
questions.text: # Timeline reconstruction: last -F # login history with timestamps lastb -F # failed logins journalctl --since="2024-01-15" -p warning # journal from incident time ausearch -ts 01/15/2024 -te 01/16/2024 -m execve # audit log commands # Find recently modified files: find / -mtime -7 -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -v /proc | sort find /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm -type f # common malware drop locations # Check for persistence mechanisms: crontab -l; cat /etc/cron* systemctl list-units --type=service | grep -v "loaded active" cat /etc/rc.local; ls /etc/init.d/ # Running processes from unusual locations: ls -la /proc/*/exe 2>/dev/null | grep -v '/usr|/bin|/lib|/sbin' # Network connections: ss -tnp # all TCP connections with PIDs ss -tnp | grep -v "127.0.0.1|::1" # external connections Incident response order: (1) Isolate (remove from network if actively compromised), (2) Preserve evidence (snapshot disk image, copy logs), (3) Investigate (timeline, modified files, persistence mechanisms, network connections), (4) Remediate, (5) Harden. Look for: SUID binaries in unexpected locations, cron entries you don't recognize, services/processes from /tmp or /dev/shm, outbound connections to unusual IPs, and unauthorized SSH keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Don't trust the running system: An attacker may have replaced system binaries (ls, ps, netstat) with rootkitted versions that hide their presence. Boot from a live CD or trusted external media for forensic investigation. Use immutable audit logs s

questions.q: "No space left on device" error — but df shows space available. What are the possibilities?
questions.text: df -h # check disk space df -i # check inode usage (THIS is often the culprit) lsof +L1 # deleted files still held open ls -la /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep "(deleted)" # same via /proc # Inode exhaustion: find directory with most files find / -xdev -printf '%h ' 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10 # tmpfs size limit: df -h | grep tmpfs # /run, /dev/shm may be full # Kernel reserved space (5% by default on ext4): tune2fs -l /dev/sda1 | grep "Reserved block" # blocks reserved for root tune2fs -m 1 /dev/sda1 # reduce reserved to 1% (on data disks) Four causes: (1) Inode exhaustion — millions of tiny files consumed all inodes; df -i shows 100% inode usage. (2) Deleted-but-open files — process holds a file open, space not freed; lsof +L1 reveals it. (3) Reserved blocks — ext4 reserves 5% for root by default; a non-root process can't use this space even if df shows it. (4) tmpfs or /run full — these are RAM-backed filesystems with their own limits. This is a common interview question because it tests whether you understand the difference between space and inodes. Fast inode cleanup: Finding and deleting millions of small files is slow with standard rm. Use find . -delete (faster than piping to rm) or rsync --delete empty_dir/ target_dir/ to bulk-delete efficiently. For mail/session queues: check application documentation for purge commands that use internal indexes rather than filesystem walks.

questions.q: SSH connection hangs or is extremely slow to authenticate — how do you diagnose?
questions.text: ssh -vvv user@host # verbose mode (shows every auth step) # Common culprits from verbose output: debug1: Trying private key: ~/.ssh/id_rsa # key being tried debug1: Authentications that can continue # what server accepts # On the server side: journalctl -u sshd -f # sshd log in real time sshd -T | grep -E "usedns|gssapi|challengeresponse" # effective sshd config # DNS reverse lookup (common culprit): UseDNS no # in /etc/ssh/sshd_config — disables PTR lookup # GSSAPI timeout: GSSAPIAuthentication no # disable if not using Kerberos # Check /etc/hosts.allow / hosts.deny (TCP wrappers): cat /etc/hosts.deny # PAM timeout (LDAP/AD unreachable): time ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no user@host # skip password auth SSH slowness causes: UseDNS=yes causing PTR (reverse DNS) lookup for the client IP (slow or failing DNS = slow login), GSSAPIAuthentication=yes trying Kerberos negotiation, PAM module timing out (LDAP server unreachable), /etc/hosts.allow timeout for TCP wrappers, or many SSH keys in agent forcing the server to try each key (use IdentitiesOnly=yes in ~/.ssh/config). The -vvv flag shows exactly which step is slow — use it first. Quick wins: Adding UseDNS no and GSSAPIAuthentication no to sshd_config (plus systemctl reload sshd) instantly fixes the majority of slow SSH login issues. These are safe to disable on most systems not using Kerberos or relying on DNS-based access control.

questions.q: How do you handle a runaway process that is consuming all disk space with log writes?
questions.text: # Identify the file being written: lsof | grep -i "REG.*<mountpoint>" | sort -k7 -rn | head -10 # largest open files inotifywait -m /var/log/ # watch directory for writes in real time # Immediate relief without killing the process: truncate -s 0 /var/log/runaway.log # empty the file immediately > /var/log/runaway.log # bash redirect to empty # Rate-limit log output (if using systemd): # In unit file [Service] section: StandardOutput=journal LogRateLimitIntervalSec=30 LogRateLimitBurst=1000 # Redirect stdout to /dev/null temporarily: gdb -p <pid> -batch -ex 'call close(1)' -ex 'call open("/dev/null",1)' A runaway logger can fill disk in minutes. The truncate trick empties the file in-place without restarting the process — the process continues writing from offset 0. This gives immediate disk relief while you investigate the root cause. Common root causes: debug logging left on in production (check log level config), a loop generating errors that each trigger a log line, or a core dump being written repeatedly. Long-term: configure log rotation (logrotate), set max log size in the application config, and set disk usage alerts at 80%. Journal filling disk: systemd-journald can fill disk if not limited. Set SystemMaxUse=2G in /etc/systemd/journald.conf. Check current usage with journalctl --disk-usage . Vacuum old entries with journalctl --vacuum-size=1G .

questions.q: How do you tune Linux kernel parameters for a Kubernetes node?
questions.text: # Required for Kubernetes networking: net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1 net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1 net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 0 # for some CNI plugins # High connection count (for services with many pods): net.core.somaxconn = 32768 net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 32768 net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 1024 65535 net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 # inotify for Kubernetes controllers: fs.inotify.max_user_watches = 524288 fs.inotify.max_user_instances = 512 # File descriptor limits: fs.file-max = 2097152 # Disable swap (K8s requires this or kubelet --fail-swap-on=false): swapoff -a; sed -i '/swap/d' /etc/fstab vm.swappiness = 0 Kubernetes nodes require specific kernel settings. The bridge-nf-call-iptables settings ensure iptables sees bridged traffic — required for pod-to-pod networking with most CNI plugins. Without ip_forward, routing between pods is impossible. Kubernetes strongly recommends disabling swap — memory limits on containers become unreliable when swap is available (a container hitting its limit swaps instead of being OOM-killed). Store these in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf for persistence across reboots. Node preparation playbook: Always version-control your node preparation steps (Ansible, Terraform user_data). Any K8s node joining the cluster should have identical kernel parameters. Drift between nodes causes subtle, hard-to-diagnose issues where pods behave differently depending on which node they land on.

questions.q: What is a Linux namespace — how do containers use them for isolation?
questions.text: ls -la /proc/self/ns/ # namespaces for current process lsns # list all namespaces on the system lsns -t net # only network namespaces # Namespace types: mnt — filesystem mounts (each container has own mount tree) pid — process IDs (container PID 1 maps to host PID N) net — network interfaces, routes, iptables rules ipc — inter-process communication (shared memory, semaphores) uts — hostname and domain name user — UID/GID mappings (rootless containers) cgroup — cgroup root view # Enter a container's namespace: nsenter -t <container-pid> -n # enter network namespace nsenter -t <container-pid> --all # enter all namespaces (like exec) Linux namespaces are what make containers possible — each container gets isolated views of processes, networking, filesystem, hostname, and IPC. cgroups (control groups) complement namespaces: namespaces provide isolation (what you can see), cgroups provide resource limits (how much you can use). Together they form the foundation of container technology. nsenter is invaluable for debugging — it lets you enter a container's network namespace to run network diagnostic tools that aren't in the container image. Debug without exec: If a container doesn't have debugging tools (distroless images), use nsenter -t $(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' <container>) -n -- ss -tlnp to run ss inside the container's network namespace from the host. No exec into container needed — you use the host's tools in the container's namespace.

questions.q: What are cgroups — how do they enforce resource limits for containers and Kubernetes pods?
questions.text: cat /proc/self/cgroup # cgroup membership of current process ls /sys/fs/cgroup/ # cgroup v1 hierarchy ls /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/ # memory controller # For a container: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/docker/<id>/memory.limit_in_bytes cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/docker/<id>/cpu.cfs_quota_us # CPU quota # Kubernetes pod cgroup: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods/pod<uid>/memory.limit_in_bytes # Check cgroup version: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/ # tmpfs=v1, cgroup2fs=v2 mount | grep cgroup # cgroup mounts cgroups (control groups) are the kernel mechanism for resource accounting and limiting. For each container, the runtime creates cgroup entries setting: memory.limit_in_bytes (OOM kill threshold), cpu.cfs_quota_us / cpu.cfs_period_us (CPU limit as a fraction — 100ms/100ms = 1 full CPU), blkio.throttle.read/write_bps_device (disk I/O limits). Kubernetes translates pod resource limits directly into cgroup settings. Understanding this explains why a container behaves differently from a VM: cgroup limits are enforced in kernel, not in the application. cgroup v1 vs v2: cgroup v2 (unified hierarchy) is default on modern kernels (5.4+, used by GKE COS nodes). Some older tools only support v1. Kubernetes fully supports v2. The memory accounting differs between v1 and v2 — cached memory counts differently, affecting OOM behavior. Verify your monitoring tools support v2 if your nodes run modern kernels.

questions.q: How do you use journalctl effectively — what are the most useful query patterns?
questions.text: journalctl -f # follow live (like tail -f syslog) journalctl -u nginx # specific service journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" journalctl -u nginx --since "2024-01-15 10:00" --until "2024-01-15 11:00" journalctl -b # current boot journalctl -b -1 # previous boot (crash investigation) journalctl -p err # error priority and above journalctl -p warning -n 50 # last 50 warnings+ journalctl -k # kernel messages only (dmesg equivalent) journalctl _PID=1234 # logs from specific PID journalctl _UID=1000 # logs from specific UID journalctl -o json-pretty -u sshd -n 5 # JSON output for parsing journalctl --disk-usage # journal size on disk journalctl --vacuum-size=500M # trim journal to 500MB journald is the central logging daemon on systemd systems — it collects stdout/stderr from all services, kernel messages, and systemd unit events. Unlike syslog, entries have structured fields (unit, PID, UID, priority) enabling precise filtering. The -b -1 flag is invaluable for crash investigations — logs from the last boot before a crash. Priority levels: 0=emerg, 1=alert, 2=crit, 3=err, 4=warning, 5=notice, 6=info, 7=debug. Persistent journal: By default, journal is stored in /run/log/journal (lost on reboot). To persist across reboots: mkdir /var/log/journal && systemctl restart systemd-journald . Or set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf. Essential for post-reboot debugging.

questions.q: How do you write Ansible-style idempotent automation versus imperative scripts?
questions.text: # Imperative (not idempotent — fails if run twice): useradd deployer # fails with "user already exists" on second run mkdir /app/data # fails with "file exists" on second run # Idempotent (safe to run multiple times): id deployer || useradd deployer # only create if not exists mkdir -p /app/data # -p = no error if exists install -m 644 -o root config.yaml /etc/app/ # sets perms atomically grep -q "setting=value" /etc/app.conf || echo "setting=value" >> /etc/app.conf # Better: use Ansible tasks which are inherently idempotent: - name: Create deployer user ansible.builtin.user: name: deployer state: present # present = ensure exists (not create) groups: docker,sudo append: yes Idempotency means running an operation multiple times produces the same result as running it once. This is critical for automation: deployment scripts run in CI/CD, Ansible playbooks run for compliance enforcement, and provisioning scripts may be re-run after failures. All Ansible modules are designed to be idempotent — they check current state before making changes and report changed/ok/skipped. In bash, implement idempotency with conditional checks before every modifying operation. Platform Engineer standard: All infrastructure automation should be idempotent. Playbooks should be runnable against production at any time to enforce desired state without fear of side effects. This is the foundation of GitOps thinking applied to OS-level configuration.

questions.q: What is the difference between CPU throttling and CPU stealing — how do you detect each?
questions.text: # CPU throttling (cgroup CPU limits exceeded): cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/<container>/cpu.stat | grep throttled # Kubernetes: check via metrics container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total # Prometheus metric kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> # current CPU usage vs limit # CPU stealing (hypervisor not scheduling our vCPU): top # %st column = steal percentage vmstat 1 5 # st column sar -u 1 5 | grep -i steal # sar history of steal CPU throttling: the container's cgroup CPU quota is exhausted — the kernel pauses the container until the next quota period (default 100ms). Even if the physical host has idle CPUs, a throttled container waits. Fix: increase the container's CPU limit or optimize the application. CPU stealing: the hypervisor is not scheduling our VM's vCPU because physical CPUs are overcommitted. The VM is ready to run but waits for a physical CPU. Fix: scale down the physical host, move to a less loaded host, or buy dedicated/reserved instances. Throttling is under your control; stealing is the cloud provider's problem. Prometheus alert for throttling: rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]) > 0.25 — alert when more than 25% of CPU periods are throttled. This is a better SLI than CPU utilization% for container workloads.

questions.q: Walk through a complete methodology for diagnosing a production Linux incident from alert to resolution.
questions.text: This is the Principal-level systems thinking question. Structure, speed, and communication matter as much as technical depth. Incident response methodology Phase 1 — Triage (first 2 minutes): uptime; free -h; df -h; ss -s # four commands, system-wide health dmesg | tail -20 # any kernel errors? systemctl list-units --failed # any failed services? Phase 2 — Identify bottleneck (next 5 minutes): vmstat 1 5 # r/b columns: CPU queue or I/O blocked? top -b -n 1 # which process is the culprit? iostat -xz 1 3 # which disk is saturated? iftop # which connection is saturating network? Phase 3 — Confirm hypothesis: strace -c -p <pid> sleep 5 # what syscalls is the process making? lsof -p <pid> # what files/sockets are open? journalctl -u <service> --since "10 min ago" # service logs Phase 4 — Immediate relief + root cause fix: # Immediate: kill/restart/scale the problematic component # Root cause: fix config, add resource, fix code Phase 5 — Validate + document: # Confirm metrics return to baseline # Write postmortem: timeline, root cause, fix, prevention Common patterns by symptom: high load + high I/O wait + D-state processes = storage bottleneck (check iostat await). High load + low I/O wait + high %sy = iptables/networking overhead (many rules, high connection rate). High load + low I/O wait + high %us = CPU-bound application (profile with perf). Memory exhausted + swap in use = OOM risk imminent (free up memory or add swap). Filesystem full + lsof shows deleted files = truncate op

questions.q: Explain process states (R, S, D, Z, T). Why can't you kill a process in D state?
questions.text: The states (column STAT in ps) R Running / runnable (on CPU or in run queue) S Interruptible sleep (waiting for an event, e.g. network, can be woken) D Uninterruptible sleep (in a kernel syscall, usually disk/NFS I/O) Z Zombie (finished, waiting for parent to reap exit status) T Stopped (SIGSTOP / job control, or being traced) # suffixes: Why D can't be killed # A process in D is blocked inside the kernel and is NOT accepting signals # (not even SIGKILL) until the syscall returns. kill -9 is queued but # won't act until the I/O completes — or never, if the device/NFS hangs. ps -eo pid,stat,wchan,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /D/' # wchan shows what it's waiting on Real cause: lots of D-state processes = stuck I/O — a dead NFS mount, a failing disk, or saturated storage. The fix is at the I/O layer (recover the mount/device), not kill -9 . Persistent D-state often needs the underlying device fixed or a reboot. Interview tip: The headline: D = uninterruptible kernel sleep, immune to signals including SIGKILL, almost always disk/NFS I/O. Zombies, by contrast, are already dead — you can't kill them; you kill or fix the parent so it reaps them. Reading wchan to see what a D process waits on shows real depth.
