questions.q: What is a zombie process and what is an orphan? How do you deal with each?
questions.text: Zombie (defunct) # Child has exited but the parent hasn't called wait() to read its exit code. # The entry stays in the process table (just a PID + exit status) -> <defunct>. ps aux | grep -w Z # or STAT shows Z # You CAN'T kill a zombie (already dead). Fix the PARENT: # - signal the parent to reap (SIGCHLD), or # - kill/restart the parent -> children get reparented to init/PID 1, which reaps them. Orphan # Parent died before the child. The child is "orphaned" and immediately # reparented to PID 1 (init/systemd), which becomes responsible for reaping it. # Orphans are normal and harmless — init handles them. When zombies pile up: a buggy parent that forks but never wait() s. A few zombies are harmless (tiny), but thousands can exhaust the PID space. In containers, PID 1 is often your app, not init — if it doesn't reap, zombies accumulate. Use an init shim ( tini , --init ) so PID 1 reaps. Interview tip: Crisp distinction: zombie = child dead, parent didn't reap (fix the parent); orphan = parent dead, child reparented to init (normal). The container angle — PID 1 must reap, use tini / docker --init — is a strong modern signal that separates you from a textbook answer.

questions.q: Explain nice, renice, and ionice. How do you deprioritize a backup job without killing it?
questions.text: CPU priority: nice / renice nice -n 19 ./backup.sh # start with lowest CPU priority (range -20..19) renice -n 10 -p 12345 # change priority of a running PID (raise = lower pri) renice -n 5 -u alice # all of a user's processes # Only root can LOWER niceness (raise priority, negative values). I/O priority: ionice ionice -c 3 -p 12345 # class 3 = idle (only gets disk when nothing else wants it) ionice -c 2 -n 7 ./backup.sh # best-effort, lowest priority within it # Classes: 1=realtime, 2=best-effort(default), 3=idle Deprioritize a backup safely # Backups are usually I/O-bound, so ionice matters more than nice: ionice -c 3 nice -n 19 ./backup.sh # CPU-idle AND disk-idle -> backup runs only with spare capacity, never killed. # Or via systemd: CPUWeight=, IOWeight=, or Nice= in the unit. Interview tip: The key insight: nice is CPU only — for an I/O-heavy job like a backup, ionice -c3 (idle I/O class) is what actually keeps it out of the way. Combining both, or using systemd's IOWeight / CPUWeight with cgroups, is the production-grade answer (resource control without killing the job).

questions.q: What are signals? Explain SIGTERM vs SIGKILL vs SIGHUP and graceful shutdown.
questions.text: Common signals SIGTERM (15) : polite "please shut down" — catchable, app can clean up. DEFAULT of kill. SIGKILL (9) : forced kill — NOT catchable, NOT ignorable, no cleanup. Last resort. SIGINT (2) : Ctrl-C (catchable) SIGHUP (1) : terminal hangup — often repurposed to "reload config" (nginx, etc.) SIGSTOP/SIGCONT : pause / resume (SIGSTOP also uncatchable) SIGCHLD : sent to parent when a child exits (used for reaping) Graceful shutdown pattern # Send SIGTERM first, give it time, THEN SIGKILL if still alive: kill -TERM 12345; sleep 10; kill -KILL 12345 2>/dev/null # This is exactly what systemd (TimeoutStopSec) and Kubernetes # (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) do: SIGTERM -> grace period -> SIGKILL. Why -9 is harmful as a default: SIGKILL gives the app zero chance to flush buffers, finish in-flight requests, release locks, or remove pid/lock files — risking corruption and orphaned resources. Always try SIGTERM first. Interview tip: Stress that SIGTERM is catchable (clean shutdown) and SIGKILL/SIGSTOP are not (no cleanup), so the correct pattern is TERM -> wait -> KILL. Tying it to systemd TimeoutStopSec and K8s terminationGracePeriodSeconds shows you understand graceful shutdown the same way orchestrators implement it. SIGHUP-as-reload is a nice bonus fact.

questions.q: How do processes communicate (IPC)? Briefly cover pipes, sockets, shared memory, signals.
questions.text: The mechanisms Pipes (|) : unidirectional byte stream between related processes (shell pipelines) Named pipes/FIFO : mkfifo — pipe with a filesystem name, unrelated processes Unix sockets : bidirectional, local-only, fast (no TCP stack) — /var/run/*.sock (Docker, databases, php-fpm use these) TCP/UDP sockets : network IPC (also works locally via loopback) Shared memory : fastest — processes map the same memory (SysV shm, POSIX, /dev/shm) Signals : tiny async notifications (no data payload beyond the signal number) Message queues / semaphores : structured messaging + synchronization Choosing # Speed vs convenience: shared memory -> fastest, but you manage synchronization yourself unix socket -> fast local, bidirectional, easy (most local services) pipe -> simple stream, related processes network socket -> when processes are on different hosts Interview tip: Know that Unix domain sockets are the workhorse for local service IPC (Docker daemon, DBs, fpm) — faster than TCP loopback because they skip the network stack. Shared memory is fastest but needs your own locking. Signals carry no data (just a number). Matching mechanism to need (local vs remote, stream vs structured, speed vs simplicity) is what's being tested.

questions.q: How do you debug a process: strace, ltrace, /proc/ , lsof? Give a workflow.
questions.text: Inspect without attaching ls -l /proc/12345/fd # open file descriptors (files, sockets, pipes) cat /proc/12345/status # state, threads, memory, uid cat /proc/12345/limits # ulimits actually in effect readlink /proc/12345/cwd /proc/12345/exe # working dir + binary cat /proc/12345/environ | tr '\0' '\n' # its environment Trace activity strace -p 12345 -f # trace syscalls (what files/network it touches) strace -e trace=open,connect -p 12345 # filter to specific calls ltrace -p 12345 # trace library calls (higher level) lsof -p 12345 # everything the process has open lsof -i :8080 # who's using a port Workflow for "process is stuck" 1. ps stat -> R/D/S/Z? (D = stuck I/O) 2. strace -p PID -> is it blocked on a syscall (read/futex/connect)? 3. /proc/PID/fd + lsof -> what file/socket is it blocked on? 4. cat /proc/PID/stack (if permitted) -> kernel stack for D-state Caution: strace significantly slows the target (every syscall is trapped) — use briefly on production, and prefer -e trace= filters. For low-overhead production tracing, reach for eBPF tools (bpftrace, perf trace ). Interview tip: Show a layered method: cheap first ( /proc , lsof , ps ), then strace to see the blocking syscall. The standout point is that strace adds heavy overhead, so on production you'd use bpftrace/eBPF instead — that distinguishes someone who's actually traced a live prod process from someone reciting commands.

questions.q: Explain fork, exec, and copy-on-write. Why is fork() cheap on Linux?
questions.text: fork + exec fork() : creates a child that is a COPY of the parent (same code, new PID) exec() : REPLACES the current process image with a new program # The classic pattern: shell forks, child execs the command, parent waits(). # That's how every command you run from a shell starts. Copy-on-write (COW) # fork() doesn't actually copy the parent's memory up front. # Parent + child SHARE the same physical pages, marked read-only. # A page is only physically copied when one of them WRITES to it. # -> fork is cheap even for large processes; you pay only for what changes. Why it matters COW makes forking a multi-GB process fast and memory-light — until it writes. This is why a big app (e.g. Redis) can fork() to snapshot: the child sees a frozen copy, and only changed pages get duplicated. But heavy writes after fork cause a memory spike as pages get copied. Interview tip: The key fact: fork is cheap because of copy-on-write — memory is shared read-only and only duplicated on write. Name the fork+exec pattern (how shells launch programs) and the Redis fork-to-snapshot example. The gotcha worth mentioning: a fork followed by heavy writes triggers mass page-copying and a RAM spike (relevant to Redis BGSAVE OOMs).

questions.q: What is the OOM killer? How does it decide what to kill and how do you influence it?
questions.text: What it does # When the kernel runs out of memory (and can't reclaim), the OOM killer # picks a process to kill to free RAM and keep the system alive. dmesg | grep -i "killed process" # see what got OOM-killed and why grep -i oom /var/log/syslog # OOM events How it chooses # Scores each process by oom_score (mostly proportional to memory used), # adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 .. +1000). Highest score dies. cat /proc/12345/oom_score echo -1000 > /proc/12345/oom_score_adj # -1000 = never kill (protect it) echo 500 > /proc/12345/oom_score_adj # more likely to be the victim Gotcha: the OOM killer often kills the biggest process, which may not be the culprit — it can take down your database instead of the leaking worker. In cgroup v2 / containers, memory limits cause a cgroup-local OOM kill (only that container's processes), which is usually what you want. Interview tip: Explain the score is memory-driven and tunable via oom_score_adj (protect critical services with -1000). The senior points: prefer cgroup memory limits so an OOM is contained to the offending container instead of the host picking a random big victim, and disabling overcommit or adding swap changes when/whether OOM triggers. Reading dmesg for the kill is the first debugging step.

questions.q: Explain inodes. What happens when you run out of inodes but still have free space?
questions.text: What an inode is # An inode stores a file's METADATA (permissions, owner, timestamps, size, # and pointers to data blocks) — but NOT the filename. The directory entry # maps name -> inode number. ls -i file # show inode number stat file # full inode metadata df -i # inode usage per filesystem (vs df -h for space) Out of inodes, space free # inodes are allocated at mkfs time (fixed count on ext4). Millions of TINY # files exhaust inodes while bytes remain free -> "No space left on device" # even though df -h shows free space. The tell: df -i at 100%. # Find the culprit directory (lots of small files): for d in /var/*; do echo "$(find "$d" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) $d"; done | sort -rn | head Classic cause: a runaway mail/session/cache dir, or millions of tiny log/temp files. The error message ("No space left") is misleading — always check df -i , not just df -h . ext4's inode count is fixed at format time; XFS allocates inodes dynamically and rarely hits this. Interview tip: The signature interview trap: "disk has free space but writes fail with ENOSPC." Answer: inode exhaustion — df -i confirms it. Inodes hold metadata + block pointers, not the name. Mention that ext4 fixes inode count at mkfs while XFS is dynamic — explaining why this bug is an ext4 phenomenon shows filesystem depth.

questions.q: Hard links vs symbolic links: how do they differ and when do you use each?
questions.text: The difference ln target link # HARD link: another name pointing to the SAME inode ln -s target link # SYMlink: a small file containing a PATH to the target # Hard link -> same inode, same data. Deleting one name leaves the data # until the link count hits 0. Can't cross filesystems or link dirs. # Symlink -> points to a path. If the target is moved/deleted -> dangling link. # Can cross filesystems and point to directories. Observing ls -li file # 2nd column = link count; same inode # = hard linked stat file # "Links:" shows hard-link count ls -l symlink # shows link -> /path/to/target find / -inum 1234567 # find all hard links sharing an inode When to use Symlinks for almost everything (cross-fs, point to dirs, human-readable, common in /etc/alternatives , current-release pointers). Hard links for space-efficient deduplication on one filesystem (backup snapshots like rsync --link-dest , where unchanged files share inodes). Interview tip: Core facts: hard link = same inode (data persists until link count 0, same-fs only, not dirs); symlink = a path pointer (can dangle, crosses filesystems, points to dirs). The practical kicker: rsync/backup tools use hard links ( --link-dest ) for dedup, and deleting a file with multiple hard links doesn't free space until the last one goes.

questions.q: A file was deleted but disk space wasn't freed. Why, and how do you recover the space?
questions.text: Why space isn't freed # On Linux, space is freed only when BOTH are true: # 1. all directory entries (names) are removed, AND # 2. no process still has the file OPEN. # If a process holds the deleted file open, the inode + blocks persist # (you'll see "(deleted)" entries). Classic: a log file rm'd while the # app keeps writing to its open fd -> disk fills, df shows full, du doesn't. Find and fix lsof +L1 # files with link count 0 still held open lsof | grep deleted # show "(deleted)" files + the holding PID # Recover space WITHOUT killing the app — truncate via the proc fd: : > /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd-number> # empties the still-open deleted file # Or, if acceptable, restart/HUP the process to release the fd. The tell: df shows the filesystem full but du of its contents is much smaller — the difference is space held by deleted-but-open files. This is extremely common with rotated logs when logrotate doesn't signal the app to reopen. Interview tip: This is a top-tier troubleshooting question. The mechanism: an open fd to a deleted file keeps its blocks allocated. Diagnose with lsof +L1 / lsof | grep deleted ; the df -vs- du mismatch is the fingerprint. Recover by truncating the proc fd or restarting the holder — and prevent it with proper logrotate copytruncate or a post-rotate reload signal.

questions.q: Explain mount, /etc/fstab, and bind mounts. How do you safely add a new disk mount?
questions.text: Mounting mount /dev/sdb1 /data # attach a filesystem at a mountpoint umount /data # detach (fails if busy; lsof /data to find users) findmnt # tree of all mounts (clearer than mount) mount --bind /src /dst # bind mount: make a dir appear at another path Persistent mounts: /etc/fstab # <device> <mountpoint> <fstype> <options> <dump> <pass> UUID=abc-123 /data ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2 # Use UUID (or LABEL), NOT /dev/sdb1 — device names reorder across reboots! blkid /dev/sdb1 # get the UUID Safely add a disk 1. mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1; blkid to get UUID 2. Add the UUID line to /etc/fstab 3. mount -a # mount everything in fstab NOW — catches typos 4. Verify: findmnt /data, df -h # CRITICAL: test mount -a before rebooting. A bad fstab line can drop the # box to emergency mode on boot. (Use 'nofail' for non-critical mounts.) Interview tip: Two safety points score here: (1) reference disks by UUID/LABEL, not /dev/sdX (which can reorder), and (2) always run mount -a to validate fstab before rebooting, since a bad entry can hang boot in emergency mode — add nofail for optional mounts. Knowing bind mounts (and that they're how containers share host dirs) is a nice extra.

questions.q: What's the difference between ext4, XFS, and Btrfs/ZFS? When would you pick each?
questions.text: The main filesystems ext4 : mature, reliable default. Fixed inode count, journaling. Shrinkable. Great general-purpose; the safe boring choice. XFS : high-performance, great for large files + parallel I/O, dynamic inodes. Default on RHEL. Can GROW but NOT shrink. Scales to huge filesystems. Btrfs : CoW, snapshots, checksums, built-in RAID, subvolumes. More features, historically less trusted for some RAID modes. ZFS : CoW, snapshots, checksums, compression, RAID-Z, self-healing. Excellent data integrity; heavy RAM use; licensing keeps it out of mainline kernel. Choosing General server / root fs -> ext4 (or XFS on RHEL) Big data, large files, DBs -> XFS (parallel I/O, scales) Need snapshots/checksums/ -> ZFS (integrity) or Btrfs (in-kernel) data integrity, NAS Need to shrink a fs -> ext4 (XFS can't shrink) Interview tip: Have a one-line opinion on each: ext4 = safe default, XFS = performance/scale (RHEL default, grow-only), ZFS/Btrfs = snapshots + checksums + integrity (CoW). The most-tested specifics: XFS can grow but not shrink, ext4 has fixed inodes, and CoW filesystems give you snapshots and end-to-end checksums (self-healing) at the cost of complexity/RAM.

questions.q: Explain file permissions deeply: SUID, SGID, sticky bit, and umask.
questions.text: Beyond rwx: special bits SUID (4xxx) : run the file AS THE OWNER (e.g. /usr/bin/passwd runs as root) shows as 's' in owner-exec: -rwsr-xr-x SGID (2xxx) : on a file -> run as the group; on a DIR -> new files inherit the dir's group (great for shared team folders) Sticky (1xxx): on a dir -> only the file's owner can delete it (e.g. /tmp) shows as 't': drwxrwxrwt chmod u+s / g+s / +t file_or_dir umask # umask SUBTRACTS permissions from defaults (666 files, 777 dirs): umask 022 -> new files 644, new dirs 755 (typical) umask 027 -> new files 640, new dirs 750 (more private; group read only) umask # show current Security: SUID-root binaries are a major attack surface — a bug in one = root. Audit them: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null . Modern systems replace many SUID binaries with capabilities (finer-grained). Never set SUID on shell scripts. Interview tip: Be precise: SUID = run as owner (the passwd example), SGID on a directory = group inheritance (shared folders), sticky bit = owner-only delete (why anyone can write to /tmp but not delete others' files). umask subtracts from defaults. The security-aware close — audit SUID binaries, prefer capabilities — is what senior interviewers want to hear.

questions.q: How do you find what's filling a disk, and handle 'No space left on device'?
questions.text: Find the big consumers df -h # which filesystem is full? df -i # OR is it inodes? (millions of tiny files) du -xh /var --max-depth=1 | sort -rh | head # -x stays on one filesystem ncdu /var # interactive disk usage explorer (fast) find / -xdev -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} \; # individual large files The deleted-but-open trap # If du is much smaller than df-used, space is held by open deleted files: lsof +L1 # or: lsof | grep deleted : > /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> # truncate to reclaim without killing the app Common culprits + quick wins journalctl --disk-usage; journalctl --vacuum-size=200M # systemd journal bloat docker system df; docker system prune # images/volumes/build cache /var/log (rotate), /tmp, old kernels, package caches (apt clean / dnf clean) Interview tip: Show a decision tree: df -h (space) vs df -i (inodes) vs df -beats- du (deleted-open files) — three different "disk full" root causes. Then locate with du -x / ncdu . Naming the usual offenders (journal, Docker, logs, old kernels) and reclaiming them shows you've actually firefought a full root filesystem.

questions.q: Explain the Linux page cache, dirty pages, and how writes are flushed to disk.
questions.text: Page cache # Linux caches file data in free RAM (page cache). Reads hit RAM, not disk. # This is why 'free -h' shows little "free" but lots of "buff/cache" — # that memory is reclaimable, NOT wasted. available is the number that matters. free -h # look at "available", not "free" Dirty pages + writeback # A WRITE first goes to the page cache (marked "dirty"), then is flushed # to disk asynchronously by kernel writeback threads -> writes feel fast. cat /proc/meminfo | grep -i dirty # Dirty: pending bytes sync # force flush all dirty pages now # Tunables: vm.dirty_ratio / vm.dirty_background_ratio control when flush starts. Durability gap: because writes are buffered, data in the page cache is lost on power failure unless fsync() has committed it. Databases call fsync /use O_DIRECT for durability. A sudden dirty_ratio -triggered flush can also cause an I/O stall ("write storm"). Interview tip: Two things land well: (1) buff/cache in free is reclaimable, so "low free memory" is usually fine — watch available instead; and (2) writes are buffered as dirty pages and flushed asynchronously, which is why fsync exists and why a power loss can lose un-synced data. Mentioning vm.dirty_ratio tuning to avoid write-storm stalls is a strong performance signal.

questions.q: The modern net-tools vs iproute2: what replaced ifconfig, netstat, route, arp?
questions.text: Old -> new ifconfig -> ip addr / ip link route -n -> ip route netstat -tlnp -> ss -tlnp (ss is faster, reads /proc directly) netstat -i -> ip -s link arp -a -> ip neigh netstat -rn -> ip route show The everyday commands ip a # all interfaces + addresses ip route get 8.8.8.8 # which route/interface/source IP is used for a dest ip -s link show eth0 # interface stats (errors, drops) ss -tlnp # listening TCP sockets + owning process ss -tn state established # established connections ss -s # socket summary stats Why it matters: net-tools (ifconfig/netstat) is deprecated and often not installed on minimal/container images. ss is dramatically faster than netstat on busy hosts (netstat parses /proc slowly). Knowing iproute2 is now table stakes. Interview tip: Just demonstrate fluency in the modern tools — ip a , ip route get , ss -tlnp , ip neigh . The single best one-liner to know is ip route get <dest> , which shows exactly which route, interface, and source IP the kernel will use — invaluable for routing/asymmetric-path debugging. Note that ifconfig/netstat are deprecated and may be absent on containers.

questions.q: How do you debug 'can't connect to a service'? Give a layered checklist.
questions.text: Work up the stack 1. DNS: getent hosts host / dig host # name resolves? right IP? 2. Route: ip route get <ip> # is there a path? right iface? 3. Reach: ping <ip> # L3 up? (ICMP may be blocked) 4. Port: nc -vz host 443 / curl -v telnet://host:443 # is the port open? 5. Listen: (on server) ss -tlnp | grep :443 # is anything bound? on 0.0.0.0? 6. Firewall: iptables/nftables, cloud SG/NACL, host ufw/firewalld 7. App: curl -v https://host/health # does the app actually answer? Read the failure mode Connection REFUSED -> reached host, nothing listening on that port (or RST) Connection TIMEOUT -> firewall dropping / wrong route / host down (no reply) No route to host -> routing/ARP problem, or firewall REJECT with icmp Name resolution err -> DNS, before any connection is attempted Interview tip: Lead with the layered method (DNS -> route -> reach -> port -> listener -> firewall -> app) and especially the refused vs timeout distinction: refused = got there, nothing listening (fast); timeout = packets dropped silently (firewall/down). A frequent gotcha to mention: the service is listening on 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 , so it works locally but refuses remotely.

questions.q: Explain iptables vs nftables and the netfilter chains. How does a packet traverse them?
questions.text: netfilter chains (the hooks) PREROUTING -> (routing decision) -> INPUT (packets FOR this host) -> FORWARD (packets THROUGH this host) -> POSTROUTING locally generated -> OUTPUT -> POSTROUTING # Tables apply at these hooks: filter (allow/deny), nat (SNAT/DNAT), mangle, raw. iptables example iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers # list filter rules + counters iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT iptables -A INPUT -j DROP # default-deny the rest # Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom; FIRST match wins. Order matters! nftables (the replacement) # nft unifies iptables/ip6tables/arptables/ebtables into one framework, # with sets, maps, and better performance. Modern distros use nft underneath. nft list ruleset nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept Interview tip: Draw the path: PREROUTING -> routing -> INPUT (to us) or FORWARD (through us) -> POSTROUTING. Stress first-match-wins and that a misplaced DROP above your ACCEPT silently blocks traffic. Note nftables is the modern replacement (sets/maps, one tool for v4+v6) and that even iptables commands now often drive the nft backend. Knowing where NAT happens (PRE/POSTROUTING) ties into the SNAT/DNAT questions.

questions.q: How do you capture and analyze traffic with tcpdump? Give a practical workflow.
questions.text: Capture tcpdump -i eth0 -nn host 10.0.0.5 and port 443 # filter by host+port (-nn no DNS) tcpdump -i any -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst) != 0' # SYNs and RSTs tcpdump -i eth0 -w cap.pcap -C 100 -W 5 # write to file, rotate 100MB x5 tcpdump -r cap.pcap -nn # read back a capture # -s0 captures full packets; add -v for more header detail. What the flags tell you SYN sent, no SYN-ACK back -> firewall drop / nothing listening / wrong route SYN -> RST -> port closed (refused) Retransmissions -> packet loss / congestion FIN/RST mid-stream -> who closed first (server vs client)? Workflow Capture on both ends when possible: if the client sends SYN but the server never sees it, the drop is in between (firewall/route); if the server replies but the client doesn't get it, the return path is broken. Move the capture to Wireshark for TCP stream analysis. Caution on prod: capture with tight filters and rotation ( -C/-W ) — an unfiltered capture on a busy host can fill the disk and add load. Be mindful that payloads may contain sensitive data. Interview tip: The pro move is capturing on both ends to localize where packets vanish (sender-side vs path vs return path). Know the flag-reading shorthand: SYN with no reply = dropped/no listener; SYN->RST = refused; retransmits = loss. Mention tight filters + file rotation so you don't take down a prod box with the capture itself.

questions.q: Explain network namespaces and veth pairs. How does container networking actually work?
questions.text: Network namespaces # A netns is an isolated network stack: its own interfaces, routes, # ARP table, iptables, ports. This is the primitive containers use. ip netns add blue ip netns exec blue ip a # run a command inside that namespace ls /var/run/netns # named namespaces veth pairs (the cable) # A veth pair is a virtual cable: two ends; what goes in one comes out the other. # One end lives in the container's netns, the other on the host (often on a bridge). ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1 ip link set veth1 netns blue # push one end into the namespace # Host end -> docker0/cni bridge -> NAT/routing to the outside. The full container picture container netns --(veth)--> host bridge (docker0/cni0) --(iptables NAT)--> eth0 -> world # "publish a port" = a DNAT rule mapping host:port -> container IP:port. # Kubernetes CNI plugins automate exactly this (plus pod-to-pod routing). Interview tip: The insight that impresses: containers aren't magic — they're network namespaces connected by veth pairs to a host bridge, with iptables doing NAT/port-publishing. Being able to say " docker run -p is just a DNAT rule" and "a pod is a netns; CNI wires the veth" shows you understand the plumbing under Docker/Kubernetes, not just the CLI.

questions.q: What is the difference between a bridge, bond, VLAN, and tunnel interface?
questions.text: The interface types Bridge : a virtual L2 switch — connects multiple interfaces/veths into one segment (docker0, br0 for VMs/containers). Bond : aggregates multiple NICs into one for redundancy and/or throughput (a.k.a. link aggregation / LACP). Survives a NIC/cable failure. VLAN : tags frames (802.1Q) to split one physical link into many logical L2 segments (eth0.100 = VLAN 100). Tunnel : encapsulates packets to traverse another network — VXLAN, GRE, IPsec, WireGuard. Basis of overlay networks. Bonding modes (most asked) active-backup : one NIC active, others standby (pure redundancy, no extra bw) 802.3ad (LACP): switch-negotiated aggregation (redundancy + bandwidth) balance-alb/tlb : load-balance without switch config Where each shows up Bridges back container/VM networking; bonds give NIC redundancy on servers; VLANs segment a datacenter L2; tunnels (VXLAN) build the overlay fabrics that Kubernetes CNIs and SDNs use to make pods on different nodes look like one L2. Interview tip: One sentence each: bridge = virtual switch (containers/VMs), bond = NIC aggregation for HA/throughput (know active-backup vs LACP), VLAN = logical L2 segmentation via tagging, tunnel/VXLAN = overlay encapsulation. Connecting VXLAN tunnels to Kubernetes overlay networking, and bonds to server NIC redundancy, shows you map these primitives to real infrastructure.

questions.q: How do you diagnose high latency or packet loss between two hosts?
questions.text: Find where it hurts ping -c 100 host # baseline RTT + loss % (watch for variance/jitter) mtr -rwzbc 100 host # per-hop loss + latency over 100 cycles (THE tool) traceroute host # path; -T for TCP if ICMP is filtered Reading mtr # Loss that STARTS at a hop and CONTINUES to the end -> real loss at that hop. # Loss at ONE middle hop but 0% after it -> that router just deprioritizes ICMP # to its own control plane (NOT a real problem) — a classic misread. # So only trust loss that persists to the destination. Local-side checks ip -s link show eth0 # interface errors/drops/overruns (bad NIC/cable/driver) ethtool -S eth0 # detailed NIC counters ss -ti # per-socket RTT, retransmits, cwnd (TCP-level loss) # Also: MTU/PMTUD black hole (big packets lost), conntrack full, NIC ring buffers. Interview tip: mtr is the headline tool, but the senior point is reading it correctly: mid-path ICMP deprioritization looks like loss but isn't — only loss that persists to the final hop is real. Separate latency (distance/queuing) from loss (errors/congestion) from jitter (variance). Checking local NIC error counters and per-socket TCP retransmits ( ss -ti ) rounds out a complete answer.

questions.q: Explain ephemeral ports, TIME_WAIT, and 'cannot assign requested address' under load.
questions.text: Ephemeral ports # Each OUTBOUND connection uses a local source port from the ephemeral range: cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range # e.g. 32768 60999 (~28k ports) # A connection is the 4-tuple: src_ip:src_port -> dst_ip:dst_port. # To ONE destination ip:port you're limited by available source ports. TIME_WAIT # The side that closes first holds the socket in TIME_WAIT (~60s) to absorb # stray packets. Under high churn, thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets tie up # source ports -> new outbound connects fail: # "cannot assign requested address" (EADDRNOTAVAIL). ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l Fixes - Use connection pooling / keep-alive (fewer, reused connections) — the real fix - Widen ip_local_port_range - net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 (safe: reuse TIME_WAIT for new OUTBOUND conns) - Do NOT use tcp_tw_recycle (removed; broke NAT) Interview tip: The chain to articulate: high connection churn -> pile of TIME_WAIT on the active closer -> source-port exhaustion -> EADDRNOTAVAIL. The correct primary fix is connection reuse/pooling, not tuning. If asked about sysctls, tcp_tw_reuse is safe but tcp_tw_recycle is a trap (NAT-breaking, removed) — knowing that difference is a strong signal.

questions.q: What is SSH multiplexing, agent forwarding, and a bastion/jump host? Show a secure setup.
questions.text: Jump host (ProxyJump) # Reach a private host THROUGH a bastion, without landing keys on the bastion: ssh -J bastion.example.com private-host # ~/.ssh/config: Host private-* ProxyJump bastion.example.com User deploy Multiplexing (reuse one connection) Host * ControlMaster auto ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p ControlPersist 10m # Subsequent ssh/scp to the same host reuse the open channel -> instant, no re-auth. Agent forwarding — and why to avoid it # ssh -A forwards your local agent so the remote can use your keys onward. # RISK: root on that remote can hijack your agent socket to impersonate you. # Prefer ProxyJump (keys never touch the intermediate host) over -A. Interview tip: Recommend ProxyJump over agent forwarding for bastions — ProxyJump tunnels through without exposing your keys on the jump box, whereas -A lets a compromised intermediate hijack your agent. Multiplexing ( ControlMaster ) is the performance win for repeated connections (Ansible uses it). Mentioning the agent-forwarding risk is a security-maturity marker. Modern shops increasingly replace bastions with SSM/IAP (no open SSH port at all).

questions.q: How do you harden SSH on a production server? Give concrete sshd_config settings.
questions.text: Core sshd_config hardening PermitRootLogin no # no direct root; sudo from a named user PasswordAuthentication no # keys only — kills brute force PubkeyAuthentication yes KbdInteractiveAuthentication no AllowUsers deploy ops # explicit allowlist (or AllowGroups) Port 22 # (obscurity only; not real security) MaxAuthTries 3 LoginGraceTime 20 X11Forwarding no AllowAgentForwarding no # unless explicitly needed Layered controls - firewall: restrict 22 to known CIDRs / VPN / bastion only - fail2ban / sshguard: ban IPs after repeated failures - MFA for SSH (e.g. TOTP PAM) for human access - short-lived SSH certificates (CA-signed) instead of static authorized_keys - centralize + monitor auth logs (failed logins, new keys) Always keep an active session open and test the new config from a second terminal ( sshd -t to validate syntax) before closing — a bad sshd_config can lock you out. Interview tip: The two highest-impact settings are PasswordAuthentication no (keys only — eliminates brute-force) and PermitRootLogin no . Then layer: firewall to bastion/VPN, fail2ban, MFA. The modern senior answer mentions SSH certificates (CA-signed, short-lived) over static authorized_keys for scalable, revocable access — and always validate with sshd -t before disconnecting.

questions.q: Explain Linux capabilities. Why are they better than SUID-root?
questions.text: The problem with SUID-root # SUID-root = the binary runs with ALL root powers, even if it only needs one. # A bug in it = full root compromise. All-or-nothing privilege. Capabilities = root split into pieces CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE # bind ports Why better Least privilege: a web server that only needs to bind port 80 gets CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE instead of running as root. A bug then leaks one capability, not the whole system. Containers use this heavily — drop all caps, add back only what's needed. Interview tip: Frame capabilities as "root chopped into ~40 independent privileges" enabling least privilege. The killer example: bind to port 80 with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE instead of full root. The container tie-in is gold: --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE , and that CAP_SYS_ADMIN is effectively root so granting it defeats the purpose.

questions.q: What are SELinux and AppArmor? How do you debug an SELinux denial?
questions.text: What they are (MAC) # Mandatory Access Control: the kernel enforces policy even root can't override, # confining what a process may access — a strong defense-in-depth layer. # SELinux (RHEL/Fedora) : label-based (every file/process has a context/type) # AppArmor (Ubuntu/SUSE): path-based profiles per program (simpler model) Debugging SELinux denials getenforce # Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled ausearch -m AVC -ts recent # the actual denials (AVC messages) sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log # human-readable with suggested fixes # Common real fix: relabel a file to the right context restorecon -Rv /web/html chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /web/file setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on # toggle a policy boolean Anti-pattern: setenforce 0 / disabling SELinux "to make it work" throws away a real security layer. The symptom "works with SELinux off" means a labeling/policy issue — fix the context ( restorecon ) or the boolean, don't disable it. Use Permissive mode to log-without-blocking while you diagnose. Interview tip: Define MAC as kernel-enforced confinement that even root obeys (vs discretionary owner-set perms). For debugging, the workflow is ausearch / sealert -> usually restorecon (wrong label) or a setsebool toggle. The maturity signal is explicitly NOT disabling SELinux — using Permissive mode to diagnose, then fixing the label/policy properly.

questions.q: How do you manage sudo safely? Explain sudoers, NOPASSWD risks, and auditing.
questions.text: Editing sudoers visudo # ALWAYS — it syntax-checks before saving # (a broken sudoers can lock out all admins) # Prefer drop-in files over editing the main file: visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy Least-privilege rules # Grant specific commands, not blanket ALL: deploy ALL=(ALL) /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp, /usr/bin/journalctl -u myapp %ops ALL=(ALL) ALL # group-based (manage membership, not rules) # NOPASSWD removes the password prompt — convenient but risky: deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp # scope it tightly! Risks: NOPASSWD: ALL means a stolen session = instant root with no second factor. Also beware commands that can spawn shells (editors, less , find -exec , vi ) — granting those effectively grants root. Restrict to exact, non-shell-escaping commands. Auditing journalctl _COMM=sudo # who ran what via sudo # sudo logs each invocation; ship these to central logging/SIEM. Interview tip: Hit three things: always use visudo (syntax check prevents lockout), grant specific commands not ALL , and be wary of NOPASSWD plus shell-escaping commands (an editor or less in a sudo rule = root). Mention auditing sudo usage to central logs. This shows you treat privilege escalation as an attack surface, not a convenience.

questions.q: How do you respond to a suspected compromised Linux server? Walk through the steps.
questions.text: 1. Contain (don't tip off the attacker) # Isolate at the network layer (SG/firewall), DON'T power off # (loses volatile evidence: memory, live connections, running procs). # Preserve: snapshot the disk/VM; capture RAM if you can. 2. Triage / investigate w; last; lastb # who's/was logged in, failed logins ss -tnp # active connections + processes (C2 beacon?) ps auxf # process tree — odd parents, miners ls -la /tmp /dev/shm /var/tmp # common dropper locations crontab -l; ls /etc/cron.*; systemctl list-timers # persistence find / -mtime -2 -type f 2>/dev/null # recently modified files grep -r authorized_keys ~ /home /root # added backdoor keys journalctl/auth.log # but assume local logs may be tampered 3. Eradicate + recover # Don't "clean" a rooted box — rebuild from known-good images/IaC, # rotate ALL credentials/keys/secrets it could have touched, patch the # entry vector, restore data from pre-compromise backups. Key principle: a compromised host can't be trusted to report on itself (rootkits hide processes/files). Investigate from outside where possible (network logs, disk image offline), and rebuild rather than clean — you can never be sure you found everything. Interview tip: Structure it: contain (isolate, preserve volatile evidence — don't just power off), investigate (connections, process tree, persistence: cron/timers/authorized_keys, recent file changes), then rebuild-not-clean + rotate all secrets + fix the entry point. The two senior insights: preserve memory/conne

questions.q: Explain disk encryption (LUKS) and file integrity monitoring. When do you need each?
questions.text: LUKS — encryption at rest cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1 # encrypt a block device cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sdb1 secure # unlock -> /dev/mapper/secure mkfs.ext4 /dev/mapper/secure; mount ... # Protects data if the DISK is stolen/decommissioned. Does NOT protect a # running system (once unlocked, data is readable to the OS). # Key management: passphrase, keyfile, or TPM/network-bound (clevis/tang) for # unattended boot. File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) # Detect unauthorized changes to critical files (binaries, configs): # AIDE / Tripwire build a baseline of hashes, then alert on changes. aide --init # baseline aide --check # compare current vs baseline -> what changed # auditd can watch specific paths in real time (watch /etc/passwd, /etc/sudoers). When LUKS for laptops, removable media, and compliance (encryption-at-rest mandates) — its real value is at decommission/theft. FIM for detecting intrusion/tampering and meeting compliance (PCI requires it). They cover different threats: confidentiality vs integrity. Interview tip: Be clear about LUKS's threat model: it protects data at rest (stolen/retired disk), NOT a live unlocked system — a common misconception. FIM (AIDE/Tripwire/auditd) detects tampering and is often a compliance requirement (PCI). Mentioning TPM/tang for unattended LUKS unlock, and auditd watches on /etc/passwd / sudoers , shows operational depth.

questions.q: How do you keep a fleet patched and find vulnerabilities? Explain CVEs and patch strategy.
questions.text: Find what's vulnerable apt list --upgradable; dnf updateinfo list security # pending security updates # Scanners map installed packages -> known CVEs: # OpenSCAP, Trivy (also containers), Grype, vendor tools (Insights, etc.) # Track severity (CVSS) + whether it's actually exploitable/exposed in your env. Patch strategy - Unattended security updates for low-risk patches (unattended-upgrades / dnf-automatic) - Staged rollout: canary hosts -> wider fleet, watch for regressions - Maintenance windows + reboot orchestration (kernel updates need reboot; or livepatch / kpatch / ksplice for no-reboot kernel patching) - Immutable infra: bake patched golden images, redeploy (don't patch in place) Prioritize, don't patch-everything-now Rank by CVSS severity × exploitability × exposure (is the vulnerable service even reachable?). A critical CVE in an internet-facing service beats a high CVE in an isolated internal tool. Known-exploited (CISA KEV) jumps the queue. Interview tip: Show a system, not "run apt upgrade": scan (Trivy/OpenSCAP) -> prioritize by severity + exposure + known-exploited -> stage (canary then fleet) -> automate low-risk + maintenance-window the rest. The modern angle is immutable infrastructure (rebuild patched golden images rather than mutate live hosts) and livepatch for no-reboot kernel CVEs. Prioritization beats "patch everything" — that's the senior judgment.

questions.q: Explain PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) and a practical use (MFA, limits, lockout).
questions.text: What PAM is # PAM is the framework that programs (login, sshd, sudo) use to AUTHENTICATE, # without each implementing auth itself. Config lives in /etc/pam.d/<service>. # Four management groups: auth -> verify identity (password, key, MFA) account -> is the account allowed/valid/expired? password -> password change rules (complexity) session -> set up the session (limits, mounts, logging) Practical examples # Add TOTP MFA to SSH (pam_google_authenticator) in /etc/pam.d/sshd: auth required pam_google_authenticator.so # Account lockout after failed attempts (pam_faillock): auth required pam_faillock.so deny=5 unlock_time=900 # Resource limits at login (pam_limits -> /etc/security/limits.conf): * hard nofile 65535 Caution: a broken PAM stack can lock everyone out (including root via console). Test changes in a separate session, and know your recovery path (single-user mode / console). Order and required vs sufficient control flow matters. Interview tip: Explain PAM as the pluggable auth layer shared by login/sshd/sudo, with stackable modules (auth/account/password/session). Give a concrete win: pam_google_authenticator for SSH MFA, pam_faillock for lockout, pam_limits for ulimits. The safety note — a bad PAM edit can lock everyone out, so test in a second session — signals you've actually touched it in production.

questions.q: What's the principle of least privilege in practice on Linux? Give concrete mechanisms.
questions.text: The principle Every user, process, and service should have the minimum access needed — nothing more. It shrinks the blast radius when (not if) something is compromised. Concrete Linux mechanisms Service accounts : run daemons as dedicated non-root users (never root) Capabilities : grant CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, not full root systemd sandbox : User=, ProtectSystem=strict, PrivateTmp=, NoNewPrivileges=, ReadOnlyPaths=, RestrictAddressFamilies=, SystemCallFilter= sudo : specific commands per user/group, not ALL MAC : SELinux/AppArmor confinement per service Filesystem : tight ownership + perms; mount data noexec,nosuid,nodev Containers : --cap-drop=ALL, read-only rootfs, non-root USER, seccomp systemd as a sandbox [Service] User=myapp NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict PrivateTmp=true SystemCallFilter=@system-service # A modern, easy way to confine a service without root or containers. Interview tip: Don't just define it — list the mechanisms: dedicated service users, capabilities over root, sudo scoped to commands, SELinux/AppArmor, and especially systemd sandboxing directives ( NoNewPrivileges , ProtectSystem=strict , PrivateTmp , SystemCallFilter ), which let you confine a plain service without containers. Framing it as "shrink the blast radius" ties everything together.

questions.q: Walk through the USE method for diagnosing a performance problem on Linux.
questions.text: USE = Utilization, Saturation, Errors # For every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check: Utilization : how busy is it? (% time in use) Saturation : is there a queue / waiting work it can't service yet? Errors : any error counts? (drops, retransmits, EIO) Per-resource quick map CPU : util=%us+%sy (top/mpstat); sat=run-queue/load, %st (steal); err=rare Memory: util=used vs available; sat=swap activity (si/so), page scan; err=OOM Disk : util=%util (iostat -x); sat=avgqu-sz/await; err=ioerrors, SMART Network: util=bandwidth vs link; sat=tx/rx queue drops; err=ip -s link errors Why a method beats poking around USE forces you to check every resource systematically instead of fixating on CPU. It quickly rules resources in or out — e.g. high disk await + low CPU points at storage, not the app. Brendan Gregg's USE method is the canonical systematic approach. Interview tip: Naming the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors per resource) signals you debug systematically, not by guessing. The high-value specifics: saturation is the early-warning sign (a queue forming before 100% util), %st steal time reveals a noisy-neighbor/overcommitted hypervisor, and disk await / avgqu-sz catch storage saturation. Pair it with the RED method (Rate/Errors/Duration) for services.

questions.q: How do you read top/htop correctly? Explain load average, %wa, %st, and the columns.
questions.text: Load average # 1/5/15-min averages of runnable + UNINTERRUPTIBLE(D) processes. # Compare to core count: load 8 on 8 cores = fully busy; on 4 cores = overloaded. # KEY: load counts D-state too, so high load can mean stuck I/O, not CPU! nproc # core count for context The CPU line %us user %sy system(kernel) %ni niced %id idle %wa iowait -> CPU idle WAITING on disk I/O -> storage bottleneck %st steal -> hypervisor took your CPU (noisy neighbor / overcommit) — VM tell %si/%hi -> soft/hard interrupts (high = network/IRQ pressure) Reading it High %us -> app/CPU bound High %sy -> syscall/kernel heavy (context switches? check vmstat) High %wa + low %us -> I/O bound (go to iostat) High %st -> you're being starved by the host (resize / move VM) High load, low CPU -> D-state processes -> disk/NFS stuck Interview tip: The two most-missed columns: %wa (CPU idle waiting on disk = it's a storage problem, not CPU) and %st (steal = the hypervisor is taking your cycles, a cloud/VM noisy-neighbor signal). And the load-average subtlety — it includes uninterruptible (D) processes, so high load with low CPU usually means stuck I/O. Always compare load to nproc .

questions.q: Diagnose a disk I/O bottleneck. What do iostat, await, and %util tell you?
questions.text: The tool iostat -xz 1 # extended, skip idle devices, every 1s # Key columns per device: %util : how busy the device is (~100% = saturated, but misleading on SSD/RAID which handle parallel I/O — high %util there isn't always bad) await : avg time (ms) per I/O incl. queue — THE latency number that hurts apps r_await / w_await : split read vs write latency aqu-sz : average queue depth — requests waiting (saturation) r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s : IOPS and throughput What points where High await + high aqu-sz -> device saturated, requests queueing (the real pain) High %util but low await -> busy but keeping up (esp. SSD/RAID) — often fine Which process? -> iotop -o (top I/O consumers) pidstat -d 1 (per-process disk I/O) Beyond the device Correlate with %wa in top (CPU waiting on I/O). Check if it's random vs sequential (random IOPS-bound), the filesystem/scheduler, or a noisy neighbor on shared cloud storage (EBS burst credits exhausted is a classic cloud trap). Interview tip: await is the number that matters (per-I/O latency including queue time) — not %util , which is misleading on SSDs/RAID that service I/O in parallel. High await + growing aqu-sz = saturation. Then attribute it with iotop / pidstat -d . The cloud-savvy bonus: exhausted EBS/burst IOPS credits cause sudden latency cliffs.

questions.q: How do you diagnose memory pressure? Explain free, swap, available, and the page cache.
questions.text: Read free correctly free -h # IGNORE the "free" column. Watch "available" — RAM apps can actually get, # counting reclaimable page cache. "buff/cache" is cached file data (good!), # reclaimed automatically under pressure. Low "free" + high "available" = healthy. Real pressure signals vmstat 1 -> si/so columns: swap IN/OUT activity = real memory pressure -> high 'r' run queue, low 'free', cache shrinking sar -B 1 -> pgscan/majflt: page scanning + MAJOR faults (hitting disk) cat /proc/pressure/memory -> PSI: % time stalled on memory (modern, precise) dmesg | grep -i oom -> OOM kills (you've gone past pressure to failure) Per-process ps aux --sort=-%mem | head # top memory users (RSS) # RSS vs VSZ: RSS = real physical RAM used; VSZ = virtual (often huge, misleading). smem -tk # PSS (shared memory counted fairly) Interview tip: The #1 correction interviewers want: low free is normal — Linux uses spare RAM for page cache; watch available and swap activity ( si/so in vmstat ), not free . Real pressure shows as swapping, page scanning, and major faults. Modern bonus: PSI ( /proc/pressure/memory ) quantifies stall time. RSS (real) vs VSZ (virtual) trips people up — cite RSS for actual usage.

questions.q: What is CPU steal time, context switching, and run queue? When is each a problem?
questions.text: Steal time (%st) # %st = time your vCPU was READY to run but the hypervisor ran someone else. # Seen only in VMs/cloud. Sustained high %st = overcommitted host / noisy neighbor. # You can't fix it from inside — resize, change instance type, or move hosts. mpstat -P ALL 1 # per-core %steal Context switches vmstat 1 -> 'cs' column (context switches/sec), 'in' (interrupts) # Very high cs/sec relative to work done = thrashing: too many threads, # lock contention, or tiny time slices. Voluntary (waiting) vs involuntary # (preempted) switches: pidstat -w shows per-process. Run queue vmstat 1 -> 'r' column = processes runnable/running. # r consistently > number of cores -> CPU saturation (tasks waiting for CPU). # This is "saturation" in the USE method for CPU. Interview tip: Steal time is the cloud signature — high %st means the hypervisor is starving you, fixable only by resizing/moving, not by tuning your app. A run queue ( r in vmstat) persistently above core count = CPU saturation. Excessive context switches (high cs ) hint at over-threading or lock contention. These three are exactly the CPU-side USE-method metrics.

questions.q: How do you profile what a process is spending CPU on? (perf, flame graphs, eBPF)
questions.text: Sample with perf perf top # live, system-wide hottest functions perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30 # sample PID at 99Hz with stacks perf report # interactive breakdown of where CPU went # 99Hz (not 100) avoids lock-stepping with periodic timers. Flame graphs # Turn samples into a visual: width = time on CPU, stacked by call hierarchy. perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > out.svg # Instantly shows the hot path — the widest tower is where the CPU goes. eBPF (low overhead, production) # bcc/bpftrace tools profile with minimal overhead, safe on prod: profile -p <pid> 30 # on-CPU profiler (bcc) offcputime -p <pid> # where it's BLOCKED (off-CPU: locks, I/O, sleep) bpftrace -e 'profile:hz:99 /pid==1234/ { @[ustack] = count(); }' On-CPU vs off-CPU: perf /flame graphs show where CPU is burned . If the process is slow but NOT using CPU, it's blocked — use off-CPU analysis ( offcputime ) to find waits on locks, I/O, or sleep. Many "it's slow" cases are off-CPU. Interview tip: perf record -g + flame graphs is the classic CPU-profiling answer; the visual makes the hot path obvious. The senior depth: distinguish on-CPU (perf) from off-CPU (blocked on locks/I/O — use eBPF offcputime ), and prefer eBPF/bpftrace on production for its low overhead vs strace. Knowing 99Hz sampling avoids timer aliasing is a nice detail.

questions.q: Explain cgroups and how systemd uses them to limit CPU, memory, and I/O.
questions.text: What cgroups do # Control groups limit + account resources for groups of processes. # cgroup v2 (unified hierarchy) is the modern default. It's the kernel # primitive behind container resource limits AND systemd service limits. systemd-cgtop # live per-cgroup CPU/mem/IO (like top, by service) systemd-cgls # the cgroup tree Limit a service via systemd [Service] CPUQuota=50% # max half a core MemoryMax=512M # hard cap -> cgroup OOM kills inside this service only MemoryHigh=400M # soft throttle before the hard cap IOWeight=50 # relative disk I/O share TasksMax=100 # limit thread/process count # Apply live: systemctl set-property myapp.service MemoryMax=1G Why it matters Without limits, one runaway service can starve the whole host. cgroups contain the blast radius: a memory leak hits a per-service OOM (only that service dies) instead of the host OOM killer picking a random victim. CPU limits also explain CFS throttling in containers. Interview tip: Tie it together: cgroups are the kernel mechanism; containers AND systemd both use them. Show you can cap a plain service with MemoryMax / CPUQuota / IOWeight — no container needed. The key benefit is blast-radius containment: a per-cgroup memory limit causes a local OOM kill, protecting the rest of the host. systemd-cgtop is the per-service top .

questions.q: How do you tune key kernel sysctl parameters for a high-traffic server?
questions.text: Common network tunables net.core.somaxconn = 4096 # max accept-queue backlog (raise for high conn rate) net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 8192 # half-open queue net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 1024 65535 # more ephemeral ports net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 # reuse TIME_WAIT for outbound net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 16384 # NIC -> kernel queue net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15 fs.file-max = 2000000 # system-wide fd limit File descriptors (per-process) # sysctl fs.file-max is system-wide; per-process is ulimit / systemd LimitNOFILE: ulimit -n # current # /etc/security/limits.conf or systemd [Service] LimitNOFILE=65535 # "Too many open files" = hit this, not fs.file-max, usually. Apply + persist sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096 # now (non-persistent) echo 'net.core.somaxconn=4096' >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-tuning.conf sysctl --system # reload all # vm.swappiness=10 (favor RAM over swap), vm.max_map_count (Elasticsearch needs high) Don't cargo-cult: measure first, change one thing, re-measure. Blindly copying "tuning guides" can hurt. The most common real fix isn't exotic — it's raising somaxconn and LimitNOFILE (the "too many open files" / connection-drop pair). Interview tip: Know the high-value few rather than reciting dozens: somaxconn + tcp_max_syn_backlog (connection bursts), LimitNOFILE / ulimit -n (the "too many open files" killer), ephemeral port range, and vm.swappiness . Emphasize measuring before/after and persisting via /etc/sysctl.d . The per-process ulimit vs system-wide fs.file-m

questions.q: An app is slow but CPU, memory, and disk look fine. How do you find the real bottleneck?
questions.text: It's probably waiting, not working # Low resource usage + slow = the process is BLOCKED, not busy. Find on what: strace -p <pid> -f -T -e trace=network,read,futex # which syscall stalls (-T = time) offcputime -p <pid> # eBPF: where it's blocked off-CPU (locks/IO/net) ss -ti # TCP rtt/retransmits to dependencies Usual hidden culprits - Downstream latency: a slow DB/API/DNS — your app waits on the network - Lock contention: threads blocked on a mutex (futex in strace; off-CPU stacks) - DNS: 5s resolver timeouts on every request (check /etc/resolv.conf, ndots) - Connection pool exhausted: requests queue waiting for a free connection - GC pauses / single-threaded hot section / external rate limiting (429s) Get end-to-end visibility Distributed tracing (or just timing each external call) localizes the slow hop. "Resources fine" almost always means the time is spent waiting on something external or on a lock — instrument the boundaries. Interview tip: The reframe is the answer: "resources fine but slow" = it's waiting , so do off-CPU analysis, not resource hunting. Name the suspects — downstream dependency latency, lock contention (futex), DNS 5s timeouts, connection-pool exhaustion. The tools that find waits are offcputime (eBPF), strace -T , and tracing. This off-CPU mindset is exactly what separates senior debugging from "check top."

questions.q: Explain LVM: physical volumes, volume groups, logical volumes. Why use it?
questions.text: The layers PV (Physical Volume) : a disk/partition initialized for LVM (pvcreate /dev/sdb) VG (Volume Group) : a pool of PVs (vgcreate data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc) LV (Logical Volume) : carved from a VG, formatted + mounted (lvcreate -L 50G ...) # disks -> pooled into a VG -> sliced into resizable LVs The killer feature: online resize lvextend -L +20G /dev/data/web # grow the LV resize2fs /dev/data/web # grow ext4 filesystem (xfs_growfs for XFS) # Or one step: lvextend -r -L +20G /dev/data/web vgextend data /dev/sdd # add a new disk to the pool first # All ONLINE — no unmount, no downtime. Why use it Flexible capacity (grow filesystems on the fly, span multiple disks), snapshots (point-in-time, e.g. for consistent backups), and the ability to add disks to a pool without repartitioning. The cost is a layer of complexity vs raw partitions. Interview tip: Explain the PV -> VG -> LV stack and lead with the practical win: online filesystem growth ( lvextend -r ) without downtime, plus pooling disks and snapshots. Mention XFS grows but can't shrink (so plan LV sizing), and that LVM snapshots enable consistent backups. This is bread-and-butter for anyone who's expanded a full data volume in production.

questions.q: How do you safely grow a filesystem that's running out of space (cloud + LVM)?
questions.text: Cloud disk (e.g. attached volume, no LVM) 1. Expand the volume in the cloud console/API (e.g. EBS modify). 2. Tell the kernel about the new size: (rescan if needed) echo 1 > /sys/class/block/sdb/device/rescan # or growpart for partitions 3. growpart /dev/nvme1n1 1 # grow the PARTITION to fill the disk 4. resize2fs /dev/nvme1n1p1 # ext4 (xfs_growfs /mount for XFS) # All online. LVM-backed 1. (If new disk) pvcreate /dev/sdd ; vgextend vg /dev/sdd 2. lvextend -r -L +50G /dev/vg/data # -r resizes the fs in the same step # Or grow the underlying disk, then pvresize /dev/sdb, then lvextend -r. Order matters disk/volume -> partition (growpart) -> PV (pvresize) -> LV (lvextend) -> filesystem (resize2fs/xfs_growfs) # You must grow each layer from the bottom up. Skipping a layer = "no space" persists. Gotcha: XFS can only grow (never shrink), and xfs_growfs takes the MOUNTPOINT, not the device. ext4 can shrink but only offline. Always have a backup/snapshot before resizing, and verify with df -h after. Interview tip: The structure interviewers want is the bottom-up layer chain: cloud volume -> partition ( growpart ) -> PV ( pvresize ) -> LV ( lvextend -r ) -> filesystem ( resize2fs / xfs_growfs ). The common failure is growing the disk but forgetting the partition or PV layer, so space never appears. Note it's all online and XFS is grow-only. This is a very common real on-call task.

questions.q: Explain RAID levels (0,1,5,6,10). What are the trade-offs and the RAID-5 rebuild risk?
questions.text: The levels RAID 0 : striping — speed + full capacity, ZERO redundancy (1 disk dies = all lost) RAID 1 : mirroring — full redundancy, 50% capacity, survives 1 disk RAID 5 : striping + 1 parity disk — survives 1 failure, capacity = (N-1) disks RAID 6 : striping + 2 parity — survives 2 failures, capacity = (N-2) RAID 10 : mirror then stripe — fast + redundant, 50% capacity (the DB favorite) The RAID-5 rebuild risk # When a disk fails, rebuild reads EVERY block on ALL remaining disks to # reconstruct parity. On large modern drives this is hours of full-stress reads, # during which a SECOND disk failure (or an unreadable sector) loses everything. # -> RAID 5 is discouraged for large disks; prefer RAID 6 or RAID 10. Operational cat /proc/mdstat # md (software RAID) status + rebuild progress mdadm --detail /dev/md0 # RAID is NOT a backup — it protects against disk failure, not deletion/corruption. Interview tip: Know the trade-off per level (0=speed/no safety, 1=mirror, 5=one-parity, 6=two-parity, 10=mirror+stripe for DBs). The senior point is the RAID-5 rebuild hole : rebuilds stress all disks for hours and a second failure/URE during rebuild is catastrophic, so RAID 6 or 10 is preferred on large drives. And always say "RAID is not a backup" — it doesn't protect against rm or corruption.

questions.q: What is swap, swappiness, and should a database/Kubernetes node have swap?
questions.text: What swap is # Disk space used as overflow when RAM is full — lets the system survive # memory spikes instead of OOM-killing, but swapped pages are SLOW (disk). swapon --show; free -h vm.swappiness = 60 (default) # 0-100: higher = swap more eagerly # Lower (e.g. 10) = prefer keeping things in RAM, swap only when really needed. Databases # DBs hate swap: a hot page swapped to disk = sudden latency cliff. # Common practice: low swappiness (1-10) so swap is a safety net, not routine. # Some disable swap entirely and size RAM properly + rely on OOM tuning. Kubernetes # Historically kubelet REQUIRED swap off (failed to start with swap on) so that # memory limits + OOM behavior were predictable. Newer K8s (1.22+ beta, GA later) # supports swap, but most clusters still run swap off for deterministic limits. Interview tip: Explain swap as an overflow safety net that trades OOM-death for severe slowness. For latency-sensitive workloads (databases), keep swappiness very low so swap stays a last resort, not routine paging. For Kubernetes, the classic answer is swap off for predictable memory limits/OOM (kubelet historically required it), while noting newer versions can support swap. The principle: swapping hot memory = latency cliff.

questions.q: How do you check disk health and predict failures? (SMART, dmesg, errors)
questions.text: SMART data smartctl -a /dev/sda # full SMART attributes smartctl -H /dev/sda # overall health PASSED/FAILED # Watch these attributes (rising = trouble): # Reallocated_Sector_Ct, Current_Pending_Sector, Offline_Uncorrectable, # Reported_Uncorrect, and (SSD) Wear_Leveling / Percentage_Used / Media_Wearout smartctl -t long /dev/sda # run a self-test Kernel + filesystem errors dmesg -T | grep -iE 'I/O error|ata|medium error|reset' # disk errors journalctl -k | grep -i error # EXT4-fs errors / "remounting filesystem read-only" = serious corruption signal. Proactive smartd (smartmontools daemon) # schedule self-tests + alert on SMART changes # In cloud, you usually don't see SMART (managed storage) — watch volume # metrics, I/O errors in dmesg, and degraded-RAID alerts instead. Reality check: SMART catches many but not all failures — disks can die with a clean SMART. Reallocated/pending sectors trending up is the strongest early warning. A filesystem going read-only or repeated I/O errors in dmesg means act now (replace + restore). Interview tip: Lead with smartctl and the meaningful attributes (reallocated/pending sectors, SSD wear) plus dmesg I/O errors and the read-only-remount red flag. The honest senior caveat: SMART isn't a guarantee — disks fail clean — so pair it with proactive smartd alerts and good backups/RAID. The cloud nuance (no SMART on managed volumes; watch metrics/dmesg) shows breadth.

questions.q: Explain NFS: how it works, common problems (stale handles, hangs), and tuning.
questions.text: What NFS is # Network filesystem — mount a remote export as if local. mount -t nfs server:/export /mnt/data # /etc/fstab: server:/export /mnt/data nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0 showmount -e server # list exports The classic problems "Stale file handle" : the server-side file/export changed/recreated under you -> remount, or the mount points to a now-invalid inode. Hard hang : with the default 'hard' mount, if the server dies, I/O BLOCKS FOREVER (processes stuck in D state, load climbs). 'soft' returns errors instead but risks data corruption. 'intr' (old) / use timeo, retrans, and consider 'soft,timeo=' carefully. Tuning + gotchas - NFSv4 (stateful, single port 2049, better security/ID mapping) over v3 - rsize/wsize for throughput; noatime to cut metadata writes - _netdev so it mounts after network; autofs to mount on demand (avoid boot hangs) - A dead NFS server is the #1 cause of D-state pileups + unkillable processes. Interview tip: The two facts that matter most: hard vs soft mounts (hard = block forever if the server dies, causing D-state hangs and rising load; soft = error out but risks corruption), and "stale file handle" meaning the server-side object changed. Tie a hung NFS server to the unkillable-D-state question. Prefer NFSv4, use _netdev /autofs to avoid boot hangs. This is a very common production failure mode.

questions.q: What's the difference between block, file, and object storage? When use each?
questions.text: The three Block : raw volumes (EBS, iSCSI, LVM). You put a filesystem on it. Low latency, attached to ONE host (usually). Like a virtual disk. File : a shared filesystem with a hierarchy (NFS, SMB, EFS). Multiple hosts mount it; POSIX-ish semantics. Like a shared network drive. Object : key -> blob + metadata over HTTP (S3, GCS). Infinite scale, durable, NOT a filesystem (no in-place edit, no POSIX). Like a giant key-value store. When to use each Block -> databases, boot disks, anything needing a real filesystem + low latency File -> shared access across many servers (legacy apps, home dirs, shared assets) Object -> backups, media, logs, static assets, data lakes, anything web-scale + accessed by URL/API. Cheapest + most durable + most scalable. Key distinctions Block = one writer, fast, you manage the fs. File = many writers, POSIX, network latency. Object = HTTP API, versioned, eventually-consistent historically (now strongly consistent on major clouds), but you can't fopen +seek-write it like a file. Interview tip: One line each: block = a virtual disk (DBs, low latency, single attach), file = shared network filesystem (NFS/EFS, many hosts, POSIX), object = HTTP key-blob store (S3, web-scale, durable, no in-place edit). The clarifying point: object storage isn't a filesystem — no partial writes/POSIX semantics — which is why you don't run a database on S3. Map each to a workload to show practical judgment.

questions.q: How do you design a backup strategy? Explain 3-2-1, RPO/RPO, and testing restores.
questions.text: The 3-2-1 rule 3 copies of the data 2 different media/storage types 1 copy OFF-SITE (and ideally 1 OFFLINE/immutable — ransomware can't encrypt it) # Modern extension 3-2-1-1-0: +1 immutable/air-gapped, 0 errors on verified restore. RPO and RTO drive the design RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much DATA LOSS is acceptable? -> dictates backup frequency (hourly snapshots vs daily vs continuous/WAL) RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long to be back UP? -> dictates restore method (hot standby = minutes; cold restore = hours) # Tighter RPO/RTO = more cost. Set them per workload by business need. Backup types + the cardinal rule Full / incremental / differential; app-consistent (quiesce/snapshot the DB, not just copy files mid-write). Encrypt backups; manage retention. # THE RULE: a backup you haven't RESTORED is not a backup. Test restores regularly # (automated restore drills) and measure actual RTO. Untested backups fail silently. Common failures: backups that were silently failing for months; file-level copies of a live database that aren't crash-consistent; backups stored only in the same account/region (ransomware/compromise takes them too). Immutable + off-site/offline copies defend against this. Interview tip: Anchor on 3-2-1 (now 3-2-1-1-0 with immutable + verified), then frame frequency/method by RPO/RTO per workload. The line that lands: "an untested backup isn't a backup" — restore drills are mandatory. Call out app-consistent backups for databases (not raw file cop

questions.q: Walk through the Linux boot process from power-on to login prompt.
questions.text: The stages 1. Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) : POST, find a boot device, load the bootloader 2. Bootloader (GRUB2) : loads the kernel + initramfs into memory, passes cmdline 3. Kernel : initializes hardware/drivers, mounts initramfs (temp rootfs) 4. initramfs : loads modules needed to find + mount the REAL root fs 5. switch_root : pivot to the real root filesystem 6. init = PID 1 (systemd): brings up the system via units/targets 7. Reaches default.target (graphical/multi-user) -> getty -> login prompt systemd's job (stage 6) systemctl get-default # the target it boots to (multi-user/graphical) # systemd activates units in dependency order (not a fixed sequence like SysV), # parallelizing where possible -> faster boot. Where it breaks No bootloader/GRUB -> "no bootable device" Bad initramfs/missing driver -> "cannot mount root" / dropped to initramfs shell Bad /etc/fstab -> emergency mode (a mount failed) journalctl -b -> this boot's logs; journalctl -b -1 -> previous boot Interview tip: Hit the chain: firmware -> GRUB -> kernel -> initramfs (loads drivers to find real root) -> switch_root -> systemd (PID 1) -> target -> login. The most useful debugging knowledge is mapping failures to stages: "can't mount root" = initramfs/driver/fstab, emergency mode = a failed mount, and journalctl -b for the current boot. Knowing why initramfs exists (chicken-and-egg: need drivers to mount the disk holding the drivers) is a great detail.

questions.q: Explain systemd units, targets, and dependencies (Wants, Requires, After).
questions.text: Unit types .service a daemon/process .socket socket activation .target a group of units (~runlevel: multi-user.target, graphical.target) .timer cron replacement .mount/.automount filesystem mounts .path activate on file change .slice cgroup resource grouping Dependency directives Requires=b.service : hard dep — if b fails/stops, this unit is stopped too Wants=b.service : soft dep — start b, but DON'T fail if b fails (preferred) After=b.service : ORDERING only — start after b (does NOT pull b in) Before= : ordering the other way BindsTo= : even stronger than Requires (tied to b's state) # KEY: Requires/Wants = "what to pull in"; After/Before = "in what ORDER". # They are independent — you often need BOTH Wants= and After=. Managing systemctl list-dependencies myapp.service systemctl cat myapp.service # effective unit file systemctl edit myapp.service # drop-in override (don't edit vendor files) Interview tip: The classic gotcha interviewers probe: After= controls ORDER, not whether the dependency starts — you need Wants= / Requires= to actually pull it in. Prefer Wants= (soft) over Requires= (hard) to avoid cascading failures. Targets replace SysV runlevels. Use systemctl edit drop-ins rather than editing vendor unit files — a real-world best practice.

questions.q: How do you create a robust systemd service? Cover Restart, dependencies, and hardening.
questions.text: A solid unit file [Unit] Description=My API After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] ExecStart=/usr/bin/myapi --config /etc/myapi.yaml Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 StartLimitIntervalSec=60 StartLimitBurst=5 # stop flapping: max 5 restarts/60s then give up Type=notify # app signals READY (or simple/exec/forking) TimeoutStopSec=30 # grace before SIGKILL [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Hardening (sandbox the service) User=myapi NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict # most of / read-only ProtectHome=true PrivateTmp=true ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapi MemoryMax=512M CPUQuota=50% # cgroup limits Restart loops: Restart=always without StartLimitBurst can hammer a crashing service forever, hiding the real failure and burning resources. Bound it so systemd backs off and the failure surfaces. Interview tip: Show you write production units, not just ExecStart : Restart=on-failure + StartLimit* (bounded restarts so flapping is visible), correct Type= (notify/simple/forking — getting this wrong makes systemd mis-track readiness), TimeoutStopSec for graceful stop, and sandboxing ( User= , ProtectSystem , NoNewPrivileges , resource limits). That breadth — reliability + security + ordering — is the senior signal.

questions.q: How do you read and manage logs with journalctl? How do you stop the journal filling disk?
questions.text: Querying journalctl -u myapp -f # follow one unit (like tail -f) journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" --until "10 min ago" journalctl -b # this boot; -b -1 previous boot journalctl -p err -b # priority err and above this boot journalctl -k # kernel (dmesg) messages journalctl _PID=1234 / _COMM=sshd # by pid / command journalctl -u myapp -o json-pretty # structured fields Disk usage control journalctl --disk-usage # how big is the journal? journalctl --vacuum-size=500M # trim to 500M now journalctl --vacuum-time=7d # keep only last 7 days # Persist limits in /etc/systemd/journald.conf: SystemMaxUse=1G MaxRetentionSec=2week Persistent vs volatile # If /var/log/journal/ doesn't exist, the journal is in RAM and lost on reboot. mkdir -p /var/log/journal && systemctl restart systemd-journald # make persistent Interview tip: Beyond basic querying, two things stand out: capping journal size ( SystemMaxUse in journald.conf , or --vacuum-size/--vacuum-time ) since an uncapped journal is a real "disk full" cause, and knowing the journal is volatile (RAM-only) unless /var/log/journal exists — so logs can vanish on reboot. journalctl -b -1 to read the previous boot after a crash is invaluable.

questions.q: A server won't boot. How do you recover? (GRUB, rescue/emergency mode, initramfs)
questions.text: Identify the failure stage No GRUB / "no bootable device" -> firmware/bootloader/disk GRUB shows but kernel panics -> kernel/initramfs/root mount Boots then drops to emergency -> a service or fstab mount failed "Give root password for maintenance" -> emergency.target (fstab is the usual cause) Recovery techniques # At GRUB: edit the entry (e) and append a kernel arg: systemd.unit=rescue.target # minimal single-user-ish (or emergency.target) init=/bin/bash # bypass init entirely -> raw shell (then mount -o remount,rw /) # Boot a previous kernel from the GRUB menu if a kernel update broke it. From a rescue/live environment # Boot live USB / cloud rescue, then chroot into the broken system to fix it: mount /dev/sda2 /mnt; mount --bind /dev /mnt/dev; mount --bind /proc /mnt/proc; mount --bind /sys /mnt/sys chroot /mnt # now fix /etc/fstab, reinstall grub (grub-install), rebuild initramfs (dracut/update-initramfs) journalctl -b -1 -p err # what failed on the last boot Interview tip: Structure it by stage (bootloader vs kernel/initramfs vs failed-mount/service), then the toolkit: edit GRUB to add systemd.unit=rescue.target or init=/bin/bash , boot a prior kernel after a bad update, and the chroot-from-rescue flow to repair fstab / reinstall GRUB / rebuild initramfs. Mentioning journalctl -b -1 to see why the last boot failed, and that a bad fstab drops you to emergency mode, shows you've done real recoveries.

questions.q: What changed from SysV init to systemd? Why was systemd adopted despite controversy?
questions.text: SysV init # Sequential shell scripts in /etc/init.d, ordered by runlevel symlinks (S/K numbers). # Slow (serial), no dependency awareness, no built-in process supervision, # each script reinvents start/stop/status. Daemons double-fork to background. What systemd added - Parallel startup with real dependency resolution -> much faster boot - Process supervision (Restart=), proper readiness (Type=notify) - cgroup-based tracking (knows ALL a service's processes — clean stop/limits) - Socket + timer + path activation; unified logging (journald) - Consistent declarative units instead of bespoke shell scripts - Sandboxing directives (ProtectSystem, NoNewPrivileges, ...) The controversy Critics argued it violates Unix "do one thing well" (it absorbed logging, networking, login, etc.), increased complexity, and centralized too much in PID 1. It won anyway because the reliability, speed, supervision, and consistency solved real operational pain that SysV scripts couldn't. Interview tip: Contrast concretely: SysV = serial bespoke shell scripts, no dependency/supervision; systemd = parallel, dependency-aware, cgroup-tracked, self-supervising, declarative. The cgroup tracking point is key — systemd reliably knows and controls every process a service spawns (clean stop, resource limits), which SysV's PID-file guessing couldn't. Acknowledging the "too monolithic / un-Unix" criticism shows balanced judgment.

questions.q: How do systemd timers work, and why prefer them over cron?
questions.text: A timer = two units # backup.service (what to run) + backup.timer (when): # /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer [Timer] OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00 # daily 02:30 (cron-like calendar syntax) Persistent=true # if missed (machine off), run on next boot RandomizedDelaySec=300 # jitter to avoid thundering-herd across hosts [Install] WantedBy=timers.target systemctl enable --now backup.timer systemctl list-timers # next/last run for all timers Why over cron + Persistent=true catches missed runs (cron just skips if the box was off — anacron needed) + Output goes to the journal (journalctl -u backup) — cron emails/loses output + Dependencies + ordering (After=) and resource limits via the .service + RandomizedDelaySec spreads load across a fleet + Same tooling as everything else (systemctl status, supervision, monotonic timers) Interview tip: The advantages that matter: Persistent=true (runs a missed job after downtime — cron silently skips, needing anacron), output in the journal (cron's lost/emailed output is a real pain), dependency ordering, resource control, and RandomizedDelaySec to de-synchronize a fleet. Also OnUnitActiveSec= for monotonic intervals. Knowing a timer is a .timer + .service pair, and systemctl list-timers , shows hands-on use.

questions.q: Explain /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/group. What's in each field?
questions.text: /etc/passwd (world-readable) name:x:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell alice:x:1000:1000:Alice A:/home/alice:/bin/bash # 'x' = password is in /etc/shadow (not here). Shell /usr/sbin/nologin or # /bin/false = account can't get an interactive login (service accounts). /etc/shadow (root-only, 0640) name:$6$salt$hash:lastchange:min:max:warn:inactive:expire # $6$ = SHA-512.
