Stateless firewalls (AWS Network ACLs, some hardware firewalls) require explicit allow rules for both directions. GCP Firewall is stateful — you only need an ingress allow rule, not an egress rule for established connections. NACLs in AWS require both inbound and outbound rules. GCP specifics: GCP Firewall rules are stateful and applied per VM via network tags or SA bindings. Default VPC allows all internal traffic and all outbound. Custom VPCs have a default-deny for all traffic — you must explicitly allow everything including intra-VPC.

questions.q: What is a DDoS attack — how do you protect cloud services against it?
questions.text: Volumetric: flood bandwidth (UDP flood, ICMP flood) Protocol: exhaust state (SYN flood — fill TCP connection table) Application layer: exhaust CPU (HTTP flood, slow loris) gcloud compute security-policies create <name> # Cloud Armor WAF/DDoS policy gcloud compute security-policies rules create 1000 --security-policy=<name> --expression="request.headers['User-Agent'].matches('bad-bot')" --action=deny-403 GCP protection layers: Global HTTP(S) LB absorbs volumetric attacks (Google's global network scrubs traffic before it reaches your backends), Cloud Armor for WAF rules and L7 DDoS protection (rate limiting, geo-blocking, OWASP rules), Google Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection for ML-based attack detection. For SYN floods: GCP's load balancers handle SYN cookies automatically — your backend VMs never see the flood. Rate limiting: Implement at multiple layers: Cloud Armor (LB level), application-level rate limiting (per-user, per-IP), and API gateway throttling. Defense in depth. A single rate limit at one layer can be bypassed by distributing requests across sources.

questions.q: What is mTLS (mutual TLS) — how is it implemented in Kubernetes?
questions.text: Regular TLS: only server presents a certificate (client verifies server identity) mTLS: both client AND server present certificates (mutual verification) kubectl get peerauthentication -A # Istio mTLS policy kubectl get destinationrule -A # Istio client-side TLS config In Kubernetes: Istio and Linkerd inject sidecar proxies that handle mTLS transparently — application code doesn't change. The service mesh CA issues short-lived certificates to each pod (using SPIFFE/SPIRE standard). Benefits: all service-to-service traffic is encrypted and authenticated, zero-trust within the cluster (even internal traffic is verified). Enable with PeerAuthentication: STRICT in Istio per namespace. Zero trust networking: mTLS + NetworkPolicies + RBAC = zero trust inside a Kubernetes cluster. Even if an attacker gets into the cluster, they can't speak to services without a valid certificate, and NetworkPolicies block unexpected traffic paths.

questions.q: What is a network proxy — how do forward and reverse proxies differ?
questions.text: Forward proxy: client → proxy → internet (hides client, used for egress filtering) Reverse proxy: client → proxy → backend servers (hides backend, used for LB/TLS termination) curl -x http://<proxy>:3128 <url> # use forward proxy env | grep -i proxy # check proxy env vars Reverse proxy use cases: TLS termination (nginx/Envoy handles TLS, backends get plain HTTP), load balancing (distribute requests across backends), caching (serve cached responses), rate limiting, and authentication (add auth layer in front of unprotected service). In Kubernetes: every Ingress controller IS a reverse proxy (nginx, Envoy/Contour, Traefik). Service mesh sidecars (Envoy) are transparent reverse + forward proxies per pod. Envoy proxy: Envoy is the de facto proxy for cloud-native networking. It powers Istio sidecars, GCP's load balancers (Envoy-based), Cloud Service Mesh, and many API gateways. Understanding Envoy's listener → filter chain → cluster → endpoint model helps debug service mesh issues at the proxy level.

questions.q: How does a load balancer distribute traffic — what are the different algorithms?
questions.text: Round Robin: requests distributed sequentially across backends (default, good for uniform load) Least Connections: route to backend with fewest active connections (good for variable request cost) IP Hash: hash source IP to backend (session affinity without cookies) Weighted: assign proportional traffic share (canary: 90% v1, 10% v2) Random with 2 choices (P2C): pick 2 random, route to less loaded (best for microservices) GCP HTTP(S) LB uses a combination of consistent hashing and session affinity. For gRPC/HTTP2 with long-lived connections, round-robin per-connection is wrong — you need per-request load balancing. Envoy in service mesh does per-request load balancing over HTTP/2 multiplexed connections, which is why service mesh L7 load balancing outperforms K8s kube-proxy (L4) for gRPC workloads. Health checks: Load balancers continuously health check backends. If a backend fails health check, it's removed from the pool. Always configure separate health check endpoints ( /healthz ) that return 200 quickly without side effects — don't use your main API endpoint.

questions.q: What is session affinity (sticky sessions) — when should you use it and what are the risks?
questions.text: Session affinity: route requests from the same client always to the same backend Methods: client IP hash, cookie-based (insert cookie with backend ID), HTTP header # GCP HTTP LB: configure affinity via backend service gcloud compute backend-services update <name> --session-affinity=GENERATED_COOKIE --affinity-cookie-ttl=3600 Use sticky sessions when: application state is stored in-process on the backend (legacy apps, websockets). Risks: hot spots (one backend gets all traffic from heavy users), failover breaks sessions (sticky session target dies — all its users get disrupted), and prevents horizontal scaling from distributing load evenly. Prefer stateless backends with shared session storage (Redis, Memorystore) — this eliminates the need for session affinity entirely. Kubernetes websockets: WebSocket connections are long-lived — once established, they stay on one pod. This is inherently sticky. Ensure the pod it's connected to is not evicted/rescheduled without graceful connection migration, or use a message broker (Redis Pub/Sub) for shared connection state.

questions.q: What is the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing — when do you need each?
questions.text: L4 (Transport): routes by IP + port only — fast, no content inspection L4 examples: kube-proxy (iptables DNAT), TCP Network LB, AWS NLB L7 (Application): inspects HTTP headers, URL, cookies — intelligent routing L7 examples: nginx Ingress, Envoy, GCP HTTP(S) LB, AWS ALB L4 advantages: lower latency (no HTTP parsing), preserves original client IP (no need for X-Forwarded-For), handles any TCP/UDP protocol. L7 advantages: URL-based routing (route /api to one service, /static to another), header-based canary (route 10% by header), TLS termination, HTTP/2 multiplexing, WebSocket upgrade handling, request/response modification. Use L4 for non-HTTP (databases, SMTP, custom protocols). Use L7 for HTTP APIs — the routing intelligence is worth the small overhead. Kubernetes services: ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer are L4 — they route by port. Ingress is L7 — routes by hostname and URL path. For gRPC load balancing, you need L7 (H2 stream-level balancing) — L4 kube-proxy only balances at the TCP connection level, which defeats multiplexing.

questions.q: What is a VPC — how does cloud VPC networking differ from traditional networking?
questions.text: gcloud compute networks create <name> --subnet-mode=custom # create VPC gcloud compute networks subnets create <name> --network=<vpc> --region=<r> --range=10.0.0.0/24 gcloud compute networks describe <name> # VPC config Traditional networking: physical switches, VLANs, hardware routers, spanning tree. Cloud VPC: software-defined, no physical topology, global (GCP VPCs span all regions — single VPC with subnets in us-central1 and europe-west1), firewall rules enforced at the VM level (not at a perimeter device), and routes are virtual. Key differences: no broadcast/multicast (ARP is handled by the hypervisor), no spanning tree, no VLANs (use subnets for segmentation), no L2 adjacency between subnets. GCP VPC is global: Unlike AWS where VPCs are regional, a GCP VPC spans all regions. You create subnets per region within the same VPC. VMs in different regions within the same VPC can communicate using internal IPs without VPC peering — a major architectural simplification.

questions.q: What is an Overlay network — how does it work in Kubernetes (VXLAN, CNI)?
questions.text: Overlay: virtual L2 network tunneled over L3 underlay (physical network) VXLAN: encapsulates L2 frames in UDP packets — allows L2 across L3 boundaries kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|flannel|cilium|weave" # identify CNI ip link show | grep -E "vxlan|cni|flannel" # show overlay interfaces In Kubernetes: each CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel) implements pod networking. Flannel uses VXLAN overlay — every pod IP is routable within the cluster via tunnels, regardless of the underlying node network. Calico can use BGP (no encapsulation overhead) if the underlay supports it. On GKE with VPC-native clusters, pod IPs are actual VPC IPs — no overlay needed, pods are directly routable from anywhere in the VPC. GKE VPC-native: GKE VPC-native clusters allocate a /24 pod CIDR per node from a reserved VPC range. No overlay — pods are first-class VPC citizens with their own IPs. This enables direct VPC connectivity to pods and is more efficient than overlay networks.

questions.q: What is a Service Mesh — how does it handle networking in microservices?
questions.text: kubectl get pods -n istio-system # Istio control plane istioctl proxy-status # sidecar sync status istioctl analyze -n <ns> # config validation kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy # sidecar proxy logs Service mesh injects a sidecar proxy (Envoy) into every pod. All traffic goes through the sidecar — the app talks to localhost, the sidecar handles actual network calls. This transparently adds: mTLS, observability (traces, metrics, access logs per request), retry policies, circuit breaking, traffic shifting (canary), and timeout enforcement. The control plane (Istiod) distributes config to all sidecars. Sidecar overhead: Every pod has an additional Envoy container consuming ~50-100MB RAM and adding ~1-2ms latency per hop. For very latency-sensitive or memory-constrained workloads, this matters. Cilium eBPF-based service mesh avoids sidecars entirely by implementing L7 policy in the kernel.

questions.q: A microservice is intermittently returning errors — walk through your systematic troubleshooting approach.
questions.text: Intermittent errors require a methodical approach — not random command firing. Follow the signal, not the noise. 1. Quantify: what % of requests are failing? Which endpoints? Since when? 2. Correlate: CPU spikes? Deploy events? Upstream changes? 3. Isolate: which component in the call chain is failing? kubectl logs <pod> -f --since=5m | grep -iE "error|warn|timeout" kubectl top pods -n <ns> # resource pressure? kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp curl -w "%{http_code} %{time_total} " -o /dev/null -s <url> # measure latency Intermittent often means: a subset of pods have an issue (check per-pod metrics), external dependency is flapping (DNS, database, third-party API), resource exhaustion under load (connection pool, file descriptors, memory), or a race condition triggered by specific request patterns. Distributed traces (Cloud Trace, Jaeger) show exactly which service in the call chain added the latency or returned the error. The 5 whys for networking: Error → which service? → which dependency? → which resource? → which config? → which change? Each why narrows from symptom to root cause.

questions.q: High network latency is reported between two services — how do you diagnose it?
questions.text: ping -c 100 <host> | tail -5 # baseline RTT and packet loss mtr --report <host> # per-hop latency + loss (run for 60s) curl -w "namelookup: %{time_namelookup} connect: %{time_connect} starttransfer: %{time_starttransfer} total: %{time_total} " -o /dev/null -s <url> ss -tin dst <ip> # TCP info for active connection: RTT, retransmits iperf3 -c <host> -t 30 # throughput test Latency sources: DNS resolution (check time_namelookup — should be <10ms within cluster), TCP handshake (round-trip to the server — baseline RTT), TLS handshake (1-2 RTT for TLS 1.2, 1 RTT for TLS 1.3), server processing time (time_starttransfer - time_connect), and response transfer time. Isolate which phase is slow using curl's timing breakdown. In-cluster latency: Pod-to-pod latency within a zone should be <1ms. If you're seeing 50ms+, check: NetworkPolicies adding iptables overhead, service mesh sidecar chains, cross-zone traffic (costs money + adds latency), or CPU throttling on the destination pod causing slow processing.

questions.q: Packet loss is occurring in the network — how do you detect and locate it?
questions.text: ping -c 1000 <host> | grep "packet loss" # detect packet loss mtr --report --report-cycles 100 <host> # per-hop loss (find the problematic hop) netstat -s | grep -i "retransmit|error|drop" # interface-level drops ip -s link show eth0 # interface rx/tx errors and drops ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i drop # NIC-level drop counters Packet loss sources: NIC buffer overflow (increase ring buffer with ethtool), kernel buffer overflow (increase net.core.rmem_max, wmem_max), CPU overload causing interrupt processing delays, network congestion (QoS / buffer bloat), or deliberate firewall drops. Distinguish random loss (congestion) from burst loss (buffer overflow) with mtr's loss pattern. In cloud VMs: packet loss is usually due to bandwidth throttling — VMs have per-VM network egress limits. TCP vs UDP loss: TCP hides packet loss via retransmission — you see latency spikes, not errors. UDP exposes loss directly. If TCP looks fine but UDP shows loss, the network has loss that TCP is masking with retransmits. Check netstat -s | grep retransmit to catch TCP-hidden loss.

questions.q: A service works from one location but not another — how do you troubleshoot path-dependent connectivity?
questions.text: curl -v <url> # from both working and failing location traceroute -T -p 443 <host> # compare network paths from both locations dig <host> # compare DNS resolution from both locations curl -H "Host: <expected-host>" http://<ip> # bypass DNS — test by IP Path-dependent issues: DNS resolves to different IPs (split-horizon, geo-routing), firewall rules blocking a specific source IP/range, routing asymmetry (request goes one path, reply goes another — stateful firewall breaks this), or geographic load balancer routing to different backends with different configs. First confirm DNS gives the same IP from both locations. Then test by IP (bypassing DNS) to isolate DNS vs routing. Cloud Connectivity Tests: For GCP, use Network Intelligence Center → Connectivity Tests to simulate the packet path from source to destination including firewall rule analysis. Far faster than manual traceroute analysis for cloud-to-cloud paths.

questions.q: How do you use tcpdump and Wireshark to debug network issues?
questions.text: tcpdump -i eth0 -n port 80 # capture HTTP traffic tcpdump -i any -n host <ip> and port 443 # filter by host and port tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap # write to file for Wireshark tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' # capture RST packets only tcpdump -i any port 53 -n # capture DNS queries kubectl sniff <pod> -n <ns> -f "port 80" -o cap.pcap # capture from K8s pod tcpdump is the primary packet capture tool for Linux. Key filters: host <ip> (either direction), src/dst host <ip> (directional), port <n> , proto tcp/udp . RST packets indicate rejected connections. Missing ACKs indicate loss. Retransmissions indicate loss or congestion. Load the pcap in Wireshark (Statistics → TCP Stream Graph for visual latency analysis) or use tshark for CLI analysis. Kubernetes capture: Use kubectl-sniff plugin or kubectl debug with a debug container sharing the pod's network namespace to capture traffic from running pods without restart. This is essential for debugging service mesh encrypted traffic at the pod's network interface (before Envoy encrypts it).

questions.q: How do you debug high CPU on a network device or high kernel networking overhead?
questions.text: top -1 # per-CPU usage — check si (softirq) column mpstat -P ALL 1 5 # per-CPU interrupt distribution cat /proc/net/softnet_stat # softirq drops per CPU sar -n DEV 1 10 # network interface throughput stats perf top -e net:* # kernel networking events (requires perf) High si (software interrupt) CPU usage indicates network interrupt processing. This happens when a single CPU core handles all NIC interrupts (IRQ affinity not configured). Fix: enable RSS (Receive Side Scaling) to distribute interrupts across CPUs, or configure IRQ affinity manually. iptables with many rules also causes high si — each packet traverses all rules. Migrating to IPVS mode in kube-proxy or Cilium eBPF eliminates most iptables overhead. Kubernetes scale: At 1000+ services, iptables kube-proxy mode has O(n) rule complexity — every new Service adds rules every pod must traverse. IPVS mode uses hash tables (O(1) lookup). Cilium replaces iptables entirely with eBPF. At scale, the networking datapath matters significantly for host CPU usage.

questions.q: What is ICMP and how is it used for network diagnostics?
questions.text: ping -c 5 <host> # ICMP echo request/reply — reachability + RTT ping -s 1400 <host> # test with larger packet (detect MTU issues) ping -M do -s 1472 <host> # don't fragment — MTU path discovery ICMP types: echo/echo-reply (ping), destination unreachable (port/host unreachable), time exceeded (TTL expired — used by traceroute), redirect (routing suggestion). Ping tests L3 reachability only — a successful ping doesn't mean the application port is open. "ICMP blocked but TCP works" is common in cloud environments where ICMP is filtered. Never conclude "host is down" from ping failure alone in cloud environments. MTU and ICMP: If large pings fail but small ones succeed, you have an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) mismatch. This causes TCP sessions to hang after the initial handshake (which uses small packets) but fail for data transfers (which use large packets). Fix: reduce MTU on the interface or enable path MTU discovery.

questions.q: What is MTU and why do MTU mismatches cause mysterious connectivity issues?
questions.text: ip link show eth0 | grep mtu # current MTU (default 1500 for Ethernet) ping -M do -s 1472 <host> # test with 1472 bytes + 28 bytes header = 1500 MTU ping -M do -s 1400 <host> # test with smaller packet (try if 1472 fails) ip link set eth0 mtu 1450 # reduce MTU (VPN/overlay use case) MTU is the maximum packet size a network can carry. Standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes. VPNs, VXLAN overlays, and GRE tunnels add encapsulation headers (50-100 bytes), reducing effective MTU to 1400-1450 bytes. If a large packet exceeds the MTU and the DF (Don't Fragment) bit is set, a router sends ICMP "fragmentation needed" back. If ICMP is blocked (common in cloud), this message never arrives — TCP stalls mysteriously. Fix: reduce MTU on the source, or ensure ICMP type 3 (destination unreachable / fragmentation needed) is not blocked. Kubernetes + MTU: CNI plugins often set pod MTU to 1450 to account for VXLAN overhead. If MTU is misconfigured (pod MTU set to 1500 but VXLAN adds 50 bytes), large pod-to-pod transfers silently fail. Always verify CNI MTU config matches the underlying network MTU minus overlay overhead.

questions.q: What is DNS negative caching and how can it cause production incidents?
questions.text: dig <nonexistent.domain> # returns NXDOMAIN with SOA TTL dig SOA <domain> | grep MINIMUM # SOA minimum = negative cache TTL # In Kubernetes CoreDNS: check negative_ttl in Corefile kubectl describe cm coredns -n kube-system | grep cache Negative caching: resolvers cache NXDOMAIN responses for the SOA minimum TTL. If a new DNS record is created but old caches hold the NXDOMAIN, clients continue to get "not found" for up to the negative TTL duration. Scenario: you create a new Service, its DNS propagates, but pods that recently got NXDOMAIN have it cached and won't retry for 30s (CoreDNS default negative TTL). Fix: reduce negative TTL in CoreDNS, or restart affected pods to flush their local resolver cache. Application DNS caching: JVM caches DNS by default (ttl = -1 in older JVMs = cache forever). A JVM app that resolved a service IP will keep using that IP even after DNS changes. Set networkaddress.cache.ttl=30 in JVM security properties. This catches many teams off-guard during rolling deployments.

questions.q: What are socket buffers and how does buffer bloat affect performance?
questions.text: cat /proc/sys/net/core/rmem_default # default recv buffer (bytes) cat /proc/sys/net/core/rmem_max # max recv buffer cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_rmem # TCP recv buffer: min default max sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=134217728 # tune for high-bandwidth, high-latency links ss -tm # show actual buffer usage per socket Send/receive buffers hold data in-flight. Too small: throughput is limited (can't fill the pipe on high-latency links). Too large: buffer bloat — data queues up in buffers, increasing latency without improving throughput. The bandwidth-delay product (BDP) formula: optimal buffer = bandwidth × RTT. For a 10Gbps link with 100ms RTT, BDP = 125MB — default Linux buffers (256KB) are too small. Increase for cross-region cloud transfers. Kubernetes pod file descriptors: Each TCP connection consumes a file descriptor. Default ulimit -n is often 1024 or 65536. High-connection pods (proxies, databases) can exhaust this limit, causing "too many open files" errors. Set ulimit -n 1000000 in container startup or adjust via pod securityContext.

questions.q: What is ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) routing — how does it affect cloud networking?
questions.text: ECMP: multiple equal-cost routes to same destination — packets distributed across paths ip route show | grep "nexthop" # show multipath routes # GCP: automatically uses ECMP for multi-NIC instances and multi-gateway VPNs ECMP distributes traffic across multiple paths using a hash of {src IP, dst IP, src port, dst port, protocol}. Benefits: higher aggregate bandwidth, redundancy (if one path fails, hash rebalances). Gotcha: TCP connections are per-flow sticky (same 5-tuple always takes same path), so ECMP doesn't help for a single large TCP connection (use multipath TCP for that). In Kubernetes: kube-proxy and IPVS use ECMP-like per-connection hashing for Service load balancing. GCP VPN ECMP: If you have two Cloud VPN tunnels to the same destination, GCP automatically does ECMP — traffic is load-balanced across both tunnels. You get ~2× the bandwidth of a single VPN tunnel. Use Active/Active VPN for throughput; Active/Passive for simple failover.

questions.q: What is a CDN — how does it work and when should you use it?
questions.text: CDN: Cache static content at edge PoPs worldwide — serve from nearest location Cache-Control: max-age=86400, public # HTTP header to make content CDN-cacheable Surrogate-Control: max-age=3600 # CDN-specific cache TTL (overrides Cache-Control) Vary: Accept-Encoding # cache different variants per encoding gcloud compute backend-buckets update <name> --enable-cdn # enable Cloud CDN CDN reduces latency (serve from edge PoP near user instead of origin datacenter), reduces origin bandwidth and load, and improves availability (CDN serves cached content even if origin is down). Use for: static assets (JS, CSS, images), cacheable API responses, video streaming. Don't use for: authenticated content (unless varies correctly), highly personalized responses, real-time data. GCP Cloud CDN integrates with Cloud Storage and HTTP(S) Load Balancer — enable with one flag. Cache key: CDN caches by URL + selected headers (Vary). A cache miss goes to origin; a cache hit serves directly from edge. Cache hit rate is the key metric. Low hit rate means content is either not cacheable, has too-short TTL, or the cache key is too specific (vary on too many headers).

questions.q: What is eBPF — how is it changing cloud-native networking?
questions.text: eBPF: extended Berkeley Packet Filter — run sandboxed programs in Linux kernel bpftool prog list # list loaded eBPF programs bpftool net show # eBPF programs attached to network interfaces # Cilium uses eBPF to replace iptables entirely: cilium status # cilium eBPF datapath status eBPF allows safe, JIT-compiled programs to run in the kernel without kernel modules. In networking: Cilium uses eBPF to implement Kubernetes Services, NetworkPolicies, and L7 observability without iptables — dramatically lower CPU overhead and O(1) rule lookup at any scale. Pixie uses eBPF for zero-instrumentation observability (automatic tracing without code changes). Falco uses eBPF for runtime security. This is the future of cloud-native networking infrastructure. Principal-level signal: Mentioning eBPF awareness — even conceptually — signals you follow infrastructure trends. Saying "we use Cilium in our cluster instead of kube-proxy for better performance at scale" is the kind of Principal-level architectural decision that differentiates candidates.

questions.q: What is Zero Trust Networking — how do you implement it in practice?
questions.text: Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. No implicit trust based on network location. Every request is authenticated and authorized regardless of where it comes from. Traditional: trust inside the perimeter, distrust outside Zero Trust: authenticate everything, encrypt everything, least privilege everywhere # Kubernetes zero trust layers: 1. mTLS (Istio) — every service-to-service call is mutually authenticated 2. NetworkPolicies — restrict which pods can talk to which 3. RBAC — restrict which services can call which APIs 4. Service accounts with minimal permissions — no broad access GCP BeyondCorp Enterprise implements zero trust for user access — users authenticate via identity-aware proxy (IAP) using device context + identity, no VPN needed. For Kubernetes: service mesh mTLS + NetworkPolicies + OPA/Kyverno policies = zero trust within the cluster. The perimeter assumption is obsolete — assume breach and design for lateral movement resistance. Interview relevance: Security-focused employers will appreciate zero trust framing. Every answer about network segmentation, access control, or service-to-service communication should reference zero trust principles — it aligns with their product philosophy and shows security-first platform thinking.

questions.q: Walk through a complete methodology for troubleshooting "the application is slow" in a cloud-native environment.
questions.text: This is the Principal-level systems thinking question. The interviewer wants to see structure, not a list of random commands. Structured methodology Phase 1 — Observe: quantify "slow" (P50/P99 latency? error rate? which endpoints?) Phase 2 — Scope: is it all users? One region? One service? After which deploy? Phase 3 — Isolate: L3 reachable? L4 port open? L7 response correct? Which hop is slow? Phase 4 — Drill down: traces → logs → metrics → code Phase 5 — Fix + verify: make one change, measure impact, confirm improvement curl -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total} " -o /dev/null -s <url> kubectl top pods -n <ns> --sort-by=cpu # resource saturation? gcloud trace list --project=<project> # distributed traces for call chain latency The breakdown: DNS lookup slow → resolver issue. TCP connect slow → routing, firewall, server overload. TLS slow → cert negotiation, OCSP. TTFB (Time To First Byte) slow → server processing, database queries, upstream dependencies. Transfer slow → throughput/MTU issue. Each phase pinpoints the layer. Escalate with data: "P99 latency is 2s, TTFB accounts for 1.8s, traced to the database query in service X taking 1.6s on cache miss." Platform Engineer framing: Don't just describe commands — describe how you'd present findings to the team, how you'd avoid recurrence (add this metric to dashboards, add SLO on this endpoint, add a test that catches this regression). That's the d

questions.q: What is MTU, MSS, and Path MTU Discovery — and how does an MTU mismatch cause a 'black hole'?
questions.text: MTU is the largest L2 frame payload a link carries (typically 1500 bytes on Ethernet). MSS is the largest TCP segment the data payload can be. PMTUD finds the smallest MTU along a path. The relationship MSS = MTU - IP header (20) - TCP header (20) = 1500 - 40 = 1460 (typical) # Overlay/VPN/tunnels REDUCE effective MTU (VXLAN ~50 bytes, IPsec more) The PMTUD black hole When a packet exceeds a link's MTU and has the Don't-Fragment bit set, the router drops it and sends back an ICMP "fragmentation needed" (Type 3 Code 4). If a firewall blocks that ICMP , the sender never learns to shrink — large packets vanish silently. Small packets (handshake, pings) work; large transfers (a big POST, a TLS cert) hang. That asymmetry is the fingerprint. ping -M do -s 1472 <host> # 1472 + 28 = 1500; bump down until it passes tracepath <host> # shows PMTU along the path ip link show eth0 # check the interface MTU Production gotcha: Classic in overlay networks (Kubernetes CNI, VXLAN) and VPNs. Symptoms: SSH connects but hangs on output, TLS handshake stalls, some HTTP works and some doesn't. Fix: allow ICMP type 3, lower the MTU, or clamp MSS. Interview tip: The senior fix is MSS clamping ( iptables ... --clamp-mss-to-pmtu or router config) so TCP negotiates a safe segment size up front instead of relying on ICMP that firewalls often drop. Mentioning the "small works, large hangs" tell shows you've debugged this for real.

questions.q: Explain NAT, SNAT, DNAT, and PAT. Where does each happen in cloud networking?
questions.text: NAT rewrites IP addresses (and ports) as packets cross a boundary. The variants differ by which side and what gets rewritten. The variants SNAT (Source NAT) : rewrite the SOURCE addr — outbound (private -> public) DNAT (Destination NAT) : rewrite the DEST addr — inbound (public -> private backend) PAT (Port Address Tr.): many private IPs share one public IP via unique source ports (a.k.a. "NAT overload" / masquerade) Where in the cloud NAT Gateway : SNAT/PAT for private subnets reaching the internet (outbound) Load balancer : DNAT inbound traffic to backend pool members Internet GW : 1:1 NAT for public IPs (EIP private IP) K8s kube-proxy : DNAT Service VIP -> pod IP; SNAT for node-to-pod return paths Gotcha: SNAT/PAT hides the original client source IP from the backend — you see the NAT/LB IP instead. Preserve the real client IP via X-Forwarded-For (L7), PROXY protocol (L4), or externalTrafficPolicy: Local in Kubernetes. Interview tip: A cloud NAT Gateway does SNAT+PAT so many private instances egress through a few public IPs — and at scale you can exhaust source ports per destination (~64k per dest IP:port tuple), causing connection failures. Knowing the source-IP-preservation problem and SNAT port exhaustion signals real cloud-network experience.

questions.q: How does ARP work, and what problems do gratuitous ARP and ARP caching cause in production?
questions.text: ARP maps an IP to a MAC address within a layer-2 broadcast domain — the glue between L3 routing and L2 delivery. The flow Host wants to send to 10.0.0.5 on its subnet: 1. Broadcast: "who has 10.0.0.5? tell 10.0.0.1" (ARP request) 2. 10.0.0.5 replies with its MAC (ARP reply) 3. Sender caches IP->MAC in its ARP table (with a timeout) ip neigh show # view the ARP/neighbor cache Gratuitous ARP (failover) An unsolicited ARP announcing "this IP is now at MY MAC" — used in VIP failover (keepalived, VRRP, cloud floating IPs) so switches and peers update their tables and traffic moves to the new active node. Production problems: Stale ARP caches after a failover (peers keep sending to the dead node's MAC until the entry ages out) cause a brief outage. ARP spoofing is a security risk (attacker claims a gateway's IP). Duplicate IPs cause ARP flapping. On large flat L2 segments, ARP broadcast traffic itself becomes noise. Interview tip: Tie gratuitous ARP to VIP failover — it's how keepalived/VRRP redirects a floating IP. The classic incident is a failover where traffic doesn't move because a peer or switch cached the old MAC; gratuitous ARP (or a lower ARP timeout) is what fixes the convergence. Cloud platforms abstract this with API-driven IP reassignment instead of L2 ARP.

questions.q: Map L2/L3/L7 concepts to cloud load balancers. What operates at each layer and why does it matter?
questions.text: Cloud networking maps directly onto OSI layers; knowing the layer of each component tells you what it can and can't see. The mapping L2 (frames/MAC) : VLANs, the VPC's underlying switching (mostly abstracted in cloud) L3 (IP/routing) : VPC route tables, subnets, NAT GW, Network LB (NLB) — IP-level L4 (TCP/UDP) : Network/L4 LB — balances by IP:port, no app awareness, fast L7 (HTTP/app) : Application LB (ALB) — sees URLs, headers, cookies, host Why the layer matters L4 LB : ultra-fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves source IP easily, can't route by path -> use for TCP/UDP, gRPC raw, extreme throughput, static IP needs L7 LB : path/host routing, TLS termination, header manipulation, WAF integration -> use for HTTP(S) microservices, content-based routing Gotcha: An L4 LB can't do path-based routing or read headers — it only sees IP:port. An L7 LB terminates the connection (two TCP sessions: client LB and LB backend), which changes source IP visibility and TLS handling. Pick the layer to match what you need to route on. Interview tip: The crisp framing: choose the lowest layer that meets your routing needs. L4 for raw speed/protocol-agnostic/source-IP preservation; L7 when you must route on HTTP attributes or terminate TLS centrally. Naming AWS NLB (L4) vs ALB (L7), or GCP's equivalents, grounds it in real cloud products.

questions.q: Compare IPv4 vs IPv6 in practice. What is dual-stack and the Happy Eyeballs algorithm?
questions.text: IPv6 solves IPv4 address exhaustion with a vastly larger space and removes the need for NAT, but adoption is gradual via dual-stack. Key practical differences IPv4 : 32-bit (~4.3B addrs), needs NAT, ARP for L2 resolution IPv6 : 128-bit (huge), no NAT needed (global addrs), uses NDP not ARP, SLAAC autoconfig, link-local addresses (fe80::/10) Dual-stack + Happy Eyeballs Dual-stack hosts have both IPv4 and IPv6. Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) is the client algorithm that races both: it fires the AAAA (IPv6) and A (IPv4) lookups, attempts connections in parallel with a slight head start for IPv6, and uses whichever connects first — so a broken IPv6 path doesn't stall the user. # Without Happy Eyeballs, a broken IPv6 route = long timeout before IPv4 fallback. # With it, the client falls back near-instantly -> resilient UX during v6 issues. Gotcha: Misconfigured IPv6 (AAAA record exists but the path is broken) causes intermittent slowness on dual-stack clients that lack Happy Eyeballs, or where the fallback timer is long. Test both stacks; don't publish a AAAA record until the v6 path actually works end to end. Interview tip: Happy Eyeballs is the detail that signals depth — it's why "my IPv6 is broken but the internet still works." In cloud, dual-stack VPCs help with IPv4 exhaustion (a real cost/scarcity issue); mention that IPv6 eliminates NAT, simplifying some architectures while complicating firewall rules.

questions.q: What is connection tracking (conntrack) and how does table exhaustion take down a busy host?
questions.text: Conntrack is the kernel's stateful table of every connection passing through a NAT/firewall host, so return traffic is matched and NAT is consistent. It's finite. Why it exists # For stateful firewalling + NAT, the kernel remembers each flow: # (src ip:port, dst ip:port, proto, state) conntrack -L | wc -l # current entries cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max # the cap cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count # current count Exhaustion failure When the table fills, the kernel drops new connections and logs nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet . Symptoms: sudden connection failures/timeouts on a busy gateway, NAT instance, or Kubernetes node — even though CPU/mem look fine. dmesg | grep conntrack # "table full" messages # Mitigate: raise nf_conntrack_max, tune timeouts (esp. TIME_WAIT/UDP), # or bypass conntrack (NOTRACK) for high-volume flows that don't need it Production gotcha: A Kubernetes node doing lots of SNAT, or a NAT gateway under load, silently drops connections at the conntrack ceiling. UDP floods and short-lived connections fill it fast. The error is in dmesg , not your app logs — so it looks like a mysterious network blip. Interview tip: This is a favorite "intermittent failures under load" root cause. The tells: failures correlate with connection volume, CPU is fine, and dmesg shows table-full. Fixes: raise the max, shorten timeouts, or use NOTRACK . eBPF datapaths (Cilium) can reduce conntrack pressure by handling some flows without it.

questions.q: Stateful vs stateless firewall — explain via AWS Security Groups vs Network ACLs.
questions.text: The stateful/stateless distinction determines whether you must explicitly allow return traffic — and it's exactly the SG-vs-NACL difference in AWS. Stateful (Security Groups) - Tracks connections: if you ALLOW outbound, the RETURN traffic is auto-allowed - Only need rules in the direction you initiate - Allow-only (no explicit deny); evaluated as a whole - Attached to ENIs/instances Stateless (Network ACLs) - No connection memory: must ALLOW both inbound AND the return path explicitly - Must open ephemeral port range (1024-65535) for return traffic! - Has explicit allow AND deny; numbered, evaluated in order - Attached to subnets Classic mistake: Adding a NACL inbound allow but forgetting the outbound ephemeral-port range for replies (or vice versa) — traffic goes one way and the response is dropped. With Security Groups you never hit this because the return is stateful. The #1 NACL bug is the missing ephemeral return range. Interview tip: Crisp summary: Security Group = stateful (return traffic implicit), NACL = stateless (must allow return + ephemeral ports explicitly). SGs are allow-only at the instance; NACLs add deny rules at the subnet for broad blocks (e.g. blacklisting an IP). Use SGs for app rules, NACLs for coarse subnet-level guardrails.

questions.q: Walk through recursive DNS resolution end to end, from a cold cache to an answer.
questions.text: Recursive resolution is how a name becomes an IP when nothing is cached, walking the DNS hierarchy from root to authoritative. The walk (cold cache, resolving www.example.com) 1. Stub resolver (client) -> recursive resolver (e.g. 8.8.8.8 / corporate) 2. Recursive -> ROOT servers: "who handles .com?" -> referral to TLD servers 3. Recursive -> .com TLD servers: "who handles example.com?" -> referral to authoritative NS 4. Recursive -> example.com authoritative NS: "A record for www?" -> the IP 5. Recursive caches each answer per its TTL, returns IP to the client Iterative vs recursive The recursive resolver does the legwork on the client's behalf; each server it queries answers iteratively (gives a referral, not the final answer) until the authoritative server returns the record. dig +trace www.example.com # shows the full root -> TLD -> authoritative walk dig www.example.com @8.8.8.8 # ask a specific recursive resolver Interview tip: The key terms: stub resolver (client), recursive resolver (does the walk + caches), root -> TLD -> authoritative hierarchy, and TTL-based caching at each hop. dig +trace is the tool that makes the walk visible — knowing it signals you've actually debugged resolution, not just memorized the steps.

questions.q: Explain the main DNS record types and the CNAME-at-apex problem (and its fixes).
questions.text: Each record type serves a purpose; the apex-CNAME restriction trips up nearly everyone pointing a root domain at a cloud endpoint. Common records A : name -> IPv4 AAAA : name -> IPv6 CNAME : name -> another name (alias) MX : mail servers TXT : arbitrary text (SPF, DKIM, domain verification) NS : delegates a zone to nameservers SOA : zone authority/metadata SRV : service location (host+port) PTR : reverse (IP -> name) The CNAME-at-apex problem You cannot put a CNAME on the zone apex ( example.com itself) — the DNS spec forbids a CNAME coexisting with the required SOA/NS records at the apex. So you can't example.com CNAME my-lb.cloud.com . # Fixes for pointing the apex at a cloud LB whose IP changes: - Route 53 ALIAS / Azure A-alias / Cloud DNS: provider-specific apex "alias" records - ANAME / flattened CNAME (some DNS providers resolve it server-side to an A record) - (Avoid) hardcoding the LB's IP in an A record — it can change Gotcha: Hardcoding an A record to a cloud load balancer's current IP breaks when the provider rotates that IP. Always use the provider's ALIAS/ANAME at the apex so it tracks the endpoint automatically. Interview tip: Knowing why apex CNAMEs are illegal (apex must hold SOA/NS, CNAME can't coexist) and the cloud-specific ALIAS fix (Route 53 alias, etc.) is a very common real-world DNS task. Subdomains ( www ) can use CNAME freely — it's only the apex that's special.

questions.q: How is DNS used for load balancing and failover? What are the limits of DNS-based LB?
questions.text: DNS can distribute traffic by returning different/multiple answers, but it's a coarse tool limited by caching. Techniques Round-robin DNS : return multiple A records, clients pick (rough spread) Weighted : send X% to one set of IPs, Y% to another (canary/migration) Latency/Geo : return the nearest region's endpoint (GeoDNS / latency routing) Failover : health-check endpoints; stop returning the unhealthy one The fundamental limits - TTL caching: clients/resolvers cache answers; a failover only takes effect after the TTL expires (and some ignore low TTLs) -> slow, uneven cutover - No real-time load awareness: DNS can't see backend load/health per request - Client behavior varies: some pin the first IP, ignoring round-robin Gotcha: Setting a 60s TTL doesn't guarantee 60s failover — misbehaving resolvers and OS/browser caches can hold answers far longer. DNS failover is best-effort and slow; never rely on it alone for fast HA. Interview tip: Position DNS LB as coarse, global traffic steering (region selection, failover, weighted migrations) layered above a real LB (L4/L7) that does precise, health-aware balancing within a region. The TTL/caching limitation is the key insight — that's why DNS failover is measured in minutes, and why you pair GeoDNS with anycast or in-region LBs for fast local failover.

questions.q: What is split-horizon DNS and when do you need it?
questions.text: Split-horizon (split-brain) DNS returns different answers for the same name depending on who is asking — typically internal vs external clients. How it works api.example.com: - internal clients (VPC/corp) -> 10.0.5.20 (private IP, direct path) - external clients (internet) -> 203.0.113.10 (public LB) # Same hostname, different view based on source/resolver When you need it - Internal services reachable privately (no hairpin through the public internet) - Same app name works inside and outside the network seamlessly - Cloud: a private hosted zone (Route 53 private zone / Cloud DNS private) overrides the public zone for VPC-internal resolvers Gotcha: Forgetting split-horizon makes internal clients route to the public IP and "hairpin" out to the internet and back — extra latency, NAT/data-transfer cost, and sometimes a security-group/path failure. Conversely, a private zone that shadows a public name can confuse debugging ("works from my laptop, fails from the pod"). Interview tip: In cloud, this is the private hosted zone attached to a VPC — internal resolvers get private IPs, the public zone serves everyone else. It avoids hairpinning internal traffic out to the public LB. Mention that mismatched split-horizon views are a common cause of "resolves differently depending on where I run it."

questions.q: Explain DNS caching layers and negative caching. Why is a stale or cached failure so persistent?
questions.text: DNS answers are cached at many layers, each with its own TTL handling — which is why both good and bad answers can stick around far longer than expected. The caching layers Application/runtime : e.g. JVM caches DNS (historically forever!), connection pools OS resolver cache : systemd-resolved / nscd / Windows DNS Client Recursive resolver : the big shared cache (8.8.8.8, corporate, NodeLocal DNSCache) Authoritative TTL : the value the zone owner sets per record Negative caching (caching the failure) NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL responses are cached too, governed by the SOA's minimum TTL. So after you create a record, a prior "does not exist" answer can linger — the record exists but clients still get NXDOMAIN until the negative cache expires. JVM gotcha: Older JVMs cache successful lookups forever ( networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1 ) — so a failover that changes an IP never takes effect for that JVM until restart. Set a finite networkaddress.cache.ttl . Connection pools that resolve once at startup have the same problem. Interview tip: Two senior points: (1) negative caching means "I just created the record but it still says NXDOMAIN" is expected until the SOA negative TTL expires; (2) application-level DNS caching (especially the JVM) defeats DNS-based failover — the app keeps hitting the dead IP. The fix is finite caching TTLs and re-resolving on connection errors.

questions.q: 'DNS works for some names but not others.' Walk through how you isolate the cause.
questions.text: Selective DNS failure points to a specific zone, resolver, or record rather than total DNS breakage. Bisect systematically. 1. Compare a working vs failing name against the same resolver dig good.example.com # works dig bad.example.com # fails — note the status (NXDOMAIN? SERVFAIL? timeout?) # NXDOMAIN = record truly missing; SERVFAIL = resolver/authoritative error; # timeout = network/resolver reachability 2. Bypass caches / try different resolvers dig bad.example.com @8.8.8.8 # public resolver dig bad.example.com @<internal-resolver> dig +trace bad.example.com # find WHERE the delegation/answer breaks 3. Common selective-failure causes - Split-horizon: internal zone missing the record the public zone has (or vice versa) - One authoritative NS out of several is broken -> intermittent SERVFAIL - search-domain / ndots: short name expands wrong (works as FQDN, fails as short) - DNSSEC validation failure on one zone -> SERVFAIL only for that zone - A specific subdomain delegated to a down nameserver Interview tip: Lead with reading the response status — NXDOMAIN vs SERVFAIL vs timeout each points somewhere different. Then bisect by resolver (internal vs public) and use dig +trace to localize a broken delegation. Selective failure almost always means one zone/resolver/record, not "DNS is down" — saying that shows structured thinking.

questions.q: What is DNSSEC and what does a SERVFAIL caused by validation failure look like?
questions.text: DNSSEC cryptographically signs DNS records so resolvers can verify answers weren't forged (cache poisoning / spoofing). The cost is operational fragility. How it works - Each zone signs its records (RRSIG); publishes public key (DNSKEY) - A chain of trust: parent zone holds a DS record hashing the child's key - Validating resolver walks root -> TLD -> zone, checking signatures - Tampered/unsigned-but-expected answer -> validation FAILS The failure mode A DNSSEC validation failure returns SERVFAIL to validating resolvers (not NXDOMAIN) — the name may resolve fine on non-validating resolvers, so it's intermittent depending on which resolver a client uses. dig +dnssec example.com # shows RRSIG records if signed dig +cd example.com # "checking disabled" — bypasses validation; # if +cd WORKS but normal FAILS -> DNSSEC issue Operational risk: Expired signatures (RRSIG has a validity window — forget to re-sign and the whole zone goes SERVFAIL), a broken chain of trust (DS record not updated after a key rollover), or a registrar that mishandles DS records. DNSSEC outages take a domain fully dark for validating clients. Interview tip: The diagnostic gem: DNSSEC failures = SERVFAIL on validating resolvers, and dig +cd (checking disabled) succeeding while a normal query fails confirms it. Stress the operational fragility — expired RRSIGs and botched key rollovers cause real outages — which is why some orgs weigh DNSSEC's benefit against its blast radius.

questions.q: Compare DNS over UDP/TCP, DNS over TLS (DoT), and DNS over HTTPS (DoH). Operational impact?
questions.text: Classic DNS is plaintext UDP (with TCP fallback); DoT and DoH add encryption, which changes privacy, security, and your ability to observe/control DNS. The transports UDP/53 : default; fast, but truncated large answers fall back to TCP/53 TCP/53 : used for big responses (DNSSEC, zone transfers) + when UDP truncates DoT : DNS over TLS on port 853 — encrypted, on a dedicated port (visible as DNS) DoH : DNS over HTTPS on 443 — encrypted AND blended with web traffic (hard to see) Operational impact + Privacy/integrity: queries can't be sniffed or trivially tampered - Visibility loss: DoH on 443 bypasses your DNS-based monitoring/filtering - Browsers shipping DoH can ignore your corporate/NodeLocal resolver entirely - Harder to enforce split-horizon / internal resolution if clients use external DoH Gotcha: A browser or app silently using public DoH can break internal name resolution (it skips your private resolver/split-horizon) and evade security DNS filtering — "works on my phone's data, fails on corp wifi" or vice versa. Enterprises often disable client DoH or point it at an internal DoH endpoint. Interview tip: The trade-off is privacy vs control/observability: DoT is encrypted but still identifiable on 853 (you can manage it); DoH on 443 is deliberately indistinguishable from HTTPS, which is great for user privacy but breaks enterprise DNS visibility, filtering, and split-horizon. Knowing why DoH specifically complicates ops is the senior point.

questions.q: Walk through the TCP three-way handshake and connection teardown. What are TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT?
questions.text: TCP establishes a connection in three steps and tears it down in four. The lingering states (TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT) are common sources of confusion and production issues. Handshake + teardown OPEN: SYN -> | (3-way) CLOSE: FIN -> | (4-way, each side closes) TIME_WAIT (the active closer) The side that closes first sits in TIME_WAIT for ~2*MSL (often 60s) to absorb stray delayed packets and ensure the final ACK arrived. Many TIME_WAIT sockets is normal on a busy client/proxy, but can exhaust local ports if it initiates huge numbers of short connections. CLOSE_WAIT (the bug signal) # CLOSE_WAIT = the OTHER side sent FIN, but YOUR app hasn't called close(). # Piling-up CLOSE_WAIT sockets = an APPLICATION BUG (leaked sockets / fds). ss -tan state close-wait | wc -l # if this grows, your app isn't closing conns Key distinction: Lots of TIME_WAIT is usually fine (it's the kernel doing its job); lots of CLOSE_WAIT is almost always your application failing to close sockets — leading to file-descriptor exhaustion and eventual "too many open files". Interview tip: Nail the distinction: TIME_WAIT is on the active closer and self-clears (tune with reuse, not the dangerous tcp_tw_recycle ); CLOSE_WAIT growth means the app isn't closing connections — a code bug, not a tuning knob. Saying that confidently separates people who've debugged this from those who haven't.

questions.q: What is ephemeral port exhaustion and how do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.text: Every outbound connection consumes a local source port from the ephemeral range. A host making many connections to the same destination can run out. The mechanism # A connection is uniquely keyed by the 4-tuple: # (src IP, src PORT, dst IP, dst PORT) # To ONE dst IP:port, you have only ~28k-64k source ports available. cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range # the ephemeral range Symptoms + diagnosis - "Cannot assign requested address" (EADDRNOTAVAIL) on connect() - Bursts of failures when connecting to one backend/DB/proxy ss -s # summary of socket states ss -tan | grep TIME-WAIT | wc -l # often TIME_WAIT eating the ports Fixes - Connection POOLING / keep-alive (reuse connections — the real fix) - Widen ip_local_port_range - net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 (safely reuse TIME_WAIT for new OUTbound conns) - Spread load across more destination IPs/ports (more 4-tuples) Gotcha: The limit is per destination 4-tuple, so a service hammering a single DB or downstream IP exhausts ports long before the host is "busy." Don't reach for the deprecated/dangerous tcp_tw_recycle (removed in modern kernels, breaks behind NAT). Interview tip: The headline fix is connection pooling — reuse instead of churn. The 4-tuple insight (per-destination limit) explains why "the host isn't even busy" yet connections fail. Cite tcp_tw_reuse (safe, outbound) and explicitly warn against tcp_tw_recycle — that distinction is a senior tell.

questions.q: Explain TCP keep-alive vs HTTP keep-alive, and how load balancer idle timeouts cause errors.
questions.text: Two different "keep-alive" mechanisms at different layers — confusing them leads to mysterious connection-reset errors behind load balancers. The two keep-alives TCP keep-alive : kernel probes to detect a DEAD peer on an idle connection (default ~2hrs — too slow to be useful by default) HTTP keep-alive: REUSE one TCP connection for multiple HTTP requests (avoids handshake per request) — an app/L7 concept The LB idle-timeout trap # LB silently drops a connection idle longer than its idle timeout (e.g. 60s). # Client thinks the (pooled, kept-alive) connection is still good, reuses it, # and gets a RST / "connection reset by peer" or 502 on the next request. This hits long-lived pools, databases behind an LB, and idle HTTP keep-alive connections. The fix — order the timeouts: client/app idle timeout < LB idle timeout < backend idle timeout. If the client's keep-alive idle is shorter than the LB's, the client recycles the connection before the LB kills it, avoiding the reset. Also enable TCP keep-alive on long-lived/pooled connections so dead ones are detected. Interview tip: The senior insight is the timeout ordering : most "random 502/connection reset behind the ALB" issues come from the app's connection-pool idle timeout being longer than the LB's idle timeout. Set the client idle below the LB idle. This is one of the most common real cloud bugs.

questions.q: What is head-of-line blocking? How do HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 (QUIC) address it?
questions.text: Head-of-line (HOL) blocking is when one stuck item delays everything queued behind it. It appears at both the HTTP and TCP layers, and each protocol generation tackles a different layer. HTTP/1.1 — application-layer HOL One request per connection at a time; a slow response blocks reuse. Browsers work around it by opening ~6 parallel connections per host (wasteful). HTTP/2 — multiplexing (fixes app-layer, not TCP) # Many streams multiplexed over ONE TCP connection -> no app-layer HOL. # BUT all streams share one TCP byte-stream: a single lost packet stalls # ALL streams until retransmit -> TCP-layer HOL blocking remains. HTTP/3 — QUIC over UDP (fixes TCP-layer too) # QUIC runs over UDP with independent streams: a lost packet only stalls # ITS stream, not the others. Also: 0/1-RTT handshakes, connection migration # (survives IP changes), TLS 1.3 built in. Gotcha: HTTP/2's win is real for high-latency/many-object pages, but on a lossy network its single TCP connection can be worse than HTTP/1.1's parallel connections because one loss stalls every stream. That's exactly the gap HTTP/3 closes by moving to per-stream delivery over UDP. Interview tip: The clean progression: HTTP/1.1 = app HOL (one-at-a-time), HTTP/2 = multiplex over one TCP (fixes app HOL, keeps TCP HOL), HTTP/3/QUIC = independent streams over UDP (fixes TCP HOL + faster handshakes + connection migration). Knowing that HTTP/2 still suffers TCP-layer HOL is the detail interviewers probe.

questions.q: Explain TCP congestion control and what BBR changes versus loss-based algorithms like CUBIC.
questions.text: Congestion control governs how fast TCP sends to avoid overwhelming the network. The big shift is from loss-based to model-based algorithms. Loss-based (Reno/CUBIC — long the default) # Ramp up until packet LOSS, then back off (loss = congestion signal). # Slow start (exponential) -> congestion avoidance (linear) -> loss -> halve. # Problem: treats ALL loss as congestion, and fills buffers (bufferbloat). BBR (model-based) # Models the path's bottleneck BANDWIDTH and round-trip propagation time, # paces sending to that estimate instead of waiting for loss. # -> high throughput on lossy/long-haul links, less bufferbloat/latency. sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control # see/set the algorithm Why it matters On long-haul or lossy paths (mobile, cross-region, satellite), loss-based CUBIC under-performs because random (non-congestion) loss makes it back off needlessly. BBR keeps throughput high and latency low, which is why CDNs and cloud providers adopted it. Interview tip: The crisp contrast: CUBIC infers congestion from loss (and bloats buffers); BBR builds a bandwidth/RTT model and paces to it, winning on high-BDP and lossy links. Mention bufferbloat and that enabling BBR is a common, low-risk throughput/latency win for cross-region or edge traffic — a practical optimization, not just theory.

questions.q: What are the SYN backlog and accept queue, and how do SYN cookies defend against SYN floods?
questions.text: Inbound TCP connections pass through two kernel queues. Understanding them explains both SYN-flood attacks and "connection dropped under load" issues. The two queues SYN queue (incomplete): half-open conns awaiting the final ACK (after SYN-ACK) sized by net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog Accept queue (complete): fully established, waiting for the app to accept() sized by min(somaxconn, app's listen() backlog) SYN flood + SYN cookies # Attack: flood SYNs, never send the final ACK -> SYN queue fills -> # legit connections dropped. # Defense: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 -> when the SYN queue is full, the kernel # encodes connection state into the SYN-ACK sequence number instead of # storing it. Validates the returned ACK -> no queue state needed. Accept-queue overflow: If the app accept()s too slowly (event-loop blocked, thread starvation), the accept queue fills and the kernel drops/resets new connections even though SYNs succeed. ss -ltn shows Recv-Q (current) vs Send-Q (max) on listening sockets — a full Recv-Q means the app isn't accepting fast enough. Interview tip: Two takeaways: SYN cookies defend the SYN queue against floods without storing per-connection state (at the cost of some TCP options); and a backed-up accept queue (slow app, low somaxconn /listen backlog) drops connections under load. Reading ss -ltn Recv-Q/Send-Q on a listener is the diagnostic.

questions.q: How does a host decide where to send a packet? Explain the routing table and longest-prefix match.
questions.text: Every packet's next hop is chosen by consulting the routing table and picking the most specific matching route — longest-prefix match. The routing table ip route # show the routing table ip route get 8.8.8.8 # show exactly which route a dest would use # Example: # default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0 (0.0.0.0/0 — catch-all) # 10.0.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel (directly connected subnet) # 10.0.5.0/24 via 10.0.0.9 dev eth0 (more specific route) Longest-prefix match If multiple routes match a destination, the one with the longest prefix (most specific, largest /N) wins. A packet to 10.0.5.20 matches both 10.0.0.0/24 ... no — it matches 10.0.5.0/24 (more specific) over the default route. The default route ( /0 ) is the last resort. Gotcha: Adding a more-specific route silently overrides a broader one — a stray /32 or a VPN pushing routes can hijack traffic you expected to go elsewhere. ip route get <dst> is the definitive answer to "which path will this actually take," rather than eyeballing the table. Interview tip: The two facts: longest-prefix-match (most specific wins) and the default route as catch-all. The killer tool is ip route get <ip> — it resolves the exact route + source IP + interface the kernel will use, ending arguments about "why is traffic going out the wrong interface." Great for debugging asymmetric routing and VPN route leaks.

questions.q: Explain CIDR and subnetting. How do you size and avoid overlap in VPC design?
questions.text: CIDR notation ( /N ) defines how many bits are the network prefix; the rest are host addresses. Subnet planning is a day-0 decision that's painful to undo. CIDR math /24 = 256 addresses (254 usable) /16 = 65,536 /28 = 16 addresses (small subnet) /8 = 16,777,216 # usable = 2^(32-N) minus reserved (network, broadcast, + cloud reserves a few) # AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet (.0 network, .1 router, .2 DNS, .3 future, .255 bcast) VPC sizing principles - Pick a large VPC CIDR (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16) with room to grow - Carve subnets per AZ + tier (public/private/data) — leave gaps for expansion - NEVER overlap CIDRs between VPCs/on-prem you intend to peer/VPN (overlapping ranges can't be routed/peered without NAT gymnastics) The cardinal sin: Using the same range (e.g. everyone defaults to 10.0.0.0/16) across VPCs or with on-prem. You can't VPC-peer or VPN overlapping CIDRs — routing is ambiguous. Plan a global IP address scheme up front; resizing or re-IPing later is a major project. Interview tip: Two senior points: (1) plan non-overlapping CIDRs across all VPCs/on-prem from the start because peering/VPN require unique ranges; (2) cloud reserves addresses per subnet (AWS: 5), and Kubernetes pod CIDRs consume real VPC IPs — so size generously. Mention that overlap forces ugly NAT workarounds, which is why address planning is a foundational architecture task.

questions.q: What is asymmetric routing and why does it break stateful firewalls and load balancers?
questions.text: Asymmetric routing is when the request and its reply take different network paths. It's fine for plain routing but breaks anything that tracks connection state. The problem # Request: client -> path A -> firewall A -> server # Reply: server -> path B -> firewall B -> client # Firewall B never saw the SYN, so the reply looks like an unsolicited packet # -> dropped by the stateful firewall (no matching conntrack entry). Where it bites - Multiple egress paths / multi-homed hosts / dual NAT gateways - Stateful firewalls or LBs in each path that must see BOTH directions - Linux rp_filter (reverse-path filtering) dropping packets arriving on an interface the route table wouldn't have used to reach the source Gotcha: Stateless routing tolerates asymmetry; stateful devices (firewalls, NAT, L4 LBs, conntrack) require seeing both directions on the same device. Symptoms: connections that establish but hang, or work intermittently depending on path. rp_filter can silently drop the asymmetric replies on multi-NIC hosts. Interview tip: The crux: state requires symmetry. Fix by forcing both directions through the same stateful device (policy/source-based routing, sticky paths), syncing firewall state, or relaxing rp_filter to loose mode on multi-homed hosts. Recognizing that "it establishes then hangs with multiple gateways" smells like asymmetric routing is a strong signal.

questions.q: What is BGP, and how do BGP issues cause large internet/cloud outages?
questions.text: BGP is the protocol that routes between autonomous systems (the internet's backbone routing). It's trust-based, which makes misconfigurations and hijacks high-impact. What BGP does - Autonomous Systems (ASes) advertise which IP prefixes they can reach - Neighbors choose best paths by policy + AS-path length - It's the glue between ISPs, clouds, and large networks - Largely trust-based historically: you believe what peers advertise How it causes outages - Route leak / fat-finger: an AS wrongly advertises prefixes it shouldn't -> traffic blackholes or detours globally (e.g. major provider self-outages) - BGP hijack: a malicious/erroneous AS claims someone else's prefixes -> traffic redirected/intercepted - Withdrawing your own routes by mistake -> your services vanish from the internet Mitigation: RPKI RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) cryptographically validates that an AS is authorized to announce a prefix (Route Origin Validation), reducing accidental leaks and hijacks. Adoption is growing but partial. Interview tip: You won't run BGP as an app engineer, but understanding that a BGP misconfiguration can withdraw a provider's own routes (causing a global self-outage) or let someone hijack prefixes explains real headline incidents. Naming RPKI / Route Origin Validation as the defense shows you understand internet-scale routing risk — relevant when reasoning about provider dependencies and DR.

questions.q: Compare VPC peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, and Direct Connect. When use each?
questions.text: These connect networks together; they differ in topology, scale, bandwidth, and whether traffic crosses the public internet. The options VPC Peering : 1:1 private link between two VPCs; NOT transitive; simple/cheap -> mesh of peerings gets unmanageable at scale (N^2) Transit Gateway : hub-and-spoke router connecting MANY VPCs + on-prem; transitive -> the scalable answer for many-VPC/multi-account networks Site-to-Site VPN: encrypted tunnel over the PUBLIC internet to on-prem -> quick, cheap, but internet-variable latency + bandwidth caps Direct Connect : DEDICATED private physical link to the cloud -> consistent low latency, high bandwidth, no public internet Choosing Few VPCs, simple -> VPC peering Many VPCs / hub-spoke -> Transit Gateway On-prem, cheap/fast set -> VPN On-prem, performance/SLA -> Direct Connect (often + VPN as encrypted backup) Gotcha: VPC peering is non-transitive — if A peers B and B peers C, A still can't reach C. People build sprawling peering meshes then hit this; Transit Gateway exists precisely to provide transitive hub-and-spoke routing. And remember: overlapping CIDRs can't peer at all. Interview tip: The two senior points: peering is non-transitive (so it doesn't scale past a handful of VPCs — use Transit Gateway as the hub), and VPN vs Direct Connect is the internet-vs-dedicated trade-off (cost/speed-to-deploy vs consistent performance, often combined with VPN as encrypted backup over Direct Connect).

questions.q: What is policy-based / source-based routing and when do you need it?
questions.text: Normal routing decides by destination only. Policy-based routing (PBR) lets you route by source, mark, port, or other attributes using multiple routing tables. The mechanism (Linux) ip rule add from 10.0.5.0/24 table 100 # traffic FROM this source uses table 100 ip route add default via 10.0.5.1 table 100 ip rule list # show policy rules (consulted in order) # Selectors: from (source), fwmark, iif, dport, etc. -> pick a routing table When you need it - Multi-homed host: replies must egress the SAME interface they arrived on (fixes the asymmetric-routing/rp_filter drop problem) - Send specific subnets/apps over a VPN or a specific gateway - Separate management vs data-plane traffic onto different links - Multiple ISPs/egress paths with per-source policy Gotcha: Without source-based routing on a dual-NIC host, replies to traffic that arrived on eth1 may try to leave via eth0's default route — asymmetric routing, and rp_filter then drops them. PBR pins the reply to the correct interface/table. Interview tip: The canonical use is the multi-homed / dual-gateway host where you must reply out the interface a request came in on — exactly the fix for the asymmetric-routing problem from the routing section. ip rule + a dedicated routing table per source is the implementation. Recognizing when destination-only routing isn't enough is the signal.

questions.q: How do you distinguish packet loss, latency, and jitter — and what does mtr tell you?
questions.text: These three degrade connections differently, and conflating them sends you down the wrong debugging path. mtr exposes all three per hop. The three Latency : time for a packet to travel one way / round trip (RTT) Packet loss : % of packets that never arrive (triggers TCP retransmits -> slow) Jitter : VARIATION in latency between packets (kills VoIP, video, real-time) mtr — traceroute + ping per hop, continuously mtr -rwzbc 100 <host> # 100 cycles, report mode, per-hop loss% + latency # Read it: loss that STARTS at a hop and CONTINUES to the end = real loss there. # Loss at ONE middle hop that DOESN'T continue = that router de-prioritizing ICMP # (cosmetic, not real loss) — a classic misread. Gotcha: A single hop showing loss while later hops show none is almost always ICMP rate-limiting on that router, NOT a real problem — many people chase this phantom. Real loss persists from the offending hop through to the destination. Also: high RTT to a far region is physics (distance), not necessarily a fault. Interview tip: Show you can read mtr correctly: loss must persist to the final hop to be real; transient mid-path loss is usually ICMP deprioritization. Match the symptom to the metric — retransmits/throughput issues = loss; slow-but-steady = latency; choppy real-time = jitter. That diagnostic precision is exactly what's being tested.

questions.q: What is hairpinning / NAT loopback and why does an internal service fail to reach itself by public name?
questions.text: Hairpinning is when traffic from inside a network goes out to a public endpoint and must "turn around" to come back to a host on the same network. Many setups don't support it. The scenario # Internal client resolves api.example.com -> the PUBLIC LB IP # Packet goes to the gateway/LB and must hairpin back to an internal backend # on the same network it came from. # Many NAT gateways / LBs don't allow this loopback -> connection fails/times out. Why it fails + fixes - NAT device won't route a packet back out the interface it arrived on - Source/dest on the same subnet confuses the NAT/security path FIXES: - Split-horizon DNS: internal clients resolve to the PRIVATE IP (no hairpin) - An internal load balancer for internal traffic - Enable NAT loopback/hairpinning on the gateway (if supported) Gotcha: The tell is "works from outside, fails from inside" (or from the same host/subnet) when using the public hostname. It's not a DNS or app bug — it's the network refusing the U-turn. This is extremely common with containers calling their own service's public URL. Interview tip: The clean fix ties back to split-horizon DNS — internal clients should resolve the name to the private endpoint so traffic never has to hairpin. Recognizing "external works, internal-to-itself fails" as NAT loopback (not DNS) demonstrates real network debugging, and the private-IP/internal-LB fix is the production-grade answer.

questions.q: What does 'connection reset by peer' (RST) actually mean, and what are the common causes?
questions.text: An RST is TCP's abrupt "this connection is over now" — unlike a graceful FIN. It signals one side tore down or rejected the connection unexpectedly. RST vs FIN FIN : graceful close ("I'm done sending") — normal teardown RST : abort NOW — no graceful close; in-flight data may be lost # Seen by the app as ECONNRESET / "connection reset by peer" Common causes - Sending to a socket the peer already closed (use-after-close) - LB/firewall idle timeout killed the connection; you reused it (the LB trap) - Backend crashed / OOMKilled / restarted mid-connection - Connecting to a port with nothing listening (RST instead of timeout) - A firewall configured to REJECT (RST) rather than DROP (silent) - Backpempt: app calling close() with unread data (SO_LINGER) sends RST RST vs timeout distinction: An RST is an active rejection (something replied "no") — port closed, app crashed, or firewall REJECT. A timeout is silence — wrong IP, DROP firewall, or network black hole. RST = someone said no; timeout = no one answered. That distinction alone narrows the cause dramatically. Interview tip: Two strong moves: (1) RST = active rejection vs timeout = silence — immediately splits "reachable but refusing" from "unreachable"; (2) the most common production RST is the LB idle-timeout + connection-pool reuse pattern from the keep-alive question. Capturing with tcpdump to see who sent the RST (and when) pinpoints it.

questions.q: Walk through the full lifecycle of an HTTPS request from URL to rendered response.
questions.text: A single HTTPS request touches DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP. Knowing each stage lets you attribute latency precisely. The stages 1. DNS : resolve hostname -> IP (may be cached at several layers) 2. TCP : 3-way handshake to IP:443 (1 RTT) 3. TLS : handshake — negotiate version/cipher, validate cert, key exchange (TLS 1.2 = 2 RTT, TLS 1.3 = 1 RTT, 0-RTT on resume) 4. HTTP : send request; server processes; sends response 5. Transfer + render Attributing latency with curl curl -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} conn:%{time_connect} \ tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n" \ -o /dev/null -s https://example.com This breaks the request into DNS, TCP connect, TLS, time-to-first-byte, and total — so you know which stage is slow. Reading it: High time_namelookup = DNS; gap between connect and appconnect = TLS; high time_starttransfer after TLS = slow server (TTFB); high total but fast TTFB = large body / slow transfer. Each points to a different fix. Interview tip: The curl -w timing breakdown is the single most useful HTTP-debugging trick — it turns "the site is slow" into "DNS is slow" or "TLS is slow" or "the server's TTFB is slow." Citing the per-phase timing variables shows you debug latency empirically, not by guessing.

questions.q: Explain the TLS 1.3 handshake and how it improves on TLS 1.2. What is 0-RTT and its risk?
questions.text: TLS 1.3 streamlined the handshake for speed and removed legacy insecure options, cutting a round trip and enabling session resumption with zero round trips. 1.2 vs 1.3 handshake TLS 1.2 : 2 round trips (ClientHello/ServerHello, then key exchange) before data TLS 1.3 : 1 round trip — client sends key share in ClientHello; server responds with everything needed -> app data after 1 RTT Also: removed old ciphers/RSA key exchange, forward secrecy mandatory 0-RTT resumption # On a RESUMED connection, the client can send app data in the FIRST flight # (0 round trips) using a pre-shared key from the prior session. # Great for latency — but... 0-RTT replay risk: 0-RTT early data can be replayed by an attacker (it's sent before the handshake completes, so there's no freshness guarantee). Only use 0-RTT for idempotent, non-state-changing requests (e.g. a GET) — never for a POST that transfers money. Many servers restrict 0-RTT to safe methods for this reason. Interview tip: Two points score well: TLS 1.3 cuts the handshake to 1 RTT (and 0-RTT on resume) while mandating forward secrecy and dropping weak ciphers; and 0-RTT's replay vulnerability means it's only safe for idempotent requests. Knowing the security caveat, not just the speed win, is the senior signal.

questions.q: How does TLS certificate validation work, and what is the 'missing intermediate certificate' trap?
questions.text: A client validates a server's certificate by building a chain of trust from the server's cert up to a trusted root CA. A broken chain causes confusing "works in browser, fails elsewhere" errors. The chain of trust Server (leaf) cert -> signed by -> Intermediate CA -> signed by -> Root CA # Client trusts the Root (in its trust store); must be able to build the full # chain leaf -> intermediate(s) -> root to validate. The missing-intermediate trap # The SERVER must send leaf + intermediate(s). If it sends only the leaf: # - Browsers often still work (they cache/fetch intermediates, AIA chasing) # - curl, Java, Go, mobile apps FAIL: "unable to get local issuer certificate" openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts # inspect the chain the server sends Classic gotcha: "It works in my browser but my service/curl/Java client gets a cert error." The server is sending an incomplete chain (missing intermediate); browsers paper over it via AIA fetching or cached intermediates, but strict clients don't. Fix: configure the server to present the full chain (fullchain.pem), not just the leaf. Interview tip: The tell "browser works, programmatic client fails" almost always = missing intermediate cert. openssl s_client -showcerts reveals exactly what the server sends. The fix is serving the full chain. This is one of the most common real TLS misconfigurations and recognizing the asymmetry instantly is a strong signal.

questions.q: Explain the difference between 502, 503, and 504 errors. How do you debug each?
questions.text: These 5xx errors come from a gateway/proxy/LB and each points to a distinct backend condition — knowing which narrows the cause immediately. The three 502 Bad Gateway : proxy got an INVALID/garbage response from the backend (backend crashed mid-response, protocol mismatch, RST) 503 Service Unavailable : no healthy backend to send to (all failing health checks, overloaded, or scaled to zero) 504 Gateway Timeout : backend accepted but didn't respond in time (slow backend, deadlock, downstream dependency hang) Debugging each 502 -> check backend logs for crashes/RST; protocol/keep-alive mismatch; OOMKills 503 -> check health checks + backend pool: are ANY targets healthy? scaled down? 504 -> check backend latency + its downstream calls (DB, API); raise/align timeouts or fix the slow dependency (don't just bump the timeout) Gotcha: A 504 often masks a downstream problem — the backend is waiting on a slow DB/API. Bumping the gateway timeout hides the symptom; find the actual slow dependency. A 502 frequently traces to the LB-idle-timeout/keep-alive reset pattern (backend closed the pooled connection). Interview tip: The crisp mapping: 502 = bad/garbage response (backend broke), 503 = no healthy backend (capacity/health), 504 = backend too slow (timeout). Tie 504 to chasing the downstream dependency rather than raising timeouts, and 502 to the connection-reset/keep-alive pattern — that connects this to the TCP section and shows systems thinking.

questions.q: Explain HTTP idempotency and safe methods. How do idempotency keys make retries safe?
questions.text: Idempotency — the same request applied multiple times has the same effect as once — is the foundation of safe retries in distributed systems. Method semantics Safe (no side effects) : GET, HEAD, OPTIONS Idempotent (repeat = same) : GET, PUT, DELETE (PUT sets a value; repeating = same) NOT idempotent : POST (each call may create a new resource) Why it matters for retries # A timeout is ambiguous: did the request succeed and the response get lost, # or did it fail? Safe to retry an idempotent op; retrying a POST might # double-charge / double-create.
