Anycast announces the same IP from many locations and relies on BGP to deliver users to the nearest, giving fast failover at the routing level. dig +short www.example.com @8.8.8.8 traceroute -n 1.1.1.1 aws route53 get-health-check-status --health-check-id <id> Interview tip: Most global platforms combine both: anycast for the edge, then application-aware routing behind it.

questions.q: How does connection reuse (keep-alive and pooling) between a load balancer and its backends change performance and failure modes?
questions.text: Reusing backend connections saves handshakes and reduces latency and CPU. But if a backend closes an idle connection just as the proxy sends a request on it, the request fails with a reset. Align idle timeouts so the proxy's is shorter than the backend's. nginx: upstream app { server 10.0.0.5:8080; keepalive 64; keepalive_timeout 55s; } curl -w '%{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer}\n' -o /dev/null -s https://example.com ss -tan state established '( dport = :8080 )' | wc -l Interview tip: The rule of thumb: the party that closes first should be the one that knows the connection is idle, usually the proxy, not the backend.

questions.q: Calico, Flannel and Cilium: how do their data planes differ and what are the trade-offs?
questions.text: Flannel is a simple overlay (VXLAN) with no network policy. Calico can run unencapsulated with BGP routing or use IP-in-IP/VXLAN and enforces policy with iptables or eBPF. Cilium uses eBPF for networking, policy, observability and kube-proxy replacement. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node cilium status calicoctl node status kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium bpf lb list | head Interview tip: Pick based on needs: Flannel for simplicity, Calico for BGP and policy maturity, Cilium for eBPF features and visibility.

questions.q: What are enhanced networking, SR-IOV and jumbo frames, and when do they matter in the cloud?
questions.text: Enhanced networking gives instances direct hardware access to the NIC (ENA, SR-IOV or Accelerated Networking), cutting latency and CPU overhead and raising packets-per-second. Jumbo frames (MTU 9001) increase throughput inside a VPC but not across the internet or many VPNs. ethtool -i eth0 | grep driver ip link show eth0 | grep mtu ping -M do -s 8973 10.0.1.20 aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types c6in.large --query 'InstanceTypes[].NetworkInfo' Interview tip: Mixed MTU paths (9001 inside the VPC, 1500 at the internet or peering edge) are a source of black-hole issues. Test the path.

questions.q: How do you give workloads a fixed outbound IP for partner allowlists, and what are the options and limits?
questions.text: Route egress through a NAT gateway or egress proxy with an elastic or reserved static IP. In Kubernetes, use a dedicated egress gateway or node pool with static IPs. Remember high availability needs several IPs and the partner must allowlist all of them. aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-1 --allocation-id eipalloc-1 gcloud compute addresses create egress-ip --region=europe-west1 kubectl get egressgatewaypolicy -A # Cilium Interview tip: One NAT gateway per availability zone means one IP per zone. Give the partner the full set, not just one.

questions.q: SERVFAIL appears for one domain on your resolver but works on a public resolver. What do you check?
questions.text: Different resolvers behave differently on broken delegation, DNSSEC validation failures, large responses over UDP, EDNS issues, or unreachable authoritative servers. Run dig +trace, check DNSSEC with +cd and delv, and compare resolvers. dig example.com @10.0.0.2 dig example.com @8.8.8.8 dig +cd example.com @10.0.0.2 delv example.com dig +trace example.com Interview tip: If dig +cd (checking disabled) works but normal fails, DNSSEC validation is the cause.

questions.q: POST requests fail with 502 occasionally after periods of inactivity, while GETs seem fine. What is the likely cause?
questions.text: A stale pooled connection: the backend or an intermediate device closed an idle keep-alive connection and the proxy or client reuses it. Non-idempotent POSTs aren't automatically retried, so the failure surfaces. Align idle timeouts and enable safe retries. curl -v -X POST https://example.com/api -d '{}' grep -E 'upstream prematurely closed|recv\(\) failed|Connection reset' /var/log/nginx/error.log sudo tcpdump -ni any 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-rst) != 0' and port 8080 Interview tip: Look in the proxy error log for 'upstream prematurely closed connection', the signature of the idle timeout race.

questions.q: Users on one ISP cannot reach your site while everyone else can. How do you investigate?
questions.text: Collect specifics from the affected users: error type, IPv4 or IPv6, resolver, and traceroute. Check DNS answers from their resolver, IPv6 reachability, MTU and BGP route visibility, then use looking glasses and RIPE Atlas probes to test from their network. dig +short www.example.com @<isp-resolver> curl -4 -sI https://www.example.com; curl -6 -sI https://www.example.com mtr -rwz -c 50 www.example.com ping -M do -s 1400 www.example.com Interview tip: Broken IPv6 paths and MTU black holes on specific ISPs are common reasons for partial outages.

questions.q: You suspect a SYN flood against a public service. How do you confirm it and mitigate it?
questions.text: Look for many half-open connections in SYN_RECV, listen queue overflows, and a flood of SYNs from many or spoofed sources. Enable SYN cookies, tune the backlog, rate-limit at the edge, and use upstream DDoS protection or a CDN. ss -ant state syn-recv | wc -l nstat -az TcpExtTCPReqQFullDrop TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtSyncookiesSent sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn' -c 20 Interview tip: Say the key point: SYN cookies avoid allocating state until the final ACK, so the backlog cannot be exhausted.

questions.q: Two hosts intermittently lose connectivity and the logs mention a duplicate IP address. How do you find and fix it?
questions.text: Two devices claim the same IP, so ARP answers alternate and traffic flips between them. Detect with arping -D, ARP tables and switch MAC tables, find the second MAC and its port, then fix DHCP overlap, static assignments or cloned VMs. arping -D -I eth0 10.0.1.50 ip neigh show 10.0.1.50 arp-scan --localnet | sort | uniq -d sudo tcpdump -eni eth0 arp and host 10.0.1.50 Interview tip: Cloud-cloned VMs with static IPs and DHCP pools overlapping static ranges are the usual culprits.

questions.q: A VPN tunnel shows as up but traffic only flows in one direction. What are the usual causes?
questions.text: Check routes and traffic selectors on both ends, security groups and firewalls for return traffic, asymmetric routing, NAT rules that rewrite addresses, overlapping subnets, and MTU. Capture on both sides to see where packets disappear. ip route get 10.20.0.5 sudo ip xfrm policy; sudo ip xfrm state sudo tcpdump -ni any host 10.20.0.5 aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=route.gateway-id,Values=vgw-1 Interview tip: Remember that a tunnel being up only proves the key exchange worked. It says nothing about routes, selectors or firewalls.

questions.q: Large file transfers between two regions are slow even though the link is rated at 10 Gbps. What do you investigate?
questions.text: Single-stream TCP is limited by window size divided by RTT, plus packet loss and congestion control. Measure with iperf3 using one and several streams, check window scaling and buffers, loss and retransmits, and consider BBR, parallel streams or a transfer tool built for long fat networks. iperf3 -c remote -t 30 iperf3 -c remote -P 8 -t 30 ss -ti dst remote | grep -E 'rtt|cwnd|retrans' sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control net.core.rmem_max Interview tip: If eight streams are much faster than one, the limit is per-flow window or loss, not the link capacity.

questions.q: Behind a load balancer, the application logs show the load balancer's IP for every request and rate limiting blocks everyone. How do you fix it?
questions.text: The app is using the peer address instead of the forwarded client address. Configure the app or web server to trust the proxy's forwarded headers (or PROXY protocol) from known proxy ranges only, and rate-limit on the real client IP. curl -s https://app.example.com/debug/headers | jq . nginx: set_real_ip_from 10.0.0.0/16; real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For; real_ip_recursive on; aws elbv2 describe-target-group-attributes --target-group-arn <arn> Interview tip: After the fix, test that a forged X-Forwarded-For header from the internet does not change the logged IP.

questions.q: A browser app calls your API and fails with a CORS error, although curl works. How do you diagnose and fix it properly?
questions.text: CORS is enforced by browsers, not servers. For cross-origin calls the server must return Access-Control-Allow-Origin, handle the preflight OPTIONS request with allowed methods and headers, and send credentials flags correctly. Check the preflight response in the network tab. curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/items -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type,authorization' curl -i https://api.example.com/items -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' Interview tip: Never answer with a wildcard origin when credentials are involved. Reflect only allowed origins from an allowlist.

questions.q: WebSocket connections drop exactly every 60 seconds. What is happening and how do you fix it?
questions.text: An intermediary, usually a load balancer or reverse proxy, closes connections it considers idle after a default 60 second timeout. Send application-level pings or heartbeats more often than the timeout and raise the idle and read timeouts on each hop. nginx: proxy_read_timeout 3600s; proxy_send_timeout 3600s; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn <arn> --attributes Key=idle_timeout.timeout_seconds,Value=3600 wscat -c wss://example.com/ws Interview tip: Every hop has its own timer: CDN, load balancer, proxy, NAT. The shortest one wins.

questions.q: After scaling out a gRPC service, one pod still receives most of the traffic. Why, and how do you fix the balancing?
questions.text: gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections that multiplex many requests. A layer 4 load balancer balances connections, not requests, so a client keeps using one connection to one pod. Use an L7 proxy, a service mesh, or client-side load balancing with headless service discovery. kubectl get svc payments -o wide # check clusterIP: None for headless kubectl exec deploy/client -- grpcurl -plaintext payments:50051 list kubectl top pod -l app=payments Interview tip: Setting MaxConnectionAge on the server forces periodic reconnects and helps rebalance after scale-out.

questions.q: A downstream API returns 429 Too Many Requests and your service's retries make it worse. How do you design client behaviour?
questions.text: Respect Retry-After, use exponential backoff with jitter, cap retries and total time, add client-side rate limiting and circuit breakers, retry only idempotent operations, and avoid retry amplification across layers. curl -si https://api.partner.com/v1/items | grep -iE 'HTTP/|retry-after|x-ratelimit' kubectl logs deploy/worker | grep -c 429 rate(http_client_requests_total{code="429"}[5m]) Interview tip: If three layers each retry three times, one failure becomes twenty-seven calls. Retry at one layer only.

questions.q: Some older clients fail TLS handshakes after you tightened the cipher and protocol configuration. How do you find who is affected and decide what to do?
questions.text: Log the negotiated protocol and cipher plus handshake failures, identify the client types, and weigh supporting them versus requiring upgrades. Test with openssl s_client forcing old versions. Keep legacy support isolated where possible rather than weakening everything. openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_1 </dev/null nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 example.com nginx: log_format tls '$remote_addr $ssl_protocol $ssl_cipher $http_user_agent'; grep -c 'SSL_do_handshake() failed' /var/log/nginx/error.log Interview tip: Collect data before and after the change. Often the affected clients are a few outdated scripts or devices, not real users.

questions.q: Visiting the site by IP or an alias hostname shows the wrong certificate or another site's content. How does SNI explain this?
questions.text: A server hosting many TLS sites chooses the certificate using the SNI hostname sent in the ClientHello. Without SNI, or with an unmatched name, it returns a default certificate or site. Check the Host header, SNI value, default server block and load balancer listener rules. openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443 -servername www.example.com </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName curl --resolve www.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://www.example.com/ -v nginx -T | grep -E 'server_name|listen 443|default_server' Interview tip: curl --resolve is the cleanest way to test a specific IP with the correct SNI and Host header.

questions.q: An attacker is hammering your login endpoint with credential stuffing. What network and application layers do you use to respond?
questions.text: Combine edge controls (WAF rules, rate limiting, bot detection, geo or ASN blocks, CAPTCHA) with application defences (per-account and per-IP throttling, lockout or step-up MFA, breached password checks) and monitoring. Block in layers, not only by IP. awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head aws wafv2 create-rate-based-rule ... grep 'POST /login' access.log | awk '{print $9}' | sort | uniq -c Interview tip: Attackers rotate IPs, so key limits on account, device fingerprint and behaviour as well as source address.

questions.q: A server with two network interfaces replies to some clients but not others. How does asymmetric routing explain it, and how do you fix it with policy routing?
questions.text: The reply leaves via the default route's interface, not the one the request came in on. Reverse-path filtering or the upstream stateful firewall then drops it. Add source-based routing tables and rules so replies use the interface that owns the source address. ip route show; ip rule show sudo ip route add default via 10.0.2.1 dev eth1 table 200 sudo ip rule add from 10.0.2.15/32 table 200 sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter Interview tip: rp_filter strict mode silently drops packets whose reverse path would use a different interface, a very common hidden cause.

questions.q: Docker or Kubernetes workloads on a host cannot reach corporate network ranges because the default bridge subnet overlaps. How do you resolve it?
questions.text: The container runtime's default bridge (172.17.0.0/16) or Kubernetes pod and service CIDRs collide with real networks, so the host routes that traffic locally. Change the bridge or CIDR ranges to unused space, and plan address allocation centrally. ip route | grep 172.17 docker network inspect bridge | jq '.[0].IPAM.Config' cat /etc/docker/daemon.json # {"bip":"10.200.0.1/24","default-address-pools":[{"base":"10.201.0.0/16","size":24}]} kubectl cluster-info dump | grep -m2 -E 'service-cluster-ip-range|cluster-cidr' Interview tip: Kubernetes pod and service CIDRs are hard to change later, so choose them to avoid all current and planned networks.

questions.q: Cross-AZ latency and data transfer costs are higher than expected for a chatty microservice setup. How do you measure and reduce them?
questions.text: Measure inter-zone traffic with flow logs and service metrics, then keep chatty services in the same zone using topology-aware routing, zone-aware load balancing and caching. Balance this against availability, because zone affinity must still fail over. kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders -o yaml | grep -E 'zone|hints' kubectl annotate svc orders service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode=Auto aws ec2 describe-flow-logs fields @timestamp, srcaddr, dstaddr, bytes | stats sum(bytes) by srcaddr, dstaddr | sort sum desc Interview tip: Zone-local routing can overload a zone with fewer pods, so keep replicas balanced per zone and allow spill-over.

questions.q: Packet captures show many retransmissions and 'TCP ZeroWindow' from the receiver. What does that tell you and what do you do?
questions.text: ZeroWindow means the receiver's buffer is full: the application is not reading fast enough. The problem is at the receiving host or application, not the network. Look at the process's CPU, blocking calls, thread pool or downstream slowness, and socket Recv-Q. ss -tnp | awk '$2>0' tshark -r cap.pcap -Y 'tcp.analysis.zero_window' | head top -H -p $(pidof app) sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_rmem Interview tip: Contrast: loss and retransmissions without zero windows point to the network. Zero window points to a slow consumer.

questions.q: A Kubernetes service cannot reach an external API only from some nodes. How do you find the difference?
questions.text: Compare the failing and working nodes: egress route and NAT gateway or IP, security groups and network ACLs, DNS resolution on the node, CNI SNAT behaviour, and node-level firewalls. Test from a debug pod pinned to each node. kubectl run dbg --image=nicolaka/netshoot --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeName":"node-a"}}' -it --rm -- curl -sv https://api.partner.com kubectl get nodes -o wide ip route get 203.0.113.50; iptables -t nat -S POSTROUTING | head Interview tip: Look at which subnet each node is in. Different subnets often use different route tables and NAT gateways.

questions.q: An application intermittently gets 'Name or service not known' during DNS-heavy workloads, and the resolver logs show timeouts. What do you investigate?
questions.text: Check resolver capacity and rate limits (cloud VPC DNS has per-ENI packet limits), UDP packet drops and conntrack, search domain amplification, caching, and retry settings. Add a local cache, reduce lookups, and use connection reuse. dig +tries=1 +time=1 api.example.com @169.254.169.253 conntrack -S | grep -i drop cat /etc/resolv.conf aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name NetworkPacketsDropped ... Interview tip: AWS limits traffic to the VPC resolver to about 1,024 packets per second per network interface, a classic cause of intermittent DNS failures.

questions.q: Security asks you to prove that production databases cannot be reached from the internet or from the web tier on unintended ports. How do you validate and document it?
questions.text: Combine configuration review with active testing: enumerate security groups, route tables and policies as code, run reachability analysis tools and authorised port scans from the web tier and from outside, and keep automated checks in CI so regressions are caught. aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=ip-permission.cidr,Values=0.0.0.0/0 aws ec2 create-network-insights-path --source i-web --destination i-db --protocol tcp --destination-port 5432 nmap -Pn -p- 10.0.3.10 # from web tier, authorised only checkov -d terraform/ --check CKV_AWS_24,CKV_AWS_260 Interview tip: Reachability Analyzer and similar tools prove intent against the actual configuration, without sending traffic.

questions.q: What is the difference between metrics, logs, and traces — the three pillars of observability?
questions.text: Each pillar answers a different question about system health. Metrics — What is happening? (quantitative time-series, cheap, fast to query) Logs — Why is it happening? (discrete events, full context per event) Traces — Where is it happening? (request path across services, latency per hop) Metrics alert you, logs explain the event, traces show blast radius. Use all three: a latency spike in metrics leads you to filter logs by trace_id, then view the trace waterfall to pinpoint the slow service. Cardinality: Keep metric label values low-cardinality (status_code, region, pod_name — not user_id). High-cardinality labels create millions of series and crash Prometheus. Use logs for high-cardinality data.

questions.q: What are the four golden signals — how do you use them to monitor a production service?
questions.text: Latency — time to serve a request (use P99, never average) Traffic — requests/second, messages/second Errors — rate of failed requests (5xx, timeouts) Saturation — how full? (CPU %, queue depth, connection pool %) # PromQL: rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) # error rate histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) # P99 Always use percentiles for latency — averages hide tail latency. If you can only have one dashboard per service, make it the golden signals dashboard. Start here: Instrument every service with golden signals before any custom metrics. If P99 latency is fine, error rate is zero, and saturation is low — the service is healthy regardless of internal details.

questions.q: What is Prometheus — how does pull-based metrics collection work?
questions.text: prometheus --config.file=prometheus.yml curl http://myapp:8080/metrics # app exposes /metrics endpoint scrape_configs: - job_name: myapp kubernetes_sd_configs: [{role: pod}] # auto-discover K8s pods relabel_configs: [...] # filter by annotation promtool check config prometheus.yml # validate config Pull model: Prometheus controls scrape rate, discovers targets via service discovery, detects targets that disappear (up metric = 0). In Kubernetes use ServiceMonitor / PodMonitor CRDs (Prometheus Operator) for GitOps-based scrape config — no central prometheus.yml editing per service. Long-term storage: Default retention 15 days. Use remote_write to Thanos, Cortex, or GCP Managed Prometheus for unlimited retention and multi-cluster global query.

questions.q: How do you write effective PromQL queries — what are the key functions?
questions.text: rate(metric[5m]) # per-second rate (use for counters) histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(duration_bucket[5m])) # P99 from histogram sum by (pod) (rate(metric[5m])) # aggregate by label topk(5, metric) # top 5 values absent(up{job="myapp"}) # alert when target disappears predict_linear(disk_used[1h], 3600*24) # predict disk full in 24h # Error rate ratio: sum(rate(requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) rate() vs irate(): Use rate() for alerts and dashboards (smoothed). Use irate() only for detecting very brief spikes. irate() uses only the last 2 data points — slow scrape intervals make it unreliable.

questions.q: What is a histogram vs summary in Prometheus — when do you use each?
questions.text: # Histogram: buckets defined upfront, percentile computed at query time histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) # Summary: percentile computed in client, not aggregatable across instances http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"} 0.42 Histograms: flexible (any percentile at query time), aggregatable across replicas (add buckets from N pods). Summaries: accurate client-side, but cannot be aggregated — useless for multi-replica services. Always use histograms for services with multiple replicas. Choose bucket boundaries around your SLO (if SLO is P99 under 500ms, add buckets at 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0).

questions.q: How does structured logging work — why is it better than plain text logs?
questions.text: # Unstructured (bad): 2024-01-15 ERROR payment failed for user 12345 # Structured JSON (queryable): {"ts":"2024-01-15T10:23:01Z","level":"error","event":"payment_failed","user_id":12345,"amount":99.99,"trace_id":"abc123"} # Query in Cloud Logging: jsonPayload.event="payment_failed" AND jsonPayload.amount > 100 # Query in Loki: {app="payments"} | json | event="payment_failed" | amount > 100 Structured logging enables filtering by any field, aggregation (count failures by error type), and correlation (join on trace_id). Always include: timestamp (ISO 8601), level, service name, trace_id/span_id (links to distributed trace), request_id. Never log passwords, tokens, or PII at any level.

questions.q: How do you build a log aggregation pipeline — ELK vs Loki vs Cloud Logging?
questions.text: # ELK: Fluent Bit → Elasticsearch → Kibana (full-text, expensive) # Loki: Promtail → Loki → Grafana (label-indexed, cheap, PromQL-like) # GCP: container stdout → Cloud Logging (zero-config for GKE) [FILTER] Name kubernetes Merge_Log On # parse JSON logs into structured fields Loki indexes only labels (not content) — typically 10-20x cheaper storage than Elasticsearch. For teams using Grafana+Prometheus, Loki is a natural fit. GCP Cloud Logging is zero-ops for GKE but vendor-locked. ELK is better for complex full-text search and compliance requirements. Cost at scale is the key driver.

questions.q: Log volume is exploding and costs are too high — how do you reduce it without losing signal?
questions.text: # Fluent Bit: drop below WARNING for noisy services [FILTER] Name grep Exclude log level debug|info # Cloud Logging exclusion filter: resource.type="k8s_container" severity # Loki per-tenant rate limiting: ingestion_rate_mb: 10 Strategies: (1) Level filtering — keep WARN+ always, sample INFO, drop DEBUG. (2) Head sampling — drop N% of healthy-looking lines at the agent. (3) Aggregation — replace N log lines with a single metric. (4) Retention tiering — hot (7 days), cold (90 days), archive (1 year). Reducing volume 80% while keeping 100% of error signal is achievable with level filtering alone. Never drop ERROR logs. Only reduce INFO and DEBUG. Error logs are the signal you need most during incidents.

questions.q: How does distributed tracing work — what is a trace, span, and context propagation?
questions.text: Trace — the entire journey of one request across all services Span — one unit of work (HTTP handler, DB query, RPC call) Parent — span knows its parent (forms a tree) # W3C traceparent header propagated between services: traceparent: 00-{traceId}-{spanId}-{flags} # Each service reads header, creates child span, passes downstream Context propagation is critical: when service A calls B, A injects trace context into HTTP headers. B extracts it and creates a child span with the same trace ID — forming a connected tree. OpenTelemetry handles propagation automatically. Without it, traces are disconnected single-service islands. Sampling: Head-based (decide at root, simple), tail-based (buffer + keep errors, smarter but expensive). GCP Cloud Trace uses tail-based sampling automatically.

questions.q: How do you implement OpenTelemetry in a production Kubernetes environment?
questions.text: helm install otel-collector open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector -f values.yaml # Configure via env vars in pod spec: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector.monitoring:4317 OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=payments-service OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 # sample 10% # Auto-instrumentation via OTel Operator annotation: kubectl annotate pod mypod instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/inject-python=true The OTel Collector acts as a local proxy — apps send spans to it, it forwards to Jaeger/Tempo/Cloud Trace. Decouples application from backend. The OTel Operator auto-instruments pods via annotation (Java, Python, Node.js, .NET, Go) with zero code changes and no Dockerfile modification.

questions.q: What makes a good alert — what is alert fatigue and how do you fight it?
questions.text: Good alert: actionable + urgent + accurate + contextual Bad alert: "CPU > 80%" fires constantly with no action needed # Every alert must have: summary: "Payment service error rate above SLO" description: "Error rate 2.3%, SLO threshold 0.1%, ~1200 users/min affected" runbook_url: "https://wiki/runbooks/payment-errors" dashboard_url: "https://grafana/d/payments?from=now-1h" Alert fatigue: engineers silence alerts without investigating, become desensitised, miss real incidents. Fix: delete alerts that never need action, raise noisy thresholds, convert informational alerts to dashboard panels, require every alert to have a runbook. If you cannot describe in one sentence what action to take, the alert should not exist. Symptom-based alerting: Alert on user-visible symptoms (error rate, latency) not internal causes (CPU%). High CPU that does not affect users is a dashboard item, not an alert.

questions.q: How does Alertmanager work — routing, grouping, inhibition, and silences?
questions.text: route: group_by: [alertname, cluster, service] group_wait: 30s routes: - match: {severity: critical} → receiver: pagerduty - match: {team: platform} → receiver: slack-platform inhibit_rules: # suppress child when parent fires - source_match: {alertname: ClusterDown} target_match: {severity: warning} equal: [cluster] amtool --alertmanager.url=http://localhost:9093 config routes test --verify.receivers=pagerduty alertname=HighErrorRate Grouping batches related alerts into one notification (10 pod failures → 1 notification). Inhibition suppresses lower-severity alerts when a higher one fires — if the cluster is down, no point getting individual pod alerts. Silences mute during maintenance windows. Test routing with amtool in CI before applying config.

questions.q: What is an SLI, SLO, and SLA — how do you define and measure them?
questions.text: SLI — the metric: fraction of successful requests, P99 latency SLO — the target: success rate > 99.9% over 30 days SLA — the contract: SLO + consequences for breach # PromQL availability SLI: 1 - (sum(rate(requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m]))) SLIs must be user-facing — not CPU utilisation. Bad SLI: CPU %. Good SLI: request success rate as seen by users. Start with your measured baseline + small improvement target. Rolling 30-day windows are better than calendar windows — always reflect the most recent 30 days of behaviour.

questions.q: What is an error budget — how does it change how you run on-call?
questions.text: SLO: 99.9% over 30 days = 0.1% budget = 43.8 min downtime allowed # Error budget remaining: 1 - (observed_error_rate / allowed_error_rate) 50% budget left mid-month = healthy, deploy freely 5% budget left on day 10 = freeze deployments, fix reliability Error budget removes the subjective argument about whether to deploy. When budget is healthy, deploy freely. When nearly exhausted, freeze deployments until it recovers. This creates natural alignment: both product and engineering teams share the same budget. The policy should be written explicitly: "if error budget drops below 10%, all non-reliability deployments stop."

questions.q: How do you implement SLO-based alerting — burn rate alerts vs threshold alerts?
questions.text: # Burn rate: are we consuming budget faster than we can afford? ALERT ErrorBudgetBurning IF ( rate(errors[1h]) / rate(requests[1h]) > 14.4 * 0.001 AND rate(errors[5m]) / rate(requests[5m]) > 14.4 * 0.001 ) # 14.4x = burns 30-day budget in 2 days (page immediately) # 6x = budget gone in 5 days (ticket) Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts: fast (14.4x, 1h+5m windows) for acute incidents, slow (6x, 6h+30m windows) for gradual degradation. Reduces false positives from brief spikes while catching sustained issues. Use google/slo-generator or SLOTH for Kubernetes-native SLO alerting implementation.

questions.q: How do you design Grafana dashboards that are actually useful during incidents?
questions.text: Row 1: Golden signals (error rate, P99 latency, traffic, saturation) Row 2: Dependencies (downstream services, DB connection pool) Row 3: Infrastructure (CPU, memory, pod restarts) Row 4: Business (order rate, checkout success) # Template variables for reuse: sum(rate(requests_total{cluster="$cluster",service="$service"}[5m])) # Add deployment annotations to see changes on timeline Design for the incident responder woken at 3am: top row gives YES/NO health in 3 seconds, drill down by scrolling. Include links to runbooks. Use stat panels for current value, time-series for trends. Dashboard as code (Grafana provisioning ConfigMap or Terraform) keeps them version-controlled and auto-restores deleted dashboards.

questions.q: What is the kube-prometheus-stack — what does it deploy?
questions.text: helm install kube-prom prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring -f values.yaml # Deployed components: Prometheus Operator — manages Prometheus via CRDs (ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor, PrometheusRule) Prometheus — metrics collection Alertmanager — routing Grafana — dashboards (25+ pre-built) kube-state-metrics — K8s object metrics node-exporter — host metrics (DaemonSet) prometheus-adapter — custom metrics for HPA Each team deploys their own ServiceMonitor alongside their Deployment — Prometheus auto-discovers it without central config changes. Pre-built dashboards cover nodes, K8s objects, etcd, coredns, and API server. Size Prometheus by series count: 1M series ≈ 3-4GB RAM. Use recording rules to pre-aggregate expensive queries at scale.

questions.q: What is Grafana Loki — how does it differ from Elasticsearch?
questions.text: helm install loki grafana/loki-stack -n monitoring # LogQL examples: {namespace="production",app="payments"} |= "error" {app="api"} | json | status_code >= 500 rate({app="payments"} |= "payment_failed" [5m]) # metric from logs Loki indexes only labels, not content — 10-20x cheaper than Elasticsearch. Tradeoff: full-text search is slower (scans lines grep-style). For most operational use cases (errors in a service/namespace/pod), Loki is sufficient. Elasticsearch excels at complex cross-service full-text search and compliance requirements. Managed: Grafana Cloud for zero-ops.

questions.q: How do you monitor Kubernetes cluster health — what metrics and alerts matter most?
questions.text: kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0 # node NotReady increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m]) > 3 # crash loop apiserver_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"} > 1 # API server slow etcd_server_has_leader == 0 # etcd no leader kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas == kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_max_replicas # HPA at max absent(up{job="myapp"}) # target disappeared HPA at maximum replicas is critical — autoscaling is exhausted and the service cannot handle more load. Certificate expiry (alert 30 days before) prevents entirely avoidable outages. absent() catches targets that stop reporting — a crash that takes the metrics endpoint with it would otherwise cause threshold alerts to miss the incident.

questions.q: How do you detect CPU throttling in Kubernetes — why is it invisible?
questions.text: # Throttling ratio (alert if > 25%): rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]) # Why invisible: container does not error or crash # It simply runs slower — requests take longer, no error logs kubectl top pod myapp # shows 0.8/1.0 CPU — looks fine # But throttling metric shows 40% of periods throttled The CFS scheduler allows a burst within the 100ms period, then throttles for the remainder. A pod using 0.8 CPU average on a 1.0 limit can still be 40% throttled if it spikes in the first 60ms of each period. Fix: increase CPU limit, reduce spike patterns, or remove CPU limits entirely (use requests only for scheduling). Always monitor throttling explicitly — CPU utilisation alone misses it.

questions.q: How does GCP Managed Service for Prometheus differ from self-managed?
questions.text: # Enable on GKE cluster: gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER --enable-managed-prometheus # Same ServiceMonitor CRDs, same PromQL, same Grafana integration # Backend: Cloud Monitoring (15 month retention, no infra to manage) gcloud monitoring metrics list --filter="metric.type=starts_with(prometheus.googleapis.com)" GMP is Prometheus-compatible (same SDKs, PromQL, ServiceMonitors) but stores in Cloud Monitoring backend — no Prometheus StatefulSets, no storage management, no HA configuration. For GKE-native teams, GMP reduces operational overhead significantly. Self-managed Prometheus: full control, open standards, multi-cloud/on-prem, no per-series ingestion cost. For a GCP-native platform team, GMP is typically the right default.

questions.q: How do you use Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace for full-stack observability?
questions.text: # Link logs to traces — set trace field in log entries: {"trace": "projects/PROJECT/traces/TRACE_ID", "spanId": "SPAN_ID"} # Cloud Logging auto-links to Cloud Trace when trace field is present # Log-based metric from error pattern: gcloud logging metrics create payment_errors \ --log-filter='jsonPayload.event="payment_failed"' # Error Reporting groups exceptions automatically gcloud beta error-reporting events list --project=PROJECT GCP observability stack: Cloud Logging ← container stdout (auto), Cloud Trace ← OTLP exporter, Cloud Profiler ← sampling profiler (zero overhead). Log entries with trace field show a "View trace" link in Cloud Logging console — one click jumps to the full distributed trace for that request. Log-based metrics extract signal from logs into Cloud Monitoring without application code changes.

questions.q: A production alert fires — walk through your structured incident response.
questions.text: Phase 1 — Detect ( Phase 2 — Triage (5-15 min): Golden signals dashboard: which signal is anomalous? Recent changes: kubectl rollout history, recent deploys, config changes Form a hypothesis before taking action Phase 3 — Mitigate: Rollback first if recent deploy (fastest recovery) Scale up if saturation issue Disable feature flag if new feature causing errors Phase 4 — Resolve: confirm metrics returned to baseline, post status update Phase 5 — Postmortem: schedule within 48 hours One incident commander coordinates (does not necessarily fix). Other engineers investigate. Rule: make one change at a time — simultaneous changes make it impossible to know what fixed the issue. Always rollback first if unsure — a known-good state beats an unknown state.

questions.q: How do you write a blameless postmortem — what structure matters?
questions.text: 1. Incident summary (severity, duration, user impact) 2. Timeline (who did what, when) 3. Root cause (5 Whys — get to systemic cause) 4. Contributing factors 5. What went well 6. Action items (specific owner + due date) # 5 Whys example: Service crashed → OOM at 2x load → Marketing campaign not communicated → No cross-team process → Fix: establish the process (not just raise memory limits) Blameless: goal is systemic improvement, not fault assignment. People make mistakes — well-designed systems prevent mistakes from causing incidents. Every postmortem must produce action items with owners and due dates. Track completion rate — below 80% means the process is broken and incidents will recur. This is a Principal-level responsibility.

questions.q: What is an SLO dashboard — how do you visualise error budget in Grafana?
questions.text: # Error budget remaining panel (PromQL): 1 - (sum(increase(requests_total{code=~"5.."}[30d])) / (sum(increase(requests_total[30d])) * 0.001)) # Error budget burn rate panel: rate(errors[1h]) / rate(requests[1h]) / 0.001 # ratio to allowed rate # Colour thresholds: green > 50%, yellow 10-50%, red An SLO dashboard has three panels: current SLI value vs target (are we in SLO right now?), error budget remaining % (how much budget is left this month?), and burn rate over time (are we accelerating or decelerating?). Green error budget with stable burn rate = healthy, deploy freely. Red budget with high burn rate = freeze deployments, fix reliability. The dashboard makes the deployment decision data-driven.

questions.q: How do you export custom application metrics from a Kubernetes pod to Prometheus?
questions.text: # Python instrumentation: from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, start_http_server requests_total = Counter("myapp_requests_total","Total requests",["status"]) latency = Histogram("myapp_request_duration_seconds","Request latency") # Expose metrics port in Service: ports: [{name: metrics, containerPort: 8081}] # ServiceMonitor CRD (Prometheus Operator picks this up): spec: selector: {matchLabels: {app: myapp}} endpoints: [{port: metrics, interval: 30s}] # Verify: kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus 9090 → check /targets ServiceMonitor is the GitOps-friendly pattern: each team deploys their own ServiceMonitor alongside their Deployment. Prometheus auto-discovers it without central config changes. Metric naming conventions: myapp_http_requests_total (counter), myapp_request_duration_seconds (histogram), myapp_active_connections (gauge). Unit in name, snake_case, _total suffix for counters.

questions.q: How do you set up PagerDuty routing from Alertmanager?
questions.text: receivers: - name: pagerduty pagerduty_configs: - routing_key: <INTEGRATION_KEY> # from PagerDuty service integration description: "{{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}" severity: "{{ .CommonLabels.severity }}" details: runbook: "{{ .CommonAnnotations.runbook_url }}" dashboard: "{{ .CommonAnnotations.dashboard_url }}" Store the integration key in a Kubernetes Secret referenced by Alertmanager. Route: critical severity → PagerDuty (wakes people up), warning → Slack (async review). Runbook and dashboard URLs in every alert — they appear in the PagerDuty incident, giving on-call engineers immediate context. This alone reduces MTTA by 50%.

questions.q: What are Grafana template variables — how do you use them for multi-cluster dashboards?
questions.text: # Variable: cluster (auto-populated from metric labels) Name: cluster Type: Query Query: label_values(kube_node_info, cluster) # Use in panel: sum by (namespace) (rate(requests_total{cluster="$cluster"}[5m])) # $__rate_interval: auto-adjusts to time range and scrape interval rate(requests_total[$__rate_interval]) # better than hardcoded [5m] Template variables make one dashboard serve all clusters. Chained variables: selecting a cluster narrows the namespace dropdown. Data links add drill-down: click a pod in the overview to jump to the pod-detail dashboard with that pod pre-selected. Use $__rate_interval instead of hardcoded time windows — it adjusts automatically to the dashboard time range and scrape interval.

questions.q: Distributed traces show high latency but you cannot find the cause — how do you debug?
questions.text: # Step 1: Find slow trace — filter by duration in Jaeger/Tempo # Step 2: Inspect trace waterfall — wide span = slow, gap = wait db.statement, http.url, db.row_count, error.message # span attributes # Step 3: Cross-reference logs with trace_id {service="payments"} | json | trace_id="abc123" # Step 4: Check resource metrics at time of slow trace container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total # was the pod throttled? Trace waterfall: width = duration, indentation = parent-child. Gap between parent starting and first child = time in parent before the downstream call (serialisation, connection pool wait). Wide span with no children = bottleneck is in that service. Span attributes (db.statement, http.url) give the exact SQL or API call. Cross-correlate with logs using trace_id to see application-level context at that exact moment.

questions.q: What is a runbook — how do you write one that actually helps at 3am?
questions.text: # Runbook structure: ## Alert: PaymentServiceHighErrorRate ### What this means: error rate above 0.1% SLO threshold ### Severity: P1 if > 1%, P2 if 0.1-1% ### Triage steps: 1. Open dashboard: [link] 2. kubectl get pods -n payments | grep -v Running 3. kubectl logs -l app=payments --tail=50 | grep ERROR 4. Check recent deployments: kubectl rollout history deployment/payments ### Mitigation: kubectl rollout undo deployment/payments ### Escalation: payments-oncall → payments-lead → CTO A good runbook assumes the reader has been woken up at 3am and has never seen this alert before. Numbered steps, exact commands to copy-paste, expected outputs, decision branches ("if step 3 shows no errors, skip to step 7"). Link to dashboards with time pre-set. Include escalation path and communication templates. Update the runbook after every incident — add the debugging steps that actually worked.

questions.q: What are the Prometheus metric types: counter, gauge, histogram and summary?
questions.text: Counters only increase, gauges go up and down, histograms bucket observations for aggregable quantiles, summaries compute quantiles client-side. rate(http_requests_total[5m]) histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) Interview tip: Always use rate() on counters.

questions.q: What is cardinality in metrics and how do you control it?
questions.text: Cardinality is the number of unique label combinations; high-cardinality labels like user IDs explode memory and cost. topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"})) metric_relabel_configs: - action: labeldrop regex: pod_uid Interview tip: Never label by unbounded values.

questions.q: How do recording rules and federation help scale Prometheus?
questions.text: Recording rules precompute expensive queries; federation or remote write aggregates data across servers. groups: - name: slo rules: - record: job:http_requests:rate5m expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) Interview tip: Dashboards should query recorded series.

questions.q: What is the USE method and how does it differ from RED?
questions.text: USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) analyses resources; RED (rate, errors, duration) analyses request-driven services. node_cpu_seconds_total rate(http_requests_total[5m]) Interview tip: USE for hosts, RED for services.

questions.q: How do you measure and alert on saturation, and why is it hard?
questions.text: Saturation is how full a resource is; measure queue depth, throttling, run queue and utilisation against limits, and alert predictively. node_load1 / count(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}) without (cpu, mode) predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[6h], 4*3600) < 0 Interview tip: Queues reveal saturation before errors do.

questions.q: How do you design log levels and what should be logged at each level?
questions.text: Error for failures needing attention, warn for recoverable anomalies, info for key business events, debug for diagnostics; avoid noise and secrets. logger.info('order_created', order_id=oid, amount=amt) logger.error('payment_failed', exc_info=True, order_id=oid) Interview tip: Every error log should be actionable.

questions.q: How do you handle sensitive data and compliance in logs?
questions.text: Do not log secrets or personal data; mask or hash at source, restrict access, set retention and audit log access. processors: - redaction: allowed_keys: [user_id, status] blocked_values: ['\\b\\d{16}\\b'] Interview tip: Redact at the source, not later.

questions.q: What is log sampling and when is it appropriate?
questions.text: Keep a representative fraction of high-volume low-value logs while always keeping errors and rare events. if hash(request_id) % 100 < 5: logger.debug(...) Interview tip: Sample by request ID to keep complete flows.

questions.q: How do you query logs effectively in Loki with LogQL or in Elasticsearch?
questions.text: Filter by indexed labels first, then line filters and parsers; avoid broad regexes over long ranges. {app="api", env="prod"} |= "timeout" | json | status >= 500 sum by (route) (rate({app="api"} |= "error" [5m])) Interview tip: Labels select streams; filters scan text.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs between agent-based, sidecar and direct logging pipelines?
questions.text: Node agents are efficient and simple; sidecars isolate per-app needs; direct SDK shipping couples the app to the backend and risks loss. kubectl get ds -n logging fluent-bit -c /etc/fluent-bit.conf Interview tip: Buffer on disk to survive outages.

questions.q: What is trace sampling and how do head-based and tail-based sampling differ?
questions.text: Head sampling decides at the start of a trace; tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so it can keep errors and slow traces. processors: tail_sampling: policies: - name: errors type: status_code status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]} Interview tip: Tail sampling needs all spans of a trace in one place.

questions.q: What is context propagation and what breaks it?
questions.text: Trace identifiers travel in headers or message metadata so spans link across services; breaks occur at async boundaries, proxies and unsupported libraries. traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01 propagators: [tracecontext, baggage] Interview tip: Instrument queues and thread pools explicitly.

questions.q: How do you use span attributes, events and links wisely?
questions.text: Attributes describe a span with bounded, queryable data; events mark moments inside it; links connect causally related traces such as batch consumers. span.set_attribute('http.route', '/orders/{id}') span.add_event('cache_miss') Link(producer_span_context) Interview tip: Use semantic convention names.

questions.q: How do you read a trace waterfall to find a latency problem?
questions.text: Look for the longest spans, gaps with no child work, serial calls that could be parallel, repeated calls and retries. traceID=<id> # open in Tempo/Jaeger sum by (span_name) (rate(traces_spanmetrics_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) Interview tip: Gaps often mean waiting, not working.

questions.q: How do you derive RED metrics from traces, and what are span metrics?
questions.text: A collector connector aggregates spans into request count, error count and duration histograms, giving metrics without extra instrumentation. connectors: spanmetrics: histogram: explicit: buckets: [5ms,25ms,100ms,500ms,2s] Interview tip: Generate before sampling to keep counts exact.

questions.q: What is multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting?
questions.text: Alert when the error budget burns quickly over both a long and short window, catching fast and slow burns while avoiding flapping. (sum(rate(errors[1h]))/sum(rate(total[1h])) > 14.4*0.001) and (sum(rate(errors[5m]))/sum(rate(total[5m])) > 14.4*0.001) Interview tip: Short window confirms it is still happening.

questions.q: How do you write alert annotations and runbook links that help on-call responders?
questions.text: Include summary, impact, severity, the dashboard and runbook URL, and likely first checks so the responder can act in minutes. annotations: summary: 'Checkout error rate above SLO burn threshold' runbook_url: https://runbooks.example/checkout-errors dashboard: https://grafana.example/d/checkout Interview tip: The alert should answer: what, how bad, what now.

questions.q: How do you reduce alert noise with grouping, inhibition and deduplication?
questions.text: Group related alerts into one notification, inhibit symptom alerts when a root-cause alert fires, and deduplicate repeated firings. route: group_by: [alertname, cluster] group_wait: 30s inhibit_rules: - source_matchers: [alertname="NodeDown"] target_matchers: [alertname="PodNotReady"] equal: [node] Interview tip: One incident should be one page.

questions.q: What is the difference between alerting on symptoms versus causes, and which should page?
questions.text: Symptoms are user-visible failures and should page; causes are internal conditions best used for diagnosis or tickets. # page: error rate and latency SLO burn # ticket: disk 80% full, node memory high Interview tip: Page on what users feel.

questions.q: How do you test alerts and make sure they actually fire?
questions.text: Unit-test rules with promtool, inject synthetic failures, use a dead man's switch, and run game days to validate the full path. promtool test rules tests.yml vector(1) # always-firing Watchdog alert Interview tip: An alert never tested is a hope.

questions.q: How do you choose good SLIs for different types of services?
questions.text: Pick indicators users feel: availability and latency for request services, freshness and correctness for pipelines, durability for storage. sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) Interview tip: Measure close to the user.

questions.q: How do you set an SLO target and negotiate it with product owners?
questions.text: Base it on user needs and historical performance, make it slightly below what users would notice, and agree what happens when the budget is spent. # 99.9% over 30 days = 43.2 minutes of error budget Interview tip: 100% is the wrong target.

questions.q: How do you handle SLOs for dependencies and composite services?
questions.text: Availability multiplies across serial dependencies; set dependency SLOs higher than yours and use redundancy, fallbacks and caching to decouple. # 0.999 * 0.999 * 0.999 ≈ 0.997 Interview tip: Serial dependencies erode availability.

questions.q: How do you report SLO status to leadership and use it in planning?
questions.text: Show compliance, remaining budget and burn trends in simple dashboards and reviews, link breaches to actions, and use it to prioritise reliability work. 1 - (sum(increase(errors[30d])) / sum(increase(total[30d]))) Interview tip: Make the budget visible weekly.

questions.q: What is the difference between SLA, SLO and SLI in practice, and what happens when an SLA is breached?
questions.text: SLI is the measurement, SLO the internal target, SLA a contract with consequences like credits; keep the SLO stricter than the SLA. # SLI: 99.95% good requests; SLO: 99.9%; SLA: 99.5% with credits Interview tip: SLA breaches cost money, SLO breaches cost focus.

questions.q: How do you structure dashboards: overview, service and deep-dive levels?
questions.text: Layered dashboards move from health overview to service RED panels to detailed resources, with consistent layout and drill-down links. # row 1: SLO status; row 2: RED; row 3: dependencies; row 4: resources Interview tip: Same layout for every service.

questions.q: What are Grafana annotations and how do they help correlate changes with incidents?
questions.text: Annotations mark events such as deploys, config changes and incidents on graphs, showing what changed when behaviour shifted. curl -X POST /api/annotations -d '{"tags":["deploy"],"text":"web v1.4.2"}' Interview tip: Most incidents follow a change.

questions.q: How do you avoid misleading visualisations such as averages, misaligned axes and missing data?
questions.text: Use percentiles or heatmaps for latency, label units, start axes sensibly, handle gaps explicitly, and show sample sizes. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) Interview tip: Averages hide tail latency.

questions.q: How do you build dashboards-as-code and manage them with GitOps?
questions.text: Define dashboards with Jsonnet, Grafonnet, Terraform or provisioning files in Git, review changes, and deploy automatically. jsonnet -J vendor dashboards/service.jsonnet > service.json terraform apply # grafana_dashboard resources Interview tip: Stop editing production dashboards by hand.

questions.q: How would you build a dashboard for a business-critical user journey, such as checkout?
questions.text: Combine funnel conversion, step latency and errors, dependency health and synthetic checks so engineering and business see the same story. sum(rate(checkout_step_total{step="payment",result="ok"}[5m])) / sum(rate(checkout_step_total{step="cart"}[5m])) Interview tip: Include a business metric next to technical ones.

questions.q: How do Thanos, Cortex and Mimir extend Prometheus for long-term storage and global views?
questions.text: They accept remote-written or sidecar-uploaded data, store it in object storage, and provide global query, downsampling and multi-tenancy. remote_write: - url: https://mimir.example/api/v1/push thanos query --store=sidecar:10901 Interview tip: Keep local Prometheus for alerting.

questions.q: What is the OpenTelemetry Collector and why use it?
questions.text: A vendor-neutral pipeline of receivers, processors and exporters that ingests, enriches, samples and routes telemetry. receivers: [otlp] processors: [batch, memory_limiter, k8sattributes] exporters: [otlphttp] Interview tip: Run agents per node and a gateway tier.

questions.q: How do you choose between self-hosted open-source observability and a commercial SaaS platform?
questions.text: Weigh cost at scale, operational effort, features, data control, lock-in and team skills; many use a hybrid with OpenTelemetry for portability. # criteria: cost model, retention, cardinality limits, compliance, support, exit plan Interview tip: Instrument with open standards either way.

questions.q: What is eBPF-based observability and what are its benefits and limits?
questions.text: eBPF programs run in the kernel to collect network, process and security telemetry with low overhead and no code changes. bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { @[comm] = count(); }' cilium hubble observe Interview tip: Needs kernel support and privileges.

questions.q: How do synthetic monitoring and real user monitoring differ and when do you need each?
questions.text: Synthetic checks run scripted probes continuously from outside; RUM measures actual user sessions in browsers. Together they show availability and real experience. blackbox_exporter probe module: http_2xx target: https://shop.example probe_success{job="blackbox"} == 0 Interview tip: Synthetics find outages at 3 a.m. with no traffic.

questions.q: How do you monitor Kubernetes control-plane health: API server, etcd and scheduler?
questions.text: Track API request latency and errors, etcd disk sync and leader changes, scheduler queue and pending pods, and controller work queues. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le,verb) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds_bucket Interview tip: etcd is sensitive to disk latency.

questions.q: How do you use kube-state-metrics and cAdvisor, and what is the difference?
questions.text: kube-state-metrics reports object state from the API; cAdvisor reports container resource usage from the kubelet. kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable > 0 rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!=""}[5m]) Interview tip: State vs usage.

questions.q: How do you find noisy neighbours and right-size workloads using metrics?
questions.text: Compare usage against requests per workload over weeks, look at percentiles and throttling, and use VPA recommendations. quantile_over_time(0.95, container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="app"}[7d]) kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="cpu"} Interview tip: Use p95 over a long window.

questions.q: How do you monitor pod restarts, OOM kills and evictions meaningfully?
questions.text: Alert on restart rate and last termination reason, not raw counts; separate OOMKilled from errors and evictions from node pressure. increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[1h]) > 3 kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"} == 1 Interview tip: Reason labels tell you the fix.

questions.q: How do you set up multi-cluster monitoring and consistent labelling?
questions.text: Add cluster, region and environment external labels, ship to a central store, and use consistent label schemas for dashboards and alerts. global: external_labels: cluster: prod-eu-1 region: eu-west-1 Interview tip: Add the cluster label at the source.

questions.q: How do you monitor serverless functions such as Lambda or Cloud Functions?
questions.text: Track invocations, errors, duration, throttles and cold starts, use structured logs and distributed tracing, and alert on error rate and concurrency limits. aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/Lambda --metric-name Errors ... gcloud functions logs read my-func Interview tip: Cold starts show up in tail latency.

questions.q: How do you control observability costs in the cloud?
questions.text: Manage cardinality, sampling, retention tiers, log volume and duplicate collection, with budgets, ownership and dashboards of telemetry spend. topk(10, sum by (job) (scrape_samples_scraped)) aws logs describe-log-groups --query 'logGroups[].[logGroupName,storedBytes]' Interview tip: Observability is often the second-largest bill.

questions.q: How do you build a cross-account or cross-project logging and monitoring architecture?
questions.text: Centralise into a dedicated observability account or project with delegated, read-only access, aggregation sinks and strict IAM and encryption. gcloud logging sinks create central-sink storage.googleapis.com/bucket --include-children --organization=ORG aws logs put-subscription-filter ... Interview tip: Write-only from workloads, read-controlled centrally.

questions.q: How do you use cloud-native tracing and profiling such as X-Ray, Cloud Trace and Cloud Profiler?
questions.text: Instrument or enable integrations to trace requests across managed services, and use continuous profilers to find CPU and memory hotspots in production. aws xray get-trace-summaries --start-time ... --end-time ... gcloud trace traces list Interview tip: Continuous profiling has very low overhead.

questions.q: How do you run an incident bridge: roles, communication and decision-making?
questions.text: Assign an incident commander, scribe, communications lead and technical leads; keep a single channel, regular updates and time-boxed hypotheses. /incident declare sev2 'checkout errors' # update every 15-30 min Interview tip: The commander coordinates, not debugs.

questions.q: How do you quickly determine the blast radius and customer impact of an incident?
questions.text: Segment errors by region, tenant, version and endpoint, check SLO burn, support tickets and synthetic checks to scope who is affected. sum by (region, version) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) sum by (tenant) (rate(errors_total[5m])) Interview tip: Slice by every dimension you have.

questions.q: What makes a postmortem action item effective, and how do you track them?
questions.text: Specific, owned, time-bound, prioritised by risk reduction, and tracked in the normal backlog with follow-up reviews. # action: add alert on queue age > 5m; owner: team-a; due: 2026-11-15; priority: P1 Interview tip: Prefer systemic fixes over reminders.

questions.q: How do you handle alert storms during a major outage?
questions.text: Silence or group symptoms, focus on the root-cause signal, designate who triages alerts, and fix the alert design afterwards. amtool silence add alertname=~"PodNotReady|HighLatency" cluster=prod-eu-1 --duration=1h --comment='incident 1234' Interview tip: Silences need an owner and expiry.

questions.q: How do you measure on-call health and reduce burnout?
questions.text: Track pages per shift, out-of-hours pages, time to acknowledge and actionable ratio; fix noisy alerts, share load fairly and give recovery time. # metrics: pages/shift, night pages, % actionable, MTTA, MTTR Interview tip: Sustainable on-call is a reliability requirement.

questions.q: How do you write an incident timeline and perform root cause analysis without blaming people?
questions.text: Reconstruct events from logs and chat, ask how the system allowed the failure using techniques like five whys, and focus on contributing factors. # timeline: 10:02 deploy; 10:07 errors rise; 10:11 page; 10:25 rollback; 10:31 recovery Interview tip: Why did it make sense at the time?

questions.q: What is OpenStack and which core services make up a typical private cloud?
questions.text: OpenStack is a set of loosely coupled services exposing REST APIs. The essentials are Keystone (identity), Nova (compute), Neutron (network), Glance (images), Cinder (block storage) and Placement (inventory), with Horizon as the UI. openstack service list openstack catalog list openstack endpoint list Interview tip: Say that services share a database and a message bus, then name the minimum viable set.

questions.q: Describe the OpenStack control-plane architecture: API, database, message queue and agents.
questions.text: API services validate tokens, persist state in Galera, and hand work to workers through RabbitMQ (oslo.messaging). The database and the queue are the shared dependencies to protect. openstack compute service list rabbitmqctl cluster_status mysql -e 'SHOW STATUS LIKE "wsrep_cluster_size"' Interview tip: Explain the failure mode: API accepts the request but no worker consumes it.

questions.q: Walk through what happens, step by step, when a user runs openstack server create.
questions.text: Keystone token, Nova API and quota, scheduler with Placement, conductor to compute, then Glance image, Neutron port and Cinder volume, and finally libvirt starts the guest. openstack server create --flavor m1.small --image ubuntu-22.04 --network private --key-name mykey web1 openstack server show web1 -c status -c fault openstack server event list web1 Interview tip: Narrate it in order, then say which log you would open at each step.

questions.q: OpenStack versus VMware vSphere versus Kubernetes: how do you position each?
questions.text: vSphere is a supported virtualisation product, OpenStack is an open IaaS API layer, and Kubernetes orchestrates containers on top of either. They are complementary, not exclusive. Interview tip: Frame it as layers, not rivals, and be honest about the operational cost of running OpenStack.

questions.q: Explain regions, availability zones, host aggregates and cells. How do they differ?
questions.text: Region: a whole deployment. AZ: tenant-visible failure domain. Aggregate: operator grouping with metadata. Cell: scaling shard with its own DB and queue. openstack availability zone list openstack aggregate create --zone az1 gpu-hosts openstack aggregate set --property gpu=true gpu-hosts Interview tip: Use the one-line summary: AZs for tenants, aggregates for operators, cells for scale.

questions.q: What is the Placement service and why was it split out of Nova?
questions.text: Placement stores resource providers, inventories, allocations and traits. Nova asks it for allocation candidates before running its filters, which is faster and less racy than the old in-scheduler accounting. openstack resource provider list openstack resource provider inventory list <uuid> openstack resource provider usage show <uuid> Interview tip: Mention allocation drift as the thing you actually debug in production.

questions.q: How does the Nova scheduler pick a host? Explain filters and weighers.
questions.text: Placement narrows candidates by raw capacity, filters reject hosts on policy, and weighers rank the remainder. The scheduler log shows how many hosts each filter removed. grep 'Filter' /var/log/nova/nova-scheduler.log | tail openstack hypervisor stats show openstack flavor show m1.small -c properties Interview tip: Say you debug no valid host by reading per-filter counts in the scheduler log.

questions.q: What are flavors and how do you design them well?
questions.text: A flavor sets vCPU, RAM and disk, and extra specs add pinning, hugepages, traits and aggregate selection. Keep a small catalogue grouped by family to avoid capacity fragmentation. openstack flavor create --vcpus 4 --ram 8192 --disk 20 m1.large openstack flavor set m1.large --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated openstack flavor set m1.large --property trait:CUSTOM_GPU=required Interview tip: A short, consistent flavor catalogue is a capacity-planning argument, not just a UX one.

questions.q: Explain the lifecycle and common states of a Nova instance.
questions.text: BUILD, ACTIVE, SHUTOFF, PAUSED, SUSPENDED, SHELVED_OFFLOADED, ERROR and DELETED. Check status, task_state and power_state together; a mismatch points at a host-side problem. openstack server show web1 -c status -c OS-EXT-STS:task_state -c OS-EXT-STS:power_state openstack server set --state active web1 openstack server shelve web1 Interview tip: Mention power_state versus status mismatch: it signals the database and the hypervisor disagree.

questions.q: How does cloud-init and the metadata service work in OpenStack?
questions.text: cloud-init queries 169.254.169.254, which Neutron proxies to the Nova metadata API. A config drive is the no-network alternative. User data is the first-boot hook. curl http://169.254.169.254/openstack/latest/meta_data.json openstack server create --config-drive true ... journalctl -u cloud-init Interview tip: Name both paths: the network metadata service and the config drive.

questions.q: How are projects, quotas and limits managed, and what happens when a quota is hit?
questions.text: Quotas cap per-project consumption and are enforced at request time. They limit but do not reserve capacity, so combine them with real capacity monitoring. openstack quota show <project> openstack quota set --cores 200 --ram 512000 <project> openstack limits show --absolute Interview tip: Be explicit that quota is a ceiling, not a reservation.

questions.q: What is the service catalog and how do endpoints work?
questions.text: Keystone returns a catalog of services with public, internal and admin endpoints per region. Clients pick by interface and region, so a stale URL breaks only the services that use it. openstack catalog show compute openstack endpoint list --service compute openstack --os-interface internal server list Interview tip: Mention interfaces and region together, since mismatches are the usual bug.

questions.q: How do OpenStack microversions and API versioning work?
questions.text: Stable major versions, with microversions adding behaviour. Clients opt in through a header; omitting it gives baseline behaviour. Pin the version in automation. openstack versions show --service compute openstack --os-compute-api-version 2.90 server list curl -s $NOVA_ENDPOINT | jq . Interview tip: Explain that pinning keeps automation stable across upgrades.

questions.q: What is oslo and why do operators care about it?
questions.text: Oslo is the shared library layer: messaging, db, config, log, policy and cache. Tuning or bugs there affect every service, which is why messaging errors are the first thing to check. grep -i 'MessagingTimeout' /var/log/nova/*.log crudini --get /etc/nova/nova.conf oslo_messaging_rabbit oslopolicy-checker --help Interview tip: Say you read MessagingTimeout errors as a queue or consumer symptom, not a service bug.

questions.q: How do you read and manage OpenStack configuration and logs effectively?
questions.text: ini files per service, reloaded by restart or SIGHUP. In containers, change configuration through the deployment tool. Follow one request across services with its req-id. grep req-<uuid> /var/log/*/*.log docker exec nova_api cat /etc/nova/nova.conf kolla-ansible reconfigure -t nova Interview tip: The request ID across services is the single best debugging tool; mention it.

questions.q: What does the release cycle look like and how do SLURP releases affect upgrades?
questions.text: Two releases a year; every other one is a SLURP release you can upgrade between directly, so one planned upgrade per year is possible. openstack --version grep -i 'upgrade' release-notes.txt kolla-ansible upgrade -i inventory Interview tip: Mention you test the exact upgrade path in staging and read the removed-options notes.

questions.q: How do you check the health of a running OpenStack cloud quickly?
questions.text: Check service and agent lists, Galera and RabbitMQ state, run a synthetic canary that boots a VM and pings it, then check capacity headroom. openstack compute service list openstack network agent list openstack volume service list Interview tip: A synthetic end-to-end canary catches what a green service list misses.

questions.q: What is Horizon and when do you prefer the CLI, SDK or API instead?
questions.text: Horizon is a UI over the same APIs. Use the openstack CLI for scripting, openstacksdk, Terraform or Ansible for repeatable automation, and clouds.yaml for credentials. openstack --os-cloud prod server list python -c 'import openstack; print(openstack.connect(cloud="prod").compute.servers())' cat ~/.config/openstack/clouds.yaml Interview tip: Say that anything repeatable belongs in code, not in dashboard clicks.

questions.q: How do images work in Glance and what formats do you use?
questions.text: Glance stores images with format and metadata properties. On Ceph, use raw so boots are instant copy-on-write clones. Keep golden images small, patched and secret-free. openstack image create --disk-format raw --container-format bare --file ubuntu.raw --public ubuntu-22.04 qemu-img convert -f qcow2 -O raw ubuntu.qcow2 ubuntu.raw openstack image set --property hw_disk_bus=scsi ubuntu-22.04 Interview tip: The raw-on-Ceph point shows you understand the storage and compute interaction.

questions.q: Explain live migration: how it works, its requirements and common failures.
questions.text: Libvirt pre-copies memory while the guest runs, then pauses briefly to finish and resume on the target. Shared storage keeps it quick; CPU model mismatches and high dirty rates are common failures. openstack server migrate --live-migration web1 nova live-migration-force-complete web1 <migration-id> openstack server migration list --server web1 Interview tip: Name auto-converge and post-copy as the answer for busy guests.

questions.q: What is the difference between cold migration, resize, evacuate and rebuild?
questions.text: Cold migrate: planned move with downtime. Resize: new flavor, may move. Evacuate: recover from a dead host. Rebuild: reinstall the root disk from an image. openstack server resize --flavor m1.large web1 openstack server resize confirm web1 nova evacuate web1 Interview tip: Frame it as planned versus failed host, and data kept versus wiped.

questions.q: What is CPU pinning and NUMA awareness, and when do you need them?
questions.text: hw:cpu_policy=dedicated pins vCPUs to cores and NUMA settings keep memory local. Great for latency-sensitive loads, but no overcommit, so isolate with aggregates. openstack flavor set rt --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated --property hw:numa_nodes=1 crudini --set /etc/nova/nova.conf compute cpu_dedicated_set 2-23 lscpu | grep NUMA Interview tip: State the trade-off: performance and predictability versus density.

questions.q: How do hugepages help, and how are they configured for instances?
questions.text: Hugepages reduce TLB misses for big or packet-heavy guests. Reserve them at host boot, set hw:mem_page_size on the flavor, and accept no memory overcommit. grep Huge /proc/meminfo openstack flavor set dpdk --property hw:mem_page_size=1GB grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args='hugepagesz=1G hugepages=64' Interview tip: Link hugepages to DPDK and NFV to show you know the use case.

questions.q: How do CPU and RAM overcommit ratios work and how do you choose them?
questions.text: Allocation ratios let scheduling exceed physical capacity. CPU 4 to 16 is common, RAM close to 1. Set per aggregate by workload and watch steal time and memory pressure. crudini --set /etc/nova/nova.conf DEFAULT cpu_allocation_ratio 8.0 openstack resource provider inventory show <uuid> VCPU sar -u 1 5 # check %steal Interview tip: Say conservative for databases, aggressive for dev, and validate with steal time.

questions.q: What are Nova cells v2 and why would you deploy them?
questions.text: Cells split compute nodes into groups with their own DB and queue under a global API database. They bound RabbitMQ and DB load and limit failure blast radius. nova-manage cell_v2 list_cells nova-manage cell_v2 discover_hosts --verbose openstack hypervisor list Interview tip: Cells are about bounding the message bus and DB, not about regions.

questions.q: A compute node dies. What is your recovery procedure?
questions.text: Verify the failure, fence the host, force the service down, evacuate instances (shared storage preserves disks), verify networking, then repair and re-enable. Automate with Masakari. openstack compute service set --down <host> nova-compute nova host-evacuate <host> openstack server list --host <host> --all-projects Interview tip: Always say fencing comes before evacuation; that is the data-safety point.

questions.q: How do server groups and affinity rules work?
questions.text: Server groups with anti-affinity spread replicas across hosts and affinity co-locates them. Strict policies fail when hosts run out, so use the soft variant when capacity is tight. openstack server group create --policy anti-affinity db-group openstack server create --hint group=<group-id> --flavor m1.large --image ubuntu db1 openstack server group show db-group Interview tip: Mention that strict anti-affinity can block live migration during maintenance.

questions.q: How do you provide GPUs to instances: passthrough versus vGPU?
questions.text: Passthrough gives a whole GPU to one guest with full performance. vGPU shares a card across guests. Use aggregates and traits to schedule precisely. lspci -nn | grep -i nvidia crudini --set /etc/nova/nova.conf pci device_spec '{"vendor_id":"10de","product_id":"2204"}' openstack flavor set gpu --property pci_passthrough:alias=a100:1 Interview tip: State the trade-off: dedicated performance versus utilisation.

questions.q: An instance is stuck in a transitional state such as BUILD or deleting. How do you fix it?
questions.text: Read fault, task_state and the compute log by request ID to learn what hung. Then reset state to error and delete or rebuild; clean up ports and volumes. Alert on long-lived transitional states. openstack server show web1 -c fault -c OS-EXT-STS:task_state openstack server set --state error web1 openstack server delete --force web1 Interview tip: Diagnose before resetting; resetting hides the cause.

questions.q: What hypervisors does Nova support and why is KVM the default choice?
questions.text: KVM via libvirt is the mainstream, best-tested driver. Others exist, such as VMware, Hyper-V and Ironic for bare metal, but KVM has the richest feature support. virsh list --all egrep -c '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo openstack hypervisor list --long Interview tip: Answer with KVM and give one reason beyond cost, such as feature coverage.

questions.q: How do you perform maintenance on a compute node without user impact?
questions.text: Disable the service, live-migrate instances in batches, handle non-migratable guests with coordination, do the work, verify agents, re-enable. Watch capacity and anti-affinity. openstack compute service set --disable --disable-reason 'kernel patch' <host> nova-compute openstack server list --host <host> --all-projects -f value -c ID | xargs -n1 openstack server migrate --live-migration openstack compute service set --enable <host> nova-compute Interview tip: Say disable first, drain, work, verify, enable, in that order.

questions.q: Explain the Neutron architecture: server, ML2 plugin, agents and mechanism drivers.
questions.text: neutron-server holds the API and DB; ML2 combines type drivers (flat, vlan, vxlan, geneve) with mechanism drivers (OVS, OVN, Linux bridge) that program the data plane; agents run per node. openstack network agent list openstack extension list --network grep mechanism_drivers /etc/neutron/plugins/ml2/ml2_conf.ini Interview tip: Separate control plane (server and DB) from data plane (driver) in the answer.

questions.q: OVS versus OVN: what changed and why do most new clouds choose OVN?
questions.text: OVN replaces the agent-based design with logical networking in OVN databases, ovn-northd translation and ovn-controller on each host.
