Fewer agents, less RabbitMQ chatter, distributed routing by default. ovn-nbctl show ovn-sbctl show ovs-vsctl show Interview tip: Name northd and ovn-controller to show you know the pipeline.

questions.q: What is the difference between provider networks and tenant (self-service) networks?
questions.text: Provider networks are operator-defined mappings to physical VLANs with routable addresses. Tenant networks are user-created overlays routed to the outside through a virtual router and floating IPs. openstack network create --provider-network-type vlan --provider-physical-network physnet1 --provider-segment 120 prov120 openstack network create tenant-net openstack router create r1 Interview tip: Give a use case for each: provider for direct addressing, tenant for self-service isolation.

questions.q: How do VXLAN and Geneve overlays work, and what is the MTU consequence?
questions.text: Overlays encapsulate guest frames in UDP between hypervisors, adding 50 to 58 bytes of header. Raise the underlay MTU or lower the guest MTU, or large packets will hang. ping -M do -s 1400 <dst> ip link show | grep mtu openstack network show tenant-net -c mtu Interview tip: The symptom-based answer: small packets work, big ones hang.

questions.q: What is DVR and when is it useful with OVS ML2?
questions.text: DVR runs routers on compute nodes so east-west and floating IP traffic avoid the network node bottleneck. Centralised SNAT remains for instances without floating IPs. OVN does this natively. openstack router set --distributed r1 ip netns list | grep qrouter ip netns exec qrouter-<id> ip a Interview tip: Say what remains centralised, which shows depth.

questions.q: How do floating IPs and SNAT work for instances?
questions.text: Routers SNAT outbound traffic and floating IPs add one-to-one DNAT and SNAT. Instances keep private addresses and security groups apply to the private port. openstack floating ip create public openstack server add floating ip web1 203.0.113.10 ip netns exec qrouter-<id> iptables -t nat -S | grep 203.0.113.10 Interview tip: Remember to say the upstream network must route the floating range.

questions.q: How do security groups work and how are they implemented?
questions.text: Stateful allow-only rules attached to ports, with default deny inbound. Implemented as conntrack-based OVS flows or OVN ACLs; port security blocks spoofing. openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 443 --remote-group app-sg db-sg openstack port show <port> -c security_group_ids conntrack -L | grep <ip> Interview tip: Mention group-to-group rules, which scale better than CIDR lists.

questions.q: What is Octavia and how does it provide load balancing as a service?
questions.text: Octavia creates HAProxy-based amphora VMs, optionally in active-standby with VRRP, and offers L4/L7, TLS termination and health monitors. The OVN provider is a lightweight L4 option. openstack loadbalancer create --vip-subnet-id web-subnet --name lb1 openstack loadbalancer listener create --protocol HTTPS --protocol-port 443 lb1 openstack loadbalancer amphora list Interview tip: Link Octavia to Kubernetes services of type LoadBalancer.

questions.q: An instance does not get an IP address from DHCP. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: Check console log, port status and binding, DHCP agent and subnet state, then capture DISCOVER/OFFER on tap, bridge and namespace. Usual culprits: agent down, binding failure, MTU, VLAN, exhausted pool. openstack port show <port> -c status -c binding_host_id ip netns exec qdhcp-<net> tcpdump -ni any port 67 or port 68 openstack subnet show <subnet> -c allocation_pools Interview tip: Narrate layer by layer: guest, port, agent, wire.

questions.q: What does a Neutron port binding failure mean and how do you fix it?
questions.text: Binding fails when no mechanism driver can bind the port on that host: agent down, wrong physnet mapping or unsupported network type. Inspect vif_type, agent state and server logs. openstack port show <port> -c binding_vif_type -c binding_host_id openstack network agent list --host <host> grep -i 'binding' /var/log/neutron/neutron-server.log | tail Interview tip: Say vif_type=binding_failed and then check agent, physnet, type.

questions.q: How do you debug network paths using namespaces, tcpdump and flows?
questions.text: Trace hop by hop: tap, br-int, tunnel or provider bridge, NIC. Use ip netns exec for routers and DHCP, and ovs-appctl ofproto/trace or ovn-trace to find the dropping rule. ovs-appctl ofproto/trace br-int in_port=tap1234,dl_src=fa:16:3e:aa:bb:cc ovn-trace tenant-net 'inport=="port1" && eth.src==fa:16:3e:aa:bb:cc' ip netns exec qrouter-<id> tcpdump -ni any icmp Interview tip: The last hop where you still see the packet is where it gets dropped.

questions.q: What is SR-IOV and how do you use it with OpenStack?
questions.text: SR-IOV assigns NIC virtual functions straight to guests for near line-rate networking. Use vnic_type direct, whitelist in Nova, and accept limits on migration and software filtering. echo 8 > /sys/class/net/ens1f0/device/sriov_numvfs openstack port create --vnic-type direct --network sriov-net sriov-port lspci | grep -i 'virtual function' Interview tip: State the trade-off: speed versus features such as migration and filtering.

questions.q: How does Neutron QoS work and what can it limit?
questions.text: QoS policies attach bandwidth, minimum bandwidth, DSCP and packet-rate rules to ports or networks. Enforcement depends on the driver, and minimum guarantees need Placement support. openstack network qos policy create gold openstack network qos rule create --type bandwidth-limit --max-kbps 100000 --egress gold openstack port set --qos-policy gold <port> Interview tip: Distinguish limits from guarantees.

questions.q: What are trunk ports and when are they needed?
questions.text: A trunk carries multiple tagged VLANs on one vNIC via a parent port and subports. Used by NFV appliances and nested container networking to avoid many NICs. openstack network trunk create --parent-port p0 trunk0 openstack network trunk set --subport port=p1,segmentation-type=vlan,segmentation-id=101 trunk0 ip link add link eth0 name eth0.101 type vlan id 101 Interview tip: Mention Kuryr or NFV as the real-world use.

questions.q: How do you handle IPv6 and dual stack in OpenStack?
questions.text: IPv6 uses SLAAC or DHCPv6 with router advertisements. Dual stack gives both address families; there is no NAT, so security groups and upstream routing of the prefix are essential. openstack subnet create --ip-version 6 --ipv6-ra-mode slaac --ipv6-address-mode slaac --network n1 --subnet-range 2001:db8:1::/64 v6 openstack security group rule create --ethertype IPv6 --protocol icmpv6 default ping6 2001:db8:1::1 Interview tip: Point out that no NAT shifts protection to security groups.

questions.q: How does Neutron integrate with BGP and dynamic routing?
questions.text: Neutron BGP speakers or OVN with FRR advertise tenant and floating prefixes to the fabric, enabling routed leaf-spine designs without stretched L2 or static routes. openstack bgp speaker create --local-as 64512 --ip-version 4 bgp1 openstack bgp peer create --peer-ip 10.0.0.1 --remote-as 64513 tor1 vtysh -c 'show ip bgp summary' Interview tip: Say leaf-spine with ECMP and per-rack L3 domains.

questions.q: What are Designate and DNS integration in Neutron?
questions.text: Designate offers DNS as a service publishing to BIND or PowerDNS. Neutron integration creates and removes records for ports and floating IPs automatically. openstack zone create --email admin@example.org example.org. openstack network set --dns-domain example.org. net1 openstack recordset list example.org. Interview tip: Mention zone ownership and delegation for tenants.

questions.q: How do you design the physical network for an OpenStack cloud?
questions.text: Separate management, API, overlay, storage and provider traffic; bond NICs across two ToR switches; jumbo MTU for overlay and storage; plan IPs and VLANs and document them. ip -d link show bond0 cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0 ethtool -S ens1f0 | grep -i drop Interview tip: Lead with traffic separation, then redundancy, then MTU.

questions.q: What is the metadata proxy path and why do some instances fail to get SSH keys?
questions.text: 169.254.169.254 requests go through a namespace proxy and the metadata agent to Nova metadata, signed with a shared secret. Failures: agent down, secret mismatch, routing or egress blocked. curl -sv http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ systemctl status neutron-metadata-agent grep metadata_proxy_shared_secret /etc/neutron/metadata_agent.ini /etc/nova/nova.conf Interview tip: Name the shared-secret mismatch, a classic cause.

questions.q: Explain the Cinder architecture and how a volume is created and attached.
questions.text: API, scheduler and per-backend cinder-volume with a driver. Attach goes through Nova and os-brick on the compute host. Volumes outlive instances. openstack volume create --size 50 --type ceph-ssd data1 openstack server add volume web1 data1 openstack volume service list Interview tip: Mention os-brick as the glue on the compute side.

questions.q: Why is Ceph the most common storage back end for OpenStack?
questions.text: Ceph unifies block, object and file storage with replication and CRUSH. Shared RBD pools give instant copy-on-write clones and shared-storage live migration. Cost is operational complexity. ceph -s ceph osd pool ls detail rbd -p volumes ls Interview tip: Say shared pools make clone-from-image instant.

questions.q: What are volume types and how do you use them for service tiers?
questions.text: Volume types map to back ends and policies through extra specs and QoS. Use them to offer tiers like ssd and hdd, and to restrict premium types to specific projects. openstack volume type create --property volume_backend_name=ceph-nvme fast openstack volume qos create --consumer front-end --property read_iops_sec=5000 fast-qos openstack volume type set --private fast Interview tip: Present types as your storage catalogue.

questions.q: What is boot from volume and what are its advantages?
questions.text: The root disk is a Cinder volume, so it persists, can be snapshotted and makes evacuation easy. It depends on the storage backend. Ephemeral still fits stateless instances. openstack server create --volume ubuntu-vol --flavor m1.small --network n1 web1 openstack volume create --image ubuntu-22.04 --size 30 ubuntu-vol openstack server create --block-device-mapping vda=<id>:::true ... Interview tip: Contrast pets and cattle to justify the choice.

questions.q: How do Cinder snapshots and backups differ?
questions.text: Snapshots are fast, same-backend point-in-time copies. Backups go to a separate target and survive backend loss. Use both, and test restores. openstack volume snapshot create --volume data1 snap1 openstack volume backup create --incremental --name bk2 data1 openstack volume backup restore bk2 data1-restored Interview tip: One-liner: snapshots share the fate of the backend; backups do not.

questions.q: A volume is stuck in attaching, detaching or error_deleting. How do you recover?
questions.text: Compare Cinder attachments with Nova block device mappings, read logs by request ID, check the host connection, then use reset-state to align them. Alert on long transitional states. openstack volume show data1 -c status -c attachments cinder reset-state --state available data1 cinder attachment-list --volume-id <id> Interview tip: Say Nova and Cinder disagreeing is the root of most stuck states.

questions.q: What is multi-attach and when is it safe to use?
questions.text: One volume attached to several instances, via a multiattach volume type. Only safe with cluster-aware filesystems or read-only use; for general shared files use Manila. openstack volume type create --property multiattach='<is> True' shared openstack volume create --type shared --size 20 shared1 openstack server add volume node2 shared1 Interview tip: Say clearly that multi-attach does not equal shared filesystem.

questions.q: How does Swift object storage work: rings, replicas and consistency?
questions.text: Proxies use a consistent-hashing ring to place replicas across zones; replicators and auditors provide eventual consistency and repair. Scales linearly for object data. swift stat swift-ring-builder object.builder openstack container create backups Interview tip: Explain the ring as consistent hashing with zones.

questions.q: What is Manila and how does it differ from Cinder?
questions.text: Manila provides shared NFS, CIFS or CephFS file systems with access rules, for many-instance sharing. Cinder gives a private block device per instance. openstack share create --share-type cephfs NFS 100 --name data openstack share access create data ip 10.0.0.0/24 openstack share export location list data Interview tip: Use ReadWriteMany for Kubernetes as the practical example.

questions.q: How do you size and monitor a Ceph cluster for OpenStack?
questions.text: Size on usable capacity after replication with 25 to 30 percent headroom, separate public and cluster networks, set failure domains in CRUSH, and monitor health, slow ops and recovery. ceph df ceph health detail ceph osd perf Interview tip: Say headroom is needed so a node failure can re-replicate.

questions.q: What are ephemeral disks, and how do Nova image backends affect them?
questions.text: Ephemeral disks live and die with the instance; the image backend (qcow2, LVM or RBD) decides where. Local is fast but host-bound; RBD enables shared-storage migration. crudini --get /etc/nova/nova.conf libvirt images_type openstack flavor show m1.small -c disk -c 'OS-FLV-EXT-DATA:ephemeral' virsh domblklist <instance> Interview tip: Tie the backend choice to your evacuation and migration strategy.

questions.q: How do you encrypt volumes and protect data at rest?
questions.text: Encrypted volume types use LUKS on the compute host with keys in Barbican, so the storage backend only sees ciphertext. Protect and back up the key manager. openstack volume type create --encryption-provider luks --encryption-cipher aes-xts-plain64 --encryption-key-size 256 --encryption-control-location front-end LUKS openstack volume create --type LUKS --size 10 secure1 openstack secret list Interview tip: Remember: lose the key, lose the data.

questions.q: How do you migrate or retype volumes between back ends without downtime?
questions.text: Retype with migration-policy on-demand copies data to the new backend; in-use volumes use a live block copy coordinated with Nova. Plan capacity, batch and verify. openstack volume set --type ssd --retype-policy on-demand data1 cinder migrate data1 host@lvm2#pool openstack volume show data1 -c migration_status Interview tip: Say in-use migrations are heavy and should be batched.

questions.q: What does Cinder replication and consistency-group support offer for DR?
questions.text: Replication-enabled volume types mirror to a secondary array, and failover promotes the replica. Groups give crash-consistent multi-volume snapshots. Driver-dependent; rehearse failover. openstack volume type set --property replication_enabled='<is> True' replicated cinder failover-host host@backend openstack volume group snapshot create group1 Interview tip: Stress rehearsal: failover plans must be tested.

questions.q: How do you provide storage QoS so noisy neighbours do not hurt others?
questions.text: Cinder QoS specs on volume types cap IOPS and throughput at hypervisor or array level; Ceph RBD QoS and flavor limits cover other paths. Monitor top consumers by latency. openstack volume qos create --consumer front-end --property total_iops_sec=3000 tier-gold openstack volume qos associate tier-gold gold ceph config set global rbd_qos_iops_limit 2000 Interview tip: Mention per-GB scaling to keep tiers fair.

questions.q: How does Keystone authentication work and what are Fernet tokens?
questions.text: Credentials produce a scoped bearer token. Fernet tokens are encrypted and not stored in the DB; rotate keys regularly and distribute them to every Keystone node. openstack token issue keystone-manage fernet_rotate --keystone-user keystone --keystone-group keystone ls -l /etc/keystone/fernet-keys/ Interview tip: Warn about key distribution: unsynchronised keys cause random 401s.

questions.q: Explain domains, projects, users, groups and roles in Keystone.
questions.text: Domains isolate identity namespaces, projects own resources, users and groups hold roles via role assignments on a scope. Policies in each service decide what roles allow. openstack domain create finance openstack project create --domain finance payments openstack role add --user alice --project payments member Interview tip: Say roles are only names; service policies give them meaning.

questions.q: What is secure RBAC and why is it replacing the global admin?
questions.text: Secure RBAC defines reader, member and admin roles across project, domain and system scopes, ending the all-powerful global admin and enabling least privilege. openstack role assignment list --system --user ops1 openstack --os-system-scope all hypervisor list openstack role add --user auditor --project payments reader Interview tip: Mention that automation assuming global admin is what breaks.

questions.q: How does federated identity work with SAML or OIDC in Keystone?
questions.text: Keystone trusts an external IdP via SAML or OIDC and maps claims to local groups and roles with JSON mapping rules, giving SSO and centralised MFA. openstack identity provider create --remote-id https://idp.example.org corp openstack mapping create --rules rules.json corp-map openstack federation protocol create --identity-provider corp --mapping corp-map openid Interview tip: Say the mapping rules are where most debugging happens.

questions.q: How would you integrate Keystone with LDAP or Active Directory?
questions.text: Domain-specific LDAP back ends read users and groups from the directory read-only, while role assignments stay in SQL. Use LDAPS, filters and caching; federation is often preferred. openstack domain create corp cat /etc/keystone/domains/keystone.corp.conf openstack user list --domain corp Interview tip: Say role assignments remain in the Keystone database.

questions.q: What are application credentials and when should automation use them?
questions.text: Application credentials let automation authenticate with a scoped, revocable, expiring secret instead of a user password, and they work for federated users. One per application, least roles. openstack application credential create --role member --expiration 2026-12-31T00:00:00 ci-bot openstack application credential list openstack --os-auth-type v3applicationcredential server list Interview tip: Say one credential per application with an expiry.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot intermittent 401 errors across OpenStack APIs?
questions.text: Look for Fernet key drift between Keystone nodes, clock skew, and memcached cache failures. Compare key checksums, check chrony and the middleware cache. md5sum /etc/keystone/fernet-keys/* | sort chronyc tracking grep -i 'could not validate\|401' /var/log/keystone/*.log | tail Interview tip: The 'works on some requests' symptom points to node inconsistency.

questions.q: How do policies work in OpenStack and how do you customise them safely?
questions.text: oslo.policy maps API actions to role and scope rules; defaults live in code and operators override via policy.yaml. Keep overrides minimal, test each persona and review at upgrade. oslopolicy-sample-generator --namespace nova --format yaml oslopolicy-checker --config-file /etc/nova/nova.conf --access creds.json --policy /etc/nova/policy.yaml git diff policy.yaml Interview tip: Minimal, version-controlled overrides survive upgrades.

questions.q: How do service users, service tokens and the service project work?
questions.text: Each service has its own Keystone user in a service project. Service tokens accompany user tokens so long operations survive user-token expiry. Use distinct, rotatable credentials. openstack user list --domain default | grep -E 'nova|neutron|cinder' grep -A6 service_user /etc/nova/nova.conf openstack role assignment list --user nova --project service Interview tip: Mention long-running snapshots as the reason service tokens exist.

questions.q: How would you make Keystone highly available and performant?
questions.text: Run several stateless Keystone nodes behind HAProxy with Galera and identical Fernet keys, cache aggressively with memcached, and watch auth latency because everything depends on it. openstack token issue --debug 2>&1 | grep -i 'elapsed' echo stats | nc 127.0.0.1 11211 | grep -E 'get_hits|get_misses' systemctl status apache2 Interview tip: Mention memcached caching, since validation volume dominates load.

questions.q: Compare Kolla-Ansible, OpenStack-Ansible and Charmed OpenStack as deployment tools.
questions.text: Kolla-Ansible runs services as containers, OpenStack-Ansible uses LXC or source installs, Charmed uses Juju and MAAS. Pick by team skills and support needs; keep config in Git. kolla-ansible -i multinode bootstrap-servers kolla-ansible -i multinode deploy openstack-ansible setup-everything.yml Interview tip: Say configuration is in Git and playbooks are the only thing that touches hosts.

questions.q: Walk me through deploying a production OpenStack cloud with Kolla-Ansible.
questions.text: Design hardware and networks, prep hosts, write inventory and globals.yml, run bootstrap-servers, prechecks, pull, deploy and post-deploy, smoke test, then harden, monitor and back up. kolla-genpwd kolla-ansible -i multinode prechecks kolla-ansible -i multinode post-deploy Interview tip: End with failure testing before onboarding tenants.

questions.q: How do you size a control plane and compute fleet for a new cloud?
questions.text: Start from workload and availability requirements. Three control nodes for quorum, compute sized by vCPU:RAM shapes and overcommit, reserve N+1 failure capacity, size storage separately. openstack hypervisor stats show openstack usage list --start 2026-01-01 ceph df Interview tip: Mention failure headroom, not just average demand.

questions.q: What are the network types and VLANs you create in a standard OpenStack deployment?
questions.text: Management, API, overlay, storage (public and cluster), external and optional provisioning and BMC networks, each with its own VLAN and addressing. ip -br addr bridge vlan show cat /etc/kolla/globals.yml | grep -E 'interface|vip' Interview tip: Offer to draw the networks and say which carry jumbo frames.

questions.q: What is Ironic and when would you provision bare metal through OpenStack?
questions.text: Ironic manages physical servers via IPMI or Redfish and PXE, exposing them through Nova flavors. Used for raw performance, HPC, GPU, and for bootstrapping compute nodes; includes cleaning and inspection. openstack baremetal node list openstack baremetal node manage node1 && openstack baremetal node provide node1 openstack server create --flavor baremetal --image ubuntu --network provision bm1 Interview tip: Mention automated cleaning, which proves you understand tenancy on hardware.

questions.q: How do you configure TLS everywhere in an OpenStack deployment?
questions.text: TLS terminates at HAProxy for public endpoints, then extend to internal VIP, RabbitMQ and MariaDB. Distribute the CA bundle to all clients and automate renewal with expiry monitoring. openssl s_client -connect cloud.example.org:443 -showcerts openssl x509 -in /etc/kolla/certificates/haproxy.pem -noout -dates kolla-ansible -i multinode reconfigure -t haproxy Interview tip: Say that renewal automation, not initial setup, is the hard part.

questions.q: How do you handle configuration management and secrets for your OpenStack deployment?
questions.text: Inventory and overrides in Git, secrets in a vault, changes applied only through the deployment tool, tested in staging, with the deploy host tightly restricted. ansible-vault encrypt /etc/kolla/passwords.yml git log --oneline -- /etc/kolla/config/ kolla-ansible -i multinode reconfigure -t nova Interview tip: The deploy host is a crown jewel; mention restricting it.

questions.q: How do you build a staging or lab cloud that mirrors production?
questions.text: Mirror release, tooling, config repo, network design and storage type at small scale; automate rebuilds; run Tempest and rehearse upgrades and failovers. Include real nodes for hardware features. tempest run --smoke kolla-ansible -i staging deploy openstack --os-cloud staging server list Interview tip: Say what you mirror (process and topology) and what you cannot (performance).

questions.q: What is DevStack and what is it not suitable for?
questions.text: DevStack builds OpenStack from source for developers and CI. It is not HA, hardened or upgradeable, so use Kolla, OSA or a vendor distribution for anything long-lived. git clone https://opendev.org/openstack/devstack ./stack.sh ./unstack.sh Interview tip: Position it as a learning and patch-testing tool only.

questions.q: How do you automate OpenStack day-two operations with Ansible and the SDK?
questions.text: Use the openstack Ansible collection and openstacksdk for idempotent onboarding, quota, network and drain playbooks stored in Git with CI. Runbooks become code. ansible-playbook onboard_tenant.yml -e project=payments python drain_host.py --host compute12 ansible-galaxy collection install openstack.cloud Interview tip: Say that runbooks should be executable code.

questions.q: How do you provision Terraform-managed infrastructure on OpenStack?
questions.text: Use the OpenStack provider with application credentials, data sources for images and networks, modules per stack, remote state with locking. Watch replace-on-change arguments. terraform init && terraform plan data "openstack_images_image_v2" "ubuntu" { name = "ubuntu-22.04" } terraform state list Interview tip: Mention data sources and replacement behaviour as the two usual gotchas.

questions.q: What is the difference between Heat and Terraform for orchestration?
questions.text: Heat is native, OpenStack-only, with HOT templates and autoscaling and no external state. Terraform is multi-platform with plan and state. Choose by scope and team skills. openstack stack create -t web.yaml webstack openstack stack resource list webstack terraform plan -out=tfplan Interview tip: Say Heat for in-cloud native use, Terraform for multi-cloud workflows.

questions.q: How would you bootstrap the first compute nodes using Ironic and MAAS or PXE?
questions.text: PXE discovery and commissioning, profile-based OS install, cloud-init or kickstart for first boot, then Ansible roles join the node. Firmware and BIOS settings are codified for repeatability. maas admin machines read | jq '.[].hostname' kolla-ansible -i multinode bootstrap-servers --limit compute13 kolla-ansible -i multinode deploy --limit compute13 Interview tip: Make scale-out an automated process, not a runbook.

questions.q: What does your day-zero checklist look like before opening a cloud to tenants?
questions.text: Smoke and Tempest tests, deliberate failure tests of controllers, compute, queue, DB and Ceph, security baseline, monitoring and backups with restore, documentation and onboarding process. tempest run --smoke rabbitmqctl stop_app openstack server list --all-projects --status ERROR Interview tip: Failure testing before launch is what interviewers want to hear.

questions.q: How would you choose between OpenStack distributions and vendor support models?
questions.text: Self-managed upstream gives flexibility but needs staff. Vendor distributions bring support and tested stacks at a cost; managed services shift operations. Decide with a PoC including an upgrade. openstack --version apt-cache policy nova-compute rpm -qa | grep openstack-nova Interview tip: Frame it as who carries the operational risk.

questions.q: How do you design a highly available OpenStack control plane?
questions.text: Three controllers, HAProxy and Keepalived VIP, Galera for the DB, clustered RabbitMQ, memcached, shared image storage in Ceph. Test by killing components. echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/lib/kolla/haproxy/haproxy.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,18 ip addr show | grep <vip> rabbitmqctl list_queues name type Interview tip: Say HA is only real if you have tested the failures.

questions.q: How do you operate a MariaDB Galera cluster for OpenStack, and what happens in a split brain?
questions.text: Synchronous replication with majority quorum. Send writes to one node via HAProxy, and after a full outage bootstrap from the most advanced node using the sequence number. Monitor cluster size and flow control. mysql -e "SHOW STATUS LIKE 'wsrep_%'" | grep -E 'cluster_size|cluster_status|local_state_comment' cat /var/lib/mysql/grastate.dat galera_new_cluster Interview tip: Never start every node at once after a full outage; bootstrap the advanced one.

questions.q: How do you keep RabbitMQ healthy at scale and recover from partitions?
questions.text: Three-node cluster with quorum queues and pause_minority, tuned oslo.messaging heartbeats, separate or drain notification traffic, and monitor queue depth, memory and consumers. rabbitmqctl cluster_status rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers | sort -k2 -nr | head rabbitmqctl list_policies Interview tip: Name notification queue buildup as the classic silent killer.

questions.q: How do you scale an OpenStack cloud as it grows from tens to thousands of nodes?
questions.text: Shard with cells, tune and split RabbitMQ and the DB, add API capacity, adopt OVN and routed networks, scale Ceph, automate operations, and measure with Rally before scaling. rally task start boot-and-delete.yaml nova-manage cell_v2 list_cells ceph osd pool autoscale-status Interview tip: Scale the measured bottleneck, and mention cells and OVN.

questions.q: What is Masakari and how does it add instance high availability?
questions.text: Masakari adds instance HA: host, process and instance monitors trigger recovery workflows such as evacuation or restart within failover segments. Pair it with shared storage and application-level clustering. openstack segment list openstack segment host list <segment> openstack server set --property HA_Enabled=True web1 Interview tip: Say it restarts instances, not applications.

questions.q: How do you design Ceph failure domains and what happens when a rack fails?
questions.text: CRUSH rules place replicas in separate hosts or racks. A rack loss leaves degraded but available data; healing needs spare capacity and enough racks. Throttle backfill and monitor degraded objects. ceph osd tree ceph osd crush rule dump ceph config set osd osd_max_backfills 1 Interview tip: Say you need spare racks and capacity for self-healing.

questions.q: How do you plan disaster recovery for an OpenStack cloud?
questions.text: Back up the platform (DB, keys, config, deploy repo) and offer tenants backups, replication and RBD mirroring across sites, with defined RTO and RPO. Practice with game days. mariabackup --backup --target-dir=/backup/$(date +%F) rbd mirror pool status volumes openstack volume backup list Interview tip: Say you separate platform DR from tenant DR.

questions.q: How do you run a multi-region OpenStack with shared Keystone?
questions.text: Regions share identity through a replicated or clustered Keystone, or federate separate ones. The catalog marks endpoints by region; cross-region workflows need tooling and Keystone is the risk to design around. openstack region list openstack --os-region-name RegionTwo server list openstack catalog list Interview tip: Name Keystone as the shared fate to design around.

questions.q: How do you prevent and handle a thundering herd of API requests on the control plane?
questions.text: Rate limit at HAProxy, tune workers and pools, cap concurrent builds, stage restarts, set quotas and watch queue depth and latency percentiles. Validate with load tests. crudini --set /etc/nova/nova.conf DEFAULT max_concurrent_builds 5 echo 'show info' | socat stdio /var/lib/kolla/haproxy/haproxy.sock | grep -i conn rally task start boot-storm.yaml Interview tip: Mention controlled restart order after a power event.

questions.q: How do you perform a rolling upgrade of OpenStack with minimal downtime?
questions.text: Rehearse in staging, back up, upgrade the control plane one node at a time, then computes in batches, run contract migrations, and canary throughout. Versioned objects allow temporary mixed versions. kolla-ansible -i multinode upgrade nova-status upgrade check nova-manage db online_data_migrations Interview tip: Mention upgrade checks and online data migrations by name.

questions.q: How do you monitor OpenStack: which metrics and alerts matter most?
questions.text: Layered monitoring: hosts, service heartbeats and API latency, RabbitMQ, Galera and Ceph health, capacity versus allocation, and a synthetic boot-and-ping canary that mirrors the tenant experience. openstack-exporter --os-client-config /etc/openstack/clouds.yaml curl -s localhost:9180/metrics | grep openstack_nova_up promtool check rules openstack.rules.yml Interview tip: The synthetic canary is the alert that reflects users.

questions.q: What are Ceilometer, Gnocchi and Aodh, and how do they relate to billing and autoscaling?
questions.text: Ceilometer collects, Gnocchi stores time series, Aodh alarms and triggers, CloudKitty rates usage. They support billing and Heat autoscaling; Prometheus often replaces them for operational monitoring. openstack metric resource list openstack alarm create --name cpu-high --type gnocchi_resources_threshold --metric cpu --threshold 70000000000 --resource-type instance --resource-id <id> openstack rating summary get Interview tip: Separate operational monitoring from usage metering.

questions.q: How do you handle capacity planning and chargeback or showback?
questions.text: Track allocation and utilisation per aggregate, forecast growth against procurement lead time, keep failure headroom, and use CloudKitty or exports for showback to change tenant behaviour. openstack hypervisor stats show openstack usage show --project payments openstack rating dataframes get Interview tip: Say hardware lead time sets your capacity thresholds.

questions.q: How do you patch the OS and kernel on hosts in a running cloud?
questions.text: Patch one failure domain at a time with health gates: drain and migrate computes, patch controllers sequentially with Galera, RabbitMQ and VIP checks, and use Ceph noout for storage reboots. ceph osd set noout kolla-ansible -i multinode stop --limit compute05 needs-restarting -r Interview tip: Mention health gates between each node.

questions.q: How do you tune the performance of a busy OpenStack cloud?
questions.text: Measure, find the bottleneck, then tune workers, DB pools and archiving, memcached, OVN, NUMA and hugepages, jumbo frames and Ceph tiers, one change at a time with before and after tests. nova-manage db archive_deleted_rows --until-complete --max_rows 10000 mysqldumpslow /var/log/mysql/slow.log | head sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max Interview tip: One change at a time, measured, is the discipline to highlight.

questions.q: How do you onboard a new tenant or team into the cloud consistently?
questions.text: Automate project creation, role assignment via IdP groups, quotas, default network and security group, and tags for owner and cost centre, with logging and a matching offboarding flow. ansible-playbook onboard_tenant.yml -e team=payments size=medium openstack project show payments -c tags openstack quota show payments Interview tip: Mention offboarding to show lifecycle thinking.

questions.q: How do you manage logs centrally and use them to troubleshoot OpenStack?
questions.text: Central log store with parsed request ID, instance and project fields; follow a request ID across services; alert on MessagingTimeout and No valid host patterns; keep debug off by default. kubectl logs -n openstack deploy/nova-api | grep req- curl -s 'localhost:9200/_search?q=req-abc123' journalctl -u docker --since '10 min ago' | grep ERROR Interview tip: Request ID correlation is the standout technique.

questions.q: How do you clean up orphaned resources and stale data in OpenStack?
questions.text: Scheduled reports of unattached volumes, idle IPs, error instances and dormant projects, notify owners with a grace period, archive and purge DB rows, and use official consistency tools. openstack volume list --all-projects --status available openstack floating ip list --status DOWN nova-manage db purge --all-cells --before 2026-01-01 Interview tip: Notify owners and keep it reversible.

questions.q: How do you manage image lifecycles and golden images?
questions.text: Build with Packer or diskimage-builder in a tested pipeline, version and rebuild monthly and on CVEs, deprecate via visibility, sign and verify, and flag instances running old images. diskimage-create -o ubuntu.qcow2 ubuntu-minimal openstack image set --property os_distro=ubuntu --tag supported ubuntu-2026-10 openstack image set --private ubuntu-2025-04 Interview tip: Pipelines, signing and deprecation are the three points.

questions.q: How do you restore service after losing the whole database?
questions.text: Stop writers, restore the last consistent backup, bootstrap Galera from it, apply binlogs if available, then reconcile hypervisor, Ceph and port reality against the restored records. mariabackup --prepare --target-dir=/backup/2026-10-20 mariabackup --copy-back --target-dir=/backup/2026-10-20 virsh list --all Interview tip: Reconciliation after restore is the step people forget.

questions.q: What does a good change-management and maintenance-window process look like for a cloud?
questions.text: Reviewed change requests with risk, test and rollback, applied from Git via the deployment tool, staged first, with tenant notice, a checklist and an abort point, then a short review. git tag change-2026-10-21 && git push --tags kolla-ansible -i multinode deploy --check openstack compute service list Interview tip: Communication is as important as the technical steps.

questions.q: How do you keep OpenStack documentation and runbooks useful and current?
questions.text: Runbooks live in Git, are linked from alerts, are turned into playbooks where possible, updated after every incident, and tested by someone who did not write them. git log --stat -- runbooks/ grep -R 'runbook_url' alerts/ ansible-playbook runbooks/restart_rabbitmq.yml --check Interview tip: Tested-by-a-newcomer is the best quality signal.

questions.q: How do you harden an OpenStack deployment?
questions.text: Secure RBAC and MFA, network isolation and TLS everywhere, hardened hosts with SELinux, secrets in a vault, encrypted volumes, audit logs and a patching process aligned with the Security Guide. getenforce openssl s_client -connect <vip>:5000 </dev/null | grep -i verify oscap xccdf eval --profile cis /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml Interview tip: Offer a layered list, then name the Security Guide.

questions.q: What is Barbican and how does it manage secrets and keys?
questions.text: Barbican stores secrets and keys with Keystone access control and pluggable encrypted back ends. It supports encrypted volumes, Octavia TLS, image signing and Magnum certificates. openstack secret store --name db-pass --payload 's3cret' openstack secret list openstack secret container create --type certificate --secret certificate=<ref> --secret private_key=<ref> --name cert1 Interview tip: Say it holds keys for many services, so it must be HA and backed up.

questions.q: How do you isolate tenants from each other in OpenStack?
questions.text: KVM guests confined by sVirt or AppArmor, separate network segments with security groups and port security, project-scoped storage and RBAC, and dedicated aggregates or bare metal for the most sensitive tenants. ps -eZ | grep qemu openstack port show <port> -c port_security_enabled openstack aggregate create --property tenant=secure secure-hosts Interview tip: Say isolation is layered: compute, network, storage, identity.

questions.q: How do you audit activity in OpenStack?
questions.text: Enable audit middleware for CADF events, centralise API, Keystone, auditd and auth logs in a tamper-resistant store, alert on role changes and failed logins, and use named admin accounts. grep -i 'audit' /etc/nova/api-paste.ini ausearch -m USER_LOGIN -ts today openstack role assignment list --names --role admin Interview tip: Named accounts and tamper-resistant storage are the key points.

questions.q: How do you respond to an OpenStack security advisory (OSSA) or a critical CVE?
questions.text: Triage exposure, assess severity, get the backported fix or a mitigation, test in staging, roll out in batches, verify the fixed version everywhere, and document. Use an emergency path for critical issues. docker ps --format '{{.Image}}' | sort -u | grep nova pip show nova | grep Version kolla-ansible -i multinode deploy --limit control Interview tip: Say exposure assessment comes before panic patching.

questions.q: How do you secure the hypervisor and the compute host?
questions.text: Minimal patched OS, SELinux sVirt, libvirt access controls and TLS, kernel and side-channel mitigations, secure boot, isolated BMC network and regular compliance scans. getsebool -a | grep virt virsh -c qemu:///system list cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/* Interview tip: Mention the BMC network; it is often overlooked.

questions.q: How do you protect the OpenStack APIs from abuse and denial of service?
questions.text: Rate limit and cap connections at HAProxy or a WAF, restrict public exposure, use quotas and middleware throttling, separate internal and public endpoints, and alert on auth failure spikes. echo 'show table' | socat stdio /var/lib/kolla/haproxy/haproxy.sock openstack application credential delete <id> grep -c ' 401 ' /var/log/haproxy.log Interview tip: Separate public and internal endpoints to contain load.

questions.q: How do you handle secrets inside instances and automation without leaking them?
questions.text: Deliver secrets at runtime from Barbican or Vault with short-lived identity, avoid secrets in images or user data, use scoped expiring application credentials, rotate, scan repos and plan for revocation. vault write auth/approle/role/app token_ttl=15m chmod 600 ~/.config/openstack/clouds.yaml git secrets --scan Interview tip: Remember user data is readable; do not put secrets there.

questions.q: Boot fails with 'No valid host was found'. How do you investigate?
questions.text: Read the scheduler log by request ID for per-filter rejection counts; check Placement inventories and allocations, disabled computes, AZ, aggregate, server group, NUMA or PCI requirements, then fix the specific cause. openstack server show web1 -c fault grep <req-id> /var/log/nova/nova-scheduler.log openstack allocation candidate list --resource VCPU=4 --resource MEMORY_MB=8192 Interview tip: Say the per-filter counts in the scheduler log tell you where it failed.

questions.q: A floating IP is associated but the instance is unreachable from outside. What do you check?
questions.text: Check the instance and security group, the router namespace NAT and gateway, then the upstream route or ARP for the floating range, and capture on the external bridge to see which side drops. openstack floating ip show 203.0.113.10 ip netns exec qrouter-<id> iptables -t nat -S | grep 203.0.113.10 tcpdump -ni br-ex host 203.0.113.10 Interview tip: The packet capture on the external bridge splits the problem in half.

questions.q: The nova-compute service shows as down but the host is running. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: Check the process, its log for RabbitMQ, DB or libvirt errors, time sync, resource exhaustion and connectivity to queue and DB; restart if needed and look for the underlying instability. openstack compute service list --service nova-compute docker logs --tail 100 nova_compute virsh list Interview tip: Restarting hides the cause; look for why the heartbeat stopped.

questions.q: Live migration fails or hangs. How do you debug it?
questions.text: Check migration status and logs on both hosts, then CPU compatibility, libvirt connectivity, storage access, port binding and capacity. For non-converging guests use auto-converge or post-copy. openstack server migration list --server web1 nova live-migration-abort web1 <migration-id> virsh domjobinfo <instance> Interview tip: Name auto-converge and post-copy as the fix for busy guests.

questions.q: RabbitMQ queues are growing and operations are slow or timing out. What do you do?
questions.text: Check cluster status and alarms, find queues with many messages and no consumers, restart or fix the disconnected service, add TTL or limits to notification queues, and check watermarks and partitions. rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers | sort -k2 -nr | head rabbitmqctl list_connections name state | head rabbitmqctl set_policy TTL '^notifications\..*' '{"message-ttl":3600000}' --apply-to queues Interview tip: Zero consumers on a full queue points to a disconnected service.

questions.q: Image upload or boot from image is very slow or fails. What do you check?
questions.text: Follow the data path: client and load balancer timeouts, Glance store health, image format (raw for Ceph clones), compute cache and bandwidth, and staging disk space. openstack image show ubuntu -c disk_format -c size rbd -p images ls grep -i 'timeout' /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg Interview tip: Raw format on Ceph is the classic fast-boot fix.

questions.q: Cinder volume creation from an image is slow or fails. What is your approach?
questions.text: Determine whether it is scheduling, image transfer or backend. Ceph clones need raw images in the same cluster; otherwise data flows through cinder-volume. Check logs, capacity and type specs. grep <req-id> /var/log/cinder/cinder-volume.log cinder get-pools --detail openstack volume show vol1 -c status -c os-vol-host-attr:host Interview tip: Say clones versus copies explains most speed differences.

questions.q: Instances lose network connectivity after a Neutron agent or OVS restart. Why?
questions.text: Restarts can flush or delay flows and lose conntrack. Check agent logs, br-int and tunnel ports and flows against a healthy host, and restart agents one host at a time. OVN is more restart-tolerant. ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | wc -l ovs-vsctl list-ports br-int | head journalctl -u neutron-openvswitch-agent --since '10 min ago' Interview tip: Compare flow counts with a healthy host as a quick signal.

questions.q: Users get random 503 or timeout errors from OpenStack APIs. How do you find the cause?
questions.text: Check HAProxy backend status and per-server errors, API worker saturation, DB pool and slow queries, RabbitMQ blocks, Keystone latency and controller resources; compare nodes if errors follow one server. echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/lib/kolla/haproxy/haproxy.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,18,42 mysql -e 'SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST' ss -s Interview tip: If it follows one controller, compare configs and keys.

questions.q: An instance has no network after a hard reboot of its compute node. What happened?
questions.text: Check the guest state, port binding and OVS or OVN wiring. Startup ordering often leaves taps unplugged; a Nova hard reboot re-plugs VIFs. Fix ordering and test host reboots in staging. openstack server reboot --hard web1 ovs-vsctl list-ports br-int | grep <tap> crudini --get /etc/nova/nova.conf DEFAULT resume_guests_state_on_host_boot Interview tip: Say hard reboot re-plugs VIFs, then fix ordering.

questions.q: Security group changes do not seem to apply. How do you verify what is enforced?
questions.text: Verify the port's groups and rule details, then the enforced state on the host (OVS flows and conntrack, OVN ACLs or iptables chains). Conntrack can keep old flows alive; test with a new connection. openstack port show <port> -c security_group_ids ovn-nbctl list ACL | grep <port> conntrack -L | grep <ip> Interview tip: Conntrack explains many rules that appear not to work.

questions.q: The Nova or Neutron database is slow and API calls take seconds. How do you respond?
questions.text: Check the process list and slow query log, connections and Galera flow control, then address deleted-row bloat, missing indexes, heavy callers and pool sizing, and tune buffer pool and disks. mysql -e 'SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST' | head -30 mysql -e "SHOW STATUS LIKE 'wsrep_flow_control%'" nova-manage db archive_deleted_rows --until-complete Interview tip: Monitoring scripts that list everything are a common hidden culprit.

questions.q: A hypervisor shows wrong resource usage compared with the real state. How do you fix it?
questions.text: Compare Nova instances, Placement allocations and libvirt domains; reconcile with nova-manage placement audit and heal_allocations; clean orphans carefully and add periodic audits. nova-manage placement audit --verbose nova-manage placement heal_allocations virsh list --all --uuid | sort > /tmp/virsh.txt Interview tip: Drift between Nova, Placement and libvirt is the root of many scheduling mysteries.

questions.q: After a controller reboot some services fail to start or stay unhealthy. What is your method?
questions.text: Work in dependency order: VIP, HAProxy, Galera, RabbitMQ, memcached, Keystone, then the rest. Read the first error, then run service lists and the canary, and update the runbook. docker ps --filter status=exited kolla-ansible -i multinode mariadb_recovery openstack compute service list && openstack network agent list Interview tip: Foundations first: DB and queue before services.

questions.q: How do you run Kubernetes on OpenStack, and which integrations matter?
questions.text: Create clusters with Magnum or Cluster API, then use the OpenStack cloud controller for Octavia load balancers, Cinder CSI for volumes, Manila CSI for shared storage and Keystone auth. Plan quotas and networks. openstack coe cluster create --cluster-template k8s-template --node-count 3 k8s1 kubectl get storageclass kubectl get svc -o wide Interview tip: Name Octavia, Cinder CSI and the cloud controller manager.

questions.q: What is Magnum and how does it differ from Cluster API?
questions.text: Magnum is the OpenStack-native container cluster API built on Heat; Cluster API is a Kubernetes-native declarative approach with a provider per platform. Choose by tenancy model and multi-cloud needs. openstack coe cluster template create --image fedora-coreos --coe kubernetes --flavor m1.medium --network-driver calico k8s-template clusterctl init --infrastructure openstack kubectl get clusters Interview tip: Frame it as OpenStack-native service versus Kubernetes-native management.

questions.q: How do you use Ceph with both OpenStack and Kubernetes?
questions.text: One Ceph cluster can back OpenStack through RBD and RGW and Kubernetes through Ceph CSI or Rook, with separate pools, keys and CRUSH rules. Watch shared failure domains and noisy neighbours. ceph auth get-or-create client.k8s mon 'profile rbd' osd 'profile rbd pool=kube' ceph osd pool create kube 128 kubectl get pv Interview tip: Say least-privilege keys per consumer.

questions.q: How would you migrate workloads from VMware to OpenStack?
questions.text: Discover and classify VMs, design flavors, networks and storage tiers, then convert or replicate disks with virtio drivers and cloud-init, migrate in waves with rollback, and rebuild with IaC where possible. qemu-img convert -f vmdk -O raw app.vmdk app.raw openstack image create --disk-format raw --file app.raw app-imported virt-v2v -i vmx app.vmx -o openstack Interview tip: Mention virtio drivers for Windows guests.

questions.q: How do you connect OpenStack to a hybrid environment with a public cloud?
questions.text: Non-overlapping addressing, VPN or dedicated links with BGP, shared IdP, common tagging and IaC tooling, unified observability, and a data placement strategy that accounts for egress cost. openstack vpn service create --router r1 vpn1 terraform apply -var cloud=openstack aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections Interview tip: Say address planning comes first.

questions.q: How do you use the openstacksdk or APIs to build automation, and what pitfalls exist?
questions.text: openstacksdk with clouds.yaml and app credentials, wait helpers, idempotent lookups, backoff on transient errors, logged request IDs and filtered queries. Use IaC for state, SDK for glue. python -c "import openstack; c=openstack.connect(cloud='prod'); print([s.name for s in c.compute.servers(status='ACTIVE')])" conn.compute.wait_for_server(server, status='ACTIVE') openstack --os-cloud prod server list --limit 100 Interview tip: Idempotence and filtered queries are the two habits to mention.

questions.q: How do you build CI/CD pipelines that deploy to OpenStack?
questions.text: Scoped short-lived credentials, build and validate, plan, apply to a test project with smoke tests, promote with variables, ephemeral per-branch environments tagged by run ID for cleanup, remote state and approvals. terraform plan -var project=test -out=plan openstack server list --tag run=1234 -f value -c ID | xargs -r openstack server delete openstack --os-cloud ci stack delete -y env-$BRANCH Interview tip: Tag everything with the run ID so cleanup is trivial.

questions.q: What is NFV on OpenStack and which features make it work?
questions.text: NFV runs network functions as software using CPU pinning, NUMA, hugepages, SR-IOV or DPDK, trunk ports and dedicated aggregates, orchestrated by MANO tools. It trades flexibility for deterministic performance. openstack flavor set vnf --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated --property hw:mem_page_size=1GB dpdk-devbind.py --status ovs-vsctl get Open_vSwitch . other_config:dpdk-init Interview tip: List the performance features together; that is the answer.

questions.q: How do you integrate OpenStack with external monitoring and ticketing systems?
questions.text: Exporters feed Prometheus and Grafana, logs go to the central stack, Alertmanager routes pages and tickets with runbook links, and requests flow from ITSM into automation. Inventory feeds the CMDB. curl -s localhost:9180/metrics | head amtool alert query curl -X POST $ITSM/api/tickets -d @ticket.json Interview tip: Say you integrate with existing tools rather than building a parallel stack.

questions.q: Why might a team choose OpenStack today instead of public cloud, and what are the honest downsides?
questions.text: Choose it for sovereignty, steady large-scale cost, performance control, open APIs and special hardware. Downsides: operational burden and fewer managed services. Often run hybrid with public cloud. openstack hypervisor stats show aws pricing get-products --service-code AmazonEC2 --max-items 1 openstack usage list Interview tip: Give the honest downsides; interviewers value balance.

questions.q: How does console access work for instances and how do you troubleshoot it?
questions.text: noVNC proxy uses short-lived tokens to reach libvirt's VNC on the compute host. Check proxy reachability, base URL and proxyclient address, WebSocket support and firewall ports; use the console log for boot errors. openstack console url show web1 openstack console log show web1 --lines 50 ss -ltnp | grep novncproxy Interview tip: The console log is often faster than the graphical console.

questions.q: How does L3 HA with VRRP work for legacy Neutron routers?
questions.text: Routers run active-standby on several network nodes, exchanging VRRP heartbeats on a hidden HA network; the backup takes over and sends gratuitous ARP. OVN uses gateway chassis priorities with BFD instead. openstack router set --ha r1 neutron l3-agent-list-hosting-router r1 ip netns exec qrouter-<id> ip a | grep -E 'inet |state' Interview tip: Say OVN makes VRRP unnecessary through gateway chassis and BFD.

questions.q: How do Glance multi-store, image import and caching improve image handling?
questions.text: Glance supports multiple stores and a staged import workflow with plugins that validate and convert images, plus API-side and compute-side caches. Ceph cloning largely removes the need for caching. glance image-import --import-method glance-direct --stores ceph <image-id> openstack image stores info glance-cache-manage list-cached Interview tip: Mention format conversion to raw on import for Ceph.

questions.q: How do you use Tempest and Rally to test an OpenStack cloud?
questions.text: Tempest verifies API functionality and compatibility, with a smoke subset after each change. Rally measures performance under load. Use both, and keep results to spot regressions. tempest run --smoke rally task start boot-and-delete.json rally task report --out report.html Interview tip: Tempest for correctness, Rally for performance.

questions.q: What is fencing (STONITH) and why does a clustered control plane need it?
questions.text: Fencing powers off or isolates a presumed-failed node via IPMI, Redfish or a power switch before resources move, preventing split brain and corruption. Evacuation needs the same guarantee. pcs stonith status pcs stonith fence node2 ipmitool -I lanplus -H bmc2 -U admin chassis power status Interview tip: Say you must be certain the old node is off before recovering.

questions.q: What are unified limits and how do they change quota management?
questions.text: Unified limits store quota definitions in Keystone as registered defaults and per-project overrides, enforced by services through oslo.limit, with hierarchical projects. Check per-service adoption before migrating. openstack registered limit create --service nova --default-limit 20 --region RegionOne servers openstack limit create --service nova --project payments --resource-limit 50 --region RegionOne servers openstack limit list Interview tip: Say Keystone becomes the single source of truth for limits.

questions.q: What does a Technical / Platform PM do that a regular PM does not?
questions.text: Customer = internal engineers + sometimes external developers, not end users Product = APIs, SDKs, CI/CD, infra services, internal tooling, golden paths Success = adoption, developer velocity, reliability, cost — not revenue/DAU directly A Platform PM builds products whose users are other engineers. The roadmap is driven by developer pain, system constraints, and leverage (one platform improvement multiplies across every team that consumes it). You trade consumer-style growth metrics for adoption, time-to-first-success, and reliability. The hardest part is that your customers can also build the thing themselves — so your product competes with "I’ll just do it myself." Interview line: "A platform PM’s job is leverage — make the right thing the easy thing, so hundreds of engineers move faster without re-solving the same problem."

questions.q: How do you measure the success of an internal platform?
questions.text: Adoption: % of eligible teams/services using it (and trend) Velocity: time-to-first-deploy, lead time for changes, onboarding time Reliability: platform SLOs, incidents attributable to the platform Cost: infra $ per unit of work; eng-hours saved vs maintained Satisfaction: developer NPS / friction surveys, support ticket volume Internal platforms rarely have revenue, so you measure leverage and friction instead. Adoption is the headline (an unused platform is a failed one), but pair it with velocity gains and satisfaction so you are not just driving mandated usage. The strongest signal is voluntary adoption — teams choosing your platform over rolling their own. Beware vanity adoption: "90% of teams onboarded" means little if half of them route around the platform for real work. Measure active, load-bearing usage.

questions.q: What is a 'golden path' and why do platform teams invest in them?
questions.text: Golden path = the supported, opinionated, well-paved way to do a common task e.g. "new service" template → repo + CI + observability + deploy, in one command Optional, not mandatory — but so good most teams choose it A golden path is the recommended route through the platform for the 80% common case: a new microservice, a new data pipeline, a standard deployment. It bakes in best practices (security, monitoring, rollback) so teams get them for free. The PM’s job is identifying which paths to pave first (highest frequency × highest pain) and keeping them genuinely the easiest option, so adoption is pull, not push. Paved roads vs guardrails: Pave the common path (make the right thing easy) and add guardrails for the dangerous edges (make the wrong thing hard). Both reduce cognitive load on product engineers.

questions.q: Build vs buy vs adopt-open-source — how do you frame the decision for a platform capability?
questions.text: Is it core differentiation? → lean build. Commodity? → buy/adopt OSS. TCO: license + integration + ongoing ops + opportunity cost of eng time Time-to-value, lock-in/exit cost, security & compliance fit, community health Frame it around differentiation and total cost. Build only what is core to your advantage; for commodity capabilities (CI runners, secrets, observability) buy a managed product or adopt a healthy open-source project. Quantify TCO honestly — engineers love to build, but a self-hosted system you maintain forever often costs far more than a SaaS bill. Weigh lock-in against the very real cost of operating it yourself. The hidden cost is operations: "We’ll just run open-source X" usually means a permanent on-call burden. Count that team-time in the TCO, not just the license you avoided.

questions.q: How do you write a good PRD for a platform/API product?
questions.text: Problem & who has it (which engineers, how often, current workaround) Goals + non-goals + success metrics (adoption/velocity targets) User stories from the consuming engineer’s POV API contract / interface sketch + key flows + failure modes Rollout, migration path, deprecation plan, dependencies, risks A platform PRD centers the consuming engineer’s experience and the interface contract. Non-goals are critical — platforms fail by trying to serve everyone. Because you have existing users on day one, the migration and deprecation plan is part of the spec, not an afterthought. Include failure modes and SLOs; for infra products, reliability is a feature. Example non-goal: "This deployment service will NOT support stateful workloads in v1." Stating it prevents scope creep and sets expectations with the loud team that wants databases on day one.

questions.q: Who are your stakeholders as a Platform PM, and how do their interests differ?
questions.text: Product engineers (users): want speed, low friction, autonomy Platform engineers (builders): want clean abstractions, low maintenance SRE/Security: want guardrails, standardization, compliance Leadership/Finance: want cost control, velocity, reduced risk Platform PM is a balancing act between groups that often want opposite things. Product engineers want flexibility; security wants constraints. Finance wants lower cost; teams want more compute. Your job is to find the design that satisfies the most important interests simultaneously — usually a paved path that is so convenient that the safe, cheap, standardized option is also the easiest one.

questions.q: Design an internal developer platform (IDP) for a 500-engineer company. Walk me through it.
questions.text: Structured product-design answer — clarify, users, pain, solution, metrics, risks. 1. Clarify: maturity? cloud? current pain? mandate or opt-in? 2. Users & jobs: ship a service, deploy safely, debug prod, manage secrets 3. Top pain: onboarding takes 2 weeks; every team reinvents CI + monitoring 4. Solution: self-service portal + golden-path templates + paved deploy + built-in obs 5. Metrics: time-to-first-deploy, adoption, lead time, dev NPS 6. Risks: forcing adoption, abstraction leaks, platform becoming a bottleneck Start by clarifying scope and the single biggest pain — do not design in a vacuum. Anchor on the developer’s jobs-to-be-done, pick the highest-leverage golden path, and design self-service so the platform team is not a ticket queue. Close with measurable success and the honest risks (the classic one: the platform team becomes the new bottleneck everyone waits on). Strong signal: Proposing self-service over a ticket-based model shows you understand that platforms scale through automation, not through the platform team doing work for others.

questions.q: How do you discover what to build when your users are engineers who don't file feature requests?
questions.text: Shadow/embed with a product team for a sprint — watch the friction live Mine signals: support tickets, Slack help channels, repeated questions Look at the data: where do builds fail? what is slow? what is hand-rolled? Developer surveys + friction logs + onboarding observation Engineers rarely write clean feature requests — they build workarounds and complain in Slack. Discovery means going to where the pain is: embed with a team, read the help channels, and look at telemetry (slow pipelines, flaky steps, repeated manual tasks). The most valuable backlog items are the workarounds teams have already built themselves — that is validated demand. "Paved-over cowpaths": When multiple teams independently build the same internal tool, that is your strongest build signal — they’ve proven the need and the design.

questions.q: Your API has 3 power-user teams demanding advanced features and 40 teams who find it too complex. Who do you build for?
questions.text: Segment by value + strategic intent, not by who is loudest Default: serve the 40 (breadth = leverage), keep an escape hatch for the 3 Layered API: simple high-level interface + low-level advanced API underneath The loud minority is not automatically the priority. Platform leverage comes from breadth, so making the product approachable for the 40 teams usually wins. But you do not abandon power users — design a layered interface: a simple, opinionated default for the majority and an advanced/low-level API for the few who need control. This is the "simple by default, powerful when needed" pattern. Don’t build only for power users: Their needs are real but narrow. Optimizing the platform around 3 teams while 40 struggle is negative leverage — the opposite of a platform’s purpose.

questions.q: How do you decide whether a capability belongs in the platform or in each product team?
questions.text: Platform if: common across many teams, undifferentiated, benefits from standardization Team if: domain-specific, fast-changing, core to that team’s differentiation Test: would centralizing it increase leverage or create a bottleneck? The line is leverage vs autonomy. Centralize what is common, commodity, and benefits from one good implementation (auth, observability, deploy). Leave with teams what is domain-specific or changes fast, where central ownership would slow them down. The failure mode in both directions: centralize too much and you bottleneck everyone; centralize too little and every team reinvents the wheel. Conway’s Law lens: Platform boundaries become org boundaries. Draw the line where a stable, well-defined interface can live — that is what one team can own without constant cross-team negotiation.

questions.q: What makes a developer-facing API 'good'? How would you evaluate one?
questions.text: Easy to start (time-to-first-call), hard to misuse, predictable Consistent naming/conventions; good errors that say how to fix Backward compatible; versioned; well-documented with examples Sensible defaults; progressive disclosure of complexity A good API minimizes the time from "I have the docs open" to "it works," and makes the wrong thing hard. Evaluate it by trying to build something real with it: how fast to first success, how clear the errors, how surprising the behavior. Great APIs have sensible defaults so the simple case is trivial, and reveal complexity progressively only when the user needs it. Errors are UX: An error that says exactly what went wrong and how to fix it is one of the highest-ROI investments in a developer product. Treat error messages as a product surface.

questions.q: Design a secrets-management product for internal teams. What matters most?
questions.text: Jobs: store, rotate, access secrets safely from apps + CI without leaking Must-haves: least-privilege access, audit log, rotation, no secrets in code/Git DX: one-line SDK fetch, local-dev story, clear migration off env-var secrets Guardrails: scanning to block committed secrets; short-lived dynamic creds Security products live or die on developer experience — if the secure path is painful, engineers route around it and paste secrets into env vars. So the design priority is making the safe path the easy path: trivial SDK access, a good local-dev experience, and automated guardrails (commit scanning) that catch leaks. Pair that with the security fundamentals: least privilege, audit, and rotation. Security UX trap: A perfectly secure system nobody can use comfortably is insecure in practice — people will work around it. DX is a security feature here.

questions.q: How do you handle a request for a feature that would help one team but hurt platform simplicity?
questions.text: Understand the underlying job, not just the asked-for feature Check generality: is this a one-off or a pattern many will hit? Options: extension point / plugin, escape hatch, or a polite no with a path Protect the core abstraction; isolate special cases at the edges Dig past the requested feature to the real need — often a simpler, more general solution exists. If it is genuinely a one-off, resist bolting it into the core where it taxes everyone; instead offer an extension point or escape hatch, or say no and explain the trade-off. Every special case added to a platform’s core is a permanent complexity tax paid by all users forever.

questions.q: What are the DORA metrics and how would you use them as a platform PM?
questions.text: Deployment frequency — how often teams ship to prod Lead time for changes — commit → production Change failure rate — % of deploys causing incidents MTTR — time to recover from failure DORA gives a research-backed way to quantify whether your platform actually makes teams faster and safer. As a platform PM you can A/B the impact: teams on the golden-path deploy pipeline vs teams self-managing — compare their DORA numbers. Improving lead time and deployment frequency without raising change failure rate is the core platform value proposition, made measurable. Tie features to DORA: "Our new canary-deploy template cut change failure rate from 9% to 3% for adopting teams" is a far stronger story than "we shipped canary support."

questions.q: You launched a new CI platform. Adoption is high but developers complain it's slow. How do you reconcile the metrics?
questions.text: Adoption ≠ satisfaction — measure both, plus the gap between them Segment: is it slow for everyone, or specific languages/repo sizes? Look at P50 vs P95 build time — the tail drives the complaints Is adoption voluntary or mandated? Mandated hides dissatisfaction High adoption with complaints often means usage is mandated, not loved — so adoption is masking a real DX problem. Dig into the distribution: average build time can look fine while the P95 (large repos, certain languages) is dreadful, and the tail is what people remember. Reconcile by treating the complaint as signal: voluntary re-adoption rate and developer NPS are the truth-tellers that raw adoption hides. Averages lie about latency: A 2-minute median build with a 20-minute P95 feels slow, because the painful builds dominate perception. Always look at the tail.

questions.q: How do you set goals/OKRs for a platform team that has no revenue?
questions.text: Objective (qualitative): "Make shipping a new service effortless" KR1: cut time-to-first-deploy from 5 days to 4 hours KR2: 80% of new services use the golden-path template KR3: platform-attributed incidents down 40%; dev NPS +15 Without revenue, anchor OKRs on leverage outcomes: developer velocity, adoption, reliability, and satisfaction. Write key results as measurable changes in those (not as feature ship-dates — "launch X" is an output, not an outcome). The best platform KRs express how much faster, safer, or happier the engineering org became because the platform exists. Outcome over output: "Ship the new portal" is an output. "Reduce onboarding from 2 weeks to 2 days" is the outcome that output is supposed to cause — commit to the latter.

questions.q: What is a North Star metric for an internal platform, and what's a good example?
questions.text: North Star = the single metric best capturing the value you deliver Good IDP example: "weekly active services successfully deployed via platform" Captures adoption + actual use + success in one number A North Star is the one metric that, if it goes up, means you are genuinely delivering value — and it should resist gaming. For an internal platform, something like weekly successful deploys through the platform combines adoption, real usage, and outcome. Avoid pure activity counts (logins, page views) that can rise without anyone actually getting value. Pick a metric tied to user success, not effort: "Services deployed successfully" beats "deploys attempted" — the former only rises when the platform actually works.

questions.q: A platform metric is going up but you suspect it's being gamed. How do you investigate?
questions.text: Pair every metric with a counter-metric (guardrail) e.g. adoption ↑ but support tickets ↑ and active-use ↓ = gaming/forced Segment the rise: which teams, is it real load-bearing usage? Talk to users — numbers tell you where to look, not why Goodhart’s Law: once a metric is a target, it gets gamed. Defend against it with counter-metrics — if adoption rises but satisfaction falls and active usage is flat, the number is hollow. Segment to find where the rise comes from, then talk to those users. Quantitative data shows you the anomaly; only qualitative work explains it. Goodhart in platforms: Mandating adoption inflates the adoption metric while teams build shadow tooling to escape. The metric looks great; the platform is failing.

questions.q: How do you measure and communicate the ROI of a platform investment to leadership?
questions.text: Cost saved: eng-hours saved × loaded cost; infra $ reduced; incidents avoided Velocity: lead-time reduction → more features shipped per quarter Risk: fewer security/compliance gaps, lower change-failure rate Frame as leverage: "1 platform team enabling N product teams" Leadership funds outcomes, not infrastructure elegance. Translate platform work into business language: hours saved across the org (multiplied by cost), faster delivery (more roadmap shipped), and reduced risk (fewer incidents, better compliance). The strongest framing is leverage — a small platform team making every product team measurably more productive. Always quantify against a baseline. Make it concrete: "Onboarding dropped from 10 days to 1 across 50 hires/year = ~450 engineer-days reclaimed annually" lands far harder than "improved developer experience."

questions.q: How do you build a platform roadmap and balance new features against reliability/tech-debt?
questions.text: Anchor on a strategy/vision → themes → initiatives, not a feature list Reserve capacity: e.g. 60% roadmap / 20% reliability / 20% debt+keep-lights Use SLOs/error budgets to make reliability a planned, visible cost Revisit quarterly; keep near-term firm, far-term loose A roadmap is a communication tool for strategy, not a dated promise list. Express it as themes tied to a vision, and explicitly budget capacity for reliability and tech debt so they are not perpetually crowded out by shiny features. Error budgets turn the reliability-vs-features fight into arithmetic: when the budget is spent, reliability work is automatically prioritized. Now/Next/Later: Present roadmaps in horizons rather than hard dates — it sets direction while protecting you from committing to estimates you can’t yet make.

questions.q: When should you deprecate a platform feature, and how do you do it without breaking teams?
questions.text: Decide: low usage + high maintenance + better alternative exists Announce early, give a long runway + clear migration guide + tooling Phases: announce → discourage (warnings) → default off → remove Track migration; offer hands-on help to the last holdouts Deprecation is a core platform skill because you always inherit users. Decide based on usage vs maintenance cost and whether a better path exists. Then over-communicate: announce early, provide a real migration path (ideally automated), and ramp pressure in phases rather than a hard cutoff. The final 10% of stragglers usually need white-glove help — budget for it rather than breaking them. Trust is the asset: One careless breaking change teaches every team never to depend on your platform again. Deprecate slowly and visibly to keep that trust.

questions.q: How do you drive platform adoption without a top-down mandate?
questions.text: Make it the easiest path (golden path) — win on DX, not policy Land a lighthouse team, prove the win, turn them into advocates Reduce migration cost: tooling, codemods, white-glove onboarding Publicize wins (metrics, testimonials); create internal pull Pull beats push. Adoption without a mandate comes from being genuinely better and easier than the alternative, proven first with one credible "lighthouse" team whose success creates FOMO. Slash the switching cost with migration tooling and hands-on help. Mandates create resentment and shadow tooling; voluntary adoption creates advocates who sell the platform for you. Lighthouse strategy: One respected team’s public success ("we cut deploys from hours to minutes") converts skeptics faster than any leadership email.

questions.q: Leadership wants to mandate your platform across all teams next quarter. You think it's too early. What do you do?
questions.text: Surface the risk with data: readiness gaps, scaling limits, support capacity Propose a staged rollout w/ readiness gates instead of a big-bang mandate Define exit criteria: SLOs met, top friction fixed, support model ready Disagree-and-commit if overruled — then de-risk the rollout hard Push back with evidence, not opinion: show where the platform isn’t ready (missing features, support can’t absorb the load, unresolved friction) and the cost of a premature mandate (a bad first experience poisons adoption permanently). Offer a credible alternative — staged rollout with readiness gates. If leadership still decides to proceed, disagree-and-commit and focus entirely on de-risking. First impressions are sticky: A forced rollout of a half-ready platform creates a cohort of users who "tried it, it was bad" — the hardest group to ever win back.

questions.q: How do you think about platform vs product-team velocity — the classic centralization tension?
questions.text: Centralize → consistency, leverage, but risk of bottleneck + loss of autonomy Decentralize → speed + ownership, but duplication + drift + inconsistent quality Resolve via self-service: central capability, decentralized usage The tension is real: too central and the platform team becomes everyone’s blocker; too decentralized and you get ten incompatible solutions. The resolution is self-service platforms — centralize the capability and the standards, but let teams consume it autonomously without filing tickets.
