questions.q: Your main API's error rate jumped from 0.1% to 8% three minutes ago. You're the on-call. What do you do first?
questions.text: Symptom You get paged: SLO burn rate is 14x on the checkout API. Customers are seeing intermittent 500s. No one has touched anything... that you know of. Investigation # 1. Don't diagnose yet — coordinate + quantify ack page; declare incident; open #inc channel; become IC # 2. Quantify blast radius which SLO? which endpoints? % of users? region-specific? # 3. THE highest-yield question: what changed in the last ~30 min? (deploy / config / flag / migration) kubectl rollout history deploy/checkout # recent deploy? git log --since='30 min ago' / check CD pipeline + flag changes ~80% of incidents are change-induced, so the deploy/config/flag timeline is the first place to look. In parallel a second responder checks dependency health (DB, downstream APIs) and the four golden signals on the dashboard. Root cause A canary deploy 4 minutes ago shipped a config that pointed 10% of traffic at a DB replica that was lagging — those requests timed out and returned 500s. The error rate (8%) roughly matched the canary slice plus retries. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate BEFORE root-causing — restore service first kubectl rollout undo deploy/checkout # roll back the canary # confirm the SLI recovers within a minute or two Prevention Once the SLI recovers, de-escalate the page (recovered ≠ resolved) and investigate the replica-lag bug calmly. First stakeholder update goes out with a 'next update by HH:MM' commitment. Interview tip: The thing they're testing is your reflex order : coordinate (IC +

questions.q: A service is 'up' (health checks green, dashboards green) but users insist it's broken. How do you reconcile that?
questions.text: Symptom Support is flooded with 'checkout fails' reports. Every internal dashboard is green. The health-check endpoint returns 200. Leadership wants to know if it's real. Investigation # Trust the user signal over the green dashboard — find the gap # Reproduce as a real user would (not the health check): curl -v https://app/checkout # full real journey, not /healthz # Compare what the health check tests vs what users actually do # Check per-dimension: region, AZ, app version, device, customer tier # Look at REAL request success, not synthetic /healthz This is a gray failure: monitoring tests something different from what users do. The health check pings a trivial endpoint that doesn't touch the broken dependency, so it stays green while the real path fails. Root cause The health check only verified the process was up; it never exercised the payment-gateway call. A cert on the payment gateway expired, so every real checkout failed — but /healthz never called it, so every probe passed. Fix / mitigation # Shift the broken subset out / fix the cert # immediate: rotate/renew the expired cert # widen the health check to exercise the real critical path Prevention Make health checks (and synthetic probes) exercise the actual user journey, not a trivial liveness ping. Add a synthetic 'checkout' transaction that would have caught this with zero traffic. Measure SLIs from the user's vantage point. Interview tip: The headline insight: when users and dashboards disagree, believe the users

questions.q: Latency spiked to 5x normal but CPU, memory, and disk all look fine. Where do you look?
questions.text: Symptom P99 latency went from 200ms to 1s. The host metrics (CPU ~30%, memory fine, disk I/O low) say everything is healthy. The service is clearly slow. Investigation # 'Resources fine but slow' = it's WAITING, not working # Find what it's blocked ON (off-CPU), not what burns CPU ss -ti # per-socket RTT/retransmits to dependencies # trace a slow request end-to-end (distributed tracing) # which span got slow? a downstream call? a lock? DNS? strace -p <pid> -T -e trace=network,futex # where it stalls # check connection pool saturation + downstream P99 Low resource usage with high latency means the process is blocked waiting — on a downstream dependency, a lock, DNS, or an exhausted connection pool. A flame graph would show little on-CPU; off-CPU analysis shows the wait. Root cause A downstream dependency's P99 had degraded, and the service had no per-dependency timeout. Requests piled up waiting; by Little's Law (L = λ×W) the rising wait time (W) inflated in-flight concurrency (L) until the connection pool was nearly exhausted — so even fast requests queued for a free connection. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate: protect the caller from the slow dependency # add/lower a timeout on the downstream call # enable a circuit breaker so it fails fast instead of piling up # scale the pool only as a stopgap (treats symptom, not cause) Prevention Bound every network call with a timeout, add circuit breakers, and size connection pools with Little's Law in mind. Add tracing so the slow hop is

questions.q: An incident started 20 minutes ago and three engineers are all investigating in parallel, stepping on each other. How do you take control?
questions.text: Symptom You join a chaotic incident call. One engineer is rolling back, another is editing config live, a third is restarting pods. No one knows what the others are doing. The SLI is still bad. Investigation # Establish command structure — this is a coordination failure # 1. Declare a single IC (you, or assign one) — one decision-maker # 2. One incident channel = single source of truth # 3. STOP uncoordinated changes — they can collide/mask each other # 4. Assign clear workstreams; a scribe timestamps actions # 5. Short sync cadence (every ~10-15 min): each lead reports The technical problem is secondary right now — the real failure is that simultaneous, uncoordinated changes make it impossible to know what's helping, and one person's rollback can collide with another's hotfix. An IC's core job is preventing conflicting simultaneous actions. Root cause Two of the parallel changes were actually fighting each other: the live config edit kept reverting the rollback. Neither engineer knew the other was acting, so the SLI never stabilized. Fix / mitigation # Freeze changes, then act deliberately under the IC # pick ONE mitigation (the rollback), let it complete, observe # everyone else stops changing prod until the IC coordinates Prevention Adopt the Incident Command System for anything above a minor: one IC who coordinates but isn't hands-on-keyboard, defined roles (ops/comms/scribe), one channel, explicit workstream ownership. Run game days so the team practices this before a re

questions.q: You roll back a bad deploy but the error rate doesn't recover. The system seems stuck. What's happening?
questions.text: Symptom A deploy caused an outage. You rolled it back immediately — but five minutes later the error rate is still pinned high even though the bad code is gone. Adding replicas isn't helping either. Investigation # The trigger is gone but the system stays down -> metastable failure # Look for a self-sustaining feedback loop: # - retry storm: failures -> retries -> more load -> more failures # - full queues / saturated connection pools that won't drain # - thundering herd of clients reconnecting in lockstep ss -s; check queue depth, retry rates, LB backlog # adding capacity FEEDS the overloaded dependency more traffic This is a metastable failure: a brief trigger pushed the system into a state its own retries now sustain. Recovery is counter-intuitive — adding servers or retrying harder pours fuel on the fire because the new capacity just generates more load on the saturated component. Root cause Clients (and internal retries) kept hammering the recovering service in lockstep. Each failure spawned retries that re-saturated it the instant it tried to come back, so it never escaped the bad state — classic retry-storm-driven metastability. Fix / mitigation # Recovery = REDUCE load, not add capacity # shed load at the edge (return 429/503 to most traffic) # temporarily disable retries / drain the queues # let the system reach a healthy steady state, THEN ramp traffic back gradually Prevention Add retry budgets (cap retries as a fraction of traffic), exponential backoff with jitter

questions.q: Disk is filling on a production host and will be full in ~30 minutes. df shows 95%, but du of the obvious directories doesn't add up. What's going on?
questions.text: Symptom A 'disk 95% full' alert fires (good — it's predictive, not at 100%). You run du on /var and /home and the numbers are far smaller than what df reports as used. Space is vanishing but you can't see where. Investigation # df > du mismatch = space held by deleted-but-open files df -h / # filesystem reports 95% used du -xh / | sort -rh | head # adds up to much less -> the tell # A process holds a deleted file open; blocks stay allocated lsof +L1 # files with link count 0 still open lsof | grep deleted # shows the holding PID + fd The classic fingerprint: df (filesystem accounting) far exceeds du (visible files). A process is still holding a file that was rm'd — usually a log file deleted by a bad rotation while the app keeps writing to its open fd. The blocks can't be freed until that fd closes. Root cause logrotate removed the app's log file but the app wasn't signaled to reopen, so it kept writing to the now-deleted inode. The file is invisible to du (no name) but its gigabytes are still allocated, visible only via lsof. Fix / mitigation # Reclaim WITHOUT killing the app : > /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd-number> # truncate the still-open deleted file # or, if acceptable, signal/restart the app to release the fd Prevention Fix log rotation to use copytruncate or a post-rotate reload signal so the app reopens its log. Add predictive disk alerts (you already had one — that's why this isn't an outage). Watch the journal, Docker, and old kernels too. Interview tip: This is a top-tier L

questions.q: Every request to your service suddenly takes exactly 5 seconds, then succeeds. Nothing is erroring. What's the prime suspect?
questions.text: Symptom Latency didn't spike randomly — it's pinned at almost exactly 5.0 seconds for a large fraction of requests, which then complete successfully. A suspiciously round, consistent number. Investigation # A consistent ~5s flat delay screams DNS timeout # Default resolver timeout is often 5s before fallback/retry cat /etc/resolv.conf # options timeout / attempts / ndots # high 'ndots' -> many failing lookups before the real one dig / getent hosts <dependency> # is resolution slow/failing? # trace a request: which span eats 5s? (likely a name lookup) A flat, round delay (5s, 10s) is the signature of timeouts, not organic slowness — most often DNS. A misconfigured resolver, a high ndots value causing many failed lookups, or one dead nameserver in the list makes every request wait out the timeout before succeeding via fallback. Root cause A high ndots:5 setting (common in some Kubernetes configs) caused each hostname to be tried with several search-domain suffixes first — each suffixed lookup hit a slow/failing resolver and waited ~5s before the real query succeeded. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate the DNS path # lower ndots / add a trailing dot to FQDNs to skip search domains # fix or remove the unhealthy nameserver # add a node-local DNS cache to absorb lookups Prevention Use FQDNs (trailing dot) for known hosts, tune ndots, run a local DNS cache (e.g. NodeLocal DNSCache in K8s), and monitor resolver latency. DNS is a dependency — give it timeouts and observability like any other

questions.q: An alert is paging every 20 minutes overnight, but each time the on-call looks, everything is fine and it auto-resolves. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Symptom The overnight on-call is exhausted — a CPU alert fires, they wake up, check, it's already back to normal, repeat. It's flapping right at the threshold. They want to just silence it. Investigation # Two questions: is the ALERT bad, or is the SYSTEM flapping? # Alert-side fixes for a threshold sitting at the normal boundary: for: 5m # require the condition to PERSIST before firing hysteresis: fire above X, resolve below Y (Y < X) # evaluate over a longer window / use burn rate, not instantaneous # Then ask: WHY is CPU brushing the line every 20 min? # a cron? a GC cycle? a batch job? a service near its limit? A flapping alert usually means the threshold sits right at normal operating range. The immediate fix is a for: duration and/or hysteresis so a momentary brush doesn't page. But a chronically flapping metric can also signal a system genuinely teetering at its capacity edge — silencing without investigating hides a brewing problem. Root cause A periodic batch job spiked CPU just over the alert line every 20 minutes. The alert was instantaneous (no duration), so each brief spike paged. The system wasn't actually unhealthy — but the alert was also masking that the box had little headroom. Fix / mitigation # Fix the alert AND check the headroom # add 'for: 5m' so transient spikes don't page # move the batch job's schedule / nice/ionice it # verify the host has enough headroom (target ~60-70% util) Prevention Run a monthly alert review: every page that fired should be ur

questions.q: A change was deployed successfully, the deploy pipeline went green, but production is now subtly broken. How do you respond?
questions.text: Symptom CI/CD reports success. The rollout completed, all pods are Ready, no alerts fired. But a key feature is returning wrong results for some users — the deploy 'succeeded' yet broke prod. Investigation # 'Deploy succeeded but broke prod' -> the pipeline's checks were insufficient # Treat it as an incident; mitigate first kubectl rollout undo deploy/<svc> # roll back to the known-good version # confirm the wrong-results behavior stops # THEN investigate why: the deploy was healthy but the BEHAVIOR was wrong # look at what the change actually altered (logic, data shape, flag) A green pipeline only proves the deploy mechanism worked and pods are live — it says nothing about correctness. The gap is missing behavioral/canary validation: there were no SLO-gated canary checks comparing the new version's real outputs against the old. Root cause The change altered a calculation that passed all unit tests but produced wrong results against real production data shapes the tests didn't cover. Liveness/readiness probes were green because the process was fine — the logic was wrong, which probes never check. Fix / mitigation # Roll back, then close the validation gap # revert to prior version (instant if blue-green / simple if rolling) # add a metrics-gated canary so the next bad change is caught at 1% Prevention Add progressive delivery: canary to 1% of traffic, watch SLOs/error budget and key business metrics, auto-rollback on regression before most users are affected. Canary catches

questions.q: Half your requests fail and half succeed, seemingly at random, right after a routine deploy. What does the 50/50 split tell you?
questions.text: Symptom Post-deploy, almost exactly half of requests return errors and half are fine, with no pattern by user or endpoint — it looks random. The deploy itself reported success. Investigation # A clean ~50/50 split points at a VERSION or INSTANCE skew kubectl get pods -l app=svc -o wide # mixed image versions? kubectl rollout status deploy/svc # rollout stuck half-done? # or: 2 replicas, one healthy one broken -> LB sends 50% to the bad one # or: 2 config versions, half the fleet has bad config # check: are the failures all hitting one subset of pods? A near-perfect 50/50 (or N/M) split that looks 'random' usually isn't random — it's a fleet partitioned into two states by the load balancer. Half the instances run the bad version/config and round-robin routing sends half the traffic there. Root cause A rolling deploy got stuck halfway: half the pods updated to a build with a broken env var, half stayed on the old good build. The Service load-balanced evenly across both, so exactly the requests routed to the new pods failed. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate by removing the bad half # roll back the deployment (or scale the bad ReplicaSet to 0) kubectl rollout undo deploy/svc # or cordon/delete the broken pods so LB only hits healthy ones Prevention Use readiness probes that actually validate the app can serve (so broken new pods never enter rotation), and metrics-gated canaries that halt a rollout when the new cohort's error rate rises — instead of a rollout blindly proceeding to 50%.

questions.q: You're paged for high memory on a host. By the time you log in, free memory is 'low' but the app is fine. Is this an incident?
questions.text: Symptom Alert: 'available memory < 10%'. You log in, run free -h, and most memory shows as used — very little 'free'. The application is responding normally. Is something wrong? Investigation free -h # don't read the 'free' column! # Linux uses spare RAM as page cache (buff/cache) — reclaimable # The number that matters is 'available', not 'free' # Real pressure shows as SWAPPING, not low free: vmstat 1 # si/so columns = swap in/out activity cat /proc/pressure/memory # PSI: % time stalled on memory dmesg | grep -i oom # any OOM kills? (past pressure->failure) Low 'free' memory is normal and healthy — Linux fills unused RAM with reclaimable page cache to speed up I/O. The alert was likely written against the wrong metric ('free' instead of 'available'). Real memory pressure manifests as swap activity, page scanning, and major faults, not merely low free. Root cause The alert thresholded on 'free' memory, which is almost always low on a busy Linux host because of page cache. There was no actual pressure: 'available' was healthy, no swapping, no OOM. It was a false alarm from a badly-defined metric. Fix / mitigation # No real incident — fix the ALERT # rethreshold on 'available' memory and/or swap activity (si/so) # alert on PSI memory pressure for a modern, accurate signal Prevention Alert on the right signal: MemAvailable, swap in/out rate, or PSI (Pressure Stall Information) — not raw free. This is also a symptom-vs-cause lesson: page on user-facing impact, not on a raw resou

questions.q: A downstream dependency you call is intermittently slow. Your service is now also slow and starting to drop requests. How do you stop the bleeding?
questions.text: Symptom A third-party API you depend on has degraded — its latency is erratic. Your service makes synchronous calls to it, and now your own threads are tied up waiting, your latency is climbing, and you're starting to shed real requests. Investigation # A slow dependency is dragging you down via resource exhaustion # 'Slow' is often worse than 'down' — it ties up your threads # Immediate levers: # 1. timeout: bound the call so threads don't hang (e.g. 1-2s) # 2. circuit breaker: trip after N failures -> fail fast, stop calling # 3. fallback: serve cached/default data for the degraded feature # 4. bulkhead: isolate that dependency's thread/conn pool Without a timeout, each slow call holds a thread until it finally returns; rising latency multiplies in-flight concurrency until your pools exhaust and you can't serve anything — the dependency's failure has cascaded into yours. The defenses (timeout, breaker, bulkhead, fallback) all exist to contain that blast radius. Root cause Your client had a very long (or no) timeout on the third-party call and shared one thread pool across all work. The slow dependency consumed the whole pool, so even requests that didn't need that dependency couldn't get a thread. Fix / mitigation # Contain it now # set an aggressive timeout on the dependency call # open the circuit breaker to fail fast + serve a fallback # (if non-critical) degrade gracefully: drop that feature, keep core flow Prevention Bulkhead each dependency with its own pool so one ca

questions.q: It's 3am, you're paged for a SEV1, and you can't figure out the cause after 15 minutes. What now?
questions.text: Symptom A full outage. You're on-call, alone, and 15 minutes in you still don't understand why. The pressure is mounting. Users are down. What's the right move? Investigation # Two parallel tracks: ESCALATE and MITIGATE BROADLY # Escalating is a strength, not a failure: # pull in secondary / specialist (DBA, network) via escalation policy # get more hands + the person who knows this system # Mitigate broadly even without root cause: # 'what changed in the last hour?' -> roll it back blindly if plausible # failover to another region/AZ; restart the suspect service # shed load if it's overload-shaped After a time-box (you've hit it), the priorities are getting help and restoring service — not continuing to solo-debug while users suffer. Broad mitigations (roll back recent changes, failover, restart) can restore service even before you understand the cause. Root cause In this case the on-call escalated, and the secondary immediately recognized a pattern from a prior incident — a specific dependency's connection pool — that the primary hadn't seen. Escalation, not more solo effort, was the fastest path. Fix / mitigation # Restore first via broad mitigation, diagnose after # roll back the most recent change even if unproven # failover to a healthy region/replica # once recovered: full investigation + postmortem Prevention Set explicit escalation policies (timeout to secondary, clear path to specialists) and a culture where escalating early is praised. Maintain runbooks and run gam

questions.q: After an incident is resolved, what do you do to make sure it doesn't happen again — and how do you run the review?
questions.text: Symptom Service is restored. The fire is out. Leadership says 'great, move on.' You know that's how the same incident recurs next month. What's the right follow-through? Investigation # Drive a BLAMELESS postmortem -> tracked action items # Blameless = focus on the system, never punish individuals # Document: summary, impact (users/duration/budget burned), # timeline, contributing factors (plural!), what went well/poorly, # where we got lucky, action items (each w/ owner + priority + ticket) # Ask 'how did the system ALLOW this?' not 'who broke it?' The incident isn't closed when service is restored — it's closed when the action items that prevent recurrence are done. Blamelessness isn't about being nice; it's about getting the truth, because engineers who fear punishment hide the details you need to fix the system. Root cause The trigger was 'someone ran the wrong command,' but the real finding was systemic: a destructive command had no confirmation, no dry-run, and no guardrail. The fix is changing the system, not the person — who did exactly what the system invited. Fix / mitigation # Convert learnings into prevention # every action item: named owner + priority + linked ticket # high-priority (SEV1) actions get scheduled, not 'best effort' # track completion rate; tie repeat incidents to skipped actions Prevention Aggregate postmortems quarterly to find systemic patterns ('40% of our SEV2s are config pushes with no validation' → build the guardrail for the whole class). Us

questions.q: CPU on all your app servers is pinned at 100% but request volume is normal. What's your approach?
questions.text: Symptom Traffic is flat versus yesterday, yet every app server is at 100% CPU and latency is climbing. Nothing was deployed. The CPU burn appeared over about ten minutes. Investigation # Same traffic + sudden CPU spike = something is doing MORE work per request # Profile what's burning CPU (on-CPU analysis): perf top # live hottest functions system-wide perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; perf report # turn samples into a flame graph -> widest tower = the hot path # also check: GC thrash? a hot loop? regex catastrophic backtracking? # any recent DATA change (not code)? a new input pattern? Flat traffic with a CPU spike means each unit of work suddenly costs more — a hot code path, GC pressure, or pathological input. A flame graph localizes it fast; the surprise is it's often triggered by data, not a deploy. Root cause A new customer started sending inputs that hit catastrophic regex backtracking in a validation function. Traffic volume was unchanged, but those requests burned exponentially more CPU, saturating every core. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate the hot path # block/throttle the pathological input pattern at the edge # hotfix or disable the offending regex/feature flag # scale out as a stopgap (buys time, doesn't fix per-request cost) Prevention Add CPU profiling that's cheap enough for production (eBPF/continuous profiling) so the hot path is one click away. Fuzz/validate inputs and bound regex complexity. Alert on CPU-per-request, not just CPU, to catch efficienc

questions.q: Two services depend on each other and both are now failing. How do you untangle a suspected cascading failure?
questions.text: Symptom Service A calls B; B calls A for some operations. Both are throwing errors and high latency simultaneously. It's unclear which one started it — they're dragging each other down. Investigation # Find the ORIGIN of the cascade + break the feedback loop # Look at timing: which degraded FIRST? (trace timestamps, deploy log) # Look for the loop: A waits on B waits on A -> mutual starvation # Check retries: are they amplifying load between the two? # Circuit breaker state, thread pools, queue depth on both Cascading failures spread through dependencies and retries; a circular dependency makes it worse because each service's failure feeds the other. The job is to find where it started and break the amplifying loop, not to fix both at once. Root cause B slowed first (a DB issue). A's calls to B timed out and retried aggressively, doubling load on B; meanwhile A's threads filled waiting on B, so A's own B-bound calls failed too. The retries between them sustained the cascade after the original DB blip passed. Fix / mitigation # Break the loop, then fix the origin # trip circuit breakers between A and B -> fail fast, stop amplifying # disable/limit retries temporarily; shed load # fix the origin (B's DB), then restore traffic gradually Prevention Avoid circular dependencies in design; where unavoidable, mandate timeouts, circuit breakers, retry budgets, and bulkheads so one service can't drag the other down. Map the dependency graph so the critical path and cycles are known bef

questions.q: A bug only reproduces under production load — never in staging. How do you debug it safely?
questions.text: Symptom Users hit an intermittent failure in prod. You cannot reproduce it in staging no matter what. It clearly correlates with high load, but you can't just break prod to investigate. Investigation # 'Only under load' = hitting a LIMIT or a race that needs concurrency # Usual suspects (check live, under load): ulimit -n / LimitNOFILE # 'too many open files'? ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l # ephemeral port / TIME_WAIT exhaustion conntrack -C # nf_conntrack table full? # connection/thread pool exhaustion; lock contention; race conditions # capture continuous metrics so you have data WHEN it happens Load-only bugs are usually a saturated resource or a concurrency race that needs real parallelism to surface. Since you can't reproduce in staging, you instrument prod with continuous sampling and correlate the failure timestamps with whichever resource saturates. Root cause Under peak concurrency the service exhausted its database connection pool: requests beyond the pool size queued and timed out. Staging never had enough concurrent load to fill the pool, so it never appeared there. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate + capture # raise the limit/pool as a stopgap; add backpressure # add tracing/metrics around pool acquisition to confirm # load-test staging to the real peak to reproduce next time Prevention Make staging load-representative (realistic concurrency, data sizes). Add soak and spike load tests in CI. Check limits before app logic for 'only under load' bugs. Continuous profili

questions.q: You suspect a recent config change caused an outage, but the change 'looks fine' and passed review. How do you confirm and act?
questions.text: Symptom An outage started right after a config push. The diff looks harmless and two people approved it. Someone argues 'it can't be the config, it passed review.' Meanwhile users are down. Investigation # Correlation with a change is strong evidence — act, then prove # Mitigate first: revert the config regardless of how it 'looks' # (a reviewed change can still be wrong — review isn't proof) git revert <config-commit> # or roll back the config version # confirm the SLI recovers -> that's your proof it WAS the config # THEN understand WHY the 'harmless' diff broke things Timing correlation with a change is the single highest-yield signal, and 'it passed review' is not evidence it's correct — reviewers miss things. The fastest path to truth is to revert and watch the SLI: recovery confirms causation faster than arguing over the diff. Root cause The config changed a value that was syntactically valid and semantically reasonable in isolation, but interacted with another setting to, e.g., shrink a connection pool below what peak load needed. No reviewer simulated the interaction under load. Fix / mitigation # Revert, confirm, then prevent # revert the config; verify recovery # add validation that would have caught the interaction Prevention Validate config in CI (linting, schema, and ideally a canary that applies it to a small slice first). Treat config changes with the same rigor as code — they cause a large share of incidents. Make config rollbacks as fast and routine as code r

questions.q: Your monitoring/dashboards themselves went dark during an incident — you're flying blind. What now?
questions.text: Symptom Mid-incident, your Grafana/metrics pipeline stops updating. The dashboards freeze. You no longer know if things are getting better or worse. The monitoring is down too. Investigation # The scariest failure: you can't see. Get ANY independent signal # Don't trust the broken pipeline — find out-of-band signals: # - direct probes: curl the service health/critical path yourself # - cloud provider's own metrics/console (independent of your stack) # - logs at the source (tail on the host) if the log pipeline is up # - external/synthetic monitor (independent vendor) + status of dependencies # - the users themselves (support volume) as a crude SLI When observability fails during an incident you must fall back to independent signals — direct probes, cloud-native metrics, source logs, external synthetics — because the system you'd normally trust is exactly what's broken. Restore a minimal signal before making blind changes. Root cause The metrics backend OOM'd from a cardinality explosion: a new deploy added a high-cardinality label (a request ID) to a metric, creating millions of series that crashed Prometheus — ironically taking out monitoring during the incident it was needed for. Fix / mitigation # Get a signal, then restore monitoring # probe the service directly to confirm current state # drop/rollback the high-cardinality metric label; restart the TSDB # verify dashboards return before relying on them again Prevention Have an independent, external monitor (different vend

questions.q: A certificate expired in production and traffic is failing. Beyond renewing it, what's the right response?
questions.text: Symptom TLS handshakes are failing across a service — an expired certificate. The immediate fix (renew/rotate) is obvious. But this is the second time this year. The interviewer wants more than 'renew it.' Investigation # Immediate: rotate the cert; confirm handshakes recover # But cert expiry is a PREDICTABLE, preventable failure class # Find every cert + its expiry, not just this one: # inventory certs (services, internal mTLS, load balancers, clients) # check for OTHER certs about to expire (don't get paged again next week) echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates Renewing fixes this instance, but expired certs are a self-inflicted, fully predictable outage — the real response is eliminating the entire class with automation and lead-time alerting, plus checking the rest of your fleet for the next ticking cert. Root cause A manually-issued certificate had no automated renewal and no expiry monitoring, so it silently aged out. Nobody knew until handshakes broke. The 'second time this year' confirms it's a process gap, not bad luck. Fix / mitigation # Eliminate the class, not just the instance # rotate now; scan for other soon-to-expire certs and pre-renew # automate issuance + renewal (e.g. cert-manager / ACME / managed TLS) # alert on expiry with weeks of lead time Prevention Automate certificate lifecycle (auto-renewal) so humans are never in the critical path, and alert well before expiry. Treat cert expiry like capacity exhaustio

questions.q: Requests are failing intermittently and the errors are spread across random users with no pattern. How do you find the needle?
questions.text: Symptom ~2% of requests fail, scattered across users, endpoints, and times with no obvious pattern. It's not a clean cohort split. Logs show varied errors. It feels like noise but it's real and steady. Investigation # Low, steady, scattered failures -> find the hidden common dimension # Slice by EVERY dimension to find what the failures share: # host/pod? AZ? node? a specific replica? a backend shard? # Use a trace/correlation ID to follow individual failures kubectl get pods -o wide # do failures map to one node/AZ? # check: one bad replica, one degraded shard, one flaky NIC/node 'Random and scattered' usually means the failures DO share a dimension you haven't sliced by yet — a single bad pod, a degraded AZ, or one unhealthy backend shard that only a fraction of requests happen to hit. High-cardinality slicing (or tracing) reveals the hidden cohort. Root cause One pod out of twenty had a degraded local disk causing occasional I/O errors. Only the ~5% of requests routed to that pod were affected, scattered across users — so it looked random until failures were grouped by pod name. Fix / mitigation # Remove the bad subset # identify and drain/delete the unhealthy pod/node kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets # or delete the pod # verify the scattered failures stop Prevention Readiness probes and node problem detectors should eject a degraded instance automatically. High-cardinality observability (per-pod, per-AZ labels) and tracing let you group 'random' failures by their

questions.q: After a database failover, the app is up but some users see stale or missing data. What happened and what do you do?
questions.text: Symptom The primary database failed and automatically promoted a replica. The app recovered — but support reports some recent writes are missing or users see old data. The failover 'worked' but data looks wrong. Investigation # Replica promotion + missing recent writes = replication lag / async loss # Determine the replication mode and lag at failover time: # async replication -> the un-replicated tail is LOST on promotion (nonzero RPO) # check replication lag metrics around the failover moment # also rule OUT split-brain: did two nodes accept writes? # (split-brain = divergent data, far worse than simple lag) With asynchronous replication, a failover promotes a replica that may be slightly behind the dead primary, so the most recent writes that hadn't replicated are gone — a real, expected nonzero RPO. The urgent secondary check is split-brain: if fencing failed and two nodes both took writes, you have divergent data to reconcile. Root cause The replica was promoted while a few seconds behind the primary under async replication. Those few seconds of writes (recent orders) were never replicated and were lost when the old primary was fenced — the failover behaved as designed, but the RPO wasn't zero. Fix / mitigation # Assess and reconcile # quantify what was lost (the un-replicated window) # recover lost writes from app logs / event stream / idempotent replay if possible # confirm only ONE primary now accepts writes (no split-brain) Prevention Decide RPO deliberately: synchro

questions.q: Traffic to your service dropped to near zero suddenly. No errors, just... silence. Is this good or bad?
questions.text: Symptom Your request rate fell off a cliff to almost nothing. Error rate is fine (there are barely any requests to error). Latency looks great. Everything is 'green' — but the traffic graph is alarming. Investigation # Near-zero traffic with no errors is suspicious, not reassuring # The failure is UPSTREAM of you -> you're not getting requests # Work BACKWARD toward the user: # is the load balancer / ingress routing to you? health checks passing? # is DNS resolving to the right place? did a DNS/routing change happen? # is an upstream gateway/CDN down or misrouting? # a dead man's switch should have caught 'expected traffic stopped' Sudden silence is often worse than errors: it means requests aren't reaching you at all, so your own green metrics are meaningless. The break is upstream — DNS, load balancer, ingress, CDN, or a gateway — and you diagnose by walking backward from your service toward the user. Root cause A DNS or ingress change routed traffic away from the service (or a CDN/gateway in front went down). Requests never arrived, so the service saw no load and no errors — looking perfectly healthy while being effectively unreachable. Fix / mitigation # Restore the path to the service # fix the DNS/ingress/LB misroute or recover the upstream gateway # verify real user requests are arriving again (traffic returns) Prevention Alert on absence with a dead-man's-switch: 'expected traffic/heartbeat stopped' should page, since absence-of-errors won't. questions.q: You're handed an incident with almost no information: 'the website is slow.' How do you turn that into an actionable investigation?
questions.text: Symptom A vague report: 'the site feels slow.' No specifics — which page, which users, since when, how slow. You need to convert this into something you can actually investigate without thrashing. Investigation # Turn vagueness into a precise problem statement FIRST # Quantify before theorizing: # WHAT exactly is slow? (which journey/endpoint) # SINCE WHEN? (correlate with a change) # WHO/WHERE? (all users? one region/device/tier?) # HOW slow vs normal? (is it even outside normal variance?) # Then: gather evidence (metrics/traces/logs) BEFORE hypotheses # change ONE variable at a time; verify assumptions, don't trust them Disciplined debugging starts by stating the problem precisely and gathering evidence before forming theories — otherwise you pattern-match to a past incident and fix the wrong thing. 'Slow' must become 'checkout P95 is 3x normal for EU users since 14:00,' which points somewhere. Root cause Once quantified, 'slow' turned out to be 'image-heavy pages slow for one region since a CDN config change an hour ago' — a precise statement that immediately implicated the CDN change, which a scattershot investigation would have missed. Fix / mitigation # Investigate the now-precise problem # with the quantified statement, correlate to the CDN change + roll back # confirm latency returns to baseline for that journey/region Prevention Bisect the problem space (which layer? which region? which change?), change one thing at a time, and verify assumptions ('is it actually the

questions.q: A previously-fixed incident has recurred — the exact same failure you wrote a postmortem for last month. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Symptom You're paged and immediately recognize it: this is the same outage you had a postmortem for four weeks ago. The 'fix' clearly didn't hold, or was never done. Users are down again. Investigation # Mitigate now (you have the runbook from last time — use it) # Then the real question: WHY did it recur? # pull the prior postmortem -> were the action items completed? # almost always: the action item was deprioritized/never shipped # OR the fix addressed a symptom, not a contributing factor # trace the recurrence directly back to the skipped/incomplete action A recurrence is a process failure as much as a technical one — you already knew how to prevent it. Mitigate fast using the existing runbook, then make the recurrence visible: it almost always traces to a postmortem action item that was never completed because reliability work lost to feature work. Root cause The postmortem's top action item (add a guardrail/validation) was created with no owner and slipped behind feature work, so it was never shipped. The latent condition remained and the same trigger reproduced the same outage. Fix / mitigation # Fix it for real this time + fix the process # apply the prior fix and actually complete the action item now # escalate: a repeat SEV is a forcing function to prioritize it Prevention Every action item needs a named owner, a priority, and a tracked ticket in the normal backlog — an action without an owner is a wish. Use the error budget policy as the lever: a repeat incident ju

questions.q: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk through how you diagnose and fix it.
questions.text: Symptom A deployment's pods keep restarting — status shows CrashLoopBackOff with an ever-growing backoff delay. The app never stays up long enough to serve traffic. Investigation kubectl describe pod <pod> # events: why is it restarting? kubectl logs <pod> --previous # logs from the CRASHED container, not the new one kubectl logs <pod> -c <init> # init container failing? # Common causes: # - app exits on startup (bad config/env, missing secret, can't reach dep) # - failing liveness probe killing a slow-starting app # - OOMKilled (check 'Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled') kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}' CrashLoopBackOff just means 'the container keeps exiting and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with backoff.' The cause is in the previous container's logs and the pod events — most often a startup failure (bad config/missing dependency), an OOMKill, or a liveness probe killing an app that simply boots slowly. Root cause The app needed ~40s to warm up, but the liveness probe had a 10s initial delay — so kubelet killed it mid-boot, every time. It wasn't actually broken; the probe never let it finish starting. Fix / mitigation # Fix matches the cause # slow start -> add a startupProbe (gates liveness) or raise initialDelaySeconds # OOMKilled -> raise memory limit or fix the leak # bad config -> fix env/secret/configmap; redeploy Prevention Use a startupProbe for slow-booting apps so liveness doesn't kill them during warmup. questions.q: A pod is stuck in Pending and won't schedule. How do you find out why?
questions.text: Symptom You deploy, but the pod sits in Pending indefinitely. It never lands on a node. No logs (the container never started). The scheduler just won't place it. Investigation kubectl describe pod <pod> # the Events at the bottom tell you EXACTLY why # Common scheduler messages + meaning: # 'Insufficient cpu/memory' -> no node has room for the requests # 'node(s) didn't match node selector/affinity' -> selector/affinity too strict # 'node(s) had taint that the pod didn't tolerate' -> missing toleration # 'no nodes available' / unbound PVC -> storage can't be provisioned kubectl get nodes; kubectl top nodes # is the cluster actually full? A Pending pod is a scheduling failure, and kubectl describe pod states the reason verbatim in its Events. The usual causes: resource requests no node can satisfy, node selector/affinity/taint mismatches, or an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim. Root cause The pod requested more memory than any node had free (requests too high), and the cluster autoscaler couldn't add a node fast enough (or had hit a quota). So the scheduler had nowhere to place it. Fix / mitigation # Resolve based on the Events reason # requests too high -> right-size requests, or add/enable node capacity # taint/affinity -> add toleration or relax the selector # unbound PVC -> fix the StorageClass / provisioner kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp Prevention Right-size requests from real usage (too-high requests waste capacity and block scheduling). questions.q: Pods are being OOMKilled repeatedly. How do you tell if it's a leak, a bad limit, or a traffic spike?
questions.text: Symptom A service's pods restart with 'OOMKilled'. Sometimes it's minutes after start, sometimes hours. You need to distinguish a genuine memory leak from an under-set limit or a load-driven spike. Investigation kubectl describe pod <pod> # Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled # Look at the memory-over-time SHAPE (from metrics): # steady climb that never plateaus -> LEAK # flat then OOM under load -> limit too low for peak working set # sawtooth (climbs, GC, climbs) near the limit -> limit too tight for GC headroom kubectl top pod <pod>; check container_memory_working_set_bytes # exceeding the MEMORY limit = OOMKill (vs CPU limit = throttle) OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit. The memory-over-time shape distinguishes the cause: a never-plateauing climb is a leak; a flat baseline that only OOMs under load means the limit is below the real working set at peak; a sawtooth hugging the limit means insufficient GC headroom. Root cause The graph showed a steady, unbounded climb regardless of load — a genuine memory leak. The limit just determined how long until each pod died; raising it only delayed the inevitable OOMKill. Fix / mitigation # Fix per shape # leak -> fix the code (the limit only changes time-to-death) # under-set limit -> raise to cover peak working set + headroom # GC sawtooth -> give headroom or tune the runtime/heap # stopgap: more replicas spreads load but won't cure a leak Prevention Right-size memory limits from observed working set (P9

questions.q: A rolling update is stuck — new pods won't become Ready and the old ones are still serving. What's wrong?
questions.text: Symptom You triggered a rolling update. The rollout is stuck partway: new pods are Running but never Ready, so the rollout won't progress, and (correctly) the old pods keep serving traffic. Investigation kubectl rollout status deploy/<svc> # confirms it's stuck kubectl describe pod <new-pod> # why isn't it Ready? kubectl logs <new-pod> # app errors on startup? # Readiness probe is failing for the NEW version -> good! it's protecting you # - new build can't reach a dependency it needs to report ready # - readiness endpoint/path changed; probe now wrong # - new config/secret missing -> app starts but never becomes ready The rollout is stuck because the new pods' readiness probe never passes, so Kubernetes correctly refuses to send them traffic or proceed (and keeps the old pods up). This is the system protecting you from shipping a broken version — the question is why the new version can't become ready. Root cause The new build required a config key that wasn't added to the ConfigMap, so it started but its readiness check (which verified that config) kept failing. maxUnavailable was 0, so the rollout safely halted with old pods still serving. Fix / mitigation # Fix the new version, or roll back # add the missing config/secret and let the new pods go Ready # or: kubectl rollout undo deploy/<svc> (abandon the bad rollout) # tune maxSurge/maxUnavailable for desired rollout safety Prevention This is readiness probes working as designed — a broken new version never receives traffic.

questions.q: A pod can't pull its image (ImagePullBackOff). How do you diagnose it?
questions.text: Symptom A new pod is stuck with ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff. The container never starts because the image won't download. Investigation kubectl describe pod <pod> # Events show the exact pull error # Decode the message: # 'not found' / 'manifest unknown' -> wrong image name/tag (typo, missing tag) # 'unauthorized' / 'denied' -> missing/expired registry credentials (imagePullSecret) # 'no such host' / timeout -> can't reach the registry (network/DNS/firewall) # rate limit (e.g. Docker Hub) -> too many pulls, need auth or a mirror kubectl get secret <pull-secret> -o yaml # creds present + correct? ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet can't fetch the image, and the describe Events name the exact reason: a bad image reference, missing/expired registry credentials, registry unreachability, or rate limiting. You read the message rather than guessing. Root cause The image tag referenced a build that was never pushed (a CI step failed silently), so the registry returned 'manifest unknown.' The deployment pointed at an image that didn't exist. Fix / mitigation # Fix per the pull error # wrong tag -> correct the image reference; ensure CI actually pushed it # unauthorized -> create/refresh the imagePullSecret + attach to the SA # unreachable -> fix network/DNS to the registry; use a pull-through mirror # rate limited -> authenticate or use a registry mirror/cache Prevention Use immutable, verified tags and ensure the image is pushed before the deploy references it (gate deploy on suc

questions.q: Service-to-service calls inside the cluster are failing intermittently. How do you debug Kubernetes networking?
questions.text: Symptom Service A calls Service B by its cluster DNS name. Most calls work; some fail with connection errors or timeouts. It's intermittent and doesn't correlate with a deploy. Investigation # Work up the stack from DNS to endpoints to pods kubectl get endpoints <svc-b> # do the Service's endpoints include healthy pods only? kubectl get pods -l app=b -o wide # are some backing pods unhealthy? # DNS inside the cluster: kubectl exec <pod-a> -- nslookup svc-b # resolves? (CoreDNS healthy?) # is one endpoint a bad pod? readiness should remove it but check # NetworkPolicy blocking some paths? kubectl get networkpolicy Intermittent in-cluster failures usually mean the Service is load-balancing across a mix of healthy and unhealthy endpoints, or DNS (CoreDNS) is flaky, or a NetworkPolicy is partially blocking. Checking which pods back the Service (endpoints) and whether they're all healthy is the fastest split. Root cause One of Service B's pods was unhealthy but its readiness probe was missing/misconfigured, so it stayed in the Service's endpoint list. kube-proxy load-balanced ~1/N of calls to the bad pod, producing intermittent failures. Fix / mitigation # Remove the bad endpoint # add/fix readiness probe so unhealthy pods leave the endpoint list # delete/drain the bad pod; confirm endpoints now list only healthy pods # (if DNS) scale/tune CoreDNS + add NodeLocal DNSCache Prevention Correct readiness probes keep unhealthy pods out of Service endpoints automatically. Run NodeLocal

questions.q: Your cluster autoscaler isn't adding nodes even though pods are Pending. Why might that be?
questions.text: Symptom Pods are Pending for 'Insufficient cpu', which should trigger the cluster autoscaler to add a node. But no new nodes appear. The cluster just stays full with Pending pods. Investigation # Why might the autoscaler NOT scale up? kubectl -n kube-system logs <cluster-autoscaler-pod> # it logs its decisions # Common reasons: # - node group at its MAX size (can't grow further) # - cloud quota / capacity limit hit (no instances available) # - pod can't fit on ANY node type the autoscaler can add (too-big requests) # - pod has affinity/taint constraints no scalable node group satisfies # - autoscaler not managing that node group / misconfigured The cluster autoscaler only adds nodes if a Pending pod would actually fit on a node it's allowed to create. It won't scale if the node group is at max, cloud quota is exhausted, the pod's requests exceed any addable node, or affinity/taints exclude the scalable groups. Its logs state the reason. Root cause The node group had hit its configured maximum size, so the autoscaler had nothing to do — it logged that scale-up was capped. The cluster genuinely couldn't grow without raising the max or quota. Fix / mitigation # Resolve the scaling block # raise the node group max (and cloud quota) if capacity is needed # right-size pod requests so they fit an addable node type # relax affinity/taints, or add a node group that satisfies them Prevention Monitor autoscaler scale-up failures and node-group headroom. questions.q: A node goes NotReady and its pods aren't being rescheduled fast enough. What's happening and what do you do?
questions.text: Symptom A node shows NotReady. The pods on it are still listed as Running for several minutes, and replacement pods are slow to come up elsewhere — so capacity is degraded longer than you'd expect. Investigation kubectl get nodes # node NotReady since when? kubectl describe node <node> # conditions: MemoryPressure? DiskPressure? kubelet down? # Why pods aren't rescheduled instantly: # - the node's pods are marked for eviction only after a toleration timeout # (default ~5 min for node.kubernetes.io/unreachable) # - StatefulSet pods won't be force-deleted (could violate at-most-one) kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> A NotReady node doesn't instantly relocate its pods: Kubernetes waits out the unreachable toleration (≈5 min by default) before evicting, to avoid thrashing on a transient blip. For StatefulSets it's even more conservative (it won't risk two instances). So there's an inherent recovery delay you must account for. Root cause The node's kubelet stopped responding (a hardware/network issue). Pods stayed 'Running' in the API until the 5-minute unreachable toleration elapsed, then they were rescheduled — the delay was the eviction timeout, not a bug. Fix / mitigation # Recover capacity # cordon + drain the node if it's coming back; delete it if it's dead kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data # for faster failover: tune toleration seconds (carefully) + keep headroom # ensure enough replicas/headroom to absorb a node lo

questions.q: Your app needs persistent storage in Kubernetes but pods keep losing data on restart. What's misconfigured?
questions.text: Symptom A stateful app (e.g. a database) loses its data whenever its pod restarts or reschedules. Each new pod comes up empty. Storage clearly isn't persisting across pod lifecycles. Investigation # Data vanishing on restart -> not actually using durable storage kubectl get pvc; kubectl describe pod <pod> # is a PVC mounted, or emptyDir? # Common misconfigurations: # - using emptyDir (ephemeral, dies with the pod) instead of a PVC # - a Deployment (shared/rescheduled) instead of a StatefulSet for stateful apps # - PVC bound but pod reschedules to another zone where the volume can't attach # - writing to the container filesystem (lost on restart) not the mount Data loss across restarts means the pod isn't backed by a PersistentVolume — typically it's using emptyDir (ephemeral by definition) or writing to the container's own filesystem. Stateful workloads also need a StatefulSet (stable identity + per-replica PVC), not a Deployment. Root cause The app used an emptyDir volume, which exists only for the pod's lifetime and is wiped when the pod is deleted/rescheduled. It needed a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by durable storage, managed by a StatefulSet. Fix / mitigation # Use durable, identity-stable storage # switch to a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates (per-replica PVC) # back the PVC with a real StorageClass (network/block storage) # ensure the app writes to the mounted volume path, not container fs Prevention Use StatefulSets + PVCs for stateful apps; reserve emptyDir for

questions.q: CPU throttling is hurting latency even though CPU usage looks low. How is that possible?
questions.text: Symptom A latency-sensitive service has P99 spikes. But CPU usage on the pods looks modest — well under the limit on average. Yet you suspect throttling. How can a 'low CPU' pod be throttled? Investigation # CFS throttling happens against the LIMIT per 100ms quota window, not the average # A bursty app can be throttled while AVERAGE CPU looks low: kubectl top pod # shows average — misleading for bursty workloads # check the real signal: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / cfs_periods_total # if throttled_periods is high -> you ARE being throttled despite low avg # a CPU limit of e.g. 500m caps each 100ms window at 50ms of CPU Kubernetes CPU limits are enforced by CFS quota per ~100ms window. A bursty service that needs a quick spike of CPU gets throttled the moment it exceeds its per-window quota — even if its average usage is far below the limit. So average CPU looks fine while latency suffers from throttling. Root cause The pod had a low CPU limit (e.g. 500m). During request bursts it briefly needed more than its 50ms-per-100ms quota and got throttled, adding latency — while the per-minute average stayed low and innocent-looking. Fix / mitigation # Relieve the throttling # raise or remove the CPU LIMIT (requests still guarantee scheduling) # many teams set CPU requests but NO CPU limit to avoid throttling # confirm cfs_throttled_periods drops + P99 improves Prevention Set CPU requests (for scheduling/guarantees) but consider omitting CPU limits to avoid CFS throttli

questions.q: After deploying a new version, you need to roll back fast. Compare your options and their gotchas.
questions.text: Symptom A new version is misbehaving in production. You need to revert quickly. The interviewer wants to know your rollback options in Kubernetes and the trade-offs/gotchas of each. Investigation # Options, fastest + safest first kubectl rollout undo deploy/<svc> # revert to previous ReplicaSet kubectl rollout undo deploy/<svc> --to-revision=N # specific revision # blue-green: flip the Service selector back to the old version (instant) # canary: just stop the rollout / scale canary to 0 # GitOps: git revert the manifest -> controller reconciles back # GOTCHA: schema/data migrations may NOT be backward-compatible! Kubernetes makes the compute rollback easy (rollout undo / flip selector / git revert), and the fastest is whatever requires the least change — flipping a blue-green selector is near-instant. The dangerous gotcha is state: if the new version ran a non-backward-compatible DB migration, rolling back the code can break against the migrated schema. Root cause The new version had applied a schema migration that dropped a column the old version still reads. Rolling back the pods alone caused the old code to fail against the new schema — the rollback wasn't safe because state had changed irreversibly. Fix / mitigation # Roll back safely considering state # code-only change -> rollout undo / selector flip is safe + instant # with migrations -> only the expand/contract pattern makes rollback safe # if a destructive migration ran -> may need forward-fix, not rollback Preventio

questions.q: A DaemonSet pod is failing on just one node out of fifty. How do you approach a node-specific failure?
questions.text: Symptom A DaemonSet (one pod per node) runs fine on 49 nodes but crashes or fails on exactly one. The pod spec is identical everywhere, so why does one node behave differently? Investigation # Identical spec, one bad node -> the NODE differs, not the pod kubectl describe pod <pod-on-bad-node>; kubectl logs <pod> --previous kubectl describe node <bad-node> # conditions, kernel, kubelet version, taints # Compare the bad node to a good one: # - different kernel/OS/driver version? disk full? clock skew? # - hardware fault (bad disk/NIC)? resource pressure unique to it? # - leftover state from a prior workload? a missing host mount/file? When one node out of many fails an identical workload, the variable is the node, not the manifest. You diagnose by diffing the bad node against a healthy one — kernel/driver versions, disk/clock state, hardware health, or leftover host state. Root cause The bad node had a full root disk (from a previous workload's leftover files), so the DaemonSet pod couldn't write its host-path data and crashed. The other 49 nodes had free space; only this node's local state differed. Fix / mitigation # Repair or replace the node # fix the node-specific issue (clear disk / fix driver / replace hardware) # or cordon + drain + delete the node and let it be reprovisioned kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets Prevention Use node problem detection and immutable, reprovisioned nodes (cattle, not pets) so a sick node is replaced rather than nu

questions.q: Your pods can't reach an external service (e.g. a third-party API) though the rest of the internet works. What do you check?
questions.text: Symptom Pods can reach most external endpoints, but calls to one external API consistently fail (timeouts or refused). DNS resolves. Other external traffic from the same pods is fine. Investigation # Narrow: is it DNS, egress routing, policy, or the remote side? kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup api.partner.com # resolves correctly? kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -v https://api.partner.com # refused vs timeout? # refused = reached it, nothing/blocked at port; timeout = dropped in transit kubectl get networkpolicy # an egress NetworkPolicy blocking this dest? # egress path: NAT gateway IP -> is it on the partner's allowlist? # is the partner rate-limiting/blocking your egress IP? Since only one destination fails while general internet works, the issue is specific to that path: an egress NetworkPolicy, the partner allowlisting your NAT/egress IP, or the partner blocking/rate-limiting you. The refused-vs-timeout distinction tells you whether you're reaching them at all. Root cause The partner API allowlists client IPs, and the cluster's egress NAT gateway IP had changed (or a new node pool used a different NAT), so the partner silently dropped the traffic — timeouts, while every non-allowlisted destination worked fine. Fix / mitigation # Restore the egress path # pin a stable egress IP (NAT gateway) and get it allowlisted by the partner # or fix the egress NetworkPolicy to permit the destination # confirm with curl from the pod that calls now succeed Prevention Use a stable, known egre

questions.q: A Helm/manifest deploy succeeded but the new config didn't take effect in the running pods. Why?
questions.text: Symptom You updated a ConfigMap (or Helm values) and applied it. The deploy reports success, the ConfigMap shows the new values — but the running pods are still using the OLD config. Investigation # ConfigMap changed but pods didn't restart -> they still hold old config kubectl get configmap <cm> -o yaml # confirms new values ARE applied kubectl describe pod <pod> # but pod started BEFORE the change # Why old config persists: # - env-var/volume ConfigMaps are read at pod START; updating the CM # does NOT restart pods or re-inject env vars # - no rollout was triggered because the Deployment spec didn't change # - (mounted CMs update the file eventually, but the app must re-read it) Changing a ConfigMap doesn't restart pods. Env-var-injected config is read once at container start, so existing pods keep the old values until they're recreated. Since the Deployment's pod template didn't change, no rollout was triggered — the new config sits applied-but-unused. Root cause The config was consumed as environment variables. Updating the ConfigMap changed the stored object but didn't recreate any pods, so every running pod still had the env vars captured at its original start time. Fix / mitigation # Trigger a rollout so pods pick up the new config kubectl rollout restart deploy/<svc> # recreate pods -> re-read config # better: make config changes auto-trigger a rollout # (checksum/config annotation on the pod template, or a reloader) Prevention Add a config checksum annotation to the

questions.q: How would you handle a noisy-neighbor problem where one tenant's workload degrades others on shared nodes?
questions.text: Symptom On a multi-tenant cluster, one team's batch job periodically spikes and starves CPU/IO on shared nodes, hurting latency for unrelated services co-located there. Investigation # One workload starving others = missing isolation / resource governance # Diagnose the contention: kubectl top pods --all-namespaces # who's consuming the node's resources? # check: are requests/limits set? are QoS classes correct? # Guilty workload likely has no/low requests -> overcommits the node # QoS: Guaranteed (req==lim) > Burstable > BestEffort (evicted first) A noisy neighbor on shared nodes is a resource-isolation failure: without proper requests/limits the offending pod overcommits the node and starves co-located pods. Kubernetes QoS classes and cgroup limits exist precisely to contain this — the batch job needs governance. Root cause The batch job ran with no resource requests (BestEffort QoS) and burst hard, consuming CPU and I/O that the scheduler never accounted for. Latency-sensitive services on the same nodes were starved during its spikes. Fix / mitigation # Impose isolation # set proper requests/limits on the batch job (cap its blast radius) # raise critical services to Guaranteed QoS (req==limit) # isolate by design: dedicated node pool/taints for batch vs latency-sensitive # use PriorityClasses + anti-affinity to separate workloads Prevention Enforce ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges per namespace so no tenant can overcommit. questions.q: A secret was accidentally committed in a container image / manifest. What's your incident response?
questions.text: Symptom During review you discover an API key (or DB password) was baked into a container image and pushed to the registry — and referenced in a manifest in Git. It may have been there for days. Investigation # Treat as a security incident: the secret is COMPROMISED, assume leaked # 1. ROTATE the secret immediately (it must be considered exposed) # 2. Assess exposure: who/what could have pulled the image or seen the repo? # 3. Check for misuse (access logs for that credential) # DON'T just delete the commit/image -> it persists in history/layers/caches git log -p / image layers retain it; rotation is the only real fix A leaked secret can't be un-leaked by deleting the file — it survives in Git history, image layers, registry caches, and anyone's local copies. The only effective response is to rotate (invalidate) the credential immediately and treat it as compromised, then investigate exposure and misuse. Root cause The secret was embedded as an image layer and referenced in a committed manifest. Removing the commit wouldn't help — the credential lived in pushed image layers and Git history that others could already have, so it had to be rotated. Fix / mitigation # Rotate, then prevent recurrence # rotate/revoke the credential NOW; confirm no active misuse # remove from history/layers as cleanup (but rotation is the real fix) # move secrets to a secrets manager injected at runtime, never baked in Prevention Never bake secrets into images or commit them — inject at runtime from

questions.q: Pods are being evicted unexpectedly. How do you find out why and stop it?
questions.text: Symptom Pods are getting Evicted and rescheduled, disrupting service. It's not a deploy. The evictions happen on certain nodes under certain conditions. Investigation kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep -i evict kubectl describe pod <evicted-pod> # eviction reason kubectl describe node <node> # MemoryPressure / DiskPressure / PIDPressure? # Eviction causes: # - node resource pressure -> kubelet evicts (BestEffort/Burstable first) # - node disk/inode pressure (image/log/emptyDir bloat) # - pod exceeding ephemeral-storage limit # - preemption by higher-PriorityClass pods Evictions come from node-level resource pressure (memory/disk/PID) where the kubelet reclaims by evicting low-QoS pods first, or from preemption by higher-priority pods. The node conditions and pod events name which pressure triggered it. QoS class determines who gets evicted. Root cause Nodes hit DiskPressure because container logs and emptyDir volumes filled the node's disk, so the kubelet evicted BestEffort pods (which had no resource requests) to reclaim space — repeatedly, as the disk refilled. Fix / mitigation # Relieve pressure + protect important pods # clear the disk pressure (log rotation, prune images, size emptyDir) # set requests so important pods are Guaranteed/Burstable, not BestEffort # set ephemeral-storage requests/limits; add node disk headroom/alerts Prevention Set resource requests so critical pods have a protective QoS class (Guaranteed pods are evicted last). Manage node di

questions.q: You need zero-downtime deploys but users occasionally get errors during rollouts. What's causing the brief errors?
questions.text: Symptom Rollouts are supposed to be zero-downtime, but during each deploy a small number of requests fail for a few seconds — connection resets or 502s — then it's clean again. Almost zero-downtime, but not quite. Investigation # Brief errors during rollout = pods terminated before they stop receiving traffic # The race: pod gets SIGTERM + is removed from endpoints, but in-flight # requests / the LB's connection list aren't drained gracefully # Checklist of the usual gaps: # - no preStop hook / no grace period -> in-flight requests cut off # - app doesn't handle SIGTERM (finish in-flight + stop accepting) # - readiness not flipped to NotReady before shutdown (still gets new traffic) # - LB/endpoint propagation lag races the pod shutdown True zero-downtime needs graceful connection draining on shutdown. The brief errors come from a race: a terminating pod is killed (or stops listening) while it's still receiving traffic because endpoint removal and in-flight requests weren't drained. SIGTERM handling + a preStop delay close the gap. Root cause On termination, pods received SIGTERM and exited immediately, but it took a moment for them to be removed from Service endpoints and for the LB to stop sending connections — so requests in that window hit a pod that had already stopped accepting them, yielding 502s/resets. Fix / mitigation # Make shutdown graceful # add a preStop hook sleep (a few seconds) so endpoint removal propagates # handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new, finish in-fli

questions.q: Your ALB is returning 5xx errors. How do you tell if it's the load balancer or your targets?
questions.text: Symptom Users get 5xx from your application load balancer. You need to localize fast: is the ALB itself failing, or are the backend targets returning errors? Investigation # ALB CloudWatch metrics split the blame for you: # HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count -> the ALB generated the 5xx (no healthy target, # timeout to target, or surge queue full) = infra/target-health side # HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count -> your APP returned the 5xx = application side # Also check: TargetResponseTime, healthy host count, RejectedConnectionCount # 502 = bad/closed response from target; 503 = no healthy targets; # 504 = target timed out (slower than ALB idle timeout) The ALB's CloudWatch metrics directly separate ELB-generated 5xx (no healthy targets, target timeout, surge queue full) from Target-generated 5xx (your app erroring). The specific code also tells the story: 503 = no healthy targets, 502 = bad target response, 504 = target too slow. Root cause HTTPCode_ELB_5XX with a healthy-host count of zero showed the ALB had no healthy targets — the app's health check was failing (it hit a dependency that was down), so the ALB returned 503 even though the app processes were 'running.' Fix / mitigation # Fix per the split # ELB 503/no healthy targets -> fix target health checks / unhealthy targets # Target 5xx -> it's your app: roll back / debug the application # 504 -> target slower than ALB idle timeout: fix latency or raise timeout Prevention Make ALB target health checks reflect real readiness (not a trivia

questions.q: An EC2 instance suddenly can't reach the internet (or a dependency) though it worked yesterday. How do you debug AWS networking?
questions.text: Symptom An EC2 instance that's been working fine can no longer reach an external dependency. No code changed on the box. The connectivity just broke. Investigation # Walk the AWS network path layer by layer # 1. Security Group: does it allow the OUTBOUND traffic? (SGs are stateful) # 2. NACL: subnet-level, STATELESS -> must allow BOTH directions incl. ephemeral ports # 3. Route table: is there a route to 0.0.0.0/0 via IGW (public) or NAT (private)? # 4. NAT gateway / IGW healthy? (private subnet needs NAT for egress) # 5. DNS (route 53 resolver) resolving? 6. is the dependency itself up? ip route get <dst>; curl -v <dep> # refused vs timeout on the box AWS connectivity is a stack of independent controls — Security Group (stateful, instance-level), NACL (stateless, subnet-level), route table, and NAT/IGW. You check each in order. A change to any one (often a NACL or route edit) silently breaks egress. Root cause A NACL was edited to add a deny rule, and because NACLs are stateless, the change blocked the ephemeral return ports for outbound connections — so new connections timed out. The instance and SG were fine; the subnet NACL broke it. Fix / mitigation # Restore the path at the broken layer # fix the NACL to allow return traffic (ephemeral ports) — NACLs are stateless! # verify SG egress, route to NAT/IGW, NAT health # confirm connectivity returns Prevention Prefer Security Groups (stateful, simpler) for most controls and use NACLs sparingly — their statelessness (must allo

questions.q: Your AWS bill spiked unexpectedly this month. How do you investigate and stop the bleed?
questions.text: Symptom Finance flags that the cloud bill jumped sharply versus last month with no obvious reason. You need to find what's driving it and stop further spend fast. Investigation # Find the driver: which service, account, region, and dimension? # Cost Explorer: group by service, then by usage type / region / tag # Look for the delta vs last month -> what's NEW or grew? # Usual spike causes: # - data transfer (esp. cross-AZ / cross-region / NAT gateway egress) # - a runaway resource (forgotten large instances, unbounded autoscaling) # - storage growth (un-lifecycled S3, orphaned EBS/snapshots) # - logging/observability ingestion exploding A bill spike is debugged like an incident: localize via Cost Explorer (group by service, then usage type/region/tag) to find the delta versus last month, which points at a specific driver — frequently data transfer (cross-AZ/NAT egress), a runaway/forgotten resource, or storage/observability growth. Root cause A misconfigured service was sending large traffic cross-AZ (and through the NAT gateway), so data-transfer charges exploded — an invisible cost that doesn't show up as 'compute' and is easy to miss without grouping by usage type. Fix / mitigation # Stop the bleed, then optimize # kill/right-size the runaway resource; fix the cross-AZ traffic pattern # add S3 lifecycle policies; clean orphaned EBS/snapshots # set budgets + anomaly detection so the NEXT spike alerts early Prevention Tag resources for cost attribution, set AWS Budgets + Cost

questions.q: An application gets 'AccessDenied' calling an AWS API despite 'having the right IAM role.' How do you debug it?
questions.text: Symptom Your app, running with an IAM role, gets AccessDenied calling an AWS API (say, reading from S3). Everyone insists the role 'has the permission.' It still fails. Investigation # IAM is deny-by-default with multiple evaluation layers — check each # 1. Is the app even USING the role you think? (which identity is it?) aws sts get-caller-identity # confirms the ACTUAL principal in use # 2. Does an EXPLICIT DENY override the allow? (SCP, permission boundary, # resource policy, session policy — explicit deny always wins) # 3. Resource policy (e.g. S3 bucket policy / KMS key policy) also allow it? # 4. For cross-account: BOTH identity policy AND resource policy must allow # decode the denied message; use IAM Policy Simulator / Access Analyzer IAM is deny-by-default and evaluates several layers — identity policy, resource policy, SCPs, permission boundaries, session policies — where any explicit deny wins. 'Has the permission' usually means the identity policy allows it, but an SCP/boundary/resource policy is denying, or the app isn't using the role you assume. Root cause An Organizations SCP (or a permission boundary) explicitly denied the action at the account level, overriding the role's allow. The role's policy looked correct in isolation, but the higher-level guardrail vetoed it — explicit deny beats any allow. Fix / mitigation # Resolve by finding the denying layer # get-caller-identity to confirm the principal # check SCPs, permission boundaries, and resource (bucket/ke

questions.q: A managed database (RDS) is suddenly slow. Walk through diagnosing it.
questions.text: Symptom Your RDS-backed app slowed down. The database is the suspected bottleneck. You can't SSH into a managed DB, so how do you diagnose it? Investigation # Use RDS-native observability (no SSH on managed DBs) # CloudWatch: CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, Read/WriteIOPS, DBConnections, # ReadLatency/WriteLatency, BurstBalance (gp2 IOPS credits!) # Performance Insights: top SQL by load, wait events (lock? IO? CPU?) # Common causes: # - a slow/expensive query or missing index (a new query pattern) # - connection exhaustion (too many app instances x pool size > max_connections) # - IOPS/burst-credit exhaustion; storage autoscaling lag Managed databases are diagnosed through their metrics and query insights, not the host. Performance Insights surfaces the top SQL and wait events (telling you if it's CPU-, IO-, or lock-bound), while CloudWatch shows connections, IOPS, and burst-credit exhaustion — the usual RDS culprits. Root cause DBConnections was pegged at the max: too many app instances each with a connection pool exceeded RDS max_connections, so new queries queued waiting for a connection — the DB wasn't CPU-bound, it was connection-starved. Fix / mitigation # Relieve the bottleneck # connection exhaustion -> add a connection proxy (RDS Proxy) / cut pool sizes # slow query -> add the missing index / fix the query # IOPS exhaustion -> move to gp3/provisioned IOPS; scale storage # read-heavy -> add read replicas (mind replication lag) Prevention Front RDS with a connection pr

questions.q: You're paged that an auto-scaling group isn't scaling out during a traffic surge. What could be wrong?
questions.text: Symptom Traffic surged and latency is climbing, but the Auto Scaling Group isn't adding instances fast enough (or at all). Capacity is stuck while demand grows. Investigation # Why an ASG fails to scale out in time: # - scaling on the WRONG metric (CPU, but the bottleneck is queue depth/latency) # - scaling policy thresholds/cooldowns too conservative -> slow reaction # - hit the ASG MAX size (can't grow further) # - hit account/instance-type capacity or quota limits (no instances available) # - launch/boot + warmup time too long for a sharp spike (provisioning lag) # - new instances failing health checks -> ASG terminates them in a loop ASGs react with a lag and only within their limits. Failures to scale come from scaling on a metric that doesn't track the real bottleneck, conservative thresholds/cooldowns, hitting max size or capacity/quota, slow boot+warmup versus a sharp spike, or new instances failing health checks and churning. Root cause The ASG was at its configured max size, so it physically couldn't add more — and even below that, the scale-out was triggered on CPU while the actual bottleneck was request queue depth, so it under-reacted to the surge.
