Fix / mitigation # Fix scaling responsiveness + limits # raise ASG max + ensure instance-type capacity/quota headroom # scale on the bottleneck signal (req/s, queue depth) not just CPU # pre-provision/pre-warm for KNOWN spikes (autoscaling lags sharp surges) # tune cooldowns; fix health checks so new instances stay up

questions.q: A multi-AZ service degraded when a single Availability Zone had problems. Isn't multi-AZ supposed to prevent that?
questions.text: Symptom Your service runs across multiple AZs for resilience. One AZ had an incident — and your service degraded anyway, which shouldn't happen if multi-AZ failover works. Why? Investigation # Multi-AZ only helps if you can actually SHED the bad AZ # Investigate why the AZ loss wasn't absorbed: # - capacity: were the other AZs sized to carry the full load? (often NOT) # - was traffic actually drained from the bad AZ? (health checks failing fast?) # - a SHARED singleton dependency in the bad AZ (a primary DB, a cache) # - cross-AZ calls still routed INTO the failing AZ # - 'gray' AZ failure: slow/degraded, not cleanly down -> health checks passed Multi-AZ protects you only if the surviving AZs have the capacity to carry full load AND traffic is actually drained from the bad AZ. Common gaps: the other AZs weren't sized for N+1 at peak, a singleton dependency lived in the failing AZ, or a gray (degraded-not-dead) AZ kept passing health checks so traffic kept flowing to it. Root cause The primary database lived in the affected AZ and didn't fail over cleanly, and the other AZs were sized for normal split load, not for absorbing 100% — so when the bad AZ degraded, the remaining capacity was insufficient and a shared dependency was impaired. Fix / mitigation # Restore + correct the gaps # drain the bad AZ (fail over the DB, pull its targets out) # ensure surviving AZs can carry full load (capacity for AZ loss) # eliminate single-AZ singletons; verify cross-AZ failover Prevention Si

questions.q: A Lambda function is timing out / throttling under load. How do you diagnose serverless-specific issues?
questions.text: Symptom A Lambda-based endpoint starts timing out and throwing throttling errors during a traffic increase. It worked fine at low volume. Investigation # Serverless-specific failure modes # CloudWatch + Lambda metrics: # Throttles -> hit concurrency limit (account/function reserved concurrency) # Duration near timeout -> cold starts or a slow downstream (often the DB) # ConcurrentExecutions -> approaching the ceiling # Cold starts: spiky latency on scale-up (VPC-attached / large package = worse) # Downstream: Lambda scales FAST and can overwhelm a non-serverless DB # (connection storm to RDS) -> the DB throttles, Lambda times out waiting Lambda failures under load are usually concurrency throttling (hit the function/account limit) or a downstream that can't keep up. A subtle one: Lambda scales out far faster than a traditional database can accept connections, so a surge spawns a connection storm that overwhelms the DB, and Lambdas time out waiting. Root cause A traffic spike scaled Lambda to hundreds of concurrent executions, each opening a DB connection — instantly exhausting RDS max_connections. The DB rejected/queued connections, so Lambdas blocked and hit their timeout; some invocations were also throttled at the concurrency ceiling. Fix / mitigation # Fix concurrency + downstream pressure # raise/managed concurrency limits (reserved + provisioned concurrency) # put RDS Proxy between Lambda and the DB to pool/limit connections # provisioned concurrency to cut cold starts

questions.q: An S3 bucket is serving stale content / a deploy to S3+CloudFront didn't take effect. Why?
questions.text: Symptom You deployed updated static assets to S3 behind CloudFront, but users still see the old version. The new files are definitely in the bucket. The CDN is serving stale content. Investigation # CDN/cache layers serve stale content until invalidated/expired # Where the old version can persist: # - CloudFront edge cache still holding old objects (TTL not expired) # - browser cache (Cache-Control headers) # - you uploaded but didn't INVALIDATE the CDN # Check the served object's headers (Age, Cache-Control, X-Cache HIT/MISS) aws cloudfront create-invalidation --paths '/*' # force edge refresh Static deploys behind a CDN are a caching problem: the new files are in S3, but CloudFront edges keep serving cached copies until their TTL expires or you explicitly invalidate. Browsers add another cache layer. The fix is invalidation plus correct cache-control headers. Root cause The deploy updated S3 but didn't invalidate CloudFront, and the objects had a long TTL — so edge locations kept serving the old cached version until you forced an invalidation. Fix / mitigation # Refresh the caches correctly # create a CloudFront invalidation for changed paths (or use versioned filenames) # set appropriate Cache-Control / TTLs # verify X-Cache shows a MISS/refetch and Age resets Prevention Use content-hashed/versioned filenames (e.g. app.[hash].js) so new deploys are new URLs that never collide with cached old ones — the cleanest pattern, avoiding invalidations entirely. Set deliberate cache

questions.q: You need to migrate a stateful workload to a new region/instance type with minimal downtime. How do you plan it?
questions.text: Symptom Leadership wants a stateful service (with a database) moved to a new region or onto new instance types, with as little downtime as possible. How do you approach the migration safely? Investigation # Plan around STATE + reversibility, not just compute # 1. Stand up the new environment in parallel (don't mutate the old) # 2. Replicate data continuously old -> new (ongoing sync, not a one-shot copy) # 3. Validate the new env under shadow/canary traffic # 4. Cut over at a low-traffic window: brief write-freeze or dual-write, # final sync, flip traffic (DNS/LB), verify # 5. Keep the old env warm as instant rollback until confident Stateful migrations hinge on moving data safely and keeping a rollback path. You build the new environment in parallel, replicate data continuously, validate with real traffic, then cut over during a quiet window with a final sync — keeping the old environment as an instant fallback rather than a one-way leap. Root cause The risky part is the data: a naive 'snapshot, copy, switch' loses writes that happen during the copy. Continuous replication plus a short final-sync (with a brief write freeze or dual-write) bounds data loss and keeps RPO near zero. Fix / mitigation # Execute the cutover safely # continuous replication -> final sync at a low-traffic window # flip traffic via DNS/LB (low TTL so you can flip back fast) # keep old env warm for instant rollback; decommission only after soak Prevention Use low DNS TTLs for a fast flip-back, validate

questions.q: Your infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) plan wants to destroy and recreate a production database. How do you respond?
questions.text: Symptom You run terraform plan for a routine change and the output says it will DESTROY and recreate your production RDS instance (or another stateful resource). Applying this would wipe data. What do you do? Investigation # STOP. A destroy/recreate of a stateful resource = data loss. Do NOT apply. # Understand WHY Terraform wants to replace it (a 'ForceNew' attribute changed): terraform plan # read the '# forces replacement' annotations carefully # common triggers: changing an immutable attribute (name, AZ, engine, # subnet group, encryption setting) -> provider must recreate # verify in state vs config what diverged A destroy/recreate plan on a stateful resource is a red alert — applying it deletes the data. Terraform shows which attribute 'forces replacement' (an immutable field changed). You never apply blindly; you find the offending attribute and avoid the recreate, often by not changing the immutable field or by moving state. Root cause A change to an immutable attribute (e.g. the DB subnet group, name, or an encryption setting) triggered Terraform's force-replacement. The intended change was harmless, but it touched a field the provider can only change by recreating the resource. Fix / mitigation # Avoid the destroy safely # revert/avoid changing the immutable attribute, OR # use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } as a guardrail on stateful resources # if the change is truly needed: do a controlled migration, not an in-place destroy # target the apply narrowly; neve

questions.q: A spot instance interruption took down part of your workload. How should you have architected for it?
questions.text: Symptom You run some workload on Spot instances for cost savings. AWS reclaimed a batch of them with a 2-minute warning, and part of your service went down because it wasn't ready for the interruption. Investigation # Spot = cheap but can be reclaimed anytime (2-min warning) -> design for it # What should have been in place: # - handle the interruption notice (drain, checkpoint, finish in-flight) # - only run INTERRUPTIBLE workloads on Spot (stateless, batch, fault-tolerant) # - diversify instance types/AZs so one capacity pool's reclamation isn't total # - mix Spot with On-Demand/Reserved for a stable baseline # - keep critical/stateful work OFF pure Spot Spot interruptions are expected behavior, not a failure — the architecture must tolerate sudden reclamation. The fixes: only run fault-tolerant/stateless work on Spot, react to the 2-minute interruption notice (drain/checkpoint), diversify across instance types/AZs, and keep a stable On-Demand baseline for critical capacity. Root cause The workload ran entirely on a single Spot instance type in one AZ with no interruption handling. When AWS reclaimed that capacity pool, a large fraction vanished at once and in-flight work was lost — there was no baseline and no draining. Fix / mitigation # Re-architect for interruption tolerance # handle the 2-min interruption notice: drain + checkpoint + reschedule # diversify instance types/AZs; mix Spot + On-Demand baseline # keep stateful/critical components off pure Spot Prevention Use

questions.q: Cross-region replication lag is causing users to see inconsistent data in an active-active setup. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Symptom You run active-active across two regions for availability. Users sometimes see stale or conflicting data because writes in one region take time to replicate to the other. Replication lag is causing inconsistency. Investigation # Active-active + async cross-region replication => inconsistency is INHERENT # Physics: cross-region distance forces ASYNC replication -> lag + conflicts # Decide per data type (CAP/PACELC): # - strong consistency needed (money, inventory) -> route writes to one region # (single-writer) or use a globally-consistent store (higher latency) # - availability/latency over consistency (sessions, carts) -> AP + reconcile # read-your-writes: pin a user's session to their write region In active-active across regions, the speed of light forces asynchronous replication, so lag and write conflicts are inherent — you can't make it both fully consistent and low-latency (CAP/PACELC). The resolution is per-data-type: strong consistency for money (single-writer or global store), availability-with-reconciliation for engagement data. Root cause Both regions accepted writes to the same records, and async replication meant a user could write in one region and read stale data from the other before it replicated — and concurrent writes to the same key created conflicts needing resolution. Fix / mitigation # Choose consistency per data flow # critical data -> single-writer region or a strongly-consistent global DB # tolerant data -> accept eventual consistency + confl

questions.q: How do you investigate and remediate a publicly-exposed cloud resource (e.g. an open S3 bucket or security group)?
questions.text: Symptom A scan (or worse, a researcher) reports that an S3 bucket is world-readable, or a security group allows 0.0.0.0/0 to a sensitive port. Sensitive data or access may be exposed. Investigation # Treat as a security incident: assume exposure -> contain, assess, remediate # 1. CONTAIN immediately: lock down the resource # (block public access on the bucket / tighten the SG to known CIDRs) # 2. ASSESS exposure: access logs — was the data actually accessed? by whom? # (S3 access logs / CloudTrail / VPC flow logs) # 3. If accessed: data-breach response (rotate any exposed secrets, notify per policy) # 4. find others like it: scan the whole estate for the same misconfig An exposed cloud resource is a security incident: contain it immediately (block public access / tighten the SG), then determine from access logs whether anything was actually reached, escalate to breach response if so, and crucially scan for the same misconfiguration elsewhere — one open bucket usually means a systemic gap. Root cause A bucket policy / ACL left public access enabled (or an SG rule used 0.0.0.0/0 for convenience and was never tightened). The remediation isn't just this one resource — it's the absence of a guardrail preventing public exposure across the org. Fix / mitigation # Remediate the instance and the class # enable account-level S3 Block Public Access; remove 0.0.0.0/0 SG rules # rotate anything that may have been exposed # add preventive guardrails so it can't recur (SCPs, Config rules, I

questions.q: Your cloud provider is having a regional incident affecting your service. What's your response when the problem is the provider?
questions.text: Symptom AWS (or your provider) is having a regional service degradation — it's on their status page. Your service depends on the affected components and is degraded. The root cause is the provider, not you. Investigation # You can't fix the provider — focus on mitigation + comms + learning # 1. Confirm it's the provider (status page + your own signals correlate) # 2. Mitigate what YOU control: # - fail over to an unaffected region (if you're multi-region) # - degrade gracefully: shed dependence on the affected service # - serve cached/static fallback for the broken capability # 3. Communicate honestly to users (status page); set update cadence # 4. Don't burn the team chasing a root cause you can't change When the provider is the cause you can't fix it, so the response is mitigation of what you control (failover, graceful degradation, fallbacks), honest communication, and not exhausting the team hunting a root cause that isn't yours. Whether you can actually fail over is determined by architecture decisions made long before. Root cause A specific regional service (say, a managed queue or a specific AZ) degraded. Single-region services were stuck; the question becomes whether you'd invested in multi-region or graceful degradation ahead of time to ride it out. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate within your control + communicate # fail over to a healthy region / degrade the affected feature gracefully # fall back to cached/default behavior; shed the broken dependency # keep users infor

questions.q: Users report 'connection refused' to your service. What does that specifically tell you, and how do you proceed?
questions.text: Symptom Clients trying to reach your service get 'connection refused' — fast, immediate errors (not hangs). What does the refused (vs timeout) distinction tell you, and where do you look? Investigation # 'Refused' is a SPECIFIC, useful signal (different from 'timeout') # Refused = the packet REACHED the host, but nothing is listening on that # port (or it actively sent a TCP RST). You got there; no one answered. # (Timeout, by contrast = packets silently dropped: firewall/route/host down) # So check the SERVER side: ss -tlnp | grep :<port> # is the process actually listening? on which address? # is it bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0? (works locally, refuses remotely) 'Connection refused' is precise: the client reached the host but nothing accepted on that port (or got an RST). That rules out firewalls/routing (which cause timeouts) and points at the listener — the service is down, on the wrong port, or bound to localhost instead of all interfaces. Root cause The service was bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, so it worked when tested locally on the box but refused every remote connection — the port was open only to loopback. Fix / mitigation # Fix the listener # bind the service to 0.0.0.0 (or the correct interface), not 127.0.0.1 # confirm it's listening on the expected port (ss -tlnp) # restart/redeploy; verify remote clients now connect Prevention Monitor that the service is listening on the expected address:port (synthetic check). The refused-vs-timeout distincti

questions.q: Connections to your service are timing out (not refused). How do you find where packets are being dropped?
questions.text: Symptom Clients get timeouts reaching your service — connections just hang and eventually fail, with no refused/RST. Packets are vanishing somewhere between client and server. Investigation # Timeout = silent drop. Find WHERE in the path packets die. # Capture on BOTH ends to localize: tcpdump -i any -nn 'tcp and host <server> and port ' # - client sends SYN but server NEVER sees it -> dropped in between # (firewall, security group/NACL, routing, network ACL) # - server sees SYN, replies SYN-ACK, client never gets it -> return path broken mtr -rwzbc 100 <server> # per-hop loss/latency along the path A timeout means packets are being silently dropped, unlike a refused (RST). The fastest way to localize is to capture on both ends: if the server never sees the client's SYN, the drop is in the path (firewall/SG/NACL/route); if the server replies but the client never receives it, the return path is broken. Root cause A firewall/security-group rule (or a stateless NACL missing the return-traffic allow) silently dropped the packets. The server never saw the SYNs, confirming the drop was in the path — not at the listener (which would have refused). Fix / mitigation # Restore the path # fix the firewall / SG / NACL rule that's dropping the traffic # (remember NACLs are stateless: allow return/ephemeral ports too) # verify with tcpdump that SYNs now reach the server and SYN-ACKs return Prevention Manage firewall/SG/NACL rules as code with review so a silent drop can't be introduced unn

questions.q: Your service works fine but is intermittently slow only for users in one geographic region. How do you diagnose it?
questions.text: Symptom Most users are happy, but users in one region (say, APAC) intermittently see high latency. Same service, same code — only certain geographies are affected, intermittently. Investigation # Region-specific intermittent latency -> the PATH or a regional edge differs mtr -rwzbc 100 <endpoint> # FROM that region: per-hop loss/latency # read mtr correctly: only loss that PERSISTS to the final hop is real # (mid-path ICMP deprioritization looks like loss but isn't) # check: is that region served by a distant origin? (no nearby edge/CDN PoP) # routing change / peering issue / congested transit on that path? # packet loss on a specific submarine/transit link -> retransmits -> latency Geography-specific latency points to the network path or edge serving that region — a distant origin with no nearby CDN PoP, a routing/peering change, or a congested/lossy transit link. mtr from the affected region localizes it, with the caveat that only loss persisting to the final hop is real (mid-path ICMP deprioritization is a false signal). Root cause That region's traffic was routed to a far origin (no local CDN edge), and a congested transit link on the long path caused intermittent packet loss → TCP retransmits → latency spikes. Nearer regions hit a local edge and were unaffected. Fix / mitigation # Improve the regional path # add a CDN/edge presence (or origin) closer to that region # work with the provider on the routing/peering/transit issue # use anycast / latency-based routing to stee

questions.q: After scaling up, your service starts failing with 'cannot assign requested address.' What's happening?
questions.text: Symptom You scaled out a service that makes many outbound connections (e.g. to a database or API). Under the higher load it begins failing with 'cannot assign requested address' (EADDRNOTAVAIL). Investigation # EADDRNOTAVAIL under high outbound connection churn = ephemeral port exhaustion cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range # ~28k ports by default ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l # piles of TIME_WAIT eating source ports # Each outbound conn to the SAME dst ip:port needs a free local source port. # High churn -> many sockets stuck in TIME_WAIT (~60s) -> ports exhausted # -> the kernel can't assign a source port for new connections This error means the host ran out of ephemeral source ports for new outbound connections. High connection churn leaves thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT (held ~60s by the side that closed), tying up the limited ephemeral range so new connects fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL. Root cause The service opened a fresh connection per request to the same backend instead of reusing connections. Under load, sockets churned into TIME_WAIT faster than they cleared, exhausting the ~28k ephemeral ports to that destination. Fix / mitigation # Fix: reuse connections (the real fix), then tune # use connection pooling / HTTP keep-alive -> far fewer, reused connections # widen ip_local_port_range; enable net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 (safe for outbound) # do NOT use tcp_tw_recycle (removed; breaks NAT) Prevention The real fix is connection reuse (pooling/keep-alive) so you don

questions.q: A large file transfer or bulk request works on the LAN but fails or hangs across a VPN/WAN. What's the likely cause?
questions.text: Symptom Small requests work fine everywhere. But large transfers (big uploads, bulk responses) succeed on the local network yet hang or fail when they traverse a VPN or certain WAN paths. Small packets fine, big ones stuck. Investigation # 'Small works, large hangs across a tunnel' = MTU / PMTUD black hole # VPN/tunnel adds encapsulation overhead -> lower effective MTU # Large packets exceed path MTU and need to fragment; if ICMP 'frag needed' # is blocked, Path MTU Discovery fails silently -> big packets vanish ping -M do -s 1472 <dst> # test if large (DF-set) packets get through tracepath <dst> # discover the actual path MTU # small packets fit -> work; large ones drop -> hang on bulk transfer This is the classic MTU/PMTUD black hole. A VPN/tunnel reduces the usable MTU via encapsulation overhead; large packets that exceed the path MTU must fragment, but if the ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages are filtered, Path MTU Discovery breaks silently — small packets pass, large ones disappear. Root cause A firewall along the VPN path blocked ICMP, so PMTUD couldn't signal the sender to reduce packet size. The tunnel's lower MTU silently dropped full-size packets, hanging any transfer large enough to send them. Fix / mitigation # Fix the MTU path # allow ICMP 'fragmentation needed' (type 3 code 4) so PMTUD works # or clamp MSS on the tunnel (MSS clamping) to fit the path MTU # lower the interface MTU on the tunnel to a safe value Prevention Enable MSS clamping on tunnels and don'

questions.q: DNS resolution is intermittently failing or slow across your infrastructure. How do you approach it?
questions.text: Symptom Services intermittently fail to resolve hostnames, or resolution is slow, causing cascading timeouts and errors across many services at once. DNS is the common thread. Investigation # DNS is a shared dependency -> its failure looks like everything failing # Diagnose the resolver path: dig @<resolver> <name> # is the resolver slow/failing/returning SERVFAIL? cat /etc/resolv.conf # options ndots/timeout/attempts; multiple servers? # high ndots -> many failed lookups (search-domain expansion) before success # one unhealthy nameserver in the list -> per-query timeout then fallback # resolver overloaded (e.g. CoreDNS under-provisioned) -> slow/dropped queries Because DNS underlies nearly every connection, a flaky resolver makes unrelated services fail simultaneously. Diagnose the resolver path: a slow/overloaded nameserver, an unhealthy server in the list causing per-query timeouts, or high ndots causing many failed search-domain lookups before the real query. Root cause The cluster's DNS (CoreDNS) was under-provisioned and overwhelmed under load, dropping/slowing queries. Combined with a high ndots value causing extra lookups per name, resolution became intermittently slow — and every service that resolves names was affected. Fix / mitigation # Stabilize DNS # scale/right-size the resolver (more CoreDNS replicas, autoscale) # add a node-local DNS cache to absorb query load + cut latency # tune ndots / use FQDNs to reduce lookups; remove unhealthy nameservers # add DNS cac

questions.q: A service behind a load balancer sees all traffic coming from a single IP (the LB), breaking rate limiting and logging. How do you fix it?
questions.text: Symptom Your app sits behind a load balancer / reverse proxy. In the app's logs and rate limiter, every request appears to come from the LB's IP — so per-client rate limiting and geolocation are broken, and logs are useless for source IPs. Investigation # Behind an L7 proxy/LB the client IP is in a HEADER, not the TCP source # The real client IP is carried in X-Forwarded-For (or Forwarded / proxy protocol) # The app/rate-limiter must read XFF, not the TCP peer (which is the LB) # BUT: XFF is client-spoofable unless you trust only the LB's appended value # configure the app to trust the LB and parse the correct XFF entry An L7 load balancer terminates the client's TCP connection and opens its own to the backend, so the TCP source IP is the LB. The real client IP is passed in X-Forwarded-For. The app and rate limiter must read XFF — but only the entry appended by your trusted LB, since clients can forge XFF. Root cause The app rate-limited on the TCP source address, which behind the LB is always the LB's IP — so all clients shared one bucket (and one client could exhaust everyone's limit). It needed to read X-Forwarded-For instead. Fix / mitigation # Use the forwarded client IP, safely # configure the app/framework to extract client IP from XFF (trusted proxy config) # trust only the LB-appended entry; strip/ignore client-supplied XFF # (for L4: use proxy protocol to preserve the source IP) Prevention Configure trusted-proxy handling so the app derives client IP from XFF append

questions.q: Your service's outbound calls to a partner intermittently fail with TLS handshake errors. How do you debug TLS issues?
questions.text: Symptom Calls from your service to a partner's HTTPS endpoint intermittently fail during the TLS handshake — not a timeout, a handshake/certificate error. Sometimes it works, sometimes not. Investigation # Debug the TLS handshake directly openssl s_client -connect partner.com:443 -servername partner.com # inspect: cert chain, expiry, SNI, negotiated version/cipher, CA trust # Intermittent handshake failures — usual causes: # - one endpoint behind the partner's LB has a bad/expired/mismatched cert # - missing intermediate cert in the chain (some clients fail, some don't) # - protocol/cipher mismatch (old TLS disabled on one side) # - SNI not sent -> wrong cert served TLS handshake failures (vs timeouts) point at certificate/protocol issues, and intermittency usually means a fleet inconsistency on the partner side — e.g. one server behind their LB has a bad or chain-incomplete cert. openssl s_client inspects the chain, version, cipher, and SNI to localize it. Root cause The partner had several servers behind a load balancer; one of them presented a cert with a missing intermediate (incomplete chain). Clients that didn't have that intermediate cached failed the handshake — but only when routed to that one server, hence the intermittency. Fix / mitigation # Mitigate + escalate # confirm which endpoint/cert fails (s_client repeatedly hits different backends) # report the incomplete chain / bad cert to the partner to fix # add retry (handshake failures may hit a good server next) +

questions.q: Your microservices mesh has high tail latency and you suspect the network layer. How do you isolate it?
questions.text: Symptom In a microservices architecture, P99 latency is poor end-to-end. You suspect network/mesh overhead but can't tell if it's the network, a proxy/sidecar, or an app hop. There are many services in the call chain. Investigation # Many hops + bad tail latency -> use tracing to find WHERE time goes # distributed tracing: break the request into spans per hop/sidecar # -> which span owns the latency? app? network? the mesh sidecar (Envoy)? # tail latency COMPOUNDS with fan-out: 1% slow per call x many calls # = most end-to-end requests hit at least one slow hop # check: sidecar/proxy overhead, mTLS handshake cost, connection pooling, # retries adding hops, per-service P99 With many hops, only distributed tracing can localize tail latency to a specific span — app logic, the network, or the mesh sidecar. The key principle: tail latency compounds with fan-out, so a 1% slow rate per dependency means most multi-call requests hit at least one slow hop, making per-dependency P99 critical. Root cause A service-mesh sidecar (Envoy) was adding latency on each hop — partly mTLS handshakes without connection reuse, partly retry-on-each-hop amplifying calls. Across a deep call chain, these small per-hop costs compounded into a poor end-to-end P99. Fix / mitigation # Reduce per-hop and tail cost # enable connection reuse/keep-alive in the mesh (avoid per-call handshakes) # tune/limit retries (retry budgets) so they don't multiply hops # reduce call-chain depth / fan-out where possible; cac

questions.q: A firewall/security-group change locked you out or broke connectivity. How do you recover and prevent it?
questions.text: Symptom Someone applied a firewall or security-group change and it broke connectivity — possibly locking out SSH/management access to instances, or cutting traffic between tiers. You need to recover without making it worse. Investigation # Recover via an out-of-band path that doesn't depend on the broken rule # - cloud serial console / Session Manager (SSM) — no network/SSH needed # - revert the change at the control plane (it's likely IaC or a console edit) # Then verify the rule logic: # - SG (stateful): allow the needed inbound/outbound; return traffic auto-allowed # - NACL (stateless): must allow BOTH directions incl. ephemeral return ports # - first-match / ordering issues; an overly-broad deny above an allow A connectivity-breaking firewall change is recovered through an out-of-band path that doesn't rely on the broken rule — a serial console or SSM Session Manager — then by reverting the change at the control plane. Understanding stateful (SG) vs stateless (NACL) is key to fixing the rule correctly. Root cause A new restrictive rule (or a NACL deny that broke stateless return traffic) cut access. Because SSH itself was blocked, recovery required the cloud serial console / SSM to get in and revert — you can't fix a network lockout over the network. Fix / mitigation # Recover then prevent # use serial console / SSM (out-of-band) to revert the rule # correct SG vs NACL semantics; verify both directions for NACLs # prevent: manage firewall rules as reviewed IaC; stage chan

questions.q: You need to debug whether a problem is DNS, network, or the application — give your systematic layered approach.
questions.text: Symptom A connection from your service to a dependency is failing and you don't yet know if it's name resolution, the network path, or the application/port. The interviewer wants your systematic method. Investigation # Walk the layers bottom-up, each test isolating one layer: getent hosts <host> # 1. DNS: does the name resolve? to the RIGHT IP? ip route get <ip> # 2. Routing: is there a path? correct interface/source? ping <ip> # 3. L3 reachability (ICMP may be blocked — not definitive) nc -vz <ip> <port> # 4. L4: is the PORT open? (refused vs timeout!) curl -v <url> # 5. L7: does the APP actually respond correctly? # refused = reached, nothing listening; timeout = dropped (firewall/route) The disciplined method isolates one layer at a time: resolve the name (DNS), confirm a route exists, test L3 reachability, test the specific port (L4), then the application response (L7). Each step rules a layer in or out, and the refused-vs-timeout distinction at L4 immediately separates 'nothing listening' from 'traffic blocked.' Root cause Working the layers showed DNS resolved to the wrong IP (a stale record after a migration), so every subsequent layer was being tested against the wrong host. Fixing DNS resolved it — a problem that 'feels like' a network or app issue but is actually name resolution. Fix / mitigation # Fix at the layer that fails # DNS wrong -> correct the record / cache / resolver # no route -> fix routing; refused -> fix the listener; timeout -> fix firewall/SG # app

questions.q: Your service is being overwhelmed by traffic that looks like a DDoS or a misbehaving client. How do you respond?
questions.text: Symptom A sudden flood of traffic is overwhelming your service — it could be a DDoS attack or a single misbehaving client/bot hammering you. Legitimate users are being affected. Investigation # First: is it malicious (DDoS) or one buggy client? and what LAYER? # identify the pattern: source IPs, user-agents, target endpoint, geographic spread # - few sources, huge volume -> one abusive client/bot (rate-limit/block it) # - many distributed sources -> DDoS (needs upstream/edge mitigation) # - L7 (app-layer floods to an expensive endpoint) vs L3/4 (volumetric) # protect the service while you sort it out: # rate limiting, load shedding (429/503), WAF rules, edge/CDN DDoS protection First classify: a few sources at huge volume is an abusive client (rate-limit/block), while many distributed sources is a DDoS needing edge/upstream mitigation; and L7 app-floods differ from L3/4 volumetric attacks. Meanwhile protect the service with rate limiting and load shedding so legitimate users still get served. Root cause A single misbehaving client (a buggy integration in a retry loop) was hammering an expensive endpoint — not a true DDoS. Per-client rate limiting and a temporary block of that source restored capacity for everyone else. Fix / mitigation # Protect, then mitigate the source # rate-limit per client/key; load-shed low-priority traffic (429 + Retry-After) # block/throttle the abusive source(s); add WAF rules for the pattern # for true DDoS: engage edge/CDN/cloud DDoS protection (ab

questions.q: Load average is 40 on an 8-core box, but top shows CPU mostly idle. What's going on?
questions.text: Symptom Alerts fire on load average >30. You log in expecting pegged CPUs, but top shows 85% idle and almost no user/sys time. Investigation uptime top # note %id high, but load high vmstat 1 5 # watch the 'b' column (uninterruptible) ps -eo state,pid,comm | awk '$1 ~ /D/' Load average on Linux counts processes in runnable and uninterruptible (D) state. Idle CPU plus high load means processes are blocked in D-state — almost always I/O wait, often a slow or hung disk/NFS mount. Root cause Many processes sit in D-state waiting on a backing store. CPU is idle because they're blocked on the kernel, not computing. This is an I/O problem masquerading as a CPU alarm. Fix / mitigation iostat -x 1 5 # %util ~100, await high on the culprit device iotop -oPa cat /proc/<pid>/stack # see where it's blocked in-kernel Prevention Alert on what matters to users (latency, saturation) rather than raw load average. Track vmstat 'b' count and per-device %util / await so an I/O stall is named as such instead of looking like a CPU fire. Interview tip: Knowing that Linux load includes D-state is a classic senior tell. Say it plainly: “high load + idle CPU = blocked on I/O, not compute,” then go to iostat / iotop .

questions.q: A process keeps getting killed and you find 'Out of memory: Killed process' in dmesg. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Symptom A service mysteriously dies every few hours with no application error. dmesg shows the OOM killer terminating it. Investigation dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' journalctl -k | grep -i oom cat /proc/<pid>/oom_score # before it dies free -m # available, not just free The kernel ran out of allocatable memory and the OOM killer picked a victim by oom_score (roughly: biggest memory user, adjusted by oom_score_adj). Your process was the fattest target, not necessarily the leaker. Root cause Total committed memory exceeded physical + swap headroom. The killed process may be the victim, not the cause — you must find what actually grew. Check whether it's a real leak, a workload spike, or another co-tenant ballooning. Fix / mitigation smem -tk # PSS per process, fairer than RSS Reduce the workload / add memory / set sane cgroup limits echo -1000 > /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj # protect a critical PID (stopgap) Prevention Run memory-critical services under cgroup memory limits (systemd MemoryMax= or container limits) so one process can't take down the host, and alert on MemAvailable trending down well before the killer fires. Interview tip: Distinguish victim from cause . Mention MemAvailable vs free, oom_score_adj for protecting critical PIDs, and that swap thrash often precedes the kill.

questions.q: ps shows hundreds of zombie processes. Are they dangerous, and how do you clear them?
questions.text: Symptom Monitoring flags a climbing process count. ps shows hundreds of <defunct> entries. Investigation ps -el | grep -w Z | wc -l ps -eo pid,ppid,state,comm | awk '$3=="Z"' # identify the common PPID — that's the negligent parent A zombie is a finished child whose exit status the parent never reaped via wait() . Zombies hold only a PID slot, not memory or CPU — but enough of them exhausts the PID table and blocks new forks. Root cause The parent process has a bug: it isn't reaping children (missing wait() /SIGCHLD handling). The zombies themselves are already dead; the real defect is in the parent. Fix / mitigation kill -CHLD <ppid> # nudge the parent to reap # if parent is broken, restart the parent — init then adopts & reaps orphans # you cannot 'kill' a zombie; it's already dead Prevention Fix the parent's child-reaping (proper SIGCHLD handler or a process supervisor). In containers, run a minimal init ( tini , --init ) as PID 1 so orphaned children get reaped instead of accumulating. Interview tip: Make the PID-1-doesn't-reap point for containers — it's the modern version of this question. And be precise: zombies consume PID slots, not RAM.

questions.q: Writes are failing with 'No space left on device' but df shows 40% free. What's the cause?
questions.text: Symptom Applications fail with ENOSPC / “No space left on device,” yet df -h shows the filesystem only 40% full. Investigation df -h /data # 40% used — misleading df -i /data # IUse% 100% — the real story for d in /data/*; do echo $(find "$d" | wc -l) $d; done | sort -rn | head Bytes are free but inodes are exhausted. Each file consumes one inode regardless of size; a directory full of tiny files (sessions, cache, mail spool) burns inodes long before bytes. Root cause Inode exhaustion. Some directory is generating millions of small files — a runaway cache, unrotated session files, or a logging bug writing one file per event. Fix / mitigation # delete/rotate the offending small-file directory find /data/cache -type f -mtime +7 -delete # inode count is fixed at mkfs time; to raise it you must reformat (-i bytes-per-inode) Prevention Monitor df -i alongside df -h , set retention/rotation on anything that creates many small files, and size bytes-per-inode appropriately at format time for known small-file workloads. Interview tip: The instant you say “ENOSPC but df shows free → check df -i ” you signal real ops scars. Add that inode count is set at format time and can't be grown live.

questions.q: The box becomes unresponsive and you suspect a fork bomb / PID exhaustion. How do you recover and prevent it?
questions.text: Symptom The host stops accepting new SSH sessions; even local commands fail with “fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable.” Investigation cat /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max ps -eLf | wc -l # threads ps -eo ppid,comm | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head # who's spawning The system hit pid_max or a per-user process limit. Once forks fail you often can't even run diagnostics — each tool needs a fork. A runaway loop or fork bomb is multiplying processes faster than they exit. Root cause Process/PID exhaustion. A user or service is forking unboundedly (a bad loop, a crash-restart storm, or a deliberate fork bomb), starving the global PID space. Fix / mitigation # use an already-running shell / a reserved root session pkill -STOP -u <baduser> # freeze the spawner, then kill the tree # systemd: systemctl kill --kill-who=all <unit> Prevention Cap fork-happy services with cgroup TasksMax= (systemd) and set per-user nproc limits in /etc/security/limits.conf so one user or unit can never consume the whole PID table. Keep a reserved root login slot. Interview tip: Emphasize prevention via TasksMax / nproc — reacting to a fork bomb is hard precisely because you can't fork. Mention freezing (SIGSTOP) the tree before killing.

questions.q: A systemd service fails to start after a config change and just shows 'failed'. Walk me through debugging it.
questions.text: Symptom After editing a unit, systemctl start myapp returns failed. The one-line status isn't enough. Investigation systemctl status myapp -l --no-pager journalctl -u myapp -n 100 --no-pager systemd-analyze verify myapp.service # syntax/dependency check systemctl cat myapp # see the effective unit incl. drop-ins status shows the exit code and last log lines; the real error is in the journal. Common causes: bad ExecStart path, a missing dependency in After= / Requires= , a permission/SELinux denial, or an edit you forgot to daemon-reload . Root cause The unit's declared state doesn't match reality — wrong binary path, an unmet ordering dependency, a sandbox directive ( ProtectSystem , ReadOnlyPaths ) blocking a write, or a stale unit because daemon-reload wasn't run after editing. Fix / mitigation systemctl daemon-reload # after ANY unit edit # fix the ExecStart path / dependency / sandbox directive systemctl reset-failed myapp # clear the failed latch before retry Prevention Validate units in CI with systemd-analyze verify , manage them via config management so edits always trigger daemon-reload , and prefer drop-in files ( override.conf ) over editing vendor units so upgrades don't clobber changes. Interview tip: The two things interviewers love here: always daemon-reload after edits, and read the journal not just status . Bonus: systemctl cat to reveal drop-ins masking your change.

questions.q: The root filesystem filled up and journald logs are the culprit. How do you contain it without losing observability?
questions.text: Symptom / hits 100%; the host gets flaky. du points at /var/log/journal consuming tens of GB. Investigation df -h / journalctl --disk-usage du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head Persistent journald grew without a cap, or a chatty service is flooding logs (a crash-restart loop emitting megabytes/sec). Unbounded journal storage will happily consume the whole root partition. Root cause No journal size limit (or one too high), amplified by a noisy unit. The fix has two halves: reclaim space now, and bound it permanently so it can't recur. Fix / mitigation journalctl --vacuum-size=2G # reclaim now journalctl --vacuum-time=7d # /etc/systemd/journald.conf: SystemMaxUse=2G RuntimeMaxUse=200M systemctl restart systemd-journald Prevention Set SystemMaxUse in journald.conf , put /var/log (or /var ) on its own partition so a log flood can't take down / , and rate-limit or fix the service that's over-logging. Interview tip: Show the both-halves instinct: reclaim with --vacuum-* now, then cap with SystemMaxUse forever. Mentioning a separate /var partition signals you've been burned before.

questions.q: An NFS-backed mount hangs and any command touching it freezes in D-state. How do you recover?
questions.text: Symptom Anything that touches /mnt/shared hangs forever — ls , df , even tab-completion. Processes pile up in D-state. Investigation mount | grep nfs # note hard vs soft, and the server cat /proc/mounts | grep nfs dmesg -T | grep -i 'nfs server.*not responding' rpcinfo -p <nfs-server> # is the export reachable? A hard -mounted NFS share whose server became unreachable blocks I/O indefinitely (by design — hard mounts retry forever to avoid data loss). Every process touching it parks in uninterruptible sleep, which you can't even kill -9 . Root cause The NFS server or the network path to it failed while the client used a hard mount. Hard mounts trade availability for correctness; the price is these hangs when the server disappears. Fix / mitigation # restore the server / network path — the cleanest fix umount -f -l /mnt/shared # force + lazy detach # mount with soft,timeo,retrans for non-critical data to fail fast instead Prevention Use hard,intr -style resilient options and sane timeo / retrans ; for non-critical reads consider soft mounts that error out instead of hanging. Monitor NFS server reachability so the cause is obvious before D-state spreads. Interview tip: The hard-vs-soft tradeoff is the whole answer: hard = won't corrupt but hangs; soft = fails fast but can lose writes. Note you can't SIGKILL a true D-state process — only fixing the I/O or lazy-unmount frees it.

questions.q: A user reports 'permission denied' on a file they own, with what looks like correct mode bits. What do you check?
questions.text: Symptom A user can't read a file. ls -l shows they own it and the mode looks right (e.g. rw-r--r-- ), yet access is denied. Investigation ls -ld /path /path/.. /path/../.. # traversal needs +x on EVERY parent dir getfacl /path/file # POSIX ACLs can override base mode ls -Z /path/file # SELinux context lsattr /path/file # immutable (+i) bit? Base mode bits aren't the whole story. Access can be denied by: a parent directory missing the execute (traversal) bit, a POSIX ACL, an SELinux/AppArmor label mismatch, the immutable attribute, or the file living on a read-only/no-exec mount. Root cause Something beyond rwx is governing access — most often a parent directory lacking +x (so you can't traverse into it) or an SELinux context denial. The visible mode bits are a red herring. Fix / mitigation chmod +x <each parent dir> # restore traversal setfacl -m u:alice:r /path/file # if ACL-driven restorecon -v /path/file # fix SELinux label ausearch -m avc -ts recent # confirm an SELinux AVC denial Prevention Standardize directory traversal permissions in your provisioning, keep SELinux in enforcing with correct contexts (don't disable it), and use getfacl / ls -Z as routine checks so the “hidden” permission layers are visible. Interview tip: List the layers fast: parent-dir +x , ACLs, SELinux label, immutable bit, mount options. The parent-directory traversal trap is the single most common gotcha — lead with it.

questions.q: The system is constantly swapping and everything feels sluggish even though there's some free RAM. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: Symptom Latency is awful and the disk light is always on. free shows swap heavily used and growing, though a little RAM appears free. Investigation free -m vmstat 1 5 # si/so columns = swap in/out per sec cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness smem -s swap -r | head # who's swapped out Active swap-in/swap-out ( si / so nonzero) means the working set exceeds RAM, so the kernel pages hot memory to disk — each fault now costs a disk seek. High swappiness can also push file-backed pages out too aggressively. Root cause Memory pressure: the sum of active working sets is larger than physical RAM, so the kernel thrashes pages between RAM and swap. The “some free RAM” is misleading — it's reclaimable cache, not headroom for the working set. Fix / mitigation # reduce memory demand: cap/limit the heaviest consumers sysctl vm.swappiness=10 # favor keeping anon pages resident (tune, don't cargo-cult) # add RAM or move a service off the host — the real fix if working set > RAM Prevention Right-size memory to the working set, set per-service memory limits so one process can't force global thrash, and alert on si / so rates (not just swap-used) since steady swap usage can be benign while active swapping is not. Interview tip: Distinguish swap used (often fine) from swapping (the si / so activity that kills latency). Tuning swappiness is a knob, not a cure — the cure is fitting the working set in RAM.

questions.q: A server fails to boot and drops to an emergency shell after someone edited /etc/fstab. How do you recover?
questions.text: Symptom After a storage change the host won't boot — it lands in an emergency/maintenance shell. The console mentions a failed mount. Investigation journalctl -xb | grep -i 'failed\|dependency' systemctl --failed cat /etc/fstab # the suspect line blkid # do the UUIDs in fstab actually exist? A bad /etc/fstab entry (wrong UUID, removed device, or bad options) fails at boot. By default a failed required mount blocks local-fs.target , so systemd stops and drops to emergency mode rather than booting half-configured. Root cause An fstab line references a device/UUID that no longer matches reality. Because the mount is marked required, its failure halts the boot dependency chain. Fix / mitigation mount -o remount,rw / # make root writable in the emergency shell # fix or comment the bad fstab line; correct the UUID from blkid # add 'nofail' (and optionally x-systemd.device-timeout=) to non-critical mounts reboot Prevention Use nofail on non-essential mounts so a missing disk doesn't block boot, reference filesystems by UUID/LABEL (stable across device renaming), and validate fstab changes with mount -a before rebooting. Interview tip: The lifesaver line is mount -o remount,rw / to edit fstab from the emergency shell, plus nofail as the preventive option. Always test with mount -a before you reboot — say that and you sound battle-tested.

questions.q: Under heavy connection load, new connections start failing and dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet'. What now?
questions.text: Symptom A busy gateway/node starts dropping new connections under load. dmesg shows nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet . Investigation dmesg -T | grep conntrack sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max conntrack -L | wc -l The kernel's connection-tracking table is full. Once conntrack_count hits conntrack_max , new flows are dropped. High connection churn (many short-lived connections) plus a default-sized table, or entries lingering in TIME_WAIT/long timeouts, fills it. Root cause Conntrack table exhaustion. The host tracks more concurrent flows than the table allows — common on NAT gateways, busy load balancers, and Kubernetes nodes with high pod-to-service churn. Fix / mitigation sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144 # raise table size (watch RAM) sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait=30 # reclaim faster # or bypass tracking for high-volume flows via iptables -t raw ... -j NOTRACK Prevention Size conntrack_max to expected concurrency (and the hashsize accordingly), tune timeouts down for short-lived flows, and on Kubernetes watch this on nodes — it's a frequent silent cause of intermittent connection failures under load. Interview tip: Naming nf_conntrack table-full as a cause of intermittent connection drops on NAT gateways and K8s nodes is a strong signal. Mention sizing max + hashsize together and NOTRACK for high-volume flows.

questions.q: A test suite passes locally but fails intermittently in CI ('flaky tests'). How do you stabilize the pipeline?
questions.text: Symptom The same commit sometimes passes, sometimes fails in CI. Engineers have learned to just hit “retry,” and trust in the pipeline is eroding. Investigation # re-run the failing job in isolation to confirm non-determinism # diff the failure set across runs — same tests or random? # check for shared state: ports, temp files, fixed timestamps, DB rows # run tests in randomized order locally to reproduce Flaky tests usually stem from non-determinism: timing/sleep races, order-dependence via shared state, real network or clock dependencies, or unfixed random seeds. CI exposes them because it's slower, parallel, and clean-room compared to a warm laptop. Root cause Tests are coupled to non-deterministic conditions — timing, ordering, external services, or shared fixtures — so they pass when conditions happen to line up and fail otherwise. The retry culture hides real signal. Fix / mitigation # quarantine flaky tests into a separate, non-blocking lane # fix root cause: inject the clock, mock the network, isolate state per test, fix seeds # add retry-with-logging to surface the failure mode, not just paper over it Prevention Track per-test flakiness rate and auto-quarantine offenders out of the blocking path, mandate hermetic tests (no real network/clock/shared DB), and treat a flaky test as a bug ticket — not a “retry and move on.” A pipeline you don't trust is worse than a slow one. Interview tip: Senior framing: flakiness is a trust problem, not a test problem. Talk about quar

questions.q: A deployment is stuck — the pipeline reports 'deploying' for 20 minutes with no progress. How do you triage?
questions.text: Symptom A deploy job hangs in the “deploying” phase far past its usual time, neither succeeding nor failing. Users are still on the old version. Investigation kubectl rollout status deploy/app --timeout=10s # if k8s kubectl get pods -l app=app # new pods Pending/CrashLoop/not Ready? kubectl describe deploy/app | sed -n '/Conditions/,$p' # check the deploy tool's own logs (Argo/Spinnaker/CD runner) A rolling deploy waits for new replicas to become Ready. If they never pass readiness (bad image, failing health check, unschedulable, or a missing dependency), the rollout stalls indefinitely rather than failing fast — by design it won't tear down healthy old pods. Root cause New instances aren't reaching a healthy/Ready state, so the orchestrator holds the rollout. The old version stays up (good for users) but the deploy never completes. The hang is a symptom; the new pods' failure is the cause. Fix / mitigation # decide: roll forward (fix) or roll back kubectl rollout undo deploy/app # fast mitigation # fix the readiness probe / image / dependency, then redeploy # set progressDeadlineSeconds so a stall fails the rollout instead of hanging Prevention Set a progress deadline so stuck rollouts fail loudly instead of hanging, make readiness probes accurate (probe a real dependency, not just process-up), and gate deploys behind smoke checks so a bad image is caught before it stalls a rollout. Interview tip: Lead with “new pods aren't Ready → rollout waits forever.” Mention progressDea

questions.q: You discover a plaintext secret (API key) was committed to the repo and is now in CI logs. What's your response?
questions.text: Symptom A code review (or a scanner alert) reveals an API key hard-coded in a commit. It has already run through CI, so it may also sit in pipeline logs and artifacts. Investigation git log -p -S '<key-fragment>' # find when it entered history # search CI logs/artifacts/caches for the same value # determine the key's scope and what it can access Once a secret is in git history (and CI logs), it must be treated as compromised — history is distributed and logs are cached. Deleting the line in a new commit does not remove it from history or from anyone's clone. Root cause A secret leaked into version control and propagated to CI. The exposure window started at commit time, not discovery time, so the only safe assumption is that it's known to attackers. Fix / mitigation # 1. ROTATE/revoke the key first — this is the only thing that truly mitigates # 2. purge from history (git filter-repo / BFG) and force-push, coordinate clones # 3. scrub CI logs/artifact caches; check access logs for misuse Prevention Rotation comes first, always. Then add pre-commit and CI secret scanning (gitleaks/trufflehog) to block leaks at the source, and move secrets to a manager (Vault, cloud secrets) injected at runtime so they never touch the repo. Interview tip: The interviewer wants to hear rotate first . Scrubbing history matters but is secondary — a leaked key is compromised the moment it's pushed. Then talk prevention via scanning + secret managers.

questions.q: Terraform apply fails with a state lock error, and you suspect drift between state and real infra. How do you proceed safely?
questions.text: Symptom terraform apply errors with a state-lock message, and a teammate mentions someone changed a resource manually in the console last week. Investigation terraform plan # read carefully: what does it want to change & why? # identify the lock holder (DynamoDB lock table / backend lock info) terraform state list # confirm what's tracked terraform refresh / plan -refresh-only # surface drift vs state Two issues: a stale lock (a previous run died without releasing it) blocks apply, and manual console changes created drift — real infra no longer matches state. Blindly applying could revert the manual change or, worse, destroy/recreate resources. Root cause The lock is a safety mechanism that outlived its run; the drift is human out-of-band change. The danger is applying without understanding what the plan will do to the drifted resource. Fix / mitigation terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> # only after confirming no live run holds it # reconcile drift: terraform import, or update code to match, or plan-revert intentionally terraform apply -target=... # narrow blast radius while reconciling Prevention Enforce remote state with locking, ban manual console changes (or auto-detect drift on a schedule), require PR-reviewed plans before apply, and use prevent_destroy on stateful resources so a surprise plan can't nuke a database. Interview tip: Two-part answer scores well: never force-unlock without confirming the holder is dead, and never apply over drift without reading the plan. Men

questions.q: ArgoCD shows an app as 'OutOfSync' and someone keeps hotfixing the cluster directly. How do you handle GitOps drift?
questions.text: Symptom Your GitOps tool reports an application OutOfSync . Investigation shows an engineer ran kubectl edit to hotfix prod during an incident. Investigation argocd app diff <app> # exactly what differs from Git kubectl get <res> -o yaml | grep -A2 managedFields # who last changed it # is auto-sync on? is self-heal on? — determines current behavior GitOps treats Git as the single source of truth. A live kubectl edit makes the cluster diverge from the repo. With self-heal on, Argo will revert the hotfix (possibly mid-incident); with it off, the drift lingers and the next sync may clobber it unpredictably. Root cause Out-of-band imperative change broke the declarative contract. The cluster and the repo now disagree, and which one “wins” depends on sync settings — a recipe for surprise reversions. Fix / mitigation # decide source of truth: codify the hotfix into Git (preferred), then sync argocd app sync <app> # reconcile to Git once Git is correct # if the live change was wrong, let self-heal revert it Prevention Make the cluster read-only to humans (RBAC), so changes flow only through Git PRs; allow a documented break-glass path for emergencies that requires back-filling the change into Git afterward; and alert on OutOfSync so drift is caught in minutes. Interview tip: The principle to state: in GitOps, fix forward by changing Git , not the cluster. Acknowledge the legitimate break-glass case during incidents — but with a mandatory codify-it-back step.

questions.q: A database migration baked into the deploy pipeline failed halfway and left the schema inconsistent. How do you recover?
questions.text: Symptom A deploy ran a schema migration that errored partway. Some statements applied, some didn't, and the app is now half-broken against an inconsistent schema. Investigation # check migration tool state (schema_migrations / flyway history) vs actual schema # was the migration transactional? (DDL transactionality is engine-dependent) # determine: which statements committed, which rolled back The migration wasn't atomic — either the engine doesn't wrap DDL in a transaction, or it spanned multiple statements/transactions. A partial apply leaves the schema in a state neither the old nor new code expects. Root cause Non-atomic migration plus a mid-flight failure. The migration tool's recorded state and the real schema have diverged, so a naive re-run may double-apply or skip steps. Fix / mitigation # reconcile the migration ledger with reality before re-running # apply the remaining steps manually if safe, or restore-and-replay from backup # verify app works against the corrected schema in a lower env first Prevention Make migrations atomic where possible and idempotent always; adopt expand/contract (backward-compatible) migrations decoupled from the deploy so a code rollback never strands the schema; test migrations against a production-like snapshot in CI. Interview tip: The senior move is expand/contract : deploy schema changes that are backward-compatible and separate from app deploys, so neither can break the other. Mention DDL transactionality varies by engine (Postgres y

questions.q: A deploy went out, errors spiked, and you need to roll back — but the previous artifact is gone from the registry. What do you do?
questions.text: Symptom A bad release spikes errors. You reach for rollback and discover the prior image was pruned from the registry by an aggressive cleanup policy. Investigation # confirm current bad version & error signature # can you rebuild the previous commit deterministically? # is the prior image cached on any node? (kubectl describe / crictl images) Rollback assumes the previous artifact still exists. An over-eager retention policy deleted it, so the fast path is gone. You're now choosing between rebuilding from the previous commit (slow, and only safe if builds are reproducible) and rolling forward with a fix. Root cause Artifact retention was tuned for storage cost without protecting the rollback target. The incident is the deploy; the rollback gap is a process failure that just made the incident longer. Fix / mitigation # fastest safe path now: roll forward with a targeted fix or feature flag # if a node still has the image cached, pin a pod to it as a stopgap # rebuild prev commit only if builds are byte-reproducible & fast Prevention Keep the last N known-good artifacts immutable and exempt from cleanup, make builds reproducible, and prefer feature flags so risky changes can be disabled without a redeploy at all — the fastest rollback is a config toggle. Interview tip: Two lessons land here: protect known-good artifacts from retention pruning, and that feature flags often beat redeploy-rollback for speed. Show you'd roll forward when rolling back isn't available.

questions.q: Builds suddenly produce broken binaries and you suspect a poisoned/stale build cache. How do you isolate it?
questions.text: Symptom Builds that worked yesterday now ship subtly broken output, with no relevant code change. A shared layer/dependency cache is suspected. Investigation # reproduce with cache disabled — does the build go green? docker build --no-cache ... # or clear the CI dependency cache # diff the resolved dependency tree vs a known-good lockfile # check for an upstream dependency that changed under a floating version A cache served a stale or corrupted layer, or a floating dependency version (no pinning) resolved to a new, broken release that then got cached. Because the cache is shared, every build inherits the poison until it's invalidated. Root cause Either cache corruption/staleness or unpinned dependencies pulling a bad upstream — both let a non-reproducible input slip into builds and persist via caching. Fix / mitigation # bust the cache: invalidate keys / docker build --no-cache # pin exact versions via lockfiles; commit them # rebuild from the verified lockfile to confirm green Prevention Pin every dependency with committed lockfiles, key caches on content hashes (so changed inputs auto-invalidate), and verify supply-chain integrity (checksums/signatures, SBOMs). Reproducible builds make “stale cache” diagnosable instead of mysterious. Interview tip: Tie it to reproducibility: pinned lockfiles + content-addressed cache keys mean a cache can't silently poison you. Mention supply-chain verification (checksums/SBOM) for the senior-plus signal.

questions.q: A canary deploy was supposed to auto-rollback on errors but didn't, and the bad version reached 100%. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.text: Symptom A progressive/canary rollout should have halted on elevated errors but instead promoted the bad build to full traffic. Now everyone's affected. Investigation # what metric/threshold was the canary analysis watching? # did the canary get enough traffic/time to produce signal? # did the metric query actually return data, or silently no-data? Canary auto-rollback depends entirely on its analysis query. Common failures: the threshold was too lenient, the canary got too little traffic to reach statistical signal, the metric query returned no data (treated as “pass”), or the error type wasn't the one being measured. Root cause The automated guardrail measured the wrong thing, lacked signal, or fail-opened on missing data — so it waved through a release it was supposed to stop. The deploy mechanism worked; the decision input was broken. Fix / mitigation kubectl rollout undo ... / promote last-good # mitigate now # fix the analysis: correct metric, sane threshold, minimum-sample gate # make no-data FAIL the canary, not pass it Prevention Treat “no data” as failure (fail-closed), require a minimum traffic/sample before a pass verdict, validate analysis queries against a known-bad replay, and watch user-facing SLIs in the canary — not just process health. Interview tip: The killer insight: most canary failures are no-data treated as success . Say you'd make the guardrail fail-closed and require minimum sample size — that's the senior reliability instinct.

questions.q: A change works in staging but breaks in production, and the diff is 'just config'. How do you find the discrepancy?
questions.text: Symptom Identical code passed staging and failed in prod. The teams insist “nothing changed but config.” Investigation # diff effective config prod vs staging (env vars, flags, secrets, scaling) # diff the environments themselves: versions, data volume, network egress, IAM # does prod hit a dependency staging mocks or never exercises? “Works in staging” failures come from environment parity gaps: prod has real data volume, real traffic concurrency, stricter IAM/network policy, different feature-flag values, or a dependency staging never truly exercises. The code is innocent; the environment delta is the bug. Root cause Configuration and environment drift between staging and prod. The deployable is the same, but the surrounding context (data scale, permissions, dependencies, flags) differs in a way the change happened to depend on. Fix / mitigation # reconcile the specific differing config/permission/flag # reproduce in a prod-like env (real data scale, real IAM) to confirm # add the missing dependency exercise to staging Prevention Drive staging↔prod parity (same topology, representative data, same policy model), manage config declaratively and diffable per environment, and shift dependencies left so staging actually exercises what prod does. Config is code — review and version it. Interview tip: Reframe “just config” as a first-class change: config differences are the #1 staging-vs-prod gap. Name the usual suspects (data scale, IAM, flags, untested dependency) to show you've

questions.q: An artifact was promoted from staging to prod but behaves differently — you suspect it's not actually the same artifact. How do you verify?
questions.text: Symptom The promoted release misbehaves in prod. You want to rule out that prod is somehow running a different build than what staging validated. Investigation # compare image digests (sha256), not tags — tags are mutable kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{..imageID}' # actual running digest # does prod pull from the same registry/repo as staging? # was the tag rebuilt/overwritten between staging and prod pulls? Tags like :latest or :v1.2 are mutable pointers — a rebuild can move a tag so staging and prod, both “on v1.2,” run different bytes. Only the content digest (sha256) proves identity. If digests differ, you never actually promoted the validated artifact. Root cause Promotion was done by mutable tag rather than immutable digest, so a rebuild silently substituted a different artifact. “Same version” was an illusion. Fix / mitigation # pin and promote by digest, not tag # re-pull the exact staged digest in prod # block tag overwrites in the registry (immutable tags) Prevention Promote artifacts by immutable digest, enable tag immutability in the registry, and sign artifacts (cosign) so prod can verify it's running exactly the bytes that passed staging. “Build once, promote the same bytes” is the rule. Interview tip: The crisp answer: compare digests, not tags , and promote by digest. “Build once, promote the same artifact across envs” is the principle interviewers want to hear.

questions.q: Your pipeline takes 45 minutes and developers are batching changes to avoid it, increasing risk. How do you approach this?
questions.text: Symptom A slow pipeline (45+ min) is changing behavior: engineers batch many changes into one big merge to amortize the wait, so each deploy is larger and riskier. Investigation # profile the pipeline: which stages dominate the wall-clock? # what's serial that could be parallel? what's rebuilt that could be cached? # test pyramid shape: are slow E2E tests gating every commit? Slow pipelines create a perverse incentive: big batches mean bigger blast radius and harder rollbacks — the opposite of safe continuous delivery. The latency itself is a reliability risk, not just a productivity annoyance. Root cause The pipeline's cycle time is high enough to discourage small, frequent changes. Likely causes: serial stages, no caching, an inverted test pyramid (too many slow E2E tests on the critical path), or full rebuilds of unchanged components. Fix / mitigation # parallelize independent stages; cache deps & build layers # move slow E2E tests off the blocking path (post-merge / nightly) # build/test only what changed (affected-targets) # fail fast: cheap lint/unit first Prevention Keep the blocking path fast (fail-fast cheap checks, parallelism, caching, change-scoped builds), push slow suites to non-blocking lanes, and track pipeline cycle time as an SLO — because batch size is downstream of pipeline speed. Small, frequent, safe. Interview tip: Connect speed to safety : slow pipelines → big batches → risky deploys. That systems-thinking framing, plus concrete levers (parallelize, ca

questions.q: Users report they save a change and it 'disappears' on the next page load. You're behind a read replica. What's happening?
questions.text: Symptom A user updates their profile, reloads, and sees the old value — then it's correct moments later. Writes go to the primary; reads are load-balanced across replicas. Investigation # check replication lag (Seconds_Behind_Master / pg_stat_replication) # trace one request: did the write hit primary and the read hit a lagging replica? # measure lag distribution, not just the average This is a read-after-write consistency violation caused by replication lag. The write committed on the primary, but the immediate read landed on a replica that hadn't received it yet, so the user sees stale data. It “fixes itself” once the replica catches up. Root cause Asynchronous replication means replicas trail the primary. Routing a user's own just-written read to a lagging replica breaks their expectation of seeing their own change. Fix / mitigation # route read-your-writes to the primary (sticky for a short window after a write) # or use causal/consistent reads: wait for replica to reach the write's LSN/GTID # alert on lag and pull replicas from rotation past a threshold Prevention Implement read-your-writes (route a user's reads to the primary briefly after their write, or track the write position and only read from a caught-up replica), and treat replication lag as a first-class SLI with alerting and auto-eviction of badly-lagging replicas. Interview tip: Name it precisely — “read-after-write consistency under async replication” — and offer the standard fixes (sticky-to-primary window,

questions.q: The app starts throwing 'too many connections' / connection pool timeouts under modest load. How do you diagnose?
questions.text: Symptom Under only moderately higher traffic, requests fail with connection-pool timeouts or the DB rejects connections with “too many connections.” Investigation # DB side: SHOW PROCESSLIST / pg_stat_activity — how many, and in what state? # app side: pool size × number of app instances vs DB max_connections # are connections idle-in-transaction (held but not working)? Connections are a finite resource. Either the pool is too small (requests queue and time out) or, more often, too large × too many app replicas, overwhelming the DB's max_connections . Idle-in-transaction connections (held open mid-transaction) silently consume slots without doing work. Root cause Connection demand exceeds supply somewhere in the chain: app pool → (optional proxy) → DB. Frequently the real culprit is leaked or idle-in-transaction connections, or simply pool_size × replicas exceeding the DB limit. Fix / mitigation # fix leaks: ensure connections are returned; set idle-in-transaction timeout # introduce a connection pooler (PgBouncer/ProxySQL) to multiplex # right-size: total app connections must be < DB max_connections Prevention Put a pooler in front of the database to multiplex many app connections onto few DB connections, set idle and idle-in-transaction timeouts, and capacity-plan so (pool_size × replicas) stays comfortably under max_connections . Connections are capacity — budget them. Interview tip: The trap to surface: people scale app replicas and forget each multiplies pool connections

questions.q: One specific query got slow over time though nothing in the code changed. How do you investigate?
questions.text: Symptom A query that was fast at launch now times out months later. No code change touched it — only the data grew. Investigation EXPLAIN ANALYZE <query> # seq scan? wrong index? bad row estimate? # check table/index growth and stats freshness # is the plan different now than before? (cached plan / stats drift) As data grows, a query that once scanned a small table now scans a large one. Either an index is missing (so it's a sequential scan), the right index exists but stale statistics make the planner avoid it, or selectivity changed so the old plan is no longer optimal. Root cause Data volume crossed a threshold where the access path that was fine at small scale (e.g. a seq scan) became pathological. Often compounded by out-of-date planner statistics choosing a bad plan. Fix / mitigation # add/adjust the index to support the query's predicates & sort ANALYZE <table> # refresh statistics so the planner chooses well # consider partitioning / archiving cold rows if the table is huge Prevention Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE in code review for queries on growing tables, keep statistics fresh (autovacuum/auto-analyze tuned), monitor slow-query logs continuously, and design indexes for actual access patterns rather than waiting for scale to expose the gap. Interview tip: Lead with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the seq-scan-at-scale story. Bonus points for naming stale statistics — the subtle case where the index exists but the planner won't use it.

questions.q: Transactions intermittently fail with deadlock errors under concurrency. How do you find and fix the cause?
questions.text: Symptom Under concurrent load some transactions abort with deadlock-detected errors. It's sporadic and load-dependent. Investigation SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS # 'LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK' (MySQL) # Postgres: log_lock_waits + the deadlock detail in logs # identify the two transactions and the lock-acquisition order each took A deadlock occurs when two transactions acquire the same locks in opposite order — each holds what the other needs. The DB detects the cycle and kills one as the victim. Inconsistent lock ordering across code paths is the usual root cause. Root cause Two transactions take locks in conflicting orders (e.g. row A then B vs B then A). Under low concurrency they rarely interleave badly; under load they collide and the engine breaks the tie by aborting a victim. Fix / mitigation # enforce a consistent lock/access ordering across all code paths # keep transactions short; touch rows in a deterministic order # add application-level retry on deadlock (they're expected, recoverable) Prevention Standardize lock acquisition order, keep transactions small and short-lived, use appropriate isolation levels, and build retry-on-deadlock into the data layer since deadlocks are a normal, recoverable outcome under concurrency — not a catastrophic failure. Interview tip: Two ideas win: consistent lock ordering prevents most deadlocks, and retry handles the rest since they're expected. Read the engine's deadlock report to recover the exact ordering conflict.

questions.q: One shard / partition is red-hot while others sit idle, causing latency spikes. How do you address the hot partition?
questions.text: Symptom A sharded datastore shows one node at 95% utilization while peers idle. Latency spikes correlate with traffic to that one partition. Investigation # identify the hot key/partition (per-shard QPS & latency) # is it one key (celebrity/hot row) or a skewed key range? # check the partition key choice vs the actual access distribution The partition key distributes data unevenly — either a single “celebrity” key concentrates traffic, or the key has low cardinality / monotonic ordering so writes pile onto one shard (the classic timestamp- or sequential-ID-as-key mistake). Root cause Poor key distribution. The shard key doesn't spread load proportional to access, so one partition absorbs disproportionate traffic — a hotspot the other shards can't relieve. Fix / mitigation # add a hot cache in front of celebrity keys to absorb reads # re-key with higher cardinality / a hashed or composite key # split the hot partition; for write hotspots, add a salt/prefix Prevention Choose partition keys with high cardinality matched to access patterns, avoid monotonic keys for write-heavy tables (hash or salt them), cache celebrity keys, and monitor per-partition load so skew is visible before it becomes a latency cliff. Interview tip: Name the two flavors — single hot key (cache it) vs skewed/monotonic key (re-key or salt). The “timestamp/auto-increment as shard key” antipattern is a great concrete example to cite.

questions.q: After a primary failover you see signs of split-brain — two nodes think they're primary. How do you handle it?
