questions.text: Symptom Following a network blip and failover, two database nodes both accept writes. Data is now diverging between them. Investigation # confirm both are accepting writes (each thinks it's primary) # check the cluster manager / quorum state and what triggered failover # assess divergence: which writes landed where since the split? A network partition let a failover promote a new primary while the old one was still alive and writable — classic split-brain. Without quorum/fencing, both sides accept conflicting writes, and merging divergent data afterward is painful or lossy. Root cause Failover happened without proper fencing or quorum, so the old primary wasn't reliably demoted/isolated before the new one took over. The partition created two writable masters. Fix / mitigation # STOP the divergence: fence/demote one node to a single writable primary # choose the authoritative copy; reconcile or replay the other's writes carefully # this is often a data-loss event — escalate and decide RPO tradeoffs explicitly Prevention Use quorum-based failover (odd member count, majority required to promote) and fencing/STONITH so a partitioned old primary is forcibly demoted before a new one is promoted. Design for it up front — split-brain recovery is far costlier than prevention. Interview tip: Show you understand quorum + fencing are what prevent this, and that recovery is often lossy (a real RPO conversation). Connect it to CAP: during a partition you can't have both consistency and ava

questions.q: A disaster strikes and you go to restore from backups — only to find the restore process has never actually been tested. What now, and what's the lesson?
questions.text: Symptom Data loss occurs. You reach for backups and discover that while backups ran , a full restore was never once tested end-to-end. Investigation # verify backups exist AND are readable/complete (not just that jobs 'succeeded') # attempt restore to an isolated environment, time it # check backup scope: schema only? missing tables? consistent snapshot? “Backups succeeded” only means the job exited zero — not that the data is restorable. Untested backups commonly fail at restore time: incomplete scope, inconsistent (non-atomic) snapshots, unreadable files, or a restore that takes far longer than the business can tolerate (RTO miss). Root cause Backups were treated as a checkbox, not a tested capability. The real recoverability — completeness, consistency, and restore time — was never validated, so its true state is unknown precisely when it matters most. Fix / mitigation # attempt the restore now in isolation; salvage whatever is recoverable # if backups are bad, pivot to other sources (replicas, WAL/binlog, app logs) # document actual RPO/RTO achieved vs what was assumed Prevention Test restores on a schedule (automated restore drills), verify backup content not just job exit codes, measure real RTO against the SLA, and store backups with independent durability (different account/region, immutable) so a single failure or ransomware can't take both prod and backups. Interview tip: The line that lands: “a backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a backup.” Talk about schedu

questions.q: A schema migration on a large table took a long lock and stalled the whole application. How should it have been done?
questions.text: Symptom An ALTER TABLE on a multi-hundred-GB table acquired a lock and blocked reads/writes for minutes, effectively an outage. Investigation # which lock did the DDL take, and what did it block? (engine-dependent) # table size & whether the operation rewrites the whole table # was it run in a transaction holding the lock for the full duration? Some DDL operations rewrite the entire table and/or take exclusive locks, scaling with table size. On a large table that's minutes of blocking — an outage. The migration was correct logically but operationally hostile because it wasn't done online. Root cause A blocking, table-rewriting schema change was run directly against a large hot table. The size made the lock duration intolerable. Fix / mitigation # use online schema-change tooling (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change) or native online DDL # or expand/contract: add nullable column, backfill in batches, then enforce # run heavy migrations in low-traffic windows with a timeout/kill-switch Prevention Adopt online/non-blocking migration tooling, prefer additive expand/contract changes with batched backfills, set lock timeouts so a migration aborts rather than queuing the whole app behind it, and rehearse migrations against a production-sized snapshot. Interview tip: Name the tools (gh-ost / pt-osc) and the expand-contract pattern, plus lock_timeout so a migration fails fast instead of stalling everything. That trio shows you've shipped schema changes safely at scale.

questions.q: A popular cache key expires and the database gets hammered by a stampede of identical queries. How do you prevent thundering herd?
questions.text: Symptom At a predictable moment, latency spikes and the DB CPU pegs. A hot cache key just expired and thousands of concurrent requests all miss and hit the DB at once. Investigation # correlate the spike with a TTL expiry of a hot key # how many concurrent identical queries hit the DB on the miss? # is every replica/instance recomputing the same value independently? When a heavily-read cache entry expires, every concurrent request misses simultaneously and stampedes the backend with identical work — a thundering herd / cache stampede. The DB, sized for cache-hit load, can't absorb the sudden synchronized miss. Root cause Synchronized cache expiry plus high read concurrency. Without coordination, N requests each independently regenerate the same value, multiplying load by N at the exact moment the cache can't help. Fix / mitigation # single-flight / request coalescing: one request recomputes, others wait # add jitter to TTLs so keys don't expire in lockstep # early/probabilistic refresh before expiry; serve stale-while-revalidate Prevention Coalesce concurrent regenerations (single-flight lock per key), jitter TTLs to avoid synchronized expiry, refresh hot keys proactively before they expire, and serve stale-while-revalidate so a miss never exposes the full herd to the backend. Interview tip: Three named techniques to drop: single-flight (request coalescing), TTL jitter, and stale-while-revalidate / early refresh. Knowing the term “thundering herd” and its mitigations is a str

questions.q: Monitoring is green but customers report wrong data — you suspect silent data corruption. How do you approach it?
questions.text: Symptom No errors, no alerts, dashboards green — yet customers report incorrect values. You suspect data corruption that no exception ever surfaced. Investigation # reproduce: pin down which records are wrong and how # trace the data's lineage: where could it have been mutated? # compare against backups/audit log to find when it diverged Silent corruption produces no exceptions — a bad migration, a race condition double-writing, a serialization bug, or bit-rot at the storage layer wrote plausible-but-wrong values. Because nothing threw, monitoring built around errors and latency stayed green. Root cause Data integrity was violated without any error signal. The corruption path wrote valid-looking but incorrect data, so error-based observability is blind to it — you need correctness checks, not just liveness checks. Fix / mitigation # stop further corruption: identify and disable the offending write path # determine blast radius; restore/repair affected records from a clean source # add an audit trail so future divergence is attributable Prevention Add data-quality and invariant checks (constraints, checksums, reconciliation jobs that compare against source-of-truth), enable storage-level integrity (checksums), keep an audit log of mutations, and alert on correctness SLIs — not just availability and latency. Interview tip: The senior insight: error-based monitoring is blind to silent corruption — you need correctness checks (constraints, reconciliation, checksums). Stopping the

questions.q: On-call is drowning in alerts and starting to ignore them. How do you fix alert fatigue without going blind?
questions.text: Symptom The on-call channel fires dozens of alerts a shift. Most are non-actionable, so engineers mute or reflexively ack them — and a real incident recently slipped through unnoticed. Investigation # pull alert volume per rule over 30 days; rank by frequency # for each noisy rule: did anyone DO something, or just ack? # measure actionability: % of alerts that led to a real action Alert fatigue comes from paging on causes and thresholds rather than on user-facing symptoms. Every static-threshold or duplicate-cause alert that doesn't require human action erodes trust until the one that matters is lost in the noise. Root cause Too many non-actionable, cause-based alerts. The signal-to-noise ratio dropped so low that humans rationally tuned out — which is how the real incident was missed. Fix / mitigation # delete or downgrade non-actionable rules to dashboards/tickets # alert on symptoms (SLO burn) not every cause # group/dedupe related alerts into one incident; add sane thresholds Prevention Adopt symptom-based, SLO-driven alerting: page humans only for user-impacting problems that need action, route everything else to dashboards or tickets, and review alert actionability regularly. Every page should be something a human must act on now. Interview tip: The principle interviewers want: alert on symptoms, not causes , and “every page must be actionable.” Tie it to SLO burn-rate alerting and a regular noise-review ritual.

questions.q: An incident happened with zero alerts — a complete monitoring blind spot. How do you find and close such gaps?
questions.text: Symptom A user-impacting outage ran for 20 minutes with no alert at all. The team found out from a customer, not the monitoring. Investigation # what failed, and what signal SHOULD have caught it? # was the metric missing, the alert missing, or the alert misconfigured? # check: did the failure mode produce any telemetry at all? Blind spots come in flavors: the metric was never instrumented, it existed but had no alert, the alert existed but had a wrong threshold/grouping, or the failure killed the very thing that emits telemetry (e.g. the metrics agent went down with the host). You can't alert on what you don't measure. Root cause The system lacked a signal for this failure mode — either uninstrumented, unalerted, or self-defeating (the outage suppressed its own telemetry). Coverage was assumed but never verified for this path. Fix / mitigation # instrument the missing signal; add a symptom-level SLO alert # add a synthetic/black-box probe that exercises the user path externally # add meta-monitoring: alert when telemetry itself stops arriving (dead-man's switch) Prevention Combine white-box (internal metrics) with black-box synthetic probes so user-facing breakage is caught even when internals lie, add dead-man's-switch alerts that fire when expected telemetry goes silent, and run game-days to discover blind spots before incidents do. Interview tip: Two ideas elevate this: black-box synthetic monitoring for the user path, and a dead-man's switch so silence itself pages you.

questions.q: Your metrics bill exploded and queries got slow after a deploy added a high-cardinality label. How do you fix it?
questions.text: Symptom Right after a release, the metrics backend slows down and the bill spikes. A new label was added that takes near-unlimited distinct values. Investigation # identify the metric with exploding series count # what label was added? (user_id, request_id, full URL, IP?) # count distinct label values = number of time series created A time-series database creates one series per unique label-set. A high-cardinality label (user ID, request ID, raw URL) multiplies series into the millions, blowing up storage, query time, and cost. Cardinality is the dominant cost driver in metrics systems. Root cause An unbounded-cardinality dimension was attached to a metric, exploding the series count. Metrics are for aggregatable, low-cardinality dimensions — per-request identifiers belong in traces/logs, not labels. Fix / mitigation # drop/relabel the offending high-cardinality label at ingest # move per-request detail to tracing or structured logs # add cardinality limits/guardrails at the ingestion layer Prevention Enforce cardinality budgets and relabeling rules at ingest, keep metrics dimensions low-cardinality and bounded, and put per-entity detail in traces and logs where it belongs. Treat “don't put unbounded IDs in metric labels” as a reviewable rule. Interview tip: The crisp rule: metrics labels must be low-cardinality ; per-request IDs go to traces/logs. Knowing that cardinality (series count) is the cost/performance driver — not data volume per se — is the senior signal.

questions.q: A dashboard shows healthy average latency, but customers complain it's slow. Why the disconnect?
questions.text: Symptom The latency dashboard shows a comfortable ~80ms average and looks healthy, yet a meaningful slice of users report the app is slow. Investigation # look at percentiles, not the mean: p50 vs p95 vs p99 # break latency down by route/endpoint and by cohort # is the tail (p99) far above the average? Averages hide tails. A low mean can coexist with a brutal p99 — if 1% of requests take 5 seconds, the average barely moves but those users have a terrible experience. Worse, a single user often makes many requests, so tail latency hits more sessions than the percentile suggests. Root cause The dashboard measures the wrong statistic. The mean masks a high-latency tail; the unhappy users live in p95/p99, which the average smooths away. Fix / mitigation # switch dashboards/SLOs to percentiles (p95/p99) and histograms # slice by endpoint & cohort to localize the slow tail # fix the tail source (slow dependency, GC pauses, cold cache, lock contention) Prevention Define latency SLOs on percentiles (and track histograms/heatmaps, not averages), because users experience the tail, not the mean. Slice by route and cohort so a slow segment can't hide inside a healthy aggregate. Interview tip: The one-liner: averages lie; track p95/p99 . Add the multiplicative point — one slow page in a many-request session ruins the whole session — to show you understand user-perceived latency, not just metrics math.

questions.q: An error occurred in production but the trace for it was never captured because of sampling. How do you handle this?
questions.text: Symptom A customer reports a failed request with a timestamp, but when you look for its distributed trace, it's missing — sampling dropped it. Investigation # what's the sampling strategy & rate? (head-based at fixed %?) # was this an error that should always be kept? # can you correlate via logs/request-id even without the trace? Head-based sampling decides whether to keep a trace at the start, before knowing the outcome — so it discards errors and slow requests at the same rate as boring successes. The interesting traces (the ones you actually need) get thrown away with everything else. Root cause Head-based (up-front) sampling is outcome-blind. It optimized for cost by dropping a fixed fraction, but that fraction included the error you now need, because the decision was made before the error existed. Fix / mitigation # switch to tail-based sampling: keep ALL errors & slow traces, sample the rest # always-keep policy for error spans and high-latency spans # correlate via request-id across logs in the meantime Prevention Use tail-based sampling so every error and slow request is retained while normal traffic is sampled for cost, propagate a request/correlation ID across logs and traces so you can stitch the story even when a trace is partial, and reserve full-fidelity capture for anomalies. Interview tip: The key distinction: head-based vs tail-based sampling . “Keep all errors and slow traces, sample the happy path” is the answer. Correlation IDs as the cross-signal fallbac

questions.q: An SLO is burning error budget fast mid-incident. How do you use burn rate to drive the response?
questions.text: Symptom During an incident, the error-budget burn-rate alert is firing. Leadership wants to know how serious it is and how to prioritize. Investigation # current burn rate = how many x the sustainable rate are we spending budget? # at this rate, how long until the budget is exhausted? # multi-window check: is it a fast burn (1h) or slow burn (6h/24h)? Burn rate expresses how fast you're consuming the error budget relative to the rate that would exactly exhaust it over the SLO window. A 14.4× burn over an hour means a month's budget gone in hours — page now. A slow 2× burn is a ticket, not a 3am page. Multi-window/multi-burn-rate alerts separate “act now” from “look soon.” Root cause The SLO is being violated fast enough that the error budget will be exhausted well before the window ends. Burn rate quantifies urgency, turning a vague “it's bad” into a concrete “act in minutes vs hours.” Fix / mitigation # fast/high burn → immediate mitigation: roll back, shed load, failover # protect the budget: stop risky deploys (freeze) while burning # slow burn → prioritized fix without heroics Prevention Define SLOs with multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts (fast-burn pages, slow-burn tickets), use remaining error budget to gate release risk (freeze deploys when budget is low), and frame incident urgency in burn-rate terms so response effort matches actual user impact. Interview tip: Show command of multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting and using the budget to gate deploys. Translating bu

questions.q: Log volume (and cost) is exploding, but you still can't find what you need during incidents. How do you fix logging?
questions.text: Symptom The logging bill keeps climbing, yet on-call still struggles to find relevant entries during incidents — too much noise, not enough signal. Investigation # what's the volume breakdown by service & log level? # how much is DEBUG/INFO noise vs actionable? # are logs structured (queryable) or free-text (grep-only)? High volume and low usefulness coexist when logs are verbose, unstructured, and undifferentiated — chatty DEBUG/INFO at full retention, free-text that's hard to query, and no correlation IDs to tie a request's logs together. You pay to store noise and still can't search it. Root cause Logging is optimized for volume, not retrievability. Without structure, levels, and correlation, more logs just means more haystack — cost rises while findability falls. Fix / mitigation # structure logs (JSON) with consistent fields + a correlation/request ID # tier retention by level; sample high-volume INFO/DEBUG # move high-cardinality detail to traces; keep logs for events Prevention Use structured logging with correlation IDs so a request's story is queryable, set log levels and tiered/sampled retention to control volume, and split responsibilities across the observability pillars — metrics for aggregates, traces for request flow, logs for discrete events — rather than dumping everything into logs. Interview tip: Connect cost and usefulness: structure + correlation IDs + tiered retention fixes both at once. Mentioning the three-pillars division of labor (metrics/traces/logs

questions.q: During an incident you can't trace a request across services because there's no correlation ID. How do you fix this going forward?
questions.text: Symptom Mid-incident, a request fails somewhere across a chain of microservices, but each service's logs are islands — there's no shared ID to follow the request end-to-end. Investigation # can you reconstruct the path manually by timestamps? (slow, error-prone) # do any services propagate ANY shared identifier? # where does the request enter, and where is context first lost? Without a correlation/trace ID generated at the edge and propagated through every hop (via headers/context), each service logs independently and there's no way to stitch one request's journey together. Debugging distributed flows by timestamp alone is unreliable, especially under concurrency. Root cause No distributed-context propagation. The system never threads a shared identifier through the call chain, so cross-service causality is unrecoverable during an incident — exactly when you need it most. Fix / mitigation # generate a trace/correlation ID at the edge (or accept inbound one) # propagate it via context/headers through every service & async hop # include it in every log line; adopt OpenTelemetry context propagation Prevention Standardize distributed tracing with context propagation (OpenTelemetry), inject a trace/correlation ID at the ingress and carry it through sync and async boundaries, and stamp it on every log line so traces and logs cross-reference. Make propagation a platform default, not a per-service afterthought. Interview tip: The answer is distributed context propagation — a trace ID

questions.q: A major traffic event (think Black Friday) is coming and autoscaling alone won't save you. How do you prepare?
questions.text: Symptom Marketing announces a flash sale expected to drive 10× normal traffic at a known time. The team's plan is “autoscaling will handle it.” Investigation # model expected peak: 10x of WHICH metric? RPS, concurrent users, writes? # what's the slowest-to-scale tier? (DB, stateful, cold caches, quotas) # how long does a new node/pod take to become ready & warm? Autoscaling reacts — it adds capacity after load arrives, with a lag (provision + boot + warm-up). For a sharp, scheduled spike that lag means you're under-provisioned exactly when it matters. And the hardest tiers (databases, stateful services, third-party quotas) don't scale on the same timeline as stateless pods. Root cause Reactive scaling can't absorb an instantaneous, predictable spike, and non-elastic tiers (DB, quotas, caches) become the bottleneck. “Autoscaling will handle it” ignores both the lag and the parts that don't autoscale. Fix / mitigation # PRE-SCALE / pre-warm before the event; don't wait for reactive scaling # load-test at 10x to find the real bottleneck (usually DB/quota, not app) # add shedding/queueing & a degraded-mode fallback for overflow Prevention Combine pre-provisioning for known events with load testing to find the true bottleneck, raise cloud/quotas and DB capacity ahead of time, warm caches and connection pools, and design graceful degradation (load shedding, queues, read-only fallbacks) so overflow degrades instead of collapsing. Interview tip: The headline: pre-scale for predictabl

questions.q: Your autoscaler is flapping — rapidly scaling up and down — causing instability. How do you stabilize it?
questions.text: Symptom Replica count oscillates every few minutes — scale up, scale down, repeat — thrashing pods and disrupting in-flight work. Investigation # what metric drives scaling, and how noisy is it? # what are the up/down thresholds — is there a gap (hysteresis) between them? # any stabilization window / cooldown configured? Flapping happens when the scaling signal is noisy and the up/down thresholds are too close, so normal metric jitter crosses them repeatedly. Each scale action then changes per-pod load, which moves the metric again — a feedback loop. No cooldown or hysteresis lets it oscillate freely. Root cause An unstable control loop: a noisy metric plus thresholds without a dead-band, and no stabilization window, so the autoscaler chases jitter and amplifies it. Fix / mitigation # add a stabilization window / scale-down cooldown (slow down, esp. on the way down) # widen the gap between scale-up and scale-down thresholds (hysteresis) # smooth the input metric (averaging) and pick a stable signal Prevention Tune the control loop like a control system: add hysteresis (separate up/down thresholds), stabilization windows (especially slower scale-down), and smoothed input metrics. Scale up fast for safety, down slowly for stability — and pick a metric that reflects sustained load, not momentary spikes. Interview tip: Frame it as a control-systems problem: hysteresis + stabilization windows + smoothed metric . The asymmetry rule — scale up quickly, down slowly — is the practical

questions.q: Capacity forecasting shows you'll run out of headroom in ~6 weeks at current growth. How do you respond?
questions.text: Symptom A trend analysis projects that a key resource (DB storage, node pool, a quota) hits 100% in roughly six weeks if growth continues. Investigation # validate the trend: linear or accelerating? seasonal? # which resource saturates first, and what's its lead time to expand? # is the growth organic, or a leak/inefficiency masquerading as growth? Six weeks is a planning window, not a fire — if you act on it. The risk is ignoring the forecast until it's an incident. The other trap is assuming you must buy more capacity when the “growth” is actually waste (a leak, unindexed bloat, retention misconfig) that should be fixed instead. Root cause Demand is on track to exceed supply within the lead time required to add capacity. Whether the right answer is “add capacity” or “reclaim waste” depends on whether the growth is genuine. Fix / mitigation # first ask: is this real demand or reclaimable waste? (cleanup may buy months) # if real: provision ahead of the lead time, not at saturation # set a headroom threshold that triggers action with buffer to spare Prevention Treat capacity as a continuous forecasting discipline: track utilization trends, define headroom thresholds that trigger action well before saturation (accounting for procurement/expansion lead time), and always check whether “growth” is demand or waste before spending. Plan capacity, don't react to it. Interview tip: Two senior moves: act within the lead time, with buffer , and distinguish real demand from reclaimable

questions.q: You lose a node (or AZ) and the survivors get overloaded into a cascading failure. How should capacity have been planned?
questions.text: Symptom An instance fails and its load redistributes to the remaining nodes — which were already near capacity — pushing them over, causing more failures and a cascade. Investigation # what was per-node utilization BEFORE the failure? # N nodes at X% — after losing one, can N-1 absorb the load? # are there resource limits / load shedding to contain overload? Running every node near capacity leaves no slack to absorb a failure. When one dies, its share lands on survivors already at their limit, tipping them over — each failure increases load on the rest, a self-reinforcing cascade. The system had no N+1 (or N+k) redundancy headroom. Root cause Insufficient redundancy headroom. Capacity was planned for the happy path (all nodes healthy) rather than for graceful operation after losing one — so the first failure became many. Fix / mitigation # immediate: shed load / add capacity fast to break the cascade # plan N+1 (or N+k): size so survivors absorb failures within healthy limits # add per-instance limits + load shedding so overload degrades, not cascades Prevention Capacity-plan for failure: provision N+1/N+k so the loss of a node or AZ still leaves survivors within healthy utilization, spread across failure domains, and add backpressure/load shedding and circuit breakers so an overload sheds gracefully instead of cascading. Interview tip: The phrase to use is N+1 redundancy / failure headroom — plan capacity for the post-failure state, not the all-healthy state. Pair it with lo

questions.q: Latency stays flat as load rises, then suddenly spikes off a cliff at a certain utilization. What's happening?
questions.text: Symptom Latency is steady and healthy as traffic grows — right up to a point, where it abruptly explodes with only a small further increase in load. Investigation # plot latency vs utilization — where's the knee? # what resource is near saturation at the cliff? (CPU, threads, connections, queue) # is a queue growing unboundedly past that point? Queueing theory: as utilization approaches 100%, wait time rises non-linearly — latency ≈ service_time / (1 − utilization). Below the knee, added load barely moves latency; past it, small increases cause huge waits as queues build. The “cliff” is the system crossing into saturation. Root cause The system is operating too close to saturation. Latency vs utilization isn't linear — there's a knee near full utilization beyond which queues grow and latency blows up. Running near the cliff means a tiny load increase triggers the spike. Fix / mitigation # back away from the cliff: add capacity to lower steady-state utilization # cap concurrency / shed load to keep queues bounded # target utilization with headroom (e.g. ~60–70%, not 95%) Prevention Operate with utilization headroom below the latency knee, use admission control / concurrency limits so queues stay bounded under pressure, and monitor utilization against the cliff (not just current latency) — because a system that looks fine at 85% can fall off at 90%. Interview tip: Cite the queueing-theory intuition — latency ≈ service_time/(1−utilization) , with a knee near saturation. The take

questions.q: A Kubernetes cluster is over-provisioned and burning money, but you're scared to lower requests/limits. How do you right-size safely?
questions.text: Symptom Cost review flags the cluster as heavily over-provisioned — nodes mostly idle — but past attempts to cut resources caused OOMKills and throttling, so the team padded everything “to be safe.” Investigation kubectl top pods --all-namespaces # actual usage vs requests # compare requests/limits to real p95/p99 usage per workload # check the VPA recommender's suggestions if available Requests reserve capacity (and drive scheduling/cost) whether or not pods use it; limits cap usage and cause OOMKill/CPU-throttle when hit. Padding requests “to be safe” strands capacity and inflates cost; setting limits too low causes the failures that scared the team. Right-sizing means matching reservations to real usage with a safety margin — not guessing high. Root cause Requests and limits were set by fear, not data — over-reserved for cost, with limits that bite when occasionally exercised. The gap between reserved and used is wasted spend; the failures came from limits set without measuring real peaks. Fix / mitigation # set requests near observed p95 usage + margin; size limits above real peaks # use VPA recommendations / historical usage to drive values # roll out changes per-workload with monitoring, not cluster-wide at once Prevention Right-size from observed usage (p95/p99 with headroom) rather than guesses, distinguish requests (scheduling/cost) from limits (the OOM/throttle ceiling), use the VPA recommender and bin-packing to reclaim waste, and change workloads incrementally wit

questions.q: Costs spiked and finance is asking why — you trace it to over-provisioning, not real demand. How do you bring it back down responsibly?
questions.text: Symptom The monthly cloud bill jumped sharply. Investigation shows usage didn't grow proportionally — resources were over-provisioned, idle instances left running, and oversized everything. Investigation # break the bill down by service/team/tag — where did the delta come from? # utilization of the expensive resources: actually used, or idle? # any zombie resources (unattached disks, idle LBs, old environments)? Cost spikes from over-provisioning come from idle/zombie resources (orphaned volumes, forgotten environments, idle load balancers), oversized instances, and on-demand pricing where committed or spot would do. The spend isn't buying reliability — it's pure waste, but cutting blindly risks an outage. Root cause Spend grew without corresponding demand: idle and oversized resources, plus no cost accountability (untagged, unattributed). The challenge is reclaiming it without trading a cost problem for a reliability problem. Fix / mitigation # kill zombie resources; right-size oversized instances from real usage # shift stable baseline to committed/reserved; bursty/fault-tolerant to spot # tag everything & attribute cost so each team sees & owns its spend Prevention Build cost observability (tagging, per-team attribution, anomaly alerts) so spikes are caught and owned early, right-size and clean up zombies continuously, and match purchasing to workload shape (committed for baseline, spot for fault-tolerant, on-demand for spiky) — reclaiming waste while protecting reliabilit

questions.q: Capstone: a system handles load fine until concurrency climbs, then throughput collapses even though CPU isn't maxed. Diagnose using Little's Law.
questions.text: Symptom Throughput is healthy at low concurrency but collapses as concurrent requests rise — yet CPU, memory, and network all look under-utilized. Something invisible is the bottleneck. Investigation # measure the three terms: throughput (λ), concurrency (L), latency (W) # Little's Law: L = λ × W — which is fixed, which is exploding? # find the real limiter: connection pool, thread pool, locks, downstream cap Little's Law (L = λ × W) ties concurrency, throughput, and latency together. When throughput (λ) is capped by a hidden limited resource — a connection or thread pool, a lock, a downstream rate limit — adding concurrency (L) can't raise λ, so latency (W) must rise instead. Requests pile up waiting for the constrained resource while CPU sits idle, because the bottleneck isn't compute. Root cause A concurrency limit somewhere (pool size, lock, or downstream cap) bounds throughput. Past that point, more in-flight requests only inflate queue time — Little's Law says if λ is pinned and L grows, W must grow. The idle CPU proves the constraint is a logical resource, not hardware. Fix / mitigation # find & raise the limiting resource (enlarge pool, reduce lock contention) # OR cap admitted concurrency to keep the system below the collapse point # add backpressure so excess load is shed, not queued into a meltdown Prevention Reason about systems with Little's Law: identify the resource that actually caps throughput (pools, locks, downstream limits — rarely raw CPU), size it delibe

questions.q: Your checkout service latency doubles every day at exactly 14:00 and recovers by itself an hour later. How do you find out why?
questions.text: Symptom p99 latency of checkout doubles daily from 14:00 to 15:00, then recovers with no human action. No deploys at that time. Investigation # line up the window with scheduled work crontab -l; kubectl get cronjob -A # compare dependency latencies in that window histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, dep) (rate(dep_duration_bucket[5m]))) # check traffic mix and batch jobs on the DB select query, calls from pg_stat_statements order by total_exec_time desc limit 5 Root cause A daily analytics export job starts at 14:00 on the primary database and competes for IO and locks with checkout queries. Fix / mitigation # move the export to a read replica pg_dump --host replica ... # or reschedule to off-peak and throttle IO ionice -c3 nice -n19 ./export.sh Prevention Inventory scheduled jobs per shared resource, run heavy reads on replicas, and add a latency SLO alert with a time-pattern annotation. Interview tip: Anything that repeats on a clock is a schedule. Look for cron, batch, certificate or cache expiry before suspecting code.

questions.q: One customer reports errors but your dashboards show a 99.99% success rate. How do you investigate a single-tenant problem?
questions.text: Symptom A single large customer sees failures. Global error rate is normal. Support has a request ID or tenant ID. Investigation # slice by tenant, not globally sum by (tenant) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[10m])) # find their traces and logs grep tenant_id=acme app.log | grep -i error | tail # compare config, data size and quotas for that tenant select count(*) from orders where tenant_id='acme' Root cause The tenant has a data volume 50x the median, so a query with no index on that tenant partition times out only for them. Fix / mitigation # immediate: raise timeout or add index concurrently create index concurrently on orders (tenant_id, created_at); # route their traffic to a larger pool if needed Prevention Track SLIs per tenant tier, alert on outliers, load test with whale-sized tenants, and add per-tenant query budgets. Interview tip: Averages hide the biggest customers. Always be able to slice by tenant, region and version.

questions.q: An incident is resolved, but the same alert returns three times the next day with a different apparent cause each time. What is going on?
questions.text: Symptom Repeat incidents, each blamed on a different cause, each 'fixed' individually. The alert keeps returning. Investigation # build a combined timeline of all four occurrences # look for a common precursor: change, load, resource kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | head -50 # check shared resources: connection pool, node, queue show max_connections; select count(*) from pg_stat_activity; Root cause A shared resource (connection pool) is near its limit, so any minor trigger tips it over. The 'different causes' were just different triggers. Fix / mitigation # raise and right-size the pool, add pgbouncer # add saturation alert at 80% pool use # fix the leaking client that never returns connections Prevention Alert on saturation, not just failures; after repeated incidents, look for a common underlying constraint instead of treating each trigger separately. Interview tip: When causes keep changing, you are probably fixing triggers. Look for the shared constraint that makes the system fragile.

questions.q: You are on call and two unrelated alerts fire at the same time on different services. How do you prioritise?
questions.text: Symptom Alert A: payments error rate rising. Alert B: internal reporting job failing. Only one on-call. Investigation # impact first check SLO burn and customer-facing impact for each # are they related? shared dependency or change? git log --since='30 min ago'; check shared DB/queue health # can anyone else take one? page secondary, declare incident for the highest-impact Root cause They were unrelated: payments degradation from a provider issue, reporting failure from an expired credential. Fix / mitigation # payments first: failover to secondary provider # ask secondary on-call to take reporting # log reporting as ticket with owner and ETA Prevention Define severities, keep a secondary on-call, and tag alerts with business impact so triage is quick under pressure. Interview tip: Triage by user and business impact, not by who shouted first. Delegate early.

questions.q: A new engineer deployed a hotfix directly to production, bypassing the pipeline, and now things are inconsistent. How do you recover and fix the process?
questions.text: Symptom Manual change on some servers only. Behaviour differs per host. Git and prod no longer match. Investigation # find drift diff <(ssh h1 sha256sum /app/bin) <(ssh h2 sha256sum /app/bin) kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}' # who and what changed grep sudo /var/log/auth.log Root cause A manual binary swap on three of ten hosts left mixed versions, and the change never went through review or tests. Fix / mitigation # bring all hosts back to the pipeline-built version ./deploy.sh --version 2026.10.3 --all # add the hotfix properly via PR + CI # document the change in the incident log Prevention Remove direct prod write access, provide a fast hotfix lane in the pipeline, use immutable infrastructure, and treat the event as a systems problem, not a personal one. Interview tip: People bypass the pipeline when it is slow or when they do not trust it. Make the right way the fast way.

questions.q: A customer-facing feature breaks only when a specific third-party script or ad blocker is present. How do you diagnose a client-side issue from the server side?
questions.text: Symptom Support reports a page blank for some users. Server logs are clean, API returns 200. Investigation # check RUM / browser error reporting filter JS errors by browser, extension, URL # reproduce with the same browser profile # compare requests with and without the extension grep -c 'Failed to load resource' rum.log Root cause A blocking extension blocks a first-party analytics script whose failure throws an unhandled exception that halts rendering. Fix / mitigation # wrap analytics init in try/catch, load async # deploy frontend fix, verify via RUM error rate Prevention Treat third-party scripts as untrusted, load them non-blocking, add RUM error tracking and synthetic checks across browsers. Interview tip: Server-side 200s do not mean the user's page works. You need real user monitoring.

questions.q: The database is healthy and the app is healthy, but a specific API endpoint returns 504 after exactly 30 seconds. Where do you look?
questions.text: Symptom 504 Gateway Timeout on one endpoint at exactly 30s. Other endpoints fine. Investigation # a round number means a configured timeout grep -R 'timeout' nginx.conf ingress.yaml kubectl get ingress api -o yaml | grep -i timeout # find the slow step inside that endpoint trace the request; check outbound calls and locks Root cause The endpoint calls a slow report generator that takes 45s; the load balancer idle timeout of 30s cuts it before the app finishes. Fix / mitigation # short term: raise LB/ingress timeout for that route nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "60" # real fix: make it async with a job id and polling Prevention Set timeouts consistently across layers, keep synchronous requests short, and design long operations as asynchronous jobs. Interview tip: Exact round-number durations almost always mean a timeout setting somewhere in the path.

questions.q: After a datacenter power event all servers came back, but some services are in a bad state. In what order do you bring things back and verify?
questions.text: Symptom Mass restart after power loss. Services started in random order, some failing on missing dependencies. Investigation # build the dependency order 1. network, DNS, NTP 2. storage/DB/queues 3. identity/secrets 4. core services 5. edge/LB # verify each layer before the next systemctl --failed; kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running # check data integrity fsck results, replication status, WAL/replay Root cause Services started before DNS and the database quorum were ready and cached failures; the database had a stale replica. Fix / mitigation # restart in dependency order, validate each tier # resync stale replica from primary # restart services that cached bad state Prevention Document and automate startup ordering, add readiness gates and retries with backoff, test cold-start recovery in drills. Interview tip: Bring up foundation services first and verify each layer. Starting everything at once creates cascading confusion.

questions.q: A Deployment shows all pods Running but the Service has no endpoints. How do you debug it?
questions.text: Symptom kubectl get pods shows Running, but requests to the Service fail with connection refused. kubectl get endpoints shows none. Investigation kubectl get svc api -o yaml | grep -A3 selector kubectl get pods --show-labels kubectl get endpoints api kubectl describe pod api-xyz | grep -i -A5 'ready\|conditions' Root cause The Service selector uses app=api but pods are labelled app=api-v2, or the pods are Running but not Ready because the readiness probe fails. Fix / mitigation # fix labels or selector kubectl patch svc api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"api-v2"}}}' # or fix the readiness probe path/port kubectl rollout status deploy/api Prevention Use Helm templates that derive selectors and labels from one helper, and add a post-deploy check that endpoints are non-empty. Interview tip: Endpoints only include pods that are Ready and match the selector. Check both conditions.

questions.q: A StatefulSet pod won't start because its PersistentVolumeClaim is bound to a volume in a different availability zone. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.text: Symptom Pod Pending with 'volume node affinity conflict' or 'had volume node affinity conflict'. Investigation kubectl describe pod db-0 | tail -20 kubectl get pv,pvc -o wide kubectl get pv <name> -o yaml | grep -A8 nodeAffinity kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone Root cause The EBS volume lives in zone a, but the only schedulable nodes (due to capacity or taints) are in zone b; block volumes cannot cross zones. Fix / mitigation # add capacity in zone a # or restore from snapshot into zone b aws ec2 create-volume --snapshot-id snap-123 --availability-zone eu-west-1b # use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer Prevention Use WaitForFirstConsumer storage classes, spread node groups per zone, and keep topology spread constraints and capacity in every zone. Interview tip: Block storage is zonal. Scheduling must follow the data, not the other way around.

questions.q: After upgrading the cluster, many pods fail with 'no matches for kind' or deprecated API errors during deploy. How do you recover and prevent this?
questions.text: Symptom kubectl apply fails: 'no matches for kind Ingress in version extensions/v1beta1'. Helm releases cannot upgrade. Investigation kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis pluto detect-files -d manifests/ helm mapkubeapis release --dry-run Root cause Manifests and Helm release history reference API versions removed in the new Kubernetes version. Fix / mitigation # update manifests to supported API versions apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 helm mapkubeapis myrelease # redeploy and verify Prevention Scan for deprecated APIs before every upgrade, read release notes, test upgrades in staging and keep charts current. Interview tip: Deprecated APIs are announced many releases ahead. Scanners such as pluto or kubent find them in minutes.

questions.q: Your cluster DNS (CoreDNS) is overloaded and pods see intermittent 'no such host' errors under load. What do you check and change?
questions.text: Symptom Random resolution failures and slow lookups, especially during traffic peaks. CoreDNS pods at high CPU. Investigation kubectl top pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns | tail kubectl exec app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf # ndots:5? kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml Root cause ndots:5 makes every external lookup try multiple search domains first, multiplying queries; CoreDNS has too few replicas and no node-local cache. Fix / mitigation # lower ndots or use FQDNs with trailing dot dnsConfig: options: [{name: ndots, value: "2"}] kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=6 # deploy NodeLocal DNSCache Prevention Run node-local DNS caching, autoscale CoreDNS with cluster-proportional-autoscaler, and monitor DNS latency and error rate. Interview tip: With ndots 5, one lookup for api.example.com can generate five or more queries. Use trailing dots for external names.

questions.q: A PodDisruptionBudget blocks a node drain during a cluster upgrade and the upgrade hangs. How do you handle it safely?
questions.text: Symptom kubectl drain waits forever: 'Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.' Investigation kubectl get pdb -A kubectl describe pdb api -n prod kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=api -o wide kubectl get deploy api -n prod Root cause PDB requires minAvailable 2 but the deployment has only 2 replicas, or an unhealthy pod already uses up the budget, so no pod can be evicted. Fix / mitigation # scale up temporarily so eviction is allowed kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=4 # fix the unhealthy replica # long term: maxUnavailable: 1 with enough replicas Prevention Set PDBs relative to replica counts, never minAvailable equal to replicas, and test drains in staging before production upgrades. Interview tip: A PDB that allows zero disruptions makes the node undrainable. Check allowedDisruptions.

questions.q: Ingress returns 502 for a few seconds after every deployment, even with rolling updates. What causes it and what do you fix?
questions.text: Symptom Short bursts of 502/503 on each rollout, then normal. Readiness probes pass. Investigation kubectl get deploy api -o yaml | grep -A8 strategy kubectl get deploy api -o yaml | grep -B2 -A10 lifecycle kubectl logs ingress-nginx-controller | grep ' 502 ' # do old pods get SIGTERM before endpoints are removed? Root cause Pods receive SIGTERM and exit immediately while the ingress still routes to them, because endpoint removal propagates asynchronously. Fix / mitigation lifecycle: preStop: exec: command: ["sleep","15"] terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 # app: stop accepting new connections after SIGTERM, drain in-flight maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 25% Prevention Standardise graceful shutdown in base charts, test rollouts under load in CI and monitor 5xx during deployments. Interview tip: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM race each other. A preStop sleep gives the proxies time to update.

questions.q: A namespace hits its ResourceQuota and new deployments fail with 'exceeded quota'. How do you resolve it without breaking other teams?
questions.text: Symptom Pods not created: forbidden: exceeded quota: requests.cpu. ReplicaSet events show failures. Investigation kubectl describe quota -n team-a kubectl top pods -n team-a --sort-by=cpu kubectl get pods -n team-a -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,REQ:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.cpu kubectl get replicaset -n team-a Root cause Over-requested CPU on idle services consumes the quota; real usage is a fraction of requests. Fix / mitigation # right-size requests using VPA recommendations # remove unused workloads # if justified, raise quota through the capacity process Prevention Review requests regularly, use VPA in recommendation mode, set LimitRanges with sensible defaults and track quota utilisation. Interview tip: Quota counts requests, not usage. Inflated requests waste shared cluster capacity.

questions.q: A critical controller or operator pod keeps getting evicted and restarted because the node is under memory pressure. How do you protect system-critical pods?
questions.text: Symptom Operator pod evicted repeatedly; custom resources stop reconciling; node condition MemoryPressure true. Investigation kubectl describe node n1 | grep -A8 Conditions kubectl get pod operator -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}' kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Evicted kubectl top node n1 Root cause The operator runs as BestEffort with no requests, so it is the first to be evicted when memory is short. Fix / mitigation # set requests=limits for Guaranteed QoS resources: requests: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi} limits: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi} priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical # fix the noisy neighbours without limits Prevention Require resource requests on all workloads, use priority classes for platform components and reserve resources for system daemons. Interview tip: QoS class decides eviction order: BestEffort first, then Burstable, Guaranteed last.

questions.q: A cronjob in Kubernetes silently stops running, no recent jobs created. How do you find out why?
questions.text: Symptom CronJob last schedule was days ago. No errors in app logs because no pods are created. Investigation kubectl get cronjob report -o yaml | grep -E 'suspend|lastScheduleTime|schedule|concurrencyPolicy|startingDeadlineSeconds' kubectl get jobs --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp kubectl describe cronjob report kubectl get events | grep -i report Root cause A previous job hung and concurrencyPolicy: Forbid prevents new runs; or more than 100 missed schedules triggered the controller to stop scheduling. Fix / mitigation # delete the stuck job kubectl delete job report-28345 # set activeDeadlineSeconds on the job # set startingDeadlineSeconds # alert on time since last success Prevention Alert on time since the last successful run, set deadlines and history limits, and avoid Forbid without a timeout. Interview tip: Monitor for absence. A job that no longer runs generates no errors, only silence.

questions.q: An AWS Lambda function suddenly starts failing with timeouts only for the first request after idle periods. How do you diagnose and improve it?
questions.text: Symptom Occasional very slow first invocation (several seconds), then normal. Users notice sporadic delays. Investigation aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/lambda/fn --filter-pattern 'Init Duration' aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name fn # look at package size, runtime, VPC config, init code # CloudWatch: ConcurrentExecutions, Duration p99 Root cause Cold starts: large package, heavy initialisation (SDK clients, config fetch) and VPC networking add several seconds when a new execution environment starts. Fix / mitigation # reduce package, lazy-load, initialise clients outside handler aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name fn --qualifier prod --provisioned-concurrent-executions 5 # consider SnapStart for supported runtimes Prevention Track init duration, set provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive paths, keep functions small and avoid blocking init. Interview tip: Provisioned concurrency trades cost for predictable latency. Use it only where cold starts hurt users.

questions.q: A cloud load balancer health check marks all targets unhealthy right after a security group change, but the app is fine. How do you recover?
questions.text: Symptom All targets unhealthy, 503 from the load balancer. Instances respond locally. Change made 5 minutes ago. Investigation aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn $TG aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-app # can LB subnet reach the health check port? aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=RevokeSecurityGroupIngress Root cause The change removed the inbound rule allowing the load balancer's security group on the health check port. Fix / mitigation aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-app --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group sg-alb # verify targets return to healthy aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn $TG Prevention Manage security groups as code with review, reference groups by ID instead of CIDR, and validate connectivity in a post-change check. Interview tip: CloudTrail tells you exactly which rule changed and who changed it, which speeds up rollback.

questions.q: Your cloud storage bucket costs spiked because of millions of tiny requests and egress. How do you find the source and stop it?
questions.text: Symptom Storage bill up 5x. Request and data transfer lines dominate. No new features shipped. Investigation aws s3api get-bucket-metrics-configuration ... aws s3api list-bucket-metrics-configurations --bucket b # enable and query S3 access logs / CloudTrail data events athena: select requester, count(*) from s3_logs group by 1 order by 2 desc limit 10 aws ce get-cost-and-usage --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE Root cause A misconfigured client polls the bucket listing every second, and an unauthenticated public object is being hot-linked by a third party. Fix / mitigation # fix the polling client to use events/notifications # block public access, restrict via CloudFront signed URLs aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket b --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true Prevention Enable cost anomaly detection, put CDN in front of public content, block public access by default and use event notifications instead of polling. Interview tip: The requester and user agent in access logs usually identify the culprit within minutes.

questions.q: A cross-account IAM role assumption suddenly fails with AccessDenied after a policy cleanup. How do you debug it?
questions.text: Symptom sts:AssumeRole denied from account A to role in account B. Worked last week. Investigation aws iam get-role --role-name target --query Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn $CALLER --action-names sts:AssumeRole --resource-arns $ROLE aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=AssumeRole # check SCPs and permission boundaries Root cause The caller's identity policy no longer allows sts:AssumeRole on the target role after a cleanup, while the trust policy requires an ExternalId that was also removed from the caller's configuration. Fix / mitigation # restore identity policy permitting sts:AssumeRole on that ARN # pass ExternalId in the assume-role call aws sts assume-role --role-arn $ROLE --role-session-name x --external-id abc123 Prevention Test IAM cleanups with policy simulation and last-accessed data, and manage roles as code with review. Interview tip: Cross-account access needs both sides: the caller must be allowed to assume, and the target must trust the caller.

questions.q: A managed Kubernetes control plane upgrade finished, but nodes are on an old version and some workloads misbehave. How do you manage version skew?
questions.text: Symptom Control plane at 1.30, node groups still at 1.28. Some pods behave oddly, new features unavailable. Investigation kubectl version; kubectl get nodes -o wide kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,VER:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion # check supported skew policy kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep <old-node> Root cause Nodes lag beyond the supported skew (kubelet can be at most a few minor versions behind the API server), so behaviour is undefined. Fix / mitigation # upgrade node groups one minor at a time, surge + drain eksctl upgrade nodegroup --name ng1 --cluster c --kubernetes-version 1.29 # pause risky deploys until aligned Prevention Upgrade control plane and nodes in one planned sequence, automate node rotation, and monitor version drift. Interview tip: Skew limits exist for a reason. Treat out-of-policy skew as an incident-in-waiting.

questions.q: Your multi-region failover test worked in staging but the real failover took 40 minutes because of DNS and stale caches. What do you improve?
questions.text: Symptom Primary region failed; traffic took 40 minutes to shift. Some clients still hitting dead region. Investigation dig +short app.example.com # TTL and answers aws route53 get-health-check-status ... # which clients cache DNS beyond TTL (JVM, mobile) # check failover record config and health check interval Root cause High DNS TTL (1 hour), slow health check thresholds and clients that cache resolution kept routing to the failed region. Fix / mitigation # lower TTL to 30-60s on failover records # health check interval 10s, threshold 2 # use anycast / global load balancer for instant shift # JVM: -Dnetworkaddress.cache.ttl=30 Prevention Run real failover game days with production-like clients, measure end-to-end RTO and fix each contributor. Interview tip: DNS failover time = detection time + TTL + client caching. Measure all three.

questions.q: Intermittent connection resets (RST) occur between two services behind a NAT gateway on long-lived idle connections. What is happening?
questions.text: Symptom Connections idle for several minutes then fail with connection reset on first use. Short connections fine. Investigation tcpdump -i any host 10.0.1.5 and 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' # NAT gateway idle timeout (e.g. 350s on AWS NAT) sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time # app connection pool max idle time Root cause The NAT gateway drops idle flows after its timeout; the client still believes the connection is open and sends on a dead flow, which gets an RST. Fix / mitigation # enable TCP keepalive shorter than NAT timeout sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time=120 # set pool max idle lifetime < NAT timeout # add retry on stale connection for idempotent calls Prevention Document infrastructure idle timeouts and configure pools and keepalives below the smallest one in the path. Interview tip: Every stateful middlebox has an idle timeout. Keepalives and pool lifetimes must be shorter than the shortest.

questions.q: Packets are being dropped between two VPCs connected by peering, but only for large payloads. How do you diagnose MTU and fragmentation problems?
questions.text: Symptom Small requests succeed, large responses hang. ICMP ping works. Path crosses a VPN or tunnel. Investigation ping -M do -s 1472 target # find max unfragmented size tracepath target ip link show eth0 | grep mtu tcpdump -i eth0 'icmp[icmptype]==3 and icmp[icmpcode]==4' Root cause A tunnel with a smaller MTU drops oversized packets with DF set, and ICMP fragmentation-needed messages are blocked by a security rule, so path MTU discovery fails. Fix / mitigation # allow ICMP type 3 code 4 # clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu # or lower interface MTU Prevention Document MTU along each path, never block ICMP fragmentation-needed, and test large transfers after network changes. Interview tip: The classic sign is: connect works, small data works, large data hangs. Think MTU.

questions.q: Users in one country can't reach your service while others can. How do you determine if it is routing, DNS, CDN or blocking?
questions.text: Symptom Reports from users in one region/ISP: timeouts or wrong certificates. Others fine. Investigation # test from multiple vantage points curl -sv --resolve app.example.com:443:<ip> https://app.example.com dig @8.8.8.8 app.example.com; dig @isp-resolver app.example.com mtr -rw app.example.com # from affected region probe # check CDN edge logs for that POP Root cause A regional ISP resolver returns an outdated IP for the domain, pointing to a decommissioned address range. Fix / mitigation # lower TTL and wait/notify ISP, publish via alternative resolvers # keep old IP responding with redirect during migration # status page + support guidance (public DNS) Prevention Keep old addresses alive through migrations for at least the max TTL, monitor from multiple geographies and test through major resolvers. Interview tip: Compare answers from public resolvers and the ISP's resolver. Different answers point straight at DNS.

questions.q: A newly added microservice cannot reach the database although security groups look right. How do you find the block?
questions.text: Symptom Connection timeout from new service to DB on port 5432. Existing services connect fine. Investigation nc -zv db.internal 5432 # check route tables and subnets for the new service aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=$SUBNET aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=$SUBNET # VPC reachability analyzer Root cause The new service sits in a subnet whose network ACL does not allow ephemeral return ports, or lacks a route to the database subnet. Fix / mitigation # add NACL rules for return traffic (1024-65535) and DB port # or place service in the correct subnet group aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry ... Prevention Define network layout in code with reusable modules and run reachability analysis in CI for new services. Interview tip: Security groups are stateful, but network ACLs are stateless. They need explicit rules in both directions.

questions.q: TLS handshakes to an internal service start failing across the fleet at midnight. Certificates look valid. What else could it be?
questions.text: Symptom x509 errors at 00:00 UTC across many clients. Server cert valid for 90 more days. Investigation openssl s_client -connect svc:443 -showcerts </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer # check the intermediate and root in the chain date -u; chronyc tracking openssl verify -CAfile ca-bundle.pem chain.pem Root cause The intermediate CA certificate expired at midnight, though the leaf certificate was valid; servers did not send the new intermediate. Fix / mitigation # install the renewed intermediate in the chain served # update trust bundles in clients if root changed # restart services to load the chain Prevention Monitor expiry for every certificate in the chain, including intermediates and roots, and test chain validation from clients. Interview tip: A valid leaf does not help if any certificate above it in the chain has expired.

questions.q: A server has plenty of free disk blocks but cannot create files because it has run out of inodes. How do you find and fix it?
questions.text: Symptom 'No space left on device' while df -h shows 30% used. Application cannot write new files. Investigation df -i find /var -xdev -type d -size +1M for d in /var/*; do echo $d $(find $d -xdev | wc -l); done | sort -k2 -n | tail ls /var/spool/mail | wc -l Root cause Millions of tiny session or cache files accumulated in one directory without cleanup, exhausting the inode table. Fix / mitigation # delete in batches to avoid blocking find /var/lib/php/sessions -type f -mtime +1 -delete # configure cleanup (tmpreaper/logrotate/app GC) # longer term: recreate FS with more inodes or use object storage Prevention Monitor inode usage as well as blocks, add retention to caches and sessions, and choose appropriate filesystem parameters. Interview tip: Deleting millions of files with rm * may fail with argument list too long. Use find -delete.

questions.q: A process is stuck in uninterruptible sleep (D state) and cannot be killed. What causes this and how do you recover?
questions.text: Symptom ps shows D state processes, load average climbing, kill -9 has no effect. Investigation ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:30,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /D/' cat /proc/<pid>/stack dmesg -T | tail -50 mount | grep -E 'nfs|cifs'; iostat -x 1 5 Root cause Processes wait on IO that never completes because a network filesystem server is unreachable or a disk is failing. Fix / mitigation # restore the storage path (network, server, multipath) # or lazy unmount as last resort umount -l /mnt/data # if hardware: fail over and replace the disk # reboot only when nothing else works Prevention Use soft/timeout mount options where safe, monitor storage latency and avoid putting critical paths on fragile network mounts. Interview tip: D-state processes count toward load average even with idle CPU, which explains high load with a quiet CPU.

questions.q: A time-sensitive application fails authentication because server clocks drifted by minutes. How do you fix time sync and prevent it?
questions.text: Symptom Kerberos / JWT / TOTP failures, log timestamps out of order across hosts, certificate 'not yet valid' errors. Investigation timedatectl status chronyc tracking; chronyc sources -v date -u; ssh host2 date -u systemctl status chronyd Root cause NTP daemon stopped after a config change and VMs drifted; firewall blocked UDP 123 to time servers. Fix / mitigation systemctl enable --now chronyd chronyc makestep # allow UDP 123 to internal NTP servers # verify offset < 100 ms Prevention Run internal NTP sources, monitor clock offset on every host, and alert when drift exceeds a small threshold. Interview tip: Prefer stepping slowly (slew) for running services; use makestep carefully since time jumps can break applications.

questions.q: After a kernel update and reboot, a server's network interface names changed and services bound to the old interface fail. What happened?
questions.text: Symptom eth0 became ens5; static config and firewall rules reference the old name; no network after reboot. Investigation ip -br link journalctl -b | grep -i 'renamed' cat /etc/netplan/*.yaml; ls /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts # console access needed if SSH is down Root cause Predictable interface naming or a changed driver/PCI order renamed the NIC; configs matched by name. Fix / mitigation # match by MAC address in netplan match: macaddress: 0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:5f set-name: eth0 netplan apply # update firewall rules to the new name Prevention Match interfaces by MAC or use persistent names, test reboots after kernel updates and keep out-of-band console access. Interview tip: Always have console or out-of-band access before rebooting a remote server after kernel or network changes.

questions.q: A Java service is repeatedly killed by the OOM killer although its heap is capped well below the container memory limit. Why?
questions.text: Symptom Container OOMKilled, Xmx=2g, limit=3g. Heap graphs look fine. Investigation kubectl describe pod | grep -A5 'Last State' jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.stat ps -o rss,vsz -p <pid> Root cause Non-heap memory (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache, native libraries) plus a high thread count pushes total RSS over the limit. Fix / mitigation # size heap to ~60-70% of the limit -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 # cap direct memory and metaspace -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m # reduce thread count / stack size Prevention Enable native memory tracking in testing, size containers using measured RSS under load and alert on container memory working set. Interview tip: The heap is only part of the JVM's memory. Budget for metaspace, threads, buffers and the runtime itself.

questions.q: A pipeline suddenly fails to pull base images with 'toomanyrequests' rate-limit errors. How do you fix it right now and permanently?
questions.text: Symptom docker pull fails: 'You have reached your pull rate limit'. Builds blocked across teams. Investigation docker pull alpine:3.20 2>&1 | head curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -I https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/ratelimitpreview/test/manifests/latest # which jobs pull most? shared runner IP? Root cause Many CI jobs behind a shared NAT IP make anonymous pulls and exhaust the public registry quota. Fix / mitigation # authenticate pulls with a paid account / token docker login -u ci -p $TOKEN # configure a pull-through cache / mirror # use internal registry for base images Prevention Mirror public images into an internal registry, pin by digest and reduce pulls with layer caching. Interview tip: A pull-through cache also protects you from registry outages and deleted upstream tags.

questions.q: A deployment succeeds but the application serves the old version for some users for hours. How do you find the cause?
questions.text: Symptom Pipeline green, new version live in some regions, others still show old behaviour. Investigation curl -s https://app/version; for r in eu us ap; do curl -s https://$r.app/version; done kubectl get deploy -A -o wide | grep app # CDN cache headers curl -sI https://app/static/main.js | grep -i 'cache-control\|age\|etag' # check image tags: latest vs digest Root cause The deployment used the mutable latest tag and a node cached the old image with imagePullPolicy IfNotPresent; the CDN also cached the old bundle for 24 hours. Fix / mitigation # deploy by immutable tag/digest image: registry/app@sha256:abc... # purge CDN and use content-hashed filenames aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id D --paths '/*' Prevention Never deploy mutable tags, use hashed asset names, and add a post-deploy check that verifies the running version in every region. Interview tip: Expose the build version in a header or endpoint so you can verify what is actually serving traffic.

questions.q: A monorepo CI run takes two hours because it builds and tests everything on every commit. How do you cut it down safely?
questions.text: Symptom Developers wait hours for feedback, merge queue backed up, teams skip tests locally. Investigation # profile pipeline stages and critical path gh run view --log | grep -E 'took|duration' # which tests fail rarely / are slowest # what changed vs what is built git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD Root cause No change-based selection, no remote cache, serial test execution and heavy end-to-end tests run on every commit. Fix / mitigation # affected-only builds with dependency graph nx affected --target=test # remote build cache # shard tests across runners in parallel # move slow e2e to merge queue / nightly Prevention Track pipeline duration as an SLO, review the slowest jobs monthly and keep a fast pre-merge tier plus a thorough post-merge tier. Interview tip: Fast feedback beats exhaustive feedback on every commit. Run the thorough suite where it counts, but still run it.

questions.q: A Terraform pipeline applied a change in the wrong order, destroying a load balancer before its replacement existed. How do you recover and design around it?
questions.text: Symptom Brief production outage: LB deleted, new LB created after; DNS now points at nothing for several minutes. Investigation terraform plan | grep -B3 'must be replaced' terraform state list | grep lb # review the plan output that was approved aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers Root cause A change forced replacement of the load balancer, and the default order is destroy then create; the plan was approved without noticing the replacement. Fix / mitigation # apply with create_before_destroy where possible lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } # use unique name_prefix to avoid conflicts # manually switch DNS to new LB, verify Prevention Review plans for replacement markers, add policy checks that block replacement of critical resources, and use blue/green for load balancers. Interview tip: Search the plan for 'replace' and 'destroy'. Make approvers look at those lines first.

questions.q: A dependency update bot merged a minor version bump that broke production because the library changed behaviour. How do you make automation safer?
questions.text: Symptom Auto-merged dependency PR passed unit tests but changed rounding in a pricing library; wrong prices shown. Investigation git log -5 --oneline package-lock.json diff old/new library release notes # what tests would have caught it? # check which services consume the lib Root cause A semantic change in a minor release was not covered by tests, and auto-merge had no canary or staged rollout. Fix / mitigation # pin and revert to the previous version git revert <bot-merge> # add characterisation tests for pricing # staged rollout of dependency updates Prevention Auto-merge only patch updates with strong test coverage, require canary deployments, and add contract tests for critical calculations. Interview tip: Semver is a promise, not a guarantee. Critical paths need tests that pin their expected behaviour.

questions.q: Replication lag on a read replica grows steadily during a nightly batch job, causing stale reads. How do you handle it?
questions.text: Symptom Replica lag climbs to 20 minutes between 01:00 and 03:00; users see missing recent updates. Investigation select now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() as lag; show max_wal_senders; select * from pg_stat_replication; # long-running transactions on the replica select pid, now()-xact_start from pg_stat_activity where state<>'idle' order by 2 desc; Root cause The batch job produces a huge volume of WAL, and long analytical queries on the replica conflict with replay. Fix / mitigation # batch in smaller transactions with sleeps # route analytics to a dedicated replica # tune max_standby_streaming_delay and hot_standby_feedback # read-your-writes: send critical reads to primary Prevention Alert on replication lag, separate workloads by replica, and design read paths to tolerate or avoid stale data. Interview tip: Replicas are eventually consistent. Decide which reads need the primary.

questions.q: A Kafka consumer group is stuck rebalancing constantly and throughput collapses. What do you check?
questions.text: Symptom Frequent rebalances, consumer lag grows, logs show 'Revoking previously assigned partitions' repeatedly. Investigation kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group g --bootstrap-server b:9092 # max.poll.interval.ms vs processing time grep -i 'rebalance\|poll timeout\|session timeout' consumer.log # pod restarts / autoscaling of consumers Root cause Message processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the broker thinks the consumer is dead and triggers a rebalance, which repeats. Fix / mitigation # reduce max.poll.records or speed up processing max.poll.interval.ms=600000 max.poll.records=100 # use cooperative sticky assignor # stop autoscaling flapping consumers # static membership group.instance.id Prevention Alert on rebalance frequency and lag, decouple slow processing with worker pools, and use static membership for stable deployments. Interview tip: Each rebalance pauses consumption for the group. Frequent rebalances turn into a throughput outage.

questions.q: Elasticsearch cluster turns yellow then red after a node restart, and search results are incomplete. How do you recover?
questions.text: Symptom Cluster health red; unassigned shards; some indices unavailable. Investigation curl -s localhost:9200/_cluster/health?pretty curl -s localhost:9200/_cat/shards?v | grep UNASSIGNED curl -s localhost:9200/_cluster/allocation/explain?pretty curl -s localhost:9200/_cat/allocation?v Root cause Disk watermark exceeded on remaining nodes so shards cannot be allocated, and replica count was zero for one index so its data was only on the restarted node. Fix / mitigation # free disk or add node; clear watermark block curl -XPUT localhost:9200/_cluster/settings -d '{"transient":{"cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.low":"90%"}}' # retry allocation curl -XPOST 'localhost:9200/_cluster/reroute?retry_failed=true' # restore missing index from snapshot if needed Prevention Keep at least one replica for important indices, maintain disk headroom, take snapshots and use allocation awareness. Interview tip: The allocation explain API tells you exactly why a shard is not assigned. Start there.

questions.q: A Redis instance used as a cache starts evicting keys and the database load triples. What is going on and how do you respond?
questions.text: Symptom Hit ratio drops, evicted_keys increases, DB CPU spikes, latency rises. Investigation redis-cli info memory | grep -E 'used_memory_human|maxmemory|evicted' redis-cli info stats | grep -E 'keyspace_hits|keyspace_misses|evicted_keys' redis-cli --bigkeys redis-cli config get maxmemory-policy Root cause A new feature stores large objects without TTL, filling memory to maxmemory so the allkeys-lru policy evicts hot keys. Fix / mitigation # add TTLs, cap object sizes # increase memory or shard redis-cli config set maxmemory 8gb # protect DB with request coalescing and rate limiting # remove the large keys Prevention Alert on hit ratio and evictions, set TTLs by default, review key patterns, and protect the database with stampede controls. Interview tip: A cache is a performance layer and often a hidden capacity dependency. Know what happens to the DB when hit ratio drops.

questions.q: A data pipeline silently produced duplicate records after a retry, and downstream reports are inflated. How do you detect, fix and prevent it?
questions.text: Symptom Revenue report 12% too high. Row counts in the warehouse exceed source counts. Investigation select id, count(*) from fact_orders group by id having count(*) > 1; # compare source vs destination counts per day # check job logs for retries / at-least-once delivery select batch_id, count(*) from load_audit group by 1; Root cause The loader uses at-least-once delivery and inserts without a unique key, so a retried batch loaded twice.
