Fix / mitigation # dedupe with window function and rebuild affected partitions delete from fact_orders where ctid not in (select min(ctid) from fact_orders group by id); # make loads idempotent: MERGE/upsert on natural key # add unique constraint / dedup in ETL Prevention Design pipelines to be idempotent, add reconciliation checks between source and sink and alert on count mismatch. Interview tip: At-least-once plus idempotent writes gives effectively-once results. Retries without idempotency create duplicates.

questions.q: Your alerts fire correctly but the on-call can't tell which customer-facing feature is affected. How do you make alerts more informative?
questions.text: Symptom Alert text: 'High error rate on service X'. Responder spends 15 minutes finding impact and owner. Investigation # review alert annotations and labels kubectl get prometheusrule -o yaml | grep -A10 annotations # do alerts link dashboards, runbooks, owners? # can we map service to user journey? Root cause Alerts have no context: no impact description, severity rationale, dashboard or runbook link, and no mapping to the user journey. Fix / mitigation annotations: summary: 'Checkout errors > 2% (card payments failing)' dashboard: https://grafana/d/checkout runbook: https://wiki/runbooks/checkout-errors labels: team: payments, severity: page # include top error and recent deploy Prevention Alert templates with required fields, and a review of alerts after every incident for missing context. Interview tip: A good alert answers: what is broken for whom, how bad, where to look, and what to do first.

questions.q: Logs from one service stopped appearing in your central logging system an hour ago. How do you find where the pipeline is broken?
questions.text: Symptom Kibana/Loki shows no logs from service payments since 10:14. Service is running and healthy. Investigation kubectl logs deploy/payments | tail kubectl get pods -n logging; kubectl logs ds/fluent-bit -n logging | tail # check agent buffer / backpressure / rejections curl -s loki:3100/metrics | grep -E 'discarded|rate_limited' # did log format or volume change? Root cause The service began emitting very large JSON lines after a deploy; the agent dropped them as oversized and the backend rate-limited the stream. Fix / mitigation # cap line size in the app, fix the log message # raise agent buffer / max line size cautiously # re-ship from node files if still available # add the stream to rate limit allowlist if justified Prevention Monitor log pipeline health (ingest rate per service, drops, lag), alert on silent services, and set size limits at the source. Interview tip: Alert on the absence of logs from services that should always log. Silence is a signal.

questions.q: Your trace sampling is set to 1% and the intermittent error you are chasing never shows up. How do you capture the interesting traces?
questions.text: Symptom Rare failures (0.05%) are invisible in traces; logs lack context to link requests. Investigation # current sampling config grep -R 'sampler\|sampling' otel-collector.yaml # are errors and slow traces force-kept? # error rate vs traces with error status Root cause Head-based random sampling decides before the outcome is known, so rare errors are almost never kept. Fix / mitigation # tail-based sampling in the collector processors: tail_sampling: policies: [{name: errors, type: status_code, status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]}}, {name: slow, type: latency, latency: {threshold_ms: 1000}}, {name: base, type: probabilistic, probabilistic: {sampling_percentage: 1}}] Prevention Use tail-based sampling to keep all errors and slow requests, add exemplars linking metrics to traces and keep trace IDs in logs. Interview tip: Sample after you know the outcome. Keep every error and every slow trace, and a small random baseline.

questions.q: After enabling debug logging to chase a bug, the application becomes slower and the log bill jumps. How should you debug in production safely?
questions.text: Symptom Latency up 20% and logging costs triple after switching the log level to debug fleet-wide. Investigation # measure overhead: latency and CPU vs log volume kubectl top pods; check log lines per second # is debug enabled everywhere or only needed paths? Root cause Debug logging was enabled globally, producing high volume synchronously on hot paths. Fix / mitigation # revert to info; enable debug for one pod or one user via dynamic log level curl -X POST app/admin/loglevel -d 'logger=payments&level=debug&ttl=15m' # use sampling and async appenders # use traces / feature-flagged diagnostics instead Prevention Support dynamic, scoped, time-limited log levels, structured logs, and rely on traces and metrics before verbose logging. Interview tip: Make debug logging expire automatically so it is never left on by accident.

questions.q: A queue consumer fleet autoscaled to 200 pods but throughput didn't improve, and the database is struggling. What went wrong?
questions.text: Symptom Lag stays high despite 10x consumers; DB CPU at 100%, lock waits and connection errors. Investigation kubectl get hpa; kafka-consumer-groups --describe select count(*) from pg_stat_activity; select wait_event_type, count(*) from pg_stat_activity group by 1; # per-message processing time vs concurrency Root cause The bottleneck is the database, not the consumers. More consumers add contention and connection pressure, reducing total throughput. Fix / mitigation # cap max replicas to what the DB can sustain # batch writes, add indexes, use a connection pooler # scale the DB or partition the workload # apply backpressure: pause consumption when DB latency high Prevention Load test the whole path to find the true bottleneck, set autoscaler maximums from downstream capacity, and implement backpressure. Interview tip: Scaling a stage that isn't the bottleneck makes the real bottleneck worse.

questions.q: Your service handles peak traffic fine in load tests but fails in production at half that load. What differences do you look for?
questions.text: Symptom Production degrades at 50% of tested peak. Staging passes with margin. Investigation # compare environments: data size, caches, topology, config # request mix in prod vs test # third-party calls mocked in test, real in prod # noisy neighbours, shared limits, DNS, connection limits Root cause The load test used a uniform request mix on a small dataset with mocked dependencies; production has a skewed mix, large data, real downstream rate limits and cold caches. Fix / mitigation # replay production traffic shape (shadow/replay) # test with production-size data # include real or realistic dependency latencies and limits # fix the discovered limit (e.g. downstream rate limit) Prevention Treat load test realism as a requirement: data volume, traffic mix, dependencies, cache state and concurrency. Interview tip: A load test is only as good as its model of production. Validate the model against real traffic.

questions.q: A latency-sensitive service shares nodes with batch jobs, and every batch run causes latency spikes. How do you isolate them?
questions.text: Symptom p99 spikes coincide with batch jobs starting on the same node pool; CPU shares and cache contention. Investigation kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep node-7 kubectl top node node-7 # CPU throttling for the latency service container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total # check QoS classes and priorities Root cause Batch pods are Burstable with low requests, consuming bursty CPU, memory bandwidth and disk IO, while the latency service lacks guaranteed resources. Fix / mitigation # dedicated node pool with taints for batch tolerations + nodeSelector for batch jobs # Guaranteed QoS and CPU pinning for latency-critical pods # priority classes; set batch requests realistically # IO limits for batch Prevention Separate workload classes by node pool, set priorities and realistic requests and monitor throttling and noisy neighbour signals. Interview tip: Shared nodes share caches, memory bandwidth and disk IO, which requests and limits do not fully isolate.

questions.q: You must reduce infrastructure cost by 30% without hurting reliability. What is your approach?
questions.text: Symptom Finance target: cut cloud spend 30% in a quarter. SLOs must stay green. Investigation # find the big spenders and waste aws ce get-cost-and-usage --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE # utilisation per resource kubectl top nodes; compare requests vs usage # idle resources, old snapshots, unattached volumes Root cause Typical findings: over-provisioned instances, idle environments running 24/7, unattached storage, no commitments on baseline, and chatty cross-zone data transfer. Fix / mitigation # rightsize instances and requests with SLO guardrails # schedule non-prod shutdown nights/weekends # savings plans for baseline, spot for tolerant batch # delete orphaned volumes/snapshots, lifecycle storage # reduce cross-AZ and egress traffic Prevention FinOps practice: tagging, showback, unit cost metrics, budgets, and regular reviews with engineers. Interview tip: Remove waste first, then optimise. Cutting capacity that is actually used trades money for incidents.

questions.q: What is SRE — how does it differ from traditional Ops and from DevOps?
questions.text: Traditional Ops: separate team keeps prod running; reactive; manual toil DevOps: culture + practices to break the dev/ops wall (CALMS, CI/CD) SRE: a specific, prescriptive implementation of DevOps using SLOs + error budgets SRE is "what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations function." It treats operations as a software problem — automating toil, defining reliability numerically with SLOs, and using error budgets to balance velocity against stability. DevOps is the philosophy; SRE is one concrete, opinionated way to do it. Interview framing: "DevOps is a set of principles; SRE is a prescriptive engineering discipline that implements those principles with measurable reliability targets." That one sentence signals you understand both.

questions.q: What are the four golden signals of monitoring?
questions.text: Latency — time to serve a request (split success vs error latency) Traffic — demand on the system (req/s, transactions/s) Errors — rate of failed requests (explicit 5xx + implicit wrong answers) Saturation — how "full" the system is (CPU, mem, queue depth, I/O) From the Google SRE book. If you can only instrument four things, instrument these. Critical nuance: measure latency of failed requests separately — a fast 500 can otherwise hide in your latency percentiles and make a broken service look healthy. RED vs USE: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is the request-centric view for services. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) is the resource-centric view for hosts/queues. Golden signals blend both.

questions.q: Define SLI, SLO, and SLA — how do they relate?
questions.text: SLI = a measured number: e.g. proportion of requests < 300ms that return 2xx SLO = internal target for the SLI: e.g. 99.9% over a rolling 28 days SLA = external contract with consequences: e.g. 99.5% or we credit the customer SLI is the metric, SLO is the goal, SLA is the promise. The SLA is always looser than the SLO — you want internal alarms to fire well before you breach a customer contract. Not every SLO needs an SLA; many internal services have SLOs with no contractual SLA at all. Common mistake: Setting the SLO equal to the SLA. If they are equal, you have zero internal safety margin — by the time you notice the SLO miss, you have already breached the contract.

questions.q: How do you choose a good SLI — what makes a metric SLO-worthy?
questions.text: Good SLI: measured at the load balancer / point closest to the user SLI form: good events / valid events (a ratio, 0–100%) e.g. (requests < 400ms AND status==2xx) / (all non-rate-limited requests) A good SLI tracks the user’s actual experience, moves predictably with user happiness, and is a simple ratio of good to total. Measure as close to the user as possible — server-side 200s mean nothing if the load balancer is timing out before requests arrive. Pick 1–3 SLIs per user journey, not one per microservice. Per journey, not per service: Define SLIs around user journeys (checkout, search, login), not infrastructure components. Users do not care that pod-7 is healthy; they care that checkout works.

questions.q: What do the nines actually mean in downtime per period?
questions.text: 99% (two nines) → 7h 18m down / month | 3.65 days / year 99.9% (three) → 43m 49s down / month | 8.77 hours / year 99.95% → 21m 54s down / month | 4.38 hours / year 99.99% (four) → 4m 23s down / month | 52.6 min / year 99.999% (five) → 26.3s down / month | 5.26 min / year Each extra nine is roughly 10x harder and more expensive. The right answer to "how many nines?" is "the fewest that keep users happy." Five nines for a back-office reporting tool is waste; three nines for a payment path may be negligence. Reliability has diminishing returns: Beyond a point, the user’s network/device is less reliable than your service — extra nines become invisible to them but cost you enormously.

questions.q: What is an error budget and how is it calculated?
questions.text: Error budget = 100% − SLO SLO 99.9% over 28 days → budget = 0.1% Total requests 28d = 50,000,000 Budget = 0.001 × 50,000,000 = 50,000 allowed bad requests Burned 30,000 so far → 60% consumed, 40% remaining The error budget is the maximum unreliability you are allowed before breaching the SLO. It converts reliability from an argument into arithmetic: "we have 20,000 bad requests left this window" is a number both product and engineering can reason about. Why it matters: The error budget reframes reliability as a shared, spendable resource. Shipping features spends it; reliability work refills it. This ends the endless "ship vs stabilize" debate with data.

questions.q: What is an error budget policy — what happens when the budget is exhausted?
questions.text: Budget healthy (>25% left) → normal feature velocity Budget low (<25%) → review risky changes, add reliability work Budget exhausted (0%) → feature freeze; only reliability + critical fixes ship Budget overspent (negative)→ all-hands on reliability; postmortem actions prioritised The policy is the pre-agreed, written response to budget states — agreed by product AND engineering BEFORE an incident, so it is not relitigated under pressure. The classic consequence: exhausting the budget triggers a feature freeze until reliability recovers. Crucially this is a policy, not a punishment — it self-corrects velocity. Get buy-in early: The hardest part is getting product leadership to sign the freeze clause in advance. Without that signature, the error budget is just a dashboard nobody obeys.

questions.q: What is burn rate — how do you alert on it?
questions.text: Burn rate = how fast you are consuming the error budget vs sustainable pace Burn rate 1 = budget lasts exactly the SLO window (sustainable) Burn rate 14.4 = entire 30-day budget gone in ~2 days # Multi-window multi-burn-rate (Google SRE recommended): Fast page: 14.4x over 1h AND 5m windows → 2% budget in 1h Slow page: 6x over 6h AND 30m windows → 5% budget in 6h Ticket: 1x over 3d AND 6h windows → slow leak Burn-rate alerting fires on how fast you are spending budget, not on raw thresholds. This gives high precision (only alert when budget is genuinely at risk) and good reset behaviour. The dual short+long window prevents flapping: the long window confirms a sustained problem, the short window confirms it is still happening right now. Why not just alert on "error rate > 1%"? Static thresholds either page too much (noise) or too late (budget already gone). Burn rate ties the alert directly to SLO risk.

questions.q: How do you alert with PromQL on a burn rate against an SLO?
questions.text: # error ratio over a window sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h])) # fast-burn alert (2-window): 14.4x burn on 99.9% SLO (budget=0.001) ( job:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001) and job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001) ) # precompute ratios with recording rules to keep alerts cheap record: job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m Use recording rules to precompute the error ratio at several windows, then the alert just compares the ratio to burn_rate × budget. Require both the long and short window to exceed the threshold so a brief blip does not page. This is the standard SRE-workbook implementation.

questions.q: What makes a healthy on-call rotation?
questions.text: Rotation size: ≥ 6–8 engineers so each person is on-call ~1 week in 6–8 Follow-the-sun for global teams → no night pages where possible Primary + secondary (escalation) on every shift Hard cap: ≤ 2 incidents per on-call shift (Google guideline) Compensation: time off or pay for on-call burden A healthy rotation has enough people that on-call is occasional, has a documented escalation path, and limits pages per shift so responders are not exhausted. Google’s rule of thumb: if a shift routinely exceeds ~2 incidents, the system is too noisy — that is an engineering bug, not an on-call problem. Pager fatigue is a reliability risk: An exhausted, alert-numbed responder misses the real incident. Protecting on-call health directly protects uptime.

questions.q: How do you reduce alert noise and fight pager fatigue?
questions.text: Every page must be: urgent, actionable, and require human judgement If an alert is not all three → make it a ticket, not a page Alert on symptoms (SLO burn), not causes (one node high CPU) Add inhibition: silence downstream alerts when an upstream cause fires Track: alerts per shift, % actionable, % auto-resolved → drive down The test for any page: is it urgent, actionable, and does it need a human now? If a machine could fix it, automate it. If it can wait until morning, ticket it. Alert on user-facing symptoms via SLO burn rate rather than on every internal cause — one symptom alert replaces dozens of cause alerts. Run an alert review: Monthly, review every alert that paged. Delete or downgrade any that were not actionable. A shrinking pager is a sign of a maturing SRE practice.

questions.q: What is the incident command system (ICS) — what are the key roles?
questions.text: Incident Commander (IC): owns the incident, makes decisions, NOT hands-on-keyboard Operations / Tech Lead: the person(s) actually investigating and fixing Communications Lead: updates stakeholders, status page, execs Scribe: timestamps every action and decision in the incident channel ICS (borrowed from emergency services) separates command from execution. The IC coordinates and decides but does not debug — that prevents the classic failure where the only person who understands the system is also trying to run the meeting. For small incidents one person wears several hats; for large ones the roles split. The IC’s job is clarity, not heroics: Track who is doing what, prevent duplicate work, decide when to escalate, and keep one source of truth. The IC can be junior — command is a skill, not seniority.

questions.q: Walk through the lifecycle of an incident from detection to closure.
questions.text: 1. Detect — alert fires (ideally SLO burn) or user report 2. Triage — assess severity, declare incident, assign IC 3. Mitigate — stop the bleeding (rollback, failover, drain) BEFORE root cause 4. Resolve — confirm SLI recovered, customers unaffected 5. Review — blameless postmortem, action items 6. Close — actions tracked to completion The order that trips people up: mitigate before you diagnose. Restoring service is the priority; understanding why it broke comes after users are safe. A rollback that fixes symptoms in 2 minutes beats a root-cause hunt that fixes it "properly" in 2 hours. Mitigation ≠ resolution: Rolling back stops user pain (mitigation). The bug still exists (not resolved). Separating these two lets you de-escalate the page while the fix proceeds calmly.

questions.q: How do you classify incident severity (SEV levels)?
questions.text: SEV1 — critical: major outage, data loss, security breach; all-hands, exec comms SEV2 — high: significant degradation, key feature down; IC + on-call engaged SEV3 — moderate: partial/minor impact, workaround exists; handled in business hours SEV4 — low: cosmetic or internal; ticket, no page Severity drives response: who is paged, whether an IC is assigned, how often stakeholders are updated, and whether it can wait until morning. Define the levels concretely (by user impact, revenue, data risk) so the on-call engineer is not guessing at 3am. Under-classifying delays response; over-classifying burns people out. When unsure, declare higher: It is cheap to downgrade a SEV2 to SEV3 once you understand it. It is expensive to discover a "minor" issue was a SEV1 an hour too late.

questions.q: What is MTTR — and why decompose it into MTTD / MTTA / MTTF?
questions.text: MTTD — Mean Time To Detect (incident start → alert) MTTA — Mean Time To Acknowledge (alert → human responding) MTTR — Mean Time To Recover/Repair (detect → service restored) MTBF — Mean Time Between Failures (reliability of the system itself) "Improve MTTR" is too blunt. Decompose it: if detection (MTTD) is slow, invest in monitoring; if acknowledgement (MTTA) is slow, fix the pager/escalation; if repair is slow, invest in runbooks, rollback tooling, and practice. You cannot improve what you cannot localise. MTTR is a distribution, not a point: A single 12-hour outage can dominate the mean. Track P50 and P90 of recovery time, and look at the long tail — that is where catastrophic incidents hide.

questions.q: Production is down. Walk me through your first 10 minutes.
questions.text: 0–2m: Acknowledge page. Declare incident. Become/assign IC. Open a channel. 2–4m: Assess blast radius — which SLO, which users, how many. Set SEV. 4–6m: Check recent changes — last deploy? config push? feature flag? (80% of incidents) 6–8m: Mitigate — rollback / disable flag / failover. Stop the bleeding. 8–10m: Confirm SLI recovering. Post first stakeholder update. Scribe logging. The structure interviewers want: coordinate first (IC + channel), quantify impact, suspect recent change, mitigate before diagnosing, communicate. Most outages correlate with a recent deploy or config change — "what changed in the last hour?" is the single highest-yield question. Say this out loud: "My first instinct is to restore service, not to find root cause. I would roll back the most recent change and confirm the SLI recovers before investigating why." That is exactly the SRE reflex.

questions.q: How do you communicate during an incident — internal and external?
questions.text: Internal: one incident channel = single source of truth; pinned status Cadence: stakeholder updates on a fixed clock (e.g. every 30 min for SEV1) External: public status page — acknowledge fast, even before root cause Template: what’s impacted | since when | what we’re doing | next update time Communication is the Comms Lead’s full-time job in a big incident. Update on a predictable cadence so stakeholders stop interrupting responders to ask "any news?". Externally, acknowledging an issue quickly (even "we’re investigating") builds more trust than silence followed by a perfect explanation. Always promise a next-update time: "Next update by 14:30" stops the flood of status pings and buys the responders space to work.

questions.q: What is a blameless postmortem and why is blamelessness essential?
questions.text: Blameless = focus on systems and contributing factors, never on punishing individuals Assume everyone acted reasonably with the info they had at the time Ask "how did the system allow this?" not "who broke it?" Blamelessness is not about being nice — it is about getting the truth. If engineers fear punishment, they hide details, and you lose the data needed to actually fix the system. The person who "caused" the outage usually did exactly what the system invited them to do; the fix is changing the system, not the person. Human error is a symptom: "Someone ran the wrong command" is the start of the investigation, not the end. Why did a dangerous command have no guardrail, no confirmation, no dry-run? That is the real finding.

questions.q: What goes into a good postmortem document?
questions.text: Summary — what happened, in two sentences Impact — users affected, duration, SLO/budget burned, $ if known Timeline — timestamped, from first symptom to full recovery Root cause(s) — technical + contributing factors What went well / what went poorly / where we got lucky Action items — each with an owner, priority, and ticket link The document exists to drive change, not to file and forget. The most important sections are the timeline (builds shared understanding) and the action items (the only part that prevents recurrence). "Where we got lucky" is underrated — it surfaces the next incident before it happens. Action items without owners die: Every action needs a named owner, a priority, and a tracked ticket. An action item with no owner is a wish, not a fix.

questions.q: How do you do root cause analysis — what is the Five Whys, and its trap?
questions.text: Symptom: checkout returned 500s for 20 minutes Why? DB connections exhausted Why? A deploy raised connections-per-pod and pod count together Why? No connection-pool limit relative to DB max_connections Why? Capacity review not part of the deploy checklist Why? No automated check links pool size to DB limits Five Whys drills past the surface symptom to systemic causes. The trap: it implies a single linear chain. Real incidents usually have multiple contributing factors that combined — a latent bug plus a config change plus a missing alert. Treat it as a tree of contributing factors, not one root. Prefer "contributing factors" over "the root cause": Complex systems fail from combinations. Naming one root cause often hides the others and gives false confidence that one fix is enough.

questions.q: What is toil — and how is it different from overhead?
questions.text: Toil is work that is: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of lasting value, and scales linearly with service size e.g. manually restarting a stuck service, applying the same fix weekly NOT toil: design reviews, writing automation, on-call strategy (overhead/eng work) Toil is the manual, repetitive operational work that grows as your service grows and produces no durable improvement. It is distinct from overhead (meetings, planning) and from real engineering. The danger of toil is that it scales linearly with the system — so without automation, growth eventually consumes the whole team. The test: "If the service doubled in size, would this work double too?" If yes, it is toil and a candidate for automation.

questions.q: What is the SRE toil budget — the 50% rule?
questions.text: Google SRE cap: ≤ 50% of an SRE’s time on toil (ops) ≥ 50% on engineering: automation, reliability projects, tooling If toil exceeds 50% → overflow goes back to the dev team, or hire/automate The 50% rule is a structural defence against the team drowning in operations. If toil consistently exceeds half the team’s time, that is a signal — either automate it away or push the operational load back to the product team that generates it. Measuring toil (surveys, ticket categorisation) is how you know you are over the line. Why the cap matters: Without it, an SRE team gradually becomes a manual-ops team, loses its engineering capacity, and can never dig out — the automation that would save them never gets written.

questions.q: How do you decide what toil to automate first?
questions.text: Score by: frequency × time-per-occurrence × error-proneness Prioritise: high-frequency + risky (e.g. manual prod failover) "Is it worth the time?" — payback = automation cost / time saved per year Quick wins first to build momentum, then the big recurring drains Not all toil is worth automating — automation has a cost too. Rank toil by how often it happens, how long it takes, and how dangerous it is to do by hand. A weekly 2-hour manual failover that occasionally causes outages is a far better target than a yearly 10-minute task. Compute the payback period honestly. Don’t automate a broken process: If the manual process is itself wrong, automating it just produces failures faster. Fix the process, then automate it.

questions.q: What is graceful degradation — give a concrete pattern.
questions.text: Recommendations service down → show generic popular items, not an error page Personalisation timeout → serve cached/default content Non-critical dependency failing → drop the feature, keep the core flow working Feature flags to shed optional load under pressure Graceful degradation keeps the core user journey alive when a non-critical dependency fails. The checkout must work even if recommendations, reviews, and personalisation are all down. Design so that a failing dependency degrades the experience rather than breaking it — fall back to cached or default responses. Rank dependencies by criticality: Map which dependencies are load-bearing for the core journey and which are optional. Optional ones should fail open (degrade); critical ones need redundancy.

questions.q: Explain the circuit breaker pattern and why it prevents cascading failure.
questions.text: Closed — requests flow normally; failures counted Open — failure threshold tripped → fail fast, stop calling the sick service Half-open — after a cooldown, allow a few probes; success → close, failure → re-open A circuit breaker stops a failing downstream from dragging callers down with it. Without it, callers pile up retrying a dead service, exhaust their own threads/connections, and the failure cascades upward. The breaker "trips" after N failures and fails fast, giving the downstream room to recover and protecting the caller’s resources. Retries make cascades worse: Naive retries multiply load on an already-struggling service. Pair circuit breakers with exponential backoff and jitter, and budget retries.

questions.q: What are timeouts, retries with backoff, and jitter — why all three together?
questions.text: Timeout: never wait forever — bound every network call (e.g. 2s) Retry: transient failures may succeed on retry — but cap attempts Backoff: wait longer each retry (1s, 2s, 4s) to let the dependency recover Jitter: randomise the wait so all clients don’t retry in lockstep delay = min(cap, base * 2**attempt) * random(0.5, 1.0) Timeouts bound how long you wait. Retries handle transient blips. Exponential backoff stops retries from hammering a recovering service. Jitter is the subtle one — without it, every client retries at the same instant after an outage, creating a synchronised thundering herd that knocks the service back down. All four work as a set. Retry budgets: Cap retries as a fraction of total traffic (e.g. ≤10%). This prevents retry storms from doubling load during partial outages.

questions.q: What is a thundering herd / cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
questions.text: Cache key expires → thousands of requests miss simultaneously → all hit the DB Fixes: request coalescing / singleflight — one fetch, others wait for it staggered TTLs + jitter on expiry early/async refresh before expiry (refresh-ahead) serve-stale-while-revalidate on backend error A thundering herd happens when many clients act at the same instant — a popular cache key expiring, or all clients reconnecting after an outage. The defence is to break the synchronisation: coalesce duplicate work so only one request rebuilds the cache, jitter expiry times, and serve stale data while a single background refresh runs.

questions.q: What is the difference between health checks: liveness vs readiness vs startup?
questions.text: Liveness — is the process alive? Fail → kubelet restarts the container Readiness — can it serve traffic now? Fail → removed from Service endpoints Startup — has a slow app finished booting? Gates the other two probes readiness should check critical deps; liveness should NOT (avoid restart loops) Confusing these causes outages. Liveness restarts a hung process. Readiness pulls a pod out of rotation without killing it (e.g. while a dependency is briefly unavailable). The classic mistake: putting dependency checks in the liveness probe — a downstream blip then triggers mass restarts, turning a minor degradation into a full outage. Liveness must be cheap and local: If liveness depends on the database, a DB hiccup restarts every pod simultaneously — the opposite of resilience.

questions.q: How do load shedding and rate limiting protect a service under overload?
questions.text: Rate limiting: cap requests per client/key (token bucket, leaky bucket) Load shedding: drop lowest-priority work when saturated to protect the rest Prioritise: shed health-check noise & batch jobs before user-facing traffic Return 429 / 503 with Retry-After rather than collapsing When demand exceeds capacity, doing some work well beats doing all work badly. Rate limiting protects against individual abusive clients; load shedding protects the system as a whole by dropping low-value requests so high-value ones still succeed. A service that sheds 10% of load and serves 90% fast is far better than one that accepts 100% and serves all of it slowly or crashes. Fail fast and explicitly: Returning 429 with Retry-After lets well-behaved clients back off. Silently queueing requests until you OOM helps no one.

questions.q: What is a bulkhead and how does it limit blast radius?
questions.text: Isolate resources so one failure can’t sink the whole ship Separate thread/connection pools per dependency Cell-based / shard-per-tenant architecture One noisy tenant or one slow dependency cannot starve the others Named after a ship’s watertight compartments. If every dependency shares one thread pool, a single slow dependency consumes all threads and the whole service hangs. Bulkheads give each dependency (or each tenant, or each shard) its own isolated resources, so a failure is contained to one compartment instead of flooding the entire service.

questions.q: What is chaos engineering — what is the experiment loop?
questions.text: 1. Define steady state (the SLI that means "healthy") 2. Hypothesise: "killing one AZ will NOT breach the SLO" 3. Inject the failure in production (or close to it), small blast radius first 4. Observe — did steady state hold? abort if it breaks 5. Fix what broke; widen the blast radius; repeat Chaos engineering proactively injects failure to find weaknesses before they cause real outages. It is a disciplined experiment, not random breakage: you start from a hypothesis about steady state, inject one fault with a tight blast radius and a kill switch, and verify the system behaves as you believed. The value is converting unknown failure modes into known, tested ones. Start in staging, then prod: The real value is in production (that’s where the real failure modes live), but earn trust first with small, well-instrumented experiments and an always-ready abort.

questions.q: What is a game day, and how does it differ from a chaos experiment?
questions.text: Game day: scheduled, rehearsed failure scenario run by the whole team Goal: test people + process + tooling, not just the system e.g. "the primary region is gone — execute the failover runbook, timed" Chaos experiment: often automated, tests the system’s technical resilience A game day is a planned drill that exercises the human side — runbooks, on-call response, communication, and the failover procedure — under realistic but controlled failure. Where an automated chaos experiment asks "does the system survive?", a game day also asks "does the team know what to do, and does the runbook actually work?". Both build confidence; game days build muscle memory. Runbooks rot: Game days catch the stale runbook, the expired credential, and the failover step that silently broke three months ago — before a real 3am incident does.

questions.q: How do you do capacity planning for a service?
questions.text: 1. Establish per-unit cost: requests/s served per replica at target latency 2. Forecast demand: organic growth + known events (launch, sale, season) 3. Add headroom: N+1 / N+2 redundancy, plus buffer for spikes 4. Load test to validate the per-unit number, don’t guess it 5. Plan lead time for provisioning (esp. on-prem / quota increases) Capacity planning matches resources to forecast demand with deliberate headroom. The foundation is a measured per-unit capacity (load test it; do not assume), a demand forecast that includes known spikes, and redundancy headroom so losing a node or an AZ does not tip you over. Always include provisioning lead time — cloud quota increases and hardware both take time. Plan for the peak, not the average: A service sized for mean traffic will fall over at the daily peak. Size for peak demand plus the loss of one failure domain.

questions.q: What is autoscaling — and what are its failure modes?
questions.text: HPA — scale pods on CPU/mem/custom metric (e.g. req/s, queue depth) VPA — right-size pod requests/limits Cluster Autoscaler — add/remove nodes when pods can’t schedule Failure modes: scale-up too slow for spikes; flapping; metric lag; node provisioning latency; scaling on the wrong metric Autoscaling adjusts capacity to demand automatically, but it is not magic. It reacts with a lag — for sudden spikes you may still need pre-provisioned headroom or pre-warming. Scaling on CPU when the bottleneck is really queue depth scales the wrong dimension. And aggressive thresholds cause flapping (scale up, down, up) that wastes resources and churns connections. Scale on the bottleneck signal: For a queue worker, scale on queue depth or age, not CPU. The right metric is the one that predicts user-facing latency.

questions.q: Why do retries and naive autoscaling sometimes make outages worse?
questions.text: Metastable failure: system stuck in a bad state even after the trigger is gone Retry storm: failures → retries → more load → more failures (positive feedback) Scale-up under retry storm just feeds the overloaded dependency more traffic Recovery requires shedding load, not adding capacity Some outages are self-sustaining: a brief trigger pushes the system into a state where its own retries keep it down even after the original cause is gone. Adding capacity or retrying harder pours fuel on the fire. The escape is counter-intuitive — shed load, drain queues, disable retries temporarily — let the system drain to a healthy state, then restore traffic gradually. This is the metastable failure trap: The instinct to "add more servers" during an overload-driven outage often deepens it. Recovery is about reducing load, not increasing supply.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs between availability and consistency (CAP) for an SRE?
questions.text: During a network partition you must choose: CP — refuse writes to stay consistent (e.g. config store, ledgers) AP — accept writes, reconcile later (e.g. shopping cart, sessions) Most real systems are tunable per-operation (PACELC: also latency vs consistency) CAP says under a network partition you trade availability against consistency. As an SRE the practical question is per-data-type: a payment ledger must stay consistent (reject the write if unsure), while a shopping cart can stay available and reconcile conflicts later. PACELC extends this: even without partitions, you trade latency for consistency on every read. Map it to the data: Don’t pick CP or AP for "the system" — pick per data flow. Money: consistency. Engagement features: availability. This nuance signals senior judgement.

questions.q: How do you set an SLO for a brand-new service with no historical data?
questions.text: 1. Start from user expectation, not current performance 2. Instrument SLIs first, run for a few weeks, measure the baseline 3. Set an achievable initial SLO near the measured baseline 4. Tighten iteratively as you learn; never set aspirational nines on day one Without data you cannot set a credible SLO, so first instrument the SLIs and observe. Set the initial SLO close to the measured baseline rather than to an aspirational number — an SLO you breach every week trains everyone to ignore it. Treat the SLO as a living target you ratchet tighter as reliability work pays off. An ignored SLO is worse than none: Set it too strict and the team learns the alert means nothing. Start realistic, earn the right to tighten it.

questions.q: How do you make sure postmortem action items actually get done?
questions.text: Each action: named owner + priority + linked ticket in the normal backlog High-priority (esp. SEV1) actions get scheduled, not "best effort" Track completion rate as a team health metric Tie repeat incidents back to unfinished prior actions in the review The graveyard of reliability is the postmortem whose actions were never done — and then the same incident recurs. Put actions in the same tracker as feature work with owners and priorities, report on their completion rate, and when an incident repeats, explicitly trace it to the action item that was skipped. That feedback loop is what gives postmortems teeth. Protect the time: If reliability actions always lose to feature work, the error budget policy is the lever — budget exhaustion forces those actions to the top of the queue.

questions.q: How do you balance reliability against feature velocity in practice?
questions.text: The error budget IS the balancing mechanism Budget healthy → ship fast, take risks, the budget absorbs them Budget low/gone → shift effort to reliability until it refills 100% reliability is the wrong target — it means you shipped too slowly Reliability and velocity are not enemies to be argued about meeting-by-meeting — the error budget makes the trade-off automatic and data-driven. A service that never burns its budget is over-invested in reliability and under-shipping. One that constantly overspends is reckless. The budget keeps you in the productive middle without politics. Say "100% is the wrong target": Interviewers love this line. The right reliability is the level that keeps users happy and leaves room to ship — usually a specific number of nines, never all of them.

questions.q: Design the reliability practice for a 30-engineer startup moving to SRE.
questions.text: Principal-level question — culture, process, and tooling, sequenced sensibly for a small org. Phase 1: Instrument golden signals; define 1–2 SLIs per critical journey Phase 2: Set realistic SLOs + error budgets from measured baselines Phase 3: SLO burn-rate alerting; delete cause-based noise; sane on-call rotation Phase 4: Incident process — IC roles, SEV levels, status page, blameless postmortems Phase 5: Error budget policy signed by product; track toil; automate the worst Phase 6: Game days + chaos experiments once the basics are solid For a small org, do not stand up a separate SRE silo on day one — embed SRE practices into the existing teams. Sequence matters: you cannot have error budgets without SLOs, and you cannot have SLOs without instrumentation. Get measurement and a humane on-call in place first, then process, then the advanced proactive work. Culture is the hard part: The error budget policy only works if product leadership signs the feature-freeze clause in advance, and postmortems only work if they are genuinely blameless. Tooling is the easy 20%; the cultural buy-in is the 80%.

questions.q: What are the main SLI types (availability, latency, throughput, correctness, freshness, durability)?
questions.text: Availability — proportion of valid requests served successfully Latency — proportion of requests faster than a threshold (a ratio, not an avg) Throughput — requests/s the system sustains (often a capacity SLI) Correctness — proportion of responses that are actually right (data pipelines) Freshness — proportion of data younger than X (caches, replicas, pipelines) Durability — proportion of stored data not lost over time (storage systems) Different services need different SLI types. A request/response API cares about availability + latency; a data pipeline cares about freshness + correctness; a storage system cares about durability. Picking the right SLI type for the service is the first design decision — measuring latency on a batch pipeline misses the point entirely. Match SLI type to the user harm: Ask "what does it mean for this service to fail the user?" A stale recommendation (freshness), a wrong total (correctness), and a slow page (latency) are different failures needing different SLIs.

questions.q: Why are averages dangerous for latency SLIs, and how do percentiles fix it?
questions.text: Avg latency 200ms can hide: 95% at 50ms, 5% at 3s (a terrible tail) P50 (median) — typical experience P95 / P99 — the unhappy tail; where real users churn P99.9 — rare but visible at scale (1 in 1000 requests) An average blends the fast majority with the slow tail into one misleading number, and a single slow outlier can swing it while a thousand can hide in it. Percentiles describe the distribution: P99 = "99% of requests were at least this fast." Users remember the slow requests, so SLOs are set on tail percentiles (P95/P99), not the mean. The fan-out trap: If one page makes 100 backend calls, a 1% (P99) per-call slowness means most pages hit at least one slow call. Tail latency compounds dramatically with fan-out — which is why P99 of dependencies matters so much.

questions.q: What's the difference between time-based and event/request-based SLO windows?
questions.text: Request-based: good_requests / valid_requests over the window (a ratio of events) 99.9% = at most 0.1% of individual requests may fail Time-based: good_minutes / total_minutes (was each minute "good"?) 99.9% uptime = at most ~43m of "bad minutes" per 30 days Request-based SLOs count individual events and naturally weight by traffic — an outage during peak burns more budget than the same outage at 3am. Time-based SLOs ask "was this minute healthy?" regardless of how many requests it held, which can over- or under-count impact. Request-based is usually preferred for user-facing APIs because it tracks actual user harm. Traffic weighting matters: A 10-minute outage that hits your busiest hour harms far more users than one at the quietest. Request-based SLOs capture that automatically; time-based ones treat every minute equally.

questions.q: How do you handle SLIs across a multi-step user journey with fan-out?
questions.text: Journey = login → search → add-to-cart → checkout (each a critical step) Option A: per-step SLIs, journey "good" only if ALL critical steps succeed Compound availability: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.996 (worse!) Option B: measure the end-to-end journey success directly when possible Reliability multiplies across a chain of dependencies, so a journey of four 99.9% steps is only ~99.6% reliable end-to-end. Either hold each critical step to a tighter SLO so the product meets target, or instrument the journey outcome directly. The key insight: you cannot set every microservice to the product SLO and expect the product to meet it. Dependencies set your ceiling: Your service can never be more available than the product of its hard dependencies. Map the critical path and budget each step's SLO so the multiplied result hits the journey target.

questions.q: What is the 'valid events' denominator and why does excluding events matter?
questions.text: SLI = good events / VALID events (not / all events) Legitimately excluded from the denominator: 4xx client errors (bad input — not your fault), rate-limited 429s, health checks & synthetic probes, requests during planned maintenance NEVER exclude: real 5xx, timeouts, your own bugs returning 200-with-wrong-data The denominator defines what you are held accountable for. A user sending malformed input (400) is not your reliability failing, so it should not burn budget. But excluding too much is gaming the SLO — if you quietly drop "slow" requests from the denominator, the SLI looks great while users suffer. Define exclusions explicitly and honestly. Watch the 429 nuance: Rate-limiting your own capacity shortfall as 429 and excluding it can hide a real capacity problem. Exclude abusive-client throttling, but count throttling caused by your under-provisioning.

questions.q: How should you treat planned maintenance and dependency outages in an SLO?
questions.text: Planned maintenance: announce windows; either exclude or budget for them explicitly — better long-term: aim for zero-downtime deploys so there's nothing to exclude Dependency outage: usually COUNTS against you (the user still sees failure) — unless you have a contractual hard dependency carve-out Users do not care whether the outage was "planned" or caused by a third party — they experienced downtime. The mature stance: count dependency failures against your SLO because that pressure drives you to add fallbacks and redundancy. For maintenance, prefer engineering away the need (rolling/blue-green deploys) over carving out exclusion windows that erode user trust. Counting dependency failures is a feature: If a flaky third party burns your budget, that is the system correctly telling you to add a circuit breaker, cache, or fallback — not an unfair penalty to exclude.

questions.q: What is an SLO dashboard and what should it show at a glance?
questions.text: Current SLI vs SLO target (are we meeting it right now?) Error budget remaining (% and absolute) for the rolling window Burn rate over multiple windows (1h, 6h, 3d) — trending up or down? Time-to-exhaustion at current burn rate History: SLI over the full window with the SLO line drawn An SLO dashboard turns reliability into something a non-engineer can read in five seconds: are we okay, how much budget is left, and how fast are we spending it. The most actionable single number is "days until budget exhausted at current burn" — it converts a trend into an urgency. Product and engineering should look at the same dashboard. Make it shared and boring: The SLO dashboard should be the neutral arbiter in ship-vs-stabilize conversations. If product and engineering trust the same numbers, the debate becomes arithmetic instead of opinion.

questions.q: Rolling window vs calendar window for SLOs — what's the trade-off?
questions.text: Rolling (e.g. trailing 28 days): budget continuously recovers as old errors age out + smooth, no artificial "reset day" gaming; − harder to explain to stakeholders Calendar (e.g. each month): budget resets on the 1st + simple to communicate, aligns with reporting; − incentivises risky behaviour late in a good month and a "fresh start" hides a bad end-of-month A rolling window is generally preferred operationally: an incident's budget impact fades gradually over the trailing period rather than vanishing at an arbitrary reset. Calendar windows are easier for business reporting but create perverse incentives — teams "spend" leftover budget recklessly before a reset, or a disaster on the 31st is forgiven on the 1st. Common hybrid: Use a 28-day rolling window for alerting/operations (no gaming, smooth) and report a calendar-month summary to leadership for alignment with business cycles.

questions.q: How do SLOs change for batch/data pipelines vs request/response services?
questions.text: Request/response: availability + latency percentiles (per request) Batch / pipeline: Freshness — output is no older than X (data lands by the deadline) Completeness — all expected records processed (no silent drops) Correctness — outputs match validation / reconciliation checks Coverage — % of input successfully processed per run You cannot put a P99-latency SLO on a nightly ETL job. Pipelines are judged on whether fresh, complete, correct data arrives by the time downstream consumers need it. The user-facing SLI is often "is the data in the dashboard/feature no more than N minutes/hours stale?" — freshness — plus correctness checks that catch silent data corruption. Silent data errors are the worst failures: A pipeline that runs "successfully" but emits wrong numbers does more damage than one that visibly fails. Correctness/reconciliation SLIs catch the failures that availability metrics never will.

questions.q: What is error budget burn during a deploy, and how does it gate releases?
questions.text: Progressive delivery gated by SLO/budget: canary 1% → watch SLI + burn rate → 10% → 50% → 100% automatic rollback if burn rate spikes above threshold during rollout Release gate: if remaining budget < threshold, block non-critical deploys Tie deploys to the budget in two ways. First, during a rollout, watch the SLI on the canary and auto-rollback if burn rate jumps — catching a bad release before it hits everyone. Second, before a deploy, if the budget is nearly exhausted, the error budget policy blocks risky changes. This makes the release pipeline reliability-aware rather than blindly shipping. The budget becomes a release valve: Healthy budget → ship freely and fast. Depleted budget → the pipeline itself refuses risky changes. Reliability enforcement moves from meetings into automation.

questions.q: How do you split or allocate an error budget across teams and dependencies?
questions.text: Product SLO 99.9% → allocate the 0.1% budget across the critical path: frontend 0.02% + API 0.03% + DB 0.02% + 3rd-party 0.03% (sums to budget) Each owner gets a sub-budget they're accountable for Shared dependencies: their failures debit the consuming team's budget When many services compose a product, the product budget must be divided so each team knows its share. Allocate sub-budgets along the critical path that multiply to the product target, and make each team accountable for theirs. This turns a vague "the product is unreliable" into "the payments service overspent its sub-budget by 3x this month." Attribution drives ownership: Without per-team budget attribution, reliability is everyone's job and therefore no one's. Sub-budgets make the responsible team visible and accountable.

questions.q: What is a 'silver bullet' / budget exception, and when is overriding the policy justified?
questions.text: Budget exhausted → policy says feature freeze Legitimate override (rare, documented, time-boxed): — a security fix or legal/compliance deadline that must ship — a fix that itself improves reliability Each override is logged, approved by a named owner, and reviewed later The error budget policy must have a defined, rare escape hatch — otherwise the first time the business genuinely must ship during a freeze, people simply ignore the whole policy and it loses all authority. A documented, approved, time-boxed exception ("silver bullet") preserves the policy's credibility while acknowledging reality. The key is that overrides are visible and accountable, not silent. Unlimited exceptions kill the policy: If overrides are easy and unrecorded, the freeze never actually happens. Make them rare, named, and reviewed — so using one has real friction and visibility.

questions.q: How do you choose burn-rate thresholds and windows for multi-window alerts?
questions.text: Goal: balance detection time, budget spent before alert, and reset time Page (fast): burn 14.4x, alert if 1h AND 5m windows exceed → ~2% budget in 1h Page (med): burn 6x, alert if 6h AND 30m windows exceed → ~5% budget in 6h Ticket (slow):burn 1x, alert if 3d AND 6h windows exceed → slow leak, no page Short window confirms "still happening"; long window confirms "sustained" The Google SRE workbook recipe: pick a small number of (burn-rate, long-window, short-window) tiers that map to how much budget you are willing to spend before being alerted. The high burn rate pages fast (an acute outage), lower burn rates open tickets (slow leaks). The short window is an AND-condition that auto-resets the alert quickly once the problem stops, preventing flapping. Why two windows per alert: The long window gives precision (real, sustained burn). The short window gives fast reset and confirms the issue is current — together they cut both false pages and stuck alerts.

questions.q: How do you account for an error budget when traffic is highly variable or seasonal?
questions.text: Request-based budgets self-adjust: more traffic → bigger absolute budget (0.1% of 100M req > 0.1% of 10M req) — peak periods get more headroom Time-based budgets do NOT adjust → a quiet-hour outage costs the same as peak Watch: a flood of cheap/abusive traffic can inflate the denominator and mask errors Request-based error budgets naturally handle variable traffic because the budget scales with volume — but that cuts both ways. A spike of low-value traffic enlarges the denominator and can hide real failures in a percentage, so monitor absolute error counts too. For seasonal businesses (e.g. retail peaks), consider tightening SLOs or pre-provisioning headroom during the critical window. Track both ratio and absolute: A 0.05% error rate sounds fine until it is 0.05% of a billion requests. Alert on burn rate (ratio) but also watch raw error counts so volume changes don't fool you.

questions.q: What's the relationship between error budgets, change freezes, and release cadence?
questions.text: Most incidents follow change → change rate is the main budget-burn lever Healthy budget → high release cadence is fine (fast feedback, small diffs) Burned budget → slow/freeze changes until reliability recovers Counter-intuitive: SMALL frequent releases usually burn LESS budget than big infrequent ones (smaller blast radius, easier rollback) Because change is the dominant cause of incidents, the error budget and your release process are tightly coupled — the budget effectively governs how aggressively you may change production. But "slow down" does not mean "big-bang releases": small, frequent, easily-reversible deploys typically burn less budget than large risky ones. A freeze is the emergency brake, not the steady state. Frequency reduces risk: Counter to intuition, deploying more often (with small diffs + canaries) is usually safer than deploying rarely. The freeze is for recovery, not a model for normal operation.

questions.q: How do you measure and report on error budget to non-technical leadership?
questions.text: Translate to business language: "We have 38% of this month's reliability budget left" "At the current rate it lasts 11 more days" "The checkout incident cost 22% of the budget = N affected orders" Tie budget state to the agreed policy consequence (ship vs freeze) Leadership does not need PromQL — they need the budget framed as a finite, shared resource with clear consequences. Report remaining budget, time-to-exhaustion, and the business impact of recent incidents in plain terms. The point is to make the ship-vs-stabilize trade-off a calm, numeric conversation that product owns alongside engineering, rather than a recurring argument. Connect budget to outcomes they care about: "This outage burned a quarter of the budget and delayed X feature" lands far better than a graph of nines. Speak in orders, revenue, and shipping capacity.

questions.q: What belongs in a good runbook, and how do you keep runbooks from rotting?
questions.text: Per alert: what it means, user impact, how to confirm, how to mitigate, how to escalate Concrete commands/links, not prose — copy-pasteable, with expected output Link the runbook directly from the alert annotation Keep fresh: update after every incident; test in game days; date-stamp A runbook turns a 3am page into a checklist instead of a research project. The best ones are specific and actionable — exact commands, dashboard links, and decision points — and are linked straight from the alert so the responder is not hunting. Runbooks rot the moment the system changes, so the discipline is updating them in every postmortem and exercising them in game days to catch the stale step before a real incident does. A wrong runbook is worse than none: A confidently-stated stale command can make an incident worse. Treat runbooks as code: review, test, and version them — and prefer linking to automation that can't drift.

questions.q: How do you onboard someone to on-call so their first shift isn't terrifying?
questions.text: Shadow shifts: ride along on a veteran's rotation before going solo Reverse-shadow: they drive, the veteran observes and coaches Start as secondary (escalation backup) before primary Provide: runbooks, architecture overview, access verified ahead of time, game-day reps Throwing a new engineer onto primary on-call cold is how you create panic and mistakes. A graduated path — shadow, then reverse-shadow, then secondary, then primary — builds confidence and surfaces gaps (missing access, unclear runbooks) while a mentor is present. Verifying their access and tooling before the shift avoids the classic "I can't even log in" failure during a real page. Psychological safety matters: Make explicit that escalating early is encouraged, not a failure, and that no one is blamed for paging for help. A responder who's afraid to escalate is a slower incident.

questions.q: What on-call metrics should you track, and what do they tell you?
questions.text: Pages per shift / per week — workload + noise (target: low, sustainable) % actionable pages — alert quality (low % = noisy, fix alerts) Pages outside business hours — burnout risk (drives follow-the-sun) Time-to-ack, time-to-mitigate — process health Repeat pages on the same cause — missing permanent fix On-call health is measurable, and the metrics double as a reliability signal. A high page volume or a low actionable-percentage means your alerting is broken, not that your people need to try harder. Repeat pages on the same root cause reveal action items that were never completed. Tracking off-hours pages protects against the burnout that quietly degrades incident response. Noise is an engineering bug: Frame a noisy pager as a defect to be fixed (delete/tune the alert, fix the flaky system), not as the cost of doing business. A shrinking, more-actionable pager is a maturing practice.

questions.q: How should escalation policies be designed?
questions.text: Primary acks within N minutes → else auto-escalate to secondary Secondary → team lead / manager → incident escalation / exec for SEV1 Severity-based: SEV1 escalates faster and wider than SEV3 Define WHO can pull in specialists (DBA, security, network) and HOW An escalation policy guarantees a page is never silently dropped: if the primary doesn't acknowledge within a timeout, it automatically moves to the secondary, then up the chain. Tie escalation speed and breadth to severity — a SEV1 should reach leadership fast, a SEV3 should not wake anyone. Crucially, define the path to specialists (database, security, networking) so responders aren't stuck when the problem is outside their domain. Escalating is a strength: The goal is the fastest path to the right expertise, not heroically soldiering alone. A well-designed policy makes "get the right person" a one-click action.

questions.q: What is follow-the-sun on-call and when is it worth the coordination cost?
questions.text: Teams in 2–3 time zones each cover their daytime → no one is paged at night Needs: ≥2 staffed regions, shared tooling, solid handoff process Handoff: documented state of ongoing incidents at each shift change Follow-the-sun routes pages to whichever region is currently awake, largely eliminating night pages and the burnout they cause. It is powerful but expensive: it requires genuinely staffed teams in multiple time zones and disciplined handoffs so an in-flight incident isn't dropped at the boundary. It is worth it when you have the global headcount and night-page volume is harming retention or response quality. Handoffs are the failure point: An incident mid-investigation at shift change can stall if state isn't transferred cleanly. A written handoff of open incidents + current hypotheses is mandatory, not optional.

questions.q: How do you handle a flapping alert that fires and resolves repeatedly?
questions.text: Add hysteresis: fire above X, resolve only below Y (Y < X) — not the same line Require a duration: "for: 5m" so a momentary blip doesn't page Evaluate over a longer window / use burn rate instead of instantaneous value If the underlying system flaps, fix the system — the alert is a messenger A flapping alert usually means the threshold sits right at the normal operating boundary, so noise crosses it constantly. Fixes: add a for: duration so the condition must persist, use hysteresis (separate fire/resolve thresholds), or evaluate over a longer window. But a chronically flapping metric often signals a real instability (a service near its limit, GC thrash) — silencing the alert without investigating hides a brewing problem. Don't just widen until silent: Suppressing a flapping alert can mask a system that's genuinely teetering at the edge of its capacity. Ask whether the flap is the alert's fault or the system's.

questions.q: What is the difference between symptom-based and cause-based alerting, and why prefer symptoms?
questions.text: Cause-based: alert on every internal cause — high CPU, disk 80%, pod restart → dozens of pages, many non-actionable, alert storm during real incidents Symptom-based: alert on user-facing impact — SLO burn, error rate, latency → one page that means "users are hurting"; causes become investigation, not pages Cause-based alerting tries to page on everything that might be bad and drowns responders in noise — and when a real outage hits, fifty cause-alerts fire at once. Symptom-based alerting pages only when users are actually affected (SLO burn rate), then you diagnose the cause. This collapses many alerts into a few meaningful ones and is the core of the Google SRE alerting philosophy. Page on the symptom, dashboard the causes: One "checkout error budget burning fast" page replaces a wall of CPU/disk/restart alerts. The causes still live on dashboards for diagnosis — they just don't wake anyone.

questions.q: How do you balance automation vs human judgement in incident response (auto-remediation)?
questions.text: Safe to automate: well-understood, low-risk, frequent (restart hung worker, clear a full temp dir, scale out on clear signal, failover a dead replica) Keep human-in-loop: ambiguous, high-blast-radius, rare, data-affecting actions Always: auto-remediation must be observable, rate-limited, and have a kill switch Auto-remediation removes toil and shrinks MTTR for known failure modes, but blind automation can amplify a problem — an auto-restart loop that masks a crash, or an auto-scale that feeds an overloaded dependency. Automate the safe, well-understood, frequent responses; keep humans in the loop for novel or destructive ones. Critically, automated actions must be logged, bounded (rate-limited so they can't run away), and overridable. Automation can hide and amplify: An auto-healer that silently restarts a crashing service every 30s turns a visible incident into an invisible chronic failure. Make auto-actions loud, capped, and easy to disable.

questions.q: How do you decide when to mitigate vs when to keep investigating?
questions.text: Default: mitigate first if a safe mitigation exists (rollback, failover, flag off) Investigate-first only when: no safe mitigation, or mitigating destroys evidence needed to stop active data loss/corruption Time-box investigation: "15 min to find it, else we mitigate broadly" The SRE reflex is mitigate-before-diagnose: a rollback that restores service in two minutes beats a root-cause hunt that fixes it "properly" in two hours while users suffer. The exception is when the safest mitigation would erase the evidence you need (e.g. wiping a corrupted node) or when no mitigation is known — then you investigate, but under a strict time box so you don't drift into an open-ended debugging session while the page burns. State your bias out loud: "Is there a safe rollback? Then we roll back now and investigate after." Interviewers want to hear restore-service-first as the instinct, with a clear exception for data-loss scenarios.

questions.q: What is blast radius and how do you limit it during an incident and by design?
questions.text: During an incident: contain spread — drain the bad node, isolate the failing shard/region, disable the feature flag, stop the rollout By design: cells/shards, per-tenant isolation, region/AZ independence, progressive rollout (1%→canary→fleet), bulkheads, circuit breakers Blast radius is how much of the system (and how many users) a failure can affect. In the moment, you shrink it by isolating the failing component — drain it, fail it over, flag it off. By design, you architect so failures are contained from the start: cell-based architecture, per-tenant/per-shard isolation, and independent failure domains mean one broken cell can't take down the whole fleet. Progressive rollouts limit the blast radius of bad changes . Cells contain failure: If users are partitioned into independent cells, a catastrophic bug hits one cell, not everyone. The cost is operational complexity; the payoff is that "total outage" becomes structurally impossible.

questions.q: How do you run an incident across multiple teams without chaos?
questions.text: One IC owns the whole incident (not one per team) — single decision-maker One incident channel = single source of truth; sub-threads per workstream IC assigns clear workstreams to team leads; no duplicated effort Regular sync cadence (e.g. every 15 min): each lead reports status to IC Multi-team incidents fail when everyone investigates in parallel with no coordination — duplicated work, conflicting fixes, and no one with the full picture. The fix is a single Incident Commander who owns the whole thing (not one IC per team), one shared channel as the source of truth, and explicit workstream ownership so each team knows its lane. A short, regular sync keeps the IC's mental model current without constant interruption. Two people fixing the same thing is dangerous: Without coordination, one engineer's rollback can collide with another's hotfix. The IC's core job is preventing conflicting simultaneous actions.

questions.q: What's the difference between mitigation, resolution, and recovery?
questions.text: Mitigation — stop user pain now (rollback, failover) — symptom gone Recovery — service/SLI back to normal, users unaffected Resolution — the underlying cause is actually fixed (the bug is gone) You can be recovered but not resolved (rolled back, bug still in the code) These are distinct states and conflating them causes premature "all clear" calls. Mitigation removes the immediate user impact; recovery means the system is healthy again; resolution means the root cause is genuinely fixed so it can't recur. A rollback mitigates and recovers but does not resolve — the bug still exists in the codebase. Tracking them separately lets you de-escalate the page (recovered) while the real fix proceeds calmly (toward resolution). De-escalate on recovery, close on resolution: Once the SLI recovers you can stand down the war room, but the incident isn't truly closed until the cause is fixed and action items are tracked.

questions.q: How do you handle a 'gray failure' where the system is partially/intermittently broken?
questions.text: Gray failure: system reports healthy but users see errors/slowness e.g. health check passes but real requests fail; one AZ degraded; 5% of pods bad Detect: measure from the USER's perspective (SLO), not internal health checks Mitigate: shift traffic away from the degraded subset; widen probes to match real usage Gray failures are the hardest incidents: monitoring says green while users suffer, because the health checks test something different from what users actually do. The defense is measuring success from the user's vantage point (end-to-end SLIs, synthetic transactions that mimic real journeys) so the discrepancy surfaces. Mitigation often means draining the subtly-broken subset (a flaky AZ, a bad deploy cohort) even before you fully understand why. Trust the user signal over the green dashboard: When internal metrics say healthy but users report failure, your monitoring has a blind spot. Believe the users and instrument what they experience.

questions.q: What are the most common incident causes, and what does that imply for prevention?
questions.text: Dominant cause: CHANGE — deploys, config pushes, feature flags, infra edits Then: capacity/overload, dependency failure, expired certs/credentials, bad data/migrations, DNS, and the classic full disk Implication: invest in safe-change tooling (canary, rollback, config validation) The large majority of incidents are triggered by a change humans made, which is why "what changed in the last hour?" is the highest-yield first question. This directly shapes prevention: the biggest reliability wins come from making change safe — progressive rollouts, automatic rollback, config validation/linting, and pre-deploy checks — plus guarding the boring recurring killers (cert/credential expiry, disk space, DNS) with proactive monitoring. Reliability is mostly change management: Since change causes most incidents, a great deploy pipeline (canary + auto-rollback + validation) prevents more outages than almost any other single investment.

questions.q: How do you preserve evidence during an incident without slowing recovery?
questions.text: Capture cheaply BEFORE destructive mitigation: snapshot the bad node/VM, grab logs/heap/thread dumps, screenshot dashboards, note timestamps Then mitigate (drain/replace) — you kept a copy to investigate later The scribe's timeline IS evidence — actions, times, decisions There is a real tension: the fastest mitigation (kill and replace the bad node) can destroy the evidence needed for the postmortem. Resolve it by capturing volatile state cheaply first — snapshot the VM, pull thread/heap dumps and logs, screenshot the dashboards at peak — which takes seconds, then mitigate freely against the copy. Recovery still comes first; you just don't throw away the corpse. One person captures, the rest recover: Assign someone to grab snapshots/dumps in parallel while others mitigate. You rarely have to choose between speed and evidence if you delegate.

questions.q: When and how do you declare a security incident differently from a reliability incident?
questions.text: Reliability incident: restore service fast, communicate openly, public status page Security incident: PRESERVE evidence first, LIMIT who knows (need-to-know), involve security/legal, do NOT tip off the attacker, careful external comms Trigger: suspected breach, data exfiltration, unauthorized access, ransomware Security incidents invert several reliability instincts. Where a reliability incident favors broad communication and fast service restoration, a security incident favors confidentiality (need-to-know to avoid alerting the attacker), evidence preservation for forensics and legal, and a different escalation path (security team, legal, possibly law enforcement). Rebooting or "cleaning" a compromised host can destroy forensic evidence and may not remove the attacker. Recognizing which type you're in changes the entire playbook. Don't run a breach like an outage: Powering off or wiping to "recover" can erase evidence and leave backdoors. Escalate to security, contain at the network layer, and follow the IR plan — not the reliability runbook.

questions.q: What are the three pillars of observability, and how do they work together?
questions.text: Metrics — cheap, aggregatable numbers over time (rates, latencies, counts) Logs — discrete timestamped events with detail (what exactly happened) Traces — the path of one request across services (where time went) Workflow: metrics tell you SOMETHING is wrong → traces tell you WHERE → logs tell you WHY (the detailed error at that span) Metrics, logs, and traces answer different questions and are strongest together. Metrics are cheap and great for alerting and dashboards ("error rate is up"), but can't explain a single request. Traces follow one request across service boundaries to localize the slow/failing hop. Logs give the granular detail at that point. The mature flow: alert on metrics, drill with traces, confirm with logs. Observability vs monitoring: Monitoring answers known questions ("is CPU high?"); observability lets you ask new questions about unknown failure modes after the fact, via high-cardinality data you didn't have to predict in advance.

questions.q: What is cardinality in metrics, and why does it cause monitoring outages?
questions.text: Cardinality = number of unique label/tag combinations on a metric http_requests{method, status, endpoint} → low, fine …{user_id} or {request_id} → MILLIONS of series → explosion Effect: Prometheus/TSDB memory blows up, ingestion slows, queries time out Each unique combination of label values creates a separate time series. Adding a high-cardinality label like user ID, request ID, or raw URL with IDs can create millions of series and OOM your metrics backend — ironically taking down the monitoring during an incident. The rule: labels must be bounded, low-cardinality dimensions (status code, method, region), never unbounded identifiers. Unbounded detail belongs in logs/traces, not metric labels. Cardinality kills monitoring systems: A single innocent {user_id} label can OOM Prometheus. Keep metric labels bounded; push per-request detail to traces and logs where high cardinality is expected.

questions.q: What is distributed tracing, and what are spans, trace context, and sampling?
questions.text: Trace = one request's journey; made of nested SPANS (one per operation) Trace context (trace_id, span_id) propagates via headers across services Sampling: keep only a fraction (head sampling) or decide after (tail sampling) tail sampling can keep all SLOW/ERROR traces, drop boring fast ones Distributed tracing reconstructs a single request's path across many services as a tree of timed spans, so you can see exactly which hop consumed the latency. It works by propagating a trace context (IDs) through request headers so each service stamps its span onto the same trace. Because tracing every request is expensive, you sample — and tail-based sampling is powerful because it can retain all the error/slow traces (the interesting ones) while discarding the routine fast ones. Tail sampling for the tail latency: Head sampling might drop the rare slow request you most need. Tail sampling decides after the trace completes, so you keep the errors and P99 outliers and throw away the cheap successes.

questions.q: How do you avoid metrics, logging, and tracing costs spiraling out of control?
questions.text: Logs: sample high-volume INFO/debug; keep all ERROR; structured + tiered retention Metrics: control cardinality; drop unused series; aggregate at the edge Traces: sample (tail-sample for errors/slow); short retention for routine traces Tiered storage: hot (days, fast) → warm → cold/archive (cheap, slow) Observability data volume grows with traffic and can rival or exceed infra cost. Control it deliberately: sample verbose logs while keeping all errors, cap metric cardinality and prune dead series, sample traces (tail-based to keep the interesting ones), and use tiered retention so recent data is fast/expensive and old data is cheap/archived. The goal is keeping the signal you'd actually query during an incident, not hoarding everything forever. Observability can cost more than the service: Unbounded log/metric/trace ingestion is a common runaway cloud bill. Treat telemetry volume as a budgeted resource: sample, aggregate, and expire deliberately.
