questions.q: What is structured logging and why does it matter at scale?
questions.text: Unstructured: log.info("user 123 failed checkout: timeout") → hard to query Structured (JSON): {event, user_id, action:"checkout", error:"timeout", trace_id} Now queryable: count by error, filter by action, JOIN to a trace_id Always include: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, request_id Structured logs are machine-parseable key/value (usually JSON) instead of free-text prose. At scale this is the difference between grepping millions of lines and running a query like "count checkout failures by error type in the last hour." The single highest-value field is a correlation ID (trace_id/request_id) that links a log line to its distributed trace and to every other log for the same request — turning three separate tools into one investigation. Correlation IDs tie it together: Propagate a request/trace ID into every log line and span. Then one ID pivots you across logs, traces, and metrics for a single user's failing request — the fastest path from symptom to cause.

questions.q: What is the RED method vs the USE method, and when do you use each?
questions.text: RED (services / request-driven): Rate, Errors, Duration → "how is this service serving requests?" USE (resources / hosts): Utilization, Saturation, Errors → "is this resource (CPU, disk, queue) healthy?" Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation) blend both views RED is the request-centric lens for services — request rate, error rate, and duration (latency) tell you how a service is treating its callers. USE is the resource-centric lens for infrastructure — utilization, saturation, and errors of a CPU, disk, or queue. They're complementary: RED tells you the service is slow; USE tells you the disk it depends on is saturated. The four golden signals are essentially the union of both. Two lenses on one system: Use RED to monitor every service uniformly and USE to drill into the resource behind a struggling service. Saturation appears in both because a saturating resource is the leading indicator of trouble.

questions.q: What are SLO-based alerts vs traditional threshold alerts in practice?
questions.text: Threshold: "page if error rate > 1%" — fixed line, no notion of budget → pages on harmless brief blips; or misses a slow steady leak under the line SLO-based: "page if burning budget fast enough to breach the SLO" → precision (only when SLO is genuinely at risk) + good reset behaviour A static threshold doesn't know how much unreliability you can actually afford. It pages on a 30-second spike that costs almost no budget, yet can stay silent during a sustained sub-threshold leak that quietly drains the whole month's budget. SLO/burn-rate alerts tie the page directly to risk of breaching the target, so you're woken when (and only when) the SLO is genuinely threatened — far higher precision and far less noise. Alert on consequence, not number: "We will breach our reliability target if this continues" is more actionable than "a metric crossed an arbitrary line." That's why mature teams alert on burn rate.

questions.q: How do synthetic monitoring and real user monitoring (RUM) complement each other?
questions.text: Synthetic: scripted probes hit critical journeys on a schedule from fixed locations + consistent baseline, catches outages even at 3am with zero traffic, pre-prod RUM: telemetry from ACTUAL users' browsers/apps + real devices, networks, geographies; catches what synthetics miss Synthetic monitoring runs controlled, scripted transactions so you have a steady signal independent of traffic — it detects a broken checkout at 3am before any real user hits it, and gives a clean baseline for trends. RUM captures the messy reality of real users on real devices and networks, surfacing problems synthetics never script. Together: synthetics for consistent, always-on detection of critical paths; RUM for the true breadth of user experience. Synthetics detect, RUM explains: A synthetic probe tells you the path is down even with no traffic; RUM tells you that 2% of users on a specific mobile network see failures. You want both.

questions.q: What is idempotency and why is it essential for retries and reliability?
questions.text: Idempotent op: doing it twice == doing it once (no extra side effect) PUT /resource/123 {state} — idempotent. POST /charge — NOT (double charge!) Make POST safe: client sends an Idempotency-Key; server dedupes by key Critical because: retries, at-least-once delivery, and network ambiguity are everywhere In distributed systems you can never be sure a request that timed out didn't actually succeed — so clients retry, and message queues deliver at-least-once. If the operation isn't idempotent, that retry double-charges the card or duplicates the order. Idempotency keys let the server recognize a repeat and return the original result instead of re-executing. This is foundational: safe retries (and thus most reliability patterns) depend on idempotent operations. The timeout ambiguity: A timeout doesn't mean the request failed — it might have succeeded and the response was lost. Without idempotency, the "safe" retry causes the very damage you feared. Design write paths to dedupe.

questions.q: What's the difference between failover, fallback, and failing open vs closed?
questions.text: Failover: switch to a standby/replica when primary dies (DB replica, secondary region) Fallback: serve a degraded alternative when a dependency fails (cached/default data) Fail open: on failure, ALLOW (e.g. auth check down → let traffic through) Fail closed: on failure, DENY (e.g. payment check down → reject) These are distinct resilience choices. Failover swaps to redundant capacity; fallback degrades gracefully to a cheaper answer. Fail-open vs fail-closed is the security/safety decision for what to do when a check can't run: a non-critical feature flag service should fail open (don't break the site), but an authorization or payment check should fail closed (deny rather than risk a breach or fraud). Choosing wrong is a classic outage or security hole. The choice depends on the harm: Fail open when blocking causes more harm than allowing (availability-first); fail closed when allowing causes more harm than blocking (safety/security-first). Decide this deliberately per check.

questions.q: How do you design for multi-region/multi-AZ resilience, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.text: Multi-AZ: spread across availability zones in one region — survives an AZ loss, low latency, synchronous replication feasible — the baseline for HA Multi-region: survives a whole-region outage — but cross-region latency forces async replication → data lag, conflict resolution, much higher cost/complexity Active-active vs active-passive (warm standby) vs pilot-light vs backup-restore Multi-AZ is the standard high-availability baseline: zones are close enough for synchronous replication, so you survive a datacenter failure with no data loss. Multi-region defends against losing an entire region but the physics of distance forces asynchronous replication — meaning potential data loss (nonzero RPO), conflict handling, and steep cost. The DR spectrum (backup-restore → pilot-light → warm standby → active-active) trades cost against RTO/RPO; pick the cheapest tier that meets the business's recovery objectives. Multi-region is not free HA: It introduces async replication lag, split-brain risk, and data-conflict resolution. Most workloads need multi-AZ; reserve multi-region for those whose region-outage cost truly justifies the complexity.

questions.q: What is backpressure and how does it differ from load shedding?
questions.text: Backpressure: signal UPSTREAM to slow down (bounded queues, flow control, TCP windowing, reactive streams) — "I'm full, stop sending so fast" Load shedding: DROP work you can't handle (return 429/503) — "I'll refuse this" Backpressure propagates the limit; shedding discards at the limit Both protect an overloaded system but differently. Backpressure pushes the constraint upstream so producers slow to the rate the consumer can sustain — bounded queues that block or signal when full, rather than growing without limit until OOM. Load shedding instead drops excess work at the overloaded service (fast 429/503) to protect throughput for the requests it does accept. Often you want both: backpressure where the pipeline allows producers to slow, shedding at the edge for traffic you can't push back on. Unbounded queues are a trap: A queue with no limit doesn't prevent overload — it hides it until memory runs out, turning a slowdown into a crash. Bound queues so they exert backpressure or shed.

questions.q: How do you make deployments safe: blue-green, canary, and rolling — trade-offs?
questions.text: Rolling: replace instances batch by batch — no extra capacity, but mixed versions run simultaneously; slower rollback Blue-green: full parallel new env, flip traffic atomically — instant rollback, but ~2x capacity during the switch Canary: route a small % to the new version, watch SLOs, then ramp — best risk control, needs good metrics + automation All three reduce deploy risk differently. Rolling is resource-efficient but you briefly run two versions and rollback means rolling back. Blue-green gives an instant, clean cutover and rollback (just flip the router) at the cost of double capacity. Canary is the safest for catching real-world problems: expose 1% of users, watch the SLO/burn rate, and auto-rollback on regression before most users are affected. Canary + automated analysis is the gold standard for high-risk changes. Canary catches what staging can't: Real traffic, real data, real scale expose bugs staging misses. A metrics-gated canary with auto-rollback limits the blast radius of those bugs to a tiny fraction of users.

questions.q: What database reliability patterns matter most: replication, failover, connection pools?
questions.text: Replication: sync (no data loss, higher latency) vs async (lag, possible loss on failover) Failover: automated promotion of a replica; beware split-brain (two primaries) Connection pools: cap connections; pool exhaustion = app-wide stall under load Read replicas for scale; mind replication lag for read-after-write consistency Databases are usually the hardest part of reliability because they're stateful. Synchronous replication avoids data loss but adds write latency; async is faster but a failover can lose the un-replicated tail (nonzero RPO). Automated failover must guard against split-brain (a fencing/quorum mechanism so two nodes never both accept writes). And the silent killer under load is connection-pool exhaustion: too many app instances × pool size exceeding the DB's max connections stalls everything — a frequent root cause in postmortems. Split-brain corrupts data: If a network partition lets two nodes both believe they're primary, you get divergent writes that are painful to reconcile. Proper failover needs quorum/fencing, not just "promote the replica."

questions.q: How do you safely run zero-downtime schema migrations on a live database?
questions.text: Expand/contract (parallel change): 1. Expand: add new column/table, backward-compatible (old code still works) 2. Migrate: dual-write + backfill data in batches 3. Switch: deploy code that reads/writes the new shape 4. Contract: drop the old column once nothing uses it Avoid: blocking locks, big ALTERs on huge tables during peak You can't take a busy database down to change its schema, and a change must be compatible with both the old and new application code during the rollout. The expand/contract pattern decouples schema change from code change: add the new structure first (non-breaking), backfill and dual-write, switch the code over, then remove the old structure later. This avoids the two classic disasters: a long-locking ALTER that freezes the table, and a migration that breaks whichever code version isn't deployed yet. Schema and code rollouts must overlap safely: Never ship a migration that only works with code that isn't fully deployed. Expand/contract guarantees every intermediate state is runnable and rollback-able.

questions.q: What is a dead man's switch / heartbeat alert, and why monitor for silence?
questions.text: Normal alert fires when something BAD happens (error rate up) Dead man's switch fires when something EXPECTED stops happening e.g. "the cron didn't run", "no heartbeat from the agent in 5m", "the monitoring pipeline itself went silent" Implement: a job pings a watchdog on a schedule; missing ping = alert Most alerting watches for bad signals — but what if the thing that emits signals dies? A crashed monitoring agent, a cron that silently stopped, or a broken metrics pipeline produces no error, just silence, and a naive system stays green. A dead man's switch (heartbeat) inverts this: it expects a regular ping and alerts on its absence. It's the safeguard that catches "the monitoring is down" and "the backup job hasn't run in a week." Monitor the monitor: The scariest outages are the ones your dashboards can't see because the dashboards themselves broke. A heartbeat to an external watchdog catches the silence that absence-of-errors would otherwise hide.

questions.q: When should you trigger a postmortem, and should near-misses get one?
questions.text: Always: any SEV1/SEV2, any customer-visible outage, any SLO breach Also: near-misses ("we got lucky") and surprising incidents, even if small Threshold should be written down so it's not a judgement call each time Define postmortem triggers in advance so they aren't relitigated under pressure: all high-severity and customer-facing incidents, and any SLO breach. The often-skipped but high-value case is the near-miss — an incident that almost happened but was caught by luck. Writing those up surfaces the latent weakness before it becomes a real outage, and it's far cheaper to learn from a near-miss than from the failure it predicts. Near-misses are free lessons: "Where we got lucky" is the section that prevents next quarter's SEV1. A culture that writes up near-misses is one that fixes problems before they bite.

questions.q: How do you keep a postmortem genuinely blameless when human action triggered it?
questions.text: Reframe "who" into "what allowed this": missing guardrail, no dry-run, no confirm Assume good intent + reasonable action given the info at the time (hindsight bias!) Use neutral language: "the deploy proceeded" not "Alice broke prod" Counterfactual test: would a competent peer likely have done the same? Usually yes When "someone ran the wrong command" is the trigger, blamelessness means treating that as the start of the investigation, not the end. The real questions: why did a dangerous command have no confirmation, no dry-run, no guardrail? Guard against hindsight bias — what's obvious after the fact wasn't obvious in the moment with partial information. If a competent engineer would plausibly have made the same choice, the system is the problem, not the person. Blame destroys your data source: The moment people fear punishment, they stop volunteering the details you need. Blamelessness isn't kindness for its own sake — it's how you get the truth that lets you actually fix the system.

questions.q: What is a 'systems thinking' view of failure vs the 'bad apple' view?
questions.text: Bad-apple (old view): failure = a flawed person; fix = remove/punish/retrain them Systems view: failure emerges from interactions, conditions, and missing safeguards the operator is one component in a system that set them up to fail Fix the conditions, not the individual The "bad apple" theory says incidents are caused by bad individuals and the fix is to find and remove them — but it predicts the next person in the same flawed system will fail the same way, and it teaches everyone to hide mistakes. The systems view (Sidney Dekker, the safety field) sees failure as emerging from the whole system: the conditions, tooling, time pressure, and missing guardrails that made the error likely. You improve reliability by changing those conditions. The second story: Behind "human error" is always a second story — why that action made sense at the time. Investigating the second story finds the systemic fix; stopping at "human error" guarantees recurrence.

questions.q: How do you aggregate learnings across many postmortems to find systemic patterns?
questions.text: Tag incidents: cause category, affected system, contributing factors, detection gap Quarterly review: cluster across incidents — same cause recurring? same blind spot? Trend: are config changes the top trigger? then invest in config validation Track action-item completion + repeat-incident rate as program health Individual postmortems fix individual incidents; aggregate analysis fixes the system . By tagging incidents with structured categories and reviewing them in aggregate, you spot the patterns invisible from any single one — e.g. "40% of our SEV2s this quarter were config pushes with no validation," which justifies a specific investment. This turns reactive postmortems into a proactive reliability roadmap and is a hallmark of a mature program. Look for the meta-pattern: One incident says "fix this bug." Ten incidents tagged the same way say "build the guardrail that prevents this whole class." Aggregate review is where the high-leverage fixes come from.

questions.q: What is the difference between proximate cause, root cause, and contributing factors?
questions.text: Proximate cause: the immediate trigger (the deploy that broke checkout) Root cause(s): the deeper systemic reasons (no canary, no rollback automation) Contributing factors: conditions that combined (peak traffic + low budget + stale runbook) The proximate cause is what visibly set off the incident, but stopping there fixes only the surface. Root causes are the systemic gaps that let the trigger cause harm. Most real incidents have multiple contributing factors that aligned — a latent bug plus a config change plus a missing alert plus peak load. Naming a single "root cause" usually hides the others and breeds false confidence that one fix is enough. Swiss cheese model: Incidents happen when holes in several layers of defense line up. There's rarely one cause — there's a stack of small gaps. Fix several layers, not just the one nearest the symptom.

questions.q: How do you balance investing in postmortem action items against new feature work?
questions.text: Put reliability actions in the SAME backlog as features, with real priority High-priority (SEV1-derived) actions: scheduled commitments, not "best effort" Error budget policy is the lever: budget gone → reliability work jumps the queue Track completion %; tie repeat incidents to skipped actions publicly Reliability work perpetually loses to feature work unless there's a forcing function — and the error budget is exactly that lever: when the budget is exhausted, the agreed policy promotes reliability action items above features automatically, removing the politics. Between freezes, the discipline is treating action items as real prioritized backlog with owners, and making the cost of skipping them visible by tracing each repeat incident back to the fix that was deferred. The budget ends the argument: Instead of debating "reliability vs features" every sprint, the error budget decides it with data — healthy budget ships features, burned budget ships fixes. That's the whole point of the mechanism.

questions.q: How do you measure toil so you actually know if you're over the 50% line?
questions.text: Categorise tickets/interrupts: toil vs engineering vs overhead Time-tracking or periodic surveys ("what % of last week was manual ops?") Track: toil hours/week, top toil sources, trend over time Tag on-call interrupts so recurring manual fixes become visible You can't manage toil you don't measure, and "it feels like a lot" won't justify automation investment. Practical measurement: categorize work (toil/engineering/overhead), use lightweight surveys or ticket tagging to estimate the toil fraction, and track the trend. The output is a ranked list of the biggest toil sources — which is exactly your automation backlog — plus an honest read on whether the team is over the 50% cap and drowning. Make toil visible to justify the fix: "We spend 14 hours/week manually doing X" turns an abstract complaint into a fundable automation project with a clear payback. Measurement is what unlocks the time to escape toil.

questions.q: What is the 'automation paradox' — when does automating make things worse?
questions.text: Automate a flaky/wrong process → it fails faster and at larger scale Over-automation → humans lose the skill + situational awareness to intervene when the automation hits a case it wasn't built for (the rare, scary incident) Opaque automation → nobody understands what it does during an incident Automation removes toil but introduces its own risks. Automating a broken process just industrializes the breakage. And the ironies-of-automation problem: the more you automate, the rarer manual operation becomes, so when the automation faces a situation it can't handle, the humans are out of practice and lack context exactly when judgment matters most. Good automation is observable, bounded, and keeps humans able to understand and override it. Ironies of automation: Automating the routine leaves humans only the hardest, rarest cases — with the least practice. Design automation that explains itself and degrades to a human gracefully, not a black box that fails baffling.

questions.q: What is 'toil debt' and how is it like technical debt?
questions.text: Each unautomated manual process is a recurring tax that compounds with scale Deferring automation = borrowing time now, paying interest every week forever Compounds: toil crowds out the engineering time needed to remove the toil The death spiral: more services → more toil → less time to automate → more toil Toil debt behaves like technical debt: every manual process you don't automate is a loan whose interest is paid in operational hours every single week, and it compounds as the system grows. The dangerous feedback loop is that toil consumes the very engineering capacity required to eliminate it — a team past the tipping point can never dig out because there's no time left to build the automation. The 50% cap exists precisely to prevent this spiral. The spiral is real and one-directional: Once toil exceeds engineering time, the team can only fall further behind. Defend the engineering-time floor aggressively — pushing overflow toil back to product teams if needed — before the spiral starts.

questions.q: How does self-service / platform engineering reduce toil at the org level?
questions.text: Toil source: SRE manually fulfilling repeated dev requests (envs, access, deploys) Fix: build a self-service platform — golden paths, paved roads, internal tooling Devs self-serve common needs safely; SRE builds the platform, not tickets Guardrails baked in → safe by default, no SRE in the loop for routine work A lot of SRE toil is acting as a manual gateway: provisioning environments, granting access, running deploys on behalf of developers. Platform engineering eliminates this class wholesale by building self-service "paved roads" — internal developer platforms where teams accomplish common tasks safely without filing a ticket. The SRE/platform team's leverage shifts from doing the work to building the system that lets everyone do it safely. Guardrails are encoded so the easy path is the safe path. From ticket-takers to platform-builders: The highest-leverage move against org-wide toil is making the common case self-service with safety built in. One paved road removes thousands of future tickets.

questions.q: What is GitOps and how does it reduce operational toil and risk?
questions.text: Desired state declared in Git; a controller (ArgoCD/Flux) reconciles cluster → Git Deploy = merge a PR; rollback = revert a commit; audit = git log Drift detection: controller flags/repairs manual changes back to declared state No manual kubectl to prod → fewer fat-finger incidents GitOps makes Git the single source of truth for infrastructure/app state and a controller continuously reconciles reality to it. This cuts toil and risk together: deploys become reviewed PRs, rollbacks become reverts, the full audit trail is the git history, and manual drift is automatically detected and corrected. It removes the error-prone manual kubectl -to-prod pattern (a common incident source) and gives you a declarative, repeatable, reviewable change process. Git as the control plane: Everything goes through review and is recorded, rollback is trivial, and the cluster self-heals toward the declared state. Reviewed-change-only is both less toil and far fewer fat-finger outages.

questions.q: How do you justify reliability/automation investment to management (ROI)?
questions.text: Quantify the toil: hours/week × loaded cost = recurring spend being wasted Quantify incident cost: downtime $ + eng-hours + churn/reputation Automation ROI: build cost vs annual hours saved → payback period Frame reliability as revenue protection + velocity (budget enables shipping) Management funds business cases, not vibes. Translate reliability work into money and time: the recurring cost of the toil being eliminated (hours × cost), the cost of the incidents being prevented (downtime revenue, engineering time, customer churn), and the payback period of the automation. Reframe reliability not as a cost center but as revenue protection and a velocity enabler — a healthy error budget is what lets the business ship features safely. Speak in payback and risk: "This $X of engineering saves Y hours/week (payback in N months) and reduces our exposure to $Z outages" gets funded. A graph of nines does not.

questions.q: What are the principles of chaos engineering (steady state, blast radius, abort)?
questions.text: 1. Define steady state as a measurable SLI (the system's "healthy" signal) 2. Hypothesise steady state HOLDS under a specific fault 3. Minimise blast radius — smallest experiment that tests the hypothesis 4. Always have an abort / kill switch ready before you start 5. Run in production (eventually) — that's where the real failure modes are Chaos engineering is disciplined experimentation, not random breakage. You start from a measurable definition of "healthy" (steady state), form a falsifiable hypothesis ("losing one AZ won't breach the SLO"), inject the smallest fault that tests it with a tight blast radius, and keep an instant abort ready. The aim is to convert unknown failure modes into known, tested ones — and the highest-value experiments run in production, because that's the only place the real failure modes live. Hypothesis + abort make it safe: Without a steady-state metric and a kill switch, you're not doing chaos engineering — you're just causing an outage. The rigor is what makes injecting failure in prod responsible.

questions.q: How do you introduce chaos engineering to a skeptical organization safely?
questions.text: Start in staging/pre-prod to build the tooling, process, and trust First prod experiments: tiny blast radius, off-peak, announced, on-call ready Begin with failures you're fairly confident you survive (prove the safety net) Show value early: each experiment finds + fixes a real gap → build credibility You earn the right to run chaos in production incrementally. Start in staging to prove the tooling and the abort mechanism work, then run the first production experiments small, off-peak, announced, with on-call standing by — and begin with faults you're reasonably confident the system already survives, so the early runs validate the safety net rather than cause outages. Each experiment that finds and fixes a real weakness builds the organizational trust to go bigger. Trust is earned per experiment: A few small, well-run experiments that quietly prevent future incidents convert skeptics faster than any slide deck. Grow blast radius only as confidence grows.

questions.q: What failure modes are worth injecting (latency, errors, resource, dependency, zone loss)?
questions.text: Latency: inject delay into a dependency → do timeouts/circuit breakers work? Errors: make a dependency return 5xx → does fallback/degradation kick in? Resource: CPU/memory/disk pressure → does autoscaling/shedding respond? Dependency down: kill a downstream → is the blast radius contained? Zone/region loss: kill an AZ → does failover hold the SLO? Network: partition, packet loss, DNS failure → split-brain? stale cache? Pick faults that exercise your resilience assumptions. Latency injection is especially valuable because slow is often worse than down — it ties up resources and reveals missing timeouts. Error injection tests fallbacks and circuit breakers; resource pressure tests autoscaling and shedding; dependency and zone failures test isolation and failover. Network faults (partitions, DNS) surface the subtle split-brain and stale-data bugs that are nearly impossible to find any other way. Latency is the sneaky one: Systems usually handle a clean "down" but choke on "slow" — a laggy dependency with no timeout cascades into resource exhaustion. Injecting latency finds missing timeouts before prod does.

questions.q: How do you plan and run an effective game day?
questions.text: Before: pick a realistic scenario, define success, brief participants, set safety bounds During: inject the failure, let the team respond via real runbooks/tools (don't help) Observe: time the response, note where runbooks/tooling/comms broke down After: blameless review → fix the gaps → schedule the next one A game day is a rehearsed, realistic failure drill that tests people, process, and tooling together — not just the system. Plan a concrete scenario ("primary region is gone — execute failover"), define what success looks like, and set safety bounds. During the drill, let the team respond with the actual runbooks and tools so you discover the stale step, the expired credential, or the broken failover before a real 3am incident does. The debrief turns those discoveries into fixes. Game days build muscle memory: The first time someone executes the regional failover should not be during a real outage. Drills make the rare procedure familiar and expose the gaps while the stakes are low.

questions.q: What's the relationship between chaos engineering and SLOs/error budgets?
questions.text: Steady state = your SLI; "experiment passes" = SLO not breached during injection Run experiments only when error budget is healthy (you can afford a surprise) A chaos-induced budget burn is a found weakness — cheaper now than in a real outage Don't run risky chaos during a freeze / depleted budget SLOs give chaos engineering its definition of success: the experiment validates that injecting a fault does not breach the SLO (steady state holds). The error budget governs when to run — you experiment while the budget is healthy enough to absorb a surprise, and you pause risky experiments when the budget is depleted or you're in a freeze. A weakness found by chaos burns a little budget on purpose, which is vastly cheaper than discovering it via a real, unplanned outage. Spend a little budget to save a lot: A controlled experiment that burns 1% of budget to expose a flaw prevents the uncontrolled incident that would have burned the whole month's. Chaos is budget well spent — when you have it.

questions.q: How do you test disaster recovery and validate your RTO/RPO are real?
questions.text: RTO = target time to restore service; RPO = max acceptable data loss Test by actually executing recovery: restore from backup, fail over the region Measure ACTUAL recovery time + data loss → compare to the targets Untested DR is a hope, not a plan — most DR plans fail their first real test RTO and RPO are just numbers on a slide until you've actually executed the recovery and measured the real results. Regularly test DR by truly restoring from backups and performing region failovers, timing the actual recovery and quantifying the actual data loss, then compare against your stated objectives — they're often far apart. The classic discoveries: backups that never restored, a failover runbook with a broken step, or replication lag that means real RPO is hours, not minutes. An untested backup is not a backup: The first real test of most DR plans is a real disaster, and that's when people learn the restore doesn't work. Rehearse recovery on a schedule and measure it against RTO/RPO.

questions.q: How do you load test properly, and what's the difference between load, stress, and soak tests?
questions.text: Load test: expected peak traffic → does it meet latency/error SLOs at that load? Stress test: ramp PAST capacity → find the breaking point + how it fails Soak test: sustained load for hours/days → find leaks, fragmentation, slow degradation Spike test: sudden surge → does autoscaling/shedding cope with the ramp? Different tests answer different questions. A load test validates you meet SLOs at expected peak. A stress test pushes past capacity to find where and how the system breaks (graceful degradation vs cliff). A soak test runs for a long time to catch problems that only appear with duration — memory leaks, connection-pool exhaustion, log-disk fill, fragmentation. A spike test checks whether reactive scaling can handle a sudden surge given its lag. Test realistically: real traffic patterns, real data sizes, production-like environment. Soak tests catch the silent killers: A memory leak or a slowly-filling disk passes every short load test and then takes down production at 2am on day three. Only sustained tests reveal time-dependent failures.

questions.q: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling, and their limits?
questions.text: Vertical (scale up): bigger machine — simple, but a hard ceiling + single point of failure Horizontal (scale out): more machines — near-limitless, but needs statelessness, load balancing, and distributed-system complexity Stateful (databases) is hard to scale horizontally → sharding/partitioning Vertical scaling is the easy first lever — just use a larger instance — but it hits a physical ceiling and leaves you with one big single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more instances for effectively unlimited growth and better fault tolerance, but it requires the workload to be stateless (or to externalize state) plus load balancing and the inherent complexity of distributed systems. The genuinely hard case is stateful data stores, which resist horizontal scaling and push you toward sharding/partitioning. Statelessness is the enabler: Horizontal scaling is trivial for stateless services and brutal for stateful ones. Pushing state into managed datastores/caches is what lets the compute tier scale out freely.

questions.q: How do you plan capacity for a known traffic spike (product launch, sale, Super Bowl)?
questions.text: Forecast the peak (not the average) from comparable past events + marketing reach Pre-provision / pre-warm — don't rely on reactive autoscaling for a sharp spike Load test to the forecast peak + margin; find the bottleneck before the event Prep mitigations: load shedding, queueing, waiting room, feature flags to shed load War room + game day rehearsal for the event For a predictable spike, reactive autoscaling alone is a trap — its provisioning lag can't match a sharp surge, so you pre-provision (or pre-warm) capacity ahead of the event sized to the forecast peak plus margin. Load test to that peak beforehand to find the real bottleneck (often the database or a downstream dependency, not the web tier). Have explicit overload defenses ready (shedding, a waiting room, flags to disable non-essential features) and rehearse the event like a game day. Don't trust autoscaling for sharp spikes: Scaling lag means you're under-capacity exactly when the surge hits. Pre-provision for known events; let autoscaling handle the gentle organic curve.

questions.q: What is Little's Law and how is it useful for capacity reasoning?
questions.text: L = λ × W L = avg number of requests in the system (concurrency) λ = arrival rate (req/s) W = avg time in system (latency, s) e.g. 1000 req/s × 0.2s latency = 200 concurrent in flight → need a thread/connection pool + capacity sized for ~200 concurrent Little's Law relates throughput, latency, and concurrency with a simple identity: the average number of requests in flight equals arrival rate times time-in-system. It's a powerful back-of-envelope tool — if you serve 1000 req/s at 200ms each, you have ~200 requests in flight, so your pools, threads, and capacity must accommodate that concurrency. It also shows why latency spikes are dangerous: if W doubles under load, concurrency doubles, which can exhaust pools and cascade. Why latency growth cascades: Little's Law says rising latency (W) raises in-flight concurrency (L) for the same traffic — so a slowdown silently consumes thread/connection pools until they exhaust. Slow turns into down.

questions.q: What is utilization vs saturation, and why target ~60-70% utilization not 95%?
questions.text: Utilization: % of a resource currently in use Saturation: queued/waiting work beyond what's being served right now Queueing theory: as utilization → 100%, latency goes to infinity (non-linearly) Headroom absorbs spikes, failover load, and variance → target ~60-70% It's tempting to run resources at 95% for efficiency, but queueing theory shows latency rises non-linearly as utilization approaches 100% — the last few percent of utilization cost enormous latency. You also need headroom to absorb traffic spikes, the redundancy load when a peer fails (N+1), and normal variance. Targeting ~60-70% steady-state utilization keeps latency stable and leaves room to survive a failure or surge without tipping into saturation. The last 10% is the most expensive: Pushing utilization from 70% to 95% saves a little money and buys a lot of latency and fragility. Reliability needs deliberate headroom, not maximal packing.

questions.q: How do you right-size resource requests/limits in Kubernetes without waste or OOM?
questions.text: Requests = guaranteed/scheduled amount; Limits = hard ceiling CPU over limit → throttled (CFS); Memory over limit → OOMKilled Set requests from observed P95-ish usage; limits with headroom (or no CPU limit) Too-high requests → wasted/unschedulable; too-low → eviction/contention Kubernetes requests drive scheduling and guarantees; limits cap usage. The behaviors differ critically: exceeding a CPU limit gets you throttled (latency spikes), while exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled. Right-size requests from real observed usage (around P95) so you neither waste capacity nor starve the pod, and set memory limits with genuine headroom since the penalty is a kill. Many teams avoid CPU limits (to prevent throttling) while keeping memory limits (to contain leaks) and rely on VPA/usage data to tune. CPU throttles, memory kills: A too-tight CPU limit silently throttles and adds latency; a too-tight memory limit OOMKills the pod outright. Tune from real usage and treat memory headroom as non-negotiable.

questions.q: What is N+1 / N+2 redundancy and how does it interact with capacity planning?
questions.text: N = capacity needed to serve peak load N+1 = one extra unit so you survive losing one (node/AZ) at peak N+2 = survive losing two simultaneously (e.g. one failed + one in maintenance) Each remaining unit must absorb the failed one's load → size for that Redundancy planning means provisioning beyond raw demand so a failure doesn't cause an outage. N+1 lets you lose one failure domain at peak load and still serve everyone — but only if the survivors can actually absorb the redirected load, which means each unit runs below 100% (tying back to the utilization headroom rule). N+2 covers the realistic case of a failure happening during planned maintenance. The mistake is sizing for N: any single failure at peak then becomes a user-facing outage. Plan for failure during maintenance: N+1 is fragile if you take a node down for patching and then lose another. N+2 acknowledges that failures don't politely wait for maintenance windows to end.

questions.q: How do you forecast capacity and detect when you'll run out (trend + lead time)?
questions.text: Track resource usage trend (CPU, mem, storage, connections, IOPS) over time Project the trend → estimate the date you hit a limit Alert with LEAD TIME: warn before exhaustion by the provisioning time + buffer Storage especially: "disk will be full in ~12 days" beats "disk is full now" Capacity exhaustion should be a forecast, not a surprise. Track usage trends for each constrained resource, project them forward, and alert predictively — far enough ahead that you can provision before you hit the wall, accounting for lead time (cloud quota increases, hardware orders, and even autoscaling have non-zero latency). "Storage fills in ~12 days at current growth" is an actionable ticket; "disk full" at 3am is an incident. Predictive capacity alerts are a hallmark of mature operations. Alert before the cliff, not at it: Lead time is everything — a predictive "you'll run out in N days" gives you a calm provisioning window, while a threshold-at-100% alert gives you an outage. Forecast the constrained resources.

questions.q: What is the relationship between SRE, DevOps, and Platform Engineering?
questions.text: DevOps: culture/philosophy — break the dev↔ops wall (CALMS, shared ownership) SRE: a prescriptive implementation of DevOps using SLOs + error budgets + toil caps Platform Engineering: build the internal platform/paved roads devs self-serve on All three: reduce friction between writing code and running it reliably These overlap but aren't the same. DevOps is the philosophy of shared dev/ops ownership and fast, safe delivery. SRE is one concrete, opinionated way to implement DevOps — with measurable reliability (SLOs), error budgets, and engineering discipline applied to operations. Platform Engineering is the more recent emphasis on building internal developer platforms (paved roads, self-service) so teams can ship reliably without deep ops expertise. In practice they're complementary lenses on the same goal: reliable software, delivered fast. One framing: "DevOps is the what/why (culture), SRE is a how (prescriptive practices with numbers), and Platform Engineering builds the tooling that makes the good path the easy path." That nuance signals you've seen all three in practice.

questions.q: What does 'reliability is a feature' mean, and how do you make that case to product?
questions.text: Unreliable product = users leave regardless of how good the features are Reliability competes with features for the same engineering time → it IS a roadmap item The error budget makes the trade-off explicit and data-driven, not political Frame in business terms: churn, trust, revenue per nine, support cost "Reliability is a feature" means it must be planned, prioritized, and resourced like any other product capability — not treated as invisible plumbing that's only noticed when it breaks. The argument to product: a product users can't depend on loses them no matter how rich the feature set, so reliability directly drives retention and revenue. The error budget operationalizes this by making reliability a quantified, shared decision rather than a recurring argument — and crucially, it also tells you when you're over -investing and should ship faster. It cuts both ways: Reliability-as-a-feature doesn't mean "always maximize uptime" — it means deliberately choosing the right level. 100% is the wrong target; the budget finds the level that keeps users happy while leaving room to ship.

questions.q: How do you think about cost vs reliability trade-offs as an SRE?
questions.text: Each extra nine ≈ 10x cost (more redundancy, more regions, more headroom) Right target = fewest nines that keep users happy (per service/journey) Levers: redundancy level, multi-region, headroom %, instance types, retention Tie reliability spend to business value of the workload (payment vs internal report) Reliability and cost are in direct tension: every additional nine demands roughly an order of magnitude more investment in redundancy, headroom, and complexity. The SRE job is not to maximize reliability but to find the right level per workload — a payment path may justify four nines while an internal reporting tool is fine at two. Past a point, extra nines are invisible to users (their own device/network is less reliable than your service) yet cost you enormously, so over-reliability is as much a mistake as under-reliability. Match the spend to the stakes: Don't run a back-office tool active-active multi-region. Reserve expensive reliability for the journeys where failure genuinely costs revenue, trust, or safety.

questions.q: What is 'defense in depth' for reliability, and how do the patterns layer together?
questions.text: No single safeguard is enough — layer independent defenses: timeouts + retries(backoff+jitter) + circuit breakers + bulkheads + load shedding + graceful degradation + redundancy/failover + progressive rollout + monitoring + auto-rollback Each layer catches what the previous one missed (Swiss cheese) Resilience comes from layering independent patterns so a failure that slips past one is caught by the next — the Swiss-cheese model applied to reliability. A timeout bounds the wait; a circuit breaker stops hammering a dead dependency; a bulkhead contains the damage to one pool; graceful degradation keeps the core journey alive; redundancy/failover handles infrastructure loss; progressive rollout + auto-rollback limit bad-change blast radius. No single pattern is sufficient, but stacked, they make catastrophic failure require many simultaneous gaps. Layers, not silver bullets: Senior answers don't name one pattern — they describe how timeouts, breakers, bulkheads, shedding, and degradation compose so a single fault can't line up holes through every layer at once.

questions.q: How do you embed reliability earlier in the lifecycle ('shift left' on reliability)?
questions.text: Design: production readiness reviews, SLOs defined before launch, failure-mode analysis Build: reliability requirements + chaos/load tests in CI, dependency/criticality mapping Deploy: canary + auto-rollback + SLO gates baked into the pipeline Run: observability from day one, error budgets, blameless postmortems → feed back to design Shifting reliability left means designing for it from the start instead of bolting it on after incidents. Concrete practices: production-readiness reviews and defined SLOs before a service launches, failure-mode analysis at design time, load/chaos tests in CI, and observability + canary + auto-rollback built into the delivery pipeline rather than added later. The postmortem feedback loop then carries operational learnings back into design, closing the cycle so each incident makes the next design better. Production readiness reviews: A checklist before launch — SLIs/SLOs defined, alerts and runbooks in place, dependencies mapped, capacity and failure modes understood — prevents the "launched then immediately on fire" pattern far more cheaply than reacting after.

questions.q: As an SRE lead, how do you build a reliability culture across engineering, not just an SRE team?
questions.text: Shared ownership: dev teams own their service's SLOs + on-call (SRE enables, not owns) Make reliability visible + rewarded: SLO dashboards, postmortem learnings shared widely Provide paved roads/platform so the reliable path is the easy path Leadership buy-in: error budget policy signed by product; blameless culture from the top Teach via game days, postmortem reviews, embedded SREs A reliability culture can't live in a single SRE silo — if SRE is the only team that cares, every other team optimizes purely for features and SRE drowns. The lead's job is to spread ownership: dev teams own their SLOs and on-call, with SRE providing the platform, tooling, and expertise (paved roads make the reliable path the path of least resistance). It needs genuine leadership buy-in — product signing the error budget policy, blamelessness modeled from the top — and continuous teaching through shared postmortems, game days, and embedded SREs. Culture is the hard 80%; tooling is the easy 20%. SRE enables; teams own: The end state isn't "SRE keeps everyone reliable" — it's every team owning its reliability with SRE providing leverage. That scales; a central team being everyone's safety net does not.

questions.q: What are the SRE principles from Google's book, and which ones do you apply first in a new team?
questions.text: Embrace risk with explicit SLOs, eliminate toil, monitor what matters, automate, simplicity, release engineering, and blameless learning. Start with SLOs and an incident process since they create shared language and priorities. # first 30 days 1. Define 2-3 SLIs per critical user journey 2. Agree SLOs and an error budget policy 3. Set up on-call, severity levels, postmortems 4. Measure toil, pick the top automation target Interview tip: Do not try to adopt every principle at once. Pick the ones that remove the biggest current pain.

questions.q: How do you decide which services deserve SRE attention and which should stay with the development team?
questions.text: Prioritise by business criticality, user impact, change rate and operational burden. Use readiness reviews and engagement tiers: full SRE support for critical services, consulting and tooling for the rest, and clear criteria to hand back. # service tiering Tier 0: revenue/safety critical -> SRE on-call Tier 1: important -> shared on-call + SRE consulting Tier 2: internal/low -> dev team owns, self-service tooling Interview tip: A production readiness review is the gate. Services that fail it stay with the dev team until they improve.

questions.q: What are common failure modes of an SRE team itself, and how do you avoid them?
questions.text: Becoming a ticket-taking ops team, no authority to say no, hero culture, ignoring toil, or being separated from developers. Avoid with an engineering mandate, toil cap, error-budget policy backed by leadership and shared ownership. # health checks for the team toil % of time (target < 50%) pages per shift (target <= 2 actionable) % postmortem actions closed in 30 days engineering project hours vs ticket hours Interview tip: If SRE only reacts to tickets, it is just operations with a new name.

questions.q: What is the difference between availability, reliability, resilience and durability?
questions.text: Availability is the fraction of time the service works; reliability is consistent correct behaviour over time; resilience is the ability to withstand and recover from faults; durability is that stored data is not lost. They need different measures. availability = good_events / valid_events durability: 11 nines = 1 object lost per 10^11 per year MTTR + MTBF -> availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) resilience: test via fault injection and failovers Interview tip: A system can be highly available yet lose data. Durability and correctness need their own SLIs.

questions.q: What is the difference between monitoring, observability and telemetry, and why does the distinction matter for SRE?
questions.text: Telemetry is the raw data (metrics, logs, traces). Monitoring checks known conditions against thresholds. Observability is the ability to ask new questions of a system and understand unknown failures from its outputs. # known unknowns -> monitoring: alert when error_rate > 1% # unknown unknowns -> observability: slice by version, region, customer, endpoint histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, version) (rate(http_duration_bucket[5m]))) Interview tip: High-cardinality, well-structured events let you debug failures you did not predict.

questions.q: How do you write an SLO document that stakeholders actually use?
questions.text: State the user journey, SLI definition and measurement point, target and window, exclusions, error budget policy, owner and review cadence, in one page agreed with product. Link it to dashboards and alerts. Service: checkout-api SLI: 2xx/3xx responses under 500ms at the load balancer / all valid requests SLO: 99.9% over rolling 28 days Policy: budget < 25% -> freeze risky releases Owner: payments-sre Review: quarterly Interview tip: If product has not signed the SLO, it is not an SLO. It is an engineering wish.

questions.q: How do you handle SLOs for dependencies, and why does a chain of 99.9% services not give 99.9%?
questions.text: Serial dependencies multiply: three 99.9% services give about 99.7%. Compute the composite, add redundancy or fallbacks for critical paths, and set your SLO below what dependencies allow or mitigate their failures. 0.999 * 0.999 * 0.999 = 0.997 (~26 h/year) parallel redundancy: 1 - (1-0.99)*(1-0.99) = 0.9999 # decide: tighten deps, cache, queue, or degrade gracefully Interview tip: You cannot promise more availability than your hard dependencies unless you add fallbacks that tolerate their failure.

questions.q: How do you implement SLOs with Prometheus recording rules and Sloth or OpenSLO?
questions.text: Define SLI ratios as recording rules over multiple windows, compute error budget and burn rates from them, and generate alerts and dashboards from a declarative SLO spec with tools like Sloth or Pyrra to avoid hand-written errors. record: sli:http_availability:ratio_rate5m expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) sloth generate -i slo.yml -o rules.yml promtool check rules rules.yml 1 - avg_over_time(sli:http_availability:ratio_rate5m[28d]) Interview tip: Generate rules from a spec. Hand-written multi-window burn rate alerts are easy to get subtly wrong.

questions.q: What are common mistakes when setting SLOs?
questions.text: Too many nines, measuring server health instead of user experience, a single average-based SLI, no business sign-off, SLOs no one acts on, windows too short or long, and never revisiting targets. # anti-patterns SLO 99.999% for a service whose users tolerate minutes of downtime SLI = CPU < 80% (not user-facing) SLI = average latency (hides tail) No policy for when the budget is spent Interview tip: An SLO nobody uses to make decisions is decoration. Tie it to alerts, release gating and planning.

questions.q: How do you set SLOs for asynchronous systems like queues, event streams and email delivery?
questions.text: Measure freshness (age of oldest message or end-to-end delay), completeness (messages processed without loss), and correctness, not request latency. Use percentile delay targets and monitor the backlog trend. histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(msg_e2e_delay_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) kafka consumer lag: kafka_consumergroup_lag processed / (produced) over 28d >= 0.9999 oldest_unacked_message_age_seconds < 120 Interview tip: Queue depth alone is misleading. Age of the oldest item tells users' real wait time.

questions.q: How do you use error budgets to negotiate with product teams about launches and risk?
questions.text: Show the remaining budget as shared data. If healthy, product can take more risk and ship faster; if low, prioritise reliability work. The budget turns an argument into a pre-agreed rule, not a personality clash. error_budget_remaining = 1 - (bad_events / (SLO_budget_fraction * total_events)) budget > 50%: ship freely, run experiments budget 10-50%: extra care, smaller changes budget < 10%: freeze risky changes, fix reliability Interview tip: Present options and trade-offs, such as launching with a feature flag and staged rollout, rather than a flat no.

questions.q: What counts against the error budget and what should be excluded?
questions.text: Count user-visible failures and slow responses from your service or its hard dependencies. Exclude client errors (4xx caused by users), synthetic probes, load tests, and agreed planned maintenance only if users were warned and the SLO document says so. good: status < 500 AND latency < 400ms bad: 5xx, timeouts, latency >= 400ms excluded: 4xx caused by client, health checks, internal test traffic sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",code=~"5.."}[28d])) Interview tip: Be careful with exclusions. Every exclusion makes the number look better than users' experience.

questions.q: How do you handle a single huge incident that consumes the entire quarterly error budget on day one?
questions.text: Follow the policy: freeze risky changes, prioritise remediation, but avoid punishing the team for the whole window. Consider whether the window is too long, analyse root causes, and use shorter rolling windows and burn-rate alerts to regain balance. budget consumed: 100% in 40 min outage action: freeze non-critical releases action: complete postmortem actions review: rolling 28d window vs calendar quarter Interview tip: Calendar windows reset all at once; rolling windows recover gradually as the bad period ages out.

questions.q: How do you use error budget burn data in capacity and roadmap planning?
questions.text: Track which causes consume budget (deploys, dependencies, capacity, bugs), then allocate roadmap time proportionally to the top drivers. Reliability work is justified by budget evidence instead of intuition. sum by (cause) (budget_burn_total) deploy-related: 38% dependency X: 25% capacity saturation: 20% unknown: 17% Interview tip: Label incidents with a cause category so you can sum the budget burn per category each quarter.

questions.q: How would you set up fast and slow burn alerts, and what are typical window and threshold pairs?
questions.text: Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: page on a 14.4x burn over 1 hour (confirmed by 5 min), also 6x over 6 hours; ticket on 3x over 1 day and 1x over 3 days. The short window confirms it is still happening. expr: (sli:burn_rate1h > 14.4 and sli:burn_rate5m > 14.4) expr: (sli:burn_rate6h > 6 and sli:burn_rate30m > 6) expr: (sli:burn_rate1d > 3 and sli:burn_rate2h > 3) expr: (sli:burn_rate3d > 1 and sli:burn_rate6h > 1) Interview tip: A 14.4x burn over one hour consumes 2% of a 30-day budget, which justifies waking someone.

questions.q: How do you handle on-call compensation, fairness and burnout prevention?
questions.text: Compensate on-call time (pay or time off), limit frequency, ensure rest after night pages, distribute load fairly across time zones, track page load per person, and give engineers time to fix causes of pages. pages per person per week night pages (22:00-07:00) on-call weeks per engineer per quarter interrupted-sleep follow-up days off Interview tip: If the same person is paged most often, the rotation is not fair and the system is not yet healthy.

questions.q: What makes a good alert, and what is the test for deciding whether something should page a human?
questions.text: A good page is urgent, actionable, user-impacting, novel and needs human judgement now. If it can wait until morning, is not actionable, or can be auto-remediated, make it a ticket, a dashboard item or automation. test 1: does it need action in the next few minutes? test 2: is there a known action to take (runbook link)? test 3: is the user impact real or imminent? test 4: could automation handle it? Interview tip: Every page should come with a runbook link and a clear description of impact. Otherwise the responder starts from zero.

questions.q: How do you structure handoffs between on-call shifts and between teams?
questions.text: A written handoff covering open incidents, active mitigations, risky changes upcoming, noisy alerts, and follow-ups, delivered in a short sync. Use a shared log so context is not lost. Pair with a primary and secondary for continuity. # handoff template Open incidents / ongoing mitigations: Temporary silences and why: Changes planned this week: Known flaky alerts and tickets: Things I'd watch: Interview tip: Temporary silences and manual workarounds are the most dangerous items to forget in a handoff.

questions.q: How do you design runbooks and automated remediation so on-call engineers do less manual work?
questions.text: Start with a runbook per alert, then script the repeated steps, then wire safe, idempotent automation with guardrails, rate limits and audit logs. Promote steps from runbook to script to automatic action as confidence grows. alert: DiskFull -> runbook: /runbooks/disk-full script: ./clean-old-logs.sh --dry-run automation: rundeck job with approval auto-remediate: rotate logs when disk > 85% (max 3 per hour) Interview tip: Add a circuit breaker to automation. A remediation that loops can make an incident much worse.

questions.q: How should a team run an effective on-call retrospective or weekly alert review?
questions.text: Review last week's pages: classify actionable vs noise, identify top sources, assign owners to fix or delete alerts, track trends in pages per shift, and celebrate reductions. Keep it short and recurring. pages by alert name, last 7 days % actionable vs non-actionable time to acknowledge / resolve per page action: delete | tune | automate | fix cause Interview tip: Delete aggressively. Alerts that never lead to action cost sleep and attention.

questions.q: How do you run an incident when the root cause is unknown and the clock is ticking?
questions.text: Stabilise first: check recent changes, roll back, shift traffic, scale or shed load. Form hypotheses, split investigators, time-box each, and keep a timeline. Mitigation matters more than finding the cause during the incident. git log --since='2 hours ago' --oneline # what changed? kubectl rollout undo deploy/api kubectl top pods; kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp # traffic shift to healthy region Interview tip: Most incidents correlate with a recent change. Roll back first, ask why later.

questions.q: What does an effective incident communication cadence look like for customers and executives?
questions.text: Acknowledge quickly, state impact and what you know, give regular updates even without news, name the next update time, avoid speculation, and close with resolution and follow-up. Separate technical channels from stakeholder updates. T+10m: 'We are investigating elevated errors in checkout. Next update 30 min.' T+40m: 'Cause identified, mitigation in progress.' T+90m: 'Resolved. Monitoring. Postmortem to follow.' Interview tip: Promise the time of the next update, then keep it, even if there is nothing new.

questions.q: How do you handle an incident that spans multiple teams or vendors, with unclear ownership?
questions.text: Declare a single incident commander, open one shared channel and bridge, list involved parties and owners, assign tasks explicitly, escalate vendors through support contracts, and keep one timeline. Resolve ownership debates after the incident. #inc-1042 channel, single bridge roles: IC, Ops lead, Comms lead, Scribe vendor: open P1 case, request named engineer, share evidence timeline doc: who/what/when Interview tip: The incident commander has authority to assign work. Arguing over ownership is for the postmortem.

questions.q: What is the difference between an incident commander and a technical lead, and why separate them?
questions.text: The incident commander coordinates, decides, delegates and communicates; the technical lead dives into diagnosis and fixes. Separating roles prevents the person debugging from losing the big picture and keeps coordination continuous. IC: owns process, priorities, decisions, delegation Ops/Tech lead: hands-on diagnosis and mitigation Comms lead: internal/external updates Scribe: timeline and decisions Interview tip: If you are the IC, resist the urge to debug. Your job is to keep everyone effective.

questions.q: How do you decide to roll back versus roll forward during a bad deploy?
questions.text: Roll back when the change is clearly implicated and rollback is safe and fast. Roll forward when rollback is risky (schema changes, data migrations) or the fix is tiny and well understood. Decide on time to restore and risk. kubectl rollout undo deployment/api argocd app rollback api 42 git revert <sha> && deploy # data migration applied? check backward compatibility first Interview tip: Design deploys to be backward compatible so rollback is always possible. Expand, then migrate, then contract.

questions.q: How do you write postmortem action items that actually reduce recurrence?
questions.text: Make actions specific, owned, time-bound and prioritised by impact: prevent, detect and mitigate. Prefer systemic fixes and automation over reminders and training. Track them in the same backlog as feature work. P0 prevent: add schema validation in CI (owner: Priya, due: 2 wks) P1 detect: alert on queue age > 5 min (owner: Sam, due: 1 wk) P2 mitigate: automate rollback on error spike (owner: Lee, due: 6 wks) bad: 'be more careful' / 'retrain team' Interview tip: If the action is 'tell people to be careful', the system is still unsafe. Fix the system, not people.

questions.q: How do you facilitate a blameless postmortem meeting when emotions are high or someone made an obvious error?
questions.text: Set ground rules, focus on how the system allowed the error, use neutral language and timeline reconstruction, ask what made the action reasonable at the time, and keep leaders from assigning blame. Safety encourages honesty. ask: 'What did you know at the time?' ask: 'What made this decision seem reasonable?' avoid: 'Why did you...?' replace 'human error' with the missing guardrail Interview tip: If people fear punishment, they hide details, and you lose the information needed to prevent recurrence.

questions.q: What is a good timeline in a postmortem and how do you build it from evidence?
questions.text: A timestamped sequence in one time zone covering detection, escalation, key decisions, mitigations and recovery, built from logs, metrics, chat and deploy records, with gaps and uncertainty marked. It shows both what happened and what people believed. 14:02 deploy 2026.10.1 rolled to 25% 14:09 error rate 2% -> 11% 14:12 page fired (detected after 10 min) 14:20 hypothesis: DB connections. Wrong. 14:41 rollback started; 14:48 recovery Interview tip: Include decision points and what responders believed, not only system events. That reveals why actions made sense.

questions.q: How do you handle postmortems for incidents caused by a third-party vendor or cloud provider outage?
questions.text: Focus on what you control: detection, your dependency design, fallback options, communication and contract follow-up. Examine why a single provider failure had that impact and what resilience investments are justified. question: why was this a single point of failure? question: did our alerts detect it before the vendor status page? question: could we have failed over or degraded gracefully? action: request provider RCA, review SLA credits Interview tip: Blaming the vendor ends learning. The question is how your system should behave when a dependency fails.

questions.q: How do you share postmortem learnings across a large organisation so other teams benefit?
questions.text: Publish postmortems in a searchable internal repository, hold regular review sessions, summarise themes in newsletters, tag by cause and component, and turn recurring lessons into checklists, templates and platform guardrails. postmortems/2026-10-12-checkout-outage.md tags: deploy, config, dependency, capacity monthly review: top 3 themes release checklist updated with lesson #7 Interview tip: The best sharing mechanism is a guardrail in the platform that prevents the same failure for everyone.

questions.q: Give examples of toil and non-toil, and explain the criteria that define toil.
questions.text: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work with no enduring value that scales linearly with service growth. Examples: manual restarts, ticket-driven provisioning. Not toil: writing automation, design, postmortems, one-off migrations. toil: manually rotating certificates every quarter toil: approving access requests by hand toil: restarting a leaking service nightly not toil: building self-service access tooling Interview tip: The key question is whether the work leaves the system permanently better. Toil does not.

questions.q: How do you quantify the ROI of automating a task, and when is it not worth it?
questions.text: Compare annual time saved (frequency x duration x people) plus error reduction against development and maintenance cost. Skip automation for rare, quick or unstable tasks, or when removing the need is better than automating it. saved = freq/yr * minutes * people = 52 * 30 * 2 = 52 h/yr cost = build 40 h + maintain 8 h/yr payback = 40 / (52 - 8) ≈ 0.9 years also: risk reduction, faster lead time Interview tip: Sometimes the best fix is to eliminate the task entirely by changing the process or design, not automate it.

questions.q: What is a self-service platform's role in reducing toil, and how do you measure adoption?
questions.text: Self-service lets developers provision and operate resources through APIs or templates without tickets, removing SRE from the critical path. Measure adoption, ticket volume, time to provision and satisfaction. ticket volume for 'new database' requests time to provision: 3 days -> 10 minutes % services on the paved road developer satisfaction (survey) Interview tip: A self-service tool nobody uses just moved the toil to its builders. Treat the platform as a product.

questions.q: How do you tackle toil that comes from a poorly designed or legacy system that nobody dares to change?
questions.text: Quantify the cost, add observability and tests as a safety net, carve out the worst pain with strangler-style improvements, get management support with data, and avoid big-bang rewrites. Reduce toil incrementally. toil log: 14 h/week on manual reconciliation step 1: add monitoring + characterisation tests step 2: automate the top 2 manual steps step 3: replace one module behind an interface Interview tip: Characterisation tests record what the legacy system does today, giving courage to change it.

questions.q: How do you design retry policies safely, including retry budgets and idempotency keys?
questions.text: Retry only transient, idempotent operations with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and use a retry budget (percentage of requests) to prevent amplification. Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent writes like payments. max_attempts: 3 backoff: 100ms * 2^n jitter: full retry_budget: 10% of requests POST /payments Idempotency-Key: 7f3a-... retry on: 503, 504, connect timeout; never on 400, 401, 404 Interview tip: Retries across several layers multiply: three layers with three attempts each make 27 calls for one failure.

questions.q: What is a service mesh's contribution to reliability, and what costs does it add?
questions.text: A mesh provides consistent retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, mTLS, traffic shifting and telemetry outside application code. Costs: extra latency and resource use, operational complexity, and another critical failure domain. istioctl proxy-status kubectl get virtualservice,destinationrule -A outlierDetection: consecutive5xxErrors: 5 interval: 10s baseEjectionTime: 30s kubectl top pods -n istio-system Interview tip: Adopt a mesh for a clear problem, such as mTLS or uniform traffic policy, not because it is fashionable.

questions.q: How do you design a graceful shutdown and connection draining for zero-downtime deploys?
questions.text: On SIGTERM, fail readiness so traffic stops, finish in-flight requests within a grace period, close connections cleanly, and use preStop delay to let load balancers deregister. Match terminationGracePeriod to the longest request. lifecycle: preStop: exec: command: ["sleep","10"] terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 server.shutdown(timeout=30) # stop accepting, drain kubectl rollout status deploy/api Interview tip: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM race each other. The preStop sleep covers the propagation delay.

questions.q: How do you build and test a disaster recovery plan for a stateful service, including RTO and RPO targets?
questions.text: Define business RTO/RPO, choose a strategy (backup-restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active) by cost, automate failover and restore, and test regularly with real restores. An untested backup is not a backup. pg_basebackup + WAL archiving -> RPO ~ minutes aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time ... time ./restore-and-verify.sh # measures real RTO dr drill: failover region, run smoke tests, fail back Interview tip: Measure the real restore time and data loss in a drill, then compare it with the target.

questions.q: What is a feature flag's role in reliability, and what are the risks of flags themselves?
questions.text: Flags allow gradual rollout, kill switches and fast mitigation without redeploys. Risks: stale flags, untested combinations, flag service outages, and config errors. Mitigate with defaults, expiry, ownership and testing. flag: new-recommendations rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% kill switch: disable feature in seconds default if flag service down: safe/off lint: flags older than 90 days Interview tip: Define safe defaults so a flag service outage does not take your application down.

questions.q: How do you run chaos experiments in Kubernetes using tools like Chaos Mesh or Litmus?
questions.text: Define steady-state metrics, write an experiment manifest (pod kill, network delay, CPU stress), scope by label and namespace, run during working hours with abort conditions, and observe whether SLOs hold. Start in staging. kubectl apply -f podchaos.yaml apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1 kind: NetworkChaos spec: action: delay delay: { latency: 200ms } selector: { labelSelectors: { app: payments } } duration: 5m kubectl get podchaos,networkchaos -n chaos-testing kubectl delete -f podchaos.yaml # abort Interview tip: Always have a one-command abort and automatic stop conditions tied to SLO alerts.

questions.q: What kinds of failures reveal the most in distributed systems: latency injection or crashes? Why is slowness harder?
questions.text: Slowness is harder than crashes because it ties up threads, queues and connections, triggers retries and cascades, and evades health checks. Latency injection exposes missing timeouts, bulkheads and backpressure. tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 500ms 100ms toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=1000 db_proxy kubectl exec pod -- tc qdisc del dev eth0 root # watch: thread pool saturation, queue depth, p99 Interview tip: A dead dependency fails fast. A slow one holds your resources hostage.

questions.q: How do you verify that failover works for databases and caches without causing a real outage?
questions.text: Rehearse in staging and then production in a controlled window: trigger managed failover, measure client reconnect behaviour, confirm no data loss, and check connection pool and DNS cache handling. Run regularly so it is routine. aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier db --force-failover redis-cli -h primary debug sleep 30 dig +short db.internal # watch DNS update psql -c 'select pg_is_in_recovery()' Interview tip: Applications often fail not because failover is slow but because they cache DNS or hold dead connections.

questions.q: How do you build a resilience scorecard or maturity model for services?
questions.text: Define criteria like SLOs, tested failover, timeouts, runbooks, capacity tests, dependency maps and chaos testing, score each service, share results, and use them to prioritise investment and gate launches. [x] SLO + burn alerts [x] Timeouts/retries reviewed [ ] Failover tested in last 6 months [ ] Load tested at 2x peak [x] Runbooks linked from alerts score: 3/5 Interview tip: Use scorecards to guide improvement, not to shame teams. Show progress over time.

questions.q: How do you perform capacity planning for a database, including connection limits, IOPS and storage growth?
questions.text: Track CPU, memory, IOPS, connections, replication lag and storage growth; project trends with headroom; load test; plan scaling steps (vertical, read replicas, sharding) well before limits, considering lead time. select count(*) from pg_stat_activity; aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --metric-name ReadIOPS ... predict_linear(db_storage_used_bytes[30d], 90*86400) pgbouncer: pool_mode=transaction default_pool_size=20 Interview tip: Connection limits are often hit before CPU. Pooling is usually the first and cheapest capacity fix.

questions.q: What are the pitfalls of autoscaling on CPU alone, and which better signals exist?
questions.text: CPU lags and doesn't reflect I/O-bound or queue-driven work. Better signals: request rate per pod, queue depth or age, concurrency, latency, or custom business metrics, plus scale-up speed and warm-up considerations. kubectl autoscale deploy api --min=3 --max=30 --cpu-percent=60 keda: ScaledObject triggers: - type: kafka metadata: { lagThreshold: "100" } metrics: - type: Pods pods: { metric: { name: requests_per_second }, target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "50" } } Interview tip: Scale on a leading indicator of load, not a lagging indicator of pain.

questions.q: How do you use load shedding priority and admission control to keep critical traffic working during overload?
questions.text: Classify requests by criticality, reject or queue lower-priority work first when saturation signals appear, return fast errors with retry hints, and protect resources for critical paths. Overload control should be automatic and tested. X-Request-Priority: critical | normal | batch if inflight > limit: shed batch, then normal HTTP 503 Retry-After: 5 envoy: overload_manager resource_monitors: fixed_heap Interview tip: Failing fast with a clear error is better than slow timeouts that hold resources and make everything worse.

questions.q: How do you account for cost in capacity decisions, such as spot instances, reservations and rightsizing?
questions.text: Match purchase model to workload: reserved or committed for baseline, on-demand for variable, spot for fault-tolerant batch. Rightsize using utilisation data, but keep headroom for failure and spikes, and track unit costs. kubectl top nodes; kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu aws ce get-reservation-utilization --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 karpenter: capacityType: [spot, on-demand] cost per 1000 requests = monthly_cost / (requests/1000) Interview tip: Cost per unit of work (per request, per user) is more useful than the raw bill when traffic grows.

questions.q: Your service's error rate jumps to 30% right after a deploy, but the canary looked healthy. What could explain this and what do you do?
questions.text: Mitigate: roll back. Then investigate why the canary missed it: low traffic share, wrong traffic type, delayed effect (cache expiry, connection pool, background job), config differences, or a dependency that only fails at full volume. kubectl rollout undo deploy/api kubectl argo rollouts abort api compare canary vs prod: traffic %, endpoints hit, data sets check cache TTLs, cron jobs, feature flag segments Interview tip: A canary is only as good as the traffic it sees. If it never exercised the failing path, it proved nothing.

questions.q: You get paged at 3 a.m. for a database CPU alert on a service you do not know well. How do you proceed?
