questions.text: Check user impact first, open the runbook, look at recent changes and top queries, mitigate (kill runaway queries, scale, shed load), escalate to the owning team if needed, and document what you did for handoff. select pid, state, now()-query_start as dur, left(query,80) from pg_stat_activity where state<>'idle' order by dur desc limit 10; select pg_cancel_backend(<pid>); git log --since='6 hours ago' --oneline escalate: page secondary / service owner Interview tip: Escalating early when you lack context is a strength. The cost of waking a colleague is lower than a prolonged outage.

questions.q: A marketing campaign will send 10x normal traffic next Tuesday and you were told on Friday. How do you prepare in four days?
questions.text: Quantify expected load, load test critical paths, pre-scale and raise limits, warm caches, protect dependencies, add load shedding and a kill switch, brief on-call, set up a war room and rehearse rollback. k6 run --vus 2000 --duration 15m checkout.js kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=40 aws service-quotas list-service-quotas ... pre-warm: CDN cache, DB connection pool, JIT Interview tip: Check quotas and third-party rate limits. They are the usual hidden ceiling in a surge.

questions.q: A chaos experiment accidentally causes a customer-visible outage. How do you respond and what changes?
questions.text: Abort the experiment immediately, restore service, communicate honestly, run a blameless postmortem, review blast radius, abort conditions and approvals, and keep the practice with stronger safeguards rather than abandoning it. kubectl delete -f experiment.yaml # abort verify steady state restored: error rate, latency postmortem: why was blast radius larger than planned? new guard: auto-abort on SLO burn > 2x Interview tip: The experiment revealed a real weakness. The failure is valuable if you learn and tighten the process.

questions.q: Your team's toil is at 70% and leadership wants new features supported. How do you restore balance?
questions.text: Measure and categorise toil, pick the top two sources by hours, propose time-boxed automation with expected payback, negotiate to cap new onboarding, hand back or stop supporting low-value services, and report progress. toil log by category (hours/week) top: access requests 12h, cert renewals 8h, manual deploys 7h plan: self-service access (3 wks), cert-manager (2 wks) negotiate: pause new service onboarding until toil < 50% Interview tip: Present it as a business trade-off with numbers: hours lost, incidents caused, and what automation will return.

questions.q: Your SLO dashboard shows 99.95% but customers are complaining about slowness and errors. What could be wrong?
questions.text: The SLI does not reflect user experience: wrong measurement point, averaged latency, excluded traffic, missing client-side failures, regional or segment issues hidden in the aggregate, or good-event definition too lenient. compare: server-side vs client-side (RUM) success rate break down SLI by region, customer, endpoint, device check latency threshold vs real user tolerance review exclusions and valid-event filters Interview tip: Cross-check SLIs against support tickets and RUM. If they disagree, trust the customers and fix the metric.

questions.q: Walk me through your framework for approaching any system design question.
questions.text: A consistent framework prevents you from going blank and shows structured thinking. Use RADIO : Requirements → Architecture → Data model → Interface (APIs) → Optimisations. Step-by-step 1. Requirements (5 min) — Functional: what does the system do? — Non-functional: scale, latency, durability, consistency — Out of scope: what are we NOT building? 2. Capacity estimation (3 min) — DAU, RPS, storage per year, bandwidth — Back-of-envelope: 1M DAU × 10 req/day = ~115 RPS 3. High-level architecture (10 min) — Draw boxes: clients, LB, services, DB, cache, queue — Identify read vs write paths separately 4. Deep dives (15 min) — Pick 2–3 hard problems, go deep — Show trade-offs at each decision 5. Bottlenecks & failure modes (5 min) — SPOF identification — Scaling levers: horizontal, caching, sharding Interview tip: Drive the conversation. Don't wait for prompts. Say "I'll now focus on the write path since that's the harder problem — is that OK?" Shows Principal-level ownership.

questions.q: How do you estimate scale requirements? Walk through a back-of-envelope calculation.
questions.text: Interviewers want to see whether you can reason about numbers, not whether you memorise them. Use round numbers and narrate your logic. Key constants to memorise 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 RPS 1 billion requests/day ≈ 11,600 RPS ≈ ~12K RPS 1 KB × 1M events/day ≈ 1 GB/day ≈ 365 GB/year SSD sequential read: ~500 MB/s Network (1GbE): ~125 MB/s RAM access: ~100 ns | SSD: ~100 µs | HDD: ~10 ms Example: Twitter-scale timeline service DAU: 300M users, 20% active daily = 60M active Avg tweets/day: 60M users × 5 tweets = 300M tweets/day Write RPS: 300M / 86400 ≈ 3,500 writes/sec Read RPS: 10× write ratio ≈ 35,000 reads/sec Storage: 300M tweets × 300 bytes = 90 GB/day → ~33 TB/year (text only) Interview tip: After estimation, say "Given 35K read RPS, a single DB won't cut it — so we'll need read replicas and a cache layer." Estimation should drive architectural decisions, not be an isolated exercise.

questions.q: Explain CAP theorem and how it affects real-world database choices.
questions.text: CAP: a distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance. Since network partitions always occur in practice, the real choice is CP vs AP . CP systems (consistent when partitioned — may reject writes): PostgreSQL (single primary), HBase, Zookeeper, etcd → Use when: financial data, inventory counts, leader election AP systems (available when partitioned — may serve stale data): Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS → Use when: social feeds, metrics, user preferences, caches CA systems (no partition tolerance — theoretical only): Single-node RDBMS — not distributed Principal answer: CAP is binary and too coarse for real decisions. Use PACELC (Partition: Availability vs Consistency; Else: Latency vs Consistency) — it captures the latency trade-off that matters even during normal operation. Cassandra is PA/EL; PostgreSQL is PC/EC.

questions.q: When do you choose SQL vs NoSQL? Give concrete decision criteria.
questions.text: Neither is universally better. Choose based on data model, access patterns, and operational requirements. Choose SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Aurora) when: ✓ Complex joins between entities ✓ ACID transactions required (payments, bookings) ✓ Schema is stable and well-defined ✓ Reporting / ad-hoc analytics ✓ Team has strong SQL expertise Choose NoSQL when: ✓ Document model (MongoDB): nested JSON, flexible schema ✓ Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): simple lookups at high RPS ✓ Wide-column (Cassandra): time-series, write-heavy, multi-region ✓ Graph (Neo4j): social graphs, recommendation engines ✓ Search (Elasticsearch): full-text, faceted search Interview tip: Say "I'd choose PostgreSQL as the source of truth for user accounts and payments — it gives us transactions and referential integrity. For the activity feed (high write RPS, time-ordered, no joins needed), I'd use Cassandra." Showing you use both is better than picking a side.

questions.q: What is consistent hashing and why do distributed systems use it?
questions.text: Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes to a ring. When a node is added/removed, only K/N keys need remapping (vs all keys in naive modulo hashing). Critical for cache clusters, distributed DBs, and load balancers. Ring: 0 ──── 90 ──── 180 ──── 270 ──── 360 Node A Node B Node C Node D Key "user:123" hashes to position 95 → assigned to Node B (next node clockwise) Remove Node B → keys 90–180 shift to Node C only. All others unaffected. Virtual nodes (vnodes) Each physical node is mapped to multiple positions on the ring. Improves load distribution. Used by Cassandra (256 vnodes per node), DynamoDB, Riak. # Without vnodes: 3 nodes, each owns 1/3 of ring # With vnodes: 3 nodes × 256 = 768 positions → much more even spread Interview tip: Mention that consistent hashing is used in Redis Cluster, Cassandra, Memcached, and CDN edge routing. Examiners love when you connect theory to real systems.

questions.q: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly). Handle 100M URLs, 10B redirects/day.
questions.text: Classic design problem. Key challenges: unique ID generation, low-latency redirects, analytics. Client → CDN / Edge Cache ↓ (cache miss) LB → Redirect Service (stateless, horizontal scale) ↓ Cache (Redis) ← hot URLs served here (95% hit rate) ↓ (cache miss) DB (PostgreSQL) — short_code → long_url, created_at, user_id ↓ Analytics Queue (Kafka) → Click Aggregator → Analytics DB ID generation — Base62 encoding # 7 chars × 62 possibilities = 62^7 = 3.5 trillion unique URLs # Generate unique int ID (Snowflake / DB sequence), encode to Base62 def encode_base62(n): chars = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ" result = [] while n: result.append(chars[n % 62]) n //= 62 return ''.join(reversed(result)) Scale: 10B redirects/day = ~115K RPS Redis cache: 99% hit rate → 115K RPS handled in memory (~1µs/lookup) Cache miss (1%): 1,150 RPS to PostgreSQL — easily handled by single read replica Write rate: 100M URLs / (365 days × 86400 sec) ≈ 3 writes/sec — trivial Principal answer: The redirect path must be P99 < 10ms. Serve from CDN edge where possible — cache 301 Permanent vs 302 Temporary based on whether the URL can change. Use 302 for analytics (forces redirect through your service every time). Use 301 for permanent links (browser caches, fewer requests).

questions.q: Design a rate limiter. Support per-user, per-IP, and per-API-key limits.
questions.text: Rate limiting prevents abuse, enforces SLAs, and protects downstream services. Key question: where to enforce (edge, API gateway, service)? Algorithm choices Token Bucket: allow bursting, refill at constant rate → Best for: API gateways, per-user limits Fixed Window: simple, cheap — but allows 2× burst at window boundary Sliding Window Log: precise, high memory (store every request timestamp) Sliding Window Counter: interpolate between two fixed windows — good balance Implementation: Redis sliding window # Redis Lua script (atomic — no race condition) local key = KEYS[1] -- "rl:user:123:endpoint:/api/search" local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1]) -- 100 local window = tonumber(ARGV[2]) -- 60 (seconds) local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, now - window * 1000) local count = redis.call('ZCARD', key) if count < limit then redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now) redis.call('EXPIRE', key, window) return 1 -- allowed end return 0 -- rejected → HTTP 429 Multi-tier rate limiting: Layer 1: CDN/Edge (IP-based, coarse — blocks DDoS) Layer 2: API Gateway (per-API-key — SLA enforcement) Layer 3: Service level (per-user, per-resource — business logic) Interview tip: Mention distributed rate limiting across multiple API gateway pods — Redis is the central store. Add response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit , X-RateLimit-Remaining , Retry-After . These are required for good API UX.

questions.q: Design a notification system (push, email, SMS) for 500M users.
questions.text: Notification systems are deceptively hard: delivery guarantees, user preferences, throttling, channel failover, and deduplication. Producers (events) → Kafka Topics (by channel type) ↓ Notification Service ├── Preference filter (user opted out? → discard) ├── Dedup check (Redis TTL key on notification_id) ├── Priority queue (critical > normal > marketing) └── Channel router ├── Push → APNs (iOS) / FCM (Android) ├── Email → SendGrid / SES → SMTP └── SMS → Twilio / SNS Key design decisions 1. At-least-once delivery via Kafka (consumer group, manual offset commit) 2. Idempotency: notification_id deduplicated in Redis (TTL = 24h) 3. Retry with exponential backoff: 1s → 2s → 4s → 16s → DLQ 4. User preference DB: per-channel opt-out, quiet hours, frequency caps 5. Rate limiting: max 5 marketing emails/user/day regardless of events Principal answer: Separate the event bus (Kafka) from the sending workers . This lets you: replay failed notifications, add new channels without touching producers, and independently scale push vs email workers (push is CPU-light, email involves template rendering). Store every notification in a NoSQL log (DynamoDB) for inbox features.

questions.q: Design a distributed job queue / task scheduler. Handle millions of jobs/day.
questions.text: Core requirements: reliable delivery, at-least-once execution, delayed jobs, priority, retries, observability. Producers → Job Queue (Redis / Kafka / SQS) ↓ Dispatcher / Broker ↓ Worker Pool (horizontal scale) ↓ ┌─ Success → mark complete in Job Store └─ Failure → retry with backoff → DLQ after N attempts Delayed jobs (scheduled tasks) # Redis sorted set — score = execution timestamp ZADD delayed_jobs 1735689600 "job:abc123" # execute at Unix time # Poller (every second): jobs = ZRANGEBYSCORE delayed_jobs 0 NOW LIMIT 0 100 for job in jobs: push to ready_queue ZREM delayed_jobs job At-least-once vs exactly-once At-least-once: Ack only after successful processing Idempotency key on the job consumer side Exactly-once: Impossible in distributed systems without 2PC overhead → Design jobs to be idempotent instead Interview tip: Celery + Redis/RabbitMQ is fine for most workloads. For 10M+ jobs/day with complex dependencies: Temporal (workflow orchestration). Mention visibility timeout — job becomes visible again if worker crashes without acking. Must be > expected max job duration.

questions.q: Design a web crawler at Google scale. Crawl 1 billion pages per day.
questions.text: Hard problems: politeness (don't hammer a single domain), deduplication, dynamic content, distributed coordination. Seed URLs → URL Frontier (priority queue) ↓ Dispatcher → Fetcher Workers (1000s, distributed) ↓ ↓ DNS Resolver Cache HTML Parser ↓ Content Seen? ──→ Yes: discard ↓ No Content Store (GCS / S3) ↓ URL Extractor → URL Normaliser → URL Seen Filter → URL Frontier Deduplication # URL dedup: Bloom filter (fast, probabilistic, no false negatives) bloom.add(url) if bloom.check(url): skip # 1% false positive rate acceptable # Content dedup: SimHash / MinHash to detect near-duplicate pages # Exact dedup: SHA-256 of content stored in distributed cache Politeness # Per-domain queue + delay # Respect robots.txt — cache it per domain (1h TTL) # Back-pressure: rate limit to 1 req/sec per domain by default # Crawl-Delay directive in robots.txt: honour it Principal answer: URL Frontier is a priority queue — prioritise high-PageRank domains. Use a multi-level queue: fresh (recrawl changed pages quickly) vs stale. DNS is the #1 bottleneck at scale — maintain a local DNS cache with thousands of entries. 1 DNS lookup per URL at 1B pages/day = ~11K DNS queries/sec.

questions.q: Design a system that achieves 99.99% availability. What does that mean operationally?
questions.text: 99.99% = 52 minutes downtime/year. 99.999% = 5 minutes/year. Every architectural decision must be justified against this budget. Availability budget breakdown (99.99% = 52 min/year): Planned maintenance: <10 min (rolling deploys, zero-downtime) Incident response: <42 min (~4 incidents × 10 min MTTR each) MTTR must be < 10 minutes → requires: • Automated alerting (PagerDuty, < 2 min to page) • Runbooks for top 10 failure modes • Feature flags for instant rollback • Health checks + auto-restart (Kubernetes liveness probe) Architectural requirements for 99.99% 1. No single points of failure — Multi-AZ deployment (lose 1 AZ, still serving) — N+2 redundancy for stateless services 2. Graceful degradation — Circuit breakers (fail fast, don't cascade) — Fallback: serve stale cache instead of error 3. Load shedding — Reject low-priority requests under overload — Rate limiting protects against thundering herd 4. Chaos engineering — Intentionally kill instances to verify recovery — GameDay exercises quarterly Interview tip: Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). To improve: increase MTBF (fewer failures) OR decrease MTTR (faster recovery). Recovery automation gives 10× more leverage than trying to make systems never fail.

questions.q: Design a distributed cache system. Handle 1M RPS with sub-millisecond latency.
questions.text: Caching is the single highest-leverage performance optimisation. Get the design right or you'll fight cache stampedes and inconsistency bugs forever. Client → Cache Cluster (Redis / Memcached, consistent hashing) ↓ miss Primary DB → write result to cache → return to client Cache patterns Cache-aside (lazy loading): App checks cache → miss → fetch DB → write cache → return Pros: only cache what's used. Cons: cold start latency. Write-through: App writes DB and cache atomically Pros: cache always fresh. Cons: write penalty, caches unused data. Write-behind (write-back): App writes cache only → async flush to DB Pros: very fast writes. Cons: data loss if cache crashes before flush. Read-through: Cache fetches from DB on miss (cache library handles it) Pros: simpler app logic. Cache stampede prevention # Problem: key expires, 10K requests hit DB simultaneously # Solution 1: probabilistic early expiration if time_to_expire < threshold and random() < probability: refresh_in_background() # Solution 2: Redis lock on cache miss if not redis.set(lock_key, 1, nx=True, ex=5): sleep(0.05); return get_from_cache() # wait for first request to populate Principal answer: Redis Cluster for 1M RPS: 6 nodes (3 primary + 3 replica), consistent hashing across slots. Each node handles ~167K RPS — well within Redis's 500K+ RPS single-node ceiling. Use pipelining for batch gets. Watch out for hot keys — a viral post accessed by millions needs key sharding or a local L1 in-process cache.

questions.q: Design a circuit breaker. When and how does a service fail fast?
questions.text: Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures — when a downstream service is slow or down, fail fast instead of queuing up requests that time out. State machine: CLOSED (normal) ──[failure threshold exceeded]──→ OPEN (fail fast) ↑ ↓ └──[success threshold met]── HALF-OPEN ←──[timeout elapsed] Implementation class CircuitBreaker: CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN = 0, 1, 2 def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, timeout=30, success_threshold=2): self.state = self.CLOSED self.failure_count = 0 self.last_failure_time = None def call(self, fn, *args): if self.state == self.OPEN: if time.time() - self.last_failure_time > self.timeout: self.state = self.HALF_OPEN else: raise CircuitOpenError("Circuit open — failing fast") try: result = fn(*args) self._on_success() return result except Exception as e: self._on_failure() raise def _on_failure(self): self.failure_count += 1 self.last_failure_time = time.time() if self.failure_count >= self.failure_threshold: self.state = self.OPEN def _on_success(self): if self.state == self.HALF_OPEN: self.state = self.CLOSED self.failure_count = 0 Interview tip: Libraries: Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), Hystrix (deprecated). In cloud-native: use Envoy/Istio service mesh — circuit breaker at the proxy layer, no code changes. Set fallback: return cached data, default response, or degrade gracefully ("show general recommendations instead of personalised").

questions.q: Design a distributed transaction system. Handle payments across microservices.
questions.text: Distributed transactions are notoriously hard. 2PC is slow and blocking. The practical answer for most systems is Saga pattern. 2PC (Two-Phase Commit) — avoid in microservices Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator asks all participants "can you commit?" Phase 2 (Commit): If all say yes → commit. If any says no → rollback. Problems: • Coordinator is SPOF • Blocking: participants hold locks during Phase 1 • Slow: 2 round trips of network calls minimum Saga pattern — the practical answer Choreography-based Saga (event-driven): OrderService → emit OrderCreated PaymentService → listen, charge card → emit PaymentCompleted InventoryService → listen, reserve stock → emit StockReserved ShippingService → listen, schedule delivery Failure: each service publishes compensating event PaymentFailed → OrderService listens → cancel order StockInsufficient → PaymentService listens → refund payment # Outbox pattern — prevents dual-write problem # In same DB transaction: BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES (123, 'pending'); INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload) VALUES ('OrderCreated', '{...}'); COMMIT; # Background process reads outbox → publishes to Kafka → marks as sent Principal answer: Choreography works well for simple flows. Orchestration (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) is better when: you need visibility into flow state, workflows are complex, or you need timeouts and compensation logic in one place. Always implement idempotency — payment services must handle duplicate events without

questions.q: Design a time-series metrics storage system (like Prometheus at scale).
questions.text: Time-series data has unique characteristics: always append-only, high cardinality, queries are usually recent data, compression is very effective. Agents (Node Exporter, cAdvisor) → Prometheus scrape / push gateway → Ingest Service → Write path: WAL → In-memory chunk → Flush to TSDB (disk blocks) → Long-term: Thanos / Cortex → Object storage (S3/GCS) → Query path: PromQL → Query Planner → Block reader → Result Storage design # Time-series: (metric_name, labels_map) → [(timestamp, value)] # High cardinality problem: {user_id="..."} label → millions of series # Delta encoding: store differences, not absolute values # e.g., [100, 101, 103, 106] → [100, +1, +2, +3] # XOR compression (Gorilla by Facebook): # Consecutive float values differ in only a few bits → 1.37 bytes/sample # vs 16 bytes uncompressed → 12× compression ratio Thanos for global scale Per-cluster Prometheus (local retention: 2h) → Thanos Sidecar → Object store (S3, GCS) → Thanos Query → fan-out queries across all Prometheus + store → Thanos Compactor → downsampling (5m, 1h resolution for old data) Interview tip: High cardinality is the #1 killer of Prometheus performance. Each unique label combination = a separate time series. Never use user IDs or request IDs as labels. Use histograms for latency (not gauges per request). Retention policy: 15 days local, compress to 5m resolution after 7 days, 1h resolution after 30 days.

questions.q: Design a real-time log aggregation pipeline. Handle 1TB/day of logs.
questions.text: Log pipelines must be: reliable (no log loss), scalable, queryable, and cost-controlled. App instances → Fluent Bit (agent, lightweight) ↓ Kafka (buffer + replay capability) ├── Topic: logs.app (structured JSON) ├── Topic: logs.infra (system metrics) └── Topic: logs.audit (compliance, long retention) ↓ Stream Processor (Flink / Spark Streaming) ├── Parse & enrich (add k8s metadata, geo-IP) ├── Detect anomalies (error spike alerting) └── Route by log level ↓ ┌── Hot storage: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch (30 days, queryable) └── Cold storage: S3 + Parquet (1 year, Athena queryable) Cost control — 1TB/day # Sampling: DEBUG logs sampled at 1%, INFO at 10%, WARN/ERROR at 100% # Compression: gzip on Kafka messages → ~5× reduction → 200 GB/day effective # Tiering: Elasticsearch for 30 days, then archive to S3 Glacier # Estimated monthly cost: ~$500 ES + ~$150 S3 for 1TB/day Principal answer: Kafka is the critical buffer — it absorbs spikes (deploy wave, incident) and allows consumer lag without data loss. Set retention to 72h on Kafka topics. If Elasticsearch is down, consumers lag but Kafka retains. Never write directly from agent to Elasticsearch — you'll lose logs on ES restarts.

questions.q: Design a search autocomplete / typeahead system. Return results in <100ms.
questions.text: Typeahead requires extremely low latency (every keystroke). The system must handle billions of queries and millions of distinct prefixes. User types "plat" → Client (debounce 100ms) → CDN edge cache (popular prefixes) ↓ miss Trie service → Redis prefix cache ↓ miss Precomputed prefix table (top-10 per prefix) ↓ Return ranked suggestions Data structure: Trie with top-K per node # Each trie node stores top-10 completions sorted by frequency # "pl" → ["platform engineer", "platform team", "playbook", ...] # "pla" → ["platform engineer", "platform team", "plan", ...] # Precomputed and stored in Redis: redis.setex("prefix:pla", 3600, json.dumps(top_10_results)) # Update frequency (offline, batch): # Kafka → Spark aggregation (hourly) → recompute top-10 → Redis update Latency budget for 100ms Network (client to edge CDN): ~5ms CDN cache hit: ~1ms (serve cached top prefixes) Cache miss → Redis lookup: ~2ms Redis miss → DB lookup: ~10ms Total (cache hit): ~6ms ✓ Total (cache miss): ~17ms ✓ Interview tip: Cache hit ratio for typeahead is very high — top 1000 prefixes cover ~80% of queries. Pre-warm the cache on deploy. Handle personalisation separately: blend global top-10 with user's recent searches client-side to avoid per-user cache fragmentation.

questions.q: Design a distributed ID generation system (like Twitter Snowflake).
questions.text: IDs must be: globally unique, sortable by time (for pagination), high throughput (100K+/sec), no central bottleneck. Snowflake ID structure (64-bit integer) Bit layout: [0] — sign bit (always 0) [1–41] — timestamp (ms since epoch) → ~69 years of unique IDs [42–51] — machine/datacenter ID (10 bits → 1024 machines) [52–63] — sequence number (12 bits → 4096 IDs/ms/machine) Max throughput: 1024 machines × 4096 IDs/ms = 4.2 billion IDs/second class SnowflakeGenerator: EPOCH = 1288834974657 # Twitter epoch (Nov 4, 2010) def __init__(self, machine_id): self.machine_id = machine_id # 0–1023 self.sequence = 0 self.last_ms = -1 def generate(self): ms = int(time.time() * 1000) - self.EPOCH if ms == self.last_ms: self.sequence = (self.sequence + 1) & 0xFFF if self.sequence == 0: while ms <= self.last_ms: # busy wait for next ms ms = int(time.time() * 1000) - self.EPOCH else: self.sequence = 0 self.last_ms = ms return (ms << 22) | (self.machine_id << 12) | self.sequence Alternatives: UUID v4 (random, not sortable, 128-bit), ULID (sortable UUID), database sequences (single SPOF). For most services, a database auto-increment sequence is fine up to ~50K inserts/sec. Use Snowflake when you need sortable IDs across shards without a central DB sequence.

questions.q: Design a multi-region Kubernetes platform. Handle active-active across 3 regions.
questions.text: Multi-region Kubernetes is the hardest class of PE design question. Focus on: traffic routing, data consistency, failure isolation, and operational complexity. Global Traffic Layer: Anycast IP (Global Accelerator / Cloud Armor LB) → Route to nearest healthy region (health check + latency-based routing) Per-region stack: GKE / EKS cluster ├── App workloads (stateless — active in all regions) ├── Local PostgreSQL primary + cross-region read replica └── Redis cluster (eventually consistent cross-region via CRDTs) Control plane: ArgoCD (one per region, sync from same Git repo) Fleet management via GKE Hub / EKS anywhere Data strategies per tier Stateless services: Deploy identical in all regions. No data concerns. User sessions: Redis CRDT (Riak) or route user to same region (sticky DNS) Transactional data: Primary in one region, failover via Aurora Global / Spanner Analytics/events: Multi-region Kafka MirrorMaker 2 → eventual consistency User-generated content: S3/GCS with CRR (cross-region replication) Principal answer: Don't default to active-active. It's 3–5× harder than active-passive. Ask: what's the actual RTO/RPO requirement? For most companies, active-passive (RPO < 1min, RTO < 15min) via Aurora Global DB + standby cluster is correct. Active-active only when regulatory requirements demand data residency in each region simultaneously, or when single-region latency is unacceptable for global users.

questions.q: Design a CI/CD platform for 500 microservices and 200 engineers.
questions.text: At this scale, the pipeline itself becomes a product. Engineers are your customers. Standardisation, speed, and self-service are the design goals. Developer push → GitHub → GitHub Actions (or Tekton on-cluster) ├── Lint + Test (parallel, cached dependencies) ├── Container build (Buildkit, layer caching) ├── Security scan (Trivy, Grype — fail on CRITICAL) ├── Push to Artifact Registry (tagged by git SHA) └── Update GitOps repo (PR to k8s-config repo) ↓ ArgoCD (per-environment) ├── Staging: auto-sync on PR merge ├── Prod: sync on manual approval + canary analysis └── Rollback: git revert → ArgoCD auto-applies Standardisation via golden path # Backstage software template: # Engineer runs: `npx @backstage/create-app` # Generates: Dockerfile, GitHub Actions workflow, Helm chart, # ArgoCD Application, PagerDuty integration, Datadog monitors # 80% of services use the golden path. 20% get custom support. Metrics that matter DORA metrics: Deployment frequency: target daily or on-demand per service Lead time for change: commit → production < 30 minutes Change failure rate: < 5% of deployments cause incidents MTTR: < 1 hour for P1 incidents Principal answer: At 500 services, the biggest problem isn't tooling — it's standardisation. Platform team builds golden paths (opinionated templates) and scores services on adoption. Enforce via Scorecard in Backstage: security scan ✓, SLO defined ✓, runbook linked ✓. Teams that score <70% get Platform team office hours, not mandates.

questions.q: Design a feature flag system for safe production rollouts.
questions.text: Feature flags decouple deployment from release. Critical for: canary rollouts, A/B testing, kill switches, and dark launches. Flag Config Store (PostgreSQL + Redis cache) ├── flag_key, enabled, rollout_percentage, targeting_rules, variants └── Admin UI → flag management SDK (embedded in each service): → Fetch flags on startup → local cache (in-memory) → Refresh every 30s via polling or SSE (Server-Sent Events) → Evaluate: is user X in rollout bucket for flag Y? Evaluation logic: 1. Is flag globally off? → return default 2. Is user in targeting rule? (beta_users group, specific user IDs) → return variant 3. Hash(user_id + flag_key) mod 100 < rollout_pct? → return variant 4. Return default Consistent bucketing def get_bucket(user_id: str, flag_key: str) -> int: # Same user always gets same bucket for same flag hash_input = f"{user_id}:{flag_key}" return int(hashlib.sha256(hash_input.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100 # user_id="abc123", flag="new_checkout" → bucket 47 # Always 47 → consistent experience across sessions and services Principal answer: Use flag SDK with <1ms evaluation latency — never make a network call per flag evaluation in the request path. Cache flags locally, stream updates via SSE. Log every flag evaluation to a data warehouse for analytics (who saw which variant, what was their conversion rate). This is the foundation of experimentation infrastructure.

questions.q: Design an Internal Developer Platform (IDP). What components does it need?
questions.text: An IDP reduces cognitive load for developers — they shouldn't need to understand Kubernetes, Terraform, or CI/CD to ship software safely. Developer-facing: ┌── Service Catalogue (Backstage) │ ├── Software templates (golden paths) │ ├── Tech docs (docs-as-code, MkDocs) │ └── Scorecards (compliance, security posture) ├── Self-service portal │ ├── Provision environment (namespace + resources) │ ├── Manage secrets (Vault UI) │ └── View logs, traces, metrics (linked from service page) └── CLI tool └── `platform new service` / `platform env create` / `platform deploy` Platform-facing (hidden from devs): Kubernetes + ArgoCD + Terraform + Vault + Crossplane The golden path contract Developer provides: ├── service name ├── tech stack (Node/Python/Go/Java) ├── resource requirements (CPU, memory, replicas) └── environment variables (plain) + secrets (references to Vault paths) Platform provides automatically: ├── Kubernetes namespace + RBAC ├── CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions workflow) ├── Ingress + TLS certificate ├── Observability (metrics, logs, traces pre-wired) ├── PagerDuty integration └── Cost attribution labels Principal answer: Measure IDP success by: time-to-first-deployment for a new service (target <1 day from zero), % services on golden path (target >80%), and developer satisfaction score (quarterly survey). Don't build what you can buy — Backstage for catalogue, Vault for secrets, Crossplane for cloud resources. Build the integration layer, not the primitives.

questions.q: Design a global CDN architecture. How does edge caching work at scale?
questions.text: CDNs reduce origin load and user latency by serving content from edge nodes close to users. Design involves: cache hierarchy, cache invalidation, origin protection, and routing. User (Mumbai) → Anycast DNS → Nearest PoP (Mumbai edge) ↓ cache miss Regional hub (Singapore) ↓ cache miss Origin shield (single region close to origin) ↓ cache miss Origin servers Cache key design # Default cache key: URL only # Vary by: Accept-Encoding (gzip vs br), Accept-Language, device type # Cache-Control headers (origin controls caching): Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable # versioned assets Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=60 # API responses Cache-Control: private, no-store # user-specific data Cache invalidation strategies 1. URL versioning (best): /app.v1.2.3.js → never expires, change URL to invalidate 2. Cache purge API: cdn.purge("/api/products/123") → instant but expensive at scale 3. Surrogate keys: tag responses with logical keys → purge by tag 4. Short TTL: max-age=60 → accept 60s staleness, no active invalidation Principal answer: Origin Shield is critical for large CDNs — it collapses all cache misses from all edge PoPs into a single PoP before hitting origin. Without it, a cache invalidation for a popular asset triggers N simultaneous origin requests (N = number of edge PoPs). With Origin Shield: exactly 1 origin request per object per cache refresh.

questions.q: Design a load balancer. Explain L4 vs L7 and when to use each.
questions.text: Load balancers distribute traffic across backend instances. L4 operates at transport layer (TCP/UDP); L7 operates at application layer (HTTP/gRPC/WebSocket). L4 Load Balancer (TCP): ├── Sees: IP, port, TCP flags — not HTTP content ├── Very fast: ~100ns decision (hardware), ~10µs (software) ├── Algorithms: IP hash, round-robin, least connections └── Use: any TCP traffic, non-HTTP, highest throughput needs L7 Load Balancer (HTTP): ├── Sees: URL, headers, cookies, body, TLS cert ├── Slower: ~1ms per request (TLS + HTTP parsing overhead) ├── Features: content routing, auth, rate limiting, WAF, health checks └── Use: HTTP APIs, A/B testing, canary routing, session affinity Health checking # L4: TCP connect probe (is the port open?) # L7: HTTP GET /health → expect 200 + healthy body # Passive: monitor real request error rates → remove if error rate > threshold # Remove from pool: 3 consecutive failures in 10s # Add back to pool: 2 consecutive successes (conservative) Consistent hashing for session affinity # Sticky sessions: route user to same backend # Option 1: Cookie (LB sets __lb_session=backend_id) # Option 2: IP hash (fragile — changes with proxies/CG-NAT) # Option 3: Consistent hashing on session token (best for scale) Principal answer: Use both in sequence. L4 (NLB/IPVS) at the front for TLS termination and connection distribution. L7 (NGINX/Envoy) behind it for routing, auth, and observability. This two-tier approach scales better than a single L7 handling all TLS connecti

questions.q: Design a WebSocket / real-time messaging system. Handle 1M concurrent connections.
questions.text: Long-lived connections at scale require stateful servers — which breaks horizontal scaling assumptions. Client ──WebSocket──→ WS Gateway (stateful, sticky LB) ↓ (Pub/Sub) Redis Pub/Sub ↑ Message Producer Services (Chat, Notifications, etc.) WS Gateway publishes received messages → Redis → all gateways → Each gateway fans out to its local connected clients Connection capacity planning # 1M concurrent connections: # Each idle WebSocket: ~40KB memory (kernel TCP state + buffer) # 1M × 40KB = ~40GB RAM just for connections # Distribute: 50 servers × 20K connections each → 800MB RAM/server ✓ # Message fan-out: if 1M users in 10K channels (100 users/channel avg) # Send to channel: 1 Redis publish → 50 WS servers receive → each fans to local subs # Cost: O(channels × servers) not O(users) — scalable Scaling challenges 1. Sticky sessions: WS connections are long-lived → LB must route to same server 2. Reconnection: client disconnects → reconnect with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s...) 3. State recovery: on reconnect, send all missed messages since last_seen_id 4. Heartbeat: ping every 30s, close if no pong in 10s (detect zombie connections) Interview tip: Redis Pub/Sub is eventually consistent — some messages may be lost on Redis restart. For guaranteed delivery use Redis Streams or Kafka. Distinguish: fire-and-forget (notifications) vs guaranteed delivery (chat history). For chat, store every message in Cassandra; WebSocket is just the delivery mechanism, not the source of truth.

questions.q: When do you use a message queue vs direct API call vs event streaming?
questions.text: This decision defines service coupling, reliability, and operational complexity. Get it wrong and you'll fight it for years. Direct API call (synchronous, point-to-point): ✓ Simple, request-response, immediate feedback ✓ Use when: caller needs the result, operation is <100ms, failure = retry immediately ✗ Tight coupling: if downstream is down, upstream fails ✗ No buffering: traffic spike propagates directly to consumer → Examples: user login validation, inventory check before checkout Message queue (async, point-to-point): ✓ Decouples producer from consumer availability ✓ Natural load levelling (workers drain at their own pace) ✓ Use when: task can be deferred, producer shouldn't wait, work is heavy ✗ Not real-time; adds latency (ms to seconds) → Examples: send email, resize image, process payment confirmation → Tools: SQS, RabbitMQ, Celery Event streaming (pub/sub, many consumers): ✓ Multiple independent consumers process same event ✓ Replay: process historical events for new consumers ✓ Use when: audit log, fan-out, event sourcing, real-time analytics ✗ Higher operational complexity (Kafka cluster management) → Examples: order events consumed by inventory + analytics + notifications → Tools: Kafka, Kinesis, Pub/Sub Principal decision rule: Start with synchronous API calls. When you see: retry queues appearing in code, caller blocking for long operations, fan-out to multiple consumers, or cross-team dependencies — introduce async. Don't over-engineer with Kafka before you ne

questions.q: Explain database sharding strategies and their trade-offs.
questions.text: Sharding partitions data across multiple database instances. The sharding key choice is the most consequential schema decision you'll ever make. Sharding strategies Range sharding: Users A–M → Shard 1, N–Z → Shard 2 Pros: range queries efficient, easy to add shards at end Cons: hot spots (all new users go to last shard), uneven distribution Hash sharding: Shard = hash(user_id) % N Pros: even distribution, no hot spots Cons: range queries hit all shards, resharding requires moving half the data Directory sharding: lookup table maps user_id → shard_id Pros: flexible redistribution, no resharding math Cons: lookup table is SPOF, extra network round-trip per query Geography sharding: EU users → EU shard, US users → US shard Pros: data residency compliance, lower latency for regional users Cons: cross-region queries complex, uneven growth if one region grows faster Resharding — the hard problem # Online resharding without downtime: 1. Add new shard (start empty) 2. Dual-write: new writes go to old + new shard 3. Backfill: migrate existing data from old to new shard 4. Verify: compare checksums 5. Cut over: reads switch to new shard 6. Remove dual-write, decommission old shard Principal answer: Shard only when you must. Most systems never need sharding — a well-tuned PostgreSQL on high-memory hardware handles 100K+ RPS with proper indexing and read replicas. Sharding adds enormous operational complexity: cross-shard joins become application logic, distributed transactions across sh

questions.q: Design a leader election system for distributed coordination.
questions.text: Leader election ensures exactly one node acts as coordinator. Required for: primary DB selection, distributed cron (run job once), cluster membership. Option 1: etcd / Zookeeper (purpose-built) # etcd lease-based leader election import etcd3 client = etcd3.client() # Try to acquire lease (TTL = 10s — leader must renew every 5s) lease = client.lease(ttl=10) # Atomic write: only succeeds if key doesn't exist success, _ = client.transaction( compare=[client.transactions.version('/election/leader') == 0], success=[client.transactions.put('/election/leader', node_id, lease=lease)], failure=[] ) if success: print("I am the leader") # Keep renewing lease — stop renewing = abdicate leadership while True: lease.refresh() time.sleep(5) Option 2: Redis (simpler, less reliable) # SET NX (set if not exists) + TTL acquired = redis.set('leader', node_id, nx=True, ex=30) if acquired: # Renew: must reset TTL before it expires redis.expire('leader', 30) Split-brain problem: two nodes think they're leader simultaneously Cause: network partition — leader A can't see quorum but still holds lease Solution: Raft consensus (etcd uses it) — Leader needs majority vote to remain leader — If A is isolated from majority, it steps down Interview tip: For Kubernetes: use Lease objects (leader-election library built into controller-runtime). For general use: etcd is the gold standard. Redis leader election is fine for advisory locks (best-effort) but not safe for cases where dual-leadership causes data corr

questions.q: Design a multi-tenant SaaS platform. How do you isolate tenants?
questions.text: Tenancy model choice affects: cost, isolation strength, compliance, and operational complexity. There's no universally right answer — it depends on customer tier and requirements. Model 1: Shared everything (silo = false) One DB, one app cluster, tenant_id column on every table ✓ Cheapest, easiest to operate ✗ Noisy neighbour, blast radius = all tenants, compliance risk (HIPAA?) → Use for: SMB SaaS, free tier, <10K tenants Model 2: Shared app, separate DB per tenant One app cluster, DB per tenant (separate schemas or instances) ✓ Data isolation, easier compliance ✗ DB sprawl (1000 tenants = 1000 DBs), connection pool explosion → Use for: mid-market, regulated industries Model 3: Dedicated cluster per tenant Separate Kubernetes namespace or cluster per tenant ✓ Full isolation, custom configuration per tenant ✗ Very expensive, high operational overhead → Use for: enterprise, government, customers who require it contractually Hybrid tiered model (recommended) Free / Starter tier: shared pool (Model 1), noisy neighbour acceptable Professional tier: shared app + separate DB schema (Model 2) Enterprise tier: dedicated namespace or cluster (Model 3) # Migrate tenant between tiers: move data, update routing config, no app code change Principal answer: Implement tenant routing at the gateway layer — every request carries tenant_id (from JWT or subdomain). Gateway resolves tenant_id → connection string → routes to correct DB. App code never deals with routing. This makes tier migration

questions.q: You inherit a monolith. How do you migrate it to microservices safely?
questions.text: The strangler fig pattern: gradually extract services from the monolith without a big-bang rewrite. The monolith keeps running and shrinks over time. Phase 1: Observe (month 1–2) Map the monolith: bounded contexts, DB tables, traffic patterns Identify extraction candidates: high-change rate, clear boundaries, team ownership Add instrumentation: trace every module call (basis for SLO baseline) Phase 2: Strangle at the edges (month 3–9) Extract peripheral services first (auth, notifications, image resizing) Use API gateway to route: /auth → new service, everything else → monolith Share the DB initially — acceptable short-term compromise Phase 3: Extract core services (month 9–18) Separate DB per service (Database Decomposition pattern) Dual-write during transition → cut over → remove monolith path Beware: distributed joins now need API calls or data denormalisation Phase 4: Retire monolith (month 18–24) Shell is empty — decommission What makes migrations fail ✗ Big bang rewrite (6 months, then nobody uses the new system) ✗ Extracting too many services simultaneously (coordination overhead explodes) ✗ Shared DB for too long (services can't evolve schemas independently) ✗ No SLO baseline before extraction (can't tell if new service is worse) ✗ Wrong first extraction (core transactional service → high risk) Principal answer: The decision to migrate should be driven by pain, not hype. If the monolith deploys weekly with a 5-person team and has 99.9% uptime — don't migrate. Migrate

questions.q: Design a news feed / timeline system (like Twitter or Instagram). Handle fan-out at scale.
questions.text: The core tension is fan-out-on-write (push) vs fan-out-on-read (pull). The right answer is a hybrid driven by follower counts. Write path (user posts): Post Service → append to user's own timeline (DB) → enqueue fan-out job (Kafka) Fan-out Worker → for each follower, push post_id into their feed cache (Redis list) Read path (user opens app): Feed Service → read pre-computed feed from Redis (O(1), already merged) → hydrate post_ids → full posts (batch get) Fan-out-on-write vs on-read Fan-out-on-WRITE (push): + Reads are cheap (feed pre-computed) - Writes expensive: a celebrity with 100M followers = 100M cache writes Fan-out-on-READ (pull): + Writes cheap (just store the post once) - Reads expensive: merge N followees' timelines on every open Hybrid (what Twitter actually does) - Normal users (< ~10K followers): fan-out-on-write (push to followers) - Celebrities (> threshold): fan-out-on-read (followers pull celeb posts at read time) - Final feed = merge(pushed posts, pulled celeb posts) sorted by rank/time Principal answer: The celebrity problem is the whole interview. Naively pushing a celeb's tweet to 100M feeds creates a multi-minute write storm and thundering-herd reads. The hybrid bounds write amplification. Mention feed ranking (ML score, not pure chronological) and that you store post_id references in the feed cache, not full posts — keeps the cache small and lets you re-rank cheaply.

questions.q: Design a distributed cache (like Redis Cluster / Memcached). Cover sharding, eviction, and consistency.
questions.text: A cache layer absorbs read load and cuts latency. At scale you need it distributed across nodes with predictable key placement. Client → consistent-hash(key) → cache node (client-side routing OR proxy like twemproxy/Envoy) Node A Node B Node C Node D [shard] [shard] [shard] [shard] ↑ replica ↑ replica (for HA reads / failover) Key design decisions Sharding: consistent hashing + vnodes → minimal reshuffle on node change Eviction: LRU (default) | LFU (better for skewed access) | TTL-based Replication: primary-replica per shard; promote replica on failure Consistency: cache-aside is eventually consistent — handle staleness explicitly Caching patterns Cache-aside (lazy): app reads cache → miss → read DB → populate cache Most common. Risk: stampede on hot-key miss. Write-through: write to cache + DB synchronously. Strong-ish, slower writes. Write-behind: write cache, async flush to DB. Fast, risk of data loss. The hard problems # Thundering herd / cache stampede → request coalescing (single-flight): only 1 request rebuilds a hot key → add jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire together # Hot key (one key = huge traffic) → replicate the hot key across nodes, or local in-process cache (L1) # Cache penetration (queries for non-existent keys) → cache negative results / bloom filter to short-circuit Interview tip: Always name the three failure modes — stampede, hot key, penetration — and a mitigation for each. Mention a two-tier cache (L1 in-process + L2 Redis) for the hottest keys to

questions.q: Design a typeahead / autocomplete search system. Sub-50ms suggestions at scale.
questions.text: Autocomplete must return ranked suggestions in < 50ms as the user types. Pre-computation and in-memory tries are the core. Client (debounced, 100–200ms) → API → Suggestion Service ↓ In-memory Trie (per shard, by prefix) ↓ (offline) Aggregation Pipeline ← query logs (Kafka) ↓ Build/rank tries nightly + hourly deltas Data structure: ranked trie # Each trie node stores top-K completions for that prefix (pre-computed) # "sys" → ["system design", "system call", "systemd"] cached AT the node # Lookup = walk prefix (O(prefix length)) → return node's top-K. No sorting at query time. Ranking & freshness Rank by: query frequency (popularity) + recency + personalization Freshness: trending terms via streaming counts; merge hourly deltas into base trie Sharding: by first 1–2 chars of prefix → route "sy*" to shard owning 's' Principal answer: Don't query a DB per keystroke. Pre-compute top-K per prefix and serve from RAM. Debounce client-side and cache popular prefixes at the CDN/edge. For typo tolerance, layer an edit-distance / fuzzy match (e.g. Elasticsearch completion suggester) behind the exact-prefix trie. Bound suggestion size and use HTTP caching headers on common prefixes.

questions.q: Design a global CDN. How does content get cached and invalidated worldwide?
questions.text: A CDN serves content from edge PoPs near users, cutting latency and origin load. Key topics: routing, cache hierarchy, and invalidation. User → DNS/Anycast → nearest Edge PoP ↓ (cache miss) Regional Shield / Mid-tier cache ↓ (cache miss) Origin (your servers / object store) Request routing Anycast: same IP announced from many PoPs; BGP routes to nearest DNS-based: geo/latency DNS returns the closest edge IP The edge tier absorbs the vast majority of requests for cacheable content Caching & invalidation Cache key: URL + select headers (Vary) + query params you choose TTL: Cache-Control max-age / s-maxage; stale-while-revalidate for smoothness Invalidation: - TTL expiry (simplest, eventual) - Purge API (push invalidation to all PoPs) — for urgent updates - Versioned URLs (/app.v3.js) — best: immutable assets, never invalidate Dynamic & large content - Dynamic content: cache micro-TTL or use edge compute (workers) - Large files/video: range requests + segment caching (HLS/DASH chunks) - Origin shield reduces origin load by funneling misses through a mid-tier Interview tip: Push hard on invalidation — it's the famously hard part. Recommend versioned/immutable URLs for static assets (cache forever, zero invalidation) and reserve purge APIs for emergencies. Mention stale-while-revalidate so users never wait on a refresh, and that cache-hit ratio is the metric that determines whether the CDN is actually helping.

questions.q: Design a notification system (push, email, SMS) delivering billions of messages reliably.
questions.text: A notification platform must be multi-channel, deduplicated, rate-limited per user, and resilient to provider failures. Producers (services) → Notification API → Kafka (ingest) ↓ Processor: template render + user prefs + dedup + rate-limit + scheduling ↓ Channel queues: [push] [email] [SMS] (per-channel workers) ↓ Provider adapters: APNs/FCM | SES/SendGrid | Twilio ↓ Delivery tracking + retries (DLQ) → status store Core requirements Dedup: idempotency key per (user, event) → drop duplicates Preferences: per-user channel opt-in, quiet hours, frequency caps Rate limit: don't spam a user — cap N notifications/hour/channel Prioritize: OTP/security (high) vs marketing (low) in separate queues Reliability: at-least-once delivery + retries with backoff + DLQ Fan-out & scheduling # Bulk campaign to 50M users → chunk into batches, spread over time window # Scheduled notifications → time-bucketed store, worker polls due buckets # Provider failover → if APNs errors spike, retry / circuit-break to backup path Principal answer: Separate transactional (OTP, alerts — low latency, high priority) from bulk/marketing (throughput-oriented) into different queues and worker pools so a marketing blast can't delay a login OTP. Make the pipeline at-least-once with idempotent delivery; track per-message state for observability. Respect user prefs and frequency caps before render to avoid wasted provider cost.

questions.q: Design a ride-sharing / location-matching system (like Uber). Match riders to nearby drivers.
questions.text: The hard parts are real-time geospatial indexing of moving drivers and low-latency matching under high update rates. Driver app → location pings (every ~4s) → Location Ingest (Kafka) ↓ Geospatial Index (Redis GEO / QuadTree / S2 / H3 cells) — updated continuously ↑ query "drivers near (lat,lng)" Rider request → Matching Service → rank candidates → dispatch → Trip Service Geospatial indexing Geohash / S2 / H3: map earth into cells; index drivers by cell id → "find nearby" = look up rider's cell + neighbor cells Redis GEO (sorted set on geohash) gives radius queries out of the box Drivers move constantly → updates dominate; keep the index in memory Matching Candidate set = drivers in rider's cell + adjacent cells, status=available Rank by: ETA (road network, not straight-line), driver rating, fairness Dispatch: offer to top driver; timeout → next; lock driver during offer Surge: per-cell supply/demand ratio → dynamic pricing signal Interview tip: Emphasize that this is write-heavy (millions of location pings/sec) — the geo index must handle high update throughput, so partition by region/cell. Use ETA via a routing engine, not Euclidean distance. Mention that matching must lock a driver atomically to avoid double-dispatch, and that you'd shard the whole system by geography since a NYC rider never matches a London driver.

questions.q: Design a distributed job scheduler / cron system. Run millions of scheduled tasks reliably.
questions.text: A scheduler must trigger jobs at the right time, exactly-once-ish, survive node failures, and scale to millions of schedules. Schedule Store (DB) ──> Scheduler (leader-elected / partitioned) (cron expr, next_run) ↓ poll "due" jobs each tick Dispatch → Task Queue (Kafka/SQS) ↓ Workers (idempotent execution) ↓ Status store + retry/DLQ Finding due jobs at scale # Don't scan all jobs every second. # Time-bucketed / sorted index by next_run_time (e.g. Redis ZSET, or DB index) # Each tick: SELECT jobs WHERE next_run <= now LIMIT N → enqueue → compute next_run # Partition the schedule space across scheduler nodes (by hash of job_id) Reliability & correctness Exactly-once trigger: claim job atomically (compare-and-set next_run) before dispatch Leader election / partition ownership: avoid two schedulers firing the same job Missed runs (downtime): catch-up policy — run once vs skip vs run-all Idempotent workers: dedup by (job_id, scheduled_time) so retries are safe Principal answer: True exactly-once is impossible across failures, so aim for exactly-once scheduling (atomic claim of the time slot) + idempotent execution. Separate the scheduler (decides WHEN) from workers (do the WORK) via a durable queue, so slow jobs never delay scheduling. Define the catch-up policy explicitly — for a billing job you run missed slots; for a cache-refresh you skip them.

questions.q: Design a real-time chat / messaging system (like WhatsApp). Cover delivery, ordering, and presence.
questions.text: Chat needs persistent connections, guaranteed delivery, message ordering, and presence — at billions of connections. Client ⇄ (WebSocket) ⇄ Connection/Gateway Servers (stateful, hold the socket) ↓ Message Service → persist (per-conversation store) ↓ Routing: find recipient's gateway → push ↓ (offline) Store + push notification (APNs/FCM) Delivery & state machine States: sent → delivered → read (the double ticks) Online: push over recipient's live WebSocket Offline: persist, send push notification, deliver on reconnect (sync since last_seen) Ack flow: client acks receipt → server marks delivered → notify sender Ordering & storage Ordering: per-conversation sequence number (monotonic), not global clock Storage: partition by conversation_id; messages are append-only, time-ordered → Cassandra/HBase fit (write-heavy, wide rows per conversation) Connection registry: which gateway holds which user's socket (Redis) Presence (online/typing) Heartbeat over the socket → TTL key in Redis (e.g. 30s) Missed heartbeats → mark offline. Don't broadcast presence to all contacts; fan-out presence only to users currently viewing the chat (bounded). Interview tip: The stateful-connection layer is the crux: millions of long-lived WebSockets need a registry mapping user → gateway so you can route a message to the right box. Use per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering (global ordering doesn't scale). For E2E encryption, mention the server only routes ciphertext. Presence is deceptively expens

questions.q: Design a payment / transaction system. Guarantee correctness with money on the line.
questions.text: Money demands strong consistency, idempotency, auditability, and reconciliation. "Eventually consistent" is unacceptable for balances. Client → Payment API (idempotency key) ↓ Ledger Service (double-entry, ACID DB — Postgres/Spanner) ↓ Payment Orchestrator → external PSP (Stripe/bank) via saga ↓ Reconciliation job ← compare ledger vs PSP statements (daily) Non-negotiables Idempotency: client sends idempotency_key; same key = same result, never double-charge Double-entry ledger: every txn = debit + credit; balances are DERIVED, immutable log ACID: use a transactional DB for the ledger; no eventual consistency here Audit: append-only ledger, never UPDATE/DELETE a posted entry Distributed payment flow (saga) 1. Reserve/authorize funds (pending entry) 2. Call external PSP 3a. Success → capture (post entry) 3b. Failure/timeout → compensating action (reverse the reservation) State machine per payment: PENDING → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED | FAILED | REVERSED Handling the unknown # PSP call times out — did it succeed? Don't guess. → store as PENDING, query PSP status (idempotent), reconcile. # Never assume failure on timeout → that's how you double-pay or lose money. Principal answer: Three pillars: (1) idempotency keys end-to-end so retries can't double-charge, (2) an immutable double-entry ledger where balances are computed from entries, never mutated in place, and (3) reconciliation against the PSP to catch drift. Use a saga with compensating transactions across the external boundary,

questions.q: Design a video streaming platform (like YouTube/Netflix). Cover upload, transcoding, and playback.
questions.text: Two very different paths: a heavy async ingest/transcode pipeline, and a globally-cached, adaptive playback path. UPLOAD: Creator → upload (resumable, to object store) → Transcode Queue → Transcoding workers: produce multiple renditions (240p…4K) + segments (HLS/DASH) → store segments in object store → distribute to CDN PLAYBACK: Viewer → manifest (.m3u8) → CDN edge → video segments (adaptive bitrate) Transcoding pipeline - Split source into chunks → parallel transcode (massively parallel) - Output ABR ladder: 240p/480p/720p/1080p/4K, each segmented (~2–10s chunks) - Generate manifests (HLS m3u8 / DASH mpd) listing segments per bitrate - This is async — user gets "processing" then "ready" Adaptive bitrate (ABR) playback Player measures bandwidth → requests next segment at suitable bitrate Drop quality on congestion, raise on recovery → no rebuffering Segments are static files → perfectly CDN-cacheable (huge hit ratio) Scale levers Storage: object store (S3/GCS) for source + renditions; cold tiers for old/rare Delivery: CDN does the heavy lifting — video is the ultimate cacheable static asset Popularity skew: pre-warm CDN for anticipated hits; long-tail served from origin Interview tip: Cleanly separate the asynchronous upload/transcode pipeline from the read-optimized playback path. Stress that video segments are static and thus ideal for CDN caching (that's how Netflix serves a third of internet traffic). Mention ABR for smooth playback, chunked parallel transcoding for fast

questions.q: Design a distributed unique ID generator. Compare UUID, Snowflake, and DB ticket servers.
questions.text: Many systems need unique IDs without a single bottleneck. The classic answer is Snowflake; know the trade-offs of each approach. Options compared UUID v4 (random): + Fully decentralized, zero coordination - 128-bit, not sortable, poor DB index locality (random inserts) DB auto-increment / ticket server: + Simple, sequential - Single point of contention; sharded ticket servers add complexity Snowflake (64-bit): [timestamp | machine_id | sequence] + Roughly time-sortable, no central coordination, compact - Needs unique machine_id assignment + clock sync Snowflake layout (64 bits) 1 bit : unused (sign) 41 bits: timestamp (ms since custom epoch) → ~69 years 10 bits: machine/worker id → 1024 nodes 12 bits: per-ms sequence → 4096 ids per node per ms → ~4M ids/sec/node, time-ordered, no coordination on the hot path The clock problem # Clock skew / NTP step backwards → could repeat timestamps # Mitigation: refuse to issue (wait) if clock moves backward; # monotonic clock; alert on large skew. Principal answer: Default to Snowflake-style IDs: time-sortable (great for index locality and pagination), compact (64-bit fits in BIGINT), and coordination-free per node. Call out the two operational gotchas — assigning unique worker IDs (via Zookeeper/etcd or config) and handling clock moving backwards. Use UUIDs only when you truly need client-side generation with zero infrastructure; their index fragmentation hurts write-heavy tables.

questions.q: Design a search engine / full-text search system. Cover indexing and ranking.
questions.text: Full-text search at scale = an inverted index, distributed across shards, with relevance ranking. Elasticsearch is the canonical implementation. INDEXING (write path): Docs → Ingest → analyze (tokenize, lowercase, stem, stop-words) → build inverted index: term → [doc_ids + positions + freq] → shard by doc_id, replicate per shard QUERY (read path): Query → analyze same way → look up terms in inverted index → scatter to all shards → gather + rank → top-K → merge Inverted index term "design" → [doc1:tf=3, doc7:tf=1, doc9:tf=5, ...] # Query "system design" = intersect postings lists for both terms # Positions stored too → phrase queries ("system design" adjacent) Ranking TF-IDF / BM25: term frequency × inverse document frequency (classic relevance) + signals: freshness, popularity, click-through, personalization + optional: vector / semantic search (embeddings + ANN) for meaning, not just keywords Scatter-gather at scale Query hits ALL shards (term could be anywhere) → each returns local top-K → coordinator merges → global top-K. Latency = slowest shard (tail latency matters). Replicas serve reads in parallel; index refresh is near-real-time, not instant. Interview tip: Lead with the inverted index — it's the heart of the answer. Explain BM25 for ranking, and that search is scatter-gather (every shard queried, results merged), making tail latency the enemy. Distinguish indexing (write-heavy, async, eventually searchable) from querying (read-heavy, latency-sensitive). Bonus points

questions.q: Design a system for exactly-once message processing. Is it even possible?
questions.text: True end-to-end exactly-once delivery is impossible in a distributed system (two-generals problem). What you achieve is at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively-once . The three delivery guarantees At-most-once: fire and forget. May lose messages. (metrics, logs) At-least-once: retry until acked. May duplicate. (most systems) Exactly-once: no loss, no dup. Impossible as pure delivery — achieved as at-least-once + dedup/idempotency. Achieving effectively-once 1. Producer: idempotent producer (dedup by sequence number, e.g. Kafka) 2. Consumer: idempotent processing - dedup table: store processed message_id, skip if seen - or naturally idempotent ops (SET x=5, not x+=5) 3. Atomic: commit offset + side-effect together (transactional outbox) Transactional outbox pattern # Problem: write to DB AND publish to Kafka atomically (no XA across them) # Solution: in ONE DB txn, write business row + an "outbox" row # separate relay reads outbox → publishes to Kafka → marks sent # Guarantees the event is published iff the DB change committed. Principal answer: Start by stating exactly-once delivery is impossible, then pivot to how it's done in practice: at-least-once + idempotency keys + a dedup store, or naturally idempotent operations. Mention the transactional outbox for the dual-write problem (DB + message broker) and Kafka's idempotent producer + transactions. The mature signal is knowing it's an end-to-end property, not something one component provides.

questions.q: How do you handle database sharding? Cover shard keys, resharding, and cross-shard queries.
questions.text: Sharding splits data horizontally across DBs when one node can't hold the data or handle the load. The shard key choice makes or breaks it. Sharding strategies Range-based: shard by key range (A–M | N–Z) + range queries easy - hotspots if keys skew (sequential ids) Hash-based: shard by hash(key) + even distribution - range queries hit all shards Directory/lookup: explicit key→shard map (flexible, extra hop) Geo/entity: shard by region or tenant (data locality) Choosing the shard key Good key: high cardinality, even access, matches query patterns Bad key: low cardinality (gender), monotonic (timestamp → hotspot on newest shard) Example: shard by user_id → user's data co-located, queries scoped to one shard The hard problems Cross-shard queries: scatter-gather (slow) — design schema to avoid them Cross-shard transactions: 2PC (slow/fragile) or saga — avoid if possible Resharding: use consistent hashing / vnodes so adding a shard moves minimal data Celebrity/hot shard: a single popular key overwhelms one shard → sub-partition it Interview tip: Spend your time on shard-key selection — it determines whether queries stay single-shard (fast) or become scatter-gather (slow). Warn against monotonic keys (they hotspot the newest shard). For resharding, consistent hashing minimizes data movement. State plainly: the goal is to make the common queries hit exactly one shard, and to denormalize so you rarely need cross-shard joins.

questions.q: Design a distributed locking system. When do you need one and what are the pitfalls?
questions.text: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive access to a resource across processes/nodes. It's subtle — naive implementations are unsafe. When you need it - Leader election (one active scheduler/worker) - Preventing duplicate work (only one node processes job X) - Guarding a non-idempotent external action # Often you can AVOID locks via idempotency or single-writer partitioning — prefer that. Implementations Redis (SET key val NX PX ttl): fast, simple - single-instance: not fault-tolerant - Redlock (multi-instance): debated safety under GC pauses/clock skew etcd / Zookeeper: consensus-backed (Raft/Zab), lease + watch + safer, linearizable; - higher latency DB row lock / advisory lock: simple if you already have the DB The classic pitfalls 1. No TTL → holder dies → lock held forever (deadlock). Always expire. 2. TTL too short → lock expires mid-work → two holders. 3. Process pause (GC/STW) → lock expires → another acquires → BOTH act. → Fencing token: lock issues monotonic token; resource rejects stale tokens. 4. Releasing someone else's lock → check-and-delete must be atomic (Lua/CAS). Principal answer: First ask whether you can design the lock away (idempotency, single-writer-per-partition). If you truly need one, use a consensus store (etcd/Zookeeper) with leases for safety-critical locks, and always pair it with a fencing token so a paused-then-resumed old holder can't corrupt the resource — the resource rejects any token lower than the highest it has seen. TTLs alone are not

questions.q: Design a feature flag / experimentation platform. Support gradual rollouts and A/B tests.
questions.text: Feature flags decouple deploy from release. The platform must evaluate flags fast, support targeting, and enable experiments. Flag Config (dashboard) → Config Store → distributed to SDKs ↓ App (SDK) evaluates locally: rules + targeting + % rollout → on/off ↓ Exposure events → analytics → experiment results Evaluation must be local & fast # Don't call a service per flag check (latency + SPOF). # SDK pulls/streams ruleset, evaluates IN-PROCESS (microseconds). # Streaming updates (SSE/poll) propagate changes in seconds. Targeting & rollout Rules: by user attribute, segment, geo, app version Gradual rollout: hash(user_id) % 100 < rollout_pct → stable bucketing (same user stays in-bucket as % grows — no flip-flapping) Kill switch: instant flag off → disable a bad feature without redeploy Experimentation (A/B) Deterministic assignment: hash(user_id + experiment_id) → variant Log exposures + metrics → statistical significance analysis Guardrail metrics + automated rollback if a variant harms key metrics Interview tip: The key insight is local in-process evaluation — flag checks happen millions of times, so they can't be network calls. Stress consistent bucketing via hashing so a user doesn't flip variants as you ramp the percentage. Mention the kill switch (the operational reason flags exist) and that exposure logging is what turns a flag into an experiment.

questions.q: Design an analytics / metrics ingestion pipeline. Handle billions of events per day.
questions.text: High-volume event analytics splits into a real-time path (fast, approximate) and a batch path (complete, accurate) — the classic lambda/kappa choice. Producers → Collector (validate, enrich) → Kafka (buffer) ├─► Stream processor (Flink/Spark) → real-time aggregates → fast store └─► Batch / data lake (object store) → warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake) → reports ↓ Dashboards / OLAP queries Ingestion at scale Buffer with Kafka → absorbs spikes, decouples producers from processors Schema + validation at edge; drop/dead-letter malformed events Partition by event-type or tenant for parallel consumption Sampling for ultra-high-volume, low-value streams Storage by access pattern Time-series DB (Prometheus/InfluxDB): operational metrics, recent, fast Columnar warehouse (BigQuery/Redshift/ClickHouse): ad-hoc analytics over history Data lake (Parquet on S3): cheap raw retention, reprocessing Pre-aggregation / rollups: hourly/daily cubes for common queries Lambda vs Kappa Lambda: separate batch (accurate) + speed (fast) layers, merge at query Kappa: single stream-processing path, reprocess by replaying the log (simpler) Principal answer: Separate by access pattern: real-time approximate aggregates (stream processor → fast store) for live dashboards, and a batch path into a columnar warehouse for accurate historical analysis. Kafka is the shock absorber. Use pre-aggregation/rollups so dashboards don't scan raw events. Mention Kappa (replayable log, one code path) as the modern simplification

questions.q: Design a system to handle the 'thundering herd' and cache stampede problems.
questions.text: A thundering herd happens when many clients hit the origin simultaneously — typically after a cache expiry, a cold start, or a recovery. Left unmanaged, it can cascade into an outage. Where herds form - Hot cache key expires → thousands of misses stampede the DB at once - Service restarts cold → every request rebuilds expensive state - Recovery after outage → all clients retry simultaneously Mitigations 1. Request coalescing (single-flight): only ONE request recomputes a missing key; others wait for its result. 2. TTL jitter: add randomness to expiries so keys don't all expire at the same instant. 3. Early/probabilistic refresh: refresh hot keys slightly BEFORE expiry, in the background. 4. stale-while-revalidate: serve the stale value while one worker refreshes async. 5. Exponential backoff + jitter on client retries (prevents retry storms). Defensive backpressure - Concurrency limits / load shedding at the origin (protect the DB) - Circuit breaker: stop hammering a struggling dependency - Queue + rate-limit the rebuild work Interview tip: Name the specific pattern for each cause: single-flight/coalescing for hot-key misses, TTL jitter so keys don't expire in lockstep, stale-while-revalidate so users never block on a refresh, and exponential backoff with jitter for retry storms (jitter is the part people forget). Top it with load shedding so the origin sheds excess load rather than collapsing.

questions.q: Design a time-series database / monitoring data store. Why not just use PostgreSQL?
questions.text: Time-series workloads (metrics, IoT, monitoring) have a distinctive shape: massive append-only writes, time-ordered, recent-data-heavy reads, and aggregation queries. Purpose-built TSDBs exploit this. Why a general RDBMS struggles - Write volume: millions of points/sec overwhelm B-tree index updates - Storage: raw rows are huge; TS data compresses ~10x with the right encoding - Retention: old data must auto-expire; deletes in RDBMS are expensive - Query shape: "avg over 5-min buckets, last 24h" wants columnar + downsampling TSDB design choices Storage: columnar + time-partitioned chunks (write to newest, read recent) Compression: delta-of-delta on timestamps, XOR on float values (Gorilla) Downsampling: roll up raw → 1m → 1h → 1d as data ages Retention: drop whole old partitions (cheap), tiered storage for history Cardinality: the killer — each unique label combo = a series; bound it! The cardinality trap # label like user_id or request_id → millions of series → memory blowup # Rule: labels must be low-cardinality (region, service, status_code) # High-cardinality dimensions belong in logs/traces, not metric labels. Principal answer: Time-series data is append-mostly, time-ordered, and read recent-first — so a TSDB uses time-partitioned columnar chunks, aggressive compression (Gorilla-style delta + XOR), downsampling as data ages, and partition-drop retention. The interview gotcha is cardinality: warn that putting a high-cardinality field (user_id, UUID) in a metric label explo

questions.q: Design a collaborative document editor (like Google Docs). Handle concurrent edits.
questions.text: Real-time collaboration needs concurrent edits to converge to the same state without locking. Two families: OT and CRDT. Client A ⇄ WebSocket ⇄ Collab Server ⇄ WebSocket ⇄ Client B (local edit applied instantly = optimistic) ↓ send op Server orders/transforms ops → broadcasts → clients converge ↓ Persist op log + periodic snapshots OT vs CRDT Operational Transformation (OT): Transform concurrent ops against each other so they apply consistently. Used by Google Docs. Needs a central server to order/transform. Complex but compact. CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type): Data structure mathematically guarantees convergence regardless of order. Peer-friendly, offline-friendly. Metadata overhead (tombstones, ids). Key mechanics Optimistic local apply: editor feels instant; reconcile when server confirms Ordering: server assigns a total order (or version vectors for CRDT) Presence/cursors: broadcast lightweight cursor positions to collaborators Persistence: append ops to a log; snapshot periodically to bound replay Interview tip: Frame the core problem as conflict resolution without locking , then contrast OT (server-centric, used by Google Docs) vs CRDTs (convergence by construction, great for offline/P2P). Mention optimistic local application for responsiveness, an op log + snapshots for persistence, and that cursor/presence is a separate low-stakes broadcast. Picking one and justifying it (OT for a central server, CRDT for offline-first) shows depth.

questions.q: How do you design for high availability? Walk through redundancy at every layer.
questions.text: HA means no single point of failure and graceful handling of component loss. You design redundancy at every tier and target a measurable availability SLO. Availability math 99.9% (three 9s) = 8.7 hours downtime/year = 43 min/month 99.99% (four 9s) = 52 minutes/year = 4.3 min/month 99.999%(five 9s) = 5.3 minutes/year # Serial dependencies MULTIPLY: two 99.9% services in series = 99.8% # Redundant (parallel) components ADD nines. Redundancy at each layer DNS: multiple providers, health-checked failover LB: redundant LBs, multi-AZ App tier: stateless, N+1 instances across AZs, auto-scaling Data tier: primary + replicas, automated failover, multi-AZ Region: multi-region (active-active or active-passive) for disaster Dependencies: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, fallbacks Eliminating SPOFs - No single instance, AZ, or region the whole system depends on - Health checks + automated failover (manual failover is too slow) - Test it: chaos engineering / game days to prove failover actually works Interview tip: Start with the SLO target (it dictates cost — five 9s is wildly more expensive than three). Show you understand serial vs parallel availability math, then walk redundancy tier by tier. The mature point: redundancy you haven't tested isn't redundancy — mention game days / chaos testing to verify failover works before a real incident.

questions.q: Design a circuit breaker and explain graceful degradation under dependency failure.
questions.text: A circuit breaker stops a service from repeatedly calling a failing dependency, preventing cascading failure and giving the dependency room to recover. Circuit breaker states CLOSED: calls pass through. Count failures. │ failure rate > threshold ▼ OPEN: calls fail fast (no call made). Return fallback immediately. │ after cooldown timer ▼ HALF-OPEN: allow a few trial calls. ├─ success → CLOSED (recovered) └─ failure → OPEN (keep waiting) Why it matters # Without it: dependency slows → threads pile up waiting → caller exhausts # its thread pool → caller fails too → cascade up the stack. # With it: caller fails fast, sheds load off the sick dependency, stays alive. Graceful degradation When a dependency is down, degrade — don't crash: - serve stale cache instead of live data - hide a non-essential feature (recommendations) but keep core flow - default/empty response with a clear partial-result indicator Example: product page loads even if the reviews service is down. Principal answer: Pair the circuit breaker with timeouts (a slow dependency is as dangerous as a dead one), bulkheads (isolate thread pools per dependency so one can't starve the others), and a defined fallback per call site. The design goal is partial availability: a single failed dependency should degrade one feature, never take down the whole request path. That's the difference between an incident and an outage.

questions.q: Synchronous vs asynchronous communication: when do you use each between services?
questions.text: Choosing sync (request-response) vs async (messaging/events) per interaction is one of the most consequential architecture decisions.
