SYNCHRONOUS (REST/gRPC, caller waits): + simple, immediate result, easy to reason about - tight coupling, caller blocked, failure propagates, latency adds up → use when: you need the result NOW to continue (read a user profile) ASYNCHRONOUS (queue/event, fire-and-continue): + decoupled, resilient (buffer absorbs spikes), scalable - eventual consistency, harder to trace, ordering/dedup concerns → use when: work can happen later (send email, process upload, fan-out) Decision heuristics Need immediate response to proceed? → sync Can it be processed later / in background? → async Want to decouple producer/consumer scale? → async Multiple consumers of one event? → async (pub/sub) Long-running work (transcode, report)? → async + status polling Hybrid: the common real pattern # Sync ack + async work: # POST /upload → 202 Accepted (sync) + enqueue processing (async) # Client polls /status or gets a webhook/websocket update when done. Interview tip: Don't pick a side globally — decide per interaction. The strongest answer is the hybrid: respond synchronously with an acknowledgment, then do heavy work asynchronously. Call out async's costs honestly (eventual consistency, harder debugging, need for idempotency) so it's clear you're not cargo-culting "async = scalable."

questions.q: Message queue vs event streaming (e.g. RabbitMQ/SQS vs Kafka). How do you choose?
questions.text: Both decouple producers and consumers, but their models differ fundamentally — queues are about task distribution, logs are about durable replayable streams. Traditional Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS): - message consumed → removed from queue - work distribution among competing consumers - per-message ack, routing, priorities, DLQ → jobs/tasks: "process this once, by someone" Log/Stream (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar): - append-only log; messages RETAINED (by time/size) - consumers track their own offset; can replay - ordered within a partition; high throughput → events: "this happened; many consumers, replayable" Choose a queue when - Task/work distribution (one job done once) - Need per-message priority, complex routing, or visibility timeouts - Don't need replay or multiple independent consumer groups Choose a log/stream when - Event sourcing, multiple consumers of the same events - Need replay (reprocess history, bootstrap a new consumer) - Very high throughput, ordered per key (partition) - Stream processing / analytics pipelines Principal answer: The deciding question is replay + multiple consumers. If many independent consumers need the same events, or you need to reprocess history, that's Kafka (the log is retained and each consumer owns its offset). If it's competing workers draining a task queue once, that's RabbitMQ/SQS. Mention Kafka's per-partition ordering and that it's not ideal when you need per-message priority or fine-grained routing.

questions.q: Design an API gateway. What responsibilities belong there vs in services?
questions.text: An API gateway is the single entry point for clients, handling cross-cutting concerns so individual services don't reimplement them. Clients → API Gateway → [auth, rate-limit, routing, TLS, transform] ↓ Service A Service B Service C ↓ (service mesh handles service↔service) Gateway responsibilities (edge concerns) - TLS termination, request routing / path-based dispatch - AuthN (validate token) — coarse authZ - Rate limiting / quota enforcement per API key - Request/response transformation, protocol translation (REST↔gRPC) - Aggregation (BFF: combine several services for one client call) - Observability: logging, tracing injection, metrics What stays in services - Business logic (always) - Fine-grained authorization (resource-level permissions) - Domain validation # Gateway = cross-cutting plumbing; services = domain. Don't leak logic into the gateway. Pitfalls - Gateway becomes a SPOF → run it redundantly, multi-AZ - Fat gateway with business logic → "distributed monolith" anti-pattern - Latency: it's an extra hop → keep it lean Interview tip: Draw the line clearly: the gateway owns cross-cutting edge concerns (auth, rate limiting, routing, TLS), services own business logic and fine-grained authorization. Mention the Backend-for-Frontend variant for client-specific aggregation, and warn against the common failure mode — stuffing business logic into the gateway until it becomes a bottleneck and a deployment chokepoint.

questions.q: Design load balancing. Compare L4 vs L7, and the main algorithms.
questions.text: Load balancers distribute traffic across backends for scale and availability. The L4 vs L7 distinction and algorithm choice are the core of the answer. L4 (transport): routes by IP:port, no payload inspection + very fast, protocol-agnostic, low overhead - can't route by URL/header, no content awareness L7 (application): understands HTTP — routes by path/host/header/cookie + smart routing, TLS termination, sticky sessions, rewrites - more CPU per request Algorithms Round robin: simple, even — ignores backend load Weighted RR: bigger boxes get more traffic Least connections: send to least-busy backend (good for long-lived conns) Least response time: factor in latency Consistent hashing: same client/key → same backend (cache affinity, sticky) IP hash: session stickiness without cookies Health & resilience Active health checks → eject unhealthy backends automatically Graceful drain on deploy (connection draining) Outlier detection: eject a backend that starts erroring Multi-LB + DNS/anycast so the LB itself isn't a SPOF Principal answer: Use L4 when you need raw throughput and protocol-agnostic routing (e.g. in front of L7 LBs, or for non-HTTP), and L7 for content-based routing, TLS termination, and canary/path splitting. Default to least-connections over round-robin for uneven workloads, and consistent hashing when backend cache affinity matters. Always pair with health checks + connection draining — a dumb LB sending traffic to a dead node is worse than no LB.

questions.q: Push vs pull architectures: when do clients pull and when does the server push?
questions.text: How does a client get new data — does it ask (pull) or does the server notify it (push)? This decision shapes latency, load, and complexity. PULL (polling): Client asks repeatedly: "anything new?" + simple, stateless, client controls rate - wasteful (empty polls), latency = poll interval PUSH (server → client): Server sends when something changes + real-time, efficient (no empty checks) - server holds connection state, harder to scale Push mechanisms Long polling: client request held open until data or timeout (easy, works everywhere) Server-Sent Events: one-way server→client stream over HTTP (dashboards, feeds) WebSocket: full-duplex persistent connection (chat, games, collab) Webhooks: server-to-server push (callback URL) Choosing Low-frequency / tolerant of delay → polling (simplest) Real-time, one-way (notifications, prices) → SSE Real-time, two-way (chat, multiplayer) → WebSocket Hybrid: pull for initial state + push for live deltas (very common) Interview tip: Match the mechanism to the need: don't reach for WebSockets when SSE or even long-polling suffices — persistent connections are expensive to hold at scale (millions of open sockets need a stateful gateway tier). The common production pattern is pull-then-push: fetch initial state via a normal request, then subscribe to live deltas. Mention the scaling cost of stateful connections explicitly.

questions.q: Design backpressure and load shedding. How does a system protect itself from overload?
questions.text: When demand exceeds capacity, a system must degrade gracefully rather than collapse. Backpressure and load shedding are how it protects itself. Backpressure Signal upstream to slow down when you're saturated: - bounded queues (reject/block when full, don't grow unboundedly) - TCP flow control / HTTP 429 with Retry-After - reactive streams (request N items at a time) # Unbounded queues are a trap: they hide overload, add latency, then OOM. Load shedding When you can't keep up, drop work deliberately: - reject low-priority requests first (shed by priority) - admission control: cap concurrent requests - fail fast with 503 rather than queueing into oblivion # Better to serve 90% well than 100% badly (or crash and serve 0%). Related protections Rate limiting: bound input rate per client Concurrency limits: cap in-flight work (e.g. semaphore per dependency) Bulkheads: isolate resource pools so one tenant can't starve others Autoscaling: add capacity — but it lags; shedding handles the gap Principal answer: The mental model is: autoscaling handles sustained growth, but it lags by minutes — so you need load shedding to survive the seconds-scale spike. Use bounded queues (unbounded queues just defer the crash via OOM), shed by priority so critical traffic survives, and fail fast with 503 + Retry-After instead of queueing requests the client has already given up on. Protecting throughput for the majority beats trying to serve everyone and toppling.

questions.q: Design a data replication strategy. Compare sync, async, and quorum replication.
questions.text: Replication copies data across nodes for durability, availability, and read scaling. The sync/async/quorum choice trades consistency against latency and availability. Synchronous: primary waits for replica(s) to ack before confirming write + no data loss on primary failure - higher write latency, availability risk Asynchronous: primary acks immediately, replicates in background + low latency, high availability - data loss window if primary dies Quorum (W+R > N): write to W replicas, read from R; tune consistency + flexible balance - more complex, still needs conflict handling Quorum math (Dynamo-style) N = replicas, W = write quorum, R = read quorum W + R > N → strong consistency (read sees latest write) W=N, R=1 → fast reads, slow/fragile writes W=1, R=N → fast writes, slow reads W=R=2, N=3 → common balanced choice (survive 1 node loss) Topologies & conflicts Single-leader: one primary, replicas follow (most common; failover needed) Multi-leader: writes to multiple regions → conflict resolution required Leaderless: any node accepts writes (Dynamo/Cassandra) → quorum + read-repair Conflict resolution: last-write-wins (lossy), vector clocks, CRDTs Interview tip: Tie the choice to the data: synchronous for can't-lose data (payments) accepting the latency, async for read-scaling and availability where a small loss window on failover is tolerable. For leaderless/multi-region, show the quorum formula W+R>N and that you still need conflict resolution (LWW loses data; vector clocks/

questions.q: How do you achieve read-your-writes and other consistency guarantees with replication lag?
questions.text: With async replicas, a user can write to the primary then read a stale replica — seeing their own change vanish. Several consistency models address such anomalies. The consistency spectrum Strong / linearizable: every read sees the latest write (expensive) Read-your-writes: you always see YOUR own writes Monotonic reads: you never see time go backwards (no flicker) Consistent prefix: reads see writes in causal order Eventual: replicas converge "eventually" (weakest) Techniques to fix lag anomalies Read-your-writes: - route a user's reads to the primary for a short window after their write - or pin reads to a replica known to have caught up (track write timestamp/LSN) Monotonic reads: - pin a user to the same replica (sticky) so they don't bounce to a staler one Version tokens: - client passes last-seen version; system serves a replica >= that version Practical pattern # After write, return a write-timestamp/LSN to the client. # On read, client sends it; router picks a replica that has applied >= that LSN, # else falls back to primary. Gives read-your-writes without all-strong cost. Principal answer: Don't reach for global strong consistency to fix one anomaly — it's expensive. Identify the specific guarantee the use case needs (usually read-your-writes + monotonic reads) and solve it surgically: route post-write reads to the primary or to a caught-up replica via a version token, and use sticky replica routing to prevent reads going backwards. This gives the UX of consistency

questions.q: Design a multi-region active-active architecture. How do you handle data and failover?
questions.text: Active-active serves traffic from multiple regions simultaneously for low latency and disaster resilience. The hard part is data consistency across regions. Users → GeoDNS / Anycast → nearest region Region US Region EU Region APAC [full stack] [full stack] [full stack] ↕ ↕ ↕ cross-region data replication / globally-distributed DB Active-active vs active-passive Active-passive: one region serves, standby on failover + simpler, no write-conflict problem - wasted capacity, failover lag Active-active: all regions serve traffic + low latency everywhere, instant failover - cross-region write conflicts Data strategies 1. Partition by geo (data residency): EU users' data lives in EU → most writes stay regional, no conflict. Great when data is user-scoped. 2. Globally-distributed DB (Spanner/CockroachDB/DynamoDB global tables) → handles replication + consistency for you (at a cost). 3. Single write-region + read replicas elsewhere (active-active reads only) Failover & conflicts Health-checked GeoDNS reroutes away from a dead region automatically Conflict resolution for multi-region writes: LWW, CRDTs, or geo-partitioning Watch: cross-region latency (~100ms+) makes synchronous global writes painful Interview tip: The cleanest active-active answer is geo-partitioning: shard data so a user's writes stay in their home region, eliminating cross-region write conflicts entirely. If data must be global and strongly consistent, name Spanner/CockroachDB and accept the latency cost of cross-regi

questions.q: Design a service discovery system. How do services find each other dynamically?
questions.text: In dynamic environments services come and go (autoscaling, deploys, failures), so hard-coded addresses don't work. Service discovery maintains a live registry of healthy instances. Service instances → register (with health) → Service Registry (etcd/Consul/Eureka) Caller → query registry → get healthy instances → call one (with LB) ↑ registry health-checks instances, removes dead ones Discovery patterns Client-side discovery: client queries registry, picks instance, calls directly + fewer hops - discovery logic in every client/language Server-side discovery: client calls a LB/router that consults the registry + clients stay dumb - extra hop DNS-based (K8s Services): query a stable DNS name → resolves to healthy pods Health & consistency Registration: self-register on startup OR third-party (orchestrator) registers Health checks: registry probes instances; remove on failure (with grace) The registry itself must be HA + consistent → backed by Raft (etcd/Consul) Stale entries are the enemy: a removed-too-slowly dead node gets traffic Principal answer: In Kubernetes this is mostly solved for you — Services + kube-dns/CoreDNS give a stable virtual IP/DNS name that load-balances across healthy pods, with the control plane handling registration and health. Explain the underlying model anyway (registry + health checks + Raft-backed consistency) and the client-side vs server-side trade-off. The recurring failure mode to mention: stale registry entries routing traffic to dead instances,

questions.q: How do you prevent and handle cascading failures in a microservices architecture?
questions.text: A cascading failure is when one service's failure propagates and topples others, turning a small incident into a system-wide outage. Microservices are especially prone to it. How cascades happen Service C slows → callers (B) block on it → B's threads exhaust → B's callers (A) block on B → A exhausts → the whole chain is down. Or: retry storms — failures trigger retries → amplify load → make it worse. Defenses Timeouts: never wait forever on a dependency (the #1 cause) Circuit breakers: stop calling a failing dependency, fail fast Bulkheads: isolate thread/connection pools per dependency Retry budgets: cap retries (e.g. ≤10% extra) + backoff + JITTER Load shedding: drop excess load to protect core capacity Fallbacks: degrade gracefully (stale cache, default response) Retry storms (the amplifier) # Naive retries during an outage MULTIPLY load on the struggling service. # Fix: exponential backoff + jitter, retry budgets, and circuit breakers # that stop retrying once a dependency is clearly down. Interview tip: Name timeouts as the root cause first — unbounded waits are what let a slow dependency exhaust caller threads. Then layer circuit breakers (fail fast), bulkheads (contain the blast), and retry budgets with jitter (so retries don't become a self-inflicted DDoS). The senior insight: retries are a double-edged sword — they help with transient blips but amplify sustained outages, so they must be bounded and paired with circuit breaking.

questions.q: Monolith vs microservices: how do you actually decide, and what's the cost of microservices?
questions.text: Microservices are not automatically better. The decision hinges on team size, domain maturity, and operational capability — not hype. MONOLITH: + simple deploy, easy local dev, no network between modules, easy transactions - scaling couples everything, large codebase, one deploy pipeline MICROSERVICES: + independent scaling & deploys, team autonomy, tech diversity, fault isolation - distributed-systems complexity: network, partial failure, data consistency, observability, deployment/infra overhead, harder transactions When microservices pay off - Multiple teams stepping on each other in one codebase (org scaling) - Components with very different scaling/availability needs - Mature domain boundaries you understand well - You have the ops maturity: CI/CD, observability, on-call, infra automation When to stay monolith - Small team / early product (boundaries still shifting) - You can't yet operate distributed systems well → Start with a well-modularized monolith; extract services when pain is real. Principal answer: Microservices solve an organizational scaling problem more than a technical one — they let many teams ship independently. They impose a real tax: distributed transactions, partial failure, network latency, and a much higher observability/ops bar. The pragmatic path is a modular monolith first, then extract services along proven seams when team friction or divergent scaling justifies the cost. Beware the "distributed monolith" — microservices that must deploy together

questions.q: Design an event sourcing + CQRS system. What problems does it solve and what does it cost?
questions.text: Event sourcing stores state as an immutable log of events; CQRS separates the write model from read models. Powerful for audit and complex domains, but not free. Command → validate → append EVENT to log (source of truth) ↓ (events published) Read model A (SQL view) Read model B (search index) Read model C (cache) ↑ queries ↑ queries ↑ queries Current state = fold(events). Read models are projections, rebuildable from the log. What it gives you - Full audit trail / history (every change is an event, immutable) - Time travel: reconstruct state at any past point - Multiple read models optimized per query (CQRS) - Natural fit for event-driven integration What it costs - Complexity: eventual consistency between write log and read models - Event schema evolution / versioning is hard (events live forever) - Replay/rebuild needs snapshots to bound cost - Steeper learning curve; over-engineering risk for simple CRUD Snapshots # Don't replay millions of events to get current state. # Periodically snapshot aggregate state; replay only events since last snapshot. Interview tip: Reach for event sourcing + CQRS only where its strengths matter — strong audit requirements (finance, healthcare), complex domains, or wildly divergent read patterns. For simple CRUD it's massive over-engineering. Be honest about the costs: eventual consistency between write and read sides, event versioning, and the need for snapshots. Showing you know when not to use it signals more maturity than knowing how.

questions.q: Design a disaster recovery strategy. Explain RTO, RPO, and the DR tiers.
questions.text: Disaster recovery plans for catastrophic loss (region down, data corruption). Two numbers drive every decision: RTO and RPO. The two key metrics RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long until you're back up? → drives your failover architecture RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data can you afford to lose? → drives your backup/replication frequency # "RTO 5 min, RPO 0" is wildly more expensive than "RTO 24h, RPO 1h." DR strategy tiers (cost vs RTO/RPO) Backup & restore: cheap; RTO hours-days, RPO = backup interval Pilot light: minimal standby (DB replicating, app off); scale up on DR Warm standby: scaled-down full stack running; promote on DR Hot / active-active: full second region serving; near-zero RTO/RPO (costliest) What a real plan includes - Cross-region backups (and test RESTORES — untested backups aren't backups) - Data corruption protection: point-in-time recovery, immutable backups - Runbooks for failover (don't improvise during a disaster) - Regular DR drills / game days to validate RTO/RPO are actually met Principal answer: Start by asking the business for RTO and RPO — they're requirements, not technical choices, and they determine cost. Map them to a tier: backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, or hot active-active. The two points interviewers reward: backups are worthless unless restores are tested regularly, and DR plans are worthless unless drilled — a plan that's never been exercised will fail when you need it. Also distinguish DR (disaster) from HA

questions.q: Design a container orchestration platform's scheduler (like the Kubernetes scheduler).
questions.text: The scheduler decides which node each workload runs on, balancing resource fit, constraints, and spreading — at scale, efficiently. Pending pod → Scheduler: 1. FILTER (predicates): which nodes CAN run this pod? resources fit? node selector / affinity? taints tolerated? volumes? 2. SCORE (priorities): rank feasible nodes least-loaded? spread across zones? affinity preferences? image locality? 3. BIND: assign pod → highest-scoring node → kubelet runs it Filtering (hard constraints) - Sufficient CPU/memory (requests fit remaining capacity) - nodeSelector / nodeAffinity match - Taints/tolerations (node says "only these pods") - Pod affinity/anti-affinity (co-locate or spread relative to other pods) Scoring (soft preferences) - Spread across nodes/zones for availability (topology spread) - Bin-packing vs spreading (cost efficiency vs blast-radius) - Image locality (node already has the image → faster start) - Preferred affinity weights Scale & advanced Resource model: requests (scheduling) vs limits (runtime cap) Preemption: evict lower-priority pods to fit a higher-priority one Descheduling/rebalancing: move pods when the cluster drifts from optimal Scale: schedule thousands of pods/sec → efficient filtering, caching node state Interview tip: Frame it as the two-phase filter-then-score pipeline — hard constraints eliminate infeasible nodes, soft priorities rank the rest. Discuss the bin-packing (cost) vs spreading (availability) tension as a scoring trade-off. Mention requests-vs

questions.q: Strong vs eventual consistency: how do you decide per feature, with examples?
questions.text: Consistency is a per-feature decision, not a system-wide one. Strong consistency is simpler to reason about but costs latency and availability; eventual scales but admits anomalies. The trade-off Strong: every read sees the latest write + correct & simple to reason about - higher latency, reduced availability under partition (CAP: CP) Eventual: replicas converge over time + low latency, high availability, scales (CAP: AP) - reads may be stale; needs conflict handling Decide by cost of being wrong Needs STRONG (correctness critical): - account balance / payments / inventory "last item" - unique username claim, booking the same seat - anything where stale data causes money loss or double-allocation Fine with EVENTUAL (stale is acceptable): - social feed, like counts, view counts - user profile, recommendations, search index freshness - analytics, notifications Mixing within one product # E-commerce checkout: # inventory decrement & payment → strong (can't oversell / double-charge) # product reviews, "customers also bought" → eventual (stale is fine) # Use the right model per data type; don't make everything strong (too slow) # or everything eventual (bugs with money). Principal answer: Frame it as cost-of-staleness. Ask: if a read is a few seconds stale, what breaks? If the answer is "money or double-allocation," go strong (and accept the latency/availability hit). If it's "a slightly old like count," go eventual and reap the scale. The strongest answers explicitly mix models i

questions.q: Design rate limiting at scale across a distributed fleet. How do limits stay accurate?
questions.text: Single-node rate limiting is easy; the hard problem is enforcing a global limit across many gateway/server instances without a bottleneck or wild inaccuracy. The distributed challenge # Limit: 100 req/min per user. Traffic spread across 10 gateway pods. # Naive: each pod allows 100 → user actually gets 1000. Wrong. # Need shared state OR a smart approximation. Approaches Centralized (Redis) counter: all pods INCR a shared key (atomic, Lua sliding window) + accurate - Redis is a hot dependency / potential bottleneck Local + sync (token distribution): each pod gets a share of the budget; periodically rebalance + fast, no per-request network hop - approximate near boundaries Tiered: coarse local limit (fast) + global Redis check for precision Algorithms (recap) Token bucket: allows bursts, smooth refill — most common for APIs Sliding window counter: accurate, bounded memory Return headers: X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After (good API citizenship) Resilience # If the rate-limit store (Redis) is down — fail OPEN or CLOSED? # fail open: don't block legit traffic (risk abuse) # fail closed: protect backend (risk blocking everyone) # Usually fail open with a conservative local fallback limit. Interview tip: The crux is shared state vs accuracy. A central Redis counter with an atomic Lua sliding window is accurate but a hot dependency; local budgets with periodic sync are fast but fuzzy at boundaries. The pragmatic answer is tiered: a cheap local limit for the common case plus a globa

questions.q: Design an internal developer platform (IDP) with golden paths and self-service.
questions.text: An IDP abstracts infrastructure so developers ship without becoming Kubernetes/cloud experts — paved roads with guardrails, self-service from day one. Developer → Portal/CLI (self-service) → Golden-path templates (service scaffold, CI/CD, observability baked in) → provision via IaC (Terraform/Crossplane) on K8s/cloud → guardrails: policy-as-code, quotas, security defaults ← golden signals dashboards auto-wired Core capabilities Golden paths: opinionated templates for the 80% common case → "new service" = repo + pipeline + dashboards + alerts in minutes Self-service: provision DBs, queues, environments without filing tickets Guardrails: policy-as-code (OPA/Kyverno), secure defaults, cost quotas Abstraction: hide YAML/cloud details behind a simple interface Design principles - Paved road, not a cage: golden path is easy; deviation is possible but owned - Reduce cognitive load: devs think in services, not pods/IAM/VPCs - Day-2 included: observability, scaling, secrets, on-call wired by default - Treat the platform as a PRODUCT: devs are customers; measure adoption Measuring success Lead time to first deploy (new service → prod) Deployment frequency, change-fail rate (DORA metrics) Golden-path adoption %, ticket reduction, developer satisfaction Principal answer: The philosophy is paved road, not cage: make the right way the easy way via golden-path templates that bake in CI/CD, observability, and security, while allowing (owned) deviation. Treat the platform as a product with de

questions.q: Design a distributed web crawler. Crawl billions of pages politely and efficiently.
questions.text: A web crawler must fetch billions of pages, avoid re-crawling, respect politeness, and distribute work — without overwhelming any single site or itself. Seed URLs → URL Frontier (priority + politeness queues) ↓ Fetchers (distributed) → download page ↓ Parser → extract links + content ↓ new links ↓ content Dedup (seen?) ──┘ Content store + index ↓ unseen back to Frontier The URL frontier (the heart) Politeness: per-domain queue + delay (don't hammer one host) Priority: crawl important/fresh pages first (PageRank-ish, change rate) Partition by domain → one host's pages handled by one worker (rate control) Dedup & freshness Seen-URL set: billions of URLs → bloom filter (memory-efficient, probabilistic) Content dedup: hash/simhash to skip near-duplicate pages Re-crawl: schedule by observed change frequency (news daily, archive rarely) robots.txt: fetch + cache per domain; respect crawl-delay and disallow Scale & traps - Crawler traps (infinite calendar URLs) → depth limits, URL pattern detection - DNS load → cache DNS aggressively - Distributed coordination → partition URL space by domain hash Interview tip: The URL frontier is the design — it encodes both politeness (per-domain rate limiting so you're a good citizen) and prioritization (crawl valuable/changing pages first). Use a bloom filter for the billions-scale seen-set, partition by domain so one worker controls a host's crawl rate, and respect robots.txt. Mention crawler traps and re-crawl scheduling by change rate to show

questions.q: Design a recommendation system. Cover candidate generation and ranking at scale.
questions.text: Recommenders predict what a user will engage with. At scale the standard architecture is a two-stage funnel: cheap candidate generation, then expensive ranking. Millions of items ↓ CANDIDATE GENERATION (fast, approximate) → ~hundreds ↓ RANKING (heavy ML model, precise) → ~dozens ↓ RE-RANK / business rules (diversity, freshness, dedup) → final list Candidate generation Collaborative filtering: users like you liked X (matrix factorization) Content-based: items similar to what you engaged with (embeddings + ANN) Graph / co-occurrence: "bought together", session sequences → Reduce millions → a few hundred candidates cheaply (often via vector ANN) Ranking Heavy model scores each candidate with rich features: user features + item features + context (time, device) + cross features Predicts P(click)/P(engage); sort by expected value. Too expensive for millions of items → that's why stage 1 narrows first. Serving & freshness Offline: train models, precompute embeddings/candidate lists (batch) Online: real-time features + low-latency ranking (feature store + model server) Feedback loop: log impressions/clicks → retrain; watch for filter bubbles Cold start: new user/item → fall back to popularity/content features Principal answer: The two-stage funnel is the key insight — you cannot run a heavy ranking model over millions of items per request, so cheap candidate generation (vector ANN / collaborative filtering) narrows to hundreds, then a rich model ranks those. Mention the offline/onli

questions.q: Design a stock-trading / order-matching engine. Low latency, strict correctness.
questions.text: An order-matching engine pairs buy and sell orders with strict price-time priority, extreme low latency, and perfect correctness — a uniquely demanding workload. Orders → Gateway (validate, risk check) → Matching Engine (per symbol) ↓ in-memory order book match by price-time priority ↓ Trades → market data feed + settlement ↓ Event log (sequenced, replayable) The order book Two sorted sides: bids (desc price), asks (asc price) Match: incoming buy ≥ best ask → trade at resting price Priority: price first, then time (FIFO at each price level) Kept fully IN MEMORY — disk/network in the hot path is too slow Latency & correctness Single-threaded per symbol → no locks, deterministic ordering (LMAX Disruptor pattern: one thread, ring buffer, micro/nanosecond latency) Sequence every event → deterministic replay → audit + recovery Partition by symbol → AAPL engine independent of TSLA engine (scale out) Reliability Replicated event log → hot standby replays the same sequence → instant failover Determinism is everything: same inputs → same outputs on the replica Risk checks pre-trade (limits, fat-finger) at the gateway, off the hot path Interview tip: Counter-intuitively, the matching engine is single-threaded per symbol — concurrency would break deterministic price-time ordering and add lock latency. Cite the LMAX Disruptor model (one thread, in-memory ring buffer, no locks → microsecond latency). Everything is sequenced and in-memory for determinism, which also gives you replay-based

questions.q: Design a system to store and serve large files / object storage (like S3).
questions.text: Object storage holds vast numbers of large immutable blobs with high durability and scalable throughput — a fundamentally different design from a database. Client → API (PUT/GET) → Metadata service (object → location, size, checksum, version) ↓ Storage nodes: object split into chunks, replicated/erasure-coded across nodes ↓ Background: repair, rebalance, integrity scrub, lifecycle/tiering Durability: replication vs erasure coding Replication (3x): store 3 copies → simple, 200% storage overhead Erasure coding (e.g. 10+4): split into 10 data + 4 parity shards → survive 4 shard losses with only 40% overhead (vs 200%) → S3-scale uses erasure coding for cost; 11 nines of durability Metadata & scale Separate metadata plane (object→chunk locations) from data plane (bytes) Metadata is small but high-QPS → sharded, replicated KV store Large uploads: multipart upload (parallel chunks, resumable) Immutability + versioning: objects are versioned, not edited in place Operational Background scrubbing: detect bit-rot via checksums, re-replicate/rebuild Rebalancing: spread load as nodes are added/fail Lifecycle/tiering: hot → cold → archive (cost optimization) Principal answer: Two big design points: (1) separate the metadata plane from the data plane — metadata is small/high-QPS (sharded KV), data is huge (storage nodes); (2) use erasure coding rather than naive 3x replication at scale — it gives the same durability (11 nines) at a fraction of the storage cost. Add multipart upload for larg

questions.q: How do you approach a system design question when you've never seen the domain before?
questions.text: Interviewers often pick unfamiliar domains deliberately — they're testing your process , not domain trivia. A repeatable method keeps you composed. The method (reduce the unknown to knowns) 1. Clarify relentlessly: turn the vague prompt into concrete requirements. "Design X" → who uses it, what are the core flows, what scale, what's out of scope? 2. Map to primitives you DO know: nearly everything decomposes into reads, writes, storage, queues, caches, fan-out, search, real-time push — patterns you've seen before. 3. Identify the hard part: what makes THIS problem non-trivial? Optimize the design around it. 4. Start simple, then scale: a working simple design beats a half-drawn complex one. Pattern-match the core challenge High write volume? → queue + partition + async Low-latency reads? → cache + CDN + pre-compute Real-time updates? → push (WebSocket/SSE) + pub-sub Massive storage? → object store + tiering Search/discovery? → inverted index / vector search Strict correctness? → strong consistency + idempotency Interview tip: Say this out loud: "I haven't built exactly this, so let me clarify the requirements and decompose it into patterns I know." Then narrate the mapping. Unfamiliar domains are won by process — clarify, decompose into primitives (reads/writes/cache/queue/search), find the one hard part, and design around it. Drive the conversation; don't freeze waiting to recall a domain you've never touched.

questions.q: Design a counter / metrics aggregation system for things like view counts and likes at scale.
questions.text: Counting seems trivial until it's billions of increments/sec on hot items. Naive UPDATE counter SET c=c+1 on a row becomes a contention nightmare. Why naive counting fails # A viral video gets 1M likes/min → 1M writes to ONE row → # row lock contention, the single row is a hotspot, DB melts. Scaling techniques 1. Sharded/striped counters: split one logical counter into N sub-counters; increment a random shard; total = SUM(shards). Spreads write contention by N. 2. In-memory aggregation + flush: increment in Redis (atomic INCR) → periodically flush to durable store. 3. Stream aggregation: emit "like" events → Kafka → stream processor aggregates → store rollups. Decouples write spikes from the counter store. Accuracy vs cost Exact counts: striped counters / stream aggregation (eventual, but exact total) Approximate (huge cardinality, e.g. unique viewers): HyperLogLog → count distinct in ~1.5KB with ~2% error Display counts can be eventually consistent — nobody needs a like count to the ms. Principal answer: Name the hot-row problem immediately, then solve write contention with striped counters (increment one of N shards, sum to read) or in-memory INCR in Redis flushed asynchronously. For unique counts (distinct viewers) at scale, reach for HyperLogLog — exact distinct-count storage is infeasible, and ~2% error is fine for a view counter. The framing that impresses: display counters tolerate eventual consistency, so trade exactness/latency for write scalability deliberately.

questions.q: Design health checks and self-healing for a large service fleet.
questions.text: At fleet scale, instances fail constantly; the system must detect and replace them automatically. Good health checking is subtler than a single /health endpoint. Types of health checks Liveness: is the process alive? failing → RESTART it (deadlock, hang) Readiness: can it serve traffic NOW? failing → remove from LB (warming up, deps down) Startup: slow-starting app → don't kill it prematurely # Conflating liveness & readiness is a classic bug: a dependency blip # flips readiness (fine) but if wired to liveness it RESTARTS healthy pods (bad). Deep vs shallow checks Shallow: "process responds" — cheap, but misses broken dependencies Deep: "can I actually query the DB / serve a real request" — catches more, but risk: a shared-dependency blip fails ALL instances at once → mass eviction → outage. Tune carefully; don't cascade. Self-healing loop Detect (health check fails) → react (restart / replace / reschedule) → verify (new instance healthy) → rebalance. Autoscaler replaces failed nodes; orchestrator reschedules pods. Guard rails: don't replace so aggressively you mask a real bug or thrash. Interview tip: Distinguish liveness (restart) from readiness (depool) from startup probes — conflating them causes the infamous failure where a transient dependency hiccup restarts your entire healthy fleet. Discuss the deep-vs-shallow trade-off: deep checks catch more but can cause correlated mass eviction during a shared-dependency blip. Self-healing is a detect→react→verify loop with guard

questions.q: Design a secrets management system. How are credentials stored, rotated, and accessed?
questions.text: Secrets (DB passwords, API keys, certs) must never live in code or plain config. A secrets manager centralizes secure storage, access control, rotation, and audit. App → authenticate (workload identity) → Secrets Manager (Vault/KMS/cloud) ↓ authorized? return secret (short-lived ideally) + audit log entry ↑ Encryption at rest (master key in HSM/KMS), encryption in transit Core requirements Encryption: at rest (envelope encryption, master key in HSM/KMS) + in transit Access control: least-privilege; identity-based (not a shared static token) Audit: every access logged (who, what, when) — essential for compliance No secrets in code/images/env files committed to git Rotation & dynamic secrets Static secret rotation: change credential + update consumers without downtime Dynamic secrets (Vault): generate short-lived, per-request DB creds that auto-expire → drastically shrinks the blast radius of a leak Lease + revoke: secrets have TTLs; can be revoked instantly if compromised Workload identity # The bootstrapping problem: how does an app prove who it is to GET secrets? # Use platform identity (K8s ServiceAccount, cloud IAM role / IRSA) — # NOT a long-lived token stored somewhere (which is itself a secret to protect). Principal answer: Three pillars: encryption (envelope encryption with the master key in an HSM/KMS), identity-based least-privilege access with full audit, and rotation. The advanced move is dynamic, short-lived secrets (Vault generating per-request DB credentials tha

questions.q: Design a system using a service mesh. What does it add over plain service-to-service calls?
questions.text: A service mesh moves cross-cutting network concerns (security, reliability, observability) out of application code into a sidecar proxy layer. Service A [app + sidecar proxy] ⇄ [sidecar proxy + app] Service B ↑ data plane (Envoy proxies handle the traffic) Control plane (Istio/Linkerd): config, certs, policy, telemetry What the mesh provides Security: automatic mTLS between services (encrypted + authenticated), zero code change Reliability: retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, load balancing in the proxy Observability: uniform metrics/traces/logs for ALL service-to-service traffic Traffic control: canary, blue-green, traffic splitting, fault injection Sidecar vs sidecar-less Sidecar (Istio classic): a proxy per pod → flexible but resource overhead + latency Sidecar-less / ambient / eBPF (Cilium): node-level proxying → less overhead Trade-off: capability/isolation vs resource cost and per-hop latency. When it's worth it Worth it: many services, need uniform mTLS + observability + traffic policy Overkill: a handful of services — the operational complexity outweighs benefit # A mesh is powerful but adds a whole control plane to operate. Interview tip: The pitch is: take retries, timeouts, mTLS, and telemetry out of every app (in every language) and standardize them in a sidecar/proxy layer with a central control plane. The big wins are automatic mTLS and uniform observability for free. Be balanced — call out the costs (sidecar latency/resource overhead, a control plane to operat

questions.q: Design a leaderboard / ranking system for millions of users in real time.
questions.text: A real-time leaderboard needs fast rank queries (top-N and a user's own rank) under constant score updates — a poor fit for naive SQL ordering. Why SQL struggles # "SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10" on 50M rows on every request, # plus "what's MY rank" = COUNT(scores > mine) → expensive at scale + churn. Redis Sorted Set (the standard answer) ZADD board score user # update score: O(log N) ZREVRANGE board 0 9 # top 10: O(log N + 10) ZREVRANK board user # a user's rank: O(log N) ZINCRBY board +10 user # atomic increment # Sorted set keeps everything ranked incrementally — no full re-sort. Scaling beyond one node Sharding: partition by region/segment; merge top-Ns for a global board Approximate global rank: exact rank among 50M is costly — bucket/percentile ("top 5%") is often enough for display Time windows: daily/weekly boards → separate keys with TTL Durability: Redis is the serving layer; persist authoritative scores in a DB too Principal answer: Redis sorted sets are purpose-built for this — O(log N) updates and rank queries, atomic increments, no re-sorting. For global scale, shard by segment and merge top-Ns; provide approximate/percentile rank for the long tail since exact rank among millions is expensive and rarely needed for display. Use separate TTL'd keys for time-windowed boards, and keep a durable copy of authoritative scores in a DB behind the Redis serving layer.

questions.q: How do you design APIs for scale and evolution? REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL, and versioning.
questions.text: API design choices affect performance, client ergonomics, and how painlessly you can evolve without breaking consumers. REST/JSON: ubiquitous, cacheable, human-readable → public APIs, broad client support gRPC/protobuf: binary, fast, streaming, strong contracts → internal service-to-service, low latency, polyglot GraphQL: client picks exactly the fields → no over/under-fetching → varied clients (mobile/web) with different data needs; complex graphs Choosing Internal high-perf RPC → gRPC Public, cache-friendly, simple → REST Many clients, flexible queries → GraphQL (mind N+1 and query-cost limits) Versioning & evolution Backward compatibility first: add fields, don't remove/rename (additive changes) Versioning: URI (/v2/), header, or content negotiation Deprecation: announce → dual-run → sunset with timelines + metrics on old version protobuf: reserve field numbers; never reuse → safe wire-compat evolution Scale concerns Pagination (cursor > offset for large sets), filtering, field selection Rate limiting + quotas, idempotency keys for writes GraphQL: depth/complexity limits to prevent abusive expensive queries Interview tip: Match protocol to use case — gRPC for internal low-latency RPC, REST for public/cacheable APIs, GraphQL when diverse clients need flexible field selection (while guarding against N+1 and runaway query cost). On evolution, emphasize additive, backward-compatible changes as the default (add fields, never repurpose them), cursor-based pagination for scale, a

questions.q: Design a system that needs both OLTP and OLAP. How do you avoid analytics killing production?
questions.text: Transactional (OLTP) and analytical (OLAP) workloads have opposite needs; running heavy analytics on your production DB will degrade or crash it. You separate them. OLTP vs OLAP OLTP: many small, fast read/write txns (orders, logins) → row store, normalized, low latency, high concurrency (Postgres/MySQL) OLAP: few huge scan/aggregate queries (revenue by region last year) → columnar, denormalized, throughput-oriented (BigQuery/Snowflake/ClickHouse) # A giant analytical scan on the OLTP DB locks/IO-starves production. Separation patterns 1. Read replica for analytics: cheap isolation; replica absorbs heavy reads (still row-store — OK for moderate analytics, not big aggregations) 2. ETL/ELT to a warehouse: batch export OLTP → columnar warehouse 3. CDC (change data capture): stream OLTP changes (Debezium → Kafka) → warehouse / lake in near-real-time, zero load on the primary 4. HTAP systems (TiDB, SingleStore): both in one — convenient, niche trade-offs Modern pattern CDC from OLTP → Kafka → stream/batch into a columnar lakehouse. Keeps production isolated, gives analysts a query-optimized copy, near-real-time. Principal answer: Never run OLAP on your OLTP database — the access patterns are opposite (row vs columnar, point vs scan). Isolate with a read replica for light analytics, or for real scale, stream changes via CDC (Debezium/Kafka) into a columnar warehouse or lakehouse. CDC is the modern default: near-real-time, zero query load on the primary, and the analysts get a store

questions.q: Design a deployment system supporting canary, blue-green, and instant rollback.
questions.text: Safe deployment minimizes blast radius and enables fast recovery. The core strategies trade infrastructure cost against risk control. Rolling: replace instances gradually (default; some mixed-version time) Blue-Green: full parallel env (green), switch traffic at once, old (blue) on standby + instant rollback (flip back) - 2x infra during deploy Canary: route a small % to the new version, watch metrics, ramp gradually + smallest blast radius, real-traffic validation - slower, needs good metrics Canary flow (the gold standard) 1. Deploy new version alongside old 2. Route 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% in steps 3. At each step: compare canary vs baseline (error rate, latency, business KPIs) 4. Automated analysis → promote if healthy, auto-rollback if not Rollback & safety Instant rollback: keep previous version ready (blue-green flip, or redeploy prev image) DB migrations: must be backward-compatible (expand/contract) — you can't roll back data → decouple schema change from code: add column → deploy code → backfill → drop later Feature flags: decouple release from deploy → flip off without redeploying Interview tip: Canary is the strongest answer — validate on real traffic with automated metric comparison and auto-rollback, minimizing blast radius. The detail that separates seniors: database migrations break the rollback story, so use the expand/contract (backward-compatible) pattern and decouple schema changes from code deploys. Pair deployments with feature flags so you can disable a fe

questions.q: Design a multi-tenant SaaS platform. Compare isolation models and the noisy-neighbor problem.
questions.text: Multi-tenancy serves many customers from shared infrastructure. The central trade-off is isolation (security, blast radius, noisy-neighbor) vs cost/operational efficiency. Isolation models (most shared → most isolated): Shared everything (pooled): one DB, tenant_id column on every row + cheapest, easiest to operate - weakest isolation, noisy-neighbor risk Shared app, DB-per-tenant (bridge): + good data isolation, per-tenant backup/restore - more DBs to manage Silo (stack per tenant): + strongest isolation, per-tenant customization - costliest, ops-heavy Tenant isolation concerns Data: enforce tenant_id everywhere (a missed filter = cross-tenant leak!) → row-level security, scoped data-access layer, tested rigorously Noisy neighbor: one tenant's load degrades others → per-tenant quotas, rate limits, resource caps, fair scheduling Blast radius: a bad deploy/incident shouldn't take down all tenants → cell-based architecture (shard tenants into isolated cells) Cell-based architecture # Partition tenants into independent "cells" (each a full stack serving a subset). # A cell failure affects only its tenants. Big tenants can get a dedicated cell. # Best balance of isolation + efficiency at scale. Principal answer: Frame it as an isolation/cost spectrum (pooled → bridge → silo) and pick per requirements — enterprise customers may demand a dedicated DB or cell; SMB tenants pool cheaply. The two failure modes to address explicitly: cross-tenant data leakage (one missed tenant_id filte

questions.q: Design a photo/media-sharing service (like Instagram). End-to-end from upload to feed.
questions.text: A media-sharing service combines object storage, async processing, CDN delivery, and a feed system — a great integrative question. Upload: client → presigned URL → object store (original) → async: generate thumbnails/sizes, extract metadata, moderation → store renditions → distribute to CDN Serve: feed request → metadata (posts) + CDN URLs for media → client loads images from nearest CDN edge Upload path Direct-to-storage via presigned URL (don't proxy big files through app servers) Async pipeline: resize to multiple resolutions, strip EXIF, content moderation Metadata (caption, author, timestamp, media refs) → DB Storage & delivery Originals + renditions → object store (S3/GCS), tiered by age Serve via CDN (images are static, cacheable → huge hit ratio) Responsive: deliver the right size per device (don't send 4K to a phone) Feed (ties to fan-out design) Feed = post metadata + CDN media URLs, hybrid fan-out (push/pull for celebs) Metadata DB sharded by user; media is just references → small feed payloads Counts (likes/views) via striped counters; comments paginated separately Interview tip: Hit the four pillars: (1) direct-to-storage upload via presigned URLs (never proxy large media through app servers), (2) an async processing pipeline for renditions + moderation, (3) CDN delivery since images are the ideal cacheable static asset, and (4) a feed that stores only metadata + media references with hybrid fan-out. This question rewards composing patterns from earlier problems

questions.q: How do you estimate cost and design for cost-efficiency (FinOps) in a system design?
questions.text: Senior designs account for cost, not just correctness and scale. Showing cost-awareness distinguishes a principal-level answer. Where the money goes Compute: often the biggest line; right-size, autoscale, use spot for fault-tolerant work Storage: tier aggressively (hot/warm/cold/archive); lifecycle policies Data transfer: egress (esp. cross-region & internet) is sneakily expensive Managed services: convenient but premium-priced; build-vs-buy math Idle/over-provisioned resources: the silent budget killer Cost-efficiency levers Caching/CDN: cuts compute + egress (cache hit is far cheaper than origin) Autoscaling: match capacity to demand; scale to zero for spiky/dev workloads Spot/preemptible: 60–90% cheaper for interruptible batch/stateless work Storage tiering: move cold data to cheap tiers automatically Data locality: keep traffic in-region/in-AZ to dodge egress charges Right-sizing: measure actual usage; trim over-provisioned requests The trade-offs Cost vs reliability: spot saves money but can be reclaimed → only for tolerant work Cost vs latency: cheaper cold storage = slower access Cost vs simplicity: a hand-rolled cheaper solution may cost more in eng time # Optimize for TOTAL cost of ownership, including engineering effort. Principal answer: Weave cost in as a first-class constraint: do a rough cost estimate (compute + storage + egress are the big three) the same way you do a capacity estimate. Lean on caching/CDN (cuts both compute and pricey egress), autoscaling, spo

questions.q: Design observability for a large distributed system. Logs, metrics, and traces together.
questions.text: Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs — essential for operating distributed systems where failures are emergent. The three pillars work together. Metrics (what & how much): aggregated numbers, cheap, alerting Logs (what happened): discrete events, detailed, debugging Traces (where & why slow): request path across services, latency breakdown ↓ ↓ ↓ Time-series DB Log store Trace store ↓ ↓ ↓ Unified query / dashboards / alerting When you use each Metrics: dashboards + alerting ("error rate > 1%", "P99 > 500ms") — start here Traces: "this request is slow — WHICH service/hop?" — distributed latency Logs: "what exactly happened in that failing request" — deepest detail Flow: alert (metric) → trace (locate) → logs (root cause). They chain. Key practices Correlation IDs: propagate a request/trace id through all services → tie the 3 together Structured logs: JSON, queryable, not free-text grep Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (alert on these) Sampling traces: 100% is expensive → head/tail sample (keep slow/error traces) Cardinality discipline: high-cardinality labels blow up metric stores Interview tip: Explain how the three pillars chain in an incident: a metric alert tells you something is wrong, a trace localizes which service/hop, and logs give the root cause. The glue is correlation/trace IDs propagated everywhere so you can pivot between them. Alert on the four golden signals, use structured logs, sample traces

questions.q: Design a system with WebSockets for millions of concurrent connections.
questions.text: Holding millions of persistent WebSocket connections is a distinct scaling challenge: the connections themselves are the constrained resource, and the connection tier is stateful. Clients ⇄ (WSS) ⇄ Connection/Gateway tier (stateful, holds sockets) ↓ registry: user → which gateway holds the socket (Redis) Pub/Sub (Redis/Kafka) for cross-gateway message routing ↓ Backend services (stateless) publish events The scaling challenges Each connection consumes memory + a file descriptor → tune OS limits (ulimit, ephemeral ports) Connections are LONG-LIVED → LB must support sticky/WS, can't freely rebalance State: a gateway holds specific users' sockets → need a registry to find them A single box maxes out around tens-hundreds of K conns → must scale horizontally Cross-node message routing # User A (on gateway 1) messages User B (on gateway 3). # Gateway 1 publishes to pub/sub → gateway 3 (subscribed for B) pushes to B's socket. # Registry maps user → gateway so you route to the right node. Resilience Heartbeats/ping-pong → detect dead connections, free resources Reconnect with backoff + resume (sync missed messages since last ack) Graceful gateway drain on deploy (migrate connections, don't drop all at once) Principal answer: The key realization is that the connection tier is stateful and the sockets are the bottleneck resource — so you scale it as a dedicated horizontal layer, tune OS limits, and use a registry (user→gateway) plus pub/sub to route messages between nodes. questions.q: Walk through a build-vs-buy decision for a major system component.
questions.text: Senior engineers don't build everything — knowing when to buy/adopt vs build is a key judgment. It's a TCO and focus decision, not an ego one. The decision framework Is it core/differentiating to YOUR business? → lean BUILD (it's your edge) Is it commodity (auth, queues, search, monitoring)? → lean BUY/adopt What's the TOTAL cost: build + maintain + operate forever, vs license + integrate? Time-to-market: buy is faster now; build is a long-term investment Opportunity cost: every engineer building commodity infra isn't building product Hidden costs of BUILD It's not just initial dev — it's maintenance, on-call, security patching, scaling, docs, and the bus-factor risk, forever. Most "we'll build it" underestimates the perpetual carrying cost by a lot. Hidden costs of BUY Vendor lock-in, pricing at scale, customization limits, integration effort, dependency on vendor reliability/roadmap, data egress/portability. → Mitigate with open standards / abstraction layers / exit strategy. Interview tip: Anchor on "is this core to our differentiation?" Build the thing that IS your product; buy or adopt open-source for commodity infrastructure (don't build your own message queue or monitoring stack to save a license fee — you'll pay far more in perpetual maintenance and opportunity cost). Be explicit that build cost is forever (maintenance, on-call, security), and de-risk buy decisions against lock-in with abstraction layers and an exit plan. This signals business judgment, not just engin

questions.q: You're given vague requirements and limited time in the interview. How do you scope and drive the design?
questions.text: Most system design interviews are deliberately open-ended and time-boxed. Managing scope and driving the conversation is itself a graded skill — often the difference between levels. Drive, don't wait 1. Clarify & scope FIRST (5 min): functional + non-functional reqs, scale, and EXPLICITLY state what's out of scope. Get agreement. 2. Propose a plan: "I'll do estimation, then high-level design, then deep-dive the 2 hardest parts. Sound good?" → you're steering. 3. Time-box yourself: don't spend 20 min on the easy CRUD part. 4. Signpost trade-offs as you go: every choice has alternatives — say them. Manage scope actively Breadth first (a complete simple design) THEN depth (deep-dive hard parts). A finished simple system > an unfinished elaborate one. Ask "is it more valuable to go deeper here or cover X?" → collaborative scoping. Watch the interviewer's cues — they'll steer you to what they want to probe. Seniority signals - Owning the structure (not waiting to be prompted) - Stating assumptions explicitly when info is missing (then proceeding) - Naming trade-offs and justifying choices, not presenting one "right" answer - Knowing what to leave out and saying why Principal answer: Treat the ambiguity as the test. Open by clarifying requirements and explicitly bounding scope, then propose and narrate a plan so you're visibly driving. Go breadth-first to a complete simple design, then deep-dive the genuinely hard parts, time-boxing the trivial bits. Continuously surface trade-offs

questions.q: How do you define functional and non-functional requirements in the first five minutes of a design interview?
questions.text: Split what the system does from how well it must do it, and confirm both before drawing anything. Functional: post, read, search, delete Non-functional: latency p99, availability, durability, consistency, scale (QPS, GB), cost Out of scope: say it explicitly Principal answer: Write numbers next to every non-functional requirement.

questions.q: How do you identify and defend the bottleneck in a design?
questions.text: Estimate load per component, find the one that saturates first, and focus the design effort there. QPS -> app tier (stateless, scales out) -> cache (hit rate?) -> DB (writes: single leader limit) Bottleneck = first component to hit its ceiling Principal answer: Name the bottleneck before you optimise.

questions.q: What latency numbers should every engineer know, and how do you use them in estimates?
questions.text: Memory is nanoseconds, SSD microseconds, network within a datacenter sub-millisecond, cross-region tens to hundreds of milliseconds. L1/L2 cache ~1-10 ns RAM ~100 ns SSD read ~100 us Same-DC RTT ~0.5 ms HDD seek ~10 ms Cross-region ~50-150 ms Principal answer: Use them to rule out designs fast.

questions.q: Explain the outbox pattern. Why is it used to publish events reliably?
questions.text: Write the business change and the event in one local transaction, then a relay publishes outbox rows to the broker, avoiding dual-write inconsistency. Service --(1 tx)--> DB: orders + outbox Relay/CDC --(2)--> Broker --> consumers at-least-once => consumers idempotent Principal answer: Dual writes cannot be made atomic.

questions.q: Compare orchestration and choreography for coordinating microservices.
questions.text: Orchestration uses a central coordinator that directs steps; choreography has services react to events. Choose by visibility versus coupling. Orchestration: Orchestrator -> A -> B -> C (central state) Choreography: A --event--> B --event--> C (no owner) Principal answer: Complex flows need a visible owner.

questions.q: What is the saga pattern and how do you handle compensation?
questions.text: A saga splits a distributed transaction into local transactions with compensating actions to undo completed steps on failure. Reserve stock -> Charge card -> Create shipment fail at 3 => Refund card -> Release stock (each step idempotent, each has a compensation) Principal answer: Compensation is semantic undo, not rollback.

questions.q: Compare batch processing, stream processing and the Lambda and Kappa architectures.
questions.text: Batch is simple and accurate over bounded data; streaming gives low latency; Lambda runs both, Kappa uses streaming with replay only. Lambda: events -> batch layer + speed layer -> serving Kappa: events -> log (replayable) -> stream job -> serving Principal answer: Prefer one code path if you can.

questions.q: Long polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets and webhooks: how do you choose?
questions.text: Match direction and frequency: SSE for one-way server push, WebSockets for bidirectional low-latency, long polling as fallback, webhooks for server-to-server. Poll: client asks repeatedly Long poll: server holds request SSE: one-way stream over HTTP WebSocket: full duplex Webhook: server calls your URL Principal answer: Consider proxies, scale and reconnection.

questions.q: How do you choose between a relational database and a document store for a new service?
questions.text: Pick by access patterns, relationships, consistency needs and query flexibility, not by trend. Relational: joins, constraints, transactions, ad-hoc queries Document: aggregate-per-read, flexible schema, horizontal scale Principal answer: Model reads first.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs of using GraphQL, REST and gRPC for service APIs?
questions.text: REST is simple and cacheable; GraphQL lets clients shape responses; gRPC is efficient and typed for internal calls. Public/web: REST or GraphQL (BFF) Internal service-to-service: gRPC (protobuf, streaming) Principal answer: Different layers can use different styles.

questions.q: How do you choose a cache strategy: cache-aside, read-through, write-through or write-back?
questions.text: Cache-aside is the flexible default; write-through gives consistency at write cost; write-back is fast but risks data loss. cache-aside: app -> cache miss -> DB -> fill cache write-through: app -> cache -> DB (sync) write-back: app -> cache -> async flush to DB Principal answer: Decide how stale reads can be.

questions.q: How do you decide between vertical and horizontal scaling and when does each break down?
questions.text: Vertical is simple but capped and a single point of failure; horizontal needs statelessness or partitioning but scales further. Vertical: bigger box (easy, limit, SPOF) Horizontal: more boxes + LB + shared/partitioned state Principal answer: Scale the simple thing first, but plan the exit.

questions.q: Design a file storage and sync service like Dropbox. How do you handle large files and sync efficiently?
questions.text: Split files into content-addressed chunks, upload only changed chunks, keep metadata in a database and sync via notifications. Client -> chunker (4MB, hash) -> upload new chunks -> Blob store Metadata DB: file -> [chunk hashes], version Notify service -> other devices -> pull diff Principal answer: Deduplicate by content hash.

questions.q: Design a hotel or ticket booking system that prevents double booking under high concurrency.
questions.text: Use transactional inventory with row locking or optimistic concurrency, short-lived holds with expiry, and idempotent payments. Search (read replica/cache) -> Hold (TTL 10m) -> Pay -> Confirm Inventory DB: UPDATE ... WHERE available>0 (atomic) Expiry job releases holds Principal answer: Correctness on the write path, speed on the read path.

questions.q: Design a maps and routing service. How do you compute fastest routes at scale?
questions.text: Model roads as a graph, use hierarchical preprocessing like contraction hierarchies, tile the map, and blend live traffic. Map tiles (CDN) <- tile service Routing: graph partitions -> contraction hierarchies -> A* Traffic: GPS probes -> stream -> edge weights Principal answer: Preprocess offline, query online.

questions.q: Design an email service that sends and receives mail for millions of users.
questions.text: Separate SMTP ingestion, queued delivery with retries, spam filtering, mailbox storage and search, with attention to reputation. Inbound: MX -> SMTP gw -> spam/AV -> queue -> mailbox store + index Outbound: API -> queue -> sender pool (IP reputation) -> remote MX Bounces/complaints -> feedback loop Principal answer: Deliverability is the hard part.

questions.q: Design a distributed file system like GFS or HDFS.
questions.text: A metadata master tracks file-to-block mappings while chunk servers store replicated blocks; clients stream data directly from chunk servers. Client -> NameNode/Master (metadata, leases) -> DataNodes: block A (3 replicas), block B ... Heartbeats + block reports; re-replicate on failure Principal answer: Keep the master out of the data path.

questions.q: Design a Kafka-like distributed log or message broker.
questions.text: Partitioned, replicated append-only logs with consumer offsets give high throughput, ordering per partition and replayability. Topic -> partitions (leader + followers, ISR) Producer -> partition by key -> append to log (segment files) Consumer group: each partition -> one consumer, tracks offset Principal answer: Sequential disk I/O is the secret.

questions.q: Design an ad click aggregation system that counts billions of clicks accurately.
questions.text: Ingest clicks through a durable log, aggregate in tumbling windows with stream processing, deduplicate, and reconcile with batch. Click -> collector -> Kafka -> Flink (dedupe, window 1m) -> OLAP store (rollups) + raw to data lake -> batch reconcile Principal answer: Exactly-once effects via idempotent sinks.

questions.q: Design a trending topics or top-K system for a social platform.
questions.text: Count events in sliding windows with approximate structures, merge partial results, and decay old counts. Posts -> stream -> per-shard Count-Min Sketch + heap (window 1h) -> merge top-K -> cache -> API Decay older windows Principal answer: Approximate is fine for trends.

questions.q: Design a flash sale or high-demand ticket release system that survives a traffic spike.
questions.text: Use a waiting room queue, cached static content, atomic inventory with strict limits, and asynchronous order processing. CDN (static) -> waiting room (token) -> API -> Redis atomic stock decr -> order queue -> DB Rate limit + bot protection Principal answer: Protect the inventory, shed the rest.

questions.q: Design a live video streaming system with chat for millions of viewers.
questions.text: Ingest via RTMP/SRT, transcode to adaptive bitrate segments, distribute over a CDN, and scale chat with a separate pub/sub fan-out. Streamer -> ingest -> transcoder (ABR ladder) -> packager (HLS/DASH) -> origin -> CDN -> viewers Chat: WebSocket gw -> pub/sub -> fan-out Principal answer: Latency vs scale: pick the protocol deliberately.

questions.q: Design a distributed build system or remote build cache for a large monorepo.
questions.text: Hash inputs to cache action results, distribute actions to a worker pool, and share artifacts through a content-addressable store. Client -> scheduler -> workers (hermetic sandbox) Action key = hash(inputs + command + toolchain) CAS (artifacts) + action cache Principal answer: Hermetic builds make caching safe.

questions.q: Design an alerting and monitoring system that evaluates millions of rules.
questions.text: Shard rule evaluation, query a time-series store efficiently, deduplicate and route alerts, and monitor the monitor. Rules -> sharded evaluators -> TSDB queries -> alert state machine (pending/firing) -> grouping/dedup -> routing -> pager/chat Watchdog heartbeat Principal answer: Alerting must be more reliable than what it watches.

questions.q: Design a webhook delivery system for third-party integrations.
questions.text: Queue events per subscription, deliver with signed requests, retry with exponential backoff, isolate slow endpoints and give visibility. Event -> subscription match -> per-endpoint queue -> delivery workers (timeout 10s, HMAC sig) retry backoff -> DLQ; circuit breaker per endpoint; delivery log UI Principal answer: Customers' endpoints are unreliable by default.

questions.q: Design a pub/sub notification fan-out for a celebrity account with 100 million followers.
questions.text: Use hybrid fan-out: push to active followers' feeds in batches, pull for the rest, and prioritise by activity. Post -> fanout service -> batch workers -> active followers' inboxes Inactive followers: pull on open Celebrity: no per-follower write; merge at read Principal answer: Avoid write amplification for hot publishers.

questions.q: How do you design retries, timeouts and budgets so retries don't cause retry storms?
questions.text: Set timeouts shorter than the caller's, retry only idempotent calls with backoff and jitter, and cap retries with budgets and circuit breakers. Client timeout 1s < server SLA Retry: max 2, backoff+jitter, only on 5xx/timeout Retry budget: <=10% of requests Circuit breaker opens on sustained failure Principal answer: Retries multiply load by the retry count at every layer.

questions.q: What is a bulkhead and how does it isolate failures between workloads?
questions.text: Partition resources such as thread pools, connection pools or instances so one failing workload cannot exhaust shared capacity. Service -> pool A (checkout, 20 threads) -> pool B (search, 20 threads) -> pool C (reports, 5 threads) Principal answer: Name the shared resource that would be exhausted.

questions.q: Design graceful degradation: what do you turn off first when the system is overloaded?
questions.text: Rank features by criticality, shed optional load first, serve stale or cached data, and keep the core path alive. Tier 0: login, checkout, payments (protect) Tier 1: search, browse Tier 2: recommendations, analytics (shed first) Fallbacks: cache, defaults, static Principal answer: Decide degradation tiers before the incident.

questions.q: Explain quorum reads and writes and how you tune N, R and W.
questions.text: With N replicas, require W acks on write and R on read; R + W > N guarantees overlap with the latest write. N=3, W=2, R=2 -> overlap, consistent reads N=3, W=1, R=1 -> fast, eventual N=3, W=3, R=1 -> slow writes, fast reads Principal answer: Tune per use case, not globally.

questions.q: How does the Raft consensus algorithm work at a high level, and when do you need it?
questions.text: A leader is elected by majority vote and replicates a log to followers; entries commit when a majority has them. Follower -> timeout -> Candidate -> majority votes -> Leader Leader: append entry -> replicate -> commit on majority 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure; 5 tolerate 2 Principal answer: Use a library, never write your own.

questions.q: Design zero-downtime deployments for a stateful service with long-lived connections.
questions.text: Drain connections gradually, version the protocol, hand off state, deploy in small batches and keep rollback ready. LB marks node draining -> no new conns Existing conns finish / migrate (reconnect hints) Rolling batch -> health gate -> next Backward-compatible protocol Principal answer: Both versions must interoperate during rollout.

questions.q: How do you design for data durability: replication, backups and protection against corruption and deletion?
questions.text: Replicate across failure domains, take immutable versioned backups, verify checksums, and test restores; replication alone doesn't protect against deletion. Primary + sync replica (AZ-b) + async replica (region-2) PITR backups (immutable, cross-account) Checksums + scrubbing + restore drills Principal answer: Replication copies mistakes instantly.

questions.q: Design a ledger or wallet system where balances must never be wrong.
questions.text: Use an append-only double-entry ledger, derive balances, enforce transactional invariants and idempotency, and reconcile continuously. Transfer(idempotency_key) -> tx: debit A entry + credit B entry (sum=0) Balances = materialised from entries Daily reconcile vs bank/provider Principal answer: Never update a balance in place without an entry.

questions.q: Design an inventory management system for an e-commerce platform with multiple warehouses.
questions.text: Track available and reserved stock per SKU and location, reserve atomically at checkout, and sync with warehouses eventually. Order -> reserve(SKU, qty, warehouse) atomic Stock = on_hand - reserved Events: received/picked/returned -> update Reconcile with WMS counts Principal answer: Separate display availability from the reservation.

questions.q: Design a fraud detection system for payments with sub-100ms decisions.
questions.text: Combine fast rules and precomputed features with a model, score synchronously, and learn from delayed labels. Payment -> feature store (velocity, device, history) -> rules + ML score (<50ms) -> allow/review/deny Events -> stream -> retrain; chargebacks = labels Principal answer: Precompute features; keep the hot path simple.

questions.q: Design a data lake and analytics platform for a company with many data sources.
questions.text: Ingest raw data into object storage, organise zones, use a catalog and table formats, and serve through query engines with governance. Sources -> CDC/batch/stream ingest -> raw zone (S3) -> clean/curated (Parquet/Iceberg) -> warehouse/BI Catalog + lineage + access control Principal answer: Governance is what makes a lake usable.

questions.q: Design a schema registry and handle schema evolution in event streams.
questions.text: Store versioned schemas, enforce compatibility rules at publish time, and let producers and consumers evolve independently. Producer -> register schema (v3) -> compat check (backward) Message = schema id + payload (Avro/Protobuf) Consumer fetches schema by id Principal answer: Add optional fields; never reuse field numbers.

questions.q: Design a sharded key-value store like DynamoDB with consistent hashing and replication.
questions.text: Hash keys onto a ring with virtual nodes, replicate to N successors, use quorums and anti-entropy for repair. key -> hash -> ring -> coordinator + N-1 successors vnodes for balance; hinted handoff when node down Merkle trees for anti-entropy; vector clocks / LWW Principal answer: Virtual nodes smooth the distribution.

questions.q: Design a metadata and search service for a large object store, such as listing and querying billions of objects.
questions.text: Keep object metadata in a sharded, indexed store separate from blob data, with prefix listing and asynchronous secondary indexes. PUT -> blob store (data) + metadata shard (key, size, etag, tags) LIST prefix -> range scan on sorted key Search -> async index (tags, attributes) Principal answer: Separate the data plane from the metadata plane.

questions.q: How do you design data retention, deletion and privacy compliance such as the right to be forgotten?
questions.text: Map where personal data lives, tag it, centralise deletion workflows, propagate to derived stores and backups, and audit. Request -> deletion orchestrator -> primary DBs, caches, search, analytics, lake, backups (expire) Data map + PII tags + audit log Principal answer: You can't delete what you can't find.

questions.q: Design a container registry and artifact repository for an enterprise.
questions.text: Store content-addressed layers in object storage, keep manifests and metadata in a database, cache regionally, and add scanning, signing and access control. push -> registry API -> layers (blob store, by digest) manifests + tags (DB) ; auth (OIDC/RBAC) pull-through cache per region ; scan + sign + GC Principal answer: Immutable tags and digest pinning.

questions.q: Design a configuration management and dynamic configuration service.
questions.text: A versioned config store with validation, staged rollout, client caching with local fallback, and audit and rollback. Config repo -> validate -> config service (versioned) Clients: poll/stream -> local cache -> last-known-good Rollout by % / env; instant rollback Principal answer: A config change is a deployment.

questions.q: Design a workflow orchestration engine like Airflow or Temporal.
questions.text: Persist workflow state, schedule tasks to workers, handle retries and timeouts, and guarantee progress after crashes. Definition -> scheduler -> task queues -> workers State store (event history) ; timers ; retries/backoff Resume from history after failure Principal answer: Durable execution needs deterministic replay or idempotent tasks.

questions.q: Design an audit logging system that is tamper-evident and queryable.
questions.text: Emit structured events at the source, ship to append-only storage, chain hashes or use object lock, index for search, and restrict access. Services -> audit events -> Kafka -> writer -> WORM storage (object lock) + hash chain -> index (search) ; strict RBAC ; retention Principal answer: Audit logs must not be editable by the audited.
