questions.q: Design a multi-region traffic management system with failover and latency-based routing.
questions.text: Use health-checked global DNS or anycast, route by latency or geography with weights, and drain regions gracefully. Users -> GeoDNS/Anycast -> region A | B | C Health checks -> remove unhealthy region Weights for canary; stateful data replicated separately Principal answer: Failover capacity must exist before the failure.

questions.q: Design a cost-aware autoscaling and capacity management system.
questions.text: Scale on demand signals with predictive and scheduled capacity, mix instance types, and use budgets and right-sizing feedback. Metrics (RPS, queue) -> HPA/KEDA -> pods Node autoscaler -> spot + on-demand mix Forecast -> pre-scale ; budgets + right-size reports Principal answer: Scaling fast is a cost lever, not just a reliability one.

questions.q: Design a DNS service and explain how resolution, caching and TTLs shape failover.
questions.text: Hierarchical authoritative servers with recursive resolvers caching answers; TTL balances load against change propagation speed. Client -> stub -> recursive resolver (cache) -> root -> TLD -> authoritative (zone) Answers cached for TTL; anycast authoritative servers Principal answer: Lower TTL before a planned change.

questions.q: Design a TLS termination and certificate management system at scale.
questions.text: Terminate at the edge with automated issuance and renewal, secure key storage, modern protocols, and monitoring of expiry. Edge LB (TLS 1.3, OCSP stapling) <- cert store/HSM ACME automation -> issue/renew -> distribute mTLS internal via mesh/SPIFFE ; expiry monitoring Principal answer: Automate renewal; short-lived certs reduce risk.

questions.q: Design an API rate limiting and quota system for a public API with tiers.
questions.text: Identify clients by key, enforce limits at the gateway using a token bucket in a shared fast store, return clear headers, and meter quotas separately. Request -> gateway -> key lookup (tier) -> Redis token bucket (rate) ; counter (monthly quota) 429 + Retry-After + X-RateLimit-* headers Principal answer: Separate burst control from billing quotas.

questions.q: Design a VPN or zero-trust access system for a distributed workforce.
questions.text: Authenticate user and device, authorise per application with least privilege through an identity-aware proxy, and log everything; avoid broad network access. User + device posture -> IdP (MFA) -> identity-aware proxy -> app (per-policy) No flat network access ; continuous evaluation ; audit Principal answer: Never trust the network; verify each request.

guides.title: Terraform Production Interview Guide (173 Q&A) — InterviewHub

questions.q: What is Terraform and how does it manage infrastructure state?
questions.text: Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool by HashiCorp that lets you define, provision, and manage infrastructure across multiple cloud providers using declarative HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) files. State management : Terraform maintains a state file ( terraform.tfstate ) that maps real-world resources to your configuration. This file tracks resource metadata, dependencies, and current values — it is Terraform's source of truth. Key state concepts terraform state list # list all tracked resources terraform state show <resource> # inspect resource attributes terraform refresh # sync state with real infra Interview tip: Mention that state enables Terraform to calculate diffs (plan), detect drift, and avoid duplicate resource creation. Remote state (S3, GCS, Terraform Cloud) is production best practice.

questions.q: Terraform state file is accidentally deleted — how would you recover?
questions.text: This is a critical incident. The recovery approach depends on whether you had backups and whether remote state was configured. Recovery steps # 1. Check S3 versioning / GCS object versioning for previous tfstate # 2. Restore from backup: aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket <bucket> terraform import <resource_type>.<name> <resource_id> # re-import each resource terraform refresh # reconcile after imports If no backup exists, use terraform import to re-import each existing resource one by one, then run terraform plan to verify no unintended changes are proposed. Prevention: Always enable S3 versioning + DynamoDB locking. Enable Terraform Cloud state history. Never store state locally in production.

questions.q: Multiple team members are working on the same Terraform code — how do you prevent conflicts?
questions.text: State locking is the core mechanism. Configure a remote backend with locking enabled. terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "tf-state" key = "prod.tfstate" dynamodb_table = "tf-lock" } } DynamoDB provides atomic lock acquisition — only one terraform apply runs at a time. Other best practices: use Terraform workspaces per environment, enforce code review via pull requests before apply, and use Atlantis or Terraform Cloud for run orchestration. Key answer points: Remote state + locking (DynamoDB/Consul), Atlantis for PR-based workflows, separate workspaces or state files per environment.

questions.q: Terraform apply failed in the middle of execution — how do you recover from a partial deployment?
questions.text: Terraform is not transactional. A mid-apply failure leaves some resources created and others not. Recovery process terraform plan # identify what's missing vs what exists terraform apply # re-run — Terraform skips already-created resources terraform state list # verify state matches reality If a resource was created outside state (partial creation with no state entry), use terraform import . For resources stuck in a bad state, use terraform taint <resource> (pre-1.0) or terraform apply -replace to force recreation. Root cause: Check provider API errors, IAM permissions, quota limits, or dependency ordering issues before re-applying.

questions.q: Terraform shows drift between infrastructure and state — how do you identify and fix it?
questions.text: Drift occurs when resources are modified outside Terraform (manual console changes, other automation). terraform plan # drift shows as "changes" in plan output terraform refresh # update state to match real infra (careful!) terraform plan -refresh-only # preview what refresh would change (TF 1.1+) To fix: either update your Terraform config to match the manual changes (then apply to align), or apply Terraform to revert the manual change back to IaC-defined values. The choice depends on whether the manual change was intentional. Production advice: Use drift detection in CI pipelines — run terraform plan on a schedule and alert on non-empty plans. AWS Config or Driftctl can augment this.

questions.q: Terraform plan shows unexpected resource changes — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: Unexpected plan changes are often caused by provider upgrades, computed attributes, or config drift. Debugging steps TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | tee debug.log terraform state show <resource> # compare state values with config terraform providers lock # check provider version pinning Common causes: provider version bump changing default attribute values, computed fields (like ARNs) changing on recreation, ignore_changes not set for externally managed attributes, or sensitive value encoding differences. Fix: Pin provider versions in required_providers . Use lifecycle { ignore_changes = [...] } for attributes managed externally.

questions.q: Remote backend (like S3) is not accessible — how do you debug backend issues?
questions.text: TF_LOG=TRACE terraform init 2>&1 | grep -i backend aws s3 ls s3://<bucket>/<key> # verify bucket access manually aws sts get-caller-identity # confirm correct AWS credentials/role Check: IAM permissions for the executing role (s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:ListBucket, DynamoDB read/write). Verify VPC endpoint or internet access if running in a private subnet. Check S3 bucket policy — it may block cross-account access. CI/CD context: Ensure the pipeline IAM role has explicit backend access. Environment variables AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_ROLE_ARN must be set correctly in the runner.

questions.q: Terraform state file is locked — how do you resolve state lock issues?
questions.text: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> # get lock ID from error message # For DynamoDB: aws dynamodb delete-item --table-name tf-lock --key '{"LockID": {"S": "..."}}' A stale lock occurs when a previous apply was interrupted (network failure, process kill). The lock ID is shown in the error message. Always verify no other apply is actually running before force-unlocking — concurrent applies corrupt state. Never force-unlock if you are unsure whether another apply is in progress. Check CI/CD pipeline status and team communication first.

questions.q: Terraform resources are getting recreated unexpectedly — what could be the cause?
questions.text: Unexpected recreation (destroy + create) is usually caused by one of these: # ForceNew attribute changed — check provider docs for which attrs trigger recreation terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan | jq '.resource_changes' Common causes: changing a resource name or ID (some resources require recreation on name change), provider upgrade altering default values, computed attributes not stored in state, or taint left from a previous operation. Use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to guard critical resources. Key trick: Read the plan's "replacement triggered by" message carefully — it tells you the exact attribute driving recreation.

questions.q: Sensitive values are visible in Terraform state — how do you secure them?
questions.text: Terraform state contains sensitive data in plaintext (passwords, keys, secrets). This is a known limitation. Mitigations sensitive = true # mark outputs/variables as sensitive (redacted in plan output) # S3 backend: enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) # Use Vault provider or AWS Secrets Manager for secrets, not tfvars Restrict state file access via IAM policies — only CI/CD roles should have S3 read access to state. Enable S3 access logging. Use Terraform Cloud/Enterprise for encrypted state with RBAC. Never commit .tfstate or .tfvars files to Git. Production pattern: Store secrets in Vault/SSM Parameter Store and reference via data sources — they never need to be in your TF config at all.

questions.q: Terraform modules are not working as expected — how do you debug module issues?
questions.text: terraform init -upgrade # refresh module sources terraform validate # syntax and reference errors TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan # trace module resolution terraform console # interactively evaluate expressions Common issues: incorrect module source path (relative vs absolute), version constraint conflicts, missing required variables, output not exposed correctly. Use terraform console to test expressions interactively. Check that module outputs are referenced as module.<name>.<output> . Registry modules: Pin module versions explicitly. Never use source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws" without version = "X.Y.Z" .

questions.q: A resource dependency is not respected — how do you handle dependency issues?
questions.text: Terraform builds a dependency graph automatically from references. When implicit dependencies are insufficient, use explicit depends_on . resource "aws_instance" "app" { depends_on = [aws_security_group.sg] } terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg # visualize dependency graph Use depends_on sparingly — it forces sequential execution and slows applies. Prefer implicit dependencies via attribute references. For module dependencies, use depends_on at the module block level. Common trap: IAM policy attachment must complete before EC2 instance launch. If the IAM role exists but the policy isn't attached yet, the instance may start without permissions. Use explicit depends_on here.

questions.q: Terraform variables are not being picked up correctly — how do you debug variable precedence?
questions.text: Terraform variable precedence (highest to lowest): 1. -var and -var-file CLI flags (highest priority) 2. TF_VAR_name environment variables 3. terraform.tfvars or *.auto.tfvars files 4. Default values in variable blocks (lowest priority) terraform console -> var.<name> # check resolved value TF_LOG=TRACE terraform plan 2>&1 | grep variable Common mistake: A terraform.tfvars is silently overriding a -var-file you intended to use. Always use explicit -var-file flags in CI/CD and avoid relying on auto-loaded files in pipelines.

questions.q: Terraform apply takes too long — how do you optimize performance?
questions.text: terraform apply -parallelism=20 # default is 10, increase with caution terraform apply -target=module.<name> # apply only specific module # Split monolith into smaller state files / root modules Root causes: monolithic root module with hundreds of resources, unnecessary depends_on causing serial execution, slow provider API calls, or large number of data sources evaluated at plan time. Break large configurations into smaller independently managed state files with remote state data sources for cross-references. Architecture fix: Separate network, compute, and application layers into distinct Terraform roots. Use terraform_remote_state data source to share outputs between layers.

questions.q: Infrastructure created by Terraform is not accessible after deployment — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: This is an application/network layer issue, not a Terraform issue per se. Terraform successfully created resources but something in the config is wrong. terraform output # verify IPs, DNS names, ports from outputs terraform state show <resource> # check security group rules, subnet config Check: security group rules (ingress/egress), NACLs, route tables, IAM roles, VPC peering, DNS resolution, health check configuration for load balancers. The resource exists in state — the problem is in its configuration values. Pattern: Compare the Terraform-created config with a known-working manually-created resource in the same region/VPC.

questions.q: Terraform workspace is not switching properly — how do you fix workspace-related issues?
questions.text: terraform workspace list # show all workspaces and current terraform workspace show # confirm active workspace terraform workspace select prod # explicit switch Common issues: workspace state stored in wrong backend path, terraform.workspace variable not used in resource naming, or workspace created in different backend config. Each workspace has its own state file at <prefix>/env:<workspace>/<key> in S3. Production warning: Workspaces share the same backend and code — they are NOT true environment isolation. For prod/stage/dev isolation, use separate root modules with separate backends.

questions.q: Terraform provider version conflict occurs — how do you resolve provider dependency issues?
questions.text: terraform providers # show provider requirements from all modules terraform init -upgrade # upgrade to latest compatible versions # In required_providers: version = "~> 5.0" (allow patch updates only) terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 # lock for CI platform Conflicts arise when a root module and a child module require incompatible provider versions. Use terraform providers to identify the conflict, then adjust version constraints. Commit .terraform.lock.hcl to Git to pin provider versions across the team. Key practice: Always commit .terraform.lock.hcl . Run terraform init in CI — never skip the lock file.

questions.q: Terraform apply fails due to API rate limits — how do you handle throttling issues?
questions.text: terraform apply -parallelism=5 # reduce concurrent API calls # Add retry logic at provider level (some providers support max_retries) AWS, GCP, and Azure all have API rate limits. Hitting them during large applies is common. Reduce parallelism, stagger deployments, split into smaller modules, or add exponential backoff via retry configuration in the provider block. For AWS: provider "aws" { max_retries = 25 } . Architecture fix: Breaking a monolithic config into smaller modules deployed sequentially is both a rate limit mitigation and a blast-radius reduction strategy.

questions.q: Terraform cannot authenticate to cloud provider — how do you debug authentication failures?
questions.text: aws sts get-caller-identity # verify AWS credentials gcloud auth application-default print-access-token # GCP ADC check TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | grep -i auth Check credential chain: environment variables → shared credentials file → IAM instance profile → IRSA (in EKS). In CI/CD, ensure the pipeline has assumed the correct role with sufficient permissions. For GCP, use Workload Identity Federation instead of service account keys. GCP context: For GCP, Application Default Credentials (ADC) flow — ensure GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS or Workload Identity is configured. Never use service account keys in CI.

questions.q: Terraform plan works locally but fails in CI/CD pipeline — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: Environment differences between local and CI are the root cause 95% of the time. # Check: Terraform version mismatch (use tfenv or .terraform-version file) # Check: Provider versions (lock file not committed) # Check: Environment variables (AWS creds, TF_VAR_*, workspace) TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan > /tmp/ci-debug.log 2>&1 Common differences: Terraform binary version, provider lock file missing/different, missing environment variables for authentication, different working directory, or network access restrictions (S3 backend, provider API endpoints) from the CI runner. Fix: Pin Terraform version in CI with a .terraform-version file and use tfenv . Commit .terraform.lock.hcl . Mirror the exact CI environment locally with Docker.

questions.q: Resources are manually modified outside Terraform — how do you detect and fix configuration drift?
questions.text: terraform plan -refresh-only # preview drift without applying changes # Schedule: run terraform plan in CI, fail build on non-empty plan # Tool: driftctl scan # open-source drift detection Drift is inevitable in large orgs. The strategic response: decide whether to reconcile to IaC or absorb the change into config. Use terraform refresh to absorb, or terraform apply to revert. Prevent future drift with SCPs (AWS), Organization Policies (GCP), or Azure Policy to restrict console-level changes in production. Process fix: Require all changes go through IaC PR process. Use Atlantis to enforce this — no manual console access in prod.

questions.q: Terraform destroy fails due to dependencies — how do you resolve it safely?
questions.text: terraform destroy -target=<dependent_resource> # destroy dependents first terraform state rm <resource> # remove from state without destroying Dependency-related destroy failures happen when resources outside Terraform depend on Terraform-managed resources (e.g., an S3 bucket with objects, a VPC with manually-created ENIs). Manually remove the blocking dependency, then retry destroy. Or use terraform state rm to detach resources from state before destroying the parent. Never force-delete production resources without confirming with stakeholders. Destroy is irreversible.

questions.q: Remote state corruption occurs — how do you recover state safely?
questions.text: # 1. Immediately lock or take the backend offline # 2. Restore from S3 versioned backup aws s3api get-object --bucket tf-state --key prod.tfstate --version-id <id> restored.tfstate # 3. Validate restored state terraform show restored.tfstate # 4. Run plan before apply to confirm no unintended changes Prevention: S3 versioning is non-negotiable for production state backends. Enable MFA delete for extra protection. Terraform Cloud provides automatic state versioning with rollback UI.

questions.q: Multiple environments (dev, stage, prod) need isolation — how do you design Terraform structure?
questions.text: The recommended pattern is separate root modules per environment, each with their own backend state. infra/ ├── modules/ │ ├── vpc/ │ └── eks/ ├── environments/ │ ├── dev/ │ ├── stage/ │ └── prod/ Each environment directory has its own backend.tf , main.tf , and terraform.tfvars . Shared infrastructure is defined in reusable modules. This gives complete blast-radius isolation — a broken plan in dev cannot touch prod state. Workspaces alone are insufficient for true environment isolation. Alternative: Terragrunt for DRY environment configs — it generates backend configs dynamically and reduces boilerplate across environments.

questions.q: Terraform outputs are not available after deployment — how do you debug?
questions.text: terraform output # list all outputs in current state terraform output <name> # get specific output value terraform state show <resource> # verify attribute exists in state Common causes: output defined in a module but not re-exported in root module, resource not yet applied (output depends on computed value), or state file not refreshed. For cross-state outputs, verify the terraform_remote_state data source path and backend access permissions. Tip: Mark outputs as sensitive = true if they contain secrets — they are redacted in CLI but still accessible via terraform output -json for pipeline use.

questions.q: Infrastructure deployment fails due to incorrect IAM permissions — how do you troubleshoot?
questions.text: TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply 2>&1 | grep -i "access denied|not authorized" aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role_arn> --action-names <action> The error message usually contains the exact missing permission. Build the IAM policy incrementally: start with a broad managed policy, run apply, capture all AccessDenied errors, then scope down to least privilege. Use AWS IAM Access Analyzer to generate least-privilege policies from CloudTrail logs. GCP equivalent: gcloud projects get-iam-policy and Policy Analyzer. For a GCP-focused role, start with roles/editor scoped to specific project, then tighten.

questions.q: Terraform cannot find required modules — how do you fix module source issues?
questions.text: terraform init # always required after changing module sources # For private registry: configure credentials in .terraformrc # For Git sources: ensure SSH key or token is configured terraform init -get=true -upgrade # force re-download modules Module sources can be local paths, Terraform Registry, GitHub, S3, or GCS. Local paths must be relative ( ./modules/vpc ). Registry modules need internet access or a private registry mirror. Git sources need SSH keys or HTTPS tokens configured in the environment. CI/CD: Use -get=true in terraform init in pipelines. Cache the .terraform directory between pipeline runs to speed up init.

questions.q: Changes are applied to the wrong environment — how do you prevent such mistakes?
questions.text: # Use separate backend configs — accidentally applying to wrong backend is immediately obvious # Require explicit -var-file=environments/prod.tfvars in CI # Atlantis: restrict prod applies to protected branches + required approvers Prevention is architectural: separate state backends per environment eliminate cross-environment contamination entirely. Add workspace/environment verification in CI with an explicit check step. Require manual approval gates before production applies. Tag all resources with environment = terraform.workspace for auditability. Process control: Production applies should require 2-person approval, be logged, and be triggered only from protected branches. Never allow direct terraform apply from developer laptops to prod.

questions.q: Terraform rollback is required after a failed deployment — how do you handle rollback strategy?
questions.text: Terraform does not have a built-in rollback command. Rollback must be planned explicitly. # Option 1: Revert git commit, run terraform apply (previous code state) # Option 2: Restore previous tfstate from S3 versioning, then apply terraform apply -target=<specific_resource> # selective rollback For stateful resources (databases, storage), rollback may be impossible or dangerous. The real strategy is forward-fix: fix the issue in code and apply forward. For immutable infrastructure (EC2, containers), blue-green or canary patterns allow instant rollback at the infrastructure level without Terraform state changes. Design principle: Build rollback into your infrastructure design (blue-green, feature flags) rather than relying on Terraform to roll back. Terraform manages desired state, not deployment history.

questions.q: How do you troubleshoot a complete infrastructure deployment failure using Terraform?
questions.text: A complete failure requires a structured incident response approach. Triage sequence TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan > debug.log 2>&1 # full trace terraform validate # eliminate config syntax errors first terraform state list # what exists vs what should exist terraform plan -target=<first_failing_resource> # isolate the failure Systematic approach: (1) isolate which resource is failing, (2) identify whether it's a config, permission, quota, or API issue, (3) fix the root cause — not the symptom, (4) apply incrementally using -target , (5) verify full plan is clean before full apply. Post-incident: Document root cause, add a plan validation step to CI, add resource-specific tests using Terratest, and improve IAM policies proactively. Share the runbook with the team.

questions.q: Explain terraform state mv, rm, and import — when do you use each in production?
questions.text: These are surgical state operations for reconciling state with reality without destroying/recreating resources. Each addresses a different mismatch. The three operations terraform state mv aws_instance.old aws_instance.new # rename/move in state, no infra change terraform state mv 'module.a.x' 'module.b.x' # move a resource between modules terraform state rm aws_instance.legacy # forget a resource (does NOT destroy it) terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abc123 # bring an existing resource under management state mv is for refactors: you renamed a resource or moved it into a module, and want Terraform to keep managing the same real resource instead of destroying and recreating it. state rm tells Terraform to stop tracking a resource without touching the real infrastructure — useful when handing ownership to another stack or removing something you will manage manually. import is the reverse: adopt an existing resource into state. Modern note: for refactors, prefer moved {} blocks (Terraform 1.1+) over imperative state mv — they are declarative, code-reviewed, and run automatically during apply, so the refactor is reproducible for everyone rather than a manual one-off.

questions.q: What are moved {} and import {} blocks, and why are they better than CLI commands?
questions.text: These declarative blocks (Terraform 1.1+ for moved, 1.5+ for import) encode state operations in code instead of as manual CLI steps, making refactors and adoptions reproducible and reviewable. Declarative refactor & import moved { from = aws_instance.old_name to = aws_instance.new_name } import { to = aws_instance.web id = "i-0abc123def" } terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf # scaffold config for imported resource A moved block means every teammate and CI run applies the rename automatically — nobody has to remember to run state mv on their machine. An import block makes adopting existing infra part of the plan/apply cycle, and -generate-config-out can scaffold the resource HCL for you. Both turn fragile, undocumented CLI surgery into version-controlled, auditable changes. Why it matters: imperative state mv only runs where someone types it — a classic source of "works on my machine, drift on yours." Declarative blocks make state changes a reviewed commit, which is the IaC philosophy applied to state itself.

questions.q: Compare S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, and Consul as state backends. How do you choose?
questions.text: The choice trades off operational ownership, locking, collaboration features, and cost. All provide remote state; they differ in what else they give you. Backend comparison S3 + DynamoDB : you own it; S3 stores state, DynamoDB provides locking; cheap, AWS-native Terraform Cloud/Enterprise : managed state + locking + run orchestration + policy (Sentinel/OPA) Consul : KV store with locking; good if you already run Consul; more ops overhead GCS / azurerm : cloud-native equivalents with built-in locking S3+DynamoDB is the pragmatic default on AWS — cheap, simple, you control encryption and access via IAM, locking via DynamoDB. Terraform Cloud adds the things teams eventually want: remote runs, a run queue, VCS integration, policy-as-code, and a state UI — at a cost and with vendor coupling. Consul only makes sense if you already operate it. Note: as of Terraform 1.10+, S3 backend supports native locking via a lockfile, reducing the need for DynamoDB. Decision framing: start with cloud-native (S3+DynamoDB/GCS) for simplicity and cost; graduate to Terraform Cloud/Enterprise when you need run orchestration, policy enforcement, and audit at team scale. State the trade-off (ownership/cost vs managed features) rather than naming a single winner.

questions.q: How do you structure state files across environments and teams to limit blast radius?
questions.text: Monolithic state is a blast-radius and contention problem: one apply can affect everything and locks block everyone. The fix is splitting state along boundaries of change and ownership. State segmentation strategies Per environment : separate state for dev / staging / prod (separate keys/backends) Per layer : networking / data / compute / app in separate states Per team/service: each owning team has its own state + backend # Cross-state references via remote state data source (read-only): data "terraform_remote_state" "network" { backend = "s3" config = { ... } } Split state by rate of change and ownership : slow-moving foundational layers (networking, IAM) in their own state, fast-moving app layers in another. This limits blast radius (an app apply cannot accidentally touch networking), reduces lock contention, and speeds up plans. Layers share data through the terraform_remote_state data source (read-only outputs) or, better, through provider data sources / SSM parameters to avoid tight state coupling. Trade-off: more state files mean more orchestration (ordering between layers) and more remote-state plumbing. Over-splitting creates a dependency web. Split where ownership or change-rate genuinely differs — not arbitrarily.

questions.q: A state file became corrupted or has stale entries. How do you safely repair it?
questions.text: State repair is delicate — mistakes can orphan or destroy real resources. Always back up first, then use targeted operations. Repair procedure terraform state pull > backup.tfstate # ALWAYS back up first aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket tf-state # find a prior good version (if versioned) terraform state rm <bad_address> # remove a stale/duplicate entry terraform import <address> <real_id> # re-attach a resource that exists but is mistracked terraform state push backup.tfstate # restore a known-good version (last resort) terraform plan # verify NO unexpected changes before applying Pull and back up the current state first — every repair is reversible if you have the prior state. For stale entries, state rm the bad address; for resources that exist but are tracked wrong, import them back correctly. If corruption is broad, restore a versioned prior state with state push . The non-negotiable final step is terraform plan showing no surprising changes before any apply. Never hand-edit the raw tfstate JSON in production unless there is genuinely no alternative — it is easy to break references and serial numbers. Prefer state rm / import /versioned restore. And confirm state versioning + locking are enabled so this is recoverable next time.

questions.q: Explain Terraform workspaces. When are they appropriate vs separate state files/dirs?
questions.text: Workspaces let one configuration maintain multiple independent states (e.g. dev/staging/prod) under the same backend key prefix. They are convenient but commonly misused for environment separation. Workspace mechanics terraform workspace new staging terraform workspace select prod terraform workspace list # reference the active workspace in config: locals { env = terraform.workspace } Workspaces share the same code and backend, switching only the state. They suit ephemeral or near-identical variations — per-developer sandboxes, short-lived test environments. They are a poor fit for prod-vs-dev when those environments diverge (different sizes, regions, accounts) or need different access controls, because the shared code and single backend make isolation weak and a mistake can hit the wrong env. Best practice for real environments: separate directories/state with explicit backends (or a tool like Terragrunt) gives true isolation — distinct access, distinct blast radius, divergent config. Reserve CLI workspaces for ephemeral or developer-scratch use. State this distinction; it is a common interview discriminator.

questions.q: How does Terraform state locking actually work, and how do you handle a stuck lock?
questions.text: Locking prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state by serializing write access. The mechanism is backend-specific; a stuck lock blocks everyone until cleared. Locking & unlock # DynamoDB: a lock item (LockID) is written before apply, deleted after # A crashed/killed apply can leave the lock orphaned: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> # remove a stuck lock (get ID from the error) # Inspect the DynamoDB lock item directly if needed: aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-lock --key '{"LockID":{"S":"..."}}' Before a state-writing operation, Terraform acquires an exclusive lock (a DynamoDB conditional put, a Consul session, etc.). If an apply crashes or is killed, the lock can be orphaned, and the next run errors with a lock ID and who/when held it. force-unlock with that ID clears it. Before force-unlocking, confirm no apply is actually running — force-unlocking an in-progress operation lets two applies run concurrently and can corrupt state. Check with the holder (the error shows who and when) first. Only force-unlock genuinely orphaned locks.

questions.q: What is terraform refresh / -refresh-only, and why was refresh-during-plan behavior changed?
questions.text: Refresh reconciles state with the real world by reading current resource attributes. Terraform 0.15.4+ added -refresh-only to make drift reconciliation an explicit, reviewable step. Refresh operations terraform plan -refresh-only # show drift (real vs state) WITHOUT proposing config changes terraform apply -refresh-only # update state to match reality, no infra changes terraform plan -refresh=false # skip refresh (faster plans; risky if drift exists) # (the standalone 'terraform refresh' command is deprecated in favor of -refresh-only) Plain terraform plan refreshes implicitly, then diffs against config. -refresh-only separates concerns: it shows you what drifted in reality and lets you accept that into state without conflating it with config-driven changes. This matters because an automatic refresh can mask or surprise you with out-of-band changes; making it explicit gives a clean, reviewable "reconcile drift" step distinct from "apply my code changes." Performance note: on large states, refresh is the slow part of plan. -refresh=false speeds CI plans but only safe when you trust there is no drift — pair it with periodic -refresh-only drift checks. Mentioning this trade-off shows operational maturity.

questions.q: How do you migrate state from one backend to another (e.g. local to S3) with zero downtime?
questions.text: Terraform automates backend migration when you change the backend block and re-init. The key is doing it carefully so no state is lost in transit. Migration steps terraform state pull > pre-migration-backup.tfstate # back up first # 1. Add/modify the backend block in terraform { backend "s3" { ... } } terraform init -migrate-state # Terraform copies state to the new backend # it prompts to confirm copying existing state terraform state list # verify all resources present post-migration terraform plan # confirm no changes proposed When you change the backend configuration and run terraform init -migrate-state , Terraform detects the change and offers to copy the existing state to the new backend. Always pull a manual backup first. After migration, verify with state list and a clean plan . There is no real downtime because state migration does not touch live infrastructure — it only relocates the tracking data. Coordinate the team: everyone must re-init against the new backend, and you should ensure no apply is mid-flight during migration. Commit the backend change and announce it so stale local backends do not cause split state.

questions.q: What is sensitive data exposure in state, and how do you protect it?
questions.text: State stores resource attributes in plaintext JSON — including secrets like generated passwords, private keys, and connection strings. Anyone with state access can read them. Protection layers # 1. Encrypt state at rest + in transit: # S3 SSE-KMS, GCS CMEK, Terraform Cloud encrypted state # 2. Restrict state access via IAM (least privilege on the bucket/table) # 3. Mark variables/outputs sensitive to keep them out of logs: variable "db_password" { type = string sensitive = true } output "endpoint" { value = ... sensitive = true } # 4. Don't generate secrets in TF at all — reference a secrets manager: data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" { secret_id = "prod/db" } Defense in depth: encrypt state at rest (KMS) and in transit, lock down access with least-privilege IAM, and mark sensitive variables/outputs so they are redacted from CLI/CI logs (note: sensitive hides them from output but they are still plaintext in state ). The strongest measure is architectural — do not have Terraform generate or hold secrets; reference a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) so the secret never lands in state. Critical misconception: sensitive = true does NOT encrypt state — it only suppresses log output. The secret is still readable in the raw tfstate. Anyone who can read your state bucket can read every secret in it. Treat state access as equivalent to secret access.

questions.q: How would you design state for a multi-account, multi-region AWS organization?
questions.text: At org scale, state design must reflect account boundaries, blast-radius isolation, and clear ownership, while enabling controlled cross-references. Design approach Per-account state backend (state lives in or is keyed per account) Layered: org/identity (slow) | networking | platform | per-service app (fast) Naming convention for state keys: <account>/<region>/<layer>/<service>.tfstate Cross-account reads via assumed roles + terraform_remote_state or SSM/Parameter Store Centralized backend bucket with strict IAM, or backend-per-account for isolation Mirror the org structure: separate state per account and per layer, with a consistent key naming scheme so any state is findable. Foundational layers (identity, networking) change rarely and many things depend on them — isolate and protect them. Cross-account/cross-layer data flows through assumed-role remote-state reads or, preferably, a shared parameter store to avoid brittle state-to-state coupling. Access to each state is governed by least-privilege IAM matching who owns that layer. Tooling: Terragrunt or Terraform Cloud workspaces help manage the proliferation of backends/state keys with DRY backend config and dependency ordering. Mention that the goal is isolation + clear ownership + controlled cross-references, and that over-centralizing state recreates the blast-radius problem.

questions.q: Explain dependency ordering: how does Terraform build its graph and where do depends_on and lifecycle fit?
questions.text: Terraform builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from resource references and walks it to parallelize independent work and order dependent work. Most ordering is implicit via references. Graph & ordering controls # Implicit dependency (preferred): referencing an attribute creates an edge subnet_id = aws_subnet.main.id # this resource now depends on the subnet # Explicit, when there is a hidden dependency Terraform can't infer: depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.app] # Lifecycle controls ordering/replacement behavior: lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] } lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [aws_instance.web.id] } Prefer implicit dependencies — referencing aws_subnet.main.id automatically orders creation. Use depends_on only for dependencies Terraform cannot see (e.g. an IAM policy that must exist before an app starts, with no attribute reference). lifecycle tunes behavior: create_before_destroy avoids downtime on replacement, prevent_destroy guards critical resources, ignore_changes stops fighting out-of-band edits, and replace_triggered_by forces replacement when a related resource changes. Interview depth: emphasize implicit-over-explicit (overusing depends_on serializes the graph and slows applies), and that create_before_destroy is the key to zero-downtime resource replacement. Visualize with terraform graph | dot -Tpng .

questions.q: What is a partial backend configuration and why use it?
questions.text: Partial backend config omits some backend settings from code and supplies them at init time — useful for keeping environment-specific or sensitive backend details out of the repo. Partial config pattern # In code: backend block with minimal/empty settings terraform { backend "s3" {} } # Supply the rest at init via a file or flags: terraform init -backend-config=prod.s3.tfbackend terraform init -backend-config="bucket=tf-state-prod" -backend-config="key=app.tfstate" # prod.s3.tfbackend: bucket=... key=... region=... dynamodb_table=... Backend blocks cannot use variables, so partial configuration is the sanctioned way to parameterize them. You keep a minimal backend block in code and inject the bucket/key/region per environment at init time via -backend-config files or flags. This lets the same code target different backends (dev/staging/prod) and keeps account-specific identifiers out of version control. Common use: CI pipelines pass the right .tfbackend file per environment, so one codebase initializes against the correct state per deploy target. Terragrunt automates this pattern (generating backend config) at scale.

questions.q: How do you handle a resource that must be replaced with zero downtime?
questions.text: By default Terraform destroys-then-creates on replacement, causing an outage. create_before_destroy inverts this so the new resource is healthy before the old is removed. Zero-downtime replacement resource "aws_instance" "web" { # ... lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } } # Force a replacement explicitly when needed: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web # replaces the 'tainted' way (modern syntax) create_before_destroy = true tells Terraform to provision the replacement first, cut over (e.g. via a load balancer or DNS that references the new resource), and only then destroy the old one — eliminating the gap. It requires that the resource can have two instances briefly (no hard uniqueness conflicts on names/IPs; handle those with naming that allows overlap). For intentional replacement, -replace= is the modern alternative to the deprecated terraform taint . Watch for conflicts: create_before_destroy fails if the new resource collides with the old on a unique attribute (a fixed name, EIP, etc.). Design names to allow two to coexist momentarily, or the create step errors and you get neither smooth cutover nor the benefit.

questions.q: Explain terraform_remote_state vs data sources vs SSM for sharing values between configurations.
questions.text: Three ways one Terraform config consumes values produced by another. They differ in coupling, access control, and how tightly they bind to Terraform. The options # 1. Remote state data source (reads another state's OUTPUTS): data "terraform_remote_state" "net" { backend="s3" config={...} } subnet = data.terraform_remote_state.net.outputs.subnet_id # 2. Provider data source (reads from the cloud API directly): data "aws_vpc" "main" { tags = { Name = "prod" } } # 3. Parameter store / SSM (decoupled, any consumer): data "aws_ssm_parameter" "vpc_id" { name = "/network/vpc_id" } Remote state is convenient but creates tight coupling — the consumer needs read access to the producer’s entire state (which contains secrets), and breaks if the producer renames an output. Provider data sources query the cloud directly (e.g. find a VPC by tag), decoupling from state entirely but depending on stable tags/naming. SSM/Parameter Store is the loosest coupling: the producer publishes values, any consumer (Terraform or not) reads them, with independent IAM. Recommendation to state: prefer provider data sources or SSM over terraform_remote_state for cross-stack values — remote state forces granting full state read (a security and coupling cost). Reserve remote state for tightly-related layers you control end to end.

questions.q: What happens during terraform init, plan, and apply internally — walk through the lifecycle.
questions.text: Understanding the phases explains where things fail and why certain operations need re-init. Each phase has a distinct job. The lifecycle init : download providers + modules, configure backend, build .terraform/ + lock file plan : refresh state (read real infra) → build graph → diff config vs state → propose actions apply : acquire lock → execute graph (parallelized) → update state after each resource → release lock # Supporting: terraform validate # static config/syntax/type checks (no API calls) terraform fmt # canonical formatting init sets up the working directory: it downloads provider plugins and modules, configures the backend, and writes the dependency lock file — required after adding providers/modules or changing the backend. plan refreshes state from the real world, builds the dependency DAG, and computes the diff into a set of create/update/delete/replace actions. apply locks state, walks the graph executing actions in parallel where independent, and writes state incrementally so a mid-run failure still records what succeeded. Why apply writes state incrementally: if apply fails halfway, the resources already created are in state — so re-running continues rather than recreating. This is why a partial-apply recovery is just “fix the cause and re-apply,” not “start over.”

questions.q: How do you safely run Terraform in CI/CD, and what are the key guardrails?
questions.text: Automated Terraform must be safe by construction: plan and apply are separated, credentials are short-lived, and applies are gated and serialized. CI/CD guardrails Plan on PR: terraform plan -out=tfplan → post plan to the PR for review Apply on merge: terraform apply tfplan # apply the SAVED plan, not a fresh one OIDC for cloud creds (no long-lived secrets in CI) State locking ensures only one apply at a time; serialize via environments/queues Policy as code: OPA/Conftest or Sentinel gates before apply Required manual approval for prod applies The core pattern is plan/apply separation : generate and save a plan ( -out ) on PR for human review, then apply that exact saved plan on merge so what was reviewed is what runs (no drift between review and apply). Use OIDC for ephemeral cloud credentials, rely on state locking plus environment serialization to prevent concurrent applies, gate with policy-as-code (OPA/Sentinel) for compliance, and require manual approval for production. Tools that productize this: Atlantis (PR-driven plan/apply with locking comments), Terraform Cloud/Enterprise (run queue + Sentinel), Spacelift, env0. Mentioning plan/apply separation + saved-plan apply + OIDC is the strongest signal of safe automation.

questions.q: A teammate ran terraform apply locally and it diverged from CI-managed state. How do you reconcile?
questions.text: Local applies bypass review and can create drift between what CI expects and what exists. Reconciliation means getting reality, state, and code back in agreement. Reconciliation terraform plan -refresh-only # detect what reality/state diverged from code terraform plan # see what CI would now change # If the local change is desired: codify it, PR it, let CI apply # If undesired: revert via apply from the reviewed code terraform state pull > current.tfstate # inspect what state believes First diagnose with -refresh-only (what drifted) and a normal plan (what CI wants to change). If the local change was legitimate, the fix is process: write it into code, open a PR, and let CI apply it so state and code agree. If it was a mistake, apply from the reviewed mainline code to revert reality. The state is shared (remote), so once code and reality align, CI is consistent again. Root cause is process, not Git: local applies against shared prod state are the problem. The durable fix is removing humans’ ability to apply to prod directly — restrict apply to CI with OIDC, lock down state-write IAM, and require PR-driven applies. Reconciling once without fixing the process guarantees recurrence.

questions.q: How do you design a reusable Terraform module? What makes a module good vs bad?
questions.text: A good module is a well-bounded abstraction with a clear interface, sensible defaults, and minimal assumptions about its caller. A bad module either does too little (a thin wrapper) or too much (a kitchen sink). Module design principles Clear interface: typed variables with descriptions, validation, sensible defaults Explicit outputs: expose what callers need, nothing internal Single responsibility: a module does one cohesive thing (a VPC, an ECS service) No hardcoded provider/region/account assumptions; pass them in Versioned + documented: README with examples, version constraints Treat a module like a function: well-typed inputs (with validation blocks and defaults), explicit outputs, and one clear responsibility. Avoid leaking implementation details or hardcoding environment specifics — callers supply those. A module that wraps a single resource adds indirection without value; a module that provisions an entire environment is too coupled to reuse. The sweet spot is a cohesive, composable unit (a VPC, a service, a database). Interview signal: “modules are functions for infrastructure” — inputs/outputs/single-responsibility — plus versioning and validation. Mention the registry pattern (root module composes child modules) and that over-abstraction is as harmful as none.

questions.q: Explain count vs for_each for resource iteration. When does each cause problems?
questions.text: Both create multiple instances of a resource, but they index differently — count by integer position, for_each by a stable key — and that difference has major consequences for state stability. count vs for_each # count: integer-indexed (aws_instance.web[0], [1], [2]) resource "aws_instance" "web" { count = 3 } # for_each: key-indexed (aws_instance.web["api"], ["worker"]) resource "aws_instance" "web" { for_each = toset(["api","worker"]) } resource "aws_instance" "web" { for_each = var.instances_map } The trap with count : removing an item from the middle of the list shifts every subsequent index, so Terraform destroys and recreates everything after it (index 1 becomes 0, etc.). for_each keys instances by a stable identifier, so adding/removing one entry only affects that entry. Use count only for truly identical, position-independent instances or simple on/off toggles ( count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 ); use for_each whenever instances have distinct identities. Classic production incident: a list with count where someone removes a middle element → mass recreation of unrelated resources. Default to for_each with a map/set keyed by a stable name. This is one of the most-asked Terraform discriminators.

questions.q: How do you version and distribute internal modules across many teams?
questions.text: Modules need versioning so consumers get reproducible, opt-in upgrades. Distribution options range from Git refs to a private registry. Versioning & sources # Private registry (best at scale): semantic versions + version constraints module "vpc" { source="app.terraform.io/org/vpc/aws" version="~> 3.2" } # Git with a pinned tag/ref: module "vpc" { source="git::https://git/org/modules.git//vpc?ref=v3.2.1" } # Always PIN the version; never float on a branch: version = "3.2.1" # exact or "~> 3.2" (>=3.2.0, <3.3.0) Publish modules to a private registry (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise or an OSS one) with semantic versioning so consumers pin via version constraints and upgrade deliberately. If using Git sources, always pin to a tag ( ?ref=v3.2.1 ), never a branch — floating on main means a module change can silently break every consumer’s next apply. SemVer signals intent: patch = safe, minor = additive, major = breaking. Never use an unpinned module source in production. source="...//vpc" without ?ref or version pulls latest — an upstream change then alters infra on your next apply with no review. Pin everything; treat module upgrades as reviewed PRs.

questions.q: Terraform plan/apply is very slow on a large configuration. How do you diagnose and speed it up?
questions.text: Slowness usually comes from refresh time (many resources, slow provider APIs), an oversized monolithic state, or excessive provider calls. Diagnose first, then attack the dominant cause. Speed-up techniques terraform plan -refresh=false # skip refresh if you trust no drift (big win) terraform plan -target=module.x # scope to a subset while iterating terraform apply -parallelism=20 # raise concurrency (default 10) if API allows TF_LOG=trace ... 2>&1 | grep duration # find slow provider calls # Structural fixes: Split monolithic state into layers/services (smaller graphs, faster refresh) Reduce data sources that hit slow APIs on every plan The biggest lever is usually state size : a monolith with thousands of resources refreshes slowly because every plan reads every resource’s live state. Splitting into layered/service states shrinks each graph dramatically. Tactically, -refresh=false skips the slow refresh (safe only when drift is unlikely), -target scopes work during iteration, and raising -parallelism helps if the provider API tolerates it. Excessive data sources that call slow APIs on every plan are a common hidden cost. Diagnose before optimizing: TF_LOG=trace reveals where time goes (refresh vs specific slow API calls). The durable fix for genuinely large infra is state segmentation, not flags — say that to show architectural thinking.

questions.q: What are dynamic blocks and when should you avoid them?
questions.text: Dynamic blocks generate repeated nested configuration blocks (e.g. multiple ingress rules) from a collection, avoiding copy-paste. They are powerful but hurt readability when overused. Dynamic block usage dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.ingress_rules content { from_port = ingress.value.from to_port = ingress.value.to protocol = ingress.value.protocol } } Use dynamic blocks when a resource has a repeatable nested block whose count/content is data-driven — security group rules, IAM policy statements, load balancer listeners. They keep config DRY. But they obscure the resulting configuration (you cannot read the actual rules at a glance), complicate diffs, and make modules harder to understand. If the nesting is fixed or small, write the blocks out literally for clarity. Readability cost: heavily nested or conditional dynamic blocks become write-only code. Prefer explicit blocks when the set is small/static; reserve dynamic blocks for genuinely variable, data-driven repetition. Over-engineering modules with dynamic-everything is a real anti-pattern interviewers probe for.

questions.q: Explain variable validation, type constraints, and how to build a robust module interface.
questions.text: A robust module rejects bad input early with clear errors rather than failing deep in a provider call. Type constraints and validation blocks are the tools. Typed, validated inputs variable "instance_type" { type = string description = "EC2 instance type" default = "t3.micro" validation { condition = can(regex("^t3\\.", var.instance_type)) error_message = "Only t3 family is allowed." } } variable "subnets" { type = map(object({ cidr = string, az = string })) } Use precise type constraints ( map(object({...})) , list(string) ) so callers get a clear type error instead of a confusing downstream failure. Add validation blocks to enforce business rules (allowed values, naming patterns, ranges) with human-readable error_message s. Provide sensible default s for optional inputs and mark secrets sensitive . This turns the module interface into a contract that fails fast and self-documents. Newer features to mention: optional() attributes in object types (with defaults) let you build flexible-but-typed inputs, and custom validation with can() / regex() catches misuse at plan time. Fast, clear failure is a hallmark of a production-grade module.

questions.q: How does Terraform parallelism work, and when would you tune it?
questions.text: Terraform walks the resource graph concurrently, processing independent resources in parallel up to a limit (default 10). Tuning trades speed against provider/API rate limits. Parallelism control terraform apply -parallelism=20 # raise from default 10 terraform apply -parallelism=1 # serialize (debugging ordering/races) # The graph dictates what CAN run in parallel; -parallelism caps how many at once The DAG determines which resources are independent; -parallelism caps how many of those run simultaneously. Raising it speeds up large applies if the provider API can handle the concurrency. Lowering it (even to 1) helps when you hit API rate limits/throttling, or when debugging suspected ordering issues. It does not change ordering — dependent resources still wait for their prerequisites. The trap: cranking parallelism on a provider with strict rate limits causes throttling errors and slower (or failed) applies, not faster ones. Tune based on the provider’s limits; sometimes lowering parallelism fixes intermittent apply failures caused by API throttling.

questions.q: How do you compose modules (root calling child modules) and pass data between them?
questions.text: Composition is the heart of scalable Terraform: a thin root module wires together child modules, passing one module’s outputs as another’s inputs. Composition pattern module "network" { source = "./modules/network" cidr = var.cidr } module "app" { source = "./modules/app" subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids # output → input wiring vpc_id = module.network.vpc_id } output "app_url" { value = module.app.url } # re-export child output The root module should be mostly wiring : instantiate child modules and connect them by feeding outputs into inputs ( module.network.vpc_id → module.app.vpc_id ). This creates the dependency graph automatically and keeps each child focused and reusable. The root re-exports the outputs callers care about. Keep business logic in children; keep the root declarative and readable. Anti-pattern to avoid: deeply nested module trees (modules calling modules calling modules) become hard to trace and slow to plan. Favor a flat-ish composition — a root composing a handful of well-bounded children — over deep hierarchies.

questions.q: What is the dependency lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) and how do you manage it?
questions.text: The lock file pins exact provider versions and their checksums so every run and every teammate uses identical providers — reproducibility and supply-chain integrity. Lock file management terraform init # creates/updates .terraform.lock.hcl terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 # multi-platform hashes terraform init -upgrade # update providers within constraints + refresh lock # COMMIT .terraform.lock.hcl to version control .terraform.lock.hcl records the selected provider versions and cryptographic checksums. Commit it so CI and every developer resolve to the exact same providers — otherwise a teammate could silently pull a newer provider with behavior changes. Add multi-platform hashes with terraform providers lock when developers and CI run on different OS/arch (e.g. Mac ARM laptops, Linux CI), or init fails on a missing checksum. Upgrade deliberately with -upgrade and review the diff. Supply-chain angle: the checksums defend against a tampered/substituted provider binary. Committing the lock file is both a reproducibility and a security control — frame it that way. Treat lock-file bumps as reviewable PRs like any dependency upgrade.

questions.q: How do you handle conditional resource creation and optional features in a module?
questions.text: Modules often need to toggle resources on/off or vary behavior by input. The idiomatic tools are count-as-toggle, for_each over conditional collections, and optional object attributes. Conditional patterns # On/off toggle with count: resource "aws_nat_gateway" "this" { count = var.enable_nat ? 1 : 0 } # Conditional set membership with for_each: for_each = var.create ? toset(var.names) : toset([]) # Optional attributes with defaults (object type): variable "cfg" { type = object({ size = optional(string, "small") }) } # Reference a count=0/1 resource safely: value = var.enable_nat ? aws_nat_gateway.this[0].id : null Use count = condition ? 1 : 0 for a simple on/off resource, and for_each over a conditionally-empty collection for variable sets. The optional() modifier in object types gives flexible inputs with defaults. Be careful referencing conditional resources: a count -gated resource must be indexed ( [0] ) and guarded so you do not dereference it when it does not exist. The footgun: referencing aws_nat_gateway.this[0].id when count is 0 errors. Always guard with the same condition ( var.enable_nat ? ...[0].id : null ). Overusing conditionals also makes modules hard to reason about — sometimes two clear modules beat one conditional-laden one.

questions.q: How do you reduce the number of provider/API calls and avoid hitting rate limits?
questions.text: Excessive data sources, oversized state, and high parallelism drive API call volume. Reducing calls speeds plans and avoids throttling. Reducing API pressure Minimize data sources that query on EVERY plan (cache values in SSM/locals instead) Split state so each plan refreshes fewer resources Lower -parallelism when the provider throttles Use -refresh=false for fast iterative plans (when drift is unlikely) -target during iteration to avoid refreshing the whole graph Every data source and every managed resource is refreshed/queried on plan. The big reductions come from fewer resources per state (segmentation) and fewer expensive data sources (publish stable values to SSM/Parameter Store once rather than querying the API on every plan). When you do hit limits, lowering parallelism and using -refresh=false / -target for iteration reduces call bursts. Provider-specific: some providers support request caching or have known rate limits; check provider docs and cloud quotas. Persistent throttling on a huge config is a signal to segment state, not just to retry harder.

questions.q: Explain locals, variables, and outputs — and the right use of each.
questions.text: These are the three data primitives of a configuration. Confusing their roles leads to messy, hard-to-maintain code. Roles variable : INPUT to a module/config (set by caller, CLI, tfvars, env) local : computed/intermediate value, DRY within a module (not an input) output : value EXPOSED to the caller or other configs locals { name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.env}" } output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.main.id } Variables are the module’s inputs — the knobs callers turn. Locals are internal computed values used to avoid repetition and to name things consistently (e.g. a derived name prefix or a merged tag map); they are not settable from outside. Outputs publish values for other modules or the root to consume. A clean module reads inputs (variables), derives internals (locals), provisions resources, and publishes results (outputs). Common smell: using a variable with a default as a “constant” that callers should never set — that should be a local . And overusing locals for trivial one-off values adds indirection. Match the primitive to the role: caller-facing → variable/output, internal → local.

questions.q: What is -target and why is it considered a code smell in routine use?
questions.text: -target limits an operation to specific resources and their dependencies. It is a legitimate recovery/iteration tool but a warning sign when used routinely. Targeted operations terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web # apply only this + its deps terraform plan -target=module.network # scope to a module terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web # targeted replacement Targeting is appropriate for recovery (apply just the resource that failed mid-run) and iteration speed on a huge config while developing. But routine reliance on -target means your normal plan/apply is unmanageable — usually a sign the state is too big (should be split) or the config has hidden coupling. Targeting also skips parts of the graph, so it can apply an inconsistent partial change that a full apply would have ordered differently. Why it is a smell: a healthy config can run a full plan / apply routinely. Constant targeting hides a structural problem (monolithic state, slow refresh). The fix is state segmentation, not normalizing -target . HashiCorp explicitly warns it is for exceptional use.

questions.q: How do you test Terraform modules? Walk through the testing pyramid.
questions.text: Terraform testing spans static checks, unit-ish plan assertions, and integration tests that actually provision. A layered approach catches different failure classes cheaply. Testing layers Static : terraform validate, fmt, tflint, checkov/tfsec (security) Native test framework (1.6+): tests in .tftest.hcl with assert blocks run "plan" { command = plan assert { condition=... error_message=... } } Integration : Terratest (Go) — apply to a real sandbox, assert, destroy Policy : OPA/Conftest or Sentinel against the plan JSON Bottom of the pyramid (cheap, fast, run on every PR): validate , fmt , tflint , and security scanners (checkov/tfsec). The middle: Terraform’s native test framework (1.6+) with .tftest.hcl files asserting on plan/apply outputs without leaving Terraform. The top (slow, expensive, fewer): Terratest spins up real resources in a sandbox account, asserts they work, and tears them down — catching issues only visible against real APIs. Policy-as-code gates compliance against the plan. Modern emphasis: the native terraform test framework (1.6+) reduced the need to reach straight for Terratest — mention it. Pyramid logic applies: many cheap static/plan tests, few expensive apply-and-verify tests.

questions.q: How do you handle Terraform with thousands of resources without applies becoming unmanageable?
questions.text: At thousands of resources, monolithic state makes plans slow, applies risky, and locks painful. The answer is architectural decomposition plus orchestration tooling. Scaling strategies Decompose state by layer (network/data/compute) and by service/team Cross-layer references via SSM/data sources, not giant shared state Orchestrate ordering with Terragrunt (dependencies) or pipelines Per-state CI plan/apply so blast radius and runtime stay bounded Use -refresh=false strategically + periodic drift checks per state The core move is state segmentation : many small, independently-applied states instead of one monolith. Each state plans fast, has bounded blast radius, and can be owned by one team. Cross-state data flows through loosely-coupled mechanisms (SSM, provider data sources). Orchestration tools (Terragrunt for DRY config + dependency ordering, or a pipeline that sequences states) manage the inter-state ordering that segmentation introduces. Trade-off to name: segmentation buys speed, isolation, and ownership at the cost of orchestration complexity (ordering, more backends, more remote-state plumbing). The skill is segmenting along genuine ownership/change-rate boundaries, not arbitrarily — that judgment is the staff-level signal.

questions.q: What are provider aliases and how do you manage multi-region or multi-account providers in modules?
questions.text: Provider aliases let one configuration use multiple instances of the same provider — different regions or accounts — and pass the right one to each module/resource. Aliased providers provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" } # default provider "aws" { alias = "eu" region = "eu-west-1" } resource "aws_s3_bucket" "eu" { provider = aws.eu } # Passing aliased providers INTO a module: module "replica" { source="./m" providers = { aws = aws.eu } } # Module declares it needs a provider via required_providers/configuration_aliases Define multiple provider blocks with alias , then assign provider = aws.eu on resources or pass providers into modules via the providers argument. This is how you build multi-region replication or multi-account deployments in one config. Modules that need a specific aliased provider declare it (via configuration_aliases ) so callers must supply it explicitly. Footgun: a module should generally NOT define its own provider blocks — that breaks reusability and complicates destroy. Pass providers in from the root via providers = {} . Self-contained provider config inside modules is a known anti-pattern that causes “provider configuration not present” errors on removal.

questions.q: Explain the difference between terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars, env vars, and -var precedence.
questions.text: Terraform sources variable values from several places with a defined precedence. Knowing the order prevents “why is my value being ignored?” confusion. Precedence (later overrides earlier) 1. Environment variables (TF_VAR_name) 2. terraform.tfvars 3. terraform.tfvars.json 4. *.auto.tfvars / *.auto.tfvars.json (alphabetical order) 5. -var and -var-file on the CLI (highest precedence) Values are applied in increasing precedence: env vars ( TF_VAR_ ) first, then terraform.tfvars , then auto-loaded *.auto.tfvars (alphabetical), and finally explicit -var / -var-file flags win over everything. Variable defaults apply only when no source sets the value. *.auto.tfvars is loaded automatically (handy for environment-specific files); a plain secret.tfvars requires explicit -var-file . Practical use: commit non-secret *.auto.tfvars per environment for auto-loading; pass secrets via TF_VAR_ env vars or a -var-file that is not in the repo. Knowing the precedence order is a common quick-fire interview check.

questions.q: What is terraform graph and how do you use it to debug or optimize a configuration?
questions.text: terraform graph emits the dependency DAG in DOT format, letting you visualize and analyze resource relationships — useful for debugging ordering and spotting unnecessary coupling. Graph inspection terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png # render the dependency graph terraform graph -type=plan # graph for a specific operation # Look for: unexpected edges (hidden coupling), long dependency chains, # resources that should be parallel but are serialized The graph reveals why Terraform orders things the way it does. Debugging uses: spotting an unexpected dependency (often an overzealous depends_on serializing work that could be parallel), confirming a resource depends on what you think, or understanding why a change ripples. Optimization uses: long serial chains or excessive cross-edges indicate coupling you can break (e.g. removing unnecessary depends_on or splitting state) to increase parallelism and reduce blast radius. When it earns its keep: on a confusing “why is this being recreated / why does apply order surprise me” problem, visualizing the graph often makes the hidden edge obvious. Pair with removing needless depends_on to restore parallelism.

questions.q: How do you structure a Terraform CI/CD pipeline with plan and apply stages?
questions.text: A safe Terraform pipeline separates plan (read-only, on PR) from apply (mutating, gated on merge), so changes are reviewed as a concrete diff before touching infrastructure. Pipeline stages terraform fmt -check # fail on unformatted code terraform validate # syntax + internal consistency terraform plan -out=tfplan # on PR: produce a saved plan artifact # post the plan as a PR comment for review (Atlantis / tf-cloud / custom) terraform apply tfplan # on merge: apply the EXACT reviewed plan Saving the plan to a file ( -out=tfplan ) and applying that exact artifact is the key safety property: it guarantees you apply what was reviewed, not a freshly-recomputed plan that may have drifted. The PR shows the diff; merge triggers apply of the approved plan. Interview tip: emphasize plan-on-PR / apply-on-merge with a saved plan artifact, plus required approvals for production. Atlantis and Terraform Cloud/Enterprise provide this orchestration out of the box; many teams also build it on GitHub Actions/GitLab CI.

questions.q: Why should you apply a saved plan file rather than re-running plan during apply?
questions.text: Running a bare terraform apply recomputes the plan at apply time against current state — which may differ from what the reviewer saw. Applying a saved plan eliminates that gap. terraform plan -out=tfplan # capture the reviewed plan terraform apply tfplan # apply EXACTLY that, no recompute # vs the unsafe pattern: terraform apply -auto-approve # recomputes; could apply unexpected changes Between review and apply, someone might change a resource manually (drift), another pipeline might alter shared state, or a data source might return new values. A bare apply would silently incorporate those into a new plan. Applying the saved plan file makes the operation deterministic and auditable: the bytes you reviewed are the bytes you apply. Production rule: never -auto-approve a freshly-computed plan in prod. Either apply a saved, reviewed plan, or require a human to inspect the apply-time plan before confirming.

questions.q: How do you manage Terraform across multiple environments (dev/staging/prod) in CI/CD?
questions.text: The two dominant patterns are directory-per-environment and workspaces . Directory-per-environment is generally preferred for production isolation. Directory-per-environment (recommended) environments/dev/main.tf # own backend key, own tfvars environments/staging/main.tf environments/prod/main.tf # shared logic lives in ../../modules/, called by each env Workspaces (use with care) terraform workspace new staging terraform workspace select prod # same backend key prefix; differentiate via terraform.workspace Directory-per-environment gives each env its own state file, backend config, and variable values — strong isolation, and a blast-radius boundary (a bad dev apply cannot touch prod state). Workspaces share one configuration and backend, which is lighter but risks cross-environment mistakes and makes per-env backend differences awkward. For production, most teams choose separate directories (or separate root modules) and wire the env into the pipeline. Interview tip: state the trade-off explicitly — workspaces are convenient for ephemeral/similar environments, but directory-per-environment is safer for prod because of isolated state and independent backends. Avoid using workspaces as the only separation between dev and prod.

questions.q: How do you run Terraform plan automatically on pull requests and surface the diff?
questions.text: Automating plan-on-PR turns infrastructure changes into reviewable diffs, the same way code review works for application code. # In CI (GitHub Actions example flow): terraform init -input=false terraform plan -no-color -out=tfplan terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt # human-readable # post plan.txt as a PR comment via the platform API or a tool Tools like Atlantis and Terraform Cloud do this natively: they detect the PR, run plan, and comment the diff directly on the PR, then let an approver trigger apply with a comment (e.g. atlantis apply ). On bare CI you replicate it: run plan, render with terraform show , and post it back. The reviewer evaluates the concrete resource changes, not just the HCL. Interview tip: the value is that reviewers see the effect (resources to add/change/destroy), not just the source change. Highlight that a "+/- destroy" in a plan comment is exactly the signal that catches dangerous changes before merge.

questions.q: A Terraform apply failed halfway through in CI. What is the state, and how do you recover?
questions.text: Terraform applies resources incrementally and records each success in state as it goes. A mid-apply failure leaves a partial apply: some resources created and tracked, others not. Recovery terraform plan # shows what's left to do (already-created resources are in state) # fix the cause of the failure (quota, permission, dependency, provider bug) terraform apply # continues from where it stopped; idempotent terraform state list # confirm what's tracked # if a resource was created but NOT recorded (rare), import it: terraform import <addr> <id> Because Terraform writes state as each resource completes, re-running plan after fixing the root cause shows only the remaining work — it will not recreate what already succeeded. The dangerous edge case is a resource that was created in the cloud but whose state write failed (e.g. lock/network issue at the wrong moment): then plan wants to create it again and you may hit "already exists." Resolve by importing it into state. Locking matters here: ensure state locking (DynamoDB/GCS) is enabled so a failed CI run does not leave a dangling lock blocking the retry. terraform force-unlock <lock-id> clears a stuck lock — use only after confirming no apply is actually running.

questions.q: How do you handle Terraform provider and module version pinning in a team?
questions.text: Unpinned versions cause "works on my machine" drift and surprise breakages when a new provider/module release ships. Pin deterministically and commit the lock file. terraform { required_version = "~> 1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.40" } } } module "vpc" { source = "..." version = "5.8.1" } # pin modules exactly # Commit .terraform.lock.hcl — it pins provider checksums across the team Use required_version and required_providers with sensible constraints ( ~> allows patch/minor but not breaking majors), pin registry modules to exact versions , and — critically — commit .terraform.lock.hcl so every developer and CI run resolves the same provider checksums. Upgrade deliberately via terraform init -upgrade in a reviewed PR. Interview tip: the lock file ( .terraform.lock.hcl ) is the detail that separates juniors from seniors here — it guarantees reproducible provider versions and verifies checksums (supply-chain integrity). Always commit it.

questions.q: How do you keep secrets out of Terraform code and state?
questions.text: Two distinct problems: secrets in code (committed to Git) and secrets in state (Terraform stores resource attributes, including some sensitive values, in plaintext state). Out of code # Never hardcode.
