Source secrets at runtime: data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" { secret_id = "prod/db" } variable "db_password" { sensitive = true } # mark sensitive # pass via TF_VAR_db_password env, Vault provider, or a secrets manager data source Out of (or protected in) state # State CAN contain secrets in plaintext — so protect the backend: # - encrypt state at rest (SSE-KMS on S3), restrict bucket access tightly # - use a backend that encrypts (Terraform Cloud, or KMS-encrypted S3) Mark variables and outputs sensitive = true so they are redacted in plan/CLI output. But understand that sensitive does not encrypt state — the value is still in the state file in plaintext. The real protection for state is a locked-down, encrypted backend with strict IAM. The cleanest pattern is to reference secrets from a secrets manager at apply time rather than passing them through Terraform at all. Critical misconception: sensitive = true only hides values in CLI output — it does NOT encrypt them in state. Anyone with read access to the state file sees the plaintext. Lock down and encrypt the backend, and prefer external secret references.

questions.q: How do you scan Terraform code for security and compliance issues?
questions.text: Static analysis catches misconfigurations (open security groups, unencrypted buckets, public access) before they are applied. Run scanners in CI as a required gate. tfsec . # security-focused static analysis checkov -d . # policy-as-code scanning (CIS, etc.) terrascan scan # compliance scanning trivy config . # misconfig + vuln scanning # Policy-as-code enforcement: # - Sentinel (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise) # - OPA / Conftest against the plan JSON: terraform show -json tfplan Scanners like tfsec , Checkov , and Terrascan flag insecure patterns (e.g. 0.0.0.0/0 ingress, unencrypted volumes, public S3) directly from HCL. For enforceable guardrails, use policy-as-code : Sentinel (in Terraform Cloud) or OPA/Conftest evaluated against the plan JSON ( terraform show -json ) so you can block, for example, any plan that creates a publicly accessible database. Interview tip: distinguish scanning (tfsec/Checkov find issues) from policy enforcement (Sentinel/OPA block merges/applies that violate policy). Mentioning evaluating policy against the -json plan output shows you know how to make guardrails truly preventive, not just advisory.

questions.q: How do you manage least-privilege IAM for the Terraform execution role itself?
questions.text: The Terraform runner often has broad permissions — making it a high-value target. Scope it tightly and prefer short-lived, federated credentials over static keys. # CI authenticates via OIDC federation (no stored cloud keys): # GitHub Actions → AWS IAM role via OIDC, short-lived STS creds # Scope the role to only what the config manages: # - per-environment roles (prod runner cannot touch dev and vice versa) # - permission boundaries to cap maximum privilege # - deny creating IAM admin / leaving the account Replace long-lived access keys with OIDC federation so the pipeline assumes a role and gets credentials valid for minutes. Give each environment its own execution role scoped to that environment’s resources, and apply permission boundaries to cap what the role can ever do (so a compromised or buggy config cannot escalate to account-admin). Separate plan (read-only) from apply (write) credentials where possible. Blast radius: a Terraform role with *:* is effectively account-admin and a single leaked credential compromises everything. Scope per environment, use permission boundaries, and federate so nothing long-lived is stored in CI.

questions.q: What does sensitive = true do, and what are its limits?
questions.text: sensitive = true marks a variable or output so Terraform redacts it from CLI/plan output and logs . It is an output-hygiene feature, not encryption. variable "api_key" { type = string sensitive = true } output "db_endpoint" { value = ... sensitive = true } # In plan output the value shows as: (sensitive value) # Terraform propagates sensitivity: anything derived from it is also redacted It prevents accidental leakage of secrets into console output, plan diffs, and CI logs, and Terraform tracks sensitivity through expressions (a value computed from a sensitive input stays redacted). Its limits: it does not encrypt the value in the state file (still plaintext), and a determined user can still extract it via terraform output -json or by reading state. It also does not stop the value from reaching the provider/API. Interview tip: frame it precisely — " sensitive protects against accidental disclosure in output/logs, not against someone with state access." That precision is what interviewers are listening for; conflating it with encryption is a common red flag.

questions.q: How would you enforce that no resource is ever created with public internet exposure?
questions.text: This is a policy-as-code problem: codify the rule and enforce it in the pipeline so violating plans cannot be applied. # Sentinel (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise) policy example intent: # deny any security_group rule with cidr_blocks containing 0.0.0.0/0 on 22/3389 # deny S3 buckets without public-access-block # OPA/Conftest against plan JSON: terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json conftest test plan.json # rego policies evaluate the planned resources # Make the policy check a REQUIRED status check before apply Generate the machine-readable plan ( terraform show -json ) and evaluate it with OPA/Conftest (open-source) or Sentinel (Terraform Cloud). The policy inspects every planned resource — e.g. reject any security group opening 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH/RDP, any database with publicly_accessible = true , any bucket missing a public-access block — and fails the pipeline so the apply never runs. This is preventive, not advisory. Interview tip: the strong answer evaluates policy against the plan (what will actually be created), not just the HCL source — because dynamic values and modules can produce public exposure that static source review misses. Wire it as a blocking gate.

questions.q: How do you handle state file security given it may contain plaintext secrets?
questions.text: State is sensitive: it can hold passwords, keys, and certificates in plaintext. Treat the backend like a secrets store. # S3 backend hardening: # - SSE-KMS encryption at rest, with a restricted KMS key # - bucket policy: deny non-TLS access, restrict to the TF role # - block all public access; enable versioning + access logging # - DynamoDB lock table with the same tight access # Terraform Cloud encrypts state and controls access via teams Because sensitive = true does not encrypt state, the defense is at the backend: encrypt at rest (SSE-KMS), enforce TLS in transit, and restrict read access to only the Terraform execution role and a minimal set of operators. Enable versioning (for recovery) and access logging (for audit). Never store production state on a developer laptop or in an unencrypted, broadly-readable bucket. Audit reminder: anyone who can read the state bucket can read every secret Terraform touched. Review who has access, encrypt with a scoped KMS key, and log access. State leakage is a full credential compromise.

questions.q: How do you implement drift detection in an automated way?
questions.text: Drift is when real infrastructure diverges from state (manual console changes, out-of-band tooling). Automated detection runs plan on a schedule and alerts on non-empty diffs. # Scheduled CI job (e.g. nightly): terraform plan -detailed-exitcode # exit 0 = no changes (no drift) # exit 2 = changes present (DRIFT) → alert # exit 1 = error # Terraform Cloud has built-in drift detection + notifications The key flag is -detailed-exitcode : it returns 2 when the plan is non-empty, which a scheduled job interprets as drift and routes to an alert (Slack/PagerDuty). Run it read-only (plan, never apply) so detection never mutates anything. Terraform Cloud/Enterprise offers this natively with health assessments. On detection, a human decides whether to revert the drift (apply) or absorb it into code. Interview tip: stress that drift detection should be read-only and scheduled , and that the response is a decision, not an automatic apply — sometimes the manual change was a legitimate emergency fix that should be codified rather than reverted.

questions.q: How do you test Terraform code? What are unit vs integration approaches?
questions.text: Terraform testing spans static checks, plan assertions, and real-resource integration tests — each catching a different class of error. Layers of testing terraform fmt -check / validate # static: syntax, formatting tflint # lint: provider-specific best practices terraform test # native test framework (.tftest.hcl), since TF 1.6 # plan-based assertions (validate values without creating resources) # integration: Terratest (Go) — apply to a sandbox, assert, then destroy checkov / tfsec # security policy tests Native terraform test (1.6+) runs .tftest.hcl files that can do plan-only assertions (cheap, no resources) or full apply/destroy against a real sandbox. Terratest (Go) is the mature integration approach: it applies real infrastructure to a throwaway account, makes assertions (HTTP checks, API calls), and tears it down. Combine with static analysis and policy scanning for full coverage. Interview tip: mention the testing pyramid for IaC — lots of cheap static/plan checks, fewer expensive integration tests that actually provision. Native terraform test (1.6+) is the current, in-the-box answer; Terratest is the battle-tested integration option.

questions.q: How do you safely roll out a change to shared modules used by many teams?
questions.text: A shared module is a published dependency — changing it can break every consumer. Version it semantically and roll out gradually. # Semantic versioning of the module + a registry (or git tags): module "vpc" { source = "app.terraform.io/org/vpc/aws" version = "~> 5.0" } # Breaking change → bump MAJOR (6.0.0); consumers opt in deliberately # Non-breaking → MINOR/PATCH; ~> constraint lets consumers pick it up Treat the module like any released library: semantic versioning (major = breaking, minor = feature, patch = fix), published to a registry or pinned by git tag. Consumers pin versions, so a breaking change does not auto-propagate — they upgrade on their own schedule, testing in dev first. Provide a changelog and migration notes for major bumps. Avoid source pointing at a mutable branch (e.g. main ), which silently breaks consumers. Anti-pattern: sourcing a shared module from a moving git branch. A merge to that branch instantly changes every consumer’s infrastructure plan with no opt-in. Always pin to immutable versions/tags.

questions.q: How do you manage Terraform Cloud / Enterprise workspaces and RBAC at scale?
questions.text: At scale, you manage many workspaces with team-based access, variable sets, and policy guardrails — ideally itself defined as code. # Workspace-per-(service x environment); group by project # Teams → workspace permissions (read / plan / write / admin) # Variable sets: share common vars/creds across workspaces centrally # Sentinel policy sets enforced org-wide (e.g. no public DBs, required tags) # Manage TFC itself with the tfe provider (workspaces/teams as code) Structure workspaces by service × environment, assign access via teams (least privilege: most users get plan, fewer get apply, admin is rare), and use variable sets to distribute shared credentials/config without copy-paste. Enforce Sentinel policy sets org-wide for guardrails. Crucially, manage TFC configuration itself with the tfe Terraform provider so workspace/team/policy setup is reviewable code, not console clicks. Interview tip: "manage the platform with the platform" — defining TFC workspaces, teams, and policies via the tfe provider is the staff-level move. It makes access and guardrails auditable and prevents console drift.

questions.q: A long-running apply is stuck holding the state lock. How do you handle it safely?
questions.text: A stuck lock blocks all other runs. The safe path is to first confirm whether an apply is genuinely still running before force-unlocking — force-unlocking a live apply corrupts state. terraform plan # will report: Error acquiring state lock + lock ID + who/when # Investigate: is a CI job / person actually still applying? # check CI run status, the lock's 'Who' and 'Created' fields # Only if you've CONFIRMED no apply is running: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> The lock error shows the lock ID, who acquired it, and when — use that to investigate. If a CI job died mid-apply (crash, cancelled runner), the lock can be orphaned and force-unlock is appropriate. But if an apply is truly still in progress, force-unlocking lets a second apply run concurrently against the same state → corruption. So confirm first, unlock second. Never force-unlock blindly. Two concurrent applies on one state file can corrupt it irreparably. Verify no apply is actually running (CI status, lock metadata) before force-unlock . Set reasonable CI timeouts so dead jobs release locks.

questions.q: How do you handle credentials and provider authentication securely in Terraform?
questions.text: Provider auth should use short-lived, environment-provided credentials — never hardcoded keys in HCL, which end up in Git and state. # DON'T: provider "aws" { access_key = "AKIA..." secret_key = "..." } # leaked to Git # DO — let the environment provide creds: provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" } # uses env / instance role / OIDC # Local dev: SSO / aws-vault / short-lived STS # CI: OIDC federation → assume-role → short-lived STS creds (nothing stored) Hardcoding credentials in the provider block commits them to Git and risks them landing in state — a classic leak. Instead let the provider pick up credentials from the environment: an instance/pod role, AWS SSO + aws-vault locally, and OIDC federation in CI so the pipeline assumes a role for minutes-long STS credentials. This keeps nothing long-lived anywhere in code or config. Interview tip: the modern best-practice answer is OIDC federation for CI (no stored secrets) plus instance/pod roles or SSO for humans. Hardcoded keys in a provider block is an instant red flag in a security-minded interview.

questions.q: Terraform plan wants to destroy and recreate a production database. How do you prevent disaster?
questions.text: A destroy/recreate on a stateful resource means data loss and downtime. First understand why Terraform wants to replace it, then protect against it. Diagnose the forced replacement terraform plan # look for '# forces replacement' next to an attribute # common causes: changing an immutable attribute (engine_version path, # availability_zone, name), provider treating a change as ForceNew terraform plan -json | jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions[]=="delete")' Protect it lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } # hard stop: apply errors instead of destroying lifecycle { ignore_changes = [<attr>] } # if the change is spurious/managed elsewhere terraform state mv ... # if it's an addressing change, not a real replace Read the plan to find the attribute that "forces replacement" — often an immutable field changed inadvertently, or a provider quirk. Add prevent_destroy = true to critical stateful resources as a safety net so any plan that would destroy them fails loudly. If the change is spurious, ignore_changes or fixing the config avoids the replacement. If it is merely a rename/move, terraform state mv updates addressing without recreating. Always run prevent_destroy on production databases, stateful volumes, and anything holding data. It converts a catastrophic silent destroy into a loud apply failure that forces a human decision.

questions.q: How do you import existing (manually-created) infrastructure into Terraform management?
questions.text: Brownfield adoption: bring already-running resources under Terraform without recreating them. Modern Terraform supports both CLI import and declarative import blocks. Declarative import (TF 1.5+, preferred) import { to = aws_instance.web id = "i-0abc123" } terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf # scaffold the HCL terraform apply # adopt into state CLI import (classic) terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abc123 # then hand-write matching HCL until plan shows no changes Import blocks (1.5+) are declarative and can even generate starter configuration with -generate-config-out , which dramatically speeds up adopting large existing estates. The classic terraform import imports one resource into state, after which you write HCL that matches reality until plan is clean. The goal in both cases: a green plan (no changes) proving config matches the real resource. Interview tip: mention import blocks + -generate-config-out as the current approach — it shows you are on modern Terraform. The success criterion is always "plan shows no changes," meaning your code now faithfully represents the imported resource.

questions.q: Two resources in state need to swap names / move into a module. How do you do it without recreation?
questions.text: Renaming a resource or moving it into a module changes its address . Without telling Terraform, it sees the old address as "destroy" and the new as "create." moved blocks and state mv avoid that. Declarative moved blocks (preferred) moved { from = aws_instance.web to = module.compute.aws_instance.web } # committed in code; plan shows a move, not destroy+create Imperative state mv terraform state mv aws_instance.web module.compute.aws_instance.web terraform state mv aws_instance.a aws_instance.tmp # for swaps, via a temp address terraform state mv aws_instance.b aws_instance.a terraform state mv aws_instance.tmp aws_instance.b moved blocks (1.1+) record the address change declaratively in code, so every collaborator and CI run applies the move consistently and reviewably — the plan shows a move with no resource churn. terraform state mv is the imperative equivalent for one-off surgery; swapping two names requires a temporary address to avoid a collision. Interview tip: prefer moved blocks over state mv — they are versioned, reviewed, and self-documenting, whereas manual state mv is an out-of-band operation others cannot see. Both avoid the destroy/recreate that a naive rename would trigger.

questions.q: A resource was deleted outside Terraform (in the console). What happens on next plan?
questions.text: Terraform compares state against reality. A resource deleted out-of-band is still in state but gone in the cloud — Terraform detects this as drift and plans to recreate it. terraform plan # shows the resource will be CREATED (it's missing in reality) terraform apply # recreates it to match config # if you intended the deletion, remove it from config + state instead: terraform state rm <addr> # drop from state (stop managing) ... # ... and delete the resource block from HCL so plan stays clean On refresh, Terraform notices the real resource is absent and reconciles by planning to recreate it (config still declares it). If the deletion was a mistake, apply restores it. If the deletion was intentional, the correct action is to remove the resource from both the HCL and the state ( state rm ) so Terraform stops expecting it — otherwise it will keep trying to recreate it on every run. Interview tip: the key insight is that state + config define desired state; reality is reconciled toward them. "Deleted in console" → Terraform recreates, because as far as it knows you still want it. This is also why drift detection matters.

questions.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime change to a load-balanced fleet with Terraform?
questions.text: Use create_before_destroy lifecycle plus health-checked target registration so new instances are serving before old ones are removed. resource "aws_launch_template" "app" { ... } # change here triggers rollout lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } # new resource up before old torn down # With ASG + LB: instance refresh / rolling update strategy # - new instances launch, pass health checks, register to LB # - only then are old instances drained and terminated The create_before_destroy lifecycle rule inverts Terraform’s default (destroy-then-create), so the replacement exists and is healthy before the original is removed — essential for anything behind a load balancer. For autoscaling fleets, pair it with the platform’s rolling/instance-refresh mechanism and connection draining so traffic shifts only to instances that pass health checks, achieving zero downtime. Gotcha: create_before_destroy requires that the new and old can coexist — unique names, no hard capacity/quota limit of 1, no conflicting fixed identifiers (e.g. a static EIP or a name that must be unique). Plan for two copies existing momentarily.

questions.q: How do you structure Terraform to limit blast radius across a large infrastructure estate?
questions.text: Blast radius is bounded by how state is partitioned. Many small, independent state files limit the damage any single apply (or corrupted state) can do. Partitioning strategy # Separate state per: environment x layer x service # network/ (VPC, subnets) — changes rarely, high blast radius # data/ (databases) — isolated, prevent_destroy # compute/ (apps) — changes often, low blast radius # Connect layers via remote state data sources or published outputs: data "terraform_remote_state" "network" { backend = "s3" config = {...} } Rather than one monolithic state for everything, split by environment, layer (network/data/compute), and service. Each gets its own state file, so a mistake or corruption in the compute layer cannot affect the network or data layers, and applies are smaller and faster. Layers reference each other’s outputs via terraform_remote_state data sources. This also enables independent change cadences — stable layers (network) change rarely; volatile layers (apps) change often. Interview tip: "one giant state file" is the anti-pattern to call out — slow plans, huge blast radius, lock contention across teams. The senior answer is partitioned state by environment/layer/service with remote-state references between them.

questions.q: A terraform apply is taking 30+ minutes and timing out. How do you diagnose and speed it up?
questions.text: Slow applies usually come from too-large state, excessive provider API calls, or serialized dependencies. Diagnose, then partition or tune parallelism. terraform plan -refresh=false # skip refresh if drift detection isn't needed now terraform apply -parallelism=20 # raise from default 10 (watch API rate limits) terraform apply -target=module.x # apply a subset (use sparingly, for triage) TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply # see where time goes (slow provider calls?) First, the structural fix: a 30-minute apply usually means the state is too big — split it into smaller, independent states (see blast-radius partitioning). Tactically, -refresh=false skips the per-resource refresh round-trips when you do not need fresh drift data, raising -parallelism speeds independent resource operations (bounded by provider API rate limits), and TF_LOG=DEBUG reveals whether a specific slow provider/data source is the bottleneck. Interview tip: lead with the root cause (state too large → partition it) and present -refresh=false , -parallelism , and targeted applies as tactical aids. -target is a triage tool, not a normal workflow — say so, since over-using it hides real dependency problems.

questions.q: How do you safely deprecate and destroy an environment without leaving orphaned resources or breaking dependents?
questions.text: Teardown must account for cross-state dependencies and protected resources. Plan it like a controlled decommission, not a single destroy . terraform plan -destroy # preview everything that will be destroyed # check for dependents in OTHER states (remote_state references) # temporarily lift prevent_destroy on resources you truly intend to remove terraform destroy # tear down this state's resources # verify no orphans: cloud-side resources not in any state (cost scanners help) Run plan -destroy first to see the full set of resources targeted. Critically, check whether other state files reference this environment (via terraform_remote_state ) — destroying a shared VPC that another state depends on breaks it. Resources with prevent_destroy will block destroy until you deliberately lift it. After teardown, reconcile against the cloud bill / a resource scanner to catch orphans — things created out-of-band or left by partial failures that Terraform never tracked. Two failure modes: (1) breaking another environment that depended on a shared resource — check remote-state references first; (2) orphaned resources still costing money because they were never in state — reconcile against the cloud after destroy.

questions.q: Terraform state has become corrupted or out of sync with reality. How do you recover?
questions.text: State corruption (truncated file, bad manual edit, conflicting writes) is serious but recoverable via backend versioning and surgical state commands. # 1. Restore a known-good version from backend history: aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket <b> --prefix <key> aws s3api get-object --version-id <v> ... terraform.tfstate # 2. Or repair surgically: terraform state pull > backup.tfstate # always back up first terraform state list # see what's tracked terraform state rm <bad-addr> # remove a broken entry terraform import <addr> <id> # re-add a missing/real resource terraform state push <fixed.tfstate> # push a corrected state (last resort) If you enabled backend versioning (you should have), the fastest recovery is restoring the last good state version. For targeted issues, always state pull a backup first, then use state rm / import to bring state back in line with reality, verifying with a clean plan . state push of a hand-corrected file is the last resort and must be done with locking and care. Prevention is the real answer: S3/GCS versioning + locking makes corruption a quick rollback instead of a crisis. Always state pull a backup before any manual state surgery, and never hand-edit state JSON directly.

questions.q: How do you handle a provider upgrade that introduces breaking changes across many resources?
questions.text: Major provider upgrades can change resource schemas, defaults, or force replacements. Upgrade deliberately in a controlled, reviewed, environment-by-environment rollout. # Bump the constraint in a dedicated PR: required_providers { aws = { version = "~> 6.0" } } # was ~> 5.0 terraform init -upgrade terraform plan # carefully review EVERY forced replacement / change # read the provider's upgrade guide for the breaking changes # apply to dev → staging → prod, validating at each step Treat it like a dependency major bump: isolate it in its own PR, run init -upgrade , and scrutinize the plan for forced replacements (a schema change can make Terraform want to recreate resources — dangerous for stateful ones). Consult the provider’s official upgrade guide for migration steps, apply moved / ignore_changes where the change is cosmetic, and protect stateful resources with prevent_destroy . Roll through dev → staging → prod, never straight to prod. Interview tip: the danger signal is a major-version provider bump silently planning to replace databases or volumes. The senior workflow: dedicated PR, read the upgrade guide, review the plan line by line, prevent_destroy on stateful resources, and a staged rollout.

questions.q: How do you manage Terraform for disaster recovery across regions?
questions.text: Multi-region DR with Terraform means parameterizing region and replicating the stack, with state and data-replication concerns handled explicitly. # Region as a variable; same root module deployed per region: module "stack" { source = "./modules/stack" region = var.region } # Provider aliases for multi-region in one config: provider "aws" { alias = "primary" region = "us-east-1" } provider "aws" { alias = "dr" region = "us-west-2" } # Separate state per region; replicate data via provider features (e.g. cross-region replication) Make region a variable and deploy the same module to each region (separate state per region for isolation), or use provider aliases to manage primary and DR regions from one configuration when they must be coordinated. Terraform provisions the infrastructure shape in both regions; data replication (DB read replicas, S3 cross-region replication, backups) is configured as resources but the actual failover/promotion is usually an operational runbook, not a Terraform apply. Interview tip: separate the concerns — Terraform reproduces the infrastructure consistently across regions (provider aliases or per-region state), but failover orchestration and data promotion are operational procedures. Mentioning that distinction shows you understand DR is more than "apply in another region."

questions.q: A count-based resource list changed in the middle, and Terraform wants to destroy/recreate many resources. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.text: count indexes resources by position. Removing an item in the middle shifts every subsequent index, so Terraform thinks each shifted resource is a different one — mass destroy/recreate. for_each avoids this. # Problem: count indexes by position resource "aws_instance" "x" { count = length(var.names) ... } # remove names[1] → indices 2,3,4 shift to 1,2,3 → churn # Fix: for_each keys by a stable identifier resource "aws_instance" "x" { for_each = toset(var.names) # keyed by name, not position ... } # migrate existing count resources without recreation: terraform state mv 'aws_instance.x[1]' 'aws_instance.x["web2"]' With count , the address is x[0] , x[1] , ... — purely positional. Deleting a middle element renumbers everything after it, and Terraform plans to destroy/recreate each shifted resource. for_each keys resources by a stable value (a name/ID), so adding or removing one item only affects that one. To migrate an existing count-based resource to for_each without recreation, state mv each from its index to its new key. Interview tip: "use for_each over count for sets of distinct, identifiable resources; use count only for truly homogeneous, order-independent copies or simple on/off ( count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 )." Knowing the positional-index pitfall is a classic senior-level distinguisher.

questions.q: How do you roll back a bad Terraform change that has already been applied to production?
questions.text: Terraform has no native "rollback" — you roll forward to the previous desired state. The mechanism is reverting the code and re-applying, with state versioning as the safety net. git revert <bad-commit> # restore the previous configuration terraform plan # confirm it reverses the bad change terraform apply # roll FORWARD to the prior known-good state # if state itself is wrong, restore a prior state version from the backend, carefully The clean path is Git: revert the commit that introduced the bad change and re-apply, so Terraform reconciles back toward the previous configuration. Because infrastructure changes are not always perfectly reversible (a destroyed resource may not come back identical, data may be lost), review the revert plan carefully — it shows exactly what reversing will do. Backend state versioning lets you also recover a prior state file if state, not just config, was damaged. Key caveat: "rollback" of infrastructure is roll-forward, and some changes are irreversible (deleted data, recreated resources with new IDs). This is why prevent_destroy , plan review, and staged rollouts matter — preventing the bad apply beats reversing it.

questions.q: How do you enforce tagging, naming, and cost-allocation standards across all resources?
questions.text: Consistency comes from a combination of provider default tags, shared modules, and policy enforcement — not from hoping engineers remember. # 1. Provider-level default tags (applied to everything): provider "aws" { default_tags { tags = { Owner = var.team Env = var.env CostCenter = var.cc } } } # 2. Naming via a shared module / locals convention: locals { name = "${var.env}-${var.service}-${var.component}" } # 3. Policy enforcement (block untagged resources): # Sentinel / OPA-Conftest against plan JSON: require Owner+Env+CostCenter Use the provider’s default_tags to stamp common tags (owner, environment, cost-center) on every resource automatically. Standardize naming with a shared locals /module convention so names are predictable and parseable. Then make it enforceable with policy-as-code that rejects any plan creating resources missing required tags — turning standards from documentation into a blocking gate that also powers accurate cost allocation. Interview tip: three layers — default_tags for automatic application, a module/convention for consistency, and policy-as-code for enforcement. Tie it to cost allocation (CostCenter/Owner tags drive showback/chargeback), which connects infra hygiene to FinOps — a strong signal for platform roles.

questions.q: How do you handle resources that must be managed partly outside Terraform (e.g. autoscaling-adjusted values)?
questions.text: Some attributes are legitimately changed by other systems (autoscaling adjusts desired_count; another tool manages a tag). ignore_changes tells Terraform to stop fighting those changes. resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "app" { desired_capacity = 3 # initial value only lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_capacity] # autoscaler owns this at runtime } } # ignore everything that drifts but you don't manage: # ignore_changes = [tags["LastScaled"]] Without ignore_changes , Terraform would revert the autoscaler’s runtime adjustments on every apply (resetting desired_capacity back to 3), fighting the system that legitimately owns that value. ignore_changes on the specific attribute(s) cedes ownership of those fields to the external system while Terraform still manages the rest of the resource. Scope it tightly to the exact attributes shared with another owner. Interview tip: the principle is "single owner per attribute." ignore_changes resolves the tug-of-war when an attribute is genuinely owned at runtime by another system (autoscaling, external automation). Over-using it to paper over real drift is the anti-pattern to avoid — scope it to specific attributes, not whole resources.

questions.q: How do you safely make changes when multiple teams share a single large Terraform repository?
questions.text: Shared-repo collaboration needs ownership boundaries, state partitioning, and gated automation so one team’s change cannot accidentally break another’s infrastructure. # CODEOWNERS routes review to the owning team per directory # State partitioned per team/service → isolated blast radius + parallel applies # Atlantis / TF Cloud: plan-on-PR, apply gated on owning-team approval # Shared modules versioned so a module change doesn't auto-hit all consumers Partition state by team/service so applies are independent and a mistake is contained. Use CODEOWNERS so changes to a directory require the owning team’s review. Run plan-on-PR with the diff posted for review, and gate apply on the right approvals. Version shared modules so updates are opt-in rather than instantly propagating. This combination lets many teams move in parallel without stepping on each other’s infrastructure. Interview tip: the themes are isolation (partitioned state), ownership (CODEOWNERS + per-team state), and gating (plan-on-PR, approvals, versioned modules). This is essentially platform-engineering of the Terraform workflow — exactly what a Platform/SRE interviewer wants to hear.

questions.q: A terraform destroy was run accidentally against production. Walk through your response.
questions.text: This is a sev-1 incident. Response is: stop further damage, assess what was lost, recover from backups/state versioning, and then do a blameless post-incident hardening. Immediate response # 1. STOP: cancel the run if still in progress; lock the state # 2. Assess: terraform state pull / cloud console — what was actually destroyed? # 3. Recover stateful data from backups/snapshots (RDS snapshots, EBS snapshots) # 4. Re-provision: terraform apply from the known-good config to rebuild resources # 5. Re-import any resources restored out-of-band so state matches reality First halt the operation and prevent concurrent applies. Then assess scope — what was destroyed, and crucially what held data (those need snapshot/backup restores, not just re-apply). Re-apply the known-good configuration to rebuild the infrastructure shape, restore data from backups, and reconcile state with reality via imports. Finally, run a blameless post-incident review focused on the guardrails that were missing. The hardening that prevents recurrence: prevent_destroy on stateful resources, requiring approval for destroy operations in CI, restricting who/what can run destroy in prod, and backups/snapshots with tested restores. The lesson interviewers want: a destroy should be hard to do by accident, and data should always be recoverable.

questions.q: How do you manage Terraform at scale with hundreds of state files and many teams (platform perspective)?
questions.text: At scale, the challenge shifts from writing HCL to operating Terraform as a platform: consistent structure, automated workflow, guardrails, and self-service. # Standardized repo/module structure + a shared module registry # Per-(service x env) state with consistent backend key conventions # Orchestration: Terraform Cloud / Atlantis / Spacelift for plan-apply + RBAC # Guardrails: org-wide policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA), required tags, no public exposure # Golden modules: opinionated, versioned modules teams compose (paved road) # Drift detection + cost estimation (Infracost) wired into PRs The platform answer: provide a paved road — opinionated, versioned "golden" modules teams compose, a standard repo/state structure, and an orchestration layer (TFC/Atlantis/Spacelift) that handles plan-on-PR, gated apply, RBAC, and state management for them. Enforce org-wide guardrails with policy-as-code and required tags, surface cost (Infracost) and drift in PRs, and manage the platform configuration itself as code. The goal is self-service infrastructure where the safe, compliant path is the easy one. Interview tip: this is the staff/principal framing — you are not just using Terraform, you are building the platform around it: golden modules, orchestration, policy guardrails, cost/drift visibility, self-service. Mentioning "paved road" and "the safe path is the easy path" signals platform-engineering maturity.

questions.q: Explain dynamic blocks and when you should (and should not) use them.
questions.text: A dynamic block generates repeatable nested blocks (like multiple ingress rules) from a collection, instead of writing each by hand. resource "aws_security_group" "x" { dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.ingress_rules content { from_port = ingress.value.from to_port = ingress.value.to protocol = ingress.value.proto cidr_blocks = ingress.value.cidrs } } } Dynamic blocks shine when the number of nested blocks is data-driven (rules from a variable, settings from a map). But they reduce readability and can hide intent, so do not reach for them when you have a small, fixed set of blocks — explicit blocks are clearer. Overusing dynamic blocks produces "write-only" Terraform that is hard to review. Interview tip: "use dynamic blocks for genuinely variable, data-driven nested blocks; prefer explicit blocks when the set is small and static." Mentioning the readability cost shows judgment, not just knowledge of the feature.

questions.q: How do you design a reusable module with a clean interface?
questions.text: A good module is a black box with a deliberate interface: well-named input variables (with types, defaults, validation), useful outputs, and no hidden assumptions. variable "instance_type" { type = string default = "t3.micro" description = "EC2 instance type" validation { condition = can(regex("^t3\.", var.instance_type)) error_message = "..." } } output "instance_id" { value = aws_instance.this.id } # expose only what consumers need; keep internals private Design the interface first: typed input variables with sensible defaults, descriptions, and validation blocks that fail fast on bad input; outputs that expose exactly what consumers need (IDs, ARNs, endpoints) and nothing more. Keep the module focused on one logical component, document required vs optional inputs, and avoid leaking provider/region assumptions — pass those in. A module should be composable and testable in isolation. Interview tip: emphasize interface design — typed/validated variables, minimal meaningful outputs, single responsibility, no hidden assumptions. Variable validation blocks (fail fast with clear messages) are a detail that signals real module-authoring experience.

questions.q: What is the difference between a root module, child modules, and how is composition done well?
questions.text: The root module is the directory you run Terraform in; it calls child modules . Good composition keeps the root thin and pushes reusable logic into focused children. # root (environments/prod/main.tf): module "network" { source = "../../modules/network" cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" } module "app" { source = "../../modules/app" subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids # wire outputs to inputs } The root module wires environment-specific values and connects child modules by passing one module’s outputs as another’s inputs (e.g. network subnets into the app module). Well-composed Terraform has small, single-purpose child modules (network, data, compute) and a thin root that just composes and parameterizes them per environment. Avoid deep module nesting (modules calling modules calling modules) — it obscures data flow and complicates debugging. Interview tip: "thin root, focused children, wire via outputs→inputs, avoid deep nesting." Mentioning that excessive nesting hurts readability/debuggability shows you have maintained real module hierarchies, not just authored toy examples.

questions.q: How does terraform_remote_state work and what are its alternatives for sharing data between configs?
questions.text: terraform_remote_state reads another configuration’s outputs from its state file, letting one layer consume another’s values (e.g. compute reads the network’s VPC ID). data "terraform_remote_state" "network" { backend = "s3" config = { bucket = "tf-state" key = "network/prod.tfstate" region = "us-east-1" } } # use: subnet_ids = data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.private_subnet_ids # alternatives: data "aws_vpc" "main" { tags = { Name = "prod" } } # query the cloud directly # or pass values via SSM Parameter Store / variables Remote state coupling is convenient but creates a hard dependency: the consumer needs read access to the producer’s state, and you are coupling to internal outputs. Alternatives that reduce coupling: data sources that query the cloud directly (e.g. look up the VPC by tag) so you depend on the real resource not its state, or a shared store like SSM Parameter Store where the producer publishes values and consumers read them — decoupling the two configs from each other’s state. Interview tip: note the trade-off — terraform_remote_state is simple but couples configs to each other’s state and requires state read access. Data sources (query reality) or a published parameter store reduce coupling and are often the more robust choice at scale.

questions.q: Explain terraform refresh, the -refresh-only mode, and why a bare refresh can be risky.
questions.text: Refresh updates state to match the real world without changing infrastructure. Modern Terraform uses plan/apply -refresh-only for a reviewable version of this. terraform plan -refresh-only # show how state would change to match reality (review) terraform apply -refresh-only # update state to match reality, no infra changes terraform plan -refresh=false # skip refresh (use cached state) — faster, but may miss drift # legacy: terraform refresh (deprecated in favor of -refresh-only) Refresh reconciles state with actual resource attributes (picking up out-of-band changes). The standalone terraform refresh is deprecated because it silently mutated state with no review; -refresh-only lets you see the proposed state changes (plan) and approve them (apply) without any infrastructure modification — useful for absorbing legitimate drift into state. -refresh=false skips refresh entirely for speed when you trust state is current. Interview tip: " -refresh-only reconciles state with reality reviewably; standalone refresh is deprecated for being a silent state mutation." Knowing the deprecation and the reviewable replacement signals current Terraform fluency.

questions.q: How do you migrate Terraform state between backends (e.g. local to S3, or S3 to Terraform Cloud)?
questions.text: Backend migration is built into terraform init : change the backend config, re-init, and Terraform offers to copy state to the new backend. # 1. Back up current state first terraform state pull > backup.tfstate # 2. Update the backend block (e.g. add the s3 backend config) terraform { backend "s3" { bucket="tf-state" key="prod.tfstate" dynamodb_table="tf-lock" } } # 3. Re-init; Terraform detects the change and prompts to migrate: terraform init -migrate-state # 4. Verify: terraform plan # should show NO changes Update the backend block to the new target, then run terraform init -migrate-state — Terraform recognizes the backend changed and offers to copy the existing state to the new backend. Always state pull a backup beforehand, and verify with a clean plan afterward (no changes = migration succeeded and config still matches reality). Ensure locking is in place on the new backend before others use it. Coordinate the cutover: migrate when no one else is applying, and make sure everyone re-inits to the new backend afterward. Two people on different backends pointing at the same resources is a recipe for divergent state.

questions.q: What are locals, and how do they differ from variables and outputs?
questions.text: locals are named values computed within a module for internal reuse — they are not inputs (variables) or exposed values (outputs). variable "env" { type = string } # INPUT from the caller locals { name_prefix = "${var.env}-myapp" # INTERNAL computed value common_tags = { Env = var.env ManagedBy = "terraform" } } output "name" { value = local.name_prefix } # EXPOSED to the caller Variables are the module’s inputs (set by the caller). Outputs are what the module exposes to its caller. locals sit in between: intermediate expressions computed once and reused throughout the module (a name prefix, a merged tag map, a derived flag) to avoid repetition and centralize logic. Unlike variables they cannot be overridden from outside; unlike outputs they are not visible externally. Interview tip: crisp framing — "variables = inputs, outputs = exposed results, locals = internal computed reuse." A common use is a common_tags local merged into every resource. Knowing locals are not overridable (unlike variables) shows you understand the data-flow model.

questions.q: Explain the difference between count, for_each, and when each is appropriate.
questions.text: Both create multiple instances of a resource/module, but they index differently — which determines stability when the collection changes. # count: positional index [0], [1], [2] ... resource "aws_instance" "x" { count = 3 } # 3 identical copies resource "aws_instance" "x" { count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 } # conditional create # for_each: keyed by map key or set value resource "aws_instance" "x" { for_each = toset(["web","api"]) } # x["web"], x["api"] resource "aws_instance" "x" { for_each = var.instances } # map of configs Use count for a number of truly identical, order-independent copies, or for a simple conditional ( count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 ). Use for_each for a set/map of distinct, individually-identifiable resources — because it keys by a stable identifier, adding or removing one element only affects that element (no positional churn). For_each is the safer default whenever the items have meaningful identities. Interview tip: the discriminator is "are the instances interchangeable copies (count) or distinct identifiable things (for_each)?" Pairing this with the count-middle-deletion churn problem (positional reindexing) demonstrates real production scar tissue.

questions.q: What is the purpose of terraform output, and how is it consumed downstream?
questions.text: Outputs expose values from a configuration — for humans, for other configs (via remote state), and for scripts/CI that need resource attributes after apply. output "lb_dns" { value = aws_lb.app.dns_name } output "db_endpoint" { value = aws_db_instance.main.address sensitive = true } terraform output # human-readable terraform output -json # machine-readable for scripts/CI terraform output -raw lb_dns # single value, unquoted (for shell use) Outputs surface computed attributes (endpoints, ARNs, IDs) that you cannot know until after apply. They are consumed three ways: by people inspecting results, by other Terraform configs through terraform_remote_state , and by CI/scripts via -json or -raw (e.g. feeding a DB endpoint into a deployment step). Mark outputs sensitive to redact them from CLI display. Interview tip: note the three consumers (humans, other configs, automation) and the formats ( -json for scripts, -raw for a single shell value). Outputs as the contract a module exposes ties back to clean module interface design.

questions.q: How does state locking work, and what happens when locking is misconfigured or absent?
questions.text: State locking serializes mutating operations so only one apply touches a state file at a time. Without it, concurrent applies race and corrupt state. # S3 + DynamoDB locking: backend "s3" { bucket="tf-state" key="prod.tfstate" dynamodb_table="tf-lock" } # DynamoDB provides atomic lock acquisition (conditional write) # (modern Terraform/OpenTofu also support S3-native lockfile locking) terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> # clear a stuck lock (only if no apply is running) When an apply starts, Terraform acquires a lock (historically a DynamoDB item for S3 backends); others attempting to apply get "Error acquiring state lock" and wait/fail. This prevents two applies from writing the state file simultaneously — which would interleave updates and corrupt it. If locking is absent (e.g. local state, or S3 without a lock mechanism), concurrent runs can silently corrupt state or create duplicate resources. Always enable locking for shared state. Its absence is invisible until two applies collide and corrupt state. A stuck lock from a crashed run is cleared with force-unlock — but only after confirming no apply is genuinely in progress, or you risk the very corruption locking prevents.

questions.q: How do you write conditional logic and handle optional resources/attributes in Terraform?
questions.text: HCL is declarative, so "conditionals" are expressed via count / for_each gating, the ternary operator, and try / coalesce for optional values. # conditional resource creation: resource "aws_instance" "bastion" { count = var.create_bastion ? 1 : 0 } # reference it safely (it may be 0): value = var.create_bastion ? aws_instance.bastion[0].id : null # optional attribute / default fallback: tags = coalesce(var.tags, {}) x = try(var.config.optional_field, "default") # optional object attributes (TF 1.3+): variable "cfg" { type = object({ size = optional(string, "small") }) } Conditional creation uses count = condition ? 1 : 0 (or for_each over a possibly-empty collection). Reference such resources guardedly since the index may not exist. For optional inputs, coalesce / try provide fallbacks, and optional() object attributes (1.3+) let you define typed inputs with defaults. The mindset shift: you do not write imperative if/else — you declaratively gate resource existence and choose values via expressions. Interview tip: show the declarative idioms — count -gating for optional resources, ternaries for values, try / coalesce for optional attributes, and optional() in object types. Mentioning the safe-reference pattern ( resource[0] may not exist) reflects real-world burns.

questions.q: When and why would you use -target, and why is it considered a smell if overused?
questions.text: -target limits an operation to specific resources. It is a legitimate triage/recovery tool but a dangerous habit if it becomes routine. terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web # apply only this resource + its deps terraform plan -target=module.network # scope to one module # legitimate uses: recovering from a partial failure, unsticking a dependency cycle, # applying an urgent fix to one resource during an incident -target tells Terraform to operate on only the named resources (and their dependencies), skipping the rest. It is appropriate for recovery — finishing a partially-failed apply, or surgically fixing one resource in an incident. But routine use is a smell: it means you are applying a partial view of desired state, which can leave config and reality inconsistent, hide dependency problems, and produce surprising drift. If you need targeting regularly, the real fix is usually to split the state. Anti-pattern: using -target as a normal workflow to "only apply my change." This bypasses the holistic plan and can mask broken dependencies. Reserve it for triage; if it is a habit, partition your state instead.

questions.q: How do you handle very large outputs or data that does not belong in state (e.g. generated files, secrets)?
questions.text: State should track resource metadata, not bulk data or secrets. Large/inappropriate data in state bloats it, slows operations, and risks exposure. # Don't stuff big blobs or secrets into outputs/state. Instead: # - write generated files via local_file only when truly needed (they go to disk, not infra) # - store secrets in a secrets manager; reference, don't embed # - put large artifacts in object storage (S3/GCS), keep only the reference in state # - mark unavoidable sensitive outputs as sensitive (redaction, not encryption) Keep state lean: it is an index of resources, not a data store. Large outputs slow every plan/apply (state is read/written each time) and big sensitive values increase exposure if state leaks. Put bulk data in object storage and keep only references (URLs/ARNs) in state; source secrets from a secrets manager rather than passing them through Terraform; generate files only when a workflow genuinely requires them. The less sensitive/bulky data in state, the safer and faster Terraform is. Interview tip: "state is metadata, not a database." The senior instinct is to keep references in state and store the actual bulk/secret data in purpose-built systems (object storage, secrets manager). This keeps state small, fast, and lower-risk.

questions.q: What is partial backend configuration and why is it useful in CI/CD?
questions.text: Partial backend config leaves some backend settings out of the HCL and supplies them at init time — useful so the same code initializes different backends per environment without hardcoding. # code: backend block with minimal/empty config terraform { backend "s3" {} } # supply the rest at init (per environment, in CI): terraform init \ -backend-config="bucket=tf-state-prod" \ -backend-config="key=app/prod.tfstate" \ -backend-config="region=us-east-1" # or: terraform init -backend-config=prod.backend.hcl Instead of hardcoding bucket/key/region (which would differ per environment), you leave them out and pass them via -backend-config flags or a per-env .hcl file at init . This lets one codebase target dev/staging/prod backends by varying the init parameters in the pipeline, keeping environment-specific backend details out of the shared HCL. Interview tip: partial backend config is the clean way to reuse one configuration across environments with different state locations — supply the backend key/bucket per env at init. It pairs naturally with directory-per-env or a pipeline that injects the right backend file.

questions.q: How do you debug a confusing Terraform plan or unexpected behavior?
questions.text: Terraform gives several inspection tools: verbose logs, the machine-readable plan, the dependency graph, and console expression evaluation. TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan # verbose internals (provider calls, decisions) TF_LOG=TRACE terraform plan # even more (rarely needed) terraform plan -json | jq ... # structured plan: inspect exact changes/reasons terraform show -json tfplan # decode a saved plan terraform console # evaluate expressions interactively terraform graph | dot -Tpng > g.png # visualize the dependency graph terraform validate # catch config errors early Start with terraform console to test expressions/interpolations in isolation, and the JSON plan ( -json or show -json ) to see precisely what is changing and which attribute "forces replacement." TF_LOG=DEBUG exposes provider API calls and Terraform’s decisions when behavior is mysterious. terraform graph visualizes dependencies when ordering or cycles confuse you. validate catches structural errors before plan. Interview tip: name the toolset — terraform console for expressions, JSON plan for "why is it changing this," TF_LOG=DEBUG for provider-level mysteries, graph for dependency issues. Knowing the JSON plan reveals the forced-replacement attribute is a particularly practical detail.

questions.q: How do you reduce Terraform plan/apply time and provider API pressure on large configs?
questions.text: Performance comes from smaller state, fewer/refresh round-trips, and controlled parallelism — plus structural partitioning when a single config grows too big. # structural (best): split into smaller independent states terraform plan -refresh=false # skip refresh when fresh drift data isn't needed terraform apply -parallelism=20 # more concurrency (mind provider rate limits) # use data sources sparingly — each can be an API call every plan # provider plugin cache to avoid re-downloading providers: export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=~/.terraform.d/plugin-cache The dominant factor is state size: a huge monolithic state refreshes and diffs slowly, so partition it . Tactically, -refresh=false avoids per-resource refresh API calls when you do not need current drift data, tuning -parallelism trades speed against provider rate limits, minimizing heavy data sources cuts per-plan API calls, and a plugin cache speeds init . Profile with TF_LOG to find the slow operations. Interview tip: lead with the structural fix (partition state), then list the tactical levers ( -refresh=false , parallelism, fewer data sources, plugin cache). Noting that data sources cost an API call per plan, and parallelism is bounded by provider rate limits, shows depth.

questions.q: How do you ensure supply-chain integrity of providers and modules?
questions.text: Providers and modules are external dependencies that execute with your cloud credentials — verify their authenticity and pin them, just like any software supply chain. # .terraform.lock.hcl pins provider versions AND checksums — COMMIT it terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 # multi-platform hashes # pin modules to exact versions/immutable tags (never a moving branch) module "vpc" { source="..." version="5.8.1" } # prefer trusted/official providers; consider an internal mirror/registry # scan IaC with tfsec/checkov; review third-party module source before adoption The .terraform.lock.hcl file is central: it records exact provider versions and cryptographic checksums, so every init verifies integrity and reproducibility — commit it and use terraform providers lock to capture hashes for all platforms your team/CI use. Pin modules to immutable versions/tags (never a mutable branch). Prefer official/verified providers, optionally mirror them in an internal registry to control what enters your environment, and review third-party module source before adopting it. Why it matters: a provider or module runs with your infrastructure credentials — a malicious or tampered one is a serious supply-chain risk. The lock file (versions + checksums), exact module pinning, trusted sources, and scanning are your defenses. An uncommitted lock file or a module sourced from a moving branch are red flags.

questions.q: Capstone: design Terraform foundations for a multi-account, multi-team organization from scratch.
questions.text: Bring together repo structure, state strategy, module strategy, workflow, security, and guardrails into a coherent platform foundation. Foundations # Accounts: separate AWS accounts per env (and per business unit) — hard isolation # State: per (account x layer x service); S3+KMS+DynamoDB (or TF Cloud); versioned+locked # Layers: network → data → platform → apps, connected via remote-state/data sources # Modules: versioned 'golden' modules in a registry (the paved road) Workflow & guardrails # CI: plan-on-PR (diff comment), gated apply-on-merge with saved plan, CODEOWNERS # Auth: OIDC federation, per-env scoped roles, permission boundaries (no static keys) # Policy-as-code: Sentinel/OPA org-wide (no public exposure, required tags, encryption) # Visibility: Infracost (cost on PRs), scheduled drift detection, audit via Git + state Start with account-level isolation (separate accounts per environment) for the strongest blast-radius boundary, then partition state per account × layer × service with an encrypted, versioned, locked backend. Provide golden modules in a registry so teams compose a paved road rather than reinventing. Standardize the workflow (plan-on-PR, gated apply of saved plans, CODEOWNERS) and auth (OIDC, scoped per-env roles, permission boundaries). Enforce guardrails with org-wide policy-as-code, and add visibility with cost estimation, drift detection, and Git+state audit trails. The objective: self-service infrastructure where the secure, compliant, cost-aware p

questions.q: What do terraform state pull and push do, and why is terraform state push dangerous?
questions.text: pull prints the current remote state as JSON, which is safe for inspection and backups. push overwrites the remote state with a local file, bypassing normal checks except a serial and lineage comparison. A wrong push can erase knowledge of real resources. terraform state pull > backup-$(date +%F).tfstate terraform state list | wc -l terraform state push -force fixed.tfstate Interview tip: Take a pull backup before any state surgery, and prefer state mv, rm and import over hand-editing and pushing.

questions.q: How do the removed block and terraform state rm differ for taking a resource out of Terraform without destroying it?
questions.text: state rm is an imperative command that forgets a resource immediately. The removed block with lifecycle destroy = false is declarative, reviewable in a pull request, and applied by the normal workflow, so everyone's state is updated consistently. terraform state rm aws_s3_bucket.legacy removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy lifecycle { destroy = false } } terraform plan Interview tip: Declarative blocks leave a code trail and work with remote execution, which is why they beat one-off commands on shared infrastructure.

questions.q: How do you use terraform plan -generate-config-out to import existing resources, and what review does the generated code need?
questions.text: With an import block that has no matching resource block, plan -generate-config-out writes starter HCL based on the real object's attributes. It is a draft: you must remove computed and default noise, parameterise values, and verify the next plan shows no changes. import { to = aws_instance.web id = "i-0abc123" } terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf terraform apply terraform plan # expect: No changes Interview tip: The success criterion for any import is a clean plan afterwards, with the config tidy enough to maintain.

questions.q: What is the difference between terraform taint and the -replace option, and why is -replace preferred?
questions.text: taint marks a resource in state as tainted so the next apply recreates it, but modifies state without a plan review. -replace=ADDRESS on plan or apply forces replacement for that run, is visible in the plan, and doesn't change state until applied. terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.web terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web terraform untaint aws_instance.web Interview tip: taint is deprecated in favour of -replace because it changes state before anyone has reviewed the consequences.

questions.q: How can large Terraform state files hurt, and what are the signs that it is time to split state?
questions.text: Large state means slow plans and refreshes, long lock times, a big blast radius, noisy diffs, and merge conflicts in review. Signs: plans over several minutes, many unrelated teams editing one root module, and fear of applying. Split by lifecycle, ownership and risk. terraform state list | wc -l terraform state list | cut -d. -f1-2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head time terraform plan -refresh=false Interview tip: Split along boundaries that change at different rates, such as network, data, platform and applications.

questions.q: What is state encryption in OpenTofu, and how does it differ from backend encryption?
questions.text: OpenTofu can encrypt state and plan files client-side using a key provider such as AWS KMS, GCP KMS or a passphrase, so even someone with read access to the bucket sees ciphertext. Backend encryption (SSE) protects data at rest only from outside the storage service. terraform { encryption { key_provider "aws_kms" "main" { kms_key_id = "alias/tf" region = "eu-west-1" } method "aes_gcm" "default" { keys = key_provider.aws_kms.main } state { method = method.aes_gcm.default } } } tofu init && tofu plan Interview tip: Be balanced: mention it is an OpenTofu feature, and that with HashiCorp Terraform you rely on backend encryption and strict access control.

questions.q: How does S3 native state locking (use_lockfile) compare with the DynamoDB lock table?
questions.text: Newer Terraform and OpenTofu versions can lock S3 state using a .tflock object created with conditional writes, removing the need for a DynamoDB table. It simplifies setup and permissions, but you must migrate carefully and make sure all users run supported versions. terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "tf-state" key = "prod/network.tfstate" region = "eu-west-1" use_lockfile = true } } aws s3 ls s3://tf-state/prod/ | grep tflock terraform init -migrate-state Interview tip: During migration you can enable both mechanisms for a while so that older clients still respect the lock.

questions.q: How do remote state backends differ on Google Cloud and Azure, and how is locking handled?
questions.text: The gcs backend stores state in a bucket and uses object generation preconditions for locking. The azurerm backend stores state in a blob container and uses blob leases. Both support encryption, versioning and identity-based auth without keys. terraform { backend "gcs" { bucket = "tf-state-prod" prefix = "network" } } terraform { backend "azurerm" { resource_group_name = "tf-rg" storage_account_name = "tfstate123" container_name = "state" key = "prod.tfstate" use_oidc = true } } Interview tip: Turn on object versioning and soft delete so a bad write can be rolled back.

questions.q: What can go wrong if different team members use different Terraform versions or backend settings, and how do you standardise them?
questions.text: A newer version can upgrade the state format so older versions can no longer read it, providers behave differently, and backend arguments drift. Pin required_version, commit the lock file, use a version manager and run through CI to keep one tool version. terraform { required_version = "~> 1.9.0" } tfenv install && tfenv use # reads .terraform-version terraform version terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 Interview tip: A state written by a newer Terraform may be unreadable by an older one, so one engineer's local apply can block everyone else.

questions.q: What is Terraform Cloud remote execution versus local execution, and how does it change who needs cloud credentials?
questions.text: With remote execution, plan and apply run on HCP Terraform workers, using credentials and variables stored in the workspace. With local execution the CLI runs on your machine and only state is stored remotely. Remote runs centralise secrets, logs, policy checks and approvals. terraform { cloud { organization = "acme" workspaces { name = "prod-network" } } } terraform login terraform plan # runs remotely and streams logs Interview tip: Dynamic provider credentials with OIDC let remote runs assume cloud roles without any stored keys.

questions.q: How do you protect Terraform state buckets from deletion, tampering and unauthorised reading?
questions.text: Enable versioning, MFA delete or object lock, bucket policies denying delete except from a break-glass role, block public access, encrypt with KMS, restrict read to pipeline roles, log access, and replicate the bucket for disaster recovery. aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket tf-state --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket tf-state --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket tf-state --policy file://deny-unencrypted-and-delete.json Interview tip: Treat the state bucket as tier-zero infrastructure, with its own account and tightly limited administrators.

questions.q: How do policy-as-code tools such as OPA Conftest, Sentinel and Checkov fit into a Terraform pipeline?
questions.text: Static scanners like Checkov and tfsec inspect HCL for known misconfigurations. Conftest with OPA evaluates the JSON plan against custom Rego rules. Sentinel does the same inside HCP Terraform. Run them between plan and apply to fail unsafe changes. terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json conftest test plan.json -p policy/ checkov -f plan.json --framework terraform_plan tfsec . Interview tip: Scanning the plan JSON catches values only known at plan time, which pure source scanning misses.

questions.q: What are ephemeral resources and write-only attributes in recent Terraform, and how do they keep secrets out of state?
questions.text: Ephemeral values exist only during a run and are never stored in plan or state. Write-only attributes accept a value to send to the provider but don't persist it. Together they let you fetch a secret from a vault and set a password without it appearing in state. ephemeral "random_password" "db" { length = 24 } resource "aws_db_instance" "main" { password_wo = ephemeral.random_password.db.result password_wo_version = 1 } terraform state show aws_db_instance.main | grep -i password Interview tip: Say it clearly: this reduces secrets in state, but the secret still needs a proper secret manager as its source of truth.

questions.q: How do you authenticate Terraform in CI to AWS, Azure or GCP without long-lived keys, and what do you restrict?
questions.text: Use OIDC federation: the CI system presents a short-lived signed token, and the cloud exchanges it for temporary credentials on a role whose trust policy limits repository, branch and environment. Use separate roles for plan (read-mostly) and apply. aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com az ad app federated-credential create --id <app> --parameters @fed.json gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create ci-pool --location=global Interview tip: Condition the trust on the exact repo and branch or environment. A loose subject claim lets any repo in the organisation assume your role.

questions.q: How do you use data sources to read secrets from Vault, Secrets Manager or Key Vault, and what are the risks?
questions.text: Data sources read secret values at plan or apply time, but the values are stored in state in plaintext. Safer patterns reference secret ARNs or names and let the application fetch them at runtime, or use ephemeral resources. Never output secrets. data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" { secret_id = "prod/db" } resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "app" { container_definitions = jsonencode([{ secrets = [{ name = "DB_PASSWORD", valueFrom = aws_secretsmanager_secret.db.arn }] }]) } Interview tip: Pass the secret's reference to the workload, not its value. Then neither state nor plan holds the secret.

questions.q: How do you verify the supply chain of Terraform providers and modules, including signatures and checksums?
questions.text: The registry provides signed provider releases and the lock file records hashes for each platform. Pin versions, commit the lock, use a private registry or mirror for modules and providers, review module source, and scan dependencies for known issues. terraform init -upgrade cat .terraform.lock.hcl terraform providers mirror ./mirror terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.60" } } } Interview tip: A filesystem or network mirror also protects builds from registry outages and tag changes.

questions.q: How do you restrict what Terraform itself can do, using IAM permission boundaries and separate roles per stack?
questions.text: Give each state its own role with only the services and resource prefixes it manages, add a permission boundary so it cannot create more powerful roles, deny destructive actions on protected resources, and use SCPs as the outer guardrail. aws iam put-role-permissions-boundary --role-name tf-app-prod --permissions-boundary arn:aws:iam::123456789012:policy/TerraformBoundary aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role-arn> --action-names iam:CreateUser s3:DeleteBucket aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn <role-arn> Interview tip: A Terraform role with AdministratorAccess is effectively a root key stored in CI. Start from last-accessed data and trim.

questions.q: What are good module composition patterns, and why prefer small focused modules wired together by a root module?
questions.text: Keep modules focused on one capability with a clear input and output contract, compose them in root modules, avoid deep nesting, and don't wrap a single resource without adding value. Pass dependencies explicitly via variables and outputs. module "network" { source = "./modules/network" cidr = var.cidr } module "app" { source = "./modules/app" subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids } terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg Interview tip: A thin wrapper around one resource is usually a smell. A module should encapsulate a decision or a pattern, not just rename arguments.

questions.q: How do you use for_each and count on modules, and what limitations apply?
questions.text: Modules support count and for_each, creating multiple instances addressed by index or key. Each instance has its own state addresses. Keys must be known at plan time, and changing a key destroys and recreates that instance unless you use moved blocks. module "service" { for_each = var.services source = "./modules/service" name = each.key config = each.value } terraform state list | grep 'module.service' moved { from = module.service["old"] to = module.service["new"] } Interview tip: Use stable keys such as names, not list indexes, so inserting an item does not shift everything.

questions.q: How does terraform test work, and what can you assert with it?
questions.text: terraform test runs .tftest.hcl files containing run blocks that apply or plan a configuration with given variables and then check assertions on outputs and resources. It can use mock providers for fast unit tests, and real applies for integration tests. terraform test terraform test -filter=tests/network.tftest.hcl run "creates_private_subnets" { command = plan variables { cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" } assert { condition = length(aws_subnet.private) == 3 error_message = "expected 3 private subnets" } } Interview tip: Use command = plan with mock providers for fast, free checks, and reserve real applies for a few key integration paths.

questions.q: When would you use terraform_data or the null_resource replacement, and what are the alternatives to provisioners?
questions.text: terraform_data is the built-in replacement for null_resource, storing input and triggering replacement on changes with triggers_replace. Provisioners are a last resort; prefer cloud-init or user data, configuration management, images, or the provider's native resources. resource "terraform_data" "bootstrap" { triggers_replace = [aws_instance.web.id, filesha256("scripts/init.sh")] provisioner "local-exec" { command = "./scripts/init.sh ${aws_instance.web.private_ip}" } } terraform state list | grep terraform_data Interview tip: HashiCorp documents provisioners as a last resort because they are not declarative and failures leave resources tainted.

questions.q: How do you design module outputs and variable types to keep interfaces stable as modules evolve?
questions.text: Expose only what consumers need, use typed objects with optional attributes and defaults, validate inputs, avoid leaking provider-specific structures, and treat outputs as a public API. Deprecate and version rather than rename or remove abruptly. variable "db" { type = object({ engine = string, size = optional(string, "db.t3.medium"), multi_az = optional(bool, true) }) } variable "env" { type = string validation { condition = contains(["dev","stage","prod"], var.env) error_message = "env must be dev, stage or prod" } } output "endpoint" { value = aws_db_instance.main.endpoint description = "Writer endpoint" } Interview tip: Adding an optional input or a new output is backward compatible. Renaming or removing one is a breaking change that deserves a major version.

questions.q: What does the provider plugin cache do, and how does it speed up CI?
questions.text: By default every working directory downloads its own copies of providers during init. Setting plugin_cache_dir (or TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR) shares downloaded providers across directories and builds, saving bandwidth and minutes, especially in monorepos with many states. export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache mkdir -p $TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR terraform init # second run reuses cached providers du -sh .terraform/providers Interview tip: Cache the directory between CI runs, keyed on the lock file hash, to avoid redownloading large providers.

questions.q: When is -refresh=false safe to use, and what are the risks?
questions.text: -refresh=false skips reading real infrastructure and trusts state, making plans much faster. It is safe when state is known to be fresh, for example in a quick re-plan after a recent apply, but dangerous for detecting drift or in production decisions. terraform plan -refresh=false terraform plan -refresh-only terraform apply -refresh=false -target=module.app Interview tip: Use it for iteration while developing, but run a full refreshing plan before the final apply.

questions.q: How can many for_each resources and large data lookups slow Terraform, and how do you design around it?
questions.text: Each instance is a separate graph node and API call set. Thousands of instances, or data sources that run for each, make plans slow and hit API limits.
