Batch via resources that accept lists, move to separate states, cache lookups with locals, and avoid per-item data sources. terraform graph | grep -c '\[label' TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | grep -c 'GET\|POST' terraform plan -parallelism=20 Interview tip: Count API calls with debug logs. The number of requests, not Terraform CPU, is usually the cost driver.

questions.q: What are the pros and cons of Terragrunt for reducing duplication, and when is it worth adopting?
questions.text: Terragrunt wraps Terraform to keep backend and provider configuration DRY, orchestrate dependencies between stacks and run commands across many directories. It adds another tool and abstraction layer, so adopt it when you have many similar stacks and environments. terragrunt run-all plan terragrunt run-all apply --terragrunt-non-interactive include "root" { path = find_in_parent_folders() } dependency "vpc" { config_path = "../vpc" } Interview tip: Alternatives: Terraform workspaces plus modules, Terraform Cloud stacks, or plain CI orchestration. Choose the simplest that fits.

questions.q: How do preconditions, postconditions and check blocks improve safety, and how do they differ?
questions.text: Preconditions and postconditions inside lifecycle blocks fail the run when assumptions about inputs or results are violated. check blocks run assertions, including on data sources, that only warn rather than stop, and are good for ongoing health validation. resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = var.ami lifecycle { precondition { condition = data.aws_ami.selected.architecture == "x86_64" error_message = "AMI must be x86_64" } } } check "site_up" { data "http" "home" { url = "https://example.com" } assert { condition = data.http.home.status_code == 200 error_message = "home page down" } } Interview tip: Use conditions for assumptions that must hold before or after change, and check blocks for monitoring-style assertions that should not block applies.

questions.q: How do prevent_destroy and ignore_changes work, and what are their pitfalls?
questions.text: prevent_destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail, a guard against accidents, but it blocks legitimate destroys until removed. ignore_changes tells Terraform to disregard drift in listed attributes, useful for fields changed by other systems, but it can hide real problems. lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"], desired_capacity] } terraform plan Interview tip: Use ignore_changes narrowly on named attributes, never on whole blocks, and leave a comment explaining who else changes them.

questions.q: What does create_before_destroy do, and what problems can it cause with unique names?
questions.text: It creates the replacement before destroying the old resource, giving zero-downtime replacement for things like launch templates, certificates and load balancer listeners. If the resource has a unique name, both can't exist at once, so use name_prefix or random suffixes. lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } resource "aws_launch_template" "app" { name_prefix = "app-" lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } } terraform plan | grep -E 'must be replaced|create replacement' Interview tip: The setting propagates to dependencies, so resources the replaced one depends on may also be forced into create-before-destroy.

questions.q: What does replace_triggered_by do, and how do you use it to roll dependent resources?
questions.text: replace_triggered_by makes a resource be replaced whenever a referenced resource or attribute changes. It is useful when something must be recreated to pick up a change that Terraform wouldn't otherwise see, like instances after a launch template or secret version change. resource "aws_instance" "app" { ami = var.ami lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [aws_launch_template.app.latest_version, terraform_data.config_version] } } terraform plan | grep 'forces replacement' Interview tip: Pair it with terraform_data holding a version value so you can force a controlled roll by bumping one variable.

questions.q: How do you design blue-green or canary infrastructure changes with Terraform, for example a new Kubernetes node group or database version?
questions.text: Create the new stack alongside the old, shift traffic gradually via weighted DNS, load balancer rules or target groups, verify health, then retire the old. Control the shift with variables or separate applies, and keep the rollback path as a one-variable change. resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "canary" { action { type = "forward" forward { target_group { arn = aws_lb_target_group.blue.arn weight = 100 - var.green_weight } target_group { arn = aws_lb_target_group.green.arn weight = var.green_weight } } } } terraform apply -var green_weight=10 Interview tip: Treat destroying the old environment as a separate, later change, after the observation window passes.

questions.q: How do you handle the Terraform lifecycle when a provider defaults or API behaviour change and cause perpetual diffs?
questions.text: Identify the attribute that differs between config and state, check provider changelogs and issues, set the value explicitly to match the API's normalised form, use ignore_changes as a targeted workaround, or upgrade the provider that fixes it. terraform plan -no-color | grep -B2 -A6 '~ ' terraform state show aws_s3_bucket.logs TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2> debug.log Interview tip: Common culprits are normalised JSON policy documents, case differences, ordering of lists and sets, and defaults the provider fills in.

questions.q: How does Atlantis work for pull-request automation, and what are its security considerations?
questions.text: Atlantis listens to pull request webhooks, runs terraform plan when code changes and posts the output, then runs apply when a reviewer comments atlantis apply. It holds credentials and executes arbitrary code, so restrict who can trigger it, require approvals, and isolate workers. atlantis plan -d environments/prod atlantis apply -d environments/prod atlantis.yaml: projects: - name: prod dir: environments/prod apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable] Interview tip: Anyone who can open a pull request can make Atlantis run code with its cloud credentials, so repo access equals credential access.

questions.q: How do you add cost estimation with Infracost to a Terraform pull request workflow?
questions.text: Infracost reads the plan or code, prices resources with cloud pricing data, and posts a diff of monthly cost on the pull request. Teams set thresholds and policies so large increases need approval, building cost awareness into review. infracost breakdown --path plan.json infracost diff --path . --compare-to infracost-base.json infracost comment github --path infracost.json --repo org/repo --pull-request 123 --github-token $TOKEN Interview tip: Usage-based costs, such as data transfer or requests, need usage estimates in a config file, or they will be underreported.

questions.q: How do you securely store, pass and verify the saved plan file between plan and apply jobs in CI?
questions.text: Write the plan with -out, store it as a protected artifact (encrypted, short retention, access-limited), and apply exactly that file so what was reviewed is what runs. The plan can contain secrets, so treat it like state. terraform plan -out=tfplan -input=false sha256sum tfplan > tfplan.sha256 terraform show -json tfplan | jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions!=["no-op"]) | .address' terraform apply -input=false tfplan Interview tip: If the state changes between plan and apply, Terraform refuses the stale plan, which is the safety you want.

questions.q: How do you detect and alert on Terraform drift on a schedule, and what do you do when drift is found?
questions.text: Run scheduled refresh-only plans with -detailed-exitcode in CI for each state. Exit code 2 means differences. Notify the owning team with the diff, then decide: revert the manual change by applying, or adopt it into code via a reviewed pull request. terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode -input=false; echo $? terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -input=false terraform apply -refresh-only Interview tip: Classify drift: benign (autoscaler fields), risky (security groups) and malicious (IAM). Route alerts accordingly.

questions.q: How do you structure a reusable GitHub Actions or GitLab pipeline for Terraform across many repositories?
questions.text: Create a shared, versioned reusable workflow or template that does fmt, validate, scan, plan and apply with standard guards, called from each repo with a few inputs. Central control means improvements and security fixes roll out everywhere through version bumps. uses: org/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/terraform.yml@v3 with: working-directory: environments/prod role-arn: ${{ vars.TF_ROLE }} terraform fmt -check -recursive && terraform validate && tflint && checkov -d . Interview tip: Pin the shared workflow to a tag or commit and update it deliberately, because it runs with your cloud credentials.

questions.q: terraform apply fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock' and the lock info shows a run from hours ago. What do you do?
questions.text: First prove no apply is running (check CI, ask the owner, read lock info). If it is stale, use terraform force-unlock with the lock ID. Then run plan to verify state integrity, and handle any partially applied changes. terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-locks --key '{"LockID":{"S":"tf-state/prod.tfstate"}}' aws s3 rm s3://tf-state/prod.tfstate.tflock terraform plan Interview tip: Forcing an unlock during a live apply can corrupt state, so verification comes first.

questions.q: After an apply you see 'Provider produced inconsistent result after apply'. What does it mean and how do you recover?
questions.text: The provider returned a value different from what the plan predicted, a provider bug or eventual consistency issue. The resource may exist but state may be tainted or partial. Re-run plan, check the real object, refresh or import, and upgrade or report the provider. terraform plan terraform state show aws_xyz.name terraform apply -refresh-only terraform providers Interview tip: This is almost always a provider bug, not user error, so check the issue tracker and try a newer or older provider version.

questions.q: Terraform fails with 'Cycle: ...' errors. How do you find and break the dependency cycle?
questions.text: Two or more resources reference each other, directly or through intermediaries, so no valid order exists. Read the cycle path in the error, use terraform graph to visualise, and break it by splitting a resource, using separate rule resources, or moving the shared value into a data source or variable. terraform validate terraform graph -type=plan | dot -Tsvg > g.svg terraform graph | grep -E 'aws_security_group.a|aws_security_group.b' Interview tip: The classic case is two security groups referencing each other inline. Use aws_security_group_rule resources instead.

questions.q: for_each fails with 'The for_each value depends on resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply'. How do you fix it?
questions.text: for_each keys must be known at plan time. Build keys from static values or inputs, not from attributes of resources not yet created. Use a stable map keyed by names, split the apply with -target as a last resort, or restructure into two layers. terraform plan for_each = { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s } for_each = toset(var.names) # not aws_subnet.x[*].id Interview tip: Keys must be known; values can be unknown. Use human-chosen names as keys and the unknown ID as the value.

questions.q: A tag or name change makes Terraform want to replace a production resource. How do you avoid the replacement?
questions.text: Check which attribute forces replacement in the plan. If it is only metadata you want to keep, restore the old value, use ignore_changes, rename in place if the provider supports it, or use moved and lifecycle controls. Never apply a surprise replacement of stateful resources. terraform plan | grep -B3 'forces replacement' terraform state show aws_db_instance.main | grep -E 'identifier|name' lifecycle { ignore_changes = [identifier] } Interview tip: Read the (forces replacement) marker. It tells you exactly which argument is immutable on the provider side.

questions.q: A secret ended up in the Terraform state and in plan output in CI logs. What is your response?
questions.text: Rotate the secret immediately, remove it from logs where possible, restrict who can read state and logs, then fix the root cause by using sensitive values, ephemeral or write-only attributes, runtime secret references, and log masking. Audit access to the state and logs. terraform state pull | jq '.. | objects | select(has("password"))' | head aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket tf-state --prefix prod/ aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=tf-state Interview tip: Rotation matters more than cleanup. Assume anyone who could read the logs or state has the secret.

questions.q: Apply fails halfway because of an account quota or service limit error. How do you proceed safely?
questions.text: Terraform records what was created, so state reflects the partial progress. Request the quota increase or reduce the change, then re-run plan and apply to finish. Check for resources created but not recorded, and avoid destroying the half-built stack. terraform apply 2>&1 | tee apply.log terraform plan aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-1216C47A aws service-quotas request-service-quota-increase --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-1216C47A --desired-value 256 Interview tip: Check quotas in the plan phase with a pre-flight script for big launches, so you do not discover limits mid-apply.

questions.q: Terraform says a resource 'already exists' on create, such as an S3 bucket, IAM role or DNS record. How do you handle it?
questions.text: The object exists in the cloud but not in your state, from a manual creation, another stack, a previous partial apply or a failed state write. Decide who owns it: import it into this state, rename yours, or remove the duplicate. Avoid deleting without checking ownership. aws iam get-role --role-name app-role terraform import aws_iam_role.app app-role terraform state list | grep app-role import { to = aws_iam_role.app id = "app-role" } Interview tip: Search other states first. Two stacks managing the same object will fight forever.

questions.q: A provider major upgrade breaks many plans, for example the AWS provider splitting S3 bucket arguments into separate resources. How do you migrate safely?
questions.text: Read the upgrade guide, pin the old version, upgrade in a branch, run plans per state to see diffs, refactor configuration to the new resource model, import or move where needed so no infrastructure is replaced, then roll out environment by environment. terraform init -upgrade terraform plan -out=upgrade.plan terraform show -json upgrade.plan | jq '[.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions|index("delete"))] | length' terraform providers lock Interview tip: The success criterion is a plan with no destroys, and ideally no changes at all, before any real apply.

questions.q: Two pipelines applied to the same state at nearly the same time and one failed or overwrote the other. How do you prevent concurrent applies?
questions.text: Locking prevents simultaneous writes if configured, but queued or retried jobs can still race on stale plans. Use CI concurrency groups per state, one apply per environment at a time, saved plans that fail when state changed, and no manual local applies. concurrency: group: terraform-prod-network cancel-in-progress: false terraform apply tfplan # fails with 'Saved plan is stale' if state changed terraform force-unlock <id> Interview tip: Never set cancel-in-progress to true for apply jobs. Cancelling mid-apply is how stale locks and partial state happen.

questions.q: Terraform init or plan fails with 403 or AccessDenied against the state backend after a role or bucket policy change. How do you debug it?
questions.text: Identify which identity Terraform used and which action was denied. S3 needs list on the bucket, get and put on the object, and KMS permissions; locking needs lockfile or DynamoDB rights. Compare the policy simulator results and CloudTrail denial events. aws sts get-caller-identity aws s3api head-object --bucket tf-state --key prod/network.tfstate aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role> --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject kms:Decrypt --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::tf-state/prod/network.tfstate aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GetObject Interview tip: KMS key policies are a frequent hidden cause. The role can read the object but cannot decrypt it.

questions.q: A data source returns multiple results or none, causing 'Your query returned no results' or 'multiple results' errors. How do you make lookups robust?
questions.text: Make filters specific and deterministic, use most_recent or unique identifiers, or avoid fuzzy lookups for critical resources by passing IDs explicitly. Add preconditions to fail clearly and pin inputs such as AMI IDs through a managed source. data "aws_ami" "app" { most_recent = true owners = ["123456789012"] filter { name = "name" values = ["app-*"] } filter { name = "tag:release" values = [var.release] } } aws ec2 describe-images --owners 123456789012 --filters Name=name,Values='app-*' --query 'Images[].ImageId' Interview tip: Moving AMI selection to an SSM parameter or explicit variable makes rollbacks possible, whereas most_recent changes under you.

questions.q: Someone applied against the wrong workspace or account and changed production while intending dev. How do you recover, and how do you prevent it?
questions.text: Stop further applies, assess the damage using the plan and cloud audit logs, restore or revert via a corrective apply or state backup, communicate. Prevent by separate backends and credentials per environment, no shared default workspace, account guards, and CI-only applies. terraform workspace show terraform state pull | jq '.serial,.lineage' aws sts get-caller-identity provider "aws" { allowed_account_ids = ["111122223333"] } Interview tip: allowed_account_ids on the provider aborts the run if the credentials point to the wrong account, a cheap and effective guard.

questions.q: A policy check blocks your pull request for a rule you believe is a false positive. How should exceptions be handled?
questions.text: Verify whether it is truly a false positive, then handle the exception transparently: a documented, scoped suppression in code with justification and expiry, approved by the policy owner, tracked, and re-reviewed. Don't disable the check globally or bypass the pipeline. checkov -d . --check CKV_AWS_18 --skip-check CKV_AWS_18 #checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_18: access logs go to central log bucket, ticket SEC-1234 conftest test plan.json -p policy/ --no-fail opa eval -d policy/ -i plan.json 'data.terraform.deny' Interview tip: Good exceptions have an owner, a reason, a ticket and an expiry date, and are visible in code review.

questions.q: HCP Terraform or your CI runs are stuck in 'pending' or queued for a long time. What do you check?
questions.text: Another run on the same workspace holds the queue or lock, a run is waiting for confirmation, an agent pool has no available agents, run triggers chain upstream runs, or organisation concurrency limits are reached. Inspect the run queue and agent status. tfe-cli runs list --workspace prod-network kubectl get pods -n tfc-agent gh run list --workflow terraform.yml --status queued terraform force-unlock <id> Interview tip: Check for a plan waiting for manual approval first. It blocks everything behind it in the workspace queue.

questions.q: You must split a monolithic Terraform state into three smaller ones without recreating anything. Walk through the process.
questions.text: Back up state, create new roots and backends, move resource addresses with terraform state mv -state-out or moved/import blocks, replace cross-references with outputs and remote state or data sources, and verify each new root shows a clean plan before decommissioning the old config. terraform state pull > monolith-backup.tfstate terraform state mv -state-out=network.tfstate module.network module.network terraform init -migrate-state terraform plan # in each root, expect: No changes Interview tip: Freeze changes during the migration, and make the old root's plan show no destroys at each step before moving on.
